South Korea Recalls Ambassador From Ukraine as Dispute Over North Korean POWs Escalates
South Korea announced on October 8 that it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine amid a diplomatic dispute over Kyiv’s disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
Reuters reported the decision, citing South Korea’s Foreign Ministry, while Yonhap provided additional details about the dispute. Seoul has demanded an official explanation and apology over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s disclosure of the prisoners’ transfer.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine to Seoul,” the South Korean Foreign Ministry stated. "We hope that various issues between the two countries will be resolved smoothly, and we will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end."
South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating an agreement to keep the transfer confidential. Seoul also objected to a statement from Zelenskyy’s office denying that such a confidentiality agreement existed.
Despite the recall, the South Korean government indicated that negotiations with Kyiv would continue as the two sides seek to resolve the dispute.
The dispute intensified earlier this week after Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha sent a message to South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun that included an apology. Cho stated on October 6 that the message fell short of Seoul’s expectations and announced that South Korea intended to take “firm measures.”
The diplomatic rupture adds to scrutiny of Seoul's stance on Russia's war, after South Korea shipped more than 176,000 tons of fuel, largely diesel, to Russia in July and August.
Seven tankers made 14 voyages from South Korean ports, including three vessels under UK and EU sanctions that declared destinations in Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
In August alone, South Korea supplied about 112,000 tons, or 31% of Russia's seaborne petroleum imports, making it Moscow's second-largest supplier after India. The shipments do not breach South Korean law, as Seoul's export controls primarily cover industrial equipment, technology, and electronics rather than petroleum products.

Russia Seeks Combined 152 Years in Prison for Eight Crimeans Accused of Ukrainian Intelligence Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:13:58 UTC
23:13:58 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Seeks Combined 152 Years in Prison for Eight Crimeans Accused of Ukrainian Intelligence Ties
A Russian prosecutor has requested a combined 152 years in prison for eight residents of Russian-occupied Crimea accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) of belonging to an alleged Ukrainian intelligence network, Ukrainian human rights initiative Tribunal. Crimean Episode reported on October 7.
According to a statement published by the organization on Telegram, the FSB described the defendants as members of a highly clandestine Ukrainian intelligence group allegedly involved in sabotage operations and preparations for attacks against Russian-installed officials in Crimea.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russian authorities claim the group operated secret channels for supplying explosives, carried out railway sabotage, installed surveillance equipment, and planned assassination attempts against Sergei Aksyonov and Vladimir Konstantinov, two senior Russian-installed officials in occupied Crimea.
However, the human rights organization questioned the credibility of the accusations, arguing that the prosecution's account began to unravel during the first court hearing due to contradictory testimony from the defendants.
Viktor Podvalnyi, whom investigators identified as the alleged coordinator of the group, told the court that he barely knew the other defendants.
Another accused, Kyrylo Barannyk, admitted to blowing up railway tracks but maintained that he had acted independently and did not know any of the other defendants. Barannyk also alleged that he had been subjected to torture during detention, including electric shocks, suffocation, and simulated drowning.
A separate defendant suggested that his arrest may have been connected to parking his vehicle near the residence of Russian-installed Crimean official Vladimir Konstantinov.
Another accused, Voynarovska, said she had signed testimony after an FSB investigator threatened to place her child in an orphanage.
The human rights initiative argued that these accounts raised serious concerns about the reliability of the evidence presented by Russian investigators and the circumstances under which testimony had been obtained.
The proceedings are being overseen by Russian judge Igor Kostin and two other judges, according to Tribunal. Crimean Episode.
The organization criticized Kostin's previous judicial record, alleging that he had earlier sentenced an innocent Ukrainian farmer to life imprisonment despite evidence establishing an alibi.
“Kostin was not the only judge involved in the trial of the Crimean residents, and the identities of the others will also be established. All of them will undoubtedly face an international tribunal for the war crimes of denying defendants access to a fair trial and complicity in unlawful imprisonment,” the organization added.
The case follows another lengthy prison sentence imposed on a Ukrainian citizen by a Russian military court. On August 4, the Crimean Tatar Resource Center reported that 30-year-old Ukrainian national Yan Haupt had been sentenced to 24 years in prison over allegations of planning and committing a “terrorist act.”
The Southern District Military Court in Russia ordered Haupt to serve the first five years of his sentence in prison, followed by 19 years in a maximum-security penal colony. The court also imposed a fine of 700,000 rubles (approximately $8,700).

Russian Oil Gets Too Expensive for India as Imports Sink to Lowest Level Since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:13:55 UTC
23:13:55 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Oil Gets Too Expensive for India as Imports Sink to Lowest Level Since 2022
Indian refiners are cutting purchases of Russia’s flagship Urals crude for November delivery as higher prices erase much of the discount that helped Russian oil capture a dominant share of the Indian market after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Bloomberg reported on October 8, citing people familiar with the matter.
The pullback is being driven primarily by economics rather than political pressure. Urals crude loaded at Russia’s Baltic ports is now being offered at a premium of more than $10 per barrel to Dated Brent, according to Bloomberg’s sources, making it far less attractive to Indian buyers than it was when Russian barrels were sold at steep discounts.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Cargoes that once undercut competing grades by a wide margin are now priced close to crude from the Middle East, prompting Indian refiners to reconsider suppliers in the Persian Gulf. Some Russian barrels originally aimed at India are also being offered to independent Chinese refiners as traders look for alternative buyers.
India, the world’s third-largest crude importer, had already begun reducing its exposure to Russian oil after the adoption of new US sanctions legislation raised the threat of punitive tariffs. However, Bloomberg’s sources said pricing has now become the more immediate factor shaping purchasing decisions.
Russia’s share of Indian crude imports fell to about 35% in September, according to analytics firm Kpler, down sharply from a peak of 56% in July. The drop reflects both growing sanctions risk and the narrowing price gap between Russian and competing crude grades.
The decline is also visible in tanker-tracking data. During the four weeks through October 4, Russian crude shipments averaged only about 310,000 barrels per day, according to Bloomberg data—the lowest level recorded since March 2022, shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
China and India remain the two largest buyers of Russian crude, although the final destination of many cargoes is not always fixed when tankers leave port. Traders often decide where to send individual shipments while the vessels are already underway, depending on prices, sanctions exposure, and demand.
Earlier, the US House of Representatives passed bipartisan legislation granting US President Donald Trump expanded authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top importers of Russian oil and gas in an effort to squeeze Moscow’s war revenue.

Tanzania's economy maintains strong growth momentum in 2026: central bank
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:24 CST
23:12:24 KST

DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Tanzania's economy has maintained strong growth momentum in 2026, with mainland Tanzania expanding by 6 percent in the first quarter and projected to grow by more than 6 percent in the second and third quarters, according to Bank of Tanzania Governor Emmanuel Tutuba.
Tutuba said Thursday that financial services, industrial production, infrastructure investment and social services supported the growth.
Zanzibar's economy grew by 6.7 percent in the first quarter and is estimated to have expanded by more than 7 percent in the second and third quarters, driven by tourism, construction and irrigation projects, he said.
Tutuba said the latest gross domestic product (GDP) rebasing exercises had raised mainland Tanzania's nominal GDP in 2025 to 234.104 trillion Tanzanian shillings (about 92.3 billion U.S. dollars), from 230.073 trillion shillings under the previous series.
Zanzibar's nominal GDP rose to 9.242 trillion shillings from 7.029 trillion shillings, Tutuba said.
He said mainland inflation rose to 4.3 percent in August from an average of 4.1 percent in the quarter ending June, but remained within the medium-term target of 3 to 5 percent.
Private-sector credit grew by an average of 32.5 percent in the quarter ending September, while foreign exchange reserves remained above 6 billion dollars, providing 4.3 months of import cover, he said.
Tutuba said the economic outlook remained favorable despite risks from elevated global commodity prices, supply disruptions and El Nino-related effects. ■

Bangladesh's inflation inches up to 8.34 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:21 CST
23:12:21 KST

DHAKA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Bangladesh's inflation edged up to 8.34 percent in September from 8.26 percent in August, according to the latest official statistics.
The consumer price index, released by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics on its website on Thursday, showed that the food inflation rate ticked up to 7.22 percent in September, the third month of the current fiscal year (July 2026-June 2027). In August, food inflation was 7.02 percent.
Inflation for non-food items edged down to 9.3 percent in September from 9.32 percent in August, the data showed.
The country's average inflation reached 8.89 percent in the last fiscal year 2025-26 (July 2025-June 2026).
In the previous 2024-25 fiscal year, overall inflation was 9.43 percent.
The Bangladeshi parliament on June 30 passed a record-high 9.38-trillion-taka (77-billion-U.S.-dollar) national budget for the 2026-27 fiscal year.
In line with the budget, the Bangladeshi government aims to reduce inflation to 7.5 percent and raise GDP growth to 6.5 percent in the current fiscal year. ■

Over 750 bear sightings reported in Mongolian residential areas since spring
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:15 CST
23:12:15 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- At least 754 bear sightings have been reported across Mongolia since spring this year, the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change said Thursday.
Of the reported sightings, 24 occurred in Ulan Bator, the capital, according to the ministry. More than 80 percent of the bears involved were cubs or female bears accompanied by cubs.
The figures were released after a man in his 40s was killed and a woman in her 50s was seriously injured in a bear attack in Ulan Bator overnight from Wednesday to Thursday.
The sharp increase in bear sightings in and around residential areas across Mongolia has prompted authorities to warn residents to remain vigilant and take necessary precautions to reduce the risk of bear encounters.
Bear-hunting permits have so far been issued in eight provinces.
Experts say encounters between bears and livestock, as well as bear sightings in residential areas, have increased in recent years. They attribute the trend to several factors, including climate change, food shortages in bears' natural habitats and the overexploitation of natural resources. ■

Economic Watch: Holiday travel, spending boom mirror vitality of China's vast market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:12:04 CST
23:12:04 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- From bustling transport hubs and crowded scenic areas to fully booked restaurants and busy shopping districts, strong travel flows and vibrant consumption during the National Day holiday highlighted the resilience and momentum of China's holiday economy.
Data from the Ministry of Transport showed that during this National Day holiday from Oct. 1 to 7, known as "Golden Week," cross-regional passenger trips reached 2.14 billion, averaging 306 million a day, slightly above the daily average recorded a year earlier.
Longer breaks, richer local experiences, rising inbound travel and policy-supported consumption... What stood out this year was not just the sheer number of travelers, but how the holiday economy was changing shape.
LONGER JOURNEYS, DEEPER EXPERIENCES
With the Mid-Autumn Festival and National Day holidays separated by only three working days this year, some travelers took three days of leave to link the two breaks into a 13-day extended holiday. Data from Trip.com Group showed that one in every 10 travelers combined the two holidays into such a break.
That extra stretch has helped reshape travel preferences, driving demand for longer-distance trips, a more relaxed pace and more immersive experiences.
Online travel platform Qunar said bookings for flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose by more than 40 percent year on year during the National Day holiday, while hotel bookings involving stays across four or more cities jumped 53 percent year on year.
Improved transport links are making long-distance trips more accessible than ever. Before the holiday, new high-speed rail sections, including the Xiong'an-Shangqiu, Xi'an-Ankang, and Harbin-Yichun lines, began operation, connecting more destinations across the country.
For families like Wang Lei's from Harbin, who traveled to Yichun to enjoy the autumn scenery, a journey that once took seven hours now takes just over one hour. "The time we used to spend on the road can now be spent enjoying the destination," Wang said.
Experts said longer breaks extend the consumption chain and expand spending opportunities, giving transport, hospitality, catering and scenic spots a longer operating window and deeper spending potential.
Official data showed that during the National Day holiday, average daily sales in service sectors rose 19.5 percent year on year, with tourism, sightseeing and entertainment services up 23.6 percent, catering services up 9 percent, cultural and arts services up 20.9 percent, and sports services up 29.4 percent year on year.
A noticeable shift unfolded during this year's National Day holiday: more travelers are looking beyond big-name cities and turning to smaller counties for their getaways.
In Mile City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, tourist Chen Jinhui from Shanghai in east China ordered a cup of local coffee and joined a community concert. "Coming to a small city, basking in the sun and relaxing -- that's the Yunnan way of life," he said.
Data from Qunar showed that hotel bookings in popular counties rose 32 percent year on year, with Jiuzhaigou County in southwest China's Sichuan and Burqin County in northwest China's Xinjiang among the most sought-after destinations.
In August, nine government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce, jointly issued guidelines to energize lower-tier markets and boost county-level consumption. The measures aim to streamline consumption channels, broaden the range of available brands, improve service quality, and create diverse and locally tailored consumption experiences in smaller cities and towns.
Small counties are no longer marginal players in the consumption landscape; they are becoming an important source of new domestic demand. McKinsey has projected that by 2030, more than 60 percent of China's personal consumption growth will come from third-tier cities and below, as well as county and rural markets.
Inbound tourism also remained robust during the holiday. Data from the National Immigration Administration showed that during the holiday, 682,000 foreign nationals entered China, of whom 505,000 arrived under visa-free policies, up 5.4 percent and 9.2 percent, respectively, from a year earlier.
As October arrives, autumn colors are spreading across Zhangjiajie National Forest Park in central China's Hunan Province. Tourists of different nationalities can be seen pausing for photos, listening to guides explain the area's unusual landscape, or watching local Tujia ethnic performances.
"Zhangjiajie is beautiful. We walked through the forest, felt close to nature, and it was very relaxing," said Noah, a tourist from Germany. He said he was especially impressed by the Tujia intangible cultural heritage performances and that the warmth of the local people made the visit truly memorable.
POLICY TAILWINDS, SMARTER SPENDING
Strong storefront demand and supportive policies are boosting consumption momentum. In the first six days of the National Day holiday, foot traffic and revenue at 78 major shopping streets and commercial districts monitored by the Ministry of Commerce rose 2.5 percent and 4.7 percent year on year, respectively.
Notably, the government's consumer goods trade-in program drove 33.48 billion yuan (about 4.97 billion U.S. dollars) in sales over the same period, benefiting 6.39 million consumers.
"During the holiday, we bought a new refrigerator. The subsidy saved us more than 1,000 yuan," said a Tianjin resident surnamed Wang.
The National Development and Reform Commission said before the holiday that it, together with the Ministry of Finance, had allocated the fourth and final batch of 62.5 billion yuan in ultra-long special treasury bonds for consumer goods trade-in programs, bringing this year's total to 250 billion yuan.
Data from the Ministry of Commerce showed that from Oct. 1 to 6, sales of embodied AI robots on key platforms surged 130 percent year on year, while sales of smart glasses doubled.
In Huaqiangbei, a sprawling electronics marketplace in south China's tech hub Shenzhen, new robots, AI translators and other tech gadgets have become popular purchases among foreign tourists.
"The number of overseas visitors has clearly increased. Most of them are buying tech products. Many come empty-handed and leave with full suitcases," said a local shop owner.
More international travelers are flocking to China to experience the country firsthand, riding a rising wave of global fascination with everything from the scenery and culture to its lifestyles and, more recently, Chinese brands and design.
From "China Travel" to "China Haul," the trend not only shows how Chinese manufacturing and innovation are winning over global visitors, but also confirms the potential and resilience of China's vast domestic market, supported by visa-free entry, expanded duty-free shopping and improved tax refund services for international visitors, said Zou Yunhan, a researcher with the State Information Center. ■

Pakistani PM pledges tech-driven disaster preparedness

ISLAMABAD, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Thursday pledged to strengthen the country's disaster preparedness through advanced technology and early warning systems, as Pakistan observed the 21st National Resilience Day.
Sharif said the government, through the National Disaster Management Authority, is integrating advanced technologies and more efficient early warning systems supported by data-based analytics into the national disaster response, reaffirming the resolve to move "from reaction to anticipation" in dealing with natural disasters.

European Commission backs Italy's bid for defense, energy spending flexibility
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:55 CST
23:11:55 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission backed Italy's request for greater flexibility under European Union (EU) fiscal rules to increase spending on defense and energy security, a Commission spokesperson said Thursday.
Italy submitted its request on Sept. 11, becoming the 19th EU member to seek activation of the national escape clause, which allows countries to temporarily deviate from EU fiscal spending requirements under certain conditions.
"Our assessment has concluded that indeed the activation of the clause does not endanger fiscal sustainability over the medium term in the case of Italy," the spokesperson told reporters. "In other words, our assessment is positive."
The request will now be submitted to the Council of the EU, which has one month to give its final approval. The clause can only be formally activated for Italy following the Council's decision, the spokesperson said.
The national escape clause is part of the EU's Stability and Growth Pact, which sets fiscal rules for members. It allows countries facing exceptional circumstances to temporarily exceed their agreed government spending limits, provided that doing so does not undermine medium-term fiscal sustainability.
The mechanism was activated for a number of EU countries in 2025 to accommodate higher defense spending, allowing additional expenditure of up to 1.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) annually over the 2025-2028 period.
Earlier this year, the EU expanded the scope of the mechanism to include certain energy security measures aimed at reducing Europe's dependence on imported fossil fuels.
Under guidelines issued by the Commission in August, eligible energy security spending can benefit from fiscal flexibility of up to 0.3 percent of GDP annually and 0.6 percent cumulatively over 2026-2028, within the existing overall ceiling of 1.5 percent of GDP. ■

China Focus: Crime drama leads China's National Day box office as market dips from last year
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:54 CST
23:11:54 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Crime drama "Traces of Justice" topped China's National Day holiday box office, in a market that fell from a year earlier, with some analysts citing the absence of a blockbuster-scale title.
The seven-day holiday frame ending on Wednesday generated 1.165 billion yuan (about 173 million U.S. dollars) from nearly 32 million admissions, according to the China Film Administration. Daily takings exceeded 100 million yuan throughout, but the total was well below last year's eight-day holiday, which grossed 1.835 billion yuan, according to ticketing platform Maoyan.
"Traces of Justice" grossed 423 million yuan. It was followed on the charts by comedy "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon," imported horror title "Resident Evil," war drama "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" and animated feature "Peppa Pig: Perfect Holiday." The top three earners accounted for more than 70 percent of total revenue.
Directed and co-written by Chen Sicheng, "Traces of Justice" is based on the life and work of renowned trace-evidence expert Cui Daozhi. The film, starring Zhang Yi, follows investigators as they solve challenging cases using forensic evidence like fingerprints and bite marks, while also tracing the development of forensic techniques in China over several decades.
A report released Thursday by the Maoyan Research Institute found that the share of multi-person movie outings during the National Day holiday fell to its lowest level in six years, while solo moviegoers made up 25.7 percent of admissions, also a six-year high.
The report said family demand was not fully met, and that the continued strength of some summer holdovers reflected a lack of new family-oriented releases.
"This year's top three films each found their own path to success, but audience interest remained relatively subdued overall because there was no blockbuster-scale title capable of generating broader excitement," said Lai Li, a Maoyan analyst.
Lai added that as audiences become more selective, there will be a greater need for innovation in both content and form.
Among the standouts was "Resident Evil," which opened on Oct. 5. Lai said the globally recognized franchise and better-than-expected word of mouth converted core fans into ticket buyers and helped boost its box office and buzz.
Other indicators were more resilient. Maoyan counted 12,800 cinemas and 79,400 screens in operation, both the highest for a National Day holiday in six years.
After a soft opening day, the market held up well, with new releases lifting daily takings on the third and fifth days. Fifth-day revenue rose 22.9 percent from the previous day to become the holiday's strongest single day, which Maoyan said underscored the role of new film supply in stimulating the market.
Chen Jin, an analyst at film data platform Beacon, expects leading titles to continue supporting the box office through mid-to-late October.
Maoyan forecasts Chinese mainland box office totals of 670 million yuan for "Traces of Justice," 550 million yuan for "Resident Evil" and 390 million yuan for "Mr. & Mrs. Pardon."
The Chinese mainland's annual box office has surpassed 30.7 billion yuan so far this year. ■

ETCS testing completed on Hungarian section of Budapest-Belgrade railway
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
22:11:52 CST
23:11:52 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Testing of the European Train Control System (ETCS) on the Hungarian section of the Budapest-Belgrade railway has been completed, marking an important step toward launching passenger services, a senior official said Thursday.
Construction of the Hungarian section is nearing technical completion, Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy said in a Facebook post. The ETCS testing followed a full-load test conducted over the weekend.
The proper functioning of the ETCS is a prerequisite for launching passenger services, he said. Based on the test results, the necessary official documentation is expected by mid-October.
Meanwhile, contractors still need to complete track adjustment work to ensure that the railway can maintain operating speeds of up to 160 km per hour over the long term.
According to the construction schedule, track adjustments on the section between Hungary's Ferencvaros and Kunszentmiklos-Tass stations are expected to be completed by the end of October, paving the way for the launch of domestic passenger services and subsequent operations.
Vitezy said that if domestic passenger services run smoothly during the first few weeks, the next phase is planned for December, when trains would operate at speeds of up to 160 km per hour and international passenger services between Budapest and Belgrade would begin.
Although extensive testing, corrective work and verification have been completed, there is further work to do, he said.
The 350-km long Budapest-Belgrade railway, linking the Hungarian and Serbian capitals, is a flagship project under the Belt and Road Initiative, jointly developed by China and countries in Central and Eastern Europe. It is also the first project to align Chinese railway technology and equipment with the European Union's railway interoperability standards.
The Hungarian section, spanning about 158.6 km, is an electrified railway designed for both passenger and freight transport, with a maximum design speed of 160 km per hour. Freight services on the section officially began on Feb. 27 this year. ■

PYONGYANG, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- A senior official of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on Thursday slammed the Republic of Korea (ROK) over its offer of medical supplies, calling the move a "grave provocation" to her country, state media said.
Kim Yo Jong, department director of the Central Committee of the Workers' Party of Korea, made the remarks in a press statement carried by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
Kim lashed out at an announcement by the South Korean authorities a day earlier that Seoul submitted to the U.N. Security Council's sanctions committee on the DPRK a request for sanctions exemption in order to offer medical supplies and the request was thereafter approved in May.
She noted that Seoul stated in the request the "lack of medicines and medical equipment and deterioration of public health situation" in the DPRK and its intention to "improve the primary medical service for the vulnerable communities" in the country, calling such statement "an insult to our state and mutant political-motivated provocation against it and a grave encroachment upon our national law," according to the KCNA report.
Saying "the medical equipment supported by the ROK cannot enter our territory," the DPRK official lambasted what she called the "sinister political calculation" behind Seoul's "farce."
Seoul is intended to "make a contrast between the ROK's 'well-meaning attitude' to offer medical supplies and the DPRK's 'conflicting attitude' to reject them," said Kim.
If the ROK really wants to improve the relations between the two countries, it should show its utmost respect and sincerity, she added in the statement.
"We have nothing to exchange or go with the ROK" and no need to deal with the country, Kim said, stressing that no change in "the hostile nature of the DPRK-ROK relations," the KCNA report said.
The ROK's unification ministry released a report which says Seoul submitted to the UN Security Council's sanctions committee on the DPRK a request for sanctions exemption in order to offer medical supplies, Yonhap News Agency reported on Wednesday.
The ROK government received approval from the sanctions committee in May for its plan to ship medical equipment, Yonhap said in the report. ■

Togo's president of Council of Ministers to visit China

JERUSALEM, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Israel has put its first hydrogen-powered bus into operation, the country's Energy and Infrastructure Ministry said on Thursday.
The launch marked a step toward expanding cleaner transportation and hydrogen technology in Israel, the ministry said in a statement.
The project, it said, will help assess the potential of hydrogen fuel cells in transportation, particularly for heavy vehicles where long travel ranges and fast refueling are important.
The Audace 1050 bus is a joint project between Chinese automotive technology company Allenbus and Brazilian coachbuilder Marcopolo.
Allenbus supplied the hydrogen powertrain and handled overall engineering, while Marcopolo provided the bus body, interior, and structural design.
The vehicle incorporates core Chinese energy technology, including 700-bar high-pressure hydrogen storage tanks, offering a driving range of up to 600 km on a single fill, alongside a high-voltage battery system developed by Chinese car battery giant CATL.
According to the ministry, the bus can be fully refueled in under five minutes, and its fuel-cell system emits only clean water.
The project, the ministry said, is part of broader government efforts to develop hydrogen infrastructure, promote alternative energy technologies, and cut emissions from heavy transportation. ■

GENEVA, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- The World Trade Organization (WTO) said on Thursday that global merchandise trade is expected to grow by 3.9 percent in 2026, up from its March forecast of 1.9 percent, driven by supply chain adaptation and strong investment in artificial intelligence (AI).
While raising the forecast for merchandise trade growth, the WTO's latest Global Trade Outlook and Statistics report lowered the outlook for commercial services trade in 2026 over the impact of the Middle East conflict.
The forecast for services trade volume growth in 2026 has been revised down to 3.3 percent from 4.8 percent in March.
In 2027, growth rates in volume terms for merchandise and services trade are expected to rise to 4.1 percent and 6.4 percent, respectively, depending on a timely resolution of the Middle East conflict, the report said.
In the report, the WTO projected global GDP growth at 2.6 percent and 2.9 percent in 2026 and 2027, respectively.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said the figures "reflect trade resilience in action."
Meanwhile, WTO Deputy Director-General Johanna Hill told a press conference held on the same day that while the system has proven resilient, that does not necessarily mean it is robust.
"Vulnerabilities remain, and WTO members are working to address them. Strengthening the multilateral trading system will help ensure that the global economy is better equipped to deal with future shocks." ■

Clashes broke out between Haredi protesters and police in Jerusalem and central Israel on Thursday as officers used stun grenades, batons and mounted units to clear hundreds of demonstrators blocking major roads in protest of renewed arrests of Haredi draft evaders.
At the entrance to Jerusalem, police forcibly removed protesters from the roadway near the Chords Bridge about an hour after the demonstrations began. Footage from the scene showed confrontations as officers used batons and stun grenades during attempts to disperse the crowd.
A soldier became trapped in his vehicle amid the blockade and was unable to continue driving. The vehicle was later extracted from the area.
Meanwhile, on Highway 4 near Bnei Brak, police used loudspeakers to order protesters to leave the roadway before moving to disperse them with stun grenades and mounted officers. Even about an hour into the protest, Haredi demonstrators remained seated on the road, chanting, “We will die and not enlist.”
Hundreds of Haredi protesters had begun gathering Thursday afternoon across the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and Jerusalem after demonstrations were called in response to the military’s decision to resume arrests of draft evaders.
Heavy congestion was already reported about an hour before the demonstrations’ announced 4 p.m. start time.
Highway 4 was blocked northbound at the Aluf Sade Interchange and southbound at the Em HaMoshavot Interchange. Police also closed the southbound highway near Bnei Brak, producing severe traffic jams in both directions.
In Jerusalem, hundreds blocked the main entrance to the city near the Chords Bridge, while dozens more gathered on Bar-Ilan Street and disrupted traffic.
“Jerusalem District police are reinforcing forces at the scene and preparing to enforce public order and clear the roads as necessary,” police said.
Police also disputed reports that a protester had been struck by a vehicle in Jerusalem. Officers said the incident was not a hit-and-run and that the man had “hung onto the vehicle of his own accord,” adding that police had footage supporting that account.
The demonstrations also caused major disruptions to Jerusalem’s light rail network.
At police instruction, the L1 line was temporarily split into two sections, operating between Neve Yaakov and Davidka stations and between Denia Square and Hadassah Ein Kerem. The L3 line was shortened to operate between Malha and the International Convention Center.
The Jerusalem Faction, a hardline Haredi group opposed to military conscription, had called for demonstrations beginning at around 4 p.m. in Jerusalem and the Tel Aviv metropolitan area. Bnei Brak was expected to be the main protest center in central Israel, with another possible demonstration near Ben Gurion Airport.
Unlike many previous demonstrations, which often involve only the group associated with Rabbi Tzvi Friedman, Thursday’s protest was expected to draw participation from across the Jerusalem Faction, potentially making it significantly larger.
Earlier Thursday afternoon, members of the faction attempted to disrupt Shas chairman Aryeh Deri as he addressed an election conference in Modi’in Illit.
Traffic congestion was reported across large parts of the country during the afternoon, including on highways 1, 2, 4, 6, 40, 41, 65, 70 and 85, as well as Route 471 and several roads in the West Bank. Some delays were linked directly to the demonstrations, while others resulted from accidents or routine congestion.
The protests followed a confrontation earlier in the week in Modi’in, where hundreds of Haredi men gathered overnight after a draft evader activated a community alert system known as “Black Alert” when military police arrived to arrest him.
Protesters entered the building where he had barricaded himself, confronted police sent to disperse them and surrounded military police officers. The standoff ended after negotiations in which protesters agreed to allow the soldiers to leave as long as the draft evader was not arrested.
The IDF recently resumed proactive arrests of draft evaders after a pause of more than two months in military police “home visits.” The military had acknowledged during a meeting with Israel’s attorney general that it had deliberately refrained during that period from proactively arresting Haredi draft evaders.
Large groups of Haredi protesters also prevented the arrest of three draft evaders in different cities overnight.
In Bat Yam, military police arrived to arrest a Haredi draft evader who activated an alert system warning that “the kidnappers have arrived.” Dozens of protesters gathered, and the military police force eventually withdrew without making the arrest. Protesters then celebrated by dancing in the street.
Military police also raided two homes in Dimona overnight in an attempt to arrest yeshiva students required to enlist. The “Black Alert” system was activated there as well, drawing dozens of Haredi protesters who prevented the arrests. As in Bat Yam, demonstrators celebrated after the military police withdrew.

====================================================================================================

The disease that once ravaged Europe still exists: could plague return to Spain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:05:28 UTC
23:05:28 KST

The death of a scientist in Russia has reignited fears of plague. Spain has seen no local cases for decades, yet the disease persists elsewhere. How real is the risk in Europe?
Plague, one of the deadliest diseases in history, has once again made headlines in recent days following the death of a scientist in Irkutsk, in Siberia. The woman died from pneumonia of unknown origin, which raised suspicions of a possible pneumonic plague infection.
However, the Russian authorities have stated that no cases of plague have been confirmed in the region and that tests carried out on the deceased woman’s contacts have come back negative. The World Health Organization (WHO) has requested additional information to clarify what happened and has offered its support to the Russian authorities.
Although no cases of routine transmission of this disease have been recorded in Europe for decades, the bacterium that causes it remains present in different parts of the world and continues to cause human infections every year.
Does plague currently exist in Spain and Europe?
Plague is not currently circulating routinely in Spain or in the rest of Europe. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the disease has been absent from the continent for more than 50 years.
This does not mean, however, that the bacterium has been eradicated from the planet. Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a microorganism that lives naturally in certain populations of small mammals, especially rodents, and in the fleas that infest them.
The bacterium can be transmitted to humans through the bites of infected fleas, contact with tissues or body fluids from infected animals and, in the case of pneumonic plague, via respiratory particles from sick people.
Therefore, although the current risk for the Spanish and European population is very low, the disease can still appear wherever there are animal reservoirs of the bacterium.
Is there a risk of plague in Spain? What the Health Ministry says
Spain has gone decades without registering locally acquired cases of plague, but it maintains active epidemiological surveillance of the disease. In April 2026 the Public Health Commission updated the national protocol, revising case definitions, the epidemiological characteristics of the infection and the information that must be collected in the event of possible infections.
This update, which predates the incident in Siberia, adds to the early-warning mechanisms already in place in Spain. For its part, the European Union examined the Russian case on 7 October, although international health authorities are still awaiting information that could clarify the cause of the researcher’s death.
Where does plague still occur in the world?
According to the WHO, plague remains endemic in several countries in Africa, Asia and the Americas. Between 2019 and 2025, most of the human cases reported to the organisation were concentrated in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. In Madagascar, for example, cases of bubonic plague are recorded virtually every year during the epidemic season, which usually runs from September to April.
The disease also appears sporadically in regions of Asia and the Americas. In the United States, an average of around seven human cases are reported each year, mainly in rural areas in the west of the country.
The persistence of the bacterium in wild animals explains why it is so difficult to eliminate the disease completely, even when human cases are rare.
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague?
Plague can present in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicaemic. Bubonic plague is the most common and usually occurs after the bite of an infected flea. It causes fever, general malaise and painful swelling of the lymph nodes, known as buboes.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and is particularly dangerous because it can be transmitted from person to person via respiratory particles. Without treatment, it can progress rapidly and prove fatal. Septicaemic plague, meanwhile, occurs when the bacterium multiplies in the bloodstream and can lead to a severe, generalised infection.
Unlike what happened during the great epidemics of the past, plague can now be treated with antibiotics. However, early diagnosis is essential to avoid serious complications and reduce the risk of death.
What risk does the Siberia case pose for Europe?
The suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia has prompted European health authorities to monitor the situation closely. The European Commission included the Russian incident on the agenda of its Health Security Committee meeting on 7 October, while the ECDC pointed out that there was no evidence of secondary cases or sustained person-to-person transmission.
The WHO has also concluded that the risk to the European region is very low. Although the disease has not been eradicated worldwide, its presence on other continents does not mean that Europe is facing a new epidemic.
Epidemiological surveillance, early detection of cases and treatment with antibiotics are crucial tools to prevent its spread. Plague still exists, but today’s health situation is very different from the one that allowed the Black Death to devastate Europe in the 14th century.

The Kremlin said Thursday that Russia believes a comprehensive settlement in Ukraine is necessary.
Speaking to journalists at a press briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Moscow has repeatedly stated that “piecemeal solutions and agreements” to the ongoing war would prevent a comprehensive settlement from being reached.
“It is a highly complex matter, and the settlement must be comprehensive,” Peskov said, noting that a “freeze” of the conflict would not help either.
“We need a solution for future generations — one that is guaranteed and safeguarded against setbacks,” the spokesman said, adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin had spoken about this, including at the Valdai Discussion Club.
He went on to express Russia’s gratitude to India for showing interest in efforts toward a settlement in Ukraine.
“We welcome any attempts or efforts by states that might in any way contribute to a settlement regarding Ukraine — or help nudge the Kyiv regime and, above all, the Europeans — toward a peaceful phase,” he added.
The Kremlin spokesman also commented on Putin’s birthday Wednesday, saying the Russian president did not receive a congratulatory telegram from US President Donald Trump.
Noting that the exact time of a telephone conversation between Putin and Trump has yet to be agreed upon, Peskov said there was no delay in coordinating such a call.
Commenting on Iran’s potential withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty, Peskov said the issue could be raised at a meeting between Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the upcoming Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) leaders’ summit in Turkmenistan on Friday.

Prison unit at Kærshovedgård could take five years to complete
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:03:41 UTC
23:03:41 KST

The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.

Danish vaccine company Bavarian Nordic has raised its forecast for revenue in 2026, citing stronger expected sales of travel vaccines.
The company now expects total revenue to reach 6.1 billion kroner this year, compared with its previous forecast of 5.7 billion kroner, Bavarian Nordic said in a company announcement Thursday.
The company attributed the increase to better-than-expected sales in its Travel Health business, particularly demand for rabies vaccines in the United States.
“Increased rabies activity among animals has resulted in a significant increase in exposure among humans and thus an increased demand,” Bavarian Nordic said in the announcement.
The company now expects revenue from its travel vaccine business to reach 3.4 billion kroner in 2026, up from its previous forecast of 3.0 billion kroner.
Third forecast increase this year
Thursday’s announcement marks the third time Bavarian Nordic has raised its revenue expectations this year.
At the beginning of the year, the company expected total revenue of between 5.0 billion and 5.2 billion kroner in 2026.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Middelfart Sparekasse, said Bavarian Nordic has gained “a new growth engine” through its travel vaccine business.
“The big question is now how much of the rabies boost will hold into 2027. Infection among animals fluctuates from year to year, so next year will face a tough comparison,” he wrote in a comment.
Bavarian Nordic sells travel vaccines against diseases including rabies, TBE and chikungunya, a disease spread by mosquitoes.
The company also sells vaccines for countries’ preparedness against outbreaks, including mpox, previously known in Danish as “abekopper.”
Bavarian Nordic will publish its third-quarter results on 13 November 2026.
Troels Lund expects Venstre lawmakers to unite on pesticide ban
Venstre chairman Troels Lund Poulsen expects the party’s parliamentary group to take a united position on a proposed national ban on pesticide spraying when the bill is considered in December.
“It is my clear expectation that Venstre’s group will vote together,” he told TV 2 News after speaking during the Folketing’s opening debate Thursday.
The statement comes after Venstre, a liberal political party in Denmark, was divided over a new fertilizer law in early September. Five of the party’s 18 members of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, voted against the party line.
The law sets quotas for Danish farmers’ nitrogen emissions into fjords and coastal waters and has caused internal disagreement within Venstre.
No Venstre members of the Folketing have so far said whether they will support or oppose the proposed spraying ban.
Preben Bang Henriksen (V) has said he “wants to see the final bill first. Hopefully, many changes can be made.”
Søren Gade (V) has declined to say whether he will vote against the bill, saying he has not yet read all the papers. He has also said he “has an expectation that if you take something from people in this country, you provide full compensation.”
The details of the proposed national spraying ban have not yet been decided.
“It is true that I support a national spraying ban. But we have not seen how a national spraying ban is to be made,” Troels Lund Poulsen told TV 2 News.
The proposed ban is intended to protect areas considered vulnerable to contamination of groundwater that can be used for drinking water.
Under the bill, the environment minister would be given authority to designate vulnerable groundwater-forming areas and establish rules for a compensation scheme.
Troels Lund Poulsen addressed the issue in his speech during the Folketing’s opening debate.
“Naturally, we must also have the opportunity to drink clean water from the tap in the future. That is also why we voted for agricultural nitrogen emissions to be significantly reduced,” he said.
“We also support the work on a national spraying ban, and we certainly also believe that we must reduce the amount of untreated wastewater that flows directly into our environment,” he said.
He ended the section of his speech with a reference to compensation.
“We will actively participate in the work to ensure better animal welfare. And all of this must happen in a way where we treat people properly and respect private property rights.”
According to the government’s legislative program, the bill on a national spraying ban is expected to be considered by the Folketing in the second half of December.
Danish Defence orders AI-supported system to coordinate responses to drone threats
The Danish Defence will receive a new command system designed to help military and civilian authorities coordinate their responses to drones.
The Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation has signed an agreement with Danish software company Systematic, the agency said Thursday.
“The construction of Denmark’s drone shield is a step closer to the goal with this agreement with Systematic,” Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said.
The system will use artificial intelligence to analyze large amounts of information and identify patterns, unusual activity and potential threats.
The Danish Defence, police and other authorities will be able to access the same information, giving them a shared operational picture from the first drone sighting until the response is completed.
Systematic’s SitaWare software will be installed at several military locations and connected to existing drone defence systems.
The agency did not disclose the agreement’s cost or when the system would become operational.
The purchase follows an August agreement with Danish defence company Terma. Terma’s system will collect information from different sensors and provide a combined overview of drone activity.
The two systems are intended to work together as part of Denmark’s response to airborne and hybrid threats. The measures follow incidents involving drones over Denmark in 2025.
Denmark records more than 1.17 million state pensioners
Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
It was the 13th consecutive month in which the number reached a new high.
The increase reflects longer life expectancy and large generations reaching the state pension age. However, many new pensioners continue working.
In July, 24.6 percent of 67-year-old state pensioners remained in paid employment, compared with 10.6 percent in July 2022.
Velliv consumer economist Thomas Gress said the rise could be connected to rules allowing people to earn income without reductions to their own or their spouse’s state pension.
“For some, retirement life is the freedom to leave work completely behind. Others want to keep their colleagues, some hours on the job, and benefit from the generous deductions and subsidies available for continuing working life once the state pension age has been reached,” Gress said.
The growing pensioner population is also increasing public spending. Statistics Denmark said social benefits cost the state 908 billion DKK last year, five percent more than the previous year.
State pensions were the largest expense in the old-age category, costing 170 billion DKK.
Velliv expects the number of state pensioners to continue rising until 2029, when roughly one in five Danes is projected to receive the benefit.

Minister expects update soon on future of Denmark’s CPR system
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates expects to provide more details soon about a security review of Denmark’s CPR system.
“I hope to be able to say something more concrete within a very short time about what the future of the CPR system will look like,” Egelund told Ritzau.
The minister announced Monday that a major security review of the entire Central Person Register, known as CPR, had been launched.
The review follows a security breach in which unauthorized people had access for ten days to CPR numbers and other personal information belonging to 8.8 million living and deceased people.
CPR numbers are the personal identification numbers used by Danish authorities and businesses.
The breach has prompted questions about whether people should receive new CPR numbers or whether the entire system needs to be redesigned.
Egelund has previously said it is too early to determine whether new numbers will need to be issued.
She said the review must first establish whether the existing system can be better protected. Authorities will then consider whether the breach warrants a broader overhaul of the CPR system.
Nearly one million Danes add credit warnings after breach of 8.8 million CPR records
The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.
About 970,000 people had registered a warning by October 7, up from just under 250,000 on October 1, the Digital Affairs Ministry said.
“The Danes have taken the situation seriously, and they have acted on the advice that has come from the government and from the authorities,” Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said.
A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.
The Agency for Societal Security has recommended warnings for people who have specific reasons to suspect fraud.
Unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system during 10 days in September.
Authorities discovered the activity after the company received an unusually large bill. Each search of the register carries a fee.
The company has not been identified, and authorities do not know who was responsible.
Egelund said it remained too early to determine whether affected people would need new CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
Man sentenced to one year in prison for assault that led to Swedish man’s death
A Copenhagen court has convicted a 31-year-old man of assaulting a Swedish police employee during a World Cup screening in June, leaving the victim with injuries that proved fatal.
The Copenhagen District Court sentenced the man to one year in prison Wednesday and imposed a one-year nightlife ban. He pleaded guilty.
The assault occurred June 30 at Islands Brygge, where spectators were watching Norway play Ivory Coast.
The defendant threw two beer cans toward a group of spectators before punching 32-year-old Christian Zedig in the head or neck.
The blow ruptured an artery, and Zedig died July 3. He left behind a wife and two daughters.
The defendant told the court he had thrown the cans because someone had thrown beer at his table.
Asked whether he had considered the consequences of punching Zedig, he replied: “No, I just hit him.”
The judge cited the defendant’s aggressive behavior, the fatal consequences and his previous convictions for attempted murder, rape and assault as aggravating factors.
Despite Zedig’s death, the man was convicted of simple assault rather than aggravated assault.
Special prosecutor Søren Harbo explained that the legal classification depends on how dangerous an attack typically is, rather than its consequences alone.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats criticized the sentence and reiterated the government’s intention to increase penalties for simple assault resulting in death.
“One can only conclude that when simple assault ends up costing a person their life, the sentence is in some cases unacceptably low,” Wammen said in a written statement.
Denmark plans two new marine nature parks with 67.8 million DKK investment
Two areas of Danish waters could receive greater protection from fishing and seabed extraction under a proposal in the government’s 2027 finance bill.
The government and Alternativet, the Alternative, propose spending 67.8 million DKK over three years to establish two marine nature national parks.
The areas would undergo active nature restoration, which could include building stone reefs and planting eelgrass on the seabed. Industrial fishing could also be banned, while seabed extraction would be removed from the areas.
“We have fantastic nature beneath the surface of the sea,” Environment Minister Maria Reumert Gjerding of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said in a statement.
“But the Danish marine environment is also under severe pressure from the way we humans have exploited the sea for decades,” she added.
Torsten Gejl, environment and nature spokesperson for the Alternative, helped negotiate the proposal and said he would like Aarhus Bay to become one of the new parks.
“It is Denmark’s second-largest city, and there is a body of water in Aarhus Bay that has enormous potential, but which is screaming for help,” Gejl told Ritzau.
He said pressures including seabed extraction, sludge dumping and trawl fishing should be removed from protected areas.
The government’s platform calls for five new marine nature national parks. The 2027 finance bill proposal provides funding for the first two.
They would be in addition to two marine nature national parks introduced under the previous SVM government in Øresund and Lillebælt.
If the funding is included in the final budget agreement, political negotiations will follow to decide where the two new parks will be established.
Denmark proposes ban on sharing AI-generated deepfakes without consent
People in Denmark could gain stronger protection against realistic AI-generated images, videos and voice recordings under a new bill introduced Thursday.
Culture Minister Zenia Stampe of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party, wants to prevent digital imitations of people’s appearance and voices, known as deepfakes, from being shared without their consent.
“With artificial intelligence, you can create manipulated videos and images with a few clicks and share them on social media. It can lead to misinformation and create doubt about what is real,” Stampe said.
The proposal would cover all citizens, including artists, whose performances and presentations could also be protected against unauthorized digital imitations.
Stampe said she had personally experienced having a photograph from her profile turned into a video that appeared to show her speaking.
She described the experience as intrusive, even when such content is labeled as satire.
The minister also pointed to SF, the Socialist People’s Party, politician Karsten Hønge, whose identity has been used in hundreds of fake social media posts about Greenland.
A central aim of the legislation is to make social media companies and other online platforms remove illegal deepfakes quickly.
Satire would remain legal, although Stampe acknowledged that distinguishing satire from unlawful manipulation could be difficult.
She said courts would have to decide whether particular content qualifies as satire or whether that label is being used to justify illegal material.
“It will certainly be difficult, but on the other hand, I also have respect for the fact that we have a very strong tradition of satire in Denmark,” she said.
Stampe hopes the legislation can take effect around the turn of the year.
Denmark expands exemptions from new nitrogen rules for fruit and vegetable growers
More Danish farmers will receive temporary exemptions from new fertilizer restrictions after concerns that the rules could make growing certain fruits and vegetables more difficult.
The Ministry of Nature and Animal Welfare announced that crops including melons, rhubarb, strawberries, table grapes and pumpkins will be exempt from the new nitrogen regulations throughout 2027.
Woody plants grown in nurseries will also be covered by the exemption.
The changes follow a review of the regulations approved by a majority in Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing, in September.
The rules, which take effect at the beginning of 2027, aim to reduce nitrogen pollution from agriculture by limiting fertilizer use.
Nitrogen runoff from farmland has contributed to the deterioration of Denmark’s marine environment.
However, agricultural experts and vegetable producers have warned that the restrictions could create significant difficulties for domestic food production.
The government initially planned to exempt mainly potato growers during the first year. The exemption has now been extended to additional fruit and vegetable producers.
“I am pleased that we have the opportunity to also exempt some berry and fruit growers who otherwise faced major challenges, so they get one more year to adapt,” Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said.
The exemptions apply only to 2027 and are intended to give affected growers additional time to adjust.
The ministry said the newly exempt crops account for a small share of Denmark’s total agricultural land.
As a result, it expects the changes to have only a very limited effect on the nitrogen reductions the regulations are intended to achieve.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.
“In practice, this means that it will normally not be sufficient to state one’s CPR number when picking up medicine,” the association said.
Customers may instead be asked to show a physical or digital health card or answer verification questions.
Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.
The changes follow recommendations from Samsik, the Danish Agency for Public Security.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” Samsik director Laila Reenberg said Tuesday.
PLO, the Danish Association of General Practitioners, which represents and advises general practitioners, has also asked its members to follow Samsik’s recommendations.
Samsik said authorities, organizations and companies should pay closer attention when CPR numbers, names or addresses are used to confirm someone’s identity and should generally use other information for identity checks.
Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency. The National Special Crime Unit is investigating the case.
Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow

He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
