Autumn holiday traffic could cause motorway delays across Denmark
Drivers should expect heavier traffic and possible delays on Denmark’s motorways at the start and end of the autumn holiday, the Danish Road Directorate has warned.
The busiest periods are expected to be Friday from 2 to 6 p.m. and Saturday from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Traffic may also be heavier than usual during the final two days of the holiday.
The directorate, Denmark’s national road authority, recommends traveling outside the busiest hours.
Routes expected to see increased traffic include the E20 motorways across western Zealand and Funen, the E45 motorway in southern Jutland and motorways around Kolding.
Drivers crossing the Vejle Fjord Bridge on the E45 should allow extra time. Maintenance work has reduced the speed limit, and queues may form during busy periods.
Those heading to the ferry terminal in Aarhus should also allow more time to drive through the city. Roadwork on Marselis Boulevard means only one eastbound lane is open.
Drivers can check traffic conditions through the directorate’s Trafikinfo service or listen to P4 Trafik, the radio traffic service.
Meny tops Danish grocery customer survey for second year as 365discount finishes last
Meny has ranked first in an annual survey of Danish grocery customers for the second year in a row, while 365discount again finished at the bottom of customers’ overall ratings.
The survey, conducted by analysis firm Loyalty Group, gathered responses from 4,255 Danish grocery customers.
Dagrofa, the company behind Meny, said in a press release that the chain had Denmark’s most satisfied and loyal grocery customers. Meny scored 71 points on the survey’s loyalty index, ahead of Rema 1000 with 69 points.
Meny also led in six of the nine areas assessed, including customer trust, organic products, service and product quality, according to Dagrofa.
“Quality pays off in the end. We invest in skilled staff and quality on the shelves. We are enormously proud of this,” Meny chain director Richo Boss said in the release.
Loyalty Group produces annual industry indexes across several sectors, offering companies insight into customer preferences.
Dagrofa highlighted service as a particular reason for Meny’s ranking. Loyalty Group research director Lars Jepsen said customers recognized a “high level of professionalism and service.”
“For the chain, it is probably worth noting that the customers’ responses show that they trust the chain, and that the experience is stable from time to time,” he said in the release.
At the other end of the survey, Coop-owned 365discount received the lowest overall customer rating for the second consecutive year, according to TV 2.
“We are of course not satisfied with the ranking, and every day we work in a targeted manner to improve the customer experience,” 365discount chain director Michael Tilsted said in a written response to TV 2.
Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.
A 31-year-old man charged with assaulting a Swedish man at a World Cup screening at Islands Brygge will appear before Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday.
The incident happened June 30 during a screening of a match between Norway and Ivory Coast. The Swedish man was punched and suffered a ruptured artery. He died July 3.
The defendant is charged with assault under a section of the Danish penal code covering less serious violence. Prosecutors are also seeking an increased sentence because of his previous convictions.
Special prosecutor Maria Cingari said in July that he could face eight to 10 months in prison.
The man has previously been convicted of rape and attempted murder. He was also convicted in another assault case last week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, criticized the possible sentence in August, saying she believed it should be harsher. The defendant is a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of Moderaterne, the Moderates, also commented after the Swedish man’s death, writing: “May the guilty party be judged harshly and fairly.”
The government has since announced plans to increase penalties in assault cases where the victim dies and the offender has previous convictions.
Prosecutors are also seeking a nightlife ban for the defendant. He has pleaded not guilty and is protected by a court-ordered name ban.
Two other people face separate assault charges in connection with the incident. One is accused of trampling on the Swedish man while he was lying down and assaulting another Swedish man. The other is accused of kicking the second man.
People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.
“In practice, this means that it will normally not be sufficient to state one’s CPR number when picking up medicine,” the association said.
Customers may instead be asked to show a physical or digital health card or answer verification questions.
Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.
The changes follow recommendations from Samsik, the Danish Agency for Public Security.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” Samsik director Laila Reenberg said Tuesday.
PLO, the Danish Association of General Practitioners, which represents and advises general practitioners, has also asked its members to follow Samsik’s recommendations.
Samsik said authorities, organizations and companies should pay closer attention when CPR numbers, names or addresses are used to confirm someone’s identity and should generally use other information for identity checks.
Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency. The National Special Crime Unit is investigating the case.
Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.
Danish government prioritizes higher early retirement benefit and Greenland defense agreement
Denmark’s government will begin the new parliamentary year by seeking approval for a Greenland defense agreement and increasing the Arne early retirement benefit.
The legislative program, published as the Folketing opened Tuesday, shows that the monthly early retirement payment will rise by 3,000 DKK. The government plans to introduce the bill in November.
Before then, parliament will vote this month on the defense agreement Denmark, Greenland and the USA signed in New York.
The agreement has broad political support and largely continues a 1951 arrangement. It also includes two bases the USA wants to establish in Greenland and gives Greenland a stronger independent position.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen thanked Greenlandic leader Jens-Frederik Nielsen for their cooperation during her opening speech.
After New Year, the government will begin legislation restoring Great Prayer Day as a public holiday from 2030.
The restoration depends on employment increasing enough to offset the additional labor created when the holiday was abolished. Socialist People’s Party leader Pia Olsen Dyhr expects the target to be reached.
The government will also reintroduce a citizenship bill covering 2,055 previously approved applicants and their children.
The original bill expired when an election was called. Applicants must undergo a complete new review.
Opposition parties have criticized the government for proceeding before completing a planned citizenship screening system.
Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.
Danish consumer group files complaint over Red Bull advertising on influencer’s platforms
Forbrugerrådet Tænk has asked Denmark’s Consumer Ombudsman to investigate whether Red Bull’s advertising through influencer Rasmus Søndergaard violates marketing law.
The Danish Consumer Council, an independent consumer organization, filed complaints against Red Bull Denmark, Søndergaard’s company and two marketing agencies.
Søndergaard publishes content on Twitch, YouTube and TikTok.
Danish law prohibits marketing energy drinks to consumers under 18 because the products are considered unsuitable for children and teenagers.
Forbrugerrådet Tænk described the Red Bull campaign on Søndergaard’s platforms as the most serious suspected violation of the Marketing Practices Act it had seen.
The organization said Red Bull products appeared frequently in his videos and argued that many viewers were younger than 18.
Miriam Michaelsen, chair of Denmark’s Media Council for Children and Young People, said Danish minors widely use the platforms carrying Søndergaard’s content.
Søndergaard rejected the complaint.
“I make content for adults, and children should not encounter advertisements that are not for them,” he said. “I completely disagree with the complaint, but we are listening, because we must protect the youngest.”
Søndergaard and Red Bull began a formal partnership in 2023.
The complaints also cover DayZeroAgency, which represents Søndergaard, and Ultra, which manages marketing and events for Red Bull.
MobilePay will change its name to Vipps in Denmark from January 12, 2027, the company behind the payment app announced Tuesday.
Some of the app’s nearly 4.7 million Danish users will begin seeing a redesigned logo during the transition.
The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.
MobilePay’s services in Denmark and Finland merged with Norwegian payment app Vipps in 2022, creating a shared Nordic platform.
Vipps MobilePay described the name change as one of the final steps toward operating under a common Nordic identity.
“We know that the new name will require a bit of getting used to,” said Jeanette Hertzum, the company’s Danish country manager.
The company wants users in Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Sweden and Finland to use the same name and logo.
The longer transition period is intended to give Danish users time to adjust before the new name takes effect.
The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.
Denmark’s parliament opens new year with royal visit and prime minister’s eighth address
The Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, opens its new parliamentary year Tuesday with a royal visit and a speech from Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
The Constitution requires parliament to open on the first Tuesday of October.
The day begins with a 10 a.m. service at Christiansborg Palace Church for lawmakers, ministers and invited guests.
The parliamentary meeting starts at noon. Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates, the longest-serving lawmaker, will initially preside. He has served in parliament since 1994.
Lawmakers will elect a speaker and four deputy speakers before Frederiksen of the Social Democrats delivers her eighth opening address.
King Frederik, Queen Mary and Princess Benedikte will attend. Members of the Royal House have attended every opening since 1966.
The government will also publish its legislative program listing bills planned for the coming year.
Frederiksen’s speech will be debated Thursday during one of parliament’s major annual political debates. Party leaders will still give initial reactions to the media Tuesday.
Henrik Frandsen of the Moderates has been nominated to replace Venstre’s Søren Gade as speaker.
Deputy speaker positions will go to the Social Democrats, Socialist People’s Party, Venstre and Danish People’s Party.
The meeting will end with Denmark’s national anthem, led by the Copenhagen Boys’ Choir, the Royal Cantory.
Southern Denmark region delays LGBTQ+ healthcare guide after parties object to gender-neutral language
The Region of Southern Denmark has delayed approval of a handbook designed to help healthcare workers provide respectful care to LGBTQ+ patients, Danish public broadcaster DR reported.
The regional Executive Committee discussed the pocket guide Monday but did not approve it after several parties objected to its language.
Venstre, Denmark’s Liberal Party, proposed revisions with support from the Danish People’s Party, Denmark Democrats, Liberal Alliance and Conservative People’s Party.
“We think that the starting point is that there are two genders, and that we should not have a woke-ideological use of language,” regional council chair Bo Libergren of Venstre told DR.
He said the guide should avoid terms including “hen,” a gender-neutral pronoun used by some people instead of “he” or “she.”
The proposed changes will be considered by the full regional council.
The handbook is part of a regional policy on LGBTQ+ patients’ experiences with healthcare, adopted in December.
Sygeplejersken, a Danish nursing publication, reported that the guide was intended to provide practical tools for treating patients with safety and respect.
It would not create new rules but provide shared knowledge and examples of situations healthcare workers may encounter.
The plan was to distribute it across regional workplaces after approval.
About eight percent of Denmark’s population identifies as LGBTQ+, according to figures cited by the Danish Institute for Human Rights.
Several wastewater discharge cases cannot be completed while Denmark’s Environmental Protection Agency reviews how it approves direct releases into waterways.
The review will also increase processing times for new permits and reassessments, the agency said Tuesday.
The action follows an August decision by the Environment and Food Appeals Board, the independent Danish body that reviews environmental rulings.
The board’s decision prompted the agency to examine its procedures for approving direct wastewater discharges.
Some cases will remain suspended until the agency develops what it called a “new administrative basis” for making decisions.
The appeals case involved chemical company Koppers Denmark.
In 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency renewed the company’s permit to discharge cooling water into Nyborg Fjord.
The Danish Society for Nature Conservation, Denmark’s main environmental membership organization, appealed the decision.
The appeals board later ruled that the agency had approved the permit using insufficient documentation.

Denmark’s cyber hotline will remain open until midnight in the coming days following unauthorized access to 8.8 million records in the national CPR system.
The hotline will operate from 8 a.m. to midnight. It normally closes at 8 p.m. on weekdays, the Agency for Societal Security said.
The hotline advises residents and businesses on digital security, fraud and cyberattacks. It can also help people whose identities have been misused.
Residents with a specific suspicion that their CPR number is being used fraudulently can receive help creating a credit warning.
A credit warning alerts companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving loans or credit, making financial identity theft more difficult.
Authorities detected irregular activity in the CPR system on October 2.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information during September.
The records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority, said automated searches appeared intended to identify valid CPR numbers.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating. Authorities have not identified those responsible.
Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates urged residents to remain vigilant.
Authorities advised people never to provide passwords or other confidential information to unsolicited callers or message senders.
Denmark says it is too early to decide whether breach victims need new CPR numbers
Denmark has not decided whether people affected by unauthorized access to 8.8 million personal records will need new CPR numbers, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said.
Egelund spoke after briefing two Folketing committees about the breach of Denmark’s national personal information register.
“I have requested a security review of the entire CPR system,” Egelund of the Moderates said.
She said the findings would determine what changes were needed to restore trust and security. No deadline has been set for the review.
Unauthorized people misused a private Danish company’s legal access to obtain names, addresses, CPR numbers and other information.
The affected records cover living and deceased people, as well as those who have moved abroad.
The CPR register can also contain details about marital status, births, family relationships, citizenship, Church of Denmark membership and guardianship.
Egelund said authorities were focused on preventing the stolen information from being used for identity theft, phishing and other digital fraud.
A website and telephone hotline have been established to advise residents about protecting themselves.
The breach has been reported to Datatilsynet, Denmark’s data protection authority.
NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit, is investigating.
Authorities have not identified who was responsible. Egelund said investigators had not ruled out any possibilities, including international involvement.
Copenhagen apartment listings exceed 2,000 as housing market begins to slow
More than 2,000 owner-occupied apartments are for sale in Copenhagen for the first time since early 2024, according to housing website Boligsiden.
At the beginning of October, 2,057 apartments were listed in Copenhagen Municipality.
That was more than five percent higher than one month earlier and almost twice the number available one year ago.
The increase gives buyers more choice and could reduce competition for individual apartments, said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Sellers must now compete with more properties for buyers’ attention, she added.
Daetz said the changing balance had also led to larger price reductions on Copenhagen apartments.
Every district recorded an increase in listings over the past year.
Copenhagen S, which includes parts of Amager, had 530 apartments for sale at the beginning of October. That was an increase of more than 150 percent from one year earlier.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at Danish bank AL Sydbank, said the figures showed that Copenhagen’s housing market was losing speed.
He pointed to slowing sales activity and smaller monthly price increases.
Across Denmark, the number of apartments for sale increased 6.3 percent over the past year.
However, listings of detached homes and terraced houses moved in the opposite direction, falling 11.9 percent nationwide.
German spy chief warns Russia is waging a ‘shadow war’
The head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service has warned that Russia is intensifying what he described as a “shadow war” against the country, saying Germany risks being drawn into a violent conflict.
“No other country poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany,” Martin Jäger said during a public hearing in the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, according to AFP.
The hearing took place before the parliamentary committee responsible for overseeing Germany’s intelligence services.
Jäger pointed to a case in August in which a drone carrying an explosive charge was found near a Ukrainian cargo plane in Leipzig. Agents with Russian connections are suspected of being behind the incident.
Germany has repeatedly accused Russia of conducting hybrid operations involving sabotage, espionage and other attempts to disrupt public order. Moscow has rejected such accusations.
Jäger said Russian intelligence services were acting “highly professionally and ruthlessly.”
“Russia is waging a shadow war against us. This undeclared war does not fit into traditional military and legal categories,” he said, according to German broadcaster Tagesschau.
“We must prepare ourselves for further attempts to intimidate us and more interference,” he added.
Germany is one of Ukraine’s largest supporters in its war against Russia.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited Kyiv on Sunday alongside senior executives from several German defense companies.
Merz, who last week also warned about continued Russian hybrid warfare, announced an additional 1 billion euros, around 7.5 billion DKK, in military support for Ukraine during the visit.
More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.
The 2026 Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands to represent friendship
This year’s Danish Christmas seal features 46 children holding hands in a design focused on friendship and community.
Christmas Seal Foundation board chair Anne Glad Wagner and artist Martin Jørgensen unveiled the seal Monday at Copenhagen City Hall.
The design is titled “The best gifts cannot be wrapped.”
Jørgensen said the children represent the supportive community that young people experience during stays at Denmark’s Christmas seal homes.
“It is about helping children, and therefore I have made them the main characters,” he said. “The Christmas seal homes help children form bonds and believe in themselves.”
Jørgensen has a background in advertising. The foundation selected him because of a graphic style that combines warmth, humor and small visual surprises.
Christmas seals are special decorative stamps sold before Christmas to raise money for the five Christmas seal homes in Denmark.
The homes support as many as 1,000 children annually who experience problems including bullying, loneliness, low self-esteem and poor well-being.
Seal sales cover about five percent of the homes’ operating expenses. Private individuals, companies and foundations provide almost all other funding.
The Christmas Seal Foundation, a Danish charity that operates the homes, has had Queen Mary as its patron since 2004.
Denmark’s Christmas seals were first issued in 1904. This year’s design is the 123rd edition. Copenhagen postmaster Einar Holbøll originally proposed the idea.
Denmark faces mild start to week before cooler and wetter autumn weather arrives
Denmark will begin the week with mild temperatures before rain, showers and cooler conditions arrive from Wednesday, according to the Danish Meteorological Institute, the national weather service.
“We will have a mild start to the week with many clouds and locally a little rain from time to time,” meteorologist Anne Borrits said.
A low-pressure system approaching from the southwest will bring more typical autumn weather during the second half of the week.
Monday will begin with some sunshine in eastern Denmark, while most other areas will remain cloudy.
Light rain is possible in Jutland, and temperatures will reach between 15 and 19 degrees Celsius. The highest temperatures are expected locally on Funen or Zealand.
Winds will be moderate to strong from the southwest. Coastal areas near the Skagerrak could experience gales Monday afternoon.
Skies will clear overnight into Tuesday, bringing dry conditions. Temperatures could fall to eight degrees in some areas, though most places will remain between 12 and 15 degrees.
Tuesday will be dry with periods of sunshine.
A low-pressure system will approach from the North Sea during Tuesday evening and Wednesday, bringing rain and later showers.
Conditions remain uncertain through Friday. Temperatures are expected to fall gradually, reaching between 10 and 15 degrees Thursday and Friday.
Strong winds are also possible along some coastal areas.
Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.
Elk dies after collision with car on motorway north of Copenhagen
An elk died after being struck by a car on the Helsingør Motorway near Nivå on Monday morning, North Zealand Police said.
A 36-year-old woman was driving north in the inside lane when the animal suddenly appeared a few meters ahead of her, according to her statement to police.
The collision occurred at 6:10 a.m. between the Kokkedal and Humlebæk exits.
The woman was apparently uninjured. The car’s windshield and rear window were shattered, while its roof and hood were damaged.
The elk was found dead about 100 meters from the vehicle.
Denmark has no naturally occurring wild elk population. However, Swedish elk were introduced to Lille Vildmose in Himmerland beginning in 2015. That population had grown to about 20 animals by 2020.
Authorities also plan to release elk into Gribskov National Nature Park in North Zealand this year.
Wild elk are occasionally seen elsewhere in Denmark. The animals can swim across the Øresund between Sweden and Zealand.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

====================================================================================================

Eye contact may act as a learning “switch” for babies’ brains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

Direct eye contact from an adult speaker appears to guide how infants choose which words to learn by aligning the baby’s brain activity with the adult’s. A new study suggests that this one-way neural coordination may help link an adult’s communicative gaze to an infant’s selective word learning. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
Infants grow up in busy environments where many sights and sounds compete for their attention, requiring them to figure out which information is worth learning. To navigate this challenge, babies rely on social signals known as ostensive cues, which are communicative acts like direct gaze or infant-directed speech that indicate an adult intends to share information. The central focus of the new study is interpersonal neural coupling, a measure of how much activity in one person’s brain predicts later activity in another person’s brain.
Past developmental research has shown that social cues play an active role in how young minds acquire language. For example, a 2003 study indicated that nine-month-old infants learned unfamiliar foreign speech sounds when interacting with a live person, but did not learn when watching identical recorded video lessons. Expanding on how social cues operate in the brain, a 2017 study found that when an adult made direct eye contact with a baby, their brainwaves synchronized more strongly than when the adult looked away.
Even so, scientists still faced an unresolved question about what this shared brain activity accomplishes. As the authors of a 2020 review noted, it remained uncertain whether brain-to-brain synchrony helps infants learn or represents an incidental byproduct of two individuals watching the same event. In a related vein, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 showed that communicative infant-directed speech heightened attention-related brain activity in toddlers and was linked to better word learning.
The research team, which included first author Wei Zhang of Nanyang Technological University and Victoria Leong, a professor in the School of Social Sciences at Nanyang Technological University and the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Cambridge, set out to address this question. “We had previously published a seminal demonstration that eye contact modulates adult-infant neural synchrony,” Leong told PsyPost. “The current study replicates (across two countries) and extends these findings to show that neural synchrony underpins infants’ selective learning in social contexts.”
The researchers tested 47 infants who were roughly nine months old, with an average age of 286 days. The sample consisted of 29 infants from the United Kingdom and 18 infants from Singapore. All infants were developing typically, with the British infants coming from English-speaking households and the Singaporean infants coming from bilingual English-Chinese families.
During the experiment, infants sat facing a monitor that displayed pre-recorded video clips of a female speaker reciting three different artificial languages. Each artificial language was constructed from four three-syllable words, like “pe-tu-do” or “di-lo-ga,” spoken continuously at a steady pace without pauses or emotional inflections. In these sequences, syllables within a word always occurred together, while syllables crossing between words occurred together only a third of the time, mimicking how real speech contains statistical patterns that help infants identify word boundaries.
To isolate the impact of eye contact, the speaker wore glasses with polarizing lenses, paired with an adjustable polarizing filter on the camera, while looking straight ahead. In the full gaze condition, the glasses appeared transparent, leaving her eyes entirely visible. In the partial gaze condition, the lenses were darkened like sunglasses, and in the no gaze condition, the lenses were made completely opaque. Adjusting only the filter on the camera allowed the researchers to manipulate how visible her eyes were while her own view remained unobstructed, so her delivery would not differ between conditions.
Each experimental block included a familiarization phase and a testing phase for each gaze condition. During familiarization, babies watched the speaker recite an artificial language for 60 seconds while their visual attention and brain activity were recorded using electroencephalography, a non-invasive technique that detects electrical signals through sensors on the scalp. During the testing phase, the infants heard either valid words from the language or artificial nonwords made by joining syllables that crossed word boundaries. The researchers measured how long babies looked at the screen, relying on the tendency of infants to look longer at less familiar sounds when they have recognized the underlying patterns.
The behavioral results showed that infants learned selectively depending on the speaker’s gaze. Infants showed evidence of learning only for the language paired with the full gaze condition, looking an average of 1.22 seconds longer at nonwords than at words, a small to moderate effect. In contrast, learning was not statistically significant for the languages accompanied by partial gaze, where the difference was 0.76 seconds, or no gaze, where the difference was 0.34 seconds.
“We let the infants listen to all three languages and it turned out they were selective in what they learned,” Leong said in a news release from the University of Cambridge. “They’re not just passive sponges. They heard all three languages, but only learned the one, which was when they could see the speaker’s eyes.”
This learning preference did not stem from differences in general visual attention. Infants spent roughly equal amounts of time watching the speaker across all conditions, averaging about 23 seconds in the full gaze condition, 21 seconds in the partial gaze condition, and 23 seconds in the no gaze condition. In addition, statistical analysis showed that the link between total looking time and learning was not statistically significant.
Kaili Clackson, a study co-author from the University of Cambridge, described the gap between looking and learning this way. “Even when the infants seemed to be staring at a screen attentively, unless there was eye contact, nothing was going in – the information washed over them,” Clackson said in the release. “The brain synchrony shows that it’s a selection process.” She added, “These cues are really powerful because when you preface new information with them, they tell the baby: this is important, you need to listen.”
When comparing the two geographic groups, Singaporean infants watched the speaker on screen longer than British infants did, which the authors suggested might reflect an interest in a speaker with unfamiliar Western facial features. However, learning performance itself did not differ significantly between the Singaporean and British infants. Both groups responded similarly to the presence or absence of the speaker’s gaze.
Leong noted that this pattern sheds light on early cognitive development across backgrounds. “This suggests that although there are already cultural differences in what we pay attention to or find novel from 9 months of age, the brain’s learning mechanisms set infants up to learn in a fundamentally similar way across cultures,” she told PsyPost.
To examine brain connections, the authors focused on alpha rhythms, a type of brainwave that in infants cycles about 6 to 9 times per second, using data from the 42 infants whose recordings were usable. Because the speaker’s brain activity had been recorded while she filmed the videos, the researchers could test whether patterns in her brain activity predicted later patterns in the infants’ brains as they watched.
This adult-to-infant coupling predicted learning better than chance, explaining about 25 percent of the variation in learning compared with about 20 percent for models built on shuffled data. The infants’ own internal brain connectivity did not predict learning, but it was linked to their scores on a parent-reported checklist of early communicative gestures, explaining about 34 percent of the variation compared with about 22 percent for shuffled data.
The team also evaluated neural entrainment, which is the tendency of a listener’s brainwaves to track the rising and falling loudness of speech. Full gaze strengthened this tracking at a few recording sites, but entrainment did not predict learning. A statistical mediation analysis suggested that adult-to-infant coupling may link the speaker’s eye contact to infant learning: coupling was stronger with full gaze than with no gaze, though not reliably different from partial gaze, and stronger coupling went along with greater learning. The authors call this result preliminary, partly because the coupling measure was selected for how well it predicted learning.
“Eye contact helps the baby decide what is important to learn in a social context, acting as a ‘switch’ to synchronize their brainwaves with those of the speaker and facilitating learning,” Leong told PsyPost.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that eye contact promotes aligned brain activity between interacting individuals. However, that earlier study examined spontaneous synchrony between familiar adult pairs rather than adult-to-infant coupling during learning.
Beyond theoretical insights into early development, the authors noted practical takeaways for parents and caregivers. “As parents, we need to be conscious of the need to use social cues like eye contact and calling your child’s name, as these cues don’t just focus your child’s attention, they activate the learning process,” Leong said in the release.
“If you’re on your phone and distracted when you’re trying to give them instructions or teach them something, there’s less of a likelihood that they’ll take it seriously or learn compared to if you put your phone down and look them in the eye,” Leong added in the release. “This is an important way of signaling your intentionality, your seriousness, that you want them to pay attention and learn something.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study involved a modest sample size of 47 infants for behavioral testing and 42 for brain recordings, meaning subtle effects in the partial gaze condition might be detected more reliably in larger groups. Additionally, the infants watched pre-recorded videos rather than interacting with a live adult, and the study did not test everyday interactions or phone use directly. Notably, infants in this study succeeded in learning statistical word patterns from video, in contrast to the 2003 findings where infants required live interaction to distinguish non-native speech sounds.
There are a few other things to keep in mind regarding the findings and measurements. The authors noted that eye contact may play a different role in communities where adult-infant interaction relies more heavily on touch and physical closeness, as observed in some Arab cultures. Methodologically, the researchers analyzed brainwaves within a single shared frequency band of 6 to 9 Hertz to meet computational requirements, even though adult alpha waves typically peak higher. Finally, while the statistical models highlight an association, experimental manipulations would be needed to establish whether neural coupling directly causes learning gains.
The study, “Adult-to-infant unidirectional neural coupling mediates selective social learning in infants from the United Kingdom and Singapore,” was authored by Wei Zhang, Kaili Clackson, Stanimira Georgieva, Lorena Santamaria, Vanessa Reindl, Valdas Noreika, Nicholas Darby, Vaka Valsdóttir, Priyadharshini Santhanakrishnan, and Victoria Leong.

Italy approves Meloni's electoral reform in confidence vote ahead of 2027 election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:00:36 UTC
23:00:36 KST

The Chamber of Deputies has passed electoral law reform by 227 votes to 164, despite possible Constitutional Court objections. Italy now formally enters the election campaign, with an early vote increasingly likely.
Italy's Chamber of Deputies approved a new electoral law on Thursday, clearing the way for its use in the next general election, due in 2027.
The legislation, backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government and formally known as the Stabilicum, - dubbed the Melonellum by opposition parties, - passed by 227 votes to 164 in a secret ballot.
The vote effectively marks the unofficial start of the election campaign. While the current legislature runs until September 2027, speculation about an early election is already circulating in the corridors of parliament, though as we explain below, a vote before 14 April remains unlikely.
The immediate political battle now shifts to alliances. Meloni has so far ruled out joining forces with National Future, the party of MEP Roberto Vannacci, while the opposition has yet to agree on a common leader. Significant divisions remain within the centre-left, particularly over the war in Ukraine, where Democratic Party secretary Elly Schlein and Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte remain at odds.
Meloni moved quickly to claim the vote as a show of unity.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right split, today we answer with facts: we are united, solid and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens," she wrote on social media.
During the sitting, opposition MPs protested, brandishing placards reading: "Rigged law", "No to the fix" and "With Meloni diesel at 3 euros".
"Seats first. That is your slogan. We will vote firmly against this electoral law, which has been designed not for voters but to protect those already elected. With our progressive alliance we will be able to win under any electoral law and change Italians’ lives," said Elly Schlein in her explanation of vote.
Five Star Movement leader Conte also used exceptionally harsh words, arguing that the law has been written to ensure victory for the current ruling coalition.
He concluded: "There is only one further detail missing to guarantee your future control of Parliament: specifying that the majority bonus goes to a prime minister with light-coloured eyes".
How the new Italian electoral law was approved
The governing majority held firm in the secret ballot. This was the third parliamentary reading, after the amendments passed by the Senate, which introduced preference voting with blocked list leaders and increased the number of signatures required from parties not represented in Parliament in order to stand in elections.
On Wednesday the Chamber had approved the third confidence motion tabled by the government on the first three articles of the law. Thursday saw the final, most delicate, vote. If this last vote had gone against the government, the text would have been rejected, but the cabinet would not formally have been obliged to resign.
The most significant changes are contained in the first two articles, which were approved through a confidence vote. They introduce preference voting alongside blocked list leaders and set out the rules for electing both the Chamber and the Senate under the new system.
The signature threshold for parties without parliamentary representation has also been raised, from 1,500 to 6,000, and the rules on gender representation have been amended.
A third article addresses single-member constituencies in the province of Bolzano, while article 8 introduces one of the most anticipated changes: the right to vote for people living away from their registered place of residence.
The confidence vote is a mechanism that allows governments to fast-track legislation and limit debate and filibustering by the opposition. Under this procedure, MPs vote on the government's text as presented, without the ability to propose amendments.
The government stakes its survival on the outcome, if the Chamber votes it down, the administration automatically falls.
The issue of first-term MPs’ pensions
Faced with the threat of a government crisis, it was widely expected that most MPs would back the reform.
There is one date that Italian political scientists are all trying to pinpoint precisely: the moment when the current legislature reaches 4 years, 6 months and one day of its total five-year term.
On that date, first-term MPs become entitled to a parliamentary pension (around 1,500 euros, payable only from the age of 65).
For the current government, that threshold falls on 14 April 2027, and Italian political history shows that it is very unlikely that an election will be called before then.
There is nonetheless concern that the Constitutional Court could overturn the reform, which would complicate the government's plans and expose the right to fierce criticism during the campaign.
The opposition has identified three potentially unconstitutional elements: the majority bonus in the Senate, the requirement for parties without an established ballot logo to gather 300,000 signatures, and the absence of any requirement that at least 40 percent of lead candidates be women.
According to critics, the law potentially leaves Italy in political deadlock.

Senior advisor to Mike Huckabee blocked and altered reports critical of Israel, investigation finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:57:48 UTC
22:57:48 KST

David Milstein, a senior adviser to U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, repeatedly blocked or substantially altered reports critical of Israel in an effort to present Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in a more favorable light to the administration in Washington, a New York Times investigation published Thursday alleges.
For the investigation, Times reporters interviewed 15 current U.S. officials who had worked with Milstein in some capacity, as well as nine former diplomats who helped provide background. The newspaper also obtained or reviewed dozens of documents, cables, memos and other internal communications that it said showed Milstein’s involvement in changing embassy reporting.
Most of those who spoke to the Times said they did so out of concern that Milstein’s actions were undermining standard diplomatic work. Some also expressed concern that, in certain cases, his actions contradicted President Donald Trump’s stated policies.
One example cited in the investigation took place in late March, at the height of the war with Iran, when Israel quietly approved more West Bank settlements at once than ever before. A sharply worded, urgent report on the move never reached the U.S. administration. According to three U.S. officials, Milstein blocked it.
A similar case occurred in April, when senior IDF officials warned that settler violence in the West Bank could ignite a new Palestinian uprising. Embassy personnel tried to relay those warnings to Washington, but Milstein prevented the reports from being sent in their original form, according to three officials.
Instead, Milstein praised Netanyahu’s “new and unprecedented initiatives” to combat violence in the West Bank. The report was titled: “Government Acts Forcefully Against Escalating Violence in the West Bank.”
Another case involved members of Congress who requested information about the deaths of nine Palestinian Americans in the West Bank over the past four years. According to multiple officials, Milstein blocked a detailed report prepared by embassy staff, effectively thwarting lawmakers’ efforts to obtain the information.
The main findings in the blocked report showed that in most cases the investigations had made very little progress, that some files had been closed and that no one had been prosecuted over the deaths, according to those officials. Instead of sending the report, Milstein argued that the embassy should send a letter stating that Israel was handling the investigations properly.
Officials who spoke with the Times said that, shortly after returning to the embassy in Jerusalem at the start of Trump’s second term in the White House, Milstein began insisting on approving outgoing correspondence from the embassy section dealing with Palestinian affairs.
The volume of reporting fell from several reports a week to only a handful a month, because some staff members stopped writing reports out of fear that Milstein would block or rewrite them, those officials said.
According to several officials, Milstein’s interventions went far beyond those of any of his predecessors. They and others said they were speaking out because they feared officials in Washington were receiving a distorted picture of Israeli actions through key diplomatic channels.
Milstein’s efforts, they said, helped shield the Netanyahu government from potentially harsher responses by the Trump administration.
The Times noted that it is unclear to what extent Huckabee was aware of Milstein’s actions. Both Huckabee and Milstein declined the newspaper’s requests for interviews. Huckabee is required to approve most major reports and decisions made by Milstein, but officials said the adviser sometimes acted on his own.
According to those officials, Huckabee at times worked with Milstein to withhold information or present it differently to the administration. In other instances, however, he believed Milstein had gone too far and stopped him.
Milstein’s efforts to influence embassy reporting were first exposed about a year ago by the online magazine of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, a Washington think tank that advocates reduced tensions and greater restraint in U.S. military policy.
The Times investigation, however, presented documented evidence and previously unreported cases in which Milstein allegedly sought to tilt information in favor of the Netanyahu government. The documented activity, the report said, continued throughout the past year.
Those who spoke with the Times included career government officials and political appointees, including strong supporters of the U.S.-Israel relationship.
Concern over Milstein’s conduct also spread to senior administration officials in Washington, including in the White House, who expressed frustration to colleagues over some of his actions, according to four people.
It remains unclear whether or how Milstein’s interventions affected White House policy toward Israel. Since Trump declared a year ago that he would not allow Israel to annex the West Bank, he has rarely spoken publicly on the issue.
In response to questions sent to the embassy about Milstein’s actions, Huckabee did not address the specific cases described in the investigation.
“The events in the investigation are so incomplete, in fact, that they are consistent with other ridiculous efforts by the Times. I personally and categorically reject the allegations presented in the investigation,” he said.
The U.S. State Department said: “The entire State Department team remains focused on advancing President Trump’s America First agenda.”
Who is David Milstein?
Milstein is a familiar figure in right-wing circles in the United States and Israel, and has repeatedly arranged meetings between Huckabee and senior Israeli officials. Still, he is not especially well known in either country, and his role as a gatekeeper for information flowing to Washington had received relatively little attention until now.
His stepfather is right-wing radio host Mark Levin, a close ally of Trump. Netanyahu has also appeared on Levin’s program several times in recent years. The connection among the three is well known in Washington and at the embassy, officials in Jerusalem and Washington told the Times.
Milstein identifies as a conservative and longtime Republican. He previously served as an aide to pro-Israel Texas Sen. Ted Cruz from 2013 to 2018, before moving to Israel to study at a Jerusalem yeshiva. In 2020, he took a job as an aide to then-U.S. Ambassador David Friedman.
As an adviser to Huckabee, Milstein is now one of the most senior officials at the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem. According to the Times, he functions as a kind of chief of staff for the ambassador.
Huckabee has authorized him to oversee much of the mission’s portfolio, particularly developments in the West Bank and Gaza. His responsibilities include reviewing and editing information sent to Washington, including the reports he allegedly softened in Israel’s favor.
Officials with professional familiarity with Milstein said he goes to unusual lengths to portray Israel positively. They said he has blocked critical reporting, rewritten reports to convey a different — sometimes opposite — message from the original, and delayed approving drafts until the issue was no longer relevant.
One prominent case cited in the investigation occurred in the summer of 2025, when dozens of Palestinians arrived at a food distribution point in Gaza run by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, or GHF, which was backed by Jerusalem and Washington.
U.S. diplomats drafted a report for the Trump administration warning that the foundation’s distribution process was chaotic and deadly, and cautioning about additional “mass casualty incidents.”
According to officials who saw the original report, Milstein rewrote it to declare the GHF operation a success, while omitting the mass casualties.
The discrepancy did not go unnoticed at the White House, which saw a striking gap between news reports and embassy reporting. As a result, White House and State Department officials sought a clearer picture of events and, on at least two occasions, contacted embassy staff directly to obtain a more reliable account.
Former U.S. diplomats who spoke with the New York Times said distorting information sent to Washington should raise serious concerns.
“The embassy should tell Washington everything — the good, the bad and the ugly,” said Dan Kurtzer, who served as U.S. ambassador to Israel under President George W. Bush.

South Africa pushes for local medicine production
South Africa is stepping up efforts to manufacture medicines and pharmaceutical ingredients locally to reduce reliance on imports and strengthen its ability to secure critical medical supplies during future health emergencies, the government has said.
President Cyril Ramaphosa, accompanied by Science, Technology and Innovation Minister Professor Blade Nzimande and Health Minister Dr Aaron Motsoaledi, toured the FuturePharma facility at the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) in Pretoria. The facility is expected to strengthen South Africa’s pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities by helping researchers move technologies from laboratories towards large-scale production and commercialisation.
”The facility will also support local API and medicine production, helping to reduce dependence on imports and strengthen security of supply,” the Government Communication and Information System (GCIS) said.
The move towards greater domestic production is aimed at giving South Africa stronger control over the availability of essential medicines while building local pharmaceutical capacity.
According to GCIS, one of the major objectives of the facility is to close the gap between scientific discoveries and medicines or pharmaceutical technologies that can be produced commercially. ”It will provide researchers, innovators and industry partners with access to specialised infrastructure and expertise to advance technologies towards manufacturing, while supporting technology transfer and skills development,” GCIS added.
This means pharmaceutical innovations developed by researchers could receive the technical support and infrastructure required to move beyond experimental laboratory stages and towards manufacturing.
The facility is also expected to form part of South Africa’s preparations for future pandemics and other major public health emergencies. The Covid-19 pandemic highlighted the risks countries face when they are heavily dependent on international supply chains for medicines, vaccines and other critical health products.

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
16:55:11 EEST
22:55:11 KST

A traffic accident can be handled without the police or paperwork — how to use the European Accident Statement in Diia and whether your “driver’s license” will be taken away
Kyiv • UNN
The European Accident Statement in Diia is available when there are no injured parties and both drivers agree. After it is completed, licenses are not confiscated and no report is drawn up.
From now on, the full process of completing a European Accident Statement can be done directly in the Diia app — without traffic jams or paperwork. This was reported by Oleksii Biloshytskyi, Head of the Patrol Police Department, according to UNN.
According to Biloshytskyi, Diia will automatically fill in the required data from official registers, which will help complete the accident report faster and avoid errors during completion.
When you can complete a European Accident Statement in Diia:
- only two cars are involved in the accident, with no trailers, and both are at the scene of the collision;
- there are no injured or dead persons;
- no property other than the cars has been damaged;
- both participants have valid compulsory third-party motor liability insurance policies;
- the drivers are sober and are not under the influence of medications that may reduce attention or reaction speed;
- the participants have reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident.
Important: if the other driver does not have the Diia app with verified documents, complete a paper European Accident Statement.
If you have not reached an agreement regarding the circumstances of the accident, call the police at 112 or 102.
Will your driver's licence be taken away after completing it?
No. You settle the situation with the insurance company without involving the police, so the driver's licence is not confiscated and no administrative report is drawn up.
How do you complete a European Accident Statement?
Diia → Services → For Drivers → European Accident Statement.
After both drivers sign via Diia.Signature, the data is sent to the Motor (Transport) Insurance Bureau of Ukraine and the insurance companies.

In attacks on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus, Russia likely used Belarusian Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14, 2026.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in a rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12.

Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28, 2026.
Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
This procedure would allow Polish forces to shoot down missiles or drones entering Polish airspace from the direction of Russia faster than previously.

A criminal investigation was opened over an alleged attempted sanctions violation and to determine who owned the coins. After the owner could not be identified, a court ordered the coins forfeited to the state.
The coins are being auctioned in small lots through Osta.ee, a local online auction site similar to eBay. Bidding on the first eight coins runs through October 14.

A top adviser to the US ambassador to Israel has systematically suppressed, delayed, and rewritten internal diplomatic cables to shield the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from scrutiny by Washington, The New York Times reported Thursday.
David Milstein, an influential gatekeeper at the US Embassy in Jerusalem since April 2025 and principal aide to US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, repeatedly stymied assessments intended for senior policymakers, according to an investigation based on interviews with more than a dozen US officials and reviews of internal State Department records.
In late March, Israel approved record-breaking occupation expansions across the occupied West Bank. Embassy personnel drafted an alert warning that the move risked violating US President Donald Trump's explicit red line against annexation. Milstein quashed the memorandum, framing the land acquisitions as a domestic matter before sending a revised text claiming the move addressed unspecified humanitarian needs of occupiers.
Milstein similarly altered reporting on surging violence in the occupied West Bank. When Israeli military commanders warned that attacks by occupiers could trigger a widespread Palestinian uprising, he blocked the dispatches suggesting that Israel failed to take action. Instead, an embassy cable authored under his name praised Netanyahu's initiatives and claimed authorities were actively combating the unrest.
The aide also suppressed a detailed embassy inquiry into the killings of nine Palestinian Americans by Israeli forces and occupiers, effectively thwarting accountability requests from members of the US Congress. Despite findings showing investigations stalled without criminal charges, the mission forwarded an alternative letter claiming active cooperation with Israeli authorities.
Milstein also edited dispatches regarding aid distribution by the US-backed Gaza Humanitarian Foundation to describe the operations as successful, removing diplomatic warnings that the process was "chaotic, deadly," and risked "mass casualty events."
Staff members noted that the interventions caused reporting from the embassy's Palestinian affairs section to drop from several weekly cables to a few per month and prompted some officials to bypass official embassy channels to obtain unfiltered ground intelligence.
"The elements of the story The New York Times is trying to assemble are so lacking in fact that it ranks up with other Times farcical endeavors," said Huckabee. The US State Department said its personnel remain focused on advancing the administration's foreign policy priorities.

GENEVA, October 8. /TASS/. Liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Middle East fell by about 47% annually during the first six months of 2026, while oil deliveries from the region dropped by about 24%, the World Trade Organization (WTO) said in its global trade prospects report.

Consequences of the energy shock related to the shortfall in supplies from the Middle East was managed to be softened and partly compensated by growing production and deliveries of other exporters, including Malaysia, Norway, and Angola, the organization noted.
According to the report, crude oil exports from the Middle East fell about 24% annually in the first half of this year. "During the same period, other suppliers (including the United States, Norway and Brazil) increased their production and shipments of crude oil, resulting in a global decline in exports of these products of around 6%," WTO added.

Bulgaria said on Wednesday it had halted its search for the crew of a ship that sank after being hit by a drone about 70 nautical miles (130 km) off its coast. Vice-Admiral Rumen Nikolov said no trace of the sailors had been found and that the rescue operation would not resume.

It remains unclear who carried out the attack.
Aloush added the authority was closely monitoring the incident and condemned the targeting of a civilian commercial vessel, saying it represented a serious violation of maritime safety and a direct threat to sailors' lives, as well as international trade routes.
He urged authorities to use all available technical means to locate and inspect the wreckage to help establish the cause of the incident, and said the case should not be closed before all available avenues had been exhausted to determine the crew's fate.
He also called on international organisations and maritime bodies to strengthen measures to protect commercial shipping and crews in the Black Sea amid growing risks to maritime transport in the region.
Russia has struck cargo ships in the Black Sea with drones and missiles during its war with Ukraine.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Wednesday that the nature of the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships could point to Russia, but said there was no evidence allowing Sofia to directly attribute responsibility.
Russia's embassy in Sofia said the merchant vessel was not among targets hit by Russian drones. REUTERS
