The imagination that began it all: The Persian-Jewish poet bringing Genesis back to life - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:30:17 UTC
22:30:17 KST

As the annual cycle of Torah reading begins anew, Israeli readers once again find themselves facing the story of Creation. We have known it since childhood: from Bible classes and ceremonies to debates on faith versus science and countless commentaries. Yet, precisely because of this deep familiarity, it can seem as though no surprises remain. The world was created, humanity was placed at its center, Eden was sealed – and we move on.
Yet centuries ago, at the far end of the Jewish world, a poet named Shahin Shirazi dared to do what we often struggle to do today: inject risk, color, and imagination back into a familiar narrative. This was not imagination as mere decoration, but as a driving force allowing us to re-examine the foundational roots of human culture.
Shahin, who lived in 14th-century Persia, was one of Persian Jewry’s greatest and most daring creators. He was not simply a poet writing on Jewish themes; he was an artist who constructed an entire cultural worldview – deeply Jewish in its roots, Persian in its aesthetic language, and Middle Eastern in the scope of its imagery. His monumental oeuvre included expansive epics, among them poetic cycles dedicated to Moses, Ezra, Esther, and the Creation. His final masterpiece, Genesis-Nama, marked his most mature work – a tapestry where memory, faith, Midrash, and fantasy converge within a single vision.
The work of Shahin Shirazi
Shahin’s adoption of the Persian epic form was by no means accidental. He understood that stories do not survive on content alone; they live through rhythm, music, metaphor, and the heroic figures that stir a culture’s soul. He harnessed the artistic tools of his environment in service of Jewish memory. He did so neither apologetically nor to assimilate, but out of a profound conviction that Judaism could engage with Iran’s great cultural landscape and speak there in its own distinct voice.
This is not merely a literary question; it is a profoundly Israeli one: Does an identity gain strength by filtering out every external influence, or by encountering another culture without losing its own essence?
In Shahin’s work, Adam is not merely a naive creature who falls. He is a figure of cosmic, almost majestic stature. The Patriarchs and leaders do not appear as static figures from a textbook, but as heroes endowed with radiance, responsibility, and a sense of destiny. Shahin reminds us of a truth that Israeli discourse often forgets: tradition is not a museum exhibit. It is a living canvas, and every generation possesses the right – perhaps even the duty – to clothe it in the imagery through which it thinks and feels.
One of the most compelling concepts in his work concerns the tension between fire and earth. Azazel, created from fire and light, looks upon the human being formed from earth and concludes that a creature’s material origins dictate its worth. To him, fire appears superior: bright, intense, impressive, and immediate. Earth, by contrast, seems humble, heavy, and devoid of glory. Shahin subverts this perspective. Earth is that which sustains, receives, nurtures, and carries life. Fire consumes itself; earth enables others to be born.
This message resonates far beyond theology. We live in an era that worships the immediate and the flashy: power, speed, virality, victory, and visibility. Whatever makes an instant impression is valued over that which is built patiently over time. Shahin proposes a different hierarchy of values: a thing’s worth is not defined by its brilliance, but by its capacity to contain and nurture. The loudest voice in the room is not necessarily the strongest; true strength often belongs to those capable of sustaining life even when it is complex, slow, and unphotogenic.
This is also a vital lesson in humility. The tragic flaw is not merely a rebellion against a command, but a failure of vision. Anyone who sees only the physical material from which a human being was formed misses the divine breath placed within them. Anyone who judges people solely by their origins, status, or appearance fails to recognize their inner potential. In this sense, Shahin’s Azazel is strikingly contemporary: he falls because he knows how to categorize, but lacks the ability to imagine.
Even the Garden of Eden in Shahin’s work is not a product of simple nostalgia for a bygone paradise. Wheat becomes a symbol of knowledge hard-won through labor, persistence, craftsmanship, and the transformation of nature into culture. This offers an almost Zionist imagery of knowledge: not an instantaneous revelation from the heavens, but wisdom acquired through dedicated effort. Human partnership, too, is presented not as an abstract ideal, but as the capacity to build a life together within physical bounds, time, and human limitations. Perfection is not found in a pure spirit hovering above the world, but in a bond that manages to endure within it.
Here lies Shahin’s unique relevance for Israel today. For decades, we have relied on a narrow narrative of Jewish culture: East versus West, tradition versus modernity, Israeliness versus Diaspora. Shahin dismantles these dichotomies. He reminds us that Judaism can be profound without being closed, faithful to itself without being defensive, and Middle Eastern without apology.
Moreover, he brings to center stage a chapter long relegated to the margins: the Jews of Iran. This is not merely a community that survived, nor simply a diaspora to be recalled on memorial days. It is a vibrant spiritual world that created, renewed, and imagined, bestowing an epic language upon our foundational stories. It is an integral part of the Jewish home, not an afterthought.
In this context, it is essential to acknowledge the dedicated individuals and patrons of culture who work faithfully to preserve and transmit Persian-Jewish heritage through the “Bama Tova” organization (www.bamatova.org). Thanks to key supporters and families, such as the Ganji family and the Mahfar family, this rich heritage does not remain locked in an archive. It continues to breathe, reach the next generation, and claim its rightful place within Israeli culture. Heritage does not preserve itself; it relies on those who believe in it, invest in it, and carry it forward.
As we open the Book of Genesis once again, perhaps we should not rush toward familiar debates over literal interpretation versus Midrash, faith versus science, or past versus present. Instead, we might ask a simpler question: What do we choose to see when we look at a human being? Do we see only earth – weakness, origins, and physical matter – or do we see the capacity to turn matter into a vessel for life?
Shahin does not call on us to return to medieval Persia. He invites us to return to the creative imagination from which all creation begins – the fundamental power that enables us to see possibility where others see only raw material, history, or limitation. In an Israel where everything seems to have already been said about Genesis, imagination may be the newest way to begin the year.
The writer is a scholar of cultures and religions, liturgical poet, filmmaker, and director of the “Bama Tova” organization.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have stepped up their deadly campaign of strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, where booms were heard on Thursday, flights were disrupted, and some office staff were told to work from home.
The Houthis said they had fired a ballistic missile at Riyadh airport and repeated a threat to force Saudi airspace to close after the kingdom gave support to the forces of Yemen's internationally recognized government in a reignited civil war.
The conflict, now an overspill of the US-Iran war, has added new chaos to a region already aflame, and threatens to draw other states into grueling mountain fighting - with Syria now considering deploying troops to assist Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has pushed for support from allied nations, including Turkey and Pakistan, even if only in a logistical or defensive capacity, as it tries to reverse Houthi gains in southwest Yemen, by the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
Those requests have taken on more urgency since Saudi authorities said on Wednesday that three people had been killed this week in strikes on Riyadh airport and Abha airport in the southwest.
Civil war reignited by conflict with Iran
The flight tracker FlightRadar24 indicated numerous delayed arrivals and departures at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport on Thursday.
Several multinational firms based in Riyadh's King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) told staff to work from home after Thursday morning's loud booms, five people familiar with the matter said, including some affected staff.
The Saudi government did not respond to a request for comment, and KAFD was not immediately available for comment.
Some diplomats said they had received warnings, and some schools in Riyadh told parents there were orders to shelter in place, though authorities did not issue a public alert. Reuters could not identify the source of the booms.
Yemen's long-running civil war, which paused with a ceasefire in 2022, has erupted again in recent weeks with the Houthis seizing stretches of the Red Sea coast last month, including along the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
The Houthis, who control many of Yemen's most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, have said they were responding to attacks from the Saudi-backed government, which the government denies.
Their threats to shipping along a waterway that has become ever more critical for Gulf oil exports since Iran's attacks in the Strait of Hormuz, and their attacks on Saudi cities and infrastructure, have drawn the kingdom back in.
This week, Saudi-backed forces launched a counterattack, taking back areas around the strait.
However, in a war with several frontlines, the Houthis have made gains of their own, surrounding Yemen's third-largest city, Taiz, by taking territory along its main mountain road to Aden.
The fighting, which pits the Houthis against a coalition of Saudi-backed forces under the internationally recognized government, has led to a humanitarian crisis in the poorest Arab state, displacing 200,000 people since the conflict resumed.
Syrian aid might be purely defensive, officials say
One US and one Syrian defense official said Syria was carefully considering options for military support, including defensive aid to protect Saudi Arabia from attacks, or an offensive deployment to help take the fight to the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia but that its focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from its own civil war.
Saudi Arabia this summer agreed to the Mecca Pact with Turkey and Pakistan, committing all three to come to each other's defense, though Ankara has yet to ratify the treaty.
NATO-member Turkey said on Wednesday it was sending mainly defensive and technical support to the kingdom to help in the fight against the Houthis. A Turkish official said this was expected to take the form of military equipment, intelligence sharing and weapons systems.
Turkey, a close ally of Syria's government and a supporter of its forces while they were still rebels fighting the government of Bashar al-Assad, previously brought some Syrians to fight in Libya's civil war in 2020.
Pakistan has flown military equipment to Aden in southern Yemen to help in the battle against the Houthis, sources in Pakistan have said, and has deployed troops within Saudi Arabia to help defend its borders.
The Saudi and Yemeni authorities did not respond to requests for comment.

The economies of the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan region are projected to contract by 2.1% in 2026, with Gulf Cooperation Council states expected to contract harder, by an average of 4.3%, according to a new World Bank report released on Tuesday.
Qatar and Kuwait are expected to be the hardest-hit GCC economies, with GDP forecast to contract by 20.9% and 14.6%, respectively, in 2026. The United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia are projected to be the least affected among GCC members, with their economies forecast to contract by 1.6% and 2.0%, respectively.
Qatar's economy, facing its weakest growth forecast in decades, has been heavily affected by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Average monthly natural gas production in Qatar fell by approximately 67% between March and July 2026, compared to the same
period in 2025.
Gulf oil production collectively has fallen from around 26 million barrels per day before to around 16 million barrels per day in March, according to the World Bank.
The disruption has also driven inflation higher across the Gulf. Qatar's food inflation exceeded 12% year-on-year as of June, while average overall inflation remained at around 2%. In Bahrain and Oman, food inflation surpassed 7%, while headline inflation stood at around 3%.
Iraq, Iran face sharp GDP declines as oil production falls and inflation surges
In Iraq and Iran, GDP is forecast to decline by 12.4% and 7.7%, respectively, with both countries operating at just 55% to 70% of their estimated oil production capacity. In Iran, inflation has also surged, rising from around 32% in mid-2024 to 89% in August 2026, according to World Bank figures.
Lebanon has also felt the economic impact of the conflict, although its inflation rate has eased from the sharp rise seen during the early months of the war and currently stands above 15%. Gasoline prices have risen by at least 40% in Lebanon, while diesel prices have increased by more than 80%. Fuel prices in the West Bank and Gaza have also risen by more than 40%.
Oil-importing economies have proved more resilient, with regional growth expected to reach 4.3% in 2026, compared with 3.9% in 2025. However, importing countries, like Egypt, Jordan, Morocco, Pakistan and Tunisia, remain vulnerable to the economic fallout of the conflict. They face higher inflation as oil and other commodity prices rise, reduced fiscal room, potentially lower remittances from Gulf economies and higher borrowing costs, driven in part by increased insurance risk premiums as the conflict continues.
World Bank forecasts 7.8% regional economic rebound in 2027 if conflict ends
Excluding Iran, the World Bank Group macroeconomic models projected that, if the conflict ended this year, regional economies would rebound sharply to 7.8 percent in 2027, driven by a recovery in hydrocarbon production, the normalization of trade routes, and base effects.
The global economy was able to absorb much of the shock from the blockade, the World Bank noted, as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the UAE bypassed the disruption and brought an additional 2.8 million barrels per day to global markets. Brazil, Kazakhstan, Venezuela and the United States also continued exporting, while inventories helped make up shortfalls and global demand fell by an estimated 5.8 million barrels per day compared with pre-conflict levels.
World Bank warns extreme weather could worsen food shortages across the region
While the impact of the blockade has so far remained manageable for most countries, the World Bank warned that El Niño could pose an additional threat to food security across the region, where families are already facing risks from declining humanitarian aid funding.
Alongside Pakistan and Afghanistan, which are directly exposed through changing monsoon conditions and heat stress, the World Bank warned that Egypt, Iraq, and Tunisia needed close monitoring given existing water stress.

WTO raises 2026 goods trade growth forecast to 3.9%, cuts services outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:26:34 UTC
22:26:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
The World Trade Organization on Thursday raised its forecast for global goods trade growth this year to 3.9% from 1.9%, as strong demand linked to artificial intelligence investment helped offset disruptions caused by the Middle East war.
The organization lowered its services trade growth projection to 3.3% from the 4.8% forecast in March, according to its Global Trade Outlook and Statistics report.
Global merchandise trade volumes expanded 3.5% in the first half of 2026, exceeding expectations despite shocks to energy, fertilizer and transport markets.
Trade in AI-enabling goods, including semiconductors and servers, surged 67% year-on-year, accounting for 47% of global merchandise trade growth during the period.
The WTO said the performance reflected the ability of supply chains to adapt, with alternative suppliers and transport routes helping maintain trade flows.
Alternative supplies cushion disruptions
Middle Eastern crude oil exports fell about 24% year-on-year in the first half, while liquefied natural gas exports dropped 47%.
Increased shipments from other suppliers helped limit the decline in global exports to 6% for crude oil and 1% for LNG.
Fertilizer markets also adjusted as alternative suppliers stepped in, while trade flows were redirected through other ports and corridors.
Global container throughput rose 3.9% year-on-year between the start of 2026 and mid-July.
The WTO expects merchandise trade to grow 4.1% in 2027, with services trade expanding 6.4%.
Gains remain uneven
The organization warned that the benefits of resilient goods trade and AI investment were not evenly distributed, with services trade and some regions more exposed to the conflict.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala said an integrated global economy and a rules-based trading system gave economies the flexibility to maintain supplies of essential goods during disruptions.
However, some economies had felt the shock more severely, while access to emerging opportunities such as AI remained unequal, she said.
She stressed the importance of ensuring the trading system continued to absorb shocks and narrow gaps so that opportunities remained open to all.

Early-onset cancer rising worldwide: Causes, risk, prevention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

Early-onset cancer: Why cases are rising in under-50s
October 8, 2026
The numbers are striking. Some cancer rates have doubled in the past 20 years. It's just not yet clear whether we're seeing a rise in actual cases or whether we're seeing more early-stage cases because of better awareness, diagnosis and treatment in hospitals.
Take, for example, colorectal (or bowel) cancer: In 2001, about one in every 26,000 people under 50 in England were diagnosed with it each year. By 2023, the rate of diagnoses was about one in 12,000. Twice what it was at the turn of the century.
That's according to the World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), an international network of charities, which analyzed registry data from England, the US and the Netherlands. It found the number of new cancer cases had risen for seven cancers in England alone.
So, rates have doubled, but the numbers overall are still small, said Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, a professor of clinical epidemiology at the Institute of Cancer Research in the UK capital London.
"Cancer is still very uncommon among young people," Berrington de Gonzalez told DW. "Three times a small number is still a small number."
But she and other scientists still want to know why this is happening, because it is a worldwide trend. Latin America is a case in point.
Early-onset cancer rates rising in Latin America
A 2025 study analyzed registry data from 50 countries and territories up to 2017. It found early-onset colorectal cancer rising in 27 of those regions.
In Latin America, rates rose in Chile, Argentina, Ecuador, Costa Rica and Puerto Rico. Chile's rise — at almost 4% per year — was among the highest.
In Brazil, the evidence comes directly from hospitals. At the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in Sao Paulo, the number of colorectal cancer patients under 50 grew by 7.6% per year between 2000 and 2023. That's a five-fold increase.
The number of patients over 50 grew even faster — at 8.1% — or about six-fold.
But since these figures came from a single hospital, they do not show whether cases are rising across Brazil. They may only reflect that this one hospital is treating more patients.
"We need better cancer registration systems," said Berrington de Gonzalez, "especially in countries like Brazil and Mexico, where obesity rates have also been increasing."
Marc Gunter, professor of cancer epidemiology at Imperial College London, said he expected Latin America to follow richer countries as diets there become more Westernized and lifestyles more sedentary. "I think it's already happening," he said.
These six cancers affect young adults most
In another study in 2025, involving 42 countries, Berrington de Gonzalez compared data from two age groups — 20 to 49 years and 50 years and older — between 2003 and 2017.
Six cancers — thyroid, breast, colorectal, kidney, uterine and leukemia — had risen among the younger groups in most countries. All but colorectal cancer were seen to rise in older adults, too.
In fact, colorectal cancer stood out. In about a third of the countries, it rose faster in younger adults than in older ones. "It is the one cancer that seems to be increasing in younger people whilst decreasing in older people," said Berrington de Gonzalez.
This has consequences for research. If cancers are rising in all age groups, the causes are likely to be widespread, so studies looking only at young people risk chasing complicated explanations with too little data to test them, she said.
Better awareness could explain the rise in diagnoses
A US study of pancreatic cancer in adults aged 15 to 39 years found the rise was almost entirely made up of early-stage tumors.
Death rates remained unchanged.
The authors said this suggested that instead of the number of cancer cases going up, it was the number of early diagnoses that had gone up. And that can be explained by better awareness in the community, with people getting checked more often.
But the data for colorectal cancer looks different: Some US studies show it rising in advanced stages of the disease as well, which suggests an increase in the number of cases, not just the number of diagnoses.
The link between cancer and obesity
Obesity is an established cause of at least 13 cancers, according to the WHO's International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC).
According to a 2021 review of existing studies, young adults with obesity were almost twice as likely to develop colorectal cancer before the age of 50.
Obesity has also spread fastest among the young. The WHO reports that obesity rates have doubled among adults since the 1990s and quadrupled among adolescents.
What you consume matters:
- Processed meat is classed as carcinogenic
- Alcohol is also considered a risk factor
- Fiber (vegetables, whole grains and pulses) lowers cancer risk
Some also say ultra-processed foods and microplastics cause cancer. But Gunter said the evidence was inconclusive.
"There's a lot of hype," Gunter said, adding that more research was needed. Berrington de Gonzalez agreed: "Diets have changed, but we don't yet know the role they might play."
How young people can lower their cancer risk
Gunter said individuals should not be blamed for living in societies built around convenience foods and desk jobs, and that lasting change needed public health policy.
But he also said that young people could lower their cancer risk by maintaining a healthy weight, moving more, eating more fiber and cutting back on processed meat.
"Going for a walk, being more physically active, eating more fruits and vegetables," he said. "Those things are maybe not so trendy, but they are really important."
For a 30-year-old reading this, Berrington de Gonzalez's message was one of reassurance: Cancer at a young age remains relatively rare.

The government lifted its full-year growth projection to 1.3%, up from its April forecast of just 0.5%, as the German economy proved more resilient than expected.
Foreign trade is expected to boost Europe's biggest economy this year.
Stronger exports helped prompt the German government to more than double its growth forecast for this year on Thursday, as it said the economy had withstood the energy shock caused by the Iran war and was benefiting from the global AI boom.
The improved outlook could take some pressure off Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is facing criticism that he has not done enough to kickstart the long-stagnant economy.
"The German economy proved more robust than projected in the spring," Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said as she announced the new forecasts.
"Despite geopolitical uncertainties, despite a global energy price shock, despite the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and despite tariffs, the economy was able to embark on a path of recovery," she told a press conference.
Germany's economy has faced years of stagnation amid weak export demand, high energy costs, US tariffs and Chinese competition, though recent indicators suggest it is starting to recover.
Reiche said foreign importers had rushed to stockpile German-made goods such as steel, fertiliser and aluminium in the months following the outbreak of the Iran war, supporting growth.
The government expects exports to grow by 3.7% this year, reversing a 0.9% decline in 2025.
German suppliers were also benefiting from the "global trend of investment in artificial intelligence", she said.
The boom in data centre construction has led to a surge in orders for German-made equipment such as lasers, semiconductor machinery and cooling systems, she said.
The economy ministry also raised its forecast for 2027 to 1.1%, from 0.9% previously, and said increased public spending on defence and infrastructure would support the economy in the coming years. Growth is expected to slow to 0.6% in 2028.
But it warned that household consumption would remain subdued as higher energy costs push up consumer prices. German inflation hit 3.3% in September, the highest level in nearly three years.
The ministry expects inflation to average 2.7% this year and rise to 3.0% in 2027, while household spending is forecast to grow by just 0.3% and 0.5%, respectively, after adjusting for inflation.
As in other countries, Germany has seen fuel costs surge amid the Iran war, prompting the government last week to announce a temporary fuel tax cut to provide some relief for drivers.
The official growth forecast for 2026 is in line with recent estimates by Germany's leading economic research institutes.

South Korea Investigates Fuel Shipments to Russia as Sanctioned Tankers Face Legal Scrutiny

- Category
- World
South Korea Investigates Fuel Shipments to Russia as Sanctioned Tankers Face Legal Scrutiny
South Korea announced on October 8 that it could take legal action if an investigation finds that fuel shipments from its ports to Russia violated domestic law.
The Guardian reported the development after previously identifying more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel loaded at South Korean ports onto tankers that subsequently traveled to Russia.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
In a joint statement, South Korea’s foreign and trade ministries and customs service stated they were “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian.” The agencies added that if violations are confirmed, the government "plans to act in accordance with the law."
The Guardian’s analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that the fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded during July and August. Seven tankers made 14 voyages to Russia’s Far East, including three vessels under UK and EU sanctions.
South Korean authorities emphasized that loading refined petroleum products at domestic ports does not, by itself, violate the country’s export controls on Russia. Seoul also stated that it had not confirmed whether the cargo was South Korean-origin fuel and reported no customs-cleared exports of diesel, aviation fuel, or motor gasoline to Russia.
The investigation will examine the tankers’ actual routes, discrepancies with their declared destinations, and the reasons for those changes. Three sanctioned tankers reportedly declared Japan or Singapore as their destinations before traveling to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under Western sanctions, loaded cargo in Ulsan three times in July and August. On each voyage, the tanker declared a destination outside Russia before later sailing there.
The dispute has also intensified tensions between Kyiv and Seoul. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry confirmed this week that it had raised the shipments through closed diplomatic channels and requested an explanation, while South Korea announced on October 8 that it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine.
The fuel shipments come as Ukrainian strikes continue to pressure Russia’s domestic refining sector. The Guardian reported that Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, while diesel output was nearly 30% lower year over year, according to the International Energy Agency.
South Korean fuel had already surfaced in Russia's supply chain weeks earlier, after retaliatory Ukrainian strikes on refineries cut aviation fuel output and pushed Moscow to temporarily ban its own jet fuel exports.
By late August, three shadow-fleet tankers had delivered about 70,000 metric tons of Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to ports in St. Petersburg and Vladivostok. The South Korean supply chain ran through UAE-based Caliph Energy Trading FZE. The fuel is suitable for Su-34, Su-35S, and Su-57 aircraft, as well as Tu-95MS strategic bombers.

Arsenal talent Max Dowman received three honors at once from Guinness World Records
Kyiv • UNN
Arsenal midfielder Max Dowman became the youngest player to make a Champions League debut and the youngest goalscorer in the Premier League. He is also the youngest English champion.
English midfielder of London’s "Arsenal" Max Dowman received three Guinness World Records distinctions at once. The young "Gunners" talent became the youngest debutant in the Champions League, as well as the youngest goalscorer in the Premier League. The Guinness World Records reports this, UNN reports.
Details
According to Guinness World Records, judge Caitlin Hiyem visited "Arsenal’s" training ground to present Max Dowman with three certificates for a record-breaking season.
Dowman received his first certificate as the youngest player in Champions League history. At the age of 15 years and 308 days, the Englishman made his debut for "Arsenal" in a Champions League group-stage match against Prague’s "Slavia," which ended 3–0.
The Englishman received his second certificate as the youngest goalscorer in the Premier League. In a match against England’s "Everton," for whom Vitaliy Mykolenko plays, Dowman broke forward on a counterattack in stoppage time, carried the ball 60 metres from his own half, and then rolled it into an empty net, sealing a 2–0 victory.

Also last season, "Arsenal" won the Premier League for the first time in 22 years. Max received his winner’s medal at the age of 16 years and 144 days, becoming the youngest footballer to win the Premier League. He surpassed the previous record held by Phil Foden of "Manchester City" by more than a year.

Russia’s Only T-90M Production Line Is Now Competing With Tanks Coming Back From the Dead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:23:50 UTC
22:23:50 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Only T-90M Production Line Is Now Competing With Tanks Coming Back From the Dead
Wrecked T-90Ms are now arriving at the same Russian factory responsible for building new ones, raising a bigger question about Moscow’s tank output: how many are actually new, and how many are rebuilt battlefield losses?
Russia’s main tank manufacturer—and the country’s only plant producing new T-90M tanks—is increasingly being used to rebuild heavily damaged vehicles recovered from the war in Ukraine, potentially diverting factory capacity from new production and complicating estimates of how many fresh tanks Moscow is actually building, according to Defence Blog on October 8.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Uralvagonzavod, or UVZ, in Nizhny Tagil is receiving battlefield-damaged T-90Ms for major overhauls, according to Defence Blog. Recent photographs showed a train carrying several badly damaged tanks toward the factory, with some vehicles displaying extensive structural damage.
Repairs may be competing with new tank production
Such work was traditionally handled by Russia’s network of military armored repair plants, known as BTRZ facilities, rather than by the country’s primary tank manufacturer.
Armor analyst Andrei Tarasenko, known as btbv.info, argues that the repair system has deteriorated to the point that UVZ is now taking on jobs outside its main production role.
“Damaged T-90Ms on the way to UVZ. Having ruined the BTRZ system, the monopoly corporation is also engaged in capital repairs that are completely outside its core business, since under factory conditions (not at a BTRZ) a repair costs as much as a new tank,” Tarasenko wrote.
Defence Blog noted that the development matters because UVZ is simultaneously responsible for manufacturing new T-90Ms and modernizing older Russian tanks.
Sending heavily damaged vehicles through the same industrial system can consume labor, workshop capacity, components, and time that could otherwise be devoted to new production.
How many “new” T-90Ms are actually rebuilt tanks?
Defence Blog noted that Oryx lead analyst Jakub Janovsky raised another issue: tanks extensively rebuilt at UVZ could make Russian production statistics harder to interpret, particularly if refurbished vehicles receive upgrades during the process.
“On the other hand, some organizations might end up counting factory repairs (and/or any additional upgrades) of these tanks as ‘new production,’” Janovsky wrote.
That distinction matters as analysts try to determine whether Russia’s defense industry is genuinely replacing battlefield losses with newly manufactured tanks or increasingly relying on restored and modernized vehicles from existing stocks.
Janovsky noted that whether a damaged tank can be recovered at all depends heavily on where it is disabled. Tanks knocked out in the contested gray zone are often struck repeatedly before Russian recovery crews can reach them, while vehicles damaged farther behind the front can be evacuated and returned to repair facilities much more easily.
Russia still shipping T-90Ms—but the production picture gets murkier
The growing repair burden comes as Russia’s armored industry continues to face pressure from Western sanctions, shortages of skilled labor, and the depletion of Soviet-era equipment reserves.
Some T-90Ms leaving UVZ have already been identified as using refurbished hulls from older T-90A tanks rather than entirely new hulls, further blurring the line between new construction, modernization, and reconstruction.
Uralvagonzavod has also publicly promoted its ability to restore heavily damaged tanks. In 2024, the company said it returned one T-90M to service in just four weeks after the vehicle had reportedly been hit by 26 drones.
The factory continues to deliver T-90Ms and upgraded T-72B3Ms to the Russian military. According to Defence Blog, earlier this week, UVZ announced another shipment of both types fitted with additional protection against drone strikes, although it did not disclose the number of tanks delivered.
Some newer T-90Ms have also appeared with the Arena-M active protection system, which Russian forces demonstrated intercepting attacking drones during the Tsentr-2026 exercise.
Earlier, Ukraine’s 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment knocked out a Russian T-54 tank, which traces its origins to the immediate post-World War II period and carries a 100mm main gun, making it one of the oldest mass-produced tank designs Russia has pulled from long-term storage and returned to wartime use.

Germany news: UK's Burnham visits Berlin for talks with Merz
Published October 8, 2026last updated October 8, 2026
What you need to know
- The 'Kensington Treaty' between the UK and Germany comes into force amid Burnham's trip to Berlin
- The UK leader and Chancellor Friedrich Merz held one-on-one talks as part of the visit
- In Berlin, the Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats have agreed to begin exploratory coalition talks after resolving differences over antisemitism and organized crime

- And a wax döner kebab is now on show at Berlin's Madame Tussauds, visitors are advised not to try to taste it
This is a roundup of the top news from and about Germany on Thursday, October 8, 2026:

German spy agency BND approved suspect's side job
Germany's foreign intelligence agency reportedly approved outside work by an employee for a former spy chief who is now suspected of illegally obtaining classified information.
According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) officially authorized Manfred D. to work for former BND head August Hanning, who became a private-sector consultant after leaving government service in 2009.
Prosecutors allege that Manfred D. supplied Hanning with nearly 2,000 internal BND documents, many of them classified, which the former intelligence chief allegedly used for commercial gain.
Investigators believe the arrangement began around 2010, when Hanning and his former chief of staff allegedly agreed that intelligence would be supplied in return for payment.
Manfred D. allegedly passed the documents to Hanning between 2010 and 2022.
Hanning, 80, headed the BND from 1998 to 2005. He is suspected of offenses including intelligence-agent activity, espionage involving state secrets and attempted treason.
Manfred D., 64, served as chief of staff to several BND presidents from March 2012 until March 2026, a position that gave him access to sensitive intelligence.
He is accused of aiding attempted treason and espionage involving state secrets.
Both men have been held in pretrial detention since this week.
According to Der Spiegel, the BND had known about Manfred D.'s work for Hanning for some time and had issued an official authorization for the secondary employment.
The agency declined to answer questions about when the authorization was granted or what activities it covered, the magazine said.
Hanning's lawyer has denied wrongdoing, saying his client was being prosecuted unjustly.
He acknowledged that Hanning had possessed confidential documents but denied he had passed on information detrimental to Germany or had done so for payment.
Merz, Burnham inaugurate new German-British friendship treaty
Chancellor Friedrich Merz received relatively new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham with military honors in Berlin.
During Burnham's visit, the new Treaty on Friendship and Bilateral Cooperation between the UK and Germany — signed last year by previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer — officially comes into force.
Aslo known as the Kensington Treaty, the 27-page document lays out a 17-point action plan for closer cooperation in the post-Brexit era, with the UK no longer a part of the EU.
Merz called it a historic day and said the deal opened up new opportunities for bilateral cooperation, particularly for students and young people.
"That's what we're doing this for," Merz said. "So that the young generation also notices when it comes to bilateral relations between Germany as part of the EU and the UK, how well we Europeans work together and how much we belong together, too."
Burnham said that the Kensington Treaty would improve security in Europe, help both economies grow and improve people's living standards.
"In challenging times, and these are challenging times, we need the strongest possible cooperation with our closest partners and Germany really is one of our closest partners," the former mayor of Manchester said.
Burnham also said that he was open to Germany joining the GCAP program, a partnership between Britain, Italy and Japan to build a next-generation multirole combat aircraft.
"I've indicated to the chancellor ... our openness to Germany joining GCAP," he said at a press conference. "That is something that we seek to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy and Japan."
A rival Franco-German plan to build a next-generation military jet, FCAS, collapsed in June.
The GCAP project has been set up to allow for different levels of involvement. It expanded in July when Canada signed up as an observer, and Saudi Arabia had also been touted as a potential interested party.
Germany already works with the UK and Italy on the joint Eurofighter Typhoon project.
Italy and Japan would need to join Burnham in indicating a willingness for Germany participating in this project.
Left-leaning parties in Berlin to begin talks on forming new government
Germany's Left Party, Greens and Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed to begin exploratory talks on forming a coalition government in Berlin, two and a half weeks after the city's state election.
The breakthrough follows an agreement on combating antisemitism and organized crime, issues that had threatened to derail negotiations before they began.
The parties said they would protect Jewish life in Berlin and reaffirmed that Israel's right to exist was "non-negotiable."
They also agreed to strengthen the police and domestic intelligence services in their efforts to protect Jewish communities.
Party and parliamentary group members who violate the agreed principles could face expulsion, with the relevant parliamentary group responsible for deciding and publicly explaining any disciplinary measures.
The three parties also pledged to maintain a clear distance from individuals and groups associated with organized crime.
The Greens and SPD had made agreements on antisemitism, racism and organized crime conditions to open talks with the Left Party.
Those demands followed controversy over positions on Israel and the Palestinians held by some members of Berlin's Left Party.
Concerns intensified after an election-night gathering organized by the Left's Neukölln branch was attended by a figure associated with a partly criminal clan and a controversial pro-Palestinian activist.
The activist is alleged to have links to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, which the European Union designates as a terrorist organization.
The Left Party emerged as the strongest party in Berlin's September 20 election, winning 25.7% of the vote.
It hopes to form a coalition with the Greens and SPD, potentially making its parliamentary co-leader Elif Eralp Berlin's first mayor from the Left Party.
Waxwork döner kebab put on the menu at Berlin Madame Tussauds
The latest exhibit at Madame Tussauds in Berlin would surely taste just as dire as all the others, but the wax replica of a döner kebab is at least supposed to look appetizing.
The kebab — obviously stuffed "with everything" or "mit alles/mit allem," depending on your level of German grammatical exactitude — is complemented by a recreation of the popular snack stop Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap in Berlin's Kreuzberg district.
Tarik Kara, who owns the restaurant, was present in the flesh for Thursday's unveiling.
The Turkish specialty has long been a mainstay of the fast food culture in Berlin and beyond, given Germany's vast and long-established Turkish diaspora, estimated at around 3 million people.

Iranian intelligence services have set their sights on US military bases in Germany, such as those in Ramstein and Spangdahlem, according to news outlet WirtschaftsWoche.
Israel recently warned US and German partners of a potential threat likely to focus on bases supporting US military operations and logistics with a connection to the conflict with Iran, the report said
The German Defense Ministry and the US forces in Germany have so far not commented on the report.
Low-cost carrier Ryanair cuts flights in Germany, with Berlin hardest-hit
Irish airline Ryanair says it will be offering 700,000 fewer seats on flights in Germany this winter season, citing the "astronomical" cost of various charges, including for air traffic control and security.
This represents a reduction of 10%.
Ryanair said Berlin Brandenburg Airport, which it has dubbed "Europe's least successful airport," would be affected the most, losing around half of its current services from the airline.
Among the 12 routes to be axed in Berlin are those to Gran Canaria, Palermo, Marseille and Thessaloniki.
The Ryanair base at the airport is set to close on October 24. Seven aircraft and their crews are to be relocated to more competitive airports in other European countries, the company said.
Passengers in the German capital will now have much less choice and considerably higher fares, according to the airline's chief executive Eddie Wilson.
Hamburg will see a cut of 5%, but Memmingen and Cologne will have their capacity expanded.
Ryanair's winter schedule also adds regional airports in Saarbrücken and Friedrichshafen.
Sick leave for mental illnesses on the rise — health insurer
The number of days of sick leave in Germany on grounds of psychological problems has risen some 42% in the last 10 years, the AOK health insurance company says.
According to AOK, there were 284 days of sick leave per 100 members in 2015, compared with 403 per 100 members in 2025.
Although absences from work are much more frequently due to respiratory illnesses, those prompted by mental illness tend to be much longer, AOK said.
It said that on average, employees took 28.5 days off on grounds of psychological problems last year compared with 5.7 days because of respiratory illnesses.
However, the AOK said there had been a slight reduction in the average number of days of sick leave taken by employees, from 23.9 in 2023 and 2024 to 23.3 in 2025.
The highest level, 24.5 days, was reached in 2022 during the coronavirus pandemic.
Berlin leftist parties agree to hold exploratory coalition talks — media
The Berlin chapters of the socialist Left Party, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) and the environmentalist Greens have agreed to hold exploratory coalition talks , media reports said on
Thursday.
The news come 2 1/2 weeks after the election for the city-state's parliament, which saw the Left Party emerge as strongest party with 25.7% of the vote.
The Greens and the SPD received 14.3% and 12.1% respectively, both below the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) on 18.8%.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) came in third, with 16.3%.
The announcement follows preliminary talks held by the three leftist parties to clarify positions amid accusations leveled at the Left Party that it was antisemitic and had alleged links to organized criminality.
According to reports, those talks have ended with an agreement satisfactory to all three parties.
Suspected Russian hacker extradited from Japan to Germany
Japan extradited on Thursday one of the suspected leaders of the Russian hacking group Qilin, which has extorted hundreds of millions of dollars, to Germany, officials said.
Herbert Reul, Interior Minister of North Rhine-Westphalia (NRW), said at a press conference that the unnamed suspect was arrested in Japan while on vacation.
The Qilin group, one of the most "aggressive" cybercrime organizations according to auhtories, has extorted about $2.9 billion from some 4,000 companies and institutions worldwide since 2024. At least 30 companies in the German state of NRW have been affected.
Hacking the hackers
German police infiltrated the Qilin group and monitored its members for several months. NRW Justice Minister Benjamin Limbach said that payments and cryptocurrency transactions were traced to individuals linked to the organization.
The Russian group is also blamed for an attack on Britain's National Health Service (NHS) that disrupted more than 10,000 medical appointments. Last year, shares of Japanese brewer Asahi fell after Qilin carried out a cyberattack that disrupted the company's ordering and delivery systems.
According to authorities, Russian cyberattacks against Germany have increased since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
My lifelong Pokemon collection is worth around €400,000, Christoph Kramer estimates
Retired midfielder and 2014 World Cup winner Christoph Kramer — now a TV presenter, podcaster and novelist — discusses another of his longstanding passions in an interview with the dpa news agency published on Thursday.
He may not have caught them all in more than a quarter of a century hunting Pokemon cards, but he's corralled a collection of creatures capable of dropping the jaw of a typical 10-year-old.
"I've been collecting pokemon cards since 1999, I have the complete first edition in English and would not give up my collection for any price," the 36-year-old said. Nevertheless he said he saw the collection as a "real investment," and said he'd estimate its value at roughly €400,000 (roughly $450,000).
"I'm wholly convinced that our generation won't be hanging classical paintings on the walls aged 50 or 60 any more, but instead will prefer to frame their Pokemon cards behind glass," he said.
Kramer, who might be best known as the World Cup winner with no memory of his finest hour on the pitch because of a concussion sustained during the 2014 final against Argentina, has quickly graduated to a senior broadcasting and punditry role since quitting football.
He's currently promoting his second novel, called "Wolkenberührpunkt," which one could perhaps translate as "the point touching the clouds." As he told dpa, he's always had a passion for collecting more generally.
"I got myself an original iPhone in its original packaging and laminated. Objects like collectors' cards, rare vintage gear or retro jerseys are, for me, the real art of our era," Kramer said. "Of course it has a lot to do with nostalgia, because these are things from my childhood I simply love."
Spanish and Turkish make gains among school language learners
Although English remains by far the most-learned foreign language at German schools, Spanish and Turkish are becoming ever more popular, while French, Latin and Russian are losing ground, new figures show.
Turkish is being learned by almost three times as many pupils as 20 years ago, with 29,230 of altogether 8.9 million school students taking the language in 2025/2026 (0.31%).
That compares with some 13,000 pupils out of 9.5 million in 2005/2006 (0.13%), according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
There are also twice as many Spanish learners at German schools compared with two decades ago.
Some 549,000 of the current 8.9 million pupils took the language as a subject in 2025/2026 (6.1%), compared with 243,400 of the 9.5 million pupils back in 2005/2006 (2.56%), Destatis said.
Fewer pupils are learning French than 20 years ago, even if the language is second only to English in the statistics.
Some 14% of pupils learned French in the 2025/2026 school year, compared with 17% in 2005/2006.
Latin and Russian are also being learned by ever fewer pupils, with the former falling from 8.1% of schoolchildren to some 6% over the 20-year period, and the latter now learned by 0.746% compared with 1.25% in 2005/2006.
English remains far ahead at the top of the language-learning table, despite a small decline over the past two decades.
It was learned by 81% of pupils back in 2005/2006 compared with 78% in 2025/2026.
Suspected puma on the loose eludes searchers
Police have so far been unsuccessful in their search for a suspicious animal sighted near Munich airport on Tuesday that is thought to possibly be a puma.
Thermal imaging cameras employed in an overnight aerial search failed to detect any sign of the animal in the Notzingermoos nature reserve in the district of Erding, a police spokeswoman said.
During the light hours of Wednesday, police also scoured the area with the help of a helicopter and drones in addition to officers on the ground but in vain.
There was one false alarm after a security guard spotted a suspicious animal on surveillance footage, with a helicopter sent to investigate.
That animal is believed to have been a domestic cat, police said.
The searches began after a hunter spotted and filmed a suspicious animal using a night-vision device late on Tuesday evening, with an expert who viewed the footage later saying it was possibly a puma.
However, local authorities have noted that there has so far been no definite identification of the animal.
Steinmeier on 'farewell' state visit to France
German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to be welcomed by French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday with military honors at one of the French capital's best-known landmarks, the Arc de Triomphe, at the start of a state visit.
Following the ceremony, the German head of state is to hold talks with Macron at the Elysee Palace, with an ensuing joint press statement.
Steinmeier will then be received for a state banquet at the palace, the official residence of the French president.
On Friday, Steinmeier is to travel with Macron to the southwestern city of Bordeaux, where the two will visit two facilities connected with atomic deterrence.
Before leaving for France, Steinmeier said he saw the trip as a kind of farewell visit to Macron, whom he described as a "committed European and a good friend."
Both men took office in 2017 and both will be stepping down early next year.
However, their roles are very different despite their having the same title: The German president has, in the main, ceremonial duties, while Macron holds wide-ranging executive powers.
UK's Burnham to meet with Merz in Berlin
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to visit Berlin on Thursday for his first face-to-face meeting with Chancellor Friedrich Merz, during which the two leaders will launch a new UK-Germany joint security partnership.
The partnership aims to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats by enhancing information-sharing and establishing coordinated monitoring, deterrence and disruption capabilities.
The initiative comes as Europe is faced by a multitude of hybrid security threats from various adversaries, especially Russia.
Ahead of the visit, Burnham said: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat."
"They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided," he continued.
"Britain and Germany are joining forces to find, expose and disrupt this activity."
The two leaders are also to discuss support for Ukraine as it faces the ongoing Russian invasion, as well as the conflict in the Middle East and the economic disruption it has caused.
They will also convene a UK-Germany Regional Growth Forum.
The platform aims to bring together British and German chief executives in a bid to promote investment and strengthen industrial partnerships between the two countries.

Solar parks driving electricity price down but could result in higher transmission charges
Sunny summers are bringing zero and negative prices to the electricity market with increasing frequency, raising questions for renewable energy developers about how they can recoup their investments.
Southern Estonia's largest solar park has begun operating at the former Raadi military airfield. With a capacity of 74 megawatts, the park could theoretically meet half the electricity needs of Tartu's households. However, summer sunshine and falling electricity prices pose a significant profitability risk for the producer.
"With projects like these, you certainly have to think very carefully about when to generate electricity, when to sell it and when to store it. There will certainly be quite a few instances when production has to be curtailed," said Kristo Seli, CEO of Estiko Group.
According to researchers, Estonia's electricity grid faces a paradox: While summer production drives down wholesale electricity prices, connecting additional power plants to the grid brings new costs for consumers.
"When we add power plants or solar parks and they generate more energy, that should bring electricity prices down. At the same time, additional equipment is being added to the grid, making it more complex, and that could lead to higher network fees," said Ivo Palu, a professor at Tallinn University of Technology's (TalTech) Department of Electrical Power Engineering and Mechatronics.
The main problem is the mismatch between when electricity is generated and when it is consumed.
"We can't take the sunshine from Midsummer Day and bring it with us to Christmas. That would require different kinds of solutions," said Toomas Plank, director of the University of Tartu's Institute of Physics.
Although energy storage is increasingly needed to balance the grid, the government does not plan to impose mandatory requirements on developers, instead leaving it to market prices to drive investment.
"It also makes much more economic sense to build hybrid parks. When the sun is shining, you can generate cheap electricity from solar panels, store it and then sell it on the market when prices peak. Both the developer and, in the long run, the consumer benefit, with consumers getting lower electricity prices," said Minister of Energy and the Environment Erkki Keldo.
Estiko plans to build a large-scale battery storage facility at Raadi by the middle of next summer. The Raadi project thus demonstrates that the future of solar energy lies in hybrid solutions that help keep electricity prices reasonable even when the sun is not shining.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Marko Tooming

India warns its citizens against joining Russian Army
India has warned its citizens against joining the Russian military again and said it is seeking information on 69 Indian nationals who are reportedly still serving. 
A total of 259 Indians are believed to have been recruited into the Russian armed forces. Of them, 139 have been discharged following India’s efforts and 51 have died, according to figures shared by New Delhi, which said it is working with Moscow to discover the whereabouts of the remaining 69. 
In its latest advisory, released on September 30, the Indian Foreign Ministry acknowledged that some Indians had sought out offers to join the Russian armed forces for financial benefits, believing they could later approach New Delhi for assistance in securing their release. 
It also said that some of the recruitment happened through non-public entities, including voluntary groups, and advised Indians to verify overseas employment agents before accepting offers. Russia has previously said its government was not involved in recruitment campaigns or fraudulent schemes targeting Indians.
The Russian Embassy in New Delhi pointed out in 2024 that Indian nationals serving with the military had entered into contracts voluntarily.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi requested the release of Indian nationals while speaking with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his Moscow visit in 2024, after which Russia agreed to work toward their early discharge.
Indian External Affairs Ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said New Delhi continued to receive reports of its Indians joining the Russian armed forces despite the repeated warnings. He urged them to stay away from such offers, saying military service carried a “grave danger to life.”

France Develops IRIFI Strike Drone With Range Of 2,000 km — Morocco to Be First Customer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:20:05 UTC
22:20:05 KST

French defense company Harmattan AI has unveiled the new long-range IRIFI strike drone, with Morocco set to be its first customer.
Harmattan AI has provided details on the new drone’s specifications.
The IRIFI UAV is designed to deliver high-precision strikes at ranges of up to 2,000 kilometers. The drones will be launched from mobile container-based launchers, allowing for rapid deployment and use in large numbers.
The drone is equipped with an autonomous navigation system that does not rely on GNSS satellite signals, as well as an optical guidance system for the final phase of flight. According to the developer, this ensures resistance to electronic warfare and strike accuracy down to one meter.
Before launch, the operator identifies the target and route, after which the drone autonomously carries out the mission without constant communication with the ground control station.
Harmattan AI positions the IRIFI as a relatively inexpensive means of delivering massive, high-precision strikes. The company has not yet disclosed the warhead’s weight, the drone’s speed, dimensions, or cost.
According to the developers’ plan, a single operator will be able to manage the deployment of dozens of such drones. Artificial intelligence will be used to plan strikes by analyzing satellite imagery. However, the decision to engage targets will remain with a human operator.
The French publication Le Desk reports that on October 7, during the Marrakech Air Show, representatives of the Moroccan Defense Ministry and Harmattan AI signed a letter of intent regarding the procurement, joint development, and production of the IRIFI within the kingdom.
As part of the collaboration, production facilities for the new UAVs are to be established in Morocco. In particular, critical technological components are planned to be developed and manufactured directly in the country with the involvement of local specialists.
At the same time, the signed document is currently a letter of intent, not a final supply contract. The number of drones planned for procurement, the cost of the program, and the timeline for the start of serial production have not been disclosed.
The new program builds on the strategic partnership established in June 2026 between Harmattan AI and the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces. The initial agreements called for the establishment of local production of autonomous defense systems, a research and development center for artificial intelligence, and collaboration with educational institutions.
Earlier, Militarnyi reported that in October 2025, Ukraine’s Skyeton and France’s Harmattan AI announced a partnership to integrate artificial intelligence technologies into Raybird drones.
In February 2026, it was also reported that Harmattan AI planned to integrate its compact Sahara synthetic aperture radars into Ukrainian drones. These radars enable reconnaissance even in cloudy and foggy conditions.

Attack risks rise for tankers as Iran vows to block more Hormuz routes
- Iran has warned it may block unauthorised Hormuz routes, raising attack risks for tankers and threatening oil exports from regional rivals.
- A tanker, the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged Acers, was hit near Qatar, with minor crew injuries and fears of a wider combat zone.
- Shipping and oil markets are under growing strain, with lower vessel traffic, tighter oil stocks, and higher costs as the conflict spreads.
AI generated
LONDON – Tankers are facing a higher risk of attacks and intimidation as they try to get critical shipments through the Strait of Hormuz after Iran issued new warnings it would block routes that it has not authorised, sources said.
Last week already saw the biggest number of attacks on tankers in the key waterway since the Iran war began – cutting the number of vessels trying to get through to the lowest in more than two months.
Iran has now warned regional countries that any attempt to open new routes for oil exports would be considered hostile, a senior regional official close to Tehran told Reuters.
It was part of a plan agreed by both Iran’s political leaders and its Revolutionary Guards, the official added.
‘Policy of fear and threats’
“Iran has absolutely no intention of allowing control of the Strait of Hormuz to slip from its hands and has plans ready to block routes that some regional countries have for exporting oil,” a senior diplomat in the region briefed by Tehran told Reuters separately.
“This could involve missile and drone attacks on ships, or sending boats to scare ships away,” the diplomat added. “It plans to continue this policy of fear and threats,” he said.
In recent months, Gulf oil producers have rushed shipments of oil through channels that hug the Omani side of the strait before transferring the oil in open waters in the Gulf of Oman with aerial support from the US, sources said.
In the latest incident in the past 24 hours, projectiles struck a tanker some 51 nautical miles off the coast of Qatar inside the Gulf, British navy agency UKMTO reported.
Maritime security sources said the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged chemical tanker Acers had been hit by multiple projectiles north of Qatar’s Madinat ash Shamal, with minor injuries sustained by its crew.
“The Acers strike raises the prospect of a wider combat area affecting approaches to Qatar, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Iraq,” maritime risk intelligence group Pole Star Global’s subsidiary Clearwater Dynamics said in a report on Oct 8.
The vessel’s operator, listed in shipping databases as Antigua and Barbuda-based Valvoria Shipping, could not be reached for comment.
“The recent spate of Iranian attacks seems to have dampened the appetite of shipowners to sail through the Strait,” said Jakob Larsen, chief safety & security officer at shipping association BIMCO.
“The Iranian threat appears to have increased.”
‘War at sea does not remain at sea’
US President Donald Trump is weighing next steps against Iran, including whether to escalate strikes before or after the November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress, as he presses a naval blockade meant to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The war – and its US$3 billion (S$3.85 billion) monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the campaign trail.
Governments and energy companies have drawn oil from stockpiles to alleviate pressure in a global oil market facing unprecedented supply disruptions in 2026, also caused by the war in Ukraine.
The amount of oil in storage that is accessible to the global market is running low, industry executives said at a forum in London this week, making the market more fragile and putting upward pressure on prices.
The impact of the crisis was increasingly rippling across the global economy. Danish shipping group Maersk said on Oct 8 it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on inland transportation in the UK and Ireland due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
“There is no going back to the old world, no harbouring back to the stability and the prosperity of the last several decades,” Major-General Paul Maynard, assistant chief of the naval staff with Britain’s Royal Navy, told a UK Chamber of Shipping Riviera conference in London this week.
“A war at sea does not remain at sea.” REUTERS

Bail of UAH 20 million set by the court as an alternative to detention has been paid in full for former deputy head of the Office of the President Iryna Mudra, who is suspected in cases involving money laundering and raiding, the High Anti-Corruption Court (HACC) told Interfax-Ukraine.
"The bail has been paid in full," the court said on Thursday.
On August 25, the HACC ordered Mudra's detention with an alternative of UAH 20 million bail. Mudra said she would try to raise the amount. The HACC Appeals Chamber subsequently upheld the decision. The bail had not been paid into the HACC account since then, and Mudra remained in pretrial detention.
On September 24, the HACC found that Mudra's rights had been violated and ordered the National Bank of Ukraine to determine why banks were refusing to accept the bail payment.
Earlier that day, the NBU said bank representatives had cited among the reasons for refusing such transactions the lack of documentary proof of the source of funds, including cash, splitting bail payments into multiple transactions and the use of shell companies to make payments.
The following day, the NBU said it had taken note of the HACC ruling concerning bail payments and would respond within its powers after receiving the official document.
On September 28, lawyers from Miller law firm, which represents Mudra, said the NBU had failed to comply with the September 24 HACC ruling ordering it to determine why banks were refusing to accept the bail.
On September 28, the HACC upheld Mudra's pretrial measure of detention with an alternative of UAH 20 million bail. Her defense had asked for the bail to be reduced to UAH 13 million, which had already been transferred to the court's account by that time.
On August 19, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) released a video about an operation codenamed Forest Gump, saying they had exposed and notified suspects of the laundering of UAH 150 million to pay bail for a suspect in the Midas case. The group included, among others, a deputy head of the Office of the President and a former member of parliament. Later that day, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree dismissing Mudra as deputy head of the Office of the President.
On August 20, NABU and SAPO released a second video concerning corruption involving the same senior officials, codenamed Femida, describing the exposure of alleged illegal acquisition of real estate and corporate assets through forged documents. Mudra, a former deputy head of the Office of the President, also features in this episode.
Later on August 20, NABU and SAPO commented on the videos released earlier under the names Forest Gump and Femida concerning alleged corruption schemes involving senior officials of the Office of the President, a former and a current member of parliament. "The activities of the criminal organization were aimed, among other things, at acquiring high-value real estate and other assets of legal entities through unauthorized interference in the operation of information (automated) networks of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine, forgery of court decisions and title documents," NABU said in a Telegram post.
NABU also said that in June 2026, certain members of the alleged criminal organization, acting in collusion with representatives and officials of a state-owned bank, had organized and facilitated the laundering of criminal proceeds.
"Based on the evidence obtained, NABU detectives and SAPO prosecutors notified members of the criminal organization and persons they had involved of suspicion under Articles 255, 191, 206-2, 209, 358 and 361 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine," SAPO said.

State budget 2027 reaches parliament with backing guaranteed by Socialist Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:18:50 UTC
22:18:50 KST

On Thursday the government submitted to parliament the draft 2027 state budget, forecasting 2% growth and a surplus between 0.1% and 0.2% of GDP. Its approval is assured by the Socialist Party, which has said it will abstain in the overall vote.
The government on Thursday early afternoon submitted to parliament the draft State Budget law for 2027, two days before the deadline, after approving it this morning in the Council of Ministers.
The document was handed over by the finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, to the Speaker of the Assembly of the Republic, José Pedro-Aguiar Branco.
The third State Budget of Luís Montenegro's government has its approval once again assured by the Socialist Party (PS).
The Socialist secretary-general, José Luís Carneiro, announced last week that the party intends to abstain in the vote on the bill in general terms, scheduled for 28 October, after the prime minister, Luís Montenegro, gave guarantees on four conditions set by the Socialists: a constitutional revision with PS and PSD playing a central role, protection of current and future pensions, funding for investment projects that remain to be carried out after the Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), and support for the recovery of municipalities and regions affected by storms.
The detailed debate and vote will take place between 29 October and 24 November, with the final overall vote set for 24 November.
The Communist Party (PCP) and the Left Bloc have already announced that they will vote against the government's proposal. Chega has also threatened to vote against (source in Portuguese)if the prime minister refuses to lower the retirement age, and has made an additional demand: a cut in VAT on fuel and the introduction of zero VAT on a basket of essential foodstuffs. These are red lines the government has already rejected.
The remaining parties have not yet announced how they will vote.
The President of the Republic, António José Seguro, said on Thursday that he expected a "fruitful debate" to improve people's lives "at a very difficult time".
Speaking to reporters in parliament after meetings with the parties on the draft budget, the finance minister, Joaquim Miranda Sarmento, refused to estimate how much room there is for negotiations, confirming that the projected surplus for next year will be between 0.1% and 0.2% of gross domestic product (GDP).
The government estimates that the economic measures already adopted, which will continue to have an impact on the public accounts in 2027, will have a 4.8 billion-euro impact next year, not yet counting any new policies to be included in the next budget.
As for the macroeconomic scenario for next year, the government is forecasting economic growth of 2%, in line with the trend of recent years, along with a budget surplus of up to 0.2%.
Pensions, public-sector wages and debt-interest payments are among the main sources of pressure, alongside tax measures such as updating income tax brackets, cutting the corporation tax rate and housing measures.
The finance minister said that the 2027 State Budget provides for a further cut in income tax, through updating the brackets, the specific tax deduction and the minimum subsistence threshold, mechanisms which by law have to be adjusted.
The PSD/CDS-PP government has decided to lower income tax rates in the first to sixth brackets by between 0.3 and 0.5 percentage points, a measure with an estimated impact of 400 million euros that will already be reflected in withholding at source in 2026.
The reduction will be 0.3 percentage points in the first bracket, 0.5 points in the second to fifth brackets and again 0.3 points in the sixth bracket.
The government has also announced a 50-euro increase in the solidarity supplement for the elderly (CSI) in 2027, with the reference amount rising to 720 euros.
The government's programme provides for this amount to reach 870 euros in 2029, compared to the current 670 euros.
A rise in the minimum wage from 920 to 970 euros is also planned. The tripartite agreement on wage increases and economic growth for 2025-2028, signed in October 2024 between the government, the four employers' confederations and the UGT trade union, revised upwards the path of the national minimum wage. The agreement provides for annual increases of 50 euros, with the aim of reaching 1,020 euros in 2028.
In the civil service, the multiannual agreement in force provides for pay rises of 2.30% in 2027, with a minimum increase of 60.52 euros.
If the planned increase in the agreement goes ahead, the minimum basic wage in the public administration should rise to 995.51 euros in 2027.
The same agreement also provides for an increase in the meal allowance, currently set at 6.15 euros, of 15 cents per year up to 2029.

India’s data silos cost up to 7% of welfare spending, threaten AI push: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:17:49 UTC
22:17:49 KST

Citing a 2025 NITI Aayog assessment, the report estimated that poor-quality data causes leakage of 4-7% of India's annual welfare spending.
NEW DELHI: Even as India processes over 20 billion UPI transactions every month and has enrolled more than 1.4 billion people under Aadhaar, fragmented government databases continue to cause financial losses, exclude eligible beneficiaries from welfare schemes and threaten the country’s AI ambitions, according to a report released on Thursday.The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change (TBI) report, From Digital Scale to Data Power: A Data Operating Model for India’s States, said India’s next digital challenge is not building more infrastructure but making existing government data accurate, accessible and usable across departments.Citing a 2025 NITI Aayog assessment, the report estimated that poor-quality data causes leakage of 4-7 per cent of India's annual welfare spending.It highlighted how past data-cleaning exercises helped remove 1.71 crore ineligible PM-KISAN beneficiaries, saving an estimated Rs 9,000 crore. Similarly, eliminating 3.5 crore bogus LPG connections saved Rs 21,000 crore over two years, while removing 1.6 crore fake ration cards is saving approximately Rs 10,000 crore annually.
Despite these gains, government databases covering health, education, land records, taxation and welfare largely operate independently, limiting their usefulness for policy decisions.
The report warned that deploying AI on fragmented or unreliable databases could amplify existing errors rather than improve public services.“Is the data good enough to trust an AI system, or a human official, to act on it? Right now, in most states, the honest answer is not yet,” said Vivek Agarwal, TBI country director and report co-author.Drawing on initiatives in Karnataka, Odisha and Rajasthan, the report proposed seven reforms, including common data standards, independent quality checks, stronger accountability and legal safeguards.It also recommended a State Data Balance Sheet to help governments track data assets and risks, arguing that reliable information must precede large-scale AI deployment in governance.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.
