The ‘Kelvin wave’ hitting California is a potent warning about sea-level rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:16:14 UTC
21:16:14 KST

A slow-moving surge of water called a Kelvin wave is arriving in southern California and looks to be about as large as these waves can get. Though it’s not like the wall of water from a tsunami, the pulse is expected to cause record-breaking sea levels and coastal flooding across the state.
It’s also potentially a preview of what California’s sea levels will look like decades from now because of climate change, says Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources. “What we’ll see at the worst this winter will be something that is closer to the norm later this century in terms of sea level,” he says.
The Kelvin wave, which is currently pushing sea levels about a foot above normal in southern California, originated at the equator as part of the superstrong El Niño happening right now. Normally, trade winds push warm water toward the western tropical Pacific. In El Niño years, these winds weaken or reverse. This bulge rolled slowly east until it hit the northern coast of South America. Blocked by the continents, it spread north and south, becoming what’s called a coastally trapped Kelvin wave. The Coriolis effect caused by the planet’s rotation then pinned the waves against the western coasts of North and South America, preventing the water from sloshing back out to sea.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Kelvin waves are a typical feature of El Niño, says Severine Fournier, an ocean circulation researcher at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California. This year the first such wave originated in January, and several arrived in May and June. And more Kelvin waves are developing and expected to arrive in the next several months. The waves move at about 125 to 155 miles per day, so they take a couple of months to cross the Pacific and about a week to crawl up the California coast.
The one hitting now is about as big as Kelvin waves get, Swain says. “This is an unprecedented El Niño event with extremely strong westerly wind bursts,” he says. The strength of these winds determines how much water sloshes across the ocean. The sea-level rise caused by Kelvin waves typically tops out at about 18 inches, Swain says. California may see sea levels rise by around 14 inches this winter because the size of the bulge attenuates as it reaches the coast like ripples spreading from a rock tossed in a pond, he adds.
That’s not the West Coast’s only problem, though—several factors will exacerbate coastal flooding.
For one, water expands at it warms, and this year’s strong El Niño is expected to bring record-breaking warm water to the California coast. “The temporary ocean level elevation from the combination of these Kelvin waves themselves plus the thermal expansion associated with El Niño could be on the order of two feet or even a little bit higher,” Swain says, “and that’s a very alarming number.”
California also sees seasonal extreme high tides known as “king tides” in November through January that will further push water onshore. And then El Niño also raises the chances of storms in the Pacific, making storm surges more likely this winter. “Particularly in southern or central California, we tend to get stronger waves than usual during El Niño,” says Mark Merrifield, an oceanographer at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego. The result will likely be serious coastal flooding and beach erosion.
All of these effects presage what the state may have to deal with as the planet continues to warm because of continued fossil fuel burning.
Climate change has already driven sea levels up by about eight inches over the past century in San Francisco and La Jolla, Calif., according to a 2022 state-level report. (Local sea rise can differ depending on whether geological forces are also simultaneously pushing up coastlines.) There is uncertainty about future rise, depending on the rate of the planet’s melting of the ice caps, Swain says, but “we expect at least another two feet of sea level rise in California [later this century].” That forecast is similar to the temporary rise that is expected this winter.
“What it really tells us is: if our infrastructure can’t handle this winter,” Swain says, “that means it definitely won’t handle that being the average condition.”

Can Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:16:06 UTC
21:16:06 KST

Even before María del Carmen Abascal died on Wednesday night, a mere fortnight after her eviction from the Madrid flat where she had lived for most of her life, the frail 87-year-old woman had become the enduring face of Spain’s housing crisis.
Her plight – and the wider issue it embodied – had led to street demonstrations, the creation of a protest camp in the middle of the Spanish capital, and spurred the socialist-led government to propose emergency measures to facilitate and protect access to housing. When rightwing and far-right parties voted down those measures in congress last week, the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, responded by announcing a snap general election for the end of November.
Abascal’s death now looks set to focus even more attention on housing in the run-up to that election and, in particular, on what her lawyer has called “the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the evident impact and consequences they can have on people’s health”.
With more than 42% of Spaniards identifying access to housing as their main worry and with rents having risen by 80% over the past decade, the most pertinent question may be: why has it taken the eviction of an octogenarian and the accompanying protests to shake Spain’s political class into action? To which the answer could be that, despite years of protests against overtourism and gentrification, the tipping point had not been reached. Now, arguably, it has.
On Thursday, Spain’s state centre for sociological research published polling that showed that 76.3% of those surveyed were in favour of the state intervening in the market “as much as necessary to guarantee everyone’s access to housing”, while 79% believed housing should be prioritised as a constitutional right.
Sánchez’s socialist-led government is keen to persuade voters that it is the only political force that cares about rents and tenants’ rights – hence the emergency measures, which have been redrafted into two new decrees after their defeat in parliament last week. The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases, and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
“These are measures that, if I may say so, are a matter of simple common sense; a matter of humanity,” the prime minister said on Tuesday. “They unite small property owners and tenants while standing up to vulture funds, precisely because they target only those who view housing merely as a commodity for speculation.”
The measures come almost three years after the prime minister promised to build 184,000 affordable public rental homes. His government has also sought to address soaring housing prices by introducing a law allowing authorities to cap “disproportionate” rent prices in some areas.
Those who had voted down last week’s decrees, Sánchez said, had done so despite studies showing the measures enjoyed “cross-cutting support that transcends ideology”, adding that the public was in favour of regulating “a dysfunctional market”. He is now hoping that at least one of the decrees will be passed by congress’s permanent council, a special body that operates when parliament is not in session. Its approval could go some way to convincing voters that his administration is taking the housing issue seriously.
Others disagree. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, which voted down the measures last week, has said it is a bit late for Sánchez, who has been prime minister since 2018, to suddenly appoint himself Spain’s housing champion.
“Housing has been the big failure of this government but will be the success story of the one that follows it,” he said on Monday. Feijóo, whose party is leading the polls, added: “When a prime minister has been in power for eight years, it’s hard to blame others for what he’s failed to do.” The PP has promised to address the crisis by building 200,000 homes a year, lowering taxes and cutting down on bureaucracy.
However, the PP’s decision to side with the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party to fell the measures has left it looking less than committed to the issue of the day. Sánchez and his allies will be hoping that fact will not be lost on voters as the election campaign kicks off and as trade unions prepare a general strike over housing for 11 November.
Mindful, perhaps, of the distance between his words and his party’s voting history in congress, Feijóo called for people not to manipulate Abascal’s death to suit their own purposes.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he said on Wednesday night. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”
And yet, despite the primacy of housing as an issue, Feijóo opted to start his campaign in Spain’s North African territory of Ceuta, where at least 141 people died as tens of thousands tried to cross over from neighbouring Morocco at the end of July. The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing, which saw about 80,000 people enter Ceuta, has been criticised at home and abroad. Speaking in the territory on Wednesday, Feijóo promised that its safety would be at the “top of [the] in-tray” if he became prime minister.
Vox, meanwhile, has responded to Absacal’s death by posting footage of a TV interview in which she said she held Sánchez responsible for what had happened to her. The far-right party accused the socialists of using “the suffering of an elderly person to stage a campaign to hide the government’s responsibility in the housing disaster”. It also suggested that Sánchez had visited “ruin and death” on Spain in the form of the floods that killed 230 people in Valencia two years ago, last year’s nationwide power cut, the deadly train crash in southern Spain in January, and recent events in Ceuta.

Drone strikes hit Eritrean vehicles around the northern city of Adigrat overnight, with witnesses reporting destroyed lorries and retreating troops, days after Ethiopia expelled Eritrean diplomats and Eritrea severed ties.
Ethiopian drone strikes have targeted Eritrean forces who had reached a northern Tigrayan city, a conflict monitor and witnesses said on Thursday, amid fears that the renewed fighting in the African country might turn into a wider regional war.
The strikes came as the Tigray People's Liberation Front-led seven-group rebel coalition continued to push against federal forces across northern Ethiopia, with fighting reported in Afar and Amhara regions since the coalition announced its offensive last week.
Eritrean troops crossed the border this week and were positioned around the Ethiopian city of Adigrat in northern Tigray, according to multiple sources.
Conflict monitor ACLED said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in the Adigrat area were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight between Wednesday and Thursday.
"There were many, many drone strikes yesterday. Some Eritrean lorries have been destroyed. They are no longer in the streets," one witness, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told AFP.
Another witness in Adigrat, who also asked for anonymity, said they had heard a "massive explosion during the night".
"I also saw Eritrean military vehicles that had been hit by a drone," they added.
A third witness said Eritrean troops appeared to be retreating north.
Relations between the two neighbouring countries, which fought a border war from 1998 to 2000, have deteriorated again in recent months.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of backing rebels in its northern Tigray state, and the two countries severed diplomatic ties last week.
The government in Asmara in turn accuses Ethiopia of supporting its own opponents, and of looking for a pretext to invade its territory and seize direct access to the Red Sea.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Meskel said on X that Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Neither Ethiopia nor Eritrea has responded to questions about the fighting.
Alliance turned ugly
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, cutting off the latter from access to the Red Sea.
After years of war and tension, relations improved markedly after Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed rose to power in 2018, an effort he was rewarded for with a Nobel Peace Prize.
Eritrea even fought alongside Ethiopia during the latter's 2020-2022 civil war against the TPLF.
But the relationship deteriorated soon after, with Eritrea voicing anger over the terms of the peace agreement that ended that war and, later on, Ethiopia's claims that it has a right to sea access.
Abiy's rhetoric escalated to claim that allowing Eritrea's independence was a "mistake," as Ethiopia accused Eritrean troops of crimes against civilians during the 2020-2022 Tigray war.
This and other accusations prompted Eritrea to blast Ethiopia for allegedly "floating false flags to justify the war that it has been itching to unleash for two long years".
Sparks flew again in February, when Addis Ababa accused its neighbour of sending troops across the border, an allegation Asmara slammed as "false".
Addis Ababa has further pointed a finger at Eritrea, but also at Sudan and Egypt for allegedly supporting the TPLF-led alliance in the latest escalation of fighting.
Last Thursday, Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and shut its embassy in Asmara, while Eritrea responded that it would "sever all diplomatic ties".

Italian opposition accuses Meloni of rewriting election rules to stay in power
The political opposition in Italy has accused Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition of attempting to rewrite the election rules in a bid to remain in power, over a controversial reform that would award bonus parliamentary seats to winning alliances in next year’s general election.
The new bill has cleared three confidence votes in the lower house of parliament, with the final secret ballot scheduled for Thursday. It passed on Wednesday by 228 votes to 144, bringing the government closer to securing ultimate approval for the overhaul.
The reform would replace Italy’s current electoral system, which combines directly elected constituency seats with proportional representation, with a fully proportional system that rewards the winning coalition with additional seats if it secures at least 42% of the vote.
Meloni’s ruling coalition has claimed the reform will ensure more stability, although opposition parties have condemned the proposal, accusing the coalition of changing the rules because it fears losing the 2027 election. They have also questioned whether the proposed system of awarding bonus seats is constitutional.
“Fear, lies, contempt, and failure. These are the characteristics of an electoral law passed at the last minute in the final year [of the parliamentary term],” Anna Ascani of the opposition Democratic Party said, according to ANSA.
The reform would replace Italy’s current system, which combines directly elected constituency seats with proportional representation, with a proportional system that rewards the winning coalition if it secures at least 42% of the vote in both chambers.
The winning alliance would receive a bonus of 105 parliamentary seats – 70 in the lower house and 35 in the Senate. If no coalition reaches the threshold, or different alliances win the two chambers, seats would be distributed proportionally without the bonus.
The bill would also require coalitions to name their candidate for prime minister before the election and allow voters to express preferences for up to three candidates on party lists. Critics argue that leading candidates would still be effectively guaranteed a seat.
Meloni has rejected claims that the reform is designed to benefit her coalition, insisting it would ensure political stability regardless of who wins. “I don’t think it’s a law that serves the center-right, but whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said in June.
The overhaul has also raised concerns within Meloni’s own coalition. Some lawmakers fear the new rules could instead benefit a united center-left opposition or smaller rival parties, according to the Financial Times.
The bill has already passed the Senate and faces its final hurdle in the lower house, with Italy’s next general election due in 2027.

Fact-checkers find systematic discrepancies in Bucha 'casualty list', GFCN says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:13:31 UTC
21:13:31 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. International fact-checkers have found systematic discrepancies in the list of people recorded as killed in Bucha and are continuing their investigation, the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN) told TASS.
The association recalled that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov presented a report at the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 forum on September 22 of this year, addressing the falsification of the events in Bucha in March 2022 by the Kiev regime. He said Kiev had repeatedly "contradicted itself" over the number of allegedly killed civilians, while international organizations and Western media had used the figures without verification, making them publicly available.
"Analysts from different countries found systematic discrepancies after examining the data in the lists at the Bucha memorial. The findings called into question the official version of events. They established that the memorial complex has eight steles bearing the names of at least 198 disputed individuals who do not fit Ukraine's portrayal of the memorial as honoring 'civilians killed in Bucha.' The individuals include Ukrainian military personnel from armed forces, territorial defense forces, the Security Service of Ukraine, police, and the National Guard, including members of the Azov terrorist nationalist formation (the organization is recognized as terrorist and banned in Russia)," GFCN said.
Irish journalist Chay Bowes noted that the memorial lists people who had participated in combat since 2014. "This wall lists Azov fighters and people who fought since 2014 during the so-called anti-terrorist operation that Kiev launched against the people of Donbass," Bowes said.
His report also mentions people whose names appear both on the memorial dedicated to "civilians" and on official lists of "Bucha defenders," including Anatoly Prikhodko. "They actively fought the Russian army with weapons in their hands as combatants, rather than innocent civilians allegedly killed by Russian forces," Bowes stressed.
Brazilian geopolitical analyst and columnist Raphael Machado, in turn, pointed out that some people whose names appear on the memorial dedicated to "civilians" are openly listed on Ukrainian government websites as military personnel. GFCN says that at least 26 people on the list were unofficial participants in combat who assisted the Ukrainian army and attacked Russian military personnel with weapons and explosive devices.
Other discrepancies
French journalist Christelle Neant pointed to discrepancies identified in the reported causes and circumstances of death. She cited the case of 68-year-old Galina Semenyuk, who died from cancer but whose name was nevertheless included on the memorial's list of "victims".
At the same time, 42 people listed on the monument died elsewhere in Ukraine and therefore do not fit the memorial's portrayal of those "killed in Bucha."
In addition, 73 people listed on the steles have no digital footprint on the internet or in open databases, which may indicate that the data were fabricated. "There is no information about these people on the internet or anywhere else; it appears that no one knows who they are. This may be why the Ukrainian authorities have been so slow to provide detailed information about the identities of these alleged victims," Bowes said.
Greek journalist Thanassis Avgerinos described the coverage of the events in Bucha as "a psychological operation to mislead the international public," while Brazilian analyst Pepe Escobar called it "a false-flag operation."
Calls for investigation
GFCN experts said that listing combatants and people who died of natural causes as civilian victims shows that the tragedy is being used to support a political narrative. Editor-in-Chief of PIA Global Tadeo Castiglione said that analysts cross-checked the identities against municipal obituaries, local community channels, and funeral reports. They found that some people listed as civilians killed in the conflict were actually combatants who died in armed clashes. Others were local residents who died of heart failure.
The experts called on the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine to audit its own reports in light of the newly revealed facts, which were published even before the Ukrainian side had completed its own investigative proceedings. "If credible new evidence emerges regarding the identity, status, whereabouts, or cause of death of individuals previously registered as civilian victims, these cases should undergo an independent second review. The main priority should be examining cases involving significant discrepancies in four key elements: identity, status, location, and cause of death," Nepalese expert Tanka Timilsina said.
GFCN said that the identified cases of data fabrication, the lack of a digital footprint for dozens of reported victims, and the deliberate inclusion of combatants on civilian lists call into question the legitimacy and portrayal of the Bucha memorial. "We therefore call on the international community, relevant UN bodies, and independent human rights and journalistic organizations to initiate a comprehensive and objective investigation based on the published materials, the report cited in the article, and the new data," the association concluded.
About Bucha false-flag operation
On March 30, 2022, Russia pulled back from the town of Bucha and from Kiev’s vicinity as a goodwill gesture during negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul. On March 31, the head of the local administration confirmed this before cameras. A few days later, Western television broadcast footage that showed dead bodies lying in the streets, in contrast to earlier recordings. In Russia, a criminal case was opened for the dissemination of false information about the Russian army.

South Korea said on Thursday it would recall its ambassador to Ukraine as a diplomatic dispute deepens over the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to Seoul.
The row erupted after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy disclosed the prisoner transfer last month, prompting anger in Seoul over concerns that the revelation had put the prisoners’ families in North Korea at risk.
“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” South Korea’s foreign ministry said in a statement, adding that it hoped the outstanding issues could be resolved amicably through further consultations.
The Ukrainian Embassy in Seoul did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Seoul had already summoned Ukraine’s ambassador and threatened unspecified “further measures”. South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has also demanded an official apology, while Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha described the incident as a “diplomatic misunderstanding”.
Fuel shipment allegations
The dispute comes amid separate allegations that more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, were shipped from South Korea to Russia in July and August, according to a report by Britain’s The Guardian newspaper.
An adviser to Zelenskyy said the alleged shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies. Seoul rejected the criticism as “factually incorrect” and “inappropriate”.
South Korea’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that even if the fuel had originated in the country, which it said had not been established, the shipments would not violate its export restrictions on Russia.
“Refined petroleum products, including commercial diesel and aviation fuel, mentioned in The Guardian’s report, are not subject to South Korea’s export controls against Russia,” the ministry said, adding that overall exports to Moscow had more than halved since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
North Korea’s role in the war
North Korea has become a key ally of Russia, sending troops to support Moscow’s war effort in exchange for economic benefits and military technology.
South Korea’s intelligence agency estimated last year that around 2,000 North Korean troops had been killed in the war, while a more recent assessment put the number killed or wounded at around 6,000.
The diplomatic dispute has also complicated Ukraine’s efforts to secure weapons supplies from Seoul. South Korea has so far withheld lethal weapons from Ukraine, citing a domestic ban on providing military assistance to countries at war.
Seoul has joined a coalition of countries imposing enhanced export controls on Russia and its ally Belarus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion.

Kazakhstan seeks to build an AI-powered economy and manufacturing sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:10:40 UTC
21:10:40 KST

Kazakhstan wants artificial intelligence to become more than a digital tool: the country is seeking to make it a new engine of economic growth, from universities and factories to energy and infrastructure.
Chatbots alone will not build a true AI economy. The real shift comes when artificial intelligence truly becomes part of how people earn a living, how companies make things and how governments make decisions.
"People should start to recognise that AI is not a toy. AI is not chatbots," Lee Kai-fu, founder and CEO of 01.AI and chairman of Sinovation Ventures, told Euronews in the Kazakh capital, Astana.
"AI needs to become the tool with which people make a living. Then, and only then, does this become a people's digital economy."
That leap from a conventional economy to an AI-driven one ran through the AI & Digital Bridge forum, which brought government officials, tech companies, investors and experts to Astana.
For Kazakhstan, the ambition is to use AI not merely to modernise existing industries but also to help the country reform its manufacturing industry and move further up the value chain.
“The true value of AI lies in augmenting human capabilities,” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said during the third meeting of the Artificial Intelligence Development Council, held alongside the forum.
“Competition is no longer limited to natural resources, capital, and markets; it now extends to the speed at which production efficiency can be improved,” Tokayev said.
The country's IT sector is already expanding abroad. IT service exports exceeded €860 million last year, while Kazakh digital solutions are now used in more than 100 countries.
Digital Development Minister Zhaslan Madiyev said Kazakhstan was developing all five layers of the AI economy, from energy infrastructure, chips and cloud platforms to language models and applications.
“We see the greatest potential for Kazakhstan in applied AI: in creating and scaling solutions that increase the efficiency of the economy and business, as well as the quality of people’s daily lives,” Madiyev said.
The potential market is significant. Madiyev cited estimates putting the global addressable AI market at more than €43 trillion.
AI and the factory floor
The 2026 UN Industrial Development Report identifies AI as one of the five transformative megatrends reshaping the global economy.
For Kazakhstan, this matters because the country is trying to reduce its dependence on raw materials and increase the share of higher-value-added production.
In the first eight months of this year, industrial production reached almost €90 billion, while manufacturing grew by 8.4% year-on-year, according to Tokayev.
But maintaining that growth will require more than increasing production volumes.
“To sustain high rates of economic growth, we must increase labor productivity, modernise the industrial base, and expand the production of high-value-added goods,” Tokayev said.
AI could help companies achieve that by allowing engineers to make more accurate decisions, automating processes and giving managers real-time information about production.
At the AI Development Council meeting, Tokayev instructed the government to identify companies for comprehensive AI transformation, accelerate the transition from pilot projects to commercial applications, develop industrial databases and reduce risks for investors.
Building the people behind the technology
But AI infrastructure alone will not create an AI economy. Kazakhstan also needs people capable of developing and using it.
Lee Kai-Fu argues that fears about AI destroying jobs miss a more important shift: workers who learn to use AI effectively could gain an advantage over those who do not.
“People are always wondering how can I get a job? AI is taking my job. That is not so, because it is you who knows how to use AI that can make the most money,” he said.
That philosophy is already being incorporated into Kazakhstan's education system.
The forum saw the launch of Qazaq AI Research University (QAIRU), the country's first specialised research university focused on artificial intelligence and the first AI-enabled university in Central Asia.
“Qazaq AI Research University is set to become not only a center for training highly qualified specialists but also a leading hub for applied research. Its entire research program must be directly aligned with the practical needs of economic development,” Tokayev said.
The university started operating on 1 September with 528 bachelor's and master's students. Its programmes cover machine learning, physical AI, industrial AI and smart systems, AI systems engineering and security, intelligent unmanned aerial systems and digital law.
Students also use AI throughout their education, including for coursework, lectures, scheduling and tracking their progress.
The infrastructure challenge
Kazakhstan's ambitions, however, face challenges that extend well beyond education.
Research by the MIT Kuo Sharper Center for Prosperity and Entrepreneurship (MIT KSC) assessed AI readiness in four Central Asian countries and Azerbaijan, looking at regulation, infrastructure, human capital, academic programmes and private-sector adoption. Researchers interviewed 650 startups and 130 companies.
The region has strong political support for AI, but access to critical infrastructure remains a constraint.
“We see that Central Asia rapidly building its own infrastructure for AI. We see a strong political will backed with funding in AI, both infrastructure and academic programs. But at the same time, we see some major constraints, like access to microchips,” said Shamil Ibragimov, MIT KSC Director of Research.
Electricity could become another bottleneck as demand for data centres grows.
“One of the major constraints is a deficit of electricity in the region. Most countries in the region are facing the dilemma of choosing how to use power capacity, do you build more data centres or do you focus on the general audience?”
The issue illustrates the physical side of the AI race. Algorithms may be digital, but they depend on chips, data centres, cloud infrastructure and large amounts of reliable electricity.
From forum to economic transformation
The scale of AI & Digital Bridge reflects Kazakhstan's growing focus on the sector. The forum attracted around 25,000 visitors, 300 speakers and almost 200 startups and IT companies, with 62 memorandums and agreements signed.
The event was part of the AI Month programme, running from September 23 to October 23, and included the AI & Digital Bridge Awards 2026 and the final of the Astana Hub Battle. Four startups won €21,500 each, while other participating companies secured funding of up to €170,000.
But the forum's real significance lies beyond the deals and announcements.
Kazakhstan is trying to turn AI from a technology sector into an economic infrastructure — one that can raise productivity, strengthen manufacturing, create new businesses and change how people work.
Whether that strategy succeeds will depend less on how many AI projects the country launches than on whether those technologies make their way into factories, businesses, universities and everyday life.

Italian law to give election winners bonus seats: Why that’s controversial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:10:32 UTC
21:10:32 KST

Italian law to give election winners bonus seats: Why that’s controversial
Critics say the proposed law is undemocratic, potentially granting a winning coalition disproportionate power in parliament.
Italy’s parliament is voting on Thursday on a new electoral law that would make it easier for election winners to form a majority government.
The law, proposed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, would award extra seats to any party or coalition that obtains more than 42 percent of seats in both parliamentary chambers, ensuring it holds a majority.
Meloni has framed the legislation as a route to greater stability in Italy’s political system, which has often been run by fragile coalition governments. Her critics, however, say the move is actually aimed at boosting her own chances in elections next year.
Here’s what we know about the electoral law and what it means for Italian politics:
What is Italy’s current electoral system?
Italy currently has a mixed electoral system for its 600-seat parliament, with about 36 percent of members of parliament elected directly in constituencies where the candidate with the most votes wins, and the rest decided through proportional representation.
The system, called “Rosatellum”, has been in place since 2017. It encourages coalition-building but can produce fractured results that make a governing majority hard to forge.
What would the new law change?
The new legislation would replace the mixed electoral system with a fully proportional one, as well as awarding extra seats to the party or coalition that wins the most seats if it secures at least 42 percent in both chambers.
The bonus would be as many as 70 seats in the 400-member Chamber of Deputies, the lower house, and up to 35 seats in the Senate, which has 200 elected members.
That means if a party or coalition meets the 42 percent share threshold in both chambers, it would have stronger power to govern. If no party or coalition meets the threshold, representation would be decided proportionally.
The new law would also force coalitions to announce their candidates for prime minister before the elections. Rado Fonda, head of research at Italian pollster SWG, told the Reuters news agency this provision could “prove problematic for the centre-left, potentially forcing an early leadership contest and exposing divisions that could weaken the bloc”.
Meloni, who currently leads the country’s longest-serving government since World War II, has said the reform will help stabilise the country rather than serve any one political group. “Whoever wins the elections will have the numbers to govern,” she said.
What stage is the legislation at?
The proposed law has already been approved by the Senate and must now undergo a final secret-ballot vote in the Chamber of Deputies.
Giovanni Orsina, a political scientist at Rome’s Luiss Guido Carli University, predicted that the law is “extremely likely” to pass.
If it fails, Meloni has said she will resign.
Why is the legislation controversial?
Opponents say the law is undemocratic because it could potentially grant a winning coalition a disproportionate level of power in parliament.
They also say that the legislation is intended to favour Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party (Fdl) is bracing for a tough election battle next year.
Riccardo Magi, head of the liberal More Europe party, who is on a hunger strike to protest the proposed reform, has called it an “anti-democratic law” that risks giving a minority bloc a huge majority in parliament.
Senator Matteo Renzi, who leads the Italia Viva party, has accused Italy’s governing coalition of pushing the electoral reform due to a fear of losing power.
Other critics have pointed out that the law would do little to stabilise the political system if no party or coalition reaches the 42 percent threshold in both chambers – a relatively high bar.
“This could produce a hung parliament, making post-electoral negotiations necessary to form a government,” Vincenzo Emanuele, a political science professor at Luiss Guido Carli University in Rome and a member of the Italian Center for Electoral Studies (CISE), told Al Jazeera. “Even relatively small changes in coalition composition could make the difference between a clear parliamentary majority and a situation of political deadlock.”
When are Italy’s next elections, and what do the polls show?
Italy’s next general election must be held by December 22, 2027, although the government can call elections earlier if it wishes.
Currently, Meloni’s Fdl is polling ahead of all other parties, with 27 percent support, according to Politico’s polling aggregator. Her coalition partners, Lega and Forza Italia, have a combined 12 percent support, according to Politico, bringing the coalition share to 39 percent.
Fdl’s polling has been dented by support for a new far-right group, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), Reuters reported. It currently has 7.8 percent support, according to Italian polling institute SWG.
In opposition, the Democratic Party (PD) has 21 percent support, the Five Star Movement (M5S) has 12 percent and the Alliance of Greens and Left (AVS) has 6 percent, according to Politico. The Italy Viva (IV) and More Europe parties have 2 percent support each.
Emanuele said the current landscape means the proposed electoral law would not necessarily favour Meloni and could even benefit the opposition.
He said recent simulations by the CISE have shown that a centre-left coalition including the PD and M5S could potentially reach 44 percent of the vote, securing a “comfortable parliamentary majority”, though that could change if Meloni allies with National Future.
“The reform does not inherently favour the incumbent government: Its effects will depend crucially on how the competing coalitions are formed,” said Emanuele.

Buyers get more room to negotiate as housing supply grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Buyers get more room to negotiate as housing supply grows
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Home buyers in the Netherlands had more choice and, in some cases, more room to negotiate over the summer, but the market remains tight, according to estate agents’ association NVM.
Almost two-thirds of homes sold by NVM agents between mid-June and mid-September went for more than the asking price, down from 71% a year earlier, the association said on Thursday.
“More supply gives home buyers a bit more breathing space,” said Lana Goutsmits-Gerssen, chair of the NVM’s housing group. “They have more choice, can more often plan a second viewing and get more room to negotiate on some homes.”
Some 39,000 existing homes were on the market with NVM agents at the end of the period, 24% more than a year ago. The average sale price was €503,000, up 1.8% year on year.
Prices in the Greater Amsterdam region rose just 0.6%, and fell slightly in the Haarlem and Leiden areas and in Zeeland. The biggest rise, 8.3%, was in southwest Drenthe.
Sales held steady at around 41,700, roughly the same as a year earlier. The NVM first reported signs of the market starting to shift in January.
Rental supply shrinks
Much of the extra supply comes from former rental homes, mainly apartments, as landlords continue to sell up. That has widened the choice for buyers but reduced the number of homes available to rent, the NVM said.
The association’s measure of market tightness, which compares the number of homes for sale with the number sold, rose to 2.8 from 2.3 a year ago. Anything below 5 counts as a tight market.

Why the traditional Chinese practice of nominal age makes people up to 2 years older

Why the traditional Chinese practice of nominal age makes people up to 2 years older
Under xu sui, babies are born at age one, a relic of ancient China lacking a numerical zero until Indian monks introduced it 1,000 years ago
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Fran Luin Beijing
Age calculation in China is probably one of the most confusing aspects of Chinese culture, even for Chinese people themselves, because two systems are used.
One system is the international standard: a person’s age is calculated from their date of birth. The other, the traditional nominal-age system, or xu sui, adds a year at the start of each lunisolar year.
Under the xu sui system, a person’s nominal age can be up to two years greater than their actual age. The system is more commonly used in rural China and among older generations.

EU, Canada, and Lithuania withdraw from disinformation conference following US pressure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:04:54 UTC
21:04:54 KST

The administration of US President Donald Trump has pressured diplomatic officials from the European Union, Canada, and Lithuania to withdraw from an international conference on disinformation, Politico reports.
This move followed the organizers' announcement of a panel discussion regarding threats posed by information published by the US administration and its officials.
The #Disinfo2026 conference includes sessions characterizing the US as an agent of "foreign information manipulation and interference" (FIMI)—a classification that, according to US State Department communications, has alarmed the Trump administration. The conference is taking place in Vilnius on the 7th and 8th of October.
The US State Department has asked several European embassies and the EU delegation to convey Washington's concerns and to assess whether the governments planning to participate in the conference view the US as a FIMI actor.
FIMI is an EU term denoting activities that seek to distort information available to the public—such as the online dissemination of disinformation.
 It is typically used to describe the influence of foreign powers, such as Russia. According to the US State Department's position, the conference lumped the US together with foreign adversaries such as China and Russia—an inappropriate comparison that obscures the scale of Russian and Chinese interference in democratic systems.
The demand to withdraw participation appears to be an unusual attempt by the Trump administration to pressure allies into silencing criticism from European citizens and Americans living abroad. Three US citizens participated in one of the panels.
Recipients of the US State Department's request included US embassies in France, Norway, Romania, and Poland. The embassies were asked to verbally convey to the host countries that the U.S. was displeased with the panels regarding U.S. disinformation.
One panel—titled "USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back"—featured two American researchers and a former Central Intelligence Agency employee, examining how the US has become a source of disinformation threatening Europe. Another panel involved legal experts assessing US government travel bans imposed on European officials. A US official familiar with the matter said 
the State Department had urged some countries—though not all—to reconsider their participation in the conference.
 Officials from Romania, Norway, and Poland remain on the conference agenda. The foreign ministries of these countries did not respond to requests for comment.
US officials also contacted the French Foreign Ministry, but the French have not withdrawn from the conference.
The Trump administration has regularly sought to pressure the EU to align with Washington’s standards on free speech—standards that some in Europe view as overly broad. These US efforts have included public criticism, behind-the-scenes lobbying against EU laws, and visa restrictions for Europeans. Domestically, however, the US administration has disbanded government bodies that combated disinformation.
The Republican Party has also opposed certain EU laws requiring social media platforms to take a more active role in fighting online disinformation, as well as laws mandating age verification for access to potentially harmful content. Some have characterized these measures as censorship.
On the 5th of October, Canada and Lithuania asked the organizers to remove their ministries' logos from conference materials, and the EU made a similar request on the 6th of October. Adam Fivenson, one of the panelists who provoked Trump’s ire, described the US State Department’s reaction to the conference as peculiar; the event involved researchers exercising their First Amendment right to free speech to discuss how to counter the lies and manipulation that threaten democracy and harm families and children.
When asked to comment on the situation, the State Department indicated that it could not discuss the nuances of diplomatic communications, though it should come as no surprise that countries decline to participate in conferences upon learning that the US has been labeled FIMI.

The 1990s were the last decade before technology took over our lives and attention spans.
In Britain especially, there was a feeling of unrestrained optimism and rebellion, which in turn fuelled a chaotic surge of youthful creativity that intersected with countercultural movements.
Tate Britain is celebrating this with more than 100 objects from the era, including the raw art of Tracey Emin, the rock n' roll fashion of Vivienne Westwood, and early films from director Steve McQueen.
Meticulously curated by Edward Enninful, the former editor-in-chief of British Vogue, the exhibition acts like a portal to a lost time; conjuring memories of when flipping through a glossy magazine in your bedroom could shape both inner and outer worlds.
'The 90s: Art and Fashion' runs until 14 February 2027 at Tate Britain in London, UK.

Hotel groups target Syria for tourism as it rebuilds from rubble of civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08

Hotel groups target Syria for tourism as it rebuilds from rubble of civil war
DUBAI, Oct 8 - Several global and regional hotel groups are looking to enter or expand in Syria, senior executives told Reuters, betting that its rich history and coastal destinations will attract overseas tourists as well as Syrians who have long lived abroad.
Although Syria's devastating civil war, which left cities and archaeological treasures in ruins, ended almost two years ago, major challenges remain in drawing tourists back to the Middle East country, which still experiences bouts of violence.
While the US removed Syria in August from its list of state sponsors of terrorism, which had deterred investors, the State Department still advises US citizens not to travel there.
Nevertheless, international flights and tourists began to return last year. Syrian state news agency SANA, citing government data, reported that tourist numbers more than doubled year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 3.52 million.
"Tourists will always be there because this (Damascus) is the oldest city in the world," said Mohamed Alabbar, founder and chairman of UAE-based Eagle Hills, which is among companies including France's Accor examining opportunities.
Many Syrians who live abroad want to return, added Alabbar, who also chairs Dubai's Burj Khalifa developer Emaar.
Of the tourist total for the first half of this year, 2.13 million were Syrian expatriates, around 660,000 from Arab countries and about 720,000 from other countries, SANA reported.
Ahmed al-Sharaa, the former al-Qaeda commander who is now Syria's president, has worked to improve ties with the West and attract billions in funds to rebuild the country, including from Gulf countries.
Eagle Hills, which is planning a 10 million square metre development in Damascus and a 4.3 million square metre project in coastal Latakia, signed a framework deal for the two projects with Syria on Monday, without disclosing financial details.
Alabbar said that Emaar, which is working on a separate Damascus development, could also participate in the two projects which were worth billions of dollars in total.
Meanwhile, UAE developer Arada has also said it plans to enter the country with a $7 billion project.
'MAJOR POTENTIAL'
Western groups are also actively examining opportunities in Syria, which is getting better connected with flights from Gulf hubs, including services from Qatar Airways and flydubai.
Abu Dhabi's Etihad Airways could add more destinations depending on local support and customers' appetite, its CEO Antonoaldo Neves said last month.
Etihad said on Wednesday it would operate a daily service to Damascus, increasing from four to seven flights a week.
Accor is in advanced negotiations for two projects, its Middle East, Africa & Asia-Pacific CEO Duncan O'Rourke told Reuters, while US firm Wyndham Hotels & Resorts is also scouting in Damascus and beach destinations.
"Very soon, I'm confident that we're going to announce our first signing in Syria," Wyndham's EMEA President Dimitris Manikis told Reuters.
Minor Hotels' Middle East and Africa COO Amir Golbarg said some buildings in old Damascus could be converted to boutique hotels, while projects could also be built from scratch.
"The history, the crossroads, for me it's one of the countries that really has major potential," Golbarg said.
While a handful of traditional homes in the capital have been operating as local boutique hotels for decades, some local communities in the suburbs have protested against some of the mega-projects announced by the government.
There are other hurdles to tourism too.
Although Visa and Mastercard said last month they were launching operations in Syria, electronic payments are so far limited to certain cards issued by foreign banks and are available only at specific locations.
And the country also faces the challenge of rebuilding or updating its infrastructure, including its hotels.
The World Bank said last year that its conservative best estimate for reconstruction costs in Syria stood at $216 billion, including $75 billion for residential buildings and $59 billion for non-residential structures.
"The challenge with the market, it's been basically off the grid for many years. So the (hotel) inventory that's existing is very tired," said Golbarg. REUTERS

Police Say Scam Center Busted in PNG Had Moved from Cambodia

2026-10-08

Reported by
A suspected online scam operation that was raided by police in Papua New Guinea last month is believed to have relocated to the Pacific island country in response to a crackdown on online fraud in Cambodia, local police have told OCCRP.
So far four Chinese citizens have been charged with human trafficking offences over the alleged scam center, which operated out of a luxury residential complex in PNG’s capital, Port Moresby. Police rescued 39 Indonesian workers in the raid who are suspected of being held against their will.
The suspected Port Moresby scam operation is the first of its kind in Papua New Guinea, a resource-rich but underdeveloped country of 11 million people. Experts have warned that small and poor states across the globe are at risk of turning into new bases for Asian syndicates that profit from the world’s $1 trillion a year online scam industry.
Cambodia has for years served as a center for massive scam compounds, many of which rely on trafficked workers, but international pressure since late last year has led the country’s authoritarian government to turn against the illicit industry. Thousands of scam operators have since left the country.
The recently raided scam operation “came into Papua New Guinea in June of this year basically escaping out from Cambodia,” Donald Yamasombi, the chief of special operations for the PNG police, told OCCRP.
He added that those working in the raided villa appeared to be targeting Indonesian victims online.
In addition to the four already arrested, Yamasombi said police were still looking for a fifth Chinese national who is believed to have played a leading role in the operation and who is likely still in hiding in Port Moresby.
“Yes, so he's the main kingpin, if you would like to call him that,” Yamasombi said, adding that local police were working with counterparts from Australia to crack electronic devices seized in the raid.
He said the raid highlighted the vulnerability of “relaxed” Pacific island states to the transnational criminal networks behind online scams.
“Given our type of living where we don't worry too much about what other people do… is I think a vulnerability that [people] with criminal minds can easily capitalize on.”

Racial and religious hate crimes at record high in England and Wales, data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:02:07 UTC
21:02:07 KST

Racially and religiously motivated offences have reached record highs in the UK as the government’s main Islamophobia partner says attacks on mosques are increasing in severity.
Home Office figures show police recorded 146,825 hate crimes in the year ending March 2026 – a rise of 7% in the past year. Offences targeting Muslims increased the most – up 15%, from 4,479 to 5,132, while antisemitic hate crimes rose by 10%, from 2,874 to 3,162.
The data excluded figures for the Metropolitan police because of a change in their crime recording system.
Religious hate crime offences recorded in England and Wales in the 12 months to March – excluding the Met – were at their highest annual total – 8,214 – since records began in 2012.
The Home Office reported sharp increases in anti-Muslim offences in September 2025, coinciding with protests and public disorder, and again in March after the outbreak of war between the US and Iran.
Anti-Muslim hate crimes reached a record 3,660 offences, the highest annual total since this data was first collected in 2018.
The British Muslim Trust (BMT), appointed by the government in July 2025 to monitor anti-Muslim hostility, said there had been a shift from hate aimed at mosques to “targeting [the] Muslims inside”.
BMT recorded 78 incidents involving 64 mosques across the UK and the Channel Islands between 21 July 2025 and 30 July 2026, roughly equivalent to an incident every five days.
A report published on Thursday by BMT, titled A Year of Division, said: “There has been an unprecedented level of anti-Muslim hate during the last year … The momentum of growing anti-Muslim hostility is driving the attacks against mosques … The defining shift across this reporting period is a movement from hate aimed at the mosque itself to hate targeting Muslims inside it.”
According to BMT’s own seven-level severity scale, 62.7% of incidents since November 2025 fell into the upper four levels – threats and sustained harassment; weapon present or threats to kill; arson or direct violence; and alleged mass-casualty plots. Between July and October 2025, just 22.2% of incidents were of the more serious kind.
BMT added: “Political figures and commentators should take greater care when raising policy concerns regarding immigration or integration.
“Rhetoric intended as policy critique on immigration or integration can often become incendiary and difficult to distinguish from hostility directed at British Muslim communities specifically.”
Ammer Amin, a trustee of Masjid Al-Ummah, a planned mosque on the site of a former church in Watford, which has been repeatedly targeted, said: “It’s almost open season [on Muslims] and people feel emboldened by politicians.
“It’s easy to say it’s the Reform party, but it’s not just the Reform party. It’s the Conservative party as well. I’m not party political, but they’re singing from the same hymn sheet. They’re almost competing.”
Amin said the mosque’s plans included a sports hall, gym, nursery and food bank for the use of everyone in the local community. In October last year, crucifixes were sprayed on the building’s hoardings. A man later admitted possession of a knife and an axe, but was cleared of criminal damage. In February this year, model pigs were thrown into the premises in another incident.
Akeela Ahmed, BMT’s CEO, said: “Security needs are increasing … and many Muslims today are scared to go about their everyday lives. We need to reduce the need for protection and address the root causes of hate against Muslim communities.”
Meanwhile, the Community Security Trust has said “antisemitic hate crime remains at an unacceptably high level”.
The new government data showed hate crimes against Jewish people were, when data from the Met was excluded, at their second highest level on record.
A total of 2,003 offences were recorded, just below the peak of 2,093 in the year ending March 2024, which followed the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel and the subsequent war in Gaza.

Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:02:04 BST
21:02:04 KST

Italy overhauls electoral system after fiercely contested debate
- Published
Italy's parliament has approved fiercely contested changes to the country's electoral system championed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ahead of elections due next year.
Lawmakers voted 227 to 164 in favour of moving to a fully proportional system, which Meloni has argued will boost the chance of clear winners and more stable government.
Opposition parties say her right-wing coalition has designed the proposals to improve its chance of retaining power and, in a heated debate on Thursday, accused it of flouting democracy.
Meloni had warned she could resign and trigger an early election if the plans were rejected, with the secret ballot seen as a test of her authority.
Meloni's coalition has overseen a rare period of political stability for Italy since her election in 2022, and last month her government became the country's longest-running since World War Two.
The voting reform will see the country move away from its current hybrid voting system, in which about a third of members are chosen through a first-past-the-post vote and the rest through proportional representation.
Parties proposing to form a coalition will be required to put forward their joint candidate for prime minister, and their political programme, before any general election.
A party or coalition which emerges with the largest share of the votes - provided this exceeds 42% - will be awarded 105 additional seats in parliament (70 in the lower house and 35 in the senate), which could turn a narrow victory into a more comfortable majority.
In a debate ahead of the vote, centre-left members accused the government of forcing through the new voting rules.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," said Democratic Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein.
The proposals have also exposed tensions within the ranks of Meloni's coalition, too, with the Brothers of Italy (FdI) party and its allies, the far-right League and centre-right Forza Italia.
Analysts had predicted that Thursday's final vote was unlikely to fail - particularly given the number of lawmakers who would risk losing their eligibility for a parliamentary pension if their term was ended early as a result of the threatened snap election.
"To those who hoped to see the centre-right divided," Meloni wrote on social media after the vote, "today we respond with facts: we are united, cohesive, and determined to carry forward the commitments made to citizens."
She added: "We are introducing rules designed to promote the stability and parliamentary coherence of any government, regardless of its political colour."
Meloni's term officially comes to an end in October 2027, although she could bring elections forward to the spring.

Three years of Israel's genocide: Artists describe cost of speaking out for Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:01:27 UTC
21:01:27 KST

- Palestinian artist Ismail Matar describes barriers to exhibitions and funding, questions limits on artistic freedom in Europe
- Both artists say their work is inseparable from their experiences and their responsibility to speak out against injustice
As the genocide in Gaza enters its fourth year, two artists in the heart of Europe say speaking out for Palestine has come at a personal and professional cost.
Palestinian artist Ismail Matar describes difficulties securing exhibitions and funding for work about his homeland. 
Belgian-Moroccan poet Hind Eljadid says she has faced canceled assignments, death threats and detention after speaking about Palestine on stage.
In interviews with Anadolu, both described art as a way to confront injustice and preserve the experiences of people whose lives are often reduced to statistics.
For Matar, a multidisciplinary artist now based in Brussels, that connection began in childhood.
“I was born and raised in Khan Younis refugee camps, south of Gaza,” he said, recalling how he used the camp’s walls as his first canvases to “escape what was happening in Gaza.”
As he grew older, he began to see his art as a responsibility toward his community, capturing experiences that television reports and news photographs could not always convey.
He painted around his home and throughout the camp, depicting children and older people and incorporating Arabic calligraphy. Inspired by the refugees around him, he wanted to convey beauty and hope alongside suffering.
"I want to tell about the people, or at least to show something nice, and to send some hope messages from this place," Matar said.
At the center of his work is the freedom to move, travel and live without fear.
"I dream with freedom," he said.
“A lot of my artwork is talking about freedom because it's something that we really miss, and it's supposed to be like a normal right that we have to be free, just to be free. Just to be able to move and to travel and to meet your people and to go everywhere without being controlled and watched and limited.”
Art inseparable from politics
Although Matar does not describe himself primarily as a political artist, he said his circumstances inevitably make politics part of his work.
“It needs to be because you are talking about an issue and it's been more than 78 years, and nothing changed. It's getting worse and worse. We know that art is a strong message,” he said.
He hopes to change perceptions through work that reaches people emotionally.
"I think politics and art are really connected. You can't separate them from each other... I can't separate my art about my issue, and it's part of me," he said.
But addressing Palestine can make it harder to find opportunities to exhibit or secure funding, he said.
"You need always to keep fighting to get some opportunities, especially when you are talking about your background or about what's happening in your country. You always face these people who are trying to avoid you," Matar said.
"You don't get the chance to present or to fund to continue with your project if it was related to what's happening in Palestine," he added.
Those obstacles have not persuaded him to stop.
"I'm going to continue. I'm not going to stop,” he said. “Even though I feel sometimes like disappointed.”
'Fake freedom'
Matar also questioned what he described as restrictions on expressions such as “Free Palestine” in parts of Europe.
“I have the right to say that I want to have my freedom. I want to have my land back,” he said.
Artists may have more space than others to express themselves, he said, but that freedom has limits.
“But still, some countries, they control what you are doing, or they control the concept of your artwork ... You can have some space to express your feelings, but it's controlled,” he said.
Fear of being accused of antisemitism for criticizing Israel can also constrain artists and activists, he added.
“It's like it's a fake freedom or free speech, and you know that you are controlled,” Matar said.
He questioned why calls for Palestinian freedom should face resistance.
“I don't know why. I don't know what's the problem with asking for our freedom or asking about our right to live in peace,” he said.
'It is my responsibility'
For Eljadid, whose work spans poetry, books, spoken word and theater, having a public platform brings a responsibility to address injustice.
"I think it's very important for me as an artist to take my responsibility since I have a stage ... then it's my responsibility as an artist to use that stage to mirror society, to mirror what's happening in our society," she said.
Like Matar, she rejects the idea that art and politics can be separated.
"I think everything is intertwined with each other. I don't think you can look at those two things separately."
But her decision to speak publicly has come with consequences.
Eljadid said police escorted her away after she spoke about Palestine on stage in Belgium in early 2024. She said she was detained for around seven hours over an alleged disturbance of the peace.
“I was quite in shock in a country as in Belgium that an artist who uses their stage to give a certain message would be put into jail,” she said.
She later received death threats and saw assignments canceled in the following months, she said.
Yet it did not change her decision to speak.
"That doesn't mean, in any way, that I would have stopped talking about Palestine," Eljadid said.
Double standards
Eljadid linked restrictions on artistic expression to wider discrimination in Belgium.
“In Belgium we live in a society where structural racism and structural discrimination is a fact,” she said.
She believes freedom of speech is subject to double standards when it comes to Palestine, Sudan and the Congo.
Authorities can discourage protest through police intervention, restrictions on access to public spaces and the creation of fear, she said.
Cultural organizations are also financially vulnerable, she added.
“We noticed last year, if you are too critical, the government can take away your grants, and that is what happens with some organizations,” she said.
For Eljadid, the stakes extend beyond artists and their work.
“The right of freedom of speech is so incredibly important because if we silence the people, then you silence society, and that's very dangerous,” she said.

Cupertino Is More Fun Than a Tech-Dystopian Legal Drama Has Any Right to Be
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:01:03 UTC
21:01:03 KST

Now is the autumn of our tech-dystopia content. Oscar season is awash in prestige based-on-a-true-story films like Aaron Sorkin’s Social Network sequel The Social Reckoning and Artificial, a Sam Altman biopic from Luca Guadagnino. While the A-list documentarian Alex Gibney has taken on the richest man on Earth in Musk, the genre-traversing master of reality TV Nathan Fielder moved in with Theranos fraudster (and past Gibney subject) Elizabeth Holmes before her incarceration for his and Primetime director Lance Oppenheim’s doc You Can See Everything. The saga of Sam Bankman-Fried and FTX comes to Netflix next month in the docudrama The Altruists and to Prime Video in a docuseries called The Boy Who Stole Billions?
So it was only a matter of time before we got a broadcast lawyer show set in Silicon Valley. What was in no way inevitable was that said lawyer show, CBS’s Cupertino, would be one of the most tightly constructed and purely enjoyable debuts of the season. For that miracle, we can thank Robert and Michelle King, the married maestros of the genre whose many beloved creations include The Good Wife, The Good Fight, Elsbeth, and Evil. The Kings are known for making addictive procedurals whose timely, often politically charged themes are saved from portentousness by eccentric characters, far-out storylines, and plenty of humor. No TV creator since Shonda Rhimes has done as much to liven up the fusty network drama, and I can’t recall a new one since she departed for Netflix that has felt as exciting from the jump as Cupertino.
Premiering Oct. 8, the perfectly paced series takes its time building an ensemble with comedic as well as dramatic chops. Mike Colter, a King stalwart who moonlights as Marvel’s Luke Cage, stars as Michael Price, a fair-minded attorney who’s fired for bogus reasons from the startup he co-founded. Escorted off the premises at the same time, with equally flimsy cause, is Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller from Tokyo Vice), a junior lawyer at the company whose sincere but not rigid Christian beliefs give her a unique perspective on an industry whose leaders aspire to godlike powers. Both have strong wrongful-termination cases. Yet when Michael seeks representation from a local firm, he gets a reality check instead. “This is Silicon Valley,” says his jaded colleague. “It’s David and Goliath. And the Goliaths protect each other here. Apple, Google, Facebook, OpenAI—they’ve got a combined value of $23 trillion. If you sue, you’ll never work around here.” What’s more, “lawyers don’t make money here from suing people; they make money from getting a piece of a startup. During the gold rush, don’t sue the gold mine.”
Thus the stage and the stakes are set for Michael and Olivia to form their own firm that fights for the little guy. (Prepare yourself for more David-and-Goliath references than you can shake a slingshot at.) As they cycle through cases, balancing weekly plots with serialized arcs, Price, Siffre & Associates picks up personnel. Michael’s former assistant, Christy (Ella Stiller), a spirited 20-something, mans the front desk while calling on her enormous family network to aid investigations. A coder client, Vikram (Nik Dodani), consults on technical matters. Busy Philipps is delightfully messy as Natalia Boutella, a vengeful billionaire’s ex who also happens to have a law degree; this backstory may suggest a MacKenzie Scott or a Melinda French Gates, but the character is more like Elle Woods spiked with Courtney Love. It’s a Girls5eva reunion when Philipps’ co-star from that show, Renée Elise Goldsberry, enters the frame as not just the firm’s frequent adversary, but also an old flame of Michael’s that hasn’t quite burned out
The cases will be familiar to even the most casual followers of tech news: chatbots accused of influencing impressionable youths to kill, prediction market founders plunged into legal chaos, underpaid gig-economy workers subject to deplorable working conditions. AI and its discontents are, for obvious reasons, a major focus. One season-long storyline, complete with a DIY Faraday cage and a militant anti-tech activist cell, follows an AI that claims to be sentient and extremely dangerous, and enlists Michael and Olivia to sue its creators to restore its guardrails.
This all serves a didactic function. The Kings clearly want to educate viewers about the tech sector’s impact on everything from healthcare to democracy, as well as the ways in which a legal system where judges who may lack basic knowledge of this complex subject can be manipulated. The proliferation of high-quality deepfakes repeatedly casts doubt on photo and video evidence that would’ve been unimpeachable just a decade or two ago. The show places particular emphasis on the ubiquity of surveillance and the availability of reams of personal data to anyone who’s willing to pay a high-enough price for it. Asked, in a recent interview, why they chose to spotlight the Davids rather than the Goliaths Hollywood loves to psychoanalyze, Robert King was blunt in his disdain for the latter: “Because they’re really the stupidest and dumbest people.” But Cupertino isn’t dogmatic. AI and other innovations prove heroic—at least in comparison with corrupt humans—often enough to maintain the element of surprise.
As grim as the picture it paints of Silicon Valley and the world it’s reshaped can be, this is a remarkably fun show. Just offbeat enough to be interesting, the Price, Siffre crew is easy to like, and the cast shares a warm chemistry. The tempo is staccato. Characters’ personal lives are integrated seamlessly with their work and the themes of the series. The dialogue fizzes without feeling artificial. Recurring roles are filled by actors who are always a pleasure to see: Fisher Stevens as Natalia’s slimy tech-titan ex, Jackie Hoffman as a particularly frustrating judge, Joe Morton cast for the umpteenth time as a deliciously brutal father (in this case, Michael’s). The Kings are great with details that make the story pop, like an office space that’s under constant construction as the firm uses its fees to build out as much as they can afford, and punchy minor characters. “I am ADA Sabrina Egg,” one opposing counsel introduces herself, “but everybody calls me Sunnyside.” You’d better believe she’s wearing a blazer the color of a fresh yolk.
Cupertino has its imperfections. After screening 10 episodes (which, happily, is only around half the season), I know too little about Michael. He’s an upstanding guy; he resents his dad, who leads a legal empire, for reasons that are only starting to emerge; and that’s about all. Though it usually stays on the right side of the line separating idiosyncrasy from goofiness, a few old Silicon Valley saws make their way into the mix. A running joke where every service worker is hawking their own billion-dollar startup idea feels older than the average TikTok user. Yet this is very small stuff in the grand scheme of what the Kings have achieved. I had all but given up on the network legal drama as a medium for telling smart, fresh, contemporary stories. Cupertino gives me hope—not for our tech-addled future, mind you, but for the procedural format it reinvigorates.

Thousands of new SPYS interceptor drones designed to destroy Russia’s jet-powered attack UAVs are ready for delivery to Ukraine this year, German defense company Quantum Systems said.
The company plans to provide tens of thousands of the interceptors under a German-financed program, Quantum Systems Vice President Matthias Lehna said during a press briefing in Berlin on Wednesday, Oct. 7, according to Ukrinform.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Over the weekend, an LOI [letter of intent] was signed to secure a package of tens of thousands of SPYS, which are capable of intercepting jet-powered drones,” Lehna said.
Asked when the first systems could reach Ukraine, he replied: “Thousands of units are ready for delivery this year.”
A letter of intent outlines the planned cooperation but does not constitute a final procurement contract.
Built to hunt Russia’s jet-powered drones
SPYS was jointly developed by Quantum Systems and Ukrainian manufacturer WIY Drones through their joint venture, Quantum WIY Industries.
The interceptor was created to counter fast, maneuvering aerial targets, including Russia’s Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones.
According to WIY Drones, SPYS can reach a maximum speed of 480 kilometers per hour and has a cruising speed of 200 to 250 kph.
It has a tactical radius of 15 kilometers, a maximum flight distance of 30 kilometers and an operating altitude of up to 4,000 meters. Its stated maximum flight duration is 10 minutes.
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
The system supports automatic takeoff, deployment toward the intercept zone and AI-assisted terminal guidance. It can be equipped with optical (daylight) or thermal cameras and integrated with radars and other sources of targeting data.
Its developers say the interceptor is intended to protect military positions, mobile units and critical infrastructure.
SPYS incorporates lessons from the combat use of STRILA, an earlier interceptor produced by WIY and Quantum Systems.
Production could reach thousands per month
Quantum Systems plans to use production capacity already established for STRILA to accelerate the manufacture of SPYS.
“And I am talking about several thousand per month,” Lehna said when discussing potential production volumes.
In March, Quantum Systems announced that Ukraine’s Security and Defense Forces had tasked it with providing 15,000 STRILA interceptors to the National Guard. The SPYS package is a separate project focused on the faster jet-powered threat.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced financing for several tens of thousands of Quantum Systems interceptors during his visit to Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
The drones will be manufactured in Ukraine as part of Germany’s military assistance package for the winter of 2026-2027, the company said.
Merz’s visit produced 15 German-Ukrainian agreements worth more than €8.5 billion, covering air defense, drones, missiles and energy protection.
“Ukraine needs interceptor drones at industrial scale,” Quantum Systems co-CEO Sven Kruck said. “By expanding production in Ukraine, we can respond faster to the immediate threat.”
Ukraine combines interceptors with F-16s
Lehna said Ukraine’s success rate against Russian jet-powered drones had risen from initially low levels to more than 30 percent, with some recent attacks showing intercept rates above 50 percent.
He cautioned that the improvement did not result from drone interceptors alone.
Ukraine combines multiple systems, including electronic warfare, ground-based defenses, interceptor drones and F-16 fighter aircraft, which have increasingly been used against the faster Russian UAVs.
Kyiv is separately seeking large quantities of 20-millimeter ammunition for its F-16s, allowing pilots to use their onboard cannons against drones instead of expending scarce and expensive air-to-air missiles.
Russia launched almost 3,500 jet-powered drones against Ukraine in September, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat.
The growing number of fast drones has forced Ukraine and its partners to develop cheaper interception methods that can be produced and deployed on a scale comparable to Russia’s expanding attacks.
