People who favor group-based inequality tend to have less gray matter in an empathy-linked brain region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:00:33 UTC
21:00:33 KST

A person’s preference for group-based inequality and social hierarchies may be linked to both brain structure and a personality trait tied to reward seeking. According to a new study published in Current Psychology, young adults who score higher in social dominance orientation tend to have less gray matter in a brain region involved in empathy and emotional processing. The findings hint that social and political worldviews may be tied partly to basic motivational and emotional differences.
Social dominance orientation is a personality trait that captures how much an individual prefers inequality between social groups over equality. People who score high on this trait view society as naturally divided into superior and inferior groups, often supporting social systems and policies that maintain these hierarchies. In contrast, those with lower scores favor egalitarian relationships between groups and oppose group-based dominance.
To explore how this mindset relates to the physical brain, researchers focused on specific areas, including the anterior insula. The insula is an island of brain tissue tucked deep within the lateral groove on each side of the brain, positioned beneath the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. Its front portion, the anterior insula, plays a central role in detecting bodily sensations and processing the emotional experiences of others.
The study was led by Jesús Adrián-Ventura, a professor at the University of Zaragoza in Spain and a researcher with the Pseudo-Lab research group.
“Despite Social Dominance Orientation—the ideological belief that some groups should dominate others—being a central construct in social psychology, its neural underpinnings have received very little attention,” Adrián-Ventura told PsyPost. “We aimed to contribute to filling this gap, while also exploring predictors related to personality and motivation. Ultimately, we sought to investigate how stable brain traits (e.g., brain anatomy) and motivational drives jointly predispose individuals to endorse social hierarchies and inequality.”
Earlier psychological work helped establish this line of inquiry. For instance, a 2013 study indicated that people who strongly favor social dominance tend to report lower empathy in general.
Other research suggested that the desire for social hierarchy may be driven less by negative feelings toward other groups than by an appetite for rewards. In particular, a 2013 paper linked social dominance orientation to positive approach motivation, which is the psychological drive to actively pursue rewards. This finding pointed to the possibility that people who endorse hierarchies might find the prospect of higher social rank and power personally rewarding.
Scientists later began asking whether these persistent psychological tendencies correspond to measurable differences in brain anatomy. In a 2023 brain imaging study of adults in Singapore, researchers observed that higher social dominance scores were tied to less gray matter, the brain tissue made up mainly of nerve cell bodies, in the anterior insula and in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex, an area just above the eye sockets involved in weighing values and regulating emotions.
Higher scores were also tied to more gray matter in the amygdala, an almond-shaped structure deep in the brain that helps process emotions such as fear. Some of those results did not hold up under stricter analysis methods, so Adrián-Ventura and his colleagues set out to test them again with refined techniques in a Spanish sample.
The researchers recruited 99 healthy young adults between the ages of 18 and 30, including 62 women and 37 men, from a university campus in Spain. All participants completed cognitive screening and filled out psychological surveys before undergoing brain scans. Two participants showed brain volume values that were potential statistical outliers and were excluded from the neuroimaging analyses, leaving a sample of 97 participants. The researchers had calculated in advance that about 84 participants would be needed to reliably detect a moderate correlation.
Participants completed an eight-item survey measuring social dominance orientation, rating statements about group equality and dominance on a scale from 1 to 7. They also completed a 24-item survey assessing sensitivity to reward, which measures how readily someone acts in response to potential incentives in daily life without worrying about negative outcomes. Brain scans were gathered using high-resolution 3-Tesla magnetic resonance imaging, a technique that produces detailed images of soft tissue without X-rays.
The team analyzed the scans using voxel-based morphometry, a computational approach that measures the volume of gray matter in specific parts of the brain. The authors analyzed predefined regions of interest based on a standardized anatomical brain atlas, adjusting their calculations for participant age and head size. They did not include sex as a separate factor, reasoning that adjusting for head size already captures much of the sex-related variation in brain volume.
The analyses indicated that higher scores on social dominance orientation were linked to less gray matter volume in both the left and right anterior insula. For the left anterior insula, the correlation with social dominance scores was r = -0.30, and for the right anterior insula, it was r = -0.29, representing moderate negative correlations after accounting for age and head size. Because testing several regions raises the odds of a chance finding, the researchers used a stricter threshold for statistical significance, and both insula results passed it.
An exploratory scan of the entire brain found no significant associations with social dominance anywhere, including the insula. The insula link appeared only in the targeted analysis of the three predefined regions.
Unlike the previous study in Singapore, the researchers did not find evidence linking social dominance to the amygdala or the ventromedial prefrontal cortex. The associations between dominance scores and gray matter volume in the amygdala were small and were not statistically significant. Similarly, the correlation with the ventromedial prefrontal cortex was not statistically significant.
“We were somewhat surprised by the absence of significant associations in the amygdala and ventromedial prefrontal cortex, which contradicted the only previous neuroanatomical study on this topic,” Adrián-Ventura noted. “Because that prior study involved Singaporean Chinese adults while ours involved a Spanish sample, we suspect this discrepancy might reflect cultural differences. It suggests that while the anterior insula’s involvement might be a universally preserved pathway, other neural mechanisms of social dominance could be highly sensitive to distinct cultural landscapes.”
In their paper, the authors note that methodological differences, such as how the brain regions were outlined, could also explain the discrepancy, and they describe the cultural explanation as speculative.
At the behavioral level, social dominance orientation was positively related to sensitivity to reward, with a moderate correlation of r = 0.33. The researchers then built statistical models that predicted social dominance scores from anterior insula volume, age, and head size before adding reward sensitivity. Among the 95 participants with complete data, the full model accounted for up to 29 percent of the individual differences in social dominance scores, with reward sensitivity adding about 10 to 11 percentage points beyond what the other factors explained.
“The effects we observed are quite substantial,” Adrián-Ventura pointed out. “Importantly, structural brain features and personality traits are highly heritable and exhibit strong stability across the lifespan. This highlights that preferences for social hierarchies are not merely transient attitudes but may be rooted in early developmental and genetic factors.”
“In this sample, people who more strongly endorsed group-based hierarchies tended to have lower gray matter volume in the anterior insula and to report greater sensitivity to rewards,” said David V. Smith, an associate professor of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University, director of the Temple University Brain Research and Imaging Center, and director of the Neuroeconomics Laboratory, who was not involved in the study.
“These findings offer interesting leads for investigating how motivational processes relate to these attitudes.” “The authors’ comparison with earlier work suggests partial support: they found a similar insula association in a different population, but no significant associations in the other two brain regions tested,” he added. “This is a useful follow-up, although I’d want larger studies before treating the pattern as well established.”
The insula findings sit in tension with earlier work by the same team. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, Adrián-Ventura and his colleagues reported that, in nearly the same group of Spanish young adults, higher scores on anti-hierarchical aggression, a facet of left-wing authoritarianism that captures hostility toward established authorities, were linked to a thinner cortex in the right anterior insula. That study measured cortical thickness rather than gray matter volume, and its attitude measure targeted hostility toward those in power rather than a general preference for group hierarchy, suggesting that quite different ideological stances may relate to the structure of the same brain region.
The authors suggest that the anterior insula findings might reflect differences in socio-emotional processing. Because the anterior insula helps people tune into the emotional distress and feelings of others, having less gray matter in this region could relate to reduced empathy. If that is the case, reduced sensitivity to others’ feelings, combined with a heightened drive toward incentives, could make individuals more comfortable endorsing social arrangements where some groups dominate others.
“We found that individuals who strongly endorse social hierarchies tend to have less gray matter volume in the anterior insula, a brain region typically involved in empathy and socio-emotional processing,” Adrián-Ventura said. “Furthermore, these individuals showed a heightened sensitivity to reward, suggesting a strong drive to pursue status that may override the negative social consequences of inequality. Together, our results reveal an underlying neurobiological and motivational predisposition associated with a higher social dominance orientation.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider. The study was cross-sectional, meaning it captured a snapshot of brain structure and personality traits at a single moment. These observations cannot establish that smaller insula volume causes someone to favor social hierarchies, nor can they determine whether adopting certain social beliefs alters brain tissue over time.
“A crucial caveat is that our study relies strictly on brain and personality measures, meaning we cannot definitively confirm that mechanisms like empathy directly mediate this relationship, although it is highly plausible,” Adrián-Ventura emphasized. “Furthermore, as this is an observational study, we cannot presume a causal direction between brain anatomy and behavioral outcomes. Finally, because our sample consisted of young Spanish adults (mostly university students), further cross-cultural research is needed to determine how well these neurobehavioral correlates generalize to other populations.”
“Lower gray matter volume does not automatically mean less empathy, and greater general reward sensitivity does not demonstrate that someone finds inequality rewarding,” Smith told PsyPost.
Smith also viewed the structural results with caution. “I would treat the anatomical findings as preliminary,” he said. “The targeted analyses and correction for multiple comparisons are strengths, but 97 participants is a relatively small sample for linking individual differences in brain anatomy to psychological traits, where estimated associations can be unstable in smaller samples. I’d also want to see whether the association holds when sex is included in the models, since adjusting for head size is not the same as adjusting for sex.”
The study was also not pre-registered, meaning the researchers did not publicly record their hypotheses and analysis plan in advance, unlike the Singapore study they sought to replicate. Future research will need to examine how sociodemographic variables such as sex and broader age distributions interact with these brain structures over time.
“More broadly, our research group investigates the neurocognitive factors associated with different belief systems—such as authoritarianism, pseudoscientific doctrines, and conspiracy theories—alongside interventions like empathetic refutation,” Adrián-Ventura said. “To advance this mission, our next steps involve examining new functional brain metrics (e.g., resting-state) and the potential mediating roles of behavioral variables such as empathy or perspective-taking. Finally, we aim to conduct longitudinal studies across more generalizable samples from adolescence to early adulthood, allowing us to track the development of these ideologies and establish causal predictors.”
Empathetic refutation is an approach to correcting false beliefs that first acknowledges the concerns behind them, while resting-state measures track brain activity when a person is not performing any task.
Smith also pointed toward experimental steps that could build upon the current findings. “I’d like to see a substantially larger, preregistered replication that directly measures empathy and tests whether people value their group being ahead of another group, even when their own group’s payoff stays the same,” he explained. “That would help distinguish a preference for relative advantage from a more general tendency to pursue rewards.”
The study, “Neuroanatomical correlates of social dominance orientation and the contributing role of reward sensitivity,” was authored by Jesús Adrián-Ventura, Angelo Fasce, Anna Miró-Padilla, Anastasia Cherednichenko, César Ávila, and Diego Avendaño.

Cold comforts: the most satisfying autumn whites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:00:18 UTC
21:00:18 KST

The wine world is full of clubs, and I’m a member of the Just-Drink-What-You-Bloody-Like club, which makes even the thought of white wines for autumn and winter feel uncomfortably prescriptive. But, for me, as the nights draw in, there’s less standing, more sitting; less chugging, more swirling; fewer sprightly aperitifs, more wine with seasonal food that demands a little more body and complexity. After months of saying yes to rosé, I’m choosing wine with more intention – it’s time to hunker down.
I’m looking for whites that are like a good cardigan, at once coddling and breathable. I want ripeness, body and freshness, and the Atlantic-influenced wines of Galicia in northern Spain – a place that’s no stranger to wind and rain – deliver. Expressive, with a saline edge, albariño from the Rías Baixas appellation has become ubiquitous in supermarkets and rarely disappoints (try Aldi’s Specially Selected one at £8.99), neither does the fuller-bodied godello from nearby Valdeorras (the Wine Society’s Exhibition range offers a good one for £14.95), while the blend of both those grapes and other local varieties from Galicia’s Ribeiro DO in today’s pick is a cool-climate humdinger for the colder months.
In October, soft greens and nightshades are out, roots and brassicas are in, and barbecues have given way to roasts; the season’s food slows us down. At my house, spiced stews and curries are increasingly on the menu, which invite aromatic central European wines such as a zippy, limey Mosel riesling. But these heartier meals also welcome something waxier, richer, warmer, such as the South African chenin blanc in my pick. Skin-contact whites, too, hold their own with these more robust flavours. Look out for wines made with Georgian grapes rkatsiteli or kisi, or those from Italy’s Friuli region. These are not budget wines, but if I drink less in the cooler months (which I do, with the obvious exception of December), that seems a good reason to spend a bit more per bottle.
There is also a small but dependable family of wines that doesn’t care about the season, and which I’ll happily drink year-round, no matter the food or mood. Gavi is often considered a summery Italian white, but the Le Marne in today’s pick is aged on the lees (the dead yeast cells left over after fermentation) for three to four months, resulting in a rounded, biscuity wine I will never tire of. But, as I said, it’s personal; if none of these appeal, just drink what you bloody like.
Five whites for the cooler months
Tesco Finest Steep Slopes Mosel Riesling £8, 11%. Hits the spot when paired with a spicy takeaway and, at this price, makes for a budget-friendly Friday night in.
Pazo do Mar Blanco Ribeiro 2025 £9.95 The Wine Society, 13%. Five native grapes work in harmony to make this food-friendly wine that sings of cool-climate Galicia.
Gavi Marne Bianco Le Marne di Carraro Federica 2023 £19 Sip Wines, 13.5%. I had this at my November wedding nine years ago, and love it more now than ever. Golden, savoury and complex.
David & Nadia Chenin Blanc Swartland 2024 £29.58 Justerini & Brooks, 12.5%. Eight vineyards, mixed soils, old oak barrels and concrete vats produce this precise, generous Swartland chenin; find me sipping it fireside.
Pheasant’s Tears Rkatsiteli Bakurtsikhe 2024 £21 Vinum, 13%. A light amber beauty that brings apricotty, honeyed sunshine to the dimmest of autumn evenings.

'I Think I'm the Best Player in the NBA.' The Excellence of Shai Gilgeous-Alexander
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander had not seen the Onion headline.
We are talking in the back of a black SUV, parked in front of his offseason home in the Toronto suburbs, when I mention the bit of satire that went viral during the Western Conference Finals in May. I hand him my phone and he laughs.
“Shai Gilgeous-Alexander Trying to Draw Foul While Shooting Free Throw,” reads the headline, which is accompanied by an image of him flailing on the foul line. “Trying to draw a foul at the free-throw line,” he says, “that would be good.”
Gilgeous-Alexander, or SGA, is known for many things—winning NBA MVP two years in a row; becoming one of the only players in league history to sweep the regular-season MVP, scoring title, and Finals MVP in the same year (Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Michael Jordan, and Shaquille O’Neal are the others); being selected four times for both the All-Star team and the All-NBA First Team; and being named the 2026 Clutch Player of the Year. But the Oklahoma City Thunder superstar who has achieved initial status—think MJ, Dr. J, or KD—has also faced backlash. Fellow players, pundits, and the NBA’s chaotic online tinderbox have accused him of “flopping”—or acting as if he were hit much harder than he really was, often falling down in the process, to goad the ref into calling a foul. The goal: get to the free-throw line for two easy points.
San Antonio’s 7-ft. 4-in. alien talent Victor Wembanyama helped unleash this anger in December when he said, after a Spurs win over the Thunder, that he was glad to suit up for a team that practiced “pure and ethical basketball.” The implication was clear: OKC is a bunch of foul merchants, with Gilgeous-Alexander, who led the NBA in free-throws-made per game for a third straight season, the top salesman. The criticism only escalated when the Thunder faced the Spurs for a spot in the Finals.
I want to gauge SGA’s feelings about all the noise. Up to this point, he has seemed almost universally admired, if not beloved—perhaps by dint of his businesslike demeanor, low-wattage Canadian upbringing, and small-market employer. Understandably, given his 30-plus-points-per-game average, 88% efficiency from the line over the past three regular seasons and playoffs combined, plethora of honors, and the $285 million contract extension he signed in July 2025, SGA is unapologetic about his approach to scoring. “Playing this game has done amazing things for my and my family’s life,” he says. “And if a narrative on social media is the worst that comes from this game for me, well, I’d take that a million times out of a million times.”
Besides, he has other priorities at the moment. Last season, Oklahoma City was on the brink of establishing a dynasty. They were the reigning NBA champions, having won a title in 2025, and had again finished with the league’s best record. Then the Spurs sent them home in that contentious seven-game series. “Awful feeling, sick to your stomach,” SGA recalls. “I tried to let it go for a little bit. Don’t obsess over it. Not yet.”
The Thunder are now the co-favorites with the Spurs—against whom they face off in the season opener on Oct. 20—to win the 2027 title, but other teams are hogging the spotlight. The New York Knicks are enjoying much of the shine after bringing the championship trophy home after a 53-year drought, and could become the first franchise in nearly a decade to repeat. Meanwhile the Philadelphia 76ers, on paper, have assembled a superteam, as LeBron James and Jaylen Brown join forces with 2023 league MVP Joel Embiid, two-time All-Star Tyrese Maxey, and VJ Edgecombe, who finished third in 2026 Rookie of the Year voting.
Gilgeous-Alexander, 28, is used to being overlooked: he’s morphed from an underhyped draft pick, and the consolation prize in a blockbuster trade, to arguably the best basketball player on earth. Through spectacularly consistent work, he has mastered basketball physics, starting and stopping and slithering his way into the lane enough to, in March, break Wilt Chamberlain’s record for most consecutive games scoring at least 20 points (126). “One person saw this happening,” says Thunder coach Mark Daigneault, who was an assistant coach when SGA joined the team in 2019. “And it was him. That’s it. If anybody else says, ‘This is what I saw,’ then it’s revisionist history.”
SGA wants to strike that dutiful descriptor—arguably—from the record. “I think I’m the best player in the NBA,” he says. “I think the production that I have night in and night out is best-player-in-the-NBA production. I think the efficiency that I do it at is best-player-in-the-NBA efficiency. I think everybody picks up a basketball or a soccer ball or a football or a tennis ball to win the game, the match, whatever it is. And I’ve done my fair share of winning in these past couple years.”
SGA credits his hometown of Hamilton, Ontario—“an underdog city”—for his work ethic, which is helpful considering the two-time NBA MVP didn’t make the JV team in ninth grade. Born to Vaughn Alexander, who won a high school city championship in Toronto, and Charmaine Gilgeous, who represented Antigua and Barbuda in the 400 m at the 1992 Barcelona Olympics, he and his younger brother Thomasi sampled all kinds of sports, including the national pastime of hockey—though never on ice. “I wanted to, but I just couldn’t afford it,” he says. But by high school, SGA was all in on basketball.
So it was a “wake-up call” when he was cut from the squad. “I thought I was this player,” he says. “I learned quickly that I wasn’t.” (In an oft-told tale, Michael Jordan’s high school coach cut him from the varsity team as a sophomore, fueling his ferocious competitiveness: the man was booed when introduced at a Jordan salute in Chicago in the mid-1990s, and Jordan referenced the slight in his Hall of Fame speech. “You made a mistake, dude,” Jordan said. SGA, on the other hand, doesn’t even recall this coach’s name. “I’ll let him off the hook,” he says.)
He sprouted from 5 ft. 7 in., with big clown feet, in ninth grade to 6 ft. 2 in. at the end of 10th. But, he says, “I was wonky. I was growing with knee pains, moving slow, hard to control my body.” So SGA and his club-basketball coach Dwayne Washington, a high school math and science teacher, spent hours in the gym developing tricks to compensate for his lack of coordination: superior ballhandling, changing speeds to deceive defenders, perfecting the art of deceleration—stopping fast on a dribble, so a defender’s momentum carries him past you. He wrote down practice instructions in a marble notebook. “He is able to sustain concentration for longer periods of time than anybody I’ve seen,” says Washington. “Everything is predicated on his inner clock to slow down, focus on tasks, and problem solve.”
By the time SGA matured into his 6-ft. 6-in. frame, and became more athletic and efficient in his movements, those tricks had evolved into lethal weapons. In order to face better competition, he and his first cousin, Atlanta Hawks guard Nickeil Alexander-Walker, who grew up in Toronto, played their last two years of high school basketball together in the U.S. They led Hamilton Heights Christian Academy, in Chattanooga, Tenn., to a Christian schools national championship. “Being able to hold your own in America is the first step to like, ‘OK, I’m on the right track,’” says SGA.
The next stop was the University of Kentucky, where he planned to do one year before entering the NBA Draft. He feels fortunate that NIL—the legal right of college athletes to cash in on their name, image, and likeness—wasn’t on the books then. Having so many options and so much money in college can sap a player’s urgency to collect a pro payday. “For me, it was so simple,” he says. “Now it’s tricky. You’re right out of high school. You don’t know anything. It’s hard to make smart business decisions. Kids have handlers, but you see it all the time: guys go down the wrong path because they’re advised by the wrong people. There’s room for error.”
In the 2018 draft, the Charlotte Hornets selected SGA with the 11th overall pick, then traded him to the Los Angeles Clippers minutes later. He had a promising rookie season, scoring 10.8 points per game, and finished sixth in Rookie of the Year voting. But Gilgeous-Alexander, along with the Clippers’ third leading scorer, Danilo Gallinari, and a boatload of future first-round draft choices, was shipped to the Thunder for Paul George, who had finished third in the MVP voting that season. “You’re never as good as you think you are, or as safe or as comfortable as you think you are,” he says. “I just use it as a chip on my shoulder.”
Playing with Hall of Famer Chris Paul in his first OKC season further enhanced his development. “I used to eat terrible,” says Gilgeous-Alexander, who strongly believes that Canadian McDonald’s is better than American McDonald’s, thank you very much. “The seriousness that he approached the things outside of the game, his diet, the weight room, recovery, everything that he did ticked towards his performance. That was pretty eye-opening to me.”
In March 2020, the pandemic shut down sports and SGA returned to Ontario. When he came back to OKC for pre-bubble workouts in June, he was visibly stronger. “It was COVID, everybody’s on Zoom calls, staying in their pajamas all day,” says Daigneault. “You’re like, ‘OK, maybe he’s in his pajamas, but if he’s in his pajamas, he’s lifting.’ He was not resting.” On a vet-laden playoff team that earned a five seed in the loaded Western Conference, it was SGA, the sophomore, who topped the Thunder in scoring.
In Gilgeous-Alexander, the Thunder had a foundational piece. But the team would take its lumps. “We had to take a longer view to get to a more sustainable level of winning,” says OKC general manager Sam Presti. The franchise lost 50 games in 2020–21 and 58 in 2021–22, before creeping back near .500, 40-42, in 2022–23. But for Presti, those years were productive: He cleared salary-cap space and used the first-round picks from the Clippers deal—plus the Thunder’s own selections—to stockpile young standouts like Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren, both drafted in 2022, and use others as trade assets. This fallow period also put the Thunder in position to better compensate their emerging stars and to add veteran role players like Isaiah Hartenstein, who joined the team in 2024.
The losing seasons never got SGA down. “I get to go out there and essentially shoot any ball that I want,” he says. “So many players don’t get this opportunity. I was so wrapped up in just playing the game that I love with that amount of responsibility that it was honestly just so fun for me that I didn’t even care.”
He was also enjoying himself off the court, establishing a reputation as one of the world’s best-dressed athletes. He showcased his fashion sense before and after Thunder games, at the Met Gala, and even on a Paris Fashion Week runway. “It’s fun to be able to play with color palettes,” says Gilgeous-Alexander, who has arrived at arenas in all-leather outfits, oversize fur coats, and various presentations of camo. “I’ve always been into arts and crafts, and it’s a way to do it through clothes.” He beat out Timothée Chalamet and A$AP Rocky for GQ’s Most Stylish Man of 2022, well before the Thunder became a national TV staple. “My parents always made sure that we looked presentable,” he says. “That was a nonnegotiable. Little things, whether it’s making sure your pants are seamed the right way, or the collar was flapped the right way.”
SGA has inspired his teammates to look good too. “He’s made me spend more money, for sure,” quips Williams. The young, chic Thunder developed a unique chemistry. Gilgeous-Alexander and Holmgren sang an off-key parody of Christina Aguilera’s “What a Girl Wants” in an AT&T commercial that ran ad nauseam during March Madness and the NBA playoffs in 2024; the next year Williams joined them in a new spot, the joke being they all wore the same outfit to an event. Players also developed a tradition of crashing postgame TV interviews with Thunder sideline reporter Nick Gallo, covering him in towels and executing other hijinks as he talks to the star of the game.
SGA sets the tone. “I was shocked at how normal he is,” says Williams. “It makes it really easy for people on the team to feel like they can be themselves.” As the accolades have piled up, he’s remained committed to meshing. “If you’re a superstar in the NBA, there’s a natural gravity that pulls you outside the team,” says Daigneault. “He wants to be one of the guys as badly as he wants to be an all-time player. He’s constantly plugging himself back into the team despite the gravity that’s pulling him out.”
After each of his MVP announcements, SGA bought gifts for his teammates: Rolexes in 2025; Audemars Piguet watches, Burberry trench coats, and golf clubs in May. “These guys don’t get to have as much fun,” he says. “I don’t ever have to think about my minutes. I don’t have to think about where my shots are coming from. Essentially, we go out there, we play my game. These guys rebound, dive on loose balls, do all the dirty work. They essentially play off of me. I just think that they deserve a little bit of credit for their sacrifice.”
After the Thunder won 68 regular-season games in 2024–25 and beat their opponents by an average of 12.9 points per game, a new NBA record, they began this past season 24-1, tying the 2015–16 Golden State Warriors for the hottest start ever. But injuries plagued them in the Western Conference Finals, as Williams and Ajay Mitchell, a second-year player who provided punch off the bench, missed key games. The 7-ft. 1-in. Holmgren had a particularly rough series: Wembanyama’s production (27.3 points per game) trumped Holmgren’s (10.7 points), and the Frenchman dunked on Holmgren minutes into Game 7. Holmgren finished that final game with 4 points, 4 rebounds, and no assists. Among fans and pundits, he took a beating.
But on the September day we spend together in Ontario, Gilgeous-Alexander says he was the one at fault. “The MVP of the league waited until Game 7 to have a good game,” he says. (While SGA’s output and efficiency did not meet his usual standard, he did shoot 50% from the field and score 30 points in OKC’s Game 2 victory over San Antonio.) “I don’t think it’s on Chet,” he says. “I carry a lot of the weight. The only way you can truly fail is if you don’t learn from the moment. I know the type of guy he is. And I know what type of worker he is. He’ll definitely do it.”
About two weeks later, I tell Holmgren that SGA blamed himself for the defeat. “I might disagree with him,” he replies. “Losing in a sh-tty fashion on the last game of the season, and f-ck-ing having that be your last game for the next three months or whatever, sucks. But he definitely checked on me. We chopped it up, trying to talk some hoops, figuring out how to use this time of the summer productively. I don’t think I’m somebody who necessarily needs to be checked in on. But it speaks to his character and his willingness and awareness to do that.”
Off Queen Elizabeth Way, not far from a Ford assembly plant that drives what’s left of Ontario’s manufacturing economy, sits the gym where Gilgeous-Alexander holes up all summer. It’s an unremarkable space—from time to time, SGA says, a shot bounces off the facility’s low ceiling. A half-dozen young men join him, a mix of former college players who offer some defensive resistance and smaller guys he’s known since grade school. They rebound and do some passing. “That’s his circle,” says Nate Mitchell, an assistant coach for the Canadian national team who works with SGA in the summers. “It doesn’t get any bigger than what you see.”
While most Ontarians are just waking up, SGA sweats through his workout, shooting dozens of three-pointers on the move. Over the past couple of seasons, he has upped his three-point attempts and efficiency, making him even more difficult to defend, though the long ball abandoned him in the Spurs series. “It’s OK, it’s OK,” he says while bobbling a pass, burying the shot anyway.
He showed up at 6 a.m. this morning, but these sessions can start as early as 4:30. The week prior, Gilgeous-Alexander flew home from Nike’s campus outside Portland, Ore., slept two hours, and was on the court before dawn. (He transferred from Converse, a Nike subsidiary, to the big brand in June; Nike plans to release a second edition of his signature shoe—the Shai 002—early next year. Asked what customers can expect, SGA, who counts drawing and tennis as hobbies, responds: “Sick design. Because I drew it. That’s all I can give you.”)
After a series of drills, he is bent over, hands on knees. “A little fatigue never hurt nobody,” says Mitchell. Gilgeous-Alexander steps to his safe space, the foul line, where he’s almost automatic. He makes nine in a row.
For the record, he does not practice falling. Yahoo! Sports basketball analyst Tom Haberstroh did yeoman’s work last spring: he tracked more than 1,300 shots taken by top scorers SGA, Wembanyama, Jalen Brunson, James Harden, and Donovan Mitchell in the playoffs and found that, indeed, SGA hits the deck at the highest rate—on both attempts that are whistled as fouls and those that aren’t. But SGA swears he’s not acting. After all, he drives to the bucket more than most, so he’s more likely to draw contact. Plus, he often lands on his tush for safety. “Sometimes I’m leaning so much and fading away so much that it’s easier for me to fall than to try to stick a landing or risk landing on someone,” he says. “It’s just natural. Your body’s in a way in the air that if you try to stick the landing, it’s unnatural. If I’m this way and my knee will have to go the other way, you’re compromising your body.”
Even with SGA healthy, OKC is no lock to top the Western Conference. Younger players like Ajay Mitchell and Cason Wallace must keep improving. And Presti traded some battle-tested cogs this summer in order to save salary and load up on more draft picks. One of them, Lu Dort, is SGA’s running mate on the Canadian national team. He’s been going up against Gilgeous-Alexander in practice for years. “I keep telling people I’m the only one that can stop him,” says Dort, who will now play with SGA’s cousin on the Hawks. SGA sees things differently. “He’s going to stand in front of me and try to stop me from going places on the basketball court, and I’m going to go places on the basketball court,” he says. “That’s just how basketball works.”
After SGA finishes his workout, he makes small talk with his team about movies—SGA has never watched a mob flick—and whether they prefer Damian Lillard or Kyrie Irving in their primes (he pleads the fifth). He’ll go back home for a lift and to hang with Ares, his 2-year-old son with his high school sweetheart and now wife Hailey Summers.
As he looks ahead to the season, SGA makes clear that he’s not out for revenge. “It’s hard to be in that state of mind that long,” he says later in the day. “Even as a kid, I was never good when I played mad. Never, never, never, never. I just don’t think you make the best decisions.” Instead, he’ll lean on his curious mind. He’s making tactical adjustments he won’t share. (Trade secrets.) He’ll troubleshoot at his own pace. “I wasn’t happy to lose,” SGA says. “But I was like, ‘OK, good, I deserved it.’ It’s my job to figure out why I didn’t deserve to win. I attack losing.”
Like many elite athletes, SGA dabbles in other pursuits. He is a part-owner of an arena in Hamilton, and according to his management team, he has also joined the ownership groups of the Spanish soccer club Atlético Madrid and the coffee brand La La Land. In September, he started a charitable foundation, and he plans on launching a media and entertainment company in early 2027. (Gilgeous-Alexander is less inclined to involve himself in politics. During the peak of the U.S.-Canada tariff war in early September, he wasn’t much interested in opining on North American trade policy, though he did offer a brief comment on President Trump’s attempt to make Lake America a thing. “It’s obviously Lake Ontario to me,” he says. “I don’t have nothing more to say beyond that.”)
But despite his many engagements, SGA assures fans that the Thunder come first. “I mean, you can’t put your time into everything in life,” he says. “I should get started sooner than later, to figure out what I’ll do after [basketball]. But while I’m in it, it gets all of me.”

EU extends Russia sanctions over hybrid attacks and destabilization abroad for another year
According to Ukrinform, the Council of the EU announced this on its website.
The decision was made in light of Russia's continued and intensified hybrid activities, including Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) against the EU and its member states and partners.
Restrictive measures in view of Russia's destabilizing activities currently apply to 80 individuals and 20 entities.
Those listed are subject to an asset freeze, and EU citizens and companies are forbidden from making funds, financial assets or economic resources available to them. Natural persons also face a travel ban that prohibits them from entering or transiting through EU territories.
The framework for restrictive measures in response to Russia's destabilizing actions was set up on October 8, 2024 to target those engaged in actions and policies by the government of the Russian Federation, which undermine the fundamental values of the EU and its member states, their security, stability, independence and integrity. The sanctions regime targets also those responsible for Russia's hybrid activities against third countries and international organizations.
The European Union stressed that it would continue to draw on the full range of tools available to protect, prevent, deter from and respond to such malicious behavior.
On October 7, the ambassadors of EU member states (COREPER) agreed on the largest-ever expansion of the sanctions list against Russia.
According to diplomatic sources, the new restrictions cover 1,569 individuals and entities, including 743 individuals and 826 companies, linked to Russia's military-industrial complex, as well as 77 individuals involved in illegitimate elections to the Russian State Duma held in the occupied territories of Ukraine.
The expansion will form part of the implementation of the sanctions agenda announced by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and is expected to be formally approved at the October 12 meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council.

Myanmar: Poverty deepens as families face multiple shocks with limited resources

Myanmar: Poverty deepens as families face multiple shocks with limited resources
Years of conflict, displacement, economic disruption and climate shocks in Myanmar have led to the “simultaneous collapse” of shelter, healthcare, schooling and livelihoods affecting millions of people, the UN Development Programme (UNDP) said in a report issued on Thursday.
The report reveals that more than two in three people now endure “multidimensional poverty” or are at risk of falling into it, with over 37 million people – 68 per cent of the population – experiencing overlapping crises.
‘Everyone is losing’
“Myanmar may no longer dominate international headlines, but the hardships facing millions of people continue to deepen,” said Kanni Wignaraja, UNDP Regional Director for Asia and the Pacific.
The UN continues to highlight multiple problems facing the people of Myanmar, which has been engulfed in civil war since the military seized power in February 2021. The country also faces macroeconomic instability, recurrent disasters and the additional impact of the devastating March 2025 earthquake.
“We are seeing a depth of poverty in Myanmar that is eroding human development itself. This is a no-win war. Everyone is losing. The core muscle of the country is being systematically eroded,” Mr. Wignaraja explained.
Dwindling resources
The report - Layers of Deprivation: Multidimensional Poverty in Myanmar, - suggests that country is confronting more than an income crisis as many buffers that helped families to absorb shocks – such as savings, stable livelihoods, access to services and social support networks – are steadily disappearing.
Deficits in health and living standards account for more than 80 per cent of multidimensional poverty. They include challenges in accessing healthcare, adequate housing, clean water, sanitation and other essential services, particularly in conflict-affected areas.
Mixed picture
Poverty also varies across Myanmar, according to the report. In some areas, conflict, displacement and restricted access to services are the main drivers, while long-standing gaps in livelihoods, education, infrastructure and public services are the chief challenges in others.
Rakhine state in western Myanmar is among the most severe multidimensional poverty hotspots. More than two-thirds of the population are multidimensionally poor and nearly a third are severely poor.
Deprivation among some stateless and displaced populations there may be understated because of limitations with collecting data by phone. This includes ethnic Rohingya communities who have faced decades of repression by the military that then UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Zeid Ra’ad Al Hussein likened to “textbook” ethnic cleansing in 2017.
The findings also challenge assumptions that poverty is primarily rural. While the Yangon region has lower poverty rates than many conflict-affected states, it is also home to one of the largest concentrations of multidimensionally poor people, reflecting deepening vulnerabilities among urban and peri-urban households.
Climate and economic shocks
The report was released at a time when roughly one in five households in Myanmar faces climate-related risks such as floods, cyclones, droughts and landslides. These shocks are expected to intensify with the coming El Niño weather pattern.
The report noted that by the end of August, roughly 600,000 people had been affected by flooding.
Communities are also feeling the strain from “external economic shocks” such as rising fuel prices linked to the Gulf crisis, inflation and increasing food costs.
Youth exodus
The report also highlights the situation of young people who are growing up amid conflict, insecurity and deep economic and social stresses. It warned that as opportunities shrink, many face limited options with regard to education, jobs, mobility and their futures.
At least one million young people may have left Myanmar since 2021, which UNDP called one of the largest losses of human capital in the country's recent history – and at a time when the population is ageing.
Meanwhile, nearly half of households that depend on casual labour are multidimensionally poor. These families, migrants and households in conflict areas face the highest poverty levels, underscoring the need for greater investment in decent livelihoods, education and essential services.
“The greatest risk facing Myanmar is not only the deepening of poverty today, but the narrowing of opportunities tomorrow,” said Mr. Wignaraja.
“Societal recovery cannot wait for a conflict to end. Investing in livelihoods, education, healthcare, local markets and basic services remains essential to preserving the fundamental human capabilities the country will need to heal and move forward”.

Why has Iraq devalued its currency, and why are some MPs against it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:59:21 UTC
20:59:21 KST

Iraq devalues its currency but some MPs oppose it
The move gives Baghdad more dinars for every dollar it earns from oil, at a cost MPs say will fall on ordinary Iraqis.
Iraq has devalued its national currency again, undoing the previous government’s move to strengthen the Iraqi dinar and prompting calls in parliament to reverse the decision.
The cabinet approved new exchange rates for the dinar on Tuesday, following an emergency recommendation from Finance Minister Falih al-Sari and the governor of the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI).
From Wednesday, banks and exchange companies have been selling dollars to the public at 1,520 dinars each, 200 higher than the previous price.
MPs who opposed the move had the agenda for Wednesday’s session of parliament cancelled in order to debate it instead.
The finance minister and the central bank governor are due to appear before parliament on Thursday to discuss the devaluation.
Here is what we know.
Why has Iraq devalued the dinar now?
Right before instituting the devaluation, Iraq’s government adopted its annual budget for 2027. It plans to spend 217 trillion dinars (about $166bn) next year, and expects a deficit of more than 40 trillion dinars ($30bn).
The massive shortfall reflects the difficult financial situation Iraq faces as a consequence of the US war on Iran. Since fighting began in late February, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted.
Iraq’s oil exports – the majority of which must transit Hormuz to reach global markets – have fluctuated throughout the war, at one point falling by 90 percent to a trickle. In August, they were at 2.34 million barrels a day, far lower than their pre-war average of 3.6 million.
Last month, Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said his country was “facing extraordinary economic challenges”, having lost about $60bn in oil revenue as a result of the disruption.
Oil revenues pay for more than 90 percent of Iraq’s federal budget. The lost income has made it harder to pay state salaries and the CBI’s foreign currency reserves fell from about $106bn before the war to roughly $80bn by late August.
Speaking to the Reuters news agency, Iraqi analyst Mohammed al-Saffar said the measure “gives the government more dinars for each dollar of oil revenue, but raises import costs and reduces households’ purchasing power”.
Why are some MPs opposing devaluation?
Iraq’s Central Bank described the decision as a “strategic step” to steady the country’s finances. But many MPs have urged the government to reverse the change, saying it will raise the cost of living for Iraqis.
In a joint statement on Wednesday, dozens of MPs opposed to the move said they had not been told how or why the decision came about – and that the CBI should have explained it to parliament before it was taken.
Speaking on their behalf, MP Aziz Nasser al-Shammari, who sits on the Iraqi parliament’s integrity body, denounced the move, saying that they had been “surprised” by the decision. “Waging war on the poor like this is wrong,” he declared.
Hassan al-Asadi, leader of the al-Nahj National Alliance bloc, rejected the measure and suggested alternative methods to balance the budget, such as cutting unnecessary spending.
MP Saba al-Saadi was also among those who rejected using a weaker dinar to plug the budget gap. She blamed the Finance Ministry and the CBI for what she called financial mismanagement and vowed to bring the matter before parliament for review.
What does it mean for ordinary Iraqis?
A weaker dinar against the dollar means that imports will become more expensive for Iraqis, raising costs that have already been elevated by regional instability.
Iraq relies on imports for much of what it consumes, from food and medicines to raw materials for industry. Last month, Iraqi consumers and business owners told Al Jazeera that prices had already risen significantly since the Iran war began, on top of delays and disruption to seaborne imports.
Opposing MPs criticised the adoption of the measure at a time when Iraqis were already facing rising prices, import fees, taxes, unemployment and delays in government salary and welfare payments.
Al-Asadi called attention to a growing gap between the official and parallel price of dollars in the country, warning it could “inflict severe harm on the poor and vulnerable”.
After the new official rate took effect on Wednesday, the rate of the dollar on the parallel market rose as well, with the gap between them widening.
In practice, most Iraqis cannot get dollars at the official rate and pay the parallel market price instead.
Has Iraq done this before?
Yes. In December 2020, Iraq devalued the dinar to 1,450 per dollar from about 1,182, after a crash in oil prices left the government short of cash.
A leaked draft budget had set out the move alongside salary cuts, prompting an outcry from state employees.
At the time, Mohammed al-Daraji, a member of parliament’s finance committee, said the weaker rate would help cover the budget gap but warned of steep price rises unless the government helped poor families.
Recalling that devaluation, al-Asadi said private banks and currency speculators, not the state, had profited from the difference between what the CBI and private banks charged for dollars.
In January 2023, after the dinar slid to about 1,670 per dollar amid US curbs on dollar flows, then-Prime Minister Mohammed Shia al-Sudani replaced the central bank governor. His government later strengthened the dinar, setting the rate for the public at 1,320.
The MPs who issued Wednesday’s joint statement also asked how citizens would be affected by the dollar rate being cut under the previous government, only to be raised again.

Free land for those who will build on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK's social housing problem? | Phineas Harper
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:56:45 UTC
20:56:45 KST

Lewisham council, in southeast London, is developing ambitious plans to transfer millions of pounds’ worth of public land to community groups in an attempt to get new social housing built in the borough. According to papers tabled at Wednesday’s council cabinet meeting, the local authority is devising a new housing strategy, which includes giving packages of public land worth up to £2m each to community-led organisations such as housing co-operatives, on the condition that they build social housing.
The Green-controlled council is further considering placing any land it gives away through the programme into community land trusts, legal instruments that lock in permanent affordability. They may also provide low-interest loans to help developments get started, and pre-approve planning permission to speed up construction. It is hoped that the proposals will take effect within a year. Together, they form the most radical suite of solutions to the housing crisis any local authority is currently putting forward. If adopted elsewhere, the approach could transform the construction of social housing not just in Lewisham, but across the entire country.
Today three in four new British homes are built by for-profit property developers. The rest are erected predominantly by housing associations, with just a paltry few built by local authorities. Unlike in comparable European economies, almost no new UK homes are being built by community organisations. To get new social housing built in their area, therefore, councils are reliant on private developers building a proportion of homes for social rent as part of larger master plans. But developers frequently use their strong bargaining position to haggle down the amount of social housing they actually deliver.
“There’s a limit to how much social housing we can realistically get private property developers to build,” says Daniel Dream, cabinet member for inclusive regeneration, planning and housing delivery in Lewisham. “We’ve got to get more creative about how to deliver social housing.” Dream, a key architect of Lewisham’s evolving new strategy, says the current system of councils haggling with developers is broken and will never produce enough social housing to meet need. Instead, he hopes to use public land to empower community-led organisations to build essential housing for themselves, or as he puts it: “enabling community to deliver community”.
Selling off public land is a fraught business even for well-meaning councils. Under a 1972 law, public bodies are obliged to accept the highest price they are offered, regardless of the buyer’s intentions. Wealthy property developers can therefore typically swoop in and outbid community groups for land, even when the community groups have far more interesting, sustainable and socially valuable ambitions. In September, for example, Somerset council voted to sell a site in Frome to the London-based investment firm Newcore Capital rather than to local community developers who had plans to build homes, workspaces, a riverside park and a lido.
However, the 1972 law has a loophole. If a local authority is selling a site worth £2m or less, the council can choose to sell it to whomever it likes, and at whatever price it pleases, even giving it away for free, provided doing so provides positive benefits for the area.
The new strategy could be especially useful in helping support more ambitious housebuilding on tricky small sites. In London a “small site” is defined as a piece of land that is under 2,500 sq metres, about the size of nine tennis courts. These plots are too modest for major developers to take an interest in, so often just sit empty. However, the potential to better use vacant small sites is enormous. The architecture practice RCKa estimates there is enough land stuck in small sites to build 850,000 new homes in the capital alone. It recently conducted a survey of Lewisham identifying space for up to 9,700 new homes across more than 3,000 potential small sites.
Improved use of small sites can also create better homes. As the research project Small Sites London shows, modest developments are generally more likely to produce high-quality housing that makes a positive contribution to its local neighbourhood than the swathes of anodyne towers put up by mainstream developers on larger sites.
Lewisham has a long history of successful projects proving the potential of community participation in housing. Beginning in the late 1970s, families on the council housing waiting list were offered the opportunity to build their own homes using an innovative construction system devised by the German architect Walter Segal. In 1997, London’s first black housing co-operative finished building Nubia Way. In 2024 a community land trust completed Church Grove, a block of 36 permanently affordable homes. But more recently the borough’s reputation for housing leadership has waned. In June, The Filigree, a major new residential and commercial development in central Lewisham, was announced joint winner of the Carbuncle Cup, an award for Britain’s worst new building. These plans to revive ambitious community-led housing could not come sooner.
Lewisham’s housing target is 30,376 homes over 15 years. Community-led development won’t be able to meet that target alone, but it marks a clear break with the failing system of squeezing piecemeal benefits from major speculative developments. If successful, the approach could better empower the council and its constituents – and if introduced nationwide, it could catalyse a genuine revolution in social housing construction everywhere.
- Phineas Harper is a writer and curator

Can emergency reserves ease the diesel crisis?
The G7 plans to release emergency fuel stocks as diesel shortages raise transport costs and squeeze household budgets.
From delivering goods to harvesting crops, much of the world’s economic activity depends on diesel fuel.
When it becomes scarce or expensive, the impact reaches far beyond the pump to food prices, household budgets and economic growth.
Right now, prices have hit record highs.
Supply has tightened as the United States-Israel war on Iran disrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Ukrainian attacks damage Russian refineries and China reportedly curbs its exports.
The Group of Seven has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from its emergency stockpiles over four months. That amount equates to about one day of global oil demand.

Alessandro Baricco in South Africa: A Journey Through the History of Opera
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:54:28 CEST
20:54:28 KST

Writer Alessandro Baricco’s South African tour concluded last night at the Baxter Theatre in Cape Town; after Johannesburg, he brought his program dedicated to the history of Italian opera to the Western Cape before a packed house. The events were organized by the Italian Cultural Institute in Pretoria with the support of the Italian Embassy in Pretoria and the Italian Consulate in Cape Town.
                                    
One of Italy’s most celebrated contemporary writers, Baricco brought two extraordinary “Opera Lecture Recitals” to South Africa. A profound and passionate connoisseur of music and opera, he presented a selection of famous arias, offering the audience glimpses into music history and anecdotes about storytelling, opera, and composers, before giving the stage to the singers of Opera UCT (University of Cape Town).
                                    
Baricco took the audience on a fascinating journey through an era when opera was, in fact, at the center of culture and social life. Composers were the true stars of the show. Baricco’s format thus made a highly successful debut in South Africa as well.
                                    
Baricco explained to the audience how music was the universal language of the time and how, in the early days, the wealthy would go to the theater partly to find a wife or husband. He then illustrated the difference between opera buffa and opera seria and how, ultimately, almost all operas revolve around a love story that may have a happy ending or end in tragedy. He also emphasized that, although composers were almost exclusively men, the true heroines and the strongest characters in the stories were often women. He even explained how music was capable of conveying emotions that could strike directly “at the heart.”
Baricco recounted with a touch of irony how Rossini was so popular that, after composing three or four operas a year for a time, he was able to retire relatively young to Paris and live off the fortune he had accumulated thanks to his success. The audience responded with great appreciation, alternating between laughter at his jokes and long rounds of applause at the end of the performance.
                                    
The Lecture Recital featured a selection of famous arias from the operatic tradition: “Io ti lascio, perché uniti,” an aria from *Il matrimonio segreto* by Domenico Cimarosa; “Madamina, il catalogo è questo” from Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s *Don Giovanni*, which was particularly appreciated by the audience for the piece’s irony; “Mira, o Norma” from Vincenzo Bellini’s *Norma*; “Una furtiva lagrima” from Gaetano Donizetti’s *L’elisir d’amore*; “Miei rampolli femminini” from Gioachino Rossini’s *La Cenerentola*.
                                    
The evening concluded with what Baricco described as the last great golden age of opera in the early 20th century, represented by “Vissi d’arte,” from Giacomo Puccini’s *Tosca*.
                                    
Joining Baricco on stage were Lisa Engelbrecht on piano, Molly Dzangare (soprano), Rosa Vita van der Dussen (mezzo-soprano), Landula Hambile (baritone), and Vuyani Halam (tenor).

Seasonal flu wave expected to start in mid-December in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:54:04 UTC
20:54:04 KST

Seasonal flu wave expected to start in mid-December in Switzerland
With the arrival of autumn, the season for respiratory infections has begun in Switzerland. While the flu and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are still circulating to a limited extent, cases of Covid-19 are already on the rise in some regions.
However, the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) does not expect a full-blown flu wave until mid-December. The scale of this wave remains difficult to predict, it told Keystone-ATS news agency. It will depend in particular on the population’s immunity, the virus variants in circulation and the weather conditions.
The same applies to Covid-19 and RSV, which can cause serious infections, particularly in young children.
+ Swiss researchers sequence genome of 1918 Spanish flu virus
For the time being, the situation is developing in line with the health authorities’ expectations. According to the Sentinella surveillance system, flu and RSV remain at very low levels, while Covid-19 is gaining ground.
A typical pattern
This trend is by no means unusual. In recent years, Covid has generally peaked in the autumn, ahead of the winter waves of flu and RSV, the FOPH notes.
In recent weeks, around 120 cases of Covid-19 have been reported each week in Switzerland and Liechtenstein, compared with 10 to 20 during most weeks of the summer. However, the circulation of the virus remains lower than during the same period in previous years. During the first week of October 2025, more than 500 cases had been recorded.
Other respiratory viruses, which are responsible in particular for colds, also circulate in autumn. This is the case with rhinoviruses, which are not, however, monitored within the FOPH’s reporting system.
At the same time, some manufacturers of flu vaccines are reporting delivery delays to doctors’ surgeries, hospitals, care homes and pharmacies.
However, this is not a shortage, but merely a delay, emphasises Simon Ming, spokesperson for the FOPH. People at risk, like the rest of the population, still have plenty of time to get vaccinated if they wish.

Over 2,000 Gazans died awaiting medical evacuation amid siege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:54:01 UTC
20:54:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Over 2,000 Gazans have died awaiting medical evacuation amid Israel's continued siege
More than 2,000 Palestinians have died while waiting to be evacuated from Gaza for medical treatment since the closure of the Rafah crossing in May 2024, the territory's health ministry said on Wednesday, as Israel's siege continues to prevent thousands of critically ill patients from accessing treatment abroad.
The ministry said 2,027 patients had died while awaiting evacuation, while approximately 21,000 others urgently require treatment outside the devastated Palestinian territory.
Among those still awaiting evacuation are 5,600 children, 2,800 patients requiring cancer treatment and 194 people whose conditions are considered immediately life-threatening.
Another 2,000 patients are classified as emergency cases, according to the ministry's latest figures.
The numbers reflect the continuing humanitarian consequences of Israel's continuing siege of the territory and the collapse of Gaza's healthcare system, nearly a year after a so-called ceasefire, which was supposed to allow the entry of humanitarian aid, came into effect in October 2025.
The Rafah crossing, Gaza's main gateway to Egypt, was closed in May 2024 following Israel's military offensive in the southern city, severely restricting the movement of patients requiring specialised treatment unavailable inside the territory.
Although limited medical evacuations have taken place through alternative arrangements, the number of Palestinians requiring treatment abroad continues to vastly exceed the capacity of evacuation programmes.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) coordinates medical evacuations alongside Palestinian health authorities and other partners, with patients requiring referrals, security clearances and arrangements with receiving hospitals before they can leave Gaza.
The ministry's latest figures come as a new report by Israeli rights organisation Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) found that Gaza's healthcare system has made only marginal progress towards recovery during the first year of the ceasefire.
According to the report, none of Gaza's hospitals has returned to full operation, while the territory remains without a functioning MRI scanner.
The number of partially operational hospitals has increased from 14 to 20 since October 2025, but intensive care capacity rose by just one bed, from 103 to 104, according to figures covering the period up to July 2026.
The report also found that dialysis services had become less accessible, with the proportion of medical facilities providing them falling from 17 percent to 12 percent.
PHRI cited earlier Gaza Health Ministry figures showing that at least 1,570 patients, including 264 children and 505 cancer patients, died while awaiting evacuation between October 2023 and 2 July 2026.
The newer ministry figure of 2,027 deaths covers the period since the closure of Rafah in May 2024 and should not be added to the earlier total.
Israeli authorities continue to prohibit the transfer of Gaza patients to hospitals in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, despite legal challenges from human rights organisations.
In July, Israel's Supreme Court declined to intervene in the policy at that stage, leaving medical evacuations dependent on arrangements with third countries.
Rights groups say that the restrictions prevent patients from accessing established Palestinian medical facilities capable of providing life-saving treatment.
The ministry said the continued delays were placing thousands more lives at risk, with Gaza's damaged hospitals unable to provide many forms of specialist and emergency care.

Israel's long road to a Gaza without Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:53:47 UTC
20:53:47 KST

Breadcrumb
With or without 7 October: Israel's Gaza endgame was always ethnic cleansing
In April 2023, six months before the 7 October attacks, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu held a meeting with Yoav Gallant, his then defence minister, and Alon Davidi, the mayor of Sderot - an Israeli city built on top of the historic Palestinian village of Huj.
Gallant and Davidi casually joked about flattening Gaza to rebuild Jewish-only settlements on its ruins. “I would also like to build in Beit Hanoun (in Gaza), but I will settle for Sderot,” said Davidi. Gallant replied, “In order to build in Beit Hanoun, you first need to flatten the area there.”
A month earlier, Israel’s Minister of Settlements Orit Strook said explicitly, “I don't know how many years it will take...returning to Gaza will take a lot of sacrifices. Gaza is part of the land of Israel, and we will return to it one day.”
Strook was reiterating what the deputy head of Israel’s Knesset, Limor Son-Har Melech, said the same day. “Our task now is to return to the settlements in Gush Katif and rebuild them,” he said, in reference to Israeli settlements in Gaza that were evacuated in 2005.
Israel’s finance minister and de facto ruler of the occupied Palestinian territory, Bezalel Smotrich, had also promised on the eve of the Netanyahu government’s formation in December 2022 that Israel would “return” to rebuild Jewish settlements in Gaza.
Three years into Israel's war, these statements now sound like prophetic declarations of intent.
Beit Hanoun was levelled to the ground during the war, just as Gallant said. Earlier this year, Limor Son-Har Melech led a group of settlers deep inside Gaza, planting trees to mark the first step towards rebuilding settlements in the enclave. He bragged: “Gaza will be Jewish, because only in this way will we ensure victory.”
Israel Katz, meanwhile, Israel’s new defence minister, has formally announced intentions to start building settlements in Gaza.
That is why Israel's military rabbi Amichai Friedman described the month of October 2023 as “the happiest month of my life”. He added, “We're finally realising who we are. All of this land is ours. The entire land, including Gaza and Lebanon. Gush Katif is tiny compared to what we will get with God’s help to achieve... We will destroy everyone.”
An ambition decades in the making
Seven months before 7 October, Israel’s former defence minister and right-wing politician Moshe Yaalon sounded the alarm that Israel’s “Jewish supremacist” ministers, whose beliefs, he said, reflected “Mein Kampf in reverse”, wanted to provoke “the final war” of “Gog and Magog.”
Yaalon warned that Smotrich and Ben-Gvir would try to provoke Palestinians, through massacres, for instance, to use any Palestinian retaliation as a pretext for the 'final battle'.
As soon as Itamar Ben-Gvir became Israel’s security minister, he rushed, as Yaalon anticipated, to abuse Palestinian prisoners to ignite that war. Some of his first decisions were to ban pita bread for detainees, reduce their shower time to two minutes per day, overcrowd their cells, and let a Palestinian hunger striker, Khader Adnan, die in solitary confinement.
The cruelty meted out to Palestinian detainees is thought to have served as one of the core justifications, and strategic drivers, for Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar to launch the 7 October attacks on Israel.
But even without Hamas’s attack, the concept of ‘transfer’, or ethnic cleansing, has long been embedded in official Israeli policymaking.
“You shall continue to live like dogs, and whoever wishes may leave… It's possible that in five years, there will be 200,000 fewer people, and that's an enormous thing,” said Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan shortly after the 1967 war.
The “live like dogs or leave” dichotomy was reiterated in 2017 by Smotrich in a manifesto Israeli pundits themselves described as “genocidal.” Smotrich gave Palestinians three options: submit to living as inferior subhumans, leave the land, or resist and get killed.
Israel has used this policy in Gaza since the 1948 Nakba. Even before it captured Gaza officially in 1967, the Israeli government sought to push for mass migration from the enclave through intimidation, bribery, periodic massacres, and destruction of vital infrastructure.
After Gaza fell under Israeli occupation, Israel used more force, coercion, destruction, intimidation, and bribery to empty Gaza.
When Israel imposed a blockade on Gaza in 2006, economic warfare and starvation were systematically imposed, punctuated by periodic “high-tech killing sprees” to inflict the maximum destruction possible in order to make the enclave uninhabitable and force its people out.
Before 7 October, about 10% of Gaza’s population (205,000 people) had already emigrated from the Strip since the blockade started. Half of that significant figure were people who left in the five years that preceded Hamas’s attack.
A senior Israeli official even bragged in 2019 that Tel Aviv was “actively pushing Palestinian emigration from Gaza.” The official said Israel was reaching out to Western and Middle Eastern countries to encourage accepting Gazan migrants and even offered to cover the costs of travel.
Israel’s focus on displacing Gaza’s population stems in part from the fact that the overwhelming majority of the Strip’s population are refugees displaced from villages in what is now Israel, leading it to view the population as a persistent potential source of insurgency.
Israel’s then defence minister Moshe Dayan said in 1956, “Why should we blame [Palestinians in Gaza] for their burning hatred for us? For eight years they have been dwelling in Gaza’s refugee camps, as before their eyes we have transformed the land and the villages in which they and their forefathers had dwelled into our own property.”
7 October gave Israel its opening
The 7 October attacks provided a powerful accelerant for Israel’s longstanding displacement of Palestinians in Gaza.
Almost immediately, Netanyahu called on Gazans to leave, while his government ordered the mass evacuation of northern Gaza. The assault also revived an older Israeli conception of the conflict as an unfinished war of national survival, with Netanyahu later explicitly invoking the 1948 War of Independence, or Nakba.
In the first days of Israel’s response, Tel Aviv, with US help, rushed to pressure neighbouring Arab countries to transfer the entire population of Gaza into the Sinai desert under the pretext of “temporary relocation until Hamas is defeated.”
When those countries refused, Israel pushed most of Gaza’s population towards Rafah at the Egyptian border in the hope of pushing them to cross into Sinai on their own. When that failed, Israel invaded Rafah and devastated the city, only to propose sending Palestinians back towards the area again - this time into a so-called “humanitarian city” that Israel’s own former prime minister Ehud Olmert described as a concentration camp.
Even after Israel signed President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan for a ceasefire - which included Hamas’s disarmament, the withdrawal of Israeli troops, and reconstruction - Israel promptly reneged on its commitments and continued to push for building the Rafah ‘humanitarian city’.
The push to empty, and resettle, Gaza
Since the ceasefire began, Israel’s Defence Minister, Israel Katz, has repeatedly emphasised that Tel Aviv’s long-term goal in Gaza remains its total ethnic cleansing.
“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration… I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” he said in September, despite Hamas agreeing to lay down its arms. Katz added that Israel remains “organised and prepared to get [Gazans] out – by sea, by air, by every way possible.”
Israel’s Security Minister Ben-Gvir presented a concrete plan in September for the ethnic cleansing of 1.86 million Palestinians in Gaza over the next 7 years, called “disengagement 710.”
Through this scheme, Israel would expel 250,000 Gazans in the first year, 1.11 million by the third year, and the entire population by 2034. During the genocide, more than 100,000 Palestinians have already left Gaza.
That is why, even in the “new Rafah” camp, Israel made clear it would not allow any permanent construction with concrete, but rather would only give the caged population temporary and portable shipping containers to live in, making clear those camps are a mere transit towards expulsion.
The Israeli defence minister made clear that all Israel now needs to “finish the job” in Gaza is a pretext. “When it becomes clear that Hamas is not fulfilling its commitment. Then we will get a green light to advance militarily, territorially, and in other areas as well,” he said.
The same applies to the West Bank, where Katz revealed on Tuesday that the Israeli army has been instructed to plan for a scenario of war with the Palestinian Authority (PA). Despite the PA being Israel’s peace partner and security subcontractor, Katz made clear that Israel is ready to replicate its ‘Gaza model’ in the West Bank.
Any war on the PA “would be short and forceful and would include the use of ground and air forces and special means, the elimination and expulsion of senior officials, the destruction of weapons, and the large-scale evacuation of residents and destruction of terror infrastructure inside the cities and in all refugee camps,” Katz said, referencing the Gaza and Lebanon “models”.
Katz’s threat to the PA is not limited to an Israeli retaliation against violent Palestinian attacks on settlers or soldiers. A “war scenario” would also be unleashed if Palestinians organise a popular uprising.
“There will not be an Intifada lasting years, as there was in the past, but rather a short and forceful war with a clear decision and a change in the reality,” he emphasised.
A political consensus on Palestinian subjugation
The upcoming Israeli election is one of the most heated and competitive in the country’s history. But the one thing that unites the Israeli ruling coalition with most opposition parties is the subjugation of Palestinians.
In 2024, the Israeli Knesset saw an unprecedented moment of bipartisanship in rejecting Palestinian statehood and self-determination. In February of that year, 99 Israeli members of Knesset from both the opposition and ruling coalition voted in favour of a resolution rejecting international recognition of Palestinian statehood. Only nine members opposed the resolution, all of whom were from Palestinian parties.
In June, another resolution passed with only the same nine members opposing it. This time, the resolution rejected Palestinian statehood in absolute terms, even if such statehood comes through negotiations and diplomacy.
In this election cycle, Israel’s former prime minister and opposition leader Naftali Bennet is campaigning on calling the Trump plan for Gaza “unworkable” and opposing the plan’s promise of returning the Palestinian Authority to the enclave.
Israel’s former defence minister Avigdor Lieberman is similarly campaigning on dismantling the PA and resuming military operations in Gaza. Israel’s former war minister and likely the next prime minister Gadi Eisenkot attacked the roadmap for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons in return for the Israeli military’s withdrawal and called it a “capitulation” to Trump “without achieving the war’s objectives.”
The 7 October attacks did not create this Israeli mainstream consensus. At most, it provided the cover of war to make it more flagrant and explicit.
Israel’s stated long-term goal in Gaza and the West Bank is the natural culmination of a settler-colonial project that was created on the premise of grabbing the “maximum land with a minimal number of Arabs.”
Palestinians have for decades been pushed by Israel into ever-shrinking confines with two options left to them: submission or departure.
The only substantial debate about this endgame in Israel’s election is about the pace and packaging of that expulsion and subjugation.
Muhammad Shehada is a Palestinian writer and analyst from Gaza and the EU Affairs Manager at Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor
