INTERVIEW - Gaza sports community seeks to revive games after genocide kills 1,000 athletes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:52:04 UTC
20:52:04 KST

Hosni Nadim and Ikram Kouachi
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
- Amputee athletes need prosthetics, rehabilitation and sports equipment to return to competition, says Mustafa Siam
- Sports seen as a tool to help Gaza’s youth recover psychologically and socially after 3 years of genocide, he says
After three years of war that killed more than 1,000 athletes and destroyed hundreds of sports facilities, Gaza’s sporting community is seeking to bring sports back to life.
Mustafa Siam, secretary-general of the Palestinian Sports Media Federation, told Anadolu that the return of sports to Gaza was not just about resuming competitions but also about helping children and young people recover psychologically and socially after three years of genocide.
“Palestinian sports have suffered extensive destruction since October 2023, and statistics show that more than 265 sports facilities have been completely or partially destroyed,” Siam said.
He said 1,014 Palestinian sports figures were killed during the war, including players, referees, coaches and administrators affiliated with the Palestinian Football Association.
Among the best-known figures were international player Suleiman Obeid, who was killed by Israeli gunfire while trying to get food, and Hani al-Masdar, coach of the Olympic team, who was killed in an Israeli strike.
Trying to bring sports back
After the implementation of a ceasefire agreement in October 2025, the Palestinian Football Association held meetings with clubs in Gaza to develop a plan to restore sports activity, Siam said.
Since then, the association has organized four tournaments for senior and youth players, as well as a beach soccer tournament.
Siam said the tournaments’ primary objective was “to restore hope and revive the spirit” among young people and athletes living in difficult circumstances.
“These young people are living in dilapidated displacement camps, and many of them have lost their families, homes, friends or coaches,” he said.
Siam said the tournaments also carried a message to the world that Palestinian youth “have the right to play football and other sports, just like athletes around the world.”
He said the Palestinian Football Association adopted an initiative in May 2024 to establish the Phoenix Cubs center for displaced children in camps. The center currently operates in Gaza City and the central governorate.
“Sports are important for strengthening the psychological and social well-being of children who have lived through difficult circumstances during the years of war,” he said.
He said football could also help preserve and develop young talent, as sports form part of education and social development.
Supporting amputee athletes
Siam said children and young people who lost limbs during the genocide need greater sporting and rehabilitation support, noting that “the number of amputees in Gaza has increased dramatically compared with the pre-war period.”
Before the war, Gaza had amputee football groups and a team, but the number of amputees has risen significantly, including among athletes, he said.
“These players need care and attention, as well as prosthetic limbs and services that can help them practice sports and football,” Siam said.
“Providing prosthetics, rehabilitation services and sports equipment could help establish a team capable of representing Palestine in international competitions.”
“Every one of these players carries a humanitarian message and a painful story they lived through during the genocide,” he said. “It is important to provide the resources necessary to help them return to sport.”
Calls for international action
Siam criticized “the failure of international sports institutions” to take action against Israel over violations affecting Palestinian athletes and sports facilities.
He said the Palestinian Football Association had requested the suspension of Israel’s membership in international sports federations as early as 2013, but no decision had been reached.
He added that campaigns by fans and coaches in Europe had called for measures against Israel.
“International sports institutions should support Palestinian sports and protect Palestinian athletes’ right to compete and represent their country internationally.”
Since October 2023, Israel's war in Gaza has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others, according to Palestinian figures, while also destroying about 90% of the enclave's infrastructure.

Opposition accuses government of borrowing to fund promises in ERR debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:51:00 UTC
20:51:00 KST

Opposition accuses government of borrowing to fund promises in ERR debate
Coalition parties say the budget deficit is being reduced, while the opposition argues that the governing parties are borrowing money to deliver on their promises.
Taking part in the studio debate were Erkki Keldo (Reform Party), Lauri Laats (Center Party), Riina Sikkut (Social Democratic Party), Rain Epler (EKRE), Aivar Kokk (Isamaa) and Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200).
Host Andres Kuusk noted that the Reform Party had promised to reduce the budget deficit by 0.5 percentage points annually, but that this target would not be met in the coming years.
Keldo maintained that the party was nevertheless reducing the deficit. He pointed out that the forecast for next year's deficit had fallen from 4.9 percent in the spring to 4.4 percent in the summer, while the state budget submitted by the government projected a deficit of 4 percent.
Keldo said the improvement had been achieved through continued spending cuts, adding that the government had already made approximately €1.5 billion in additional cuts.
Aivar Kokk of Isamaa accused the government of concealing spending in the budget. He criticized the submission of a second supplementary budget to the Riigikogu, saying the government was bringing expenditures forward from next year, including €28 million for Rail Baltica rails without knowing where they would be used.
Kokk also argued that the Reform Party's income tax exemption was being financed through borrowing, with the government taking on debt both this year and next to fulfill the party's election promise.
Center Party member Lauri Laats described the state budget currently being prepared as a disaster and called for a comprehensive overhaul of Estonia's tax system.
He criticized the country's reliance on consumption taxes, which he said accounted for 40 percent of tax revenue. Laats said the Center Party would reduce consumption taxes, particularly VAT on food.
Social Democrat Riina Sikkut said her party would not engage in political blackmail when deciding whether to support the budget.
However, she stressed that certain expenditures, including funding for specialized care services, were not ideological matters. She cited a Supreme Court ruling stating that shortages of funding or available places did not absolve the state of its responsibility to guarantee people's fundamental rights.
Sikkut said the Social Democrats planned to submit amendments aimed at supporting vulnerable groups and hoped to secure backing from both coalition and opposition parties.
"These are measures to support vulnerable groups, things the government has left out but which we believe are absolutely essential to address next year," she said.
Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200) expressed hope that future governments would continue reducing the budget deficit by 0.5 percentage points annually.
He said maintaining that pace would eventually stabilize the national debt and allow it to begin declining, although the process would take time. Uibo acknowledged that even achieving a 0.5 percentage-point reduction had been difficult and that a substantial deficit could not be eliminated in a single year.
Rain Epler (EKRE) argued that Estonia had a spending problem and that there were areas where further cuts could be made.
He accused the Reform Party of driving up government expenditure, pointing out that the state budget had grown by more than 50 percent over the past five years while gross domestic product (GDP) had increased by just 4 percent.
Sikkut also criticized the government's approach to spending cuts, arguing that it had reduced expenditure only on paper by shifting some costs into future years.
She said the government's room for maneuver had been limited by its decision to abandon a planned income tax increase that was originally intended to finance the elimination of the income tax "hump."
Estonia switched from a gradual basic exemption reduction scheme to a flat €700 exemption for everyone recently, costing the state in excess of €500 million annually.
"They made the numbers work on paper," Sikkut said, adding that the government had instead chosen to finance the tax change through borrowing.
Sikkut also accused the government of failing to comply with domestic budget rules, which require an annual improvement of 0.5 percentage points throughout the state budget strategy period.
Keldo, however, maintained that eliminating the income tax "hump" had been the right decision.
The debate also covered Rail Baltica, potential spending cuts and excise tax increases.

Semitic, semantic, whatever
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:50:58 UTC
20:50:58 KST

Semitic, semantic, whatever
« previous post |
Last Tuesday's post "Pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever" was based on a New York Post headline announcing that "Trump calls reported pneumatic plague outbreak ‘big problem for Russia’". It was implicit in the discussion that the headline writer was ignorant or careless or both.
But yesterday, Bob Ladd pointed out to me that Science magazine committed a similar error in the references to a paper dated 9/25/2026 (Morvai, Boglárka, Kinga G. Tóth, Marianna Boros, Dorottya S. Rácz, Ivaylo Iotchev, Kitti Szabó, and Attila Andics. "Neural evidence that dogs segment the speech they hear with a humanlike consonant bias." Science (2026).
The paper's second reference was to John McCarthy's 1979 PhD thesis, Formal problems in Semitic phonology and morphology — and "Semitic phonology and morphology" is rendered as "semantic phonology and morphology".
Bob's email:
I was going to add a somewhat off-topic comment to your latest post, but I thought you might be interested in this as a separate LLog item.
There's a recent article in Science about how dogs listening to Saffran-style nonsense syllable sequences can pick out recurrent patterns based on detecting regularities in transition probabilities, and that they show the same bias as human subjects do in favour of detecting CONSONANT regularities rather than VOWEL regularities. (I was led to this article by a news story in New Scientist which which kind of garbled the details of the experimental stimuli, so that I went to the original article to figure out what the researchers had actually done.)
The opening sentence of the Science paper begins "Across many languages, consonants are more useful for word identification than vowels…" and goes on to cite work by the likes of Anne Cutler and Jacques Mehler that explored psycholinguistic aspects of this asymmetry. The Science study aimed to see if dogs exhibit the same bias as humans for attending to consonants in speech segmentation, and it reports that they do. Conceivably this would be worth a LLog post for the interest of all those readers who used to annoy Geoff Pullum.
However, what's relevant for "pneumatic, pneumonic, whatever" is that one of the sources for the statement in the paper's opening sentence about consonants and vowels is a reference to John McCarthy's PhD thesis, which is cited as “Formal problems in semantic phonology and morphology.”
The Science paper and its human background deserve a full post, which I hope that Bob will provide for us.
The conceptual gap between that paper and its coverage in the New Scientist should also be mentioned, perhaps with glance at the rest of the (extensive) coverage in popular media (BioTechniques, Neuroscience News, Discover, WaPo, El Pais, Newser, Science Alert, the Times, Earth.com, the Independent, etc. etc.).
There's also the obvious observation that the neuroscience of talking to dogs is one of the most clickbait-y possible current topics, maybe minus only the neurological verification that cats are more aloof, and that some AI agents are developing neurologically optimized vocalizations to steal the loyalty of our pets.

Rubio says US committed to Mediterranean undersea power cable

Rubio says US committed to Mediterranean undersea power cable
ATHENS, Oct 8 - The US supports an EU-backed undersea power cable scheme in the eastern Mediterranean and will use diplomacy to try to remove any possible hurdles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a Greek newspaper.
Greece's power grid operator IPTO is developing the €1.9 billion scheme, which aims to link the European mainland to Cyprus and later Israel, but progress has been slow amid a dispute between Greece and Turkey over the maritime area that will be designated for laying down the cable.
Greece wants to resume seabed surveying to determine the route soon, a move Turkey says would need prior coordination between the two countries as it crosses an area under a 2019 maritime deal with Libya, which Athens has rejected.
Rubio said in the interview with Kathimerini newspaper, published on Thursday, that the US was "very committed" to the project as it promotes energy supply diversification, which he said was necessary due to Russia's war in Ukraine and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz.
"We understand there are some potential impediments, there are some things standing in the way, and we intend to use our diplomatic efforts to remind all parties how important this is to us and why this matters. And I hope to find resolutions," he said.
French investment group Meridiam signed in August an agreement to become the majority shareholder in the project.
Cyprus is the only EU country that has no link to other members' electricity markets, and the cable aims to improve its energy security. REUTERS

Russian Drones That Entered Poland Were Carrying Polish SIM Cards, Investigation Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:48:48 UTC
20:48:48 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Drones That Entered Poland Were Carrying Polish SIM Cards, Investigation Finds
Polish investigators found SIM cards belonging to Polish mobile operators inside some of the Russian Gerbera drones that violated Poland’s airspace during a large-scale Russian strike on Ukraine in September 2025, according to RMF24 on October 8.
The finding emerged after Polish prosecutors completed their investigation into the incident, which saw Russian drones penetrate NATO airspace during the night of September 9-10.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Prosecutors have not disclosed how the Polish SIM cards ended up inside the Russian UAVs, including whether they were stolen, purchased through intermediaries, or obtained illegally through another method. That part of the investigation remains classified.
The presence of local SIM cards is particularly notable because unmanned systems can use cellular connectivity for communications, telemetry, navigation support, or other data functions, depending on how the aircraft is configured.
Polish prosecutors ultimately closed the investigation after failing to identify a specific individual directly responsible for the airspace violation. Investigators nevertheless concluded that Poland’s armed forces acted in accordance with established procedures during the incident and were legally authorized to destroy hostile drones entering the country’s airspace.
The incursion occurred during one of Russia’s largest aerial attacks against Ukraine at the time. Polish forces detected the first airspace violation at around 11:14 pm on September 9, while the final intrusion was recorded at approximately 6:30 am the following morning.
On September 12, Marcin Przydacz, head of the Polish president’s International Policy Bureau, said information available to the presidential office indicated that 21 drones had crossed the Polish border.
Authorities later found wreckage from intercepted or crashed drones across several parts of the country, including the Lublin, Masovian, and Łódź regions. One falling object damaged a residential building, although no deaths or injuries were reported.
Earlier, reports emerged that the Kremlin had been preparing for cross-border attacks since at least July 2025, when Polish SIM cards were discovered inside Russian drones shot down in Ukraine.

Gabriele Moreno Locatelli Remembered in Sarajevo

The Italian Ambassador to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarah Castellani, commemorated Gabriele Moreno Locatelli on the 33rd anniversary of his death. The Italian priest and pacifist, a volunteer with the association “Blessed Are the Peacemakers,” was killed by a sniper on the Vrbanja Bridge on October 3, 1993. “In a world marked by conflict, his legacy as a pacifist remains particularly significant,” said Castellani, offering her thoughts to his family, friends, and the community of Canzo, Locatelli’s hometown. 
The ambassador emphasized how his legacy continues to inspire those who promote reconciliation and interethnic dialogue in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in support of the country’s stability and prospects for European integration, which Italy supports.
                                    
“Gabriele Moreno’s sacrifice is a further reminder to reject all forms of denialism that offend the victims and poison the future,” she concluded. The ceremony was attended by Deputy Mayor Predrag Puharić, citizens, members of the Italian community, military personnel from the EUFOR mission, and representatives of local civil society. Also present were Italian deputies and senators who had arrived in the country as part of the parliamentary assemblies of the OSCE, the Council of Europe, and NATO to monitor last Sunday’s general election.Among the members of the Italian parliamentary delegation, Eugenio Zoffili paid tribute on behalf of the Lombard community, noting that a monument and a street in Canzo are dedicated to Locatelli. “His sacrifice serves as a reminder for our daily work in the service of parliamentary diplomacy, which acts as a tool for dialogue among peoples,” he said. Locatelli was crossing the bridge along with other volunteers to symbolically call on the warring parties to cease hostilities. At that same spot, in April 1992, Suada Dilberović and Olga Sučić—the war’s first two civilian victims—had been killed during a demonstration against the conflict. Shot by a sniper, Locatelli died in the hospital a few hours later.

Fresh day of student protests across France as rally planned in Paris

11:47:38 UTC
20:47:38 KST

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday evening in an effort to ease the crisis, promising the government would share a plan to respond to the situation by the end of October.
France is braced for another day of protests as high school students across the country continue to demonstrate against teacher shortages, poor facilities, and overcrowded classrooms.
Students and unions are taking to the streets once more on Thursday as they say the government is failing to listen to their demands, with a major rally planned in Paris.
Students have blocked access to high schools since late September, setting fire to bins and erecting blockades as part of the movement.
A Euronews journalist on the ground in Paris' 5th arrondissement on Thursday morning reported that the streets were already filled with students, some of whom had been dragging bins into the streets and chanting since 6:30 am.
One student outside the prestigious Lycée Henri-IV told Euronews that they had come to stage a blockade "to show our full support for the suburban secondary schools."
"They were the ones who started this movement and were immediately cracked down on by the police," they said.
Another student from a technological school in the 5th arrondissement said: "For six months we’ve had no teacher, there’s no supply teacher, and we’re sitting our baccalauréat in that subject."
"At school, to be honest, our living conditions aren’t great," they continued, adding: "Personally, I don’t think it’s normal to finish at 5.45 pm – or rather, 6 pm."
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu addressed the nation on Wednesday evening in an effort to ease the crisis, promising the government would share a plan to respond to the situation by the end of October and denying that law enforcement officers had been "instructed to confront secondary school pupils."
"Their role is to protect property, but above all people; to ensure that the law is upheld; and to allow access to schools," he said.
Education Minister Édouard Geffray also announced on Thursday that he would present an "emergency plan" to address teacher absences within the "coming hours or days."
Protests have at times descended into violent clashes with riot police, resulting in a number of serious injuries, including one teenager who lost his hand.
Unions, rights groups, and students have accused officers of using disproportionate force, but French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has defended the response to the protests and said that authorities would "continue to do what we are doing: maintaining order and intervening proportionately whenever violence breaks out."
France has nevertheless moved to temporarily suspend the use of stun grenades in policing the demonstrations.
Anne Savinel-Barras, the president of Amnesty International France, welcomed the decision but said further action was needed.
"Protests should not be battlefields. Stun grenades are designed to shock, disorient, and sow panic, often among dense crowds at demonstrations," she said. "Some can cause permanent hearing loss as well as life-changing mutilations due to the blast and shrapnel."
Thousands of people - the majority minors - have been arrested since the protests began.

The wife of ousted Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro was set to be back in court Thursday, where her lawyers will urge a judge to free her from jail and put her under house arrest because she has heart problems.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been behind bars in New York since early January when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid.

Her lawyers said she had lost 25lbs (11kgs) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn and had been told that she might need heart surgery. They said she also suffered from “lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath” and might have suffered a minor heart attack in July.
Prosecutors opposed the bail request. In a court filing, they wrote that Flores would pose an “extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released. They also said she had been taken from the jail to get treatment at a local hospital, when care was needed.
Donald Trump’s administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a “surgical law enforcement operation”. Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.
Flores is charged with participating in a cocaine importation conspiracy with Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture by US forces in January.
Lawyers for Flores said she was no threat to flee because she is “intent on supporting her husband with her constant presence”.

Ukraine and Romania opened a new crossing point over the Tysa River
Kyiv • UNN
The "Bila Tserkva–Sighetu Marmației" crossing point has opened in Zakarpattia for passenger cars—up to 400 vehicles per day. Trucks and buses will be allowed through later.
A new road border crossing point, "Bila Tserkva – Sighetu Marmației," has opened in Zakarpattia at the border with Romania. At the first stage, it will operate for passenger cars and be able to process up to 400 vehicles per day. This was reported by the Ministry for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine, UNN writes.
Details
To launch traffic from the Ukrainian side, an access road was built and modular infrastructure for border and customs control was installed. On the Romanian side, a border crossing point and a new bridge over the Tysa River were built, connecting the two countries.
"The opening of the new border crossing point is a tangible result of our systematic work to develop the western border. For Zakarpattia, it is an additional route to Romania, while for the entire transport system, it is another opportunity to redistribute flows and reduce the burden on existing border crossing points. It is especially important that we continue developing border infrastructure even during the war. The next stage is to create a fully fledged border crossing point here for trucks and buses," said Mykola Kalashnyk, Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport of Ukraine.
It is noted that this is only the first stage. Development of the border crossing point will continue. Once full construction is completed, up to 400 trucks and 50 buses per day will be able to undergo processing here.

India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:45:17 UTC
20:45:17 KST

India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US have put forward proposals for ceasefires in bid to protect global energy and shipping.
Ukraine says it has received proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States to broker talks with Russia. The offers come as the two adversaries escalate attacks on each other’s energy and port infrastructure with their war now in its fifth year.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha revealed the four proposals at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday and singled out New Delhi’s. “The most comprehensive is India’s proposal,” he said, adding that India had signalled a willingness to play a role for the first time.
None of the proposals aims to end the war. Each seeks a narrower truce, covering energy facilities, ports or commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Here’s what we know:
What is India proposing?
India has not made its plan public. Quoting unnamed sources, however, Indian media have reported it has three parts. According to the Hindustan Times, it would aim to protect infrastructure, keep grain and energy supplies moving through Black Sea ports, and ensure the safety of commercial shipping.
The first part – mutually halting strikes on energy facilities and ports – matches what Kyiv has been demanding. Sybiha said any deal must be a complete energy truce that covers port infrastructure as well.
The second part builds on the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkiye and the United Nations mediated in 2022 but Russia abandoned in 2023.
The third part, protecting merchant ships and their crews, is particularly important to India because Indian sailors have been killed or harmed on Black Sea routes.
The sources were quoted as saying India’s plan goes further than the other three proposals because it covers infrastructure and shipping together. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that it incorporates elements of the Turkish, Egyptian and US initiatives. The Kyiv Post reported that Sybiha also described the plan as addressing a possible ceasefire along the front lines, although other accounts said he gave no specifics.
The proposal likely took shape during Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar’s first visit to Ukraine last month and in a later meeting with Sybiha at the UN General Assembly in New York, also in September. Jaishankar said New Delhi was “trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue”.
What do we know about the Turkish and Egyptian proposals?
Very little. Neither Ankara nor Cairo has published details. Both reportedly focus on keeping Black Sea grain supplies moving by suspending attacks on commercial shipping. Some reports said the two countries proposed a grain truce jointly while others described two separate plans.
Turkiye has done this before. With the UN, it steered the 2022 grain deal, one of the few narrow truces of the war to hold for any length of time. Ankara and the UN are now organising new Black Sea talks with a round planned for October.
Beyond its Black Sea focus, almost nothing is known about Egypt’s proposal. Its interest, however, is clear: Egypt relies on Ukraine for nearly one-third of its grain supplies.
What is the US pitching?
According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Washington has proposed three steps: a mutual halt to energy strikes, a reopening of the grain corridor and a trilateral meeting with Ukraine and Russia, possibly in Abu Dhabi.
The latest effort began in early September when US President Donald Trump’s envoys visited Kyiv and Moscow and secured an agreement in principle for a trilateral meeting. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on September 5 while Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the US twice in September.
The trilateral meeting has since been pushed back. It had been expected to take place in the United Arab Emirates in early October. Washington now wants it in late October, and people close to the talks blamed the delay on Russia.
Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida, in December. “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. The Kremlin said no decision has been made.
At the same time, the US is applying pressure to try to end the war. Trump recently signed a law giving him sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy.
He has also called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian diesel facilities amid a diesel prices crisis in the US, where Trump faces tricky midterm elections next month. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” he said on September 13. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.” This drew much criticism that Trump instead should focus his comments on Russia, which began the war with its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
He is reportedly sceptical about his own government’s latest diplomatic initiative. People familiar with his thinking have told US media that he doubted Putin would agree to an energy truce before winter.
How have Russia and Ukraine responded?
Sybiha said Ukraine would agree to a truce but with conditions. It would accept an energy and Black Sea shipping ceasefire, but only as a combined package, he said.
He added that Kyiv is also open to an unconditional ceasefire along the current front lines. Zelenskyy backs the US-proposed meeting but stressed it needs “not only Ukraine but also the Russian side” to support it.
Moscow has been warm in tone but has committed to nothing. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia would welcome India’s peace efforts while Putin said Modi has “very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions”, but he did not elaborate.
In private, Moscow appears to have said no. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that Russia has rejected India’s proposal although this has not been confirmed publicly. Ukraine’s agriculture minister said Russia had rejected every Black Sea ceasefire option the mediators have presented.
Why are Global South countries becoming more involved?
Food supplies, the lives of their citizens and fuel prices are all at stake.
“I think it’s clear to many countries that this war is not a localised war, but it’s a war that has these global consequences,” Fredrik Wesslau, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told Al Jazeera.
Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of global wheat shipments, and their attacks on each other’s ports helped push wheat futures to a three-year high in August.
Sailors from countries with no links to the war are being killed. At least five Indian seafarers have died in strikes on Black Sea shipping in recent months along with seven Azerbaijani crew members since June. On Saturday, a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged ship in a port in the Odesa region killed a crew member. Ukraine, for its part, has targeted tankers it links to Russia’s shadow fleet since July.
The energy war is also being felt in global markets. Ukraine reported more than 194 drone attacks on Russian refineries this year, hitting all 11 of the largest. Bloomberg News estimated that Russia’s fuel output has fallen by more than 30 percent. With Middle East supply already down as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran, global diesel markets are more exposed to the loss of Russian supplies.
Maximilian Hess, a nonresident senior fellow in the Eurasia Program at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said energy is at least as important as grain in driving the diplomatic efforts. He pointed to a “clear frustration” among many countries over high oil prices, which reflect both the Russia-Ukraine war and the crisis in the Middle East.
“Of course, Ukrainian grain is important for them, but the oil-price factor is important there as well,” he told Al Jazeera. “I think it is those commodity-shock concerns that are pushing them to re-embrace this rhetoric, rather than anything else.”
What are the challenges ahead?
Every previous attempt at diplomacy has failed to end the Russia-Ukraine war. A US-brokered, 30-day energy truce in early 2025 collapsed amid accusations of violations on both sides. At talks in Istanbul in May 2025, Zelenskyy complained that Russia had sent a junior delegation with no authority to sign a ceasefire.
In August 2025, a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska yielded no results despite Trump claiming to be close to a deal ahead of it.
Wesslau said Washington’s efforts have faltered partly because Trump – who had boasted he would end the war within 24 hours of taking office in January 2025 – has appeared unwilling to put real pressure on Moscow. “The Russians see this, and they conclude that they can continue this war,” he said.
Deep distrust remains. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said: “Putin never keeps agreements.”
Moscow’s actions on the ground suggest it is in no hurry, Wesslau said “They’re trying to strangle Ukraine, strangle the economy, and make it unliveable ahead of the winter,” he said. He added that Moscow’s occasionally softer rhetoric was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and “has always proved to be a bluff”.
Russia’s terms are another obstacle. Hess said Moscow’s demands have not softened at any point since it launched the war and at times have grown. Putin has demanded all of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia regions, including territory Russian forces have never controlled, as well as a buffer zone in northern Ukraine. Moscow is also seeking sanctions relief and military concessions for any Black Sea deal.
“I don’t think it’s a question of who actually mediates. I think it’s really a question of the calculation in Moscow,” Wesslau said. “Fundamentally, the problem is that Putin doesn’t want a ceasefire or a peace agreement. He wants to continue the war. He believes that he can win.”
Analysts said only greater economic pressure is likely to change that calculation.
Wesslau said if Europe can close down Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers, “this would be a massive blow to Russia’s war economy.” Hess said the country best placed to shift things quickly is China, rather than the US, by cutting its purchases of Russian oil. However, he added: “I don’t think Beijing is interested in doing so.”
Hess said that unless there is an outside shock, the war “is much more likely to last another four years than another four months”.

====================================================================================================

Security in the Black Sea region: is Bulgaria the weak link in Europe's defense against threats from Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:45:00 UTC
20:45:00 KST

Black Sea security: Is Bulgaria the weak link?
October 8, 2026
Security in the Black Sea, a frontline in Russia's war in Ukraine, is a complex issue for several reasons, but two incidents in recent days have highlighted just how precarious the situation there is.
On October 6, drones struck two cargo ships, the Alfa Watan and the Able, in the Bulgarian exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea.
The Alfa Watan sank, and its crew has not been recovered. Bulgaria conducted a search and rescue operation, which was called off on Wednesday morning.
The crew of the Able, which was damaged, was rescued by a passing Bulgarian ship. Two crew members were taken to the military hospital in Varna.
The day before, another cargo ship, the Royad Mammadov, was struck by a drone and sank off the coast of Romania, killing two crew members.
Multiple recent attacks on ships
These are not isolated incidents. In the past few months, there have been multiple attacks on cargo ships carrying grain from Ukraine.
As a result, doubt is increasingly being cast on the belief that the western part of the Black Sea — the area off the coast of Bulgaria and Romania — is relatively safe.
"Тhe Black Sea front is clearly expanding, and we should no longer look only to the Baltic Sea as a potential avenue for escalation and aggressive actions," said Ruslan Trad, global security expert and non-resident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab.
PM downplays drone attacks
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev downplayed the attack on the ships, remarking that ships are constantly being sunk in the Black Sea and that Tuesday's drone attacks were "probably not the most serious incident."
Bulgaria's government called Tuesday's attack on the two vessels an "absolutely unacceptable violation of international law" but refrained from calling on Russia to end its war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on the other hand, was unequivocal. He said that the Ukrainian military had assured Bulgaria that it was not responsible for the attack and pointed the finger squarely at Russia.
After a meeting of the National Security Council on Wednesday, a declaration was issued, which once again did not name the source of the threat in the Black Sea.
Radev stated that the cargo and the direction of travel of the ships "logically speaking" provide grounds for a hypothesis pointing to Russia but stressed that there is no concrete evidence. He also contradicted Zelenskyy, saying no such conversation had taken place.
Earlier he said that "if the war is not brought to an end in due time, it will continue to expand."
Similarly, Bulgaria's Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said that "we need to support all possible diplomatic efforts to bring this war to an end."
The refusal to state clearly that it is Russian aggression that is putting the region at risk is not new for the Radev administration.
Is Bulgaria a 'weak link' in European defense?
For Rumena Filipova, chairperson of the Institute of Global Analytics, this is an example of how Bulgaria seems to be a weak link in Europe's defense against malicious influence from Russia and China.
"This weakness stems from the lack of a serious institutional response to hybrid attacks of any kind, the absence of appropriate measures and a general tendency to downplay incidents," she told DW.
"The perpetrator is not named explicitly, even though our partners in the European Union and NATO have already issued numerous warnings about what aggressive steps Russia could take against Europe," she said.
According to Filipova, the Bulgarian government's narrative about peace without actually specifying the conditions or consequences for Ukrainian and European security is a demonstration of its leniency toward Moscow and raises the question of Sofia's geopolitical orientation.
No smoking gun
One of the surviving members of the Able's crew has said that he believes it was a Russian strike because the ship was carrying Ukrainian grain.
Trad, the global security expert, says that the crew member's testimony is an eyewitness hypothesis, not hard proof.
"The logic of motive, however, points toward Russia, as it is the state systematically threatening navigation to Ukrainian ports," he told DW, adding, "Until more concrete data is revealed the most accurate phrasing is 'probable but unproven Russian responsibility' without excluding other possibilities."
Trad also pointed out that Bulgarian institutions lack experience in attributing maritime drones in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone (EEZ). "When the system is uncertain, the safest institutional reaction is to say nothing until certainty is achieved," he said. "That is caution, but it is also a political choice."
Economic consequences
A direct military response or the triggering of NATO's Article 5, which guarantees collective defense in the event of an attack on any member state, should not be expected.
Bulgaria's EEZ in the Black Sea is not Bulgarian sovereign territory and, as such, the strikes on the ships in this zone do not constitute a direct attack on Bulgaria — or on Romania in the case of the Royad Mammadov.
Nevertheless, Trad thinks these three incidents shatter the illusion that the western part of the Black Sea is a safe zone because of the distance between it and the frontlines in Ukraine.
"This will increase pressure for tighter maritime monitoring, anti‑mining capabilities, coordination between coastal guard services and intelligence‑sharing among allies," he said.
"The real effect will be a hardening of the shipping regime: stricter routing recommendations, higher insurance premiums and more difficulty hiring crews. Economic repercussions for local businesses can also be anticipated — imagine the impact on fishermen if they have to stay in ports constantly due to fear of further attacks. That is the intended effect of such strikes," he added.
Rumena Filipova believes that although Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey strengthened their Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group at this year's NATO summit in Ankara, this is not enough.
She says there are far more substantial gaps in naval defense capabilities: "Modernization of Bulgaria's naval forces must be improved, much greater coordination — especially with Romania — is required. Yet, for more than a decade, Bulgarian authorities have downplayed or ignored the idea of developing joint naval defense forces and coordination, and that trend continues today," she said.
Turkey's leverage and China's role
Another question is how Turkey will react to recent developments. All three ships were owned by Turkish firms and some of the crew members were Turkish nationals. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday spoke to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the security of navigation in the Black Sea.
Trad notes that Ankara has several levers of influence in the Black Sea: control of the Straits under the Montreux Convention, the largest fleet in the Black Sea and its role as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.
"A realistic scenario is intensified diplomacy, coordination with Bucharest and Sofia, and pressure for safe navigation, probably within the existing trilateral anti‑mining cooperation. If it turns out that Turkish citizens were killed in a deliberate attack, Ankara's stance could become markedly tougher," he said.
Filipova thinks that Black Sea security is already being perceived as a core issue — not only for the region but for NATO as a whole.
In her view, there's not enough coordination between the countries in the region, which means that any response to threats does not come from a united front — something she feels has to change urgently.
Filipova says that China's influence in the region and how it's connected with Russia is another factor.
"We see not only the concrete military threat from Russia but also a subtler threat from China, which is less publicly discussed. But Beijing is trying to acquire strategic assets in ports, thereby gaining influence over both trade and critical infrastructure," she said. "Given that China and Russia cooperate closely, this constitutes a double threat for the Black Sea region."

French police arrest 5 suspects over Renoir museum theft
October 8, 2026
French police have arrested at least five suspects in connection with the theft of two Renoir paintings from a museum in southern France last month, local media reported.
Two burglars cut through a fence and smashed a window to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on September 8. They then used an electric saw to cut through the frame mountings, according to the local mayor.
The thieves initially took four Renoir artworks, valued together at around €9 million ($10.5 million), but dropped two in the museum's garden as they fled from police who had been alerted by the alarm system.
The daily Nice Martin newspaper, which first broke the news of the arrests, said six people were taken into custody, including the two suspected burglars.
Prosecutors in Marseille, who are leading the investigation, declined to comment.
What happened to the artworks?
The two paintings stolen from the museum were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886).
Nice Martin reported that the whereabouts of the artworks was not immediately known.
Founded in 1960, the Renoir Museum is located in the former home and studio of French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir on the Cote d'Azur. The property houses 12 of his artworks and is surrounded by gardens and olive trees.
The heist in Cagnes-sur-Mer was the latest in a series of museum robberies, including the daylight theft of the French crown jewels from the Louvre Museum in Paris last year.
Four suspects have been arrested over that case, but the jewels they are accused of taking, with a value of around $100 million, have not been recovered.

Assistant US Attorney Amanda Elbogen told the court that Zhang received NT$6.05 million from an “unregistered cryptocurrency exchange” business, with the money deposited into a Chinese bank account. Prosecutors also said she has hundreds of thousands of US dollars in additional funds in China that she could access.
Zhang, who lives in Orange County, California, is accused of traveling to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese government officials to surveil Lai Ting-yu (賴廷與), the president’s eldest son, and his family. The FBI arrested her Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport and charged her with acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government in the US.
Prosecutors told the court that one of Zhang’s brothers had previously worked for the Chinese government, while her parents and siblings currently live in China, CBS reported. Investigators also found that Zhang owns a business in China and that her Chinese bank accounts regularly receive deposits.
Elbogen also confirmed that Zhang has a Chinese passport that investigators have not located. FBI agents did not find the passport during a search of her California residence.
Zhang is a naturalized US citizen, while China’s Nationality Law does not recognize dual nationality. Under Article 9, a Chinese national who settles abroad and voluntarily acquires foreign nationality automatically loses Chinese nationality.
Prosecutors argued that Zhang’s family and financial ties to China created a flight risk if she were released, according to CBS. Kim ultimately sided with prosecutors and ordered Zhang to remain in federal custody.
Presidential Office Spokesperson Karen Kuo (郭雅慧) on Monday said the alleged surveillance was a typical case of transnational repression.
“We strongly condemn such barbaric acts that disregard human rights and the sovereignty of countries, suppress and threaten people who advocate for freedom and democracy, and even harm them or their family members,” Kuo said.

Taiwan insurance coverage cuts severe vision-loss risk to 19.6%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:43:48 UTC
20:43:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Doctors said at a press conference Wednesday that expanded national health insurance coverage for intraocular injections has helped cut the rate of severe vision deterioration among macular degeneration patients from 41.4% to 19.6%, CNA reported.
Macular degeneration has two main forms. The dry form accounts for about 85% of cases and involves the deterioration of light-sensitive cells in the macula. The wet form accounts for about 15% and involves fragile, abnormal blood vessels that can leak or bleed, potentially causing rapid and severe vision loss.
Taiwan Retina Society and Taiwan Association of Professors of Ophthalmology Chair Chen Jiann-torng (陳建同) said vision lost after the optimal treatment window may be difficult to recover. Taipei Veterans General Hospital physician Weng Chang-chi (翁章旂) said the condition may initially develop in one eye and be difficult to notice because people use both eyes to see.
Weng said injections can suppress abnormal blood vessel growth and leakage. Before 2020, national health insurance covered up to seven injections per eye. Coverage was then expanded to 14 injections, with eight available upon initial approval, cutting the treatment discontinuation rate from 45% to 23% and the rate of severe vision deterioration from 41.4% to 19.6%, he said.
Love Eye Association Chair Wu Chien-liang (吳建良) said patients often stop treatment entirely when they feel better or because they fear the injections. It is a serious condition that requires long-term monitoring, he said.

At least 10 people were killed and 45 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 8.
In Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed and six others injured, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Two of those people died in Zelenye. In Sloviansk, one person died and three were injured, while a high-rise building, an administrative building, a shop, a service station, a gas station, a car, and a bus were damaged. In Veselia Hora, Novodonetska community, one person died, and a private house was damaged. One person was injured in Zolote Prudy, and a private house, a car, and a truck were damaged. In Druzhkivka, a person was injured.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of which were jet-powered overnight on Oct. 8, Ukraine's Air Force said. The Air Force said it shot down or suppressed 126 drones.
In Ukraine's capital city Kyiv, four people were killed and 21 others injured, including four children, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said.
In Solomianskyi district, a UAV fell on the roof of a five-story residential building, causing a fire, while elsewhere in the district falling debris injured one person. In Desnianskyi district, falling drone debris also caused a fire in a 12-story residential building.

In Kharkiv Oblast, three people were injured overnight, said regional governor Oleh Syniehubov. In the city of Kharkiv, a 67-year-old woman was injured, while a 62-year-old man was injured in the city of Dergachi, and a 70-year-old woman was injured in the village of Dobrenka.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks injured five people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russian forces also struck critical and social infrastructure, residential areas, in particular, a high-rise building and four private houses, as well as private cars.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, three people were injured by Russian attacks over the last day, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said. He said he knew of 84 reports of damage to housing, cars, and infrastructure in the oblast.
In Odesa Oblast, the Russian attack damaged the territory of a parking lot, damaging several cars, and an animal shelter, killing one of the animals inside, regional governor Oleh Kiper said. Damage to civilian enterprise, settlements, and a bus were also reported in Dnipropetrovsk and Rivne oblasts.

Türkiye's METU plans to send homegrown lunar rover to Moon in 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:42:46 UTC
20:42:46 KST

Türkiye’s Middle East Technical University (METU) is planning to launch the homegrown lunar micro-rover ‘Cheri’ to the Moon in 2030, the rector told Anadolu.
Ahmet Yozgatligil, speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) held in the southwestern province of Antalya, stated that the prototype of the rover has been completed and the craft is undergoing testing.
The Cheri project includes two autonomous vehicles powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and developed in collaboration with the China National Space Administration (CNSA).
The twin rovers were designed to operate in extreme cold and with limited sunlight at the lunar south pole, running simultaneously to conduct topographic studies and analyse rock samples via remote sensing.
“Our two Cheri rovers will work together and even take a ‘selfie’ of the mission, while carrying out mapping activities at the sites they discover, which we’re very excited about,” he said.
The prototype of the Cheri micro-rover was presented to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan by the head of the Higher Education Council (YOK), Erol Ozvar, during the opening ceremony of the national academic year.
“Over 120 of our students are working on this project alongside faculty members, while as a part of the EU’s ‘Go Space’ programme, our students are also focused on developing communications protocols for satellites in space, stations to be established on the lunar surface, and orbital stations,” he said.
Yozgatligil noted that the faculty is also contributing to the space sector through initiatives like the Aselabs Programme in collaboration with the defence firm Aselsan.
He mentioned that METU recently joined the microgravity research collaboration established between leading European and US universities, after signing a deal with Axiom Space.
“The most important international project we’re carrying out is the METU Space Technology Park, which will be a hub for space sector research and commercialisation activities,” he added.
The premier aerospace event IAC 2026 kicked off on Monday and will run until Friday. It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and SAHA Istanbul defence cluster and organised by the Industry and Technology Ministry.

Black Sea countries on alert after deadly vessel attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:40:40 UTC
20:40:40 KST

Bulgarian authorities take an injured crew member to a hospital after two commercial vessels were attacked in the NATO member's Black Sea economic zone on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, Varna, in what was the first such attack on shipping in the area. (AP File Photo)
Countries bordering the Black Sea have stepped up security measures following a series of deadly attacks on commercial vessels this week, with Bulgaria announcing plans to hold urgent consultations with Türkiye and Romania on steps to ensure the safety of navigation.
Bulgaria’s President Iliana Iotova said on Oct. 7 that Sofia would propose urgent consultations with Türkiye and Romania aimed at taking joint measures to prevent further attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea and safeguard freedom of navigation.
The announcement came after an extraordinary meeting convened in Sofia to discuss maritime security in the Black Sea.
Iotova also proposed that Bulgaria launch a diplomatic initiative involving all six Black Sea littoral states — Bulgaria, Türkiye, Romania, Ukraine, Russia and Georgia — with a view to reaching agreement on a moratorium aimed at halting hostilities in the Black Sea.
The initiative seeks to turn the Black Sea into a “common security area,” according to proposals outlined following the meeting.
Bulgaria will also push for the establishment of a framework mechanism under the European Union’s Black Sea strategy to ensure free and secure maritime traffic in the region.
Sofia is additionally expected to call for increased NATO air and maritime surveillance capabilities in the Black Sea, stronger coastal defenses and the deployment of additional anti-drone systems.
It also wants allies to step up their contribution to Black Sea security under NATO’s “Eastern Sentry” activities.
Iotova said, however, that launching special consultations under Article 4 of the NATO treaty was considered “unproductive” at this stage, as it would not provide any additional measures.
The latest diplomatic push came after drones struck two commercial vessels in the Black Sea early on Oct. 6, marking the latest fallout from the Russia-Ukraine war to hit civilian shipping in the region.
One of the vessels caught fire, while the other sank. Eighteen Turkish and Indian crew members were rescued from the vessel that caught fire, while crew members aboard the sunken ship remain missing.
The attack took place within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone and was described by Bulgarian authorities as a serious breach of maritime law and the rules governing navigation. Both vessels were Turkish-owned.
Neighboring Romania also reported on Oct. 5 that a grain carrier had caught fire and subsequently sank in the Black Sea.
Ukraine blamed Russia for the attack on the Turkish-owned ship. The vessel’s Azerbaijani captain was killed, while another Azerbaijani crew member remains missing.
Following the attacks, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Russian President Vladimir Putin held a phone call on Oct. 7, during which Erdoğan stressed the importance of efforts to ensure navigational safety in the Black Sea.
More than 200 civilian and commercial vessels have come under attack in the Black Sea since the start of the Russia-Ukraine war in February 2022, with the vast majority of the incidents occurring this year, according to the Turkish Chamber of Shipping (IMEAK DTO).

SOS meals – the food to cook for friends that shows you care
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:40:18 UTC
20:40:18 KST

I lost my beloved cairn terrier Wilf a couple of weeks ago, and when I say lost, sadly, I don’t mean I mislaid him yet again on Hampstead Heath. Rather, after 13 and a half years of (mostly) civil disobedience, we had to make the tough but ultimately kind decision to say a final goodbye. Since then, I have been bombarded with kindness. Friends and family have rallied round to take me out for breakfast, lunch, dinner and coffee, clearly worried that the bereavement might affect my appetite – well, apart from the one who responded by having a baby a week early, and who now requires me to provide for her.
It got me thinking about the part food plays in big life events. We so often cook, or otherwise provide for people in the aftermath of such shocks, be they happy or sad, as a way both to offer practical help and to show them how much we love them. Such tokens of affection tend to fall into two camps. The first is high-energy food that can be easily eaten with one hand while the other is holding a baby or clutching a sodden handkerchief, or simply when you’re just too busy to sit down. Just this morning, I received a picture of the new mother tucking into my extremely wholesome fruit and nut-packed granola with her daughter sleeping on her arm, but Melissa Hemsley’s five-ingredient flapjacks (pictured top) would fall into this category, as would Meera Sodha’s chaat masala popcorn and Thomasina Miers’ dark chocolate and toasted walnut banana bread. Like Anna Jones’s chocolate chip cookie power bites, Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall’s spiced nuts or my own kale chips, they’re full of good things, and tempting enough to compete with the less nutritious options that are so easy to reach for instead. (That said, no one should judge anyone for the choices they make at times of stress.)
The second consists of home-cooked meals that you hope will make them feel looked after, even when you can’t be there to do it yourself. I’ve already promised to make a batch of my massaman curry for the new parents by special request, because I usually fall back on either my ragù alla bolognese (vegan version here), or chicken cacciatore. Bundle the clearly labelled plastic containers with a big bag of nice pasta, too, as well as a block of hard cheese, perhaps, and I figure the recipients are never more than 10 minutes from a good dinner – though, in this case, I’ll splash out on microwaveable sachets of rice instead. Go for a pie, however, and they don’t even have to cook any carbs to go with it. At this time of year, Nigel Slater’s cauliflower cheese number would be delicious, as would Calum Franklin’s keema-spiced shepherd’s pie or Jeremy Lee’s classic chicken version. Thomasina’s ricotta, courgette and spinach dumplings, meanwhile, come with their own tomato sauce, and freeze brilliantly, as would Blanche Vaughan’s Lancashire hotpot.
And, if in doubt, take round a roll or two of Tamal Ray’s freezer cookie dough, so they’re always prepared for last-minute guests or late-night sugar crashes. After the past fortnight, I can confirm there’s very little to match the comfort of a nice cup of tea and a biscuit.
My week in food
On the subject of tea … | I found myself dogless but hungry in Henley-on-Thames on Saturday evening, after talking with wine writer Olly Smith about our respective culinary-themed novels at the town’s literary festival (which runs until Sunday). Happy chance led me to Bijan’s Kitchen, a Persian restaurant that served the most delicious and enormous lamb kebabs on naan, as well as thick, garlicky yoghurt with cucumber and mint, and olives covered in a rich paste of walnuts, pomegranate molasses and garlic, plus a lovely Iranian black tea perfumed with rose petals. Best of all (for me), it’s also dog-friendly – Wilf would have loved it.
Apple turnover | A reminder, should you need it, that although the weather (at the time of writing) feels more like summer, British apple season begins to wind down towards the end of October, so if you value the more unusual varieties rarely found in supermarkets (I got some lovely Charles Ross and Blenheim Orange fruits on Sunday), now is a good time to stock up at the farmers’ market, farm shop or pick-your-own orchard. Dry the apples well, if necessary, and store them, preferably in a single layer, in a slatted crate, cardboard tray or on open shelves (air flow is vital) and keep them somewhere cool, dry and dark, where they should keep until Christmas. So long as you don’t eat them all first.
Not worth dying for | The start of Celebrity Traitors has proved a welcome distraction for me – and, as usual, I found myself most interested in what the cast is actually eating during the dramatic daily breakfasts in the castle, and what they’re awkwardly picking at from the buffet later in the day. This article sheds a little light on the on-set catering, and confirms that I would be a terrible contestant: there’s only so long I could put up with dry croissants and rationed wine before I confessed all just to get out of there.
Fishy business | As a devotee of the much-maligned kipper (a cold-smoked herring), I was delighted to discover that Waitrose now does a hot-smoked version in place of the Scottish mackerel it’s removed from shelves in response to warnings of imminent population collapse in the north-east Atlantic Ocean. Herring numbers, which suffered from similar problems in the 1970s thanks to over-fishing, are now more robust in the North Sea – though check it’s been responsibly sourced, because numbers have dwindled farther west. Anything you can do with smoked mackerel, you can do with herring, from flaking it into potato salads to whizzing it into paté. Just ask any of our northern European neighbours.

How a multibillion-dollar oilfield has ignited UK-Argentina feud over the Falklands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

How an oil project reignited UK-Argentina Falklands dispute
October 8, 2026
Home to fewer than 4,000 people and located in an isolated corner of the South Atlantic Ocean, the Falkland Islands don't often feature in global business headlines.
However, a UK-Israeli oil exploration project in the North Falkland Basin is stoking long-running tensions between Argentina and the people of the archipelago.
Argentina has laid claim to the islands, which it calls Las Malvinas, for two centuries. In 1982, the dispute over the islands' sovereignty led to a war between the UK and Argentina, though British control was quickly restored after Argentine forces invaded the islands.
A 2013 sovereignty referendum on the islands returned a 99.8% vote in favor of remaining tied to the UK as a self-governing British Overseas Territory.
The Sea Lion oilfield project has brought the issue back to the surface. Last month, Argentine President Javier Milei threatened to launch an international legal challenge against the UK unless the project was stopped within two weeks.
The oil project is being run by Israeli company Navitas Petroleum and the UK's Rockhopper Exploration and has the full support of the Falkand Islands Legislative Assembly, which has pursued the project since 2010. The companies plan to begin extracting oil from the Sea Lion oilfield by early 2028.
Milei says the project is "the illegal plundering of our resources" and that he will take the matter to the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea, an independent judicial body responsible for the application of the United Nations' Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Rally around the flag?
Stacy Bragger, a member of the Falklands Islands' 12-member assembly, told DW that the dispute was "nothing new" and that Argentina is using the oil project as "a vehicle to pursue their sovereignty claim."
He thinks Milei may be stepping up rhetoric ahead of the 2027 elections in Argentina.
"When there's elections coming up, the Falklands is a very convenient tool to use in order to rally people together and distract them from domestic problems," he said.
Henry Ziemer, an analyst with the Americas program at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington, says the Falklands is "a perennial sore spot in Argentine politics" and that since the 1980s, various governments have raised the issue in an attempt to rally support and to "stoke the fires of nationalism."
Howerver, he thinks Milei's intervention is noteworthy given that he had previously been open to better relations with the UK on the issue. He agrees that it may be a strategy to "boost approval ratings at a time when the government is under a lot of strong domestic pressure."
Potentially transformative for the Falklands
Even if Milei sees political gain in the issue, the possibility of the Sea Lion project being successful would significantly raise the economic stakes for all concerned.
The project has a budget of $1.8 billion (€1.6 billion) and could generate revenues of more than double that for the Falkland Islands. The companies hope that at its peak, the field will produce up to 50,000 barrels per day and could last for up to 35 years.
That would substantially increase the Falklands' current annual GDP, which is almost entirely dependent on the volatile fishing sector and tourism. The administration is even looking into the possibility of creating a sovereign wealth fund if the oil project is successful.
"It's a very significant project for us with a lot of potential for our future," said Bragger. "It's been a big effort to get to this point and assuming all goes to plan, we want to retain as much value as possible."
However, beyond playing to domestic politics, Milei may also spy an opportunity for Argentina to position itself as an energy player amid the war in Iran and the troubles in the Strait of Hormuz.
Argentina's own domestic oil sector is growing, with production surging at Patagonia's Vaca Muerta, one of the world's largest shale developments. Were Milei's legal efforts to prove successful, there may be further gains.
"When natural resources overlay existing territorial disputes and bad blood, that tends to galvanize a lot of conflict," said Ziemer.
However, Bragger counters that Milei and Argentina have no legitimate claim to either the Falklands or whatever oil wealth may be extracted over the coming years.
"They don't respect our right to self-determination," he added. "They don't respect our right to develop our own resources. They just want to colonize us."
More economic pressure from Argentina
Milei plans to put pressure on the Falklands by stepping up existing economic sanctions. Andrea Clausen, chief executive of the Falklands since 2025, recently described this campaign as "economic warfare."
Many international suppliers and shipping companies already refuse to supply the Falklands for fear of angering Argentina. Now, Milei's government has initiated sanctions against 60 people involved in the Sea Lion project.
In a televised address last month, the Argentine president also vowed to sanction the companies involved in the project. Such a move could cast doubt on the project, which previously collapsed in 2014 and 2020, due to financing troubles, oil-price weakness and delays caused by sanctions.
Navitas this week confirmed that two contractors had pulled out of the project due to sanctions concerns, and that it was replacing them. There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."
Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.
While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.
"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.
Edited by: Tim Rooks

Gallery: A portrait painting of President Alar Karis unveiled at Kadriorg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:40:00 UTC
20:40:00 KST

Gallery: A portrait painting of President Alar Karis unveiled at Kadriorg
On Thursday, a portrait painting of President Alar Karis was presented at the Office of the President, created by painter Tõnis Saadoja at Karis's request.
The portrait gallery of heads of state located in the President's Office in Kadriorg carries forward the continuity of Estonian statehood. The tradition of shaping the gallery began during President Lennart Meri's term in the 1990s, when portraits of earlier Estonian heads of state starting from 1918 began to be gathered in Kadriorg, including heads of state who fulfilled presidential duties in exile during the occupation period. The portraits of earlier heads of state were created by Tiit Pääsuke, Miljard Kilk, Nikolai Guli and Olev Subbi.
Of the presidents of re‑independent Estonia, Lennart Meri's portrait was painted by Jüri Arrak, Arnold Rüütel's portrait by Valli Lember‑Bogatkina, Toomas Hendrik Ilves's portrait by Kaido Ole, and Kersti Kaljulaid's portrait by Alice Kask.
Each head of state has chosen their own artist; the artists have been able to create their own approach and choose their aesthetics. Thus the gallery reflects, in addition to Estonia's political history, the different styles of Estonian portrait art and artists.
--
Editor: Mari Peegel, Argo Ideon

There are also concerns that Milei could try to garner international support in favor of his position, with US President Donald Trump recently suggesting that US support for the status quo on the islands was "under review."
Bragger played this down, pointing to recent comments from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirming support for the Falklands. Ziemer said it would be "very shocking" if the US came down on the side of Argentina.
While uncertainty reigns over whether the oil project ultimately gets going or not, there is little expectation that the dispute could lead to a return of armed conflict like in 1982.
"That's a step too far, and the situation would have to dramatically deteriorate before we would see the potential for military conflict," said Ziemer.

Only 1 in 3 EU counter-drone programs expected to deliver by 2030: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:39:32 UTC
20:39:32 KST

Melike Pala
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Only around one-third of European Union counter-drone and very short-range air defense programs are expected to be delivered by 2030, despite a sixfold increase in investment between 2024 and 2025, according to a confidential European Defence Agency (EDA) report obtained by Euronews on Thursday.
The 2026 annual defense readiness report, which assesses EU member states’ military capabilities, highlights persistent gaps in Europe’s ability to counter the growing threat posed by unmanned systems.
“Investment in counter-drone and very short-range air defence capabilities grew sixfold between 2024 and 2025 in response to the growing threat posed by unmanned systems, although only around one third of programmes are expected to deliver by 2030,” the report said.
The document was shared with European governments last week.
The report comes as countries along the EU’s eastern flank, stretching from the Baltic region to the Black Sea, face growing concerns over drone threats, including drone-related incidents.
EU countries are expected to invest €18.9 billion ($21.1 billion) in drone technologies between 2024 and 2029, according to the report.
“Despite the high level of attention paid to the acquisition of drone and counter-drone capabilities, significant capability gaps and external dependencies continue to affect overall European readiness,” it said.
The EDA also identified significant shortcomings, including fragmented procurement at the national level, limited interoperability, insufficient capacity for experimentation and inadequate industrial surge capacity, particularly for weaponized drones.
The report said addressing these gaps would require relatively modest investment compared with other defense capabilities but would depend on sustained funding and a more agile and integrated approach.
According to the report, the sector could expand by as much as 140% by next year if supported by an appropriate investment framework.
It warned that the rapid pace of technological development is creating a growing risk that military systems could become outdated before they are deployed.

Reported by
The U.S. State Department announced Thursday it had designated for “significant corruption” Zhao Fugang, a Chinese Communist Party-backed businessman in Fiji that OCCRP has previously revealed to be a top organized crime target of Australian law enforcement.
Zhao, a China-born Fiji citizen, is a leading member of the Pacific island country’s Chinese business community and heads the Overseas Chinese Service Center in the capital, Suva. OCCRP and Australia’s Nine media have previously reported that Australia placed the businessman on its top tier list of criminal targets in 2023 on suspicion that he is a senior member in a syndicate involved in drug smuggling, money laundering, and human trafficking.
Zhao has not been charged with a crime and no evidence has been publicly presented against him. He denies any wrongdoing.
The State Department said in a statement that Zhao had “abused his public position by paying bribes to Fijian citizens to advance China-based government, business and criminal interests.” The designation restricts Zhao or his family members from entering the U.S.
The State Department did not provide further details on who Zhao is suspected of bribing. OCCRP has previously reported that Zhao has enjoyed public ties to senior Fijian government and law enforcement officials.
“Mr. Zhao denies the allegations, he was never given a chance to respond to the allegations,” Zhao’s lawyer, Nikheel Nambiar, told OCCRP.
“The allegations are unsubstantiated without any supporting evidence,” Nambiar said.
In a post on Facebook, the U.S. Embassy in Suva described Zhao’s purported actions as part of a pattern of “systemic geocriminality” in which Beijing uses organized crime figures as proxies to pursue its interests in the Pacific, a vast and strategically important region.
OCCRP has previously reported on other instances in which questionable businesspeople and organized crime figures have helped to push Beijing’s interests in Pacific island nations.
The Fiji police and prime minister’s office did not respond to requests for comment.

Estonia's national e-calculation contest draws 10,700 participants
Unknown

2026-10-08

20:38:00 KST

Estonia's national e-calculation contest draws 10,700 participants
A total of 10,739 people took part in the third nationwide online math challenge during its first three hours. Of those, 375 answered all the questions correctly, more than in previous years.
Getter Põru won the €1,234 grand prize provided by SEB Bank. The grand prize was drawn from among all participants who answered every question correctly. Participants had to solve one problem for each school grade, for a total of 12 problems, prepared by Hele Kiisel, Helen Kaasik and Kristel Tamm of the Estonian Mathematical Society's school mathematics association.
Taking into account the time spent solving the problems, this year's rankings by category were as follows:
Upper secondary school students:
- Jasper Vähk
- Mattias Mahlakas
- Egert Pähkel
Basic school students:
- Karl Miko Põdra
- Märt Mattias Alas
- Mia Väinsar
University students:
- Romet Martjan
- Getlin Juhe
- Sergei Baumer
Teachers, lecturers and researchers:
- Rainer Bõkov
- Mikk Põdra
- Ekke-Markus Muttika
General participants:
- Hendrik Nigul
- Mihkel Kree
- Hannes Valk
The top upper secondary school student will be able to enroll in a bachelor's degree program of their choice at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech), with the exception of architecture, while the top adult participant in the general category will have the opportunity to enroll in a TalTech microdegree program of their choice.
Participants could also take part in the math challenge together with family members, classmates, teammates or colleagues. A total of 378 groups registered. The largest was from Nõo Sciences High School, with 220 participants.
"The success of the third online math challenge shows that interest in mathematics is strong in Estonia. We are on the right track, but we need to see improvements in math skills more quickly. Large cohorts of upper secondary school graduates are currently entering universities, but considerably smaller age groups lie ahead. This makes it all the more important that we help every young person develop their abilities," said TalTech Rector Tiit Land, who completed the challenge at Võru High School.
The online math challenge is organized by Tallinn University of Technology, ERR and SEB Bank. All of this year's math challenge problems will remain available to solve until next year's competition.
