UK Jerusalem consulate prepares for Israeli closure deadline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:37:27 UTC
20:37:27 KST

Breadcrumb
UK removes plaques, signs from consulate in East Jerusalem, as Israeli deadline for closure looms
Staff at the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem removed signs and plaques from the exterior of the building late on Wednesday, as a 30-day deadline from Israel to shutter the premises inched closer, with advocacy groups warning that Palestinians will be harmed as a result.
Local media reported that workers were seen removing a sign that read “British Consulate General” from the building. A statement from UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband on Thursday said that the consulate would continue providing services and would be known from now on as the "UK Mission".
“This response from the Israeli state is not surprising. It is emblematic of an increasingly shrill reaction by Israeli leadership to any international effort to comply with international law,” Zena Agha, director of the British Palestinian Committee, told The New Arab.
“The purpose is to punish Palestinians who rely on the UK Consulate in East Jerusalem. It’s a way of saying to the UK Government ‘sanctioning us will end up harming Palestinians’ - which only provides further evidence of the injustice and violence of the Israeli occupation which controls much of Palestinian daily life,” Agha continued.
Israel last month ordered the UK to close its consulate within a 30-day period, and remove its diplomats from Jerusalem, in response to the UK announcing sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and a trade ban on goods from settlements.
The latest move has signalled what appears to be a deterioration in relations between the UK and Israel.
The UK has attempted to keep the consulate open through various efforts, including sending the British national security advisor to Israel last week for talks; however, the Israeli government has not changed its course.
The set closure of the consulate, which is in the Palestinian neighbourhood of Sheikh Jarrah, will not affect the British Embassy in Tel Aviv, which manages diplomatic relations between Britain and Israel.
The closure would affect around 30 British diplomats and their family members.
The statement from Ed Miliband on Thursday appeared to hit back at the Israeli decision.
“We have been clear that we do not accept that the Government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years. The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory,” the statement reads.
“Following discussions with the Government of Israel, our Consulate General building will not be closing, and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from today. The UK Mission, Jerusalem is independent, operational, and will continue to deliver vital services and our work with Palestinian people,” the statement added.
We retain our long-standing presence in Jerusalem. My statement: https://t.co/ABnaopUBwU
— Ed Miliband (@Ed_Miliband) October 8, 2026
Miliband noted that the UK had temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and their families for their safety and security, adding that in the coming months it will work to build up its presence again.
Earlier this week, a spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office told The New Arab, "We will not go into detail on live discussions about the future of the British Consulate General in Jerusalem. The protection and wellbeing of our staff is our priority."
While the attempted closure of the consulate is illegal under international law, the UK has limited legal options to fight the Israeli decision.

JFCA study reveals how Hamas hid its October 7 invasion plans from Israeli intelligence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:36:59 UTC
20:36:59 KST

Hamas’s leadership planned to use strategic deception to lull Israel into a false sense of security before the October 7 attacks, activating double agents as late as the eve of the invasion to feed the Shin Bet (Israel Security Service) false information, as revealed in a new study by Lt.-Col. (res.) Yehonatan Duhoch-Halevi published on Wednesday by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
A core part of Hamas’s strategy was conceived in early 2022 and sought to create the impression that Israel’s “carrot and stick” policy, which combined threats to assassinate senior Hamas leaders with economic relief for Gaza, was working, according to the research.
Through the evening of October 6, Israeli intelligence was fed the impression that conditions in Gaza were routine, thus allowing Hamas to conceal its plans while arming and concentrating its forces, according to a senior figure in Hamas’s military wing.
According to the terrorist’s testimony, Hamas identified an Israeli espionage network in 2017 and was able to recruit some members of the network to become double agents operating under Hamas’s direction.
The IDF investigation into the failures leading up to the massacre noted that, on October 6, indications of a Hamas attack were received alongside reassuring signs, although the investigation did not explain what those reassuring signs were. The Shin Bet investigation reported that “human intelligence sources,” or intelligence agents, had confirmed that the terror group was operating routinely.
Hamas officials have since acknowledged the use of deception as part of the preparations for the attack. In a late 2023 interview with Ammar Taqi, senior Hamas official Khaled Mashal admitted that, ahead of October 7, Hamas carried out strategic and tactical deception, including conveying "reassurance" messages.
“Regarding the aspect of strategic deception and the method of deception, as I mentioned, there was a general feeling that [Gaza] [under Hamas leadership] was focusing on its affairs, and wanted to bring in a certain amount of fuel, electricity and aid, meaning [Gaza] was licking its wounds and pains because of the blockade imposed on it, and after the 21 war [Hamas] did not respond to the escalation [in actions] carried out by the occupation in al-Quds and Al-Aqsa,” Mashal said.
“For example, as I mentioned, during the previous Ramadan, in this year 2023, on days 13 or 14 in the middle of Ramadan, they [the Israelis] broke into Al-Aqsa, and the public [wondered] where was Gaza? The enemy began to analyze and thought that Gaza was occupied with itself. The holidays came from September 15 to October 6 [2023], and then, behold, the movement's leadership wisely sent deception messages to the enemy once again. We know some of them.”
Hamas inspired by Egypt's deception during Yom Kippur War
“The [Jewish] holidays came from September 15 to October 6 [2023], and then, behold, the movement’s leadership wisely sent deception messages to the enemy once again. We know some of them.”
Mashal also admitted that he took inspiration from Egypt’s strategy during the Yom Kippur War, when Egypt attacked Israel on a religious holiday and shared that Cairo had told soldiers to go on a religious pilgrimage to Mecca to lull Jerusalem into believing that no war was coming.
“A message, in order to fulfill its purpose, must be an indirect message, meaning messages that will not be understood [by the enemy] to be deception messages, which the enemy will swallow. The enemy also uses deception against others, and the resistance succeeded in deceiving the enemy, and it picked up false messages,” Mashal said at the time. “After that, there was concealment, meaning avoiding exposing the preparations: Of course, the tunnels...”
The JCFA study noted that Hamas-affiliated political commentator Issam Shawar said that Hamas had been taken by surprise by a similar strategy a few months earlier when Israel began Operation Shield and Arrow against Palestinian Islamic Jihad (PIJ) in May 2023. According to Shawar, one day before the launch of the operation, Israel carried out a deception operation by informing Hamas that it would allow the transfer of the financial grant from Qatar to pay the salaries of public-sector employees.
The use of deception by Hamas was also noted by Palestinian journalists immediately after the October 7 attack. On October 8, 2023, JCFA noted that Palestinian journalists had commented on Hamas’s use of deception tactics.
Fadi Ramadan noted that Hamas had carried out two separate deception operations.
The first created a false impression in Israel that the planned attack would come through the tunnels, whereas Hamas launched a ground invasion.
The second involved conveying to Israel that the “carrot and stick” policy had been effective.
JCFA also suggested that former Palestinian Authority (PA) minister for prisoner affairs Sufian Abu Zayda had been deceived by Hamas’s plans.
Explaining that the terror group had a channel of contact with Israel through Zayda, JCFA said that the former PA official was enlisted to negotiate a deal with Israel to release Palestinian prisoners for the bodies of Israelis already held in Hamas captivity before October 7.
Zayda had reportedly met with Ghazi Hamad in Gaza, who confirmed that now-assassinated Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had authorized the deal. After his return to Israel, Zayda contacted a retired Shin Bet officer who arranged a meeting between him and active Shin Bet personnel in Ashkelon.
In July 2022, Zayda met with Sinwar in Gaza, in the presence of Rawhi Mushtaha, where Sinwar presented his priorities regarding a possible agreement with Israel concerning the release of prisoners.
Sinwar-Zaida meeting led to increased Israeli interest in deal with Hamas
According to Duhoch-Halevi’s assessment, the meeting between Sinwar and Zayda strengthened Israel’s interest in a deal, and Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar personally met with Zayda to hear from him the conditions set by Hamas for a possible deal.
Zayda claimed Bar asked him to convey a message to Sinwar that Israel would be willing to advance far-reaching economic measures in Gaza.
The negotiations between the sides advanced to the stage of deliberations over the names of the prisoners to be released as part of the deal, and drafts were exchanged between the sides.
On September 14, 2023, two days after Hamas conducted its major annual military exercise, Zayda met with Sinwar, again in the presence of Mushtaha, and Sinwar dictated a message to Zayda for the Israeli side, according to which “by the end of September we will put cards on the table that will cause an earthquake regarding the negotiations, and they should prepare to empty the prisons.”
Zayda was asked to convey this message verbatim to the Shin Bet representatives who were in contact with him, and another meeting with Yahya Sinwar was scheduled for October 8. Abu Zayda traveled to Israel, conveyed the message to Shin Bet personnel, and returned to Gaza on October 5, ahead of another planned meeting with Sinwar.
“It appears that Abu Zayda was a component of the deception plan operated by the Hamas leadership in an attempt to convince Israel that it was serious in its intentions to reach an agreement for the exchange of Palestinian prisoners for Israelis (living and dead) held in Gaza, as a move that would lead to the regulation of relations between Israel and the Hamas government on the basis of economic relief on Israel’s part and infrastructure development in the Gaza Strip,” Duhoch-Halevi said, adding that it was “reasonable” to think Sinwar’s scheduled meeting with Zayda on October 8 “served as a smokescreen for the secret continuation of military preparations.”

Turkey does not expect any particular change in Israel's foreign policy after the country's elections, scheduled for October 27, regardless of the outcome, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday.
Fidan also discussed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and Turkey's role in the defensive pact signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.
Turkey assessing ways to assist Saudi Arabia against Houthi threat
Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi terrorists under a joint defense pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defense commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Mecca pact defensive rather than offensive
Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defense, electronic warfare and technical support.
"Yemen's legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them," Fidan said.
"But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defense. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory," he said.
Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia's operational defense needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.
On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help it fight Houthi terrorists.
Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint defense pact.
Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament's approval and that they aimed to send it "as soon as possible."
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defense industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea.

Three sisters who drowned in Brighton took their own lives, inquest finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:35:40 UTC
20:35:40 KST

Three sisters who drowned in the sea in Brighton collectively decided to end their own lives, a coroner has ruled.
The bodies of Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, all from London, were recovered from the sea off Brighton in the early hours of 13 May.
An inquest into their deaths heard on Thursday that in the days before they died, the three women made a trip together to Birmingham to visit the former home of their mother, who died by drowning in 2010.
The inquest at Woodvale coroner’s court in Brighton heard that the sisters travelled by taxi to Birmingham on 11 May and were dropped off at 11.36pm at Linton Walk. The address is close to Brookvale Park Lake, where their mother, Janice Adetoro, died. They were picked up to return to the flat they lived in together in Greenford, west London, at 1.28am on 12 May.
DCI Mark Cullimore, of Sussex police, told the hearing there was no CCTV to show what the women did in the time they were in Birmingham.
On the evening of 12 May, they took a pre-booked taxi to Brighton and arrived near the seafront at 10.21pm. They are thought to have last been seen alive on CCTV from the beach at 2.42am on 13 May.
The bodies of Jane Adetoro and Christina Walters were located by a RNLI lifeboat crew; Rebecca Walters’ body was recovered from the shoreline on Brighton beach.
The senior coroner Penelope Schofield told the court on Thursday: “In hours of darkness, they entered the sea at Brighton, they could not swim and sea conditions were adverse.”
A postmortem found all three women had drowned. There was no evidence of any drugs or alcohol in their bodies and no evidence to suggest they had been subjected to violence.
The coroner concluded that the medical cause of death for all three women was drowning and that they had died by suicide.
Schofield told the court: “These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private. We don’t know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known.”
The inquest heard that Christina Walters had suffered from anxiety and depression since her mother’s death, but no such issues were recorded for her sister Rebecca. Adetoro was not registered with a doctor.
The women’s father, Joseph Jacobson, who attended the hearing by video link, said in a written statement: “There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. To lose all three of my precious daughters, Jane, Christina and Rebecca, is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined.”
He said he could not understand why their lives had ended so suddenly, adding: “You were my daughters, you will always be my daughters and I will love you for the rest of my life. May your beautiful souls rest in perfect peace.”

Russian Bombing Forces Tuaregs to Retreat from Kidal, Mali
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:34:49 UTC
20:34:49 KST

The Azawad Liberation Front (ALF) announced the forced withdrawal of its forces from the city of Kidal in northern Mali.
The group’s spokesperson, Mohamed Elmaouloud Ramadane, announced the withdrawal in an official statement.
The decision was made following massive airstrikes by the ruling military junta and mercenaries from Russia’s Africa Corps, which destroyed most of the civilian infrastructure.
The Tuareg command stated that leaving the settlement was a temporary measure aimed at preserving its personnel and logistics.
The city of Kidal has been a key political and military center of the Tuareg movement since the start of the 2012 rebellion for Azawad’s independence, when rebels first drove the Malian army out of the city.
In 2013, as part of Operation Serval, French troops and a Chadian contingent entered the city, driving out radical groups and handing control to moderate Tuareg forces.
In May 2014, an attempt by the Malian army to storm Kidal ended in defeat, after which the city remained under the full control of the Tuareg alliance for years.
From 2015 to 2022, the status quo in the city remained largely unchanged: the UN’s MINUSMA mission was deployed there, while de facto control was exercised by local Tuareg forces.
In November 2023, Malian government forces, backed by Wagner Group mercenaries, managed to temporarily seize the city after a prolonged offensive.
The rebels later regained control of Kidal, launching active operations against government forces and defeating a Russian convoy near Tinzaouaten, which shifted the balance of forces in the war.
In July, Mali’s junta forces, together with the Africa Corps, regained control of the city of Anefis in the north of the country.
The city is located approximately 100 km from Kidal and holds significant strategic importance for controlling Mali’s northern regions.

New Italy election law puts fragile opposition unity to the test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:34:41 UTC
20:34:41 KST

New Italy election law puts fragile opposition unity to the test
ROME, Oct 8 - A new electoral law approved by Italy's parliament on Thursday was conceived by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's coalition as a way to cement its grip on power after the next election, opposition politicians say.
Yet analysts say the reform, which rewards broad alliances rather than individual parties, could ultimately benefit Meloni's centre-left foes if they can overcome their internal divisions and rally behind a single leader.
The reform gives a parliamentary majority bonus to the largest alliance if it wins more than 42% of the vote, encouraging rival parties to join forces before an election. Meloni says it is intended to increase the prospect of stable government.
OPPOSITION RIVALS CLASH OVER LEADERSHIP
When Meloni drew up the bill, her own conservative coalition was ahead in the polls, but its advantage has been eroded by the emergence of a new far-right group, National Future, allowing a cluster of centre-left parties to edge ahead.
However, a requirement in the new law for coalitions to nominate their candidate for prime minister before any election has laid bare divisions between Elly Schlein and Giuseppe Conte, the leaders of the two main opposition groups, the Democratic Party (PD) and the 5-Star Movement.
"The leadership belongs to the party that gets one vote more. That's not hegemony, it's democracy," Schlein, 41, told a PD meeting last week, making clear she believes the largest opposition force should lead the alliance.
"If there are those who do not recognise this democratic principle, then we will hold primaries," she added.
Conte is indeed pushing for primaries, arguing that voters, not party rankings, should choose the coalition's candidate for prime minister. But a showdown would expose sharp policy differences within the centre-left bloc and personal rivalries.
"Primaries will probably make life worse for the left, because they are a contest in which one person says, 'I’m better than the other,' and that doesn't make cooperation any easier," said Piero Ignazi, a professor of comparative politics at the University of Bologna.
Schlein struck a defiant note in parliament on Thursday as the reform was approved despite centre-left opposition.
"Go ahead and change the electoral law, we will win in any case under any voting system," Schlein said.
SUPPORT FOR UKRAINE DIVIDES THE LEFT
Conte, 62, was prime minister from 2018 to 2021 in back-to-back administrations and has made it clear he wants his old job back. He spent much of the summer courting left-wing voters and challenging PD policy positions -- particularly the group's continued support for helping Ukraine's war effort.
Schlein, who has no national government experience, says the PD's lead over its opposition allies in opinion polls means its views must be given more weight.
Latest polls put the PD on about 20% against 12.5% for 5-Star, making it the second most popular party in Italy after Meloni's Brothers of Italy, which is on around 28%.
Alessandro Di Battista, a former senior 5-Star politician who no longer belongs to the party but retains a following among its supporters, said Schlein would struggle to win over parts of the 5-Star base.
"There is a section of citizens who support the 5-Star Movement who wouldn't vote for Schlein even under torture," he told Canale 9 television on Saturday.
Warning that the increasingly bitter rivalry between Schlein and Conte risked playing into the government's hands, he added: "Meloni is already the favourite ... but if they continue like this they may as well not hold the election."
However, Ignazi predicted that despite 5-Star doubts over her leadership credentials, Schlein would win an eventual primary.
"The Democratic Party has many more supporters, who are much more active than 5-Star, so she is the clear favourite," he said.
LESSONS FROM 2022 DEFEAT
The last national election in 2022 used a hybrid voting system that mixed proportional representation with first-past-the-post constituencies dotted around the country.
The PD and 5-Star did not run together, dividing the opposition vote and handing power to the conservative bloc, an experience former Prime Minister Matteo Renzi says should galvanise rather than discourage the opposition.
Renzi, whose small centrist party hopes to join a future centre-left alliance, urged the opposition to embrace any primary contest as a way to expand the coalition's appeal rather than allow it to shred their sense of unity.
"Let's get moving, organise these blessed primaries and turn them into a celebration of democracy," he said last month. REUTERS

Australia's bushfire crisis linked to colonial land-use change: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:34:17 CST
20:34:17 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Forest expansion and thickening after British colonization created landscapes more prone to burning, amplifying the influence of climate change and propelling Australia's bushfire crisis, new research finds.
Researchers from the University of Melbourne, in collaboration with Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation, reconstructed the past 1,000 years of vegetation, fire and erosion in Croajingolong National Park, one of southeastern Australia's most fire-prone forests, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
Published in Nature, the study found that colonization drove cascading changes, including increased fire temperatures, a fourfold increase in eucalypt cover, the transformation of open woodland into forest and increased soil erosion.
The findings provide scientific evidence for the value of cultural burning and the need to integrate Indigenous knowledge into contemporary fire management, said lead author Michael-Shawn Fletcher, a professor at the university.
Climate records showed similarly dangerous fire-weather seasons had repeatedly occurred before colonization, but cultural burning helped maintain open landscapes and limit catastrophic fires, Fletcher said.
"When colonization ended that care, the forest expanded and thickened across the region, loading the landscape with fuel. It is that transformation that has handed control of fire to climate," he added.
Researchers found that the land-use changes predated human-driven climate change, indicating that the current vulnerability of southeastern Australia's eucalypt forests to wildfire has been strongly influenced by colonial land-use legacies.
Sediment records showed that hot fires were followed by a fourfold surge in eucalypts, thickening the landscape and increasing fuel loads. Infrared analysis of charcoal showed that cooler or low-intensity cultural fires before colonization were replaced by hot wildfires afterward. ■

Hungarian section of Budapest-Belgrade railway passes European safety testing
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:34:15 CST
20:34:15 KST

BUDAPEST, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Testing of the European Train Control System (ETCS) on the Hungarian section of the Budapest-Belgrade railway has been completed, marking an important step toward launching passenger services, a senior official said Thursday.
The ETCS must function properly before passenger services can launch. Hungarian Minister of Transport and Investment David Vitezy said contractors still need to complete track-adjustment work to ensure that the railway can maintain operating speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour over the long term.
This final procedure corrects ballast settlement following construction and load testing and ensures track geometry meets design specifications before a new railway enters service.
According to the construction schedule, track adjustments on the section between Hungary's Ferencvaros and Kunszentmiklos-Tass stations are expected to be completed by the end of October, paving the way for the launch of domestic passenger services and subsequent operations.
Vitezy said that if domestic passenger services run smoothly during the first few weeks, the next phase is planned for December, when trains would operate at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour and international passenger services between Budapest and Belgrade would begin.
He added that although extensive testing, corrective work and verification have been completed, further work remains.
The Budapest-Belgrade railway, linking the Hungarian and Serbian capitals, is a flagship project under the Belt and Road Initiative jointly developed by China and countries in Central and Eastern Europe. It is also the first project to align Chinese railway technology and equipment with the European Union's railway interoperability standards.
The Hungarian section, spanning about 158.6 kilometers, is an electrified railway designed for both passenger and freight transport, with a maximum design speed of 160 kilometers per hour. Freight services on the section officially began on Feb. 27 this year. ■

Former senior disciplinary inspector sentenced to 12 years in jail for bribery

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:33:47 CST
20:33:47 KST

NINGBO, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese court on Thursday convicted Xu Chuanzhi, previously a senior disciplinary inspector, of taking bribes and sentenced him to 12 years in prison.
Xu, a former senior member of a disciplinary inspection team of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, was fined 2.5 million yuan (about 370,000 U.S. dollars), according to a verdict issued by the Intermediate People's Court of the city of Ningbo in east China's Zhejiang Province.
All illicit gains and related proceeds will be recovered and turned over to the state treasury, the court said.
From 2001 to 2023, Xu took advantage of his official positions to provide assistance to relevant organizations and individuals in matters such as project contracting, handling of cases and personnel arrangements. In return, he accepted money and property worth 10.72 million yuan, either personally or through a third party, the verdict noted.
From 2023 to 2025, after his retirement, Xu also used the influence derived from his former positions via the acts of other state functionaries to help others in project contracting. In exchange, he accepted another 25.87 million yuan in bribes, the court ruling said.
The court said Xu received a lenient sentence because he truthfully confessed to his crimes and disclosed additional bribery facts previously unknown to investigators, while some of the bribery offenses were attempted rather than completed. He had also pleaded guilty, expressed remorse, and actively returned illicit gains, with almost all illegal proceeds already recovered, the ruling said.
The court stated that these circumstances warranted leniency in sentencing.
The case was heard publicly on July 23. ■

STOCKHOLM, October 8. /TASS/. The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded to Canadian author Anne Carson, the Nobel Committee for Literature at the Swedish Academy said.
Carson is awarded the prize "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature".
"Anne Carson has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities. Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work," the committee pointed out.
Carson, a native of Toronto, is an English-language writer, poet, essayist, and translator. Born in 1950, she studied at the University of Toronto and has taught at universities across the United States and Canada.

China's highway NEV charging volume posts strong growth over National Day holiday
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
19:33:35 CST
20:33:35 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- China's highway new energy vehicle (NEV) charging volume rose sharply during the recent week-long National Day holiday, data from the National Energy Administration showed on Thursday.
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, the country's highway NEV charging volume reached 163 million kilowatt-hours, averaging 23.26 million kilowatt-hours daily, up 51.42 percent year on year.
These figures reflect both the rapid growth of China's NEV fleet and the growing number of highway charging facilities.
China is the world's largest NEV market. NEV sales and ownership have climbed steadily, partly supported by trade-in programs and increasingly competitive domestic models.
Official data show that China's NEV ownership has reached 48.97 million, or 13.19 percent of all vehicles, with NEVs accounting for nearly half of new vehicle registrations in the first half of 2026.
China has been accelerating the expansion of charging infrastructure as part of its broader push to promote NEVs and cut carbon emissions.
The total number of charging connectors in China has surpassed 24 million, making it home to the world's largest electric vehicle charging network.
About 89,000 charging facilities have been installed at expressway service areas. From January to August this year, these service areas added around 11,000 high-power charging units, roughly equal to the cumulative total before this year.
The National Day holiday, often called "Golden Week," is one of China's busiest travel periods. A total of 2.14 billion cross-regional passenger trips were made over the seven days this year, averaging more than 300 million a day.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), China aims to upgrade and retrofit charging facilities at expressway service areas to build an intercity charging network that effectively meets mid- and long-distance travel needs, while also raising the share of fast-charging facilities.
By 2030, the total number of charging facilities is expected to exceed 40 million units, including approximately 300,000 high-power charging facilities, providing enough charging capacity to support more than 110 million electric vehicles. ■

China

SYDNEY, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- Eighty-eight percent of Australian parents surveyed support the country's under-16 social media ban, despite the majority using social media every day themselves, new research has found.
The report by Edith Cowan University (ECU) and Playgroup WA in the state of Western Australia (WA) surveyed 726 WA parents of children aged 0 to 8 about their social media use and its impact on parenting, according to an ECU statement on Thursday.
It found social media is deeply embedded in family life, with parents relying on it daily for information, support and connection, while increasingly recognizing its risks and backing stronger protections for children online, the statement said.
Of the 92 percent of respondents who used social media, 96 percent said they used it daily, with 99 percent accessing it via mobile phones, according to the report, which found 44 percent of parents believed social media had a somewhat or extremely negative impact on their lives, compared with 22 percent who reported a positive impact.
Parents cited concerns about children's vulnerability, brain development, bullying, addiction and online predators when supporting delayed access to social media, it said, adding that nearly half said children should be at least 16 before having an internet-enabled smartphone.
The findings highlight a striking contrast between parents' own social media habits and what they want for their children, said Catherine Archer, a senior lecturer at ECU who conducted the research.
"The same experience that makes social media useful for parents also appears to make them more aware of the risks it can pose to children," Archer said.
However, the study found 67 percent of parents reported posting photos of their children online, despite concerns about children's privacy. ■

Medium-term borrowing costs for the UK government hit a fresh 19-year high today, as investors continued to offload global bonds amid fears of rising inflation – stoked by the oil price soaring more than 5% at one stage.
Recent dramatic moves in government bond markets have been driven by international factors, but will increase the pressure on John Healey ahead of his first budget as chancellor on 28 October.
The yield, or interest rate, on 10-year UK government bonds jumped as much as 0.07 percentage points (7 basis points) by lunchtime in London, to 5.515%. That was the highest level since July 2007, when the global financial crisis was starting to unfold.
Yields on 20- and 30-year UK government bonds, which are known as gilts, climbed to their highest levels since 1998. Yields go up when bond prices go down. The 20-year gilt yield reached 6% for the first time since March 1998 and the 30-year gilt yield also topped 6%.
The bond selloff has eased somewhat, though, and the 10-year gilt yield is now up 2bps at 5.459%.
Eurozone and US government bond yields also rose sharply earlier today, especially those in France, where the government is under huge pressure to tackle its debt position and pass its 2027 budget.
The French benchmark 10-year bond has dipped slightly to 4.86% while the US 10-year Treasury bond yield is also down a tad, at 5.29%.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, leapt more than $5 to over $105 a barrel, and is now trading 4.4% higher at $104.6 a barrel, up $4.43.
Analysts pointed to growing attacks on tankers around the strait of Hormuz, including an attack on a vessel near Qatar yesterday, coupled with cuts to US oil output as a tropical storm approaches and is expected to turn into a hurricane.
UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said:
Renewed tensions in the Middle East, with vessel strikes occurring well beyond the strait of Hormuz, have revived concerns about the sustainability of higher transit volumes through the chockepoint.
UK and European natural gas prices also jumped, but the increases later eased.

Lisa Barber, tech editor of the consumer group Which?, says customers’ search history is useful to hackers, so they can launch convincing ‘spear phishing’ attacks.
It’s deeply concerning to learn that hackers have not only obtained customers’ personal details, like email addresses and phone numbers, in the Asos hack, but also their search history.
While many of us would assume that our search history would be uninteresting to a hacker, it can in fact be incredibly useful for criminals hoping to target you with extremely convincing, personalised phishing attacks. This technique, known as ‘spear phishing’, can be hard to spot, as criminals will tailor the communication specifically to you, often using data gleaned from social media accounts and, unfortunately, data breaches.

Eurozone finance ministers, ECB to urge France to pass budget to calm bond markets
Eurozone finance ministers and the European Central Bank will urge France today to pass its 2027 budget to calm bond markets, as French borrowing costs hover at 25-year highs, senior euro zone officials told Reuters.
France is at the centre of a bond market storm, fuelled by worries over the country’s large budget deficit and looming presidential election next year.
Its 10-year bond yield has jumped nearly 80 basis points (bps) since the start of September and hit its highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. That is driving up the government’s borrowing costs and making things even harder.
Eurozone finance ministers and the ECB meet in Luxembourg this afternoon for monthly talks and the surge in French borrowing costs will be discussed.
But asked if the European Commission or ECB would take any action, a senior eurozone official told Reuters:
I think the clear answer is “no“. I would expect the Eurogroup to recognise that France has all the means to respond. The proper response is to agree on a budget. That’s kind of a no-brainer. So I would expect this to be the main message.
The ECB can buy bonds of a eurozone country on the secondary market if their prices move in an unjustified way to protect the proper transmission of monetary policy. But officials said this does not apply to what is currently happening in France. A second senior eurozone official said:
Everybody has their own mandate. The European Central Bank has a mandate to maintain price stability, and governments have a mandate to maintain the fiscal stability of their countries. Everybody should do their own job.
France said last month that its budget deficit will exceed the government’s target of 5% of GDP this year. It plans to sell a record €340bn of bonds in 2027 to fund the government and refinance Covid-era debt.
Eurozone officials said there was concern about French borrowing because it created conditions for a broader crisis, but added there was no sign of contagion yet to other countries in the currency bloc.
Since the creation of the euro in 1999, France – the European Union’s second biggest economy and a key political player – has only had a budget deficit below the EU’s ceiling of 3% six time.
Supermarket shake-up: why Asda or Morrisons could vanish within a decade
Our retail expert Sarah Butler has also looked at the UK’s big supermarkets.
They may be two of the most recognisable brands in Britain, with a combined 188 years serving shoppers, but industry watchers agree that either Asda or Morrisons – or both – could disappear within a decade.
This week, it emerged that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons – the UK’s second- and sixth-largest supermarket chains – had held merger talks between last November and February, before the larger player decided to walk away.
News of the potential deal has relaunched speculation that the UK grocery market is now ripe for consolidation and revealed that the Sainsbury’s boss, Simon Roberts – who has been in post for six years – is at least willing to consider the possibility of buying one of his troubled rivals.
Sainsbury’s, which has 600 supermarkets and almost 900 convenience stores, has until recently been seen as wary of trying to revive merger talks with its rivals after its bid to buy Asda for £7bn in 2019 was blocked.
However, industry experts say Asda and Morrisons’ owners have held informal talks with each other – and both with Sainsbury’s team – and predict that talks could restart.
“The three of them, one way or another, are talking to each other,” one said. He suggested that a combination of Asda and Morrisons could happen but was likely to be a weaker deal than a Sainsbury’s takeover of either, as both businesses struggle with costs and interest on debt piles.
Gold and crude oil are currently telling two very different stories about the macro backdrop, says Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.
Gold remains under pressure near $4,100–4,150 an ounce, weighed down by elevated Treasury yields, a firm dollar and a Federal Reserve that remains reluctant to declare victory over inflation. Brent, meanwhile, has climbed back above $100, with renewed attacks on shipping in the Gulf rebuilding part of the geopolitical premium that had faded as US-Iran negotiations showed signs of progress.
Gold: safe-haven demand vs yields
Gold has struggled to find sustained support despite an increasingly complicated geopolitical backdrop. Prices are trading around $4,130, close to their lowest levels since August and significantly below the late-August peak around $4,650.
The main problem is the bond market. The US 10-year Treasury yield remains around 5.3%, while the 30-year is close to 5.7%. More importantly for gold, real yields are exceptionally high: the Federal Reserve’s latest data put the 10-year inflation-indexed yield around 2.9%. That significantly raises the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset such as bullion.
For many investors, Treasuries can now fulfil part of the defensive role traditionally occupied by gold while simultaneously offering a substantial real return. That helps explain why geopolitical uncertainty has not translated into the kind of sustained gold rally normally associated with an escalation in the Middle East.
Fed hawkishness adds another headwind. Wednesday’s Federal Reserve minutes reinforced the hawkish position. The September meeting produced a unanimous 25bp hike to 3.75–4.00%, and the minutes showed broad agreement that inflation remains too high. The disagreement was less about whether inflation was a problem and more about why rates needed to rise: some policymakers viewed the hike as insurance against energy and other supply shocks, while a more hawkish group worried that price pressures were increasingly becoming demand-driven.

Meanwhile, the bond sell-off continues, as the Brent crude oil price jumped more than $5, taking it above $105 a barrel and stoking inflation fears.

This has pushed bond yields sharply higher, increasing borrowing costs for the UK government. The benchmark 10-year yield has gone above 5.5%, rising 6 basis points to 5.515%, the highest since July 2007

This will only ramp up the pressure on Andy Burnham and John Healey in the run-up to the budget on 28 October, analysts said.
As AJ Bell’s head of financial analysis Danni Hewson points out:
Rising bond yields are bad news for stocks for several reasons. One is they increase the cost of companies’ own borrowing, which eats into their profitability. Another is that when yields on low-risk government bonds are higher, they compare more favourably with the stock market, which is widely perceived as being a higher-risk option. This makes the latter a less attractive place for people to put their cash.
For consumer-facing businesses there is a further challenge. Higher government bond yields feed into increased mortgage and credit costs, putting the squeeze on their customers and affecting their ability to spend.

I am delighted that nearly half a million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters.

Gwyn Topham
London’s High Court today refused claimants permission to appeal against its verdict in the UK dieselgate trial, which broadly found in favour of some of the world’s biggest carmakers.
Lady Justice Cockerill, who in July ruled against most allegations that certain cars were fitted with illegal “defeat devices” that concealed their true emissions, said that claimants would have to apply directly to the Court of Appeal.
The trial, which began in October 2025, was a group action for 1.6 million drivers against 16 car manufacturers, based on test cases against Mercedes, Ford, Renault, Nissan, and Peugeot/Citroën, and potentially extending to claims against many others.

Most of the increase in gilt yields since the pandemic is justified by the return of interest rates to normal levels as policymakers no longer need to set them close to zero to generate sufficient demand. However, the extra increase in yields this year is predicated on four Bank of England interest rate hikes, which we do not think are necessary to prevent another bout of persistent high inflation.
If these lofty expectations are not met, the 10-year gilt yield will probably reverse much of its 2026 surge in 2027. We expect the 10-year yield to drop to 4.7% by end-2027.

The Iran war has hit two mainstays of Gulf business: energy exports and aviation. The disruption extends to Europe, where buyers have had to replace missing gas supplies.
The World Bank expects the six Gulf Cooperation Council economies to shrink by an average of 4.3% this year, as the impact of the Iran war continues to hit the region’s trade and business.
Higher oil prices have not compensated for lower export volumes, which have cut output and government revenues, the bank said in its regional update published on Tuesday.
Middle Eastern crude exports exceeded pre-war levels on 14 days in September, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing provisional Kpler data. Those shipments included oil sent through Hormuz and via alternative routes.
The World Bank’s forecast covers the full year and includes sectors beyond oil.
Some gas shipments are also getting through. Reuters reported on Monday that four vessels carrying Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG) had reappeared outside Hormuz around 2–3 October.
Italian energy company Edison said on 28 September that QatarEnergy had extended its force majeure notification to early December, saying it could not deliver further scheduled cargoes.
The notice brought the total number of cargoes affected between April and early December to 35, equivalent to about 4.6 billion cubic metres of gas destined for Italy’s Adriatic LNG terminal.
Edison said it had bought replacement supplies and remained able to meet its commitments to customers.
Airlines face weaker demand
Passenger traffic on Middle Eastern airlines fell 14.6% in August from a year earlier, according to figures published by the International Air Transport Association on 30 September.
The measure accounts for both the number of paying passengers and the distance travelled. Available capacity fell 9.3%, leaving a larger share of seats empty as traffic declined faster.
But regional airlines are taking some passengers whose flights have been cancelled by European and other carriers.
Aviation consultant Omar Hashmi said Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad serve passengers connecting through their hubs as well as visitors to the Gulf.
Longer routes also add fuel costs, he said.
“When airspace is closed, and routes become longer, there is also the headache that flight timings change,” he told Euronews.
Qatar warned at a briefing in Doha on Tuesday that the “whole world is paying” for the conflict, as diplomatic efforts to advance talks between Washington and Tehran continued.
The World Bank warned that damaged infrastructure and postponed investment could continue to hold back growth after the immediate disruption has passed.

A former CIA official pleaded guilty Tuesday to wire fraud in a scheme that used fictitious classified programs to finance purchases of Florida real estate and gold with nearly $200 million in government money, CBS News reported.
David Rush entered the plea in federal court in Virginia and faces a maximum prison sentence of 20 years.
His plea agreement provides for the forfeiture of at least $194 million. Assets listed include four Florida homes, 298 gold bars, 35 luxury watches and two BMWs, according to the report.
Court documents cited by CBS describe how Rush invoked classified government activities to authorize spending, direct contractors and gain control of the assets they acquired.
Prosecutors said the property and gold purchases were parts of a single fraud scheme, despite involving different intermediaries and transactions.
About $145 million was routed through companies to purchase properties in Palm Beach and Hobe Sound, Florida, which Rush intended to sell for profit, according to the filings.
To arrange the gold purchases, he told contractors that a top-secret project required deliveries of valuable commodities to unidentified recipients. A contractor’s $45 million transfer to a holding company in January formed the basis of the wire fraud charge. 
'Master manipulator'
The investigation began with a CIA referral to the FBI, the two agencies previously said.
Prosecutors said Rush could access “highly sensitive and classified government programs,” although the charging document did not identify his employer. An earlier affidavit described him as a former employee at the Senior Executive Service level at a government agency in eastern Virginia.
Rush was arrested in May.
During a search of his home, FBI agents seized gold bars valued at about $40 million, along with luxury watches and $2 million in cash. Prosecutors said roughly $38.6 million was still in a holding company’s account.
A federal judge ordered him to remain in custody in June, citing a severe risk that he would flee.
Justice Department lawyers called him a "master manipulator" at the detention hearing, saying he "cannot be trusted" and was "fully willing and able to skirt the rules."

Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said.
Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Russia’s technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline and leading to potential online service disruption.
Separately, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow.
Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified.

Canadian poet Anne Carson wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:28:16 UTC
20:28:16 KST

Anne Carson was among the bookies' favourites to win this year, as her body of work eschews easy categorisation.The Nobel Prize committee singled out her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson has been awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for 2026, “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
The 76-year-old writer is known for her hybrid style, combining poetry and prose, as well as contemporary stories with ancient myth.
The Academy stated: “Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work.”
Among Carson’s best-known works are her 1986 debut "Eros the Bittersweet", a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature; her 1998 work, often heralded as her greatest, "Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse", a queer coming-of-age story that reworks a Greek poem about Heracles; "The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos" (2001); and "Norma Jeane Baker of Troy" (2019), which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
Her most recent work is "Wrong Norma", which was published in 2024.
By winning the Nobel Prize, Carson becomes only the 19th woman to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, with recent winners including Han Kang in 2024, Annie Ernaux in 2022 and Louis Glück in 2020.
As of today, the literature prize has been awarded by the Nobel committee of the Swedish Academy 119 times to a total of 123 winners (four literature prizes have been shared between multiple laureates).
Last year's prize was won by postmodern Hungarian author László Krasznahorkai “for his compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.” Susan Sontag previously described the author as “the contemporary Hungarian master of apocalypse.”
The literature prize is the fourth to be announced this week, following the 2026 Nobels in medecine, physics and chemistry.
Each prize this year comes with 12 million Swedish kronor (€1.07 million). The winners also receive an 18-carat gold medal and a diploma.
The winner of the Nobel Peace Prize will be announced on Friday and the final prize, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences, is to be announced on Monday.
Nobel Prize award ceremonies are held on 10 December, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death in 1896.

Seoul said Kyiv's public disclosure of the repatriation of two North Korean prisoners endangered their families in North Korea, where relatives of those who fall into enemy hands face punishment. Ukraine has rejected South Korea's accusations.
South Korea recalled its ambassador to Ukraine on Wednesday over Kyiv's public disclosure of the repatriation of two North Korean prisoners of war, in a continued public dispute between the two countries.
Seoul's foreign ministry announced it was recalling ambassador Park Ki-chan, citing the unauthorised disclosure of information about the handover.
The ministry said it hoped to resolve outstanding issues through continued consultations and that the South Korean embassy in Kyiv would remain open.
The dispute began on 23 September, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated at the UN General Assembly that North Korean soldiers captured fighting on Russia's side had been repatriated.
Seoul argues the disclosure endangered the soldiers' families in North Korea, where the regime is known to punish the relatives of defectors and those who fall into enemy hands.
Ukraine rejected the accusations. Zelenskyy's adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said at the end of September that no confidentiality agreement existed.
"There was no such agreement, that is not true. And it would be wrong to conceal what happens to particular prisoners," he wrote on social media.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described it as a diplomatic misunderstanding and expressed hope for a swift resolution.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung had previously warned of "additional measures" if Kyiv did not acknowledge a breach of a confidentiality agreement and issue a public apology.
On Tuesday, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said Seoul had received an apology from Ukraine, but it fell short of what his country expected.
Oil shipments to Russia a further complication
Reports indicate that South Korean ports shipped more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel oil, mostly diesel, to Russia in July and August, based on port documents and vessel-tracking data published by The Guardian.
Seven tankers, three of which are subject to UK and EU sanctions, made 14 voyages over the two-month period, according to reports.
Vladyslav Vlasjuk, Ukraine's presidential envoy on sanctions policy, said the timing was no coincidence.
"These deliveries began precisely when Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries reduced processing volumes and caused a fuel shortage in the Russian Federation. In other words, imports from South Korea effectively helped Russia offset the consequences of losing its own refining capacity," he wrote on social media.
Kyiv's reaction came despite Seoul joining the coalition of countries that imposed enhanced export controls on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022.
In 2024, South Korea expanded its list of controlled goods to more than 1,400 items and tightened restrictions on so-called Common High Priority Items, components Russia procures through third countries for use in missiles, drones and other weapons.
Seoul has also sanctioned Russian ships, companies and individuals involved in military cooperation with North Korea.
In response to reports, South Korea's foreign ministry said Seoul "supports and is actively participating in global efforts to end the war in Ukraine and restore peace."
It declined to comment on specific shipments or the arrival of sanctioned vessels, saying the country strictly observes its own export-control measures against Russia.

====================================================================================================

Mathematicians invented a knitting stitch that stops mistakes from spreading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:25:51 UTC
20:25:51 KST

Despite its tranquil reputation, knitting is anything but boring. One stitch slip-up can cause a defect that spreads across the entire fabric. But does it have to be that way? In a recent paper in Physical Review X, a team of researchers mathematically investigated knitting to invent a new, more resilient stitch.
Knitting is a special form of fabrication in which the two ends of the yarn remain outside the fabric. In knitting, loops from the middle of an entangled yarn are slipped through one another so the yarn holds its position but isn’t knotted together. The knitting process is portable and easy, but the structure also means a tug on one loose end can quickly unravel the whole project. It’s also vulnerable to other quickly spreading errors.
Daisuke S. Shimamoto, a physicist at Ritsumeikan University in Japan, and his colleagues wrapped a three-dimensional model of a single jersey knit stitch—a simple beginner’s stitch—around a doughnut shape called a torus, which preserves the pattern without including any edges at the top or bottom. It basically converts the knit pattern into one giant knot that can be analyzed with knot theory. The scientists projected multiple knit rows on the torus to reveal how defects from one row of stitches spread until the entire fabric unravels. The process is called defect propagation, and the researchers say it’s one of the defining characteristics of knittable fabrics.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Researchers have mathematically described stitch defects in the past, says applied mathematician Alexander Omelchenko of Constructor University in Germany, but only as static objects. This study shows how defects move dynamically across a textile. “It’s a very original approach,” says Omelchenko, who wasn’t involved in this study but originated the topological analysis method used.
One common type of defect propagation is “laddering,” in which a single missed loop slips down a column of stitches, unraveling the whole column along the way. “If one unit cell is disentangled, the cell just below that cell is disentangled, and it is repeated, and it propagates endlessly,” Shimamoto says.
After his topological analysis of the jersey knit, Shimamoto used moves from basic knot theory to design a knittable stitch in which defect propagation can still happen but not endlessly. This “robust knit” is a complex stitch with sweeping loops that cross over through two stitches rather than one, and it reduces propagated defects row by row until they stop. Defects expand only when there is more than one slipped stitch in a row.
Omelchenko appreciates the study authors’ ability to translate math to real life but notes that fully evaluating the possibilities of new stitches by using torus diagrams would be impractically expensive to compute. Shimamoto hopes his work with the robust knit, as a proof of concept, can one day inspire stronger fabric design for manufacturing.
Besides a fascination with fabric, the two researchers have another thing in common: both consulted their mothers’ knitting advice for their papers, and Shimamoto even gave his mother an author credit as a thank you for teaching him how to knit. According to Omelchenko, “It sometimes was a little bit more useful to talk with her rather than textile researchers.”

Britain will update the design of its banknotes — bumblebees, hedgehogs and other animals will be depicted on the pound notes
Kyiv • UNN
The Bank of England selected four animal species for the new series of banknotes following a vote by nearly 500,000 people. The design will be developed over several years.
The Bank of England has identified four species of animals that will become the central images on a new series of banknotes. They were chosen through a public vote. This is reported on the Bank of England website, writes UNN.
Details
The next series of banknotes will feature a barn owl, a buff-tailed bumblebee, a European hedgehog and an Atlantic puffin. Each animal will become the central design element of one banknote of a different denomination.
The selection was based on a vote in which nearly 500,000 people took part. Residents chose from a list compiled by wildlife experts.
The barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and hedgehog were clear leaders in their respective categories. At the same time, the Atlantic puffin was chosen to add diversity and represent the country's marine wildlife and coastline, although other animals received more votes in the overall ranking.
The Bank notes that the process of designing, testing and printing the banknotes will take several years. Portraits of historical figures first appeared on British money in 1970. The new series will preserve this tradition: the portrait of the reigning monarch will also remain on the banknotes.

====================================================================================================

Two-thirds of young Europeans suffered childhood trauma, with lasting life impact, WHO finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:21:21 UTC
20:21:21 KST

Two-thirds of European children experienced trauma that ‘follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships’.
More than two-thirds of young people in Europe have experienced childhood adversity ranging from domestic violence to the death of a parent, exposing them to poorer mental health and quality of life years later, according to a new report from the World Health Organization Regional Office for Europe.
More than one in five young adults reported experiencing four or more adverse childhood experiences.
“When a child grows up around violence or a household in crisis, we shouldn't be surprised that it follows them into the classroom, job market and their relationships years later,” said Natasha Azzopardi-Muscat, director of health systems at the WHO/Europe.
She added that the extent of the problem is often overlooked and the consequences expand to several aspects of people's lives.
“This isn't a mental health issue in isolation. It's a social and economic one, and it needs every sector at the table, not just health services,” said Azzopardi-Muscat.
The report surveyed more than 26,000 young adults aged 18 to 30 across Europe between November 2025 and January 2026. It measured exposure to nine forms of adversity, such as physical, emotional or sexual abuse, physical neglect, household substance use, household mental illness, parental separation or death, and witnessing domestic violence during their childhood.
“The findings are remarkably consistent. Adverse childhood experiences are at the root of poorer health, social and economic outcomes among young adults across Europe,” said Mark Bellis, from Liverpool John Moores University and academic lead for the study.
The most common experiences were parental separation or death, witnessing domestic violence or suffering emotional abuse.
Exposure to chronic stress in early childhood, which can be caused by these adverse experiences, disrupts brain development, impairs emotional regulation and alters physiological stress response systems, the report noted.
Young adults reporting four or more adverse experiences suffered significantly higher rates of physical pain or discomfort, difficulties with everyday activities like work or study, impaired mobility and self-care difficulties.
Among those who reported exposure to four or more adverse experiences, 76.3% felt they had needed professional mental health support in the previous year, compared with 36.7% of those who reported none.
However, young people most exposed to harmful experiences were also more likely to report that they had not received the mental health support they felt they needed, the report warned.
Breaking the cycle
Without effective prevention and early intervention, harmful experiences tend to recur across generations, the authors warned.
Adults affected by childhood adversity face higher risks of raising their own children in conditions marked by financial stress, domestic violence, and parental mental ill health.
Despite this stark picture, the report noted that even those exposed to more adverse experiences could still achieve positive outcomes.
The good news, Bellis said, is that adverse childhood experiences can be prevented and their impacts reduced.
“With support from policymakers, investment in safer and more nurturing childhoods will help deliver healthier populations, stronger communities and a more prosperous future for Europe,” he added.

Euronews Next exclusive: A driverless shuttle now carries aircraft workers and spare parts at Tallinn Airport, with no safety agents on board.
Autonomous cars and shuttles are no longer rare on city streets, but airports with their extraordinary safety rules are a different matter.
At Tallinn Airport, Estonian company Auve Tech is now running its MiCa shuttles on routes passing close to parked aircraft — for the first time, without a safety operator on board. It is a step the company hopes will make driverless transport pay for itself and perhaps spread to other airports.
The Tallinn shuttles serve Magnetic MRO, an aircraft maintenance firm with hangars on opposite sides of the airfield. They move workers, tools and spare parts between the sites throughout the day.
Getting here took years. Auve Tech began testing their tech at the airport in 2023, and the commercial service started in 2025, first with a required safety operator on board. Taking that person out was the hard part.
"When conducting a drive inside the airport, that's a whole other story. You have so many layers of safety rules that you have to comply with," Deivis Sepp, Fleet Operations Lead at Auve Tech, told Euronews Next. "That's why getting the permit is kind of a miracle."
Sepp said the airport's safety board has been reviewing the shuttles' performance data every week throughout the test period.
"Terabytes and terabytes of data have been gathered," Sepp told Euronews Next. "They are not giving us the permit like, 'Hey, just go ahead and do your thing, do the innovation.' It doesn't work like that."
How MiCa works
MiCa is a small electric shuttle that Auve Tech unveiled in October 2022. It is designed for last-mile transport in pre-mapped areas, and it carries up to eight passengers. MiCa is rated Level 4 for self-driving — meaning it can drive itself without a human at the wheel, but only within defined conditions, such as a mapped route.
To ”see” its surroundings, the shuttle uses ten cameras and seven laser-based sensors, which give it a 360-degree view. It does not roam freely between the planes — it follows a fixed route with rules built in and reacts immediately to any potential obstacle.
"It will see enough ahead to make a decision," Sepp told Euronews Next. "We are at a cross section, looking from one place to another, and if it's safe to move, it will go."
The shuttle also reacts to small hazards. Euronews' reporter had to grab a handrail when the shuttle braked hard midway through the ride, apparently for a bird crossing its route.
“Small birds are flying around here, and it detects everything near it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "So of course safety comes first for us."
Humans are still part of the system, but from a distance. The vehicle makes its own decisions, and a remote operator in a tele-monitoring room watches over it.
"The vehicle decides what to do, whether to do it and when to do it," Sepp told Euronews Next. "But if some glitch happens, it will ask permission from the tele-monitoring operator."
Making the sums add up
For Auve Tech, removing the on-board operator is a crucial economic step. Taavi Rõivas, Chairman of the Supervisory Board and a former Estonian prime minister, said a safety operator on board "doesn't make much sense commercially".
"Regulatory needs are there to still have a human in the loop, but one human can supervise or remotely monitor several vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
He put the break-even point at around three vehicles per remote operator.
"If you look at three vehicles at the same time, see what they're doing, and if necessary give some minor guidance, then we can match the price of human-driven vehicles," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
"Once we can roll out this service in this way, I believe the scaling of autonomous vehicle transportation will be very, very rapid."
Their main client already sees the benefit in cost and reliability. Risto Mäeots, CEO of Magnetic Group, said his company drives "almost 50,000 kilometres every year" between its hangars. Before the shuttles, they had to only use human drivers, which sometimes brought problems of their own.
"We faced a lot of reliability issues. For example, people can get sick, and there was staff turnover," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "It turned out to be a big challenge."
He described transport as a cost centre for a maintenance business, not a source of revenue. He also said the company, which competes with much larger aviation players, has to be inventive to survive.
"We half-joke that we don't have a right to exist because we are a small company against major aviation players," Mäeots told Euronews Next. "So for us to exist, we have to really think out of the box."
"We thought it was going to be predominantly used by people, but now we see an equally important part is spare parts being delivered between the hangars," Mäeots told Euronews Next. Bulky items still travel by conventional vehicles because of the size limits.
Auve Tech now wants to take the model elsewhere. Rõivas said the immediate target is the large number of last-mile shuttle services running in closed environments, such as corporate campuses, where regulators find it easier to allow vehicles without safety operators.
"Globally there are hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of last-mile shuttle services, only in closed environments," Rõivas told Euronews Next. "We see that we can either match the price or outperform the price of the current service."
Interest is coming from Europe, Japan, Abu Dhabi and the US, he said. Other airports’ representatives are visiting Tallinn "pretty much one airport per week" to see the service working. Some consider carrying VIP passengers or move people between gates in such shuttles.
"We are expecting to have, very soon, announcements that much bigger airports than Tallinn will have a similar service up and running," Rõivas told Euronews Next.
Sepp is confident about the direction. "I believe within the next 10 years, autonomous transportation solutions inside the airport will be a common thing to see," he told Euronews Next.
