US-led coalition exit shifts more counter-ISIS burden to Iraq and Syria - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:20:08 UTC
20:20:08 KST

The US-led coalition formally ended its Operation Inherent Resolve mission in Iraq on September 30 as its remaining forces and equipment completed their withdrawal, shifting primary security responsibility to Baghdad and raising new questions about how Iraq and Syria will monitor their long frontier against ISIS.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
US Central Command said the transition was part of a planned move toward a bilateral defense relationship between Washington and Baghdad. Combined Joint Task Force-Operation Inherent Resolve remains active, with its headquarters relocated to Jordan, while coalition forces continue counter-ISIS operations in Syria.
For Damascus, the shift follows another major change. US forces completed their departure from the al-Tanf garrison in southeastern Syria in February as part of a broader military repositioning. CENTCOM said at the time that American forces would remain capable of responding to ISIS threats in the region and supporting partner-led operations.
The transition raises a central question along the Syrian-Iraqi frontier: Can forces on both sides maintain effective surveillance and intelligence sharing as the coalition’s military footprint changes?
Istanbul-based Iraqi journalist Ali al-Khazali told The Media Line that the most important change after the coalition mission ended has not been a major increase in troop numbers, but a higher state of readiness and greater responsibility for Iraqi forces.
Before the transition, he said, Iraq had worked to build a multilayered defensive system along the Syrian border involving border guards, the Iraqi army, and the Popular Mobilization Forces, backed by fortifications and aerial and technical surveillance.
“Baghdad tried before the coalition’s departure to make the border less dependent on the foreign military presence and to ensure that Iraqi forces themselves hold the ground and manage the file directly,” al-Khazali said.
Iraqi authorities had already expanded concrete barriers, trenches, barbed wire, thermal cameras, observation towers, and drone surveillance along the frontier.
Stronger fortifications, al-Khazali said, do not mean Baghdad can fully replace everything the coalition provided.
Iraqi forces are now capable of handling much of the operational burden inside the country and conducting operations against ISIS cells, he said, but advanced technical and intelligence capabilities remain a more difficult challenge.
US capabilities difficult to replace in short term by Iraq
According to al-Khazali, the United States provided aerial surveillance, drones, intelligence imagery, and sophisticated systems for tracking targets and rapidly integrating information from multiple sources - capabilities that will be difficult to replace completely in the short term.
“Iraq can compensate for a large part of the coalition’s military role, but it has not yet reached the point where it can fully dispense with US support, particularly in intelligence, surveillance, and long-range reconnaissance,” he said.
On the Syrian side, political analyst Firas al-Allawi described similar concerns about surveillance and intelligence capabilities.
Al-Allawi told The Media Line that there are no clear indications of a broad Syrian military deployment or a major increase in troop numbers along the Iraqi border, although limited redeployments may have taken place recently.
“What is available so far does not indicate the transfer of large numbers of troops or major changes along the Syrian-Iraqi border,” al-Allawi said.
Coordination between Damascus and Baghdad exists, particularly in the exchange of security information, he said, but it has not yet reached the level of an integrated strategic security partnership.
Al-Allawi believes some intelligence cooperation is taking place away from public view, with a significant portion occurring within a broader framework that still involves the United States.
“I believe an important part of the information exchange takes place within a broader intelligence cooperation umbrella in which Washington participates, rather than through deep, direct Syrian-Iraqi cooperation,” he said.
A degree of mistrust and caution remains between Damascus and Baghdad, according to al-Allawi, making it premature to describe their cooperation as a fully developed joint security system.
Al-Khazali offered a similar assessment from the Iraqi side. Direct communication channels, information sharing, and meetings between border officials exist, he said, but publicly available information does not indicate that the two countries operate a permanent joint operations room or fully integrated intelligence center.
“What exists is direct communication channels, information exchange, and coordination in some operations,” he said. “But transforming that cooperation into a permanent joint security system is still a work in progress.”
Iraqi officials have previously said Baghdad coordinates directly with Syrian authorities to prevent ISIS infiltration, combat smuggling, and exchange security information.
ISIS operating through small cells, individual operatives, in shift since 2014
The nature of the threat has also changed considerably since 2014.
ISIS no longer needs to move large columns of fighters across the border or capture cities and crossings to pose a danger. The group can operate through smaller cells, desert routes, logistical and financial networks, and individual operatives capable of exploiting gaps in surveillance without the kind of large-scale military breakdown seen during its territorial expansion.
“The most dangerous gap today is not an open stretch of border or the collapse of fortifications,” al-Khazali said. “The biggest danger is the intelligence gap between the two sides of the border.”
The desert corridor between Iraq’s Anbar province and Syria’s Deir ez-Zor region remains particularly sensitive, he said, because small cells and smuggling networks can exploit vast distances and the difficulty of maintaining continuous surveillance.
Al-Allawi identified a similar weakness on the Syrian side.
Syria’s Badia desert and the broader desert belt extending toward Iraq still suffer from limited aerial surveillance and incomplete intelligence capabilities, he said, while the vast geography makes sustained control difficult.
“The area generally remains fragile from both a security and strategic perspective, and the length of the Syrian-Iraqi border makes it even harder to control,” al-Allawi said.
Increasing troop numbers insufficient to rein in ISIS, analyst says
Although ISIS is far weaker than at the height of its territorial expansion, scattered cells in desert areas could use surveillance gaps to regroup or move personnel, money, and equipment.
For that reason, al-Allawi said increasing troop numbers alone will not be enough. Syria needs more advanced surveillance and reconnaissance technology, aerial support, improved equipment, and personnel with greater training in border security, counter-infiltration, and desert operations.
Al-Allawi said improved border security will also require broader cooperation with Iraq, the United States, the international coalition, and Jordan rather than relying solely on a larger Syrian military deployment.
The ISIS detainee issue further ties Syrian and Iraqi security together.
During a 23-day operation that began January 21, US forces transferred more than 5,700 adult male ISIS detainees from facilities in northeastern Syria into Iraqi custody. CENTCOM said the operation was intended to keep the detainees securely held and reduce the risk of an ISIS resurgence.
The end of the coalition mission in Iraq does not sever Iraq’s security concerns from Syria. Iraq now has responsibility for thousands of ISIS detainees transferred from Syrian facilities, while Damascus must prevent remaining ISIS cells in the Badia from using the frontier for movement and reorganization.
Iraqi and Syrian sources agree on one central point: Securing the frontier depends not only on walls, trenches, troops, and surveillance equipment, but on whether information can cross the border faster than ISIS operatives do.

SDE demand €100 million worth of changes in exchange for supporting the state budget
The Social Democrats are prepared to vote in favor of the state budget if the coalition backs their proposed amendments, worth up to €100 million, without negotiations.
The Social Democrats voted in favor of sending the budget to the plenary session of the Riigikogu in the parliament's Finance Committee, although they do not intend to support its final passage in its current form. Ahead of the second reading, they plan to submit a raft of amendments, which they expect to be backed without negotiations.
The Social Democrats' demands total up to €100 million. They include larger increases to the salary funds for teachers, police officers and rescue workers, as well as additional funding for special care services and healthcare.
"About €40 million is currently set to be cut from healthcare. We are not prepared to vote for a budget that reduces access to medical care," Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets said.
"If we look at specialized care services, they will need an additional €30 million next year. There may ultimately be a few more proposals on top of these," Läänemets noted.
According to Läänemets, funding could be found for all their proposals. First, the state should take more serious action to tackle the shadow economy. Second, tax breaks for remote gambling should be reversed. Third, the government's reserves should be reviewed.
Õnne Pillak, chair of the Reform Party's Riigikogu group, said the coalition was prepared to reach an agreement if funding sources could be identified.
"It's no secret that specialized care services are an issue close to all our hearts. The budget actually sets aside €37.5 million to reach these agreements. I think this is work we need to get done. I'm glad that at least the Social Democrats are showing a willingness to contribute ideas and put forward substantive proposals," Pillak said.
The Reform Party has also held talks with other opposition parties and unaffiliated MPs. However, there is a fairly clear understanding in the Riigikogu that the Social Democrats are being considered the most seriously, as another MP could leave Eesti 200 before the final budget vote.
The support of an entire party would give the minority government a bigger buffer than that of a handful of unaffiliated MPs. Unaffiliated Riigikogu member Tõnis Mölder said the Social Democrats know this and have set their price very high.
"It has been clear in this building for a long time that the Social Democrats are very keen to join the coalition," Mölder said. "What the Social Democratic Party also needs to understand is that all parties in the Riigikogu actually support increasing funding for special care services. The issue is rather that this budget must not turn into a preelection spending spree. It has to be responsible."
According to Mölder, unaffiliated MPs will take a closer look at the budget over the coming weeks, but their priorities include relief from high energy prices and scrapping the fuel excise duty. On these issues, the government has recently been sending largely positive signals.

Two of Britain’s new E-7 aircraft airborne
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:18:20 BST
20:18:20 KST

Both of the Royal Air Force’s delivered Boeing E-7 Wedgetail aircraft were flying at the same time on Thursday afternoon, the first occasion on which the two have been airborne together.
WT001 came south from RAF Lossiemouth for the orbit areas in the South West using the callsign Boeing 31, while WT002 was out of MOD Boscombe Down as Boeing 38. Between them they represent two thirds of the entire future British airborne early warning fleet. The second aircraft was still being outfitted by STS Aviation at Birmingham Airport as recently as January, so its appearance out of Boscombe Down marks its arrival in the flight test programme alongside the first aircraft.
The Wedgetail is built on the Boeing 737 Next Generation airframe, the same basic aeroplane as the RAF’s Poseidon maritime patrol fleet, and carries the Northrop Grumman Multi-role Electronically Scanned Array radar in the distinctive dorsal fin above the fuselage.
The array has no moving parts, which is the main departure from the rotating radomes of earlier airborne early warning aircraft, and it allows the operator to concentrate the radar’s attention on a particular sector while continuing to scan elsewhere.

The most recent milestone before this one came on 21 May, when WT001 landed at RAF Lossiemouth for the first time, flown by a mixed Boeing UK and Royal Air Force crew. The station has spent a long time preparing for it.
Group Captain Sarah Brewin, the station commander at Lossiemouth, said at the time: “We have been working hard to get ready to operate these aircraft.”
Stu Voboril, Boeing’s vice president and programme manager for the E-7, said: “We look forward to continuing test and evaluation as the aircraft moves closer to entry into service.”
That test and evaluation phase is split between Boscombe Down and Lossiemouth, which explains Thursday’s pattern of one aircraft working out of each. Boeing UK hands the aircraft over to the Royal Air Force once the phase is complete, at which point 8 Squadron takes them on.

Flydubai attack: Israel's Transport Ministry sought crew data only after three years of requests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:17:39 UTC
20:17:39 KST

Despite repeated requests from the Israel Tax Authority over the past three years, the Transport Ministry's security division sought access to information on airline crews only after a closed-door Knesset hearing into the attempted flydubai cockpit attack, ynet has learned.
The request came after a confidential meeting of the Knesset's Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee on Tuesday, which examined the attempt by Omani pilot Hamam al-Hammami to crash a flydubai passenger aircraft. Following the hearing, the Transport Ministry's security division requested immediate access to the National Passenger Assessment Center, seeking information about the nationalities of airline crew members.
The Tax Authority confirmed that it had contacted the ministry several times before the attempted attack, explicitly asking it to fulfill its responsibility to appoint an authorized representative who could retrieve information from the center.
Despite those requests, the ministry had not taken the necessary steps to obtain access during the preceding three years.
After finally authorizing a representative, the Transport Ministry was informed that the system was not technically capable of providing airline crew nationality data 48 hours before departure, as required under the legislation governing the center.
Instead, the information becomes available only close to departure, at a stage when it can no longer be effectively used for security screening.
Transport Ministry officials complained about the limitation. However, according to the Tax Authority, the procedure under which crew information is transmitted shortly before flights had already been established with the knowledge and approval of Transport Ministry representatives.
The Transport Ministry disputed the allegation that its security division had failed to appoint a representative despite repeated requests.
"The security division continues to participate in a series of previously scheduled meetings of the National Passenger Assessment Center's steering committee, in order to help define the system and take part in it once it becomes operational," the ministry said.
"Claims that the security division was asked to send a representative and failed to do so are completely detached from reality, since a representative of the division is a member of the center's steering committee."
The ministry added that, regardless of the dispute over representation, the system remained unable to provide information about airline crews sufficiently far in advance.
"In any event, even at this stage, the system is unable to provide the information about airline crews ahead of time, as noted," the ministry said.
The conflicting accounts highlight a dispute over responsibility for obtaining aviation security information, particularly the distinction between participating in the center's steering committee and appointing an authorized official to retrieve operational data.
The revelations come as Lahav 433, the Israel Police's national crime investigation unit, opened a preliminary inquiry Wednesday into suspicions involving senior Transport Ministry officials responsible for aviation security.
The inquiry concerns allegations that officials responsible for security oversight, particularly the screening of pilots arriving in Israel, also worked for foreign airlines, including flydubai, the airline involved in the attempted attack.
Two senior officials are at the center of the inquiry: Avraham "Avri" Cohen, head of the Transport Ministry's security division, and Dvir Rubinstein, director of the ministry's Aviation Security Operations Center. The examination was launched following information provided to police by officials within the Transport Ministry.
The National Fraud Investigations Unit, which operates under Lahav 433, is handling the inquiry, including suspicions of potential conflicts of interest involving ministry employees and the operations of foreign airlines in Israel.
Meanwhile, the investigation into the actions of Omani pilot al-Hammami remains underway. Saudi Arabia is continuing its investigation into the security incident aboard the flight, while the United Arab Emirates is conducting a separate criminal investigation in which Israel's Shin Bet security agency is participating.
Israel has also offered to participate in any aviation safety investigation led by Saudi authorities, but has not yet received an invitation.
Ofer Vaknin, head of the Transport Ministry's aviation safety investigation authority, told Reuters that Israel was prepared to assist with such an investigation. "We are still waiting for an invitation from Saudi Arabia," he said.
Separate investigations are also underway in Australia and New Zealand concerning periods during which the Omani pilot stayed in those countries.
The growing number of inquiries comes as Israeli authorities face questions not only about the attempted attack itself, but also about the aviation security information available before the incident and whether existing procedures were adequately implemented.

Dragon Capital slashes outlook, sees Ukraine GDP dropping 0.5% in 2026, 1.0% in 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:16:25 EEST
20:16:25 KST

The intensification of Russian attacks since July 2026 has inflicted significant damage on Ukraine's economy, prompting leading Ukrainian investment company Dragon Capital to substantially downgrade its macroeconomic forecast: it now expects real gross domestic product (GDP) to decline by 0.5% this year and by 1.0% next year, whereas before the escalation it had forecast possible growth of 1.5% this year and 0.5% next year.
"These estimates are based on the assumption that Ukrainian air defenses will eventually be able to counter jet-powered drones more effectively, but the shortage of interceptors for ballistic missiles will remain a significant problem," the company said in a press release published Thursday.
Dragon Capital recalled that, taking into account the initial consequences of the escalation, it cut its forecast for real GDP growth in 2026 by 0.5 percentage points (p.p.) in early August, to 1.0%, but the latest developments, in particular the expansion of the range of targets attacked by the enemy, indicate that the negative impact on the economy will be more substantial.
A significant part of Ukraine's territory where major industrial assets, including metallurgical enterprises, are concentrated is within the range of ballistic missiles, it said. Although damaged production assets can likely be repaired, the threat of repeated strikes will prevent steelmakers from resuming full-scale operations.
"We believe that grain exports by sea may resume next year as a result of a diplomatic agreement similar to the 'grain corridor' that operated in 2022-2023. However, reaching an agreement covering a broader range of facilities, including the widely discussed 'energy truce,' appears unlikely," the press release said.
According to Dragon Capital, a blockade of Black Sea ports could reduce real GDP by 2.2%, provided that agricultural exports are partially redirected to alternative routes, particularly to Danube ports. If grain exports by sea are unblocked before the start of the spring sowing campaign, these losses could be reduced by 1.5 p.p., to 0.7%.
However, another 1.5% of GDP will be lost due to the shutdown of steel production and, consequently, a reduction in iron ore mining, since it is impossible to redirect these shipments to export under conditions in which the seaports are blocked, the release said.
As reported, the World Bank recently downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's economic growth in 2027 from 4% to 1.5%, while maintaining its estimate for growth this year at 1.2%.
At the end of September, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's GDP growth in 2026 to 1.5% and in 2027 to 2.5%.
Economy and Environment Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said at the end of September that he was allowing for a downward revision of the 2027 GDP growth forecast by 0.3-0.5 p.p. from the already incorporated pessimistic scenario (from 1.3% to 0.8-1%) and for 2026 to 0.5%, compared with the current forecast of 1.6%.
The National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its estimate for real GDP growth this year to 1.1-1.2%, compared with its estimate of 1.8% at the end of July this year.

Aliyev’s foreign policy messages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:16:00 UTC
20:16:00 KST

Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev (AA File Photo)
Ilham Aliyev’s speech at the 8th Congress of the New Azerbaijan Party on Oct. 2 was noteworthy not only in terms of Azerbaijan’s domestic political agenda, but also for understanding Baku’s foreign policy line.
The most widely discussed parts of the speech were the messages directed outward. His statements that “no one should interfere in our affairs,” that “they should not stick their noses into our way of life,” that “we do not need a patron,” that “we have never played a double game,” and that Azerbaijan had acquired its weapons using its own resources quickly gave rise to various interpretations. In particular, on social media in Türkiye, interpretations that these remarks were directed at Ankara came to the fore.
However, there is an important question here: Should we read a political speech solely through the words themselves, or should we also consider the developments that immediately preceded those words?
When Aliyev’s speech is considered as a whole, a broader framework emerges. The president was explaining Azerbaijan’s determination to make independent decisions, its position against external interference, and the country’s understanding of security. He regards ideological security as important as physical security and emphasizes that, particularly in the age of the internet, cyberattacks and artificial intelligence, externally directed influences constitute a new area of risk for the state.
Yet in politics, chronology is often at least as important as the words themselves.
Just three days before Aliyev’s Oct. 2 speech, on Sept. 29, an Azerbaijani delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev was in Tehran. Mustafayev met with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and subsequently held a meeting with Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. During the meetings, relations between the two countries, regional developments and, in particular, security issues in the context of attacks against Iran were discussed. The Azerbaijani side also explicitly stated that its territory had not been used against Iran.
This meeting does not mean that Azerbaijan-Iran relations are poor. On the same day, the two sides spoke of friendship, good-neighborly relations and cooperation in the fields of economic and trade relations, transportation and energy. However, Aliyev’s speech that followed immediately afterward led some of his remarks to be read within a different political context.
Especially when Rezaei’s statements in previous years regarding Azerbaijan’s security policy, its relations with Israel and the United States, the Zangezur Corridor and regional balances are taken into consideration, Baku’s emphasis that “we make our own decisions” becomes more meaningful.
Aliyev’s statement that “we bought all our weapons with our own money; no one gave us weapons for free” is also noteworthy in this context. The emphasis that Azerbaijan built its security and defense capabilities with its own resources can be seen as a direct response to claims of external patronage or political tutelage.
Likewise, the message that “there are two superpowers: the United States and China. We have strategic agreements with both” can be read as a foreign-policy formula conveying that Azerbaijan is not a political extension of any particular center of power. Baku’s approach is not to take sides with one party, but to establish relations with different centers of power on the basis of its own interests.
Relations between Azerbaijan and Türkiye are not limited to day-to-day political statements. The alliance between the two countries has been institutionalized in the fields of defense, energy, transportation and security. Therefore, stronger grounds would be needed to regard the message that “we do not want outside interference” as a warning directed specifically at Türkiye.
Another important aspect of the Oct. 2 speech was the emphasis that Azerbaijan does not “play a double game.” This statement summarizes the foundation of Baku’s foreign-policy approach in recent years: working simultaneously with different centers of power while not allowing any of them to become decisive over Azerbaijan’s domestic and foreign-policy decisions.
For this reason, reading the speech simply as a “message to Türkiye” narrows the picture too much, in my view. Likewise, it would not be accurate to link all of the harsh statements to a single country. The broader thesis put forward by Aliyev is this: Azerbaijan now wants to act on the basis of its own strength, its own decisions and its own national interests.
Yet in politics, sometimes the address of a message is revealed not so much by the message itself as by what happened before it.
When the contacts that took place in Tehran on Sept. 29, Rezaei’s previous statements, Azerbaijan’s sensitivities regarding regional security, and the discussions over way of life that followed immediately afterward are considered together, it becomes possible to offer a different reading of why the Oct. 2 speech was framed in such a strong tone.
This does not mean that the remarks were directed at a particular party. That is precisely the nature of diplomatic messages: Sometimes no name is mentioned, yet the political chronology speaks for itself.
*Leman Abdulla is a Baku-based journalist.

Open an office in Ukraine, officer tells defence firms
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:14:26 BST
20:14:26 KST

Companies that want their equipment used by Ukrainian units should put staff and an office inside the country and begin by asking soldiers what the problem is, the chief unmanned systems officer of the 2nd Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Oleksii Krymeniuk, whose corps is known as Khartiia and numbers up to 35,000 personnel across formations ranging from infantry to uncrewed systems units, was asked how feedback from operators reaches developers and what makes the cycle work.
His answer put the burden squarely on the supplier instead of on the units doing the fighting. “The main actor in this kind of feedback loop and in this kind of conversation between the unit and the industry is the industry, because this unit is constantly fighting, and unfortunately we don’t have enough time and enough resources to communicate and to ping pong and to talk to this industry,” he said.
Turning up a couple of times a year for a demonstration does not count, in his view. “They should hire the guys in Ukraine, have a Ukrainian office, and they should constantly communicate about the challenges that that unit can encounter, because some challenges that you think are challenges in Ukraine, they are not challenges, and some challenges you even didn’t hear,” he said.
He was candid about the companies that arrive with a solution already decided. “I’ve seen some companies that came to us, they propose some solutions to some problems, but for us it’s not a problem. They just want to sell us something, and they want to get this kind of approved by Ukrainian unit sign, and then it would be much easier for them to sell their products in the international market,” he said.
The example he reached for was the first-person-view drone, the product most often carried into Ukraine by visiting firms. “I’ve seen a number of companies that came to us trying to sell us FPV drones, but we have an enormous number of companies inside of Ukraine that already sell us these drones, and they’re much cheaper than the drones that we can get from international markets,” he said.
Companies willing to work that way should expect frank conversations and not take them personally. “Some of these words, they couldn’t be very polite, because sometimes it could be very rough and straightforward as any military. But it’s not that we don’t want to help you,” he said, explaining that there is simply not time for a longer version of the conversation.
His own corps has met industry halfway by standing up a small team whose only job is talking to companies and sorting what is relevant from what is not, since the number of firms now approaching units has become very large. “So it’s a two-way situation,” he said.
Asked what advice he would give a national armaments director, he returned to where equipment gets proved. “First of all, you should buy some stuff that is tested in Ukraine and fully combat tested. Not the guys who came to a very safe zone, made a couple of flights there, and say okay, it’s completely tested in Ukraine. I think it should be truly tested on the front line,” he said.
His second point was about what a buyer should be planning for. “I think there is still a belief in the decisive battle as a concept, that we can buy very expensive stuff and it will be one battle and you will win,” he said. “But from the experience of Ukraine, and from history, each war is a war of attrition, and if you can achieve mass production, mass usage of it on the ground, you’ll be successful.”
Several of the companies on the panel described doing precisely what he asked for. Helsing has around fifty people in an office in Ukraine, Ark Robotics has seventy per cent of its workforce in the country with teams embedded in frontline units, and Havoc also keeps people there.

Russia says reports of second case linked to Siberian plague lab are false
MOSCOW, Oct 8 - Russia's health regulator denied on Thursday that someone had fallen ill after coming into contact with a worker at a plague research laboratory in Siberia who died last week.
In a statement published by Russian news agencies, the regulator denied what it called "fake information circulating on social media regarding a second case of illness".

Russian authorities say there is no risk of an epidemic breaking out, but their response so far has failed to allay international concerns.
The WHO said on Wednesday it had asked Russia to verify "media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause".
The WHO based its request on two reports - one by Russian outlet starhit.ru, which mostly covers celebrity news, and the other on a story citing unnamed Russian media from a British newspaper, the Daily Mail. REUTERS

EU debt could hit €1 trillion by 2027 as spending errors rise, auditors warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:13:48 UTC
20:13:48 KST

EU auditors said 3.8% of the bloc's spending last year breached funding rules, warning that borrowing could hit €1 trillion by 2027 and that the next long-term budget risks repeating the flaws of the COVID-era recovery fund, as the Commission defended its controls.
The European Union's financial watchdog has flagged swelling debt and a rising spending error rate in its latest report, released on Thursday.
It urged policymakers haggling over the 2028-2034 budget to avoid the weaknesses of the pandemic-era stimulus scheme that the proposed budget would largely mirror, while the European Commission argued that robust checks keep its money safe.
The European Court of Auditors (ECA), the EU's independent external auditor, estimated that 3.8% of last year's EU budget spending, excluding the recovery fund, breached EU or national funding rules, up from 3.6% in 2024 and well above its 2% threshold for error.
The figure does not measure fraud, though the auditors separately reported 17 suspected fraud cases to EU authorities.
While the accounts again received a clean opinion, EU budget spending received an adverse one, for a seventh consecutive year, meaning errors were material and widespread.
Error rates were highest in cohesion funding for jobs, growth and regional development, up from 5.7% to 6.6%, and in agriculture and the environment, up from 2.6% to 3.9%.
The European Commission, which oversees the EU budget, put its own cohesion estimate at 2.3%, but the auditors said its figures were "likely to be underestimated".
The Commission said on Thursday that the error rate was "comparable" to the previous year's and "significantly lower" than in 2023 and 2022, when the auditors placed it at 5.6% and 4.2% respectively.
Its estimates and the auditors' "are not directly comparable due to their distinct mandates," it added, citing €9 billion in preventive and corrective measures last year, and an estimated final error rate below 2% for cost-based programmes after corrections.
Debt heading for €1 trillion
Outstanding EU borrowing jumped by more than 20% to €738.9 billion last year and could reach €1 trillion by 2027, the auditors said, largely because of the NextGenerationEU (NGEU) recovery package.
NGEU debt must be repaid between 2028 and 2058.
For the 2028-2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF), the EU's next long-term budget, the Commission has proposed a fixed €24 billion a year to repay debt raised for NGEU grants, with interest paid first.
However, interest alone could be around €93 billion over seven years, more than half the €168 billion total.
"Expected NGEU borrowing costs for the current MFF remain double the initial estimates," the auditors wrote, noting that "the Commission has not published an overall repayment strategy for NGEU until 2058".
Liabilities backed by the EU budget, mostly loans including those to Ukraine, could reach up to €664 billion by 2027.
If borrowers fail to repay, the Commission can call on member states for extra cash.
Recovery fund lessons
The Commission's almost €2 trillion proposal for the next MFF would channel much of its money through national and regional plans largely modelled on the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF), NGEU's centrepiece, which pays out when governments hit agreed milestones and targets rather than reimbursing costs.
Yet nine of the 37 RRF grant payments made last year breached the stipulated rules and conditions, including requirements on milestones and targets, public procurement and state aid.
"The Commission has nevertheless made the corresponding payments," the report said.
In its response, the Commission said that RRF spending "carries a low level of risk", as it checks milestones before paying and "does not pay all or part of the financial contribution" if it finds they were not met.
Some governments were allowed to water down their commitments, the auditors found.
Of 32 changes examined, 29 lacked sufficient evidence, with 13 of 20 milestones and targets changed after payment was requested.
"This poses the risk that countries could receive EU money for delivering less than originally promised," the ECA warned.
More than €122 billion, over a third of the RRF's grants, remained unpaid going into its final year.
Only France, Austria and Croatia had received 80% or more of their grants.
"Ambitious budgets demand equally ambitious safeguards," said ECA President Tony Murphy, urging the EU to "learn from experience" if it switches to paying for milestones rather than costs.
Pressure on national budgets
New borrowing under the Commission's plans could also put pressure on national treasuries.
"Such planned borrowing may require member states to increase national contributions to service the debt amid already strained budgets," Murphy wrote.
France's 10-year borrowing costs hit their highest level since 2002 last week, while International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva on Wednesday urged high-debt advanced economies to adopt credible deficit-cutting plans.
Germany, Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden, all net contributors to the EU budget, want several hundred billion euros cut from the Commission's current proposal, a call they renewed last month.
Seventeen others, including Spain and Italy, want a more ambitious budget to protect farm and regional funding.
"At a time when virtually all member states are undertaking painful fiscal consolidation, the EU budget cannot be an exception," the six "frugal" leaders said in August, but Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pushed back on Tuesday.
Aware of "the difficult budgetary situation in Member States", she told the European Parliament: "I would like to caution against large cuts. It would risk cutting deep into critical priorities that we all together have agreed on."
She also called for new EU revenue sources, saying "we have to do the hard work on the revenue side".
Most governments want a deal this year ahead of elections in 2027, including the first round of France's presidential election on 18 April, which EU diplomats are calling a "political minefield".
Leaders will discuss the budget's financing at a Brussels summit on 15-16 October.
Without new revenue, the auditors warned, the EU budget could fall significantly short, forcing capitals to pay in more or scale back its ambitions.

Canadian author Anne Carson received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature
Kyiv • UNN
Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. The committee recognized her bold creative work.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded to Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson. The Nobel Committee announced this on October 8, UNN reports.
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature has been awarded to Canadian author Anne Carson "for her bold and inventive oeuvre which, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, creates new forms for contemporary literature"
This year's Nobel Prize laureate Anne Carson was born in 1950 in Toronto, Canada. In 1981, she published her doctoral dissertation in the journal "Classics " under the title "Odi et Amo Ergo Sum" and throughout her career combined writing poetry with translation work and teaching at various universities.
"Almost all of her literary work is focused on the intersection of the philologist's obsession with words and the poet's quest for new meaning. She herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work," the committee noted.
The new Nobel Prize laureate Anne Carson published a series of distinguished works in the 1990s. Among them was "The Glass Essay" in the collection "Glass, Irony, and God" (1995), "which demonstrates the potential of the long poem, where the boundaries between genres become blurred."
In the same decade, another work was published that is often called Carson's greatest, titled "Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse" (1998).
"Throughout her career as an author, Carson explores the possibilities of writing with a light touch, a process through which the literary sketch has become particularly valuable to her. Her collaboration with visual artists and choreographers, as well as with opera and theatre directors, demonstrates the freedom with which she approaches literary expectations and systems of rules. This lies at the heart of the outstanding significance her work since the 1990s has had for the international artistic and literary scene," the committee's statement says.

The European Commission said Thursday
that it is in favour of granting Italy's request to use the
national escape clause under which EU allows greater budget
leeway for investments in defence and energy.
                                    
"We received a request for activation from Italy on September
11, and our assessment concluded that, in Italy's case, the
activation of the clause does not actually jeopardize fiscal
sustainability in the medium term," a Commission spokesperson
said.
                                    
"Our assessment is positive.
                                    
"The dossier now goes to the Council, which will have one month
to give its final approval; only then can the clause be
officially activated for Italy".
                                    
Originally the escape clause, brought in last year following
Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, gave member States the
option of running extra deficit of up to 1.5% of GDP for three
years for defence investments only.
                                    
But Premier Meloni's government successfully lobbied the
European Commission to allow for extra spending on energy
investments too after the Iran war led to a spike in fuel
prices.
                                    
In August Giorgetti said the government would request the
maximum level of flexibility for energy security of 0.6% of GDP
and 0.9% for defence.
                                    
Under pressure from US President Donald Trump, Italy and its
NATO allies have pledged to increase defence and security
spending up to 5% of GDP.

Government establishes explosives factory spatial plan in Western Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Government establishes explosives factory spatial plan in Western Estonia
The government has approved a national designated spatial plan for a defense industry park in Piirsalu, Lääne-Nigula Municipality. The state will invest more than €6 million in developing the park's basic infrastructure.
An explosives plant operated by state-owned company Hexest Materials is planned for Piirsalu.
According to current plans, the explosives plant will begin production in 2028. The investment required to establish production is estimated at €150 million and the plant is expected to create approximately 75 jobs in Piirsalu.
"Establishing RDX explosives production in Estonia is strategically necessary. Against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine, the need to expand Europe's defense industry production capacity has increased dramatically and NATO countries currently face a shortage of explosives production capacity. The plant to be built in Piirsalu will give Estonia an opportunity to help alleviate this shortage," Defense Minister Martin Herem said.
"The plant's impact will not be limited to national defense. New jobs and additional economic activity will also generate additional tax revenue for the region. At the same time, the state is investing more than €6 million in developing the park's basic infrastructure," he added.
The national designated spatial plan takes into account questions and proposals raised by local residents and other stakeholders, the Government Communication Office said. One of the key conditions for the development is compliance with environmental and safety requirements.
For example, to address concerns raised by local residents during public discussions, it has been decided that waste from explosives production will not be burned in the open air during normal operations, as is common practice in European countries. Instead, a specialized enclosed incinerator will be purchased.
The company operating in the area will also be required to continue monitoring the ecological condition of the Piirsalu River and to monitor water levels and quality in drinking water wells near the industrial park, in cooperation with the local community and Lääne-Nigula Municipality.
In addition to establishing the defense industry park, the Ministry of Defense and its agencies will support development in the Piirsalu area. Plans include supporting the construction of a pedestrian and bicycle path along the Risti–Kuijõe highway in Piirsalu village. The ministry is also prepared to support the establishment of a community resilience center and a public shelter in the village.
Piirsalu is the third area where a national designated spatial plan has been approved for the development of a defense industry park. Such plans have previously been approved for Ermistu in Pärnu County and Põhja-Kiviõli in Ida-Viru County. The planning process is also continuing for the Aidu area in Ida-Viru County.

How Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' reshaped Lebanon 3 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:07:55 UTC
20:07:55 KST

Breadcrumb
Hezbollah and the 'Gaza support front': cost of ongoing Israeli war on Lebanon, three years on
The third anniversary of Hezbollah launching what it describes as "the support front for Gaza" falls on 8 October 2023. Its repercussions continue for Lebanon, amid ongoing Israeli attacks and an expanded occupation over more than 60 villages and towns.
Today, many in Lebanon remain afraid of a third round after the September 2024 and March 2026 Israeli offensives.
On the third anniversary, Hezbollah issued a statement, saying: "The enemy has failed to eliminate Hamas, the resistance factions or the people of Gaza, and has failed to achieve peace, or even a temporary truce and stability. The situation remains open to developments whose repercussions will extend beyond the Gaza Strip to the future of the entire region, the Palestinian cause, and international security and peace."
"Hezbollah in Lebanon, which believes in the justness of the Palestinian cause and does not hesitate to support its resisting and oppressed people, renews its strong condemnation of the blatant Zionist genocide that exposes the false values of the international community and holds the US administration and Western countries that remain silent about condemning Zionist crimes responsible, whether those involving genocide or crimes against humanity," it further said.
"We stand firmly with all these resistance factions so that they remain steadfast and united around their vision and position against the enemy's project, its supporters and those complicit with it. We also warn the region's rulers that remaining silent, accommodating and flattering the enemy and its allies will only lead to the undermining of their authority, weakening them and enabling the enemy to determine the future of their countries and peoples," it added.
Victims of the two support wars
Hezbollah's 'Gaza support front' began on 8 October 2023 and was initially confined to south Lebanon. But the geographical scope, consequences, human losses, and economic cost gradually expanded, particularly after September 2024.
More than 8,900 people have been killed and more than 30,000 injured by Israel since 8 October 2023, while the forced displacement of thousands of families continues, whether because their homes were damaged, their villages were occupied or destroyed, or some were destroyed by more than 90%.
Additionally, financial losses are estimated at more than $27 billion, mostly in the south, as well as damage in the Bekaa and Baalbek-Hermel in eastern Lebanon, Beirut, the southern suburbs of Beirut, and other areas to varying degrees.
The war also brought radical changes.
First for Hezbollah, with the loss of its first- and second-tier leaders, most notably its Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September 2024 and his successor Hashem Safieddine on 3 October 2024.
It was also subjected to one of the largest cybersecurity operations, with the explosions of "pagers" and "walkie-talkies" on 17 and 18 September 2024.
The Islamic group found its military capabilities significant declined, while it also lost key supply lines, most notably the Syrian route, after the fall of the Assad regime on 8 December 2024, and its external support, particularly Iranian support, decreased.
Moreover, Israel is targeting Hezbollah's financing networks, foremost among them the Al-Qard Al-Hassan Association.
Hezbollah's political position was also impacted with a decline in its influence in state centres and institutions with the beginning of the new era under President Joseph Aoun on 9 January 2025, which came with broad US support, sovereignty-focused slogans and historic decisions.
The most important of these decisions was the cabinet's approval of a measure to restrict weapons in Lebanon and its tasking of the Lebanese army with drawing up a plan to implement this, in August 2025, with progress recorded in implementation south of the Litani River.
This came before Hezbollah's security and military activities were banned on 2 March, after it supported Iran by launching six missiles from Lebanon at Israel, following the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, along with other decisions that also affected the Iranian side.
The choice of launching "support fronts", for Gaza and Iran, also affected Hezbollah's alliances, particularly through the "disengagement" between it and the Free Patriotic Movement headed by MP Gebran Bassil, as well as its relationship with the Amal Movement headed by Nabih Berri, amid differences and varying views that emerged in approaching the issue.
Hezbollah and Amal have continued to seek through ongoing meetings to maintain coordination and cooperation, amid some tensions in southern areas associated with both sides.
This followed media reports about attempts by Hezbollah to establish positions and launch platforms in some towns politically associated with the Amal Movement.
Another major shift is that Lebanon and Israel began direct negotiations for the first time on 14 April 2026, resulting in the signing of a framework agreement in Washington on 26 June, and subsequently encouraged political and media discourse calling for normalisation and peace with Israel, marking a major breaking of taboos.
This was particularly evident with Lebanese channels conducting interviews with Israelis and showing blatant bias towards Israeli narratives, eventually leading to direct cooperation between a Lebanese platform and an Israeli one.
Addressing the cost of the ongoing war for Lebanon, Nasser Yassin, director of the Beirut branch of the Arab Centre for Research and Policy Studies, told The New Arab that estimates indicate that the cost since 8 October until today has exceeded $27 billion.
These losses are divided between direct losses related to the destruction and damage to homes, residences, buildings and infrastructure, as well as losses related to the agricultural, commercial and economic sectors, among others.
Yassin noted that most losses are concentrated in the south, alongside damage also recorded in the southern suburbs of Beirut and the Bekaa in eastern Lebanon.
He pointed out that the number of homes destroyed or requiring complete demolition in this war had reached about 132,000, more than those recorded during the July and August 2006 war, when the number of destroyed homes reached around 12,000.
He also said there are currently about 65 occupied villages and towns in the south where destruction and land levelling are taking place continuously.
Yassin was environment minister in the government of former Prime Minister Najib Mikati, during which indirect negotiations with Israel led to a ceasefire agreement on 27 November 2024.
However, Israel violated it thousands of times while insisting on remaining at five southern positions.
The expanded offensive then resumed on 2 March, increasing Israeli control over southern villages and sites.
Yassin noted the 27 November 2024 agreement was based on Resolution 1701, which brought an end to the Israeli offensive against Lebanon in summer 2006.
Under the agreement, Lebanon affirmed its commitment to the deployment of the Lebanese army and the state's exercise of sovereignty through its own forces in the south, particularly south of the Litani River, while Israel was to withdraw from positions it occupied at the time.
"Today, the situation is different. There is a security zone, Israeli occupation and control over about 65 villages, and an area that Israel has completely eradicated and destroyed. Therefore, the discussion is now taking place in a different context," he said.
As for whether the negotiations could produce the anticipated solution, Yassin acknowledged it is unclear whether the negotiations currently underway will lead to an outcome.
However, Lebanon has no option other than negotiations to achieve a withdrawal, whether directly, indirectly or through Arab or international mediators.
Yassin said the negotiating performance should be better and should primarily place Israel's withdrawal at the top of any framework, since Israel is occupying another country's land, namely Lebanon, thereby violating international law.
Therefore, he added, the withdrawal should not be linked to measures and issues as happened in the framework agreement, even though these are important.
Domestic repercussions
Regarding the domestic repercussions, particularly for Hezbollah, political writer Khaldoun Al Sharif told The New Arab that "[the support front] led to major Israeli breaches that affected Hezbollah, beginning with the pager and walkie-talkie operations and the assassination of Nasrallah and ending with the occupation of a large area of the south."
Al Sharif noted that "the assassination of Nasrallah, the symbolic leader of Hezbollah, along with the assassination of leaders in the Radwan Force, the party's elite force, and military officials, fundamentally changed the equation. This included the leadership, capabilities, military capacity and material resources."
At the popular level, Al Sharif does not believe the support for the war changed much.
There had been no national, international or governmental support for the party's constituency, which led to its continued attachment to the party.
He also noted that it is impossible to assess changes at this level or among the opposing Shia constituency because the usual measure is parliamentary elections, which were postponed because of the war.
According to Al Sharif, the war inevitably affected domestic alliances because political forces in Lebanon only agree on specific interests, rather than principles or values.
"The Amal Movement remains committed to its alliance with the party because the fall of the duo, in one way or another, would lead to the Shiite community being left alone. Therefore, the issue of Shiite unity remains fundamental for both of them regardless of the repercussions," he said.
Al Sharif also said the decisions taken by the government in August 2025 and March 2026 have not been implemented to date, adding that what matters is implementation.
However, he noted there is no doubt that these decisions were taken after the balance of power changed, particularly following the assassination of Nasrallah.
Al Sharif argued that there is a division between two camps in Lebanon, with only a small percentage of people in the middle: "the Iranian camp," which has been left alone, and the US camp and its allies.
He said that before the situation in the Gulf and Iran becomes clear, it is difficult to determine where Lebanon will go.
"If Iran is crushed, we will face a new equation. If it is not crushed, the equation will be different. Therefore, today we are in a state of 'status quo', particularly since the latest round of negotiations held in Rome last August. Whether we like it or not, Lebanon has become tied to the existing regional equations and the international equations that will impose new balances of power in this region," he remarked.
Hezbollah alliances in decline
Mahend Al Hajj Ali, a researcher at the Malcolm Kerr-Carnegie Middle East Centre, told The New Arab that the war weakened and destabilised the political alliances Hezbollah had built since 2005.
Presently, there is a threat emerging against the alliance it also established with the Amal Movement.
This is one of the repercussions at the political level, in addition to its relationship with Christian, Sunni and Druze forces that had been allied with it but are no longer as they were and have become distributed among a group of regional powers that are not allied with the party.
Al Hajj Ali said that at the social and demographic level, the repercussions have been enormous for the community that supports Hezbollah, namely Lebanese Shias, who, as a result of the war, have been subjected to ethnic cleansing that displaced them from their homeland across a large part of Jabal Amel in southern Lebanon.
Currently, the other part north of the Litani River is also exposed to ethnic cleansing, and in his view it has begun and could continue if a third war breaks out, which is very possible.
Al Hajj Ali also highlighted the changes that have taken place at the regional level, including the change in the situation in Syria and the collapse of the Syrian regime, which had repercussions for Lebanon and Hezbollah.
He also pointed to the establishment of a new era and a new government in Lebanon, following a line opposed to that of Hezbollah and based on the principle that weapons come first.

Buried answers: Gaza families' unbearable wait for missing continues amid three years of Israel's genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:06:06 UTC
20:06:06 KST

As the Gaza war enters its fourth year, thousands of Palestinian families remain without answers about loved ones who disappeared amid three years of Israeli attacks and destruction.
The scale of the task is immense.
The UN estimates the war has generated millions of tonnes of debris across Gaza, while Palestinian Civil Defense estimates that more than 8,000 people remain missing beneath the rubble.
For many families, even knowing where to search is impossible. Missing relatives could be buried beneath destroyed buildings, detained or otherwise unaccounted for, leaving families unable to hold a burial or know whether to keep hoping for their return.
Pat Griffiths, spokesperson for the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Jerusalem, described seeing families gather at hospitals when buses carrying released Palestinian detainees arrive in Gaza.
Some hold photographs of missing relatives, not knowing whether the person they are searching for has been detained or killed.
ICRC psychologists describe what those families experience as "ambiguous loss.”
"You don't know if your loved one you haven't heard from ... is alive or if they've been killed. You don't know if they're detained or not," he told Anadolu.
"Thousands of people live with this limbo. This pain of not knowing what to do or how to feel exactly. They're stuck."
Amani Al Naouq, ICRC spokesperson in Gaza, said families repeatedly bring the organization the same question.
"We just want to know what happened to them," she recalled them saying. "'If they are dead, we can be relieved. But the fact that we don't know if they are dead or alive' – that's one of the most difficult things for them."
Al Naouq told Anadolu that some families keep contacting the ICRC even when they know there may be no immediate answer, simply because they need somewhere to share what is weighing on them.
Others, she said, eventually begin to accept that a missing relative is dead despite having no confirmation.
The uncertainty is unfolding amid an enormous recovery challenge, with much of Gaza's built environment destroyed or damaged and human remains believed to lie within the ruins alongside unexploded ordnance, hazardous materials and potential evidence relevant to investigations into international crimes.
The cost of removing and managing more than 68 million metric tons of debris in Gaza exceeds $1.7 billion, according to the April 2026 Gaza Strip Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment by the European Union, UN and World Bank.
The effort also requires access to heavy machinery and specialized equipment, along with consistent fuel supplies – conditions that are currently far from being met.
Al Naouq said recovery teams have extremely limited heavy machinery, sometimes relying on one or two excavators contracted from private suppliers, while much of the work is carried out with small equipment and by hand.
With limited capacity, teams depend heavily on families to pinpoint where relatives were last seen – the building, the room and who was with them. That forces families to relive moments when they were unable to reach or save their loved ones, Al Naouq said.
"It's actually back again an open wound for these families," she said.
Griffiths, who recently spent a week in Gaza, described seeing "kilometers and kilometers just mountains of rubble," much of it posing dangers from unexploded remnants of war.
The ICRC supports the rental of two excavators for recovery teams, he said, but that is "a drop in the ocean."
"The scale of the task ahead of them – it's daunting. It's huge."
Griffiths said the problem is compounded by access restrictions, with search-and-recovery teams unable to reach much of the Gaza Strip to carry out their work safely.
DNA testing is also currently unavailable in Gaza, according to the ICRC.
Forensic teams instead rely on information including age, sex, height, previous injuries, dental information, clothing, personal belongings and where remains were recovered.
But time can erase those clues through decomposition and skeletonization, while moving rubble can separate remains from their original location.
"The more time passes, the harder identifying the deceased gets," Griffiths said.
Drawing on ICRC experience in conflicts including Syria, Iraq, Afghanistan and the Balkans, he said searches for missing people can continue for years or even decades.
"It's one of the tragedies of armed conflict," he said.
Mayy El Sheikh, of the UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory, recalled interviewing a 37-year-old woman with a disability whose husband remained missing after an attack on his family home in northern Gaza in 2023. The couple have a 5-year-old son.
Almost every member of her husband's family was killed, El Sheikh said. Some were recovered, but her husband was not.
The woman believes she knows the mound of rubble containing him but cannot reach it because it lies beyond the deployment line for Israeli forces – the so-called "yellow line."
Recalling all of this was "excruciatingly painful" for her, El Sheikh said. "She felt that she couldn't support her son recovering as well because he has no grave to visit, and that she failed her husband, that she was not able to honor him."
"For her, the war is not over until her husband is found," she added.
Other families have believed missing relatives were dead only to later recognize them alive in images or videos from Israeli prisons, El Sheikh said.
"It's that level of uncertainty, not knowing even if your loved one is alive or dead," she said.
Concerns over the fate of potential evidence within Gaza's rubble have recently been raised by UN Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territory Francesca Albanese, who warned that the removal, crushing and relocation of debris in areas under Israeli military control could destroy human remains and potential evidence of alleged international crimes.
El Sheikh also warned about what may be disappearing as Gaza's ruins are disturbed.
"It is almost inevitable that evidence is being lost, damaged, or disturbed as we speak," she said, citing the scale of destruction, access restrictions, reported rubble removal and crushing, and shortages of heavy machinery and forensic identification capacity.
She said large parts of Gaza remain inaccessible to independent observers and investigators, particularly areas under Israeli military control, making it difficult to establish what is happening to human remains and potential evidence there.
El Sheikh said there have also been repeated reports since the announcement of the ceasefire of remains being returned to Palestinian authorities without information that could be critical to identification and establishing what happened.
"They have returned remains to the Palestinian authorities, sometimes even partial remains with no identification and no clarity on where they were recovered or how they were killed," she said.
Griffiths said that if remains are moved with rubble, their original location – an important piece of identification evidence – can be lost, while remains may also become fragmented,
Srinivasan Muralidhar, chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, said the commission has received reports of rubble removal and the possibility of evidence being destroyed.
"We are concerned that the removal of rubble could result in evidence getting lost forever," he said.
Muralidhar compared evidence gathering to assembling a jigsaw puzzle, saying material recovered from the rubble could complement witness testimony and medical and forensic evidence.
Its loss would not prevent investigators from establishing alleged crimes, he said, but could leave important gaps.
Its importance goes beyond potential prosecutions, Muralidhar added.
"In international law, there is a known concept of the right to the truth. Every family wants to know what exactly happened."
For relatives who have waited years without recovering their loved ones, information about what happened can be "very, very valuable as a piece of memory and most importantly for closure," he said.
Griffiths said that resolving the fate of Gaza's missing will require greater humanitarian access and significantly more resources for search-and-recovery teams.
He called for more heavy machinery, including excavators, to be allowed into Gaza so teams can scale up recovery operations, while also stressing the need for safe access to areas they currently cannot reach.
"Humanitarian access for the purpose of search and recovery work – it's also really important," he said.
Muralidhar also called for international cooperation to accelerate the process.
"We have to have cooperation across countries to help clear the rubble quicker," he said, stressing the importance of not creating more rubble.
“This is a huge task right in front of us, and if the attacks do not stop now, things might get further worse and go beyond a point when we'll all be just shrugging our shoulders and watching helplessly,” he warned.
For one family encountered by Griffiths and Al Naouq, that answer eventually came.
The ICRC has supported the establishment of a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, part of efforts to preserve information about remains that cannot immediately be identified.
Griffiths said that after remains are recovered, forensic teams seek to collect as much identifying information as possible and create a corresponding file. When identification is not possible, the remains can be laid to rest in an individual grave marked with a unique serial number linked to that information.
The ICRC is also supporting efforts to establish an information-sharing system between recovery teams, forensic authorities and those managing cemeteries so that information collected about remains is preserved for possible future identification.
The aim is to preserve both the dignity of the dead and the possibility of identifying them in the future, including if DNA testing eventually becomes available in Gaza.
During a visit to a cemetery for unidentified dead in Deir al-Balah, they met a young woman whose husband's remains had eventually been identified through forensic methods available in Gaza.
Griffiths recalled what finally having a grave meant to her.
"She could visit his grave, she could stand at his grave, to be near him," he said.
It gave her "a sense of closure, a way to mourn."
For thousands of families still searching for someone who disappeared during the war, even that remains out of reach.

Dozens Killed In Russian Strike On Passenger Buses In Kramatorsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:04:33 UTC
20:04:33 KST

KRAMATORSK, Ukraine -- Dozens of people were killed in a Russian strike on the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk on October 8, according to local authorities, a day after another deadly barrage killed at least 25 people across Ukraine.
The death toll from the Kramatorsk attack has risen to 33, with 18 others wounded, according to the latest reports from regional authorities and the prosecutor's office.
Footage taken by RFE/RL correspondent Serhiy Horbatenko, who visited the site shortly after the attack, showed two passenger buses burned out by the strike, with bodies strewn around the scene.
"The bodies are lying right in the middle of the road," the RFE/RL correspondent said while describing the aftermath of the deadly attack.
The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor's Office said the Russian strike hit two buses that were carrying passengers at the time of the attack.
The prosecutor's office said Russian forces likely used guided bombs to strike the vehicles.
The strike came a day after at least 25 people nationwide, including two in the capital Kyiv, were reported killed in the October 7 barrage.
The bombardment was part of near-daily attacks that have steadily increased in frequency and ferocity as the Kremlin struggles on the battlefield front line.
In Pryluky, about 150 kilometers east of Kyiv, rescuers searched through the rubble of a destroyed apartment building in northern Ukraine for survivors following a Russian missile attack on October 7 that killed 22 people, including five children.
Russian forces "destroyed" a residential building "as a birthday 'gift' to Putin," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post to X, calling it one of the "most vile" attacks in recent memory. He noted that the October 7 attacks across Ukraine occurred on the birthday of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
At least 10 other such buildings were damaged elsewhere, along with Ukraine's energy infrastructure, one of Moscow's other "key targets," he said.
"The fire was right in front of my eyes. There were explosions. I was screaming in my apartment. Extremely scary. I can't describe it," one woman, who gave her name as Lidiya, told Current Time at the scene in Pryluky.
"So many people have died. I knew everyone here," she added, holding back tears.
With a fifth wartime winter approaching, Russian strikes on Ukraine have become a daily occurrence.
Moscow has previously sought to pressure Kyiv into accepting its hard-line demands by attacking the country's energy infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid freezing temperatures.
Since this year, however, Kyiv has increasingly responded to Russian attacks with a campaign of long-range strikes targeting military and energy sites inside Russia and middle-range strikes targeting its key logistics in Ukraine's occupied eastern and southern regions.
According to monitoring Telegram channels, Ukrainian drones struck a Yandex data center in Russia's Ryazan region on October 8, causing a fire and forcing the company to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers.
Yandex, Russia's leading AI and technology company, confirmed the attack on its Sasovo hub, one of its five large data centers. It said it was restoring affected services.
Ukrainian forces also struck the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Bashkortostan on the same day, sparking a fire, according to Ukraine's military.
Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 399 Ukrainian drones overnight, Russia's Defense Ministry reported on October 8.

Cuban actors insist the show must go on despite blackouts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:04:24 UTC
20:04:24 KST

Cuban actors insist the show must go on despite blackouts
HAVANA, Oct 8 - When blackouts in an upscale neighborhood of Havana began approaching 24 hours a day, morale plummeted at one of the Cuban capital's many niche but celebrated theater groups.
"It became impossible for the actors to arrive on time; they were exhausted and struggling to cope," said Linda Soriano, director of theater group Impulso Teatro. "I told them they were free to leave."
But the group's members decided the show must go on — and they kept turning up.
Cuban theater, alongside music and ballet, has long been hailed as a cultural hallmark of an island with a tradition of promoting the arts that spans centuries.
However, many of the island's youth — actors, artists and musicians — have left the country in a record-breaking exodus since the COVID-19 pandemic.
Since January, when the US imposed a fuel blockade on Cuba in a bid to upend the communist-run government, those who remain have had to contend with blackouts spanning days, food, fuel and water shortages, and a lack of public transportation.
On a recent Friday evening, actors dripping with sweat pranced about the stage, voices echoing across a large room in a converted mansion in Havana's Vedado business district. Candles flickered outside the theater hall, while the inside was lit by an array of rechargeable lights in all shapes and sizes — similar to those found in many Cuban homes.
There was no electricity, no air conditioning, and no sound system. All the drama was dependent on the acting.
"What keeps us making theater is the determination to ensure ... that it does not die out," said 88-year-old Carlos Perez, a winner of Cuba's national theater prize and by far the oldest of this small company of 14 actors. "But it comes at a cost."
Many actors and stagehands work multiple jobs to make ends meet in a country where prices have soared alongside the plummeting local peso currency, Perez said.
"I don't know if I could have managed if I had been in their shoes at 25," he said.
Amanda Feijo, attending a recent performance at the makeshift theater, said the show had provided its own snippet of light amid all the darkness.
"To see that there is an audience seeking to nourish their souls, despite the truly lamentable situation unfolding right now," she said. "It is heartening." REUTERS

Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Canada’s Anne Carson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:04:18 UTC
20:04:18 KST

Nobel Prize in Literature awarded to Canada’s Anne Carson
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson on Thursday by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. Toronto-born Carson, 76, draws from ancient Greek and Roman literature for her works blending elements of poetry, essay and fiction. She will receive 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million) alongside the prestigious award.
Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in Literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature”.
Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win.
Toronto-born Carson draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction.
“She was very taken by surprise,” Carlberg said.
Her books include “Eros the Bittersweet”, a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel “Autobiography of Red”, “Men in the Off Hours”, a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy”, which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.
Carson also has translated works of classical Greek literature that, the Swedish Academy said, “may be regarded as independent works in their own right.” They include “If Not, Winter,” based on poem fragments by Sappho, Sophocles’ tragic plays “Electra” and "Antigone” and Euripides’s “Bakkhai.”
“Almost all her literary production has centered upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the literature committee.
Carson has taught classics at several North American universities and has lived in Iceland, where she and her husband, Robert Currie, were granted citizenship in 2022.
The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.
Last year, Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humour, won the Nobel Prize in Literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror”.
Read moreLaszlo Krasznahorkai: Hungary's 'master of apocalypse'
Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognised a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognised two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
This week ends with Friday's peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organisation.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

School protests, blockades resume in France despite PM’s promise to act
