Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:53:48 UTC
19:53:48 KST

Naval expansion propels India to world’s No. 2 arms importer – Russian think tank
India was the world’s second-largest arms importer in 2025, partly aided by a historically large naval buildout, according to a Russian think tank that tracks weapons purchases and military expenditures.
The South Asian nuclear power has been rapidly building up its armed forces following a brief clash with neighbor Pakistan last year, triggered by a terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir.
India’s identified military imports were worth $6.97 billion, or 5.83% of the global total, and the country is projected to retain the position through 2029, the Moscow-based Center for Analysis of World Arms Trade (CAWAT) said.
Poland came in first with $11.91 billion, while Australia was narrowly behind India at $6.96 billion.
Among the major Indian deliveries cited by CAWAT was the Russian-built frigate Tamal, which joined the Indian Navy in July 2025. Two more Project 11356 frigates are being built at India’s Goa Shipyard with assistance from Russian state arms exporter Rosoboronexport. 
India also commissioned the Vaghsheer, the sixth and final Kalvari-class submarine built by state-owned Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders under license from France’s Naval Group. The six-submarine program was valued at $3.6 billion, according to CAWAT.
The Indian Navy is undergoing its largest expansion in history, with plans to induct or commission 18 warships this year. 
New Delhi imported $25.44 billion worth of arms in the 2022-2025 period, placing it third behind Saudi Arabia and Qatar in CAWAT’s four-year rankings. Its annual imports rose from $3.87 billion in 2024 to $6.97 billion last year. 
The think tank projects India’s arms imports at $45.65 billion over 2026-2029, keeping the country in the second position. Poland is expected to remain at the top with $55.32 billion worth of imports, followed by Germany at $36.48 billion. The forecast is based on existing contracts, officially announced procurement plans, and expected tenders as of December 2025. 
Poland’s rise has been particularly sharp. Its arms imports climbed from $2.17 billion in 2022 to $11.91 billion in 2025, driven by major purchases including US-made Abrams tanks and South Korean K2 tanks.
CAWAT projects global arms imports at almost $633 billion over the 2026-2029 period, up 52.5% from in the preceding four years. The center expects Europe to take a larger share of global demand during the period.
The ranking covers identified commercial arms deliveries and does not include weapons supplied free of charge, including Western military aid to Ukraine.
CAWAT’s methodology differs from that of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI), which measures the volume of major weapons transfers using a trend-indicator value rather than their sale price. SIPRI says its figures should not be directly compared with the financial value of arms transfers.

====================================================================================================

Portuguese hospital lets pets visit owners on wards: a new model?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:53:08 UTC
19:53:08 KST

In northern and central Europe, pets stay outside hospitals. São João's flexible model unites clinical benefits and safety, with no infections yet. "There is too much fear," says the doctor who helped draft the project's rules.
Since 9 July, São João, one of Portugal's leading public university hospitals, has been opening the doors of its wards to visits from pets.
The "Pets and Company" project brings together different professionals from the One Health São João (source in Portuguese) programme, as well as from the Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance Prevention and Control Unit and the hospital's Humanisation service. The initiative is part of a strategy aimed at breaking isolation and relieving the exhaustion of prolonged hospital stays.
The therapeutic potential of animals is far from a recent discovery. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany have used them in psychiatric and physical rehabilitation treatments for humans since the 19th century. The term "pet therapy" (animal-assisted therapy) was scientifically recorded in the 1960s by a US psychologist who fortuitously discovered the healing benefits of these interventions.
In Portugal, trained and certified dogs for emotional support sessions have been working in hospitals for several years, including at São João, in partnership with volunteer handlers from associations.
On 30 May 2023, a 77-year-old patient admitted to Cascais Hospital, recovering from a haemorrhagic stroke, received a visit from her own dog, in a reunion that took place in an outdoor area of the health unit.
This unprecedented experience is now being expanded by São João through a comprehensive protocol created from scratch, which goes a step further and normalises the practice of bringing pets into inpatient areas, recognising them as part of the patient's immediate family and giving those who have been away from home for a long time moments of comfort under safe sanitary conditions.
What does the protocol say?
Visits are requested by the health professional (doctor or nurse) in charge of the patients, who is responsible for flagging each case, and they are not available to everyone in hospital. A tailored assessment is always made of the risks and benefits.
Once informed, the team responsible for the programme assesses whether there is a clinical need and whether the infection-control conditions at the chosen location allow the visit to go ahead. Other patients in the ward are also asked whether they feel comfortable with the presence of animals.
Once authorisation is given, the patient's family must submit a veterinary medical certificate proving that the animal's vaccinations and deworming are up to date and that it has behaviour compatible with the demands of remaining in a hospital setting.
"Any professional, from security staff to a doctor or nurse, who sees that something is not in line with the protocol can interrupt the visit," said Filipa Ceia, spokesperson for the One Health São João Group, to Euronews.
If the animal is "anxious" because of the "noise on the ward", appears "aggressive" or is "visibly dirty", the visit is "immediately called off", the infectious disease specialist and vet warns.
Dogs, cats and even "more exotic species" are allowed, as long as "all the conditions are met", says Filipa Ceia. While in hospital areas, the animal must be accompanied by an adult.
Each patient can enjoy these half-hour meetings once every seven days. The project gives priority to those who are terminally ill or in long-term hospitalisation.
To the team's surprise, it is male patients who have most often requested that their four-legged companions be allowed into the hospital, although the small sample does not allow for definitive conclusions. "Men may be more fragile when they are ill. They realise that there are things that really matter in life and want to have them close during their hospital stay," notes Ceia.
Benefits for patient and animal
Studies on interventions assisted by trained animals report clear improvements in patients' clinical condition: blood pressure falls and the production of hormones linked to stress and anxiety is inhibited. When the family pet is involved, there is "an even greater benefit", stresses Filipa Ceia.
Euronews followed the visit of Princesa, who went to São João for the second time in 15 days to ease the longing for her owner, António, who has been in hospital for three months. The dog was taken to the hospital by the patient's wife, who led her on the lead to the ward.
As soon as the lift doors opened, Princesa could not contain her excitement – and neither could António.
"My heart was pounding with joy. She is like family. She is like a daughter to me," confessed the 65-year-old man, who is undergoing rehabilitation because of balance and walking difficulties.
The diagnosis is still not confirmed, but doctors suspect he suffers from a rare blood disease. The reunion with the dog, who was given to him five years ago after being rescued from the street, is a balm for the soul.
"It makes me feel I want to walk better and everything. This is the joy a person gets," he said. These reunions bring "smiles, cooperation with treatment and an incentive to leave hospital", notes Filipa Ceia, who also identifies benefits for the animal itself and even for health professionals.
"Residual risk"
This initiative was launched at the beginning of July and, so far, no infections have been recorded.
The team behind the project wants to review the protocol at a later stage to correct any shortcomings. Given the procedures in place, a scenario involving "incidents" is nevertheless "highly unlikely", points out Filipa Ceia.
In northern and central Europe, infection-control and public-health rules are stricter. Assistance dogs are prioritised and, when visits by patients' own animals are authorised (usually for patients in palliative care), they take place in isolated facilities, namely in open courtyards or gardens adjoining the main building.
Take the example of Sint-Trudo Hospital in Sint-Truiden, Belgium. In July 2023, this health unit opened an independent pavilion (source in Portuguese), connected to but separate from the main building, so that terminal patients or those in long hospital stays could interact with their pets. The access (source in Portuguese) for the animals is via the outside, through a courtyard, and they are strictly forbidden, under any circumstances, from passing through the interior of the hospital.
Instead of erecting physical barriers with secondary structures, São João has drawn up a set of rules which, while maintaining clinical rigour, are part of an agile protocol shaped by scientific evidence.
"There is an excessive fear of zoonotic transmission which is not borne out by the studies," says Filipa Ceia. In fact, the infectious disease specialist notes, "it is easier for most diseases to be transmitted from human to human than from an animal to a human".
"Because we do everything we can to preserve safety and because, once they go home, patients will be living with their animals, the risk really is residual. We have to ask whether, in trying to mitigate the risk, we are not depriving patients of the benefit," she adds.
The boldness of São João lies not only in the balance between empathy and sanitary control, but also in its autonomy and ability to humanise care without waiting for lawmakers, unlike in Italy, for example, where the move was driven by decrees from regional governments.

Survey: 62% of Ukrainians believe neither side is currently winning war
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:53:00 EEST
19:53:00 KST

Survey: 62% of Ukrainians believe neither side is currently winning war
A majority of Ukrainians (62%) believe that neither Ukraine nor Russia is currently winning the war, while 26% say Ukraine has the upper hand and 6% say Russia does.
Source: the results of a survey conducted by Rating Group on 3-5 October 2026
Quote: "An absolute majority believes that currently neither Ukraine nor Russia is winning the war (62%). A quarter speak of Ukraine's advantage (26%), and 6% of Russia's."
Details: The survey also found that 57% of respondents support a cessation of hostilities and seeking a compromise through negotiations. Meanwhile, 13% favour continuing the fighting until the lines of control as of 23 February 2022 are restored. Another 21% support continuing the fighting until the territories of Donbas and Crimea are liberated.
A total of 57% of respondents see seeking a compromise with the involvement of other countries in the negotiations as a realistic way to end the war, while another 26% favour direct negotiations.
Some 35% of respondents oppose territorial concessions in exchange for long-term peace. Meanwhile, 56% would accept such concessions if they were accompanied by security guarantees from the US and European partners, including funding for Ukrainian forces and weapons. Another 3% would accept concessions without any preconditions, while 6% were undecided.
If territorial concessions become a condition for peace, 68% of respondents believe the final decision should be made by the people in a nationwide referendum. Some 17% believe it should be made by the president, while 9% say the Verkhovna Rada (parliament) should decide.
For reference: The survey was conducted on 3-5 October 2026 using computer-assisted telephone interviews (CATI) among 1,000 Ukrainians aged 18 and over.
Respondents were selected through a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all oblasts except for temporarily occupied territories and areas without Ukrainian mobile coverage at the time of the poll.
The results were weighted using current data from the State Statistics Service. The sample is representative by age, gender and type of settlement. The margin of error does not exceed 3.1 percentage points with a 95% confidence level.
Background: A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology showed that 62% of Ukrainians, like the majority of Kyiv residents, are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary, whereas 23% are ready to continue fighting for only a few months or up to six months.

Ryanair CEO sees no European jet fuel shortages into summer 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:58 UTC
19:52:58 KST

Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary expects Europe to have enough jet fuel through next summer, but warns that high prices will persist for another 12 to 18 months.
Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said on Thursday that he did not expect jet fuel shortages in Europe this winter or into summer 2027, even as the Iran war disrupts supply chains.
"There is no question, I think, over availability of jet fuel in Europe this winter, or frankly into next summer either, unless there's some unforeseen event," O’Leary said at a press conference organised by Airlines for Europe (A4E) in Brussels.
His comments offer reassurance on supplies, but airlines and passengers still face persistently high fuel costs.
Euronews Business previously reported that lower seasonal demand from November and increased imports from Asia were expected to keep Europe supplied in the coming months. According to Kpler, nearly 900,000 tonnes of jet fuel from Asia were scheduled to arrive over that period.
Those shipments could help prevent shortages, but are unlikely to bring much relief on prices.
“Jet fuel will likely be subject to higher prices, especially as it is deeply linked to the diesel market, which is becoming even tighter and experiencing record prices recently,” George Shaw, Kpler’s senior insight analyst for distillate markets, told Euronews on 23 September.
The European Commission also said on 8 September that increased EU refinery output and alternative imports were meeting European demand for jet fuel, although further disruption in the Middle East could tighten supplies.
Separately, the G7 agreed last Friday to speed up the release of 100 million barrels from strategic reserves to ease pressure on energy markets. On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency clarified that these barrels were part of the emergency stock release agreed in March.
Its members supported accelerating the remaining releases and prioritising diesel because of tight supplies, although the announcement did not specify a release of jet fuel.
Jet fuel prices double
Jet fuel prices have risen faster than crude prices since the war began, as attacks on refineries have disrupted production and widened the gap between the cost of crude and the price of the finished fuel.
According to the International Air Transport Association’s latest fuel price monitor, Europe and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), which includes several former Soviet republics, had the highest average jet fuel price of any region.
Prices averaged $195.95 a barrel in the week ending 2 October, more than double their level a year earlier. Although they fell 1% that week, the global jet fuel premium over crude remained roughly three times its year-earlier level.
"Historically, jet fuel was about somewhere between 10 per cent and 15 per cent more expensive than Brent crude. It's currently running at about 50 per cent more expensive," O’Leary said.
He expected that premium to persist for another 12 to 18 months, citing attacks on Russian and Middle Eastern refineries, along with constraints on tanker availability and refining capacity.
Ryanair said last month that it would reduce its winter flight schedule to limit its exposure to higher fuel costs, cutting its full-year passenger target to 214 million from 216 million.

Lower House gives final approval to new election law
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:52:44 CEST
19:52:44 KST

The Lower House on Thursday gave
final approval to a bill presented by the parties of Premier
Giorgia Meloni's ruling coalition for a new election law, giving
it the green light with 227 votes in favour and 164 against.
                                    
The ruling alliance says the new system will make it more likely
that elections produce a clear winner.
                                    
But opposition politicians held up signs calling it a "scam law"
and a "con", when the result of the vote, a secret ballot, was
announced.
                                    
The opposition say the ruling alliance has changed the system
because it fears losing the general election set to take place
next year and wants to minimize the chances of this happening.
                                    
Under the law the old system, a mix of first-past-the-post and
proportional representation, has been replaced with a
proportional-representation system with bonus seats for the
coalition that obtains the most votes, as long as it reaches a
threshold of 42%, to ensure it has a working majority in
parliament.
                                    
If no coalition reaches the threshold, or the votes for the
Lower House and the Senate produce different results, a purely
proportional system is used.
                                    
The opposition have said that, among other things, the system of
bonus seats is unconstitutional and are ready to appeal to the
Constitutional Court.
                                    
Coalitions will have to say who their candidate to be premier is
before the election.
                                    
The opposition said this is the government's way to bring in a
reform that it promised by has not delivered so far, the direct
election of the prime minister, by the back door.
                                    
The bill will also give voters the option to express preferences
for up to three candidates out of six on a party list in which
candidates names must alternate according to gender.
                                    
The opposition says that in reality this gives "fake
preferences" as the head of the ticket would always be
"blocked", arguing this was also be a step back for equality,
as, in theory, it would be possible for all the ticket heads to
be men.
                                    
The current system does not give voters any option to express
preferences about which of the candidates on a party list they
want to represent them.

As Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian data centers, could Ukraine soon be offline?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:52:00 UTC
19:52:00 KST

Ukraine is not likely to go offline despite attacks
October 8, 2026
Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs.
Since early September, Russia has been targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically.
Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting.
Why is Russia targeting Ukrainian data centers?
The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly.
Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians."
Could Ukraine go offline?
Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks, experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized.
"The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services."
He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world."
At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly.
Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook.
How can data and devices be protected?
Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained.
He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon.
Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained.
Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers.
"We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change."
Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

ASEAN and China adopted a nonbinding declaration governing conduct in the disputed waters in 2002, but negotiations on a substantive agreement have continued for years.
Manila has repeatedly accused Chinese vessels of dangerous maneuvers against Philippine ships, while Beijing maintains its maritime claims.
ASEAN and China aim to conclude CoC negotiations by the end of 2026.

françois prost photographs the facade as a machine for manufacturing desire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:50:58 UTC
19:50:58 KST

françois prost photographs the facade as a machine for manufacturing desire
the french photographer traces how nightclub facades turn borrowed images and popular fantasies into architectural promises that remain visible long after the spectacle has disappeared.
Building the idea of a night out
A club facade is an image before it is a place.
It was probably this idea that led me, more than a decade ago, to start photographing nightclubs. It began in 2011, during a bike ride along a canal in Burgundy. On a small road cutting through the fields, I came across an old farmhouse that had been transformed into a nightclub. A lightbox sign had been screwed above the door, a laser installed on the chimney, and fluorescent stars added around the entrance. On the gravel lay shards of broken glass and torn flyers. The party had just ended. Standing there with my bike under the bright Saturday morning sun, I was struck by the contrast between the frenzy of the night before and the ordinary light of day.
The club was closed. Nothing was happening. There was no music, no crowd, no colored light. Yet the building was still trying to tell me what kind of place it was supposed to be.
I think this was the beginning of my fascination with these facades. Since then, I have pursued this work across France, Europe, and eventually far beyond. Different cultures and contexts emerged, but I kept encountering something remarkably familiar: buildings trying to transport us somewhere else. A palm tree can suggest the tropics. A column can evoke ancient Greece. Neon can summon Las Vegas. Faux marble can suggest luxury. A few golden letters can make an ordinary building feel prestigious. Even the name of a club can be enough to trigger an image in the mind: Copacabana, Le Mirage, L’Acropole. The facade does not necessarily describe the place behind it. It promises it.
Borrowed images, imagined worlds
This is what interests me in these buildings. They borrow images from elsewhere – from cinema, tourism, advertising, architecture – and assemble them into a kind of popular visual language. Sometimes the result is carefully designed; sometimes it is improvised, almost clumsy. But the intention is usually very clear. The building has to be understood immediately. In that sense, these facades are not so far from advertising. They are large-scale images designed to produce desire. They don’t tell you exactly what will happen inside. They give you an idea of how you might feel there.
A nightclub in the middle of the French countryside can become a tropical paradise. A building on the outskirts of a Spanish town can pretend to be somewhere in Las Vegas. A club can borrow the architecture of a Greek temple, a palace, a casino or a Miami hotel. For a few hours, these borrowed images create the possibility of another world. Perhaps this is also why I became interested in photographing them during the day. In daylight, the illusion is exposed. The lights are switched off. The music has stopped. The people are gone. What remains is the physical object: the sign, the columns, the painted walls, the fake palm trees, the entrance, sometimes the traces of years of modifications and repairs.
The spectacle has been dismantled, but the machinery that produced it is still there. Photographing these places this way changes their meaning. I am not trying to document nightlife itself. I am interested in what nightlife leaves behind – the architecture of its promise.
Popular fantasies, built in plain sight
There is also something very democratic about these buildings that I find moving. They do not necessarily rely on architects, designers or institutions to construct their visual identity. They use whatever images are available in the collective imagination. A palm tree, a Greek column, a neon sign, a name borrowed from a distant city: these are simple tools, but they are powerful because we already know what they mean.
Their apparent naivety is therefore part of what makes them interesting to me. I don’t see these façades as ridiculous objects or as failed architecture. I see them as records of a popular visual culture – evidence of the way people construct fantasies from the images that surround them.
Over the years, this search has gradually led me towards other architectures built around desire: American gentlemen’s clubs, Japanese love hotels, and clubs in Côte d’Ivoire. Their functions and cultural contexts are very different, but the same mechanism keeps appearing. Buildings become images. Images become promises. The strange thing is that these images often become most visible when nobody is using them. In the morning, when the party has disappeared and the building returns to its ordinary surroundings, the facade is left alone with its promises. That is when I like to photograph it most.
François Prost is a parisian photographer and art director born in 1980. When he’s not working for editorial or commercial clients, he spends his time on personal photography projects, documenting facades of local French nightclubs, machine gun shops in the US, Chinese scooters, or similarities between European cities and their Chinese replicas. His work has been awarded and exhibited internationally and published in 6 monographic books, including After Party, Gentlemen’s Club, Club Ivoire, and Love Hotel, which are distributed by D.A.P./Artbook in North America, Antenne Books in the UK and worldwide, and Interart in France.
project info:
photographer: François Prost | @francoisprost

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia’s newest electronic warfare (EW) system, the Yastreb-S, is being modernized to jam Starlink satellite communications used by Ukrainian drones, Igor Potapov, an official representative of its developer, NPP Design Bureau, told TASS.
"The Yastreb system itself is currently undergoing testing. The Yastreb-S version requires modernization to shift frequencies to the operating bands of Starlink systems for maximum suppression of all possible threats. The frequency shifter has already been made, and all that remains is to integrate it and begin testing," he said, calling the system the "Starlink killer."
He added that this will deprive enemy attack unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) of satellite communications.
Potapov said earlier that the Yastreb 1.0 system is undergoing final testing, and Russian troops will begin using it in November. According to the expert, the Yastreb 1.0 has no analogues in its class. The system covers a wide frequency band from 100 to 6,000 MHz. The system’s electronic intelligence capabilities include video interception with image transmission to the operator’s network.

Firefighters: Narva nursing home met fire safety rules in fatal blaze
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:49:00 KST

Firefighters: Narva nursing home met fire safety rules in fatal blaze
Firefighters say they found no fire safety violations at a Narva nursing home where an elderly woman perished in a fire Tuesday evening.
The cause of the fire, which was confined to a smoking area has so far been put down to possible lack of care when smoking, is still under investigation, the Rescue Board (Päästeamet) said.
The board said as well as fire safety features being in place the facility's staff responded promptly, but the woman could not be revived.
Around a quarter of the home's 130 residents smoke, the board added.
Staff at the nursing home on Rahu põik were dealing with the aftermath of the blaze and the fatality on Wednesday morning.
Fire doors and containment features meant the fire did not spread elsewhere in the building and no evacuation was required; when firefighters arrived at the scene just minutes after being notified shortly before 9 p.m. Tuesday, all that remained for them to do was ventilate the premises and conduct checks.
"The nursing home staff managed to respond to the fire promptly and quickly, extinguishing it. All that remained for the firefighters was to check the scene and, unfortunately, confirm that a person had died in the fire. But if fire safety had not been in order, the consequences would have been even more serious," said Denis Duškin, head of the Narva fire station.
According to nursing home staff, the deceased woman used a wheelchair but was otherwise fully independent and mentally alert, requiring neither assistance nor special treatment.
Staff said the woman often wore clothes made from synthetic fibers, which may have caught fire while she was smoking.
The nursing home is considering restricting access to the smoking room in the evenings, when fewer people are moving around the building, but added it cannot close the room permanently and cannot send its residents outside to smoke.
"It is very difficult to forbid an elderly person from doing something they have been accustomed to doing for years. For this reason we maintain the smoking room so that residents can smoke indoors. If people started smoking outside, there would be several times more cases of colds and other respiratory illnesses," said Tatjana Stolfat, head of the Narva Social Work Center.
A total of 23 fire fatalities have been reported in Estonia so far this year.

Photos: Protests erupt after 87-year-old evicted woman dies in Madrid
Nationwide outrage grows after the death of woman whose eviction sparked protests and political tensions.
The death of an 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home ignited nationwide outrage has intensified Spain’s debate over housing and pushed the country into a political crisis.
Maria del Carmen Abascal, known widely as “Maricarmen”, died in hospital on Wednesday, her lawyer confirmed, weeks after televised images showed police removing her on a stretcher from the flat where she had lived for seven decades. Activists said her case exposed the human cost of soaring rents and aggressive evictions.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez led tributes online, calling her “a symbol” of renters struggling with Spain’s affordability crisis and writing on X: “All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. … Rest in peace.” Protesters gathered near parliament chanted: “Maricarmen lives. The fight goes on!”
Her lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said activists were devastated, calling the eviction “shameful violence” that showed “the impact it can have on people’s health”. Housing groups stressed that although a deal was eventually reached allowing her to return home, the agreement came “too late” after a “harrowing ordeal”.
Spain’s average rent has almost doubled in a decade, and the government said more than a quarter of tenants spend about 40 percent of their income on housing and utilities – more than double the EU average.
Abascal’s removal from her home so the property could be relet at a higher price set off protests across Spain, a planned general strike next month and mounting pressure on politicians. After failing to pass emergency housing measures, Sanchez called an early election for November 29, hoping to channel public anger into support for his Socialist Party.
Conservative opposition leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo also offered condolences, urging “respect” and warning against using Abascal’s death for political gain.

Poland launches €114m fund to support space technology firms

Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector.
The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence.

According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle.
The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski.
Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings.
“The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said.

Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”.
The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said.
Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence.
In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners.
KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets.
Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News.
Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”.
“The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl.
Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund.

Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems.
A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight.
The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security.
In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience.

EXPLAINER - What will Türkiye’s first spacecraft to the Moon actually do?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:45:44 UTC
19:45:44 KST

- The spacecraft will study the Moon from orbit, test autonomous navigation and collect scientific data before a controlled descent
- 'We are developing an image-based navigation system' to help the spacecraft navigate autonomously around the Moon, the mission’s project manager explains to Anadolu
Türkiye is preparing to send its first spacecraft beyond Earth orbit, a mission designed not only to study the Moon but also to test whether satellite technologies can operate autonomously in deep space.
The spacecraft is targeted for launch in the second quarter of 2027, according to the mission’s project manager. It will travel for about two months before entering a circular polar orbit roughly 100 kilometers (62 miles) above the lunar surface. It is expected to operate there for at least three months, with the mission potentially extended to up to 1.5 years depending on performance.
“We will obtain important images from the Moon, have high-resolution cameras and collect scientific data,” Burak Yaglioglu, project manager for the mission at the Scientific and Technological Research Council of Türkiye’s Space Technologies Research Institute (TUBITAK UZAY), told Anadolu at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
The mission is the first phase of Türkiye’s Lunar Research Program, one of the 10 strategic targets of its National Space Program. Its broader purpose is to move the country’s space capabilities beyond Earth orbit and prepare the technology and experience needed for more ambitious lunar missions.
A first step beyond Earth
Türkiye has developed and operated Earth-orbiting satellites for years, including the IMECE Earth-observation satellite and the TURKSAT 6A communications satellite.
But working around the Moon is a substantially different challenge.
The lunar spacecraft, weighing about 3.5 tons, has a domestic content rate of more than 80%, according to TUBITAK. Production, assembly and integration were completed in September, and the spacecraft has now entered system-level environmental testing ahead of its launch.
The spacecraft uses the TstarD-100 platform developed by TUBITAK UZAY specifically for deep-space missions. Of its 65 mission-critical components, 56 were manufactured using domestic capabilities, while several systems draw on technology previously developed for Türkiye’s IMECE and TURKSAT 6A programs.
“For the first time, we will enter the orbit of a body other than Earth and conduct operations there,” Yaglioglu said.
He said the team designed the spacecraft and mission architecture itself and that its software is also being developed domestically.
The point, he said, is not simply to reach the Moon but to demonstrate that Türkiye can design, operate and extract scientific data from a spacecraft operating deep in space.
How will it find its way around the Moon?
One of the mission's more ambitious technology demonstrations involves autonomous navigation.
A spacecraft orbiting the Moon cannot rely on GPS in the way a vehicle on Earth can. Instead, Türkiye is developing an image-based navigation system that will use recognizable features on the lunar surface, including craters, to determine the spacecraft’s position and orientation.
“We are developing an image-based navigation system,” Yaglioglu said. “These will determine the position and orientation of our spacecraft by looking at craters on the lunar surface, so our spacecraft will be able to carry out autonomous operations in lunar orbit.”
That capability could become particularly important for future missions in which a spacecraft needs to navigate with less reliance on commands from Earth.
The spacecraft will also carry four scientific payloads. Two were developed domestically, while two were developed through international cooperation with researchers in Sweden and China. The instruments will study, among other things, the interaction between solar wind and the lunar surface, the Moon’s local magnetic environment and processes related to water formation.
Its imaging system is designed to provide panchromatic images at resolutions of up to 0.7 meters, alongside wide-area RGB imaging and video.
What happens after the science?
The first mission is not designed to make a soft landing.
After completing its planned scientific operations in lunar orbit, the spacecraft is expected to be deliberately sent toward the lunar surface through controlled maneuvers using its propulsion system. TUBITAK describes this as a hard landing at the end of the first mission.
A hybrid propulsion system developed domestically with Turkish company DeltaV will be used for key maneuvers, including raising the spacecraft’s orbit and the final controlled descent.
The distinction matters because the soft landing comes later.
Türkiye’s second lunar mission is planned to build on the first mission’s experience and attempt a controlled landing on the Moon, followed by the deployment of a rover for surface exploration.
Yaglioglu said the two missions are therefore being considered together.
"The second mission involves a soft landing and taking a rover to the surface," he said. While working on the first mission, he added, the team has also been planning for the second, designing its systems around an architecture suited to landing and surface exploration.
Why does the mission matter?
For Türkiye, the lunar program is intended as a test of a much broader technological capability.
The country’s National Space Program was unveiled in 2021 and includes goals ranging from developing domestic satellite technologies to sending a spacecraft to the Moon. Türkiye also carried out its first human spaceflight mission in 2024, when astronaut Alper Gezeravci traveled to the International Space Station.
The lunar mission takes the next step: operating a spacecraft in an environment far beyond Earth orbit.
Yaglioglu said the spacecraft’s communications, power systems, flight computers, software and other components will gain what the industry calls “flight heritage” -- operational experience that can inform future missions.
“This has also given us important experience,” he said, referring to the development of the first spacecraft and the preparations for the second mission.
For Türkiye, that experience may ultimately be as important as the scientific data gathered from the Moon.
The spacecraft is now undergoing acoustic, vibration, thermal-vacuum and electromagnetic-compatibility testing designed to simulate the conditions it will face during launch and in space. If testing and final preparations proceed as planned, it will be transported to the Kennedy Space Center in the US where a SpaceX launch vehicle will carry it into Earth orbit.
The spacecraft will then use its DeltaV propulsion system to begin its journey toward the Moon.
Türkiye aims to become the ninth country to carry out a lunar mission, according to Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacir.
As Yaglioglu put it, the objective is not simply to go to the Moon but to turn the technologies, engineering and scientific capabilities developed for the journey into a foundation for Türkiye’s next generation of deep-space missions.

Russian strikes kill 33 in street in east Ukraine stronghold
A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said on Thursday, describing it as a targeted strike on civilians in the key stronghold sought by Moscow.
Another 18 people were wounded in one of the largest single attacks this year, which took place on a street where police said two city buses were operating at the time of the strike. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy described it as a bus stop.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus.
"For them (the Russians), a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one strike can kill as many people as possible," regional governor Vadym Filashkin said on the Telegram app.
There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the attack. Russia denies targeting civilians, though it has regularly pounded Ukrainian cities, towns and other targets during its full-scale invasion that began in February 2022.
Intensifying strikes
Moscow's forces have stepped up drone and guided-bomb strikes on Kramatorsk and other cities in Ukraine's "fortress belt", local officials say, the backbone of its defences in the Donetsk region.
Russia has demanded that Ukraine cede the rest of the region still under its control before it stops fighting, which Kyiv refuses to do. The pace of Moscow's battlefield gains in the region has significantly slowed this year.
Filashkin said he had ordered city authorities in Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, another key fortress-belt city, to halt public transport, saying "we have no right to risk" citizens' lives.
Thursday's attack came a day after dozens were killed in a massive Russian air attack across Ukraine, primarily targeting the country's power grid.
Separately on Thursday, three people were killed and 14 wounded in morning drone strikes on the capital Kyiv, said Mayor Vitali Klitschko. Russian forces have unleashed frequent waves of attacks on Kyiv amid a shortage of Ukrainian air defences.

NEW DELHI: The government on Thursday decided to cap trade margins at 30% of the maximum retail price (MRP) for all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs, according to official sources cited by ANI.The decision will cover branded and generic medicines, as well as domestic and imported drugs, including patented and non-patented medicines. The government said the move is aimed at addressing excessive trade mark-ups and improving the affordability of life-saving cancer medicines while ensuring their continued availability.According to the official sources, the measure could result in up to 70% reduction in the MRP of the affected medicines and is expected to generate estimated annual savings of around Rs 2,500 crore for patients.Under the decision, the trade margin on all non-scheduled anti-cancer medicines will be capped at 30% of their MRP. The measure covers a wide range of medicines, irrespective of whether they are branded or generic, manufactured domestically or imported, or patented or non-patented.The government said the intervention is intended to tackle excessive mark-ups in the distribution and sale of cancer medicines and reduce the financial burden on patients.
The move is also expected to lower out-of-pocket expenditure for cancer patients, according to official sources cited by ANI.The government has projected that the intervention could bring down the MRP of affected medicines by up to 70%.
According to official estimates, the trade-margin cap is expected to result in annual savings of approximately Rs 2,500 crore.The savings are expected to accrue to patients through lower prices for the affected anti-cancer medicines.The government has also framed the measure as part of its broader effort to improve access to affordable medicines while maintaining the availability of essential treatments.The latest decision builds on a similar government intervention introduced in 2019.According to official sources cited by ANI, the 2019 measure resulted in reported annual savings of Rs 984 crore across 526 brands.The government said the latest intervention reinforces its focus on affordable and accessible healthcare, particularly for patients requiring expensive cancer treatment.The latest cap extends the approach to all non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs and covers medicines across different categories, including branded, generic, domestic, imported, patented and non-patented products.

This involves not only expanding the military-industrial complex but also ideologically brainwashing their own populations to embrace Russophobia and the idea of 'inevitable conflict.' This is precisely what the Russian president has addressed in his repeated statements."
Zakharova pointed out that should such aggression originate from Western Europe or the EU, a response would follow. "As for the nature of that response, you need only re-read the president's relevant statement," she concluded.

'Heroic actions': Magen David Adom mourns first responders who served, were murdered on Oct. 7

Magen David Adom mourned its first responders who were murdered during the October 7 massacre earlier this week to mark three years since Hamas terrorists infiltrated Israel and murdered over 1,200 Israelis.
According to MDA, 20 members of the emergency services were murdered during the massacre, including seven who were murdered while treating the wounded under fire.
Three MDA personnel were abducted into the Gaza Strip. Among them were volunteer Emergency Medical Technicians Ronen Engel from Kibbutz Nir Oz and Lior Rudaeff from Kibbutz Nir Yitzhak, whose remains were returned to Israel for burial in October and November 2025, respectively.
MDA said that its ambulances and motorcycles were targeted by terrorists, with 18 ambulances damaged during October 7 and the following days, including eight that were completely destroyed.
"Tragically, some of those who answered the call to save lives never returned home, losing their own lives in the line of duty," MDA Director-General Eli Bin reflected.
"Three years later, we remember every member of our MDA family who was lost and honor their courage, dedication, and sacrifice."
As reports that morning accumulated of rocket fire, casualties, and terrorist infiltrations into military bases and communities, MDA leadership assembled in the early hours at the National Integrated Dispatch Center.
For MDA to mobilize as many available resources as possible, rapid internal decisions were made, such as the initial decision to keep the night shift on duty rather than release personnel as the morning shift arrived.
MDA immediately raised its national alert to the highest level, staffed every available ambulance and emergency dispatch position, and deployed armored ambulances from across the country to southern Israel, while maintaining reserve capacity in case of escalation on the northern front.
MDA received over 21,600 emergency calls during October 7 massacre
More than 21,600 emergency calls were received by its dispatch centers, approximately five times the daily average, said MDA. Hundreds of MDA ambulances operated in southern Israel, evacuating scores of casualties from the Gaza border communities and their surrounding areas.
MDA said that its helicopters also played a critical role in evacuating the wounded. During the morning hours of October 7, MDA said that its helicopters were the only helicopters in the air evacuating wounded people from the affected areas. However, one MDA helicopter was ultimately struck by rocket shrapnel. MDA also coordinated with the Israel Air Force for medical evacuations.
MDA Blood Services also played a critical role from the earliest hours of October 7. Blood collection activity was expanded, including at protected donation sites, to increase blood reserves and ensure a continuous supply of blood units to hospitals and the defense system.
Since then, they have also "pioneered a whole blood protocol" that has "significantly reduced battlefield deaths," according to MDA.
In the days following October 7, thousands of people came forward to donate blood. The Marcus National Blood Services Center, Ramle, enabled MDA to process and distribute blood donations under wartime conditions.
Three years after massacre, MDA has greatly expanded emergency response capacity
Three years on, MDA honored those it lost while pointing to a major expansion of its emergency response capacity, including a fivefold increase in its armored ambulance fleet.
When the October 7 massacre occured, MDA had 20 armored ambulances. Today, it has more than 100 armored ambulances and approximately 2,000 ambulances in total. Its helicopter fleet has also expanded from three helicopters to five.
Additionally, MDA has established community-based initiatives, including expanded midwife services and the Magen Project, which has trained over 17,800 civilians to provide immediate first aid when emergency medical teams are cut off. The organization has also reportedly expanded training, blood collection, humanitarian assistance, and emergency preparedness.
According to MDA, around 5,000 new volunteers have joined the organization since the war broke out on October 7, and the organization's vehicle fleet and its operational and community capabilities have continued to grow.
Since the massacre, MDA has expanded its response capabilities through initiatives designed to strengthen emergency preparedness and bring lifesaving care closer to communities.
“October 7 showed the courage, dedication, and leadership of Magen David Adom’s medics under circumstances unlike anything we had experienced before,” said Bin.
“Our teams went out under heavy fire to treat and evacuate the wounded, putting their own lives at risk while their families sheltered from the attack,” he added.

"Well, unfortunately, it seems to be going into its fifth year, which was never the original plan. I don’t think that was Putin’s plan for this war, so it hasn’t gone the way he planned it. "We are prepared to play whatever role we can in making that happen. And we have tried in the past, but so far it’s been elusive. The United States is also closely monitoring the risks of escalation with great concern.
"Just yesterday, some ships were attacked in the Black Sea through a coordinated drone attack. We’re worried about a sabotage operation in a neighboring country that can spiral out of control," Rubio said.
He added that there are clear indications that Russia will use the upcoming winter as something they want to use to destroy what remains of the electric grid in Ukraine and force them into capitulation. Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown more effective in its ability to conduct long-range strikes deep into Russia.
"So, we share the same concern. The whole world is going about this thing like something that could escalate and perhaps become a broader conflict. So, we stand prepared to facilitate and continue to explore any opportunity for a negotiated settlement. We think it would be good for Russia and Ukraine, but so far, it’s proving elusive," Rubio said.

Limits changed in money laundering, terrorism finance fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:40:47 UTC
19:40:47 KST

Türkiye raised the threshold for jewelry transactions to 370,000.
Türkiye has raised monetary thresholds for identity verification and introduced new security rules for digital customer validation used by financial institutions to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.
The amendment, published in the Official Gazette, reorganized ID checks that banks, factoring companies, brokerage houses, portfolio management firms and payment entities must perform during transactions.
The verification threshold for cash, foreign exchange and jewelry transactions rose to 370,000 Turkish Liras ($7,517). Institutions must identify customers, verify information and take measures to establish the ultimate beneficial owner when single or linked transactions reach 370,000 liras ($7,517). The previous limit was 185,000 liras ($3,759).
Meanwhile, the limit for electronic transfers, digital identity verification and simplified measures doubled from 15,000 liras ($305) to 30,000 liras ($610).
The legislation also introduces new provisions for verification through internet or mobile channels using a one-time password (SMS OTP) sent to previously verified mobile numbers.
Any verification method must match the transaction’s nature and risk level, provide sufficient assurance that the user is a previously identified customer and include safeguards against unauthorized transactions.
Financial institutions may waive physical signature requirements for verification through internet or mobile channels or SMS OTP, provided the chosen method meets the stated security and risk criteria.

Two dead after 7-story building partially collapses in Istanbul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:38:49 UTC
19:38:49 KST

(AA Photo)
Search and rescue operations are underway in Istanbul’s Maltepe district after a partial collapse of a seven-story building early on Oct. 8 left two dead and two others trapped beneath the rubble, with crews operating amid warnings of further collapse.
The building in the Cevizli neighborhood was constructed in 1987. Its ground floor and two upper floors collapsed before dawn, while the remaining four floors tilted to one side. The ground floor housed a textile workshop.
Istanbul Governor Davut Gül said 33 people were officially registered as living in the building, which contained 12 apartments. Four apartments on the collapsed floors were registered as housing 14 people.
Ten people, including three children, were rescued alive, while the bodies of two others were recovered. Two people were still being sought in the rubble.
Rescue operations were temporarily halted after teams detected movement in the structure, raising concerns that the remaining section could collapse. Nearby buildings were also evacuated as a precaution. Firefighters were deployed with 56 vehicles, 175 personnel and a search-and-rescue dog, while the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD) sent five vehicles, 25 personnel and two search dogs.
While Gül noted that municipal records show no prior safety complaints against the building, Maltepe Mayor Esin Köymen stated that an initial archive review revealed the top two floors were constructed illegally after the occupancy permit was issued.
An investigation has been launched into the collapse. A deputy chief prosecutor and two prosecutors, along with two inspectors, were appointed to examine the building’s planning, construction and renovation history and determine whether any public officials had been negligent or responsible.
The incident has also renewed concerns over Istanbul’s aging and potentially unsafe building stock. The city has been carrying out an urban transformation program aimed at replacing buildings vulnerable to earthquakes, particularly those constructed before the 1999 Marmara earthquake.
Following the devastating 2023 earthquakes in southeastern Türkiye, applications for Istanbul’s municipal rapid building-screening program surged into the thousands per day. Demand has since fallen to about 500 applications a day.
The Istanbul Municipality says it has conducted rapid risk assessments on about 40,000 buildings out of 170,000 applications, identifying 18,800 pre-1999 structures as high or very high risk.
The rapid screening program assesses a building’s concrete and reinforcement quality, structural design and compliance with its approved plans to estimate its earthquake safety. The assessment is not legally binding and requires unanimous approval from residents to apply.

Benin demands France return cultural treasures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:38:44 UTC
19:38:44 KST

Benin demands France return cultural treasures
Benin has renewed its demand for the return of 35 cultural artifacts and archival materials held in France, including a sacred statue taken during the colonial era, Benin Web TV reported on Tuesday.
President Romuald Wadagni raised the issue during talks with French counterpart Emmanuel Macron in Paris on Monday. The requested objects include a carved wooden divination tray at the Quai Branly-Jacques Chirac Museum, a statue of Gou, the Vodun god of iron and war, and the throne of King Toffa of Porto-Novo.
The statue of Gou was taken to France during its conquest of Dahomey in the late 19th century. Benin had previously sought its return under former President Patrice Talon, but the sculpture was not among the objects handed back by France in 2021.
Benin could receive an initial response from Paris by mid-October, RFI reported on Wednesday, citing informed sources. Further discussions are expected to determine whether France will return all 35 objects or only some of them.
The renewed request comes after France introduced a new legal framework in May to simplify the repartriation of cultural objects acquired unlawfully during the colonial period.
France previously returned 26 royal treasures to Benin in November 2021. They had been seized by French troops during the conquest of the Kingdom of Dahomey in 1892 and were held in French museum collections for more than a century.
African countries have repeatedly called for the return of cultural artifacts taken under colonial rule. Nigeria has secured agreements with European countries, including Germany, for the restitution of the Benin Bronzes looted by British troops in 1897.
In June, three Swiss museums returned 18 Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, including 14 from the University of Zurich. The handover followed a formal request submitted by the Nigerian authorities in 2024.
Guinea has made similar demands. In September, Culture Minister Moussa Moïse Sylla urged France to set a clear timetable for returning objects belonging to anti-colonial leader Samory Toure and the remains of Bocar Biro and his companions.

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Russia’s Prosecutor General’s Office has sent the Netherlands a request for the extradition of nine representatives of the International Criminal Court (ICC) who were convicted in absentia in Russia, including ICC President Piotr Hofmanski and Prosecutor Karim Khan, the Russian supervisory authority’s press service said.

They were sentenced to prison terms ranging from three and a half to 15 years.
The Prosecutor General’s Office recalled that, citing the political bias of the International Criminal Court, the Russian president issued an order in November 2016 declaring Russia’s intention not to become a party to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. Notification of this intention was sent to the UN secretary-general. Russia has never been and is not a party to the ICC Rome Statute and does not recognize its jurisdiction.
"Despite this, ICC Prosecutor Khan unlawfully brought criminal charges against Russian citizens in The Hague. The ICC Presidency, in the absence of legal grounds, instructed the chamber’s judges to issue manifestly unlawful arrest warrants against them. These decisions were made in violation of fundamental principles and norms of international law and without any evidence that the individuals in question had committed the alleged crimes," the Prosecutor General’s Office said.

Russia believes that agreements regarding Ukraine must be guaranteed for generations to come and safeguarded against collapse, he continued: "We need a solution for future generations -- one that is guaranteed and safeguarded against collapse. The president has repeatedly spoken about this, including at the [recent] Valdai forum."
Freezing the Ukrainian conflict will not help resolve it, Peskov argued: "Let’s put it this way: a temporary halt or a freeze won’t help either."
On Iran potentially exiting NPT
The possibility of Tehran pulling out of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) may be raised at talks between President Putin and his Iranian counterpart, Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines of the upcoming CIS summit, the Kremlin spokesman said: "If Iran finds it necessary to brief us of it and if these plans are really being implemented, then [the issue] will certainly [be brought up at the meeting]. However, it’s crucial to understand if this is really [on the agenda], because we have heard statements from lawmakers. Those aren’t always, say, in line with the country’s actual foreign policy plans."
On CIS
The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) has proved to be beneficial for its member countries in decades of its history, Peskov maintained: "The CIS format itself has proved to be beneficial to its member countries and quite relevant for more than a decade of its history."
It has been a platform for more advanced integration processes, he said: "The CIS format has paved the way for more advanced forms of integration, which is also very important."
Putin will meet with all participants in the upcoming CIS summit in Turkmenistan on the sidelines of the event, Peskov announced: "The president will have [an opportunity] to communicate with all other participants on the sidelines of these cultural events tonight. It means that he will talk with almost everyone on the sidelines [of the summit]."

Helsinki will not ban face coverings in schools, but tightens guidelines
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:37:07 EEST
19:37:07 KST

The City of Helsinki will not ban the wearing of items such as headscarves, balaclavas and other face-covering garments in schools and colleges.
However, the city will instead add a requirement to schools' safety guidelines stating that a student must be identifiable during instruction and assessment.
The decision follows a meeting of Helsinki City Council on Wednesday, which dealt with a motion submitted by the Finns Party calling for a ban on the wearing of headscarves in schools and colleges.
National Coalition Party (NCP) councillor Seida Sohrabi also filed a separate, but almost identical, motion.
Sohrabi said face coverings such as niqabs, burqas, and balaclavas should be banned because they make it impossible to identify a child. The Finns Party wanted to extend the headscarf ban to include school staff, particularly teachers.
City councillors did not however vote in favour of an outright ban. The Finns Party also lost a vote calling for the motion to be reconsidered.
Only for a justified reason
The City of Helsinki has been preparing a new safety guideline for schools, and the majority of the city's councillors said this reworking is a sufficient means of dealing with the matter.
The guideline regarind face coverings will stipulate that a student's face must be visible during lessons in order to ensure interaction, participation, legal protection and safety.
The guideline will however not be rolled out as a universal rule — rather as a case-by-case policy — but the main principle is that there must be a justifiable reason for requiring a student to show their face in a given situation.
The requirement for the face to be visible must not be related to the student's appearance, clothing or other personal characteristics, the guideline also emphasised.
Satu Järvenkallas, executive director of the city's education division, told Yle via email that the clarified safety guideline will be put into use in schools as soon as possible.
The issue has been widely debated in Finland since Minister of Social Security, Sanni Grahn-Laasonen (NCP), wrote last year in a post on X that "burkas and niqabs — scarves and veils covering the face — are not suitable for school".
Earlier this year, the cities of Tampere and Vantaa both announced plans to ban face coverings in their schools.

The Liberia-flagged Aframax Rio, a 246-meter (807-feet) long and 107,113-ton deadweight vessel built in 2004, is sanctioned by Ukraine as a shadow tanker Russia uses to evade Western oil export sanctions. The Aframax was southbound when it was hit and set fiercely afire in an early Tuesday evening drone attack.
The blaze under clear skies some 15 nautical miles (30 km) off the shore of Sochi – the heart of the “Russia Riviera” Black Sea resort region – was observed by thousands of local residents and tourists.
Video of the burning ship showed flames engulfing the entire top deck, with the fiercest fires concentrated around the middle of the tanker. Imagery of the fire and its expansion recorded live from shore on Wednesday showed the blaze most concentrated in the central portion of the ship’s upper deck, an area often targeted by Ukrainian airborne drones attacking tankers in the past. Ukrainian sea drone attacks in past strikes on tankers have focused on engine rooms and propellers near the stern.
The Russian local news platform Sochi Radar reported that the Aframax Rio was fully loaded and that so much oil had spilled into the water and caught fire that firefighters were prevented from moving to extinguish the blaze quickly.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, in his Wednesday evening broadcast, said the Ukrainian military had attacked and badly damaged a tanker in the Black Sea, but he did not name the vessel, nor did he specify the type of drones used in the attack.
Local Russian news platforms identified the Ukrainian military as having operated the drones that attacked the tanker.
The US-based shipping information platform Marine Executive, in a Thursday article, said that the fire started in the center of the ship in the cargo tank area and then spread aft down the starboard side. Later that evening, the report said burning oil that had escaped from the tanker’s holds was visible on the water, beneath a towering column of smoke.
According to the world civilian vessel tracking group MarineTraffic, the last time the Aframax Rio turned on its transponder was Oct. 5 off the coast of Georgia, and since then its location has not been visible to satellite tracking. Its registered owner is Rio Enterprises SA, a Marshall Islands company.
The Greek news platform Protothema, in its Wednesday article, reported the tanker “is linked to Andreas Hadjiyiannis’ Hellenic Tankers.” As of Thursday, no major ship tracking platform showed the ship’s location.
Marine tracking platforms showed past port destinations for the vessel included Sapsun, Turkey and Sika, India.
According to Kyiv, both countries help Russia evade sanctions by receiving shadow tankers loaded with Russian crude, which is then refined into legitimate product not subject to sanctions.
The Black Sea shipping tracker Blackseanews.net showed the vessel’s operator as Hellenic Tankers Co LTD, an Athens-headquartered business, and its last officially recorded voyage as from Russia’s Novorossiysk port to Saudi Arabia’s Rabigh port in May 2026.
On Sept. 22, Robert “Magyar” Brovdi, commander of Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), claimed his strike forces had attacked and disabled 300 Russian “shadow-fleet” tankers since July 6, with 134 strikes in the Sea of Azov and 166 in the Black Sea.
The most environmentally damaging Russian shadow fleet tanker sunk in those waters was the Vologaneft-212, which went down in a December 2024 storm near the resort port of Anapa with more than 4,000 tons of heavy fuel oil aboard.
Leaking product souked hundreds of kilometers of resort beaches and sensitive wetlands on the Russian Black Sea coast and in Russia-occupied Crimea. The most intense period of the Black Sea storm season is from late October through March.
A press release from the ship’s declared operator, a Singapore-based company called Executive Ships Management, said all 23 crew members were safe ashore after the drone strike. The company said it was investigating the ship’s current status, including any potential threat it might pose to navigation, waters or the shoreline in the area.
