‘Israeli false flag’: Tucker Carlson pushes Oct. 7 conspiracy theory, accuses Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:36:48 UTC
19:36:48 KST

American right-wing commentator Tucker Carlson marked the third anniversary of the October 7 massacre by promoting a conspiracy theory that the Hamas attack was an Israeli "false flag" operation, suggesting that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu knew about the impending assault and allowed it to happen to preserve his political power.
In a special episode released Wednesday with commentator Dave Smith, Carlson revived early speculation by the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk, presenting his remarks as evidence that the October 7 attack, in which more than 1,200 Israeli civilians and soldiers were killed, had served Netanyahu's political interests.
Carlson offered no evidence that Netanyahu knew of Hamas' plans in advance or ordered Israeli forces not to intervene.
The approximately 95-minute episode was promoted with a description asserting that Kirk had suspected from the beginning that October 7 was an Israeli false flag, a term for an operation designed to appear as though it was carried out by another party.
Carlson played a clip from an October 12, 2023, interview in which Kirk questioned the Israeli military's delayed response to the attack.
Kirk described Israel as a heavily fortified country with extensive security capabilities and pointed to the political turmoil surrounding Netanyahu's government's judicial overhaul, which had sparked months of mass protests.
He questioned how Hamas terrorists had been able to operate for hours before Israeli forces reached some of the massacre sites. "Was there a stand-down order?" Kirk asked twice. However, Kirk explicitly stopped short of accusing Netanyahu of deliberately allowing the massacre. He acknowledged that he did not know whether the Israeli prime minister had been aware of the attack in advance.
His comments were made just five days after the massacre, when the circumstances surrounding Israel's intelligence and military failures were still unclear. Carlson nevertheless portrayed Kirk's questions as supporting the theory that Netanyahu had allowed the attack to proceed because it helped his government survive a political crisis.
The commentator argued that the massacre had effectively saved Netanyahu's administration and enabled him to remain in office.
Carlson's use of Kirk's remarks was particularly striking given the conservative activist's relationship with Israel. Kirk, who founded the conservative youth organization Turning Point USA, was murdered in September 2025 while appearing at a university in Utah.
Following his death, Netanyahu described him as a "courageous friend of Israel," said they had spoken approximately two weeks earlier and revealed that he had invited Kirk to visit the country. Carlson argued during the episode that Netanyahu and others had effectively hijacked Kirk's memory by portraying him as an unwavering supporter of Israel.
Yet the October 2023 interview Carlson cited also included Kirk's acknowledgment of the murder of women and children during the Hamas assault and his recognition of Israel's right to act against those responsible. Kirk's original remarks were speculative questions about the security failures surrounding October 7, rather than an assertion that Netanyahu had deliberately enabled the attack.
Carlson also used the October 7 massacre to challenge the justification for American involvement in Israel's security.
He claimed that he had been unable to identify a single American killed in the attack who did not also hold Israeli citizenship, suggesting that the deaths of dual nationals should not carry the same significance for the United States.
He then turned to Edan Alexander, the former Hamas hostage who grew up in the United States and holds American citizenship. Carlson claimed Alexander was "not even technically American" and accused President Donald Trump of lying when he described the former hostage as an American citizen. Alexander's American citizenship is not negated by his connections to Israel or his Israeli citizenship.
Throughout the episode, Carlson linked the October 7 massacre to subsequent wars in the region, criticized American military and financial assistance to Israel and attacked Netanyahu personally.
He described the Israeli prime minister as a liar who believes Israeli blood is worth more than American blood.
Carlson also claimed that between 190,000 and 200,000 people had been killed in Gaza, asserting that the figure was apparent from satellite imagery. He presented no evidence substantiating that estimate. The commentator further criticized what he described as the use of accusations of antisemitism to silence criticism of Israel.
The October 7 episode was not Carlson's first confrontation with Israel or Jewish organizations. Last year, he hosted Nick Fuentes, a far-right activist known for antisemitic statements, on his program.
In February, Carlson traveled to Ben Gurion Airport to interview U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee. Following the visit, Carlson alleged that he and members of his team had been detained and questioned by Israeli authorities.
The Israel Airports Authority rejected his characterization of the incident, saying the visitors had been asked routine questions in a separate room in the VIP lounge to protect their privacy.
During the same interview, Carlson made an unfounded allegation involving President Isaac Herzog and the private island owned by convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. He subsequently apologized for the claim.
Carlson has also generated controversy over comments about World War II. In an interview with a former British member of Parliament published last weekend, Carlson questioned whether Britain had been justified in fighting Nazi Germany.
He suggested that Adolf Hitler's invasion of Poland had stemmed from a legitimate territorial dispute and argued that Britain had no reason to become involved. "Who cares if you were speaking German now?" Carlson asked the visibly astonished former lawmaker.

India cut its purchases of Russian oil due to rising prices and competition with China - Bloomberg
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
13:36:21 EEST
19:36:21 KST

India cut its purchases of Russian oil due to rising prices and competition with China - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Indian refineries reduced their purchases of Russian oil due to the rising price of Urals and competition with China. Supplies from the Middle East increased.
Indian oil refineries have reduced purchases of Russian crude for November delivery, as growing competition from China is driving up prices at a time when buyers can use alternative supplies from the Middle East. UNN writes about this, citing Bloomberg.
Details
According to sources familiar with the situation, the reduction in purchases was prompted by a sharp increase in the price of Russia’s flagship Urals crude, loaded in the Baltic region, which is the main feedstock for Indian refineries. Economic factors outweighed pressure from Washington on New Delhi to reduce purchases from Russia, the country’s largest oil supplier, the publication writes.
Russian crude is being offered at a premium of more than $10 per barrel compared with Brent, sources said. Previously sold at steep discounts, the crude is now being sold at nearly comparable prices to Middle Eastern grades, prompting Indian refineries to turn back to suppliers from the Persian Gulf, the sources said. Some of these cargoes are also being offered to independent Chinese refineries.
Refineries in the world’s third-largest oil-importing country had already reduced purchases of Russian crude after a sweeping U.S. sanctions law increased the threat of punitive tariffs.
According to Kpler, Moscow’s share of India’s oil imports fell to about 35% in September from 56% in July. According to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg, supplies averaged just 310,000 barrels per day in the four weeks to October 4, the lowest level since March 2022.
China and India remain the largest buyers of Russian crude, with many cargoes receiving their final destination only after they are already in transit.
"Over the past few months, China’s imports of Russian crude have increased, intensifying competition for barrels that would otherwise have been available to Indian refineries," said Sumit Ritolia, a senior modeling manager at Kpler. "This has partly coincided with China’s reduced access to Iranian oil."
According to sources, New Delhi did not ask refineries to reduce imports from Russia in response to risks related to U.S. tariffs. India’s Ministry of Petroleum did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Meanwhile, supply volumes from the Middle East have increased, as more tankers pass through the Strait of Hormuz despite the continuing risks associated with Iranian attacks on vessels, which have become more frequent. According to Shell Plc Chief Executive Officer Wael Sawan, volumes have recovered to approximately 80% of prewar levels. In addition, oil from the Persian Gulf benefits from shorter voyages and lower transportation costs, increasing its appeal to Indian buyers amid rising tanker freight rates.
Along with China, India became an important market for Russian oil after Western sanctions redirected exports away from Europe following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. India’s shift toward Middle Eastern oil could intensify competition for crude from the Persian Gulf, as Asian refineries secure supplies for the final months of the year.
"India is certainly diversifying its sources of oil by increasing supplies from the Middle East and the Americas," Ritolia said.

The First Year: A reckoning with the media's coverage of Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:35:33 UTC
19:35:33 KST

Breadcrumb
The First Year: A searing takedown of the media's coverage of Israel's genocide in Gaza
When playwright and director Sînziana Cojocărescu began working on the play The First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) in 2023, she could not have imagined that the genocide in Gaza would be ongoing three years later.
Hamas’s large-scale attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 was quickly presented by mainstream media in the UK and beyond as the starting point of Palestinian-Israeli history, with every depraved act of Israel’s genocide in Gaza reported as being committed in retaliation for, and in relation to, that attack.
This recalibration of history was the impetus behind The First Year, which, in its world premiere run at the New Diorama Theatre in London, excavates this flimsily constructed timeline of violence and challenges establishment media’s obfuscation of facts.
"The idea for the show came incredibly early, as soon as the genocide started, really," Sînziana tells The New Arab of the play’s origins.
"I saw how people who, before 7 October, might have said, ‘Oh yeah, it’s a shame what’s happening in Israel and Palestine, it’s so complicated,’ suddenly had it all simplified for them. The way the media reported 7 October and the genocide after that almost took the issue off the shelf for them. They didn’t have to think about it, because they were helped to make up their minds. This made me think about the huge responsibility the media has in shaping public perception and, basically, enabling genocide," Sînziana adds.
How the media became part of the story
Sînziana is the artistic director of British Romanian theatre company Bezna, whose modus operandi is political and uncompromising theatre-making.
For The First Year, Bezna worked with researchers from its frequent collaborators Shadow World Investigations and the International State Crime Initiative to create a comprehensive timeline of the events of the first year of the genocide in Gaza.
"We looked at that timeline and compared the events as they were reported with how the journalists in Gaza we interviewed experienced them," Sînziana says.
Condensing the enormity of the first year of this genocide – in which almost 42,000 people were killed – and the media’s warping of events into a 90-minute play posed a huge challenge.
"We’ve had to cut a lot and think, OK, we can’t make every single point. We can just make a couple of points, but let’s make those points strongly," Sînziana says.
"Hopefully, giving an insight into how the media operated during that year will make our audiences want to find out more and really question things they have heard or seen."
The play’s all-Palestinian heritage cast enact some of the most farcical instances of reporting we saw in the year after 7 October 2023.
In one scene, they grill a flustered representative of the BBC on its breaches of the values of impartiality and objectivity that it claims to hold so dear.
For The First Year, Bezna also collaborated with three writers – Ahmed Masoud and Hannah Khalil, who are both Palestinian, and an anonymous playwright.
These writers created short, on-theme scenes based on the skeleton of the play that Sînziana had put together. They ask if a mathematical value can be placed on Palestinian life (an academic almost combusts on stage in an attempt to do so), and lend voice to a Palestinian mother’s dreams (a house with a swimming pool, by the beach).
Elsewhere, an account of the Nuseriat massacre of June 2024 by an Israeli soldier, as reported by the BBC, brought to life on stage with Hollywood vocal affectation and sepia-toned lighting, sits next to a chilling and sombre account of that same massacre by a Palestinian eyewitness.
Here, the parallels between biased journalism and the storytelling of theatre and cinema are laid bare. "Journalism is responsible for creating an image and telling a story," Sînziana says.
"The story we have seen told since 7 October, where context was only given from one point onwards, where the history behind it was never mentioned, where the words occupation and apartheid were mentioned only a few times in one year, where passive language continuously masked the perpetrator… that feels like a performance. It feels like telling a particular story," Sînziana adds.
"I think that’s where we are trying to use the theatrical tools at our disposal to uncouple the actual story from the way the story was told."
Theatre that stays with you
At the play’s end, a message on a screen reads: There will be no bow. As happens upon revelation of a big truth, The First Year makes for a disorienting viewing experience; the head swims for a long while after you leave the theatre, before clearing to leave just a sobering truth: we have been lied to repeatedly by supposed arbiters of fact.
"I think the play is a hard watch, and it should be a hard watch, because it basically clarifies and sharpens an image that has been blurred in the media," Sînziana says.
"When the occupation is over, that is the only catharsis. We feel that a bow at the end is a moment of catharsis. It says, ‘Oh, the fiction has ended!’ None of our work is fiction," Sînziana continues.
"We feel that the work we make should always stay with people, and that they should take it with them. They should be moved to action, moved to organise by what they see and experience."
The First Year (of the Gaza Genocide in the Media) runs until 10 October at New Diorama Theatre in London.
Shahla Omar is a freelance journalist based in London. Follow her on Instagram: @shahlatan

Asos says customer data accessed by hacker posing as trusted contact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:35:16 UTC
19:35:16 KST

Asos hackers gained access to millions of customers’ recent search histories as well as names, addresses and phone numbers, the online fashion retailer has revealed.
Terms typed in by customers such as “glamorous wide fit” and “Asos petite” were in the data accessed in the cyber-attack, which emerged on Tuesday after app users received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link to the Telegram messaging service.
After carrying out a “detailed, 48-hour investigation” into the incident, Asos confirmed on Thursday that basic personal information had been accessed by an unidentified third party. This included delivery and email addresses, names and phone numbers.
Experts said the extra information could help attackers devise “highly convincing” phishing scams targeted at customers.
Hackers gained access to a database of one of Asos’s third-party service providers by impersonating a “trusted contact” to gain access to one of its employee’s accounts, the retailer said.
Asos said they had also gained access to “certain non-personal account related information”, which are understood to include shoppers’ recent search history on the app, as first reported by the BBC which was contacted by the hackers.
Payment card details and passwords had not been accessed, the retailer added. It said in a message to customers on Thursday: “We discovered that an unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain login credentials. Those credentials were then used to access information on certain third-party platforms used by Asos.
“The affected platforms were immediately locked down, ensuring that no further information could be accessed, and a full investigation was launched with the support of both internal and external cyber experts. We are also working with the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities.”
Asos said its website and app continued to be safe to use, that customers did not need to take action and that it had “already taken additional steps to further strengthen security controls”.
However, the company warned: “Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos. We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call.”
Charles Allen, an analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence, said the hack might “temporarily cap the pace” of Asos’s attempt to revive sales and profits, after the Covid pandemic led to a period of boom followed by a sharp drop in trade. “The loss of customer trust could weigh on efforts to rebuild its client base,” he said.
Asos pledged to contact customers directly once its investigation was complete and “where we believe additional information, support or action may be required”.
The Telegram channel operated by the purported hackers, who have named themselves the Xuanye Group, to which users were directed on Tuesday carried a message assuring Asos customers that “payment information is not affected”.
Experts said they had not heard of the group before and that the push notification could have been an attempt to gain wider attention.
Simon Phillips, the chief technology officer at the cybersecurity firm CybaVerse, said the admission that a wider array of customer information was accessed than previously thought could lead to more persuasive phishing attempts.
“Given the information contained search data, and that Asos regularly sends customers reminder emails about the items they search for on the site, attackers could have used this data to send highly convincing scams which are disguised as the emails they typically receive from Asos,” he said.
Lisa Barber, the tech editor for the consumer watchdog Which?, said: “Shoppers should be especially wary of unexpected phone calls, texts, messages and emails they receive in the coming weeks and months.”
She said that if shoppers were unsure who they were speaking to, they should end the conversation and contact the company directly.
It is possible to dial 159 to speak to your bank’s fraud team, or use the number on the back of your card. If you have been called by a possible fraudster, wait at least 15 minutes before calling or use a different phone to ensure the scammer is no longer connected to the call, she said.
The hack comes after a number of British retailers, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods, suffered damaging cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages, and the former was forced to shut down its website for several weeks while it ensured its systems were clean.

Elderly Spanish housing protest icon dies after forced eviction

Elderly Spanish housing protest icon dies after forced eviction
Maria del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction sparked massive housing protests across Spain, has died in a Madrid hospital after a protracted legal battle with a real estate firm over the home she had lived in for seven decades.
Her death was announced by the Madrid Tenants’ Union, prompting hundreds of protesters in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square to hold a minute of silence for Abascal, widely known as ‘Maricarmen’.
Abascal became a symbol of growing anger over Spain’s housing crisis, where the average rent has almost doubled over the past decade, with protests often blaming investment “vulture funds” – such as Blackstone and BlackRock – for the trend.
The protests erupted in force on September 23, when riot police dispersed hundreds of activists attempting to prevent Abascal’s removal from her Madrid apartment, with images of an elderly woman being taken away on a stretcher fueling public outrage.
An 87-year-old pensioner whose eviction sparked protests in Madrid is now being allowed to return home. Last week, police evicted Maricarmen Abascal on a stretcher from her home of more than 70 years. https://t.co/Kdz2eDwbSI
— Channel 4 News (@Channel4News) September 29, 2026
Three days later, tens of thousands marched through the Spanish capital, establishing a camp in Puerta del Sol square and sparking a major political crisis.
Abascal’s family first rented the apartment in 1956, with the tenancy passing from her father to her mother and eventually to her. In 2018, the real estate company Urbagestion purchased the property and later challenged her right to remain. Following a lengthy court battle, the company offered her a new rent contract at around €1,600 ($1,800) per month, compared with the roughly €500 she had previously paid from her monthly pension of €1,400.
While three attempts to evict her were postponed due to resistance from local activists, the fourth succeeded. Following the backlash, Urbagestion agreed to let Abascal return to the apartment at a rent close to her previous payments. However, she died before she could sign the agreement and move back.
Abascal’s cause of death is unclear, but multiple local media outlets reported that her physical condition had worsened amid the legal battle.
Commenting on her death, the Madrid Tenants’ Union called Abascal’s situation “a turning point in the history of this country.” 
“Speculation costs lives, and today rent profiteering has finished killing our colleague Maricarmen,” the union’s spokeswoman said.
Some of the messages laid at an impromptu memorial read, “it’s not a death, it’s a killing,” and “the fight will continue.”
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also weighed in, expressing condolences. “All my affection to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones. A hug also to everyone who today feels this loss as our own. Rest in peace,” he wrote on X.
The Spanish have struggled with soaring rent costs for years, with 26% of renters spending at least 40% of their income on housing and utilities, according to government figures. Meanwhile, A 2024 investigation by the nonprofit Civio identified more than 185,000 rental properties held by large corporate landlords in the regions surveyed, around half linked to US banks and investment funds.
US giant Blackstone controlled nearly 19,600 rental properties, while BlackRock has indirect exposure through its stake in Ares Management, another major investor in Spanish housing.
The protests sparked a major political upheaval in Spain. After parliament rejected emergency housing decrees, Sanchez called a snap general election for November 29. His government subsequently approved a revised 21-measure package, including stronger eviction protections, rent controls and restrictions on speculative property purchases, though it has yet to be ratified.

Kids turning to chatbots to disclose online sexual victimisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:30:29 UTC
19:30:29 KST

AFP chief says policing alone can't fix rise in online child abuse
In short:
More than one in three children turn to AI chatbots for help when they are sexually victimised online, or keep quiet entirely, data shows.
The AFP commissioner says software cannot replace human support and that parents need to encourage children to speak up.
What's next?
A welfare tool that triages reports of harm for human assessment is being developed.
More than one in three Australian children who are sexually victimised online either tell no-one or turn to an AI chatbot for help, according to data from Adelaide University.
The data has prompted Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett to warn law enforcement cannot be the only safety net for vulnerable young people.
In an interview marking her first year in the top job, Commissioner Barrett stopped short of directly endorsing an extension of the federal government's under-16 social media ban to AI chatbots, but stressed that "anything that helps to keep our kids safer is obviously something we support".
The study, an initiative between Adelaide University and the AFP-led Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, has delivered sobering data on how generative tools are altering youth safety.
Amid a sharp increase in children as young as 12 being manipulated through AI-altered nude images and sadistic online exploitation, the study found 35 per cent of children sexually victimised online confided in an AI chatbot or did not tell anyone.
More than 15 per cent of young people report seeking personal or counselling advice from AI at least once a week.
Among victimised boys, two in five disclosed their experiences solely to an AI bot or kept quiet entirely.
Commissioner Barrett called the trend "heartbreaking" and warned that automated software cannot provide the human support or protection vulnerable youth require.
"Young people are turning to AI more and more for advice and for support and for guidance and that should be concerning to all of us, not just parents,"
she said.
Addressing the limits of police intervention when children reach out to AI instead of adults, Commissioner Barrett was realistic about the role of law enforcement.
“We're right at the end of the suite of tools here, and we're a pretty blunt object. Let's be honest, by the time we become involved, the options are reduced," she said.
When pressed on whether the federal government should extend its landmark social media ban for under-16s to conversational AI tools to protect young people, Commissioner Barrett cautioned that legislative bans were not a panacea.
"I won't speak specifically to what government should or shouldn't do," she said.
"I would just say generally that anything that helps to keep our kids safer is obviously something that we support."
Bans were "not the whole solution," she added, noting that while regulatory limits were effective for "starting conversations in households around dinner tables," they could not replace community vigilance.
How parents and communities can step up
Comissioner Barrett said parents, carers, family, educators and community leaders were best placed to notice when a child began to withdraw or alter their behaviour.
"It starts in the home, it starts with parents knowing what their kids are doing online, creating those safe opportunities for conversations,” she said.
“You remember when you're at that age, it is awkward talking to your parents about anything, but we need to create that trust in those safe spaces, because as we know, AI technology, it's not a human."
While the use of artificial intelligence in the exploitation of young people was a major concern for the AFP, Commissioner Barrett was just as emphatic that AI had a place in policing.
To help identify potential exploitation earlier, the AFP is working with Monash University's AiLECS Lab on a welfare tool that triages reports of harm to the Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation and refers them to a human for assessment.
“It's quite forward leaning. This is something that we need to be doing more and more: partnering with academia, and with tech companies around how do we bring all of our knowledge, expertise and access together to come up with these solutions.”
The AFP released its first AI strategy last month, a "human-led" approach to matching the "scale and pace" of offending, particularly in child exploitation and youth radicalisation.
Extremist material and counterterrorism
On counterterrorism and the rise of violent extremism, Commissioner Barrett said the bulk of the AFP's terrorism caseload was still predominantly religiously motivated, but police were increasingly seeing more "mixed and unclear ideologies".
“Sometimes, particularly with our young people, what we see is perhaps they're not actually driven by a particular ideology, they are driven by a grievance,” she said.
“They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose.”
Comissioner Barrett said the rapidly evolving threat environment had validated her decision to establish national security investigation teams designed to target the "grey zone" of radicalisation, including hate crimes, misogyny, and online hostility that fell just below statutory thresholds for joint counterterrorism charges.
The teams have charged 65 people since they were created at the end of last year and she expects those volumes to increase.
"We're going through doors and arresting and charging people very quickly after we receive the reports," Commissioner Barrett said.
Asked whether she believed the definition of terrorism needed to be changed to reflect the evolving security environment, Commissioner Barrett said violent extremist material laws were already working well as a key preventative measure.
"That legislation gives us the ability to go and conduct a search warrant, to seize the devices, to intervene early," she said, describing the possession of extremist material as frequently being the start of a continuum that can lead to violence.
Commissioner Barrett said it also provided police with more options "around how we deal with a young person who's come to our attention".
She said most young people in the extremism cases showed behavioural warning signs before they came to police attention, and called on parents and carers to watch out for these.
"I don't want to be arresting and charging young people. We want to be intervening earlier and we want to be getting them the assistance and the support that they need," Commissioner Barrett said.
In 2026, 23 juveniles and 24 adults have been charged for possessing violent extremist material.
The commissioner is working to strengthen ties with other nations and is scheduled to travel to Tokyo later this month.

Life Is Asymmetric. The Scientists Who Figured Out Why Won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.
Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.
Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”
In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.
The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.
At the beginning of the last century, the German chemist Willy Marckwald designed an asymmetric reaction capable of producing a slightly greater amount of one of the two versions. He achieved this using a chiral catalyst—a substance that facilitates a chemical reaction without being consumed and favors the formation of one of the enantiomers. The ratio between the two variants, however, only changed a little.
Later, in 1953, theoretical physicist Charles Frank proposed a mathematical model that outlined three conditions for reproducing homochirality. First, there must be an asymmetric reaction capable of favoring one of the two versions; that imbalance has to be amplified; and the reaction itself has to produce the catalyst that drives it. This last characteristic is called autocatalysis and generates a kind of positive feedback loop, in which a small initial advantage can cause one of the variants to assemble at an ever-faster rate until it dominates the reaction.
This framework formed the basis of Henri Kagan’s research. Beginning in the early 1980s, he focused on refining asymmetric reactions through a detailed study of the catalyst. At that time, scientists typically used catalysts consisting of a metal atom that acted as the reaction’s driving force and a chiral substance that ensured the process was asymmetric. They assumed that if they used a mixture containing equal amounts of the two versions of that chiral molecule, the result would also be a balanced mixture.
Kagan began to question that idea. He realized that the metal atom likely did not interact with just one enantiomer but with both at the same time. This meant that, by mixing versions A and B, three different combinations could form: A-A, B-B, and B-A. The first two would produce molecules that were mirror images of each other. But the A-B combination could behave differently during the reaction.
The A-B combination, the scientist discovered, could slow down the reaction, indirectly favoring the formation of one of the two versions of the final molecule. The phenomenon was called the “nonlinear effect” and represented a new way to manipulate chemical reactions.
“In addition to their practical interest, nonlinear effects are a very valuable tool for studying reaction mechanisms and the nature of catalytically active species,” explained José María Andrés García, a professor in the Department of Organic Chemistry at the University of Valladolid, in a statement reported by SMC Spain.
Inspired by Kagan’s findings, Kensō Soai sought to create a reaction in which the product itself would act as a catalyst and help produce more molecules identical to itself—one of those theoretical conditions for the homochirality. He conducted a test with a substance known as 5-pyrimidylalkanol. At the beginning of the experiment, one version was just 2 percent more abundant than the other version of the molecule. By the end of the reaction, that advantage had jumped to 87 percent.
In the years that followed, Soai worked toward achieving reactions that resulted in the near-absolute purity of one enantiomer, replicating the molecular state inside living organisms. Finally, in 2003, he engineered a reaction in which the starting substances had no defined orientation, but as they reacted, a slightly greater amount of one enantiomer appeared by chance. That tiny difference then produced many more molecules of the same variant. Gradually, that form came to dominate the reaction, accounting for up to 99.99 percent of the final product.
In other words, the reaction formed only one of the two possible enantiomers. As the Nobel Committee stated, “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat.”
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Israeli prisons since 2023: sites of torture and 'extermination'
Unknown

2026-10-08

Breadcrumb
Israeli prisons since 2023: Palestinians face abuse, torture and 'extermination'
Three years into Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, organisations representing Palestinian prisoners say a "parallel extermination" is taking place inside Israeli prisons, where abuse, torture, starvation and medical neglect have intensified.
More than 100 Palestinian prisoners have died in Israeli custody over the past three years, while around 9,300 remain imprisoned in increasingly harsh conditions, according to Palestinian prisoners' rights groups.
For Nisreen Abu Ghraibeh, those three years have been marked by constant fear for her son Fadi, who is being held by Israel.
Her anxiety grows with every court hearing, the only opportunity she has to see her son, who appears via video link.
Israel has increasingly used video hearings since October 2023, further isolating Palestinian prisoners from their families, who often struggle to obtain even basic information about their detained relatives.
Speaking during a weekly protest at the Al-Bireh Cultural Centre, near Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, Abu Ghraibeh told The New Arab that her son, like other prisoners, had faced systematic repression while his family received only limited information about his condition.
One of her greatest fears is the spread of disease in Israeli prisons, particularly skin conditions such as scabies. Families have also recently received reports of other illnesses, including mpox.
Whenever Abu Ghraibeh hears that another Palestinian has died in custody, she fears her son or other prisoners could be next.
'Parallel extermination'
At a press conference marking three years since the start of Israel's war on Gaza, Palestinian prisoners' organisations warned of a growing gulf between international legal protections and the reality faced by detainees.
Abdullah al-Zaghari, head of the Palestinian Prisoners' Club, said Israeli prisons could not be viewed separately from the wider context of the war.
"The prison cannot be viewed as a place separate from the context of extermination, but rather as one of the tools through which violence and control over Palestinians are reproduced and perpetuated within a closed system," he said.
Zaghari said testimonies gathered by prisoners' groups and human rights organisations over the past three years provided an important record not only of abuses inside Israeli prisons, but also of the failure of the international system to protect victims and uphold international law.
He warned that allowing violations to continue without accountability risked normalising such practices far beyond the Palestinian context.
Zaghari called for implementation of the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion declaring Israel's occupation unlawful, including the dismantling of what he described as a discriminatory military judicial system used to legitimise repression and collective punishment against Palestinian prisoners.
He also called for greater international pressure on Israel over the death penalty for Palestinians.
Lawyer and prisoners' rights activist Sahar Francis said the past three years had also seen a dangerous shift at the legislative level, including the introduction of the death penalty and the establishment of a new military court to try Gaza detainees accused of involvement in the 7 October 2023 attack.
Francis questioned what Palestinian institutions, political parties and prisoners' families could do in the face of what she described as the failure of international legal mechanisms and states to uphold their obligations.
Helmi al-Araj, director of the Hurriyat Centre for Defence of Liberties and Civil Rights, accused Israel of pursuing a policy of "slow death" against prisoners through systematic torture, starvation and medical neglect.
He said the treatment of prisoners over the past three years was unprecedented and called for greater public mobilisation around their plight.
Al-Araj also held the UN Secretary-General largely responsible for providing legal protection for prisoners and ensuring international protection for Palestinians from violations by Israeli forces and settlers.
More than 100 deaths in custody
In a report examining the abuses suffered by Palestinian prisoners since October 2023, prisoners' organisations said detainees had faced attacks unprecedented in their severity and scale.
They highlighted the introduction of legislation imposing the death penalty on Palestinian prisoners in March 2026 as among the most serious developments.
More than 100 Palestinian prisoners have died over the past three years, according to the report. The identities of 92 have been announced, while Israel continues to conceal information about the fate of dozens of detainees from Gaza and retains the bodies of dozens of Palestinians who died in custody.
Deaths over the past three years account for around 28% of all recorded Palestinian prisoner deaths since 1967, the organisations said.
Around 26,000 arrests have been recorded in the occupied West Bank since October 2023, alongside thousands more in Gaza.
Some 9,300 Palestinians are currently held by Israel, including 118 serving life sentences, 91 women and 350 children.
Another 3,101 Palestinians are being held under administrative detention without charge or trial.
Israel also classifies 1,419 detainees as "unlawful combatants", a category that includes prisoners from Gaza as well as detainees from Syria and Lebanon.
For families such as Abu Ghraibeh's, the figures compound three years of uncertainty over what their relatives are enduring behind prison walls.

Leaked Russian Blueprint Counts 1,000 Weapons to Freeze Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:28:34 UTC
19:28:34 KST

An alleged Russian document calculates that three Kinzhal missiles could be used against each combined heat and power plant and 20 attack drones against each single boiler facility as part of a wider campaign to deprive Ukrainian cities of electricity, heating and water.
The Ukrainian investigative project Schemes, run by RFE/RL, said on Thursday, Oct. 8, that it obtained a copy of the document from sources in Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The file outlines approximately 60 critical targets and calculates that Russia would need roughly 1,000 weapons to disable them: up to 770 drones and drone-missiles, 170 guided aerial bombs and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles.
The document does not constitute a confirmed order for attacks. Experts consulted by Schemes described it as an analytical estimate that could be used to justify weapons production and establish how many munitions would be required for a future operation.
Russia calculates weapons for each target
The document is titled “Analytical Brief: Analysis of Ukraine’s Energy Generation and Utilities” and is dated August 2026.
Its authors are not identified, its metadata has been altered and some pages are missing. It also does not specify which Russian officials received the presentation before Ukrainian intelligence allegedly intercepted it.
Schemes said the file relies partly on publicly available information from OpenStreetMap, Worldometers and the websites of Ukrenergo, Ukrhydroenergo, Kyivteploenergo, the Energy Ministry and DTEK. Other assessments are attributed only to unnamed Russian military experts or a “working group.”
Poland Ends Russian Drone Probe After Failing to Identify Perpetrator
The document names four priority sectors: electricity generation and distribution, water supplies, sewage systems and heating.
Its list of 60 targets includes hydroelectric and thermal power plants, combined heat and power facilities, electricity substations, cross-border interconnectors, boiler houses, water-treatment facilities and pumping stations.
According to the calculations:
- Equipment connecting each of Ukraine’s three operating nuclear power plants to the grid would require two Iskander missiles to disable.
- Each major hydroelectric power plant could require up to 25 Molniya, Geran or Dan-T/Banderol drones, or three Kinzhal missiles.
- Each combined heat and power facility could require 25 drones or three Kinzhals. The document also considers approximately 25 FAB-500 guided bombs and five Iskander-M missiles for each facility.
- A substation or electricity interconnector could require 15 drones or three Kinzhals.
- A boiler house could require 20 Geran or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The authors acknowledge that boiler houses are close to residential areas and state that using other weapons against them could cause civilian casualties.
Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa are principal targets
The document identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa as the main target cities. It also lists Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia and Ivano-Frankivsk as priorities.
Kyiv’s energy system receives particular attention. Although the capital has an extensive network, the authors identify five substations forming part of the “Kyiv ring” as potential weak points.
According to the calculation, disabling 12 key substations serving Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa could halt as much as 90 percent of their electricity supply. The document estimates that this would require 40-50 Molniya drones and 130-140 Geran-4 or Dan-T/Banderol weapons.
The same material was previously examined by The New York Times, which reported that Moscow’s apparent objective was to cause a humanitarian emergency by cutting large cities off from electricity, heating and water.
The proposed campaign reportedly begins with attacks on interconnectors through which Ukraine imports electricity from Europe, followed by attacks against 10 major hydroelectric plants and equipment connecting the South Ukraine, Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants to the national grid.
Not a final attack order
Energy Research Center Director Oleksandr Kharchenko cautioned that the document should not be interpreted as a direct combat order.
“This is not a combat directive,” he told Schemes, describing it as a presentation intended to demonstrate the concept to senior Russian officials.
A Ukrainian defense-industry representative who had seen the material before being contacted by journalists offered a similar assessment. The source said the calculations could support requests for manufacturers to produce certain quantities of weapons.
An actual operational plan would be a separate document specifying how weapons would be distributed and when attacks would take place, the source said.
Schemes could not independently establish who prepared the file. The defense-industry representative assessed that it probably originated in the Russian Defense Ministry or one of its subordinate bodies.
Ukraine’s military intelligence, Foreign Intelligence Service and Security Service had not formally authenticated the document by the time the investigation was published.
“Cold terrorist calculation”
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented Russia’s alleged preparations to European partners during a G7+ energy meeting in Paris on Sept. 17.
Shmyhal described the material as a “cold terrorist calculation,” saying it contained tables specifying the weapons considered necessary to destroy individual facilities.
Since the full-scale invasion began, Ukrainian prosecutors have opened investigations into 3,374 Russian attacks affecting 1,177 energy facilities, according to figures provided to Schemes.
At least three facilities attacked during Russia’s large-scale barrage on Sept. 30 – two combined heat and power plants in Kyiv and a thermal power plant in the Kyiv region – also appeared in the document.
On Oct. 7, Russia launched 70 missiles and dozens of attack drones across Ukraine, hitting energy infrastructure and residential buildings. The nationwide death toll later rose to at least 32, including five children.

Pakistan joins Saudi airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthis: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:27:41 UTC
19:27:41 KST

- A senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times that Pakistani fighter jets have carried out strikes against Yemen’s Houthis.
- A second official called it air support against Houthi drone and missile threats and ruled out a Pakistani ground offensive inside Yemen.
Pakistan Air Force fighter jets are being used in strikes against Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a senior Pakistani military official told The New York Times, the first indication from inside Pakistan’s military that its air force has joined Saudi Arabia’s renewed war against the Iran-backed group.
A second Pakistani official told the newspaper that Pakistan’s role is expected to focus on degrading Houthi drone and missile threats through air support, and not on a ground offensive in Yemen. Neither official said how many aircraft are involved, which targets have been hit, when the strikes began or whether the jets are striking inside Yemeni territory, and Pakistan’s military declined to comment.
Col. David O. Smith, a former U.S. Army attaché in Pakistan and former Defense Intelligence Agency analyst, told the Times that analysts broadly estimate about 8,000 Pakistani troops have deployed to Saudi Arabia, including Pakistan Air Force and Army air defense units. He said they would likely help protect oil infrastructure and were unlikely to fight the Houthis directly, given Islamabad’s effort to preserve its relationship with neighboring Iran.
The report follows Monday’s decision by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey to activate the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, a mutual defense pact the three countries signed on Aug. 7. At an emergency meeting in Riyadh, they agreed to put collective deterrence measures into effect and rapidly deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, the first time the pact had been invoked. Hours later, Pakistani Defense Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part, although when reporters asked him on Sept. 30 whether Pakistani forces had joined strikes in Yemen, he did not answer directly.
Pakistan’s military spokesman, Lt. Gen. Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, confirmed this week that Pakistani troops are stationed in Saudi Arabia but declined to say whether they would operate across the border in Yemen, telling CNN that any involvement would be defensive in nature.
Over the past several days, Saudi Arabia said Houthi missile and drone strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and Abha International Airport in the south killed three people, two women at Abha and a Sudanese man at King Khalid, and injured 36. The Saudi-led coalition said it retaliated by hitting dozens of Houthi military sites in Yemen, including missile storage sites and command centers, and on Thursday residents of Riyadh reported hearing several explosions whose cause was not immediately clear.
The Houthis declared a blockade of the Red Sea in July and attacked shipping there, then seized Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive last month, routing Saudi-backed government forces. The Saudi-led coalition says 100 fighter jets are now supporting a counteroffensive by Yemen’s internationally recognized government to retake that territory, and a United Nations agency said nearly 200,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since early September.
Islamabad has long kept its distance from the Yemen war: in 2015, when Saudi Arabia launched its original campaign against the Houthis and asked Pakistan for jets, ships and troops, Pakistan’s parliament voted to stay neutral. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said on Sunday it hoped reports of a Pakistani deployment for the war in Yemen were untrue.
Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a separate bilateral mutual defense agreement in September 2025, declaring an attack on either country an attack on both, and the Mecca pact extended that commitment to Turkey, whose parliament has not yet ratified it.

Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:26:46 UTC
19:26:46 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza 3 years on: The unfinished fight for Palestinian workers
Three years after Israel began its genocide in Gaza, the fate of Palestinian workers detained after 7 October remains unclear, though their odyssey of humiliation, torture, and, on occasion, murder is beyond doubt and is mostly documented by their Israeli tormentors on social media and aired live by the far-right Minister of National Security Itamar Ben-Gvir.
Gazans who had crossed the Green Line desperate to earn a living, mostly in blue-collar jobs, were stripped of their permits, rounded up, and held without contact with lawyers or families. Their treatment should push one to wonder what international trade unions did when fellow workers in this part of the world were imprisoned and abused.
Israel closed the crossings and revoked Gazan workers’ permits, turning people previously authorised to work into supposed illegal residents. Thousands were detained in Israel and the occupied West Bank. On 3 November 2023, more than 3,000 were released into Gaza, where bombardment continued. Release offered no guarantee of safety.
Workers described, in testimonies published by Human Rights Watch in January 2024, beatings, electric shocks, humiliation, and deprivation of food and water. The rights watchdog also independently documented mass detention without contact with the outside world.
International allies
Warnings of the ongoing abuse were already coming out earlier. On 11 October 2023, the Palestinian Democracy and Workers’ Rights Centre denounced violence against Gazan workers. On 25 October, it demanded their immediate release and appealed to the international labour movement. The workers’ predicament was already being placed before their supposed international allies.
Their case cuts through the claim that Palestine is somehow outside a union’s remit. These Gazan workers had employers, wages, and families dependent on their earnings. Stripped of work permits, thrown in torture dungeons for weeks, should have triggered a global public outcry among trade unionists and industrial organisers everywhere.
Calling the subsequent response universal silence would be inaccurate. The International Trade Union Confederation’s 2024 Global Rights Index described thousands of workers held in illegal detention, denied basic rights and legal representation. It recorded reports of abuse and degrading conditions, alongside two deaths in custody. The world’s principal union confederation had publicly acknowledged the violations.
Australia’s Union Aid Abroad–APHEDA published Palestinian union allegations of torture deaths in January 2024. In March 2025, the International Labour Network of Solidarity and Struggle endorsed reports from the Arab Workers Union in Nazareth concerning disappeared Gazan workers, torture and deaths in detention. These were clear acts of solidarity, but circulating allegations is only the beginning.
On 27 September 2024, nine global unions filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation detailing the draconian working conditions of more than 200,000 Palestinian workers in Israel. The nine organisations condemned “widespread wage theft due to the suspension of work permits and the unilateral termination of their contracts.”
Signatories included the ITUC, IndustriALL, Education International, Public Services International, UNI, and the international federations representing transport, construction, food workers and journalists. The OECD’s Trade Union Advisory Committee also joined. Its stated legal focus was wage protection; however, not accountability for torture.
The demands of Palestinian unions
While such a solidarity move is worth applauding, it still exposes a long-running problem of “economism” that has long marred the trade union movement.
What resources went toward locating missing workers, supporting survivors, securing independent investigations and pursuing those responsible? A complaint about stolen wages surely matters enormously to impoverished families. It cannot substitute for a “political” campaign against imprisonment, torture, military occupation and genocide.
Palestinian unions had also identified what their counterparts could do. Their 16 October 2023 appeal asked workers to refuse to manufacture or transport weapons for Israel, challenge complicit companies and pressure governments to stop military trade. This was an action plan for international unions. Were the latter ready to organise around those demands and protect members prepared to act?
The wider response to Gaza shows that stronger positions were possible. The World Federation of Trade Unions was calling for an end to genocide by October 2023. IndustriALL’s executive committee explicitly condemned the continuing genocide in May 2024 and urged affiliates to support boycott, divestment, and sanctions.
Education International’s 2024 congress demanded an end to arms transfers to Israel. These were formal positions of international organisations, not merely statements by dissident branches.
Other unions organised material support. In November 2023, the International Transport Workers’ Federation created a Palestine Solidarity Fund. Public Services International established its Gaza fund in March 2024. By August 2025, European Union federations were demanding sanctions, suspension of the EU–Israel Association Agreement, and an end to economic relations with Israeli settlements.
Influential national unions in several countries also took a firm position in solidarity with the Palestinians, sometimes aligning with their governments’ stated positions and sometimes opposing them.
South Africa’s teachers’ union SADTU explicitly condemned genocide in 2023. Ireland’s ICTU demanded economic sanctions, while Britain’s TUC called for ending arms licenses and suspending the trade agreement. Canada’s CUPE described the assault as genocide and supported Palestinian workers’ rights organising.
In July 2024, seven US unions demanded an immediate halt to military aid: UAW, UE, SEIU, the postal workers’ APWU, flight attendants’ AFA, painters’ IUPAT and National Education Association. Their demand confronted the material support sustaining Israel’s assault, even if a letter alone could not stop it.
Disrupting the deadly occupation machine
Workplace action offered another, certainly more effective, route. A trade union representing workers in 11 major Indian ports refused to handle weapons shipments for Israel. France’s CGT endorsed workers at Fos and Roissy who refused to facilitate arms deliveries. Such examples show where unions’ distinctive power lies: in their capacity to interrupt production and transport.
Italian unions took action to another level by organising a general strike explicitly in solidarity with Gaza. On 22 September 2025, USB and other grassroots unions organised a nationwide stoppage against the genocide, disrupting transport, schools and ports.
Following Israel’s interception of the Global Sumud Flotilla, CGIL and USB called another general strike on 3 October. According to CGIL, the stoppage disrupted major services, and more than two million people rallied across over 100 cities.
Such organising efforts developed across borders. Italy’s USB, Greece’s ENEDEP, the Basque union LAB, Turkey’s Liman-İş and Morocco’s ODT called a joint ports action for 6 February 2026, demanding an end to arms shipments feeding the genocide and a trade embargo on Israel. Their initiative connected solidarity with opposition to militarisation and the erosion of dockworkers’ conditions.
But other union leaders shamefully obstructed solidarity. In October 2023, the AFL-CIO intervened against a ceasefire resolution adopted by Washington state’s Thurston-Lewis-Mason labour council. The federation eventually, under pressure, called for a negotiated ceasefire on 8 February 2024.
Germany’s DGB declared solidarity with Israel after the Hamas attacks. Its position cannot fairly be reduced to unconditional approval of everything Israel subsequently did: a July 2025 resolution demanded an end to attacks on civilians and supported a ceasefire. Yet the same resolution sharply defended Histadrut against criticism within international union bodies.
The Histadrut, for its part, is hardly an ordinary “trade union.” It has been the backbone of the settler colonisation of Palestine from the start, and a major instrument of segregation and discrimination against Arab workers. The international labour movement should isolate, boycott, and deplatform it.
Union members everywhere need to hold their own leaders accountable for these decisions. Those who blocked solidarity or defended Israel’s actions should face a challenge from below, with their record on Gaza brought into branch meetings, congress debates, and leadership elections. Members can demand disclosure of their unions’ ties to Histadrut and organise to sever them.
The fight is far from over. Missing workers must be accounted for, survivors supported, stolen wages recovered, and those responsible for torture and deaths held accountable. These demands belong alongside the struggle to end the occupation and dismantle the structures that leave Palestinian workers dependent on those who dispossess and exploit them.
The strikes and port actions point toward what comes next: sustained organising to stop arms shipments, challenge complicit employers, and defend workers who face retaliation for taking action. Every solidarity resolution needs an organising plan behind it. Palestinian workers deserve a labour movement prepared to use its power, and a rank and file ready to act when its leaders refuse.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.

UK airport e-gates to become passport-free and contactless by early 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:24:53 UTC
19:24:53 KST

UK airports have begun rolling out contactless e-gates. The technology allows eligible travellers to pass through without having to show their passports.
The UK has begun rolling out a new contactless border system across its airports. The move means eligible passengers arriving in the country will soon be able to pass through airport e-gates without presenting their passports.
Initially only available for British citizens, the initiative was launched at East Midlands Airport in England this week. In a statement, the government said it plans to upgrade all the country’s e-gates by early 2027 and expand its accessibility to other eligible nationalities.
“We’re delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless e-gates introduced by Border Force,” Steve Griffiths, Managing Director of East Midlands Airport, said. He added that any technological innovation that can make customers’ journeys “smoother, swifter and simpler” is welcomed.
According to tests, the new contactless system is up to 25% faster compared to presenting a physical passport. Phil Douglas, Director General of the UK's Border Force, said the digital push builds on work from the summer period to extend e-gates to children aged eight and older. This will make life “a little easier” for families, he added.
How does it work?
The contactless system uses facial comparison technology to verify a traveller’s identity. Upon arrival, passengers will approach an e-gate where their photo is taken. The system then checks the live image against verified immigration, travel and passport information. And, if all clear, the barrier will automatically open, meaning the checks are complete.
If further checks are needed, however, travellers will be required to place their passport on the reader or be directed to a Border Force officer.
Officials advise that travellers keep their passport with them at all times, nonetheless. Further, the UK government added that Border Force officers will remain at hand monitoring all e-gates and offering assistance.
For dual British nationals, the advice is to return to the UK with a valid British passport or hold a Certificate of Entitlement to avoid any potential delays at the border.
Which UK airports have the new contactless e-gates?
Currently, a handful of contactless e-gates are available to use at East Midlands Airport.
As part of the phased rollout, however, the technology will also be available across Birmingham, Bristol, Cardiff, Edinburgh, Gatwick, Glasgow, Heathrow, London City, Luton, Manchester, Newcastle and Stansted airports.
The UK has more than 290 standard e-gates in place at 15 air and rail ports. This technology is available to UK or Irish citizens, as well as travellers eligible to obtain an Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) to travel to the UK.
Introduced in February, the ETA allows officials to identify potential security risks before someone travels to the country.

At least 12 people were killed and 14 others wounded on Oct. 8 when Russia struck two passenger buses in Kramatorsk near the frontline in eastern Ukraine, authorities said.
“According to preliminary data, 12 people are known to have been killed as of now. Additionally, 14 people are believed to have sustained injuries,” the local prosecutor’s office said.
“The final toll of the enemy attack is being determined,” it added, posting photos of bodies and debris strewn across a road in front of the burning metal shell of a bus.
Ukraine’s national police said Russia had hit the buses with a glide bomb.
Kramatorsk is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” which troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern edge, which has prompted calls for civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Oct. 8's strike, which happened at 10 a.m., came a day after a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the northern region of Chernigiv, killing 22, including five children.
Kramatorsk City Council said it was “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population.”
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.

Sozanovsky joined the team of PrJSC Inter TV Channel in November 2023 and, over the course of three years, participated in implementing the strategic objectives of Inter Media Group.
