Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:19:24 UTC
19:19:24 KST

Putin just turned 74. Russia’s State Duma isn’t getting any younger either. Here’s how the country’s parliament has aged over the past three decades.
In late September 2026, after reviewing the results of elections to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, Russia’s Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said:
The Duma has gotten a little younger. It wasn’t old to begin with, but it’s gotten younger.
To support her claim, Pamfilova cited the lawmakers’ average age at the end of the previous session and the start of the new Duma: 57 and 53, respectively.
That comparison is incorrect, however. The newly elected lawmakers are indeed younger on average than those who served during the spring sitting of the eighth, outgoing session.
Comparing lawmakers’ ages at the start of each session shows the State Duma has been steadily aging, according to Meduza’s calculations. BBC Russia reached the same conclusion.
The State Duma’s first session was elected in December 1993, and lawmakers convened for their first meeting in January 1994, when their average age was 45.8. By the second session, the average age had risen to 47.2.
In the fifth session, which began work in 2007, the average age exceeded 50 for the first time.
Since then, the average age has continued to rise, reaching 54.3 in the ninth session. The difference from the first session is 8.5 years.
How we calculated this
Meduza compared lawmakers’ ages as of the date of each session’s first meeting. Vacant seats were not counted, which is why some previous Dumas had fewer than 450 members. The fourth session, for example, began work with 447 lawmakers after the “against all” option won in three electoral districts, leaving those seats vacant until repeat votes were held several months later.
Meduza calculated lawmakers’ average and median ages using their dates of birth, rounding the results to the nearest tenth of a year. The lists of lawmakers and their dates of birth were compiled from Central Election Commission documents, State Duma records, and other published biographies.
Age is calculated as of the day of each session’s first meeting, and party affiliation is based on faction membership on that same date.
Each successive session is older than the last
Nearly one in three lawmakers in the new Duma has already turned 60. United Russia has the most lawmakers in that group: 109, out of 349 seats the party won overall.
United Russia’s lawmakers age 60 and older alone outnumber all lawmakers from every other party combined: only 101 lawmakers in total were elected to the rest of the Duma, including members of Russia’s Communist Party (KPRF), New People, the LDPR, A Just Russia, and Rodina, along with four independent candidates.
Almost a quarter of the Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — have already reached retirement age (currently 64 for men and 59 for women); 81 of them were elected from United Russia.
How we calculated retirement age
Russia carried out a pension reform in 2019, so Meduza used the retirement age in effect for each given year when calculating the number of retirees in the Duma. Women born between 1964 and 1968 and men born between 1959 and 1963 follow a transitional retirement schedule. The thresholds are listed on the Social Fund’s website.
Northern work experience and other benefits were not factored in.
Lawmakers’ average age depends directly on the Duma’s oldest members: the older they are, the higher the overall figure. To rule out the possibility that a few outliers are driving the increase, Meduza also calculated the median age.
In the first session, the median age was 45.3: half the lawmakers were younger, half older. In the current session, it is 54.2, a difference of almost nine years.
This means aging has affected every age segment of the Duma, though the trend has not been uniform: in 2011, for example, the median age dipped slightly.
The change is visible even without averages. In 1994, 127 lawmakers under 40 were elected to the Duma’s first session, almost a third of the original lineup that convened for its first meeting. In the new Duma, only 51 lawmakers are under 40, or one in nine.
There are now almost as many lawmakers age 70 and older: 49. Just 10 years ago, at the start of the seventh session, there were only 19, and in the Duma’s first session there were none at all.
The record for age at the start of a session had previously belonged to KPRF member Vladimir Dolgikh, who was 87 when the sixth Duma began work in December 2011. In the ninth session, United Russia’s Vladimir Resin broke that record; he turned 90 in February.
Before being elected to the State Duma, Resin spent many years heading Moscow’s construction sector and served as first deputy mayor of Moscow under Yuri Luzhkov. LDPR leader Leonid Slutsky likely owes his career to Resin: in private conversations, he calls Resin “Dad.”
The Duma’s oldest lawmaker has a special duty: under the Constitution, he is the one who opens the first meeting of a new Duma. In January 1994, LDPR lawmaker Georgy Lukava opened the first session at age 68. This year, 90-year-old Resin ceded the right to open the meeting to his United Russia colleague, 79-year-old Yuri Petrov.
Petrov is actually only fourth by age: older than the United Russia member are his party colleague Valentina Tereshkova, 89, and KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, 82. During his remarks, Petrov asked each of his older colleagues in turn, “Shall we open the meeting?” All three agreed, after which Petrov thanked them “for the trust placed in him,” the Russian business daily Kommersant wrote.
The youngest lawmaker in the new Duma is Georgy Arapov, the former head of New People’s regional branch in Irkutsk region, who turned 27 in September.
Arapov has set the lower end of the age range for elected lawmakers over the past five years: he was also the youngest lawmaker in the previous Duma, when the New People member was only 22.
The record for this metric, however, belongs to 21-year-old Vasily Vlasov, elected to the seventh session of parliament from the LDPR in 2016. Before his election, he worked as an aide to Vladimir Zhirinovsky and headed his secretariat. In March 2021, when Vlasov was 25, he became first deputy head of the LDPR faction. In November 2023, a year and a half after Zhirinovsky’s death, Vlasov lost his parliamentary mandate over absences from meetings.
More about Vasily Vlasov
In August 2017, Yuri Dud asked Zhirinovsky about Vlasov’s path to the Duma on the party’s ticket: “What did he do to become a lawmaker at 21?” The LDPR leader pointed to the legally permitted age for election, 21, and explained: “He knows better what young people his age want.”
Vlasov’s rise within the party caused discontent among its members. According to the Russian business outlet RBC, Zhirinovsky’s son, State Duma Deputy Speaker Igor Lebedev, opposed the appointment. On the independent Russian broadcaster TV Rain, Zhirinovsky denied any conflict with his son and explained his choice of Vlasov simply: “It benefits us [that] he’s good at his job.”
Vlasov now works at the Russian University of Sport in Moscow, where he oversees youth policy.
More than three-quarters of pension-age lawmakers were elected from United Russia
Almost a quarter of the new Duma’s lawmakers — 106 of 450 — are already old enough to retire. A large share of them belong to United Russia.
The KPRF has 16 pension-age lawmakers out of 37 in the faction, A Just Russia has five out of 17, the LDPR has two out of 24, and Rodina has one. New People has none.
A total of 109 United Russia lawmakers are starting their work at 60 or older, compared with 35 in the other parties combined.
Despite the increase in the retirement age, United Russia now has more pension-age lawmakers in the new Duma than before: 81, up from 75. The other factions now have fewer: 25, down from 36 in the previous session.
Over the past three sessions, the share of seats held by lawmakers age 60 and older has grown from 26.9% to 32%. The number of lawmakers in that age group was 121 in 2016, 126 in 2021, and is 144 now.
The number of pension-age lawmakers in the Duma as a whole has fallen. Ten years ago, almost one in three lawmakers fell into this group. Now, about one in four do. The decline, however, is directly tied to the increase in the retirement age — under the pre-reform rules, more than a third of the Duma would now fall into this group.
This last change is particularly telling. Compared with the start of the previous session, the number of lawmakers age 60 and older across the whole Duma has grown by 18. All of that increase came from United Russia, which gained 23 lawmakers over 60. In the other parties, the number is actually five lower.
In 2016, only 19 lawmakers had already turned 70. By 2021, there were 33, and in the current session there are 49, or one in 10. Of these, 34 are United Russia members, 11 were elected from the KPRF, two from A Just Russia, one from the LDPR, and one ran as an independent candidate.
Despite their age, many remain politically active, supporting Putin and the war in Ukraine.
For example, 82-year-old KPRF leader Gennady Zyuganov and his party colleague, 78-year-old Vladimir Kashin, are involved in organizing supplies for the Russian military. In August 2026, the KPRF announced that the two had helped send another convoy to the combat zone. According to the party, along with food and medicine for soldiers, the communists sent drones, thermal imaging devices, camouflage netting, SUVs, and motorcycles.
A Just Russia leader Sergei Mironov is now 73. In January 2023, he received a sledgehammer bearing the insignia of the Russian mercenary group Wagner as a gift from Yevgeny Prigozhin. Wagner mercenaries used a sledgehammer to kill their own comrade at the front, former convict Yevgeny Nuzhin. Even after Prigozhin’s march on Moscow and his death in a plane crash, Mironov said he would keep the gift “in a place of honor” as “a sign of fellowship.”
However, since late August 2026, Mironov has stopped attending party events in person. He said he is being treated for an injury sustained during a trip to Altai. His fellow party members stood in for him during the pre-election debates. Nevertheless, on September 28, Mironov was unanimously reelected as faction leader. He joined the meeting via video link and said he would continue working remotely for now.
The Kremlin openly uses the standing of other experienced lawmakers for its own purposes. For example, in March 2020, Valentina Tereshkova proposed a constitutional amendment allowing Putin to run for president again. She was 83 at the time and is starting the new Duma at 89.
A source in the State Duma told Meduza that Tereshkova’s remarks had been written in the Kremlin. Kommersant wrote that the amendment had been drafted in advance, with Tereshkova’s name added by hand. A source who spoke to Kommersant, close to Russia’s Presidential Administration, said Tereshkova was close to State Duma speaker Vyacheslav Volodin.
After Tereshkova’s remarks, Volodin called on all factions to defend her from criticism: “The attacks being made on Tereshkova today are attacks on our country.”
Hi, I’m Yulia.
I’m an editor at Meduza, and for almost five years now, I haven’t been sleeping well for one reason: I’m worried about my colleagues in Russia.
I’m often woken up by messages from our freelance reporters inside the country. They sometimes work late at night or early in the morning, and they message me at all hours. I never silence my phone at night in case of an emergency. Every notification jolts me awake. Half-asleep, my first thought is always the same: they’re texting me because the police have come to search their home. In Russia, you can go to prison for working with Meduza. Sometimes I have nightmares about my reporters being interrogated by the FSB. Some of those nightmares have come true.
Meduza’s reporters risk their freedom to tell the world what’s happening inside Russia. They believe their work can help make a better future possible, and they refuse to leave. Please donate so they can keep reporting.
New People remains the youngest party. But it’s aging too
The youngest faction, as in the previous session, is New People. Founded in 2020, this was the party’s second electoral cycle, but it, too, has aged in the meantime: the average age of a faction lawmaker was 39.9 in 2021 and is 42 in the current session.
At the same time, the party’s makeup in parliament has changed. The nine lawmakers elected to the Duma for the first time are noticeably younger than their more experienced colleagues: the newcomers average 39.7, compared with 43.8 for the others.
The oldest faction in the new Duma is the KPRF, whose lawmakers average 61.5 years old. The faction has aged by 11.3 years since the first session, though there have been periods in the KPRF’s history when it got younger — after the 2021 election, for example, the average age of the communists fell, though it remained higher than in 1994, when it was 50.2.
Right now, 37 communists have been elected to the Duma. Eleven of them have already turned 70, and another eight have turned 60.
There is only one communist lawmaker under 40: 38-year-old Alexander Ivachev of the Sverdlovsk region. He heads the region’s party branch and previously served as deputy speaker of the regional legislative assembly. Ivachev is known, among other things, for his statements against the Yeltsin Center and his fight to preserve a bas-relief of Stalin on the Officers’ House building in Yekaterinburg, calling the arguments of those who wanted it removed “the sick fantasies of ‘victims of repression.’”
The LDPR faction has aged by 8.2 years over the past 10 years, the largest increase among the four parties represented in the last three sessions. This trend only emerged in recent years — the LDPR used to be one of the youngest parties. In 2000, lawmakers elected from the Zhirinovsky Bloc began their work with an average age of about 40.
A Just Russia lawmakers have gotten an average of 10 years older over five sessions: the figure was 49 in 2007 and is now 59.1.
United Russia’s average age, 54.1, is lower than that of the KPRF and A Just Russia. Within the party, the share of members age 60 and older rose from 26% at the start of the previous session to 31% in the current one.
Some lawmakers have aged along with the Duma. Three of them have voted on bills for almost 33 years in a row.
More than half the lawmakers in the current Duma — 269 of 450 — also served in the previous session, and 143 took part in all three of the last sessions.
A total of 172 people received a Duma mandate for the first time in 2026. About one in eight of them, 21 lawmakers, have already reached retirement age, roughly the same share as five years ago. The average age of newcomers has not changed since the start of the previous session, either: it is about 48.
Overall, lawmakers entering the Duma for the first time are younger than their experienced colleagues, but the incoming generation that has already made it into parliament is not getting any younger from one election to the next.
Not all newcomers, though, help make the Duma younger. For example, former minister and current adviser to the head of Bashkortostan Gennady Bukayev ran for the State Duma for the first time this year. He had turned 79 by the start of the new Duma’s work.
And some of those who received their first mandate already at retirement age have since spent five or 10 years in parliament. United Russia lawmaker Galina Danchikova came to the Duma in 2016, at 62, and is now starting her third session at 72. Her fellow party member Nikolai Doluda became a lawmaker for the first time in 2021, at 69, and had turned 74 by the start of his second session.
Three lawmakers in the current Duma were part of the starting lineup in all nine sessions, including the very first: KPRF member Gennady Zyuganov, his party colleague Nikolai Kharitonov, and A Just Russia member Anatoly Greshnevikov. In 1994, they were 49, 45, and 37, respectively. Now they are 82, 77, and 70.
The Duma’s age makeup does not closely reflect Russia’s population. The most noticeable gap is the shortage of lawmakers under 40: more than a third of Russia’s adult population is under 40, but in the new Duma, only one in nine seats went to a lawmaker that age. Nationwide, there are three times as many people ages 18 to 40 as there are lawmakers in that age group: 35.1% versus 11.3%.
Lawmakers ages 40 to 64 hold more than two-thirds of the seats, even though they make up less than half of the country’s adult population. The share of people 65 and older is nearly the same in parliament and among the population overall, about one in five.
In the new State Duma, 11% of lawmakers are under 40. In Germany’s Bundestag, after the 2025 election, the figure was 28%, and in France’s National Assembly, after the 2024 election, it was 25%. The U.S. House of Representatives, however, had even fewer young lawmakers than Russia at the start of 2025 — only about 8%.
By the end of the ninth session, the average age of State Duma lawmakers is projected to reach 59.3.

U.S. Air Force shows Morocco the F-35A it reportedly wants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:18:46 UTC
19:18:46 KST

- U.S. Air Force F-35As flew with Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, which runs Oct. 7-10.
- Morocco’s first new F-16 Block 72 flew on Oct. 6, and reports say Rabat has discussed buying F-35s, though no sale has been approved.
U.S. Air Force F-35A Lightning II stealth fighters flew alongside Moroccan F-16s on the opening day of the Marrakech Airshow, putting the jet in front of a country that has been reported to be interested in buying it and that already fields a growing list of American weapons.
The airshow runs Oct. 7-10 at a Royal Moroccan Air Force base in Marrakech. Lockheed Martin, which builds both aircraft, posted that Morocco’s F-16s and the U.S. Air Force F-35As took to the skies to open the four-day event. According to the U.S. Department of War, the F-35A flyby is the centerpiece of about 45 U.S. military personnel taking part. The fighters come from the 48th Fighter Wing at RAF Lakenheath in England, the largest U.S. fighter wing in Europe, which flies both F-35As and F-15E Strike Eagles.
The U.S. contingent also includes two aircraft on static display: an HC-130J Combat King II search-and-rescue plane from the Alaska Air National Guard’s 176th Wing at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, and a KC-135 Stratotanker aerial refueling aircraft from the Utah National Guard’s 151st Wing. The Utah National Guard has been paired with Morocco since 2003 under the State Partnership Program, which links U.S. National Guard units with foreign militaries for regular training and exchanges.
“It is an honor to be at Marrakech ahead of the 250th anniversary of the U.S.-Moroccan Alliance,” said U.S. Air Force Brig. Gen. Matthew J. French, Air National Guard assistant to the commander of U.S. Air Forces in Europe and Air Forces Africa. “Hosted by the United States’ oldest Ally, this forum best illustrates our goal of establishing strong and enduring Allied and partner forces for an evolving security environment. It makes us stronger in both our individual and combined capacities.”
Morocco was the first country to recognize U.S. independence, in 1777, and Washington designated it a major non-NATO ally in 2004.
Morocco’s air force is about to receive a major upgrade of its own. On Oct. 6, Lockheed Martin said the first of 25 new F-16 Block 72 fighters built for Morocco had made its maiden flight in Greenville, South Carolina. The U.S. approved that sale, worth an estimated $3.8 billion, in 2019, along with a separate package of about $985 million to upgrade Morocco’s 23 existing F-16s to a similar standard.
Rabat has also been one of the steadier buyers of American ground equipment in Africa, including M1 Abrams tanks, AH-64E Apache attack helicopters and HIMARS rocket launchers. In 2024, the U.S. State Department approved the sale of 612 Javelin anti-tank missiles to Morocco for an estimated $260 million.
Morocco’s interest in the F-35 has surfaced repeatedly. Reports since 2025 have said Rabat was in talks for up to 32 of the stealth fighters. The U.S. government has not announced any approval of an F-35 sale to Morocco, and neither government has confirmed negotiations.
“The Marrakech Air Show is a world-class exhibition of aviation innovation and a powerful testament to the enduring, nearly 250-year friendship between the United States and the Kingdom of Morocco. For decades, our nations have flown side-by-side, from our vital pilot training pipelines to our complex joint operations. The United States remains deeply committed to standing with our Moroccan partners, delivering cutting-edge aerospace capabilities and working hand-in-hand to promote regional peace, stability, and shared prosperity across the African continent,” said Duke Buchan III, the U.S. ambassador to Morocco.

Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge
- Published
At least 30 people have been killed in a Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in the eastern front line city of Kramatorsk, rescue officials say.
Authorities said three people were also killed in the village of Bilenke, part of the Kramatorsk community.
Another 18 people were wounded, said Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin, accusing Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill as many civilians as possible.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Slovyansk are part of a so-called fortress belt that Moscow is trying to seize as part of Russian President Vladimir Putin's claim to the entire Ukrainian industrial region of Donbas.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said: "This strike will not go without our response."
In a post on Telegram, he said: "Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this. React harshly - exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have caused."
Images posted by local prosecutors showed the burning metal shell of the bus along with debris and some of the victims on the road.
Moscow is yet to comment on the latest attack. It follows a dramatic surge in Russian attacks across the country and a heavy increase in civilian casualties.
According to the UN, Ukraine saw more civilians killed by August this year than were killed in all of 2025.
In one single attack that destroyed a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky east of Kyiv early on Wednesday, 22 people were killed, including five children. Three of the children were only one year old.
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, meeting Zelensky in Kyiv on Thursday, said the attack in Pryluky showed Putin's "evil intent and evil strategy".
He announced "more sanctions on Russia, on the war machine of Putin, on the shadow fleet, on the oil companies, on the crypto, on the financing of the war" and told Zelensky the UK would stand with Ukraine "as long as it takes for you to prevail in this conflict".
After the deadly attack on Kramatorsk, Donetsk regional head Filashkin appealed to anyone who was still in the eastern front line region to move to safer parts of Ukraine.
Given the sharp deterioration of security in the two neighbouring cities, he said all public transport had been ordered to stop. The safety of civilians was paramount, and "we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers", he said.
Moscow has often cited the "liberation" and "protection" of the predominantly Russian-speaking Donbas as justification for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It is made up of two regions - Luhansk and Donetsk - and with most of Luhansk under Russian control, the Kremlin is also aiming to capture remaining 20% of Donetsk territory still held by Ukraine.
For much of the war Kramatorsk acted as a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military, however it has now come under almost daily Russian attack as its military moves closer to the east of the city.
Glide bombs in particular have been launched at Slovyansk and Kramatorsk. The bombs are fitted with winglets so they glide towards their target rather than simply fall. In late August as many as nine glide bombs were fired at Kramatorsk in one day.
Kramatorsk City Council described the strike as a "horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population".
"Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets," it said.

Russia is also launching constant air raids on the capital Kyiv, with sirens ringing throughout the day.
Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko said attacks on Thursday had killed three people, with 14 others injured. Two of the eight injured are in a critical condition.
The attacks are forcing schoolchildren out of classes into shelters, shuttering businesses, and disrupting public transport.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, particularly on its energy grid, are causing power outages already and are even affecting the water supply. Local water authorities in the capital warned on Thursday that pressure was dropping across the city's right bank due to power cuts.
Zelensky offered his condolences to families and loved ones affected by the latest attack and said Ukraine's partners needed to provide "concrete action through new defence packages for the protection of Ukraine".
Ahead of the Pryluky attack, the Ukrainian leader had warned this week of intelligence suggesting plans for a major Russian onslaught, and in Kyiv families responded by heading to metro stations for shelter.
Such warnings are for now one of the only defences Ukrainians have.
Interceptor missiles are in short supply around the world, so Ukraine has little chance to stop incoming Russian ballistics.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, with Russian attacks targeting Ukrainian data centres and logistics warehouses.

DEHRADUN: As many as 39,815 rural families in Uttarakhand have been provided pucca houses under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) since 2022, with Udham Singh Nagar recording the highest number of houses constructed, according to state government figures.Udham Singh Nagar accounted for 4,882 houses, followed by Haridwar with 4,493 and Rudraprayag with 4,032. Chamoli recorded 3,900 houses, while Pithoragarh and Pauri accounted for 3,386 and 3,195 houses respectively. Uttarkashi saw 3,057 houses constructed under the scheme.Chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami has been seeking additional housing allocations from the Centre under both the rural and urban components of the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana. The state government said Uttarakhand has also received national-level recognition for its performance under PMAY-Urban 2.0.Launched in 2016, PMAY-G aims to provide pucca houses with basic amenities to homeless families and those living in kutcha or dilapidated houses in rural areas. Under the scheme, eligible beneficiaries receive financial assistance of Rs 1.30 lakh per house through direct benefit transfer into their bank accounts.The state has also increased assistance for purchasing kitchen utensils and other kitchen-related items from Rs 5,000 to Rs 6,000 from 2022-23 onwards.
Beneficiaries are provided an additional Rs 12,000 for toilet construction under the Swachh Bharat Mission through MGNREGA/SWajal.Under the BB Ramji Yojana, beneficiaries are also provided 95 days of wage employment for construction of their houses. The housing support is supplemented with access to basic services such as drinking water, LPG connections under the Ujjwala scheme and electricity connections.
“Under the guidance of Prime Minister Narendra Modi ji, our government is committed to providing a pucca house to every needy family. We are continuously working to ensure that the benefits of PMAY-G reach every eligible family,” Dhami said.Other districts covered under the scheme include Dehradun with 2,839 houses, Champawat with 2,789, Bageshwar with 2,279, Tehri with 2,134, Nainital with 1,480 and Almora with 1,349 houses.

Russian attack on bus kills at least 30 people near Ukraine frontline

Unknown Publisher

A Russian missile strike on a bus in the eastern city of Kramatorsk has killed at least 30 people, officials have said, in one of the worst attacks by Moscow on Ukrainian civilians this year.
The regional prosecutor’s office in the Donetsk region said on Thursday the vehicle had been hit at 10am by an aerial bomb. “As of now, the death toll from this morning’s attack has risen to 30. Eighteen people were wounded,” it said, adding that all local public transport had been suspended.
Images posted by police showed bodies strewn across a street littered with debris, as well as a charred shell of what appeared to be a bus. A second bus had also caught fire, officials said. The strike targeted an area next to a dental clinic on the city’s Yuvileina Street.
Three people had also been killed by shelling in the village of Bilenke, outside Kramatorsk, they added. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Kremlin had deliberately targeted an “ordinary public transport stop”.
Some of those killed could not be identified because of the severity of their injuries, Ukraine’s president added. He said the number of victims could “sadly rise”, as doctors fought to save the lives of those wounded.
He said: “This strike will not go unanswered. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and a response from the world is a must. A forceful response – exactly as the Russians deserve for all the deaths they have brought. May all those killed rest in peace.”
The bombing follows a gruesome Russian strike on Wednesday on a five-storey block of flats in Pryluky in the northern Chernihiv region. The building collapsed, entombing those inside. At least 22 people were killed, including five children, aged between one and eight.
Visiting the scene with Ed Miliband, the British foreign secretary, Zelenskyy urged the US to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage so that Ukraine could hit targets inside Russia such as launch sites. So far, Donald Trump and Elon Musk have refused Kyiv’s request.
Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict” than this week’s murderous attacks. He said: “Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield. He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Writing earlier on social media, Zelenskyy called on western allies to take “concrete steps” to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences, amid a round-the-clock Russian onslaught in recent weeks featuring ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones.
“Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft, and investments in interceptors – all of this is directly helping save lives every day. Important talks with our partners will take place today and tomorrow,” Zelenskyy said.
Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk form part of a “fortress belt”. They are the last two big cities in northern Donetsk under full Ukrainian military control. Russia has been trying to capture them for more than a decade, after a brief period in which Russian forces occupied Sloviansk in 2014.
The cities are home to thousands of civilians, as well as Ukrainian soldiers. In recent months, roads have been festooned with nets to protect traffic from marauding enemy drones. These defences offer little protection, however, against aerial bombs.
“These are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army,” the Donetsk regional governor, Vadym Filashkin, said on Telegram after Wednesday’s strike. “Russia comes to Ukrainian land with death.”
He added: “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians. For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.
“Russia deliberately flouts every conceivable rule of warfare and the norms of international humanitarian law. It selects targets where it can inflict the greatest suffering on civilians.”
There was criticism of the White House’s policy of engaging with Vladimir Putin, whom Donald Trump has invited to December’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida. The Kremlin has yet to say if Russia’s leader will take part.
The former US ambassador to Moscow Michael McFaul said on social media that Russia was guilty of terrorism. “There is no other word for it. Putin is running a terrorist state. That officials from my country call this terrorist a nice guy is deeply embarrassing for me.”
Putin has demanded Ukraine cede the rest of the eastern Donbas region still under its control. Kyiv refuses to hand over its territory, believing Russia will take any concessions and carry on fighting.

ISIS-inspired pharmacy student charged with plotting mass killing of Jews using poisons

Mohammed Shalabi, 22, a pharmacy student from the Beit Hanina neighborhood in eastern Jerusalem, planned to carry out terrorist attacks against security forces and Jewish civilians using explosive devices and deadly poisons, with the aim of causing mass casualties, according to an indictment filed against him Thursday in the Jerusalem District Court.
According to the indictment, filed by attorney Amihai Marx of the Jerusalem District Attorney's Office, Shalabi, a third-year pharmacy student at al-Quds University in Abu Dis who also worked as a pharmacy assistant, underwent a process of ideological radicalization, partly in response to the events of October 7 and the subsequent war.
During this period, he systematically consumed content associated with the Hamas and ISIS terrorist organizations and decided to use the knowledge he had gained through his studies and his access to chemicals to carry out deadly terrorist attacks.
In early 2025, angered by parking tickets issued to worshippers near a mosque in the Beit Hanina neighborhood, Shalabi planned to plant an explosive device at a location where enforcement officers regularly stationed.To prepare for the attack, he monitored their activities for about two months and downloaded bomb-making instructions from the internet. The plan was never carried out because enforcement officers stopped coming to the area.
Shalabi subsequently planned a large-scale terrorist attack in which he sought, in his own words, to kill "lots of Jews." To prepare for the attack, he joined Telegram groups associated with terrorist organizations, including an ISIS-affiliated group, and downloaded dozens of files containing instructions for making bombs, explosives and deadly poisons.
He also copied formulas for producing poisons capable of causing death through skin contact, inhalation or ingestion into a notebook and documented substances that could be used to make explosives.
Chemical experiment in bathtub
According to the indictment, Shalabi went beyond planning and took concrete steps to prepare for the attacks. He traveled to Ramallah on two occasions, purchasing chemicals and equipment while splitting up the purchases to avoid raising suspicion, and stored the materials in his bedroom at home.
He later conducted a chemical experiment in his bathtub, igniting a mixture he had prepared to test the chemicals. Shalabi also deleted files and search history from his phone in an effort to conceal his activities.
The indictment charges Shalabi with preparing to commit a terrorist murder and undergoing training for terrorism. Prosecutors have asked the court to keep him in custody until the end of his trial.
The investigation was conducted by the Jerusalem District Police Central Unit and the Shin Bet security agency.

So that no hospital has to stop operating: the Kyiv City State Administration explained how preparations for winter at medical facilities are progressing

So that no hospital has to stop operating: the Kyiv City State Administration explained how preparations for winter at medical facilities are progressing
Kyiv • UNN
The capital's hospitals are receiving backup generators, supplies of fuel, water, medicines, and food. The work is expected to be completed by the end of November.
Preparation of the capital’s healthcare facilities within the capable network is ongoing. At the same time, as Tetiana Mostepan, director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, said on air at KyivFM , work is currently underway to improve what has already been done, reports UNN.
Of course, we are strengthening the entire healthcare system, and accordingly, we are not expecting anything good from this winter. Therefore, all facilities are not only equipped with generators, but also with backup generators. We have planned for no facility to stop operating, regardless of any scenarios that may unfold in the city of Kyiv. This concerns engineering networks, generators, fuel supplies, medication supplies, and food supplies. In other words, all areas have been fully taken into account, and each healthcare facility in the city of Kyiv within the capable network, in accordance with its schedules, response plan, and everything else, is not merely preparing… We have already been improving all these things because we have been ready for this for a long time, but now, understanding the vulnerabilities that may arise, we are strengthening every possible area
As UNN wrote, full autonomy includes not only provision with backup power sources, but also autonomous heating (its own boiler rooms or the ability to quickly connect to mobile boiler rooms in the event of interruptions in centralized heating), as well as its own water source.
At the same time, Mostepan acknowledged that there had been certain delays in strengthening the autonomy of some healthcare facilities. These are hospitals located in the historic part of the city, where preparing project documentation, for example, for drilling a water well, requires bureaucratic issues to be resolved. However, she said that 17 wells have now been launched at 13 healthcare service locations.
"We clearly understand that a well is not simply water for people to drink; it is the operation of surgical units, the functioning of departments and sterilization units, and the operation of emergency departments," Mostepan explained.
Work is also continuing to strengthen hospitals’ autonomy in terms of heat supply.
"Last winter, we used the mobile boiler rooms of the city of Kyiv, but given the scale of the needs and the risks of outages resulting from this, of course, each such boiler room is extremely important for the city of Kyiv. Therefore, we are trying to make every healthcare facility completely independent of everything," Mostepan said.
According to the director of the Kyiv City State Administration’s Department of Health, the city allocated substantial funds to strengthen the resilience of healthcare facilities, while the Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization also provided assistance.
According to Mostepan, work to strengthen autonomy at all facilities within the capital’s capable network is expected to be completed by the end of November.
We remind you
As the director of the Kyiv Perinatal Center, Professor Dmytro Hovsyeiev, said in an interview, the facility had installed its own autonomous boiler room even before the start of the full-scale invasion.
"Even before the full-scale invasion, we were offered the installation of a pellet boiler room independent of the centralized heating supply. It is also cheaper.
Today, we are probably the only maternity hospital that can operate completely autonomously. Our own boiler room. Our own well—the water is always available, even when there is nothing else. Water reserves. A food unit that operates without an external power supply. Generators at every branch," he said .
The facility also has fully equipped shelters operating at two of its branches, where doctors can deliver babies and perform operations.

Confessional confidentiality and journalistic sources to be given greater protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:13:00 UTC
19:13:00 KST

Confessional confidentiality and journalistic sources to be given greater protection
The Ministry of Justice wants to explicitly enshrine in law the right of lawyers, journalists, notaries and clergy to refuse to provide information or testify in criminal proceedings.
Estonia already recognizes the concept of professional confidentiality and members of certain professions have the right to refuse to testify. However, Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta (Eesti 200) says the relevant provisions in existing legislation are too narrow and unclear.
"Our idea is to establish clear professional privileges. This is different from professional confidentiality. Professional privilege specifically means that people working in certain professions who may come into possession of information that could, for example, be relevant to a criminal investigation are not required, and in some cases are not permitted, to disclose that information to investigative authorities," Pakosta explained.
Such clearly defined professional privileges could apply to lawyers, notaries, victim support workers, bankruptcy trustees, clergy, journalists and patent attorneys.
Estonian Bar Association President Imbi Jürgen said such violations of privacy in criminal proceedings are not merely a theoretical threat.
"The biggest concern at present is the interception of calls between lawyers and their clients during surveillance operations. This is a very serious problem and disputes concerning the issue have also reached the Supreme Court," Jürgen said.
Justice Minister Pakosta acknowledged that protecting members of these professions would also make certain crimes more difficult to investigate.
"If the state wants to convict someone, it must gather all the evidence itself. It cannot assume that just because someone has told their story to a journalist, that means they can be convicted on that basis the following day," Pakosta said.
Chief State Prosecutor Taavi Pern said the Prosecutor's Office welcomes the proposal, as the law governing these professions has so far been relatively unclear.
"Both the Bar Association and the Prosecutor's Office have been telling the Ministry of Justice for years that this bill and more precise regulations are needed," Pern said.
According to Pern, the bill will increase the Prosecutor's Office's workload.
"If we have to carry out various investigative procedures involving people covered by professional privilege, such as conducting searches or arguing in court over whether the contents of certain emails are protected by professional confidentiality, this will add to our workload," Pern said.
Despite the additional workload, the state does not plan to allocate any extra funding to the Prosecutor's Office. This could mean that prosecutors will have to reorganize their work.
"Given how complex criminal proceedings have become, it would be welcome if discussions about any legislative amendments also included consideration of how many resources, for example, the Prosecutor's Office or the courts would need to implement them," Pern said.

U.S. Army updates logistics tool with Iran war lessons
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:10:58 UTC
19:10:58 KST

- The U.S. Army upgraded its LOADOUT transportation software with changes based on lessons from Operation Epic Fury.
- New features include customizable dashboards, real-time capacity visibility and a Priority 1 banner, with monthly reviews planned with theater sustainment commands.
The U.S. Army has updated LOADOUT, its software for requesting and tracking military cargo and troop movements, with changes drawn from lessons of Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. campaign against Iran that began in February.
The Army’s Combined Arms Support Command at Fort Lee, Virginia, which develops the system, said the latest upgrades respond to a common complaint from soldiers: too much time spent hunting down where a shipment stands and too little spent moving it. The command developed the changes with the 1st Theater Sustainment Command, which oversees Army logistics in the Middle East, the 8th Theater Sustainment Command in the Pacific, U.S. Army Japan and other units.
LOADOUT handles Transportation Movement Requests, the formal requests units submit when they need equipment, supplies or people moved. The system walks a request through each stage, from submission and coordination to execution and closeout, so units and sustainment staff can see its status without chasing it down through phone calls and email.
The new version adds dashboards that users can customize to show their own movement requests, cargo manifests that can be exported line by line, and improved tools for uploading and assigning a unit’s equipment and deployment lists. A Movement Board now shows available transportation capacity in real time, and a banner flags Priority 1 mission-critical requests so they stand out.
According to the command, LOADOUT also replaces separate workarounds that individual theaters had built for themselves with a single Army-wide system, giving leaders a common picture of transportation requirements across the geographic combatant commands. The Army said the data helps commanders judge how much transportation capacity they need to support Army and joint operations.
Operation Epic Fury put heavy demands on U.S. military logistics. The campaign involved more than 50,000 U.S. troops, and U.S. Transportation Command has said it used AI tools to replan routes after Spain closed its airspace to U.S. military aircraft at the start of the operation.
CASCOM held its first Functional Review Working Group for LOADOUT on Sept. 24 with leaders from the 1st and 8th Theater Sustainment Commands to review the completed upgrades and set priorities for the next round. Theater partners will now meet monthly to refine the system.
Next steps under discussion include interim tracking of diplomatic and customs clearances, which units often need before cargo can cross borders. Over the longer term, the Army plans to link LOADOUT to its ARTEMIS capability suite so movement information can be handed off automatically between systems.

NEW DELHI: The INDIA bloc's confrontation with the Election Commission escalated on Thursday as Opposition leaders regrouped in Delhi for a third consecutive day, with Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi saying around 300 MPs from both Houses wanted to stage a peaceful protest but had been stopped for two days.Rahul Gandhi, who was detained during Wednesday's protest, said the Opposition would continue its campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and alleged that the government and the Election Commission had "hijacked India" and "stolen votes". The latest mobilisation follows a tense day in Delhi on Wednesday when INDIA bloc MPs attempted to proceed towards Jantar Mantar to protest against Gyanesh Kumar and the SIR process.Delhi Police stopped the march, after which Opposition leaders staged a sit-in. RIYADH – Diplomats stationed in the Saudi capital were sheltering in place and international schools took safety measures on Oct 8, diplomats and residents told AFP, after explosions echoed across the city.
The explosions heard in Riyadh came hours after the Houthis in Yemen, which borders Saudi Arabia, claimed their latest attack on the kingdom.
The Iran-backed fighters have launched a wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia since they began a major offensive in Yemen against the internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government there.
Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have struggled to contain the Houthis’ advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around a waterway that is crucial to global energy flows.
In Riyadh, home to a large number of non-Saudis, diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, diplomats told AFP.
Several residents, meanwhile, said that international schools were taking precautions, with at least one facility sending children into a basement for safety.
The measures came after repeated blasts were heard in the city, one of the loudest disturbances there since the start of the Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February.
Two people working in Riyadh’s business hub – the King Abdullah Financial District – told AFP that some companies were evacuating staff from the area.
200,000 people displaced
While the Yemen war predates the Iran war, it had come to a near-standstill in recent years, until September, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive against government forces.
They seized large swathes of territory, including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key waterway for global shipping and, crucially, Saudi oil exports.
The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional conflict, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the beleaguered Middle East.
In Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, it is ordinary civilians paying the price, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.
After declaring a counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen’s government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Saudi Arabia, the latest blasts came a day after the Houthis claimed attacks on two international airports, while repeating a warning to airlines to avoid Saudi airspace.
“On Tuesday and Wednesday... Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport were subjected to attacks targeting their facilities,” Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said.
An Egyptian and an Algerian national were killed at Abha airport, while a Sudanese national was killed at Riyadh airport, the agency said.
The attacks wounded 36 people, it added.
In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed a response.
“The brutal attacks by the Terrorist Houthi Militia on civilian and civilian objects in the Kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished,” it wrote on X.
‘Terrified’
On Oct 7 in Yemen, clashes left at least 62 combatants dead, including 37 Houthis, military sources from both camps told AFP.
Yemeni state news agency Saba also reported that a Houthi missile wounded five civilians in Taiz, a city held by government forces.
“We went out into the street to check on the wounded and saw young civilians who had been hit,” resident Al-Fateh al-Eisaei told AFP.
“The Houthi shell landed in the middle of the street, right in an area crowded with civilians.”

Lunar resource management, permanent human presence expected in coming years: UAE deputy space chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:09:49 UTC
19:09:49 KST

Emirhan Yilmaz and Emir Yildirim
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
A new era of industrial space exploration, including lunar mining and a permanent human presence on the Moon, will become a reality in the coming years, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Space Agency’s deputy director general told Anadolu.
Ibrahim Hamza Al Qasim, speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in the southwestern Turkish province of Antalya, said upcoming missions will focus on extracting space resources, including rare metals and raw materials “that are limited on Earth but abundant in space.”
“The UAE started in space about 30 years ago, 1997 is when we first entered the space race, and we built incredible capabilities over the last three decades, then we started our deep space exploration programs for the Moon, Mars, and the asteroid belt that we’re launching in the first quarter of 2028,” he said. “We have quite an ambitious astronaut corps of four, two of which have flown to the ISS (International Space Station) or to other places.”
Al Qasim said the agency is placing much greater emphasis on private sector involvement rather than relying on government funding.
“We noticed that the tipping point is happening already within the UAE’s ecosystem -- we see that most of the funding, well over 50%, coming towards space comes from the private sector,” he added.
He noted that advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and next-generation robotics are lowering barriers to entry, allowing emerging space programs to achieve results beyond their traditional capabilities.
“I think over the next decade you’ll see incredible missions, humans going back to the service of the moon, a permanent presence for people on the Moon, but more importantly, I think you will probably see programs that not only explore space, but look at exploiting space resources and bringing back rare metals and and resources that are very limited on Earth,” he said.
“It’s a very exciting time to be working in space -- I think we are fast approaching a time when we could have all the resources we need on Earth to really drive a new era of industries,” he added.
The IAC 2026 kicked off Monday and will run until Friday. It is co-hosted by the Turkish Space Agency (TUA) and the SAHA Istanbul defense cluster and organized by the Industry and Technology Ministry. Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.

CNN, MS NOW, Politico to urge judge to block White House ban long-term
NEW YORK, Oct 8 - CNN, MS NOW and Politico are due in Washington federal court on Thursday as they urge a judge to extend their protection against being banned from the White House on President Donald Trump’s order.
Trump’s revocation of the outlets’ access for publishing what he said was “FAKE NEWS” was the latest escalation of his pressure campaign against media coverage he dislikes. He said he might ban other outlets but was unsure it would hold up in court.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily blocked the ban on September 24, finding it likely violated the outlets’ right to fair treatment under the Constitution's Fifth Amendment. He did not rule on the outlets’ claim that the ban violated their First Amendment free speech rights.
The outlets have asked for an order blocking the ban until a final ruling. They say the revocation of their passes was unlawful retaliation for their coverage and accused the administration of coming up with meritless national security concerns to justify the ban.
Justice Department lawyers say the outlets endangered national security by publishing classified information, citing stories about construction of Trump's White House ballroom and turnout at the recent Republican midterm convention.
Kelly was skeptical of the government’s arguments at a September 23 hearing. Kelly blocked Trump during his first term from revoking CNN reporter Jim Acosta’s White House pass, finding the decision was not transparent or fair.
The legal battle comes just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump's job approval ratings are at the lowest of his political career in opinion polls amid concerns over the Iran war and inflation. REUTERS

High explosive payloads keep a human in the loop
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
11:09:21 BST
19:09:21 KST

Where a person sits in the decision depends on what the system is carrying, and anything with a high explosive payload will keep a human in the loop, a panel on autonomous mass heard at the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Freddie Bradshaw, head of business development at the Estonian company Ark Robotics, said the use case has to come before the autonomy question, because the answer changes completely between a one-way strike vehicle and a resupply run.
He said: “We’re certainly seeing that it’s very important to have human in the loop when it comes to a one-way strike effector, for instance. If you’ve got a system that has a payload of high explosive, the chances are we aren’t going to allow AI to be controlling that, and we need to have some sort of human in the loop.”
Further back from the front the balance shifts, and that is where he sees autonomy earning its place, taking the cognitive burden off a commander and handing it to the system so that one person can manage a fleet.
Antony Quinn, the Europe director of Havoc, argued that the vocabulary needs tightening before the debate can go anywhere, since human in the loop and human on the loop get used interchangeably and mean different things. Adding waypoints and watching a vessel follow them round makes the operator the bottleneck, which defeats the point of mass in the first place.
Three things have to be right in his account before any of it works, the first is the human interface, which should use simple accessible language and let an operator give intent and supervise instead of constantly intervening or monitoring camera feeds. The second is trust, earned by designing, testing and assuring the system the way trust is extended to an officer commanding a tactical unit. The third is policy and doctrine, which he does not think needs reinventing.
He said: “There is a point at which the system, whatever it is, is trusted to the person or computer you have trained, with its boundaries and actions on, and doctrine already supports this. So yes, humans are critically important in or on the loop, but a lot of it is not that unfamiliar, actually.”
Mr Bradshaw made a related point about interfaces, saying his company works to ensure its own plugs into a number of command and control systems so it can be operated through NATO compliant architectures, and that it has to be easy enough to use that scaling is possible at all.
From the user’s side, Oleksii Krymeniuk, the chief unmanned systems officer of the 2nd Corps of Ukraine’s National Guard, gave the position a name. “I’m not a huge believer in full autonomy. I’m more a believer in something that could assist our guys in the staffs and on the ground and help them make faster and more efficient decisions,” he said.
What he wants next is one operator running many drones, which he was careful to distinguish from swarming. The arithmetic is what makes it matter, since a mission needing dozens of aircraft currently needs dozens of operators, and bringing that ratio down multiplies what a unit of fixed size can achieve. Mr Bradshaw agreed that ground autonomy has not arrived yet, saying there is still a way to go in the uncrewed ground vehicle domain.
Mike Wilmot, head of UK land at Helsing, came at it from the opposite direction, arguing that there are tasks where an automated process deserves more confidence than a person does, with air defence engagement the obvious case. He drew an ethical conclusion from that.
He said: “There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms.”
None of the four speakers argued for removing the person altogether, and the disagreement between them was about where the line falls, not whether there should be one. Mr Quinn’s closing advice to anybody buying this technology was that the decision making does not need to change as much as people fear, and that a degree of the caution around it is unjustified.

Israel shuts British E. Jerusalem consulate as diplomatic rift grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:09:00 UTC
19:09:00 KST

Israel announced Thursday that the British Consulate in East Jerusalem has "ceased to function," forcing 20 staffers to leave the country and deepening the worst diplomatic rift between the allies in decades.
The sign outside the consulate was taken down, but Britain said the building remains open and a core staff will continue to deliver "vital services” and work with Palestinians.
The U.K. government said it would not retaliate by expelling Israeli diplomats as it seeks to rebuild its staff.
The dispute began last month when the United Kingdom banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations and much of the international community consider all settlements as illegal.
"Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said in a statement, adding that the building would continue to operate with a "task force" of seven diplomats and a "very limited” scope of activity. Twenty British diplomats will leave Israel, including the consul general.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement that the building "will be known as the U.K. Mission, Jerusalem" after discussions with Israel’s government, and a small team of diplomats would continue to operate there.
"This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the U.K.'s role in support of a two-state solution," Miliband added.
Britain had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if the consulate was closed, but said it would not do so for now because it's in talks with Israel about expanding the mission.
"We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence," Miliband said.
Meanwhile, "our diplomats are going to be able to carry out their important work in relation to, for example, relations with the Palestinians, but also supporting British nationals visiting the area," Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty told Times Radio.
Miliband made clear that Britain does "not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years."
The foreign secretary added that the U.K. government reiterates its view that East Jerusalem "is occupied territory."
The U.K. and Israel continue to have close defense and security cooperation, but diplomatic relations have deteriorated over Israel’s conduct of its genocidal war on Gaza and Britain’s decision last year to recognize a Palestinian state.
Last month’s announcement of the ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank marked a significant toughening of Britain’s stance toward a longtime ally.
Doughty, the Middle East minister, said the U.K. has "a strong and ongoing relationship with Israel."
Israel captured and occupied the West Bank, along with Gaza and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Mideast war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state.
Since then, the Israeli government has built scores of settlements that are home to well over 500,000 illegal Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble fully developed suburbs.

Polish prosecutors have closed an investigation into last year’s mass Russian drone incursion after failing to identify who ordered or directed the operation, while investigators found Polish SIM cards in some of the drones.
The military section of the Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office discontinued the investigation into the violation of Polish airspace, prosecutor Marcin Kozak told Rzeczpospolita.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Most of the case files, including the reasoning behind the decision, remain classified.
“The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime involving the violation of Polish airspace and thereby creating a threat to public safety was not identified,” Kozak said.
The investigation concerned the overnight incursion of more than 30 Russian Gerbera drones into Polish airspace on Sept. 9-10, 2025. The drones entered Poland from the east and were found in 27 locations across the country.
The investigation sought to determine who was personally responsible for directing the operation. Prosecutors ultimately could not identify the person responsible, leading to the case being closed.
The circumstances surrounding the operation remain partly classified.
Polish SIM cards found in some drones
Investigators also found SIM cards belonging to Polish mobile operators in some of the drones, according to the report.
The investigation did not establish publicly whether the cards had been stolen or obtained through illegal purchases. That part of the case remains classified.
Russia Is Targeting Kyiv’s Bridges: How Resilient Are They?
The finding is not entirely new: Ukrainian defense analysts had previously reported the discovery of Polish and Lithuanian SIM cards in Russian drones found in Ukraine. Rzeczpospolita reported that at least one previously identified card belonged to T-Mobile Poland.
Polish military cleared over response
Another key finding of the investigation concerns the Polish military’s response to the drone attack. Prosecutors concluded that the armed forces responded properly and followed the applicable procedures, having the right to shoot down hostile objects.
“The use of weapons was authorized and justified. This part of the investigation was discontinued after it was determined that there were no grounds to establish a prohibited act, meaning no crime,” prosecutor Marcin Kozak said.
He declined to disclose which specific unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) were shot down.
The investigation also established that missiles were launched from fighter aircraft to destroy some of the incoming drones. According to the prosecutors, an incident involving “an explosion of explosive material contained in missiles fired, on the decision of the Operational Commander of the Armed Forces, from combat aircraft” occurred in Poland’s Lublin region.
The missiles missed their intended targets and unintentionally struck a field in the village of Choiny and a forest plot in Krzywowierzbie Kolonia, as per the report.
Separately, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into a missile that struck a residential building in Wyryki, also in the Lublin region. Rzeczpospolita reported that an allied missile fired by a Dutch F-35 pilot at an incoming drone destroyed the house.
Investigators concluded that the pilot had acted within the scope of his authority, although the investigation did not establish whether the incident resulted from human error or a technical failure.
Investigators examine possible motive behind drone incursion
Another unresolved question is why the Russian drones entered Polish airspace in the first place.
According to Rzeczpospolita, the answer is contained in a classified section of the investigation. The newspaper reported, citing its sources, that investigators are leaning toward the assessment that the drones were deliberately launched to test Poland’s air-defense procedures and force NATO and Ukrainian systems to expend missiles.
Most of the drones were reportedly unarmed and did not carry warheads or explosives. However, the investigation has not publicly established what payloads, if any, were carried by the drones that were shot down.

SIM cards from Polish mobile operators were found in some of the Russian Gerbera UAVs that violated Polish airspace in September 2025.
This became known after the Polish prosecutor’s office concluded its investigation, RMF24 reports.
At the same time, the agency has not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.
This part of the investigation remains classified.
The Polish prosecutor’s office closed the investigation because the individual directly responsible for the airspace violation could not be identified.
At the same time, investigators concluded that Polish military personnel acted in accordance with established procedures during the attack and had the right to destroy enemy UAVs.
On the night of September 9–10, 2025, Russia carried out one of its largest attacks on Ukraine, during which Russian Gerbera drones violated Polish airspace.
Polish military personnel detected the first incursion at around 11:14 p.m., while the last was detected at around 6:30 a.m.
On September 12, 2025, Marcin Przydacz, head of the International Policy Bureau at the Chancellery of the President of the Republic of Poland, said that according to data received by the presidential office, 21 drones had crossed the Polish border.
Fragments of downed and crashed drones were later found in various parts of Poland.
The crash sites included settlements in the Lublin, Masovian, Łódź, and other voivodeships. One residential building was damaged due to a crash with no casualties or injuries reported.

Gas stocks in European underground storage facilities reach 73%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:07:41 UTC
19:07:41 KST

MOSCOW, October 8. /TASS/. Gas reserves in European underground gas storage (UGS) facilities have risen to 73%, though injection rates are slowing as temperatures in the region drop, according to TASS calculations based on data from Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE).
While average gas injection rates into EU storage facilities this October remain the highest in four years, Europe has already missed the summer months most favorable for replenishment.
As of October 6, European UGS facilities were 72.97% full (15.11 percentage points below the five-year average for this date), compared to 82.9% a year earlier. This remains the lowest level recorded for this date since data collection began in 2011. EU storage facilities currently hold approximately 79.9 billion cubic meters of gas, which is 11.6 billion cubic meters less than last year's levels and the lowest volume since 2013. Gazprom previously forecast that European UGS inventories might not even reach 75%, warning that the region faces a challenging autumn-winter season.
TASS previously reported that Europe risks entering the heating season with record-low gas stocks. By the traditional start of the autumn-winter period, EU countries may only manage to fill their storage facilities to 70-75% capacity, marking an all-time low for the start of a heating season. Since the summer season began in April 2026, net gas injection (the difference between injection and withdrawal volumes) into EU facilities has reached 49 billion cubic meters. Consequently, Europe has so far secured only 72% of the volume required for the upcoming winter.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must ensure their storage facilities are 90% full between October 1 and December 1 each year, with a 10% margin of flexibility allowed for challenging conditions. Thus, net injection into European storage must total at least 68 billion cubic meters by the start of the 2026-2027 autumn-winter period to meet the standard. However, anticipating a mild winter, the European Commission is reportedly prepared to lower this threshold to 80% for the current year.

pedrali converts temporary wooden pavilion into permanent community hub

Unknown Publisher

10:07:12 UTC

pedrali converts temporary wooden pavilion into permanent community hub
pedrali transforms its temporary wooden pavilion in bergamo, italy into a permanent venue for public events, exhibitions, and outdoor design.
AMDL CIRCLE and Michele De Lucchi transform Pedrali Pavilion
Pedrali has transformed the Pedrali Pavilion, adapting it for permanent use and turning the structure from a one-off architectural wonder into a permanent gathering place for the community.
Looking back, few architecture lovers have not heard of the Crystal Palace. Built in London’s Hyde Park for the Great Exhibition of 1851, the vast iron-and-glass structure was a technical statement that set a precedent and inspired countless later buildings.
In a similar way, Pedrali marked its 60th anniversary in 2023 with a major architectural undertaking: the Pedrali Pavilion. Designed by AMDL CIRCLE and Michele De Lucchi to host the anniversary exhibition at the company’s headquarters in Mornico al Serio, Bergamo, the timber structure stood out not only for the technical complexity of its large wooden roof, supported by legs of the same material, but above all for its sustainable approach, based on reversibility and reuse. Rather than being conceived as an ephemeral structure to be demolished once the anniversary celebrations were over, the Pavilion was designed from the outset to be dismantled, relocated and reused.
In the end, however, the brand chose a different path for the structure’s next life. Pedrali has decided to keep the Pavilion standing and transform it into a permanent place that supports its values around art, education, design, architecture and community.
all images courtesy of Pedrali, photography by Filippo Romano
new layout of the Pedrali Pavilion
The Pavilion is made of PEFC-certified spruce wood and measures 50 meters long, 12 meters wide and nine meters high. Its silhouette is defined by arched portals connected by horizontal beams. Throughout the structure, natural materials such as wood and stone strengthen the relationship with the landscape afforded by its open design.
The team has worked to preserve this skeleton and its characteristic lightness. The most visible change is the replacement of the original wooden roof with a new brass covering. A burnishing and satin-finishing treatment has been applied to the metal, generating tonal variations that echo the natural appearance of aged wood in a nod to the Pavilion’s original composition. The shingles retain the same dimensions, shape and pattern as the original wooden ones.
Visitors are welcomed by an arena that serves as both a gathering space and an antechamber to the upper floor. Upstairs, the timber structure is preserved to host a new auditorium designed for events, conferences and exhibitions. In this space, whose layout has been slightly modified, wood is used generously, from matte-finished oak flooring to larch paneling, a choice that recalls the building’s origin and creates an intimate atmosphere.
On the ground floor, the former open space is transformed into a new showroom dedicated to Pedrali’s outdoor collections. Glass plays a leading role, allowing nature to be seen from every point of the Pavilion. The showroom, designed by DWA Design Studio, features a light structure with glossy soft-sand partitions that reflect the light and is further enhanced by photographs by Alecio Ferrari.
In addition, a geothermal system will provide heating and cooling inside the Pavilion, adapting it to improve visitor comfort while also serving the offices and future production areas.
From ephemeral installation to permanent project
The Pavilion’s new life turns it into a space for gatherings, conferences, art exhibitions and community life. This change of use has required a second construction phase, aimed at weatherproofing and technically reinforcing the structure to enhance its durability, without compromising its architectural value.
The new Pavilion does not simply move from ephemeral to permanent. Its use will also change significantly: from hosting the exhibition Pedrali60, we design a better future, curated by Luca Molinari Studio, to accommodating public moments of exchange between local initiatives and professionals from the art and design sectors.
This new use fits naturally within Pedrali’s long-standing commitment to cultural projects and local initiatives. The brand’s interest in moving beyond manufacturing and creating value for people has been made clear through initiatives such as #pedrali4art, aimed at supporting and enhancing significant artistic and cultural initiatives; #pedrali4design&architecture, which seeks to disseminate design culture; and #pedrali4community, dedicated to local communities and their surrounding area.
As a project within the initiative of #pedrali4education, which is focused on the education of younger generations, the former roof has not been discarded but reused. Elements from the original roof have been repurposed through the design workshop A New Life, developed with students from La Traccia Art High School Centre in Calcinate, Bergamo. Using craft techniques, the young participants have created a series of decorative objects and evanescent walls from the original wooden shingles.
new surroundings Beyond architecture
The adaptations do not begin and end with the Pavilion. The landscape intervention introduces a system of pathways and gathering spaces, where Luserna stone paving creates a sense of continuity between architecture and landscape. As visitors approach the pavilion, they discover green terraced seating areas flanked by seasonal trees.
Pedrali has created Pedrali Path, a pedestrian route that runs around the headquarters in Mornico al Serio as part of the Workplace Health Promotion (WHP) Programme, an initiative the brand joined in 2024 to promote healthy lifestyles among employees.
The transformation of the Pavilion into a permanent architectural element is not merely an addition to the local community. It has turned a workplace into an ode to human connection and culture. An essential stop for design lovers in Bergamo.
project info:
exhibition name: Pedrali60
company: Pedrali | @pedralispa
pavilion design: AMDL CIRCLE and Michele De Lucchi | @micheledelucchi
showroom design: DWA Design Studio | @dwa_design_studio
photography: Filippo Romano
location: Pedrali Headquarters in Mornico al Serio, Bergamo, Italy

I’m worried about the number of offenders being released into communities. At the moment we’re arresting two or three early release offenders a week who are being recalled to prison or doing further offending.
That’s been since the start of August we’ve been capturing that data. We’re getting increasing numbers of tag breaches to enforce that probation is sending to us – it’s now over 100 tag breaches a day in London… and rising.

UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report
Peter Walker
The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.
Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence.
The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.
Starmer’s then defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.
It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.
