More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.

A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.

The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.

“The construction of Denmark’s drone shield is a step closer to the goal with this agreement with Systematic,” Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said.
The system will use artificial intelligence to analyze large amounts of information and identify patterns, unusual activity and potential threats.
The Danish Defence, police and other authorities will be able to access the same information, giving them a shared operational picture from the first drone sighting until the response is completed.
Systematic’s SitaWare software will be installed at several military locations and connected to existing drone defence systems.

Denmark records more than 1.17 million state pensioners
Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
It was the 13th consecutive month in which the number reached a new high.
The increase reflects longer life expectancy and large generations reaching the state pension age. However, many new pensioners continue working.
In July, 24.6 percent of 67-year-old state pensioners remained in paid employment, compared with 10.6 percent in July 2022.
Velliv consumer economist Thomas Gress said the rise could be connected to rules allowing people to earn income without reductions to their own or their spouse’s state pension.
“For some, retirement life is the freedom to leave work completely behind. Others want to keep their colleagues, some hours on the job, and benefit from the generous deductions and subsidies available for continuing working life once the state pension age has been reached,” Gress said.
The growing pensioner population is also increasing public spending. Statistics Denmark said social benefits cost the state 908 billion DKK last year, five percent more than the previous year.
State pensions were the largest expense in the old-age category, costing 170 billion DKK.
Velliv expects the number of state pensioners to continue rising until 2029, when roughly one in five Danes is projected to receive the benefit.

Nearly one million Danes add credit warnings after breach of 8.8 million CPR records
The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.
About 970,000 people had registered a warning by October 7, up from just under 250,000 on October 1, the Digital Affairs Ministry said.
“The Danes have taken the situation seriously, and they have acted on the advice that has come from the government and from the authorities,” Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said.
A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.
The Agency for Societal Security has recommended warnings for people who have specific reasons to suspect fraud.
Unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system during 10 days in September.
Authorities discovered the activity after the company received an unusually large bill. Each search of the register carries a fee.
The company has not been identified, and authorities do not know who was responsible.
Egelund said it remained too early to determine whether affected people would need new CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.

Two areas of Danish waters could receive greater protection from fishing and seabed extraction under a proposal in the government’s 2027 finance bill.

The government’s platform calls for five new marine nature national parks. The 2027 finance bill proposal provides funding for the first two.
They would be in addition to two marine nature national parks introduced under the previous SVM government in Øresund and Lillebælt.

Denmark proposes ban on sharing AI-generated deepfakes without consent
People in Denmark could gain stronger protection against realistic AI-generated images, videos and voice recordings under a new bill introduced Thursday.
Culture Minister Zenia Stampe of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party, wants to prevent digital imitations of people’s appearance and voices, known as deepfakes, from being shared without their consent.
“With artificial intelligence, you can create manipulated videos and images with a few clicks and share them on social media. It can lead to misinformation and create doubt about what is real,” Stampe said.
The proposal would cover all citizens, including artists, whose performances and presentations could also be protected against unauthorized digital imitations.
Stampe said she had personally experienced having a photograph from her profile turned into a video that appeared to show her speaking.
She described the experience as intrusive, even when such content is labeled as satire.
The minister also pointed to SF, the Socialist People’s Party, politician Karsten Hønge, whose identity has been used in hundreds of fake social media posts about Greenland.
A central aim of the legislation is to make social media companies and other online platforms remove illegal deepfakes quickly.
Satire would remain legal, although Stampe acknowledged that distinguishing satire from unlawful manipulation could be difficult.
She said courts would have to decide whether particular content qualifies as satire or whether that label is being used to justify illegal material.
“It will certainly be difficult, but on the other hand, I also have respect for the fact that we have a very strong tradition of satire in Denmark,” she said.
Stampe hopes the legislation can take effect around the turn of the year.
Denmark expands exemptions from new nitrogen rules for fruit and vegetable growers
More Danish farmers will receive temporary exemptions from new fertilizer restrictions after concerns that the rules could make growing certain fruits and vegetables more difficult.
The Ministry of Nature and Animal Welfare announced that crops including melons, rhubarb, strawberries, table grapes and pumpkins will be exempt from the new nitrogen regulations throughout 2027.
Woody plants grown in nurseries will also be covered by the exemption.
The changes follow a review of the regulations approved by a majority in Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing, in September.
The rules, which take effect at the beginning of 2027, aim to reduce nitrogen pollution from agriculture by limiting fertilizer use.
Nitrogen runoff from farmland has contributed to the deterioration of Denmark’s marine environment.
However, agricultural experts and vegetable producers have warned that the restrictions could create significant difficulties for domestic food production.
The government initially planned to exempt mainly potato growers during the first year. The exemption has now been extended to additional fruit and vegetable producers.
“I am pleased that we have the opportunity to also exempt some berry and fruit growers who otherwise faced major challenges, so they get one more year to adapt,” Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said.
The exemptions apply only to 2027 and are intended to give affected growers additional time to adjust.
The ministry said the newly exempt crops account for a small share of Denmark’s total agricultural land.
As a result, it expects the changes to have only a very limited effect on the nitrogen reductions the regulations are intended to achieve.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.

Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.

The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.

“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.

Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.

A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Greenland municipality imposes temporary alcohol ban
The Greenlandic government, Naalakkersuisut, has introduced a temporary ban on the sale and serving of alcohol in the southern Greenlandic municipality of Kujalleq.
Naalakkersuisut writes this on Friday, when the ban took effect, in a press release.
The ban comes following a request from the municipal council in Kujalleq.
– The purpose of the temporary closure of alcohol sales and serving is to eliminate the threat to children’s welfare and the safety of the population.
– Furthermore, Kommune Kujalleq has expressed concern and insecurity among the municipality’s population in recent times as a result of the fatal incidents that are a direct consequence of alcoholic beverages, the press release states.
It is not specified further which alcohol-related incidents have taken place in the municipality.
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, who is mayor of Kujalleq, confirms in a post on Facebook that she has asked Naalakkersuisut to temporarily halt the sale of alcohol in the municipality.
– Based on the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, we can no longer defend the way we use alcohol, she writes.
In a press release, according to the Greenlandic media outlet Sermitsiaq, she elaborates further.
– We can no longer stand passively by and watch the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, and merely wait for another serious incident to happen in our society, the mayor writes according to the media outlet.
The ban on the sale and serving of alcohol will last until the executive order is repealed, it is stated.
Thus, it is not clear how long the ban will remain in effect.
It is not the first time that an alcohol ban has been introduced in parts of Greenland.
At the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic, a ban was introduced for a period on the serving of alcohol with an alcohol percentage above 2.25 percent in Nuuk, Kapisillit, and Qeqertarsuatsiaat.
At that time, it happened with the justification that they wanted to protect children who were at home during the pandemic.
RITZAU
Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

Does nail length shape how attractive you are? New research suggests it might
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:54 UTC
19:00:54 KST

A new study suggests that small grooming choices, such as the length and color of a person’s fingernails, can shape how others judge their physical appeal and romantic desirability. Observers tended to view medium-length nails and white nail polish as the most attractive options, while long nails and darker shades received less favorable marks. The findings were published in EvoS Journal: Evolutionary Studies and Higher Education.
Nail adornment involves altering the length, shape, or color of the hard protective plates on the tips of human fingers using cosmetic tools, lacquers, and polishes. While people in the United States alone spend billions of dollars each year on manicures and professional salon treatments, scientists know relatively little about how these cosmetic changes influence everyday social impressions. Evolutionary perspectives suggest that personal grooming acts as a nonverbal cue, communicating clues about a person’s health, hygiene, and investment in their appearance.
Past research has examined how different physical traits influence attraction. For instance, a 2011 study on hand attractiveness indicated that overall grooming and the condition of the skin around the nails influence how appealing people find someone’s hands. In addition, a 2008 study found that the color red can make women appear more sexually appealing to men, suggesting that color choices carry social meaning.
Although nail styling often serves personal emotional purposes, such as boosting mood and relaxation as suggested by a study covered by PsyPost in 2023, its impact on external observers remains less explored. Sara DeMichele, who began the project as an undergraduate at Bucknell University and is now pursuing a doctorate in psychology at Liberty University, conducted the research with T. Joel Wade, a presidential professor of psychology and director of the neuroscience program at Bucknell.
“My interest in the social psychology of nail adornments began with campus observations of how ‘getting your nails done’ functioned as a ritual far greater than just grooming,” DeMichele, the study’s lead author, told PsyPost. “Specifically, the practice appeared to serve as a practice for self-expression and social presentation.”
“Despite mainstream recognition of the nail care industry, there was surprisingly limited psychological research examining how specific nail characteristics influence social perception, or why individuals select particular colors and designs. This gap motivated me to investigate whether nail length and color systematically affect perceptions of physical attractiveness and seek to understand how subtle dimensions of appearance shape interpersonal judgments.”
“There is a dearth of research examining hand attractiveness,” Wade explained. “This research adds to the literature on hand attractiveness, and adds to the literature on ornamentation and attractiveness showing that hand ornamentation can also affect perceptions of attractiveness.”
To examine these impressions, the researchers collected responses from 342 adults through an online survey shared across social media and email platforms. The participant group included 214 women, 98 men, and 4 nonbinary individuals, with an average age of 30 years. Most participants identified as White (262 individuals), with smaller numbers identifying as Asian (26), Hispanic (13), Black (9), or other racial backgrounds (8). A majority of 275 participants identified as heterosexual, while the rest identified with various non-heterosexual sexual orientations.
Each participant viewed digital illustrations depicting hands with identical skin tone and shape, ensuring that only the nails varied between pictures. In the first phase, participants evaluated three different nail lengths: short, medium, and long. In the second phase, they looked at four different polish colors applied to the nails: red, white, black, and blue.
Participants rated each image using an eight-point scale ranging from zero, meaning not at all, to seven, meaning very much. The questions measured physical attractiveness, cuteness, sexual appeal, and how desirable the person seemed as a casual date, a romantic partner, or a marriage partner. The researchers then analyzed the scores to see how changes in length and color influenced these ratings.
The results indicated that nail length affected social impressions, with medium-length nails consistently scoring highest. On a scale from 0 to 7, participants gave medium nails an average physical attractiveness score of 5.10, compared to 3.20 for short nails and 2.50 for long nails. Medium nails also led the ratings for cuteness at 4.80, sexual appeal at 4.30, and partner desirability at 4.20, while long nails received the lowest scores across every measured category.
Nail color also swayed evaluations, though the pattern differed from traditional expectations regarding the allure of red. White nails earned the highest average marks across the board, scoring 4.60 for physical attractiveness and 4.70 for sexual appeal. Red polish followed with an average attractiveness score of 3.80, whereas darker shades scored lower, with blue receiving an average of 2.50 and black receiving 2.30. The paper reports an overall effect of color but does not report statistical comparisons between individual colors, so the ranking reflects average scores.
The lower standing of red polish came as an unexpected outcome for the team. “One finding that surprised our team was the relatively lower attractiveness ratings associated with red nails,” DeMichele said. “Red is frequently discussed in color theory literature as leading to initial attraction and sex signaling, which made me expect it to receive strong ratings.”
The researchers also looked at whether preferences varied by participant background. Medium-length nails received the highest ratings in every racial group, though some groups were very small, such as the 9 Black and 13 Hispanic participants. When it came to color, heterosexual participants rated white nails highest, whereas non-heterosexual participants, who were combined into a single group because each orientation had few members, gave higher ratings to black polish.
The preference for intermediate nail lengths aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which examined eyelash length rather than fingernails and similarly observed that moderate feature lengths were judged as most attractive compared to short or long extremes.
The authors suggested that medium-length nails may strike an appealing balance between routine grooming and functional practicality. Extremely long nails may be viewed as impractical or exaggerated for daily life, while very short nails might be perceived as lacking grooming effort. Similarly, the high ratings for white polish may stem from cultural associations between lighter colors, cleanliness, and simplicity. The authors describe the overall effects as modest.
“The primary ‘takeaway’ was that nail presentation may influence how people perceive others, although the effects should not be interpreted as universal rules about what is or is not attractive,” DeMichele told PsyPost. “Importantly, these findings suggest that seemingly minor aspects of appearance can contribute to broader social judgments. They do not mean that one particular nail length or color is objectively more attractive, instead highlighting that aesthetic tweaks can influence perceptions within certain social contexts.”
Regarding how strongly these features guide human perception, DeMichele cautioned against overstating the findings. “I would characterize this as an introductory investigation of an understudied form of appearance-based social perception,” she explained. “The findings are useful for identifying patterns and generating hypotheses, but they should not be interpreted as evidence that one nail length or color determines overall ‘attractiveness’. Replication with larger and more diverse samples would be important for determining the robustness and practical magnitude of these effects in larger populations.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study used digitally edited drawings of hands rather than actual photographs of human hands in real-world settings. This controlled design allowed the researchers to isolate specific traits, but it may not fully capture how people respond to real hands during everyday social interactions.
DeMichele also pointed to the sample itself. “I would emphasize that this was an introductory study and that the sample was predominantly WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) which limits how broadly the findings can be applied,” she noted. “Preferences surrounding appearance and adornment are likely shaped by cultural norms, gender, sexuality, age, and other nuanced experiences.”
In addition, the researchers focused strictly on length and a small selection of four solid colors. Other common styling elements, such as intricate nail art, artificial textures, or varying nail shapes like almond or stiletto, were not assessed and could influence attractiveness differently.
Looking ahead, DeMichele has already begun investigating how these cosmetic choices affect the individuals wearing them. “My master’s thesis at Florida Southern College extended this line of study by examining whether nail length and color influence confidence and self-efficacy,” she stated. “The preliminary findings suggested that short- and medium-length nails, along with particular nail colors, were associated with higher levels of confidence and self-efficacy. Longer term, I will continue to expand on how and why nail adornments influence self-perception, interpersonal communication, and even professional judgment.”
Self-efficacy refers to a person’s belief in their ability to succeed at tasks. Those thesis findings have not yet been published.
“I think one of the most interesting aspects of this research is that it examines something people encounter every day but rarely consider from a psychological perspective,” DeMichele reflected. “Nail presentation is a relatively small component of appearance, yet it may communicate meaningful information about individual identity. I hope this research encourages further examination of the subtle ways appearance-related behaviors influence both how we see ourselves and how others perceive us.”
The study, “The Power of Polish: Effects of Nail Length and Color on Perceptions of Attractiveness,” was authored by Sara DeMichele and T. Joel Wade.

How much does France spend on education compared with the rest of Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:21 UTC
19:00:21 KST

How much does France spend on education compared with the rest of Europe?
Amid student protests, Al Jazeera visualises how French spending stacks up against defence and healthcare.
French high school students have been protesting for more than two weeks over conditions in schools, including overcrowded classrooms and staff shortages, and they show no sign of stopping.
The unrest began on September 21 when pupils blockaded a school in the Paris suburb of Creteil, and within a week, their protest had spread across the country with students and police clashing violently.
On September 29, the demonstrations coincided with a nationwide public sector strike, in which teachers joined other state workers against a proposed pay freeze. More than 6,100 people have since been arrested.
With the government under pressure to rein in spending as its debt rises, Al Jazeera looks at how much France invests in education, how it compares with the rest of Europe and how it measures up against what the country spends on healthcare and defence.
How much does France spend on schooling?
According to the latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP). That figure does not include private spending, such as school fees paid by families.
The French Ministry of National Education uses a broader measure, known as domestic expenditure on education, which counts all the money that goes into education, whether from the state, local authorities, businesses or households. As well as teaching, it covers adult and continuing training and related costs such as school meals, boarding and transport.
By this measure, France spent 199.2 billion euros ($223bn) on education in 2025, equivalent to 6.7 percent of its GDP and 2.4 billion euros more than in 2024, according to provisional ministry figures.
Spending has more than doubled since 1980, even after accounting for inflation. But the economy has grown too, so education spending’s share of GDP is lower today than it was in the mid-1990s.
Secondary education accounted for the largest share of spending at 73.7 billion euros (37 percent), followed by primary education at 60 billion euros (30 percent), higher education at 45.6 billion euros (23 percent) and adult and continuing education at 19.7 billion euros (10 percent), according to the National Education Ministry.
How much do other European countries spend on education?
Among European countries, Sweden spends the largest share of its GDP on education at 7.3 percent in 2024, followed by Iceland (7 percent) and Belgium, Estonia and Finland (6.3 percent each), according to Eurostat.
The lowest spenders are Ireland (2.7 percent), Greece (3.9 percent), Romania and Italy (4 percent each), and the United Kingdom and Spain (4.1 percent each).
At 5.1 percent, France is joint 13th, level with the Netherlands and Slovakia, and above the EU average of 4.8 percent.
But above-average spending has not shielded France from a problem affecting much of the developed world. Teacher shortages are growing across countries in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, according to the OECD’s latest Education at a Glance report.
Rather than leaving posts empty, many countries are filling them with teachers who lack full qualifications. In the 2024-2025 school year, 9 percent of primary and secondary teachers across the OECD were not fully qualified.
In France, the strain is most visible in secondary schools. About 11 percent of secondary teachers are not fully qualified, compared with less than 3 percent in primary schools. Furthermore, lower secondary classes average 26 pupils, compared with 23 across the OECD.
That echoes what pupils have been saying during the latest protests: Classes are large, and absent teachers are not being replaced. Some also described dilapidated buildings, a shortage of tables and chairs and, in some schools, rodent infestations. The intense heatwaves that hit France this year exacerbated existing problems in neglected buildings, many of which have no air conditioning, students said.
Teachers also feel undervalued. Only 4 percent said their profession is valued in society, the lowest share of any country surveyed and far below the OECD average of 22 percent.
How much has spending changed?
Historical UNESCO data showed France’s education spending slipped from 5.5 percent of GDP in 2017 to 5.3 percent in 2022 although it remained the ninth-highest among 29 European countries with data. A brief rise to 5.7 percent in 2020 reflected the pandemic shrinking the economy, not extra spending.
France was one of 14 countries where the share fell. Norway and Denmark saw the steepest drops while Slovakia, Slovenia, Lithuania and the Czech Republic recorded the biggest rises.
What else are these nations spending on?
The protests have coincided with nationwide public sector strikes over the government’s proposed 2027 budget, which seeks 54 billion euros ($61.3bn) in savings as French President Emmanuel Macron’s government tries to rein in a large public deficit.
Unions and public sector workers object in particular to a plan to freeze state employees’ salaries, which is expected to save about 2 billion euros ($2.27bn).
Across Europe, most governments spend more on education than on defence, but healthcare takes the largest share of national income of the three, according to 2022 data from the World Bank and UNESCO.
France spent 11.9 percent of its GDP on healthcare in 2022, one of the highest shares in Europe.

My latest discovery? You can eat the skin of a kiwifruit – and the benefits are myriad | Adrian Chiles

Unknown Publisher

19:00:17 KST

Every day’s a school day, honestly. How on earth did I get to just short of my 60th birthday before finding out that you could eat the skin of kiwifruit? Astounding, just astounding. What a revelation. It’s odd, because of all fruit skins, it’s probably the one that looks least appetising. Nice clean oranges and bananas almost beg to be troughed, skins and all, yet we know this is a no-no. But it turns out that all of this small, hairy, boringly coloured object can go down the hatch. Admittedly, I have been slicing the ends off first, but I might start eating them, too.
The first time is the hardest. You need to set aside years of prejudice against that hairy skin that you’ve been so painstakingly removing. Mind over matter. Initially, I sliced my kiwis longways and then each half into four. Now, I’m just eating them like apples. Sometimes three bites, usually two, occasionally just the one. I promise you, a lifetime’s fear of the fur evaporates in an instant. At least, for me it did. I have to report that when I talked my mum into giving it a try, she gagged alarmingly and swore at me with some venom as she fought to expel bits of skin from her mouth. Perhaps it’s not for everyone, after all.
The health benefits are many, apparently. Plenty of furry fibre (I’m sure the furry type is the best) and all kinds of nutrient blah as well. This wasn’t the appeal for me, so much as the dispensing of the faff, all the peeling and paring. That said – and I apologise for oversharing – increasing the furry fibre intake made short shrift indeed of a recent bout of constipation. Highly recommend.
The kiwifruit’s trade association needs to get this out there – the easy eating, that is, not the laxative effect. I think it’s possible it doesn’t even know. In Lidl in Stourbridge this week, I saw some badged up as “easy peelers”. What? No need! If there had been anywhere to give them a wash, I’d have commenced an eat-it-whole demonstration there and then. Seriously, this is marketing gold. My kiwi consumption has gone from every now and then to every other hour. Once the word gets out, all that pent-up demand will be unblocked. Get yourself out there and panic-buy, while stocks last.
Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation | Margaret Sullivan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:16 UTC
19:00:16 KST

When you hate the mainstream press as much as Donald Trump does, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.
Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.
And certainly not any awareness of how the first amendment is supposed to function in American democracy.
This week, his revenge tour took yet another turn.
He barred one of his most disfavored media organizations – Politico – from boarding Air Force One, where it was supposed to provide “pool coverage” to the rest of the press corps as Trump traveled to Nebraska for a campaign stop on Monday afternoon.
That move was met with a strong show of solidarity by several media outlets, who decided not to fill the Politico spot.
And the White House was defiantly delusional, claiming that Trump will “continue to grant an unprecedented level of access to the press”.
This latest chapter came with the usual blast of venom at the mainstream media, though not specifically aimed at Politico.
“The New York Times and many other Artificial Media Outlets should be arrested for their dishonesty and disservice to our Country,” he posted on Truth Social.
The episode follows Trump’s effort in mid-September to ban Politico, CNN and MS Now from the White House. Those organizations quickly sued, charging that Trump’s action was unconstitutional.
Trump-appointed judge Timothy Kelly came down on the side of the media, issuing a temporary restraining order that ordered the White House to reinstate the press badges that had been taken away.
And since then, CNN has been kept off Air Force One repeatedly, using the rationale that access to the White House is one thing, but access to the president’s plane is another.
“The law is absolutely clear,” Ted Boutrous, the first amendment lawyer who is representing the three news organizations said in a statement. “The harm to our clients, the first amendment and the public as a whole is profound.”
The Trump administration’s position is that traveling with the president is a privilege not a right.
The fight is not over, since Kelly will conduct a hearing later this week over the media outlets’ request for a preliminary injunction – a stopgap measure to protect press access in advance of a possible trial.
Trump, of course, has been picking fights with individual journalists and entire news outlets for years. At this very moment, there are court fights involving the Associated Press, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and Disney, which owns ABC News and a number of local ABC affiliates.
So far, there’s been a rare display of support among news organizations that are normally each other’s competition. Columbia Journalism Review called it “a striking and heartening show of solidarity from the White House Press Corps”.
When the three outlets were kicked out of the White House last month, the other networks in the press pool decided not to replace CNN in the rotation, thus suspending coverage for a time.
Peter Baker of the New York Times noted that for the first time in his 30 years covering the White House, “the president will not have a network TV camera covering his everyday official actions and travels”.
What’s more, about 50 media organizations backed up the lawsuit by the three who had been singled out by filing an amicus brief.
It’s hard to understand exactly how less coverage and this constant squabbling benefits Trump, but apparently, he is making a different calculation.
His anti-press actions get a lot of attention, which is the very oxygen he requires to breathe. It doesn’t matter that much of the attention is negative.
Meanwhile, he has entered a phase of saying and doing ever more outrageous things, like his statement this week at a rally that his war in Iran was necessary to protect the world. Trump appeared to suggest that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego if it develops a nuclear weapon which prompted California’s Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, to call the president “deranged and dangerous”.
Trump exudes a sense of desperation these days, with the midterm elections only weeks away and his approval ratings under water.
His war against the press is something of a reflex for him – it’s what comes naturally, especially when he doesn’t like the shape of reality.
The press corps’ newfound solidarity is encouraging. It’s been a long time coming from a group that, in the past, has responded to this president’s constant abuse with deference and dinner invitations.
Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day.
Standing together will be a necessity in the weeks and months ahead.
- Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

Sam Altman says AI will make ‘bad things’ happen. Exhibit A: needless death | Moustafa Bayoumi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:16 UTC
19:00:16 KST

Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, has some words for you about his company and the future of artificial intelligence.
“One of the differences between us and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency [to use it],” Altman told Politico’s new technology podcast and newsletter Decoded.
Yikes. This statement – and the approach it represents – is, well, problematic, to say the least. It’s also emblematic of precisely the kind of world-building and world-destroying that is happening with today’s technology in front of all our eyes, with precious little input from the rest of us.
Altman’s mention of the “bad things” that AI might bring makes it sound like AI’s failures mistakenly create innocent, minor problems or even silly little episodes, such as the time when Google’s “AI Overviews” told users to put non-toxic glue on pizza so the cheese will be less likely to slide off. Good advice is helpful. Bad advice? Chalk it up to being a bad thing.
But culinary adventurism is hardly the only realm that AI operates in and the damage AI is inflicting has already and repeatedly proven itself to be dangerous and even potentially deadly to humans.
OpenAI is embroiled in a lawsuit after the tragic suicide of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old student who initially began using OpenAI’s ChatGPT for homework help. The family’s lawsuit alleges that the teenager took his own life with the chatbot’s encouragement. (OpenAI has claimed Raine misused the platform.)
And Raine’s action is hardly the only one. OpenAI is facing multiple lawsuits filed by different families of victims of suicide and self-harm.
Nor is suicide the only “bad thing” to emerge in the AI universe. In February of this year, on the first day of the war in Iran, two Tomahawk missiles struck the Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary school in the city of Minab, killing at least 120 children. (A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the US was likely responsible for the strike.)
In a recent investigation into the attack, Bloomberg News reported that an AI-linked system was used to target the school. In this case, the system is called Maven, and it is made by Palantir.
Unnamed defense officials told Bloomberg that “inside Centcom, which conducted the US attack, some personnel relied too much on the artificial intelligence embedded in Maven Smart System”. The report also adds that “in the past year, the Defense Department has rapidly made Maven a cornerstone of the US military apparatus”.
AI is helping to produce these tragic and needless deaths, but bad things happen, I guess.
Or there’s the little detail that the US may have come within a hair’s breadth of starting a major war against a superpower, all due to an AI error.
In September, CNN reported that an unidentified AI chatbot used by the US military decided that a Chinese ship in Middle Eastern waters was carrying components of a nuclear weapons program. According to CNN, US planes took off on an interception mission and US military personnel were preparing to board the ship.
Only then did the military look more closely at the report they were basing the mission on and realize the chatbot’s mistakes.
Also found in CNN’s frightening story is that the analyst who used the chatbot to come up with the shoddy analysis then used AI again to write the report, which set the whole thing in motion. A twofer of bad things, I suppose.
Why does it seem that these technologies, which, in the words of Trump’s White House, are “empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor”, get such serious stuff so wrong and so often?
And isn’t it true that the more we rely on AI, the more dangerous these little mistakes become? And why were we never consulted about any of this in the first place?
Could it be that what’s behind the artificial intelligence revolution may be less about the utopian or dystopian future (take your pick) that’s just around the corner and more about the enormous amount of money that is being poured into these companies in the present?
AI may be the only thing keeping Trump’s economy afloat right now. And it’s paying dividends. According to the New Yorker, OpenAI “is reportedly preparing for an initial public offering at a potential valuation of a trillion dollars” and Sam Altman “may become one of the wealthiest and most powerful people on the planet”.
Those bad things? They only happen to other people.
Meanwhile, we are being warned almost every day that AI systems are getting so smart that they’ll end humanity.
But maybe the real worry here is not that the machines are taking over.
It’s that the humans are giving up, ceding control and responsibility in the name of hyping up a product that has shown itself as being really good at taking jobs away from people, stealing the intellectual property of others, writing some piss-poor undergraduate essays, spying on you and your license plates and bringing us to the brink of world war three because God forbid humans should actually question the output from machines. Or the makers of those machines.
What we need is real, tangible and enforceable government oversight over these technologies, which are quickly becoming a dominating force in all our lives. We must collectively have the right to decide how AI should be used. And despite what you may hear, China already regulates its AI companies quite aggressively.
Instead, Donald Trump, Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta and Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia believe that the AI companies should simply regulate themselves, so they have come up with something called the AI Accords.
Signed by leaders of Meta, Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, xAI, and OpenAI, the accords ask tech companies to “implement robust internal controls and monitor the capabilities and alignment of its models”, among other things. “Over time,” the agreement states, “it may make sense to codify these steps into laws or regulations.”
I’m not holding my breath.
Trump, who has ordered the term artificial intelligence be discarded for “super intelligence”, posted the accord on social media on 29 September. The document, titled The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, can still be seen on his account and the White House’s official account. It’s signed by all six tech leaders and Trump, who in the document is labeled “President of the Unites States.”
Super intelligence, indeed.
