Trump Administration Proposes $70K Fee for International Students to Work in U.S.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The Department of Homeland Security on Wednesday proposed a rule that would charge schools $70,000 per international student seeking to work in the U.S. through a program known as Optional Practical Training. It marks the Trump Administration’s latest attempt to curb foreign enrollment.
The proposal, published Thursday in the Federal Register and open for comment until Nov. 9, aims to crack down on OPT—a temporary employment authorization that lets students work in jobs related to their field of study and that DHS has claimed has “ballooned into an uncontrolled guest worker pipeline” and become a “magnet for fraud.”
Under the current system, students pay about $500 to apply and are generally permitted to work in the U.S. for up to a year during or after their study, while those in the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields may get work period extensions.
Under the proposal, schools would have to pay $70,000 for a student’s initial participation—and another $30,000 for each additional program participation—though DHS said it recognizes schools “may pass the financial obligation of this proposed fee” to students or employers. Collected fees would be deposited in the U.S. Treasury.
A DHS spokesperson said in the announcement of the proposed fee that OPT “was never meant to be a back door into the American workforce, a subsidy for cheap labor, or a prize for those who game the system,” and that “American workers should not have to compete against a program that has been turned into a pipeline for cheap foreign labor.”
International students have been in the crosshairs of the second Trump Administration as part of the President’s wider anti-immigration agenda. The Administration has revoked thousands of student visas and heightened vetting of applicants, including by reviewing their social media activity. It also pressured universities and colleges to agree to a compact that includes capping the number of undergraduate students on foreign visas, and it tried to limit the stays of international students to only four years. The Administration has zeroed in particularly on Chinese students amid national security concerns.
While the Administration champions policies discouraging foreign student enrollment as a means to benefit Americans, experts have said that such policies could hamper U.S. competitiveness in the long run.
Why DHS is cracking down on OPT
Since 1947, federal regulations have allowed foreign students to work in cases where employment for practical training is required or recommended by their schools.
But DHS in May alleged it found more than 10,000 foreign students “who claim to be working for highly suspect employers,” and, upon further OPT-linked investigations across multiple states, said it found “empty buildings and locked doors at addresses where hundreds of foreign students are allegedly employed.” Investigators also alleged fraudulent activities, such as “phantom employees,” and suspicious financial transactions.
In its proposal for the new fee, DHS claimed that the program’s growth in the last few years “has exponentially outpaced the number of companies” which it could review and investigate. It said that 194,554 students were granted employment authorization documents in 2024, compared to 160,627 in 2023. The department reasoned that “without the fees proposed in this rule, it cannot operate OPT consistent with its focus on preventing fraud and may shut down the program entirely.”
It also said the fee was “necessary to ensure that schools, students, and employers participate in OPT for its intended purpose instead of a means to circumvent the H-1B visa program,” which refers to the work visa that allows American employers to hire foreign workers in specialty occupations such as technology, engineering, education, healthcare, and finance. OPT has often served as a bridge for students seeking work under H-1B visas, which the Administration has similarly targeted with higher fees.
DHS said it believes that the proposed fee would put the onus on schools “to exercise greater oversight and selectivity” when recommending students for OPT, and it would thus reduce fraud.
Critics call proposal illegal—and anti-American
The proposal, however, like previous attempts to curb foreign enrollment, is expected to face legal challenges. On Oct. 5, educational organizations took the Administration to court following its efforts to limit a similar program, Curricular Practical Training. A $100,000 H-1B visa fee has also been blocked in courts.
“Don’t Panic: DHS has no authority to slap a $70k fee on international students,” Doug Rand, director of the Talent Mobility Fund, an advocacy group for attracting foreign STEM talent, posted on LinkedIn. “Let’s not overreact—this proposed rule isn’t going to fare well in the courts, just as the $100k H-1B fee and other restrictionist policies have been struck down.”
Todd Schulte, president of the immigration reform advocacy group FWD.us, said that if the proposal passes, the U.S. “is intentionally pricing itself out of the global market for top talent, especially in STEM fields.”
Results of a survey by the D.C.-based think tank Institute for Progress released Tuesday found that most international students plan to use OPT, but 80% fewer students said “they would likely try to stay” if the proposed fees were implemented. For STEM students eligible for OPT, the survey found that only 15% would likely try to stay. “DHS assumes that for STEM grads, there will be ZERO change in participation,” the think tank’s director for immigration policy, Jeremy Neufeld, posted on X.
Zuzana C. Wootson, deputy director of federal policy at nonprofit organization Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, said in a statement that such exorbitant fees would push prospective students to competitor countries. But she also warned that the consequences “would extend well beyond international students. Declining international enrollment would strain institutional budgets, increase tuition pressure on American students, and diminish the educational experience for everyone.”

The ghetto on the lagoon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Listen to this essay
25 minute listen
On 29 March 1516, the Venetian Senate voted to create the world’s first ‘ghetto’. All Jews then living in the city – as well as any others who might come later – were ordered to move immediately to a small island in the northeastern sestiere of Cannaregio, a neighbourhood known as the geto novo. It was anything but appealing. Previously used as a dumping ground for the communal copper foundry, it had been converted into a residential quarter for local workers. From the outside, it already looked ‘like a castle’ – ringed by canals and bounded by perilously tall tenements. But by the time Venice’s Jews were herded in, it seemed more like a prison. All outward-facing doors and windows were blocked up; extra walls were built to close off access to the water; and a pair of sturdy iron gates were placed at either end of the bridge leading to Cannaregio. These were closed at sunset and opened in the morning at the ringing of the marangona bell. And just to be sure that no one could sneak out when they weren’t supposed to, four guards – paid for by the Jews themselves – patrolled the canals around the Ghetto ‘day and night’.
It was not the first time that Jews had ever been confined to a separate quarter, of course. By the early 16th century, Jews in France and in German lands had already been living in designated neighbourhoods, physically distinct from the surrounding areas, for close on 300 years. Nor was it even the first time Venice itself had toyed with the idea of Jewish confinement. Back in the 13th century, it had already obliged Jews in its Cretan colony’s capital Candia (now Heraklion) to live in a separate area.
What made the Ghetto unusual was its name. Etymologically speaking, of course, the word geto had nothing to do with Jews. Derived from the verb gettare, meaning ‘to throw’ or ‘cast’, it was just the local name for a foundry (geto) – and, by extension, for the dump next door. But even after the Venetian government moved the foundry elsewhere, people kept on calling the area by its old name. And when the Jews moved in, the island soon lent its name to the institution of segregation, too – a bit like how, today, we can use ‘the White House’ to refer both to 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and to the administration that’s based there.
This was no small matter. Before then, Jewish quarters had been known by all sorts of different names (Judenstraße, Judengasse, Juiverie, etc). But none of them had ever broken through into common parlance as a way of describing segregation per se. They were either too closely associated with a specific geographical feature – a street or a square – or so imprecise that they could refer to just about anything. ‘Ghetto’ offered something different. Precisely because the word was being used metonymically, rather than just geographically, the word ‘ghetto’ could be used to describe any Jewish segregation anywhere. And soon enough, that’s exactly what happened. In around 1562, people started calling the Jewish quarter in Rome a ‘ghetto’; and less than 10 years later, another ‘ghetto’ was established in Florence. And so it went on – right through the 17th century, down to the eve of the French Revolution.
That was just the beginning. After Jewish segregation was abolished in Italy, in the wake of the Napoleonic invasions, the word ‘ghetto’ came to be applied even more widely. Now that its link with a specific type of Jewish segregation was broken, it could denote many more varieties of confinement, marginalisation and exclusion. Brought to the United States in the late 19th century, it was used to describe the poverty and precarity of any migrant group. And after the Nazi invasion of Poland in September 1939, it was applied with terrifying potency to sites of captivity and genocide. Even today, its meanings continue to multiply. Open a newspaper or shuffle your playlist, and you’ll find it used to stigmatise an ‘other’ – or, more often, to reclaim a lost power. And though all these ‘ghettos’ are very different, they all trace their origins back to Venice.
When the Venetian Ghetto was established, of course, no one could have foreseen that it would have such a lasting legacy. Its founders never meant to lay down a marker for the future. It wasn’t the result of a long-term plan. In fact, it almost didn’t happen at all. It was a compromise that emerged out of a period of confusion, experimentation and failure – an attempt to balance the apparently irreconcilable demands of religious prejudice and economic need. It was a paradox, born of war and migration, fear and uncertainty. And, to understand how it came into being, we have to go right back to the arrival of the very first Jews in the Venetian lagoon.
By the time the Ghetto was founded, Jews were already a familiar presence in the Venetian lagoon. As early as the 10th century, Jewish merchants from the eastern Mediterranean are known to have travelled on board Venetian ships; and at least a few spent some time in the city itself. They were, however, a transitory presence, staying only for as long as it took to unload a cargo or conclude their business, and then moving on to harbours new.
Towards the middle of the 14th century, however, a new wave of Jewish migrants began arriving from Germany. These ebrei Tedeschi (German Jews) were not visitors, pausing in the middle of a journey, but refugees. Having been forced to flee their native land by the waves of persecution unleashed by the Black Death, they came to Venice in search of safety – and in the hope of sharing in its commercial might. They first settled in Mestre, just across the lagoon from the city. And they quickly flourished. Some became labourers, others merchants, tailors or jewel-cutters. There were even a few doctors. But it was as money-lenders – or, more properly, pawnbrokers – that they found their niche.
Their success was hardly accidental. Since the mid-12th century, Christians had been forbidden to lend each other money at interest (a practice known as usury). To be sure, some enterprising souls had found a way round this – at least insofar as larger sums were concerned. Were a banker to lend a merchant 2,000 ducats to speculate on wood, for example, he could always dress up the loan as a ‘partnership’, and pretend that the interest was just his share of the profits. But smaller loans were another matter. If a sailor needed to borrow 2 ducats to buy food for his family, and agreed to pay it back, with a bit extra, a month later – well, that was usury, pure and simple. And that’s where the Jews of Mestre came in. As the Fourth Lateran Council had noted, usury was forbidden only between people of the same faith. Provided interest rates were not ‘excessive’, however, there was no reason why Jews couldn’t lend money to Christians. So, by lending small sums – the equivalent of today’s payday loans – the ebrei Tedeschi were able to fill a major gap. And the Venetian government was only too glad for them to do so. More likely than not, in 1366, several German Jews signed a contract (condotta) with the chief magistrate of Mestre, granting them protected status, in exchange for keeping their interest rates down.
No sooner had Venice recovered its prosperity than the ‘need’ for toleration of Jewish migrants began to wane
However, what the ebrei Tedeschi really wanted was to live in Venice itself. But the Venetians were having none of it. Although they were happy enough to borrow money from Jewish bankers when it suited them, they still regarded the same bankers with undisguised hostility. In the Venetians’ eyes, Jews posed a clear and present danger to the Christian faith. If they were allowed to take up residence in the city, the thinking went, they could easily ‘infect’ unsuspecting believers – and thereby undermine the health of Christian society as a whole. There was no question of them being allowed in.
It didn’t take long for Venice to change its mind, though. After a devastating war with Genoa, the Venetian economy was in ruins. Trade had dropped, food prices had soared, and poverty was rising fast. With more people borrowing than ever before, interest rates skyrocketed. If Venice was to stand any chance of getting back on its feet, it needed cheap credit – and fast. Therefore, it put pragmatism ahead of prejudice. In February 1382, the Venetian government offered any banker who would agree to lower their interest rates the chance to live in the city for a period of five years. Theoretically, anyone could apply; but, with only one exception, all those who signed up were Jewish.
It worked like a dream. Little by little, the Venetian economy began to recover. The government was so happy, in fact, that just three years later it voted to offer the ebrei Tedeschi a new condotta, allowing them to go on living in Venice for another decade, after the last arrangement expired. And that wasn’t all. The Venetians were so keen to attract more Jewish bankers to the city that the government even decided to set aside a quarter especially for Jews. In the event, nothing came of this – but the intention was clearly to give Jews a more settled status, and to make Venice a more attractive home for Jewish migrants. A bright future seemed to lie ahead.
But no sooner had Venice recovered its prosperity than the ‘need’ for such toleration began to wane and prejudice once again reared its ugly head. Disagreements sprang up. Threats were made. And, after briefly reviving the plan to create a separate Jewish quarter – albeit to segregate, rather than to welcome the community – the Venetian government decreed that, when the condotta expired in 1397, the Jews would have to leave.
With no other choice, the ebrei Tedeschi dolefully made their way back to Mestre. Although they were not forbidden to visit Venice, they would be allowed to stay only for 15 days at a time and were required to wear a yellow circle on their outer clothing at all times, so that they could be clearly identified – an obligation that had already been foisted on their coreligionists in Sicily, and which would subsequently be imposed in many other Italian cities.
However, the Venetian government quickly realised that it had made a mistake. Although it had seemed easy enough to get rid of the Jews, it proved almost impossible to do without them. Even at a time of economic recovery, ordinary people still needed Jewish loans – and, despite everything, the Jewish moneylenders still wanted their business. It did not take the ebrei Tedeschi long to find a way round the ban. After their 15 days in Venice were up, they simply took a boat to Mestre, stopped for as short a time as was needed to reset the clock, and then went straight back to the city. In this way, they were able to maintain an almost permanent presence in Venice – without ever ‘officially’ residing there.
Naturally, the Venetian authorities tried to clamp down on such infractions. In 1402, they decreed that, after the 15 days were up, Jews could not return to the city for another four months. But there were so many exceptions that it was virtually impossible to enforce. Therefore, even though the Venetian government had no intention of revoking the Jews’ expulsion, it had to reconcile itself to the fact that a Jewish presence of sorts was inevitable – even desirable. As such, its approach shifted from expulsion to containment. Efforts were made to enforce the wearing of the yellow circle, to prohibit acts of worship, and to prevent ‘sexual pollution’. By the 1420s, however, there were just as many Jews in Venice as ever.
Such pragmatic ambiguity might easily have continued indefinitely, had a new wave of antisemitic hostility not swept Europe in the mid-15th century. In response to a complaint from King John II of Castile about the ‘scandalous’ offences Jews were supposedly committing against Christians in his kingdom, Pope Eugenius IV promulgated a bull – Dudum ad nostram audientiam (1442) – that attempted to separate the two religions as completely as possible. All the privileges Jews had previously enjoyed were annulled; harsh new legal restrictions were imposed; and the opportunities for social interaction were cut down to an absolute minimum. Officially, this was intended to apply only to Castile; but in Italy, the mendicant orders were not slow to pick up on its implications. Wandering from town to town, itinerant friars like Domenico da Leonessa preached against Jewish usury and urged municipal authorities to expel Jewish populations once and for all.
This was easier said than done. As Venice had already recognised, most towns depended so much on Jewish credit that it was difficult to imagine doing without them. The friars therefore proposed a solution. With the papacy’s approval, they proposed that towns should set up monti di pietà (‘banks of compassion’). Funded by voluntary donations, these would offer small loans to the working poor on a charitable basis – that is to say, either without asking for any interest at all, or charging rates no higher than they needed to cover their running costs. In principle, this would then relieve Italian towns of the need for Jewish moneylenders, while still respecting the prohibition on Christians lending money.
Several towns had already banned Jews from lending money, or expelled them outright
The first reliably attested monte di pietà was established in Perugia in April 1462. Over the subsequent decades, dozens more followed across Italy and, in most cases, they worked pretty much exactly as the friars had hoped. Once a ‘bank of compassion’ was operating, Italian towns generally didn’t waste much time before ordering the local Jews to leave.
In the Republic of Venice, the friars’ message struck a chord. Since the 1420s, many of Venice’s nearby subject towns on the Italian mainland had grown increasingly hostile to their Jewish residents. Shortly after the promulgation of Dudum ad nostram audientiam, several of them had already banned Jews from lending money, or expelled them outright. And that was just the beginning. When, in 1475, the Jews in Trent (now Trentino) were arrested on suspicion of having ritually murdered a toddler named Simon, a new wave of antisemitic fury was unleashed. Encouraged by preachers like Bernardino da Feltre and Marco da Montegallo, this led to the establishment of monti di pietà in Vicenza, Brescia and Verona just a few years later.
Venice itself seemed close to following suit. Although the Jews’ contribution to the city’s financial stability ultimately prevented the government from taking any precipitous steps just yet, a growing number of patricians were anxious to see them gone. To many of them, it must have seemed like a matter of when, not if.
Their confidence was misplaced, however. When King Charles VIII of France set out to conquer Naples in 1494, Italy was plunged into a series of devastating wars that would rage, on and off, for much of the following 65 years. Venice could not help being drawn into the fray. Yet if it hoped to profit from the fighting, it was cruelly mistaken. It was woefully unprepared. And as its military position worsened, it found that it had no choice but to call on the Jews for help. Heavy taxes and loans were asked of Jewish communities throughout the terraferma (mainland); and, with food prices rising by the day, Venice did whatever it could to keep Jewish credit flowing. On 14 January 1503, the government offered the Jewish bankers of Mestre a new condotta on unusually generous terms. Provided they continued to lend money at reasonable rates of interest, they would be allowed to come and go as they wanted, to rent houses in Venice, and to observe their rites. Most importantly, they were also given an assurance that, if the war on terraferma threatened their safety at any point, they would be allowed to take refuge in Venice itself, and to remain there as long as necessary.
This last clause was probably just meant to be a sweetener. Although Venice was struggling on the battlefield, things were not so bad that anyone seriously expected the bankers of Mestre to flee. But, before long, all that would change. Following a catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Agnadello on 14 May 1509, Venice’s control over the terraferma suddenly collapsed. As French troops advanced on the lagoon, refugees began to stream into the city – including hundreds of Jews from Mestre and other subject cities. The bankers who had signed the 1503 condotta came with the government’s blessing, but a great many more did not.
Terrified that this sudden influx of people would cause a shortage of food, the Venetian government tried desperately to expel anyone who did not have permission to stay. But the frightened refugees refused to budge – and no amount of cajoling could persuade them to do otherwise. Quite suddenly, Venice found itself confronted with precisely the Jewish presence it had tried for so long to avoid.
Even the Jews’ most ardent detractors had to admit that having Jewish bankers in the city at a time of crisis was something of a boon
A paradoxical situation now began to unfold. As the months passed, pressure on the government to expel the Jews – or even worse – only grew. Despite a few fleeting moments of hope, Venice’s position remained critical; and more than once, the city itself was threatened with a direct assault. In the eyes of its inhabitants, every setback began to assume a religious significance. Encouraged by preachers, they came to believe that their misfortunes were a form of divine punishment and that the Jews were ultimately to blame. At Eastertide – when Jews were traditionally held responsible for Christ’s crucifixion – the calls for retribution became intense. On 2 April 1511, for example, Fra Rufin Lovato suggested that the best course of action would be ‘to deprive [Jews] of everything they owned and put them to the sack’.
At the same time, it was increasingly clear to the government that it would not just be difficult to remove the Jews – but positively dangerous to do so. Even the Jews’ most ardent detractors had to admit that having Jewish bankers in the city at a time of crisis was something of a boon. The diarist Marin Sanudo the Younger is a case in point. Although he complained bitterly about the ‘great number’ of Jews he saw in the street, he acknowledged that it was impossible to say anything because ‘they are needed’. And the more the war dragged on, the more essential they became.
The question facing Venice therefore shifted. Instead of focusing on how the Jews might be expelled, the government now began to ask itself how best it could take advantage of the Jews’ presence, while minimising the ‘risk’.
It was not long before a new ‘solution’ presented itself. On 23 April 1515 – 18 months after the Venetian defeat at the Battle of Schio – Giorgio Emo, an important member of the Collegio – the nearest thing Venice had to a cabinet – proposed that the Jews should be confined to the island of Giudecca. It seemed to be a reasonable compromise. There, Emo argued, the Jews would be kept far enough away from the Christian population to prevent religious ‘infection’ from spreading, yet close enough that they could keep the wheels of finance turning. Naturally, the Jews were appalled. They protested that, if the Jewish community was forced to move to Giudecca, it would be in danger of being attacked by the mercenaries billeted there. They therefore suggested the island of Murano instead. But when this, too, turned out to be unworkable, Emo’s proposal was quietly shelved. The principle of segregation was not in any doubt, though. It was just that, for the moment, the government didn’t have the time – or the inclination – to find a more suitable location.
It didn’t take much for that to change. The following year, the Emperor Maximilian invaded the Duchy of Milan, threatening the security of Venice’s remaining possessions on terraferma. In Venice itself, public anxiety rose. That Easter, Fra Lovato once again railed against the Jews. His sermons were apparently no more violent than before. But it was enough to revive the idea of segregation – and stirred the government to action. On 26 March 1516, the Venetian patrician Zaccaria Dolfin presented a proposal to the Collegio similar in outline to that put forward by Emo the previous year. Dolfin stressed that the Jewish presence was the source of Venice’s ills. Given that the Jews could neither be expelled nor confined too far from the city’s markets, he therefore proposed that they should be sent to live on the island of the geto novo in Cannaregio. Despite strong opposition from the Jewish community, the Collegio approved the proposal and, three days later, the Senate confirmed its decision. On 1 April, city criers read the decree in public, and by 25 July, all Venice’s Jews, without exception, were in the geto novo. The Ghetto had been born.
The Ghetto was never meant to be anything more than a temporary measure – a quick fix for a passing ‘problem’. But over the decades that followed, the persistence of war and an abiding reluctance to establish a monte di pietà in Venice prevented the government from ridding itself of the city’s Jewish quarter. In fact, as time wore on, the steady decline of Venice’s fortunes not only guaranteed the Ghetto’s endurance – it also paved the way for its expansion. Later, two further ghettos would be created – the Ghetto Vecchio (1541) and the Ghetto Nuovissimo (1633) – each intended to accommodate different groups of Jewish migrants from the Iberian peninsula (those who came via the Ottoman Empire being known euphemistically as ‘Levantines’, and those who subsequently arrived by a more direct route as ‘Ponentines’), whose involvement in international trade increasingly sustained Venice’s faltering commercial standing. And though the Ghetto itself would endure its own decline, it would not be abolished until after the arrival of Napoleon in 1797.
The Ghetto was, from its inception, a site of exclusion. As the centuries wore on, efforts were repeatedly made to reinforce the barriers – both real and metaphorical – that separated its inhabitants from the Christian world beyond. Yet at no point was it ever hermetically sealed. Its very existence was founded on the necessity of exchange, interaction, even co-existence. The credit market, and later international trade, required there to be a constant to-ing and fro-ing between Jews and Christians. Exactly the same was true of cultural life. In a city as intellectually vibrant as Venice, where humanists were as fascinated by anything Hebrew as they were by Latin and Greek, the exchange of ideas was inevitable. And this is to say nothing of the fact that identities in early modern Venice were often so complicated that it was virtually impossible to separate any communities completely.
In some ways, then, the Ghetto is a reminder of the paradox that lies at the heart of all forms of social exclusion, even today. It speaks to the fact that any attempt to marginalise a community ultimately arises out of ties that bind – and speaks more eloquently to the failures of those doing the marginalisation than it does to any perceived ‘differences’.
Yet perhaps the Ghetto’s most powerful lesson for our own times lies in its contingency. The path to its foundation was not travelled in giant leaps, but in hesitant steps. It was made up of small, incremental decisions, each of which was contested – and all of which seemed conditional, at best, in the moment. At any stage, it could have been stopped. Venice could have reversed its steps or chosen a different road. And this is where its real message lies. Today, antisemitism is once again on the rise, influenced by wars beyond our reach, and events beyond our control. It is built on paradoxes and contradictions, prejudices and failures. And it advances by small steps – steps that we tell ourselves are isolated or unrepresentative in themselves. A piece of graffiti, a shouted slogan, a casual assault in the street. But Venice shows where those steps lead – and reminds us that every one can, and must, be fought.

He's Running In a District Trump Won By 21 Points. Democrats See an Opening

2026-10-08

The odds are still stacked against Justin Pearson.
When the Democratic state representative announced that he would continue to run for Congress in a gerrymandered district five months ago, it was seen by many in Tennessee and Washington as more symbolic than viable. Pearson had originally planned to run in a majority-Black district in the Memphis area, challenging Rep. Steven Cohen, a ten-term Democratic incumbent. Then in May, the Republican-controlled state legislature redrew Tennessee's congressional map, splitting off parts of Memphis and combining it with 14 rural counties. Pearson is now running to represent a district that Trump carried by more than 21 points in 2024.
“We knew this was going to be a harder race after they rigged the maps,” Pearson says in a phone interview. “ It has not deterred us at all.”
This week, Democrats’ House campaign arm gave Pearson’s bid against Republican state Sen. Brent Taylor a vote of confidence, adding Tennessee’s 9th district to its coveted “Red to Blue” list. Campaigns on the list receive “organizational and funding support,” as well as staff resources, training, and strategic guidance, according to a DCCC press release.
The late support comes against the backdrop of a broad national trend of key races shifting in Democrats’ favor. In late September, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report said House Democrats are on track to pick up five to 15 seats. Though Cook still rates Tennessee’s 9th District as a “Solid Republican” seat, emboldened Democrats see a potential blue wave significantly expanding the races in play.
There has been little publicly available polling on the race. A recent poll sampling 400 voters and commissioned by a Democratically-aligned group found Pearson trailing Taylor by four percentage points.
Pearson sees the addition of his scrappy campaign to the "Red to Blue" program shows the party’s leaders see it as more than just a protest against GOP gerrymandering. He says he’s campaigned in all 15 counties in the new district, holding three to four campaign events daily.
“We've been having listening tours, road-to-victory rallies, meet and greets, fundraisers, and of course we're visiting barber shops and beauty shops and churches here in Memphis and Shelby County too, because we're not going to leave any of this to chance,” Pearson says,
A growing backlash in Tennessee to President Trump and the Iran War is also helping, he says, pointing to rural voters who previously voted for Trump that are now canvassing for him. “There are a lot of people who voted conservatively in the past who are farmers, who are very frustrated by the tariffs and what they [the Trump administration] have done with beef imports,” Pearson says. “There are people who are having to spend $1,000 a day on their machineries, diesel fuel, and they know that's a direct correlation to the Iran War.”
Closing the gap
Pearson made national headlines in 2023 for getting expelled from the Tennessee legislature for leading a gun reform protest from the House floor. His opponent, Taylor, has sought to brand Pearson as a “democratic socialist” who is too liberal for the district.
“He causes chaos everywhere he goes, and that’s why the voters in Tennessee’s District 9 will vote for competence over chaos,” Taylor said in a statement to TIME.
Pearson has argued Taylor can’t be trusted to represent the interests of the district’s voters. He highlighted donations Taylor accepted from Elon Musk’s SpaceX. A subsidiary company, SpaceXAI, is seeking to build a massive data center in the Memphis area despite local residents' concerns over environmental impact.
“My opponent…is about making more money for himself rather than protecting and serving the people in our community and in our state,” Pearson says.
Taylor, a former owner of funeral homes who is mostly self-funding his campaign, told TIME he sold his business four years ago and retired at age 54 before running for state Senate. He also accused Pearson of never having a real job and being “a paid protester.”
Capitalizing on voters’ energy
When the Supreme Court issued a ruling in April that undermined a major provision of the Voting Rights Act, it prompted multiple Republican-controlled states to quickly redraw its congressional lines. Tennessee was the first to act, with the legislature quickly approving a new map erasing Tennessee's only majority-Black district. Efforts by civil rights groups to convince the courts to block the new map have so far failed.
Yet the map switch appears to have jolted many of the state’s Democratic voters during the primaries. The Washington Post reported that a fifth of active registered voters in Shelby County, which includes Memphis, cast a ballot in three Democratic primaries for U.S. House seats, the highest level of voter turnout in a decade.
Pearson says Black voters in Tennessee are showing they refuse to be deterred by Republicans’ efforts to dilute their political power.
“This is just another challenge that we are going to face, and we're going to face it together,” he says. “And we're going to show up more than we have in decades. We're going to participate more than we have in decades because our voting rights are on the ballot.”

Judge holds critical hearing in Trump’s attempt to ban CNN, MS Now and Politico from White House
The federal judge who issued a temporary restraining order, pausing Donald Trump’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House, is set to hold a hearing at 11am ET today.
Timothy Kelly, a Trump-appointee, previously blocked the president from carrying out the ban for two weeks. Today we’ll see whether that pause is extended on the administration’s latest attempt to strip access from members of the press whose coverage it claims to be negative and inaccurate.
However, at his initial hearing, Kelly was skeptical of the administration’s argument to bar the three outlets from the White House grounds, expressing that they received no prior warning. He also pointed to existing precedent, which shows the high standards needed to prevent press-pass holders from accessing the White House – including a written notice with the reasons for denial.
The three newsrooms have since requested for Kelly to extend his pause while the litigation plays out.
Since the Kelly’s initial injunction, there have been several reports of the affected outlets still being barred from covering the president. Most recently, a reporter from Politico was prevented from traveling on Air Force One to cover Trump’s rally in Nebraska on Monday. While CNN journalists were also stopped from also traveling on the jet at the end of September to report on the president’s trip to Tennessee. A reminder: these outlets are part of the press pool, an almost century-old system in which news organisations take turns covering the president’s daily movements. When Trump returned to office, the White House took control of the pool rotation, which previously was managed by an independent association. Kelly’s temporary block technically doesn’t apply to Air Force One or the Oval Office – smaller spaces that only those on pool duty have access to on any given day.

Riyaz ul Khaliq
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Pakistan and Bahrain on Thursday emphasized de-escalation in the Middle East amid the US-Iran war and conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthi group as Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar hosted his Bahraini counterpart, Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, in Islamabad.
Dar said discussions with Al Zayani covered the evolving situation in the Gulf, adding that they "emphasized the importance of restraint, dialogue and de-escalation."
“We discussed the need to ensure safety and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb given their importance for regional and global food and energy security,” said Dar.
He said Pakistan “remains committed to efforts for peace and stability in the region.”
The Middle East has seen an escalation of conflicts since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran, triggering retaliation by Tehran, which hit American military bases and assets across Gulf nations, including in Bahrain.
Amid the US-Iran war, conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis intensified in September when the Yemeni group seized strategic positions in the provinces of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz, including the port city of Mokha, before advancing to Mayyun Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Islamabad has played a mediating role between the US and Iran, securing a ceasefire and then hosting the highest-level talks between the warring parties in April earlier this year, and has called for an end to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Bahraini Foreign Minister Al Zayani said the meeting in Islamabad comes while “the crisis in our region remains unresolved and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz is under daily threat.”
Bahrain “strongly condemns” Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's airports, saying that targeting airports and civilian infrastructure “is a criminal act, flagrant violation of international law,” he said.
Saudi Arabia’s security “is an integral part of the security of Bahrain and of the GCC (Gulf Council Cooperation),” the Bahraini foreign minister said.
He said he discussed with Dar the situation around the two straits, "underscoring the importance of freedom and safety of navigation and respect for international law."
Tehran has closed Hormuz since the US and Israel initiated the war while the Pentagon has imposed a military blockade of Iranian ports since April.
“We highly value Pakistan’s constructive role” of hosting Islamabad Talks between the US and Iran and "its continued efforts for dialogue and de-escalation,” said Al Zayani.
"We respect each other... we are consistent in our relationship... we feel safe in this relationship," said Al Zayani about Bahrain's ties with Pakistan, stressing: "we understand the constraints on each other."
Boosting ties
After the two foreign ministers co-chaired the third session of the Pakistan-Bahrain Joint Ministerial Commission, Al Zayani said the ties between the two nations have “gained significant momentum.”
Reaffirming “mutual resolve” to strengthen bilateral cooperation in key areas, the two nations next week will mark 55th years of diplomatic relations and have set target of $1 billion in trade transactions.
Bahrain is home to some 134,000 Pakistani citizens and the joint ministerial commission covered cooperation across more than 15 fields as the two sides stress on enhancing people-to-contacts.

Yle poll: Finns Party overtakes Prime Minister Orpo’s party
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
12:56:31 EEST
18:56:31 KST

The Finns Party has overtaken Prime Minister Petteri Orpo’s National Coalition Party (NCP) in Yle’s latest opinion poll, marking the first time the two governing parties have exchanged positions during the current parliamentary term.
The poll, published on Thursday, 8 October, puts the Finns Party in second place with 16.5 per cent support, ahead of the NCP on 16.3 per cent. The opposition Social Democratic Party (SDP) retains its lead with 22.7 per cent.
The Finns Party, led by Finance Minister Riikka Purra, gained 0.2 percentage points from the previous survey, while support for Orpo’s NCP fell by 0.7 points.
The gap between the governing parties stands at just 0.2 percentage points, well within the survey’s margin of error of 1.8 points.
According to Yle, the NCP has not recorded such a low level of support in its polling series since late 2020. The Finns Party last ranked ahead of the NCP when both parties were in opposition at the beginning of the decade.
Tuomo Turja, research director at polling company Taloustutkimus, attributed the NCP’s decline partly to the government’s spending cuts.
"It was not surprising that support for the biggest governmental party declined. The government's saving measures are now fully showing at this stage of the mandate," Turja told Yle.
He said the NCP was losing former supporters to the Finns Party, while some voters remained undecided.
The survey also found that support for the NCP among women had fallen to 12.1 per cent. The SDP leads among female voters with more than 27 per cent, followed by the Left Alliance with more than 16 per cent.
The Finns Party has recovered nearly six percentage points since its low point in spring 2025, continuing a rise that has lasted more than a year.
Meanwhile, the Left Alliance reached a record 12.4 per cent, gaining 0.7 percentage points and closing the gap with the Centre Party, which fell to 12.6 per cent.
Turja told Yle that the Left Alliance had attracted voters from the SDP and Greens. The party has also distinguished itself by refusing to join a cross-party agreement on a debt brake intended to restrict government borrowing.
The Greens received 8.3 per cent support, followed by the Swedish People's Party on 3.6 per cent, the Christian Democrats on 3.4 per cent and Movement Now on 2.1 per cent.
The Centre Party, which previously held third place in Yle's polling, has seen its support settle at around 13 per cent despite criticism of the government over fuel prices.
Taloustutkimus conducted the survey for Yle between 7 September and 5 October, interviewing 2,807 people. Of those, 2,089 expressed a party preference. The margin of error is 1.8 percentage points in either direction.

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:56:02 BST
18:56:02 KST

South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
- Published
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.
It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.
The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.
South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.
And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.
But on Wednesday, Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told reporters at a media briefing that its Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha had not apologised, according to Ukrainian news site Liga.
In a statement on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".
- Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia 
  - Published11 January 2025
Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".
It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.
President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.
But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.
The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.
Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.
Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.
After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.
This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.
Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.
South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.
Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute

Unknown Publisher

UK scales back Jerusalem consulate after Israel dispute
October 8, 2026
Britain has withdrawn diplomats from its consulate in East Jerusalem after reaching an agreement with Israel over the future of the diplomatic mission.
According to Israel, the consulate had ceased operating in its previous capacity. Britain insisted that the building would remain open under the name UK Mission, Jerusalem.
The move follows a diplomatic dispute over British measures targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
What has happened to the British consulate?
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said 20 British diplomats, including the consul general, were ending their assignments and leaving Israel.
Seven diplomats would be allowed to continue working from the building, although their activities would be "very limited," he said.
The consulate's diplomatic emblem and sign were removed from the building on Thursday.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said London had temporarily withdrawn some staff and their families to ensure their safety.
He insisted the mission would remain independent and operational, continuing to provide "vital services" and work with Palestinians.
Miliband said Britain did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which was established in 1838.
Why did Israel order the consulate to close?
Israel ordered the closure on September 8 in retaliation for British measures against Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
Britain joined other countries in announcing trade restrictions and sanctions targeting settlements and individuals linked to settler violence against Palestinians.
Israel condemned the measures as a diplomatic attack.
The British consulate has traditionally handled relations with Palestinians in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, separately from Britain's embassy in Tel Aviv.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in 1967 and subsequently annexed it, a move not recognized by most countries, including Britain.
Miliband said Britain would not take retaliatory diplomatic action while talks with Israel continued.
He reaffirmed London's support for a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Number of victims of Russia’s strike on buses in Kramatorsk has doubled - public transportation services suspended
Kyiv • UNN
A Russian attack on two scheduled buses in Kramatorsk has claimed the lives of 30 people, while another 18 were injured. Public transportation has been suspended in the cities.
As many as 30 people have already been killed as a result of Russia’s morning strike on scheduled buses in Kramatorsk on October 8, the Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office reported. Against this backdrop, as stated by Donetsk Regional Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin, public transport services in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk are being suspended, UNN writes.
As of now, the death toll from the morning attack on scheduled buses has risen to 30. Eighteen people were injured
According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the occupiers attacked scheduled buses in Kramatorsk on October 8 at 10:00.
"Two scheduled buses were at the epicenter of the strike, which the enemy most likely attacked using a UMPB D-30 SN glide bomb," the statement said.
Public transport services in Sloviansk and Kramatorsk are being suspended due to Russia’s deliberate attacks
"In view of the sharp deterioration in the security situation, I ordered the Kramatorsk and Sloviansk city military administrations to suspend public transport services. The Russians are deliberately striking civilians. For them, a bus carrying passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible. Today’s tragedy in Kramatorsk is yet another piece of evidence: the Russians killed 30 people and injured 18 more in an instant," Donetsk Regional Military Administration Head Vadym Filashkin wrote on social media on October 8. "I ask you to treat this decision with understanding. This is a forced step dictated by the actions of the enemy, for whom public transport has become yet another way to kill Ukrainians."

South Korea decided to recall its ambassador from Ukraine, the South Korean Foreign Ministry announced on Oct. 8, amid ongoing deterioration in Kyiv-Seoul relations.

Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 6, injures 17, disrupts electricity, water supplies
Russian drone strikes on the morning of Oct. 8 have killed six people and injured at least 17 in Kyiv, the city's authorities said.
A Russian drone struck a four-story commercial building in Solomyanskyi district, killing two and injuring two, and leading to a fire, while the wreckage of another fell on the Holosiivskyi district, Klitschko said.
Prior to that strike, Klitschko said that Russian attacks on the capital this morning had killed one person and injured 11 others.
A fourth person died of their injuries in hospital, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said in the afternoon.
Klitschko raised the number of injured to 14, eight of which were hospitalized, in an update on 13:11 a.m. local time.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said that two more people had died and three more were injured after another Russian strike on Solomyanskyi district destroyed a metal hangar for storing paint.
At 10:00 a.m. local time, Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm DTEK announced emergency energy shutdowns in Brovary, Buchanskyi, Vyshgorod, and Boryspil districts of the oblast.
Shortly after, KMDA announced that the right bank of Kyiv may experience interruptions in water supply, as the power decrease in the electricity grid also meant a decrease in pressure of the water supply network. This applied especially to the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
DSNS also said that a fire broke out at a logistics facility in the Buchanskyi district in Kyiv Oblast following a Russian drone strike.
Overnight, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv had already killed four people and injured 21 across four districts, KMDA said.
In Solomyanskyi district, a UAV fell on the roof of a 5-storey residential building, causing a fire, while elsewhere in the district falling debris injured one person.
In Desnyanskyi district, falling drone debris also caused a fire in a 12-storey residential building.
At the time of writing, Klitschko said there had been a further strike on Shevchenko district, emergency services were dispatched.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of them jet-powered, on the night of Oct. 8, Ukraine's air force said. The Air Force said that air defense shot down or suppressed 126 of these drones.

California's Proposition 40: the world's first billionaire tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:33 UTC
18:53:33 KST

Breadcrumb
What is California's Proposition 40, the world's first billionaire tax?
Proposition 40 (or Prop 40), also known as the California billionaire tax or the California wealth tax, is a measure that appears on the upcoming California’s 2026 ballot in the United States.
Its aim is to impose a one-time 5% tax on the state’s 200 to 250 billionaires (by net worth) and use 90% the funds for healthcare and the remainder for other social services.
How did Prop 40 come about?
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare have led to charge to get the measure on the ballot.
Working class advocates have long been pushing for a tax on billionaires, particularly after the 2025 Big Beautiful Bill that redirected funding for healthcare to immigration enforcement.
California has long had an extreme rate of wealth inequality. This was exacerbated during the pandemic, when some of the state’s top billionaires saw their wealth multiply. The state’s billionaires became $500 billion richer last year. Of the 100 wealthiest people in the world, around 85 reside in California as of September 2026.
Who supports Prop 40?
The measure is supported by former Democratic House Speaker Nancy Pelosi of California, Representative Ro Khanna of California, whose district has one of the highest concentrations of billionaires, and Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont (an Independent who caucuses with the Democrats). Sanders is currently touring the state to advocate for Proposition 40.
“Once California passes Proposition 40, trust me, that will not be the end,” Sanders said at a recent rally in California. “If Ro and I have anything to say about it, and we do, we will enact a national wealth tax."
Other politicians, including Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts are pushing for similar measures. At a recent rally in California, Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was asked if he supported the measure, he said he wouldn’t comment on California legislation, but that he would support a similar initiative (if it were proposed) in Michigan.
In addition, six Nobel prize-winning economists support the proposition.
Who opposes Prop 40?
Aside from the billionaires who would be taxed, the main opponents are California Governor Gavin Newsom, the California Police Chiefs Association, and the California Medical Association.
The billionaire opponents are spending over $200 million on TV ads against Proposition 40. Google founder Sergey Brin alone has spent $100 million opposing the measure.
In their ads, they say Proposition 40 has loopholes that would allow for middle-class tax increases. Sanders says that no one with less than a billion dollars would see a tax increase under the measure.

Russian, Ukrainian strikes leave at least 56 dead, over 100 injured
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:09 UTC
18:53:09 KST

Russian and Ukrainian authorities reported deadly attacks on cities and infrastructure on Thursday as Moscow and Kiev continued to target each other amid escalating hostilities.
In Ukraine, a Russian missile attack on the northern city of Pryluky killed 22 people, including five children, and wounded more than 50, Chernihiv Governor Vyacheslav Chaus said on Thursday.
“Twenty-two people died in Pryluky. Among them were five children. Four died at the impact site, and one child died in the hospital,” Chaus said in a statement on Telegram.
Chaus also said a Russian strike hit the regional capital of Chernihiv on Wednesday, setting fire to a three-storey building. Ukraine’s Air Force said its air defences had shot down 117 of 130 strike drones and at least 44 ballistic and cruise missiles launched by Russia overnight.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a Russian Kh-101 missile had struck a residential building in Pryluky, renewing calls for additional air defence systems and ammunition.
“The threat is there every day, and every day, our air defence batteries need to have missiles ready,” Zelenskyy said, adding that Kiev was counting on prompt deliveries and sufficient production by its partners.
A separate Russian strike on two passenger buses in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk has killed 30 people and wounded 18, local authorities said on Thursday.
The Donetsk regional prosecutor’s office said the death toll from the morning attack had risen to 30. The regional governor’s office confirmed the same toll and said public transport had been suspended.
Ukrainian drone attacks reported in Russia
Meanwhile, Russian authorities said a Ukrainian drone attack on the southern port city of Novorossiysk in the Krasnodar region killed four people, including a child, and wounded 29 others. Three of the injured were in serious condition, regional governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
Kondratyev accused Ukraine of targeting civilians, saying damage was reported to three private homes, five apartment buildings, a church and a kindergarten.
Drone debris also damaged homes and a kindergarten in the nearby town of Anapa, though no casualties were reported there.
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed its air defences had shot down 596 Ukrainian drones over 11 regions, as well as over the Black Sea and Ukraine’s Russian-annexed Crimea region.
Ukraine’s General Staff said it had struck the Novorossiysk naval base overnight, causing fires at the base and at an oil terminal in the city’s seaport. It described the base as an important hub for the Russian Black Sea Fleet’s ship basing, maintenance and logistical support. The claim could not be independently verified.
Fire sparked at Yandex data centre
A separate drone strike also sparked a fire at a data centre operated by Russian technology company Yandex in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, Russian state media TASS reported.
Yandex said the attack damaged part of its infrastructure, forcing it to suspend operations at the facility and potentially disrupting some services. The company reported no injuries.
Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov said two drones had been shot down over the region overnight, adding that a fire broke out at a local enterprise and windows were blown out in several private homes.
Moscow and Kiev have increasingly targeted each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, saying their attacks are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Lithuania plans 4.8 billion euros for defence in 2027, substantial budget deficit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:53:00 UTC
18:53:00 KST

Lithuania plans to allocate about 4.8 billion euros to defense next year, or slightly more than 5% of gross domestic product, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Thursday.
The planned allocation would be about 36 million euros higher than this year’s military budget. But because of economic growth, defence spending would account for a smaller share of GDP than this year, when the budget provided for 5.38%.
“The priorities for 2027 are to maintain 5% of gross domestic product for defence. As we mentioned, being in the 5% club remains our goal and will be implemented,” Sinkevičius told reporters.
He said the exact figure was still being discussed by the governing coalition and with Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, who wants defence spending to reach 5.1% of GDP.
“The actual amount, compared with this year’s allocated amount, will still grow, the percentage will decrease, but the actual amount allocated for defence and security will increase,” Sinkevičius said.
He stressed that increasing military spending must be accompanied by efficient and transparent use of the funds.
“Is the budget growth sufficient? You can say that the more, the better probably, but I say we need efficient, transparent, meaningful spending,” he said.
Among the government’s main priorities are air defence, the deployment of a German brigade in Lithuania and development of a national division, Sinkevičius said.
He added that 43.92% of this year's defence appropriations had been spent so far.
Lithuania has sought to maintain defence spending at 5% of GDP as it strengthens its military capabilities in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and deepens NATO cooperation.
Deficit expected to exceed EU limit
Lithuania’s general government budget deficit is expected to reach about 3.8% of GDP next year, Sinkevičius said.
“It seems that the variation is currently about 3.8%,” he said at a news conference when asked about the projected deficit.
That would put Lithuania above the 3% deficit limit set under the European Union's fiscal rules.
Sinkevičius said the government had already made about 1.5 billion euros in planned spending cuts after negotiations to keep the deficit from rising further.
He has previously said that without allowing a larger deficit, the government would not be able to meet its commitments on military spending and other planned increases in expenditure.
The EU’s Maastricht criteria generally require member states to keep their general government deficit below 3% of GDP.

Lithuania plans to allocate about 4.8 billion euros to defense next year, or slightly more than 5% of gross domestic product, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Thursday.
The planned allocation would be about 36 million euros higher than this year’s military budget. But because of economic growth, defence spending would account for a smaller share of GDP than this year, when the budget provided for 5.38%.
“The priorities for 2027 are to maintain 5% of gross domestic product for defence. As we mentioned, being in the 5% club remains our goal and will be implemented,” Sinkevičius told reporters.
He said the exact figure was still being discussed by the governing coalition and with Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas, who wants defence spending to reach 5.1% of GDP.
“The actual amount, compared with this year’s allocated amount, will still grow, the percentage will decrease, but the actual amount allocated for defence and security will increase,” Sinkevičius said.
He stressed that increasing military spending must be accompanied by efficient and transparent use of the funds.
“Is the budget growth sufficient? You can say that the more, the better probably, but I say we need efficient, transparent, meaningful spending,” he said.
Among the government’s main priorities are air defence, the deployment of a German brigade in Lithuania and development of a national division, Sinkevičius said.
He added that 43.92% of this year's defence appropriations had been spent so far.
Lithuania has sought to maintain defence spending at 5% of GDP as it strengthens its military capabilities in response to Russia’s war against Ukraine and deepens NATO cooperation.
Deficit expected to exceed EU limit
Lithuania’s general government budget deficit is expected to reach about 3.8% of GDP next year, Sinkevičius said.
“It seems that the variation is currently about 3.8%,” he said at a news conference when asked about the projected deficit.
That would put Lithuania above the 3% deficit limit set under the European Union's fiscal rules.
Sinkevičius said the government had already made about 1.5 billion euros in planned spending cuts after negotiations to keep the deficit from rising further.
He has previously said that without allowing a larger deficit, the government would not be able to meet its commitments on military spending and other planned increases in expenditure.
The EU’s Maastricht criteria generally require member states to keep their general government deficit below 3% of GDP.

Ancient volcanoes, dinosaurs and healing mud in Pomorie’s planned geopark

News
Ancient volcanoes, dinosaurs and healing mud in Pomorie’s planned geopark
Thursday 8 October 2026 11:53
Thursday, 8 October 2026, 11:53
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Ancient volcanoes, traces of the age of dinosaurs and healing mud are among the attractions of a planned geopark on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. The project, which would bring together natural, cultural and historical sites in what could become the country’s first geopark, was presented at the Dechko Stoev City Art Gallery in Pomorie. Developed by the Pomorie Local Action Group, it aims to attract more tourists and create new opportunities for local businesses.
“We have been working on this project for two years and will also apply for inclusion in UNESCO’s Global Geoparks Network,” said Pomorie Mayor Ivan Aleksiev. He hopes the geopark will give visitors more to see and do, while drawing tourists to places beyond the town’s best-known attractions.
The planned geopark will cover the whole of Pomorie municipality, as well as an area near the village of Golitsa in Dolni Chiflik municipality, Varna region. Among the sites it will include are three ancient volcanoes near Dabnik, Kableshkovo and Kamenar, the Pomorie Lagoon, Lake Pomorie, the salt pans and deposits of therapeutic mud.
Also included is an area near the village of Kozichino, where geological traces of events dating back some 66 million years have survived. They tell the story of one of the great turning points in Earth’s history – the mass extinction that brought an end to the age of the non-avian dinosaurs.

====================================================================================================

US probes EU carbon border tax over potential trade barriers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:50:58 UTC
18:50:58 KST

The EU's carbon border tax was designed to prevent companies from shifting production abroad to countries with weaker environmental rules — but the US says it amounts to a discriminatory trade rule.
Washington is investigating whether the European Union's carbon border tax is harming US trade and whether plans to expand it would create unfair barriers for American companies, according to an official document published on Thursday.
The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) took effect in January 2026, covering imports of aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, iron and steel.
It aims to level the playing field between European manufacturers and foreign competitors while preventing carbon-intensive production from shifting to countries with weaker climate rules.
Shortly after its launch, several EU countries sought temporarily exemptions for fertilisers, warning that the tax would push up prices and could undermine food security.
Under CBAM, EU importers must monitor and report emissions generated in producing the goods they bring into the bloc. Washington argues that the system is creating financial liabilities for American companies, raising the prospect of fresh trade tensions with President Donald Trump's administration.
The timing is significant. Brussels is negotiating plans to extend CBAM to more products, including washing machines and car parts, while tightening rules to prevent companies from circumventing the tax.
"The USTR (Office of the United States Representative) is seeking comments on the impact of the CBAM on US trade with the EU, as well as the potential impact of the EU’s proposals to expand CBAM coverage. Such comments will help inform continued USTR and US government engagement with the EU on CBAM," the document says.
Washington will examine the impact on costs, regulatory burdens and access to the EU market for American producers, as well as direct and indirect exports and overall trade with the bloc. US companies have until November 9 to submit their views.
The move comes shortly after the World Trade Organisation (WTO) agreed to establish a panel at Russia's request to examine the legality of CBAM. Moscow argues that the carbon border tax creates "significant trade barriers" for goods entering the EU.
Russia also claims that free carbon allowances granted to some heavy industries under the EU's Emissions Trading System (ETS) amount to an "export subsidy" designed to give European manufacturers a competitive advantage, according to the WTO.
EU splits
Within the EU, governments and the European Parliament remain divided over plans to expand CBAM, particularly over which products should be covered, according to a Council document seen by Euronews.
The European Commission says the expansion is intended to prevent carbon-intensive imports from escaping the bloc's climate rules.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency and is brokering negotiations, says both governments and Parliament consider the Commission's proposed expansion too narrow. But they disagree over which additional products to include.
Belgium Green MEP Sarah Matthieu told Euronews that the EU should include critical clean tech goods such as solar panels and heat pumps.
Such a move would protect European manufacturers, but critics argue it would also push up prices for businesses and consumers.
The Irish Presidency, which wants to seal the deal at a key meeting on 20 October, has asked EU capitals to identify which Parliament proposals they could accept and where they would be ready to compromise.
Dispute over carbon calculations
Another sticking point is the Commission's proposal to allow certain goods to be temporarily exempted from CBAM in "serious and unforeseen circumstances".
MEPs oppose the measure, arguing that it could weaken the mechanism and give the Commission excessive powers without sufficient parliamentary scrutiny. Instead, they favour financial support for affected industries through redistribution from EU funds.
MEPs also want a tougher system to automatically apply default carbon values to high-risk goods and origins unless specific exceptions are met.
The Council is more flexible, allowing companies to continue using their actual emissions data if they can provide sufficient evidence.
CBAM's default values are calculated using country-specific, sectoral and energy data to estimate the emissions generated in producing imported goods.
Washington, however, argues that the "EU adds a punitive markup" to these estimates, effectively penalising companies that do not provide their own emissions data.
The Irish Presidency has asked governments whether Parliament's approach could create practical difficulties for importers and national authorities – concerns also raised by Washington.
According to the US document, Washington will assess the Commission's original proposal and the competing positions of the Council and Parliament to determine how each could affect American companies compared with their European rivals.
The Commission did not respond to a Euronews request for comment at the time of publication.

Fewer targets, more waves: jet-powered Gerans partly free Russia to concentrate missiles, ISW says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:49:50 UTC
18:49:50 KST

Russia is concentrating missiles on a smaller, more specific set of targets, and its jet-powered attack drones are part of the reason, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed. Its combined attack overnight on 7 October killed 22 people in Pryluky, the State Emergency Service (SES) said as of the morning of 8 October. Russian milbloggers noted the shift the same day.
Russia often uses concentrated drone and missile strikes to overwhelm localized Ukrainian air defenses and destroy urban centers, ISW noted. Pryluky, where the strike killed children, was one of the areas a Russian channel says drew a significant share of the Kh-101s that night. With winter close, ISW expects the same pattern against Ukraine's energy grid, with jet drones partly letting Russia keep its missiles for priority targets without firing many more.
Missile waves on a few areas, Russian channels claim
Russia launched 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K, and Kalibr cruise missiles overnight on 7 October, Ukraine's Air Force reported. It also fired ballistic missiles, Zircon and Oniks anti-ship missiles, and 130 strike and decoy drones, 46 of them jet-powered Shahed-type models.
Russian milbloggers claimed the same day that Moscow had grouped a large part of its missile salvo into repeated waves on a few areas, while other weapons kept stretching Ukraine's air defenses elsewhere. The pro-war Russian Telegram channel Dva Mayora described the change as a switch from striking with splayed fingers to a series of hits with missile "fists." Defenders must then absorb a sharply rising load around one chosen site as one wave follows another, the channel claimed.
Citing Ukrainian monitoring channels, it claimed that roughly 30 or more Kh-101 cruise missiles flew toward Pryluky, Kremenchuk, Svitlovodsk, and Oleksandriia in Chernihiv, Poltava, and Kirovohrad oblasts. It put the Kremenchuk group at up to 15 missiles, Kh-101s and Kalibrs among them, aimed at the area of Kremenchuk and its hydroelectric plant.
Jet drones take some of the load off Russia's missiles
ISW said the jet-powered versions penetrate Ukrainian air defenses deeper and more reliably than propeller models. In ISW's assessment, that partly lets Russia concentrate cruise and ballistic missiles on priority targets without significantly raising missile use. Russia builds about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) told Militarnyi in August.
Ukraine spent three years learning to catch Russian drones—so Russia made them fly faster
ISW expects Russia to apply the pattern in a likely brutal winter campaign against energy infrastructure. Russia likely intends to make city life untenable and force Ukraine to capitulate to its demands, ISW assessed. Such tactics have not worked before and are unlikely to work now, analysts added.
They called cheap countermeasures to jet drones and small cruise missiles vital, alongside Western air defense aid such as US-made Patriots, which can stop ballistic missiles. Ukraine has already paired a Soviet-era Kub launcher with American RIM-7 interceptors to catch jet drones.
