Only a third of EU counter-drone programmes will deliver by 2030, leaked report warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:37:32 UTC
17:37:32 KST

EU counter-drone investment grew sixfold in 2025, but only a third of programmes will deliver by 2030, a confidential EU report seen by Euronews says, citing fragmented procurement and industry struggling to keep pace with fast-moving drone technology.
Investment in counter-drone technology across the EU surged sixfold between 2024 and 2025, but only a third of the programmes are expected to deliver by 2030, according to a confidential EU report obtained by Euronews.
The 2026 annual defence readiness report, a European Defence Agency (EDA) assessment of national military capabilities, exposes persistent gaps in Europe's defences against drones and urges member states to step up investment in drone and counter-drone technology.
"Investment in counter-drone and very short-range air defence capabilities grew sixfold between 2024 and 2025 in response to the growing threat posed by unmanned systems, although only around one third of programmes are expected to deliver by 2030," reads the report, which was shared with European governments last week.
The EU's eastern flank, stretching from the Baltic to the Black Sea, faces a growing threat from drones, some of which have strayed from the battlefield in Ukraine. On Tuesday, drones struck two commercial vessels in Bulgaria's territorial waters, sinking one.
The EDA found that most member states are investing in drones for surveillance, reconnaissance and target acquisition, while other types of unmanned aircraft continue to attract limited funding despite their growing importance on the battlefield.
EU countries are investing €18.9 billion in drone technologies over 2024-2029, the report says.
"Despite the high level of attention paid to the acquisition of drone and counter-drone capabilities, significant capability gaps and external dependencies continue to affect overall European readiness," the document continues.
Spain, Denmark, Croatia, Latvia and the Netherlands are leading a joint EU project to buy drones and anti-drone systems together and to set up a technology hub to centralise innovation and testing.
However, the EDA points to significant shortcomings: procurement fragmented at national level, limited interoperability, a lack of experimentation capacity and insufficient industrial surge capacity, notably for weaponised drones.
Closing these gaps would cost comparatively little next to other defence capabilities, the report notes, but would demand sustained funding and an agile, integrated approach.
"Industrial capacity has yet to reach the scale and responsiveness required for protracted high-intensity operations, as the pace of technological innovation is outstripping traditional acquisition cycles, creating a persistent risk that capabilities become obsolete before they can be fielded," the report adds.
In short, it says drone technology is evolving so quickly that equipment risks becoming obsolete before it even reaches the battlefield.
The report says current plans and programmes address these challenges but must be paired with adequate doctrine and training.
The EDA also found more than 200 companies producing drone and counter-drone technologies in the EU, a dynamic but fragmented ecosystem that could expand by up to 140% by next year with the right investment framework.
"Industrial readiness in this sector requires agile production ecosystems maintained at the cutting edge of technologies and organised for rapid and massive scaling rather than building up large stockpiles," the report reads.

‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:37:15 UTC
17:37:15 KST

‘Nature can recover’: Inside the race to rescue world’s crisis-hit wildlife
There is a spark of hope for a natural world beset by crisis, as conservation efforts succeed amid a 73 percent drop in wildlife numbers.
Beneath the dense forest canopy of Uganda’s Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, a troop of gorillas is being quietly observed by a group of tourists who have each paid $800 for the privilege of the experience.
In villages around the park, a thriving economy has grown off the back of the gorillas’ presence here, from the sale of wood carvings to visitors and the provision of accommodation for up to 40,000 tourists a year.
In the national park, which sprawls along the edge of the Rift Valley and the border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), there are many local jobs for rangers and guides.
But deeper into the forest, more mountain gorillas live away from human contact, quietly enhancing the natural world around them through their daily routines of foraging, nest building and dispersing seeds.
And, crucially, by increasing their own populations.
In the 1980s, the mountain gorilla was on the fast track to extinction. Now, there are more than 1,100 living in thriving populations in Uganda, Rwanda and the DRC.
Theirs is a story of conservation success that spills beyond the species themselves, into the nature they live in, and the human communities they exist alongside.
“The mountain gorilla story shows us that conservation can work,” Tara Stoinski of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund tells Al Jazeera. “It’s a really important example of the effort that’s needed to make that happen – decades of sustained conservation action that includes direct protection, science-informed management and meaningful community support and involvement.”
When science and policy align
This is welcome news for a natural world beset by crisis.
According to this year’s Living Planet Report by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF), over the past 52 years, there has been a 73 percent decline in the average size of monitored wildlife populations. Across the world, habitats have been degraded and lost as overexploitation, climate change, pollution and invasive species take their toll.
But the report also highlights important recoveries in populations of green turtles, bluefin tuna, tigers and Southern African elephants. “For too long nature has been undervalued,” says Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at the Zoological Society of London, who helped produce the report. “But these declines are not inevitable and change is possible. Nature can recover, and these stories are a powerful reminder of this.”
The WWF says these conservation successes demonstrate how international partnerships drive results. Intergovernmental commitments from tiger range countries, including India, Bhutan, Nepal, Laos and China, helped increase global wild tiger numbers by more than 70 percent between 2010 and 2025.
In 2025, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from “endangered” to “least concern” on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature Red List. That reflected 50 years of species research, active protection of nesting females and eggs, measures to reduce fishing gear and sustained community engagement.
Professor Brendon Godley is a leading conservation scientist at the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Research Centre in the United Arab Emirates and has spent much of his career dedicated to researching and protecting sea turtles. “Conservation success stories are hugely important because they demonstrate that declines are not inevitable,” he tells Al Jazeera.
“The recovery of species such as green turtles shows that when science, policy, enforcement and public support align, populations can rebound, sometimes remarkably so. However, they are not grounds for complacency.”
Small battles – where hope comes from
Indeed, these conservation triumphs are small battles won in an ongoing war against the degradation of nature. The WWF’s Living Planet Report highlights the three systems that are primarily driving the destruction of nature: the global food system, which is the leading cause of habitat loss as areas are cleared to grow crops; the energy system, which fuels climate change through burning fossil fuels; and the finance system, which bankrolls harmful activities, for example, large-scale infrastructure or mining projects.
Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF, says these industries and systems need to be transformed. “Progress is already under way,” she tells Al Jazeera. “Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible.”
The return of a species can have a powerful effect. In 2010, Atlantic bluefin tuna populations had declined by 80 percent and the species was listed as endangered. They had disappeared from much of their historical range, including UK waters. Yet today they are returning in numbers not witnessed in generations, perhaps ever.
“What makes this story particularly powerful is that the recovery is visible,” says Tom Horton, research fellow at the University of Exeter. “Coastal communities, fishers and sea-users who had never seen a bluefin tuna in British waters are now encountering them regularly. It transforms conservation from an abstract concept into something tangible.”
These successes serve as inspiration for other conservation projects in the fight against species decline, like that of the largest primate on Earth, the critically endangered Grauer’s Gorilla. Its home range lies within the vast remote forests of the DRC, living in a landscape beset by instability and habitat loss. Its numbers have dropped by an estimated 60 percent to just 6,800 today.
Urbain Ngobobo, country director for the Dian Fossey Fund in the DRC, explains that the challenge of restoring numbers there is significant but so is the opportunity.
“Every forest we help communities protect,” he says, “every gorilla we are able to monitor and every young Congolese person who develops the skills to become a conservation leader, represents progress.
“That is where hope comes from – not from assuming the future will be easy, but from knowing that our actions today can change what is possible tomorrow.”

Analysis. Russia Is Targeting Kyiv’s Bridges: How Resilient Are They?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:36:00 UTC
17:36:00 KST

Russia is systematically targeting Ukrainian bridges.
Kyiv’s South Bridge has been targeted at least three times in recent days, while the North Bridge has been targeted twice. Both are crucial parts of the capital’s complex transport infrastructure. The South Bridge has six traffic lanes and carries the “green” metro line, while the North Bridge has eight traffic lanes. On Oct. 6, a new bridge in Zaporizhzhia was also targeted.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
So why has Russia begun attacking bridges? Could these strikes destroy them? And what broader risks do they pose?
                                                                                                                                                                         The blast after a drone strike on Kyiv’s North Bridge (Screenshot from open sources)                              
Hard to destroy, but possible to disable
The recent spate of attacks on these bridges has not caused significant damage; only the road surface was affected. Repairs caused traffic jams, but road crews patched the damage very quickly.
                                                                                                                                                                         Typical traffic on Kyiv’s Paton Bridge (Photo by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)                             
Engineers who spoke to Kyiv Post were clear and unequivocal: destroying bridges with drones is practically impossible. The load-bearing structures of Kyiv’s bridges contain dozens of tons of reinforced concrete. Neither a drone nor even a missile can penetrate them easily.
Kyiv’s AI Turrets Provide ‘Last-Level’ Protection, Defense Advisor Says
“Individual UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] strikes cannot cause significant damage to massive bridge structures. However, Russia is using a tactic of ‘small cuts,’ in which numerous small strikes can force bridges to close temporarily for inspection and repairs, while also creating a cumulative effect,” says Armed Forces of Ukraine Major Artem Bilyk, a member of the General Staff’s ad hoc expert group coordinating engineering protection solutions for critical infrastructure and a leading co-author of the “Fortress Country” concept.
He notes that the main concern may be the precision of the strikes. In particular, if Russian forces can repeatedly hit vulnerable points in a bridge’s structure, serious problems could arise even if the bridge remains standing.
“Bridges have sensitive parts – nodes, joints and tensioned elements – that are particularly vulnerable to strikes, especially given that the enemy uses UAVs in a guided configuration through MESH modems. Repeated UAV strikes can disable a bridge even without causing its complete collapse,” Bilyk says.
This raises another question: what would happen if Russia used missiles? So far, there have been no attempts to target the bridges specifically with missiles.
That is not because Russia lacks missiles, says certified architect and Kyiv-based infrastructure researcher Oleg Grechukh. Rather, missiles lack the necessary accuracy, and bridges are narrow structures – no more than 15-20 meters wide – making them very difficult to hit.
“First, a direct frontal hit on the road surface will not cause critical damage. Second, even a ballistic missile with an accuracy of 10 meters can very likely miss the bridge. In that case, it will not cause any damage at all, because the missile will not even produce a significant spread of fragments or a shock wave, as it will land in the deep waters of the Dnipro,” Grechukh says.
One example of missiles being used against a bridge was the AFU’s HIMARS strikes on the Antonivskyi Bridge near Kherson in the summer of 2022. HIMARS were used several times in an effort to destroy the only bridge across the Dnipro and prevent Russian forces from escaping Kherson, which was surrounded by Ukrainian troops. Yet even after the missiles hit the bridge, they caused only limited damage, and Russian forces were able to withdraw almost all their soldiers from Kherson before they could be trapped.
The conclusion is that strikes are unlikely to destroy the bridges or seriously damage them. So why target them?
Exploiting Kyiv’s transport weak point
Russia’s objective may lie elsewhere. The apparently random pattern of strikes – first on petrol stations, then internet providers, food warehouses and shops – may look chaotic. In reality, it appears more like a search for vulnerabilities.
After several strikes on petrol stations, only a handful of Kyiv’s nearly 700 operating stations were damaged. They were quickly restored.
Then came strikes on internet providers. Within hours, however, all had resumed operations, and despite concerns, internet and mobile communications in Ukraine remained available.
There was no panic over food in supermarkets either.
Now – bridges.
The bridge strikes, by contrast, caused enormous traffic jams. Public reaction was anxious: many people chose not to travel to work, while repairs brought parts of the transport network to a standstill and left motorists stuck in traffic for hours.
Russian propaganda quickly seized on the disruption. “Our goal is to scatter brains from those who try to cross these bridges,” wrote popular Russian blogger and war observer Ilya Tumanov, known as Fighterbomber.
                                                                                                                                                                         Screenshot from Fighterbomber Telegram page                             
Such tactics are nothing new for Russia. In 1999, Russian forces destroyed Grozny, the capital of the Chechen Republic; in 2017, they helped destroy Aleppo, one of the world’s oldest cities, in Syria.
Russia has, in effect, found Kyiv’s pressure point – one that was never a secret.
Ukraine’s capital straddles the broad Dnipro river, which is 600 to 1,000 meters wide within Kyiv and is one of Europe’s largest rivers. Almost 3 million people live on the two banks of the Dnipro within Kyiv; including the suburbs, the figure is close to 4 million. It is a large urban agglomeration with a distinctive imbalance.
Residents are split between the two banks at a ratio of roughly 55:45, meaning that almost equal numbers of people live on the left and right banks.
                                                                                                                                                                         The Dnipro river, with its bridges clearly visible. The right bank is on the western side; while the left bank is on the eastern side. (Screenshot: Google Maps)                             
Jobs are not distributed as evenly between the two banks as the population. Some 85% of jobs are on the right bank, which is home to the headquarters of the largest companies, the biggest industrial zones, the government center, foreign embassies and the service sector that supports them.
The left bank is not “wild,” as Kyiv residents sometimes joke, but it is predominantly residential.
This imbalance, combined with limited public transport on the left bank – especially the metro – creates enormous daily commuter flows.
Every morning, hundreds of thousands of left-bank residents travel to the right bank; in the evening, the flow reverses.
“Every day, the bridges are crossed by at least 100,000 cars – not counting public transportation,” Grechukh says.
Only six bridges carry cars: the North Bridge, Podilskyi Bridge, Metro Bridge, Paton Bridge, Darnytskyi Bridge and South Bridge.
A traffic accident on any one of them during the morning or evening rush hour can cause a jam on that bridge. Drivers then divert to the others, which can trigger a wider “transport collapse.” Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, this could happen regularly.
                                                                                                                                                                         Typical traffic jam in Kyiv in 2019 (Screenshot by Sergii Kostezh/Kyiv Post)                             
The problem has plagued Kyiv since the mid-2000s. Many solutions have been proposed: building new bridges, dispersing jobs by encouraging new business centers on the left bank, improving public transport and cycling infrastructure, and encouraging people to drive less. Yet little of substance has been done by 2022.
The problem therefore remains. What can be done now?
Can anything replace bridges over the Dnipro river?
The infrastructure minister proposed building pontoon crossings between the two banks to ease pressure on the bridges, an idea which has some appeal, especially because the Ukrainian military has gained extensive experience building river crossings during the war.
Kyiv also has a history of pontoon crossings. During World War II, both Nazi Germany and the Red Army built such crossings after all the bridges across the Dnipro were destroyed in 1941.
The engineers consulted for this article, however, do not believe this proposal would work.
Because the crossing would have to span such a wide section of the Dnipro, the pontoon bridge would probably be limited to a single traffic lane.
“Their capacity would not come close to that of a bridge. There would be one lane with reversible traffic, and speeds would be lower. Moreover, if something happened on the pontoon – erosion by the river or a strike – it would be much harder than on a bridge to reach vehicles stranded there quickly,” Grechukh says.
Kyiv Post sources in the Kyiv City Administration agree.
“A pontoon is not simply placed on level ground. It needs ramps and exits, which require complex and substantial engineering work. Traffic must also be organized around it, which is difficult given the existing road network,” a source in the Kyiv City Administration says.
Another idea embraced by activists is to complete the “Stalin tunnels.” Kyiv has two unfinished sections, in the north and south. Built between 1938 and 1941 during the Stalin era, they were intended to provide trains with a safer wartime alternative to bridges.
                                                                                                                                                                         An unfinished section of Kyiv’s Stalin-era tunnel (Photo by Valentyna Latko/Facebook)                             
But Andriy Shvachko, a senior lecturer at Kyiv National University of Construction and Architecture, says completing them now makes no sense.
“From a security perspective, a bridge and a tunnel are equally vulnerable. A tunnel cannot be bombed along its entire length, but its entrance can be struck. From an engineering perspective, completing the ‘Stalin’ tunnels also makes no sense: each was designed for a single-track railway, while Ukrainian railways today are double-track. It would be expensive, time-consuming and uneconomical, and it would not solve the problem. The tunnels also have no provision for road vehicles or pedestrians. They cannot be widened, which is where they lose out to bridges,” Shvachko says.
Engineers note that consoles can sometimes be added to an old bridge to accommodate pedestrians and cyclists, if it does not already have such provision. Widening a tunnel, however, is technically unrealistic.
“There is a case for designing and building new tunnels, but Ukraine does not have the resources for that now. Completing structures abandoned during Stalin’s lifetime is simply absurd,” one of the capital’s design engineers tells Kyiv Post.
How can Kyiv protect its bridges?
Bilyk believes that no alternative can match the carrying capacity of bridges, arguing that they should be protected as effectively as possible.
“First and foremost, the most critical nodes, key elements and supports of bridges should be reinforced using gabions, blocks and steel sheets. It’s also advisable to install special metal lattice anti-detonation screens around the carriageways. This makes it possible to move the point of the UAV explosion farther away and reduce damage to the bridge. Particular attention should be paid to fire resistance and the protection of flammable or vulnerable elements of bridge infrastructure, which should be enclosed in fireproof armored casings,” Bilyk says.
The question is whether Ukraine has sufficient resources – particularly metal – to do this.
Recent reports following Russian strikes say that the last of Ukraine’s metallurgical plants has shut down. Before the Russian invasion, the country had five operating plants and numerous factories. Ukraine thus stopped producing steel despite having both iron ore and coal – everything needed for production – and despite being one of the few countries with a fully integrated mining and metallurgical complex.
Ukrainian steelmakers, however, are confident that enough metal will be available.
“Ukraine still has sufficient capabilities in the design, manufacture and installation of bridge structures, as well as their repair and restoration; missing components can be delivered from abroad if necessary. Ukrainian steel construction plants are certified according to European standards for manufacturing. It should be understood that the enemy began searching for unprotected infrastructure facilities to strike, such as power transmission line supports and bridges, precisely because during the period from 2023 to 2026, hundreds of protective structures were built and security measures were implemented for energy facilities – transformers, generators and other equipment,” says Anna Hontarenko, executive director of the Ukrainian Steel Construction Center association.
There may still be a silver lining. One proposal for addressing the crisis includes decentralizing jobs and encouraging industrial and commercial development on the left bank. Another is to revive river transport, including ferries, which ran between the two banks during the Soviet era but declined in the 1990s during the transition to a market economy.
Even in difficult circumstances, Ukrainians continue to look for opportunities and seek asymmetric solutions. Could this new wartime crisis ultimately drive changes that make Kyiv better?

Lithuania considers tax on streaming platforms to support local film industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:35:00 UTC
17:35:00 KST

Lithuania is considering requiring major digital streaming platforms to contribute part of their subscription revenue collected in the country to support local cinema and other audiovisual arts, Culture Minister Lukas Alsys said.
Alsys said a Culture Ministry study conducted over the summer found that a fund-based model could be used to encourage major audiovisual platforms to contribute to Lithuania’s creative industries.
Under the proposal, platforms such as Netflix, which collect subscription revenue from customers in Lithuania, would allocate a portion of that income to the country’s cultural sector. The money would be administered through existing infrastructure to avoid creating additional bureaucracy, Alsys said.
The ministry is currently considering a levy of 3.5% of revenue collected by the platforms in Lithuania, he said.
The proposal would effectively create a so-called Netflix tax, a model already under consideration elsewhere in the Baltics. Latvia is considering a similar levy, with relevant draft legislation currently being debated in parliament. Estonia is also considering introducing such a contribution from major streaming platforms.
Alsys said the Lithuanian proposal is aimed at strengthening the country’s audiovisual sector and ensuring that global platforms benefiting from the local market also contribute to the development of domestic cultural production.

INTERVIEW- Arab voters to determine Israel’s next prime minister, says Balad leader
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:33:50 UTC
17:33:50 KST

- 'There is complete agreement among all the Arab parties that we want to prevent these criminals from returning to power,' says Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh
- 'The issue is not changing the person in charge. We want to change Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies,' he says
Arab voters could determine Israel’s next prime minister, said Sami Abu Shehadeh, head of the left-wing National Democratic Assembly (Balad) party, stressing that the goal of Arab parties is to prevent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming a government.
“The Arab vote in this election, according to all opinion polls over the past two years, will determine who will be prime minister in Israel,” Abu Shehadeh told Anadolu.
“We are therefore very concerned in this racist society about efforts to disqualify the Arab vote and remove us from the political arena altogether. The closer we get to Election Day, the greater our concern becomes,” he said.
Palestinians in the territories occupied in 1948 make up more than 20% of Israel’s population of 10 million.
Opinion polls indicate that Arab lawmakers will win 12 to 14 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
“There are around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel eligible to vote. A Knesset seat requires roughly 40,000 votes. We expect turnout to be between 62% and 73%,” Abu Shehadeh said.
“We therefore expect Palestinian Arabs to win around 14 to 16 seats in the Knesset. If we reach these numbers, Netanyahu and his criminal gang will not be able to form a coalition in the next phase,” he added.
Preventing Netanyahu’s return
Abu Shehadeh said bringing down Netanyahu’s government and preventing him from forming a new one is the strategic objective of Arab parties in the upcoming election.
“There is complete agreement among all the Arab parties that we want to prevent these criminals from returning to power,” he said.
“These criminals are the most difficult governing coalition we have dealt with since the Nakba (1948)," he said.
Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition bloc will be able to secure enough seats to form a government.
A government requires the support of at least 61 members of the 120-seat Knesset.
According to the polls, the Jewish opposition would need the support of Arab parties to form a government.
However, most leaders of Jewish opposition parties reject relying on Arab parties for support in forming a government.
Asked if Arab lawmakers would be open to forming a government with these Jewish opposition parties, he said: “I wish there was a real opposition (in Israel)."
"I wish someone was pushing a different political agenda from racist Netanyahu. A candidate who was ready to end the occupation," he said, adding so far a genuine candidate has not come forward.
“The issue is not changing the person in charge. We want to change Benjamin Netanyahu’s policies.”
 
Raising turnout
Abu Shehadeh said the Joint List, an alliance of the Balad, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality and the Arab Movement for Renewal, will work to increase Arab turnout.
“We are in a very difficult election campaign and are working at every level to raise turnout. We expect it to be very high compared with the past 30 years,” he said.
According to estimates, a sizeable Arab turnout could threaten the chances of small right-wing parties of winning seats, which would reduce Netanyahu’s chances of forming a government.
 
Disqualification attempts
Abu Shehadeh also discussed recent attempts to prevent Arab parties from participating in the election.
“There was a serious attempt by Netanyahu and his gang to remove all the Arab parties from the political arena, and we stopped that in the Supreme Court,” he said.
“Nevertheless, I was personally disqualified as head of Balad, but we are continuing. We will not stop. We will continue our just struggle for freedom, justice and equality for the Palestinian and Israeli people,” he added.
“They are trying to disqualify us and silence our votes, and we will work to silence the voices of racism and racists,” he said.
On Sept. 23, the Israeli Central Elections Committee decided to disqualify the Joint List, led by Yousef Jabareen , as well as the United Arab List led by Knesset member Mansour Abbas.
The decision also included Abu Shehadeh and Knesset member Ofer Cassif of the Joint List, before Israel’s Supreme Court overturned the committee’s decision.
However, the court signaled that it could uphold Abu Shehadeh’s disqualification, prompting him, following consultations, to withdraw his candidacy before a judicial ruling was issued against him.
So-called only democracy in Middle East
Observers say preventing Arabs from participating in the election would have dealt a blow to Israel’s claims of being “the only democracy in the Middle East.”
Despite withdrawing his candidacy, Abu Shehadeh continues to campaign for the Joint List with the aim of preventing Netanyahu from forming a government.
“We are continuing, as we told our people directly after the Supreme Court decided to disqualify us and remove us from this contest,” he said.
“We will not derive our legitimacy from the criminal Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, from the Israeli court or from any other Zionist party. As leaders of our people, our legitimacy comes solely from the sons and daughters of our people,” he added.
“I will do everything I can to ensure the Joint List succeeds,” Abu Shehadeh said.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, in a government described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.
The election on Oct. 27 is considered critical to Netanyahu’s political future as he faces corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust.
Alongside the domestic corruption proceedings, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu since 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity related to the war in Gaza.

How Gaza war sped up India’s shift towards Israel under Modi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:31:44 UTC
17:31:44 KST

Gaza war sped up India’s shift towards Israel under Modi
As even Israel’s traditional allies are distancing themselves from Netanyahu, Modi’s India has embraced the country.
New Delhi, India – The United Kingdom, France, Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Norway had already banned the entry of Bezalel Smotrich, Israel’s far-right finance minister, who had advocated the ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in Gaza and the annexation of the occupied West Bank.
But in September 2025, as the European Union was planning bloc-wide sanctions against him and his fellow far-right colleague Itamar Ben-Gvir that it would eventually announce late that month, Smotrich was welcomed with garlands and a multi-city trip to India. In New Delhi, he signed a trade deal; in Mumbai, he visited the stock exchange; and in Gujarat – the home state of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi – he travelled to a new investment hub.
As Israel was conducting its genocidal war on Gaza, bombing and killing dozens on the very days he was visiting India, New Delhi was ready to expand business with Israel like never before. For decades, India had been one of the world’s staunchest supporters of Palestine, and Europe one of Israel’s closest backers. India’s position has shifted firmly since 2014, when Modi and his Hindu majoritarian Bharatiya Janata Party came to power. But analysts say the optics of Smotrich’s visit underlined something even more dramatic: At a time when even Europe, traditionally seen as backing Israel, has veered away from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government, the genocidal war on Gaza appears to have escalated India’s embrace of Israel.
In February this year, Modi visited Israel as Netanyahu – who faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over war crimes carried out in Gaza – faced growing isolation in the international arena.
“You are a great friend of Israel. You are more than a friend. You are a brother,” Netanyahu told Modi when both leaders addressed the Israeli parliament in Jerusalem.
How October 7 attack changed tones
Three years of Israeli attacks have killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children. That is about one in every 30 people, or 3 percent of the pre-war population.
Historically, India has argued that diplomacy and dialogue are the way forward to resolve conflicts – whether between Russia and Ukraine, the US and Iran, or Israel and Palestine. New Delhi has maintained that war doesn’t solve anything.
But investigations by Al Jazeera and other reporting have revealed that New Delhi exported weapons to Israel during the ongoing genocidal war on Gaza. Meanwhile, under Modi, India has become Israel’s largest weapons buyer.
Just hours after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, India’s Modi unequivocally condemned the “terrorist attack”, adding that he was “deeply shocked”. When he visited Israel in February this year, Modi referred to the Mumbai attacks in 2008, carried out by Pakistani fighters, which New Delhi has blamed on the Pakistani government. “Like you, we have a consistent and uncompromising policy of zero tolerance for terrorism with no double standards,” Modi said.
Analysts believe that the framing of Israel as a country under attack has helped Modi justify pushing India closer to it. For decades, much of the politics of Modi’s BJP “has hovered around Islamist expansionism or Islamic terrorism”, said Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi.
“So it helps [in relationship with Israel],” Kidwai said, pointing to the link between Modi’s Israel policy and his domestic politics. “Take this relationship as an extension of the domestic narrative that one sees in India.”
The Indian Hindu right has long supported the ideology of Zionism, analysts note. Modi’s BJP has roots in a philosophy, Hindutva, which ultimately seeks to transform India into a Hindu nation and a natural homeland for Hindus anywhere in the world – similar to Israel’s view of itself as a Jewish homeland.
Since the October 7 attacks on Israel, Kidwai noted, “the anti-Muslim sentiments fill in that block in India.” This feeling is, of course, coupled with “pragmatism in New Delhi because Israel is a potent international player”.
Navdeep Suri, a former Indian diplomat who served as ambassador to Egypt and the United Arab Emirates, told Al Jazeera that people-to-people ties are also a central pillar of the India-Israel relationship, “particularly within a section of Indian society that has strong admiration for the muscular policy that Israel adopts”.
Time and again, there have been calls from within Indian right-wing echelons for Modi to adopt more Israel-like policies, from clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir to attacking neighbouring Pakistan.
Suri noted that a shift towards Israel predates the ongoing genocidal war in Gaza. “Under PM Modi, a relationship that was largely covert or under the carpet has become a much more open relationship,” the former Indian diplomat said.
“There has been a recognition in Delhi that Israel has been a very strong defence and intelligence partner,” he told Al Jazeera, referring to another pillar of the bilateral relationship. “There’s a genuine convergence when it comes to the perceptions on security.”
India ‘should take principled positions’
Even several of Israel’s closest European allies have moved from criticism of the genocidal war on Gaza and expansive illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank to concrete measures. At least 11 European countries and Canada have imposed trade measures against products from illegal Israeli settlements. Many have imposed sanctions on settlers and networks accused of conducting pogroms against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, as well as on ministers like Smotrich and Ben-Gvir.
India, for its part, has avoided anything more than homilies and mild opposition to war and West Bank attacks.
Diplomatically, New Delhi still backs a two-state solution and has called for aid access and peace in the region. Suri, the former Indian diplomat who served in the Middle East, said New Delhi “should be able to take more principled positions on these things”.
However, from his experience in office, Suri added, “there is such a close alignment at the political levels between the governments in Israel and India that there is a reluctance [in India] to criticise Israel.
“That reluctance manifests in various aspects,” Suri explained to Al Jazeera. “The refusal to criticise the settlers’ attacks; refusal to criticise the brutal use of force in Gaza; refusal to criticise the attack on Iran and point out violation of international norms.”
Unlike Western countries, India’s current leaders “lack that kind of dynamic thinking and are rather far more dogmatic”, said Kidwai, the political analyst.
India’s shift and Modi’s calculus
Netanyahu’s disruptive and fatal assault on Gaza has drawn ire from even the White House in Washington, where Israel enjoys bipartisan support. United States President Donald Trump has previously threatened to cut off support for Israel’s bombing of Lebanon – even while signing off on huge weapons sales to Israel.
However, nothing has moved Modi’s bonhomie with Israel’s Netanyahu.
In fact, Modi’s February visit on the eve of the joint US-Israel attacks on Iran appeared “as almost a personal favour to Netanyahu by boosting his image as an international statesman just as Israeli election campaigning is getting under way”, Max Rodenbeck, Israel/Palestine programme director at the Washington-based International Crisis Group, had told Al Jazeera.
Such an act would have been unthinkable from an Indian leader in previous decades.
In 1948, India opposed the creation of Israel. A relationship with Israel was once frowned upon in New Delhi – a legacy of India’s anti-colonial past – though the two had clandestine ties since at least the 1970s.
India backed the 1975 United Nations General Assembly resolution calling Zionism a form of racism, was the first non-Arab nation to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization, and was among the first in the world to recognise Palestinian statehood. It only established diplomatic ties with Israel in 1992, and though governments since then slowly built up relations, Modi, in 2016, was the first Indian PM to visit that country.
The Congress party that’s now in opposition, but ruled India for most of its post-independence period before Modi, also viewed its support for Palestine as helpful with Muslim voters – only Indonesia and Pakistan have more Muslims than India – said Kidwai. Modi’s Hindu-first politics, by contrast, thrives on othering Indian Muslims.
“Modi’s party believes it stands to gain nothing from a pro-Palestine posture,” Kidwai told Al Jazeera. “Instead, Modi has sought to link the attack on Israel with the so-called reign of terror and Islamic extremism and make a case against Muslims – and within those realms lies the justification of everything.”

2026-10-08
08:29:54 UTC
17:29:54 KST

The claims came as witnesses reported several explosions across the Saudi capital, a day after a separate Houthi drone attack on the same airport killed one person and caused flight delays that continued into Thursday.
Yemen's Houthis said on Thursday they targeted King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh with a missile for a second time, as the group escalated its strikes on airports across the neighbouring kingdom.
"Our armed forces targeted King Khalid Airport in Riyadh at midday with a ballistic missile that hit its target," said the Houthis' military spokesman Yahya Saree.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said earlier on Thursday it had intercepted two missiles fired at the kingdom's capital, coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki posted on X.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defence agency reported "material damage" to buildings from falling shrapnel after the interceptions. Riyadh has not disclosed any further information on damage or casualties.
Several explosions echoed across Riyadh on Thursday morning, witnesses said.
Diplomats were instructed to shelter in place in their respective embassies, as witnesses said international schools were also taking precautions. Meanwhile, King Khalid Airport in Riyadh asked departing passengers to contact their airlines before coming to the airport.
"We would like to inform passengers of the necessity to contact their airlines directly and check their flight status before proceeding to the airport," it said in a statement posted on X.
A drone attack on the same airport earlier this week killed one person, with another two killed in a separate strike on the airport in the southwestern city of Abha, Riyadh said on Thursday, as flight delays continued into the second day.
The attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 other people, while the attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, officials said.
The Saudi General Authority for Civil Aviation did not blame any party for the attacks at the two international airports.
In a subsequent statement, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis blamed them for the strikes and vowed a response.
"The brutal attacks by the terrorist Houthi militia on civilian and civilian objects in the kingdom, most recently targeting (the two airports) will not go unpunished," it wrote on X.
The spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, Major General Turki al-Malki, said forces intercepted a ballistic missile north of Riyadh and destroyed a platform in Yemen’s capital of Sana'a that had been used to launch attacks on the Saudi capital.
The group formally known as Ansar Allah has claimed repeated attacks targeting Saudi airports in recent days, along with salvos aimed at critical infrastructure and military sites across the kingdom.
Saree on Thursday also called on staff at oil facilities in Saudi Arabia to leave to avoid being targeted.
"Employees at all oil facilities must leave areas that are targets for our forces, so as not to endanger their lives," Saree wrote on X, also issuing a warning "to airlines, airports, travelers and their staff".
Strikes on Saudi facilities pose a threat to crucial shipping alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war.
In an earlier post, Saree warned international airlines "for the last time" over operating flights in Saudi airspace "which has become a theatre for our military operations, with the exception of the airspace over the sacred areas in Mecca ... and Medina."
Saudi Arabia has previously accused the Houthis of targeting Islam's holiest sites in Mecca and Medina, allegations the group rejected as "fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal al-Saud regime."
The Houthis are Zaydi Shia Muslims, a specific branch of Islam historically rooted in northern Yemen that is theologically distinct from both the Twelver Shia Islam dominant in Iran and Saudi Arabia's Wahhabi-influenced Sunni tradition.
Any confirmed attack on either Mecca or Medina would put the perpetrators beyond the pale in the eyes of virtually the entire Muslim world, Shia and Sunni alike.
Houthi strikes have further escalated as Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces launched a major ground and air offensive aimed at retaking territory that the group seized a month ago along Yemen’s western Red Sea coast and on the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
On Monday, officials said forces of the Saudi-led coalition recaptured several key areas around the strait, through which about 12% of global trade transits.
“The Houthis believe that they can maximise Saudi economic costs and compel Saudi Arabia to surrender to Houthi demands by striking civilian infrastructure, such as oil facilities and airports,” the Washington-based Institute for the Study of War think tank wrote in an analysis.
The fighting in Yemen has in recent weeks become the most active front of the wider regional war, which for months has seen violence repeatedly shift focus across the beleaguered Middle East.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since the Yemen war escalated again in July, according to UN data.

Egypt charges six journalists with 'terrorism'

Breadcrumb
Egypt charges six journalists with 'terrorism' offences
Egyptian prosecutors accused six journalists from an independent fact-checking platform on Wednesday of terrorism-related offences, alleging they worked for the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and received foreign funding to spread "false news".
The journalists, who make up the entire newsroom of Matsadaash, were arrested during raids across several governorates on 28 and 29 September, according to the outlet's management and rights groups.
Matsadaash, whose name means "Don't Believe It" in Arabic, has operated since 2018 and often investigates statements by officials and state bodies.
The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), which represents the journalists, said they had reported torture following their arrests, allegations denied by the Interior Ministry.
In a statement on Wednesday, prosecutors said the case stemmed from investigations into activities by Brotherhood leaders abroad.
They alleged those leaders had directed members to create online platforms to spread "rumours and false news and statements", undermine confidence in state institutions and incite people to take part in demonstrations.
The statement identified Matsadaash as "one of the group's media platforms" operated from abroad.
Investigators also alleged the defendants received "monthly funding" in foreign currencies through transfers from a company owned by a Brotherhood member living overseas.
According to the prosecution, one defendant admitted that he and the others had been instructed to publish "false news about state institutions and their officials in preparation for bringing them down".
Another defendant allegedly admitted the platform was used to "highlight shortcomings" by state officials in a way that fuels public discontent.
Prosecutors said an examination of two journalists' social media accounts found posts "supporting the terrorist Muslim Brotherhood group".
Matsadaash and its co-founder, Abdelrahman Mansour, a prominent activist from Egypt's 2011 uprising now based in New York, deny the allegations.
The Muslim Brotherhood was banned in Egypt in 2013 following the overthrow of late Islamist president Mohamed Morsi.
A conviction on charges of belonging to the group can carry a sentence of up to life imprisonment.
The arrests have drawn condemnation from dozens of rights and press freedom groups, who have called for the journalists' release.
Egypt, which has long faced criticism over restrictions on media activity, is now holding 26 journalists in connection with their work following the latest arrests, according to EIPR.

Earth quakes in West Flanders for first time since 2011
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:27:47 UTC
17:27:47 KST

A minor earthquake with a magnitude of 1.9 occurred in Ruiselede (Wingene – West Flanders) at around 10 pm last night.
The minor earthquake has been the subject of lively discussion on social media in recent hours. Many residents not only felt it but also heard it.
The tremor was centred on Ruiselede, but residents of nearby Meulebeke, Izegem and Ardooie – and even as far afield as East Flanders – have reported hearing something.
Already more than 200 reports
Details of the earthquake can be found on the website of the Royal Observatory of Belgium. There, you can also report that you felt the earthquake. So far, more than 200 people have done so.
Most of them report having felt an intensity of 3. At this level, the tremors can be felt indoors. People at rest feel a slight sway or tremor. Suspended objects swing slightly from side to side, but the tremor causes no damage.
From pressure wave to acoustic wave
“Many people don’t make the connection with an earthquake when they hear the sound that could be a loud lorry passing by,” says weather presenter Geert Naessens. So how exactly is that sound produced? “In the case of a shallow earthquake like this, a pressure wave that travels towards the Earth’s surface is generated.”
“You can imagine a pressure wave like that as a pulling and shoving of matter. As soon as that pressure wave reaches the Earth’s surface, it transforms into an acoustic wave – in other words, a sound wave. That is why you hear a sound but do not feel any vibration.”
Anyone who was close to the earthquake probably experienced the sound as a dull thud. Those further away were more likely to have heard a rumbling. “Just like a lorry, in other words.”
Unusual?
Just how unusual is this, actually? “A minor earthquake like this occurs about 10 to 20 times a year,” says seismologist Koen Van Noten. “But usually, nobody feels a thing. The fact that people have actually felt it this time is quite unusual.”
‘It doesn’t happen very often, particularly not in West Flanders,’ explains Van Noten. ‘The rock there lies in a much deeper layer of the earth. It is precisely in that rock that earthquakes occur. The fact that so many reports about the earthquake are now coming in is certainly due to the fact that people in West Flanders are absolutely not used to it.’
The previous earthquake in West Flanders took place on 2 August 2011 in Veldegem (Zedelgem). “Back then, we also received 500 reports,” adds Van Noten.

As of October 7, Ukrainian farmers had sown 2.52 million hectares with winter grain crops, or 48.4% of the projected area, and 1.041 million hectares with winter rapeseed, or 94.2% of the forecast, the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food reported on its website Wednesday.
In particular, wheat and triticale (a hybrid of wheat and rye) had been sown on 2.253 million hectares (49.6% of the forecast), barley on 209,900 hectares (35.4%), and rye on 57,800 hectares (75.3%).
Over the past week, the area sown with grain crops increased by 925,700 hectares, compared with an increase of 853,200 hectares the previous week.
Last year, by this date, 2.572 million hectares had been sown with grain crops, just 2% more than this year. The area sown with wheat was 4.2% larger, while barley and rye sowings were larger this year, by 17.1% and 26.5%, respectively.
As for rapeseed, its sowing season is nearing completion: over the past week, the area increased by just 22,900 hectares, compared with 59,200 hectares the previous week. This year's rapeseed sowings as of this date are 5.6% larger than last year's.
The Agriculture Ministry specified that the leading regions by area sown with winter grain crops are: Mykolaiv region with 368,800 hectares, including 288,000 hectares of wheat and triticale, 79,300 hectares of barley and 1,500 hectares of rye; Dnipropetrovsk region with 284,600 hectares, including 262,100 hectares of wheat and triticale, 21,200 hectares of barley and 1,300 hectares of rye; and Poltava region with 200,100 hectares, including 191,900 hectares of wheat and triticale, 3,200 hectares of barley and 5,000 hectares of rye.

EBU warns Lithuanian probe into LRT could threaten editorial independence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:25:00 UTC
17:25:00 KST

The European Broadcasting Union said Tuesday it is “deeply concerned” about an investigation by Lithuania’s General Prosecutor’s Office into the editorial policies of the country’s public broadcaster, LRT, concerning covert information gathering.
The EBU said authorities have a right to ensure compliance with the law and protect people’s rights, but argued that examining how a news organisation makes individual editorial decisions could interfere with its independence.
“The decisions about whether and how to conduct an investigation are editorial decisions,” the EBU said. “The European Media Freedom Act protects media outlets from state interference in editorial policy and decisions and ensures the editorial and functional independence of public service media.”
The General Prosecutor’s Office has asked LRT Director General Monika Garbačiauskaitė-Budrienė for information about the broadcaster’s rules governing secret recordings. Prosecutors say they are examining whether the rules could violate the public interest, including people’s constitutional right to privacy.
The prosecutor’s office submitted 15 questions about LRT’s procedures. They include who can request permission for covert audio or video recording, what evidence must be provided, how editors assess whether covert recording is justified, whether information could be obtained by other means and how permissions are issued.
Prosecutors also asked how covert recordings are supervised, how their results are reported to editors, who decides whether allegations have been substantiated and whether recordings should be destroyed or retained.
The EBU said the questions could expose confidential journalistic sources or unpublished investigations by requiring information about proposed investigations, evidence and access to journalistic material.
“Investigative journalism depends on journalists and sources knowing that sensitive editorial processes will remain protected,” the EBU said. “This risks chilling investigations before they even begin.”
LRT’s editorial policy permits journalists to gather information covertly, eg record people without their knowledge, only in exceptional circumstances, when there is evidence that the conduct being recorded could demonstrate illegal or dishonest actions involving a clear public interest. It also requires prior authorisation from a responsible editor.
The EBU called on prosecutors to ensure their investigation remains necessary and proportionate, respects LRT’s editorial independence and does not seek information that could reveal confidential sources or unpublished investigations.
Reporters Without Borders, another international organisation, has also expressed concern, saying the investigation could expose confidential journalistic sources. It said covert recording can be a legitimate journalistic method when used exceptionally, proportionately and in the public interest.
The General Prosecutor’s Office said the investigation was launched on a prosecutor’s initiative to determine whether LRT’s rules comply with Lithuania’s Constitution and laws governing the media and covert information gathering.
Prosecutor’s Office spokeswoman Elena Martinonienė rejected the suggestion that the investigation threatens media freedom.
“From the prosecutor’s office’s perspective, journalists’ freedom and the public interest are ensured precisely when editorial rules governing journalists’ activities raise no doubts about their compliance with the Constitution and laws,” Martinonienė told LRT.lt last week.
She said prosecutors would decide whether there were grounds to take measures to protect the public interest only after receiving all the information necessary for their assessment.
The EBU, which represents public service media organizations in Europe and beyond, said it supports LRT and is ready to help facilitate dialogue with Lithuanian authorities to protect fundamental rights and media freedom.

LONDON — The U.K. and Israel have stepped back from the diplomatic brink by securing a compromise to prevent the full closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Most diplomats will leave what will now be operating as a “U.K. Mission” in the occupied territory — but Israel has stopped short of closing it entirely ahead of Thursday’s deadline.
Both sides were presenting this as a good outcome Thursday, in a diplomatic tussle over the U.K.’s plans to impose sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Advertisement
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the diplomats and their families were being “temporarily withdrawn” to secure their safety, but he said the mission will remain independent, operational and continue to work with the Palestinian people.
“We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence, and we will not take reciprocal action while such discussions are underway and credible,” he continued, in a statement released as he was visiting Ukraine.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar set out a list of diplomatic actions taken against Britain, adding: “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response.”
Sa’ar said the consulate would be “closing its operations today” and that the “sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed.” Twenty British diplomats, including the consul general, will be leaving East Jerusalem.
The dispute over the consulate has been the latest marker of declining relations between Israel and the U.K. under its Labour government. Israel threatened to close the consulate within 30 days of Sept. 8, in retaliation against Andy Burnham’s government announcing a ban on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank.
Advertisement
A person familiar with Israeli government thinking, granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter, told POLITICO the mission is “basically an empty shell” that cannot issue visas, renew passports or liaise with the Palestinian Authority. Britain does not tend to issue visas or passports in consulates.
“The seven diplomats there, their work is basically to maintain the building and hold the Union Jack in place,” they said.
A British official presented the deal as a “good outcome” nonetheless. After three weeks of hard-fought negotiations, a feared spiral of tit-for-tat expulsions has been avoided.
The U.K. has told Israel it is keeping the possibility of retaliation open, however, after Israel threatened to expel British diplomats from Israel. The Israeli government had been demanding that the U.K. rolls back its pending package of sanctions on West Bank settlements, but British ministers are holding firm.
Miliband maintained Thursday that Britain does not accept Israel has a “legal right” to shutter the site that has been there for nearly 200 years, because East Jerusalem is deemed “occupied territory.”
The hope in the U.K. Foreign Office is that maintaining a presence will make it easier to build back up after elections in Israel on Oct. 27.
U.K. National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell traveled to Jerusalem last week as part of efforts to persuade the Israeli government not to shut the consulate, but a breakthrough wasn’t reached until Wednesday night.

Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:19:50 UTC
17:19:50 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data.
The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013.
Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%.
The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030.
At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%).
After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU.
In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%).
And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%).
Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states
For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6

The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%.
The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation.
At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts.

US drone firm urges Taiwan to buy autonomous surface vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:19:29 UTC
17:19:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former US official and Saronic executive Mira Resnick said Wednesday that Taiwan should expand its fleet of autonomous surface vessels to deter Chinese incursions, CNA reported.
The Taiwan External Trade Development Council hosted the 2026 Aerospace and Defense Strategic Forum, a one-day event featuring speakers from defense contractors including Anduril, AeroVironment, and Saronic. Resnick, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state and now Saronic’s senior director for global policy and defense cooperation, spoke about the importance of multipurpose autonomous surface vessels.
Resnick said most of the unmanned boats Taiwan plans to procure are intended for one-way attack missions. She said China has consistently used gray-zone attrition tactics to exhaust Taiwan’s maritime forces and suggested that Taiwan instead purchase multipurpose autonomous surface vessels as more effective deterrents.
Resnick said Taiwan should prioritize lethal, mobile, reliable, and cost-effective weapons systems. She added that Taiwan plans to purchase more than 200,000 unmanned systems, but only about 1,300 are boats intended for one-way missions that would be deployed only during wartime.
Resnick cited an Oct. 1 defense ministry report that recorded 23 PLA aircraft, seven PLA Navy ships, and seven Chinese government vessels around Taiwan during the preceding 24 hours. She added that China uses dredgers and maritime militia vessels to probe Taiwan’s waters, including those around Kinmen and Matsu.
Resnick said China prefers attrition to a full-scale invasion, wearing down Taiwan’s Navy and Coast Guard fleets. She suggested investing in autonomous surface vessels rather than continuing to chase Chinese ships.
Multipurpose autonomous surface vessels can perform round-trip missions such as monitoring, escorting, and relaying signals, Resnick said. Their modular designs allow them to perform different tasks and free personnel for more critical duties, she added.
Resnick highlighted two important aspects of autonomy. First, China is investing heavily in electronic warfare and anti-satellite technology that could render drones useless by disrupting their communications. Second, remotely controlled vessels still require skilled operators, whereas one person should be able to oversee a fleet of autonomous vessels.
Resnick said the government should field-test all vendors to verify performance amid unusual radar returns, fishing nets, and rough seas. She added that US vendors should integrate Taiwanese sensors and command-and-control systems and establish local maintenance capacity rather than simply selling complete vessels.
This would support joint production and help Taiwan develop an autonomous operational system while balancing speed and sovereignty, she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s optical communications firms reported strong revenue growth in September as demand for high-speed connectivity driven by AI data centers continued to increase.
LandMark Optoelectronics Corp. reported September revenue of NT$540 million (US$16.9 million), up 190.16% from the same month a year earlier. TrueLight Corp. posted revenue of NT$121 million, an annual increase of 140.31%, according to CTEE.
As AI data centers handle growing volumes of data, conventional electrical signals face greater signal loss and power consumption at higher transmission speeds. Optical communications address these limitations by using light-based signals to transmit data, enabling higher bandwidth and lower signal loss over long distances, according to Pocket Securities.
Other companies in the sector also benefited from stronger demand. Elite Advanced Laser Corp. reported revenue of NT$1.3 billion, up 99.78% year on year.
Apogee Optocom Co. posted revenue of NT$65 million, an annual increase of 52.96%. IntelliEPI Inc. reported revenue of NT$108 million, up 11.37% from a year earlier, according to FTNN.
With 800G technology gradually becoming a mainstream standard for high-speed optical communications, adoption of 1.6T technology is also increasing. Analysts expect demand for high-speed AI interconnects to support further growth across Taiwan’s optical communications supply chain.
For the fourth quarter, Goldman Sachs forecasts continued revenue growth for LandMark, supported by the rollout of next-generation AI server racks, the shift to faster 1.6T optical modules, and the company’s ongoing capacity expansion. The investment bank also expects higher demand for optical communications components such as continuous-wave lasers as AI servers require faster data transmission, supporting growth in the sector, according to TechNews.
TrueLight has expanded into back-end optical communications manufacturing as demand for high-speed laser-related products increases. The company expects contract manufacturing to account for a growing share of its revenue this year.
According to market research firm Yole, demand from AI data centers is driving rapid growth in optical transceiver modules with speeds of 400G and above. Shipments of these products are expected to reach 102 million units this year, up 79.7% from the previous year.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan could begin distributing its planned NT$10,000 (US$315) cash payment as early as Jan. 26, with foreign nationals holding permanent residency among those eligible.
The Cabinet said Thursday that it has allocated NT$235.7 billion in the proposed 2027 central government budget to share the economic gains and increased tax revenue generated by the booming AI industry with the public. The government said the spending would not crowd out other policy priorities and would adhere to the principles of fiscal discipline, no net new borrowing, and legal and constitutional procedures.
Foreign nationals with permanent residency in Taiwan will be eligible for the payment, as will citizens with household registration and nationals without household registration who hold residence permits. Spouses of Taiwanese citizens from China, Hong Kong, Macau, or other countries who hold residence permits are also eligible.
The eligibility rules generally follow those used for the government’s 2023 and 2025 cash handouts. Taiwanese government employees stationed overseas on official duty and their dependents who hold Taiwanese nationality will also qualify.
The government plans to distribute the money through five channels: bank-account registration, ATM withdrawals, post office withdrawals, direct deposits, and roster-based payments. Shanghai Commercial & Savings Bank is expected to join the ATM network, bringing the total number of participating financial institutions to 17, per UDN.
If the legislature passes the 2027 central government budget by Jan. 5 and the president promulgates it by Jan. 20, the finance ministry plans to open pre-registration on Jan. 20 and registration for bank deposits on Jan. 25, UDN reported. The first payments through pre-registration, direct deposits, and roster-based distribution could begin Jan. 26.
ATM cash withdrawals are expected to begin Feb. 15, 2027, while withdrawals at post offices are expected to begin Feb. 22. The general claim deadline will be Aug. 31, 2027, while newborns born by the end of 2027 will have until Jan. 31, 2028, to claim the payment.

Researchers: International plague outbreak highly unlikely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:18:41 UTC
17:18:41 KST

In the Russian city of Irkutsk, a laboratory worker at a plague research institute has died of pneumonia of unknown origin; Russian authorities have stated that the death is unrelated to her professional duties, the BBC reports.
Darya Shipilova, 28, died on the 2nd of October following possible exposure to pathogens, and nearly 200 of her contacts were subsequently placed in quarantine. While officials have sought to allay concerns, various speculations regarding the incident are circulating online.
Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Plague Research Institute. Unconfirmed reports suggest she fell ill and developed symptoms characteristic of pneumonia either after dropping a test tube containing the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis or following a research trip to the Buryatia region near the Mongolian border, where the plague is endemic among animals.
As of the 7th of October, the cause of Shipilova's death had not been officially confirmed, and laboratory investigations were ongoing. One thing is clear, however: experts believe that even if the death was caused by pneumonic plague, it is unlikely to lead to an international outbreak of the disease. Plague is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Clinically, it manifests in three forms: bubonic plague, pneumonic plague, and septicemic plague (which represents the fatal outcome of all clinical forms of the disease). 
Bubonic plague is the most common form and is transmitted by infected fleas; the incubation period ranges from two to eight days.
The bacteria enter the lymph nodes, and a painful bubo develops within six to eight hours. Human-to-human transmission of bubonic plague is rare, but the bacteria can enter the bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, or the lungs, causing pneumonic plague.
Unlike the other two forms, pneumonic plague can be transmitted to other people via respiratory droplets. If not detected early and treated with antibiotics, pneumonic plague is also fatal; furthermore, it has a much shorter incubation period—as little as 24 hours.
The so-called Black Death—caused by bubonic and pneumonic plague—killed more than 25 million people in 14th-century Europe, wiping out between one-third and two-thirds of the population. The spread of the plague was facilitated by new trade routes and the transport of grain and flour by ship, which also attracted rodents.
However, modern conditions are far less favorable for the spread of the plague.
 First, although Yersinia pestis is almost always fatal if left untreated, it can now be easily eliminated with simple, widely available antibiotics. Piero Olliaro, Professor of Poverty-Related Infectious Diseases at the University of Oxford, noted that there are two drugs that are highly effective against bubonic plague.
Another reason why a widespread pandemic is virtually impossible is that—unlike COVID-19—pneumonic plague is infectious only after symptoms have appeared; these symptoms usually manifest within 24 hours and are severe and obvious. This means that an outbreak can be quickly detected, and individuals can be isolated and treated before transmission occurs. Zania Stamataki, a professor of immunology at the University of Birmingham, stated that pneumonic plague is not something easily overlooked—the sort of illness where an infected person might board a plane and manage to spread the disease across half the globe.
According to information from the World Health Organization, all of Shipilova’s contacts have been identified and are being monitored, and none are showing symptoms of the disease. In a risk assessment published on the 6th of October, WHO representative Christian Lindmeier rated the risk of an outbreak in Irkutsk as moderate to low, in Russia as low, and for the WHO European region as very low.
In general, contracting the disease in a laboratory setting is a very rare occurrence, as strict operating protocols are usually in place.
 Stamataki noted that these are highly specialized laboratories with a range of protective measures in effect. The professor explained that researchers wear full protective gear and handle samples inside special safety cabinets that maintain negative air pressure; this means air is drawn inward and away from the researcher, so that even if a sample breaks, the contents remain inside the cabinet rather than escaping into the air around the researcher. Even when the test tube is being moved, it is placed inside another container to prevent the contents from escaping into the external environment.
One of the main reasons the plague had such devastating consequences in the 14th century was the living conditions of the time. Streets accumulated waste and food scraps, creating ideal conditions for black rat nests—and, consequently, for fleas. People lived in close proximity to one another, and merchants on ships spent months in extremely cramped quarters. Today, living conditions in most parts of the world are far better.
However, it is important to understand that the plague is not a disease of the past. It remains endemic in rodent populations across Africa, Asia, South America, and even parts of the United States. Human cases are still detected annually; for instance, an average of seven cases of plague are reported in the US each year. Localized outbreaks occur sporadically in some parts of the world, with instances of human-to-human transmission of pneumonic plague also being recorded.

SMEs drive AI job market boom in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
08:17:54 UTC
17:17:54 KST

SMEs drive AI job market boom in Switzerland
Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities in the Swiss labour market. However, not everyone is benefiting equally from the growing demand for AI specialists.
The job market for artificial intelligence (AI) is booming in Switzerland. Between July 2025 and June 2026, just under 5,000 AI vacancies were advertised. This was 32% more than in the previous year, as shown by a study published on Thursday by the Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts (HSLU).
Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) were the main drivers of this boom. They accounted for 76% of the growth in job vacancies. “AI is no longer just the preserve of large technology companies, but is increasingly being integrated into the processes and services of established SMEs,” said the study’s author, Curdin Derungs, according to the press release.
The IT sector offered the most jobs, with 1,211 vacancies (+49 per cent). However, AI specialists were also sought after by banks and insurance companies such as Axa, Julius Bär and the Swiss National Bank, as well as by pharmaceutical firms such as Roche, Novartis and Lonza. In the engineering sector, Siemens, Hitachi Energy and ABB are among the leading employers.
+ As big pharma meets AI, new career paths open in Switzerland
The public sector recorded the strongest growth at 67%. The largest employers in this sector include the Canton and City of Zurich, as well as the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH). “The growth in AI roles within the public sector in particular suggests that policymakers and public authorities are strengthening their confidence in AI as a technology of the future,” said Derungs.
Regionally, Zurich was clearly in the lead with 2,181 vacancies, accounting for 45% of all AI roles. It was followed by the cantons of Geneva with around 620 and Bern with around 590 roles.
A challenging situation for those starting their careers
There was particular demand for experienced professionals capable of developing and implementing AI systems. The number of vacancies for experienced specialists rose by 42%. For those starting their careers, however, the market remained challenging. Only 5% of the vacancies were for permanent junior roles.
Even for entry-level positions, two to three years’ professional experience was often required, according to the study. University graduates told the authors of months-long job searches and dozens of unsuccessful applications.
“New entrants to the labour market describe the job market as extremely competitive,” study author Derungs added. He was surprised to find that even experienced professionals were increasingly facing difficulties in their job searches.
