Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water this winter?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
10:00:00 EEST
16:00:00 KST

Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
On the night of 29-30 September – ten days earlier than last year – Russia's winter campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure officially began. Ekonomichna Pravda (EP) sources say Russian ballistic missiles and drones have been primarily targeting energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region. Their targets include thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, hydroelectric power plants and electricity transmission infrastructure.
Last winter demonstrated the problems that massive strikes on critical infrastructure can cause in people's everyday lives. This year Ukraine is heading into the heating season better prepared. Power generation has been restored, backup power sources secured, security measures strengthened, equipment stocked up, and repair crews replenished.
But as everyone knows, no level of protection can fully shield the power grid from Russian attacks, meaning that Ukraine is highly unlikely to get through the winter without some disruptions to electricity, heating and water supplies.
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin has no desire, and certainly no plans, to agree to an energy truce any time soon, given that he sees further strikes as a means of exerting pressure on the Ukrainian authorities and influencing Kyiv's position ahead of possible negotiations.
Moscow is likely to focus its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine's most densely populated city, in an attempt to influence the public mood in the capital – something the Ukrainian authorities cannot afford to ignore.
The Kremlin's overall objective is to bring about a humanitarian catastrophe and render the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable. Read on to find out how Kyiv is preparing for the heating season, what challenges lie ahead, and what its residents should expect.
Resilience Plans
In early March, Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council approved Comprehensive Resilience Plans for regions and major cities. The plans set out step-by-step roadmaps to prepare critical infrastructure for the next heating season.
EP has looked at what the plans involve, how much they are expected to cost to implement, and whether they can all feasibly be put into practice before the cold weather arrives. The plans cover four key areas, some of which may overlap.
- The first area concerns protection for critical infrastructure. It covers air defence measures and the completion of Level 2 protective shelters at facilities belonging to Ukrenergo (Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator), Naftogaz (the largest national oil and gas company), the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine, and regional electricity distribution companies.
- The second area involves building 1.5 GW of distributed generation capacity, primarily in the city of Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Poltava and Kyiv oblasts. Distributed generation refers to smaller power generation facilities located closer to consumers, rather than centralised in a small number of large plants.
- The third and fourth areas are about ensuring uninterrupted heating and water supplies.
At the heart of the plans is a simulation of a total blackout, designed to answer a crucial question: how would the city keep its heating and water systems running if that were to happen? "The concept has been dubbed 'Dark, but warm.' In other words, the lights might go out after a bombardment, but there must always be water and heating," Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Centre for Energy Research, told EP.
Immediately after the government adopted the Resilience Plans, energy sector sources told EP they were overly ambitious and optimistic and said they doubted that all the measures could be implemented before winter.
Three years would be a more realistic timescale for completion of the work, the sources said. What has been achieved so far, and how is Kyiv preparing to go into the heating season?
What will happen to the electricity supply?
Before Russia began to attack its power grid, Ukraine had a significant electricity surplus. Generation comfortably exceeded domestic demand.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says Ukraine currently has over 15 GW of generating capacity available during the evening, when demand is at its highest. And that's with only six of Ukraine's nine nuclear reactors in operation (the other three are undergoing maintenance). The plan is to increase available generation capacity to 19.6 GW by 1 November and 21.4 GW by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, electricity consumption last week ranged from 6,800 MW at its lowest to 10,200 MW at its peak. The sharp drop in consumption across the country is linked to Russia's constant attacks on major metals companies, which have been forced to halt production.
Electricity consumption will obviously go up in winter, but if all the planned repairs are completed, power generation should be sufficient to keep the system balanced in normal winter temperatures, a source at an energy company told EP.
"However, we have to factor in that the energy sector will come under attack," the source noted. "We had enough generation capacity on paper at the end of last September too, but after several waves of attacks, we ended up with a shortfall of 5,000-6,000 MW."
So the main risk this winter is not a shortage of generation capacity at the outset, but how quickly that capacity could be lost due to further Russian attacks.
For Kyiv, this is particularly important. Russian attacks have already destroyed a significant portion of the capital's power generation capacity. Some of that capacity is slated to be restored, but once brought back online, the facilities will become priority targets again.
The second major area of preparation is therefore to ensure a reliable electricity supply for the capital. The Kyiv energy ring is built around four 330 kV substations, supported by dozens of smaller 110 kV substations.
The Resilience Plan envisages providing Level 2 protection for these sites. According to sources who spoke to EP, some of the work is already complete and the remainder is due to be finished by the end of the year, despite government statements about a freeze on capital expenditure. Level 2 protection is designed to withstand drone attacks, but not ballistic strikes.
Another part of Kyiv's Resilience Plan is establishing backup power sources. A document seen by EP puts the capital's peak winter load at 2 GW. Critical infrastructure accounts for around 280 MW, and a reserve of generators and cogeneration units is to be set up specifically to keep those facilities supplied.
EP sources say around 150 MW of the planned 200 MW of distributed generation capacity has already been commissioned. According to an energy market source, the city could have 180-185 MW available by the end of the year. Privately owned facilities with a combined capacity of 55-60 MW could also come online before winter; around half of them are ready to start operating.
The main function of distributed generation is to keep critical infrastructure running if the main generation sources or the grid are damaged.
In other words, if there is an electricity shortage, priority will be given to water supply systems, boilerhouses, hospitals, communications, transport and other essential services. For ordinary consumers, emergency or hourly power outage schedules will be in place, as they were last year. What will this mean for the public?
A senior manager at a state-owned energy company told EP: "If temperatures fall below -10°C and some generation capacity can't be brought back online in time, we could be looking at around eight to ten hours of power cuts per day. That's assuming there are no further attacks.
Then there's the pessimistic scenario – heavy strikes and widespread destruction. In that case there might be only four hours of electricity a day, leaving Kyiv without power for up to 20 hours," the source added. Even so, EP sources say Russia will not be able to plunge Kyiv into a total blackout.
In other words, the worst-case scenario for the capital is prolonged power cuts for most consumers, but critical infrastructure kept powered up.
The source concludes: "No one can give an accurate forecast right now. The situation depends on many factors. It will depend on where and how the attacks happen, which power plants are still working, and how quickly they can be brought back online."
What are the risks to Kyiv's heating supply?
Heating is a more complex issue. Kyiv's heat supply system has historically been highly centralised: around 70% of the city is heated by three large combined heat and power (CHP) plants.
That is why backup heat sources are one of the key priorities of the Resilience Plan: modernising old boilerhouses, building new ones, installing cogeneration units, and creating connections between different sections of the heating network.
The idea is that if a major CHP plant goes down, individual districts will be able to receive heat from alternative sources. The problem is that Kyiv's huge CHP plants cannot be fully replicated in just a few months.
"Kyiv's CHP plants have a capacity equal to that of several regional capitals. They were built over decades, when the Soviet Union had virtually unlimited resources," a source in the Kyiv city administration told EP.
For that reason, Kyiv will not be able to fully protect its heating supply system from losing heat this year. An EP source close to the government said that between 2,500 and 3,000 apartment blocks may be left without a backup heat supply this winter. Another source believes the number could be even higher. There are 12,000 apartment blocks in Kyiv.
"It's hard to say exactly which apartment blocks might be left without heating, but potentially the areas at risk are parts of the Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi and Pecherskyi districts, Teremky, Berezniaky, parts of the Dniprovskyi district, part of Troieshchyna, and even the Obolonskyi district," Kharchenko says.
As with the power supply, what happens next will depend on the scale of the attacks.
The optimistic scenario assumes that the main heat sources will be partly operational and any damage would be repaired quickly, in which case Kyiv should get through the winter without widespread heating disruptions. Backup boilerhouses and bypasses should help localise any problems.
But if the Russians launch massive strikes on thermal power stations and large boilerhouses, heating problems are inevitable. "There are three major plants in Kyiv that have already been attacked. You don't need a crystal ball to know that they're going to be attacked again," says an EP source at an energy company. On 30 September, Russian forces launched relentless strikes on one of the capital's CHP plants.
If this happens, the city will switch to emergency mode. Backup boilerhouses, generators, emergency response teams and mobile equipment will be deployed wherever possible. Critical infrastructure will be prioritised above all else.
But some residential buildings will have no backup heat supply. In the worst-case scenario, the city will have to rely on electricity to make up for the shortfall in heating.
"As a last resort, if some areas have no heating, they should be exempt from rolling blackouts, or at least the power cuts there should be shorter than in the rest of the city. And people will rely on electric heaters to keep warm, just as they did last year," the source explains.
"There are no guarantees that Kyiv will have heating," the source in the city administration told EP. "Ballistic strikes mean there can be no guarantees in principle. A lot will depend on how intense the attacks are."
But one thing is different from last winter. According to Kharchenko, Kyiv will be more resilient to attacks even in the most challenging scenario, as backup boilerhouses, generators, hospitals, staff and invincibility centres are now better prepared. [An invincibility centre is a heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist residents facing hardships due to power cuts – ed.]
Kyiv will not be left without water, but there are some caveats
Water is another critical part of the picture, as Russia could target the capital's water supply in an attempt to trigger a humanitarian disaster.
Kyiv's Resilience Plan focuses on keeping the water utility running even if the power goes out. To achieve this, pumping stations and other key water supply and drainage facilities must be equipped with backup power sources.
According to EP sources, almost half of the planned 40 MW of backup power has now been commissioned. The rest is due to be completed by the end of the year.
The good news is that most of Kyiv's water infrastructure is underground, so it is more resilient to attacks. However, the water supply system cannot be fully protected from the effects of massive strikes.
"Most of the infrastructure is underground," an EP source in the government notes. "Even at water intakes and large water treatment plants, a significant part of the infrastructure is underground. But concentrated ballistic strikes could still cause serious damage."
According to the source, even major damage to the system would not automatically leave the entire city without water. In the worst-case scenario, the problem would be water quality and the supply to some districts.
Another EP source did not rule out the possibility that in certain circumstances, some areas of the city could be without water for a week or longer. Residents are therefore advised to ensure they have stocks of drinking water at home.
* * *
To sum up, Kyiv is heading into this winter objectively better prepared than it was a year ago. The city has more backup generation capacity, better-protected facilities, alternative heat sources, generators, and well-rehearsed plans for dealing with large-scale attacks.
But that doesn't mean the winter will be easy. None of these measures offers a cast-iron guarantee, because the scale of future attacks and the damage they will cause cannot be predicted in advance.
So the main question is not whether there will be problems – there will be. The question is how quickly the city can bring damaged facilities back online and whether its backup capacity and reserves will be enough to prevent local problems from turning into a city-wide crisis.
For Kyiv, as for the country as a whole, the biggest unknown is something that can't be predicted or controlled: the scale and intensity of future Russian attacks.
Mykola Topalov

Malaysia promises Myanmar help toward full ASEAN reintegration

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday his government would do "whatever possible" to reintegrate Myanmar into ASEAN following a meeting with the country's leader, Min Aung Hlaing.
Anwar also pledged to continue working with Myanmar, including on the repatriation of thousands of Myanmar nationals from Malaysia – a move the United Nations and rights groups have widely criticized, citing risks from an ongoing civil war.
Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing is on a two-day visit to Malaysia as he seeks greater international legitimacy after becoming president in April following an election that Western nations and rights groups widely criticized as a sham.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since 2021 when Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup against a democratically elected government, triggering armed conflict across much of the country.
Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been barred from attending ASEAN summits after failing to adhere to an ASEAN-brokered peace plan following the coup, but some member countries have sought to reestablish ties.
Since becoming president, Min Aung Hlaing has also visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.
Malaysia's Anwar acknowledged ongoing concerns about democratic processes in Myanmar but said differences should be respected, adding Min Aung Hlaing had shown a willingness to collaborate.
"We in Malaysia will do whatever is possible to make sure that we enhance this collaboration and, ultimately, take Myanmar as part of our community of nations, without prejudice and particularly in the context of ASEAN," Anwar told a news conference following the meeting.
Anwar also expressed appreciation to Min Aung Hlaing for accepting the repatriation of 10,493 Myanmar nationals from Malaysia so far.
Malaysia has said it can no longer take in refugees from Myanmar, saying they had become a financial burden and a security risk. Malaysia is not a party to the United Nations refugee convention and treats asylum-seekers as illegal migrants.
The country last month sent back around 1,500 people on Myanmar naval ships, part of a wider repatriation program that could see as many as 5,000 people deported.
Min Aung Hlaing said at Thursday's news conference Myanmar citizens currently held at Malaysian immigration detention centers would be brought back as soon as possible.
"Because the current weather is favorable, I will send navy ships to repatriate them," he said, adding he would formally request Malaysia allow the repatriation.
He also extended an invitation for Anwar to visit Myanmar "when the time is right."
Anwar and Min Aung Hlaing did not mention if their discussions included plans to repatriate Rohingya Muslim refugees, many of whom fled Myanmar after a brutal 2017 military crackdown in the country's Rakhine state that is now the subject of a genocide case at the International Court of Justice.
Muslim-majority Malaysia widely criticized the crackdown at the time.
But public sentiment has turned in recent years, with the Rohingya in Malaysia facing increasing harassment and scrutiny amid a surge of online hate speech and misinformation. Anwar has said he would push for Myanmar to accept Rohingya refugees.
There are more than 193,000 refugees and asylum-seekers from Myanmar in Malaysia, about 65% of them Rohingya, according to the United Nations refugee agency.
Buddhist-majority Myanmar does not recognize the Rohingya as one of its official ethnic groups and denies citizenship to most.

As big pharma meets AI, new career paths open in Switzerland

As big pharma meets AI, new career paths open in Switzerland
Switzerland is one of the world’s leading pharma hubs, but it’s also a growing hot spot for AI research, start-ups and major technology companies. The combination is giving pharma professionals in the country opportunities beyond traditional drugmakers.
Pharmaceutical companies like Swiss giants Novartis and Roche are betting big on artificial intelligence to discover and develop new drugs. In 2025, the top 20 pharma firms spent some $29.5 billion (CHF24.5 billion) on AI drug discovery deals, up from $15.4 million the year before, accordingExternal link to consulting firm McKinsey.
Meanwhile AI giants like Anthropic and OpenAI are racing to develop tools for the data-heavy scientific, clinical, and commercial work of the drug industry. In June, the CEO of Microsoft’s AI division, Mustafa Suleyman, calledExternal link healthcare “the most important application of AI”.
For pharma professionals based in Switzerland, the convergence of pharma and AI is opening new career paths. Basel is already one of the world’s top pharma hubs while Zurich is emerging as a centre of AI innovation, thanks to top universities and funding for AI research as well as start-ups that have attracted big names in AI.
OpenAI, which created ChatGPT, along with Anthropic have set up operations in Zurich. Isomorphic Labs, the AI drug discovery company spun out of Google DeepMind, opened its first office outside the United Kingdom in Lausanne.
More
Big Pharma steps up race for AI-discovered drugs
Nives Rombini is one of a small but growing number of scientists who spent years working for pharmaceutical companies and are now being drawn to AI, believing they’ll make more impact in a tech company than in traditional pharma.
The Swiss-Italian national studied immunology at the University of Bern and was always interested in the life sciences industry. But she also has a passion for data and automation, spending time after her studies as a trainee at the telecom provider Swisscom.
Rombini joined US pharmaceutical company Bristol Myers Squibb (BMS) in western Switzerland in 2021, becoming a senior scientist in 2023, making sense of patient data to help the company decide what research areas to pursue.
But in 2024, at age 29, she quit her job, frustrated by how inefficiently pharma companies process large-scale data, and co-founded Zurich-based tech start-up Navis Bio.
“At Navis, I have almost the same job processing data as I did in big pharma, but now I can build a platform to do it,” Rombini told Swissinfo.
Her startup’s AI-powered software automates the monumental task of analysing thousands of clinical trials, patents, and scientific papers to help drugmakers identify target diseases. Building such software would be hard to do inside pharma.
“It’s almost intrinsic in the type of business that pharma does, that they cannot really move fast and break things,” said Rombini. “It’s structurally hard to really push the frontiers in big pharma. And this is what we are trying to do.”
It takes on average more than a decade and $2.3 billion to develop a drug, and only 10% of drugs that enter clinical trials are successful. AI-driven R&D efforts could deliverExternal link time and costs savings of at least 25-50% in the drug discovery phase, according to Boston Consulting Group. To tap this potential, dozens of AI-driven drug discovery companies, such as HAYA Therapeutics, Onena Medicines and Adaptiv Bio, have set up in Switzerland in the last decade.
Beyond the scientist
AI isn’t only opening new career paths for laboratory scientists and researchers. Professionals with pharma experience across a range of functions, such as pricing, reimbursement, market access and customer strategy, are finding opportunities with specialist AI service providers.
This is because of the way AI is being applied across the entire chain: from analysing biological data to identifying potential targets and refining candidate medicines, to designing clinical trials and supporting manufacturing, regulatory, pricing and commercial decisions.
More
Basel’s world-beating pharma hub fights for place in new global order
“You always had scientists in pharma, leaving to create biotech companies,” said David Vanni, who spent seven years working for Novartis, most recently as associate director for global customer strategy in oncology. “What you see now is pharma talent moving into AI startups, from different roles, bringing the business context into AI solutions.” Previously, this was only possible if you went to work in a consulting firm, he said.
Vanni, who worked in commercial, marketing, and customer-strategy roles in Shanghai and Basel, saw potential for AI to streamline processes and bring more evidence into commercial decision-making. After executive training in AI, he thought, like Rombini, that he had a better chance to address these gaps as a technology provider to big pharma.
In July, he joined Singapore-headquartered start-up CHOIR, which develops AI business intelligence solutions for pharmaceutical companies, leading its global sales and marketing activities from the company’s new Zurich offices.
There are now a host of start-ups combining AI and pharma expertise that seek to bring greater efficiency into pharma companies. Basel-based Lyfegen is using AI to help with pricing and reimbursement, Bern-based Risklick offers AI-driven solutions for developing clinical trial protocols and US company iFactory uses AI to flag quality problems and improve productivity in drug manufacturing.
More
How artificial intelligence is shaping the Swiss job market
Bigger tech companies like Anthropic or Microsoft that are trying to target pharma with tools also need people who understand the industry’s science, regulatory and business processes. Anthropic recently listed 16 roles related to life-sciences across legal, computational, and sales teams. Although they are just a fraction of the nearly 600 open positions on its careers page and most are US-based, they offer highly competitive salaries.
Long-term potential
Just how significant the crossover of pharma talent into AI will become is hard to estimate. The numbers are still fairly small in Switzerland and globally, said Maurice Thornton who heads the Zurich-based life science recruitment agency headcount AG.
“What we see more of is AI companies bringing on higher level, very experienced pharma people to join their boards or as advisors to help build out their healthcare business,” he said. One example is Vas Narasimhan, the CEO of Novartis, who joined the board of Anthropic in April 2026.
The scale of opportunities in the long-term depends on the endgame for AI companies, said Christian Hein, previously vice president of digital transformation at Novartis and now an independent advisor on AI in life sciences and healthcare.
More
AI’s next pharma challenge: tackling costly and risky clinical trials
“It isn’t clear yet whether AI-native drug discovery companies stay platforms or become more traditional biotechs with their own pipelines,” said Hein. “If it is the latter, there are likely to be more people moving from pharma into these companies.”
He is sceptical that the large frontier AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic will become direct competitors to pharmaceutical companies when it comes to attracting talent.
“The moment you get into clinical development, it’s quite a different business model from the technology and software market,” he said. “I see the big AI labs much more as enablers and accelerators of science and pharma processes.”
Thornton agrees. He expects more partnerships between pharma and AI companies and with that, more cross-pollination of talent. For traditional pharma hubs like Switzerland, this makes it even more important to attract AI talent.
The country already has an advantage – Swiss federal institutes of technology, ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne, are some of the best training grounds for AI talent. “The marriage of pharma and AI in this country is a huge opportunity,” said Thornton.

Russian sabotage costs UK up to £2.5bn a year
The economic impact of Russia's hostile activities against the United Kingdom amounts to at least £2-2.5 billion a year, according to a new report by the vice-chair of the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) on rearmament.
Source: Financial Times
Details: The new report, entitled "The Putin Tax", estimates the costs of the disruption, recovery and investment in resilience caused by Russia's hybrid warfare against the UK.
However, the study by Labour MP Graeme Downie, published on Wednesday 7 October, suggests that the true figure is likely to be "vastly higher" than his estimate. He warned that gaps in government-published data make it impossible to accurately calculate the cost of hybrid warfare linked to Moscow.
The overall estimate of £2-2.5 billion comprises three components: £400-500 million in average annual losses from major incidents since 2022, such as attacks on Jaguar Land Rover, the Royal Mail and National Health Service suppliers; £1.47 billion in losses from Russia-linked cyberattacks, based on industry analysis and threat intelligence; and £250-500 million in losses from damage to undersea communications cables and related infrastructure.
The report also emphasises that the UK lacks a coherent system for assessing the economic impact of hostile state activity and that the cost of many serious incidents has yet to be calculated, leaving both MPs and the public without a clear picture of the financial consequences.
Background: Danish intelligence has reported that Russia launched sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying goods to Ukraine after concluding that broader destabilisation efforts had failed to curb military support.

Faisal Mahmud
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
New Zealand on Thursday confirmed a new measles case in the capital Wellington, linked to recent international travel.
Health New Zealand, the public health agency, said it was supporting the infected person and identifying close contacts.
Dr. Craig Thornley, medical officer for Greater Wellington, warned that international travel during school holidays increased the risk of imported infections.
"With many people travelling or returning from overseas during the school holidays, this case is a timely reminder that measles can be brought into New Zealand at any time," Thornley said.
He urged residents to monitor symptoms, including fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes and a rash, and seek medical advice if they suspected exposure.
Authorities advised anyone developing symptoms to remain home and contact healthcare providers before visiting medical facilities to prevent further transmission.
Thornley also emphasized the importance of vaccination, saying two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine provide effective protection.
Health New Zealand urged residents to regularly check its website for updated exposure locations and public health advice.
New Zealand's Immunisation Advisory Centre warned in July that the country remained vulnerable to fresh outbreaks despite the conclusion of its 2025 measles outbreak.

Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, finds UN study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:58:57 UTC
15:58:57 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte.
The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study.
“Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte.
📉Facts matter.
Refugees from Ukraine contributed 2.4% of Poland’s GDP in 2025, says new analysis by UNHCR and Deloitte.
This is what happens when people forced to flee are given the opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity.
The full report: https://t.co/egUp8jjCwc pic.twitter.com/CSNONqdKGU
— UNHCR Polska (@UNHCRPoland) October 1, 2026
The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025.
Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further.
The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before.
The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data.
The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens.
However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens.
Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland.
Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise.
The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million.
Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026
Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity.
Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”.
At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives.
Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work.
Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded.
The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2025
The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status.
Meanwhile, surveys show a weakening of refugees’ intentions to eventually return to Ukraine. Research by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) found that the proportion who plan to settle permanently in Poland rose from 21% to 25% between 2024 and 2025.
However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine.

Can a picture make healthy food irresistible to teens?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:58:56 UTC
15:58:56 KST

Even without any single “problem” food, simply eating a very large meal is one of the strongest triggers. Holiday dinners, big restaurant plates, or second helpings that push the meal into the heavy category regularly led to that classic “food coma.”
NEW DELHI: A bowl of millet porridge may not sound as tempting as a burger, but put it through a social-media makeover and teenagers may look at it differently. An Indian Council of Medical Research-National Institute of Nutrition (ICMR-NIN) study involving 203 adolescents found that the visual appeal of food images was significantly associated with their willingness to consume the food.Researchers showed adolescents attractive “foodporn” images of healthy foods on Instagram for 15 days and compared them with regular images. The strongest differences were seen for millet porridge and boiled chana salad, whose attractive images generated about 50% and 10% more positive responses, respectively, than their regular counterparts. The difference was statistically significant for the millet and pulse categories.The study used 15 food images divided into three categories: unhealthy foods presented as “foodporn”, healthy foods presented in an attractive “foodporn” format, and healthy foods shown as regular pictures. The researchers also conducted in-depth interviews with 19 adolescents to understand what made food images appealing.Researchers found that the intervention showed a broader positive trend, with adolescents reporting more favourable attitudes towards healthy foods, greater consumption and stronger intentions to eat them, although not all changes were statistically significant.
Intentions to consume millet porridge and chana salad were 9% and 15% higher, respectively, for attractive images than regular ones, but neither difference was statistically significant.Visual appeal appeared important, with adolescents citing colour, presentation, ingredients, angle, texture, glossiness, balance and symmetry as factors that made food images more appealing. Even before the intervention, 60% said they were willing to try foods seen on social media, while 56% said attractive food images made them crave them.
Adding nutritional information did not significantly alter responses, suggesting that adolescents paid more attention to the visual presentation than accompanying text.The findings suggest that making healthy foods visually appealing could help counter the dominance of attractive unhealthy-food content online, with potential applications in school canteens, restaurants and cafes. However, the study did not establish that attractive food images change actual eating behaviour. The intervention was short, relied partly on self-reported responses, and could not establish causality.

Rampant mortgage fraud used by gangs to buy up homes around NL
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Rampant mortgage fraud used by gangs to buy up homes around NL
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Between 6,000 and 11,000 homes in the Netherlands have been bought with forged documents in recent years, according to an unpublished report on mortgage fraud.
The report, by the Financial Expertise Centre (FEC), a partnership of regulators and law enforcement agencies, has been with the justice ministry for more than six months, sources told broadcaster NOS. It was due to be completed in March.
According to NOS, the report says criminal groups use mortgage fraud to acquire properties which they then use for other illegal activities.
Fraudsters forge documents such as pay slips, employer statements, annual accounts and tax returns to obtain mortgages. MPs, the Dutch banking association NVB and the notaries’ professional body KNB have raised concerns about the issue for several years. The previous cabinet commissioned the FEC to investigate.
NVB chair Medy van der Laan told a parliamentary hearing on organised crime on Wednesday that the homes are used for money laundering, illegal renting, labour exploitation and drug crime. “Mortgage fraud is happening more and more,” she said, adding that it undermines the quality of life in neighbourhoods.
Banks and notaries want to be able to check applicants’ income data with the tax office. “We respect all the sensitivities around privacy. We just want to check whether the information we have been given is correct,” Van der Laan said.
Left-wing Pro MP Hanneke Mutluer has called for the report and its recommendations to be sent to parliament as soon as possible. MPs are due to debate the issue next week.
In 2024, the Financieele Dagblad reported that a criminal network had used forged mortgage papers to buy hundreds of homes in the Amsterdam area between 2018 and 2023. The properties were used to store cash and drugs and to house foreign workers.
Last October, Amsterdam police arrested a Zaandam real estate agent and seven others suspected of falsifying mortgage papers for criminals. Police said at the time that mortgage fraud was rampant.
They have long called for banks to be allowed to check applicants’ income against tax office data.

Apple's age-verification feature welcomed by Pornhub owners
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:57:21 UTC
15:57:21 KST

In short:
Pornhub has returned to Australia after Apple introduced a new age-verification process targeted at eliminating minors' exposure to explicit content.
Australian iOS users will be prompted to confirm they are 18 or older in order to access adult content.
What's next?
Aylo, the parent company behind many popular adult platforms including Pornhub, has welcomed the move.
Pornhub, the world's most popular porn site, has returned to Australia after Apple introduced a new age-verification process targeted at eliminating minors' exposure to explicit content.
The adult site was barred from Australian devices in March after sweeping age-restricted safety codes came into effect.
Australia joins the United Kingdom in the latest roll-out of Apple's age-verification standard after widespread concern related to children's online safety.
A report released by the eSafety Commission in 2023 found about 10 per cent of children accidentally came across online pornography by the age of 10.
The number climbed to almost 30 per cent by age 13.
In 2026, eSafety said it was prioritising "systemic safety failures" over individual incidents of children accessing sensitive materials.
The commission said it was taking enforcement actions against AI chatbots generating sexually explicit content in addition to monitoring online services like search engines and app stores, and pornography providers were enforcing safe user experiences.
Accordingly, companies found in breach of the online safety codes would face civil penalties of up to $49.5 million.
Under Apple's new account management requirements, adults over 18 will need to "take certain actions on their account".
Among the requirements, Apple users will need to confirm their age with a credit card, passport, driver's licence or government-issued ID.
Apple said it would verify account-holders' ages via existing card details or other "eligible methods".
"Debit cards and gift cards aren't supported," Apple's support page read.
Alex Kekesi, vice-president for brand and community at Aylo, the parent company behind many adult entertainment platforms including Pornhub, welcomed the news.
She said Apple's verification process had "set a benchmark by enabling child safety features automatically for users who have not verified that they are adults, ultimately, making every phone or tablet kid-safe as a starting point".
Ms Kekesi said Aylo had advocated for "device-based verification" for years.
She said it was "the most effective and privacy-protecting approach to help prevent minors from accessing age-inappropriate content online".
"In our view, Apple’s Australian device-level age-verification update offers one of the strongest and hardest to circumvent protections currently available.
"Moving forward, age-verified iOS users in Australia reaching Pornhub will be served a standard adult user experience."
She said the technology also avoided users turning to virtual private network apps to circumvent blocks.
VPN usage skyrocketed in the days leading up to Pornhub's ban in Australia, the Guardian reported at the time.

What we don't know about the government's private health rebate changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:57:08 UTC
15:57:08 KST

Key Points
- Older migrants could face higher health insurance costs.
- Rebate cuts may affect two million low-income Australians.
Older migrants could be among the hardest hit by proposed private health insurance rebate cuts, with concerns that the government has not modelled how the changes would affect people paying higher premiums under Lifetime Health Cover rules.
Under the plan, people aged 65 and over, who receive a higher private insurance health rebate than the general population, would have that rebate reduced, with expected savings of $3 billion redirected into aged care beds and home care services.
Treasury has forecast that of the three million people receiving the higher rebate, just 44,000 would be pushed into the public health system after it was reduced.
But new health department data, reported by the ABC, shows more than two million on an annual income below $37,000 will lose the discount. The government's plan is opposed by both the Coalition and the Greens.
The government appears not to have modelled the impact on migrants whose private insurance history can differ from Australian-born people of the same age and income.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
A Labor-led Senate committee, which received 665 submissions, reported on Wednesday that the reforms should proceed despite warnings that pensioners may downgrade or dump their cover and move into the stretched public healthcare system.
Medical, insurance and seniors groups argued the higher rebate should continue; otherwise both patients and hospitals will be harmed. Academics and think tanks, including the left-wing Australia Institute, said the discounts should be retired because statistical evidence shows it is a poorly-targeted subsidy paid mostly to people who will hold onto their insurance regardless.
The Members Health Fund Alliance said older Australians who drop their cover face higher costs and fewer products if they try to come back under the Lifetime Health Cover (LHC) loading rules. For some, leaving is "effectively irreversible".
Catholic Health Australia modelling estimated one in five people aged 65 and over will change their level of cover, instead of the one-in-75 assumed by government models. They calculated a 70-year-old pensioner dropping cover in 2027 who rejoined aged 73 may face an LHC loading of up to 70 per cent.
Andrew and Irene Aves told the committee that when they arrived in Australia on parent migrant visas in 2014, they paid over $70,000 to the immigration department, which then provided them with Medicare access. Not wanting to be a burden on the health system, they took out health insurance and became Australian citizens in 2019.
But as retirees, their UK state pension was frozen at 2013 rates when they left the UK. The extra cost of health insurance without the higher rebate may make their cover unaffordable, they wrote.
The government did not answer questions about how its reforms would affect older migrants, but a spokesperson said the changes will make private health insurance rebates fairer.
"These changes mean all Australians will now receive the same private health insurance support, based on their income, not age," the spokesperson said.
"The current additional rebate is simply not the best way to spend precious taxpayers' dollars on behalf of older Australians when we need to do so much heavy lifting in aged care.
"Every dollar will be reinvested to deliver more aged care beds, more packages and better care for older Australians."
Opposition health and aged care spokesperson Senator Anne Ruston said the policy is an "aged pensioner penalty, pure and simple".
"A government that believes it must cut health funding to pay for aged care is a government that has lost control of its own budget," she said.
"Evidence from older Australians, their advocates, doctors and other healthcare professionals agreed this ill-conceived policy would have a profound impact on vulnerable older Australians."
She said no state or territory supported the changes, with most saying they expect longer elective surgery wait lists and extra costs for state taxpayers.
The Greens may negotiate a change to the legislation by exempting pensioners.
Intergenerational equity will not be helped by making cover more expensive for people over 65 on low incomes, the Greens wrote in a dissenting report.
"Pensioners and part-pensioners generally live on fixed incomes and have limited capacity to absorb additional costs," the Greens wrote.
"The committee heard that many may struggle to meet higher private health insurance premiums, potentially forcing people to downgrade their level of cover or to cut back on other essentials such as heating, cooling and putting food on the table."
What are the private health changes and when will they start?
The rebates are subsidies paid by the federal government to help people cover the costs of their private health insurance.
The rebates give an extra 4 per cent discount on private health insurance for people aged 65–69 and 8 per cent for people over 70.
Starting 1 April 2027, the rebates will be based solely on household income.
People under 65 receive a standard base or a tiered discount, which decreases as their income rises and phases out completely for high-income earners.
The government's modelling predicted about 99 per cent of over-65s would keep their cover, about 44,000 people.
But Private Healthcare Australia commissioned polling that found 39 per cent of insured older Australians would be more likely to drop their cover.
That figure represents about one million people. But when the government proposed means-testing the private health insurance rebate over a decade ago, similar health industry polling estimated 1.6 million people would drop their cover — instead, the opposite happened and coverage rose slightly.

German exports fall in August as shipments to US decline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:57:08 UTC
15:57:08 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Germany’s exports fell 0.8% in August from the previous month, while imports increased, narrowing the country’s trade surplus, official data showed on Thursday.
Europe's biggest economy saw its exports amount to €137.6 billion ($154.1 billion), while imports rose 0.9% to €118.1 billion, according to provisional figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
The trade surplus narrowed to €19.5 billion ($21.8 billion) from €21.6 billion in July, but exceeded the market expectation of €19 billion ($21.3 billion). The surplus stood at €17.6 billion in August last year.
Compared with August 2025, exports increased 6.2% and imports rose 5.5%.
Shipments to the US, Germany’s largest export destination in August, dropped 6.3% from July to €13.5 billion. However, exports to the country remained 22.6% above their level a year earlier.
Exports to the UK jumped 16.7% month on month to €7.9 billion, while shipments to China increased 4.7% to €5.9 billion.
Meanwhile, imports from China, Germany’s largest source of imported goods, surged 11% to €16.8 billion. Imports from the US declined 0.5% to €8.1 billion, while those from the UK fell 3.8% to €3.2 billion.
German exports to EU member states decreased 0.6% to €77.5 billion, while imports from the bloc fell 0.4% to €59.3 billion.
Within the EU, exports to euro area countries rose 0.8%, while shipments to member states outside the currency bloc declined 3.5%.
Exports to countries outside the EU fell 1.1% to €60 billion, while imports increased 2.2% to €58.8 billion.
In the first eight months of 2026, Germany’s calendar and seasonally adjusted exports totaled €1.09 trillion, up 4.4% from the same period last year.

Pentagon wants a robot dog that maps toxic air in 3D
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:56:03 UTC
15:56:03 KST

- The Defense Threat Reduction Agency plans a sole-source contract with Rocky Mountain Unmanned Systems for one prototype robot that maps hazardous gases in 3D.
- The robot will fuse data from a government chemical detector, a commercial quadruped, a 3D lidar and a mesh radio into one live map.
The Defense Threat Reduction Agency plans to pay a Utah company to build a prototype four-legged robot that can walk into hazardous areas on its own and produce a live 3D map of dangerous gases, according to a contract notice the agency posted on October 7.
DTRA, the U.S. Department of War agency responsible for countering chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats, said it intends to award a firm-fixed-price, sole-source contract to Rocky Mountain Unmanned Systems of Centerville, Utah, for a single prototype. The notice does not give a contract value or delivery date.
Under the plan, the government will supply a multi-gas chemical detector, and the contractor will provide a commercial quadruped robot, a survey-grade 3D lidar sensor and a tactical mesh networking radio, then fuse the data from all four into a single real-time “hazardous atmosphere map” showing operators where dangerous gases are inside the space the robot has scanned. DTRA called this software integration the core of the work but did not say which quadruped platform or chemical detector will be used.
The agency said market research found Rocky Mountain Unmanned Systems to be the only company that already has a proprietary software framework and demonstrated experience fusing these specific data streams into such a map. Although the hardware is commercial off the shelf, DTRA said no other source has shown the same pre-existing software capability and that the government does not own a technical data package it could use to hold a competition.
Because the notice is not a request for competing bids, other companies can only submit capability statements, proposals or quotes by noon MDT on October 22, and they must provide clear evidence that they already have the required data-fusion software. DTRA’s western contracting office at Kirtland Air Force Base, New Mexico, is handling the work, which is classified as applied research and development.
Rocky Mountain Unmanned Systems, founded in 2014, sells and integrates drones, public safety quadruped robots and gas imaging tools for government and commercial customers.
Robot dogs fitted with chemical and radiological sensors have seen limited military use for several years: in 2024, the U.S. Space Force said its CBRN detection robot, nicknamed CHAPPIE, was one of only two quadruped ground robots in the military dedicated to that mission, and the U.S. Air Force has tested a CBRN detector-equipped robot dog at Barksdale Air Force Base, Louisiana.

Tesco lifts profit forecast and says consumer confidence is resilient
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:52:40 UTC
15:52:40 KST

Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war.
The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn.
Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said growth had been helped by strong online sales, which were up 8%, and a 9% jump in revenue from its premium own-label Finest range.
He said: “Consumers in the UK have been pretty resilient in an uncertain environment and there is a sense that customers want to enjoy Christmas, given everything that is going on in the world.”
The retailer had bought more stock of “key Christmas lines”, understood to be foods such as turkey and mince pies, and added 10% more delivery slots for its online grocery business. It is also ramping up its in-house rapid delivery service, Whoosh, and has signed new partnerships, including with Deliveroo.
Murphy said he expected Britons to seek out a “marginally healthier Christmas” with higher sales of low-alcohol and no-alcohol drinks, including ready-mixed mocktails, but that families would still treat themselves as “customers do love to indulge”.
He said he was not expecting food supplies to be hit by this summer’s drought. Tesco had also hedged its energy costs into next year and was making savings across the business to help keep prices down for shoppers.
He said the business still had room for growth despite being almost twice the size of its nearest rival, Sainsbury’s, with a 28% market share, and that he did not “dwell too much” on the possibility of its closest rival acquiring another leading supermarket.
Sainsbury’s is understood to have walked away from merger talks in January with the UK’s sixth-biggest supermarket, Morrisons, prompting consolidation chatter across the industry.
“Whatever happens in the market we will respond to it,” Murphy said. While Tesco is expanding its reach with financial services and more fashion, he said its strategy “begins and ends in winning in food”.
The company added: “While consumer confidence has remained relatively resilient in the first half of the year, ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to create uncertainty and we remain focused on helping customers get the best possible value.”
Earlier this year, Tesco warned that profits could fall in the year ahead, citing increased uncertainty caused by the conflict in Iran, which began in late February. However, some economic indicators have suggested that the war has not yet had a significant impact. Last week, official estimates for UK growth in the second quarter were upgraded.
The company said it now expected to make underlying annual profits of between £3.15bn and £3.3bn. That represents an upgrade from its previous expectation of at least £3bn in profits but the bottom end of the range would still mark a fall from a year earlier.
Sales at established UK Tesco stores were up 1.5% as food sales motored, but the group’s Booker wholesale arm continued to struggle, with sales falling 2.6%.
The supermarket said it was increasingly using artificial intelligence across the business, including in a meal-planning assistant that was tested from April with 280,000 staff before being launched for customers in September.
It said AI was also helping to cut costs by making in-store stock replenishment more efficient and improving energy efficiency in its supermarkets.
Tesco shares rose 4% on Thursday morning.

British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:51:05 UTC
15:51:05 KST

Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general building in East Jerusalem as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel, with only seven to remain in the building. Among those leaving is the consul general, Helen Winterton.
The change was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those who aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two-state solution as the best means of ending the Israel-Palestine conflict.
Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign.
There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics.
Israel had ordered the British consulate in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.
The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”
Miliband said the mission remained independent, by which he meant it will continue to report directly to the UK Foreign Office in London rather than through the UK embassy in Tel Aviv.
One former Foreign Office diplomat said: “Israel has always wanted to shut the consulates in Jerusalem […] Israel will come for the French next.”
Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn. “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.”
He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”.
Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that, having withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the staffing at the mission in future months.
He said Britain would not take any reciprocal action against Israel while the two sides engaged in talks, in effect suspending discussions until a new Israeli government is formed.
UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and that it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt, regardless of the imminent election outcome.
The sources emphasised that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory. It was thought not feasible to defy Israel since the UK diplomats would have no security protection.
Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to provide vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal.
Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.”
Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.
The incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.
The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the UN and most of its members as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel, as Britain has become increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seems prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments have thought is unachievable through his methods.
The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel, and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believed this a matter for international courts to determine.

Yemen’s government needs tribes to defeat the Houthis. Will they join?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:50:08 UTC
15:50:08 KST

Yemen’s government needs tribes to defeat the Houthis. Will they join?
Yemen’s tribes could prove crucial to government’s fight against the Houthis, but many may wait for evidence of sustained military gains before choosing sides.
Sanaa, Yemen – The Yemeni government’s new military offensive against the Houthis is testing more than the balance of forces in the country – it is also testing whether the government can persuade powerful tribes in Houthi-controlled areas that the balance of power is beginning to shift.
For years, many of the tribes hostile or wary of the Iran-backed Houthis have stopped short of openly confronting the movement, deterred by their military strength and by previous failed uprisings. Those same tribes are now looking to the internationally recognised government’s newly-activated frontlines – on the Red Sea coast, Marib and al-Jawf primarily – to see if the limited advances made since the Dawn of Yemen military operation launch this week can turn into sustained gains.
The offensive by the Saudi Arabia-backed government forces follows major Houthi gains in September, when the armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) swept across the country’s Red Sea coast. The Houthis captured vital trade corridors, including the port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.
While airstrikes have inflicted losses on Houthi forces over the past few days, pushing towards Houthi strongholds where the group has been entrenched since the war started in 2014, including Sanaa, Saada, and Amran, remains a formidable challenge.
With the government declaring an all-out war on the Houthis, pledging to recapture Sanaa, tribal distrust of the government may diminish, prompting tribes to shift positions at the right time, experts say. The role of the tribes could therefore prove critical to the government’s ability to advance deeper into Houthi-controlled territories.
On Monday, Marib governorate – the government’s stronghold in the north – saw a large tribal rally attended by tribal sheikhs and local anti-Houthi fighters from tribes such as the Jadan from Marib, Nihm from Sanaa and other allied tribes.
The rally announced a general mobilisation to support the armed forces in the battle to “restore the state and topple the Houthi coup”.
“If this tribal support translates into actual mobilisation and sustained participation in the battle, tribes will help government troops advance toward Houthi-controlled areas and the Houthi heartland, including Sanaa,” said Adel Dashela, a researcher at the Sana’a Center for Strategic Studies.
Over the past decade of war in Yemen, tribes have repeatedly mobilised against the Houthis at a local level, but deep divisions and a lack of sustained outside backing have prevented the emergence of a unified tribal front. Nevertheless, tribes can potentially be a key source of manpower and influence for the government.
“Tribal fighters remain indispensable to any future campaign against the Houthis. But to be effective, their military engagement must occur through formalised state and coalition command structures, rather than as an independent vanguard,” Dashela said.
‘Wait for the right time’
Tribes in Yemen do not want to risk confronting Houthi forces without support, and they “wait for the right time” to act, Abdulsalam Mohammed, chairman of the Yemeni Abaad Studies and Research Center, said.
“The tribes seek a powerful state, and once they find the state reliable, they can side with it,” Mohammed said.
He added that tribes do not want to repeat mistakes made by tribes that had rebelled against the Houthis, and then not received enough support from the government.
“Those tribes revolted against the Houthis, and they were crushed amid the absence of the government’s effective role,” Mohammed said.
In January 2019, fighting broke out between the Houthis and the Hajoor tribe in northwest Yemen’s Hajjah, lasting several weeks. The Houthis eventually captured the Hajoor areas in March of the same year.
At the time, Saudi Arabia dropped food, medical supplies and weapons to besieged Hajoor fighters, but this did not prevent the tribe’s defeat by the Houthis.
Mohammed said that even in areas where the Houthis have local support, some tribes could gradually shift their allegiance towards the government, if they saw it as serving their interest.
“Not all tribes fighting for the Houthis are staunch supporters. Their motivations range from pragmatism to ideological loyalty and material necessity,” Mohammed said.
‘A friend of the tribe’
Over the past decade, the Houthis have weakened traditional tribal power structures in areas under their control, co-opting some leaders and replacing others with loyalists. They have defeated tribal challenges, and have withstood not only conflict with the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia, but also bombing by the United States, the United Kingdom and Israel. All of that has reinforced a perception among tribes that the Houthi military capability had become “invincible”.
A tribal sheikh in northern Yemen, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that the Houthi military “supremacy” in the country over a decade-long war has “dwarfed the political and military role of the tribe”.
“Before the Houthi takeover of power, the government was like a friend of the tribe,” he said. “Today, the tribe is subordinate to the Houthis.”
The Houthis, according to him, used three tactics to tighten their grip on territories under their control: military force, financial incentives and their public identification with the Palestinian cause.
“The Houthis used military force if negotiations or financial incentives failed to win the tribes’ backing. Moreover, the Houthi military support for Palestine has earned the group additional popular and tribal support,” said the tribal figure.
As the Houthis built up enormous military and financial power over the past few years, the tribal sheikh said tribes acting alone could not match the group’s power. He also said that the government’s reported gains on some frontlines could not by themselves be taken as a sign that the Houthis were collapsing.
“A concrete government advance on the battlefields would reassure some Yemeni tribes that the Houthis have lost ground,” the tribal sheikh said. “Once this materialises, anti-Houthi and neutral tribes can feel confident and begin confronting the group.”
