Lithuanian government extends temporary protection for Ukrainian refugees until March 2028 – Interior Ministry
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:32:52 EEST
15:32:52 KST

The Government of the Republic of Lithuania has decided to extend temporary protection for Ukrainian citizens who fled the full-scale Russian aggression until March 4, 2028, the Ministry of the Interior of Lithuania reported on Wednesday.
The decision aligns national legislation with the European Union Council's decree prolonging the temporary protection mechanism for an additional year.
"The war in Ukraine continues, so we need to ensure clarity and stability for the people who have fled it and currently live in Lithuania. The extension of temporary protection allows them to continue legally living, working, and building their lives in Lithuania until it is safe to return to Ukraine," Minister of the Interior Martynas Katelynas stated.
The ministry reported that the Migration Department has already begun the process of replacing digital temporary residence permits for Ukrainians with documents valid until March 4, 2028, starting October 5. The procedure remains standard, is carried out free of charge, and entails no additional requirements.
Applications are submitted through the MIGRIS electronic migration system, after which applicants must visit any convenient customer service branch of the Migration Department by prior appointment to present their original documents.
According to the Lithuanian migration authority, more than 52,000 Ukrainian refugees currently hold valid temporary residence permits in the country under temporary protection, and nearly 109,000 Ukrainians have registered in the MIGRIS system since the beginning of the Russian full-scale invasion.

====================================================================================================

Portuguese hospital lets pets visit owners in wards: a paradigm shift?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:32:20 UTC
15:32:20 KST

In northern and central Europe, pets stay outside hospitals. São João's flexible model unites clinical benefits and safety, with no infections yet. "There is too much fear," says the doctor who helped draft the project's rules.
Since 9 July, São João, one of Portugal's leading public university hospitals, has been opening the doors of its wards to visits from pets.
The "Pets and Company" project brings together different professionals from the One Health São João (source in Portuguese) programme, as well as from the Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance Prevention and Control Unit and the hospital's Humanisation service. The initiative is part of a strategy aimed at breaking isolation and relieving the exhaustion of prolonged hospital stays.
The therapeutic potential of animals is far from a recent discovery. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany have used them in psychiatric and physical rehabilitation treatments for humans since the 19th century. The term "pet therapy" (animal-assisted therapy) was scientifically recorded in the 1960s by a US psychologist who fortuitously discovered the healing benefits of these interventions.
In Portugal, trained and certified dogs for emotional support sessions have been working in hospitals for several years, including at São João, in partnership with volunteer handlers from associations.
On 30 May 2023, a 77-year-old patient admitted to Cascais Hospital, recovering from a haemorrhagic stroke, received a visit from her own dog, in a reunion that took place in an outdoor area of the health unit.
This unprecedented experience is now being expanded by São João through a comprehensive protocol created from scratch, which goes a step further and normalises the practice of bringing pets into inpatient areas, recognising them as part of the patient's immediate family and giving those who have been away from home for a long time moments of comfort under safe sanitary conditions.
What does the protocol say?
Visits are requested by the health professional (doctor or nurse) in charge of the patients, who is responsible for flagging each case, and they are not available to everyone in hospital. A tailored assessment is always made of the risks and benefits.
Once informed, the team responsible for the programme assesses whether there is a clinical need and whether the infection-control conditions at the chosen location allow the visit to go ahead. Other patients in the ward are also asked whether they feel comfortable with the presence of animals.
Once authorisation is given, the patient's family must submit a veterinary medical certificate proving that the animal's vaccinations and deworming are up to date and that it has behaviour compatible with the demands of remaining in a hospital setting.
"Any professional, from security staff to a doctor or nurse, who sees that something is not in line with the protocol can interrupt the visit," said Filipa Ceia, spokesperson for the One Health São João Group, to Euronews.
If the animal is "anxious" because of the "noise on the ward", appears "aggressive" or is "visibly dirty", the visit is "immediately called off", the infectious disease specialist and vet warns.
Dogs, cats and even "more exotic species" are allowed, as long as "all the conditions are met", says Filipa Ceia. While in hospital areas, the animal must be accompanied by an adult.
Each patient can enjoy these half-hour meetings once every seven days. The project gives priority to those who are terminally ill or in long-term hospitalisation.
To the team's surprise, it is male patients who have most often requested that their four-legged companions be allowed into the hospital, although the small sample does not allow for definitive conclusions. "Men may be more fragile when they are ill. They realise that there are things that really matter in life and want to have them close during their hospital stay," notes Ceia.
Benefits for patient and animal
Studies on interventions assisted by trained animals report clear improvements in patients' clinical condition: blood pressure falls and the production of hormones linked to stress and anxiety is inhibited. When the family pet is involved, there is "an even greater benefit", stresses Filipa Ceia.
Euronews followed the visit of Princesa, who went to São João for the second time in 15 days to ease the longing for her owner, António, who has been in hospital for three months. The dog was taken to the hospital by the patient's wife, who led her on the lead to the ward.
As soon as the lift doors opened, Princesa could not contain her excitement – and neither could António.
"My heart was pounding with joy. She is like family. She is like a daughter to me," confessed the 65-year-old man, who is undergoing rehabilitation because of balance and walking difficulties.
The diagnosis is still not confirmed, but doctors suspect he suffers from a rare blood disease. The reunion with the dog, who was given to him five years ago after being rescued from the street, is a balm for the soul.
"It makes me feel I want to walk better and everything. This is the joy a person gets," he said. These reunions bring "smiles, cooperation with treatment and an incentive to leave hospital", notes Filipa Ceia, who also identifies benefits for the animal itself and even for health professionals.
"Residual risk"
This initiative was launched at the beginning of July and, so far, no infections have been recorded.
The team behind the project wants to review the protocol at a later stage to correct any shortcomings. Given the procedures in place, a scenario involving "incidents" is nevertheless "highly unlikely", points out Filipa Ceia.
In northern and central Europe, infection-control and public-health rules are stricter. Assistance dogs are prioritised and, when visits by patients' own animals are authorised (usually for patients in palliative care), they take place in isolated facilities, namely in open courtyards or gardens adjoining the main building.
Take the example of Sint-Trudo Hospital in Sint-Truiden, Belgium. In July 2023, this health unit opened an independent pavilion (source in Portuguese), connected to but separate from the main building, so that terminal patients or those in long hospital stays could interact with their pets. The access (source in Portuguese) for the animals is via the outside, through a courtyard, and they are strictly forbidden, under any circumstances, from passing through the interior of the hospital.
Instead of erecting physical barriers with secondary structures, São João has drawn up a set of rules which, while maintaining clinical rigour, are part of an agile protocol shaped by scientific evidence.
"There is an excessive fear of zoonotic transmission which is not borne out by the studies," says Filipa Ceia. In fact, the infectious disease specialist notes, "it is easier for most diseases to be transmitted from human to human than from an animal to a human".
"Because we do everything we can to preserve safety and because, once they go home, patients will be living with their animals, the risk really is residual. We have to ask whether, in trying to mitigate the risk, we are not depriving patients of the benefit," she adds.
The boldness of São João lies not only in the balance between empathy and sanitary control, but also in its autonomy and ability to humanise care without waiting for lawmakers, unlike in Italy, for example, where the move was driven by decrees from regional governments.

Can Europe's return hubs work without breaking its own human rights rules?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:30:54 UTC
15:30:54 KST

The EU has approved a legal basis for sending people with no right to stay to centres outside the bloc. Governments say rights will be respected. Rights groups warn the safeguards on paper may not hold up in practice.
EU home affairs ministers gave their final approval to a new Return Regulation in Luxembourg on October 1. The regulation replaces the 2008 Return Directive and includes a legal framework for "return hubs" in non-EU countries.
What governments say
The Council of the EU presents the rules as a way to make returns work. Ireland's Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, Jim O'Callaghan, whose country holds the presidency, pointed to the gap between decisions and departures. "Around two in three people ordered to leave the EU do not actually leave. The revised return rules adopted today will help member states implement swift returns effectively."
The Council says the rules complement the Migration and Asylum Pact and that all return measures must respect fundamental rights. They set obligations on people with no right to stay, who must leave and cooperate with authorities. Non-compliance can bring sanctions from reduced benefits to financial penalties.
People posing a security risk can face an indefinite entry ban or detention beyond 24 months, where justified and proportionate. A European Return Order lets states recognise one another's return decisions, voluntarily at first, with a reassessment after three years.
Hubs require an agreement or arrangement with a non-EU country that respects international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement. Unaccompanied minors are excluded. Separately, Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece, and the Netherlands are pursuing a joint hub in Africa. Greece's migration minister, Thanos Plevris, said the aim is to open a facility in 2027. Rwanda is reported as a possible frontrunner.
A promise on paper
Human rights NGOs worry whether the rights guaranteed in the EU can be enforced once a person has left the bloc’s territory.
Marta Welander, EU Advocacy Director at the International Rescue Committee (IRC), has no doubts. "The proposed idea of return hubs is cruel, costly and counterproductive,” she told Euronews. "No amount of additional funding, training or monitoring design changes the fact that a transferred person's protection would depend entirely on a state outside the EU's legal reach, so proper oversight, rights to appeal and protection from refoulement cannot be guaranteed the way they can be inside EU jurisdiction," Welander continued.
Chiara Catelli, Advocacy Officer at PICUM, said that "no safeguard can make deportation centres a legitimate tool to manage migration." She argues that the transfer itself is a rights issue. "The very fact of sending people to places they don't even know, far from the life they were trying to build, goes against the right to private and family life."
The gaps in the text
Catelli points to what the regulation doesn’t include. "The Return Regulation doesn't say anything about living conditions or timeframes for detention in the return hubs, nor who will monitor the respect of and enforce any safeguards."
The Council's description confirms that details are left to individual deals, like an "agreement or arrangement." This is where the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner, Michael O'Flaherty, objected. In letters published in July to the five countries pursuing the joint initiative, he called for four guardrails.
These include a risk assessment before any hub opens, independent and continuous monitoring with the power to suspend cooperation, legally binding agreements with enforceable human rights clauses, and publication of agreements and findings so parliaments and courts can scrutinise them. These are his recommendations, not clauses of the regulation.
Welander doubts that monitoring is realistic. "It is hard to see how effective monitoring could work in a third country where the EU has no courts, no jurisdiction and no enforcement power at all."
The IRC points to Italy's detention centres in Albania, often described as a blueprint for return hubs, which it has visited twice. "What has been witnessed in Albania includes widespread psychological distress among those detained without proper mental health care, including extremely troubling reports of self-harm."
Who is responsible?
Catelli says responsibility cannot be handed over along with the detainees. "What is clear is that the EU and its member states cannot just outsource their responsibility to protect people's fundamental rights, or to prevent and address violations, especially when those violations are a direct consequence of policies they have put in place."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk made the same point after Parliament adopted the text in June. "EU States cannot simply outsource their human rights obligations to third States in this context."
Welander argues the real bottleneck lies elsewhere. "A major factor behind slow returns is third countries' willingness to cooperate on readmission and document verification - this is widely cited as a bigger constraint than coordination at EU level."
Rights groups do not dispute that the rules apply. They dispute if the new powers can uphold them in practice. With no host country confirmed, the answer will emerge from the agreements governments sign, and from whether those agreements are made public.
The "safe third country" label carries much of the weight, and Catelli says it should not. "A country could be considered safe by the EU and still be unsafe for certain people, depending on their individual circumstances."

Acclaimed Indian actor Nana Patekar dies aged 75
Patekar won three National Film Awards and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honours.
Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker known for his fiery performances in Bollywood films and theatre, has died aged 75.
Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest at his home in Goa, the Press Trust of India news agency reported on Thursday, quoting a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead.
His son, Malhar Patekar, confirmed his death, saying the actor died of natural causes. A medico-legal case was registered, and a post-mortem examination will be conducted, officials said.
Patekar’s career spanned nearly five decades across Hindi and Marathi cinema, theater and filmmaking.
Born in 1951 in India’s western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi- and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters.
Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film Gaman, and later earned acclaim for Parinda and Krantiveer. He gained wider international recognition with filmmaker Mira Nair’s Oscar-nominated Salaam Bombay!
He won three National Film Awards, India’s highest film honours, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honours.
‘One of those rare actors’
Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar’s death, praising his “intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence” as an actor.
“He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations,” Modi wrote on X.
He played a variety of roles, sharing screen space with actors such as Amitabh Bachchan and Shah Rukh Khan and excelling in both serious and comic roles.
“He was one of those rare actors who never needed to do too much to make you sit up and watch. That voice, that intensity, that honesty in every performance… he was completely his own,” said actor Akshay Kumar, who starred with Patekar in several movies.
In 2018, as the #MeToo movement swept the world, Patekar was accused by an Indian actress of sexual harassment during the making of a film in 2008. He denied the allegation and a court in Mumbai dismissed the case last year.
Patekar’s death came days after he appeared at a theater event in Goa, where he spoke about the importance of keeping the performing arts alive.
Patekar is survived by his wife, from whom he was separated, and a son.

Angus Taylor tries to find his place on the migration middle road
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:30:17 UTC
15:30:17 KST

analysis
Angus Taylor tries to find his place on the migration middle road
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.
Angus Taylor arrived at the three-corned migration battle this week with a plan aimed at the middle road between One Nation and the government.
Vowing to slash Australia's temporary workforce by 650,000 people over four years, the opposition leader was trying to land the twin objectives of bringing the fight to One Nation while also presenting an economically sound policy.
With a top line designed to grab headlines — "the largest cut to immigration in Australia's history" — the opposition has pledged deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas should Taylor get handed the keys to the Lodge.
The opposition is the last to join the migration debate. Labor released its own policy several weeks ago, forging ahead with changes to reduce the Net Overseas Migration figure to its Treasury forecasted cap of 225,000 people. One Nation got out of the blocks first, though, flagging a period of negative migration before its policy settles at 130,000 people per year.
The Coalition hit the middle: two years at 100,000 before rising to 160,000 in the fourth year.
That's a deeper cut than Peter Dutton proposed ahead of the last election. So far, Taylor has done a better job at selling the plan than his predecessor. Dutton's pitch was mired in confusion as he struggled to explain which visa categories would be targeted.
But time will tell if the Coalition's revamped policy stacks up. Business groups claimed the plan would harm economic growth, concerns dismissed by Taylor as being made by "vested interests". The aged care sector also raised the alarm.
"I think the problem is that whenever any party talks about immigration they use these sort of flashy headline numbers that … appeal hugely to people who want less immigration, terrify everybody who relies on immigration, and we get this sort of big swirling debate and we need to stop doing that," Aging Australia chief Tom Symondson told ABC's Radio National this morning.
The policy wasn't formally costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), despite senior figures insisting they worked closely with the independent watchdog. Taylor's office modelled the policy and asked the PBO to confirm if it was budget neutral.
The Australian Financial Review reported that Taylor's team had told MPs not to say the migration policy was officially costed. Of course, the PBO can't discuss what it's working on. It declined to comment when asked on Wednesday.
Loading...
It's a far cry from Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam's declaration last month that the Coalition would do the work One Nation failed to do.
He argued this morning that it would be done. Just not right now. That job will be completed closer to election day and by that time Duniam will be well out of the political fray, having confirmed he'll be exiting politics by the end of the year.
The shadow of One Nation looms large over the policy. Both the Coalition and One Nation have used the term "breathing space" to describe why Australia requires the cuts. The blueprint was also released just days before Taylor is scheduled to headline the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane.
He's the first Liberal leader to attend. Flyers promoting CPAC placed the opposition leader in a trio alongside Pauline Hanson and Nationals leader Matt Canavan.
A storm in a coffee cup
While the government largely stayed out of the migration debate this week, it was facing another storm over a decision to wind back surcharges.
A ban on additional card payment fees, announced earlier this year by the Reserve Bank, came into effect last week. The move was originally championed by Labor MP Jerome Laxale before the RBA even started looking at the issue.
The central bank expanded it beyond Laxale's original focus on debit cards, arguing the change was a win for consumers. As such, the government started selling it as a cost-of-living measure, with Anthony Albanese and other MPs taking to social media to herald the change.
But within days the sentiment began to shift — turbocharged by the Australian Tax Office's decision to jump on board and ban credit card payments on tax bills. That opened another can of worms.
The business backlash was fierce. The ATO refused to budge, despite holding a crisis meeting about the issue on Wednesday. It argued that only 2.3 per cent of payments to the ATO are via credit.
So far, the government has shown little interest in helping the ATO solve the problem. Labor may be a little relieved that it's the tax office that's become the focus of the story, rather than the additional 50 cents many people are paying for their coffee. At least for now.
Loading
COP that
So, where has the prime minister been this week? He's been off in Fiji and the low-lying atolls of Tuvalu where Australia had organised an international conference to highlight the impact of climate change on the Pacific.
Albanese made the promise way back when climate change was front of mind for the public and Australia's relationship with Pacific neighbours was lagging. The idea was to bring world leaders to the region to see what's going on for themselves.
But the years have chipped away at that promise. First, Australia wasn't able to secure the right to host the UN climate summit, known as COP, in its own right. Albanese and minister Chris Bowen had to settle for a precursor to the main event in Türkiye in November.
One by one, world leaders declined the invitation to come and, as time went on, the government had to accept that mostly ministers and other officials would visit Tuvalu.
In all, 36 people boarded the plane to Tuvalu. Mauritius's Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam and East Timor President José Ramos-Horta were the sole leaders from outside of the Pacific to attend.
Both Albanese and Bowen have defended the poor showing, arguing world leaders don't typically attend pre-COP, which is hardly the main event.
So, was it a flop? That was the question foreign affairs reporter Stephen Dziedzic tackled this morning — a recommended read if you have a spare moment this afternoon.
He argues that it's hard to say for certain just yet. We'll have to wait to see if there are concrete outcomes from COP31 held next month. But the gap between what the government hoped the event would be and what was delivered is hard to ignore.

Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
09:30:00 EEST
15:30:00 KST

Russia's winter campaign against energy infrastructure has begun. Will Kyiv be left without electricity, heating and water?
On the night of 29-30 September – ten days earlier than last year – Russia's winter campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure officially began. Ekonomichna Pravda (EP) sources say Russian ballistic missiles and drones have been primarily targeting energy facilities in Kyiv and the surrounding region. Their targets include thermal power plants, combined heat and power plants, hydroelectric power plants and electricity transmission infrastructure.
Last winter demonstrated the problems that massive strikes on critical infrastructure can cause in people's everyday lives. This year Ukraine is heading into the heating season better prepared. Power generation has been restored, backup power sources secured, security measures strengthened, equipment stocked up, and repair crews replenished.
But as everyone knows, no level of protection can fully shield the power grid from Russian attacks, meaning that Ukraine is highly unlikely to get through the winter without some disruptions to electricity, heating and water supplies.
Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin has no desire, and certainly no plans, to agree to an energy truce any time soon, given that he sees further strikes as a means of exerting pressure on the Ukrainian authorities and influencing Kyiv's position ahead of possible negotiations.
Moscow is likely to focus its attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine's most densely populated city, in an attempt to influence the public mood in the capital – something the Ukrainian authorities cannot afford to ignore.
The Kremlin's overall objective is to bring about a humanitarian catastrophe and render the Ukrainian capital uninhabitable. Read on to find out how Kyiv is preparing for the heating season, what challenges lie ahead, and what its residents should expect.
Resilience Plans
In early March, Ukraine's National Security and Defence Council approved Comprehensive Resilience Plans for regions and major cities. The plans set out step-by-step roadmaps to prepare critical infrastructure for the next heating season.
EP has looked at what the plans involve, how much they are expected to cost to implement, and whether they can all feasibly be put into practice before the cold weather arrives. The plans cover four key areas, some of which may overlap.
- The first area concerns protection for critical infrastructure. It covers air defence measures and the completion of Level 2 protective shelters at facilities belonging to Ukrenergo (Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator), Naftogaz (the largest national oil and gas company), the Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine, and regional electricity distribution companies.
- The second area involves building 1.5 GW of distributed generation capacity, primarily in the city of Kyiv and Dnipropetrovsk, Odesa, Poltava and Kyiv oblasts. Distributed generation refers to smaller power generation facilities located closer to consumers, rather than centralised in a small number of large plants.
- The third and fourth areas are about ensuring uninterrupted heating and water supplies.
At the heart of the plans is a simulation of a total blackout, designed to answer a crucial question: how would the city keep its heating and water systems running if that were to happen? "The concept has been dubbed 'Dark, but warm.' In other words, the lights might go out after a bombardment, but there must always be water and heating," Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Centre for Energy Research, told EP.
Immediately after the government adopted the Resilience Plans, energy sector sources told EP they were overly ambitious and optimistic and said they doubted that all the measures could be implemented before winter.
Three years would be a more realistic timescale for completion of the work, the sources said. What has been achieved so far, and how is Kyiv preparing to go into the heating season?
What will happen to the electricity supply?
Before Russia began to attack its power grid, Ukraine had a significant electricity surplus. Generation comfortably exceeded domestic demand.
Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal says Ukraine currently has over 15 GW of generating capacity available during the evening, when demand is at its highest. And that's with only six of Ukraine's nine nuclear reactors in operation (the other three are undergoing maintenance). The plan is to increase available generation capacity to 19.6 GW by 1 November and 21.4 GW by the end of the year.
Meanwhile, electricity consumption last week ranged from 6,800 MW at its lowest to 10,200 MW at its peak. The sharp drop in consumption across the country is linked to Russia's constant attacks on major metals companies, which have been forced to halt production.
Electricity consumption will obviously go up in winter, but if all the planned repairs are completed, power generation should be sufficient to keep the system balanced in normal winter temperatures, a source at an energy company told EP.
"However, we have to factor in that the energy sector will come under attack," the source noted. "We had enough generation capacity on paper at the end of last September too, but after several waves of attacks, we ended up with a shortfall of 5,000-6,000 MW."
So the main risk this winter is not a shortage of generation capacity at the outset, but how quickly that capacity could be lost due to further Russian attacks.
For Kyiv, this is particularly important. Russian attacks have already destroyed a significant portion of the capital's power generation capacity. Some of that capacity is slated to be restored, but once brought back online, the facilities will become priority targets again.
The second major area of preparation is therefore to ensure a reliable electricity supply for the capital. The Kyiv energy ring is built around four 330 kV substations, supported by dozens of smaller 110 kV substations.
The Resilience Plan envisages providing Level 2 protection for these sites. According to sources who spoke to EP, some of the work is already complete and the remainder is due to be finished by the end of the year, despite government statements about a freeze on capital expenditure. Level 2 protection is designed to withstand drone attacks, but not ballistic strikes.
Another part of Kyiv's Resilience Plan is establishing backup power sources. A document seen by EP puts the capital's peak winter load at 2 GW. Critical infrastructure accounts for around 280 MW, and a reserve of generators and cogeneration units is to be set up specifically to keep those facilities supplied.
EP sources say around 150 MW of the planned 200 MW of distributed generation capacity has already been commissioned. According to an energy market source, the city could have 180-185 MW available by the end of the year. Privately owned facilities with a combined capacity of 55-60 MW could also come online before winter; around half of them are ready to start operating.
The main function of distributed generation is to keep critical infrastructure running if the main generation sources or the grid are damaged.
In other words, if there is an electricity shortage, priority will be given to water supply systems, boilerhouses, hospitals, communications, transport and other essential services. For ordinary consumers, emergency or hourly power outage schedules will be in place, as they were last year. What will this mean for the public?
A senior manager at a state-owned energy company told EP: "If temperatures fall below -10°C and some generation capacity can't be brought back online in time, we could be looking at around eight to ten hours of power cuts per day. That's assuming there are no further attacks.
Then there's the pessimistic scenario – heavy strikes and widespread destruction. In that case there might be only four hours of electricity a day, leaving Kyiv without power for up to 20 hours," the source added. Even so, EP sources say Russia will not be able to plunge Kyiv into a total blackout.
In other words, the worst-case scenario for the capital is prolonged power cuts for most consumers, but critical infrastructure kept powered up.
The source concludes: "No one can give an accurate forecast right now. The situation depends on many factors. It will depend on where and how the attacks happen, which power plants are still working, and how quickly they can be brought back online."
What are the risks to Kyiv's heating supply?
Heating is a more complex issue. Kyiv's heat supply system has historically been highly centralised: around 70% of the city is heated by three large combined heat and power (CHP) plants.
That is why backup heat sources are one of the key priorities of the Resilience Plan: modernising old boilerhouses, building new ones, installing cogeneration units, and creating connections between different sections of the heating network.
The idea is that if a major CHP plant goes down, individual districts will be able to receive heat from alternative sources. The problem is that Kyiv's huge CHP plants cannot be fully replicated in just a few months.
"Kyiv's CHP plants have a capacity equal to that of several regional capitals. They were built over decades, when the Soviet Union had virtually unlimited resources," a source in the Kyiv city administration told EP.
For that reason, Kyiv will not be able to fully protect its heating supply system from losing heat this year. An EP source close to the government said that between 2,500 and 3,000 apartment blocks may be left without a backup heat supply this winter. Another source believes the number could be even higher. There are 12,000 apartment blocks in Kyiv.
"It's hard to say exactly which apartment blocks might be left without heating, but potentially the areas at risk are parts of the Solomianskyi, Holosiivskyi and Pecherskyi districts, Teremky, Berezniaky, parts of the Dniprovskyi district, part of Troieshchyna, and even the Obolonskyi district," Kharchenko says.
As with the power supply, what happens next will depend on the scale of the attacks.
The optimistic scenario assumes that the main heat sources will be partly operational and any damage would be repaired quickly, in which case Kyiv should get through the winter without widespread heating disruptions. Backup boilerhouses and bypasses should help localise any problems.
But if the Russians launch massive strikes on thermal power stations and large boilerhouses, heating problems are inevitable. "There are three major plants in Kyiv that have already been attacked. You don't need a crystal ball to know that they're going to be attacked again," says an EP source at an energy company. On 30 September, Russian forces launched relentless strikes on one of the capital's CHP plants.
If this happens, the city will switch to emergency mode. Backup boilerhouses, generators, emergency response teams and mobile equipment will be deployed wherever possible. Critical infrastructure will be prioritised above all else.
But some residential buildings will have no backup heat supply. In the worst-case scenario, the city will have to rely on electricity to make up for the shortfall in heating.
"As a last resort, if some areas have no heating, they should be exempt from rolling blackouts, or at least the power cuts there should be shorter than in the rest of the city. And people will rely on electric heaters to keep warm, just as they did last year," the source explains.
"There are no guarantees that Kyiv will have heating," the source in the city administration told EP. "Ballistic strikes mean there can be no guarantees in principle. A lot will depend on how intense the attacks are."
But one thing is different from last winter. According to Kharchenko, Kyiv will be more resilient to attacks even in the most challenging scenario, as backup boilerhouses, generators, hospitals, staff and invincibility centres are now better prepared. [An invincibility centre is a heated premises stocked with food and power banks to assist residents facing hardships due to power cuts – ed.]
Kyiv will not be left without water, but there are some caveats
Water is another critical part of the picture, as Russia could target the capital's water supply in an attempt to trigger a humanitarian disaster.
Kyiv's Resilience Plan focuses on keeping the water utility running even if the power goes out. To achieve this, pumping stations and other key water supply and drainage facilities must be equipped with backup power sources.
According to EP sources, almost half of the planned 40 MW of backup power has now been commissioned. The rest is due to be completed by the end of the year.
The good news is that most of Kyiv's water infrastructure is underground, so it is more resilient to attacks. However, the water supply system cannot be fully protected from the effects of massive strikes.
"Most of the infrastructure is underground," an EP source in the government notes. "Even at water intakes and large water treatment plants, a significant part of the infrastructure is underground. But concentrated ballistic strikes could still cause serious damage."
According to the source, even major damage to the system would not automatically leave the entire city without water. In the worst-case scenario, the problem would be water quality and the supply to some districts.
Another EP source did not rule out the possibility that in certain circumstances, some areas of the city could be without water for a week or longer. Residents are therefore advised to ensure they have stocks of drinking water at home.
* * *
To sum up, Kyiv is heading into this winter objectively better prepared than it was a year ago. The city has more backup generation capacity, better-protected facilities, alternative heat sources, generators, and well-rehearsed plans for dealing with large-scale attacks.
But that doesn't mean the winter will be easy. None of these measures offers a cast-iron guarantee, because the scale of future attacks and the damage they will cause cannot be predicted in advance.
So the main question is not whether there will be problems – there will be. The question is how quickly the city can bring damaged facilities back online and whether its backup capacity and reserves will be enough to prevent local problems from turning into a city-wide crisis.
For Kyiv, as for the country as a whole, the biggest unknown is something that can't be predicted or controlled: the scale and intensity of future Russian attacks.
Mykola Topalov

In Poland, the investigation into the incursion of Russian drones—some of which had Polish SIM cards—has been completed
Kyiv • UNN
Polish prosecutors failed to identify those responsible for the incursion of Russian drones and closed the case. The army acted according to procedures; some of the drones had Polish SIM cards.
The Polish prosecutor’s office has completed a months-long investigation following the incursion of Russian drones into the country’s airspace, but it was unable to establish who was responsible for the attack. RMF24 reports, according to UNN.
Details
The military prosecutor’s office conducted an investigation for many months, attempting to establish who was personally responsible for the attack. Unfortunately, as reported by Prosecutor Marcin Kozak, spokesperson for the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, the investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator could not be identified.
The investigation was discontinued because it was not possible to identify the perpetrator of the crime, which consisted of violating Polish airspace and thereby creating a threat to public safety
The investigation also examined the Polish army’s response to the drone attack. The prosecutor’s office unequivocally established that the military responded appropriately and in accordance with the applicable procedures. The service members had the right to use combat means and shoot down the hostile objects. The investigation was also discontinued in this regard—no violations were found.
One of the investigation’s most unexpected findings was the presence of Polish SIM cards in some of the downed drones. Investigators are not disclosing whether the cards had been stolen or acquired illegally—this version remains confidential.
Recall
On September 10, 2025, dozens of drones violated Poland’s airspace. As reported by the Operational Command of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Poland, some of the drones were shot down.

Israel ordered Britain in September to close the consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including a trade ban on goods made there.

zaha hadid’s former london headquarters reopens as a public hub for architecture and art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

zaha hadid’s former london headquarters reopens as a public hub for architecture and art
thirty years of architectural experimentation give way to a new public chapter, where the late architect's legacy is anything but static.
ZAHA HADID FOUNDATION OPENS ITS LONDON STUDIO TO THE PUBLIC
Ten years after Zaha Hadid’s passing, the Zaha Hadid Foundation is opening the doors of the architect’s former London headquarters to the public. Located at 10 Bowling Green Lane in Clerkenwell, the Victorian schoolhouse that housed her practice for more than three decades has been transformed into a cultural space dedicated to architecture, design and the arts. Opening on November 3rd, 2026, following a preview on October 29th, the refurbished building will accommodate galleries, a lecture hall, learning facilities and collection displays, alongside exhibitions, workshops and creative residencies. What was once the nerve center of one of architecture’s most experimental practices is preparing to welcome a rather different audience.
The renovation, led by Studio KA, founded by Katherine Nolan and Alex Butterworth, takes a careful approach to the Grade II-listed building, originally constructed in the early 1870s. The ground floor has been reorganized to improve circulation, while original fireplaces and doorways have been reopened and new finishes introduce colors drawn from Hadid’s paintings. Rather than erasing the building’s more recent history, the intervention preserves distinctive details introduced during her occupation, including Z-shaped door pulls and shard-like flooring insets. Furniture and objects created by Zaha Hadid Design also inhabit the refurbished interiors, ensuring that the architect’s unmistakable visual language remains part of the everyday experience.
ZAHA HADID’S STAGE DESIGNS ON DISPLAY
The opening program looks beyond the buildings that made Hadid famous, beginning with Zaha Hadid: Architecture of Performance, the Foundation’s first collection-based exhibition devoted to the architect’s stage and set designs. Curated by Catherine Howe and guest curator Libby Sellers, the exhibition traces her experiments with performance environments across dance, opera and pop music. Projects range from her 1989 collaboration with choreographer Rosemary Butcher and the Music Video Pavilion in Groningen to stage designs for the Pet Shop Boys’ Nightlife World Tour and Mozart’s Così fan tutte at Walt Disney Concert Hall. Together, they reveal how her investigations into movement, abstraction and spatial geometry extended well beyond conventional architecture.
In the second gallery, London-based artist LionHeart presents The Rebar Beneath, a commissioned 11-minute, dual-channel video installation combining film, poetry and performance. Developed through research into Hadid’s archive, the work examines the structures beneath visible forms through layered projections and fragmented spatial compositions. Meanwhile, Pulitzer Prize-winning illustrator Mona Chalabi contributes The Completely Exhausting Inexhaustibility of Zaha Hadid, a visual timeline mapping the architect’s life and creative output. Installed in the foyer, the animated work is projected onto a textile surface inspired by an Issey Miyake coat once worn by Hadid. The program also includes public talks, tours, workshops and a pop-up AA Bookshop.
EXPERIMENTAL JETSET REIMAGINES ZAHA HADID’S IDENTITY
The reopening comes with a new graphic identity by Amsterdam-based Experimental Jetset, extending Hadid’s appetite for experimentation into the Foundation’s visual communications. Rather than relying on a static logo, the designers have developed a flexible typographic language shaped by a distorting grid, allowing letters and compositions to shift across different applications. The system draws on ideas of transformation and continuous questioning that characterized Hadid’s practice, translating them into a contemporary graphic framework. A redesigned website by London-based Made by ON, scheduled to launch during the week of October 12th, will incorporate the identity while offering expanded access to the Foundation’s programs and archive.
To mark this new chapter, the Foundation joins the Architectural Association and Serpentine for 89° of Zaha Hadid, a two-day symposium taking place across their respective London venues on October 30th and 31st, the latter marking what would have been the architect’s 76th birthday. The initiative reflects a broader ambition to activate the Foundation’s archive through research, education and exchanges with emerging creative voices. As Rana Hadid, Chair of the Foundation’s Trustees, explains, the intention is to ‘preserve her legacy while carrying her ideas forward.’ With a former schoolhouse turned architectural studio now becoming a public cultural destination, the Foundation is treating that legacy as something to keep experimenting with, rather than simply preserve behind glass.

visual identity: Experimental Jetset | @jetset_experimental
location: Clerkenwell, London, UK

Spanish autopilot maker taps satellite signals for drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:22:22 UTC
15:22:22 KST

- UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía is researching how drones can navigate using low Earth orbit communication satellite signals when GPS is jammed or denied.
- The ESA-funded project will integrate the satellite-derived data into the company’s autopilot and validate it in a flight-representative environment.
Spanish drone autopilot maker UAV Navigation-Grupo Oesía is working with the European Space Agency on a way for military drones to navigate using signals from low Earth orbit internet satellites when GPS and other satellite navigation signals are jammed, spoofed or unavailable, the company said on October 8.
The research is funded by ESA’s NAVISP Element 2 program, which supports European navigation technology projects. The company did not disclose the value of the funding, the project’s timeline or when the technology could reach operational drones.
The idea is to use satellites that were never designed for navigation. Broadband constellations in low Earth orbit transmit powerful communication signals, and the project aims to extract position and navigation data from them, particularly in the Ka-band, so a drone can still work out where it is when GNSS signals such as GPS or Galileo are degraded or denied. In the industry, such borrowed signals are known as signals of opportunity.
UAV Navigation’s part of the work is to feed this satellite-derived data into its autopilot. The autopilot’s navigation software will combine it with inertial sensors, air data, GNSS when available and camera-based navigation to estimate the aircraft’s position. The company says this approach is meant to keep a drone on its mission in contested airspace, particularly during beyond-line-of-sight flights for defense, security and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance work.
A central element is drawing position estimates from the multibeam, electronically steered antennas that drones would need to communicate with new broadband constellations such as the European Union’s planned IRIS² network. The company says these highly directional antennas are inherently harder to jam or spoof than the omnidirectional antennas used for standard GNSS reception.
Inster-Grupo Oesía, another company in the group, leads the consortium. It also includes the Catalan research center CTTC and engineering firm SICWAVE.
IRIS² is the EU’s planned secure communications constellation for government, defense and emergency users. Under an implementation agreement signed in August 2026, it is set to comprise 348 satellites, including 330 in low Earth orbit and 18 in medium Earth orbit, with first launches planned for 2029 and services starting from 2030.
UAV Navigation, which has built guidance, navigation and control systems for unmanned aircraft since 2004, is part of Grupo Oesía, a Spanish engineering group that says it employs about 4,000 people and works on avionics for European programs including the Eurofighter, A400M, Eurodrone and the Future Combat Air System. UAV Navigation already markets autopilots designed to keep flying in GNSS-denied conditions and has been selected as a technology provider for the European Defence Fund-backed VANTAGE drone project.

Group of Friends of Global Governance calls for respect for int'l rule of law
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:17:04 CST
15:17:04 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- The Group of Friends of Global Governance on Wednesday called for respect for the international rule of law.
The rule of law is a hallmark of the progress of human civilization, providing an essential legal safeguard around which societies are built and international order is shaped, the group said in a joint statement delivered by China on its behalf at the UN General Assembly.
Noting that the international order is again facing turbulence and instability, the group said the rule of law at the international level is under serious strain, risking undermining global peace and security.
"The foundation of the international rule of law lies in faithful adherence to the purposes and principles of the UN Charter," said the statement. "All parties should defend the authority and integrity of international law and jointly uphold the international order based on international law."
The group stressed that all states enjoy equal rights and bear equal obligations under international law, firmly rejecting double standards and the selective application of international rules.
It urged countries to refrain from unilateral economic, financial and trade measures inconsistent with international law and the UN Charter and that impede economic and social development, particularly in developing countries. It also called on parties to settle disputes through peaceful means of their own choice and opposed the threat or use of force in international relations.
International law must keep pace with rapidly advancing technology and provide guidance for its governance, it said, urging all parties to strengthen global governance in emerging areas such as cyberspace, outer space, the deep sea, the polar regions and artificial intelligence, preventing them from becoming new arenas for rivalry and instead making them avenues for cooperation.
The group stands ready to work with all parties to uphold the UN-centered international system and an international order based on international law, while advancing the rule of law, fairness and justice at the national and international levels, said the statement. ■

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- U.S. universities on Wednesday saw pro-Palestinian protesters gather at campus gates for demonstrations marking three years since the war in Gaza began.
Dozens of protesters gathered Wednesday at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), chanting slogans including "Stop the genocide" and "Free Palestine."

Most of the fall was in ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman, where cargoes move between tankers, they added.

S. Korea's August current account surplus hits 2nd-highest at 46.11 bln USD
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:16:50 CST
15:16:50 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 8 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's August current account surplus hit the second-highest on record thanks to explosive growth in semiconductor and tech-related exports, central bank data showed Thursday.
The current account balance, or the broadest measure of cross-border trade, recorded a surplus of 46.11 billion U.S. dollars in August, marking the second-highest figure and trailing only the historic high of 49.73 billion dollars seen in June, according to the Bank of Korea (BOK).
The monthly surplus comfortably stayed above 40 billion dollars for three consecutive months.
For the first eight months of 2026, the cumulative current account surplus reached 279.20 billion dollars, almost a fourfold increase compared to 69.67 billion dollars tallied during the same period last year.
Trade surplus for goods posted its second-highest at 46.81 billion dollars in August, just behind 47.89 billion dollars in June.
Exports jumped 82.1 percent year-on-year to 104.80 billion dollars in August, topping 100 billion dollars for a third straight month on the back of soaring demand for semiconductors and solid-state drives (SSDs).
Imports advanced 23.8 percent to 57.99 billion dollars, led by capital goods and raw materials.
Service account deficit totaled 1.68 billion dollars in August, lower than a deficit of 1.97 billion dollars in the previous month.
Within services, the travel deficit widened in August compared to July, but improvements in the transport and the intellectual property balances helped curb the overall deficit.
The primary income account, including monthly salary and investment income, registered a surplus of 1.92 billion dollars amid seasonal quarterly dividend payouts to foreign investors.
The net assets of financial account, which gauges cross-border capital flow without transaction in goods and service, grew by 40.23 billion dollars in August.
Overseas direct investment by domestic residents climbed by 6.22 billion dollars, while foreign direct investment in South Korea decreased by 1.61 billion dollars.
For portfolio investment, which includes stock and bond trading, overseas investment by local residents gained by 16.60 billion dollars, but foreign investment in local stocks and bonds shrank by 4.85 billion dollars. ■

Poland concludes investigation into Russian drone incursion: some had Polish SIM cards
An investigation into a large-scale incursion of Russian drones into Polish airspace in September 2025 has been closed because those responsible could not be identified.
Source: Lublin District Prosecutor's Office; European Pravda, citing RMF24
Details: The military prosecutor's office spent months investigating the attack, trying to establish who was responsible.
Unfortunately, as reported by prosecutor Marcin Kozak, a spokesperson for the Lublin District Prosecutor's Office, the investigation has been closed because the perpetrator could not be identified. Most of the case materials, including the justification for the decision, are classified.
"The investigation has been closed because it was not possible to identify the perpetrator of the crime, which constituted a violation of Polish airspace and thereby posed a threat to public safety," prosecutor Kozak said.
The investigation also examined the Polish military's response to the drone attack. The prosecutor's office unequivocally concluded that the military had responded correctly and in accordance with the procedures in force. The soldiers had the right to use military force and shoot down hostile objects. The investigation was also closed on this matter, as no violations were found.
One of the investigators' most surprising findings was the presence of Polish SIM cards in some of the downed drones. The investigators have not disclosed whether the cards had been stolen or illegally purchased, and this information is classified.
Background:
- During the first large-scale incursion of Russian UAVs into Poland on 10 September 2025, around 20 drones entered the country. Debris was found in various parts of the country, with some drones flying almost 300 km from the eastern border.
- On 13 September, NATO launched Operation Eastern Sentry in Poland in response to the incident.

How October 7 redrew the map of the Middle East
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:11:24 UTC
15:11:24 KST

Map of Middle East redrawn after October 7
Three years of war have upended alliances, weakened US influence and reshaped the region’s power balance.
In the past three years, following the October 7 attacks and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, the wider region has been marked by conflict, economic turmoil, and a shattering of the balance of power.
The network of alliances maintained by Iran, long central to its regional power, has been hit hard and severely weakened. Yemen’s Houthi rebels remain one notable exception.
Israel has made gains. Many of the leaders of the Lebanese group Hezbollah and the Palestinian group Hamas have been killed, while Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was also assassinated in February. Israel occupies most of Gaza, where it has also killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and reduced much of the enclave to rubble.
Its military aggression has come at a cost, isolating it from its traditional allies and making it globally unpopular, including in the United States. The potential for more normalisation deals with Arab countries seems unlikely, at least in the short term.
Instead, Israel continues to launch attacks across the region, crossing previously held red lines – such as the 2025 attack on Doha, Qatar – and making many governments around the world view it as the primary source of unrest in the Middle East.
US not a protector
“Before October 7, the US’s entire policy in the Middle East rested on normalising Israel’s presence in the region through its so-called Abraham Accords,” HA Hellyer of the Royal United Services Institute said, referring to the normalisation deals with several Arab states, including the United Arab Emirates. “Israel’s response to the October 7 attack ended that.”
Instead, rather than a stable Middle East with Israel at its centre, the US entered into a war with Iran this year, and has since looked on as Tehran targeted US allies across the Gulf, shattering the perceived security of the US security umbrella.
Drones and missiles hit Qatar’s Ras Laffan gas hub and started fires near Dubai airport and at Fujairah’s oil zone. In September, the Houthis surged down Yemen’s Red Sea coast, taking the port of Mocha and nearby islands. Their gains tightened their grip on the Bab al-Mandeb strait, threatening a key route for global trade and energy supplies that had become even more important amid disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
“There’s been a loss of faith in the US as a singularly sufficient security guarantor,” Hellyer continued.
“This is why you’re seeing many in the region talk to other external actors, in addition to continuing, and in some cases deepening their US ties, as well as initiatives such as the Mecca security pact as states in the region look elsewhere for ways to safeguard their security,” he said, referring to the defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan, signed in August, agreeing that an attack on one was to be regarded as an attack on all.
Alliances
Alongside the loss of confidence in the US as a security guarantor has come a dramatic reordering of alliances and rivalries. Much of Iran’s network – most notably Hezbollah, whose reputation had long served as a deterrent against Israeli attack – appeared to buckle under Israeli pressure.
That, in turn, emboldened an Israeli military push that saw troops invade Lebanon in October 2024 and again in March 2026, and seize Syrian territory during the brief power vacuum that followed Bashar al-Assad’s ouster in 2024.
“The Middle East has always been multi-aligned. However, now it’s even more so,” Sanam Vakil, the director of the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House, said of the increased leverage given to external actors, such as Turkiye in Syria and China’s involvement in negotiations over the end to war on Iran, as Beijing finds its own energy supplies under threat.
“It’s ironic, since October 7, it’s Israel that has emerged as the revisionist power and Iran almost as the status quo power,” she said of the apparent reversal in status of the two belligerents, with Tehran seemingly more focused on regaining the ground it has lost in the last three years rather than advancing beyond them.
However, none of this was to overstate Israeli influence, or liken it to a regional superpower, Vakil cautioned. “Israel may currently be the preponderant military power in the Middle East, but real power is typically classed as being able to project stability, which Israel hasn’t shown itself able or willing to do,” she said.
Clogged arteries
While Israel and the US hoped February’s attacks would swiftly topple Iran’s government, they have instead opened a new front. Tehran now wields economic leverage over Israel, the US and their partners through the Strait of Hormuz, which borders Iran and typically carries about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas, and through Bab al-Mandeb, which is now threatened by its Houthi allies.
Whatever Tehran’s intentions, the economic pain has been uneven. The West, cushioned by emergency reserves, record US oil production and supplies from countries such as Norway, has so far avoided the turmoil of the 1970s oil shocks, when US drivers queued for petrol, even though the current disruption is on a greater scale. In April, the International Monetary Fund trimmed its 2026 global growth forecast only slightly, to 3.1 percent from 3.3 percent.
Gulf exporters, in contrast, have fared far worse. The same assessment cut its forecast for Saudi Arabia from 4.5 to 3.1 percent, and turned Qatar’s from growth of 6.1 percent into a contraction of 8.6 percent.
“It’s curious, in many ways the West’s reduced need for Gulf oil has increased the degree to which Israel has become a liability for the US,” Israeli political economist Shir Hever told Al Jazeera, referring to a diplomatic alliance between the two states long underpinned by Israel’s strategic position in an oil-rich region central to US interests.
“There’s a train of thought in Israel that the current crises may push the Gulf states into allying with it,” he said, while noting the irony that Israel had been the main aggressor in the conflicts that followed October 7. “Though that seems fairly unlikely.”

Will AI replace traditionally Jewish jobs? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:09:49 UTC
15:09:49 KST

Every few months, someone declares that artificial intelligence is about to hollow out the professions that Jewish families have built their American lives around: medicine, law, and finance. Basically, the trades that reward brains and relationships over brawn.
It's a scary headline, sure, but it’s also asking the wrong question. The real dividing line forming isn't AI vs humans, it's professionals who use AI vs professionals who don't – and the ones who don't are the ones who should be worried.
Take radiology, the profession AI was supposed to kill first. In 2016, AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton told the world to stop training radiologists, insisting machines would out-read them within five years.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang later went further, calling radiology the first job AI would "destroy and eliminate." Neither prediction held up. The number of radiologists in the United States has grown, not shrunk, since those warnings, and the American College of Radiology projects the workforce could expand by as much as 40% by 2055.
Huang himself has since reversed course, arguing that people confuse a job's tasks with its purpose: AI got faster at reading images, so hospitals could run more scans, which meant more patients, which meant hiring more radiologists, not fewer. The task moved to a screen, and the job didn't disappear… it multiplied.
AI, despite its benefits, still cannot hold accountability for its output
Think about it: AI is very good at consuming and organizing information, such as reading a scan, drafting a memo, transcribing a deposition, or summarizing a contract. What it cannot do – at least not yet and not in any way a court, a regulator, or a patient would accept – is hold accountability.
A radiologist, not an algorithm, signs the report. A lawyer, not a chatbot, is disbarred for bad advice. Nobody sues Anthropic or OpenAI for advice a doctor or a lawyer chose to act on: the license, the malpractice exposure, and the judgment call all still sit with a human being.
That's probably why AI is already displacing paralegals, junior analysts, and note-takers faster than it will ever displace the doctors, lawyers, and accountants sitting above them: the jobs most exposed are the ones with the least responsibility attached, not the highest income.
That matters for the Jewish community specifically, given its high levels of educational attainment. Pew Research Center’s 2020 survey found that nearly six-in-10 Jewish adults were college graduates, compared with roughly three-in-10 American adults overall. Twenty-eight percent held postgraduate degrees, vs 11% of the general adult population. For those working in law and other professions entrusted with public responsibility, that accountability carries particular weight.
Those statistics aren’t a coincidence of history: They reflect generations of families pushing their kids toward professions where they get paid for judgment, not just for labor. Those are the same professions AI is currently worst at fully owning because judgment implies liability and liability is a human category.
Where AI is a genuine threat is to the tasks underneath those professions, like the associate work, the intake, the scheduling, the note-taking.
And here's the part that should change how we talk about this: That threat is also an opportunity, especially for anyone entrepreneurial enough to grab it first. A solo attorney or a small accounting practice that used to need three junior hires to keep up with paperwork can now run leaner, using AI for transcription, drafting, and research, and put the savings into growth instead of headcount.
But the opportunity isn't limited to people who already own the firm. The same tools can make it dramatically cheaper for someone starting out to build a practice, launch a service business, or take on work that once required a small team. A young accountant can serve more clients, for example, and a freelance writer can research and produce at a scale that once required an editor and researcher. An aspiring entrepreneur can also test an idea before spending heavily on employees, software, or outside help.
Does that sound like jobs disappearing? The story is more about smaller operations suddenly being able to compete with bigger ones – which is exactly the kind of leverage that has historically helped push a striving middle class into the upper middle class. And for a community with a long history of starting businesses, building professional practices, and creating opportunities for the next generation, that is extremely important: AI can lower the barrier to entry, not just raise the bar for existing workers. Jewish communal life has always prized entrepreneurship as much as credentialed professions; AI, used well, is a force multiplier for exactly that instinct.
The pattern holds outside the big three professions, too. Bankers and financiers aren't being replaced by AI models that can price a deal; they're using those models to move faster while the actual business still runs on relationships, trust, and the willingness to push into a new market or a new client base nobody's approached yet. That's a human sales act, not a data-processing one.
Jewelers are using AI to render and iterate on designs in minutes instead of days, but nobody's algorithm is building the relationship with a bride's father or spotting the untapped niche in a new city. The idea has to come from a person willing to take the risk; AI just lets them execute it faster.
Even the most futuristic version of automation makes the same point: Elon Musk isn't promising a driverless economy that runs itself. He's selling regular people the chance to own a robotaxi and put it to work. Someone still has to buy the car, manage the fleet, handle the insurance, and build the business around it. The car drives itself, sure, but the business sure doesn’t run itself.
So will AI replace the Jewish jobs? No, but it will replace the people of any background who refuse to use it. The professions themselves aren't going anywhere because responsibility isn't something you can automate away.
What's actually being tested right now is whether people treat AI as a threat to hide from or a tool to build with. Given how the Jewish community has approached every previous wave of economic change, I know which way I'd bet.

American, Russian officials meet on bringing US investor into Nord Stream gas pipeline to Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
06:09:48 UTC
15:09:48 KST

Top Russian and US officials, including US Special Envoy Jared Kushner, have held talks about bringing a US investor into the Nord Stream pipelines that delivered gas to Germany before Russia invaded Ukraine, five people with knowledge of the situation said.
The discussions included Kirill Dmitriev, a close adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Kushner, the son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, the people said.
Kushner, who has been trying to broker a truce between Russia and Ukraine, views doing business as central to restoring peace. Such a deal would enable US investors to profit from energy flows to Europe once the war ends.
Dmitriev and Kushner have met in Moscow and New York in recent weeks. While it was unclear to what degree they discussed Nord Stream on those occasions, the topic remains on the agenda, two of the people told Reuters.
"Any deals will have to be negotiated by Russia with DFC (US International Development Finance Corporation) and Treasury and must benefit United States taxpayers and companies," a White House official said when asked about the pipeline discussions.
There had been "no Nord Stream discussions recently," the official told Reuters.
Dmitriev, who has campaigned for a resumption of Russian gas sales to Germany, met last month with US Energy and Treasury Department representatives to discuss potential US-Russia energy initiatives. A representative for Dmitriev declined to comment.
It remains unclear how interested Washington is in pursuing the restarting of Russian gas flows to Germany, which is Europe's biggest energy consumer.
A US official said that given the obstacles, a deal is unlikely in the medium term. The US and the EU have sanctioned the Nord Stream gas pipelines, making any restart illegal.
Trump could waive or soften US sanctions, but if Democrats win control of Congress in next month's midterm elections, this would become harder.
Germany and other European countries, which are spending billions of euros to rebuild their militaries to defend themselves from Russia, would strongly resist reopening Nord Stream.
A spokeswoman for Germany's economy and energy ministry said Europe had sanctioned Nord Stream and Russian gas and that Germany had found alternatives. She said any reopening of the pipelines would require government approval, and that was not desired.
Before Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Germany bought more than half of its gas from Russia through the two Nord Stream pipelines. They were mothballed after Moscow throttled supply to Europe and were blown up in a series of underwater explosions in September 2022.
Europe distrusts Russia as Washington-Moscow talks continue
Talks between Moscow and Washington are taking place against a backdrop of deep European mistrust of Russia's motives.
Earlier this year, the heads of five European spy agencies told Reuters that Russia did not want to end the war quickly and was using US talks to push for business deals instead.
Relations between Russia and Germany, which is among the biggest providers of military support to Ukraine, have hit a low ebb, as officials in Berlin have accused Russia of mounting a systematic campaign of hybrid attacks.
Some German lawmakers say that business deals would bolster Moscow as it pursues war with Ukraine.
"This threatens to be a dirty deal that will cost Europe dearly," said Michael Kellner, a lawmaker who led German energy policy in the aftermath of the Ukraine invasion.
"Americans and Russians will share the profits," he said.
While Germany's coalition government opposes restarting the pipeline, Alternative for Germany (AfD), the country's most popular political party, wants to do so.
Dmitriev will meet the AfD leadership early next year to discuss selling Russian gas again.
But selling ownership of the company that controls the Nord Stream gas pipelines to a US investor or restarting Russian gas faces hurdles.
The company is 51% owned by Russian state energy giant Gazprom, with a further 31% split between two German entities and the rest in the hands of a French and a Dutch firm.
The two German shareholders are seeking to keep their shares to maintain German influence if Gazprom sells its stake, another person said.
Days after the Moscow meetings, Kushner said in Kyiv he had spoken to European counterparts about how the war pushed up energy prices, advocating "prosperity agreements" to encourage peace and give "leaders... something to look forward to."
Germany, Europe split over potential Russia gas deal
While a gas deal would please the Kremlin, it would split German public opinion, which is divided over buying Russian energy, and Europe, where Poland and the Baltic states are particularly vulnerable to Russia and reject energy ties.
Poland's political leadership is watching the discussions to reopen the pipeline but remains firmly opposed, one person with knowledge of the government's thinking said.
Kushner and Dmitriev have also been discussing the sale of a collection of businesses, from oil refineries to petrol stations in Europe and elsewhere, owned by Russian energy company Lukoil, two other people familiar with the matter said.
Under that plan, a consortium of the DFC federal investment agency and investors from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates would buy the assets, while US authorities would lift sanctions, those people said.
"On Lukoil, Steve (Witkoff) and Jared (Kushner) worked with DFC to negotiate a substantial upfront payment and profits interest for the United States," said a White House official.
Lukoil and Gazprom did not respond to requests for comment.
