====================================================================================================

Menopause patients left without treatment: what is happening in Spain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:04:57 UTC
14:04:57 KST

The shortage of Lenzetto has had a domino effect on other menopause hormone treatments in Spain and other European countries. Spain's Health Ministry expects supplies to improve in November, but Spain's Medicines watchdog warns the timetable is still unclear.
Hundreds of thousands of Spanish women have spent months encountering problems getting hold of some of the hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms.
What began as an issue with a single medicine — Lenzetto, a transdermal estradiol spray — has finally triggered a domino effect in the market for hormone replacement therapies (HRT).
The shortage of Lenzetto drove up demand for other estradiol formulations, such as patches and gels, which were not prepared to absorb it. Over recent months, Aemps has recorded supply issues affecting medicines such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva.
The result has been months of supply problems, patients searching for their medication from pharmacy to pharmacy, and authorities trying to find alternatives.
November could mark the start of an improvement, although there are still doubts about when supply will truly return to normal.
The Secretary of State for Health, Javier Padilla, told Euronews on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein in Austria that the situation should start to ease from next month.
Spain's Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Aemps), however, warns that the forecasts communicated by Lenzetto's manufacturer, Gedeon Richter, "have not always been accurate".
Gedeon Richter confirmed to Euronews that it expects Lenzetto to be available again in Spanish pharmacies starting in the second half of November. However, the company acknowledges it may not be able to fully meet demand throughout 2027 due to global supply constraints, though it expects to gradually meet demand starting in the second half of 2027.
European issue
The problem is not confined to Spain. According to Padilla, a sharp surge in demand has outstripped manufacturers' production capacity in several European countries. Aemps also considers this to be an international supply issue affecting, to varying degrees, different European Union member states.
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has confirmed to Euronews that it has been informed of the supply issues regarding Lenzetto and is considering possible coordinated measures at the EU level to mitigate the impact. The matter will be addressed in upcoming meetings of the European group responsible for medicine supply issues.
The EMA further notes that it is aware of recent supply problems involving other estradiol-based medicines in the EU. However, these cases have not been deemed critical at the European level and are being managed by national authorities.
The crisis mainly affects women who use these therapies to alleviate symptoms associated with the menopause, although estradiol is also used in other clinical situations, including the prevention of osteoporosis and gender-affirming hormone treatments for trans women.
From Lenzetto to a domino effect
The crisis was brewing for months. Aemps began receiving reports from users about difficulties in finding Lenzetto in February and contacted pharmaceutical company Gedeon Richter at that point. Initially, the company insisted it was meeting demand as normal.
The situation changed soon afterwards. The laboratory reported that it was facing a surge in demand it could not meet immediately and problems with the device used to administer the medicine. Weeks later it announced that it had run out of stock and that the issue was affecting all its markets throughout 2026.
Aemps also maintains that the company failed to meet its obligation to notify in advance of incidents that could disrupt the continuous supply of the medicine. Consumption of Lenzetto had risen very rapidly. In Spain, distributed units rose from around 13,000 in 2018 to about 123,000 in 2024.
Gedeon Richter explained to Euronews that demand had outstripped its manufacturing capacity and that the availability of the applicator used to administer the medication could not keep pace with the growth. The company emphasises that the shortage is unrelated to any quality or safety issues with the medication.
To increase supply, the company states that it is maximising its current capacity and developing new manufacturing options and suppliers. Furthermore, it is establishing a new plant and a new production line.
Spain raised the price, but it was not enough
The government has tried various ways to increase the availability of these medicines. Among them, as Padilla explained, raising the regulated price in an attempt to attract more supply to the Spanish market. But the measure failed to resolve the problem. The Secretary of State stressed that the difficulty goes beyond price: manufacturers do not have sufficient capacity to cope with the sharp rise in demand.
The Health Ministry then explored another option. It contacted manufacturers of alternative treatments that are not reimbursed by the National Health System and signalled its willingness to consider funding them in order to widen the options available to patients.
According to Padilla, this route has also not delivered the expected results so far. The companies told the government that they did not have enough production capacity to increase supply, even if their products were to be publicly funded. Aemps confirms that the Health Ministry has held talks with the holders of these alternatives, although no reimbursement requests have yet been formalised.
More than 25,000 signatures reach the Health Ministry
While the authorities look for solutions, patients have begun to mobilise. More than 25,000 people have supported, in barely three weeks, a petition calling on the government to take urgent action over the supply problems. Its organiser, 49-year-old Rebeca Marín, who uses hormone replacement therapy, is due to submit the signatures this Tuesday, 6 October, at the Health Ministry.
The petition calls on the authorities to act preventively in the face of future supply problems and to ensure that when a medicine is unavailable, there are accessible alternatives for patients regardless of where they live. The financial aspect is particularly important. Some of the existing alternatives are not covered by the public system, forcing patients to bear the full cost.
The Institute of Women demands "urgent" action
The issue has also reached the Institute of Women, which has asked the Health Ministry and Aemps to tackle "as a priority and urgently" the supply problems. The body acted after receiving complaints from individuals and women's associations concerned both about the difficulty of maintaining their treatments and about the price of some of the available alternatives.
Catalonia turns to pharmacies
In view of the prolonged shortage, Catalonia has decided to prepare an alternative solution. The regional government plans to allow pharmacies to prepare magistral estradiol formulas if supply problems persist.
The measure would allow individualised treatments to be made up from the active ingredient and on the basis of a medical prescription. Compounding pharmacies have estradiol in stock as a raw material, so this route could serve as an alternative when industrially produced medicines are unavailable.
The proposal has, however, opened up a divide between health authorities and pharmacists. Aemps believes magistral formulas should be used only as a last resort, as their absorption can be more variable than that of authorised medicines. The General Council of Official Pharmacists' Associations, by contrast, advocates their use in the current shortage.
The Health Ministry is also studying, together with scientific societies and laboratories, other measures to tackle the shortage, including the possibility of setting criteria to prioritise certain patients if necessary.
When will the shortage end?
For now there is no definitive answer. The situation differs from one medicine to another. For some Evopad presentations, Aemps expects new batches in October and a return to normal from November.
The outlook for Lenzetto is more uncertain. Gedeon Richter has informed Aemps that it will distribute new units over the course of November and will gradually resume supply from that month and throughout 2027.
It is precisely this uncertainty that qualifies the forecast passed on by Padilla to Euronews. November may mark the beginning of recovery, but not necessarily the end of the crisis.

From tigers to turtles: The conservation success stories that prove there’s still hope for wildlife
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:02:07 UTC
14:02:07 KST

“Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an alarming pace, yet amid these steep declines there are grounds for hope.”
Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an “alarming pace” – but experts insist there are still grounds for hope.
New research from the WWF and the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) warns that there has been an average 73 per cent drop in the size of monitored wildlife populations over a 52-year period.
The Living Planet Index (LPI) tracks how species populations are faring around the world and is based on almost 35,803 population trends and 5,790 species of vertebrates (amphibians, birds, fish, mammals and reptiles).
Its latest findings, published in WWF’s Living Planet Report (LPR) 2026, show an average decline of monitored wildlife populations of 2.5 per cent between 1970 and 2022.
The LPI uses changes in population sizes to establish whether, on average, the relative abundance of monitored vertebrate species has increased, decreased or stayed the same. It does not mean that there are 73 per cent fewer wild animals in total today than in 1970.
What is causing wildlife population declines?
The new research warns that habitat loss and degradation are the most frequently reported threats affecting monitored wildlife populations, followed by overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease.
“These threats are, in turn, driven by broader systemic failures across the food, energy and finance systems,” the report states.
The steepest declines are seen in Latin America and the Caribbean, Africa and Asia and the Pacific.
In both Europe and North America, large-scale impacts on nature had already taken place and biodiversity was in a poorer state by the baseline year of 1970, which explains why there is less of a negative trend in these regions.
‘Progress is already underway’
Despite the stark findings, the report highlights the effectiveness of conservation efforts – arguing that there is still time to buck the trend.
Tigers are one of the clearest examples. In 2010, only around 3,200 wild tigers remained and the species seemed to be heading rapidly towards extinction. But by last year, the population had grown to roughly 5,700 – marking a 70 per cent increase.
Atlantic bluefin tuna were also destined for a similar fate, with numbers collapsing from decades of overfishing. Now, populations have recovered to the point where neither is considered threatened.
Over in South Africa, elephants are stable or growing in many of the places where local communities lead the management of the land they share with them.
And last year, the green sea turtle became the first marine turtle ever to be downlisted from Endangered to Least Concern, following decades of conservation efforts.
“Biodiversity continues to be degraded at an alarming pace, yet amid these steep declines there are grounds for hope,” says Dr Kirsten Schuijt, director general of WWF International.
“The report highlights evidence that many species populations are stable or recovering, alongside inspiring stories that show nature can rebound and change is possible.”
Dr Schuijt credits years of “sustained collective conservation” for recoveries in populations of tigers, tigers, bluefin tuna and green turtles.
She adds: “To continue and expand these conservation successes, the industries and systems that drive nature loss need to be transformed.
“Progress is already underway. Not everywhere, and not yet at the scale required, but enough to demonstrate that change is possible. It's time to accelerate the scale of those systemic changes already underway and work together in harmony with nature to build a more sustainable, equitable and resilient world.”
The three systems driving biodiversity loss
While the report acknowledges the importance of these recoveries, it argues that they sit inside a “much larger set of forces” driving biodiversity loss in the opposite direction. The first: the way the world produces and uses energy.
“Burning coal, oil, and gas to power homes, transport and industry generates roughly three-quarters of the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change, which has now become a driver of biodiversity loss across every ecosystem on Earth,” the report says.
The second is the way the world produces and consumes food. Agriculture is the single largest cause of habitat loss and degradation and the leading driver of biodiversity decline.
“The third is the financial system,” the report explains. “Capital allocation – the decisions about which industries receive investment and which do not – determines which activities grow and which shrink.”
In 2023, around $7.3 trillion (€6.5t) flowed into activities that harm nature, while just $220 billion (€197b) went towards activities that protect or restore it.
“Until that ratio shifts, the underlying drivers of biodiversity loss will continue to be funded,” the report says.
Positive tipping points
Experts say that transforming these systems, even if it feels “impossible”, can trigger positive tipping points. This occurs when a threshold is crossed and change accelerates.
The clean energy transition is a clear example of this. Decades ago, a technology like solar power was used in pocket calculators and satellites.
Now, it is the cheapest source of new electricity generation in most countries – one that is cushioning Europe’s energy price shock from the war on Iran.
Last year, solar generated 13.1 per cent of EU electricity, outpacing coal and coming close to competing with gas. Together with wind, solar generated more EU electricity than fossil fuels for the first time in 2025.
“Every phase of the transition has produced resistance from industries and political interests whose dominance is threatened by it,” the report says.
“In recent years, that resistance has intensified in some parts of the world. The pushback is part of how transformations work, and it indicates that the change has become disruptive enough to matter. Moving through this phase takes resilience, a willingness to adjust and the determination to keep going.”

Aegean, Ryanair and Austrian ranked highest in new 10-year European Airline Safety Index
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:56 UTC
14:00:56 KST

In its newly-released European Airline Safety Index, AirAdvisor has ranked the top 20 carriers across a decade’s worth of research data.
Aegean Airlines, Ryanair and Austrian Airlines have been ranked in the top three positions of a new 10-year safety index of 20 major European airlines.
Released by AirAdvisor, the 2026 European Airline Safety Index assessed the 10 largest eligible low-cost and 10 largest eligible mainline carriers operating in Europe, based on 2025 flight volumes reported by EUROCONTROL.
Each airline was scored out of 100 across six weighted categories:
- 40%: safety record, based on accidents published in the IATA Safety Report between 2016 and 2025 inclusive
- 20%: certification and audit, including audit history and International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) data on the effectiveness of national aviation oversight
- 15%: operational safety systems
- 10%: fleet age and technical profile
- 10%: pilot training
- 5%: financial stability
Scores for operational safety, fleet, training and financial stability were based on publicly available regulatory and company information, AirAdvisor said, adding that the index is “comparative and should not be read as a measure of whether any individual airline is safe or unsafe”.
In the final rankings, Greek flag carrier Aegean scored 89/100 with no qualifying accidents in the 10-year period, ahead of Ryanair (86/100) and Austrian Airlines (85.5/100).
Aegean achieved a perfect 40/40 for its safety record and also scored highly on operational safety (13/15), fleet (9/10) and financial stability (5/5).
A perfect safety record alone “was not enough to reach the top”, said AirAdvisor. “British Airways, SAS and Eurowings also scored 40/40 in that category but finished outside the top five, because the index weighs six factors together.”
Low-cost carriers rank high
Three of the top five airlines in the 10-year safety index were low-cost carriers: Ryanair (second), Norwegian (fourth) and SunExpress (fifth). Across the full study, low-cost airlines averaged a score of 79.2/100, compared with 82.8/100 for mainline carriers – a gap of 3.6 points.
"Many travellers assume that a cheaper ticket means accepting more safety risk, but the data doesn't support this," Anton Radchenko, CEO of AirAdvisor, said to Euronews Travel.
"Low-cost and mainline airlines have very similar accident records, and their safety management systems scored the same on average. In other words, the price of a ticket tells you very little about how safe an airline is.”
Low-cost carriers outranked mainline airlines on their fleet age and technical profile, with the former scoring 7.8/10, while the latter scored 7.1/10. Low-cost carriers tend to have a younger fleet, with Wizz Air and Pegasus scoring 10/10 in this category.
"A young fleet can bring technological and efficiency advantages, but aircraft age should never be treated as a safety rating on its own," Radchenko said in the report. "An older aircraft that is properly maintained can continue operating safely for decades."

UK motorists can now see live fuel prices on Google Maps

2026-10-08
05:00:11 UTC
14:00:11 KST

Drivers will be able to see live petrol prices on Google Maps for the first time from Thursday, in a move that will help motorists shop around for the cheapest fuel.
Millions of motorists will be able to find the cheapest petrol and diesel prices by searching for a local forecourt in the Google app, in what could prove to be “a major development” in making fuel prices more fair, according to campaigners.
The tech company will use data from the government’s Fuel Finder platform, which displays real-time prices at 99% of forecourts, to show Google Map users the cheapest in their local area.
It is expected to make forecourt pricing more transparent and encourage competition between fuel retailers, as millions face record-high road fuel costs due to the global squeeze on supplies prompted by the US-Israel war on Iran. The average price of diesel in the UK recently hit a record £2 a litre, having risen by more than 40% since late February.
Edmund King, the president of motoring group the AA, said: “Getting transparent fuel prices on to Google Maps is a massive step forward and means most drivers will have easy access to pump prices. Hopefully, this high-level pump-price transparency will also encourage more competitive prices from retailers.
“More transparent prices should reduce the extent of rampant price-matching between fuel stations that is currently seen in many areas. Those competitive forecourts that break rank and offer lower fuel prices can be found if drivers look hard enough and will now stand out more.”
The government’s Fuel Finder scheme was launched in February to help drivers get more competitive fuel prices after a recommendation by the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) in 2023. It is already available via apps including Waze, PetrolPrices, the AA, Confused.com and RAC Fuel Watch.
Luke Bosdet, a spokesperson for the AA, said the Google launch would not necessarily dampen interest in the existing apps, such was “the demand for fuel price information”.
However, the development could “signal trouble for the fuel trade by revealing the forecourt pricing tactics which keep local prices artificially high in their full horror, he said.
The CMA cautioned fuel retailers in August that many were still slow to pass on falls in wholesale diesel prices. These “passive pricing strategies” may have dented competition in the market and kept household costs higher than they needed to be, the watchdog said.
Polly Billington, the minister for energy consumers, said: “Accessing the cheapest fuel should be simple, which is why it is a gamechanger for near real-time fuel prices to be shown on Google Maps for the first time in the UK, helping drivers find the best deal and save money at the pump.”

‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones

From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.
“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.
Outside, on the day after a shadow Conservative Home Office minister had claimed there were “no-go zones” for white people in Luton, there was a hum of activity on Dunstable Road, a thoroughfare lined with restaurants, jewellery stores and shops selling pakoras and other snacks. Further along, shoppers of different races trundled trolleys through the car parks of Sainsbury’s and Lidl.
Blake Stephenson, the MP for Mid Bedfordshire, who lives in a village 15 minutes away from Luton, had claimed at the Tory party conference on Monday that the town was “a very dangerous place” where some communities “live in ghettoes”. “There are parts where white people won’t go,” he said. “They are like no-go zones.”
His comments have been roundly condemned in Luton, but they echo the longer-term far-right framing of the English town as a poster child for the supposed dangers of Islamism and multiculturalism.
As the home town of the far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, it is also where the English Defence League (EDL), the street movement he used as a springboard to semi-celebrity status in likeminded circles, was launched. International far-right figures have eagerly seized on his depiction of the town. The Australian senator Pauline Hanson joined him there in July for a walkabout filmed by a major Australian TV network.
The 2021 census found that 54.8% of Luton’s population were non-white, making it one of four places outside London at that time where the majority of the population was from minority groups.
A day after Stephenson’s comments, there was little sign if any that Bury Park was a place where any group might fear to tread – even those giving out parking tickets.
Among a smattering of white faces on Dunstable Road was a traffic warden, who declined to give their name but said: “I’ve always felt perfectly safe, and if ever there has been a minor incident, generally a member of the public or a shopkeeper has come to my aid.”
Joshua Bozier, 36, a homeless man, said: “To be honest, I feel safer here in Bury Park than in the town centre. I know everybody here, whereas I’ve been spat at and urinated on in the centre. I’ve lived all over and Luton’s not what it’s made out to be.”
He said Robinson “spilled a lot of shit”, but he did point to the past conduct of some Islamist activists in the area, who in 2009 demonstrated against the Royal Anglian regiment’s homecoming parade from Afghanistan.
Only a tiny proportion of the town’s Muslim community were involved, but the incident became a useful symbol for the far right.
Dr William Allchorn, an associate professor at Richmond American University and an expert on the far right, said the relationship between the EDL and the Islamist activists “was mutually reinforcing and for people looking for a European example of the supposed consequences of multiculturalism, Luton came with an unusually ready-made set of images, personalities and stories.
“A series of confrontations occurred at exactly the moment when a new anti-Muslim form of street politics was developing, and an unusually effective political entrepreneur in Tommy Robinson was able to turn those local events into a national and eventually international story.”
Sarah Owen, the Labour MP for Luton North, accused Stephenson of pushing the same “rightwing nonsense” as Robinson. The police and crime commissioner for Bedfordshire, Labour’s John Tizard, wrote to the Tory MP to say: “These statements are not supported by evidence and bear a troubling resemblance to far-right agitators seeking to divide communities.”
Luton’s independent mayor, Javed Hussain, said he was baffled by Stephenson’s claims as he strolled through Bury Park, pointing out Christian, Sikh and Muslim places of worship and emphasising local regeneration.
“I’m at a loss to know why he is saying this because Luton is a very multicultural, diverse town, as well as very vibrant one, so it’s disheartening,” he said.
“Yes, in this area there may be a large number of people from an Asian background, but people from all over do travel here for all sorts of reasons, whether to shop or eat.”
Research by the council has also found that cohesion was strong enough for the town to avoid the fractures that led to violence in other English towns in the past, though there were warnings that more needed to be done, such as broadening cultural experiences for school pupils.
Not unsurprisingly, community relations are never far from the lips of local policymakers. While proud of the aspirational ethos among second- and third-generation British Asians in Luton, including his own family, Hussain said: “Look, if there was something I wish we could do more of, it would be to support children from council estates that are predominantly white. There is always more to do.”

Stockpile food – and wash your hands: is that really how to prepare for environmental catastrophe? | George Monbiot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Would you mind fixing the NHS? And while you’re at it, could you please build an anti-missile system in your garden? Then regulate the banks, replace the water mains, tax the very rich and use the proceeds to rebuild our schools. Well, come on people: what are you waiting for?
I exaggerate, but this isn’t very far from the approach taken by the government’s Prepare campaign. Crucial functions, way beyond the scope of individual action, are dumped on our doorsteps while those in power fail to act. As a result, our national resilience is arguably lower than at any time since the second world war. At the Labour conference last week, Andy Burnham promised “a Britain where people feel the country has got their back again”. To make good on that pledge, he will have to change almost everything.
It’s not that the advice offered by Prepare – a government campaign designed to promote readiness for emergencies – is irrational. But when the state is absent or working against us, households and communities cannot fill the gap. The campaign tells us, for example, to conserve water during droughts by turning off the tap while brushing teeth, or taking a shower instead of a bath. For sure. Every citizen should do their duty. But the government has at the same time declared datacentres “nationally significant infrastructure projects” that can be forced through the planning system, despite two startling facts. The first is that even Water UK – the body representing water companies, those paragons of environmental responsibility – has said there isn’t enough water to support the new datacentres. The second is that, as a freedom of information response reveals, the government has no idea what they are being used for. You could be turning off your taps so the water can be used to nudify celebrities.
Talking of droughts, the government’s National Risk Register seems seriously out of whack. It estimates the risk of a drought with a moderate impact occurring in the next five years at just 0.2-1%. What?? It also estimates the risk of heatwaves with a “significant” impact – by which it means between 200 and 1,000 deaths – at only 1-5% over the next five years. The government estimates there were 2,877 heat-associated excess deaths in England during this year’s hot weather in May and June. There were a similar number of deaths in the heatwave of 2022.
But never mind: the Prepare campaign advises that “if you live in a home that is more likely to overheat … contact your local council, your letting agency or Citizens Advice to find out what help and support they can provide”. Good luck with that. In the meantime, the “future homes standard” is at last due to come into force in March 2028, but thanks to lobbying by the building sector, according to some practitioners it still won’t deliver new homes matched to the climate challenges we face. And local authorities have been blocked from demanding anything better, thanks to the same corporate pressure.
Survive floods, the Prepare campaign tells us, by “packing a ‘grab bag’ of essentials in advance”, moving “valuable items upstairs” and making “changes to your property to reduce the damage flooding can do”. But one in nine new homes are being built in areas at risk of flooding according to data from Aviva, and a recent high court judgment reveals that the law prevents local authorities from blocking such developments, even if they fail a crucial safety test.
These are not the starkest examples of public exhortation colliding with government failure. The Prepare campaign tells us to help stop the spread of avian flu by washing hands “with soap and water” after feeding wild birds. Fine. But at the same time, at the behest of lobbyists, the government is pushing a “poultry sector growth plan”. This will multiply the number of super-incubators of avian flu: namely the factory farms rearing chickens. As the Scientific Task Force on Avian Influenza and Wild Birds points out, poultry farms are where highly pathogenic bird flu first arose. Through their growth and intensification, the spreading of their manure on fields and its runoff into rivers, we could scarcely devise a better formula for generating new variants of the virus and the attendant ecological disasters. Oh hang on, we could: the shooting industry is still allowed to breed tens of millions of pheasants and partridges in similar conditions each year, then release them into the countryside to mingle with wild birds. But do wash your hands.
You’re also advised to “reduce your exposure to air pollution”. How? The government is allowing new homes to be equipped with wood-burning stoves, building huge and arguably pointless new roads and consulting on radically delaying the transition to all-electric vehicles. All, once again, in response to lobbying.
As for food resilience, the Prepare campaign scarcely mentions it, except to say we should stock some “non-perishable food that doesn’t need cooking” in our homes. Last week, a group of anonymous senior food executives warned that, in the face of “material reductions in yield, quality and reliability of supply”, their industry was “defaulting to quick-fix crisis management” rather than taking a strategic, long-term approach. “At present, we are seeing companies either consistently lobby against necessary regulations or stay silent,” they said. The result is a likely failure to address an existential threat.
There was much in Burnham’s speech that delighted me, especially his listing of deregulation as one of the five great evils putting Britain on “the wrong path”. That’s a break with 47 years of policy, in which all governments have dismissed essential public protections as “red tape” that must be cut. The Tories were still at it in their own conference this week – telling us, in effect, they are here to burn it all down. But, like Keir Starmer, Burnham has tied his own hands by pledging to “stick to our fiscal rules”. These rules did not come from government. They were developed by Westminster junktanks and pushed into being by the media. As Larry Elliott has argued persuasively, they are unnecessary and self-defeating.
The threats to our resilience are the same as the threats to our democracy: what Burnham called “that sense of the powers-that-be pulling against the people, not with them”. We’ve had five decades of lobbyists shaping policy, with devastating consequences for our ability to withstand crises. Willing to play our part as we may be, we cannot do the work of government.
- George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist

Rachel Roddy’s recipe for cheese and bread balls | A kitchen in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:10 UTC
14:00:10 KST

Sadly, I’m never going to be able to recreate the cheese and bread balls I made a few weeks ago, because, of the four cheeses used, I recognised only two of them: a bit of gorgonzola and a slice of precious Montgomery cheddar, bought from Da Corrado, a stall on Testaccio market. The other two lumps of cheese, both wrapped in white waxed paper and both quite dry, were, I think, a piece of grana padano and the end of the pecorino we brought back from Umbria. But I can’t be sure, because I didn’t really examine them. Even if I had, it would have been hard to guess; the description “heels of cheese” is appropriate here. What I do know, however, is that the combination of those four grated cheeses with two eggs and enough breadcrumbs to turn the mix into a soft, malleable dough made for fantastic deep-fried balls.
The inspiration for using up the uncertain contents of the cheese box was pallotte cacio e ova, which translates as “little cheese and egg balls”, a typical and much-loved thing in both Molise and Abruzzo, which were, in fact, one region until 1964. Pallotte are resourceful, and were surely invented as a way of using up scraps of cheese (almost certainly local pecorino) and bread. Whatever combination of cheese you use, though, the important thing is to add enough soft white breadcrumbs – anything from 80g to 120g – to turn the mixture into a soft dough that you can then mould into balls, but not so compactly that the tenderness is lost. Like meatballs, cheese balls benefit from a rest in the fridge, so they can firm up before frying. The rest in the fridge also ensures that they are cold, which is important, because the thermal shock of the cold surface meeting the hot oil helps create a crisp shell.
It’s not just my fridge that was (and remains) chaotic; our whole kitchen, which is still missing four cabinets since they fell off the wall, is disorderly to say the least. One of my various justifications is that I am in a suspended state until I finish editing my next book, an exuberant regional recipe book that includes a fair bit of frying. Editing and testing means I’m also feeling pretty fluent in my frying advice. I fry in a smallish, high-sided frying pan, so a litre and a half of oil comes 8cm up the sides; I use a mixture of one-third olive oil (which gives great flavour) and two-thirds neutral peanut or sunflower oil, and keep the temperature around 180C (and certainly not much hotter). Good fritti need a good set-up, too: the pan with oil positioned safely at the back of the stove; a slotted spoon and pair of tongs; a plate lined with kitchen towel to blot excess oil, or a wire rack set over a tray to catch drips; and a big serving plate.
Pollette are a perfect pre-dinner snack, or turn them into a light meal by serving with a mixed salad. Either way, just-fried and steaming-hot cheese and bread balls call for a drink: beer, lemonade, wine. Just make sure it’s cold.
Cheese and bread balls
Makes 24 small or 12 larger balls
2 eggs 
150g grated cheese (whatever you have)
Nutmeg
80-120g soft white breadcrumbs 
1½ litres sunflower or peanut oil, or 1 litre sunflower or peanut oil and ½ litre olive oil
Working in a bowl, beat the eggs lightly, then add the cheese and a good grating of nutmeg, and mix well for a sticky mixture. Add enough breadcrumbs to turn the mix into a soft dough that you can mould into balls.
It pays to weigh the dough, then weigh the first “example” lump as a guide – the lumps need to be about 15g if you are making 24 marble-sized balls, or 30g if your plan is to make 12 ping-pong balls). Roll the lumps of dough between your palms to make smooth, compact balls, then put in the fridge to rest and chill for at least an hour.
Fry in batches in hot oil (180C) until deep golden, then use a slotted spoon to lift them on to the kitchen towel to blot.

Lithuania eyes payouts to bring back diaspora
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Lithuania is considering payments of between €2,000 and €5,000 for families returning from abroad, depending on their size. Returnees would also be offered an integration allowance of up to €1,000 for language courses or help toward the cost of a private nursery.
The owners of the KasKanda dog grooming salon moved to Jauniūnai in eastern Lithuania from Ireland and England five years ago. Since returning to Lithuania, they have not only expanded their family but also set up a business, turning the wife’s parents’ former shop into a dog grooming salon.
“We came back with two Yorkshire terrier puppies and needed somewhere to have them groomed. Eimantė wasn’t working at the time and was expecting a baby, so she said, ‘I’ll groom them myself.’ Well, she didn’t do it quite as she should have, and that made her determined. She said, ‘I want to learn how to groom dogs,’” said Rimantas, co-owner of the KasKanda salon in Jauniūnai.
Rimantas spent 16 years in Ireland but never really felt that he belonged there.
“It doesn’t matter whether you speak the language or integrate into society – you are still a foreigner, someone from another country, and you still feel that you don’t really belong,” he said.
The past six years have been a positive period for Lithuania, with more people returning than leaving. Last year alone, more than 19,000 Lithuanians returned home.
More than 1,000 people moved to each of Vilnius, Kaunas and Klaipėda. Kaunas district was also particularly popular with newcomers, attracting more people than Panevėžys, Šiauliai or Vilnius district.
The fewest newcomers moved to the municipalities of Neringa, Birštonas and Rietavas. Meanwhile, 106 emigrants returned to Širvintos district.
“Širvintos is facing a problem – there are very few flats available. Two apartment blocks are currently being built near the waterfront, another two near the main road, and one more will also be built by the shore,” said Ingrida Baltušytė, director of the Širvintos district municipal administration.
The government is also looking at ways to help people returning to Lithuania settle in.
The Social Security and Labour Ministry’s family support package proposes a €2,000 payment for couples without children who have lived abroad for at least five years. Families returning with one child would receive €4,000, while those with two or more children would receive €5,000.
“The payment could be made in two instalments. The first would be paid when the family returns, and after they have lived here for at least a year, another €1,000 could be provided to help with their integration,” Social Security Minister Inga Ruginienė said.
“Some families return without even having a home to live in. That can hold them back. I think some financial support would certainly help, at least during the period when they are settling in,” said Rimantas, the recent returnee.
But the Širvintos official is not so sure.
“Financial support is welcome, of course, but I doubt it would be enough to persuade people to return. I think people are attracted by other things: the overall economic situation, the political situation and how good life is here,” said Baltušytė.
People who work with emigrants say the government should provide support regardless of a person’s family status.
“Lithuania needs everyone. What about single parents, or people who have never married but have children – would they also be considered? What about older people, whose experience is very valuable? Could they receive support as well? And what about students whose parents remain abroad?” said Agnė Skučaitė-Leonavičienė, coordinator of the Gal į Lietuvą? Initiative that aims to encourage diaspora to return.
According to the ministry’s calculations, the return payment could help 2,000 families move back to Lithuania. The proposal is still being discussed and will still need to be approved by the government and then by the Seimas.

Housing as a Human Right and an Exhibition Reassessing Le Corbusier: This Week's Review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

The week began with World Architecture Day, drawing attention to the global housing crisis as a fundamental element of human dignity, inclusion, and well-being. In a joint message between the UIA and the United Nations, this year's call is to focus disciplinary efforts on building not only residential structures but also systems to better distribute and use what already exists, proposals that enable new ways of living and alternatives for a more sustainable industry. Aligned with this concept, we featured three projects where reuse and representation converge, and three others that help establish a dialogue between what we consider old and what we can expect from the new. On this week's radar, we find another instance to reexamine the canons of modern architecture in Switzerland, the start of construction on a translucent yet hurricane-resistant building in the United States, and a winning entry for a mixed-use urban complex in Austria.
Traveling Structures: National Representation and Reuse on Temporary Ground
Under the twin ideas of reuse and representation, structures are traveling around the world for temporary settings. The timber-framed U.S. Pavilion designed by Marlon Blackwell Architects for the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale, an exercise in national representation originally presented in the Giardini as part of PORCH: An Architecture of Generosity, will be reconstructed at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, in late 2027. In a different kind of movement, TAELON7's Limbo Engawa installation traveled from Limbo Museum in Accra, Ghana, to Art Omi's Sculpture & Architecture Park in Ghent, New York, drawing a parallel between two very different contexts while retaining its architectural language across each site. And in Amsterdam, Ammodo Architecture announced the first edition of Ammodo Architecture Days, a two-day program on November 9 and 10 organized around six themes, including Reuse and Heritage, alongside a symposium, exhibition, publication launch, and award ceremony at Westergas.
Related Article
On World Architecture Day 2026: A Call to Build Better, Build Differently, and Share Resources
Building on What Came Before: Heritage, Memory, and a Carbon Tool
A cultural institution, a design event, and a digital platform each build their own bridge between what is old for us and what is new this week. In material terms, Design Museum Gent reopened within Ghent's UNESCO World Heritage city center, with a new wing by Carmody Groarke and ATAMA linking the museum's historic buildings, the eighteenth-century Hotel de Coninck among them, into a single visitor route built around a restored garden courtyard. On a more disciplinary level, Amman Design Week returned under the theme "Accumulations," examining how everyday materials, memories, and practices settle into a place over time and come to shape it, staged across the city's historic Hangar building, public spaces, and archaeological landscapes. And toward making that dialogue more actionable, HENN launched CarbonBudget, a free digital tool for European building projects that calculates project-specific CO2 budgets to help architects design within the Paris Agreement's 1.5°C target.
On the Radar
"Remettre les Pendules à l'Heure": Villa Le Lac Hosts an Exhibition Reassessing Le Corbusier's Legacy
Running from June 26 to October 25, 2026, "Remettre les pendules à l'heure" (translated as "Setting the Record Straight") is a bilingual French-English exhibition currently on view at Villa Le Lac in Corseaux, Switzerland. Designed by Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret between 1923 and 1924 for Le Corbusier's parents, the 64 sqm lakeside house on Lake Geneva is itself a landmark of early modernism, anticipating three of the architect's future "five points of a new architecture." The exhibition takes a position against what it describes as a wave of historical revisionism surrounding Le Corbusier, reassessing his legacy alongside the roles of figures including Eileen Gray and Charlotte Perriand, and reexamining works such as the Villa E-1027 in Roquebrune-Cap-Martin. Drawing on more than 25 years of research by historians including Arnaud Dercelles, Jean-Louis Cohen, Jacques Sbriglio, Tim Benton, and Robert Belot, the exhibition argues for a history grounded in contextualized sources and historiography, countering narratives it attributes to the distorting mechanics of social media and post-truth culture.
Snøhetta Breaks Ground on Sweetbird North, a Mixed-Use Office and Retail Building in Miami's Design District
Snøhetta has broken ground on Sweetbird North, an eight-story, approximately 11,150 sqm mixed-use office and retail building in Miami's Design District. The building's defining feature is a custom-engineered veil of coiled stainless-steel mesh, draped and tensioned to a structural frame, which functions simultaneously as sunshade, guardrail, and hurricane-resistant exterior screen. Due to Miami's stringent hurricane code, the design integrates required impact glazing, reinforced concrete, and protective screening into a single architectural system. The mesh appears nearly transparent from head-on, becoming increasingly opaque at oblique angles and shifting throughout the day as light conditions change, while reducing solar gain to lower mechanical cooling loads. Each office floor opens onto its own planted terrace, with vegetation transitioning from tropical planting at the lower levels to flowering bougainvillea above, and a landscaped roof crowning the building. At street level, metal-clad columns and extended canopies frame the retail bays. With groundbreaking complete, foundation work is set to begin in the coming weeks. A full-scale mock-up of the façade veil is planned to test performance ahead of fabrication, with installation of the veil system scheduled for the final phase of construction.
Klinglmüller, HENN, and a-stud.io Win Competition to Expand Sparkasse OÖ's Urfahr Campus in Linz, Austria
The consortium formed by Klinglmüller, HENN, and a-stud.io has been selected as the winning entry in the competition to expand Sparkasse Oberösterreich's Linz-Urfahr location. The new building is positioned to the south of the existing office tower, a local landmark since 1979, recognizable for its seemingly floating glass cubes, extending the campus while responding to the scale of the surrounding residential and cultural neighborhood north of the Danube. The addition is composed of three horizontally interlocking rectilinear volumes, each subtly rotated off-axis, whose varying heights rise toward the existing tower. A glazed incision in the northern block references the original floating cube concept. The façade combines glass, recycled concrete, and timber. Internally, a light-filled atrium links all parts of the building: the northern section houses the BusinessCenter with flexible open-plan workspaces and meeting rooms, the central volume accommodates shared facilities including a marketplace, a Future Lab, and a rooftop garden, and the lower southern volume contains a kindergarten and fitness area. At ground level, a public plaza connects the campus to the city.

From Desert Heat to Northern Winters: How Container Architecture Adapts Across the United States
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Far from simply transporting goods from A to B, shipping containers have become a go-to building material across the US, forming the basis of everything from tiny homes to container pools, site offices to workshops. But given the size of the country, and the range of climates found within its borders, the approach to container architecture can vary significantly from state to state, even county to county.
A container conversion in the desert Southwest faces very different conditions from one in New England, while projects along the Gulf Coast must account for humidity, storms, and salt air. These regional differences can influence everything from insulation and ventilation to roofing, foundations, and exterior protection. Let's take a closer look at these regional approaches, the local climate challenges to consider before a build, and the adaptations that can address them.
Regional Approaches to Climate Adaptation
The Arid Southwest
Challenges: Container conversions in Southern California, Arizona, New Mexico, and Nevada must handle extreme heat and UV exposure, along with rapid overnight temperature drops.
Solutions: White or reflective roof coatings can reduce the amount of heat that accumulates within the steel. A secondary roof (ramada) with plenty of overhang can go a step further, preventing the sun from hitting and heating the container directly. Insulation and ventilation are critical, and a climate control system can be a wise addition.
The Icy North
Challenges: The Northern Plains, the Upper Midwest, and New England all face bitterly cold winters, severe freeze-thaw cycles, and heavy snow loads on roofs.
Solutions: For insulation, a combination of exterior cladding and internal spray foam or rigid insulated panels (R30-R60, depending on local climate and applicable codes) can help isolate the steel from the cold. A sloped roof is recommended to shed heavy snow, while flat roofs may need to be suitably reinforced.
The Humid South
Challenges: Container conversions in southern states must deal with storms, extreme humidity, potential hurricane-force winds, and salt-spray corrosion if built near the coast.
Solutions: Closed-cell spray foam insulation can help maintain a comfortable temperature inside the container while keeping humidity out to prevent the damaging effects of condensation. For the exterior, containers are made from weathering steel designed to develop a protective layer of rust, but a marine-grade protective coating adds an extra layer of protection. For high winds, heavy-duty corner castings can be anchored to concrete footings.
High-Density Hubs
Challenges: From New York to LA and Chicago to Miami, container builds must deliver climate mitigation within strict local planning rules and severely limited space.
Solutions: Stacking containers vertically maximizes space while also offering a small amount of insulation, particularly for containers sandwiched in the middle. In hotter regions, a living sedum green roof can help prevent heat buildup and help to accommodate city mandates for stormwater retention.
Permitting, Sourcing, and Siting
Beyond climate, other key container conversion considerations include:
- Code compliance: Conversions must align with local zoning ordinances, building standards, and regional energy codes (e.g., California Title 24).
- Procurement: When sourcing shipping containers in the United States, choose a vetted local supplier to minimize transport costs and carbon footprint.
- Foundation/site access: Depending on soil stability, the container may need screw piles, pier footings, or a gravel pit foundation. There must also be enough clearance for positioning with a truck or crane.
Conventional Construction Is Often the Better Option
While shipping containers can adapt remarkably well to a range of environments and conditions, extreme climates may push modification costs past a tipping point.
When a build demands extensive structural alterations—from additional insulation to custom roofing—the initial cost and efficiency gains offered by a shipping container conversion can be canceled out. Traditional builds can be the better option for designs with open plans, intricate geometries, or particular aesthetics.
Ultimately, containers excel as a building material when regional climate adaptations complement their core strengths: modular prefabrication, adaptability, and that uniquely industrial aesthetic.

Authorities alarmed as Estonian teens climb restricted buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:59:00 UTC
13:59:00 KST

Authorities alarmed as Estonian teens climb restricted buildings
Young people are competing for attention by slipping into abandoned buildings and infrastructure sites, prompting concerns that the urban‑exploring craze may pose real security risks.
In recent years, social‑media content has sharply increased in which youngsters outdo one another, breaking into empty buildings and poorly guarded sites and performing feats there. One thing is adrenaline hunting and chasing fame, on the other hand it is often vandalism and theft, and according to experts hotheads may in extreme cases even be used in hybrid warfare.
The former Harju District Court building in Tallinn, the emptied Swedbank headquarters, Viimsi winter garden, but also the Paldiski nuclear site or Levira's television and communication mast at Valgjärve. These are only a few examples of startling videos shared in communities dedicated to the subject.
"Above all, attempts are made to find such places where people have no access. Then it is filmed, it is especially cool if in that video there is some kind of entry method that could be especially complicated," described Anders Allandi, head of the Ida‑Harju proceedings unit of the Northern Prefecture.
One of the most popular places where sometimes neck‑breaking tricks are done is the gigantic elevator in Hiiu, Tallinn, which has stood empty for almost 20 years and whose tower rises far above the surrounding buildings.
Jan‑Erik Moon, with an IT background, has been mapping old buildings for 20 years already, and Raigo Kotkas, who earns a living project‑based, got hooked six years ago and today even run a corresponding YouTube channel. The hobby carries internationally the name urban exploring or briefly urbex, which can be translated as discovering the urban environment. In Estonia it originally meant mainly exploring old military installations or shelters. Jan and Raigo call themselves rather hobby historians and photographers and emphasize that they try to visit sites correctly. Jan has even conducted official tours in the Hiiu elevator with the owners' agreement.
What bothers Jan and Raigo is that when for a long time the circle of enthusiasts in Estonia was quite small, then in the last couple of years an explosion occurred. If earlier enthusiasts were motivated by history, architecture and the joy of discovery, then now the average age has come down a lot and there is outdoing one another.
Let's be clear — urbex is not fundamentally a negative phenomenon and there are also more correct practitioners, but lately in TikTok alone there are in Estonia about 500 accounts connected with the urbex topic, where thousands and thousands of clips have been uploaded, a large part of which is clearly the illegal activity of rascals.
Separate sub‑types are roofing, that is, climbing in high places, and diggers, who explore tunnels and other underground structures.
The police have also noticed a clear rise, confirms Anders Allandi, head of the Ida‑Harju proceedings unit.
"Everything starts with simple and accessible buildings, like the music high school, the Liivalaia courthouse, some other abandoned building that is visible and known to everyone. From there it moves to more extreme. For example some kinds of masts, excavators, building roofs," he said.
According to Marko Künnapas, sales manager of the Riigi Kinnisvara (RKAS), their portfolio contains across Estonia about 600 properties with altogether around a thousand buildings. Among them is the music high school complex in Kivimäe, Tallinn, which has stood mostly empty for about ten years and consists of five buildings. A large number of break‑in and rampage videos have been recorded there. RKAS has indeed made efforts to protect the buildings, and at the dormitory one can even read young people's "feedback."
"The headache is that this involves resources that are spent on it, and it involves costs, and these costs per site can reach tens of thousands," said Künnapas.
The videos show a clear dynamic: when the first break‑in has occurred and becomes known, a mass invasion and decline follows. For example the former Viisnurk factory in Pärnu, where skis were once produced.
"At some point all the security systems were broken there and basically the entire archive contents were thrown down from the fourth floor into the stairwell," said Jan.
Or the once popular Mereranna sanatorium in Narva‑Jõesuu. "Where actually at the beginning of this year everything was still quite in order, they broke in, smashed all the security there and in just the past summer there were a whole 14 fires," said Raigo.
Because social media requires public sharing, paradoxically the pranksters themselves document their crimes. There are videos where a crowbar, an angle grinder is used or a hole is smashed in a stone wall with a hammer. A vivid example is the Soviet‑era shelter in Õismäe. In the end the owner had no choice but to place multi‑ton concrete elements in front.
In the videos there is also quite a bit of teasing owners, security firms and even the police.
"In places where there is security, they have a so‑called five‑minute rule, meaning within five minutes you basically have to be gone from the site. You have to be able to run through the building with sirens blaring," said Raigo.
Allandi admits that probably only a fraction of cases reach the police, but when they do, it is formally a break‑in, which is a misdemeanor and may involve a fine. If the break‑in perpetrator is under 14, the matter usually ends with a conversation with the culprit and their parents.
A separate issue is that for damaged property a civil claim may also threaten. One thing is financial damage, but everyone highlights the physical dangers, which begin with mold, inhaling which is harmful, up to the possibility of falling to one's death. In one music school video, for example, a boy trips and flies through a door glass.
One thing is young people's risk behavior, but lately more and more videos have come from sites that can be called vital infrastructure. For example a clip from the end of August, where a masked group breaks into the Valgjärve television and communication mast.
It is still light outside and one worker's car stands in front of the building, but at the same time the guys stroll on the roof. In the end the intruders admire the sunset 350 meters above ground at the top of the mast, through which among other things ETV's picture is transmitted into many homes.
It is also noticeable that urbex enthusiasts have clearly climbed, without owners' knowledge, for example to the top of the chimney of the Iru thermal power plant, accessed the Paldiski nuclear storage, Tallinna Vesi and several Eesti Raudtee sites, which should be quite well guarded.
Just last week a video was posted of how a stranger climbed in the dark into the crane cabin at the Rail Baltic terminal construction in Ülemiste. Experts warn that on the one hand in the current era of hybrid war videos may provide information, on the other hand hotheads may be used for some mischief.
"I think that danger may be great, we actually see in the context of hybrid war very many acts that we could not yet yesterday think of in hybrid war. These acts develop at tremendous speed and all the more we ourselves must be careful how or what we do," said Allandi.

Real wages set to fall in major European economies, except Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:57:10 UTC
13:57:10 KST

Italy, Spain, France and the UK are projected to see declines in real wages between the first quarters of 2026 and 2027, while Germany is expected to record growth. Euronews Business looks at what is driving the divide.
Real wages — pay adjusted for inflation — are projected to fall in Italy, Spain, France and the UK between the first quarters of 2026 and 2027, while rising in Germany, according to the OECD’s Employment Outlook 2026. In Italy and Spain, they are expected to remain below their early 2026 levels until at least the end of 2027.
“In the future, geopolitical uncertainties and a time-limited increase in energy costs may significantly weaken labour markets while exerting further upward pressure on inflation, which likely will depress wages,” the report said.
The report notes that projections are “based on the assumption that the disruptions from the conflict in the Middle East are sizeable but limited to a relatively short period of time”.
Alexandre Georgieff, an OECD economist and one of the report’s authors, said differences in projected real wage growth can be explained by different outlooks for inflation, unemployment and labour market slack.
Unless otherwise stated, all figures below compare real wages with their level in the first quarter of 2026.
Across the eurozone as a whole, real wages are expected to fall by 0.4% in mid-2026 and return to their early 2026 level by the first quarter of 2027. By the end of 2027, they are projected to be 0.7% higher.
Italy sees the largest fall
Italy is expected to record the largest decline in real wages among the five countries, falling 1.9% below its early 2026 level in the third quarter of that year.
A slow recovery is expected to follow. The decline narrows to 1.4% in the first quarter of 2027. By the end of 2027, real wages in Italy are still projected to be 0.6% below their early 2026 level. Italy's annual inflation rate was estimated to reach 4.1% in September.
“In Italy, high energy costs are expected to wipe out recent real wage gains, reflecting the country's heavy dependence on imported oil and gas,” Georgieff told Euronews Business.
“Its recovery in 2027 is expected to be limited because few collective wage agreements are due for renewal that year and slack remains in the labour market.”
Spain shows no recovery
Spain's decline is smaller, but it lasts. Real wages slip 0.4% in the third quarter of 2026 and 0.7% in the fourth.
Spain's decline is smaller but more persistent. Real wages are projected to fall 0.4% in the third quarter of 2026 and 0.7% in the fourth.
They then remain 0.7% below their first-quarter 2026 level through all four quarters of 2027.
By the end of 2027, Spain is projected to have the largest decline among the five major economies, at 0.7%.
Georgieff said that Spain is expected to see strong job creation, but continue to face high inflation, largely driven by energy prices. Prices in Spain were estimated to be 5% higher in September compared with the year before.
Italy and Spain are the only two countries among the five where real wages are projected to remain below their early 2026 levels at the end of 2027.
UK falls fast then recovers
The UK has the second-largest projected drop after Italy. According to OECD projections, real wages fall 0.6% in the second quarter of 2026 and 1.5% in the third. They bottom out in the fourth quarter at 1.6% below their first-quarter level.
The recovery is quicker. The decline eases to 1.1% in the first quarter of 2027 and 0.4% in the second. Real wages then move above their early 2026 level, up 0.4% in the third quarter and 1% by the end of 2027.
With annual inflation rising to 3.1% in August, pay remains under pressure.
"The outlook for real pay growth in the UK remains challenging. The UK is particularly exposed to energy price volatility as a result of the conflict in the Middle East. This means inflation is expected to remain higher for longer than in comparable European economies into 2027,” Charles Cotton, senior reward and performance adviser at the CIPD, told Euronews Business.
He noted that the CIPD's Labour Market Outlook suggests employers are becoming increasingly cautious about future pay awards. Rising employment costs, including higher employer National Insurance contributions and increases to minimum wage rates, combined with wider cost pressures such as rising supplier costs, are constraining pay budgets.
France sees a smaller decline
France reaches its lowest point earlier, with real wages projected to fall 0.5% in the second quarter of 2026. The gap then narrows. Real wages return to their first-quarter 2026 level in the second quarter of 2027 and end 2027 just 0.1% higher.
September’s estimated annual inflation rate of 3.4% was below the eurozone’s 3.8%.
“In France, inflation remains relatively low thanks to nuclear power, but wages are expected to adjust only slowly as unemployment continues to rise,” Georgieff said.
Real wages are projected to fall year-on-year in these four major economies between the first quarters of 2026 and 2027.
Germany is the exception
Germany is the only country among the five where real wages are projected to rise throughout the period, despite annual inflation reaching an estimated 3.3% in September.
The gain is small at first, at 0.1% in the second quarter of 2026 and 0.5% by the end of the year.
Growth accelerates in 2027, with real wages projected to be 1.1% higher by the second quarter and 1.7% higher by the fourth. This is the strongest result among the five.
Georgieff noted that Germany's wage projections are boosted by a comparatively tight labour market, with skilled labour shortages and better unemployment prospects. A large debt-financed fiscal expansion is also supporting activity.
Why are real wages growing in Germany?
Enzo Weber, a professor at the Institute for Employment Research (IAB), noted that real wages in Germany were particularly weak in the first years of the 2020s due to surging inflation. “Afterwards, nominal wages started to catch up, supported by collective wage bargaining. What we see at the moment is still driven by this development,” he told Euronews Business.
He noted that the minimum wage increased by 8.4 % at the beginning of 2026 and will increase by a further 5% in 2027.
“Germany witnessed several stagnation years. Now the business cycle recovers with capacity utilisation clearly increasing. This boosts productivity and creates more room for wage increases despite the crisis in manufacturing,” he said.

LIAA to lead efforts to boost Latvian defence companies’ exports and attract investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:54:38 UTC
13:54:38 KST

A subgroup of the Defence Industry Advisory Council has begun work under the leadership of the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) to help Latvian defence companies reach international buyers and support the development of manufacturing in Latvia. At its first meeting in Riga on 6 October, representatives of public institutions, industry associations and chambers of commerce outlined priorities for cooperation on exports, investment attraction and the planning of international events.
Demand for defence technologies is opening up new opportunities for Latvian companies, but competition for contracts, investment and a place in international supply chains is intense. The subgroup’s task is to facilitate information sharing, consider industry proposals and coordinate the work of participating institutions and organisations in line with companies’ needs.
“The defence technology sector offers Latvia an opportunity to develop high-value-added manufacturing, create skilled jobs and increase exports. The Advisory Council’s subgroup allows us to bring everyone around the same table to discuss businesses’ needs and agree on how each institution can help. LIAA’s role is both to help companies reach international buyers and partners and to attract investment for manufacturing development in Latvia. Business initiative is also essential — clearly defined target markets, cooperation with our overseas representatives and regular information sharing. This enables us to work together on concrete business opportunities,” emphasises LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere.
The subgroup will coordinate support from LIAA, the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Economics, drawing on the experience and contacts of industry associations, business organisations and chambers of commerce. At the inaugural meeting, participants reviewed the proposed working model and suggested topics for further work.
Export connections and a broader Latvian offering
The discussion focused particularly on the quality of business meetings at international exhibitions and trade missions. Participants proposed organising dedicated defence industry delegations, approaching potential international partners well in advance and helping companies prepare clear, compelling proposals.
“An international industry event held in Latvia allows us to showcase our manufacturing capabilities far more extensively than we can at a single exhibition abroad. The Drone Summit provides a strong foundation for presenting a broader Latvian defence industry offering — from technologies and finished products to components and assemblies. It also gives mechanical engineering and metalworking companies an opportunity to meet international buyers and enter defence supply chains. Through the subgroup, we can coordinate this work in advance to show international partners both our companies’ areas of expertise and the opportunities for cooperation,” says Ivars Eniņš, Vice-President of the Latvian Confederation of Industry Development.
Participants emphasised that defence supply chains also offer opportunities for companies that manufacture components and assemblies or provide the technologies and services defence manufacturers need. Cooperation among several Latvian companies could also enable them to combine their offerings into broader, integrated solutions.
Cooperation with LIAA’s overseas representative offices, Latvian embassies and military attachés is essential to building export connections. The meeting also addressed the need to update the defence industry catalogue regularly so that it serves as a practical tool for presenting Latvian companies and their offerings to international partners.
Participants reviewed the calendar of international activities for 2026 and 2027, which includes trade missions, Latvian national pavilions and industry events in Europe, North America, Australia and South Korea. The discussion highlighted the importance of coordinating events well in advance and attracting international buyers, partners and investors.
From investment plans to production
Alongside exports, the meeting focused on establishing new manufacturing facilities and expanding existing production in Latvia. Companies were encouraged to inform LIAA about regulatory and administrative barriers that hinder development or influence investment decisions. LIAA can refer these issues to the relevant ministries for consideration.
The forthcoming defence industry investment roadmap was proposed as one of the tools for further work. It examines the investor’s journey from an initial idea to project implementation in Latvia, with particular attention to regulatory requirements and stages where practical improvements are needed.
Participants proposed involving a wider range of finance providers to ensure that companies at different stages of development have access to suitable funding sources — from business angels and venture capital to bank financing for manufacturing expansion. They also suggested establishing clear performance indicators to track the sector’s development and assess the benefits of these activities for businesses.
The subgroup is expected to meet twice a year, with thematic working meetings and information exchanges organised between sessions as needed.

Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin

UK and Germany will face threats together, says Burnham in Berlin
- Published
The UK and Germany will face threats together, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said as he reaffirmed a series of defence and security partnerships.
On his first official European trip, apart from visits to Ukraine, Burnham met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and was greeted with military honours in Berlin.
Speaking to reporters at the German capital's Federal Chancellery, the prime minister said both countries were facing hybrid attacks "on a regular basis" and "it makes sense" to take them on together.
The pair formally ratified the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity.
Burnham said the treaty would "improve our security here in Europe" but also help grow the economy and living standards.
He added that the UK government would now "seek to progress" Germany joining Gcap, the Global Combat Air Programme led by Italy, Japan and the UK to develop a next-generation fighter aircraft.
He outlined partnerships "countering hybrid attacks" and "countering interference in our democratic processes".
He mentioned collaboration on quantum technology and space, adding he was aiming to host the first joint meeting of the UK and German cabinets next year.
The Berlin talks come after intelligence services warned of rising threats, including last month when Germany accused Russia of launching a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Meanwhile, French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the European Union, in an interview with the BBC's economics editor Faisal Islam.
Ahead of a UK-EU summit next month, Burnham said he was "very committed to securing deeper cooperation" and to "see if we can bring the UK closer to Europe".
He told reporters a closer relationship with Europe was in the interests of growth and tackling irregular migration.
In recent weeks he has mentioned the prospect of eventually rejoining the bloc.
The German leader replied: "From our German side, I can assure you that we will do anything what we can do to bring the UK closer and closer back to Europe, to the European continent, to the European Union."

The meeting comes as European leaders have been warning that the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified.
Hybrid attacks can include potentially destabilising activity such as cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.
Sir Mark Lyall Grant, former UK national security adviser, explained that hybrid warfare "falls somewhere between peace and war - it's in that sort of grey zone, an area where Russia has been extremely active for some time".
He told Radio 4's Today that while Russia had posed a threat to the UK since Vladimir Putin became president in 2001, there had been an "intensification" in response to European support for Ukraine following Russia's invasion.
"We know Russia has been mapping undersea cables in the North Sea; that's something I'm sure Andy Burnham will be talking to Chancellor Merz about because it affects both the UK and Germany," he added.
Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport, while the EU's foreign affairs chief also summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels.
It is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.
Meanwhile, questions have been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage.
The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.
Burnham replaced Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister in July, after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.
Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections.
Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.
