South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:45:07 UTC
13:45:07 KST

South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
Guardian analysis of port records and ship-tracking data found that in July and August over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, was loaded at several South Korean ports on to seven tankers that made 14 voyages to Russia’s far east.
Three of the tankers were under UK and EU sanctions. One of them took on about 26,000 tonnes through a ship-to-ship transfer at an anchorage off the southern port of Yeosu.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Finnish thinktank, said the trade “undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea’s support for Ukraine.”
Russia’s capacity to refine oil has been severely disrupted by Ukrainian drone strikes. Its refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% on last year, according to the International Energy Agency.
Thursday’s statement from Seoul said the refined petroleum products involved were not covered by South Korea’s export controls on Russia, which apply mainly to industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
“As reported by the Guardian, the loading of refined petroleum products at our ports does not constitute a violation of our domestic law”, it said.
The government said whether fuel of South Korean origin, such as diesel, had been exported “has not been confirmed”, adding that no diesel, aviation fuel or motor petrol had been “exported” from South Korea to Russia through customs clearance.
It is unclear who owned or sold the fuel, which South Korean port records do not show publicly.
The government also cautioned that the “mere fact that a vessel did not proceed directly to the final destination country stated on its declaration and instead moved to another country makes it difficult to conclude that there is a suspicion of false declaration of destination”.
It said it would examine the tankers’ actual routes, any divergence from their declared destinations and the reasons for them, before judging whether the law had been broken.
The three sanctioned tankers told South Korean authorities they were bound for Japan or Singapore before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Aram Khachaturian, which is not under western sanctions, loaded at Ulsan three times in July and August and on each occasion gave a destination other than Russia before sailing there.
An adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said this week that the shipments stood in “sharp contrast” to South Korea’s sanctions policies.
On Wednesday South Korea’s presidential office said those remarks were “contrary to fact and inappropriate”, and asked Ukraine to refrain from public comment that could damage South Korea’s international credibility.
Ukraine’s foreign ministry reportedly said on Wednesday that it had raised the fuel shipments with Seoul through closed diplomatic channels and asked for an explanation.
Its spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said Kyiv also had “our own data on such activity”.
Seoul, which has also been at loggerheads with Ukraine since Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, on Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv.
“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the foreign ministry said in a statement. “The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”

'Live on forever': Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:42:16 UTC
13:42:16 KST

In short:
Craig Lowndes says the legacy of legend Peter Brock remains powerful, as Australian motorsport marks the 20th anniversary of his death.
Lowndes, who was a close friend of Brock, won the Bathurst 1000 with Jamie Whincup in 2006 just weeks after Brock's death.
What's next?
ABC Sport will have a live blog of the Bathurst 1000 from lights out to the chequered flag on Sunday, October 11.
Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.
It is just that this year's Great Race feels a bit more special, with Australian motorsport marking 20 years since the nine-time Mount Panorama conqueror's tragic death.
A long-time protege of Brock, seven-time Bathurst 1000 winner Lowndes will line up for his 33rd bid at claiming the holy grail of Australian motorsport.
The 52-year-old will share the number 15 Team 18 wildcard with Super2 racer Bayley Hall after Triple Eight Racing Engineering ditched Chevrolet for Ford last year.
Lowndes has paired with rookies since former Triple Eight teammate Jamie Whincup's retirement in 2021, a move that helps the three-time Supercars champion pass on Brock's legacy.
"I'm somewhat gone full circle," Lowndes said today.
"Bayley, we did a track walk the other day, and I literally recalled everything that Peter taught me; from Turn 1, from Hell Corner, all the way around to Murray's Corner.
"For me, I'm hopefully passing on that legacy in some way … it is a milestone year. There's no doubt about that."
Ask Lowndes what he remembers of Brock's counsel, and he will condense his knowledge of the track's 23 corners into a minute: advice like doing all your braking over Skyline or looking for the kink on the inside of the Elbow for your turn-in point.
"Peter was more than just a teammate," Lowndes said.
"His legacy will live on forever. He was bigger than the sport in some regards.
"He was just very much a person that could capture people's attention, hold their attention, but also inspire them for greatness.
"Those are the parts that I miss 20 years on."
Just weeks after Brock died in 2006, Lowndes roared to an emotional Bathurst 1000 win with an up-and-coming Jamie Whincup to pay tribute to his great mate.
"History shows that the gap at the end of the day was 0.5, and that was Brock's number for a long time," Lowndes said.
Whincup added: "The minute's silence, I'll never forget that."
"You generally got someone on the hill yell out or whatnot, but that day, even the birds stopped chirping.
"It was my first (Bathurst) win for the team and a memory that I'll take to the grave."
Seven-time champion Whincup won't be on the grid for the first time since his 2002 debut, making way for Nick Percat to link up with title contender Broc Feeney, and allowing him to focus on his duties as Triple Eight team principal.
Feeney and Percat will be smarting after a horror outing at last month's The Bend 500, finishing 24th out of 26 cars at the Bathurst 1000 curtain-raiser.
The Triple Eight star has never won the 1,000km epic and is second in the standings behind last year's race winner and Grove Racing star Matt Payne.

Naked, gilded Trump statue goes on display at EU Parliament

A gilded statue of US President Donald Trump naked went on display in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg on Tuesday.

Veteran actor Nana Patekar dies at 75
Nana Patekar, a well-known Indian actor and filmmaker, died on Thursday after what Indian media reported was a severe heart attack. He was 75.
Patekar passed away at his home in the scenic state of Goa but was later taken to a hospital where doctors pronounced him dead, news agency Press Trust of India reported.
It said Patekar was found unconscious in his apartment and could not be revived despite 45 minutes of cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Authorities will conduct postmortem procedures to ascertain the cause of the death, the report said.
Patekar's film career
Born in 1951 in the western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built his career over five decades, largely in Hindi and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for his intense, often complex roles, punctuated with unconventional comedy.
In his early work, he earned acclaim for movies like "Parinda" where he played a ruthless crime lord in the menacing setting of the underworld-dominant Mumbai. One of his better-loved movies includes "Khamoshi" — a musical in which Patekar portrays Joseph, a loving yet stubborn deaf and mute father to the lead actress.
India's millennials saw the actor in lighter, comedy dramas like "Taxi No. 9211" where he played a taxi driver who wrecks havoc in a rich man's life after accidentally coming in possession of the key to the latter's wealth. Still, one of his most memorable roles will be that of underworld boss Uday Shetty in the 2007 movie "Welcome." His iconic dialogue from the movie are often meme-d and casually repeated among groups of friends.
Patekar was the recipient of three National Film Awards, several Indian Cinema Awards and state awards. He also received a Padma Shree, India's fourth-highest civilian honor.
#MeToo allegations
In 2018, during India's #MeToo movement, an actress accused Patekar of sexually harassing her on the sets of a movie in 2008.
The actress alleged that he was present on the sets of song which did not feature him and tried to physically get close to her under the pretext of teaching dance moves.
Authorities had launched a formal investigation into the claims, which Patekar consistently denied. The probe was closed approximately a year later due to the lack of sufficient evidence.
India denies bias after Musk's 'oligarchs' jab, says satellite rules 'fair'
India on Thursday defended its satellite internet approval process, hours after US tech mogul Elon Musk accused unnamed "oligarchs" of blocking Starlink's launch in the country.

"You can guess who they are... This is a crime against the people of India!" he added.
India's telecom market is currently dominated by billionaires Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Jio and Sunil Mittal's Airtel. Both their satellite internet ventures, along with Musk's Starlink, have secured early approvals in India but are awaiting spectrum assignments.
For Starlink, this wait has stretched on for four years.
"The suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," officials said in a statement. "Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees. As and when this process is completed for a licensed entity, it may proceed to the next step," the statement read.
Musk has previously too been at odds with Mittal and Ambani over how India should assign spectrum reach.
FYI: spectrum refers to the invisible radio frequencies which enable mobile calls, text messages, and data transmission.
For Musk's Starlink, at stake is access to a satellite broadband market which Deloitte forecasts will be worth $1.9 billion by 2030.
Starlink's India saga also features a layer of India-US diplomacy. Washington has pushed for greater access for Starlink as a goodwill marker in trade talks with countries burdened with President Donald Trump's tariffs. All of this while New Delhi and Washington are yet to finalize a trade deal since reaching an interim framework in February.
Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout
Foreign workers, mostly Indian, building a vast new US consulate compound in Milan, Italy, signed agreements on Wednesday securing payouts averaging tens of thousands of euros each.
The payout is over alleged labor abuses while working for an American construction company.
Over 60 laborers signed the deal to receive their share of a €31 million (nearly $35 million) settlement with Alabama-based Caddell Construction. Prosecutors say this is the largest-ever settlement over labor exploitation in Europe.
The payouts include unpaid overtime, reimbursement for housing illegally deducted from their pay and other hefty damages sought by the prosecutors.
Dilip Ram, a 43-year-old mason from India who worked at the Milan site for over two years, said that the money would go a long way to help his family of five in the Indian state of Bihar.
"Things are better now than before …we get more rest now," Ram said, after signing the deal. "This has led to a lot of change. This settlement will be good. Because the workers had troubles, that’s why this settlement has been applied."
Prosecutors alleged that workers were paid less than $2 (€1.8) an hour, were illegally docked money for housing and denied overtime for working up to 10 hours a day, six days a week. They were reportedly also subjected to threats and not given proper medical care when injured on the job.
While most of the workers were from India, others were from Nigeria, Kenya and Bangladesh.
The Indian workers reported having to pay €5,000 ($5,600) to recruiters to get the jobs. However, the current settlement could not address abuses in India as that is out of its jurisdiction.

Cockroach party claims 1000s of volunteers detained across states ahead of Delhi march
While India's opposition is protesting against the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC), so are other activists and student groups.
One such group is pressure group the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) which has already led a protest demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation in western city of Mumbai, earlier this week. They are scheduled to participate in a similar protest in Bengaluru today and lead one in Delhi on October 10.
CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka on Thursday claimed that thousands of the group's volunteers had been detained across states like Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal "on the grounds that they were planning to attend the October 10th protest."
"How many will you arrest? There are over 250 million cockroaches," he said on X, using the group's chosen term for its supporters.
"Modi thinks he can silence dissent by putting people behind bars. The more people you detain, the more people will show up!" CJP Founder Abhijeet Dipke said in a post on X.
Police authorities in these states have not commented on the matter so far.
All you need to know about the protests
What prompted the protests?
Pressure on Kumar intensified in September after the Indian Express newspaper reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally raised concerns over aspects of the Special Intensive Revisions (SIR) at least 14 times over the past 10 months.
The objections relate to new voter registrations, deletion and restoration of voters in the rolls, filing of appeals against orders restoring voters in the SIR process and the custody and security of the entire electoral roll itself, the report said.
In one of the objections, Commissioner Sukhbir Singh Sandhu reportedly complained that the Kumar acted against the written advice of himself and Commissioner Vivek Joshi and claimed his actions was "unauthorized and illegal."
However, the Election Commission of India (ECI) issued a statement dismissing concerns of an internal rift, saying differing views were a "normal" part of deliberations and that all its actions were lawful.
How many people were excluded?
According to Election Commission data cited by Indian media, over 130 million names have been excluded from the draft electoral rolls since the revision began in October 25. That's roughly the population of Mexico. In India, it adds up to about 15% of the electorate.
Not all the exclusions are contested as they also took double entries and deaths into account.
A clearer idea of wrongfully excluded voters can only emerge after the exercise is complete across the nation.
How has the election body responded?
After denying a rift, the ECI has since taken a number of measures to improve internal procedures and transparency. It has also directed a "special drive" in 20 states and union territories to include voters who have been left out of the rolls due to solvable errors.
How do these protests relate to Modi and his party?
The protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar are partially being viewed as renewed pressure on Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The reason behind it may not be immediately obvious since the ECI is meant to be an independent body. But this might help:
The commission is responsible for overseeing elections and related projects such as the SIR exercise, which is meant to remove redundancies in India's electoral rolls.
Opposition leaders and critics have argued that those struck off in the exercise include a heavy proportion of minority voters and that Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP is using it as a tool to secure future electoral wins. They have also accused ECI chief Kumar of doing the central government's bidding even though the institute is meant to maintain its independence.
The BJP has dismissed those claims, arguing that those removed largely involve dead voters and illegal infiltrators, thereby protecting India's democracy.

Female rage inspires new adaptation of classic novel Little Women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:30:33 UTC
13:30:33 KST

Little Women and Romeo + Juliet adaptations lead Queensland Theatre Company's 2027 season
When Kathryn Marquet was 18, she wasn't interested in anything but making art.
"If anyone had told me at 18, 'You have to get married now', I'd have been like, 'What are you talking about?'" the Brisbane-based actor and playwright says.
"I had other stuff to do first."
Marquet is tapping into that feeling as she co-adapts Louisa May Alcott's Little Women for the stage for Queensland Theatre Company (QTC)'s 2027 season.
In Little Women, Jo March, the second-eldest of four sisters, yearns for a creative life while rejecting the constraints of her gender and the expectation of marriage.
It follows recent adaptations of other coming-of-age novels about young women, from the My Brilliant Career musical to A Room with a View.
These classic stories are finding audiences as young women today continue to grapple with ideas around feminism and choice: from trad wives to the myth of "having it all", she says.
"These characters have other passions, other obsessions and an inner world that exists far beyond the need of a husband," Marquet says.
"We're told we can have a job, children, this and this, but the reality is it's profoundly difficult."
The playwright is excited to explore these ideas through Jo, a character with whom she's always identified.
"Jo feels very out of place in the world she inhabits," Marquet says. "She struggles with her anger because she wants so much more than is being offered to her.
"I think a lot of young women have that experience and aren't sure where they fit in the world."
Marquet sees Jo's fiery temper as resonating with today, when, she explains, "female rage isn't an acceptable sin".
"We're encouraged to be sweet and kind and together, so what do you do with your rage?"
A cozy world
On the flip side of rage, Marquet and her co-writer, fellow Brisbane playwright Maxine Mellor, have been grappling with the question of how to be a good person in a time of crisis, like Jo March.
In Little Women, she tries to figure out how to help as her father serves in the Union Army in the American Civil War. That also has parallels with today.
"All these terrible things are happening overseas and we want to help, but we don't quite know what to do," she says.
"The challenges of being a good person in a complex world are still as relevant today as they were when Louisa May Alcott first wrote Little Women."
While there are contemporary resonances to Little Women, part of the appeal for Marquet of adapting a book that is so well-known and loved is in offering a kind of balm to an audience.
"We want to create this beautiful, cozy world where people can go into the theatre and have a moment of escape and feel safe and feel all the good things about the human condition," she says.
For QTC artistic director Daniel Evans, commissioning a new Little Women was about getting together a group of artists he admires. Not just Marquet and Mellor, but Brisbane director Bridget Boyle and Brisbane actor and playwright Courtney Cavallaro, who will play Jo.
It reflects Evans's appreciation of the local independent scene in which he developed as a writer and director.
"I grew up and came of age surrounded by amazing women, particularly in the independent sector," he says.
"I'm only here because of them, so it's a bit of a gift or a love letter or acknowledgement of these incredible makers of enormous heart and enormous talent."
Difficulties facing drama in Queensland
Little Women is one of two new adaptations by artists from Queensland in QTC's season, alongside a new Romeo + Juliet from First Nations theatre-makers Isaac Drandic and Kamarra Bell-Wykes.
The idea for an all-Indigenous Romeo + Juliet came from Drandic, the company's Head of First Nations Theatre.
Evans is excited to see a First Nations dramaturgical lens applied to one of the world's most famous plays.
"You can't understand through a Western European dramaturgical lens the way a First Nations culture experiences time, love, fraternity and connection," Evans explains.
"That wrestle is where the bravery and excitement of that project is for me."
Making space for local theatre-makers, like Marquet, Mellor and Drandic, is important to Evans.
"I'm constantly in dialogue with everyone, going, 'How do we put Queensland front and centre?'" he says.
"I spend a lot of my job advocating for Queensland and for Queensland artists, while trying to punch up into that national conversation as well."
He's heartened by the depth of talent and skill throughout the Queensland arts community, but aware of the constraints facing the industry.
Evans points to the dwindling of theatre and technical production courses across the country, including Queensland University of Technology cutting the state's only degree in technical production.
It's one of 48 creative arts degrees across Australia that were discontinued between 2018 and 2025.
"Young school leavers being able to enter the industry, to study a technical trade or design course, is difficult," Evans says. "That's something that weighs on my mind."
At the same time, across the country, enrolments in high school drama courses fell by 39 per cent in the eight years to 2023.
In Queensland, the number of schools offering drama fell by 22 per cent, from 323 to 253 between 2020 and 2025, with enrolments falling 39 per cent, from 3,576 in 2020 to 2,194 in 2025.
Those statistics emphasise the importance of QTC education programs such as The Scene Project, in which the company commissions a new short play that is then workshopped and performed by high school students from 130 schools across Queensland.
"Things like The Scene Project and our Young Company [an ensemble of performers in years 9 to 12] have to continue," Evans says.
"When things do tighten, those are the things we have to keep on the table, otherwise we're not going to have a future generation of makers."
Dreaming bigger
It's all part of the answer to the central question for Evans when planning QTC's 2027 season, his second since becoming artistic director: What does the industry need?
"Right now, we need to dream a bit bigger," he says.
"The best thing I can do for Queensland artists, technicians and audiences is just to punch and swing big."
Those big swings include the Brisbane premiere of An Iliad, starring David Wenham, after its sell-out season in Sydney this year; producing a musical, Sweeney Todd, at a time when some commercial theatre productions are cutting runs of major musicals short; and bringing S Shakthidharan's three-hour epic Counting and Cracking to Queensland for the first time.
"The cast sizes are big, the worlds are really epic, and all the stories are quite high stakes, or the characters are at an emotional crucible," Evans says.
The season also includes a new Australian play, the just-announced winner of the $30,000 Queensland Premier's Drama Award: My Roman Empire by Alberto Di Troia.
It's the story of a queer man travelling to his ancestral home in rural Italy and finding it's not "the Eat Pray Love, La Dolce Vita [he] thought it would be". Instead, his long-lost family are neo-fascists.
Evans's sense of ambition also extends to co-productions with other companies: Stereophonic with Melbourne Theatre Company and Belvoir St Theatre in Sydney; and Miss Fisher's Murder Mysteries: Death by Deckchair with Sydney Theatre Company. Evans will direct both.
"These big works we're all staging together [like Stereophonic] are our way of going: 'We want to bring the best theatre in the world to you,'" he says.
At the same time, those collaborations meet Evans's aim of creating pathways for local artists.
"We get to send and showcase some of our amazing Queensland actors and creators to southern states, and that's worth a lot," he says.

Country diary: The changing face of stubble fields, those shortcuts of my youth | Nicola Chester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:30:09 UTC
13:30:09 KST

Stubble fields, those post-harvest acres of short straws, seem to be lasting longer into the season, as farmers respond to changing practices. I have a wistful attachment to stubble fields: for so long a kind of temporary commons where, for a few redundant weeks before autumn or winter ploughing, you could shortcut across them, the dew-filled straws flicking water up the inside of your legs. But today, stubble fields aren’t all equal.
Below Cleve Hill Down, a tractor is drilling winter wheat directly into bare seedbed between the stubble. Regularly sprayed with herbicide, it is free of weeds or any green – a pale-gold spread of machine-knitted tweed. A hundred years ago, the stubble would be left, full of weeds, birds and insects, until midwinter ploughing, allowing frosts to break down the clods.
The next field over, on another traditional farm, is another piece of arable history. Just over 30 years ago, it was the last stubble field to be burned in Berkshire; burning killed pernicious weeds, but a lot else besides. Many farmers had already given up the polluting practice when it was banned in 1993. Today, the stubble here remains while a cash crop of winter wheat begins to germinate – better for soil structure than ploughing. But, being otherwise bare, it’s at risk of erosion from wind and rain, having already been baked to death, and holds no value for wildlife.
Over the hill at Wexcombe, the Hosier family are farming regeneratively to improve soil health rather than deplete it. Even to the untrained eye, their stubble looks different, the standing straws almost lost among the lush, green leaves – it’s a rarity in this landscape. George Hosier takes time to explain that the stubble was drilled with a cover crop – fodder radish, phacelia, buckwheat, clover, vetches – in August while the combine was still in the field, harvesting wheat planted last winter. It’s what he delightfully calls a “five-minute fallow field”.
Some of those cover crops are beginning to flower now, their roots feeding, covering and protecting the soil. Wexcombe’s outdoor-living cows will graze some over winter (fodder they might dream about) before spring barley is planted around April. All that time, the soil – a living, complex resource – will be replenishing, and providing shelter and food for wildlife.

Shiranthi Rajapaksa has been jailed pending investigation into alleged corruption. Authorities accuse her of misusing donation funds during her time as first lady of the island nation.
The wife of Sri Lanka's powerful former President Mahinda Rajapaksa was detained on Wednesday on allegations of misusing donations received for her charity when she was first lady.
Police questioned Shiranthi Rajapaksa at her home and later took her before a court, which ordered her detention for a week pending investigations. Police then escorted Rajapaksa, who had one eye bandaged from recent surgery, to a vehicle to be taken to a jail.
Rajapaksa was accused of misusing funds that her charity received as a donation from a state bank earmarked for the purchase of a scanner for a government hospital.
The then-head of the bank also was arrested for allegedly circumventing procedures in releasing the money to the charity. The court later released him on bail.
The former first couple's son, lawmaker Namal Rajapaksa, has also been detained on charges of bribery.
Ex-President Rajapaksa and his family were adored by the country's majority ethnic Sinhala Buddhists after he and his brother Gotabhaya Rajapaksa led a military campaign to defeat the now-defunct Tamil Tiger rebels and end a 26-year civil war in the island nation in 2009.
His popularity declined after his re-election in 2010 however, over rampant allegations of bribery, corruption and the stifling of freedoms, leading to his defeat while seeking a third term in 2015.
His family had wielded unbridled power — with his son, brothers, nephews and nieces holding top government positions.
The family made a comeback in 2019 when security emerged as a key concern following Islamic State-inspired suicide bomb attacks that killed 267 people in churches and hotels on Easter Sunday.
Gotabhaya Rajapaksa was elected president later that year, but then the country suffered an economic crash brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic, a tourism downturn and his economic decisions.
He was forced to resign and flee the country amid massive public protests.
Anura Kumara Dissanayake later replaced him and became president, for which he campaigned on an anti-corruption ticket in 2024, promising to take action against anyone suspected of corruption in the Rajapaksa family and administrations that preceded them.

Local think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation has urged the government to deepen its collaboration with mainland cities to assist the growing number of Hong Kong residents retiring in Guangdong. 
This would include helping retirees purchase specialist medical services in the Greater Bay Area as an alternative care option.
In its latest research, the think tank noted that there are more than 111,000 Hong Kong residents aged 65 or above residing in Guangdong — an increase of nearly 60 percent compared with a decade ago.
Following a survey of around 1,000 people aged 36 and above who are interested in retiring in the GBA, the foundation found that nearly half face significant barriers when trying to access specialist medical care in the province.
Among respondents over 50, the foundation stressed that the primary hurdle was finding appropriate care rather than affordability.
To address this, the foundation suggested the government purchase high-demand specialist services — such as cataract surgery, knee replacements, and diagnostic imaging — from accredited private healthcare providers on the mainland.
The initiative could, the foundation stressed, provide a viable alternative for elderly residents with urgent medical needs who cannot afford local private healthcare.
It also proposed creating a "Hong Kong-based GBA Care Navigator Network" in partnership with mainland organisations to give retirees dedicated touchpoints and support.

Prison unit at Kærshovedgård could take five years to complete
The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.

Bavarian Nordic sells travel vaccines against diseases including rabies, TBE and chikungunya, a disease spread by mosquitoes.

Danish Defence orders AI-supported system to coordinate responses to drone threats
The Danish Defence will receive a new command system designed to help military and civilian authorities coordinate their responses to drones.
The Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation has signed an agreement with Danish software company Systematic, the agency said Thursday.
“The construction of Denmark’s drone shield is a step closer to the goal with this agreement with Systematic,” Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said.
The system will use artificial intelligence to analyze large amounts of information and identify patterns, unusual activity and potential threats.
The Danish Defence, police and other authorities will be able to access the same information, giving them a shared operational picture from the first drone sighting until the response is completed.

Denmark records more than 1.17 million state pensioners
Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
It was the 13th consecutive month in which the number reached a new high.
The increase reflects longer life expectancy and large generations reaching the state pension age. However, many new pensioners continue working.
In July, 24.6 percent of 67-year-old state pensioners remained in paid employment, compared with 10.6 percent in July 2022.
Velliv consumer economist Thomas Gress said the rise could be connected to rules allowing people to earn income without reductions to their own or their spouse’s state pension.
“For some, retirement life is the freedom to leave work completely behind. Others want to keep their colleagues, some hours on the job, and benefit from the generous deductions and subsidies available for continuing working life once the state pension age has been reached,” Gress said.
The growing pensioner population is also increasing public spending. Statistics Denmark said social benefits cost the state 908 billion DKK last year, five percent more than the previous year.
State pensions were the largest expense in the old-age category, costing 170 billion DKK.
Velliv expects the number of state pensioners to continue rising until 2029, when roughly one in five Danes is projected to receive the benefit.

Nearly one million Danes add credit warnings after breach of 8.8 million CPR records
The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.
About 970,000 people had registered a warning by October 7, up from just under 250,000 on October 1, the Digital Affairs Ministry said.
“The Danes have taken the situation seriously, and they have acted on the advice that has come from the government and from the authorities,” Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said.
A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.
The Agency for Societal Security has recommended warnings for people who have specific reasons to suspect fraud.
Unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system during 10 days in September.
Authorities discovered the activity after the company received an unusually large bill. Each search of the register carries a fee.
The company has not been identified, and authorities do not know who was responsible.
Egelund said it remained too early to determine whether affected people would need new CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.

Denmark proposes ban on sharing AI-generated deepfakes without consent
People in Denmark could gain stronger protection against realistic AI-generated images, videos and voice recordings under a new bill introduced Thursday.
Culture Minister Zenia Stampe of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party, wants to prevent digital imitations of people’s appearance and voices, known as deepfakes, from being shared without their consent.
“With artificial intelligence, you can create manipulated videos and images with a few clicks and share them on social media. It can lead to misinformation and create doubt about what is real,” Stampe said.
The proposal would cover all citizens, including artists, whose performances and presentations could also be protected against unauthorized digital imitations.
Stampe said she had personally experienced having a photograph from her profile turned into a video that appeared to show her speaking.
She described the experience as intrusive, even when such content is labeled as satire.
The minister also pointed to SF, the Socialist People’s Party, politician Karsten Hønge, whose identity has been used in hundreds of fake social media posts about Greenland.
A central aim of the legislation is to make social media companies and other online platforms remove illegal deepfakes quickly.
Satire would remain legal, although Stampe acknowledged that distinguishing satire from unlawful manipulation could be difficult.
She said courts would have to decide whether particular content qualifies as satire or whether that label is being used to justify illegal material.
“It will certainly be difficult, but on the other hand, I also have respect for the fact that we have a very strong tradition of satire in Denmark,” she said.
Stampe hopes the legislation can take effect around the turn of the year.
Denmark expands exemptions from new nitrogen rules for fruit and vegetable growers
More Danish farmers will receive temporary exemptions from new fertilizer restrictions after concerns that the rules could make growing certain fruits and vegetables more difficult.
The Ministry of Nature and Animal Welfare announced that crops including melons, rhubarb, strawberries, table grapes and pumpkins will be exempt from the new nitrogen regulations throughout 2027.
Woody plants grown in nurseries will also be covered by the exemption.
The changes follow a review of the regulations approved by a majority in Denmark’s parliament, the Folketing, in September.
The rules, which take effect at the beginning of 2027, aim to reduce nitrogen pollution from agriculture by limiting fertilizer use.
Nitrogen runoff from farmland has contributed to the deterioration of Denmark’s marine environment.
However, agricultural experts and vegetable producers have warned that the restrictions could create significant difficulties for domestic food production.
The government initially planned to exempt mainly potato growers during the first year. The exemption has now been extended to additional fruit and vegetable producers.
“I am pleased that we have the opportunity to also exempt some berry and fruit growers who otherwise faced major challenges, so they get one more year to adapt,” Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen said.
The exemptions apply only to 2027 and are intended to give affected growers additional time to adjust.
The ministry said the newly exempt crops account for a small share of Denmark’s total agricultural land.
As a result, it expects the changes to have only a very limited effect on the nitrogen reductions the regulations are intended to achieve.
Serum Institute expects high flu levels this winter
Influenza infections are expected to reach a high level in Denmark this winter, according to Statens Serum Institut (SSI).
“We expect a winter where influenza will once again be prominent, while COVID-19 appears to remain at a lower level,” Bolette Søborg, chief physician and head of section at SSI, said in an update published by the institute.
SSI expects both influenza A and B to circulate during the coming season.
“Both the number of influenza cases and influenza-related hospitalizations are assessed to potentially reach a high level,” the institute said.
Influenza A has dominated recent seasons, while influenza B has circulated at relatively low levels. SSI said this may mean that the population has less naturally acquired immunity to influenza B, which could make it account for a larger share of infections this season.
COVID-19-related hospitalizations, meanwhile, are expected to remain at a low to medium level.
People aged 65 and over are being offered free vaccinations against both influenza and COVID-19. SSI said the vaccines are expected to provide good protection against the two respiratory infections.
The institute also expects vaccination against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, to reduce serious illness among infants.
Since October last year, the Danish Health Authority has offered RSV vaccination to pregnant women. SSI said hospitalizations among infants fell by about 70% during the latest transmission season compared with previous years.
“We therefore also expect that the vaccination will significantly reduce the burden of disease among the youngest infants this winter,” Søborg said.
RSV is still expected to circulate among older children and adults, although for most people the infection causes symptoms similar to a common cold, including coughing.

Denmark proposes up to four years in prison for mediation councils that seek to prevent prosecution
The Danish government has introduced a bill that would make it a criminal offense to participate in a mediation council with the aim of preventing public prosecution of a crime.
The proposed penalty is a fine or up to four years in prison. The bill targets councils that attempt to settle criminal matters outside the Danish justice system.
Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen, a Social Democrat, introduced the proposal on Wednesday, arguing that such councils undermine the rule of law.
“It must come to an end that, for example, imams or prominent criminal families can exploit their position to act as judges of law and order and attempt to override the Danish rule of law,” he said.
The proposal revives a bill from the previous government that was not passed before a general election was called in February.
Police have encountered councils in Aarhus
Wammen said several police districts were aware of mediation councils, although he could not give a figure for how many exist.
In 2024, Jyllands-Posten reported that East Jutland Police had encountered such councils in western Aarhus for several years. The newspaper described them as widespread among groups with other ethnic backgrounds.
One anonymized police interview report described a case from 2020 in which a group of “important men” visited the parents of a man who had reported a violent assault.
The visitors wanted to avoid police involvement and suggested compensation for the assault, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Under current rules, a victim and perpetrator can agree to settle a conflict without police involvement, provided there is no criminal conduct such as coercion or witness intimidation. This has made it difficult for police to act against the councils.
The proposed law would also criminalize participation in a council when the purpose is to evade prosecution.
“What we are doing with this bill is that we are taking targeted action against those who sit at the head of the table,” Wammen said.
He cited wiretapping as a tool police could use to establish whether an illegal council was taking place.
“That is because this is something that takes place behind closed curtains and in environments that do not want to talk to the police. That is why we need better tools to combat it,” he said.
The government still needs a majority in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, to pass the bill. It is intended to take effect on January 1, 2027.

Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.

Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.

The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.

Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.

Electric bicycle injuries reach six-year high as imports approach 100,000 in Denmark
Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Greenland municipality imposes temporary alcohol ban
The Greenlandic government, Naalakkersuisut, has introduced a temporary ban on the sale and serving of alcohol in the southern Greenlandic municipality of Kujalleq.
Naalakkersuisut writes this on Friday, when the ban took effect, in a press release.
The ban comes following a request from the municipal council in Kujalleq.
– The purpose of the temporary closure of alcohol sales and serving is to eliminate the threat to children’s welfare and the safety of the population.
– Furthermore, Kommune Kujalleq has expressed concern and insecurity among the municipality’s population in recent times as a result of the fatal incidents that are a direct consequence of alcoholic beverages, the press release states.
It is not specified further which alcohol-related incidents have taken place in the municipality.
Malene Vahl Rasmussen, who is mayor of Kujalleq, confirms in a post on Facebook that she has asked Naalakkersuisut to temporarily halt the sale of alcohol in the municipality.
– Based on the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, we can no longer defend the way we use alcohol, she writes.
In a press release, according to the Greenlandic media outlet Sermitsiaq, she elaborates further.
– We can no longer stand passively by and watch the negative consequences that alcohol consumption has on our surroundings, and merely wait for another serious incident to happen in our society, the mayor writes according to the media outlet.
The ban on the sale and serving of alcohol will last until the executive order is repealed, it is stated.
Thus, it is not clear how long the ban will remain in effect.
It is not the first time that an alcohol ban has been introduced in parts of Greenland.
At the beginning of the coronavirus pandemic, a ban was introduced for a period on the serving of alcohol with an alcohol percentage above 2.25 percent in Nuuk, Kapisillit, and Qeqertarsuatsiaat.
At that time, it happened with the justification that they wanted to protect children who were at home during the pandemic.
RITZAU
Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:25:14 UTC
13:25:14 KST

One of Swedish pop group ABBA’s best-known songs is getting its own exhibition in Stockholm, half a century after its release in 1976.
ABBA The Museum will open an exhibition Sunday celebrating the 50th anniversary of “Dancing Queen,” according to news agencies NTB and TT.
The exhibition will explore how the song was created and why it continues to attract listeners across generations, using music, photographs, objects and personal stories.
“‘Dancing Queen’ is a song that many have a personal relationship with,” museum director Hanna Kimblad Einarsson said in a statement.
“It has accompanied people through parties, weddings, and other major moments in life, at the same time as new generations discover it.”
Among the exhibits are recreated outfits inspired by clothing worn by ABBA members Agnetha Fältskog, Benny Andersson, Björn Ulvaeus and Anni-Frid Lyngstad during a 1976 performance at Stockholm’s Royal Opera.
The performance celebrated the wedding of Sweden’s King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia.
The king has previously named “Dancing Queen” his favorite song, including at the 2022 London premiere of the virtual concert production “ABBA Voyage.”
“It comes as a shock – bang! It has been just as good throughout all the years. It is spot on,” he said at the time, according to NTB.
Before receiving its final title, “Dancing Queen” was known by the working name “Boogaloo.”
The museum also plans to examine how the song has taken on different meanings over time.
“A museum is not just about looking back. We also want to show what happens when music lives on and gains new meanings over time,” Einarsson said.

Denmark plans two new marine nature parks with 67.8 million DKK investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:25:09 UTC
13:25:09 KST

Two areas of Danish waters could receive greater protection from fishing and seabed extraction under a proposal in the government’s 2027 finance bill.
The government and Alternativet, the Alternative, propose spending 67.8 million DKK over three years to establish two marine nature national parks.
The areas would undergo active nature restoration, which could include building stone reefs and planting eelgrass on the seabed. Industrial fishing could also be banned, while seabed extraction would be removed from the areas.
“We have fantastic nature beneath the surface of the sea,” Environment Minister Maria Reumert Gjerding of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said in a statement.
“But the Danish marine environment is also under severe pressure from the way we humans have exploited the sea for decades,” she added.
Torsten Gejl, environment and nature spokesperson for the Alternative, helped negotiate the proposal and said he would like Aarhus Bay to become one of the new parks.
“It is Denmark’s second-largest city, and there is a body of water in Aarhus Bay that has enormous potential, but which is screaming for help,” Gejl told Ritzau.
He said pressures including seabed extraction, sludge dumping and trawl fishing should be removed from protected areas.
The government’s platform calls for five new marine nature national parks. The 2027 finance bill proposal provides funding for the first two.
They would be in addition to two marine nature national parks introduced under the previous SVM government in Øresund and Lillebælt.
If the funding is included in the final budget agreement, political negotiations will follow to decide where the two new parks will be established.
Prison unit at Kærshovedgård could take five years to complete
The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.

“Increased rabies activity among animals has resulted in a significant increase in exposure among humans and thus an increased demand,” Bavarian Nordic said in the announcement.
The company now expects revenue from its travel vaccine business to reach 3.4 billion kroner in 2026, up from its previous forecast of 3.0 billion kroner.
Third forecast increase this year
Thursday’s announcement marks the third time Bavarian Nordic has raised its revenue expectations this year.
At the beginning of the year, the company expected total revenue of between 5.0 billion and 5.2 billion kroner in 2026.
Jacob Pedersen, an investment strategist at Middelfart Sparekasse, said Bavarian Nordic has gained “a new growth engine” through its travel vaccine business.
“The big question is now how much of the rabies boost will hold into 2027. Infection among animals fluctuates from year to year, so next year will face a tough comparison,” he wrote in a comment.
Bavarian Nordic sells travel vaccines against diseases including rabies, TBE and chikungunya, a disease spread by mosquitoes.
The company also sells vaccines for countries’ preparedness against outbreaks, including mpox, previously known in Danish as “abekopper.”
Bavarian Nordic will publish its third-quarter results on 13 November 2026.

The Danish Defence will receive a new command system designed to help military and civilian authorities coordinate their responses to drones.
The Danish Ministry of Defence Acquisition and Logistics Organisation has signed an agreement with Danish software company Systematic, the agency said Thursday.
“The construction of Denmark’s drone shield is a step closer to the goal with this agreement with Systematic,” Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said.
The system will use artificial intelligence to analyze large amounts of information and identify patterns, unusual activity and potential threats.
The Danish Defence, police and other authorities will be able to access the same information, giving them a shared operational picture from the first drone sighting until the response is completed.
Systematic’s SitaWare software will be installed at several military locations and connected to existing drone defence systems.
The agency did not disclose the agreement’s cost or when the system would become operational.
The purchase follows an August agreement with Danish defence company Terma. Terma’s system will collect information from different sensors and provide a combined overview of drone activity.
The two systems are intended to work together as part of Denmark’s response to airborne and hybrid threats. The measures follow incidents involving drones over Denmark in 2025.
Denmark records more than 1.17 million state pensioners
Denmark had a record 1,175,187 state pensioners in August, according to figures from the Jobindsats statistical database reviewed by pension company Velliv.
It was the 13th consecutive month in which the number reached a new high.
The increase reflects longer life expectancy and large generations reaching the state pension age. However, many new pensioners continue working.
In July, 24.6 percent of 67-year-old state pensioners remained in paid employment, compared with 10.6 percent in July 2022.
Velliv consumer economist Thomas Gress said the rise could be connected to rules allowing people to earn income without reductions to their own or their spouse’s state pension.
“For some, retirement life is the freedom to leave work completely behind. Others want to keep their colleagues, some hours on the job, and benefit from the generous deductions and subsidies available for continuing working life once the state pension age has been reached,” Gress said.
The growing pensioner population is also increasing public spending. Statistics Denmark said social benefits cost the state 908 billion DKK last year, five percent more than the previous year.
State pensions were the largest expense in the old-age category, costing 170 billion DKK.
Velliv expects the number of state pensioners to continue rising until 2029, when roughly one in five Danes is projected to receive the benefit.

Nearly one million Danes add credit warnings after breach of 8.8 million CPR records
The number of Danes with a credit warning in the national CPR register has almost quadrupled since authorities disclosed a major data breach.
About 970,000 people had registered a warning by October 7, up from just under 250,000 on October 1, the Digital Affairs Ministry said.
“The Danes have taken the situation seriously, and they have acted on the advice that has come from the government and from the authorities,” Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said.
A credit warning makes it harder for someone to obtain loans or credit in another person’s name. It tells companies to conduct additional identity checks before approving applications.
The Agency for Societal Security has recommended warnings for people who have specific reasons to suspect fraud.
Unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people by misusing a small Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system during 10 days in September.
Authorities discovered the activity after the company received an unusually large bill. Each search of the register carries a fee.
The company has not been identified, and authorities do not know who was responsible.
Egelund said it remained too early to determine whether affected people would need new CPR numbers, which are Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
