Danish companies and organizations should use other methods to verify people’s identities after unauthorized parties accessed information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register, authorities said Tuesday.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” said Laila Reenberg, director of Samsik, the Agency for Public Security.
“You can no longer count on that if you receive a CPR number, you have identified a specific citizen. That is the consequence of this leak.”
Unauthorized parties collected information over 10 days in September through a small Danish company that had access to the CPR system. Authorities discovered the activity when the company was invoiced for the large number of searches.
The CPR system contains information on people living in Denmark as well as people who have died or moved abroad.
CPR numbers are sometimes used to identify people when they call their doctor or collect prescription medicine from a pharmacy.
Samsik recommends using other forms of identification, including MitID, two-factor authentication or one-time codes sent by text message or email.
“You cannot use it to authorize buying something or receiving sensitive personal data,” Reenberg said about CPR numbers.
Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization, said an overall security review of the CPR system is being launched.
“It is important to emphasize that the information accessed is name and address. There is also other information that has not been accessed,” Leihardt said.
“As a system, CPR is intact.”
Reenberg said authorities have also introduced measures covering critical state IT systems.
A 31-year-old man charged with assaulting a Swedish man at a World Cup screening at Islands Brygge will appear before Copenhagen City Court on Wednesday.
The incident happened June 30 during a screening of a match between Norway and Ivory Coast. The Swedish man was punched and suffered a ruptured artery. He died July 3.
The defendant is charged with assault under a section of the Danish penal code covering less serious violence. Prosecutors are also seeking an increased sentence because of his previous convictions.
Special prosecutor Maria Cingari said in July that he could face eight to 10 months in prison.
The man has previously been convicted of rape and attempted murder. He was also convicted in another assault case last week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of Socialdemokratiet, the Social Democrats, criticized the possible sentence in August, saying she believed it should be harsher. The defendant is a Danish citizen who came to Denmark from Congo as an infant.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of Moderaterne, the Moderates, also commented after the Swedish man’s death, writing: “May the guilty party be judged harshly and fairly.”
The government has since announced plans to increase penalties in assault cases where the victim dies and the offender has previous convictions.
Prosecutors are also seeking a nightlife ban for the defendant. He has pleaded not guilty and is protected by a court-ordered name ban.
Two other people face separate assault charges in connection with the incident. One is accused of trampling on the Swedish man while he was lying down and assaulting another Swedish man. The other is accused of kicking the second man.
People collecting prescription medicine in Denmark may be asked to show identification as pharmacies respond to unauthorized access to information on 8.8 million people in the CPR register.
Danmarks Apotekerforening, the Danish Pharmacists’ Association, which represents the country’s pharmacies, said pharmacies are increasing checks when dispensing medicine and health information, particularly medicine with a risk of abuse.
“In practice, this means that it will normally not be sufficient to state one’s CPR number when picking up medicine,” the association said.
Customers may instead be asked to show a physical or digital health card or answer verification questions.
Additional checks may also apply when collecting medicine for another person. The association said bringing that person’s health card or other identification would be the easiest option. Otherwise, pharmacies may ask verification questions.
The changes follow recommendations from Samsik, the Danish Agency for Public Security.
“One must expect that one can no longer identify oneself with CPR,” Samsik director Laila Reenberg said Tuesday.
PLO, the Danish Association of General Practitioners, which represents and advises general practitioners, has also asked its members to follow Samsik’s recommendations.
Samsik said authorities, organizations and companies should pay closer attention when CPR numbers, names or addresses are used to confirm someone’s identity and should generally use other information for identity checks.
Unauthorized people collected information on 8.8 million living, deceased and emigrated people over 10 days in September by abusing a private Danish company’s legal access to the CPR system.
The incident has been reported to Datatilsynet, the Danish Data Protection Agency. The National Special Crime Unit is investigating the case.
Around 687,000 people in Denmark currently owe money to the public sector, down from more than 1.1 million in 2023, according to the Danish Debt Collection Agency.
That represents a decline of 454,000 people. The debt can include money owed to the police, municipalities or tax authorities.
Søren Bork Hansen, deputy director at the agency, said several factors have contributed to the decline.
“It is due to a combination of people being able to log in to ‘Mit gældsoverblik’ and pay the debt, but also that we can write off the debt if we have attempted to get the debt paid, and it is for a low amount,” he told Ritzau.
The agency can also recover debt through tax refunds or deductions from a person’s salary.
Debts can be written off when the amount is small, generally below a few thousand DKK, and collection has been attempted for at least a year. In such cases, the cost of collecting the money can be too high.
People living in Denmark owed the public sector around 108 billion DKK in total as of June 2025. Including businesses, deceased and missing people and people living abroad, the figure was 164 billion DKK in June 2026.
Since 2023, around 690,000 people have become debt-free, while others have accumulated new public-sector debt, resulting in the net decline of 454,000.
In the second quarter of 2026 alone, 110,000 people became debt-free while 62,000 took on public-sector debt, the agency said.
Danish government proposes prison unit at Kærshovedgård departure center for convicted residents
Denmark’s government wants to build a prison unit at Kærshovedgård for departure center residents who receive prison sentences.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen announced the proposal Tuesday during her speech opening the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The unit could hold residents convicted of repeatedly violating requirements to report to authorities.
“Those residents who are sentenced to prison must be able to serve their sentence behind lock and key in a prison unit located in connection with Kærshovedgård,” Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said.
Kærshovedgård houses foreign nationals who have been ordered to leave Denmark or whose asylum applications were rejected but who cannot or will not return to their countries of origin.
Some say they would face persecution or torture. In other cases, their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities on returns.
Frederiksen said residents had caused problems for people living near the center, including theft, drug dealing and dangerous driving.
Authorities have previously introduced stricter reporting duties, removed some residents’ driving licenses and established electronic ankle monitoring.
The Danish People’s Party and others have called for all residents to be confined at the center.
The government rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving criminal sentences cannot legally be detained under international agreements.
The planned locked unit would apply only to residents convicted of crimes and sentenced to prison.

Large search bill alerted Danish authorities to breach of 8.8 million CPR records
An unusually large invoice led Danish authorities to discover that unauthorized people had accessed personal records on 8.8 million people, an official said Tuesday.
A small Danish company had legal access to search the national CPR register. Each search carries a fee, and extensive activity produced a large bill.
“There is a very large amount being invoiced, which makes one aware that there has been a lot of activity,” said Mikkel Leihardt, a department head at the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization.
Unauthorized users abused the company’s access for about 10 days in September.
Authorities have not identified the company.
The accessed information consisted mainly of names and addresses, Leihardt said. The CPR system is Denmark’s national register of personal information.
Authorities do not yet know who was responsible or how the company’s access was compromised.
“It is too early to say at this point who is behind it and what method has been used,” said Henriette Erbs of NSK, Denmark’s National Special Crime Unit.
She said cases of this type often involve cross-border crime.
Laila Reenberg, director of Denmark’s Agency for Public Security, said digital fraud was an obvious possible motive.
However, she said authorities did not yet know who collected the data or how they intended to use it.

The app’s functions will not change. Contacts, payment agreements, transaction history and other features will remain available.
MobilePay’s services in Denmark and Finland merged with Norwegian payment app Vipps in 2022, creating a shared Nordic platform.
Vipps MobilePay described the name change as one of the final steps toward operating under a common Nordic identity.
“We know that the new name will require a bit of getting used to,” said Jeanette Hertzum, the company’s Danish country manager.
The company wants users in Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Sweden and Finland to use the same name and logo.
The longer transition period is intended to give Danish users time to adjust before the new name takes effect.
The app will retain MobilePay’s blue color in Denmark and Finland. The logo will change to include the smiling symbol already used by Vipps in Norway and Sweden.
Hertzum said some users would adapt quickly, while others might need more time. The company said assistance would be available to people who need help with the change.

More than seven in 10 Danish cancer patients survive at least five years
Just over seven in 10 cancer patients in Denmark are alive five years after diagnosis, according to the Danish Health Data Authority.
The latest figures cover patients diagnosed from 2023 through 2025 and five-year survival was slightly above six in 10 during 2011 to 2013.
“Survival is still increasing, even though it is not happening at the same pace as previously,” authority deputy director Jesper Juel-Helwig said.
Lung cancer showed the largest improvement for both sexes.
Among women, five-year lung cancer survival increased from 21 percent in 2011 to 2013 to 39 percent in the latest period. For men, it rose from 14 percent to 29 percent.
Survival also improved for some of the deadliest cancers. Five-year survival among men with liver cancer doubled from 10 percent to 20 percent.
Among women with pancreatic cancer, it increased from nine percent to 16 percent.
Kræftens Bekæmpelse, the Danish Cancer Society and the country’s main cancer organization, welcomed the progress but said further improvement was needed.
“We have gone from being at the bottom in Europe to being up near the top,” managing director Jesper Fisker said.
Fisker linked the improvement to national cancer care programs introduced almost 20 years ago and a stronger focus on research and coordinated patient treatment.
Dementia patients wait five times longer than legal limit for assessment
Nearly 25,000 people have waited more than the statutory 30 days for a dementia assessment over the past four years, according to a new report from Denmark’s National Audit Office.
The Public Accounts Committee has now issued sharp criticism of the country’s regions over the delays, using the second-highest level of criticism on its scale.
Under Danish law, patients should be assessed within 30 days. In practice, however, the average waiting time nationwide was 165 days last year, more than five times the legal limit.
“The Public Accounts Committee sharply criticizes that 84 percent of patients are not assessed for dementia within the 30 days prescribed by law,” the committee said.
The criticism follows a report by the National Audit Office, which found significant differences in both waiting times and the quality of assessments across Denmark.
In the Region of Southern Denmark, the average waiting time was 133 days. In Region Zealand, it was 244 days.
“The report shows that we are very far from the target of patients being assessed for dementia within 30 days, and that waiting times are growing,” the Public Accounts Committee said.
“There are far too large differences between our regions and between citizens with a strong and a weak social background when it comes to the quality of the specialized assessment and access to necessary examinations. We sharply criticize this.”
The report also found that social background can influence how quickly patients receive an assessment.
On average, the assessment process was 24 days shorter for patients with what the National Audit Office defines as a strong social background.
This includes people with greater wealth and medium- or long-cycle higher education, as well as those who have a partner and adult children with a similar level of education.
Patients with a weak social background are defined as people with debt, no vocational qualifications and no partner or adult children.
The Public Accounts Committee said the reasons behind these differences should be investigated.
“The Public Accounts Committee agrees with the National Audit Office’s recommendation that the causes of differences in the quality of assessment and the differences in assessment waiting times and quality for patients depending on their social background should be investigated,” it said.
Mads Duedahl of the Liberal Party, chairman of Danish Regions, which represents Denmark’s five regional authorities, said the criticism was justified.
“Waiting time is often very burdensome for both patients and relatives, and therefore the regions will make every effort to get more people assessed,” he told Danish Regions’ website.
Duedahl said the system needs to be “rethought” to increase assessment capacity. One option under consideration is to allow general practitioners to carry out more dementia assessments.

Stolen CPR data could make phishing attacks more convincing, cybersecurity expert warns
Personal information obtained through unauthorized access to Denmark’s CPR register could help criminals create more convincing phishing attacks, a cybersecurity expert said.
Names, addresses, identification numbers and birth dates can be used to make fraudulent emails and text messages appear to come from authorities, Aarhus University professor Jens Myrup Pedersen said.
“The more data you have about people, the more realistic attacks you can also create,” he said.
Phishing is digital fraud in which criminals pretend to represent a company, public authority or police force to obtain sensitive information.
Denmark’s Digitalization Ministry said Monday that unauthorized people had accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people.
CPR numbers are Denmark’s personal identification numbers. The register includes living and deceased people, as well as former residents.
Pedersen said the information should not be sufficient by itself to obtain loans in another person’s name. Service providers cannot assume that someone knows a person’s identity simply because they possess a CPR number, he said.
However, the information could support other forms of identity misuse and might be sold or combined with publicly available data and photographs.
Pedersen described the breach as unusually extensive.
Unlike a 2015 incident in which records on more than five million Danes were mistakenly delivered to a visa company, the new unauthorized access appears deliberate, he said.
Danish minister says security was inadequate after access to 8.8 million personal records
Security surrounding a private company’s access to Denmark’s national personal information register was inadequate, Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund said Monday.
Unauthorized parties used the small Danish company’s legal access to obtain records on 8.8 million people over about 10 days in September.
“It is clear to me that the security measures surrounding this company’s access to CPR have not been good enough,” Egelund of the Moderates told the Danish news agency Ritzau.
The accessed information includes names, addresses and CPR numbers, Denmark’s personal identification numbers.
The total exceeds Denmark’s population of about six million because the records also cover deceased people, emigrants and others registered in the system.
An employee in the CPR administration detected unusual activity Friday, October 2. Authorities had established by Saturday that a security incident had occurred.
The company had permission to search the CPR register, but unauthorized people abused its access. That access has since been closed.
Egelund acknowledged that warnings should have been triggered sooner because the activity continued for several days.
“It is a serious incident. It should not be able to happen,” she said.
The minister declined to identify the company or say whether authorities believe those responsible had criminal intentions, citing the ongoing investigation.
Authorities have not disclosed who accessed the records or how the company’s credentials were compromised.

Electric bicycle injuries in Denmark reached their highest level in six years as imports of the vehicles continued to rise.
In 2025, 200 electric bicycle riders were injured in traffic, including 133 who were seriously injured. Eleven riders died, according to Danish Road Directorate figures analyzed by insurance company Alm. Brand.
Electric bicycles can reach higher speeds and usually weigh more than standard bicycles, potentially making injuries more serious, said Mathias Kjær Sigvaldason, Alm. Brand’s accident insurance director.
Denmark imported 98,078 electric bicycles in 2025, up from 40,216 in 2017, Statistics Denmark reported.
Imports of standard bicycles fell from slightly more than 500,000 in 2017 to about 350,000 in 2025. Electric models now represent more than one in four imported bicycles.
The figures cover imports, not consumer sales, for which no combined national data are available.
The Danish Road Safety Council, an organization working to prevent traffic injuries, wants helmets to become mandatory for electric bicycle riders.
It also called for illegal electric bicycles to be removed from cycle paths.
Standard electric bicycles may assist riders up to 25 kilometers per hour and follow ordinary bicycle rules.
Approved speed pedelecs may assist riders up to 45 kilometers per hour. Helmets and lights are legally required when using them.
Most Danes support blocking social media for teenagers during overnight hours
A majority of Danes support requiring social media platforms to block teenagers ages 15 to 17 from viewing content between midnight and 6 a.m., a new survey found.
Voxmeter conducted the poll among 1,034 representative Danish adults for Digitalt Ansvar, an organization promoting responsible use of digital technology.
A total of 62.3 percent agreed or strongly agreed with an overnight block. Another 15.9 percent were neutral, while 17.4 percent disagreed or strongly disagreed.
The European Union’s proposed Kids Act includes an overnight block for users ages 13 and 14.
Digitalt Ansvar wants the measure expanded to include teenagers through age 17.
Director Ask Hesby Holm said nighttime social media use harms sleep and can leave students unprepared for school.
Aarhus University research found that more children arrive at school tired and that tiredness is linked to poorer academic results.
Previous studies reviewed by the researchers associated screen use, particularly before bedtime, with later, shorter and lower-quality sleep.
Digital Affairs Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said action was needed but questioned whether a complete ban was the right solution.
“Social media should not be allowed to take our night’s sleep,” she told Danish broadcaster TV 2.
The EU estimates that young Europeans spend four to six hours daily using screens.

Professor: Old IT makes universities hacking targets
Danish universities hold vast amounts of personal data while some continue to rely on ageing IT systems that may not meet modern security standards, a cybersecurity professor warns following the major attack on DTU.
Old IT systems combined with large amounts of sensitive personal data make Danish universities particularly vulnerable to cyberattacks, according to Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor of cybersecurity at Aarhus University.
His warning comes after the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) revealed Friday that hackers had gained access to its user database and extracted a large amount of data.
“Universities possess a very large amount of personal data,” Pedersen told Ritzau.
“And then it is my impression that several universities have quite a few older systems that probably do not have the security level one can expect in 2026.”
Pedersen stressed that he cannot comment specifically on the quality of DTU’s IT security.
But he said the attack raises important questions about how universities protect access to sensitive information.
“The question is which accounts have had access to all this personal data, and how well they are protected,” he said.
Another key question, according to Pedersen, is whether university IT systems can detect when unusually large amounts of data are being extracted and trigger an alarm before the damage becomes more extensive.
Universities face a ‘very high’ cyber threat
The problem extends beyond DTU.
Danish universities have been targeted by hackers several times in recent years, while a 2025 assessment from the Danish Agency for Societal Security (Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed) rated the cybercrime threat against Danish universities as “very high”.
Universities can be attractive targets because they combine extensive personal databases with large and complex IT environments used by thousands of students, researchers and employees.
The latest attack has brought renewed attention to whether security measures have kept pace with that complexity.
More than 200,000 potentially affected at DTU
As previously reported by The Copenhagen Post, more than 200,000 people could be affected by the DTU attack.
Unauthorised parties compromised several DTU user profiles and used them to access the university’s user database. DTU says a large amount of data was extracted and that the information involved could include CPR numbers, home addresses and telephone numbers.
The university has not yet determined exactly what information was taken or how many people are affected.
The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency (Datatilsynet), while the National Special Crime Unit (NSK) is in contact with DTU about the case.
It has not been disclosed who is suspected of carrying out the attack.

Kosovo lawmakers elect Justina Pula as president in late-night vote to avert snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:14:57 UTC
13:14:57 KST

The late-night parliamentary session ended a more-than-19-month legislative deadlock in the country. Pula’s election to the post makes her the third woman to hold that office since Kosovo’s post-war independence from Serbia.
Lawmakers in Kosovo elected economist and academic Justina Shiroka Pula as the country’s new president in a marathon late-night session, moments before a constitutional deadline that would have forced a snap election.
The election late on Tuesday was a significant moment in a political crisis in the small Balkan nation that has caused legislative deadlock for over 19 months and two early parliamentary elections.
Just before Shiroka Pula was elected, lawmakers also approved a law limiting the powers of a special court in The Hague, which was set up to investigate and prosecute war crimes committed by the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the country's 1998-1999 war for independence from Serbia.
During the extraordinary session in parliament, Shiroka Pula secured 81 votes in the 120-seat parliament. Outside, thousands of protesters had gathered demanding that the legislature pass the law limiting the powers of the war crimes court, known as the Specialist Chambers.
Shiroka Pula recently served as president of the Academy of Sciences and Arts of Kosovo. She is now Kosovo’s third female president since the country’s post-war independence was declared in 2008.
She was a last-minute consensus candidate backed by the ruling leftist Vetevendosje or Self-Determination party and the largest opposition party, the centre-right Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK).
The president of Kosovo plays an important role in foreign policy and serves as commander-in-chief of the security forces, while also approving laws passed in the national assembly, among other powers.
One of Shiroka Pula's first responsibilities will be to endorse the law limiting the Hague court's power for it to become binding.
In her speech after taking the oath of office late on Tuesday, Shiroka Pula said she accepted the appointment "with great honour and full responsibility".
“This mandate does not belong to one person alone, it belongs to our citizens, our institutions, and the state for which many generations have sacrificed,” she said.
Shiroka Pula’s election came after over two weeks of protests following a verdict by the Hague-based court convicting four of Kosovo's wartime rebel leaders of war crimes, including the country's former President Hashim Thaçi.
The court sentenced them to between 13 and 25 years in prison.
Many Kosovars believe the verdicts were unjust because the KLA — which Thaçi was one of the leaders of before entering politics — had fought against Serbian oppression, fearing that the court ruling would tarnish Kosovo’s independence struggle.
More than 13,000 people, mostly ethnic Albanians, were killed during the conflict in Kosovo, while about 1 million ethnic Albanian Kosovars were driven from their homes during the fighting.

Lithuanian Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said continued assistance was essential not only for Ukraine’s survival but also for Europe’s security.

Funding Ukraine’s recovery and reconstruction
The €10 million ($11.2 million) contribution to SPUR 2.0 will support a World Bank financing mechanism designed to mobilize additional resources for Ukraine’s recovery.
Established in June 2026, the program allows donor contributions to generate approximately three times their value in concessional lending.
According to Lithuania’s Finance Ministry, $2 billion in donor contributions could unlock around $6 billion in loans to Ukraine on favorable terms.
The program also includes a private-sector component aimed at encouraging investment and supporting Ukraine’s economic recovery.
Lithuania previously contributed €10 million ($11.2 million at the Oct. 7, 2026 exchange rate) to the original SPUR program in 2023.
The remaining €5 million ($5.6 million) will go to the EIB’s EU4U Fund, which finances critical infrastructure reconstruction and projects strengthening Ukraine’s economic resilience.
The EIB requested additional contributions from member states in July after previously committed funding for Ukrainian projects was nearly exhausted.
Lithuania also contributed €10 million to the EU4U Fund in 2023.
Lithuania reaffirms long-term commitment to Ukraine
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, Lithuania’s Finance Ministry has allocated more than €93 million ($104.2 million) to Ukraine through international financial institutions and EU mechanisms, alongside €26 million ($29.1 million) in bilateral assistance.
Valys said Ukraine’s financial requirements and the international community’s continued assistance would be among the central issues discussed at next week’s annual meetings of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund.
During a September meeting with Ukrainian Ambassador Olha Nikitchenko, Valys said Ukraine’s security was inseparable from Europe’s and reaffirmed that assistance to Kyiv would remain a priority during Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027.

Britain removes East Jerusalem consulate signage as Israeli shutdown order expires
JERUSALEM – Workers removed signs and plaques at the British consulate in East Jerusalem overnight after Israel ordered it shut by Oct 8 over London’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank, further damaging strained ties between allies.
Reuters journalists saw workers in the consulate remove a plaque reading “British Consulate General” and another sign for its consular section. The British flag was still flying over the building. There was no immediate comment from the consulate.
Israel in September ordered Britain to close the consulate within 30 days and remove its diplomats from the city, after Britain announced sanctions targeting Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including a trade ban on goods made there.
The United Nations and most countries consider the settlements to be illegal under international law. Israel disputes this.
Israel has been adamant the consulate will close even as Britain sought to keep it open, including sending the country’s top national security adviser to Israel last week for talks.
Britain’s presence in the city dates back almost 200 years, long before the State of Israel was established in 1948. The closure order does not affect Britain’s embassy in Tel Aviv, which handles diplomatic relations with Israel’s government.
The consulate, in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East Jerusalem, handles Britain’s relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem, as well as in the West Bank and Gaza. It also provides consular services to Palestinians.
Britain’s Foreign Office on Oct 7 declined to comment when asked whether the consulate was still operating or any British diplomats working there had returned to Britain.
Sources have said the order to close the consulate affects around 30 British diplomats along with their family members.
Britain is considering expelling Israeli diplomats from Israel’s embassy in Britain in response to any closure of the consulate, Reuters reported on Oct 6, citing sources.
It would be a highly unusual step for the allies to expel each other’s diplomats. Despite the current strains, Britain and Israel are close economic, security and intelligence partners.
The British sanctions announcement, and Israel’s order to close the consulate, mark a new low in a relationship that has deteriorated over the past three years. Britain has repeatedly criticised Israel over its actions in the war in Gaza and over Israeli settler attacks on Palestinians in the West Bank.
Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has accused Britain’s governing Labour Party of being hostile towards Israel. REUTERS

South Korea pledges legal action over alleged fuel exports to Russia
Ukrainian reports of South Korean fuel exports to Russia come amid strained tensions between Seoul and Kyiv.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has said the government will take legal action over illegal fuel shipments to Russia if allegations from an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy are confirmed.
The Foreign Ministry said on Thursday it had not confirmed whether South Korean fuel, including diesel, had been exported to Russia.
It added that exports of some products, such as diesel and jet fuel for commercial purposes, were not included in a South Korean exports control list to Russia.
On Wednesday, the South Korean presidential office dismissed a statement by Vladyslav Vlasiuk, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on sanctions policy, that 176,000 tonnes of fuel were shipped from South Korea to Russia via sanctioned tankers in July and August.
Ukraine’s top sanctions official said the alleged findings run counter to South Korea’s sanctions policy towards Russia.
“Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, our government has consistently implemented sanctions and export controls against Russia in close cooperation with the international community,” South Korean presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said on Wednesday, according to the Yonhap news agency.
“We ask that Ukraine also refrain from distorting the relevant policies of the Republic of Korea without sufficient verification of the facts and making public remarks that can damage international trust,” she added.
Relations between South Korea and Ukraine have been strained for the past couple of weeks after Seoul accused Zelenskyy of having “unilaterally disclosed” to the United Nations General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.
Seoul Korea demanded an official apology from Kyiv, claiming the Ukrainian president had breached a non-disclosure agreement. Kyiv said no such agreement was in place.
Pyongyang and Moscow, meanwhile, have deep ties, with the two countries having signed a mutual defence treaty in 2024. According to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, about 14,000 to 15,000 North Korean soldiers were sent to support Russia’s war efforts against Ukraine.
North Korea and South Korea remain technically at war because the 1950–1953 Korean War ended in an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Yageo posted multiple revenue records as demand for passive components used in AI-related applications remained strong.
The company reported September revenue of NT$17.1 billion (US$535.4 million), up 46.1% year-on-year. The result rose 4.5% from August, marking Yageo’s seventh consecutive monthly record, according to Anue and FTNN.
Third-quarter revenue reached NT$49.5 billion, also a quarterly record, up 49.7% from a year earlier. Revenue for the first nine months totaled NT$132.2 billion, a record for the same period and 36.3% higher year-on-year.
Yageo’s main business is passive components, which regulate or store electrical energy in electronic circuits rather than generate it. The company said shipments of both standard and specialty products increased steadily in September, while demand from end-use applications showed moderate growth.
Looking ahead, Yageo said the growing adoption of AI is driving structural changes in the industry. Geopolitical uncertainties remain, but customer inventories are at healthy levels, it added.
AI servers are changing not only the number of passive components used, but also their specifications and applications. One example is the growing use of multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), which help stabilize voltage and filter electrical noise in electronic circuits, according to UDN Money and Sinotrade.
Next-generation AI accelerator platforms place greater demands on power stability, signal integrity, and long-term reliability, driving the use of higher-end versions of these components. On some platforms, these components are replacing aluminum electrolytic and tantalum capacitors during the validation process, resulting in several-fold increases in their use.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Puma Shen (沈伯洋), the DPP’s mayoral candidate in Taipei, said in a televised interview Wednesday that he would not push for drug decriminalization and does not support legalizing cannabis in Taiwan.

Jaw served one term as a Taipei city councilor before being elected to the Legislative Yuan in the 1990s and was the KMT’s vice-presidential nominee in the 2024 election.
Shen, a criminology professor at National Taipei University, said that to tackle illicit drug use, it is crucial to understand why people start using drugs in the first place.
“Putting people who use drugs in prison to help them quit is not the most effective strategy,” he said. “The key is education,” adding that Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) had supported this idea when he was a legislator before becoming mayor.
Shen, who is running against Chiang in November, added that policy should also focus on treating people who use drugs rather than forcing them to be hospitalized.
Currently, it is common practice for healthcare facilities in Taiwan to prevent people who use drugs from contracting the HIV virus by supplying clean needles and substitute treatments, he explained.
He also proposed hot spot policing, concentrating police resources in specific areas where crime is clustered, as a way to address illicit drug use.
Asked about his view on cannabis, Shen cited people’s fear over the substance as a reason why he does not believe Taiwan should move toward legalization.
“If we rush to legalize cannabis, it will only become more stigmatized,” he said.
In the interview, Jaw also brought up the campaign last year by civic groups to remove 31 KMT legislators from office in a series of recall elections, all of which ended in failure.
Jaw asked Shen what responsibility he believed he should bear for leading the failed campaign and whether he was sowing social division as its leader.
Shen responded by denying his role as the initiator of the recall campaign. Recalling elected officials, he said, is a right guaranteed by the Constitution and does not in itself amount to dividing society.

Eslite Hotel chef crafts date-friendly cuttlefish pasta in Taipei
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:12:05 UTC
13:12:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Eating cuttlefish pasta on a date used to be a high-stakes gamble for your smile, but Executive Chef Allen Lu (呂芳坤) of Eslite Hotel has officially eliminated the black-ink hazard.
Located near the Taipei Dome, The Chapter restaurant on the ground floor of Eslite Hotel has launched its new menu inspired by the relaxed rhythm of Mediterranean dining, anchored by Lu's stain-free, date-friendly cuttlefish pasta.
To solve the messiness typically associated with the dish, Lu kneads rich, highly concentrated imported cuttlefish paste directly into the pasta dough during production rather than tossing cooked noodles in liquid ink before serving.
"If I were a girl eating cuttlefish pasta across from a crush, having a mouth full of black ink would be completely embarrassing," Lu said with a smile.
By incorporating the paste straight into the dough, the cooked noodles maintain a springy texture and deep seafood flavor while absorbing sauce cleanly, leaving diners with spotless teeth and lips throughout their meal.
However, the labor-intensive process severely limits daily availability. Between preparation, kneading, and portioning, making the fresh pasta takes over seven hours daily.
Because the kitchen avoids artificial preservatives and fresh seafood dough deteriorates quickly when exposed to air, the restaurant caps output to roughly 10 portions per day.
Despite the tight limit, it has quickly become the top-selling main course on the menu.
Beyond the signature pasta, Lu emphasized that the menu's true core lies in its traditional Italian antipasti.
Following a culinary exchange tour across top Italian establishments in Taipei, Lu said that a genuine Italian meal always begins with shared appetizers.
Unlike the formal structure of French fine dining, Italian food culture centers on relaxed sharing, where friends and family gather over small plates paired with wine, slowly awakening their palates through lively conversation.
The appetizer lineup balances traditional recipes with modern adaptations, including tomato burrata, Florentine stewed tripe with tomato, Ligurian white wine prawns, spiced almond stuffed green olives marinated for three days, and a crispy durum wheat fried seafood platter.
Lu said that because Taiwanese diners often prefer lighter profile meals, his team refined traditional Italian techniques into lighter, healthier dishes without sacrificing authentic Mediterranean flavors.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s stock market has overtaken South Korea’s as the world’s top-performing major market, as investors increasingly favor Taiwanese shares amid the global AI boom.
Taiwan’s benchmark TAIEX gained about 23 percentage points more than South Korea’s Kospi last quarter, marking its largest quarterly lead this century, per Bloomberg. Earnings estimates for Taiwanese companies also rose more than those for South Korean companies for the first time since March 2025.
In a Bank of America survey last month, about 40% of fund managers said they were overweight on Taiwanese stocks, while 25% took the same position on South Korean shares. Data compiled by Bloomberg showed earnings estimates for TAIEX rose about 19% in the September quarter, compared with a 15% increase for Kospi.
Taiwan also emerged as the clear favorite when investors were asked which market would benefit most from the next phase of the AI cycle. About 35% of respondents selected Taiwan, compared with just 5% who chose South Korea.
The optimism reflects Taiwan’s broader exposure across the AI supply chain and a more favorable earnings outlook, Bloomberg reported. Taiwan offers investment opportunities across chip design and manufacturing, packaging, networking, and servers, giving investors more ways to benefit as AI spending expands.
Taiwan also trades at a significant valuation premium to South Korea, with the TAIEX at about 18 times forward estimated earnings versus roughly 5.5 times for the Kospi. Brief Asia said investors appear willing to pay the premium for greater visibility into sustained volume growth, while concerns over the cyclical nature of the memory-chip market have kept South Korean stocks at a discount.
Vikas Pershad, a portfolio manager at M&G Investments in Singapore, told Bloomberg, “The distinction for us is not simply the amount of AI exposure, but the nature of the earnings supporting it.” Taiwan’s earnings are driven more by volume, resulting in broader and more durable earnings upgrades, while South Korea’s near-term earnings growth is driven more by prices, he said.
The TAIEX is expected to rise 72% in 2026, making it the best performer among more than 90 stock indexes tracked by Bloomberg. The Kospi ranks second with a gain of about 65%.
Samsung and SK Hynix, two of the Kospi’s largest stocks, fell 19% to 33% in the three months through September after six straight quarters of gains. Their earlier rally was fueled by higher memory-chip prices, which boosted earnings and led analysts to raise their profit forecasts.
TSMC shares rose 2.9% in the three months through September, marking their sixth consecutive quarterly gain, according to Bloomberg. About 10% of TAIEX constituents had at least doubled in value this year as of Wednesday, compared with 4.1% of Kospi stocks and 5.7% of Nikkei 225 constituents, highlighting the breadth of Taiwan’s rally.

Political ‘firewall’ breached in eastern Germany – AfD
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:07:52 UTC

Political ‘firewall’ breached in eastern Germany – AfD
The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has secured the office of state parliament president in Saxony-Anhalt, with its successful candidate claiming he received backing from members of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in a historic first.
Despite emerging as Germany’s most popular party in recent polls, the AfD has for years been subjected to the so-called ‘firewall’ policy, under which mainstream parties refuse to cooperate with it.
The largest opposition faction in the Bundestag, the AfD campaigns on an anti-immigration platform and is highly critical of the German government’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
The party won last month’s regional election in Saxony-Anhalt with 43.8% of the vote, narrowly falling short of an absolute majority in the regional legislature. Merz’s CDU finished a distant second with 17.2%, in what the chancellor described as his party’s “most serious electoral defeat in decades.”
On Tuesday, the AfD’s Tobias Rausch was elected president of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament, becoming the first AfD politician to head a German state legislature.
Ahead of the secret ballot, representatives of the left-wing Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) announced that they would support Rausch. Together, the AfD and BSW hold 44 seats.
Rausch, however, received 48 votes, with 29 lawmakers voting against him and five abstaining. The result means he secured four more votes than the combined AfD-BSW total, although the secret ballot makes it impossible to establish who cast them.
The CDU parliamentary leadership had advised its lawmakers to abstain, while the SPD, the Greens, and The Left said they would vote against Rausch in keeping with the firewall policy.
Following his victory, Rausch said he believed CDU lawmakers had backed him. Asked directly whether he had received CDU votes, he replied: “Yes.”
“The era of political ‘firewalls’ should be a thing of the past,” Rausch proclaimed.
AfD co-chairs Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla similarly declared that the “years of ostracism against our party have finally come to an end today,” and called on the CDU to cooperate with the AfD.
In recent months, several establishment political figures, including Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, have backed a potential ban on the AfD over claims that it poses a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
Following the party’s victory in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s regional election in September with 38.2% of the vote, the SPD renewed calls for a formal review that could pave the way for a ban.
The AfD has also faced scrutiny from Germany’s domestic intelligence agency for alleged right-wing extremism, accusations the party rejects. Some regional branches, including in Saxony-Anhalt, have been subjected to particularly extensive monitoring.
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published earlier this month put public support for the AfD at a record 30% nationwide. Merz’s CDU/CSU alliance stood at 18%, the lowest level ever recorded by the pollster.

Trump has repeatedly attacked El-Sayed since his primary win. El-Sayed brushed aside those attacks, saying Trump was "more interested in saying my name in an interesting way" than in solving Michigan's problems, and urging the president to focus on his affordability agenda.
"I invite the president to focus on what I'm saying. I want to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket, and pass Medicare for all," El-Sayed said in an interview with CNN in August.

El Nino forecast to reach record strength as global heat, weather risks rise: WMO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:04:44 UTC
13:04:44 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
An ongoing El Nino event is strengthening rapidly and is forecast to push key Pacific sea-surface temperatures to record levels, increasing the risks of extreme heat, drought and flooding around the world, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said Thursday.
In its latest Global Seasonal Climate Update, the UN weather agency said there is a near-100% likelihood that El Nino will persist through February 2027, with the event expected to peak around December.
“El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly," WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said, warning it will potentially be "one of the strongest since at least 1950."
For October-December, the average sea-surface temperature anomaly in the Nino 3.4 region of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific is forecast to reach about 3.7C (6.7F) above normal, which the WMO said would be "the highest since observations began."
The previous record was 2.6C (4.7F) above normal during the November 2015-January 2016 period.
The WMO said El Nino is likely to bring above-average temperatures across large parts of the globe while significantly shifting rainfall patterns.
Wetter-than-normal conditions are forecast in areas including the Greater Horn of Africa, parts of Central and East Asia, northern parts of the Arabian Peninsula, parts of North America and southeastern South America.
Drier-than-normal conditions are expected across the Indian subcontinent, southern Central America, parts of the Caribbean and northwestern South America.
Saulo said El Nino does not create additional planetary heat but releases heat already stored in the ocean, warning that the ocean from which the current event is drawing is “the warmest we've ever measured it.”
The WMO said national meteorological services and regional climate forums are providing regular updates to governments and humanitarian partners to support preparedness and risk management.

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK
- Published
French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the EU, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled a second Brexit referendum was "possible" in a future Labour election manifesto.
Lescure said being in the bloc comes with some difficulties, but it enables members to better address the challenges facing the world.
Last week, Burnham said the UK needed to "consider the options", ranging from staying as is, rejoining the customs union or single market, or going "all the way".
Asked about the PM's comments, Lescure told the BBC: "British people decided, and that's obviously their 100% right, and if they're willing to come back, they will have to decide."
He added: "But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime."
Burnham recently warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK.
The prime minister expressed concerns about how British industry and supply chains could be affected by the planned Made In Europe scheme.
The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its own supply chains.
Asked about the possibility of Britain being kept out of the scheme, Lescure said: "Come back, and you'll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together."
'Our duty is to listen to young people'
The finance minister's interview with the BBC also touched on French domestic matters, including the student protests that have swept the country, with more than 500 schools fully or partially shut as of Wednesday.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been taking to the streets to call for better conditions in schools.
Lescure said it was a "tough world" for young people, saying he understood why they were anxious and that "our duty as leaders is to listen to them".
"It's hard to tell young people we're not going to have the money for you because we're spending a lot on health and pensions," he acknowledged.
"We're getting people more healthy. People live longer. But we cannot just say 'this is fine' and then we don't have money left for the kids, so we need to rebalance that."
In France's upcoming budget he said he will cut back on health spending and ask retired people to accept a below-inflation rise to their pension next year.
While he said "not all" French schools were crumbling, he promised further investment in education, adding: "If we need to do more, we'll have to see."
Public deficit is 'alarming'
Other challenges France is currently facing include its budget deficit, and markets pushing up borrowing costs.
Lescure acknowledged that France's annual public borrowing of over 5% of its gross domestic product (GDP) was "alarming", and said "that's why we need to act now" to avoid being forced to act later.
Asked about the possibility of an intervention from the eurozone's central bank, Lescure said his job was to make sure France did not have to "go there".
With significant rises in French borrowing costs, especially the premium paid over its eurozone partner, Germany, Lescure acknowledged it was "more expensive" to borrow but said there was "no issue" with issuing its debt.
He said that his budget "will pass" a fractious French parliament and there were "lots of different ways" to ensure that.

Next UK banknotes to feature barn owls, bumblebees, puffins and hedgehogs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:00:11 UTC
13:00:11 KST

Bees, barn owls, puffins and hedgehogs have been picked to feature on the next generation of banknotes, the Bank of England has announced.
The quartet of creatures were selected after a large-scale consultation settled on wild animals as the theme, with members of the public then asked to pick their favourites out of 18 options divided into three categories.
The buff-tailed bumblebee got the most votes in the insects, fish and amphibian group; the barn owl won the bird division; and the European hedgehog was named top mammal. The Atlantic puffin was added to celebrate Britain’s coastline, the Bank said.
It is as yet undecided which species will adorn which banknote. An image of King Charles will continue to be represented on the other side of the £5, £10, £20 and £50 notes, which are expected to take several years to design.
Victoria Cleland, the Bank’s chief cashier, said: “I am delighted that nearly half-a-million people responded to our wildlife imagery consultation, showing that cash still matters.”
She said the public had chosen “four distinct and inspiring animals” that not only showcased the great variety of wildlife in the UK but would “also enhance the security of our banknotes”.
Among the species losing out were the basking shark, the common frog and the red fox – the last celebrated in David Attenborough’s recent Wild London documentary, but seen as a pest by some.
Atlantic puffins, with their distinctive multicoloured beaks, spend much of their lives at sea, coming ashore in summer to nest in burrows on clifftops on the coast including on the Farne Islands and Lundy.
With their numbers declining, the bird is classified as “vulnerable” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s red list of threatened species.
The decision to replace the historical figures on the banknotes – including Winston Churchill and Jane Austen – prompted a backlash when first announced in March, with the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, accusing the Bank of “erasing our history”.
Badenoch called it “a silly thing to do”, adding: “I absolutely do not support it.” Her Reform UK counterpart, Nigel Farage, described the move as “absolutely crackers”.
The Liberal Democrat leader, Ed Davey, joined in, issuing a social media video in which he brandished a fiver and claimed that Churchill deserved “better than being replaced by a badger”.
The badger was not among the 18-strong shortlist of animals eventually published by the Bank in June.
That selection prompted the RSPCA to complain about the choice of animals on offer, calling for less obviously cute creatures to be included.
“Gulls, badgers, rats and pigeons all divide opinion, but this would have been a great opportunity to discuss these fantastic animals,” it said.

Germany is right to rearm. But Europe has well-founded fears about that | Paul Taylor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:00:11 UTC
13:00:11 KST

When the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, visited the White House earlier this year for a high-stakes meeting with Donald Trump, he invited a Washington-based German researcher little known outside expert circles to a private dinner.
Liana Fix had caught his eye with a forthright essay in the journal Foreign Affairs warning of the perils of Germany becoming “Europe’s next hegemon”, whose military dominance may come to scare its neighbours and divide Europe once again. That concern might seem far-fetched after three decades since the fall of the Berlin Wall, during which a peace-loving reunited Germany let its armed forces wither and rust, prided itself on being a “civil power” and preached a gospel of military restraint.
Yet the combination of a sudden surge in German rearmament, growing doubts over the United States’ willingness to remain the guarantor of European security through Nato, and the rise of the far-right nationalist Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party, currently leading in opinion polls, has reignited old anxieties among Berlin’s neighbours, especially Poland and France.
Fix, a historian and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, has built her argument into a timely and incisive book, Germany Rearmed: The Return of War and the End of Illusions. Among the fallen myths she skewers are not just the delusion that economic interdependence would make Russia a benign partner for Europe, which collapsed with Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, but also the end of what she calls “the illusion of the west”, which had been central to Germany’s identity and foreign policy since 1945. “It is not that Germany wants to leave the west, but the west seems to be abandoning Germany, in particular the US-led western order,” Fix told me in an interview.
To guard against any hegemonic temptation, she urges Berlin to anchor its future military power in closer European unification by helping to finance European defence through joint defence bonds, embracing a Europeanisation of the continent’s national arms industries, and deepening the integration of the Bundeswehr into European armed forces.
There is little sign so far that Merz, whose first defence strategy, released in April, vowed to make Germany Europe’s strongest conventional army by 2039, is heeding her advice.
Struggling with unpopularity, economic stagnation and a rising cost of living, the conservative chancellor has ruled out issuing eurobonds to fund European defence. His government scrapped two big arms cooperation projects with France – a next-generation fighter aircraft and a tank. Planned arms purchases worth €123.3bn notified to parliament last month are overwhelmingly from national and US industries, with only scraps for European partners.
To be sure, all Berlin’s armed forces are committed to Nato, unlike France’s, and it has invited allies to join its European Sky Shield air and missile defence programme. Germany is the biggest donor of financial and military assistance to Ukraine. It is working with the UK on deep precision strike weapons. And it has stationed a brigade in Lithuania to help protect Europe’s eastern flank in the first permanent deployment outside its territory since 1945.
Defence industrial nationalism is by no means confined to Germany. France and the UK are equally protective of their national arms makers. The EU’s defence commissioner, Andrius Kubilius, laments that up to 80% of European defence purchases are made by direct awards with national prime contractors without a competitive tender, exploiting a security exemption in the EU treaty.
The fact that German rearmament coincides with a severe slump in core manufacturing industries such as cars, chemicals and machinery is an extra reason to “buy national”. But Berlin, once on the frontline of east-west confrontation, is now cushioned by a buffer zone of central European allies and should have an interest in helping them invest in their own defence. For practical reasons, it’s better to help equip friends and neighbours to intercept drones and missiles before they reach Germany rather than waiting to shoot them all down over Berlin and Frankfurt.
Fix is right to argue that because of its dark history and its weight in the middle of Europe, Germany must do more than others to reassure its neighbours and to embed its rearmament in common European industrial, political and military structures. As Timothy Garton Ash has argued in the Guardian, that is what Helmut Kohl achieved a generation ago by anchoring German reunification in a common European currency.
Otherwise, the question of German power and its political uses is bound to return sooner or later, especially if the Russia-friendly AfD, which opposes assistance for Ukraine and advocates withdrawal from the EU, continues to gain ground in German elections.
“The German question is not dead,” Fix told me. “It’s dead in the sense that a militaristic Germany will not re-emerge under a centralised government. But the German question can also just be a question of dominance and of balance. And this is the thinking we unfortunately have to revive.”
- Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre

Teenager becomes first person to have testicular tissue transplant in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
04:00:10 UTC
13:00:10 KST

Surgeons have performed the first testicular tissue transplant on a teenager in the UK, offering hope that boys left infertile by chemotherapy could one day have biological children.
The 19-year-old had his tissue removed and frozen three years ago before undergoing treatment for a serious blood disorder. He said he was “incredibly grateful” to the medical team behind the pioneering procedure, which represents a potential breakthrough for male fertility preservation.
Chemotherapy can permanently damage the cells needed to produce sperm, leaving children who undergo it at risk of infertility in adulthood. Three years after his chemotherapy, tests showed he had no sperm in his semen.
Now a team of NHS medics in Edinburgh have transplanted his previously frozen testicular tissue back into his body, in the hope that it will begin to produce sperm.
The operation is the first of its kind in the UK, and only the second reported to have taken place worldwide. “Fertility is something I’ve struggled with personally for a long time,” said the patient, who asked to remain anonymous.
“I’ve always wanted to have children of my own but at some point, I found myself starting to slowly accept that that might never be possible for me. Having this procedure has given me genuine hope for the future.”
The student added: “We don’t know yet whether it will work, but knowing that there is now even a possibility means more to me than I can really put into words.
“I’m incredibly grateful to everyone for giving me this opportunity and for all the work that has made it possible. I also hope that being part of this research means that, in the future, other young people in the same position can have that hope too.”
Freezing semen is an established fertility preservation method for older teenagers and adult men.
But for pre-pubescent boys this is not an option. The new treatment potentially opens a door to fertility preservation for children needing cancer care and other treatments which require the use of chemotherapy.
The tissue taken for transplant contains spermatogonial stem cells, which are responsible for producing sperm from puberty onwards.
Doctors should know in a matter of months whether the procedure, which took place in August, has enabled the 19-year-old to produce viable sperm.
The transplant, carried out by medics at NHS Lothian and backed by funding from Children with Cancer UK, follows a decade of research by the University of Edinburgh.
Rod Mitchell, professor of developmental endocrinology at Edinburgh’s Institute for Regeneration and Repair, and a consultant paediatric endocrinologist at NHS Lothian, said: “This is a big step towards helping boys facing treatments that damage their fertility to have children of their own.
“Ten years ago, we started our research programme to freeze and store pieces of testicle from boys before they start chemotherapy, to preserve their fertility.
“We are beginning to see some of these young men return to explore their fertility options. This study offers real hope for future fertility in boys facing cancer treatment.”
Tracey Gillies, the medical director at NHS Lothian, said the operation was a “landmark procedure” and marked an important step forward for children whose fertility may be affected by treatment they needed to overcome serious illness.
She added: “We are grateful to the patient and his family for helping advance research that could transform care for others in the future.”
In May, the Guardian reported how a man whose testicular tissue was frozen before he had chemotherapy as a child and retransplanted 16 years later had been able to produce sperm.
More than 1,200 patients in the UK and 3,100 worldwide had had testicular tissue stored for potential future use, the University of Edinburgh said.
