‘I carried God in my pocket’: Reservist who identified Oct. 7 victims recounts horrors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:50:15 UTC
09:50:15 KST

For two years, Shlomo Efrati served as a reservist at Camp Shura, the military facility near Ramla where the bodies of those murdered in the Oct. 7 massacre were brought for identification and, later, where fallen IDF soldiers from the ground campaign in Gaza were prepared for burial.
The exposure came at a severe psychological cost. Yet Efrati, 39, says he does not regret answering the call on Oct. 7.
“I would have been willing to pay this price another thousand times if necessary. I’m talking to you after four nights without sleep,” he told Ynet. “I wish none of it had happened, all the suffering of those who were murdered and their families. But once it did happen, I feel that my service at Shura was the mission of my life.”
During the first two weeks after the Hamas-led attack, Efrati and his fellow reservists took fingerprints from about 700 murdered civilians from the Nova music festival, the Gaza border communities, Zikim Beach, Sderot, Ofakim and elsewhere, helping identify victims so their families could bury and say goodbye to their loved ones.
He later began handling the bodies of fallen IDF soldiers and preparing them for burial.
His experiences at Shura have now been collected in the Hebrew book Bein Chalal Lechalal (“Between the Fallen”), published by Yedioth Books, a harrowing poetic diary edited by Yondav Kaplan and illustrated by Barak Toito.
On Oct. 7, 2023, Efrati was called up under an emergency reserve order to the IDF’s casualty data collection unit, part of the Military Rabbinate command responsible for handling the fallen. His reserve commander contacted him after the Simchat Torah holiday ended that Saturday night.
“I drove to Shura and had no idea what I was going to encounter,” he recalled. “There was a long line of refrigerated trucks at the entrance and lots of stretchers with bags on them.”
“I was trying to understand how this was supposed to work. They gathered us together and I sat next to someone. I asked his name and he said, ‘Oded.’ I told him, ‘I’m Shlomo, and from now on we’re together.’ From that moment until the end of our reserve service, we were inseparable. His name is Oded Kind, and I dedicated the book to him.”
In one poem, written after the birth of his daughter Ori Sheva in July 2025, Efrati juxtaposed the blood of childbirth with the blood he remembered from Shura:
After the birth of my daughter, Ori Sheva, yesterday, as I rolled the metal crib down the corridor, with the baby inside, I noticed: my shoes were stained with blood. from the birth I remember well another metal bed and other blood staining my shoes.
A lack of coordination between IDF and police records meant Efrati and his colleagues were asked to help identify murdered civilians by taking fingerprints from their bodies.
“A very high percentage of those murdered were identified that way,” he said.
Returning to what he saw remains emotionally difficult, but Efrati believes testimony matters, particularly in a world where some deny the Oct. 7 massacre.
He describes victims who arrived with their legs bound and bodies bearing signs of gunfire and severe injury around the groin and genital areas.
“When victims came to me with their legs tied, I could only imagine where they had been taken from, where they had been and exactly what had happened,” he said. “I remember people whose legs were tied with ropes, or who had bruising in the groin area, or bullets in those areas.”
“Sometimes there was a severed hand or a severed leg. Some bodies arrived completely burned. We couldn’t take fingerprints from them, but under the procedures we still had to go in and examine them.”
The terrorist’s body
In his book, Efrati describes how the body of a Palestinian terrorist who participated in the attack was mistakenly brought to his team.
Three grenades and an opened package of condoms were found in the man’s pockets, Efrati said. He also recalled that the man was wearing flip-flops, leading him to believe he may have been a civilian who joined the terrorists entering Israel rather than a trained member of Hamas’ Nukhba force.
In a passage written on Oct. 28, 2023, he described the encounter:
One day in the valley of slaughter, the body of a terrorist arrived by mistake. How much darkness entered the room. The body lay helpless on the table. How vulnerable he is now, I thought. And in his pocket was the essence of evil: three grenades and a pack of condoms. Suddenly, an ancient melody from the Yom Kippur prayer began playing in my head: Have mercy upon Your creations. How much compassion is missing from our world. What a tragedy that there are people imprisoned for an entire lifetime inside this evil. I am uncomfortable admitting it, but I felt pity for him. Not for his death, but for the life he lived, for his ability to choose good and for the choice he made: evil.
“Everyone treated him respectfully, just as they treated every other body, but the conversations among the guys were difficult,” Efrati said.
He found himself separating the terrorist’s choices in life from the body left behind after death.
“He chose to do the worst things a person could possibly do with his life. But once the soul is no longer in the body, only the second part remains, his body. And the body contains what we call tzelem, the image of God.”
“At that point, his body is like my body. I see a human being lying in front of me, and the part that chose to commit the atrocities is no longer there.”
“This is a person who, in my eyes, represents absolute evil, without question, and it is good that he died. It would have been better if he had died before committing the terrible acts he committed. But after he dies, his body still bears the image of God, and it must be treated with sanctity and respect.”
Asked about writing that he even felt pity for the man, Efrati described what was found in his clothing.
“It was terribly difficult. We emptied his pockets and he had grenades, a lighter and an opened packet of condoms. He also had a small Quran, like those pocket-sized editions of Psalms.”
“You see absolute evil there. This man came to murder and rape. That is what he came to do. In my internal dialogue with God, I said: How does a person reach a point where this is his choice in life? How does that happen?”
For Efrati, the question became inseparable from his faith.
“Just as there is an encounter with God through good, there is an encounter with God through what is not good,” he said. “I walked around Shura with God in my pocket.”
“Of course I had grievances. I have a profound grievance with God. At the same time, I have a deep recognition of the value of my life and of the soul inside a human being. I have profound gratitude for the privilege of living this life and accomplishing whatever can be accomplished here.”
The bitter contradiction, he acknowledged, is that the terrorist himself may also have believed he was acting in God’s name.
“That’s absolutely right. Religion is the most wonderful thing in human existence and the most terrible thing in human existence,” Efrati said.
“It is responsible for a great many wars, atrocities and hatred between people, and it is also responsible for a great many good deeds and for people’s desire to do good. It depends on where you take it.”
Efrati distinguishes religion from the spiritual experience he underwent at Shura.
“Religion is clothing. I am a religious person, but that is my clothing. It is the mother tongue I grew up speaking. My way of speaking with God is through religious elements, prayers and commandments, and that is how I am raising my children.”
“But it is one language, and I do not fool myself into believing it is the only language that exists. I have great respect for people who speak other languages.”
Oded Kind, who served alongside Efrati, confirmed to Ynet the details Efrati described, including the objects found on the terrorist’s body and the signs of abuse and severed limbs encountered by the unit.
On the edge of infinity
Efrati lives in Harish with his wife, Maayan, and their five children. Their youngest daughter, Ori Sheva, was born during the war.
He grew up in Givat Shmuel in a religious Zionist household, and his writing is steeped in Jewish texts and imagery.
He previously served as assistant director-general of the Harish municipality, director-general of the West Bank community of Etz Efraim and director-general of the Oranit local council. Today he works independently advising local authorities on large-scale projects.
During his mandatory IDF service, Efrati originally enlisted in the Nahal Brigade. Knee problems during advanced training led to his transfer to the Military Rabbinate, where he served in a religious affairs role. Only during his reserve service was he assigned to casualty identification work.
The pieces in his book were originally written as messages on his phone.
“It was the most readily available outlet I had for unloading what I was going through,” he said. “At first I wrote in a WhatsApp group with my siblings, then with some friends from the reserves.”
Some of the writing later appeared in Haaretz’s culture and literature supplement. Former supplement editor Benny Ziffer compared Efrati’s work to Haim Nahman Bialik’s poem “In the City of Slaughter,” written after the Kishinev pogrom.
The first poem in the book was written on Oct. 8, 2023, after his first night at Shura.
“In the morning I step outside for a moment / and there is light in the sky! / As if, thankfully, at least this / the Holy One remembered today / to do as He should.”
“That was written at the end of the first night,” Efrati said. “We had entered a conveyor belt. We didn’t even have time to sit down and breathe.”
“More and more bodies kept arriving. We saw things I never imagined I would see in my life. At some point I felt as though I had entered a loop and that night would never end. Like I had entered an episode of ‘Black Mirror’ and it was going to continue forever. Then suddenly there was light in the sky.”
Despite all the unanswered questions, Efrati still defines himself as a believer.
“My conversation with God is not one of doubt, but obviously these were days of a tremendous hiding of God’s face,” he said.
“Every fallen person there tells a story through their clothing or their tattoos. You try for a moment to categorize them: She is an elderly woman from Ofakim, he is a cool guy from the party with long hair, she has glitter around her eyes.”
“Every body tells a story. But at the same time, the body has been separated from the soul. It emphasized to me that a living human being is a divine creation, a creation of the soul, because I know what the body looks like without a soul.”
“When you spend so much time on the edge of the abyss, on the edge of infinity, life can no longer be taken for granted. A living person is not something to take for granted.”
‘The triggers are endless’
Like many who served at Camp Shura after Oct. 7, Efrati was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder and recognized by Israel’s Defense Ministry as a disabled IDF veteran. He was eventually released from reserve duty along with the rest of his unit.
Even mundane moments can bring the images rushing back.
“Lots of everyday situations remind me of Shura,” he said. “I have a thing about gel nail polish because of the fingerprints we took.”
“I can remember Shura when I stretch sheets over my children’s beds. It can remind me of burial shrouds. In the community garden below my home there are long wooden garden beds where I grow tomatoes, and they look exactly like coffins.”
“The triggers are endless. For two years I handled many hundreds of bodies. There was a time when I took a phone out of a soldier’s pocket and saw that his mother was calling.”
‘They abused the Thais too’
Some passages in Efrati’s book concern Thai agricultural workers murdered in the Gaza border communities.
“There was severe abuse of the Thai victims’ bodies,” he said. “You could see that they had been sprayed with gunfire, including long after they were dead.”
“You see it and think about the person who did it: Seriously, what is wrong with you? What do you have against the Thais? Why? What did they do to you?”
“You came to fight over land, fine. Leave the Thais alone. What do you have against them? Say you didn’t like that they received a paycheck from the Zionists, so you killed them. Fine. Why abuse their bodies?”
“There was something there that made clear to me how much of it was simply evil. How much of it was sitra achra,” he said, using the Aramaic Jewish term for the forces of evil. “There is a sitra achra in the world.”
In another poem, written in February 2025, he wrote:
Dear doctor, I need a prescription for breathing. And while we’re at it, if possible, how does one breathe inside a dream?
Much of Efrati’s writing has now been translated into English and was published on Oct. 7 in a digital edition of the journal Liberties. The intention is eventually to publish the full book in English.
“At the deepest level of what we do in this world, we did not come here in order not to suffer,” Efrati said. “We came here to fulfill our souls, to let our souls shine. I felt this was my life’s mission.”
Asked whether that meant all the large municipal projects he had managed now seemed insignificant compared with his work at Shura, Efrati went further.
“I was assistant director-general of Harish when they were building the city. We implemented projects worth billions. We built schools, kindergartens, roads, streets and neighborhoods. I was part of a national project, and in my eyes that is nothing compared with this mission.”
“I felt there was nothing better on earth that I could be doing at that moment than being there and caring for those who had been murdered. I feel I was given a different internal, spiritual language.”
Amid colleagues doing everything they could to respect the dead and allow families to say goodbye, Efrati says he reached another conclusion.
“I understood that good is infinite, and what is not good is infinite too,” he said.
“Humanity is constantly trying to create technology that is more sophisticated and advanced, and the artificial intelligence that erupted during these years is the ultimate technology, the ultimate machine.”
“In that situation, what remains for a person is to make their soul shine. If all knowledge exists and a machine can tell me everything, now is the time to define what I know how to do. What do I know how to say? What can the divine part within me create in this world?”
In other words, AI is pushing you to be more fully human?
“Exactly. You were created, so create. Make art,” he said. “Publishing the book and having the text recognized as possessing artistic value makes me think I need to answer that call and reveal my art to the world.”
Despite everything, Efrati remains optimistic about Israel’s future.
“In the story of the war and the way it developed, you see God speaking with us,” he said. “The pager operation and Hezbollah, Syria, Iran. Just as God blinded our eyes for several hours on Oct. 7, God knew how to open them and show us which room in Iran Haniyeh was in and when to eliminate him.”
“It is clear to me that the story with Iran is not over. Evil wants to destroy itself. What did Sinwar think, that he would manage to destroy us? Evil has some deep death wish.”

Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro

Brazil: Thousands of students march against Bolsonaro
October 8, 2026
Thousands of people joined a student march in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on Wednesday to protest the possibility that Flavio Bolsonaro could become president after the far-right candidate came out on top in the first round of the country's presidential election on Sunday.
Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, won about 2 million more votes than the incumbent president, the left-leaning Lula da Silva.
But since neither reached the 50% hurdle to win the presidency, the pair will face off in a run-off on October 25, in which Bolsonaro is considered the favorite.
"If Bolsonaro wins, Brazil will become a colony of the United States," said 20-year-old literature student Joao Victor Vieira, voicing the fear of many on the left in Brazil that Bolsonaro is too ideologically aligned with US President Donald Trump.
Brazil: 'Never again Bolsonaro'
Other marchers held signs with messages such as "Brazil isn't anyone's backyard," "I don't vote for someone who sells Brazil," and "Never again Bolsonaro" – all against a soundtrack of drums, fireworks and chants.
"We're fighting for Brazil, not for Lula," said Talita Amaral, a 19-year-old environmental sciences student, wearing Brazil's iconic yellow and green football shirt, often worn by nationalist Bolsonaro supporters but which opponents have been aiming to reclaim for themselves.
"We don't have time to be sad, we need to be doing this, occupying the streets, sending messages in WhatsApp groups, trying to convince people," she told the Associated Press.
For Alice Carneiro, a 25-year-old maritime shipping administrator, the prospect of another Bolsonaro conjures fears of far-right policies which will discriminate against Brazil's minorities – such as her transgender wife.
"I'm here because I believe in democracy," she told the AFP news agency. "Because I'm scared."
Witnesses reported that the march was notably more crowded and animated than President Lula's rally on the same street on Friday, the culmination of a lackluster campaign ahead of the election.
After the third, fourth and fifth places all went to right-wing candidates, who polled over eight million votes between them, Lula and the left appear to have a mountain to climb in the run-off.
The incumbent's campaign has shifted its focus to social media, where the far-right dominates but Lula has largely been absent, arguing he "like[s] to say only what is essential." But on Wednesday, the president convened leftist influencers who won legislative seats on Sunday to advise his campaign.

US President Donald Trump was interrupted by 12 people during the first 45 minutes of his speech to supporters in Texas, which is considered one of the key Republican-leaning states, the White House press pool reported, noting that the American leader continued his speech nevertheless.
Police escorted one of the protesters out of the venue in handcuffs. Others were escorted out without handcuffs, or left on their own. How kidnappings are hitting Nigeria’s Borno families hard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:47:32 UTC
09:47:32 KST

How kidnappings are hitting Nigeria’s Borno families hard
Across Borno, abductions are leaving families with depleted savings, missing loved ones and disrupted education.
Maiduguri, Nigeria – When Musa Abdullahi Wakawa learned that his wife and seven-year-old son had been abducted, disbelief quickly gave way to fear.
Then came the question confronting many families caught in Nigeria’s kidnapping crisis: How could he raise the ransom demanded for their release?
For days, Musa searched for a way to bring his family home, confronting the financial burden imposed by the kidnappers.
Across northeastern Nigeria, families sell livestock, seek loans, dispose of property and exhaust savings in the hope of securing the release of loved ones.
In Borno State, kidnapping has become more than a security threat. Families are losing money, living with the trauma of abduction and, in some communities, keeping their children away from school.
‘Please just help me with your prayers’
Laraba Dauda, 45, still remembers the last conversation she had with her younger sister.
Her sister was abducted on January 13, 2026, along the Biu–Buratai road, according to Laraba.
Shortly after the abduction, the phone rang. Her sister was calling from somewhere in the bush.
“Aunty, unknown people have kidnapped us and taken us somewhere in the bush. We don’t know where they are taking us. At this moment, Aunty, please just help me with your prayers,” Laraba recalled her sister saying.
The call ended in tears.
Her sister has not returned home.
Months later, Laraba and her family still do not know where she is being held or whether she is safe.
Laraba is calling on the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to rescue those still in captivity.
“We need the government to come to our aid and help rescue our relatives who have spent more than six months in captivity,” she said.
A journey that never reached Maiduguri
For Anjikwi Hena, his son’s disappearance came just as the family was looking towards a better future.
His son was abducted on March 30, 2026, according to Hena.
He had completed his education and was preparing to travel to Maiduguri in search of work. His father encouraged him and prayed for his success.
Instead, the young man disappeared into captivity.
Hena said their close relationship has made the uncertainty especially painful.
When schools become unsafe
The kidnapping crisis is also threatening education in communities already weakened by years of rebellion.
In Askira-Uba Local Government Area of Borno State, only 56 of 113 primary schools are currently functioning, according to Fasuma Askira, the local government education secretary.
Before the May attack in Mussa, 76 primary schools were operating. The threat of violence subsequently forced authorities to close another 20, leaving only 56 functioning.
On May 15, suspected rebel fighters attacked Mussa and abducted dozens of children. A register later obtained by news services identified 40 missing children, although figures provided by the community and government have varied.
The Borno State government has more recently referred to about 44 children still missing from Mussa.
Then, on June 29, armed rebels attacked the Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking National Examinations Council examinations.
Some students were recovered shortly after the attack, but 36 students and a teacher have been reported as remaining in captivity.
The attacks have deepened fears among parents and teachers already living with the threat of rebel violence.
The education authority moved junior secondary students from Mussa to a government boarding school in Uba and advised the local government to deploy community vigilantes around schools.
Soldiers have also been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes, according to the Askira.
For families in these communities, keeping children in school now means weighing access to education against the risk of further attacks.
Borno’s crisis reflects a national problem
The situation in Borno is part of a wider kidnapping crisis across Nigeria.
Amnesty International Nigeria says at least 1,100 people were abducted across the country between January and April 2026, while warning that the actual figure could be considerably higher because many incidents in remote communities go unreported.
“Apart from killing people, gunmen are now on a rampage of abductions, largely for lucrative ransom,” said Isa Sanusi, director of Amnesty International Nigeria.
“Some stay months at the mercy of gunmen in punishing situations.”
Amnesty says victims can face torture, starvation and sexual violence, while families are often forced to raise money under extreme pressure.
The organisation has also warned that fear of abduction is pushing children out of school, particularly in rural communities.
Government says security and humanitarian measures are under way
Borno State Commissioner for Information and Internal Security Usman Tar said the government was using both military and nonmilitary measures to confront insecurity.
He acknowledged that the state has several security hotspots, including the Biu-Buratai axis and the Biu-Damboa-Sabon Gari area.
“We are putting in place both kinetic and non-kinetic measures in order to overcome the problem,” Tar said.
He said the state government was working closely with the armed forces by providing additional logistical support and civilian volunteers to assist field operations.
“This has enabled us to dominate the hotspot axis,” he said, adding that attacks had reduced in some affected areas.
The government is also using technology as part of its response, including drones equipped with thermal capabilities to monitor the movement of criminals, Tar said.
Authorities, he added, were advising commuters to avoid dangerous routes where necessary, and working to ensure that people involved in kidnapping and other criminal activities were prosecuted.
Tar acknowledged the humanitarian and psychological impact on families.
He said senior government officials had visited affected families to offer condolences and reassurance, while authorities also provided financial assistance through the State Emergency Management Agency and the state humanitarian agency.
“There are fixed sums that are provided through the State Emergency Management Agency and the State Humanitarian Agency,” Tar said, adding that other legitimate mechanisms were also used to make funding available to affected families.
He said the government viewed “terrorism and criminality” as problems that required more than military action.
“Terrorism is a multinational problem,” he said.
He pointed to poverty, unemployment and illiteracy as socioeconomic factors that can contribute to insecurity, saying federal and state governments were working to improve people’s access to necessities while ensuring that criminals face the law.
When kidnapping becomes a business
Security analyst Professor Khalifa Dikwa described the kidnapping situation as “pathetic”, warning that there were no clear signs that the crisis would end soon.
He said kidnapping for ransom had “metamorphosed into a profit-making venture”, with different armed groups competing for territory and, at times, fighting for dominance in forest areas.
According to Dikwa, ransom payments help sustain criminal networks, finance weapons purchases and attract younger recruits.
That creates a cycle in which communities already struggling with poverty are forced to finance the groups terrorising them.
Families may sell possessions to secure one relative’s release, only to face another ransom demand when someone else is abducted.
Dikwa argued that the government needs stronger intelligence- and technology-driven operations to locate armed groups and disrupt the movement of ransom money.
He also called for security agencies to receive modern weapons, night-vision equipment and tracking technology, alongside improved welfare for soldiers and other security personnel operating on the front lines.
For families, paying ransom may be the only immediate way to try to save someone they love. For armed groups, successful ransom payments can provide the resources and incentive to carry out further abductions.
The cost of waiting
Musa is waiting for his wife and young son. Laraba is waiting for her sister. Hena is waiting for the son who was preparing to leave home in search of work.
In Askira-Uba, 20 primary schools have closed since the Mussa attack, while dozens of children remain unaccounted for.
During their final phone call, Laraba’s sister told her:
“This is my last communication.”

Margaret Hamilton, trailblazer whose software powered Apollo 11 moon landing, dies at 90
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:40:37 UTC
09:40:37 KST

Margaret Hamilton, the computer pioneer whose software powered the first moon landing, has died, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) announced on Wednesday. She was 90.
In an era before titles such as software engineer and computer scientist became mainstream, Hamilton, who died on 30 September, learned to program under the tutelage of a renowned MIT meteorologist.
She continued to perfect the craft in an MIT laboratory, writing software that could detect enemy aircraft. When the institute received a Nasa contract to develop the Apollo onboard flight software, she jumped at the opportunity.
“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she told the Guardian in 2019.
In 1969, minutes before the Apollo 11 spacecraft was set to make history by landing on the lunar surface, an onboard computer’s alarm rang, indicating an emergency.
Faced with a decision of whether to abort the mission, the spacecraft continued on. The software was working just as Hamilton and her team intended.
“It quickly became clear the software was not only informing everyone that there was a hardware-related problem but was compensating for it – restarting and re-establishing the highest priority tasks. The error detection and recovery mechanisms had come to the rescue,” Hamilton said.
Barack Obama referenced the incident when he presented her with the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.
“Our astronauts didn’t have much time, but thankfully they had Margaret Hamilton,” he said.
Hamilton is survived by her daughter, a son-in-law, two grandsons and four great grandchildren, according to MIT.
Reflecting on the mission, in a 2009 interview with MIT News, Hamilton said: “Looking back, we were the luckiest people in the world; there was no choice but to be pioneers; no time to be beginners.”

US city council opens with ‘Hail Satan’ prayer (VIDEO)
An Iowa city council meeting erupted into controversy after opening with a Satanic invocation that ended with the words “Hail Satan,” prompting a local pastor to demand that officials “reverse this curse.”
Matt Dalbey, an Ottumwa resident and former city council member, delivered the invocation at Tuesday’s meeting under a policy allowing residents of different religions and belief systems to open council proceedings with a prayer or reflection.
Dalbey began by addressing a “dark father” and invoking what he called the “Luciferian impulse” before concluding: “It is done. Hail Satan.”
The invocation immediately drew objections from New Life Center pastor Rick Bick, who interrupted the proceedings.
“That was a curse put on the city,” he said. “Most of you know that, and we need to just stop and reverse it… ‘Hail Satan’ is not welcome here.”
Mayor Benjamin Foote then called for a 30-second moment of silence “to reflect on whatever it is we need to reflect on at this time.”
Dalbey’s invocation was permitted under a policy adopted by the council in January. The measure states that Ottumwa, a city of some 25,500 people, seeks to respect “the diversity of both organized and unorganized religious denominations, as well as other faiths, belief systems, or the lack thereof.”
Council member Cara Galloway had specifically warned that a Satanic invocation could happen when she cast the only vote against the policy in January. “Opening with an invocation means allowing viewpoints that may not reflect our own,” she said, warning that selectively objecting to one now could expose taxpayers to legal liability.
The city said Wednesday that it had been flooded with calls over the prayer, many of them “rude and full of profanities,” but stressed that officials cannot discriminate between denominations or belief systems.
The recording of the meeting had drawn more than 12,000 views on the city’s YouTube channel by Wednesday afternoon, making it the most-watched video ever posted there.
Dalbey is scheduled to deliver another invocation at the council’s November 3 meeting. He told the Ottumwa Courier that the prayer is used by the Satanic Temple of Iowa, of which he is a member, but “has nothing to do with the belief in a satanic deity.” The organization describes itself as non-theistic.

A 194-year-old tortoise, world’s oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:30:00 UTC
09:30:00 KST

A 194-year-old tortoise, world’s oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
- Scientists say Jonathan, a 194-year-old Aldabra giant tortoise on St Helena, may live so long because of helpful genetic traits and youthful cell systems.
- Researchers studied his genome and epigenome, finding links to DNA repair, mitochondria, insulin control and telomere function, plus 287 unique genes and extra cancer-fighting copies.
- Jonathan, now mostly blind but still hungry, is a beloved island symbol of resilience; scientists say his case may also help explain ageing in humans.
AI generated
The world’s oldest-known terrestrial animal, an Aldabra male giant tortoise named Jonathan which is estimated to be about 194 years old, may owe his extraordinary longevity to a combination of genetic traits and an ability to keep key cellular systems functioning in a more youthful way, according to scientists.
Members of this species are known to live more than 100 years, but Jonathan has far exceeded that.
Brought to the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena as a fully grown animal in 1882, likely from the Aldabra Atoll or the Granitic Seychelles, the tortoise resides in a paddock at Plantation House, the governor’s residence.
“Other Aldabra tortoises have been claimed to have lived as long as Jonathan, but he has the most documentary evidence supporting his age,” said Benjamin Vaisvil, a researcher affiliated with the organisation Kallel and co-lead author of the study published on Oct 7 in the journal Science Advances.
Scientists have studied Jonathan to explore the secrets of the animal’s amazing longevity, sequencing its genome and analysing its epigenome – the chemical markers that control which genes switch on and off.
“We found changes in Jonathan’s genome in pathways associated with longevity, like DNA repair, mitochondrial function, insulin regulation and telomere function,” Vaisvil said.
Mitochondria are structures considered the powerhouse of a cell. Insulin is a hormone that helps regulate levels of blood sugar by letting it enter the body’s cells for energy. Telomeres are protective caps at the ends of chromosomes, structures that carry genetic information inside cell nuclei.
Researchers compared Jonathan’s epigenome with those of four other Aldabra tortoises, ranging from juveniles to older adults.
While pretending to feed Jonathan, they waited until the tortoise began biting the air, then wedged his mouth open with a gloved hand and scraped under the tongue with a specialised kit. St Helena officials restrict blood draws to prevent infection risks.
To explain the finding, Vaisvil compared the genome to a cookbook and the epigenome to handwritten notes in the margins.
“As the cookbook ages, those notes become more difficult to read clearly. We can think of that as methylation entropy,” Vaisvil said, referring to a metric for disorder in a certain biochemical process.
Most of the notes in Jonathan’s “cookbook” look very old. But in certain regions, stretches of DNA that act as switches controlling whether genes are turned on or off, Jonathan’s methylation entropy was lower than that of every tortoise studied except a five-year-old juvenile. These regions controlled genes that influence longevity.
The researchers identified 287 genes with variants unique to Jonathan, including some linked to tumour suppression and DNA repair. The tortoise also carries extra copies of a gene that encodes a protein that hunts down ageing and cancerous cells.
‘Gentle giant’
When he was younger, Jonathan was known for mischievous antics including overturning chairs and lying on croquet balls, according to the tortoise’s longtime veterinarian and study co-author Joe Hollins. Cataracts have since left him mostly blind. Hollins describes Jonathan today as “a gentle giant”.
Determining how long giant tortoises can live is challenging because reliable historical records are scarce and many outlive researchers.
Record-keeping before the 20th century was also problematic. While a young tortoise’s age can be estimated from growth rings on the plates that form the animal’s shell, ascertaining the age of adults is more difficult. The new study involved only one exceptionally old tortoise, making it hard to determine whether the traits identified are unique to Jonathan or common among long-lived tortoises.
“We cannot say for certain that what we found is the reason for his longevity,” Vaisvil said.
Environmental factors also may have contributed. Jonathan lives on a tropical island with an optimal diet carefully managed by trained veterinarians.
The research findings broadly match patterns documented in studies of exceptionally long-lived people, suggesting that some mechanisms of ageing may be shared across species.
Vaisvil noted that a recent study of a 117-year-old woman found unusually efficient mitochondrial function, echoing findings in some of Jonathan’s regions.
Voracious appetite
Despite his age, Jonathan retains a voracious appetite, Hollins said, lifting his head and stretching out his long neck when the veterinarian calls out his name.
“I know he knows me, knows my voice and my handling, and I also know it isn’t love on his part but a recognition of the arrival of a feast,” Hollins said. “And yet I, of course, don’t mind. I have a huge affection for him.”
“He is a remarkable symbol. Icon, I know, is an overused word, but Guinness World Records has just given him ‘icon’ status this year,” he added.
Beloved by island residents, Jonathan has lived through world wars and the rise and fall of empires.
“He is symbolic of resilience, longevity, endurance, a persistent presence throughout huge historic events,” Hollins said. REUTERS

“That is deeply disappointing, despite all due respect for France.”

The agreement also caused controversy within the European Union, with Ukraine strongly opposing sanctions relief for businessmen linked to the Kremlin while Russia continues its war.

“While there is still a chance, we must save at least some of those who will not survive imprisonment,” Orlov said, according to AFP.
He urged French lawmakers to take responsibility for individual prisoners and publicly follow their cases.
“It would be very important for members of parliament to take symbolic responsibility for specific political prisoners, to monitor their fate, and to speak about them publicly.”
According to Memorial, more than 1,800 people are recognized as political prisoners in Russia, while approximately 5,700 are imprisoned or facing prosecution for politically motivated reasons.

Mia Schem slams ‘pro-Palestinian sheep,’ Drake as she recounts Hamas captivity

09:17:34 KST

Three years after she was abducted to the Gaza Strip, Mia Schem is recounting the terrifying moments of the morning of October 7, the horrors she endured in Gaza and what she calls a mentality of “pro-Palestinian sheep.” In an interview with the Daily Mail, Schem, the first hostage whom Hamas featured in a psychological warfare video, released on October 16, spoke about the rising wave of antisemitism and her disappointment with musician Drake.
'I think people don’t understand anything. People follow what others say, like sheep. They follow one another,” she said of the rise in antisemitism and anti-Israel sentiment around the world. “They follow what they see in the news. The news presents what it wants people to see. I can only tell you what I know from my own experience: I was kidnapped from my country and taken into Gaza. I know how they treated me there.”
That treatment, she said, was particularly cruel: “They teach their children from the very beginning to hate, to become terrorists and to glorify death. If you kill Jewish people, your parents in Gaza are proud of you. You have brought pride to your family. I thought perhaps the women would be different. Woman to woman, I thought there might be a little humanity. But there was nothing. It was worse with the wife of the man who held me captive. She hated me because I was being kept in the same room as her husband, the man who had kidnapped me. She was jealous and so cruel. Sometimes she would give me food only once every two or three days. I would get one bottle of water, perhaps two, for the whole week. It was only enough to keep me alive, not because they cared about me.”
The children of the terrorist who held her captive were also cruel to her. “They would tease me with food: "Do you want food?" Then they would not give it to me. They treated me like an animal in a cage.”
Schem added in the interview: “I know what it means to be Israeli and Jewish. In the Torah, we are taught, first of all, to be a good person, a good human being. After that comes the other things. Being a good person is what matters. What I experienced in Gaza was completely different. I saw people glorifying death. When a terrorist dies after carrying out an attack, his family can be proud of him.”
Speaking about Drake, whose latest song includes the line “we pray for Gaza,” Schem said: “I loved him very much. He even gave me a sweater, a jacket from his brand. But I was shocked by the song he released about Gaza.'”
In the Daily Mail interview, she also described the physical and emotional scars left by her captivity: “Listen, the fact that I am sitting here in front of you is a miracle. Even talking about it now, I find myself getting stuck on the words. It is beyond anything I can explain. Look at my hand. This arm is shorter than the other because they shot me at point-blank range. My arm was almost completely disconnected. Only a small part of it was still attached to my body. I picked up my own arm from the floor and carried it with me. I screamed. I still cannot get my head around it. I lost an enormous amount of blood — something like five litres. It’s a miracle that I’m alive. And they gave me nothing. Nothing at all.”
Schem arrived at the Nova music festival with her close friend, Elia Toledano. “Everything happened so fast. Five minutes earlier I was dancing with my best friend. It was as though I closed my eyes and opened them again, and I was in Gaza. It happened so quickly that I couldn’t take it in. There were Hamas terrorists everywhere, so I didn’t see the face of the person who shot me. I'’m only starting to feel it now. Sometimes I can talk about what happened, and then suddenly I have to stop. But I think that is good for me. I want to understand what happened to me and how I can go on from it. I just can’t talk about Elia. It is very hard. He was someone extraordinary. People say that God takes only the good people. It is not a lie. It really is true. He was an angel.”
Describing her abduction to Gaza, she said: “There were seven Hamas terrorists with me in an ordinary private car with five seats. They dragged me by my hair, pushed me into the car and forced my head down. That is all I can say. I really cannot talk about the rest of it today.”
Despite all the horrors she endured during her 55 days in captivity, Schem said she wants a different future.
“I don’t want to spend my life being sad, constantly reminding myself of what happened just to feel sad again.  I want to build a home in Israel. I want to get married. I want to build a home in Israel. I want to be happy. Having children is my biggest dream. I don’t have a boyfriend. I think I will only be able to open my heart to somebody else when I am in a good place within myself. Right now, that is a process.”

Microsoft pushes AI vision with new, expensive Surface laptop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:17:00 UTC
09:17:00 KST

Microsoft pushes AI vision with new, expensive Surface laptop
- Microsoft launched the Surface Ultra, a new AI laptop with Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. It costs US$2,599 and ships on 16 October.
- The company says “hybrid intelligence” will mix local and cloud AI. Satya Nadella and Jensen Huang said AI should work across all devices.
- The move helps Microsoft compete with Apple, Intel and AMD. It also fits Microsoft’s wider plan to cut its dependence on OpenAI.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Microsoft is pushing a “hybrid intelligence” future with a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than US$2,500 (S$3,200), the company announced Oct 7.
The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud data centres, where running AI is slower and more expensive.
It also sees Nvidia, whose data centre processors power the AI revolution, make a move into personal computing, a sector dominated for decades by chips from Intel and Qualcomm.
“The trajectory for me is so clear. There will never be a moment where we will go and look and say: ‘Oh, this runs locally, this runs in the cloud.’ You will expect this hybrid intelligence to be everywhere and pervasive,” chief executive Satya Nadella said at an event in San Francisco.
He was joined onstage by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who echoed the idea that AI will be integrated into all computing going forward and on all devices.
Agentic AI, in particular, will be central to software development, Huang said, referring to systems programmed to be autonomous and perform tasks without supervision.
With all the changes from AI, “the computer has to be revolutionised”, Huang said.
The partnership between the two US-based tech titans helps them compete with Apple, Intel and AMD in the personal computing market.
Apple unveiled two desktop computers in September, the Mac mini and Mac Studio, which it touted as powerful new options capable of processing AI software locally.
Microsoft has been working on building “AI PCs” since at least 2024, when its laptops were powered by Qualcomm chips.
The new Surface Ultra will use Nvidia’s state-of-the-art AI chip, RTX Spark, which the semiconductor giant announced earlier in 2026.
It will cost US$2,599 and begins shipping on Oct 16.
Some AI computing power and data will be processed locally or on the device, while other applications are still handled remotely via Microsoft’s cloud computing services.
“We built it for developers and creators pushing the limits of performance,” Pavan Davuluri, Microsoft executive vice-president of Windows and device, said on Oct 7.
The news comes just a couple of weeks after Microsoft announced it would integrate Word, Excel and PowerPoint into its AI-powered assistant Copilot, in an effort to make AI the entry point for its famous suite of productivity software.
OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, and Claude-maker Anthropic each launched their own document creation tools in recent months.
The two San Francisco-based AI labs are also key suppliers for Microsoft, since Copilot runs primarily on their models.
Microsoft’s in-house models currently power only a few products, such as GitHub’s Copilot coding tool.
In June, Microsoft also unveiled its own cutting-edge artificial intelligence models – a crucial step toward reducing its dependence on OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT.
Microsoft, the first company to have invested massively in OpenAI and its largest corporate shareholder, has for several years been seeking to reduce its reliance on its Sam Altman-led partner.
It renegotiated their alliance in 2025 and retains only a non-exclusive licence on its technology until 2032.

How Indonesians Are Being Recruited Into the Russian Army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:17:00 UTC
09:17:00 KST

On September 18, Indonesia’s ambassador to Russia, Jose Tavares, told the state news agency Antara that his embassy had taken dozens of calls from families who believed their relatives had been recruited into Russia’s army by agents on social media promising large salaries. Jakarta has so far dealt with these cases one by one, in line with standard consular procedures. On September 19, the Indonesian embassy sent a note verbale, a formal diplomatic letter, asking the Russian Foreign Ministry to verify the names, and bring home those who failed Russia’s medical examination. Arrmanatha Nasir, the career diplomat who was sworn in as foreign minister on October 1, has inherited that approach.
However, the current approach is ill-equipped to handle a problem that has arisen alongside President Prabowo Subianto’s efforts to build a close relationship with Vladimir Putin’s Russia. Indonesian institutions have been promoting Russia as a labor destination, including in a special economic zone that assembles attack drones, even as they warn their citizens against the job offers that might lead to the frontlines in Ukraine. Meanwhile, Jakarta counts the personal closeness between Prabowo and Putin as an asset, yet it has made no public use of that closeness to aid the citizens caught in this recruitment trap.
Most of the public record on these cases comes either from one of the warring parties or from the recruits and their families. Ukraine’s foreign intelligence service said on August 27 that it had documents on at least eight Indonesians who were recruited into Russia’s army. However, Kompas noted that the documents are Russian e-visa notices, while Russia’s embassy in Jakarta called the release a disinformation campaign. Meanwhile, a man who told Republika that he was among those named said that an agent had promised him a security job and then pushed him into a military contract, although he had failed his medical examination in Moscow. He was in hospital when he spoke to the newspaper, after a Ukrainian drone had taken one of his fingers. In Natuna, the parents of a 30-year-old man said that a comrade had reported him killed by a Ukrainian drone on September 20, which the regent of Natuna still called uncertain and unclear 10 days later.
The cases point to three problems, the first of which is that recruitment follows the logic of labor migration long before it turns into military service. Hartyo Harkomoyo, Indonesia’s deputy ambassador in Moscow, told RRI that most recruits are promised civilian jobs, some of them as drivers, builders, cooks, or nurses under Russia’s Defense Ministry. Some are recruited from Indonesia through social media, and others from among Indonesians already in Russia, especially students. A content creator from Central Java told Republika that a Russian contact on social media had offered him a post in a government ministry or a large company and paid for his flight and his e-visa. The contract he was handed in Moscow was a military one, written in Russian, which he could not read. An Indonesian man filmed by Ukrainian soldiers after his capture in early September said he had been working as a cleaner when he was put into uniform and sent to the front.
The case of the man from Natuna shows the same path from a civilian job to the frontline. According to his family, the young man had worked as an electrician in the Philippines before going to Russia with seven other Indonesians. He believed he had been hired to deliver food to the troops. The head of his neighborhood said that he refused a transfer to a combat unit because it was not in his contract. He could not leave because his passport was being held. And yet, the migrant-worker protection office in his province found no record of him as a registered worker.
The second problem concerns the fact that Indonesian institutions themselves opened a formal labor channel to Russia this year. In January, the Ministry for the Protection of Migrant Workers (KP2MI) welcomed a plan by the aluminum producer RUSAL to take 50 vocational-school graduates, with departures scheduled for September. They presented it as part of Prabowo’s “SMK Go Global” program. A month later, KP2MI named Russia a new placement destination in manufacturing and shipbuilding. It also said it had received a draft Memorandum of Understanding from Russia’s Federal Service for Labor and Employment. In the same meeting, the deputy minister received a warning from the defense attaché in Moscow that Indonesians should beware of well-paid job advertisements for private military companies, suggesting that the Ministry knew of the risk from the start.
The West Java provincial labor office went further in June, when its one-stop service for migrant workers advertised jobs for women aged 18 to 24 in Russia’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone, with salary in dollars and a flight paid by the employer. The United States Treasury sanctioned the company that runs the zone in February 2024 for producing Iranian-designed Geran-2 attack drones under a contract with Russia’s military. An Associated Press investigation found that young African women recruited there, with offers of work in hospitality and catering, ended up assembling drones. The West Java advertisement, now marked closed, names no employer and gives no number of applicants or departures. No documented recruit is known to have left through these channels. Their effect is to present Russia, including the defense industry, as an ordinary destination for Indonesian workers.
In July, Indonesia’s embassy in Moscow warned Indonesians against taking job offers on tourist visas and signing contracts in a language they could not read. The warning did not mention military service, and a month later the embassy’s own job fair for Indonesians in Russia, held on August 17, listed Alabuga SEZ among the employers, beside RUSAL, En+ Group, and Rusagro. The ambassador presented the fair as a way to widen Indonesians’ chances to work and build careers in Russia. Indonesia’s national placement system still listed 76 places in Russia on October 1. Among them, 60 places are for fishery workers whose placement permits were issued on September 1.
The third problem is that Jakarta’s response to these recruitment traps has treated the issue as a series of separate cases. The Foreign Ministry’s spokesperson said on September 18 that the government would look into claims of fraud and exploitation, protect any Indonesians found to be victims, and prosecute recruiters. She added that any verified service in a foreign army would be seen as an individual act that does not represent the policy of the Indonesian government. Tavares described the embassy’s note verbale to the Russian Foreign Ministry as a request for verification and clarification. Meanwhile, KP2MI’s deputy minister, Christina Aryani, said the recruits had been lured by advertisements and declined to treat the cases as trafficking without proof of exploitation, thereby leaving any kind of repatriation for the Foreign Ministry to negotiate. Moreover, as of press time, the ministry’s online travel advisory for Russia still said nothing about recruitment.
I would suggest that the reason for this restraint lies in the relationship itself. Prabowo has met Putin five times since taking office, and in Vladivostok last month, he offered Indonesia to Russian businesses as a natural entry point to ASEAN. A government that has invested this much in the relationship at the presidential level is unlikely to seek a public quarrel with Moscow over a few dozen citizens. Therefore, it treats each case as a matter of individual choice and consular care. Friction between KP2MI and the Foreign Ministry, visible in Aryani’s remarks, explains why the cases pass between agencies, but not why no one has raised them with Moscow at the political level. The cost of that restraint falls on the men themselves, because Moscow has little reason to act on the cases of a partner that has not raised them at the political level publicly.
It is true that not every Indonesian in Russia’s army was deceived by a job offer. Among the eight named by Ukraine is a former activist and party cadre from Aceh whose friends told Generasi.co that he had spoken of going to Russia to fight if a business project failed, and Harkomoyo distinguishes recruits who were tricked from those who signed knowingly and were aware that they could lose their citizenship. Aryani made the same point when she compared the recruits to Indonesians who had knowingly taken jobs in scam compounds in Cambodia. However, the choices of individual recruits do not explain why Indonesians became a target in the first place, which is a question about Jakarta’s dealings with Moscow.
An investigation published by Germany’s public broadcaster in July suggests an answer. Tagesschau’s reporters followed an agency called WorkVia, which ran Instagram videos addressed to Indonesians and paid Facebook advertisements offering $3,200 a month and a $30,000 signing bonus for a contract with Russia’s army. Posing as an Indonesian applicant, one reporter was told by the agency’s recruiter that the job was risky but well paid. Since February 2026, according to the investigation, WorkVia has addressed mainly men from Cambodia and Indonesia, two countries from which Russia had hardly recruited before. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry told the reporters that Russia keeps 36 countries off its recruitment lists to avoid negative reactions from their leaders, and a version of that list obtained by the independent Russian outlet iStories includes India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, and Laos (although it does not mention Indonesia and the Philippines). iStories links the list to diplomatic pressure: Nepal, India, and Sri Lanka have appealed to Moscow since mid-2024, and Jordan was added after making similar demands in November 2025. Read together, the two findings suggest that recruiters moved toward countries whose governments had not objected, and that Indonesia was one of them.
Other governments have raised the issue with Moscow, and several have obtained concessions. Nepal suspended work permits for Russia and Ukraine in January 2024, after nine of its citizens were killed in the war. Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Putin in July 2024, after which New Delhi said Russia had promised to discharge all Indians in its army. India reported 139 of its nationals released by the end of July this year, although New Delhi says its citizens are still being recruited despite its warnings. Sri Lanka’s foreign minister obtained an assurance from Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in June 2024 that no further recruitment from the island would take place, and South Africa’s president secured Putin’s support for the return of 17 men in a telephone call in February. Colombia formally asked Russia and Ukraine in September to stop enlisting its citizens. None of these governments had to break with Moscow to do so.
Jakarta’s first step should be political, since its leverage lies in the relationship itself. Prabowo, or his new foreign minister, can ask Moscow to stop recruiting Indonesians and to release those already under contract. India and South Africa, fellow BRICS members, made such requests at the highest level. Putin, for his part, has called Indonesia one of Russia’s trusted friends in ASEAN. A partner that close should have no difficulty in asking for the same treatment as others. The recruiters’ stop-list suggests that Moscow adjusts when a government’s leaders object.
Jakarta should also bring its own labor channels into line with its warnings. Until Russian employers can be checked, KP2MI and the provincial labor offices should stop placing Indonesians with firms tied to Russia’s defense industry, beginning with the Alabuga SEZ. The embassy in Moscow should not invite such firms to its job fairs. The draft labor memorandum with Russia’s Federal Service for Labor and Employment is the place to write that exclusion down. The cost would be small, since the national placement system lists more than 2,200 places in Slovakia and more than 1,400 in Poland, against 76 in Russia.
Indonesia’s warnings also need to reach the people whom the recruiters already reach on social media. WorkVia found Indonesians through Instagram videos and paid Facebook advertisements, although Meta has barred advertising from Russia since 2022, while the embassy’s warning was posted on a ministry website. The Foreign Ministry and KP2MI could run Indonesian-language warnings on the same platforms where the advertisements appear. The Communications Ministry could also ask Meta to enforce its own ban. Colombia offers a working model, since its Foreign Ministry has added an awareness campaign to a screening protocol in its passport offices for applicants who say they intend to fight abroad.
Lastly, Indonesia need not act alone, since other states in the region face similar recruitment challenges. The Philippines, which is also missing from the recruiters’ stop-list, said in September that it was verifying reports of Filipinos recruited into foreign armed forces, in terms close to Jakarta’s own, and WorkVia has turned to Cambodia as well. Indonesia, the Philippines, and Cambodia could take the matter up together in ASEAN, which would raise the political cost to Moscow of recruiting in Southeast Asia.
As I have argued elsewhere, calling these men mercenaries narrows the protection Indonesia can still give them. Treating them as a series of individual cases narrows it in the same way, because it leaves the routes that brought them to Russia intact. A government that offers itself as Russia’s entry point to Southeast Asia is well placed to ask Moscow to keep its recruiters away from Indonesians. It should make that request at the level at which the relationship itself is conducted, which is the presidential one.

Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:16:41 UTC
09:16:41 KST

Russia dismisses reports of second plague case as ‘false information’
Senior WHO official urges Russia to to provide more information on the suspected pneumonic plague case.
What we know about Russia’s suspected plague case
Russia has dismissed media reports of a second suspected case of pneumonic plague in Siberia, as the World Health Organization (WHO) urged Moscow to formally respond to its inquiry regarding the reports.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that “the vast majority of what the media is reporting regarding this situation is false information”, in response to a question about reports of a second case.
Peskov said that information on the suspected cases should be derived from official statements by Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor.
Russia’s health regulator said there were no infections detected among staff after a plague institute worker died from pneumonia. The origin of the illness remains unknown, prompting international concern that the case could involve the plague.
Russia acknowledged on Sunday that a 28-year-old woman employed at a plague research institute in Siberia’s Irkutsk died after she was diagnosed with a “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, prompting global concern over a suspected plague case.
The United States, the European Union and the WHO have all called on Russia to be transparent about the situation.
US President Donald Trump told reporters on Wednesday when asked whether it’s possible the infection was from a bioweapon, “We do not think so.”
“They are saying it is very much under control,” he said, adding “Russia is not saying much either.”
Trump confirmed he has spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and when asked about what US intelligence agencies are reporting, Trump said the two sides are “in very deep discussions” and that they would likely be able to provide an update “probably tomorrow.”
More information needed
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus urged Russia to clarify “media reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause” at the Irkutsk institute.
“We have received information from two media outlets, one of them is Russian,” Tedros said in a briefing on Wednesday, adding, “We asked Russia to respond to that.”
“We cannot ignore any reporting that comes,” the WHO chief said.
WHO Director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said the UN agency does not know the “causative agent” behind the death in the first suspected case.
In a briefing, Van Kerkhove said, “We don’t understand how she was infected.”
“We need information in a timely way. We need regular information. We need answers to the follow-up of the questions that we have asked,” she added.
Low US risk
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the risk to the United States from the suspected pneumonic plague case as “extremely low”.
CDC Director Erica Schwartz said on Wednesday that the US agency is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State, Defense and other agencies to monitor people travelling from the area.
The CDC has a health station at New York City’s John F Kennedy International Airport that can screen travellers coming from the Siberian region, she added.
About 200 people per year travel from the Siberian region to the United States, a Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson told the Reuters news agency.
Direct flights between Russia and the US have been suspended since the start of the Ukraine war in 2022.
“What we’re doing from a whole of government standpoint is we’re making sure that we understand exactly what that threat is,” Schwartz said at the Wall Street Journal’s The Future of Health event in Washington, DC.
“At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely,” the CDC said in a separate statement.

In corporate trading, Caterpillar led the Dow lower, dropping 5.75 percent after the Federal Trade Commission and the U.S. Department of Agriculture announced a public inquiry into farm-equipment markets. The FBI has arrested an 18-year-old man who had been plotting to carry out a mass shooting at the Mall of America near Minneapolis in the name of ISIS, according to court filings.
He was arrested on Tuesday after an FBI undercover agent sold the Minnesota man, Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, an AK-47, ammunition and magazines for $600, according to the complaint. Mohamud told the informant he planned to use the items to kill 30 to 60 people at an event at the mall in late October.
Mohamud was charged with one count of knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition in order to commit an act of terrorism. His lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
According to the complaint, Mohamud told an FBI source on various messaging platforms that he intended to travel overseas to fight on behalf of al-Shabaab, a designated foreign terrorist organization. He said if he couldn't travel, he planned to conduct a mass shooting. He later said he wanted to join ISIS.
He also allegedly expressed support for a man who rammed a truck into a crowd in New Orleans on January 1, 2025, killing 14, before being killed in a shootout with police.
Plan for attack at the Mall of America

The Mall of America is the largest mall in the United States, with a theme park, an aquarium, and more than 500 stores.
On Tuesday, Mohamud allegedly bought the AK-47, four 30-round-capacity magazines, and about 200 rounds of ammunition from an FBI undercover agent. Soon after, FBI agents arrested him.

00:08:02 UTC
09:08:02 KST

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew to the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday and praised the resilience of sailors who endured an extended, wartime deployment that drew scrutiny over suicide attempts on board.
The Lincoln, which is due to dock on Thursday in San Diego, is the flagship of a carrier strike group that had eight suicide attempts among US sailors during its time at sea, according to the Navy. Its deployment included more than 260 continuous days without a port call, a record, according to the Pentagon.
Hegseth, whose speeches regularly target the media, accused reporters of trying to turn the crew of the Lincoln strike group into symbols of dysfunction or of a failed mission instead of heroes of the conflict, and presented a citation from President Donald Trump for their achievements during the Iran war.
The Lincoln's accomplishments included sinking 64 Iranian warships, destroying 21 anti-ship cruise missiles, executing 3,693 combat sorties, launching 450 Tomahawk land attack cruise missiles and firing 1.37 million pounds of ordnance against Iran, Hegseth said.
Despite the fast pace of combat operations, it suffered no casualties and had no aircraft mishaps, Hegseth said.
"What makes the US military and the US Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome - you finish the mission nonetheless," Hegseth told the crew. "Yes, it's hard. That's why you're here. You do difficult and hard things."
Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months but can be extended during times of conflict. Mental health issues on long deployments have long challenged the US Navy.
In August, amid reports of low morale and supply shortages on board, Trump was asked whether he thought the Lincoln had been deployed too long. Trump responded: "No, no, no. Not nearly long enough."
Hegseth acknowledged some challenges on board, saying "there wasn't an easy resupply."
Ahead of the carrier's return to port, Hegseth joked that he was "the only thing standing between you and home" and that he was also the one who signed the orders repeatedly extending the deployment.
"You deserve to see your families and see them as soon as possible," Hegseth said, adding he just wanted to see them for "a moment on the route, on the way in, just to say thank you."
Crossroads in US-Iran war
The carrier's return comes at a crossroads in the US-Iran war, which has jolted global energy markets and become a political liability for Trump and fellow Republicans ahead of November midterm elections.
The war — and its $3 billion monthly price tag — has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Higher energy prices have put Trump and Republicans on the defensive in competitive states that will decide control of Congress.
Trump is weighing next steps against Iran, including whether to escalate strikes before or after the elections, as he presses a naval blockade meant to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
Vice President JD Vance told Reuters on Monday that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' seven-month war.
Hegseth said the crew of the Lincoln had helped ensure the US objective of preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.
"You have changed the arc of history," he told them on Wednesday.

China’s crackdown on house churches: An interview with Su Ziming, wife of detained Chinese pastor Wang Lin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
00:01:00 UTC
09:01:00 KST

On 9 October 2025, Pastor Wang Lin was taken away by police during a crackdown on Zion Church. Zion Church is a “house church” – in other words, one of the primarily protestant churches in China that operate independently of the state-approved religious system and therefore lack official registration. Wang Lin’s case highlights ongoing concerns about religious freedom for independent Christian communities in China. In the months that followed Wang’s arrest, his wife Su Ziming and their young son and daughter endured constant surveillance and harassment, restrictions on their ability to leave China, and prolonged family separation. Today, Su and her children live in the United States, while her husband remains detained in China.
Here, Su tells Amnesty International how the crackdown changed the course of her family’s life and describes the wider repression faced by China’s “house churches” and its faith-based communities.
How did your husband end up a faith leader?
Before becoming a pastor, Wang Lin worked as a lawyer. In 2006, after he became a Christian, he left the legal profession, enrolled in seminary, and spent several years in the US pursuing theological studies. We returned to China at the end of 2017 and Wang Lin became a faith leader at Beijing Zion Church.
As a pastor, his greatest joy came from being with others.
In 2018, the Chinese authorities shut down Beijing Zion Church. What happened next?
After the shutdown, many members were driven out of Beijing by authorities through harassment, including coerced evictions, or concerns about their jobs. A congregation that had once worshipped together found itself scattered across the country.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, believers stayed connected through Zoom services and online Bible studies. Gradually, the church became a network spanning multiple provinces rather than a single congregation based in Beijing.
And did the authorities allow this?
No! At the same time this network developed, surveillance and repression intensified.
I think the authorities have tried for a long time to bring house churches fully under their supervision.
When house churches refuse government control and wish to exercise their beliefs freely, the governments see this as a problem. And they’re not afraid to use trumped up charges under existing criminal law to solve that problem. At the end of the day, whatever charges they use, their ultimate goal is to crush the church and make it disappear.
What are some of the tactics used by the authorities to target the Zion Church?
In the case against Zion Church, authorities accused church leaders of receiving “fraudulent proceeds”, treating believers’ tithes and offerings as unlawfully obtained funds. They also characterized church training programmes and seminary courses were deemed as engaging in “illegal business activities.” My husband Wang Lin has been charged on both counts.
I think the charges against Zion Church reflect a broader trend in recent years. While some church leaders, like many human rights defenders, are prosecuted on national security charges, authorities have increasingly used charges such as “fraud” and “illegal business operations” to target the normal actions and management of the institutions and communities themselves.
What activities are being targeted with these allegations?
In the Zion case, the authorities have defined believers’ voluntary offerings as money obtained through fraud. They see it as money that was obtained from people through deception. And as to the theology courses, this was a discipleship training programme within the church. It was never intended to make money. I don’t think this was about actually finding problems with our financial activities; it was aimed at faith communities themselves.
What’s been the impact of these allegations?
A lot of human rights activists, and very high-profile church leaders, face serious criminal charges like “inciting subversion of state power”. But a lot of damage can be done with these ordinary or more “minor” criminal prosecutions. Not least because it affects the ability of parishioners and believers to exercise their right to freedom of religion.
These charges not only stigmatize normal religious activities but also obscure the broader issue of freedom of religion. By treating voluntary offerings as “fraudulent proceeds” and church training programmes as “illegal business activities”, the authorities are effectively criminalizing the peaceful exercise of religious freedom, making it easier to target church leaders and entire faith communities.
What about the family members of those targeted – how has it affected you and your family?
Even before my husband’s arrest, we were living under immense pressure. We had to move repeatedly, we’d get evicted for no reason, we couldn’t finalize a contract to buy our own home.
Wherever we went, it seemed like someone was watching.
The most painful thing was seeing our children unable to 
get an education.
Su Ziming
Obviously, this had an effect on our children, too. But the most painful thing was seeing our children were unable to get an education. One afternoon, a teacher packed up all of our children’s books and supplies and sent them home. My son asked: “Mom, why do we always have to take our things home?” Even he had begun to realise that this was not the first time our family had faced such disruption. How can I explain?
It’s terrible that in China today, simply because of their father’s work, my children don’t have the right to go to school.
And so, you decided to leave?
Yes. When I tried to leave with our two children in November 2025, we were stopped after entering the airport in Shanghai. The airport security took me aside and escorted me to an interview room; they said I was under an exit ban. They refused to show me any legal documents to justify their actions until hours later – at around 4 in the morning, when I copied down the details of the restriction. Our children were there and saw everything: their mother confronting a room full of police officers.
Following sustained international attention and pressure, the authorities eventually lifted the exit ban, allowing us to leave China. But I know this experience has taken an emotional toll on our children. Even here safe in the US, the trauma remains. They often ask: “What if you get arrested too?” It’s a question no mother ever wants to answer.
Why have you and other family members decided to go public with this case and the challenges facing Christians, among many faith communities, in China?
There have been other church cases that received little public attention over the years, and we have heard reports that people detained then were subjected to abuse and mistreatment. Another house church leader, Yang Rongli, was sentenced to 15 years in prison on fraud charges. But we think that if a case becomes internationally known, authorities often become more cautious in how they treat those in custody.
This would be important for the family members of Zion Church, but also to other house churches and believers facing persecution because of their faith. You – international NGOs, governments, the media, the UN – your voices can be the strongest support.
Would you like to share a message for your husband?
Our children and I will stand with you. I will always believe in you. And no matter if you get sentenced, or for how long, our children and I will wait for you.
Amnesty International continues to document the ways in which human rights defenders and others, including faith-based leaders, are targeted with punitive measures by the authorities – and the ways this extends to their family members, despite them not being accused of any crime themselves. Amnesty is concerned about the new Entry-Exit Regulations and the risk that they codify a persistent use of de facto travel and exit bans to constrain freedom of movement for activists and their families.
