Christa Pike ‘angry and confused’ about Tennessee’s failed execution effort, lawyers say
- - Christa Pike woke up in hospital “angry and confused” after Tennessee’s failed execution, which left her critically ill, swollen, and unable to swallow or move her arms.
- - A judge ordered Tennessee to preserve syringes, drugs, and internal records after the botched execution, as Pike’s lawyers pushed for more transparency and chemical testing.
- - The case has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in Tennessee, and Governor Bill Lee has paused all executions while investigators review Pike’s case and another failed execution.
AI generated
NASHVILLE - Christa Pike, sentenced to death for a 1995 murder, awoke “angry and confused” in a hospital this week with a long recuperation ahead after surviving Tennessee’s botched effort to execute her, her lawyers said on Oct 7.
A week ago, Pike, 50, was taken from the execution chamber to a Nashville hospital, unconscious, critically ill and with severe arm injuries after two injections of the caustic barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution.
As late as Oct 5, her lawyers believed Pike was brain dead and that life support would be removed the next day following the second botched execution in Tennessee this year, which has renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US.
“But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone, including me, including her team, and including the medical team, Christa woke up and began talking,” Randall Spivey, one of her lawyers, told reporters after a court hearing on Oct 7, where a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve syringes and other evidence from the botched execution.
“She is angry and confused about everything right now,” Spivey said.
“She is very aware that the state tried to execute her.”
Governor Bill Lee has suspended all executions for the rest of the year while investigators look into the botched executions of Pike and of Tony Carruthers in May, when prison officials were unable to set up intravenous lines.
Pike remains very sick and shackled to her hospital bed, facing a long road to recovery, her lawyers said.
She cannot swallow or eat, has pneumonia, cannot move her “tremendously swollen” hands or arms, and it is unclear if she will regain her lost mobility, they said.
Although she still has “cognitive confusion,” the lawyers said, she has been speaking with those around her.
“She has wanted to know what’s happened, and she’s asked about several people,” Spivey said. “She’s asked about the victim’s family.”
Pike was sentenced to death for her role as a teenager in the 1995 torture and murder of her 19-year-old schoolmate Colleen Slemmer.
She is the first person known to have survived a “completed execution attempt” in the US, her lawyers say, calling it a violation of the Constitution’s prohibition on cruel and unusual punishments.
A unique case
Pike’s lawyers are unexpectedly continuing their litigation against state officials, seeking to pierce the secrecy that normally surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states.
Earlier on Oct 7, a judge in Davidson County Chancery Court, I’Ashea Myles, agreed to order Tennessee officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous lines and gurney restraints.
The all-female execution team requested by Pike used at least seven needles during a gruelling ordeal that lasted more than two hours, and one needle was bent 90 degrees when it was pulled out, her lawyers said.
Myles largely sided with Pike’s lawyers at the end of the Oct 7 hearing, describing the litigation, which began in January in an effort to prevent the scheduled execution, as unusual because no one had anticipated Pike surviving.
“This case is unique, to say the least,” Myles said.
She also ordered the state to preserve internal communications about the attempted execution, including incident reports, witness accounts and encrypted messages.
She has yet to rule on a request by Pike’s lawyers that the Tennessee Department of Correction let them take any residual traces of the execution drugs for chemical analysis.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has opposed what it says is a “duplicative and unnecessary” preservation order, arguing it is already legally required to preserve all evidence and that it was already willing to share most, if not all, of what Pike’s lawyers sought.
Tennessee and other US states have long struggled to acquire execution drugs. They cannot be obtained from major pharmaceutical companies because of a European trade ban on companies that sell products for use in torture or executions.
Tennessee, like other states, has turned to small, largely unregulated compounding pharmacies to make small batches of the drugs, promising to hide their identity.
“Today’s hearing was about transparency, about why Christa, the courts, the media and the public should not simply take the state’s word about what happened last Wednesday,” Luke Ihnen, another lawyer for Pike, told reporters after the judge’s ruling.
He repeated the demand that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee commute Pike’s sentence to life in prison and never attempt to execute her again. A spokesperson for Lee, who denied a clemency appeal two days before the failed execution, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Pike’s lawyers had sought an alternative to lethal injections, saying her small veins and related medical conditions made her afraid that something would go wrong. REUTERS

56 Ukrainians still missing as Nepal ends flash flood search-and-rescue operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:18:21 UTC
06:18:21 KST

56 Ukrainians still missing as Nepal ends flash flood search-and-rescue operation
Fifty-six Ukrainians remain missing after Nepal ended its search-and-rescue operation following August's deadly floods, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 6.
Devastating flash floods ravaged Nepal after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on Aug. 26, drowning villages in mud and debris. At least 1,455 people were killed in the floods, and over 5,200 people were unaccounted for.
While active rescue operations have been suspended, the search and identification of remains continue, the ministry said.
"Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, (the missing Ukrainians) have still not been found among either the dead or the injured," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Out of the missing Ukrainian citizens, 46 were traveling together in a tour group. Contact with the group was lost when the flash flooding began. Rescue efforts have been ongoing for over 40 days, but none of the missing Ukrainians have been identified.
While there have been no official reports of Ukrainians killed, Nepalese officials said they were considering commencing the legal process of declaring missing persons as dead.
"We are initiating due processes to complete required legal formalities," Phanindra Paudel, chief of the National Emergency Operation Centre, told Reuters.
These formalities would allow families of the missing individuals to complete relevant administrative tasks, such as filing life insurance claims, in their home countries.
The Ukrainian embassy in India has contacted relevant authorities concerning procedures for official documentation, the ministry said.
The Ukrainian National Police is also working to finalize a database of DNA profiles of those missing in the floods to share with Nepalese authorities.

Iran says response to US proposals aimed at ending war will be delivered through mediators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:09:56 UTC
06:09:56 KST

Sahin Demir
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Iran said Wednesday that its response to US proposals concerning efforts to end the conflict will be delivered through mediators while announcing progress with Oman on establishing safe shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran had clearly outlined its “considerations and conditions” for ending the war on all fronts and restoring security to the Gulf region and the Strait of Hormuz, according to state-run IRNA news agency.
“The necessary response to the proposals of the other side will also be provided through the mediators,” Baghaei said, adding that messages between Iran and the US are being exchanged through intermediaries.
Baghaei also responded to remarks by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier Wednesday that Iran had failed to take advantage of “multiple opportunities” to reach an agreement with Washington over its nuclear program. Rubio made the remarks during a visit to Athens.
“Distorting historical facts cannot erase from public opinion the reality of the United States’ repeated breaches of its commitments,” Baghaei said.
He cited the US withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement in 2018, what he described as Washington’s disruption of diplomatic processes and military attacks against Iran during negotiations.
Baghaei accused the US of responsibility for the current insecurity in the region and its economic consequences in the US and around the world.
On navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, he said Iran and Oman had made progress in consultations aimed at restoring maritime security.
He said the two countries had agreed on the geographical coordinates of safe inbound and outbound shipping routes through the strategic waterway.
The two sides also reached an understanding on how the arrangement would be communicated to the relevant international body, a step Baghaei said would take place “soon.”
Baghaei also said that Iran would continue its efforts to strengthen trust and engagement among countries in the region.

French mayor caught in viral video clash says student protesters 'could be my children'
SAINT-DENIS, France, Oct 7 - In a video that has gone viral on social media, Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of the French town of Saint-Denis, stands facing police at a march in Paris on Tuesday, shielding young protesters and shouting "stop."
Bagayoko said he has been supporting the students in his working-class Parisian suburb and on Tuesday was asking the police not to charge.
"They had decided to charge and effectively go after the students, many of whom had shown no aggressive behaviour whatsoever toward the police officers," Bagayoko, who is part of the hard-left France Unbowed party (LFI), told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday at his town hall office in Saint-Denis, on the northern outskirts of Paris.
In the end, the police fired tear gas at the group, including the mayor, he said.
The wave of student protests, which began in Paris' marginalised suburbs, has been going on for more than two weeks and has exposed widespread public anger six months ahead of an election to replace French President Emmanuel Macron.
There have been more than 6,000 arrests and dozens of student injuries since the protests began. Rights groups and unions accuse the police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flashball guns. Authorities say hundreds of police officers have also been injured, schools have been burned or ransacked, and teachers and members of the public have been attacked.
The town of Saint-Denis, where poverty levels are more than double the national average, was one of the first sites of student protests in late September over overcrowded and unsanitary classrooms, teacher shortages and unequal opportunities.
"Protests are not new here, they happen at every start of the academic year," Bagayoko said. "The Republican promise (of equality) — in particular for the working-class neighbourhoods, and also rural areas — is not respected."
He said the government should prioritise investing in education and levy heavier taxes on billionaires.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on Wednesday that the government would review demands made by students and present proposals at the end of October, but gave no details.
The government has suggested that LFI politicians were behind the protests, an accusation that Bagayoko dismissed as insulting to the young protesters.
A father of four, he said that "the high school children who were in the street could be my children ... it is my responsibility to be at their side." REUTERS

Germany’s far-right AfD and left-wing populist BSW party now hold a majority in an eastern state parliament. Their first joint proposal: End aid to Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:06:08 UTC
06:06:08 KST

Germany’s far-right AfD and left-wing populist BSW party now hold a majority in an eastern state parliament. Their first joint proposal: End aid to Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and the left-wing populist Union for Social Justice plan to pass their first joint resolution soon, calling for an end to military aid to Ukraine, Reuters and Deutsche Welle reported. Together, the parties hold a majority in Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament following the election.
The resolution’s authors call on the state parliament to declare that the policy of imposing sanctions on Russia and providing arms and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. They say further escalation in Ukraine must be prevented and call for “a policy that promotes peace.”
The authors call for “an immediate ceasefire and the start of peace talks with Russia,” as well as restoring normal economic relations between Germany and Russia and lifting sanctions.
A vote on the resolution is scheduled for October 14. DW and Reuters said it will be symbolic because state governments have no influence over Germany’s foreign policy. Reuters reported, however, that the initiative underscores the AfD’s persistent push to end German support for Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.
Representatives of the Union for Social Justice said Germany needs policies that prioritize Köthen, a town in Saxony-Anhalt, over Kyiv.
In early September, Alternative for Germany won the election in Saxony-Anhalt with its best-ever result — 43.8% of the vote. The party took 39 of the state parliament’s 83 seats. Together with the Union for Social Justice, it holds 44 seats.
The AfD said it was already in talks with Russia about resuming gas supplies to Germany. The party’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, discussed the issue with Gazprom chief Alexey Miller.

'One student, one day': CUET-UG 2027 may get shorter, simpler
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:05:49 UTC
06:05:49 KST

NEW DELHI: CUET-UG 2027 could see some of its biggest changes yet - fewer subjects, shorter papers and a new grouping system aimed at ensuring that a student can finish the entire entrance test in a single day instead of making repeated trips to examination centres.The ministry of education, University Grants Commission and National Testing Agency are working on a formula to shorten the overall examination cycle and simplify the experience for candidates, sources said.At present, a candidate can take up to five subjects in CUET-UG, with each paper lasting 60 minutes.
Under one proposal being examined, the duration of individual papers could be reduced so that even a student taking five subjects can complete all tests within about 180 to 200 minutes.
CUET-UG also mulls reducing number of subjects from 5 to 4
Another option under discussion is whether the maximum number of subjects should be reduced from five to four. Sources said senior officials of the education ministry, UGC and NTA recently discussed the proposed changes and asked officials to examine how the examination could be compressed without affecting university admission requirements.A key part of the plan is to create subject groups based on commonly chosen combinations.
This would allow NTA to schedule related papers together and complete a candidate’s examination in one sitting or on the same day.For example, physics, chemistry and biology could form one group for those seeking admission to science programmes. General studies could be added as a fourth paper where universities give weightage to its score. The idea is to bu-ild these groups around eligibility rules followed by universities.
For instance, a student seeking admission to physics (Hons) at DU could choose the relevant three-subject combination rather than taking papers not required for the course.Officials believe such grouping could reduce the number of examination days and make scheduling easier. It could also end the problem of students having to travel to examination centres on different days for different papers. The proposals will depend on consultations with universities and the testing agency.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Germany Plans New Naval Port in Emden as Navy Expands
Germany plans to build a new naval port in Emden on the North Sea as it expands naval capacity for operations in the North Atlantic and High North, according to the joint press release posted on the City of Emden website on October 5.
Germany’s Defense Ministry, the state of Lower Saxony, the Federal Institute for Real Estate, and the City of Emden signed a letter of intent supporting the project and further planning.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The decision reflects NATO defense plans, Germany’s national military requirements, and the expected expansion of the Bundeswehr. The navy will need additional berths, support infrastructure, accommodation, and training facilities as new ships and personnel enter service, the press release stated.
Germany currently has only one naval port on the North Sea, in Wilhelmshaven. According to the statement, that base will not be able to meet future requirements for berths, pier capacity, and logistical support linked to operations in the North Sea, Atlantic, and High North.
After examining several possible locations, the navy identified Emden as the strongest option because of its geography, infrastructure links, and access to the Atlantic and High North.
“The navy is growing. New ships and boats need berths. Our soldiers need accommodation and training facilities. That is why we need a new naval port. And we want to build it in Emden,” German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius stated.
“The navy carried out an intensive review, and Emden offers ideal conditions, including rapid access to the Atlantic and the High North,” he added.
The agreement is not legally binding, and a final decision has not yet been made. Further feasibility studies are expected to be completed before construction can formally proceed, according to the joint press release.
Germany has been steadily increasing its naval role within NATO. In September, the German Navy tested a ship-launched LORA ballistic missile in the North Atlantic, while German and Dutch forces had earlier established a joint command center in Estonia as part of NATO’s eastern-flank defense.

Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

"They hit us bad": Newly obtained footage, witness accounts detail Iran attack, and U.S. retreat, at major post in Kuwait
Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.
The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.
The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.
The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.
"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.
Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.
CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.
Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.
Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.
"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."
While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.
"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."
A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.
The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.
No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.
Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.
"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"
The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.
In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.
CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

Gene therapy can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers reveal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:01 UTC
06:00:01 KST

A type of gene therapy based on Nobel prize-winning science is safe and can partly restore sight in blind people, researchers have revealed.
The approach, known as optogenetic therapy, harnesses the technique for turning nerve cells on and off using light that scooped the 2026 Nobel prize in physiology or medicine.
It was first shown to partly restore vision in a single blind person in 2021. Now researchers have reported the results from a larger trial involving the original patient and a further nine people.
“What we can say for sure is that the concept of optogenetics is valid for vision restoration,” said Prof Botond Roska, director of the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel and a lead author of the study.
Roska added the aim is now to work towards restoring high-resolution vision, with the hope of achieving the goal in five to 10 years.
All 10 of the trial participants had advanced retinitis pigmentosa – a group of genetic disorders thought to affect more than 1.5 million people worldwide.
In these disorders, light-sensitive cells in the retina gradually lose their function. However, ganglion cells in the retina, which send visual information to the brain, deteriorate less quickly.
“These cells are not the primary cells targeted by the disease, so that’s why they are good candidates for the therapy,” said Dr José-Alain Sahel, another lead author of the study from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center in the US.
The gene therapy involves giving a single injection into the eye. This injection contains a harmless, synthethic virus that delivers the genetic instructions for producing a light-sensitive protein into a ring of surviving ganglion cells. As a result, these cells are made light-sensitive.
Each patient then receives a pair of light-stimulating goggles. These capture images of the world around the patient and convert them into pulses of light of a single wavelength These pulses activate the ganglion cells that have been made light-sensitive, allowing the wearer to perceive a monochrome image.
Crucially, the technique does not depend on the exact genetic cause of the patient’s sight loss.
Writing in the New England Journal of Medicine, the researchers report how for each patient they treated only the eye with the worst vision, adding participants’ outcomes were then followed for up to five years.
Only one severe eye-related side-effect occurred, but this was resolved within minutes, while there were no side effects related to the therapy in the rest of the body.
However, six of the 10 participants had clinically meaningful improvements in light sensitivity after the treatment.
What’s more, some of the participants showed improvements in a range of tasks when wearing the light-stimulating goggles after the gene therapy – such as detecting, locating and touching a notebook, locating a door and walking on a line.
The team added that participants who spent more time training with the goggles tended to do better on the tasks.
However, the study has limitations.
“[Patients] can detect objects, but they cannot yet detect faces,” said Roska. That, the team say, is down to the treated ganglion cells being in a ring-like arrangement around the fovea – the tiny pit in the retina responsible for sharp central vision.
Mark Hankins, professor of Visual Neuroscience at the University of Oxford, who was not involved in the work, welcomed the study, noting it provides reassurance on the safety of the approach and its application to people who still have some residual vision.
“We’ve gone from one patient to 10 patients, we’ve seen improvement in their light sensitivity … and we’ve seen that we can give a stable restoration of some visual function, some light sensitivity, that lasts for four or five years in these patients,” he said. “They’re baby steps, but they’re critical.”

‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:01 UTC
06:00:01 KST

Ahmed Ishtaiwi has six chairs. They are cheap and plastic and battered, but they are among the 43-year-old driver and mechanic’s most valuable possessions.
Ishtaiwi lives in a tent near Deir al-Balah in central Gaza with his two daughters. Their former home is far to the north, in the now ruined town of Beit Lahiya, uninhabitable and impossible to reach.
“When I sit on those chairs, I remember sitting in the garden at home, having breakfast and drinking tea. They remind me of my life there,” he said last week.
Wednesday is the anniversary of the raid on 7 October 2023 by Hamas militants into southern Israel that killed 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and triggered a relentless Israeli military offensive that killed 73,000 Palestinians, mostly civilians, wounded many more and reduced swathes of Gaza to rubble.
When Layan al-Jbour, a 15-year-old from the southern city of Khan Younis, tries to bring some order to the crowded makeshift shelter she shares with her parents, brothers and sisters in al-Mawasi, a strip of coastline at the southernmost end of Gaza, she recalls life before the war.
“When I tidy the tent, I remember our home and how I used to tidy it. I remember my room and how I used to make my bed. When I put a sheet over a table and arrange the bedding, the place looks like our old home,” al-Jbour said.
“We hardly took anything with us from our home. We left everything behind, and the only thing I took was my schoolbag. It is the most precious thing I own now. It reminds me so much of my school days. I loved going to school and meeting my friends there.”
Across Gaza, Palestinians describe daily routines full of challenges that nothing in their former lives prepared them for: shortages of water and of nourishing food, minimal healthcare, disease, unemployment, economic collapse and the continuing threat of death or injury.
Despite a ceasefire a year ago, Israel’s airstrikes continue. Palestinians who have approached the “yellow line” that divides Gaza into zones controlled by the Israeli military and by Hamas have been shot dead. In the last year, the overall death toll has risen by a further 1,400 people.
In recent days, Israeli attacks have intensified, killing at least two Palestinians in Gaza on Tuesday, according to health officials. The Israeli military said the strikes targeted militants.
On Wednesday, Gaza medics said at least two Palestinians were killed and others wounded in airstrikes in Beit Lahiya and Khan Younis.
“It is what we feared … a ceasefire that just isn’t a ceasefire,” said one international aid worker now based in Amman, Jordan, who worked in Gaza throughout much of the conflict. “Daily life is horrible. People aren’t hungry any more but they are still malnourished. Our local staff are telling us that this is just the next stage of the conflict.”
Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s humanitarian coordinator for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, told the UN security council last month that despite the increase in supplies entering Gaza, the health situation remained critical, with “infectious diseases … widespread amid overcrowded displacement sites and inadequate water, sanitation and hygiene conditions”.
Inadequate funding for relief efforts exacerbated the “shortages of medical supplies, fuel and the overall humanitarian response”, Alakbarov said, while “restrictions on the entry of critical humanitarian items imposed by Israel” were slowing preparations for cold weather.
Israeli authorities deny shortages and say adequate supplies are reaching Gaza, with more than 600 trucks entering the territory each day.
Saleh Kilani, 70, from Beit Lahiya, used to have a farm and olive trees before the war. “Around this time of year, I used to press about 60 containers of olive oil. But I lost all of that too. If I go to my home I may die, and if I go to my farm, I may die too. This is not a life. We are exhausted and we have lost hope.”
Kilani said life before the conflict seemed very distant. “We never used to think twice about seeing orange and peach trees, green fields, grapes and figs. These things were simply part of our lives. Now when we see them, we are surprised,” he said.
Hamas, which swiftly reimposed its authority over the 2.3 million Palestinians who live in the third of Gaza not under the control of the Israeli military, has rebuilt a rudimentary administration which provides patchy education, some healthcare services and limited policing based on deterrence through often arbitrary punishment.
Donald Trump’s plan to definitively end the war in Gaza has stalled, with little progress towards disarming Hamas, securing the withdrawal of Israeli troops and beginning the vast job of reconstruction.
“My biggest fear is that this situation will continue. We are living through a period that can be described as neither war nor peace,” said Kilani.
The only time Esraa Abu Taiba recalls her life before the war is when she gets to practise her former profession: beautician.
The 26-year-old lived in Bani Suheila, a town to the east of Khan Younis and now within the zone controlled by Israel. Of her five brothers, two were killed in the conflict, two were wounded, and one is among the more than 1,500 Palestinians from Gaza in detention in Israel.
“Before the war my life was quiet and good,” she said. “I could go wherever I wanted without fear or restrictions. We lived in our own home. We had a washing machine, a tap and a garden. The house belonged to us and we lived there comfortably.
“Now we live in a tent. Our lives depend on carrying water and getting food from the community kitchen. A water truck comes to the end of the street and … I go to collect it because my mother cannot carry it.”
Like most Palestinians in Gaza, her family was displaced multiple times during the conflict, and they have lost everything from their former home – except a house key, which her mother keeps close.
“The only thing I still do from my old life is some beauty work. I cut girls’ hair in the tents around us and do their makeup for weddings,” said Abu Taiba.
“It takes me back to a beautiful and happy period of our lives, when we used to celebrate weddings and other happy occasions before the war. It takes me away from the misery we are living through, even if only for a little while.”

Elon Musk’s America PAC Is Quietly Funding November’s Most Consequential Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Elon Musk’s America PAC is focusing its war chest on the most consequential Senate races this midterm cycle—and doing so by financing attack ads on Democrats, as voters nationwide sour on the Trump administration’s agenda.
The trend of political parties and outside groups focusing on trashing their opponents is not a new phenomenon. But America PAC's approach has been unusual: for every dollar it has spent supporting GOP Senate candidates, it has spent almost three dollars attacking Democrats.
To monitor America PAC's spending on digital ads and mailers this cycle, our ace team at WIRED has created a live tracker that updates daily and highlights where Musk's political contributions are heading as we enter the waning years of Trump’s second term.
The political stakes are especially high for Republicans this midterms cycle because of the possibility of Democrats taking the majority in the US Senate, should the party flip four battleground races and retain three of the Senate seats it currently holds.
For Musk, the implications of a Democratic-controlled Senate would also be far-reaching, as he personally could become the target of congressional investigations, while his companies might be affected by bills related to tech and AI regulation.
Texas Senate Race
For the critical Texas Senate race, America PAC has poured more than $9.4 million into ads opposing Democratic candidate James Talarico and roughly $1.8 million into ads backing Republican candidate and state attorney general Ken Paxton.
The lopsided spending here is perhaps the least surprising of all of the close Senate contests. Paxton comes with so much personal baggage—from facing impeachment charges that were eventually dropped to having his wife (who has since endorsed him with an ad that doesn’t mention him by name) file for divorce on “biblical grounds”—that trying to boost him with ads highlighting his background is tough.
Republicans in Texas also cannot realistically do positive ads of President Donald Trump and Paxton together, since both men have terrible approval ratings.
The largest single expenditures by America PAC have been two $1.3 million digital media buys opposing Talarico. America PAC has not put any money into television ads, which is being handled by other groups, like MAGA Inc., the Trump-affiliated super PAC.
Meanwhile, the Senate Republican Conference–affiliated Texas PAC has so far booked the lion's share of television ads. Punchbowl News reported last month that Texas PAC has booked around $120 million and was looking to buy $100 million in ad slots before November 3.
Ohio Senate Race
In Ohio’s Senate race, America PAC has spent $3.3 million against Democrat Sherrod Brown compared to $1.6 million supporting Republican candidate Jon Husted.
Husted has been struggling to distance himself from supporting data centers at a time when voters in the state have become fed up with rising costs associated with the projects. Husted has been tagged as "the face of data centers" because of a planned Nvidia data center project in Ohio that will be leased by OpenAI, and for his past support for data centers when he served in the state government.
The effort by Brown to cast Husted as the champion of data centers has in fact been so effective that a memo by the Senate Republicans' campaign arm in August said it was tying an anchor around the neck of Husted's public polling.
At a rally this week in Ohio, despite the cratering public support for data centers, Trump could not help himself and declared to the crowd: “We want them.” Husted’s campaign quickly replied that it should be a “local decision.”
Iowa Senate Race
In Iowa, America PAC has spent $1.5 million hitting Democratic candidate Josh Turek, while only spending roughly $100,000 supporting the Republican candidate Ashley Hinson—the biggest disparity, according to the WIRED tracker.
To put that another way: To date, Musk's political operation has spent a staggering 14 times more attacking Turek than supporting Hinson.
This could be because Hinson has taken great pains to distance herself from Trump's agenda. She recently called on Trump to ban diesel exports and end the Iran war (after previously voting six times against the House resolution to end the conflict), after Turek called for both of those measures.
To illustrate the upside-down nature of this race, Hinson recently launched attack ads against Turek, accusing him without evidence of having “received tens of millions in support from men in the Epstein files,” a remarkable situation given that Trump has sought to tamp down any mention of the files because of the negative blowback on him personally.
Once again, pro-Republican ads are likely not helpful when the candidate is trying to run a race apart from Trump and is barely ahead in the polls in what should be a safe Republican seat. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, Hinson was just one single, solitary point ahead of Turek.

Gene therapy and special goggles give some blind people limited sight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Some blind people can now find a doorway or spot an object with the help of an experimental treatment and custom goggles.
Participants in a new study had blindness caused by a genetic disease called retinitis pigmentosa, which progressively kills off light-sensing cells in the retina. The treatment improved seven of 10 people’s light sensitivity, researchers report October 7 in New England Journal of Medicine. The findings build on a 2021 report that the same approach helped one blind man see and count objects.
The treatment is based on optogenetics, a technique that uses genetic instructions to make cells respond to light. Rather than repair the retina’s damaged light detectors, it gives that ability to retinal ganglion cells that normally relay visual signals to the brain.
“This is a proof of concept that optogenetics can bring back some visual activity [and] object sensitivity,” says Botond Roska, neuroscientist at the Institute of Molecular and Clinical Ophthalmology Basel in Switzerland.
Pioneering work on optogenetics snagged the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on October 5.
Scientists have been experimenting with optogenetic therapies to rewire the eye and restore vision to people with degenerative eye diseases for more than a decade. Just as in the 2021 study, in the new work Roska and his colleagues injected genetic instructions for ChrimsonR, a light-sensitive protein derived from algae, into participants’ worse-seeing eye. The treatment made retinal ganglion cells in that eye sensitive to amber light. A camera in the custom goggles detected changes in brightness in what was in front of a study participant, and the goggles projected those changes onto the retina as pulses of amber light, activating the treated cells.
Four of the eight study participants who completed behavioral testing after treatment were able to find a doorway or follow a line while wearing the goggles. No patient gained the ability to read visual words or see faces, but Roska and his colleagues hope to tackle that next.
But there’s a limitation to this work. The approach requires a working optic nerve to carry signals to the brain, says study coauthor José-Alain Sahel, an ophthalmologist at the University of Pittsburgh. It relies on cells in the retina communicating to the brain, so it cannot restore vision when that connection is damaged.

Labour Send changes at risk as parents rush to secure support, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:00:00 UTC
06:00:00 KST

Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.
The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.
The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.
The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.
The Guardian recently reported that councils and schools have reported a surge in applications for EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.
Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.
“There’s a ‘use it before you lose it’ dynamic, as schools and parents have an incentive to secure EHCPs before they are phased out, because there’s a lot of uncertainty about what these new specialist packages of support will contain and who will be eligible for them,” she said.
Dellar said the government’s plans added new resources in order to reduce the need for families to seek EHCPs, the individualised packages of support agreed between parents and local authorities that can be enforced by specialist tribunals.
But Dellar said budgets for the additional resources for special educational needs and disabilities (Send) would be eroded if demands for EHCPs shot above the government’s own forecasts, with councils saying they have to keep issuing EHCPs until the existing legislation is repealed.
She said: “The government has a lot riding on the reforms taking effect before they fully kick in – its spending plans for the parliament have some assumptions about savings baked in that are based in particular on them being able to slow the growth or the trajectory of numbers of pupils with EHCPs.
“It has a lot politically riding on it as well, and of course in terms of the wellbeing of the children and families involved.”
A Department for Education (DfE) spokesperson said: “The figures in this report are speculative and there is no evidence that proposed reforms are driving additional EHCP demand.
“We inherited a Send system with record numbers of EHCPs and families waiting months for support. We are already investing to change that, backing schools to improve inclusion, widening access to specialists and rolling out training for every teacher to better support children before needs escalate.
“It is vital that we take the time needed to get this right, but we are completely committed to the implementation timelines set out in the schools white paper and will announce next steps soon.”
The changes announced in February under Keir Starmer’s administration promised to overhaul a system that parents have denounced for forcing them to seek EHCPs to secure specialist support or a place in a special school.
Many parents said the EHCP application process – introduced by the Conservatives in 2014 – required lengthy waits for NHS assessments for conditions such as ADHD or autism, or great expense for those who could afford private assessments. Families then face bureaucratic delays from schools and local authorities, or legal appeals to a specialist Send tribunal to override councils’ objections.
Mark Franks, the director of welfare at the Nuffield Foundation, which funded the report, said: “While there is broad agreement that the current system is under strain, uncertainty and concern remain about whether future levels of investment and the nature of reform will be sufficient to provide high-quality support for all children and young people.”
The IfG said the additional costs of Send provision could erode the extra funding being offered for state schools in England, saying it could absorb “around two-thirds of the generous schools funding uplift over this parliament”.
The package of changes would see mainstream schools given greater support for pupils with special needs, including the creation of specialist bases, allowing pupils to attend local schools and reduce pressure on special schools.
The DfE also wants individual support plans to replace many EHCPs, which would be retained for children with the most profound needs.
The IfG said: “It is not clear exactly how the reforms will slow the growth in EHCPs before the new system is fully in place.”
Dellar said: “The government is making investments now, in early intervention and in specialist bases. But the whole way the government is approaching these Send reforms is deliberately to take a slow, phased approach – largely because it knows that those investments are going to take a while to have an effect.
“Its investments in early assessment are going to take a little time to bear fruit. It has not yet properly set out exactly what preventative support it wants schools to put in place. So until schools have that, it’s unclear that they will actually be able to start doing the work the government wants them to do.
“On top of that, the system is tightly bound by existing legislation. Local authorities [LAs] in particular have quite strict guidelines, and tribunals suggest that there are often disputes over eligibility for EHCPs but LAs are likely to be pulled towards the law as it stands until the law changes.”

María del Carmen Abascal, symbol of Spain’s housing protests, dies aged 87
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:57:51 UTC
05:57:51 KST

María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis, has died.
News of her death came two weeks after Maricarmen, as she had come to be known across Spain, was evicted from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than seven decades.
The pensioner, whose apartment had been purchased by an investment firm who sought to hike her rent by 230%, swiftly became a symbol of the many left behind by Spain’s surging housing market.
Scenes of the eviction, which saw police use rounds of teargas as they carried out the order, made headlines across Spain. The shocking images – showing Abascal being forcibly removed from her home on a stretcher, flanked by protesters and police – swiftly crystallised into anger.
About 10,000 people took to the streets of Madrid hours later, wielding signs such as “Shame” and “We’re all Maricarmen”. From Spain’s north to the south, people poured into plazas to protest the suffering wrought by rents that had soared 80% in the span of a decade while house prices had climbed 63%.
From the hospital where she was being treated for severe exhaustion, Abascal cheered on the fledgling movement. “I would like to be there with you all,” she said in a video shot from her hospital bed. “But I’m not that lucky. So from here, I ask you all for courage and to fight and defend what is yours.”
As encampments began springing up across the country, the investment firm that bought Abascal’s home said she could return. The deal did little to quell the anger that had boiled over in the wake of the eviction.
This week the wave of outrage led the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to call a snap general election after rightwing and far-right parties voted down two emergency decrees his government had proposed to address the housing crisis.
The Madrid tenants’ union said the solution had come too late for the octogenarian. “This was a completely preventable situation following an agonising ordeal,” it said in a statement announcing that Abascal had died in hospital, reportedly hours before she was due to sign a new lease with the investment firm that had evicted her.
“The events triggered by the injustice of her eviction undoubtedly mark a turning point in the history of this country: massive demonstrations, encampments in the squares, an early election, and the call for a general strike,” it added. “The housing debate is at the center of it all, but the cost of getting to this point has been too high.”
Sánchez offered his condolences to Abascal’s family and friends. “A hug also to everyone who’s feeling this loss today as their own,” he wrote on social media. “Rest in peace.”
Spain’s health minister, Mónica García, said Abascal’s plight had “served to awaken awareness across all of Spain, lighting a fuse that cannot be put out”, and adding that her “dignity and courage” had shown the way.
The Podemos MEP and former equalities minister Irene Montero was more blunt. “This isn’t a death; it’s a murder,” she wrote on social media. “Such bloody anger. Thank you for fighting, Maricarmen.”
Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party (PP) – which voted against last week’s emergency housing measures – also offered his condolences.
“No campaigning, no political parties, no partisan ends, no more bricks in the wall,” he wrote on social media. “When a person dies there should be nothing but respect.”
Her death came a day after Sánchez’s cabinet approved two new housing decrees intended to “maintain the spirit” of the two previous decrees that were voted down in parliament last week by the PP, the far-right Vox party and the rightwing Catalan pro-independence Junts party.
The 21 measures include facilitating renting or buying a new home; extending eviction protections for vulnerable residents; regulating room rentals; imposing a new tax on seasonal rentals; prohibiting speculative real estate purchases; and granting tax breaks to property owners and tenants who pay on time.
With the lower and upper houses of parliament dissolved following the calling of the snap election, the decrees will be voted on by the permanent council of congress, a special council that operates when parliament is not in session.
The body’s 69 members are distributed proportionally among the various parliamentary groups to reflect the composition of the lower chamber, meaning Sánchez will probably have enough support to get at least one of the decrees passed.
In the heart of Madrid, where campaigners have set up a giant protest camp, news of Abascal’s death was met with a moment of silence. Soon after, hundreds marched from the camp to the country’s parliament chanting: “Maricarmen lives on, the fight continues.”

B-21 Testing, Manufacturing Ramp Up: ‘We’re Moving Fast’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:57:40 UTC
05:57:40 KST

Northrop Grumman has broken ground on a major new production facility for the B-21 Raider, the company and the Air Force announced Oct. 6. The construction comes as a top service official said testing on the bomber is going well in the lead up to its planned introduction into the operational fleet in 2027.
“It’s more than construction,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink wrote in a social media post. “We’re moving fast to build B-21s!”
The Air Force Test Center has likewise been moving quickly to test the bomber ahead of its introduction into service next year. Brig. Gen. Mark Massaro, head of the Air Force Test Center at Edwards Air Force Base, Calif., gave an enthusiastic thumbs-up when asked about the program at an Oct. 6 event. The aircraft first flew in 2023, and two bombers are currently known to be undergoing testing at the base.
“I can’t give you many details about specifics on how it’s going, but I am very closely tied into that program and have been getting regular updates,” Massaro said during a discussion hosted by AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “We are actively testing right now.”
Less than 30 miles away, Northrop is already building B-21s at its Air Force Plant 42 facility in Palmdale, Calif., but the new construction will add 1 million square feet of production space. Meink said it will be the “final assembly line” for new bombers.
In February, Air Force officials said they had agreed on a plan with Northrop to increase B-21 production capacity by 25 percent, using $4.5 billion from the “One Big Beautiful Bill” legislation passed in 2025. Northrop is also investing $2.5 billion of its own money in bolstering B-21 production, CEO Kathy Warden said in April.
The new groundbreaking, which occurred Sept. 29, is “a significant step toward expanding production capacity for the B-21 Raider and delivering combat capability to the Joint Force faster,” the service wrote in a photo caption provided of the groundbreaking.
Increased production capacity is likely—but not confirmed—to lead to more B-21s overall. While the official program of record is for a minimum of 100 bombers, U.S. Strategic Command boss Adm. Richard Correll and U.S. Pacific Command head Adm. Samuel Paparo have advocated for a larger B-21 buy, and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told lawmakers in April that the Air Force will need “a lot more” than 100 B-21s in the future.
The Air Force has yet to formally commit to more than 100 bombers, but top leaders have indicated they are open to doing so.
“At some point in the future, we’ll consider additional buys,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach told Air & Space Forces Magazine in July when asked about increasing the size of the future B-21 fleet. “One of the things we’re talking to Northrop about is how could we do that in a way that doesn’t stretch out.”
Exactly how many the service may buy will likely come out with the Air Force’s 2028 budget request, expected in spring 2027, Air Force Deputy Chief of Staff for Plans and Programs Lt. Gen. David H. Tabor said earlier this year.
Meanwhile, at Edwards, the Air Force is pushing a novel approach to testing by having developmental test pilots fly alongside operational test pilots, the head of the Test Center said.
“One of the areas that we’re really getting into, which we have done in the past, but in a big way, we’re moving forward in programs like the B-21 … is that integrated test,” Massaro said, which is “making sure that the warfighter and our operators have earlier insight into a lot of the developmental test work to be able to get information to make comments and understanding of what things might need to change earlier in a development cycle, but then also influence and discuss how this is going to be operated best. You’re bringing that operator in earlier into the Test Center test execution phase.”
“That integrated test construct is something that we’ve been very much focused on more often in a lot more programs, and that is something on the B-21 that I would like to highlight,” he added.

My target is 100 FIRs against me. Every FIR a medal: Rahul

However, Delhi Police said restrictions imposed under BNSS’s Section 163 were in force in the New Delhi area, which is why the protesters were detained. “As Section 163 is in force here… protest marches or demonstrations are not allowed without permission,” DCP Sachin Sharma said.

My target is that there should be 100 FIRs against me. Every FIR against me is a medal for me.” Rahul said the opposition decided to demonstrate at Jantar Mantar, which is the designated protest site, as govt told them that dharna couldn’t be held at places like Election Commission.
While some of Congress’ allies were absent from the lunch, party spokesperson Jairam Ramesh said the decision for lunch was taken late Tuesday night, and the absence was understandable.On Samajwadi Party, O’Brien said there was a minor miscommunication, which was addressed swiftly, and Samajwadi Party will join the protest Thursday.Sources said Congress had reached out to certain opposition parties to make it clear there was some misunderstanding and the decision to enter Akashwani Bhavan Tuesday was taken on the spur. Left and TMC functionaries were also dismissive of any lingering differences.

Details
According to the official, the situation on the Lithuanian border is currently calm, and the involvement of the military is a preventive measure.
This is a preventive measure, taking into account several factors — yesterday's incident on the Latvian border and, at the same time, publicly available information about possible mobilization in Russia, which those who genuinely do not want to be mobilized may try to enter illegally
In turn, Lithuania's Minister of National Defense Robertas Kaunas said that the order would be carried out immediately and that the army would assist the border guards for several weeks.

WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump, who waged war with Iran and has yet to broker peace in Ukraine, said on Oct 7 that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize but acknowledged doubt about his chances.
“I don’t know what their decision is going to be,” Trump said of the 2026 award, which the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce on Oct 9. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me.”
Since his return to the White House in 2025, Trump has repeatedly said he deserves what may be the world’s most prestigious award.
“It is about that time,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. “But I was very honoured to receive it indirectly last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump.”
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado gave her 2025 Nobel Peace Prize medal to Trump in January as she sought US support for her efforts in Venezuela.
Trump said he should get the prize after wading into eight conflicts since taking office in January 2025.
The leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan have said they nominated Trump, though there is no way of verifying that.
Parties to some conflicts Trump claims to have resolved dispute the US President’s diplomatic role, and fighting has flared again in some of those regions, including the Democratic Republic of Congo and along the border between Cambodia and Thailand.
A resolution to Russia’s war in Ukraine has eluded Trump, who promised to end it on the first day of his second White House term. US-Israel strikes on Iran have led to a seven-month simmering conflict that has upended global energy supplies and driven petrol prices up before November’s midterm elections.
Pope Leo XIV, the International Criminal Court and the special rapporteur for the Palestinian Territories are among the favourites to win in 2026. REUTERS

Yemeni government forces say they seize Kahbub front near Bab al-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:48:05 UTC
05:48:05 KST

Aziz Al-Ahmadi and Sahin Demir
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Yemeni government forces said Wednesday that they took full control of the Kahbub front in the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area in western Yemen following clashes with the Houthis.
The government-aligned Nation’s Shield Forces said on the US social media platform X that their troops, alongside the Giants Brigades and Joint Forces, established “full control” over the Kahbub front.
It said the advance was part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” operation.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the claim.
Kahbub, administratively part of the southern Lahj province, is strategically important because its mountainous terrain overlooks the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Fighting between Yemeni government forces and their allies and the Houthis continued on several fronts Wednesday, the third day of the “Dawn of Yemen” operation.
Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi announced the launch of the operation Monday, saying it aimed to restore state institutions, retake the capital Sanaa and end the Houthi takeover.
The latest offensive comes amid a broader escalation in Yemen that began in July after a period of relative calm following a UN-brokered truce that took effect in April 2022.
Fighting intensified in September, when the Houthis seized strategic positions in the provinces of Al-Hudaydah and Taiz, including the port city of Mokha, before advancing to Mayyun Island overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in September 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

US consumer credit growth slows in August as revolving borrowing falls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:48:00 UTC
05:48:00 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US consumer credit rose $8.3 billion in August, slowing from the previous month as revolving credit declined, according to Federal Reserve data released Wednesday.
Total outstanding consumer credit reached approximately $5.2 trillion, with borrowing growing at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 1.9%, down from 4.1% in July.
Revolving credit, which includes credit cards, fell $4.8 billion, an annualized decline of 4.2%. That reversed a 2.5% annualized increase in July.
Nonrevolving credit, including automobile and student loans, increased $13.1 billion, expanding at an annualized rate of 4.1%.
Outstanding revolving credit stood at approximately $1.35 trillion, while nonrevolving credit totaled $3.84 trillion.
The release also showed that commercial banks charged an average interest rate of 21.19% across credit card accounts in August. For accounts assessed interest, the average rate was 22.36%.
Average rates on 60-month new automobile loans stood at 7.54%, while rates on 24-month personal loans averaged 11.90%.

French prime minister says government not indifferent to students' concerns in TV address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:47:55 UTC
05:47:55 KST

In a televised address from his official residence the French prime minister acknowledges young people's anger 'doesn't come from nowhere' and promises a plan to respond to the crisis
As expected Sébastien Lecornu addressed young people in particular in his televised speech, and said the country could not be "indifferent" to the concerns of high school students, acknowledging that the "anger of young people does not come from nowhere".
However, he said French security forces do not have orders to "confront" protesting high school students, as allegations of police brutality mounted following days of protests that have shaken the country.
Hundreds of students, police and teaching staff have been injured since the movement demanding better conditions in high schools began, and more than 6,500 people -- mostly minors -- have been arrested.
After Tuesday's demonstrations, the mobilisation is not letting up. Several education unions have called for another day of strikes and protests on Thursday, raising fears of further disruption. Secondary school students are demanding, among other things, more resources, enough teachers, improvements to the condition of school buildings and changes to Parcoursup – the platform used to apply for first-year higher education courses – which they regard as opaque and unequal.
The government has already begun to respond. A consultation with secondary school students is under way and several projects have been launched by the executive, notably on covering for absent teachers, repairing school premises, organising the school timetable and, again, Parcoursup.
In Wednesday's address Lecornu promised the government would present a plan to respond to the crisis at the end of October.
The head of government also says that Agora, an app launched to gather young people's grievances, has already received 30,000 anonymous contributions.
France suspends use of stun grenades at secondary school protests
Other initial measures taken after the demonstrations concern public-order policing. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has confirmed the suspension of the use of stun grenades in the context of the secondary school movement, after a 15-year-old boy was seriously injured in Lens, in northern France.
The student whose hand was torn off by a police grenade has undergone amputation and remains in hospital.
Some police unions have already reacted coolly to the measure, invoking their right to withdraw from duty and explaining "their inability to respond" in the event of unrest.
Fuels, agriculture and public finances
Turning to wider economic issues, Lecornu also promised to release diesel stocks in a bid to bring down fuel prices, and reiterated an aim to cut the country's soaring debt to five percent of GDP next year.
The French government is wrestling with multiple crises including the protests and its 2027 budget, as well as a looming election next year to choose Macron's successor, with far-right candidate Marine Le Pen riding high in the polls.
The price of diesel has once again exceeded 2.36 euros per litre, fuelling concern over purchasing power. At the same time, the farming sector is still facing the consequences of a severe drought and has been calling for answers from the state for several weeks.
Wine-production forecasts, for example, have been revised "slightly" upwards, to almost 35 million hectolitres, a level that remains historically low, according to the Agriculture Ministry.
In other words, behind the immediate demands voiced by the protests across the country lies the question of how much room for manoeuvre the government really has to calm anger on the streets.
A much-awaited response on resources
It is therefore on concrete measures that expectations are focused. The list of demands is long, while the government must contend with highly constrained public finances and a risk of deadlock in Parliament.
The draft 2027 budget provides for an increase in education spending, but at the same time the executive has to find several tens of billions of euros in savings to repair the public accounts.

The World Health Organization has said it does not have the “full picture” from Russia following the suspected death from plague last week of a 28-year-old laboratory worker in Siberia.
Darya Shipilova died two days after falling ill with cold-like symptoms. She was an employee at the anti-plague research institute in the eastern city of Irkutsk, with some reports suggesting she was infected after a workplace accident.
The Russian authorities have denied a connection with the institute and say Shipilova died from “pneumonia of an unknown aetiology”. They insist there is no danger of a plague outbreak and have described the “sanitary and epidemiological” situation in the region as stable.
At the same time, officials have imposed sweeping quarantine restrictions at the lab where Shipilova worked and in nearby hospitals. Staff were locked down inside the institute for three days, sleeping on the floors and on chairs, while tests were conducted.
On Wednesday the WHO director general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said: “We don’t yet have the full picture of this event and we’re not able to conduct a full risk assessment.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public risks.”
Tedros said he also wanted more clarification from the Russian government following unconfirmed media reports of “a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause”.
“We assess any reporting from the community,” he said. “We asked Russia to respond to that. We’re waiting for an answer.”
The WHO’s director of epidemic and pandemic management, Maria Van Kerkhove, said the agency still did not know how Shipilova became infected in the first place – and with what viral disease. If pneumonic plague was ruled out, “what did she actually die from?” Kerkhove asked.
In an interview with local media, Shipilova’s 64-year-old mother, Svetlana, discounted the theory that her daughter had been infected after smashing a test tube. “I know the truth. I’m fending off stupid friends who believe this. A test tube is unbreakable, even if you throw it against the wall,” she said.
She described her daughter as a dedicated worker and “pure person” devoted to her job.
Former classmates are also sceptical she was infected at her workplace. One reportedly said: “They’ve smeared a woman without properly investigating. Knowing how hard-working and responsible she was, it just doesn’t add up for me.”
The Kremlin has sought to downplay the incident and has brushed aside an offer of assistance made earlier this week by Donald Trump, the US president. The White House has pressed Moscow for more details of the case, while stressing the risk to the US is very low.
On Tuesday Trump said he would speak about the plague issue “very soon” with Vladimir Putin, who celebrated his 74th birthday on Wednesday. The Kremlin said no call had been arranged but could be quickly organised.
According to the Baikal Medical Journal, health officials in Irkutsk have taken extensive measures to stop a potential outbreak from spreading. Neighbours said workers in white protective suits and gas masks disinfected the two-storey brick building where Shipilova lived several times after her death last Friday.
“The smell was unbearable and very pungent,” a woman in her 40s said. “A woman knocked on our door. I said: ‘What are you treating here?’ I already knew about the plague rumours.
“She said: ‘It’s for cockroaches.’ But we don’t even have any cockroaches in our building. I saw her packing her overalls into a bag. I was like, ‘Well, I get it.’”

The Science Behind the Nobel-Winning Technology That Controls Neurons With Light
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:40:00 UTC
05:40:00 KST

The Karolinska Institute awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Medicine to researchers Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University, Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin, and Georg Nagel of the University of Würzburg. Their discoveries led to the development of optogenetics, a technique where scientists can turn individual nerve cells on or off using beams of light.
According to Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for Medicine, “Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of.” No other technique allows for such precise study of a living brain, helping researchers better understand the functions of our nervous systems as well as various neurological diseases and disorders.
But this prize is not just a celebration of neuroscience. It also serves as a triumphant example of what can happen when different disciplines of biology converge, as the findings that served as the basis for the development of optogenetics emerged from research in microbiology.
At the end of the last century, Peter Hegemann began a series of studies to understand how the single-celled alga Chlamydomonas is able to detect and react to light. Previous research documented that Chlamydomonas has an “eye spot,” a small orange dot on its surface that contains a light-sensing molecule called retinal.
Hegemann used tiny electrodes to measure the electrical signals generated by the alga and to expand our understanding of this structure’s rapid response. The scientist discovered that the organism was capable of producing an electrical impulse about 0.5 milliseconds after receiving light. This response time is 20 times faster than that of the human eye, whose light detection process takes at least 10 milliseconds.
Hegemann suggested that light detection in the alga must be the result of a much simpler process than that identified in the human eye. In the early 1990s, he proposed that the eye spots contained a protein that both detected the light and responded to it, likely opening as a channel to let ions through. At the time, this hypothesis sparked controversy. Many ion channels had been documented up to that point, but none could respond to light on their own.
To test his theory, the scientist attempted to isolate the light-sensitive proteins from the eye spot. However, when removed from their natural environment, these proteins became unstable. Later, a group of Japanese researchers sequenced the complete DNA of Chlamydomonas, which allowed Hegemann’s team to identify two genes that would create proteins with the expected characteristics of a possible light-sensing channel.
Georg Nagel took the next step of verifying the function of the genes. He introduced copies of each of the identified genes separately into different groups of frog eggs. The eggs began to produce the corresponding proteins, which eventually localized to the cell membranes. Nagel then turned on the lights.
Both proteins functioned as ion channels that opened when exposed to light. He named the genes channelrhodopsin-1 and channelrhodopsin-2. Further experiments showed the protein produced by this second gene—called ChR2 for short—opened especially quickly, the flow of ions occurring in just 0.2 milliseconds. It explained the extraordinary speed of the light reaction originally observed in Chlamydomonas.
When the researchers introduced the gene into mammalian cells—which do not normally respond to light—the cells generated an electrical signal when illuminated. This is what got the neuroscientists particularly excited.
Ion channels are important across many types of cells, but they do some especially heavy lifting in our nervous systems. The electrical impulses that neurons use to communicate with one another, as well as other tissues in our body, are mediated by the flow of ions in and out of the cell. If you can control the ion channels, you can control the neuron.
This is where Karl Deisseroth comes in. Deisseroth was searching for a method that would allow him to toggle the activity of specific nerve cells in a living brain. In his view, this tool could expand our understanding of brain functions and open new avenues for treating conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.
Following the discovery of ChR2, he asked Nagel for the DNA sequence so he could introduce it into rat nerve cells. The neurons, growing in dishes, produced ChR2 and, when illuminated with blue light, reacted immediately—sending an electrical impulse that propagated to other neurons. This result, obtained in 2005, was decisive in establishing ChR2 as a tool for neuroscience.
In the following years, Deisseroth, Hegemann, and Nagel collaborated to identify other proteins capable of activating or deactivating neurons using different wavelengths of light. With this toolkit, researchers can now design experiments where one group of neurons is turned on by one wavelength of light and another set of neurons is controlled by a different wavelength.
The term optogenetics was coined in 2006 and has since been implemented in a variety of studies. “Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders. In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment,” the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute stated in a press release.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.
