Following the riots in Modi’in during a failed attempt to arrest an ultra-Orthodox draft evader, and amid the resumption of arrests of draft evaders, the Jerusalem Faction, a hard-line ultra-Orthodox group opposed to military conscription, announced mass protests for Thursday afternoon in Jerusalem and central Israel, at around 4 p.m.
“Following the arrests in recent days by military authorities of students at yeshivas, Jewish religious seminaries, and married men engaged in full-time advanced Jewish religious study, and their abandonment by the ultra-Orthodox establishment, our revered rabbi, Rabbi Ezriel Auerbach, instructed the public to launch mass protests across the country against the desecration of the honor of the Torah and those who study it,” the Committee to Save the Torah World said in a statement.
“Speaking to the committee’s rabbis, the rabbi sharply criticized the abandonment of yeshiva students by those who had previously declared that they would stand by them at such a time. The rabbi noted that the protest is also over the terrible desecration of God’s name caused by yeshiva students and married kollel students being thrown into prison while no one speaks out.”
The protest is expected to include all components of the Jerusalem Faction. Its demonstrations usually include the group known as the “Ratzapnikim,” named after Rabbi Tzvi Friedman, the group’s leader. This time, however, the entire Jerusalem Faction may take part, meaning the protest could be larger and more disruptive.
The protest announcement came after hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men were summoned to Modi’in overnight Monday into Tuesday after an ultra-Orthodox draft evader activated the “Black Alert” system, used to mobilize supporters when authorities attempt to arrest draft evaders. Protesters then entered the building where he had barricaded himself in an effort to prevent his arrest.
The ultra-Orthodox extremists clashed with police who arrived to disperse them and surrounded Military Police soldiers. The protesters ultimately declared victory in the confrontation after negotiations with police resulted in an agreement allowing the soldiers to leave on condition that the draft evader was not arrested.
A police review obtained by ynet found that, contrary to procedure, the small Military Police force that arrived at the scene did not immediately remove the draft evader after locating him, instead giving him time to prepare. As he stalled, rioters began gathering at the scene. Only then were police called in to help extract the military force and restore order.
On Tuesday, the IDF acknowledged during a meeting with Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara that it had refrained from carrying out proactive arrests of draft evaders “in the recent period,” without specifying exactly when. It said this was done “against the backdrop of concentrating efforts at border crossings and adjustments for the holiday period.”
The IDF’s acknowledgment contradicts what it told the media just two weeks earlier. At the time, the IDF Spokesperson’s Unit said reports that the military had stopped carrying out proactive arrests were “incorrect,” adding that the Military Police was conducting proactive enforcement operations in population centers and at border crossings.
However, in an update submitted to the High Court of Justice on behalf of Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara, the military acknowledged that it had generally not carried out proactive enforcement or arrests in recent weeks. Military officials said enforcement efforts had instead been focused on border crossings, with additional adjustments made for the High Holiday period.
The document added that the military would resume proactive arrest operations during October.
Deputy Attorney General Gil Limon reprimanded the military, saying, among other things, that “the fact that for a considerable period no proactive operations, including arrests, have been carried out against draft dodgers is inconsistent with security needs, particularly in light of the senior military command’s clarification that expanding the standing army is a strategic necessity. It is also inconsistent with the principle of equality, the state’s commitments to the High Court of Justice and the court ruling that determined that the law preventing the arrest of yeshiva students must be struck down.”
The document also shows that as part of the military’s “concentration of efforts” at border crossings in September, 212 draft evaders and draft dodgers were arrested. An estimated 163 of them were ultra-Orthodox.
All 212 detainees were prosecuted, most in disciplinary proceedings. Of the 188 people arrested at Ben Gurion Airport, 64 were apprehended only upon returning to Israel, raising concerns about possible “loopholes” in enforcement of the ban on leaving the country.
The Population and Immigration Authority said that identified “loopholes” were quickly closed and that cases involving anyone suspected of the criminal offense of illegally crossing the border were referred to Israel Police or the IDF.
The IDF Spokesperson’s Unit later said: “The claim that we provided information that was untrue is incorrect. It should be clarified that during the High Holiday period, policing teams and preparations for the arrest of draft dodgers and draft evaders were reinforced at various border crossings, in addition to routine activity and presence. During the holidays, more than 200 draft evaders and draft dodgers were proactively arrested at border crossings.
“At the same time, proactive arrests were also carried out by the Military Police, all in coordination with the police. During September, the Military Police Corps carried out 15 proactive attempts to arrest draft evaders and draft dodgers. Eight draft evaders and draft dodgers were ultimately arrested.”

Tenants unable to pay higher rental prices, Domain data finds
In short:
Despite severe rental shortages, landlords are struggling to increase rents due to tenants hitting their affordability limit.
New data shows rent is flatlining in most capital cities and has even fallen in a few in the past three months.
What's next?
Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising to 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago.
Australia's rental market is beginning to lose steam despite rents remaining at record highs.
It is the rapidly emerging disconnect that experts say could suggest tenants are being pushed to the brink as rents flatline and even fall across most of the major capitals.
New data from Domain shows capital city house rents were unchanged at $700 a week over the September quarter, while unit rents rose by 1.5 per cent despite very low levels of rental properties available on the market.
That slowdown is challenging the long-held relationship between tight rental supply and growth, according to Domain's chief residential economist Nicola Powell.
"Tenants' ability to absorb further increases is really the dynamic that is limiting further rental growth," she told The Business.
"There's almost a disconnect now between where vacancy rate sits and what is occurring for rental growth."
Loading...
Lack of supply not translating into rent rises
Dr Powell said although it was still "a landlords' market" in all major capitals and regional areas, the severe supply shortage was not necessarily transferring into rental increases as tenants hit their ceiling.
Rents for houses are at or near record highs, with Sydney, Darwin and Perth the most expensive cities to live in.
But most of that growth occurred earlier in the year.
The new data from Domain found rents in Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide flatlined over the past three months.
And housing rents fell in Sydney and Canberra by $5 and $10 respectively, erasing gains in June.
Only Darwin and Hobart bucked the trend across the capital cities in Domain's dataset, recording rises of 5.3 per cent and 1 per cent respectively in houses in the past quarter.
Although the market is slowing, with the national vacancy rate rising by 0.1 percentage points to rest at 1 per cent, it is still much tighter than it was a year ago.
Renters compromise to avoid higher rent
Cameron Kusher of Kusher Consulting, an independent property economist, said renters were finding other ways to survive as the market squeezed them for all they were worth.
"Because rents have increased so much over the last few years, what people are doing is they're renting in a less ideal location," he said.
"So they're opting for a cheaper rental, maybe not ideally where they want to live but basically a trade-off that they're having to make."
Other ways include share housing or adult children staying at home longer.
Migration cuts floated to curb rent rises
The figures came after One Nation released new modelling for its migration plan on Wednesday, saying it could save Australian renters almost $3,000 a year.
The party has pledged that, if elected, it would cut 750,000 temporary visas over three years to reduce rental inflation by 6.5 per cent.
"I don't know that that's enough to significantly improve rental affordability given how much rents have increased over recent years," Mr Kusher said of the policy.
"But I feel like, at this point, renters would probably take any win that would lower their rent."
He also said changes in this year's budget that made property investment less attractive were still flowing through the system.
But at this stage, Mr Kusher said they did not seem to be causing the massive rent increases initially feared.

Air Force Mulls Adding a Missile Warning System to F-15EX
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:36:19 UTC
05:36:19 KST

The Air Force is looking for ways to add an integrated missile warning system into the F-15EX Eagle II fighter for the first time.
The Air Force Life Cycle Management Center posted a sources sought notice Sept. 29 as part of a market research effort, looking for potential vendors for a missile launch and approach warning system that could be quickly installed on the F-15EX.
The system has to be able to alert the fighter’s aircrew about missile threats without distracting them with too many false alarms, the notice states. It also has to use the F-15EX’s six preexisting sensor locations already earmarked for missile warning, as well as the jet’s data cables, power cables and cooling capabilities. And it has to be able to be quickly and easily installed or removed in the field by Air Force maintainers, without requiring any changes to the aircraft itself aside from installing line replaceable units in the six sensor locations, per the notive.
The notice did not say how much such a system could cost or how long the contract could last, but said those details will be in line with what such work typically requires.
The Boeing-made F-15EX is a more advanced version of the F-15E Strike Eagle, with upgrades including fly-by-wire controls and a new electronic warfare system. But while the jets are built with the features necessary for a missile warning system, they do not actually come with that capability, even though other variants like Saudi Arabia’s F-15SA and Qatar’s F-15QA do.
The F-15EX does have the Eagle Passive Active Warning Survivability System, an advanced electronic warfare suite that can jam enemies’ radar systems and thus defend against radar-guided missiles. But a new missile warning system would help defend against infrared-guided vehicles.
Other Air Force fighters have missile warning systems that can detect infrared-guided threats—the F-35 has the AN/AAQ-37 Distributed Aperture System, built by Northrop Grumman, and the F-22 has the AN/AAR-56 Missile Launch Detection system.
Years ago, the F-15C was supposed to be equipped under the Common Missile Warning System, a joint program between the Army, Navy, and Air Force. But the Air Force dropped out of that program in 2000, according to a report from the Institute for Defense Analyses. The Common Missile Warning System eventually became the AN/AAR-57, built by BAE Systems. The F-15SA has the CMWS from BAE.
The threat of infrared-guided missiles was underscored during Operation Epic Fury, when an F-15E Strike Eagle, the EX’s predecessor, was downed over Iran in April. President Donald Trump said Iran used a shoulder-fired missile—often called a man-portable air defense system or MANPADS—to hit the fighter, and MANPADS often use infrared sensors.
While the Air Force is not committing to buying a new system, the request shows it is giving serious consideration to adding it at a time when the service’s plans for the F-15EX are rapidly expanding. Just this past April, the Air Force announced it was expanding its planned fleet size from 129 aircraft to 269.
AFLCMC wants potential respondents to say what military aircraft their missile warning systems are already approved on for operational use, whether the system is currently in active production, and how many months after the contract award could the companies start delivering the system, among other issues.
Companies have until Nov. 12 to submit unclassified white papers on their systems’ technical capabilities to the Air Force.

“We’ll send you to your cozy Gulag”.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:36:16 UTC
05:36:16 KST

Folkston D. Ray James ICE Processing Center. Photo from the Geo Group website
Russian asylum seekers, some held without charge for more than two years, are among dozens of detainees on hunger strike at a privately-run immigration jail in the U.S. state of Georgia. A report written by two of the Russians and shared with Mediazona alleges medical neglect, mouldy food and threats from the warden, who they say promised to send them to “your cozy Gulag”.
Detainees at the Folkston D. Ray James ICE Processing Center in southern Georgia began a hunger strike on October 6, a spokesperson for the Campaign to Shut Down FIPC told the local broadcaster WSAV. The centre is run by the private prison company GEO Group under contract with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Advocates estimate that at least 73 people have joined, according to the Guardian.
One of the strike’s organisers, Idris Makhmudov, is a Russian citizen who has been detained since July 2024. He has reportedly been placed in solitary confinement, according to Monica Whatley of the “Campaign to Shut Down the Folkston ICE Processing Center”, who spoke to the Guardian.
The strikers want to be released while their asylum cases continue, seek protection from re-detention and deportation, as well as reunification with loved ones. Makhmudov drafted an open letter in June that was signed by 45 men, eight of them Russian citizens, who had been held for between 16 and 32 months at the time. “We are those who have been imprisoned for years, yet have never been accused of any crime,” it reads.
The men asked for asylum on arrival to the United States, so they are classed as “arriving aliens” and treated in law as if they were still at the border. Many say bond requests, parole, custody reviews and habeas corpus petitions have all failed. “For those of us held here in Georgia, it feels like rights exist only on paper,” the letter says.
A report written in Russian by two detainees, Aleksei Kovalko and Aleksandr Borovkov, describes life inside. It is dated September 14 and signed by 14 men. “The aim of this prison is to deport as many people as possible and to create conditions in which it is impossible to defend your case in immigration court,” they write.
The authors accuse the warden, whom they do not name, of “open xenophobia”. They say that earlier this year he told Russian-speaking detainees, in Russian: “Don’t worry, we’ll send you to your cozy Gulag.” On another occasion, Kovalko says, the warden told a group of detainees: “None of you will be released into freedom in America—all of you will be deported.”
The report says meaningful medical care is effectively absent and that there is no dentist. Kovalko says his complaints of toothache over almost two years were never logged. One of the authors recalls a doctor telling him: “It is not my job to cure you; what matters to me is that you don’t die.” In January 2025, he says, after he fainted during a blood test, staff at the neighbouring Folkston ICE Processing Center left him for hours in a cold concrete cell with no mattress.
The authors describe mattresses little more than a centimetre thick, mouldy lettuce and tortillas. They say the drinking water smells bad, while staff drink bottled water that detainees cannot buy. TVs blare until the early hours. Kovalko says he was sent to the disciplinary isolation unit for switching one off at 2 a.m. after a guard ignored his requests.
The authors say post from lawyers is withheld or delayed, sometimes past court deadlines, and that evidence stored on detainees’ phones cannot be copied or printed. Kovalko says he has been allowed to speak to his wife, who was detained in Louisiana, four times in two years.
Borovkov says ICE refused his written requests for his own arrest and detention records, even though, he says, the agency’s detention standards require it to provide them. He says an officer told him he was not allowed to defend himself.
GEO Group’s operation in Folkston has failed federal oversight before. In 2022, the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general reported on an unannounced inspection of the neighbouring Folkston ICE Processing Center and its annex. It found violations of detention standards on medical care, facility conditions, grievances, segregation, communication between staff and detainees, and the handling of detainees’ property, and made 13 recommendations to ICE.
ICE’s own inspectors rated D. Ray James “good” after their first visit in June 2026. They found it compliant with 22 of 24 detention standards, including medical care, food, grievances and segregation, and none of the 28 detainees interviewed alleged mistreatment; however, the facility had been given four weeks’ notice of the inspection. Inspectors did flag two “priority” failures: suicide-watch checks logged up to 58 minutes apart instead of every 15, and detainees kept in units that did not match their security classification. One detainee told inspectors he was being treated for tooth pain with painkillers while on a waitlist for an outside dentist.
Good internal ratings have long been the norm. A May 2025 review by the Government Accountability Office, Congress’s watchdog, found that ICE inspectors rated detention centres “acceptable” or better in 238 of 241 inspections between 2022 and 2024, despite recording more than 5,400 deficiencies. Facilities are usually told of inspections four weeks in advance. The Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, which carried out unannounced inspections, was dissolved this year.
An investigation by the Project On Government Oversight found this August that ICE has never given a failing grade to a facility that, like D. Ray James, holds only ICE detainees.
GEO Group referred the Guardian’s questions to ICE, and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to them.

Target unprecedented and extraordinary goals: Modi
Modi’s speech on his 25 years as head of govt came amid the opposition’s protest in Delhi over the SIR row, but he did not join the issue, except for a sideswipe at his rivals when he said a big tragedy for the country had been that it was divided for votes due to political expedience.Water crisis in agriculture or power shortage does not hit any particular caste or community, Modi said.
“When a problem troubles everyone, then the solution too should cover everyone,” he said, adding this was why his govt linked good governance and saturation to inclusion.
Reiteration of his “tireless” resolve to make India a leading player in a gamut of sectors, including tourism, education, sports, entertainment and science, ran through the nearly hour-long speech as its central theme.“Our pilot (Smit Machchhar) is being discussed globally today. Made-in-India planes will be discussed tomorrow... It will be an injustice to the country if we set small and easy goals. We should target unprecedented and extraordinary goals,” Modi said.“Viksit Bharat by 2047: we will do it. Top three economy: we will do it. Self-reliant: we will do it,” he said.
Addressing the criticism that his target of “Viksit Bharat by 2047” is too far into the future, he said the idea of an independent India two decades before 1947 had looked improbable. India has 140 crore citizens now as against less than 40 crore then and is much more capable, he said.Modi said the Indian economy was considered a “gone case” when he took office in 2014, and the picture had completely changed now.Lauding RSS volunteers and BJP members, he recalled his rise from a humble background, saying he was always driven by a desire to learn. “No incident was a waste for me. Those who helped me win taught me humility. Those who brought me down taught me to stand up. Those who opposed me taught me the power of democracy. Every crisis was a test of my patience,” he said.Modi said he was never driven by ambition but mission, adding he never intended to contest elections and was busy helping others fight polls as a senior organisational functionary in BJP before being asked to take over as Gujarat CM.

07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US stocks closed lower Wednesday as elevated Treasury yields weighed on markets and Federal Reserve minutes signaled another interest rate increase would likely be appropriate before year-end.
The Dow Jones industrial average fell 341.41 points, or 0.66%, to 51,179.87.
The S&P 500 declined 17.16 points, or 0.22%, to 7,801.77, retreating from Tuesday's record close. The Nasdaq composite also lost 61.20 points, or 0.22%, to 27,538.69.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield stood at 5.286%, up about 1.5 basis points, after reaching 5.365% earlier in the session, its highest level since April 2002.
Yields eased from their intraday highs following a $39 billion auction of 10-year Treasury notes, helping stocks pare earlier losses.
Higher yields increase borrowing costs and can put pressure on equity valuations.
Housing data released Wednesday highlighted the impact of rising borrowing costs.
The average rate on 30-year fixed mortgages climbed to 7.49% in the week ending Oct. 2, its highest level since November 2023, from 7.30% a week earlier, according to the Mortgage Bankers Association.
Mortgage applications fell 4.2% from the previous week.
The association attributed the rise in mortgage rates to higher Treasury yields and widening mortgage spreads amid increased interest rate volatility.
Fed signals further tightening
Minutes of the Fed's Sept. 15-16 meeting, released Wednesday, showed most participants assessed that another rate increase would likely be appropriate by year-end.
Officials emphasized that future decisions would depend on incoming information, the economic outlook and the balance of risks.
The Fed unanimously raised its benchmark rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4% at the September meeting.
Many participants judged that financial conditions remained supportive of growth despite higher longer-term Treasury yields.
In other markets, the dollar strengthened against the euro, with the exchange rate falling 0.56% to 1.12.
Gold declined 1.4% to $4,107.50 per ounce, while West Texas Intermediate crude fell 0.54% to $88.96 per barrel.
European stocks close lower
European markets also closed lower amid concerns over France's public finances and geopolitical uncertainty.
The benchmark Stoxx Europe 600 fell 1% to 630.25.
Italy's FTSE MIB dropped 2.51% to 49,972.25, while Germany's DAX declined 1.35% to 25,104.36.
France's CAC 40 lost 1.22% to 7,769.21, and Britain's FTSE 100 fell 0.79% to 10,458.5.
Spain’s IBEX 35 also dropped 1.68% to end at 19,118.

87-year-old symbol of Spain’s housing crisis dies 2 weeks after eviction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:31:26 UTC
05:31:26 KST

Alyssa Mcmurtry
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Maricarmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked housing protests across Spain, died on Wednesday.
She died at a Madrid hospital, where she had remained since her Sept. 23 eviction, according to a joint statement from the Madrid tenants’ union, her family and her lawyer, reported by Spanish media.
“Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return to her home, this solution came too late,” the statement said.
Known publicly as Maricarmen, she had lived for around seven decades in the apartment in Madrid’s Retiro district.
She was taken from her home on a stretcher and hospitalized after police carried out the eviction despite crowds trying to prevent it.
Her removal galvanized demonstrations and protest camps, turning her into a symbol of the country’s housing crisis.
Her case became a rallying point as the government sought stronger tenant protections. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez announced early elections for Nov. 29 following parliament’s rejection of housing measures.
The government approved two revised housing decrees this week, while unions prepared a housing-related general strike for Nov. 11.
The statement announcing Maricarmen’s death said the mobilization had marked a turning point but added that “the cost of getting here has been far too high.”
She had spent years fighting efforts by the property’s owner, Urbagestion, to evict her.
According to El Pais newspaper, she received a monthly pension of €1,400 ($1,567), while the company sought rent of €1,600. She had continued paying her longstanding rent and bills, totaling around €500 a month.
Public pressure eventually led the company to agree to a new rental arrangement that would have allowed her to return. She never made it home.
She had described how the prolonged dispute affected her health.
“It has affected every aspect of my life. I’m not myself anymore,” she told El Pais two days before the eviction.
From the hospital, she continued encouraging protesters who had gathered in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol and other Spanish squares.
“I would like to be there with you, accompanying you in your camp, in your struggle, but I don’t have that good fortune,” she said in a message reported by the newspaper.
“Fight, defend what is yours and, please, take care.”

Key Event
'[China] housing won't find a floor this decade': Oxford Economics
Oxford Economics has penned a note on the struggling Chinese housing market.
Here are the key takeaways.
- We’re more pessimistic than the consensus about when a floor will form.
- Housing inventories are near record highs, developer financing has been squeezed further, and the exposure of banks to more insidious forms of real estate lending has risen markedly. We expect housing to subtract ~1.6ppt to GDP growth this year and ~1.1ppt next year.
- Against that, the authorities continue to offer incremental demand-side housing support. With recent price recoveries in tier-1 cities proving limited, we also see growing evidence that the property market’s problems are feeding into weaker economic activity – and the reverse is becoming more evident, too, creating an ugly feedback loop.
- But there’ll be no single trough, as resale transactions should recover before prices, and construction will likely bottom out before the housing stock has fully repriced. Less a conventional property cycle and more a structural repair of various balance sheets, the housing adjustment is increasingly likely to take the form of repeated temporary stabilisations rather than a clean cyclical turn.
- Recent mortgage subsidies are too narrowly targeted, and, by our calculations, cheaper financing still can't fully offset expected capital losses. Some frontloaded buying may materialise given the one-year subsidy application window, but more debt isn’t likely given consumers’ currently low appetite for risk.
- Nor can China simply build through the downturn. We estimate total structural demand for housing will be roughly half 2019’s levels by 2035 and fall by another 50% by 2060.

BCCC working to help banks stop making the lives of grieving families harder
So, I've discussed some of the shortcomings of the Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) in an earlier post.
Here's some of the positive elements coming out of its annual report.
"Strengthening management" of deceased estates
Ever since the "I Fee Dead People" scandals uncovered in the Hayne royal commission, banks have tried to stop charging customers that it knows are dead fees for services that can only be accessed by the living.
A further issue has been the at-times diabolical treatment of the relatives of people who have died.
This is not ancient history:
- Between 1 July 2019 to 30 September 2023, ANZ charged fees and interest to deceased estate accounts in error.
- To remediate, ANZ paid approximately $3,253,646 to 18,852 impacted estates.
- In February 2022, ANZ identified a backlog of 7,329 delayed cases of deceased estates.
- ANZ sent approximately 10,604 apology letters to representatives of the estates affected by potential delays. (Some got a small amount of compensation
The bank received the harshest punishment available to the BCCC: it published the name ANZ alongside a report about the wrong-doing. In other cases, it doesn't name the institution.
"We decided to apply a sanction to name ANZ and publish details of its non-compliance on our website and in our Annual Report."
In this year's annual report, the BCCC talks about what it has achieved across the sector, regarding this problem.
"Our report of July 2026, 'Managing deceased estates – a follow-up review', showed that most banks reported changes to their systems, processes, staff training and monitoring arrangements.
"These changes point to more structured and accountable practices, including better identification of relevant products, stronger staff capability and closer oversight.
"Improvements should support more timely processing, reduce the risk of inappropriate fees and other errors, and provide representatives of deceased customers with clearer and more consistent service at a difficult time.
"We found that progress remains uneven, though.
"Some banks still rely on manual processes and have fragmented accountability, while gaps in training and monitoring may limit the impact of the improvements they have made.
"We will continue to monitor the progress of this issue, with a focus on banks that reported changes still under development or not yet fully embedded"

19,551 breaches, $47 million in financial impact: regulator of banking's code tallies industry problems
The annual report of the Banking Code Compliance Committee (BCCC) has been released.
It notes 19,551 breaches of the Code and $47 million in financial impact on customers.
Breaches of the Code must be reported when they affect more than 20 customers or result in more than $20,000 in financial impact
I've written previously about the BCCC, a well-meaning body that does good work but has few powers and rarely uses them.
The committee was set up in the wake of epic failures with the industry exposed at the Hayne royal commission. It holds members to standards set out in a Banking Code of Practice, a set of guidelines that has no weight in law but is written into the contracts when you buy a product from a bank.
I hope you're sitting down: it's most substantial power is to publish the name of the organisation that it has found in breach of the Code.
And it doesn't even do it that often.
It is funded entirely by the banking industry's key lobby group, the Australian Banking Association, and a few years ago asked for the ability to routinely name banks in breach of the rules, and to force them to publicise it (such as a note on the bank's website).
The ABA said... no thanks.
So it's a body that does solid behind the scenes work but is in no way a watchdog.
Here's what the BCCC's report says about the model of self-regulation that it operates under:
"The Code is a fundamental element of successful self-regulation.
"Self-regulation involves the industry setting its own standards of conduct and enforcing these standards through breach identification, reporting, and remediation.
"This model allows the industry to demonstrate a commitment to ethical and responsible behaviour, helping to build trust with customers.
"It also reduces the need for costly and time-consuming regulatory intervention.
"Our work monitoring the Code is crucial to the success of the self-regulation model working to its full potential."
So either a win for the reduction of red tape, a safeguard for customers, a weak system that shows the strength of the banking lobby in avoiding regulation or a little of all three.

The residential construction industry is the latest to attack the Australian Taxation Office (ATO) over an announcement that it will withdraw individuals and businesses being able to pay tax debts by credit card from December 1.

Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning Is a Brisk, Old-School Journalism Thriller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:29:48 UTC
05:29:48 KST

In the months leading up to the release of The Social Reckoning—a sequel to David Fincher’s 2010 film The Social Network, which covered the rise of Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook—movie people, at least, spent a fair amount of time grumbling about the fact that the film’s writer-director, Aaron Sorkin, is no David Fincher. That, of course, is demonstrably true. Sorkin wrote the script for The Social Network and won an Oscar for it. Fincher was for a time in talks to direct The Social Reckoning, but ultimately that gig landed with Sorkin, and the grousing began. Sorkin specializes in crackling dialogue and heartfelt, if often self-righteous, liberal views, but the movies he has directed (The Trial of the Chicago 7, Being the Ricardos) haven’t been considered particularly dynamic. His excessive earnestness can be both a plus and a minus: While it’s great that he cares, too much caring can be exhausting.
Which is why it’s something of a surprise that The Social Reckoning moves along as briskly as it does. This is an account of how Wall Street Journal writer Jeff Horwitz (played here by Jeremy Allen White) cracked the story of how, ahead of the 2020 election, Facebook founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg essentially encouraged the amplification of extremist views, a factor that fed directly into the violent January 6 attack on the Capitol. Horwitz can’t write that story alone; he enlists the clandestine help of a loyal Facebook engineer—part of the organization’s civic integrity team—who has become skeptical of certain company policies. Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) at first offers only minimal information; she loves her job and doesn’t want to lose it. But the deeper she digs into Facebook’s sinister practices of promoting rage bait to increase engagement, the more disenchanted she becomes.
The Social Reckoning is at its core an old-school shoe-leather journalism thriller. Sorkin’s point seems to be that even in the digital age, there aren’t really any new ways to be a thorough, ethical journalist—all the old rules still apply. His script is dense with information, and the story—which opens in 2019 with Horwitz’s joining the paper’s San Francisco bureau and more or less wraps up with the publication of his Pulitzer-winning multi-part 2021 expose the Facebook Files—leapfrogs from one year to another and back again. (The time shifts are helpfully indicated by a sliding timeline appearing at the bottom of the screen.) Sorkin’s approach to telling this story is somewhat professorial—there’s a lot of telling without much showing. But cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth—the frequent Fincher collaborator who also shot The Social Network—gives the picture a handsomely polished look. Somehow, the runtime slips by faster than you might have expected.
Maybe that’s thanks, in part, to Sorkin’s casting choices. Zuckerberg is played by shapeshifter du jour Jeremy Strong, who radiates a kind of robotic clamminess. In many of his scenes, he’s ensconced in a mock Congressional hearing, overseen by a “crisis specialist” (played by a take-no-prisoners Wunmi Mosaku) who has been hired to make him more likable, a Sisyphean task if ever there were one. He sits, straight-backed and tense, in a dark suit, working terrifically hard at the task of appearing human. At one point in the film, when he’s grilled about his company’s role in promoting the views of hate groups, he snaps, “We’re a corkboard. We don’t control what people pin to it.” Strong is attracted to playing unlikable people, and he’s good at it, though often—as with his portrayal of fixer extraordinaire Roy Cohn in The Apprentice—he offers a dash of tempered sympathy to remind us that these people are actually human. Not so with Zuckerberg: he focuses almost solely on the tech oligarch’s calculating, evasive nature. It’s the right choice.
As Horwitz, White serves up a classic, muted portrayal of a guy so dedicated to his job that he’s seriously fun-deprived. Oddly enough, it takes a smart, ultra-serious tech engineer to loosen him up, and his scenes with Madison, in which their characters banter and spar, are the movie’s best. At one point he refers to Frances as a Cassandra, citing the story of the cursed Trojan princess who has the gift of predicting the future, though no one believes her. Only he’s mangled and misapplied the myth; Frances sets him straight, and fills him in on the correct metaphorical meaning of Chicken Little and the Boy Who Cried Wolf as well. It’s Madison who anchors the movie. Frances wears studious-schoolgirl glasses, and she suffers from neuropathy: In chilly San Francisco, she needs to bundle up in chunky leg warmers and wristlets to keep numbness at bay—this garb gives her a waifish air. At one point she describes herself as “the girl in class with her hand raised that nobody wants the teacher to call on.” That’s a mouthful of classic Sorkinese if ever there were one, but as she spins the words out, Madison is so plaintive that she makes you see that girl. Frances Haugen is the conscience and the true hero of The Social Reckoning, and Sorkin knows it. He practically hands the movie over to Madison, and even in a movie filled with talking—and often with guys talking—it’s her stalwart yet unassuming presence that makes it sing.

Venezuela’s Maduro to face new US charges over alleged torture of Americans, official says
WASHINGTON - Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores are expected to face new criminal charges in the United States over allegations that Americans detained in Venezuela were tortured, a US official said on Oct 7.
The new charges could come as soon as Oct 8, according to the official, who was briefed on the investigation.
Maduro, who led Venezuela for 13 years, and Flores were captured by the US military from their home in Caracas on Jan 3 and brought to New York to face drug trafficking charges. They have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial starting June 1, 2027.
A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.
Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Oct 7.
Details of the new charges, including the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available.
Maduro’s tenure was marked by tensions with the United States. Washington accused his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions such as relief from financial sanctions.
Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during Maduro’s tenure included five oil executives arrested on graft charges. They were freed in 2022 in exchange for two of Flores’ nephews, who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking.
Others detained included two former US Army Special Forces members who were arrested in Venezuela in 2020 in connection with a botched raid aimed at ousting Maduro. They were freed in 2023 as part of another prisoner swop.
Since Maduro’s capture, Venezuela has been led by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodriguez, who has increased cooperation with the Trump administration.
Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been held in a federal jail in Brooklyn.
Flores is due to appear in Manhattan federal court on Oct 8 to urge US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein to release her from jail before trial for health reasons. Prosecutors oppose her release. REUTERS

What three years of the Gaza war reveal about Israel and the world

What three years of the Gaza war reveal about Israel and the world
On October 7, 2023, Hamas and other Palestinian resistance organizations launched an attack out of the Gaza Strip and into Israel under the code name “Al-Aqsa Flood.” Israeli and Western mainstream media and politicians rapidly labelled this a massive act of terrorism and flooded the world with tales of horrific atrocities allegedly perpetrated by the Palestinians, such as sadistically murdering children and women and committing mass rape.
We now know that these atrocious tales were lies calculated to generate domestic and international outrage against the Palestinian resistance and Palestinians in general. They were part of the same poisonous Israeli narrative that labeled these people “Amalek” – a reference to a perversely “exemplary” genocide in the Old Testament – and denied that they were human beings. They were taking steps, in other words, to start a genocide.
These atrocious propaganda lies were made up and spread by, for instance, Israel’s Zaka activists and Western mainstream journalists, such as the New York Times, high public officials such as the UN’s Pramila Patten, and activists. For instance, former Meta executive Sheryl Sandberg acted as a Zionist propagandist, who chose to rely on Israeli disinformation.
In reality, there were no mass rapes, there were no sadistic baby murders by beheadings or in microwave ovens, no pregnant woman was found killed with a headshot, with her baby stabbed and still attached to the umbilical cord. It “simply didn’t happen,” as a detailed investigation by Israeli newspaper Haaretz found.
What did happen on October 7, 2026 was not a savage, sadistic rampage but a daring military resistance operation. It was also a mass break-out from the Gaza Strip, which was under a long Israeli siege so brutal that Israeli sociologist Baruch Kimmerling had already called the Strip the “world’s largest concentration camp ever” almost a quarter-century ago.
The core of this offensive targeted Israel’s Gaza Division, which, according to high-ranking Israeli officers was “overpowered.” In the process, Palestinian resistance fighters killed and captured Israeli military personnel. While Israel’s propaganda has done its best to obfuscate this fact, these actions were neither “terrorism” nor hostage-taking but legitimate acts of armed resistance under international law.
The Palestinian fighters also attacked a music festival as well as several settlements. There, according to an Amnesty International summary in early 2024, they did commit crimes, including the deliberate killing of civilians and the taking of hostages, that is, civilians, not soldiers, whose capture makes them POWs and not hostages. A crime, in any case, is a crime even if it’s only realistic to recognize plenty of mitigating circumstances in the immense injustice, dispossession, and often sadistic and humiliating violence Palestinians have suffered from Israelis over decades.
Honesty also dictates that we take three key facts into account: First, the leader of the pro-Israeli UAE, has revealed that he warned Israel’s leader Benjamin Netanyahu personally of Hamas’s plans. In a similar vein, Qatar’s leader claims that Hamas was ready to free all civilian hostages immediately after the attack (which would have left it with only military prisoners). Yet the Israeli leadership ignored the warning and rejected the offer to free all civilians.
It’s almost as if it wanted the attack to happen, as a pretext to initiate a massive ethnic cleansing-by-genocide campaign, and for the civilian hostages to stay in Gaza, as a pretext for continuing that campaign.
Second, it has long been clear that Israeli authorities activated an expanded “Hannibal Directive”: Usually prepared to kill their own soldiers rather than let them be captured, on October 7, Israeli forces also killed Israeli civilians and, most likely, in large if unknown numbers, deploying tanks as well as helicopter gunships to – in the words of an Israeli officer – “mass Hannibal” their own. Of the roughly 1,200 casualties on 7 October, hundreds are likely to have been due to Israeli-on-Israeli violence; others were soldiers and as such legitimate targets.
And finally, a simple point all too often drowned out by Israeli and pro-Israeli propaganda: A legitimate military force does not lose its overall legitimacy – or that of its goals – even when some of its members commit crimes. If that were the case, most armies in this world would have to be dissolved because none of them have a history entirely free of crimes. Armed Palestinian resistance is fundamentally legitimate under international law – and morally, too, obviously – and remains so. In fact, in the future, the outnumbered, outgunned, and abandoned Palestinian defenders of Gaza will be remembered as heroes, as they should.
Things are different, as a matter of fact, if we look at the actions of the Israeli military since October 7. Unlike with anything that individual Palestinian resistance fighters may have done, in the case of Israel’s euphemistically mis-labeled Defense Forces – a “citizen army [and] representative sample” of Israeli society – we are looking at a clear case of a whole, large organization deliberately and enthusiastically dedicated to committing every war crime and crime against humanity in every book, including ethnic cleansing and genocide.
Because that is a precise description of what Israel has been doing to the Palestinians of Gaza – and not only – since October 7, 2023. It is also by now the consensus among honest observers, including the global community of genocide experts. This, indeed, has been the most public genocide in human history, despite Israeli attempts to seal Gaza off and mass murder its journalists under false pretexts.
Israeli perpetrators – high and low – have proudly advertised their own crimes. Israeli society as a whole, virtually continuous polling has shown consistently, supports the genocide. In a world of real-time media and social media, the reality of Gaza could not be hidden. Only recently, Google has finally adjusted its maps to reflect it.
The nature and extent of Israel’s crimes is obvious and exceedingly well documented, and that is a very important thing. Humanity owes an enormous debt of gratitude to those Palestinians and others who have undertaken the harrowing task of compiling and analyzing the evidence, such as, to name only a few, UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese or the tireless staff of the Electronic Intifada.
What needs at least as much attention is what the Gaza genocide says about our world as a whole: namely that genocide is not only possible – it was before – but can take place over years and in full view of the global public, with the active support of most of the establishments of virtually the entire West and the passive acquiescence of the elites of most other countries.
In a more or less sane world, fulfilling its obligations under the short and clear UN Genocide Convention of 1948 – it bears recalling – the Israeli genocide perpetrators would long have been stopped by a combination of diplomatic, economic, and, of course, military intervention. That would have been the minimum of what both international law and basic ethics obviously demand.
Yet, instead, we live in a world, where – apart from the Palestinian resistance itself – only a handful of states and political organizations have done anything at all to interfere with Israel’s mass murder campaign: Iran, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Ansarallah – the Houthis – in Yemen.
Think about the above what you want, like or dislike their politics, it is a fact that no one else has even remotely tried to apply the Genocide Convention in practice. If that is irritating, don’t blame Ansarallah, for instance, but blame the many who have failed to act.
But failure to act has been only part of this real-life horror story. In the West, many governments and mainstream establishments, including in the media and academia, have pro-actively supported Israel. This is a shameful history of criminal collaboration and complicity still to be written. Indeed, in the worst cases, such as the elites of the US, the UK, and Germany, complicity seems too weak an expression: they are better described as genocide co-perpetrators.
The obvious inference from this state of the world is that international law does not matter. There is no more devastating attack on the very idea of international law and a law-based order than the impunity of Israel and its accomplices. Benjamin Netanyahu, with an International Criminal Court warrant to his name, has been able to brazenly deny his and his country’s crimes at the recent UN General Assembly and even repeat the Amalek reference, as Craig Mokhiber has pointed out. Outside, meanwhile, his critics were being arrested.
Annalena Baerbock, in her time as one of Germany’s most embarrassing foreign ministers ever, also justified, shielded, and supported Israel; she has just finished her ill-begotten sinecure as the UN General Assembly’s president and made a lateral move to an absurdly undeserved position at Columbia University. The examples could be multiplied endlessly: the elites of the West, including American presidents Joe Biden and Donald Trump, have devastatingly compromised themselves by their complicity with Israel. And yet, they keep thriving.
So, not only has international law been discredited as literally never before, but international establishments also have, and in particular those of that part of the world that still has the arrogance to claim global leadership as if it were some kind of birthright, the West.
Now add the fact that Israel has not “only” been committing the Gaza genocide. It has also escalated ethnic cleansing terror in the West Bank, invaded Syria and Lebanon, attacked Yemen, participated in and triggered brutal assaults against Iran that have also tanked the world energy economy, and, in general, has followed its usual modus operandi of assassination, subversion, torture, rape, and relentless aggression. And yet it faces no discernible consequences beyond ludicrously inappropriate, purely symbolical measures at best and, of course, massive continued support.
Meanwhile, those in the West who dare be human and show their solidarity with the Palestinians and other victims of Israel and its accomplices and co-perpetrators are harassed, beaten up by police, arrested, and blacklisted.
What the Gaza genocide has shown with respect to the world as a whole is simple: Those who rule us will go much farther, much more shamelessly and openly than most of us, even the pessimists, used to be able to imagine. More importantly, they will get away with it, and they will let each other get away with it. Gaza is not an exception. It is a harbinger of a world of horrors. Resistance is not an option; it is the only one.

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:47 UTC
05:27:47 KST

US Republicans, independents express low trust in election integrity: Poll
A Gallup survey highlights a deep – and historic – partisan divide over confidence in the country’s elections.
With less than a month to go before the United States’ pivotal midterms, a new survey found that most independent voters and supporters of President Donald Trump’s Republican Party do not believe the elections will be honest.
Polling from the research firm Gallup, released on Wednesday, found that 37 percent of Republicans and 35 percent of independents have confidence in the country’s electoral system, significantly lower than the rate for Democrats, at 63 percent.
The numbers highlight a deep, historic partisan divide over confidence in US elections.
The survey also suggests a counterintuitive relationship wherein the US voters who approve of Trump’s leadership also distrust the electoral system.
“Since 2025 and Trump’s return to the White House, the relationship between leadership approval and confidence in elections has disappeared,” Gallup wrote in a statement highlighting the results.
The firm added that the US is the only country out of more than 100 polled annually over the past 15 years to show this pattern: Trust in US election integrity is markedly higher among those who disapprove of the country’s leadership under Trump than those who approve.
That marks a shift in voter sentiment. In 2025, at the start of Trump’s second term, confidence in US elections “was nominally higher among approvers (51 percent) than disapprovers (45 percent)”, according to Gallup.
Now, 52 percent of those who disapprove of Trump’s leadership express confidence in US elections, compared with 41 percent of those who approve.
Overall, 49 percent of Americans said they were confident in the honesty of elections, while 51 percent said they were not. Those figures are unchanged from the country’s last midterm election in 2022.
Michael McNulty, the senior policy director at Issue One, a nonprofit that tracks the role of money in politics, has worked on more than 30 elections across the world.
He said the numbers, especially among Republicans, do not point towards problems in the US election system itself.
Rather, he blames Trump for sowing distrust in the election system among his base, particularly ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
“The fact that Republicans trust elections less really is exactly the result of that false fraud narrative perpetrated over many years,” McNulty said. “I think Americans can trust the people who run their elections.”
Still, the US perspective towards election integrity appears to be a global outlier.
In more than 100 countries where Gallup tracks views of national leadership and confidence in elections, people who approve of their governments have generally been more likely to trust their country’s elections.
In 2025, a median of 70 percent of people across those countries who approved of their national leadership expressed confidence in the honesty of their elections, compared with 30 percent among those who disapproved.
“The current US pattern is highly unusual compared with the rest of the world,” Gallup wrote.
Under former US President Joe Biden, 81 percent of Americans who approved of the government also expressed confidence in elections, compared with just 30 percent of those who disapproved.
Gallup said this year’s unusual divide could have implications for the November elections, raising questions about whether some voters will view the results as legitimate.
Over the course of his second term in office, Trump and members of his administration have taken steps to upend the US voting system, including by launching investigations into the 2020 election, issuing executive orders to change voting procedures and demanding voter data from states.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Monday, Trump once again claimed that mail-in voting was prone to fraud, without providing evidence.
“No, vote by mail … I’d rather have a vote in person. But they can vote by mail if they want, because we seem to have no choice,” Trump said.
“What we’re concerned about is … there is a lot of cheating in vote by mail,” he added.
McNulty said Trump’s remarks are part of what he describes as an “election takeover playbook” aimed squarely at the president’s supporters.
“You use these false fraud narratives. You sow chaos. You undermine confidence, particularly among his own base and his own voters, because they’re the ones listening to him,” McNulty explained.
“And then you use that narrative to justify efforts” against the US electoral system, he added.
McNulty said voting organisations like his are preparing for the “very real threat” that Trump or Republican-aligned groups could challenge the midterm results.
But he is “confident” the US electoral system will stand up to any possible attempts to undermine it.
In response to a request for comment from Al Jazeera, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis instead blamed any decline in election-season trust on the Democratic Party’s refusal to implement Trump’s changes.
“Every American should be asking why the radical Left continues to fight against commonsense election integrity measures, like Voter ID and citizenship verification,” Bis wrote.
“President Trump has made clear: Anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable.”
State and federal law already prohibits non-citizen voting in federal elections. Critics, however, have accused Trump of seeking to implement further restrictions that would discourage or prevent citizens from exercising their legal right to vote.

Historical records cast doubt on Zack Polanski’s family Nazi escape story
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:27:40 UTC
05:27:40 KST

Zack Polanski, leader of Britain’s Green Party, is at the center of a public controversy after historical records contradicted his account of his ancestors fleeing the Nazis. The party has made headlines in recent days after passing a motion declaring Zionism to be racism and following revelations that one of its members is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist.
In his keynote speech at the party conference in Bournemouth last year, Polanski, 43, said his Jewish ancestors fled pogroms in Latvia and Ukraine, made their way to Nazi-occupied Poland and ultimately escaped to England, where they encountered antisemitism. However, a review of public birth, marriage and census records from 1891 and 1901 found that his family had settled in Britain in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Despite the records, Polanski repeated the story of his family fleeing the Nazis on several occasions, including on “The Rest Is Politics” podcast and the BBC’s “Question Time” in December. The Daily Mail reported that the mystery deepened last month when Polanski himself acknowledged, during a podcast interview with Iain Dale, that his great-grandparents had arrived in Britain “way before the Second World War.”
In the same interview, he said they changed their surname from Polanski to Paulden to escape antisemitism in Britain, not the Nazis. Polanski, who was born David Paulden in 1982, changed his name to Zack Polanski to reconnect with his Jewish heritage and distance himself from his stepfather.
The Green Party declined to explain the discrepancy to the Daily Mail. A party spokesperson said that “Jewish family history is often confusing and muddled, as Zack has acknowledged” adding that “it’s astonishing that the only current Jewish leader of a British political party is having his family history raked over by the press in an attempt to discredit him.”
The controversy comes as the Green Party opens its 2026 conference in Brighton and less than a week before Polanski is due to contest a parliamentary election in Holborn and St Pancras in north London, a seat held by Labour since 1983 and previously represented by Keir Starmer, who stepped down as prime minister.
This is not the first time Polanski, who serves as a member of the London Assembly and earns nearly £66,500 ($88,000) a year, has faced scrutiny over contradictory statements. Earlier this year, he apologized for an “unintentional mistake” after failing to pay council tax on a residential property because of “financial hardship.”
In May, he admitted that he had not voted in local elections because he was not registered to vote, despite publicly promising his party’s candidate that he would vote for him. His spokesperson had claimed he had done so by postal ballot. The party attributed the incidents to a “misunderstanding.”
Anti-Zionism and ties to terrorists
The Green Party on Sunday approved a controversial motion declaring Zionism a form of racism. The wording of the motion implies a call for the effective elimination of the State of Israel. In response, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar decided to bar Polanski from entering Israel.
The approved motion calls for the establishment of “a single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital.” It also calls for a sweeping boycott of Israel and broad sanctions similar to those imposed on South Africa’s apartheid regime, arguing that “Zionism has created, and seeks to maintain and, where possible, expand, a system of apartheid between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea.”
On Tuesday, Britain’s Telegraph reported that party member Lubna Speitan, who spearheaded the motion, is a close friend of an al-Qaeda terrorist who plotted a suicide attack at Heathrow Airport that was intended to kill hundreds of people, with a particular focus on passengers arriving from Israel or the United States.
According to the report, Speitan had previously offered to testify in defense of the terrorist, Minh Quang Pham, who was convicted in the United States of membership in al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, and of plotting the attack. Court documents from 2015 described her as a “close friend” of his.
Speitan has previously said Hamas should not be designated a terrorist organization. She has also called for Zionism to be “dismantled from the world” and said the time would come when Zionists would be “hunted down as the Nazi oppressors were hunted down.”
When initially asked about her relationship with the terrorist, Speitan called the question “insulting” and said it had “no relation to the work that I’m doing.” She accused the “mainstream media” of seeking to “demonise” Palestinians and suggested that Pham had been wrongfully accused.
Asked about his 44-year prison sentence, she said: “People are demonised for all sorts of things and wrongfully accused of all sorts of things.”

Life in Gaza, three years after October 7
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night
In the three years since the October 7 massacre, the state of Israel and the region as a whole have changed beyond recognition. The same applies to the Gaza Strip. According to the most recent available satellite imagery, roughly 80% of all buildings in Gaza have been damaged or destroyed during the war.
Israeli forces currently control 63% of Gaza's territory. In the remaining 37%, some two million Gazans live in the densely populated city centers and tent cities across the Strip. And life there is uncertain, with many fearing a resumption of the fighting as Hamas refuses to concede power and disarm.
The prevailing mood is one of frustration and despair. For three years, residents have waited for the war to end and for the technocratic committee meant to run Gaza to begin operating there. That moment still seems distant. "Three years have passed with people hoping that the war would end, but it hasn't, and we are still stuck," one woman in Gaza told i24NEWS. "As you know, people have been living in tents for three years, and this is extremely difficult."
Tension rose in the days leading up to the anniversary, as many families stockpiled food in case of an emergency. The fear that a major military operation could see the IDF take over what remains of the Strip has not gone away. "We don't feel stable, and honestly, we don't feel that there is any real hope for peace," she said.
Hamas operatives largely keep a low profile, but armed men still appear in the streets at night. Residents often cannot tell whether these men belong to Hamas or to one of the armed groups operating from behind the Yellow Line. "To be honest with you, we don't know who they are," she said.
Residents also say Hamas finances itself in part by imposing various taxes on residents and merchants, which some describe as extortion. "Here, we know very well that Hamas must hand over all its weapons," the Gazan said. "The people of Gaza want to get rid of Hamas and its rule, so that this situation we are living through and suffering from can finally come to an end."
Food and basic goods are available, the woman said. "There is no famine at all. Food and other goods are available, but not everyone has the means to buy them. The poor and those who don't have jobs depend on free aid and on groups that cook free food in the streets and distribute it to them."
Work in Gaza is scarce. Many of the available jobs in the various NGOs operating in the Strip are subject to Hamas's approval, as it decides who can get hired. If you're not affiliated with Hamas, chances are you won't find work.
Despite criticism in Western and Arab capitals, where Israeli plans to encourage emigration from Gaza have been branded "ethnic cleansing," the woman who spoke with i24NEWS said she hopes to leave at the first opportunity. "I intend not to return," she said.

This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual assault.
A congressional candidate in Arizona says she was attacked and raped in August while trying to repair one of her damaged campaign signs.
Bernadette Greene-Placentia, a trucker and small-business owner, shared her account with the Phoenix New Times, a local publication. The assault took place on 14 August, according to the campaign.
The Democratic candidate, running in a district that includes parts of Phoenix, told the newspaper that she was walking across a parking lot just after 2am to fix a campaign sign when an attacker smashed her over the head, causing her to black out.
Greene-Placentia told the newspaper that she awoke to find a man on top of her and discovered he was raping her. She recalled another man coming over and pushing her leg, at which point she said she swung her foot at him. The man said, “Not even worth it”, and the two attackers left, leaving her face down in the parking lot, she recalled.
The candidate said her memory of the incident and its aftermath was hazy, telling the newspaper she did not remember picking herself off the pavement or returning home.
“It’s just these little tiny flashes of things that I do remember,” Greene-Placentia told the Phoenix New Times. “As much as I don’t want to remember, I’ve tried very, very hard to remember more stuff. But that’s where I’m at.”
She said she may have had a concussion as a result of the attack and that her body was covered in bruises. She said she initially wanted to forget what had happened and felt “embarrassed”, at first choosing not to report the assault. But she told the paper that on the campaign trail, she often spoke about fighting for Arizonans, “and I didn’t feel like I could keep saying that if I weren’t also fighting for women that are victims of sexual assault”.
Greene-Placentia told her campaign staff and husband about the assault days after it happened and reported it to the Maricopa county sheriff’s office two weeks later, according to the Phoenix New Times. The newspaper interviewed Greene-Placentia’s relatives, friends, campaign staff and landlord about the aftermath of the assault.
“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokesperson told the Guardian on Wednesday after the Phoenix New Times story was published. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”
The spokesperson added: “She hopes the focus remains on supporting survivors and making sure people who have experienced sexual violence know they are seen, heard and supported.”
“I need to let women know that it’s OK to talk about it,” Greene-Placentia told the newspaper.
Stephanie Simacek, a state representative and friend of Greene-Placentia, said the congressional candidate told her of the assault in early September, telling the Phoenix New Times, “I felt sick to my stomach, and it was extremely disturbing. It was a big wake-up call for me. I think oftentimes, as candidates and electeds, we think that it’s not going to happen to us.”
A Maricopa county sheriff’s spokesperson declined to comment, saying the investigation was ongoing.
Greene-Placentia is running against an incumbent Republican member of Congress, Abraham Hamadeh.

precious while melting: jewelry that turns scarcity into spectacle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:19:44 UTC
05:19:44 KST

silver bead necklace comes with seven ice cubes that sweat, shrink and eventually vanish
developed by GOLEM's ariel andré and laila el mehelmy, the ooOoooOoooOh la l’ice necklace turns water into a piece of wearable art that measures time on the body.
GOLEM and LAILA EL MEHELMY TURN ICE INTO WEARABLE JEWELRY
There is jewelry designed to last generations, and then there is ooOoooOoooOh la l’ice, a necklace whose most conspicuous components are destined to disappear within the hour. Developed by artist and jeweler Laila El Mehelmy and architect Ariel André, founder of Paris-based studio GOLEM, the piece threads seven ice cubes onto a chain of solid-silver beads. A custom silicone tray allows the wearer to freeze the necklace on demand; removed from its mold, it becomes a slightly impractical but highly effective piece of wearable theater. Without the ice, the silver strand can still be worn as a conventional necklace or doubled into a choker.
Its origins are appropriately less conventional. The idea emerged during a 24-hour party at Club der Visionaere in Berlin, amid one of Germany’s intensely hot summers. As temperatures climbed, partygoers began taking ice from the freezers and rubbing cubes over one another to cool down. For El Mehelmy and André, the scene hovered somewhere between pleasure and apocalypse: bodies dancing, sweating and consuming frozen water simply to remain comfortable. The next day, that sweaty survival tactic became the starting point for a discussion about scarcity and value. As the designers put it, ‘water is turning from an overlooked commodity into one of the most sought after luxury goods.’
THE BODY TURNS THE ICE-CUBE NECKLACE INTO A CLOCK
That interaction with the wearer is particularly relevant to El Mehelmy’s practice. Originally trained as an industrial designer, the Saudi artist shifted her attention towards jewelry precisely because of its tactile relationship with the body, exploring how physical contact can transform the work itself. Here, that transformation could hardly be more literal. Skin warms the seven frozen blocks, water begins running across the chest, and the necklace slowly edits itself in public. The ice takes around 30 minutes to disappear against bare skin, or roughly an hour when worn over clothing.
Together with GOLEM, the jeweler developed the ooOoooOoooOh la l’ice necklace as a ‘time-piece’, although there is no dial and punctuality would probably be asking too much of it. Instead, time becomes visible through loss. Every drop records the warmth of the body, while the wearer inadvertently performs the object’s disappearance for everyone around them. ‘The choreography of a dancing body wearing it while the precious solid water stones melt away makes it an event,’ the designers explain. Once the ice is gone, larger beads along the silver chain indicate the empty positions where the frozen ‘stones’ previously sat — traces of something absent until the necklace is returned to its mold and frozen again.
WATER SCARCITY REWRITES THE LANGUAGE OF LUXURY
The necklace also borrows the visual codes of conventional luxury only to make them behave badly. Its ice cubes become what El Mehelmy and André call ‘solid water gems’, replacing permanent stones with one of the world’s most ordinary — and increasingly contested — resources. The project deliberately sets water against the culturally constructed desirability of diamonds, asking what preciousness might mean when abundance can no longer be taken for granted. In their reading, permanence is almost the problem: rather than promising forever, these gems sweat, shrink and vanish. The value of the object lies not in resisting change but in forcing its wearer to watch it happen.
That makes the necklace less a static accessory than a small spectacle with an audience, even when that audience consists only of whoever happens to be standing nearby at the party. The wearer activates it, heat completes it, and disappearance becomes part of its design language. The process also folds the human body into the natural water cycle: solid becomes liquid, runs over skin and eventually evaporates, ready — at least conceptually — to begin again. El Mehelmy and André describe the piece as a materialization of the evanescence of water, adding that ‘its beauty results from its temporality.’ Perhaps that is its neatest inversion of luxury: the necklace becomes most itself at precisely the moment it starts ceasing to exist.

 name: ooOoooOoooOh la l’ice
designer:  Ariel André/ GOLEM | @golem.digital, and Laila El Mehelmy
photography: Guillaume Blondiau | @billy_blond

Democratic FCC member warns of AI robocall misinformation risks in US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:14:35 UTC
05:14:35 KST

Democratic FCC member warns of AI robocall misinformation risks in US
FCC commissioner warns against AI robocalls, citing risks of misinformation before crucial midterm elections.
Anna Gomez, the Democratic member of the United States Federal Communications Commission, has urged the federal agency not to allow robocalls generated with artificial intelligence in the lead-up to the midterm elections in early November.
On Wednesday, the commissioner pushed back against a petition from Club for Growth, a national conservative fiscal policy organisation, to allow AI-generated robocalls.
The petition, filed on August 31, requested that the federal agency allow political groups to make automated phone calls to people without their prior permission. The group said it would limit calls so that the same person would not receive more than three calls over the course of 30 days and would be presented with the option to opt out.
The FCC’s public comment period began on September 4, with the deadline for comments on Monday. Responses to those comments are due October 19, and the FCC has yet to decide whether it will approve the request.
Robocalls have been used in political campaigns for years. The FCC prohibits such calls to cellphones and pagers without the called party’s prior express consent, but they are permitted to landlines.
The concern with the use of AI is that it can sound like a real person and make it easier to impersonate someone. On the back of a rising number of scams using the technology, the FCC, in February 2024, banned it, saying, “this action now makes the act of using AI to generate the voice in these robocalls itself illegal.”
“[If] the FCC allows a dark money group to flood Americans’ phones with AI-generated robocalls they never agreed to receive, it would bring chaos so close to Election Day,” commissioner Gomez told the Reuters news agency on Wednesday.
She told The Associated Press that removing the FCC’s consent requirement could lead to a rise in unwanted robocalls and misinformation.
Representatives for Gomez did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment.
The concerns are not unfounded. In advance of the 2024 New Hampshire primary, voters received a robocall featuring an AI-generated version in the voice of President Joe Biden, the Democrat incumbent, telling them not to vote.
The FCC said that political consultant Steve Kramer, who was working for long-shot primary challenger Dean Phillips, was responsible and could face $6m in fines. He was later acquitted of voter suppression charges.
At the state level, Louisiana, Tennessee and Vermont passed laws this year requiring disclosures for AI-generated campaign phone calls. More broadly, 25 states have passed laws concerning the use of AI-generated materials in elections since 2019.
AI election concerns mount
Concerns about AI robocalls underscore broader concerns about AI in the run-up to the midterm elections.
According to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll, 57 percent of registered voters said that the administration of US President Donald Trump has not taken the risks of AI seriously enough, with 54 percent saying the same about congressional leadership.
Late last month, the White House convened leaders from leading AI companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google, to sign a voluntary pact in which the companies agreed to put more safeguards in place around the development of their most advanced AI systems. Its non-compulsory nature has not appeased critics.
“The White House Accord on Super Intelligence is ‘morally binding’ only, allowing AI companies to design their own controls, select their own evaluators, and determine whether their own procedures are being followed,” Tom Wheeler, visiting fellow in governance studies with Center for Technology Innovation (CTI) at the think tank Brookings Institution, wrote about the decision.
“History suggests voluntary commitments from these companies are unreliable, as Facebook, Google, and Twitter have all walked back or violated previous self-imposed standards.”
