Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:13:45 UTC
05:13:45 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Builds Airless Wheels to Keep Ground Robots Moving After Battlefield Damage
Ukrainian companies Print&Live UA and iSCALE 3D have developed lightweight airless wheels for unmanned ground vehicles operating on the front line.
Militarnyi reported the development on October 7, citing the companies behind the project. According to the outlet, the wheels are designed specifically for ground robotic systems, where conventional pneumatic tires remain vulnerable to punctures and battlefield debris.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new design eliminates the need for compressed air, allowing a wheel to remain functional after damage that could disable a conventional tire, Militarnyi added. The developers also focused on reducing the wheel's weight, an important factor for smaller robotic platforms with limited payload and battery capacity.
According to Militarnyi, the project combines Print&Live UA’s experience in additive manufacturing with iSCALE 3D’s work on large-format 3D printing. The technology allows components with complex internal structures to be manufactured without using traditional tire-production tooling.
Airless wheels use a flexible structural body rather than air pressure to support the vehicle’s weight and absorb impacts. For military ground robots, this can reduce the risk of losing mobility after running over fragments, nails, or other sharp objects common on the battlefield.
Militarnyi noted that such components are particularly relevant for unmanned ground vehicles used for logistics, evacuation, and other missions in areas where recovering a disabled platform can expose personnel to additional risk.
Wheel resilience matters because Ukrainian ground robots are taking on an increasing share of frontline work.
On September 30, Ukrainian defense company Frontline Robotics unveiled Frodo, a six-wheeled unmanned ground vehicle with a range of up to 150 kilometers and a chassis designed to stay mobile even after losing a wheel.

As the Fiji Airways flight carrying dignitaries to Tuvalu sat on the airport runway at the heart of its tiny capital, Funafuti, an official struggled with a broken umbrella in the driving rain.
A pile of sodden brollies lay next to him as locals prepared to ferry leaders, ministers and assorted bigwigs out of the plane, across the tarmac, through the downpour, and into a traditional welcome ceremony.
The rather forlorn image seemed to fit neatly with the headlines back home in Australia, which had already declared the pre-COP summit a farce and a failure, particularly as the government had only managed to coax two non-Pacific leaders to fly to Tuvalu to see the climate emergency up close.
On the face of it, this might seem a little unfair.
By all accounts, the vibe on the ground was not nearly so grim.

Housing institute hits back at One Nation's rental and migration claims
The Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute (AHURI) has distanced itself from One Nation, after its research was used for the party's latest policy on migration and rents.

This would reduce rent inflation by 6.5 per cent and save $2,818 a year on average for a renter by the third year of the party's immigration cuts, according to One Nation.
The party said the internal modelling relied on rental figures from the AHURI, to assume a substantial reduction in demand for rented properties as a result of the migration cuts.
The AHURI said in a statement to the ABC that it was not consulted, the research attributed to it was actually ABS 2021 data, and to be cautious about the modelling claims.
"AHURI was not consulted on, or involved in, the modelling One Nation has undertaken, so we are unable to comment on its reliability or validity," its managing director Tom Alves said.
"We would encourage caution when interpreting this ABS data. For example, it should not be assumed that each temporary migrant occupies an entire property, as several people may share a single home.
"Some temporary migrants may also live in accommodation owned or provided by their employer or education provider, which may not be available or practical for the general rental market."

Mamdani marks Oct. 7 by accusing Israel of genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:11:51 UTC
05:11:51 KST

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani marked the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack Wednesday by mourning the Israelis killed and abducted before accusing Israel of committing “genocide” and “apartheid” in Gaza, drawing sharp criticism from Israeli diplomats as commemorations were held across New York.
“This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers,” Mamdani wrote in a statement. “It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7.”
Mamdani said Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 people in the attack. “We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss,” he wrote.
But the mayor immediately turned to the war in Gaza, saying “the suffering did not begin nor end that day” and accusing the Israeli government of carrying out a “devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza.”
Mamdani said more than 74,000 Palestinians, including more than 21,000 children, had been killed and claimed more than 1,400 Palestinians had been killed since what he called the “so-called ceasefire.” He also accused Israel of bombing ambulances outside hospitals, targeting residential buildings and journalists with drone strikes and turning away food aid at border crossings.
The figures and allegations were presented by Mamdani in his statement. Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza and has said its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties.
“Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them — all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes,” Mamdani wrote.
He also accused the U.S. government of complicity through arms shipments to Israel.
“Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment,” he said. “To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.”
Mamdani issued a similarly structured statement on the anniversary last year. He began then by describing the Hamas attack as a “horrific war crime,” cited the Israeli death toll and said he was praying for the return of the hostages before turning to Gaza and accusing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his government of waging what he called a genocidal war. He also accused the U.S. government of complicity and called for an end to what he described as “occupation and apartheid.”
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul issued a separate statement Wednesday focused on the victims of the Hamas attack and the Jewish community.
“It’s hard to fathom that it has been three years since the October 7 Hamas massacre,” Hochul wrote. “Three years since the deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust.”
“The pain of that dark day has not faded. But neither has the strength, resilience and enduring hope of the Jewish people,” she added. “Today, we remember the innocent lives stolen, stand with the survivors and the families forever changed, and pray for a lasting peace.”
Mamdani’s statement drew condemnation from senior Israeli representatives in the United States.
Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations, Danny Danon, accused the mayor of attempting to appropriate the anniversary to attack Israel.
“‘Mamdani-ism’ — an attempt to hijack the anniversary of October 7 and turn it into yet another propaganda attack against Israel,” Danon said. “It is like turning September 11 into a day of mourning for al-Qaeda terrorists.”
“We will remember those who were murdered, and we will never forget who was behind this massacre,” he added.
Ofir Akunis, Israel’s consul general in New York, also sharply criticized Mamdani, saying the mayor “should be ashamed of himself.”
“It’s a shame that on October 7, the day that the Hamas monsters brutally murdered, raped and burned our people alive, Mamdani responded in this way,” Akunis said.
Akunis invited Mamdani to attend a screening later Wednesday of footage documenting atrocities committed during the Hamas attack, saying it was “not too late to come and watch the horror film and see the truth.”
Mamdani was scheduled to attend an anniversary gathering at Union Square later Wednesday organized by Israelis for Peace. Organizers described the event as an evening of “quiet reflection and mourning” for those killed in 2023 and for the “bloody aftermath” of the attack.
After the memorial, Mamdani was scheduled to meet with Palestinian residents of New York, as the mayor sought to engage communities deeply divided over the war.
It was to be Mamdani’s second year attending the Union Square commemoration. He attended the previous year while running for mayor alongside Brad Lander, then New York City comptroller.
In his first statement after the 2023 attack, Mamdani did not explicitly condemn Hamas and focused largely on Israel’s response. He later condemned the killing of civilians and subsequently denounced Hamas directly, calling the Oct. 7 assault a “horrific war crime.”
Pro-Palestinian groups, meanwhile, were organizing campus strikes and a protest outside City Hall on Wednesday, accusing Mamdani of “betraying his values” and bowing to what they described as Zionist pressure.
Memorial events across New York
A series of other events were held across New York to mark three years since the attack.
The Marlene Meyerson JCC Manhattan organized what it called a “day of remembrance, music and community,” including an exhibition of drawings by Israeli artist Zeev Engelmayer.
UJA-Federation of New York unveiled “Rooted” at the Museum of Jewish Heritage, a public installation made from thousands of dog tags and pins bearing messages calling for the return of the hostages.
At 92NY on Manhattan’s Upper East Side, Jonathan Dekel-Chen, father of former hostage Sagui Dekel-Chen, was taking part in a discussion with Palestinian father Jasser Abu Musa. The conversation was moderated by Claire Shipman, who previously served as acting president of Columbia University.
Former hostage Omer Shem Tov was scheduled to speak Wednesday evening at Yeshiva University’s memorial ceremony, while the Park Slope Jewish Center in Brooklyn was hosting testimony from Atir Vinikov, a survivor of the massacre at the Nova music festival.
Protest targets Jewish organization in London
The anniversary was also marked by tensions outside the United States.
Earlier Wednesday, masked protesters demonstrated outside the London headquarters of the Board of Deputies of British Jews, hours before the organization was due to host a major memorial event.
The protesters, some draped in Iranian, Palestinian and Irish flags, gathered outside the Board of Deputies’ offices in Camden for about 20 minutes.
They chanted “stop killing babies” and carried signs accusing the organization of genocide denial. Other signs described the umbrella organization representing British Jews as “Israel’s mouthpiece” and a “shield for Israel’s crimes” and accused it of weaponizing antisemitism.

US gasoline stocks fall in most regions despite national increase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:11:06 UTC
05:11:06 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Gasoline inventories fell in four of the US’ five petroleum reporting regions last week, according to Energy Information Administration (EIA) data released Wednesday, underscoring an uneven supply picture as G7 economies move to release emergency reserves to ease energy market pressures.
Midwest stocks decreased by 421,000 barrels to 41.41 million for the week ending Oct. 2, leaving inventories 12.7% below their year-earlier level.
The Gulf Coast recorded the largest weekly decline, with stocks falling 1.83 million barrels to 75.04 million barrels. Inventories also decreased on the West Coast and in the Rocky Mountain region.
An East Coast increase of 2.8 million barrels offset the declines, lifting nationwide gasoline inventories by 382,000 barrels to 204.74 million.
Despite the weekly increase, US stocks remained 6.5% below a year earlier. All five regions held less gasoline than during the comparable week of 2025, with the Midwest recording the steepest annual decline.
G7 leaders agreed Oct. 2 to implement a coordinated release of 100 million barrels through the International Energy Agency over four months, including a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days.
The statement linked the release to implementing commitments made in March, taking account of volumes already released.
Leaders also pledged to coordinate refinery maintenance to prevent simultaneous shutdowns and temporarily increase utilization rates where feasible, while encouraging greater global production of refined products, particularly diesel.
The group reaffirmed its commitment to avoid restrictions on energy exports between G7 countries and urged producers to refrain from bans that could worsen market tensions.

Former Tottenham Hotspur and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega announced Wednesday his intention to challenge FIFA President Gianni Infantino, who is seeking reelection next year.
"I am standing to reunite the global football family, deliver genuine and lasting reform, modernise FIFA for the 21st Century, restore stability and credibility, and rebuild the trust that our game urgently needs," Vega said in a statement.
"Football does not belong to presidents, confederations or administrators. Football is greater than any position, any individual or any institution," said the 55-year-old.
"It is the people's game and belongs to everyone: the players, coaches, referees, supporters, volunteers, clubs, leagues, associations and communities that give football its life."
Vega accused FIFA's leadership of damaging trust in the governing body and demanded changes to its governance.
"The current leadership has demoralised the game. Weak governance has damaged FIFA's credibility and eroded trust across the global football family," he said. "Football is in the emergency room, on life support. We cannot wait any longer. FIFA needs a new direction and fundamental reform."
Infantino has faced demands to step down following the collapse of a controversial plan involving the sale of a stake in commercial and ticketing rights to FIFA competitions to private investors.
Vega considered running for the FIFA presidency in 2015, telling the BBC at the time that he was weighing a candidacy.
Four years later, he announced plans to challenge Infantino but failed to secure the backing of five FIFA member associations required to appear on the ballot.
Candidates seeking to challenge Infantino in the 2027 election have until Nov. 18 to declare their intention to stand.
Vega earned 23 caps for Switzerland and played for clubs including Tottenham, Celtic and Watford before retiring in 2004. He later pursued a career in finance.

US President Donald Trump has said that he welcomes an agreement by Türkiye and Pakistan to provide military support to Saudi Arabia as part of a new collective defence arrangement involving the three countries.
Speaking to reporters at the White House on Wednesday before departing for Texas, Trump was asked about the decision by Türkiye and Pakistan to send military forces to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Defence Alliance.
"I think they want to help Saudi Arabia, and I think that’s great," he replied.
‘Defence and dialogue together’
Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan moved to strengthen their joint defence framework on Monday as senior political and military officials met in Riyadh for an emergency session.
Türkiye’s foreign minister Hakan Fidan said the three countries discussed steps to support Saudi Arabia's defence while also examining ways to resolve regional issues peacefully through dialogue.
The alliance was established in August by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, with the three countries subsequently agreeing to build permanent institutions and strengthen collective deterrence and defence capabilities.
According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the three countries agreed that military forces and capabilities could be rapidly deployed in Saudi Arabia under the alliance's framework.
The sides also condemned attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Madinah and reaffirmed their commitment to confronting attacks against Saudi Arabia and Islamic holy sites.
Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said the alliance remains committed to confronting attacks and protecting the kingdom, while collective deterrence measures would be used against threats and those responsible.
The Turkish government will submit a defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan to parliament within days, a spokesperson for the governing Justice and Development (Ak) Party said, setting the stage for a ratification process that could pave the way for a possible deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks
The Houthis have claimed responsibility for several recent attacks in the kingdom, including strikes targeting Saudi Aramco facilities, airports and military sites.
Saudi Arabia has also reported Houthi attempts to target the holy cities of Mecca and Medina over the past nine years, including two incidents in September, drawing condemnation from Arab and Muslim countries.
Confrontations between Yemen's internationally recognised government forces and the Houthis have escalated since early July following years of relative calm.
The country has been engulfed in war since the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, before a Saudi-led Arab coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognised government.
The Houthis have been engaged in renewed fighting with government forces since Yemen's civil war reignited in July, when the group declared a maritime blockade on Riyadh and began targeting its ships in the Red Sea.

US midterms: Is Trump campaigning at taxpayers' expense?
October 7, 2026
It's neither a joke nor fake news but a real report from earlier this week: Donald Trump has backed down. On Monday, the US president announced that a series of advertisements aired in September promoting him and his administration would no longer be funded with taxpayer money.
"The radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our great USA, and paying for them with USA money," Trump wrote on his platform Truth Social.
He went on to claim that funding partisan ads with public money was a "rather standard thing to do," before adding that future ads would be paid with money raised from donations.
The ads themselves have caused some controversy in the United States. They ran in September between popular shows such as Saturday Night Live and football games, marked with the line: "paid for by the US government" — that is, paid with tax dollars.
The commercials showed scenes such as when US troops captured Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro earlier this year but they mostly consisted of images and videos of Trump himself, along with combative messages that he would "expel the warmongers" or "throw off the sick political class," and ensure that the US did not become a communist state.
Public funds for personal praise
Political opponents and a series of NGOs responded to the campaign with sharp criticism. Not only does US law prohibit the use of taypayer funds for political advertisements, but the ads also appeared shortly before the midterms — elections held near the midpoint of a president's four-year term.
On Tuesday, the US broadcasting network CBS reported that, according to contracting records, the US Department of Homeland Security had paid an agency $20 million (€17.9 million) for a "national media campaign."
The "rather standard" practice that Trump referred to actually applies to public service announcements, but this is not what the campaign ads are, argued the US non-profit consumer advocacy group Public Citizen.
"Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising," the organization wrote in a public complaint to the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) ."Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump's recent campaign ads."
Independent experts have also voiced concerns. Patrick Malone, a professor in the department of Public Administration and Policy at American University in Washington DC, said the timing of the videos was problematic.
"You're not supposed to use taxpayer dollars to pay for anything that's campaign-related," he told DW. "Technically, [Trump] is not campaigning. He's not saying 'Vote for me!' The thing that's created the challenge here is the timing. Weeks before the midterms, this is a real big issue."
Will the Republicans keep their majority after midterms?
Voters do not choose presidents in the midterm elections but members of Congres, which comprises the Senate and the House of Representatives and is the legislative branch of the federal government. On November 3, those eligible to vote will cast their ballots for all the seats in the House of Representatives, and roughly a third of the seats in the Senate. Some states will also be choosing governors.
Republicans have not been faring well in recent polls, which may be why Trump has been trying to promote his party's achievements. The Republicans currently hold a majority in both houses, with 53 of 100 seats in the Senate, and 219 of 435 seats in the House of Representatives. This has enabled Trump to pass a large number of his proposals fairly easily.
But a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday indicates that this could soon change. "Voters age 50 or older preferred Trump's party over the Democratic Party by just 2 percentage points — 44% to 42% — compared to an 8-point Republican advantage in December," it found. This age bracket "is particularly important for midterm elections, when older Americans historically have made up large shares of the electorate."
Meanwhile, among voters under the age of 50, "Democrats led by 18 points," the survey showed.
The poll also found that opinions on Trump himself were low, with "32% of Americans giving a thumbs up to Trump's presidency." This level of approval, the study highlighted, was unchanged from an earlier poll "that saw the leader's rating at the lowest of his political career."
Republicans shy away from Trump's support
This could also be one of the reasons why Republican candidates do not seem so keen on making public appearances with the president, usually a highlight of a campaign trail.
Many US citizens associate Trump with high living costs, or the war with Iran, which has dragged on for over half a year now.
One Republican operative told the news website Politico on condition of anonymity that if the the president were to visit a battleground state — where Democratic and Republican support is fairly equal among voters — to campaign for his party, they suspected their "candidates would come down with COVID" to avoid having to attend.
In September, a number of Republicans skipped Trump's big party convention — typically reserved for presidential, not midterm elections — even though the event could have offered them a platform for their campaign.
Susan Collins from Maine and Dan Sullivan from Alaska, are just two examples of Republican senators whose seats are on the line and who did not attend. Neither did candidates for the House of Representatives from the swing states Arizona, Iowa and Michigan.
Trump promises $5,000 payout if Republicans win
Those who skipped the event missed the president repeating an unusual campaign message: To encourage more people to vote, Trump urged supporters to "pretend" he was on the ballot.
And if that wasn't enough, he also promised each US citizen eligible to vote a $5,000 payout if Republicans maintained their majority in both houses of Congress.
Keeping that pledge could cost the federal government over $1.2 trillion, but observers doubt it would ever come to that.
"He has no money to do that with. It would have to be authorized and appropriated by Congress," Mallone explained. "I think the likelihood is very slim," he added. "It's one of those things like 'Mexico is going to pay for the wall.'"
Whether Trump's commercials or promised payouts will be enough to rally majority Republican support remains to be seen.

A US real estate firm announced on Wednesday it is buying the Chrysler Building and will undertake a vast makeover of the art deco landmark that dominates New York’s skyline.
The Chrysler Building, which was opened in 1930 as a symbol of exuberance and modernity, had faced several years of uncertainty over its ownership.
Tishman Speyer, a commercial landlord, said it and other investors will inject US$235 million into the property to refurbish its ageing interior and exterior.

Drinking problems remained a risk factor for reoffending even among men with stronger social skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:00:25 UTC
05:00:25 KST

Alcohol-related problems and difficulties with social and cognitive skills were each associated with reoffending among men who had perpetrated intimate partner violence, but the two did not appear to combine in a way that further increased risk, according to a study published in Applied Cognitive Psychology. Some skills that would normally be expected to protect against reoffending were unexpectedly linked to higher odds of a new violent offense.
Problematic alcohol use is common among men who perpetrate intimate partner violence, and alcohol can impair judgment, weaken behavioral control and make people more prone to impulsive reactions. However, alcohol is not the sole cause of violence. Other factors, including hostility, impulsivity, poor problem-solving, difficulty understanding another person’s perspective and trouble controlling behavior, are also linked to violence against partners and to reoffending.
Researchers have suggested that alcohol might be especially dangerous for people who already have these difficulties. For example, alcohol could make it harder for someone with poor impulse control to pause before acting or could intensify hostile interpretations of a partner’s behavior, while stronger skills might help buffer against alcohol’s effects. Few studies had tested whether these factors actually interact to predict reoffending, and most had looked at only a handful of skills.
The study was led by Crystal J. Giesbrecht and Kaila C. Bruer of the University of Regina in Canada. The team analyzed existing assessment and follow-up data from 7,781 men in Alberta who had perpetrated intimate partner violence and had started community supervision between 2009 and 2012. The men ranged in age from 18 to 84, with an average age of about 35, and about 27% were Indigenous.
The data came from the Service Planning Instrument, a risk assessment that correctional staff complete when a person begins serving a sentence under supervision in the community. Staff score it using interviews, criminal records, previous assessments and information from people such as family members, partners and employers. The researchers then examined whether the men had any recidivism within three years, which included new charges as well as violations such as breaching release conditions or failing to appear in court, and whether they had a new violent offense, such as assault or uttering threats.
Alcohol use was measured in three ways: how often the men drank, whether drinking had disrupted their work, family life, friendships or health, and whether alcohol use contributed to their criminal behavior. Staff also rated eight social and cognitive skills: impulsivity, hostile attributions (the tendency to read neutral actions as hostile), consequential thinking (thinking ahead about the results of one’s actions), perspective-taking, problem-solving, behavioral control, interpersonal skills, and goal-setting and planning. The researchers classified each skill as either a risk area or not.
Alcohol use was widespread: 93% of the men used alcohol, and about a third drank at least three days a week. For about half the men, alcohol contributed to their criminal behavior, and for 27% it had disrupted their functioning. Within three years, 38% of the men had some form of recidivism and 20% had a new violent offense.
After accounting for the other factors in the analysis, men whose drinking had disrupted their functioning had about 27% higher odds of any recidivism and 28% higher odds of violent recidivism. Alcohol-related criminal behavior was linked to similar increases for both outcomes. Frequent drinking was associated with higher odds of any recidivism compared with not drinking, but not with violent recidivism.
Among the skill measures, men rated as having problems with impulsivity were more likely to have both types of recidivism, and those with weaker goal-setting and planning were more likely to have any recidivism. Hostile attributions were linked to higher odds of violent reoffending. Problem-solving, behavioral control and interpersonal skills were not reliably linked to either outcome once the other factors were taken into account.
Two results ran in the opposite direction from what the researchers expected. Men rated as having no problems with perspective-taking had higher odds of any and violent recidivism, and those with no problems in consequential thinking had higher odds of violent recidivism. The authors suggested that such skills, without adequate self-control or prosocial goals, might help some people manipulate others or navigate the justice system in self-serving ways, though the pattern could also reflect factors the data did not capture.
Alcohol problems and skill deficits tended to go together: men whose drinking disrupted their lives or contributed to their offending were more likely to be rated as having deficits in every skill area. But the researchers found little evidence that the two interacted to predict reoffending. In other words, alcohol problems and skill deficits each mattered, but having both did not produce an extra increase in risk beyond what each contributed on its own. The models explained only about 3% of the variation in any recidivism and about 2% for violent recidivism, which the authors note is typical of research predicting a behavior as complex as reoffending.
“This indicates that problematic alcohol use may represent a stand-alone criminogenic need that remains salient even among individuals with relatively strong cognitive or social skills,” the authors wrote. Criminogenic needs are risk factors for reoffending that can change over time, which makes them targets for treatment.
The researchers recommend screening for both alcohol problems and social and cognitive skills when people enter supervision, and building alcohol treatment into intimate partner violence programs. Such programs often exclude people who are actively using substances, and access to them in Canada is limited and inconsistent.
There are a few things to keep in mind. Because the dataset contained no victim information, the researchers could not tell whether new offenses were committed against an intimate partner, so the findings concern general and violent reoffending rather than repeat partner violence specifically. Canada’s Criminal Code also has no specific offense for intimate partner violence, which makes such cases hard to identify in official records.
The study relied on existing assessment data, so the researchers could not add measures or check for errors, and recidivism was based on official records, which miss offenses that never come to the attention of authorities. Because the data are observational, the findings show associations rather than evidence that alcohol or skill deficits cause reoffending. The authors also suggest that future research account for differences among men who perpetrate partner violence, since alcohol may be more closely tied to violence for some types of perpetrators than for others.
The study, “The Connection Between Alcohol Use and Social and Cognitive Skills for Men Who Have Perpetrated Intimate Partner Violence,” was authored by Crystal J. Giesbrecht and Kaila C. Bruer.

Brazil's Bolsonaro pledges broad review of Lula-era taxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:59:25 UTC
04:59:25 KST

Brazil's Bolsonaro pledges broad review of Lula-era taxes
BRASILIA, Oct 7 - Brazil presidential candidate Senator Flavio Bolsonaro said on Wednesday his team was studying constitutional amendments to revise parts of a planned consumption-tax reform — alongside other fiscal measures — arguing the current design would leave the country with an excessively high tax burden.
"There are several constitutional amendments that are possible," Bolsonaro told reporters, citing "aspects of the tax reform" among measures he would pursue if elected, alongside lowering the age of criminal responsibility, ending presidential reelection and implementing a political reform.
In 2023, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva approved the consumption-tax reform, a long-awaited overhaul of Brazil's tax system, set to begin taking effect next year, which will consolidate multiple levies into a dual value-added tax administered at the federal and regional levels.
"I support modernizing our tax system, which is genuinely too complex," Bolsonaro said.
The reformed consumption tax's effective VAT rate — estimated to be about 28% by economists but not yet finalized by the government - would be too high, Bolsonaro said.
Bolsonaro also said he wanted to reduce payroll taxes and ensure that "more of Brazilian workers' income stays with them rather than the government."
On Tuesday, the senator's top economic adviser, Daniella Marques, told local media that a Bolsonaro administration would review a broad range of tax measures enacted under Lula, including a dividend tax that took effect in January.
Marques served in the elder Bolsonaro's government. She said that administration had previously only proposed taxing dividends alongside a reduction in corporate income taxes.
Bolsonaro would also eliminate the 12% tax on crude oil exports introduced this year by Lula's government, Marques said, describing the levy as an "aberration."
Lula introduced the tax to help finance fuel-tax relief for Brazilians amid a global oil-price spike linked to the US-Israeli conflict on Iran.
Other tax measures on the chopping block include reversing increases to the Financial Transactions Tax (IOF) on corporate credit operations, foreign-exchange transactions, and certain private pension investments, Marques said.
By contrast, Lula's platform pledged to deepen efforts to promote "tax justice" and reduce inequality through the elimination of tax distortions and privileges, while implementing the consumption-tax overhaul approved during his administration.
Lula this year introduced a tax on dividends to help finance an tax exemption on higher income for middle-income earners, while his administration has argued for further cuts to tax exemptions and the elimination of what it views as inefficient tax incentives.
Bolsonaro, the eldest son of ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, outperformed expectations to finish ahead of leftist incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in Sunday's first round. The rivals go head-to-head in an October 25 runoff.
DEBT RESTRUCTURING
Amid near-record levels of household debt in Brazil, Senator Bolsonaro also said his government would buy debt from over-indebted consumers and refinance it through state-owned lender Caixa Economica Federal.
Borrowers would also gain access to new credit lines to help finance small businesses, he said.
Lula, like Bolsonaro, has also pledged to purchase debt as part of a campaign promise.
The government said it will hold an auction in November to buy and restructure household debt, spending 15 billion reais to acquire up to 150 billion reais of delinquent loans at discounts of at least 90%. The program is expected to cover about half of the debt stock deemed eligible.
Households would then be able to clear overdue obligations at the discounted value, with the full benefit of the write-down passed through to borrowers. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Most Americans Want to Stop Changing the Clocks. Here’s Why Senators Are Hesitating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:59:00 UTC
04:59:00 KST

In less than a month, most of the U.S. will fall back an hour, continuing the cycle of biannual clock changes. Some lawmakers are trying to end that practice—but are facing pushback from others.
In July, the House passed a bill with bipartisan support that would instate Daylight Saving Time year-round across the U.S.—the latest step forward in a yearslong effort to eliminate the clock change. President Donald Trump has repeatedly urged Congress to pass the bill. But the legislation now faces an uncertain future in the upper chamber. Earlier this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told POLITICO that there is no “consensus” among his colleagues on whether to advance the measure.
“The President feels strongly on it like he does a lot of issues,” Thune said. “It’s something we’re having conversations about, but there’s no clear path forward or consensus on it yet.”
Here’s what the bill would do, why some senators are backing it, and why others aren’t.
What would the Sunshine Protection Act do?
Most of the country follows the practice of changing the clocks twice a year, jumping forward an hour every March when Daylight Saving Time begins and falling back every November when it ends to observe Standard Time.
The system is widely unpopular. Polling conducted by the Associated Press/NORC last year shows that more Americans oppose the current biannual clock change than those who support it—47% compared to just 12%.
Americans are a bit more divided on whether they would rather observe Daylight Saving Time or Standard Time year-round, though the former tends to garner more support. Fifty-six percent support permanent Daylight Saving Time, compared to 42% for Standard Time, according to last year's AP/NORC poll.
Currently, federal law allows states to forgo Daylight Saving Time and stay in Standard Time throughout the year; Hawaii and most of Arizona have chosen to do so. States aren’t allowed, though, to observe Daylight Saving Time permanently.
The legislation that passed the lower chamber over the summer, called the Sunshine Protection Act, would change that.
If the bill succeeds in the Senate and is signed into law by the President, it would make Daylight Saving Time permanent nationwide—though it would allow states to opt out if they choose.
Why are some senators supporting permanent Daylight Saving Time?
Senators who have expressed support for making Daylight Saving Time year-round in the past have argued that most Americans dislike the biannual clock changes, calling the practice “antiquated.”
They have also pointed out that remaining in Daylight Saving Time permanently would mean that the sun would appear to set later throughout the year, rather than just in the summer, which, they claim, would encourage people to engage in more outdoor activity.
Florida Republican Sen. Rick Scott is one of the most vocal backers of the Sunshine Protection Act. In a statement last year, when he introduced a version of the bill in the upper chamber, Scott said that he hears from constituents that “they are sick and tired of changing their clocks twice a year—it’s an unnecessary, decades-old practice that’s more of an annoyance to families than benefit to them.” He added that he believes this is a “common-sense change that will simplify and benefit the lives of American families.”
“For many Americans, an extra hour of daylight means more time to play outside with their kids, walk their dog, or spend time with neighbors,” he said in a post on X on Wednesday. “Americans work hard, and they deserve more free time to enjoy all the outdoors has to offer. It’s time to pass my Sunshine Protection Act [so] they can enjoy every ounce of sunshine.”
In July, Sen. Patty Murray, a Democrat from Washington, applauded the House for passing the bill, saying that the lower chamber “delivered on something Americans all across the country actually want: to never have to change their clocks again.”
“It’s not lost on me that Republicans still refuse to do literally anything to make life more affordable for families or to hold the Trump administration accountable for its daily abuse of power, but if Congress can enact permanent Daylight Saving Time, I will take this opportunity to make it happen,” she said in a statement.
She went on to say that, in her home state, it often gets dark around 4 p.m. in the winter months. Her constituents, she said, have “made it abundantly clear” that they want to observe Daylight Saving Time year-round.
When Scott introduced a version of the bill last year, other senators from both parties also expressed their support for the measure.
“The head-spinning ritual of falling back and springing forward has a very real impact on our economy, our health, and our happiness,” Sen. Ed Markey, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said in a statement at the time. “Let’s say goodbye to 4pm winter sunsets and pass the Sunshine Protection Act for permanent Daylight Saving Time—permanently springing forward for brighter evenings year-round.”
Why are some senators against permanent Daylight Saving Time?
While it’s true that permanent Daylight Saving Time would mean later sunsets year-round, what that would look like for Americans depends on where in the country they live.
Some places already experience sunrises and sunsets an hour or so after other places in the same time zone do, which means that some parts of the U.S. wouldn’t see daylight until much later in the morning than others. In Indianapolis, for instance, residents would only see the sunrise after 9 a.m. local time on Jan. 15, 2027, if Daylight Saving Time were made permanent, AccuWeather predicted, while other parts of the country would see the sunrise around 8 a.m. their time.
Because of that discrepancy, some senators have objected to legislation that would establish year-round Daylight Saving Time. The most vocal opponent of the Sunshine Protection Act in the upper chamber has been Sen. Tom Cotton, a Republican from Arkansas, who has previously said that observing permanent Daylight Saving Time would “again make winter a dark and dismal time for millions of Americans.”
Cotton has also pointed out that the U.S. has unsuccessfully tried this move before. In 1974, the U.S. began observing Daylight Saving Time year-round, but it was unpopular among Americans and Congress repealed the legislation that had instituted the change just months after it took effect.
“No one likes changing the clock, me included,” Cotton acknowledged in a social media post on Saturday. But he argued that permanent Daylight Saving Time would result in “absurdly late sunrises in the winter.”
“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he continued.
Read More: Daylight Saving Time Is Bad For Your Health. This Canadian Province Just Made It Permanent
Sen. Roger Wicker, a Republican from Mississippi, told reporters on Monday that he was aware that some people have “safety concerns in the more northern and rural states where children get on the school bus in very early hours.”
Sleep experts have opposed the idea of year-round Daylight Saving Time because they argue that Standard Time aligns best with people’s circadian rhythms. Organizations such as the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, have pushed for making Standard Time permanent instead, arguing that it would be better for health and safety.

Former Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing indigenous men in Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:57:14 UTC
04:57:14 KST

Former Catholic bishop sentenced for abusing indigenous men in Australia
The Catholic Church in Australia has been marred by abuse allegations in recent years.
A former Roman Catholic bishop has been sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young indigenous men in Western Australia.
Seventy-six year old Christopher Saunders was sentenced by the District Court of Western Australia and showed no reaction during Wednesday’s sentencing hearing.
In August, a court found Saunders guilty of one count of sexual penetration without consent and 12 counts of indecent assault.
The offences took place between 2010 and 2019 when he was bishop of Broome, a remote diocese in northwestern Australia.
Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, president of the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, issued a statement apologising for the pain and suffering Saunders inflicted on victims, saying their trust had been “profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church”.
Saunders was ordained a priest in 1976 and initially worked at mission stations in outback regions from the 1970s onwards. In the 1990s, he was appointed bishop of Broome by Pope John Paul II.
Following the abuse allegations, Saunders suspended his duties in 2020 and in August 2021 Pope Francis accepted his resignation. The clergyman has consistently denied the allegations.
It was revealed in court that the bishop had groomed his victims.
He is said to have regularly invited young indigenous Aboriginal men and teenagers to a beach house or a Catholic Church residence, providing them with alcohol and cigarettes, and giving them money and mobile phones.
The assaults on the two young men reportedly took place while they were heavily intoxicated.
Royal Commission and history of abuse
In 2013, Australia’s government set up a Royal Commission, a high-level inquiry into institutional child sexual abuse, after a series of scandals involving the Catholic Church.
In 2017, the commission revealed that most of the abuse took place in churches, with seven percent of Catholic priests accused of abusing children in Australia between 1950 and 2010. It said allegations were almost never investigated.
It found that 4,444 alleged incidents of child sexual abuse had been reported to church authorities. In some dioceses, more than 15 percent of priests were perpetrators.
The commission also heard testimony from the Vatican’s former finance chief Cardinal George Pell, who was found guilty in 2018 of sexually abusing choirboys in Melbourne, Australia in the 1990s.
Pell – who had been Pope Francis’s anti-corruption tsar – was released from prison in 2020 after a court quashed his conviction. He died in Rome on January 10, 2023, at the age of 81 due to heart complications following hip surgery.

Fenerbahce Tarfin defeated hosts CIMSA CBK Mersin 79-71 to win the FIBA SuperCup Women title Wednesday for the third time.
The reigning EuroLeague Women champions from Istanbul secured their third SuperCup crown after lifting the trophy in 2023 and 2024.
Mersin, the reigning EuroCup Women champions, were competing in the SuperCup for the first time.
The opening quarter was close, with the teams level at 11-11 midway through before Mersin edged ahead 21-19 at the end of the quarter.

Fenerbahce, however, held their nerve from the free-throw line to secure the 79-71 victory and become only the second club to win the SuperCup Women three times.

The warning comes as Ethiopia continues to face security challenges in several parts of the country, with the US government regularly updating travel and security guidance for Americans.

Oct. 7 terrorist trials face delays, Rothman calls to accelerate process for early 2027 indictments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:49:48 UTC
04:49:48 KST

Implementing the law to prosecute perpetrators of the October 7 Hamas massacre has faced recent setbacks, with estimates suggesting indictments for terrorists could be delayed until 2028, though MK Simcha Rothman called on Wednesday for the process to be accelerated.
He called for the initial indictments against the perpetrators of the attacks to be filed in the first half of 2027.
“It is an attainable target, and I call on you to make every effort to achieve it,” Rothman said.
Rothman, who chairs the Knesset Constitution, Law and Justice Committee, where the discussion took place, made the remarks to a panel of lawmakers and representatives from the Defense Ministry, Israel Prison Service, and the State Attorney’s Office, who provided an update on the ongoing process of implementing the legislation.
The Knesset committee meeting was held on the third anniversary of the massacre.
There has not yet been a full accounting for the events of October 7 in a criminal courtroom. Special legislation has been passed for military tribunals that has not yet been implemented.
The Knesset passed a law in May to prosecute terrorists involved in the attacks, granting authority to impose the death penalty and conduct public trials for the perpetrators of the attacks at a Jerusalem military court.
Later, in June, the government approved a budget of over NIS 1 billion to carry out the military tribunals, as the law’s proposal consists of a broad framework for implementing the trials and building a full complex for them to take place.
Committee meeting vowed to resolve budget issues in prosecution
The committee meeting discussed delays in moving forward with the prosecutions, largely due to stalled budget issues.
MK Yulia Malinovsky (Yisrael Beytenu), who sponsored the bill with Rothman, vowed to resolve any existing issues holding back the legislation from being implemented.
“If there are problems, we will solve them, and if we need to bang on the table, we will, but we want results. The people of Israel deserve answers,” she told the panel.
“We did what we needed to do; we passed the law, and now every official needs to put personal whims and disagreements aside and rise to the occasion. Regardless of the election results and who sits in this chair, we will not let up. We owe this to the families,” she added.
Building infrastructure for October 7 military tribunal is underway
In June, Rothman said bulldozers had begun preparing the Atarot site in northern Jerusalem, where the dedicated military tribunal is slated to be built. The announcement marked the first public sign that the law had crossed into the implementation stage.
The infrastructure to be built for the trials includes the court complex, prosecution offices, and an IDF headquarters facility.
The legislation to prosecute the terrorists also includes ensuring that key moments of the trial for the military courts can be filmed and broadcast on a dedicated website.
It establishes provisions concerning judicial panels, public access to proceedings, audiovisual documentation of hearings, and the broadcasting of parts of the proceedings to the public.
The law further proposes establishing specific arrangements for appointing judges to the court, including sitting and retired judges.
It calls for establishing special arrangements regarding victims’ rights, legal representation for defendants, and the conduct of hearings via video conference.
Military tribunal likened to Eichmann trial
The legislation also proposes the creation of a special guard unit to secure the military court in Jerusalem.
It mandates administrative preparations for conducting the proceedings, periodic reporting to the Knesset, and the promulgation of regulations concerning the implementation of the death sentence.
Capital punishment has only been carried out twice in the history of the State of Israel. The last person to be executed by Israel was Nazi Holocaust architect Adolf Eichmann, who was hanged in 1962. He was the only person ever executed following a civilian trial in the Jewish state. (The other was the case of an IDF captain, Meir Tobianski, hastily court-martialed and executed by firing squad for treason in 1948 but posthumously exonerated by David Ben-Gurion and reburied with full military honors.)
Lawmakers, from both the coalition and opposition, who sponsored the bill likened it to the Eichmann trials in 1961, which broadcast live and recorded testimonies of Holocaust survivors throughout Israel and numerous other countries before Eichmann’s hanging took place.
During the October 7 massacre, Hamas terrorists brutally massacred over 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and kidnapped 251 hostages into Gaza. The attacks included sexual violence and rape.
Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

How Israel’s political parties plan to fix the public transportation crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:48:22 UTC
04:48:22 KST

Who will get us out of the traffic jam? In 20 days, Israelis will head to the polls as the daily reality on the country’s roads becomes increasingly unbearable. We examined how the parties plan to tackle the serious problems facing public transportation in Israel and which will continue to oppose buses and trains operating on Shabbat (Saturday). We also looked at what civil society organizations are urging politicians to do to genuinely address the difficult transportation challenges Israelis face every day.
Delays and rising costs
Transportation Minister Miri Regev’s tenure has been marked by a fare reform that drew criticism for favoring certain sectors, with further price increases expected. At the same time, numerous projects have been delayed, entire cities look like construction sites and political tensions, along with changes among the ministry’s professional staff, have held up critical initiatives.
While some parties did not address transportation at all in their platforms, those that addressed it are proposing different approaches to resolving the crisis. The Beyachad party has presented the most comprehensive and detailed plan, drafted by Keren Terner, a former director general of both the Transportation Ministry and Finance Ministry who is seeking to become transportation minister in the next government.
The key innovation in Beyachad’s plan is an overhaul of the way public transportation companies are compensated, based on the “Amsterdam model.” The state currently pays operators according to the number of kilometers traveled, a model that incentivizes the creation of long, winding routes that often run largely empty. The plan proposes shifting to compensation based on the actual number of passengers and strict service-quality metrics, including punctuality, cleanliness, seat availability and passenger satisfaction. It also calls for broad decentralization of authority to local governments and for the private sector to take over implementation of major infrastructure projects.
The Democrats have placed a sweeping budgetary and environmental commitment at the center of their transportation platform: allocating 80% of the Transportation Ministry’s budget to public transportation development, alongside a plan to acquire 4,000 new electric buses. The party is proposing a distinctive model for transitioning to clean, green transportation within cities, pledging to pass legislation establishing metropolitan transportation authorities and implement a national emergency plan to address the driver shortage, including direct pay raises and designating drivers as public employees.
Yisrael Beytenu is focusing on infrastructure solutions, connecting outlying areas and reducing travel times. At the heart of the party’s approach are more frequent train and bus service, dedicated public transportation lanes on major intercity and urban roads and the advancement of modern mass-transit projects.
The Yashar! party is placing regulatory and structural change at the center of its transportation platform. The party has pledged to immediately pass legislation establishing metropolitan transportation authorities, arguing that only by transferring management and planning powers to local and regional governments can public transportation routes be adapted to residents’ actual needs.
Likud continues to favor centralized government planning and management. Its platform focuses on “connectivity,” linking outlying areas with central Israel through the development of rail networks, high-speed trains and major national infrastructure projects while keeping management and budgetary authority in the hands of the central government.
The Shabbat issue
Public transportation on Shabbat also features prominently in some of the parties’ platforms. While parties including the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu and Beyachad support allowing local governments to operate public transportation on weekends in accordance with the character of their communities, Likud opposes such a move in order to preserve the status quo.
In an appeal to all parties running in the election the Public Transportation Forum presented a firm position paper aimed directly at shaping the next coalition agreements. The organizations stressed that resolving the crisis will require more than additional funding and will instead demand fundamental changes to management, planning and compensation methods.
One of the forum’s main proposals is to break up the Transportation Ministry’s centralized control. The ministry in Jerusalem currently attempts to manage thousands of bus routes across the country, creating cumbersome bureaucracy, delays and services that do not adequately reflect local needs. The forum is calling for the establishment of metropolitan transportation authorities that would assume those powers.
The forum is also demanding a sweeping overhaul of public transportation tenders and a transition to a compensation system based on service quality and the actual number of passengers. Another critical solution at the center of the organizations’ proposals is a national emergency plan to address the severe shortage of some 5,000 bus drivers. The plan would include higher wages, upgrading drivers’ status to that of public employees, improving welfare facilities at route terminals and accelerated training programs.
Sivan Shmuelovitz, CEO of 15 Dakot, an Israeli advocacy organization dedicated to improving public transportation in Israel, said: “There are deep gaps in the system that ultimately affect our wallets, the cost of living and our quality of life. We are proposing practical solutions that can work for everyone, some of which can be implemented almost immediately.”
She emphasized the direct connection to the cost of living: “Good public transportation determines whether a person can get to a good job without owning a car, whether a family can live in the periphery and still have access to opportunities and whether we spend our lives sitting in traffic instead of spending time with our families.”
Even after the next government is formed and a new transportation minister is appointed, implementing the necessary reforms will not be simple. The main obstacle the incoming government is expected to face is structural and bureaucratic resistance within the Transportation Ministry itself, including concerns about relinquishing authority and budgets to local governments. In addition, the depth of the ministry’s management crisis, following an exodus of professional staff and senior officials in recent years, poses a significant obstacle to implementation.
According to Shmuelevitz, after the election, the real test for the next transportation minister will not be ceremonial declarations or campaign promises, but the ability to move immediately to implementation, mobilize professional officials and build a reliable, efficient and safe transportation system.
Shmuelevitz concluded: “There are deep gaps in the system that ultimately affect our wallets, the cost of living and our quality of life. We are proposing practical solutions that can work for everyone, some of which can be implemented almost immediately.”

Bundeswehr Begins Testing Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak Without Planned Natter Weapon Station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:47:47 UTC
04:47:47 KST

The Bundeswehr has received the first two prototype Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak engineering vehicles and is beginning their testing. However, the vehicles were delivered without the Natter remotely controlled weapon station, which was originally planned for installation on German Kodiaks.
Hartpunkt reports this, citing the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support (BAAINBw).
The two prototypes were delivered to the Bundeswehr at the end of August 2026. They will now undergo testing at the relevant technical centers of the German Ministry of Defense.
A BAAINBw representative confirmed that the vehicles were indeed delivered without the weapon station. The agency has not disclosed the reasons for the change in configuration, citing ongoing negotiations.
Rheinmetall also declined to comment on the situation due to restrictions related to the procurement procedure.
It is not yet known whether production Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiaks will be equipped with a different weapon station.
Hartpunkt notes that, theoretically, alternatives could include the FLW 200 remotely controlled weapon station from KNDS Deutschland or the Protector RS4 from Kongsberg, both of which are already in service with the Bundeswehr.
Both systems can be equipped with heavy machine guns or automatic grenade launchers and have already been integrated with heavy tracked platforms. However, there is no official decision to install either system on the Kodiak.
BAAINBw has not disclosed whether the decision to remove the Natter will affect delivery timelines, the cost of the program or the testing schedule.
The Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak is a heavy engineering vehicle based on the Leopard 2 chassis, which Rheinmetall began developing in 2002 at the request of the Swiss Army together with RUAG.
In addition to Switzerland, the Kodiak is already in service with the Netherlands, Sweden and Singapore.
The vehicle is equipped with a centrally mounted excavator arm, two winches with a pulling capacity of nine tons each, and a large dozer blade.
Using pulley blocks, the winches can move loads weighing more than 60 tons.
Various tools can be mounted on the excavator arm, including a bucket, grapple or hydraulic concrete-breaking tool. The tools can be replaced under armored protection.
According to Rheinmetall, the Kodiak’s excavator arm can move about 200 cubic meters of heavy soil per hour. The arm can lift a load of approximately 3.5 tons at a maximum reach of up to nine meters.
Some versions can also be fitted with a mine-clearing system instead of the dozer blade.
The Bundeswehr began procuring new engineering vehicles in 2019.
The German military allocated 44 Leopard 2A4 chassis for the program.
Rheinmetall with the Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiak and FFG Flensburger Fahrzeugbau Gesellschaft with the WiSENT 2 competed for the contract.
In May 2021, BAAINBw awarded Rheinmetall Landsysteme a contract for 44 Pionierpanzer 3 Kodiaks worth approximately €295 million.
The contract also includes training, an initial spare parts package, special tools and other equipment required to operate the vehicles.
The initial schedule called for the delivery of prototypes in 2023–2024 and the first production vehicles in 2026.
Under the plans at the time the contract was signed, the Bundeswehr was to receive five production Kodiaks in 2026, 14 in 2027, 17 in 2028 and the final six vehicles in 2029.
The delivery of the two prototypes in August 2026 indicates that the program is behind its original schedule.

Gunfire hits UNIFIL position in southern Lebanon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:47:39 UTC
04:47:39 KST

The UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) said on Wednesday that several rounds of small arms fire struck its position near Kfar Shouba in southern Lebanon, hitting accommodation units and UN vehicles.
It occurred in the morning along the Blue Line in Sector East, the mission said in a statement on Telegram. The Blue Line is a temporary boundary that was established by the UN in 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon after a two-decade occupation.
All peacekeepers stationed at the position took shelter shortly after the first round of firing, and no one was injured.
Most rounds struck the perimeter wall, while some hit accommodation units and UN vehicles inside the base. Several were recorded at the post, said UNIFIL.
“It is unacceptable that firings continued towards a clearly marked UNIFIL position. Such deliberate attacks put the lives of peacekeepers at serious risk,” it said.
Possible war crime
UNIFIL said it launched an investigation to determine the circumstances of the incident. The statement did not identify who fired the shots.
“We strongly remind all actors of their obligations under international law to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel and properties at all times,” it said. “Any attack on UNIFIL peacekeepers constitutes a grave violation of international humanitarian law and of the Security Council Resolution 1701 and may amount to a war crime.”
The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 1701 in August 2006 following a 33-day war between Israel and Hezbollah.
The resolution calls for a complete cessation of hostilities between Lebanon and Israel and for an area between the Blue Line and the Litani River in southern Lebanon to be free of weapons and armed personnel, except those of the Lebanese army and UNIFIL.
Israeli attacks despite ceasefire agreement
The Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,386 people and wounded 12,407 others since March 2, according to Lebanese official figures.
On June 26, Lebanon and Israel signed a US-sponsored Framework Agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory and the deployment of the Lebanese army to areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israel has continued to carry out attacks in southern Lebanon and maintains a military presence in parts of the south, including territory it has occupied for decades and other areas seized during more recent wars and military operations.

Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were apprehended by police on Wednesday as they marched towards Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in India’s capital, New Delhi.
A live feed on the YouTube channel of Gandhi’s Congress Party showed police taking him into a vehicle and driving away. Authorities also detained several other opposition lawmakers and protesters.
Opposition parties, their student units and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the poll body he heads of benefiting Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party.
India’s Election Commission has so far removed more than 130 million names from the voter lists, with millions appealing the removals. About 969 million people were eligible to vote in the 2024 election.
Protesters allege the changes disproportionately removed voters who support opposition parties while preserving or adding voters more likely to back Modi’s party.
The commission and government deny the allegations. They say the revision has no political motive but is aimed at removing duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain registered.
Opposition lawmakers led by Gandhi protested on Tuesday as well, before police broke up their gathering and briefly detained them.
Speaking before his detention on Wednesday, Gandhi said protesters showed up unannounced after Delhi police “stopped” their gathering the day before.
“We will go to the designated protest site, sit there, and tell the country that, for us, Gyanesh Kumar is not the legitimate commissioner,” he told reporters, referring to Jantar Mantar.
“The people who have done this [vote theft] are traitors … Gyanesh Kumar will have to resign,” he added.
There was no immediate comment from the police on the detentions.
The demonstrations present a new political challenge to Modi midway into his third term, just months after similar protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party youth movement forced the resignation of his education minister over exam paper leaks.
The “Cockroach” protests, one of the most visible signs of public dissent against Modi’s government in recent years, reflected growing anger over job scarcity, corruption and a lack of government accountability.

EU drops sponsorship of disinformation conference at Trump officials’ request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:38:24 UTC
04:38:24 KST

The Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands.
The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab.
Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website.
Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste.
Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference.
Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”. The document says Washington was “grateful” Lithuania supposedly found a panel framing the US as a foreign information threat “reprehensible and surprising” and welcomed its decision to limit involvement in the conference.
That panel – called “USA as a FIMI threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back”, with the acronym FIMI referring to “foreign information manipulation and interference” – took place Wednesday. It explored how Europe’s disinformation community could rebuild resilience without Washington, and is the first time the conference appears to have entertained the idea that the US could be a disinformation actor in Europe. Sources and the internal document indicate the state department was explicitly focused on this panel, which included three American speakers, among them a former CIA officer.
According to one person familiar with the deliberations, other communications appeared to originate from the office of Sarah B Rogers, the US undersecretary of state for public diplomacy.
Nina Jankowicz, a former US official and disinformation expert who in 2022 briefly headed the Biden administration’s Disinformation Governance Board, which Republicans assailed as a vehicle for policing Americans’ speech, said she understood that Washington had pressured Lithuania and Canada to withdraw from the conference. The Guardian understands that France was contacted as well.
“What this amounts to is a purported defender of free speech at the state department using the enormous power of the US government to try to pressure Americans from criticizing their government,” said Jankowicz.
In statements, Lithuania, Canada and the EU said the program of the conference did not align with their official views on the US role in disinformation – although that program had been in place for months before they withdrew their support, since June.
“Lithuania has cancelled its participation in ‘Disinfo 2026’ as several parts of the conference programme differ from the official position of the Government,” Lithuania’s foreign ministry wrote in a statement.
Global Affairs Canada “carefully assesses participation in, and sponsorship of, external events on a case-by-case basis,” GAC spokesperson Samantha Lafleur said. “Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference.”
Canadian officials are still participating in the conference, Lafleur added.
An EU spokesperson confirmed that the European External Action Service had decided to withdraw its support from the conference because “the organisers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU.”
EU officials, the Guardian understands, did not agree with the characterisation of the US as a disinformation actor.
Despite withdrawing its branding as an official supporter, the EU continues to fund the conference.
In its latest report on foreign information manipulation and interference threats, published in March, the EU’s diplomatic service named Russia and China as “threat actors” without any negative reference to the US.
A diplomatic source at France’s foreign ministry said “there’s absolutely no reason for us to change our commitments” when it came to supporting the conference.
“We stick to supporting civil society. It’s not just principled, it’s operational,” she said, adding that the conference was a “laboratory” that helped Europe develop key policy around disinformation.
The US state department has taken an increasingly interventionist posture towards free speech and civil society in Europe over the past year. The Guardian has revealed that the state department is awarding millions of dollars in non-competitive grants to organisations across the continent supportive of Trump’s agenda.
Lithuania’s withdrawal comes just after the prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevicius, said Lithuania would pay for a permanent US military base if the US agreed, a day after Trump said he would consider the request. Sinkevicius called a lasting American presence a critical guarantee of deterrence against Russia.
“They are great people, so we will certainly look at it,” the US president said on Monday.
Sinkevicius said he first proposed the idea in a meeting with Trump’s envoy John Coale, and called it a “critically important guarantee of deterrence and security.” Lithuania, a member of the EU and Nato, borders Russia and its close ally Belarus.
The US has kept a rotating armoured battalion of almost 1,000 troops in the country since 2019, the US Army has noted.
