Putin Pushes Russia’s 2026 War Spending to $200 Billion—Matching Next Year’s Record Budget
Russia is set to spend around 17 trillion rubles ($200 billion) on its war effort in 2026—nearly matching the record level Moscow had planned to reach only next year—after Vladimir Putin ordered a major increase in military expenditures, Bloomberg reported on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new estimate is roughly 40% above the Russian government’s original 2026 spending plan and comes just days after Moscow unveiled a record $200 billion military allocation for 2027.
According to Bloomberg, Putin ordered the government to increase war-related spending by nearly $60 billion after the Kremlin concluded that negotiations involving US President Donald Trump were unlikely to end the war on terms acceptable to Moscow.
Putin had initially expected that talks with Trump could pressure Ukraine into an agreement and allow Russia to avoid another major increase in military spending, a person familiar with the matter told Bloomberg.
By January, however, the Kremlin had concluded that no breakthrough had been achieved. The government subsequently accelerated advance payments to Russia’s defense industry and increased other military expenditures throughout 2026.
As a result, spending is now expected to reach around 17 trillion rubles ($200 billion) by the end of the year, according to two people close to the Russian government cited by Bloomberg.
The figure effectively brings Russia’s 2026 war spending to the level Moscow had presented as a new record for 2027. Russia’s draft budget for next year allocates 17.1 trillion rubles ($201 billion) to defense-related spending, representing roughly 35% of total federal expenditure.
Russia had initially budgeted roughly 12.1 trillion rubles ($142 billion) for defense in 2026, although actual military expenditures are classified and additional war-related spending is distributed across other parts of the federal budget.
The acceleration was already visible during the first half of the year. According to calculations by Janis Kluge of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs cited by Bloomberg, Russia spent 10.687 trillion rubles ($126 billion) on the war during the first six months of 2026, approaching its original full-year target.
The surge is also adding pressure to Russia’s public finances. The federal budget deficit is now projected to exceed 7 trillion rubles ($82 billion) in 2026, compared with an earlier target of 3.8 trillion rubles ($45 billion).
Earlier, senior Russian financial officials warned Putin that the country’s war spending was becoming unsustainable, with the Finance Ministry and Central Bank raising concerns that rising military expenditures could further widen the federal budget deficit.

ST. PETERSBURG, October 7. /TASS/. Russia has achieved full technological sovereignty in hydropower, with domestic manufacturers capable of producing the equipment required for every stage of hydroelectric power plant construction and modernization, RusHydro First Deputy CEO and Chief Engineer Sergey Kondratyev told reporters on the sidelines of the 18th scientific and technical conference Hydropower. Hydraulic Engineering. New Developments and Technologies.
"Overall, I can say with confidence that we have 100% technological sovereignty in Russia’s hydropower sector. In other words, from the very beginning of developing a dam site and constructing the dam, we can fully provide both the equipment and all the control systems using the capabilities of Russian industry," he said.
Power Machines Deputy CEO and Head of the Hydropower Division Vladimir Demyanov previously told TASS, the company is capable of producing a full range of equipment for hydroelectric power plants annually, with production capacity of up to 10 equipment sets totaling up to 2 GW.
Russia’s General Scheme for the Development of Electric Power Facilities through 2042 envisages the commissioning of 6.7 GW of new hydropower generation capacity, comprising seven hydroelectric power plants and four pumped-storage power plants. A total of 37 hydropower units of various capacities will be required. According to the document, the nearest commissioning dates for such units are scheduled for 2031, when eight hydropower units are due to come online, and 2032, when 13 units are scheduled for commissioning.
RusHydro is Russia’s largest energy company by installed capacity, bringing together more than 600 generating facilities. The total installed capacity of the company’s power plants stands at 38.7 GW.
RusHydro’s largest shareholders are the Russian Federation with a 62.2% stake, VTB Bank with 12.37%, and En+ holding company with 9.61%.

Will you really get 'left behind' if you don't use AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Avoiding AI won't 'leave you behind', but ignoring it could
Whether it was from the mouth of a tech leader or celebrity, you've probably heard that "if you don't use AI, you'll be left behind".
I guess you'll find me somewhere in the dust then.
I've used ChatGPT a handful of times, mainly to see what the hype was about, and ask very important water-guzzling questions like: "What would I look like with curtain bangs?"
I worry generative AI is bad for our brains, creativity and the planet.
They're common concerns. Most Australians think the risks of AI outweigh the benefits, and almost two-thirds believe it's moving too fast.
But will avoiding AI really leave me or you behind? I asked three AI academics who shared their advice for avoiders like me.
They all agreed on one thing: you don't have to use it, but you do need to understand it.
Do you believe people who don't use AI will be left behind?
Professor Mirjalili: In my experience, most people who say they do not use AI already use it every day. They are just not aware of it.
AI filters their spam emails, suggests the fastest route on their maps, recommends their next show, and flags suspicious bank transactions.
The real question is not whether you use AI. You definitely do. It is whether you use it knowingly and well.
In many jobs, there is a real risk to not adopting AI. If others can use AI to complete certain tasks faster and improve their quality, someone doing things manually may find it harder to keep up.
But not using AI does not automatically make someone less capable or less valuable.
The impact depends on the work and whether AI actually improves it.
Producing more content is not necessarily the same as producing better work.
Dr Ciriello: The inevitability narrative is very much being pushed by big tech companies.
It's in their interest to make the case we must all use it otherwise we will get left behind.
If the goal is simply to maximise speed and productivity, then people who don't use generative AI may well be disadvantaged compared with those who do.
But the harder question is deciding where we actually want to be, and what we want to become better at, and that's not something we can easily automate.
What are we racing towards? Faster is not automatically better. And productivity is not an end to itself.
Historically, modern society has tended to optimise for efficiency and productivity without necessarily considering the consequences or whether those ends are legitimate.
Professor Shafiabady: To me, using AI is similar to driving. Some people do not learn to drive and do not want to drive or they are scared of driving.
If you don't drive you will survive of course, but you won't have the convenience of taking your car and going where you like. You have to take public transport, it will be slower.
But I think it's very important that every individual is aware and in control of the reason they are doing things.
For example, if I'm writing an article for a media outlet, I prefer to start writing with my own thoughts and not use AI for that.
If I'm doing research for the ease of some work, I use AI and I just say "find this for me" … to make my life easier in accessing information.
I think we all have to learn how to use it ethically and responsibly.
Are there positive consequences to not adopting AI?
Professor Mirjalili: Yes. Doing work yourself gives you opportunities to improve your skills, develop your own ideas, and build deeper knowledge.
In 2025, a study found that experienced doctors became noticeably worse at spotting early signs of bowel cancer on their own after only a few months of working with an AI assistant.
You can fall behind by refusing to learn about AI, but you can fall further behind by letting AI do all your learning for you.
Dr Ciriello: Technology has often been deployed to serve the interest of a privileged few, while imposing harms and costs on society as a whole.
The resistance can be a good thing because it forces decision-makers and governments to consider the collective will of the people.
If enough people come together and say: "We don't want this on these terms," … it can be a signal to teach people in power what the people are not ready to participate in, and therefore, they need to find a better way.
And so much content and writing is now looking the same.
By not using AI, you might actually be able to differentiate yourself as someone who has a unique style and niche.
Professor Shafiabady: I love programming and coding. I have spent my career coding and developing algorithms.
But at the same time, I am against computers. And if it was up to me, I would ban them because it's changing the way we live.
The way we are not thinking about the consequences of what we are doing is killing our planet.
What advice do you have for AI avoiders?
Professor Mirjalili: Start with curiosity rather than fear.
You can start experimenting to see where and how it increases your productivity.
I suggest starting with a small, low-risk task and assess the result. Did it save time? Did it improve the quality of your work? How much checking or correcting did it require?
If checking and fixing the output takes longer than doing the task yourself, it does not make you more productive.
My advice is to learn enough to make an informed choice.
Knowing where and when not to use AI is also part of AI literacy.
Dr Ciriello: There's a difference between saying: "I'm not going to use ChatGPT to write my articles," versus: "I'm not going to bother looking into this at all."
Learning about these tools safeguards against misconceptions.
If you want to learn about the ethical use of AI or what it means for society … you can read about what other critical thinkers in this space have said about AI.
If you want to play around with tools, there's many more than ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. There are tools being developed by communities for communities without that strong commercial incentive behind them.
See if AI can help you, and if not, that's perfectly fine. You might be doing a service to society.
Professor Shafiabady: The best thing to do is think about the ways AI can help each of us ethically and responsibly, and keep an open mind on that.
Each of us have to think about what can help us in our lives, in what we want to be in our careers, in the person we want to become, the goals we want to achieve, how it can help us ethically and responsibly.
And then we start learning how to use it in those ways.

Aaron Sorkin takes on Facebook again, and this time he's furious
Two statistics are outlined in Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning, and they will follow you out of the cinema. The first: 64 per cent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent there by Facebook. The second: 32 per cent of teen girls said Instagram made them feel worse about their bodies.
2010's The Social Network won Aaron Sorkin an Oscar for screenwriting but David Fincher was in the director's chair. This time Sorkin does both, delivering a damning, journalistic drama about how Facebook whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) exposed what Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his senior team knew.
As the film tells it, the platform was addictive and harmful, yet they tweaked the algorithm to boost content designed to make users angry, because angry content gets re-shared and re-shares keep people scrolling and on the platform. Madison (who won an Oscar for her role as Ani in Anora) presents a welcome change of register as Haugen, while White is mercifully off The Bear's boil, playing a composed reporter.
From a network to a reckoning
Comparisons to The Social Network are inevitable, but this film stands on its own, even if it satisfies fewer people. It holds your attention but it's better written than it's made. The film is not a sequel in that almost nobody has returned except for cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth, who keeps the dark tonality of the film consistent with the earlier film; while Trent Reznor's and Atticus Ross's score has given way to Alexandre Desplat's slightly less memorable version of synths and unsettling piano.
For the most part, this is a good thing. After all, we're in an unprecedented chapter of social media.
Jeremy Strong, who opted for method acting throughout production, replaces Jesse Eisenberg and nails Zuckerberg's mannerisms and voice. We are 16 years on from Sorkin's original portrayal of Zuckerberg — young, flawed and, at moments, vulnerable, maybe even potentially redeemable. Now, he's a shell of a person, even ridiculous (apparently he has a bulletproof couch in his office, to hide behind in an attack). The film presents him as a villain, even if Sorkin says he isn't.
Yet, Sorkin's real target is us. How do you shock an audience who have already scrolled past the evidence? You open with proof. The film's prologue, which is wryly titled White Girl Wasted, begins with an alt-right Karen meltdown: a drunk white woman recording a viral video and screaming at two police officials of colour, claiming she's being targeted for being a white woman. We soon learn she was recently a progressive and a friend of Haugen, but has now been radicalised by Facebook. Are you angry yet? It's a human example in place of a statistic that would slide off.
The film hops between 2019 and 2022, sometimes to jarring effect. Haugen, a data scientist in Facebook's now-disbanded civic integrity team and a true believer in its mission, begins to question what she sees after this video. Horwitz, a beat reporter covering Facebook, who isn't even on Facebook (a true millennial), emails every civic integrity team member, attempting to cultivate an ongoing credible source. Haugen is the only one to reply, and she starts feeding him information, then evidence, including the algorithm change, palatably named MSI (meaningful social interactions).
Facebook, IRL
The Social Reckoning is a film about Facebook, but we don't actually meet Zuckerberg until roughly 30 minutes in, during deposition preparation in a mock hearing room with his press team, led by Raya (played by Oscar-nominated Wunmi Mosaku) and his advisers, including Bill Burr's Charlie, who urges him to fact-check political ads.
Zuckerberg simply responds with "we respect our users" to make their own mind up about content presented. Sorkin's quips and rapid-fire dialogue come alive here, and anyone who misses The Newsroom series will feel at home with the back-and-forth banter as the camera bounces between speakers. In another scene, a fellow journalist tells Jeff he's joined the last two minutes of print journalism, earning a chuckle, but fewer lines land with as much conviction and satisfaction as they did in The Social Network.
To its credit, the film doesn't glamorise journalism, and there's no romance between its leads, a trope we're usually handed. The only remotely sexy moment is when Haugen turns up at Horwitz's hotel room dressed, supposedly in disguise, as if she's on a date; it feels like a thinly veiled excuse to see Madison in tight clothing. In a film about platforms engineered to hold our gaze, it's an odd moment to catch Sorkin engineering one.
During my viewing of the film, I was wondering if it might have been more effective with more real-life consequences on screen. Then it reached the events of January 6, 2021, which is, arguably, enough. In the war room, as the frightening riot rages on at the Capitol in Washington, DC, they're asking Zuckerberg to block the sitting president on the platform (Trump is never named) from inciting more violence. We watch in disbelief as he hesitates.
Another potent moment comes when Haugen has a scare, thinking she's been outed as the source, and for a split second questions whether what Facebook is doing with the algorithm is even really a big deal and who is she to be a whistleblower? Horwitz says he isn't angry about apps like Facebook seeping into mainstream news, or even threatening his own future as an investigative journalist; he's angry because they're doing his job so badly and, yes, it is a big deal. This Wild West lack of regulation and the feeding of misinformation are actions he can't abide, and we shouldn't either.
Where do we go from here?
Sorkin has said in recent interviews he wants the film to be evergreen, and his reverence for American institutions and the media still stands. That's hardly new for him, but the cynic in me leans towards distrust.
But as our protagonists take risks, believing in journalism's ability to "cause pain" for the right reasons (as Horwitz puts it) and hold people accountable, it gives hope that there may still be goodness in media reporting.
Interestingly, Sorkin withholds a real-life postscript. Since the events of the film, Meta (the name change came three weeks after the release of the Journal's "Facebook Files"), has agreed to make major changes to Facebook and Instagram, and to pay up to $US18 billion to settle claims from dozens of US states over teen addiction. Perhaps even Sorkin knows there's more work to be done.
The Social Reckoning is for the cynics and the numbed. See it, then put your phone away on the walk home.
The Social Reckoning is in cinemas now.

The US president says the Mexican leader rang him to urge him not to rename the Gulf of Mexico. Trump justified the change with coastal data that available figures do not support.
US President Donald Trump again referred on Tuesday to his decision to rename the Gulf of Mexico as 'Gulf of America' and mocked Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum's reaction, according to his account.
Speaking at an event with members of the US Navy in Baltimore, Trump said that Sheinbaum had called him to ask him not to alter the name. The president re-enacted the alleged conversation in front of those present and said he had told the Mexican leader that the decision was already made.
"It was a slightly tricky moment when I did that. I received a call from the president of Mexico. She was a very nice woman, beautiful, with a lovely voice, and she said to me: 'No, no, Mr President. Please, please, tell me that isn't the case**'**".
Trump defended the change by claiming that the United States accounts for 93% of the Gulf coastline, compared with barely 7% for Mexico. However, the available data do not support that ratio.
The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and calculations published by Mexico's National Commission for the Knowledge and Use of Biodiversity (Conabio) point to a much more balanced split. According to Conabio, using geospatial data from the Flanders Marine Institute, Mexico represents 47.67% of the Gulf's maritime area and the United States 44.75%.
Sheinbaum rejects the new name
Sheinbaum has repeatedly opposed the change pushed by Trump and has insisted that the internationally recognised name remains Gulf of Mexico. The president has even responded to the controversy with irony, floating the idea of referring to the United States as 'Mexican America'.
Trump ordered the name to be changed to 'Gulf of America' in 2025, a decision that has since caused friction with the Mexican government over which name should be used.

Vovk said Gasilin died on October 4 in Moscow. The cause of death has not been disclosed.
The Voice Mag (formerly Cosmopolitan) reported that Gasilin “popularized blanket coats and made dresses in sophisticated shades and designer cuts affordable for many Russian women.”
Vovk called Gasilin “a great artist — someone with a vision of his own who had a major influence on Russian fashion and on how we think about the cut of contemporary clothing”:
His clothes were always recognizable — understated, precise, yet with a distinctive fluidity. He knew how to work with shape and color so that even the most complex pieces looked natural. He developed that attention to construction in part during an internship at the Paris haute couture house Dominique Sirop. Later, his passion for well-cut clothes became one of the foundations of his own label, which he founded in 2007.
In addition to creating fashion collections, Gasilin designed costumes for the Tokyo National Ballet’s program “The Afternoon of a Faun and His Nymph.” In 2020, he also worked with Alexander Vasilyev, a fashion historian and host of the television show “Modny prigovor” (“Fashion Verdict”), to design costumes for a production of “My Fair Lady” at the Russian Theater in Tallinn (now the Südalinna Theater). In 2023, he designed costumes for the ballet “La Bayadère” at the Tbilisi State Opera and Ballet Theater.

Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh were targeted in two separate attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The attack on Abha International Airport killed two female residents, a Moroccan and an Algerian, and injured 28 others, GACA reported.
The attack on King Khalid International Airport in the capital Riyadh killed a Sudanese citizen and injured eight residents, including five Saudi citizens.
GACA said it is working “in full integration and continuous coordination with the relevant security authorities” to assess the damage and take all necessary measures to ensure the safety of passengers and workers.

Previous attacks on Saudi airports

On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards the airport in Riyadh from Yemen.
A day later, on September 19, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport.
Saudi-backed Yemeni forces from the country’s internationally recognised government are locked in escalating combat with Iran-aligned Houthi forces who seized a broad swathe of territory astride the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Meanwhile, the United States embassy in Riyadh has issued another security alert for Americans in Saudi Arabia due to the ongoing security situation, reminding “all US citizens to exercise heightened vigilance”.

Most Americans oppose Trump’s taxpayer-funded ‘golden age’ ads: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:27:09 UTC
03:27:09 KST

Most Americans oppose Trump’s taxpayer-funded ‘golden age’ ads: Poll
Trump says he will pay for future advertisements, but the White House says taxpayers will not be reimbursed for past ones.
The Trump administration says its taxpayer-funded television advertisements are about patriotism, reminding people why they should love the United States and why it is worth defending. But an overwhelming majority of Americans say they should not be paid for with taxpayer dollars.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll suggested that 86 percent of Americans, including four out of five Republicans, believe it is inappropriate to use public money for election-related television advertisements featuring US President Donald Trump or members of his cabinet.
The poll comes as Trump says he will stop using taxpayer money to fund the advertisements. On Monday, he said he would instead pay for them himself and with money raised by MAGA Inc, his political action committee.
What remains unclear is whether he will reimburse taxpayers for advertisements that have already aired. The White House said on Tuesday that the president would only pay for future advertisements, but Trump later appeared to leave the door open to reimbursing the government, telling reporters, “The ads were really good. They were promotion for the country, done by many presidents before. So, we’ll decide.”
The Trump administration faces mounting criticism about a number of government-funded advertisements that have been airing in the run-up to November’s midterm elections, celebrating what they describe as a “golden age of America”.
In one, a choir sings “love me” over a montage of Trump as he declares the US will “never be a communist country”. Another uses images of Mount Rushmore as Trump heralds a new “golden age of America”. The third is darker: Trump walks towards the camera in black and white, warning of a “final battle” against the “deep state” and other perceived enemies.
All three end with a disclaimer saying they were “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
The advertisements have already cost taxpayers at least $1.4m, according to media tracking firm AdImpact, and have aired across network and cable television, including during high-viewership programmes, such as NFL games, as well as streaming services.
Democratic lawmakers have said the White House transferred $20m in Department of Homeland Security funds to pay for the campaign and have called for independent investigations.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer criticised the advertisements in a Senate floor speech, saying, “Americans sat down to watch football, not to be force-fed Trump’s propaganda on their own dime.”
But criticism has also come from within Trump’s own party.
“It shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars,” Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters last month.
The White House has defended the advertisements as public service announcements, pointing to government-funded campaigns under previous administrations promoting Medicare, Affordable Care Act subsidies and COVID-19 vaccinations. It says the Trump advertisements are similarly intended to remind Americans to “love their country and understand what makes it worth defending”.
But critics say there is a key difference: those advertisements were tied to specific government programmes or policies, while Trump’s are not.
“There’s nothing in here about a particular policy that’s at all focused,” Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told The Associated Press news agency.
Experts interviewed by The AP also pointed to potential legal issues, as the advertisements may violate federal restrictions on using congressionally appropriated funds for “publicity or propaganda,” as well as rules limiting partisan political activity by government employees.
“You watch all three ads; they’re sheer propaganda,” said Painter. “This is increasingly looking like what authoritarian governments do to promote their leaders.”

In El Salvador’s mass trials, lawyers struggle to defend hundreds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:26:07 UTC
03:26:07 KST

In El Salvador’s mass trials, lawyers struggle to defend hundreds
Human Rights Watch says defendants face proceedings where lawyers have struggled to access case files.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) has released a report documenting widespread violations as part of El Salvador’s mass trials, in which hundreds of people can be tried and convicted together.
The report, released on Wednesday, reviews four indictments covering more than 600 defendants and a single court ruling that involved more than 120 people.
It also includes interviews with 15 defence lawyers, who say their clients were denied their due process rights and were therefore unable to adequately defend themselves at trial.
The report concludes that defendants in the mass trials face vaguely defined charges, weak evidence and faulty proceedings. In some cases, defence lawyers have reportedly been restricted from viewing their clients’ case files and communicating privately with the defendants.
“El Salvador’s mass trials are a mockery of justice,” said Juanita Goebertus, the Americas director at HRW, in a statement. “These hearings are designed to produce guilty verdicts, not to weigh evidence under due process.”
The mass trials are part of President Nayib Bukele’s sweeping security crackdown, launched in response to a surge in organised crime in the country.
Bukele first issued a state of emergency to address the crime wave in March 2022, suspending certain civil liberties in favour of greater powers for law enforcement officials. Those efforts included mass arrests.
The following year, El Salvador’s Congress passed a bill clearing the way for mass trials as well, allowing courts to decide cases involving hundreds of individual defendants.
The Salvadoran government has defended the trials as necessary to dismantle gangs, given the scale of crime in the country. But critics have repeatedly warned that such tactics violate basic human rights and have led to unlawful imprisonment.
Bukele himself has acknowledged that innocent people have been swept up in his crackdown. In 2024, he said some 8,000 people who had been arrested were later released.
“We are going to free 100 percent of the innocent people,” he pledged at the time, arguing that no system was perfect.
More than 93,000 people, including more than 3,000 children, have been detained under El Salvador’s emergency order, which has been renewed multiple times since 2022.
An estimated 120,000 people are currently imprisoned in El Salvador, equivalent to about 2 percent of the country’s population. The country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world.
HRW noted that many convictions in the mass trials are secured by accusing the defendants of being “collaborators” with gangs, a vague legal standard.
In a single trial reviewed by the group, more than 120 people were convicted of unlawful association and sentenced to 30 or 45 years in prison. No one was acquitted, HRW said.
HRW reported that, for the vast majority of prisoners convicted on such charges, the only evidence connecting them to a gang was a statement by one of two anonymous witnesses, who had received immunity from prosecution.
“Prosecutors say a person is a gang member because a police officer says so,” one lawyer anonymously told HRW. “The prosecutor relies on the police report, and the police report relies on unspecified official intelligence or public rumours.”
There have also been questions about the system overseeing the mass trials.
The cases have been presented before the Tribunals Against Organized Crime, a court system overseen by El Salvador’s Supreme Court that critics accuse of a lack of transparency.
The identities of the tribunals’ judges have not been disclosed, even to the lawyers involved in the proceedings.
Still, despite concerns about human rights in the country, Bukele’s government has historically enjoyed a relatively high approval rating in public polls.
Bukele has cited such statistics as a sign of public support for his anti-crime tactics.
In April, Attorney General Rodolfo Delgado also defended a mass trial of nearly 500 alleged MS-13 members, saying in a social media post that the gang had operated systematically for years, causing “fear and mourning among Salvadoran families”.
The Salvadoran government did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In its report, HRW called for independent reviews of cases brought under the state of emergency. It also demanded that people detained without credible evidence be released.

Australian bishop sentenced for abusing young indigenous men

Australian bishop sentenced for abusing young indigenous men
A former Australian Catholic bishop has been sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young indigenous men over the course of a decade.
76-year-old ex-bishop Christopher Saunders is one of the most senior Australian clerics to be convicted in a series of scandals that have shaken the Catholic Church for decades. In August, Saunders was found guilty on 13 out of 19 sexual abuse charges pertaining to two accusers he victimized between 2008 and 2019.
Saunders narrowly dodged a harsher punishment, with all the charges related to his alleged sexual relations with minors flopped in court. Four charges related to the alleged abuse of a child younger than 13 were dropped on the first day of his trial, while he was acquitted of six further charges involving a 16-year-old child.
All the crimes were perpetrated by Saunders when he led the remote Broome Diocese between 1996 and 2021, when he resigned from the position over allegations of sexual misconduct. While the territory of the diocese covers an area larger than France, it has a population of only some 50,000, predominantly indigenous people.
The cleric fell under the Vatican’s crosshairs in 2022, when it launched an internal probe into his predatory behavior. While the report was never made public, the Holy See shared its findings with the Australian authorities the next year, and Saunders was ultimately charged in 2024.
The scale of sexual misconduct by the ex-bishop was likely significantly greater than the crimes he was convicted of. The Church’s internal report was leaked to Australia’s Seven Network and indicated that Saunders likely sexually assaulted at least four and groomed a further 67 indigenous minors and young men.
The sentencing has been welcomed by the Australian Catholic Bishops Conference, with its president, Archbishop Timothy Costelloe, insisting it reflected the gravity of the crimes committed.
“To each victim and survivor who courageously revealed what they had endured, we want to say this: We are sorry for the pain and suffering that was inflicted on you. We are sorry that your trust was so directly and profoundly betrayed by a leader of the Church,” Costelloe said in a statement.

Syria weighs military aid for Saudi Arabia amid Yemen war, sources say
RIYADH, Oct 7 - Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia amid an escalating war against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.
Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the sources said.
The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis.
In response to a request for comment to the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government's primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country's civil war.
"Should Saudi Arabia request any military cooperation or exchange of expertise, this would take place exclusively through official channels and within the framework of the bilateral agreements governing relations between our two brotherly countries," the diplomat said in a statement.
The Saudi government media office and Yemen's information minister did not respond to requests for comment.
Saudi Arabia has been requesting assistance far and wide, from the US to Europe and the Middle East, for both defensive and offensive support in a renewed war against the group that follows weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on the kingdom.
The war is being led on the ground by a patchwork of Yemeni government forces with Saudi air support. They have made limited advances since the campaign was launched on Monday.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa made a public visit to Riyadh on Tuesday and met Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, also known as MbS. He discussed potential Syrian military assistance for the kingdom, among other matters, the US official said.
Footage broadcast by Syrian state media showed that he was escorted back to his plane by Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, a brother of the crown prince who has overseen the Yemen file.
DEPLOYMENT COULD DEEPEN TENSIONS WITH NEIGHBOURS
Syrian fighters from opposition groups that battled former leader Bashar al-Assad in the country's civil war have in past years been recruited as mercenaries for other conflicts, notably Libya's internal conflict and the Russia-Ukraine war.
But for Damascus, any potential deployment carries risks.
The militias that made up the armed opposition are now under the nascent Syrian state, which has adopted a policy of avoiding engagement in conflict, including the Iran war, to focus on recovery from the 14-year Syrian civil war.
The state is still piecing together its army from the various militia groups from the former rebel coalition that toppled Assad, which included many hardline Sunni Islamist and foreign fighters, and trying to contain tensions with minorities including the Alawites, a Shi'ite offshoot to which Assad belonged.
A conflict between that army and the Houthis, who are also adherents of an offshoot of Shi'ite Islam, could have divisive religious undertones that the Syrian leadership and its Western partners want to avoid, the US official said.
It is for this reason that it previously rejected a US request to help fight Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Involvement in a battle against the Iran-backed Houthis could also be viewed as a hostile act by Iran and its allies Hezbollah in Lebanon and militias in Iraq, with which the Syrian rebels-turned-rulers have a history of conflict.
KEEN TO SHOW SUPPORT
At the same time, Sharaa is keen to show the country's support for Saudi Arabia and MbS, who played a decisive role helping the former jihadist gain international legitimacy, including by brokering a May 2025 meeting between Sharaa and US President Donald Trump.
Saudi Arabia has also provided financial assistance to Syria and a Syrian show of support could result in that increasing, the US official said.
"A new Syria sending defensive personnel of a very small number to the most holy places in the Islamic world, alongside technical support to neutralise incoming drones, would be tremendously and positively symbolic," said H.A. Hellyer, senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
"But anything beyond, particularly in terms of Syrian boots on the ground, I think would be a wholly different proposition, and one I think Damascus would avoid, given the priorities they need to focus on in Syria," he said. REUTERS

Botched execution of Christa Pike: judge orders Tennessee to preserve syringes and other evidence
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

21:23:01 EEST

Botched execution of Christa Pike: judge orders Tennessee to preserve syringes and other evidence
Kyiv • UNN
Christa Pike survived two botched injections and remains in the hospital. The judge ordered the state to preserve evidence and documents.
A judge in Nashville said she would order Tennessee state officials to preserve all evidence related to last week’s failed execution attempt of Krista Pike (who was convicted of a 1995 murder), including syringes and other instruments used during two unsuccessful attempts to administer the lethal injection, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
Pike, 50, was taken to a Nashville hospital unconscious, in critical condition and with severe injuries to her arms after two injections of the caustic barbiturate pentobarbital failed to kill her at the Riverbend maximum-security prison last Wednesday.
According to her attorneys, as of Tuesday she had regained consciousness and was talking, but remains shackled to a hospital bed as her defense team seeks to pierce the veil of secrecy that typically surrounds execution procedures in Tennessee and other states.
The attorneys argue that the failed execution — already the second in Tennessee this year — effectively constitutes torture and violates the U.S. constitutional ban on cruel or unusual punishment.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for participating, while still a teenager, in the torture and murder of her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1995, is the first known person in the United States to survive a "completed execution attempt," her defense attorneys say.
They asked Davidson County Chancery Court Judge Aisha Miles to order state officials to preserve all evidence from the failed execution, including syringes, drug packaging and lot numbers, catheters, intravenous infusion sets and straps used to restrain her on the gurney.
At the end of Wednesday’s hearing, Miles largely sided with Pike’s attorneys. She called the legal proceedings — which began in January to prevent the scheduled execution — unusual because no one had anticipated that Pike would survive.
"This case is unique, to put it mildly," Miles remarked.
She also ordered the state to preserve internal records and correspondence concerning the execution attempt, including incident reports, witness statements and encrypted messages.
The judge has not yet ruled on Pike’s attorneys’ motion to allow the Tennessee Department of Correction to provide them with the remaining drugs used during the execution for chemical analysis.
The Tennessee Department of Correction opposed what it described as a "duplicative and unnecessary" preservation order, arguing that it is already legally required to preserve all evidence.
Christa Pike is awake after failed execution - attorneys07.10.26, 09:41 • 5030 views
In addition
Tennessee and other U.S. states have long struggled to obtain execution drugs. They cannot obtain them from major pharmaceutical companies because of a European ban on trade by companies that sell products for use in torture or executions.
Tennessee, like other states, turned to small, largely unregulated compounding pharmacies that produce small batches of drugs, promising to conceal their identities.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican who rejected Pike’s request for clemency and to have her sentence commuted to life imprisonment, called the failed execution a tragedy. He suspended executions for the rest of the year and promised to conduct an investigation.
Pike’s attorneys sought an alternative to lethal injection, saying their warnings that her small veins and related medical conditions could create a risk of complications had been ignored.

US Supreme Court hears challenge to air force UXO detonations in Guam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:16:07 UTC
03:16:07 KST

US Supreme Court hears challenge to air force UXO detonations in Guam
Advocacy group claims military sidestepped review of impact, says case highlights lack of representation in US territories.
The United States Supreme Court has begun hearing arguments in a case that could determine whether the US air force can continue to use a beach in Guam to detonate unexploded ordnance.
Wednesday’s hearing stems from a challenge by a Guam conservation group, Prutehi Guahan, which argues that the longstanding use of Tarague Beach to dispose of munitions may harm the ecosystem, damage an important cultural and historical site, and threaten the island’s water resources.
The case has gained attention for raising broader questions over the rights of residents of US territories, who cannot vote in presidential elections and have limited representation in the US legislature.
Guam became a US territory in 1898, in the wake of the Spanish-American Civil War. It has also served as a key US military hub in the western Pacific, hosting both Andersen Air Force Base and US Naval Base Guam.
The island has an estimated population of about 170,000.
Here’s what to know about the case:
What’s being challenged?
The case before the Supreme Court hinges on whether the US air force followed proper environmental procedures before applying for a new permit to continue to dispose of and destroy hazardous munitions – including bombs, landmines and missiles – at Tarague Beach.
The air force has used the beach for the detonations since 1982 and applied for a permit to continue in 2021. Guam’s Environmental Protection Agency did not “deny or approve” the permit, and detonations have continued.
At the centre of Prutehi Guahan’s challenge is whether the air force followed the law.
In applying for the permit, the air force adhered to the 1976 Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, which requires environmental regulators in US states and territories to regulate hazardous waste disposal.
Prutehi Guahan has also maintained that the air force must adhere to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, which requires federal agencies to conduct environmental impact assessments, including receiving community input, before undertaking major decisions.
What is the threat to Guam?
In court filings, Prutehi Guahan, which means Protect Guam in the Chamorro language, said the air force disposal range is located “on ancestral land that the military seized from local families after World War II”.
It added the beach is “adjacent to culturally significant fishing locations – upon which local families depend for sustenance – and contains sites for collecting traditional medicines”. The area is one of the oldest occupied sites in the region, with archaeological evidence dating back to the 2nd millennium BC, Prutehi Guahan noted.
Prutehi Guahan also said the detonation site sits “above an aquifer that provides drinking water to over 80% of the island’s population”.
The court filing detailed studies that found munition disposal and detonation can send fragments into the surrounding ocean and reef, while releasing toxic chemicals.
What has the air force said?
Government lawyers have maintained that the air force followed environmental review procedures under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, arguing the process “displaces” any requirements under the National Environmental Policy Act.
They have further argued that, because the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in Guam has not issued a final determination on the 2021 permit, the challenge from Prutehi Guahan was premature.
A US district judge initially sided with the air force and threw out the case after Prutehi Guahan filed its challenge in January 2022. The US Court of Appeals’ Ninth Circuit, the country’s largest federal court, later determined the case could move forward.
The air force then appealed to the US Supreme Court.
Why is the case significant?
Prutehi Guahan has underscored the significance of public feedback, which is required as part of environmental assessments under the National Environmental Policy Act.
In its filing, it pointed to a history of US government decisions about Guam made without input from residents, as well as a legacy of environmental damage. That includes two designated heavily polluted Superfund cleanup sites linked to navy and air force hazardous waste dumping.
“Decisions the military made nearly a century ago caused damage that still requires extensive and expensive cleanup,” the filing said. “And military decisions made more recently compound the damage Guam already bears”.
Writing for the SCOTUSblog which covers the US Supreme Court, Right to Democracy co-founders Neil Weare and Adi Martinez Roman said the case underscores the “unbalanced political relationship” between residents of US territories and the federal government.
“The people of Guam have little power or agency to influence federal decisions that impact their lives – which makes community consultation through federal laws like NEPA [National Environmental Policy Act] all the more important,” they wrote.

Trump administration plans to charge international students US$70,000 for work authorisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

03:14:13 KST

Trump administration plans to charge international students US$70,000 for work authorisation
- - The Trump administration plans to make international F-1 students pay at least US$70,000 for Optional Practical Training, or US$30,000 for extra work training.
- - DHS says the fee will “combat fraud” and protect US workers, but students now pay about US$500 and the move could block many from working in the US.
- - The rule may face legal challenges, and it must pass 30 days of public comment before a 60-day wait and possible final rollout.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed that international students pay at least US$70,000 (S$90,000) in training fees if they want to work in the country, according to a government notice posted online on Oct 7, as part of the Trump administration’s wider crackdown on foreign visa holders.
Under the proposal, non-immigrant students with F-1 visas would be required to pay US$70,000 to a certified institution for on-the-job training, known as Optional Practical Training (OPT), and US$30,000 for any additional work training.
DHS said the new rules were meant “to combat fraud, strengthen the integrity of the immigration system and protect US workers”.
Under the OPT system, foreign students can engage in work training for up to 20 hours a week while school is in session and for a limited time after graduation, with an additional allowance for those with degrees in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). Those who enrol are currently expected to pay around US$500.
“DHS is now setting a fee to ensure employers, students and institutions are engaging in appropriate activities consistent with admission as an F-1 non-immigrant,” the agency said.
Such training programmes often serve as a bridge for students seeking work under H-1B visas, which the Trump administration has also targeted with increased fees.
For decades, the H-1B programme has allowed young engineers and scientists from across the world, especially India and China, to turn years of study at US universities into high-paying jobs and a path to permanent US residency. Leading US tech companies have come to rely heavily on these workers to fill skilled positions.
When campaigning in 2024, President Donald Trump vowed to make it easier for foreign students to remain in the country, suggesting that they be automatically awarded a green card after graduation.
Like similar DHS proposals, the rule change is likely to face swift legal challenges.
“This proposed rule isn’t going to fare well in the courts, just as the US$100,000 H-1B fee and other restrictionist policies have been struck down,” Doug Rand, director of the Talent Mobility Fund, which works to attract foreign STEM professionals, wrote on LinkedIn on Oct 7.
The proposal is subject to 30 days of public comment before it can be finalised.
DHS said it would wait 60 days after the rule is finalised before putting it into effect to allow schools, students and employers time to prepare. REUTERS

Visiting Greece, Rubio says Western civilization is ‘at an inflection point’

Visiting Greece, Rubio says Western civilization is ‘at an inflection point’

====================================================================================================

US Secretary of State Rubio applies classical Greece’s lessons to modern political decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:13:06 UTC
03:13:06 KST

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke in Greece on the third anniversary of October 7, 2023. He spoke Wednesday against the epic backdrop of the Parthenon on the summit of the Acropolis in Athens. In his speech, he sought to channel the world of the ancient Greeks and contrast it with today’s world. His message was clear: It is in Athens and the Greek city-states that Western civilization has its roots. We must look to those roots, the way the Romans once looked to their swords after the sack of Rome in 390 BCE, to renew and defend our way of life.
Rubio’s speech is emblematic of the attempt of the American administration’s attempt to highlight the Trump doctrine. Rubio wanted to articulate the Trump administration’s underlying ideology and give a resounding speech that will live into the future.
This is a symbol of our time, like US president John Kennedy going to Berlin or US ambassador to the UN Adlai Stevenson speaking at the United Nations during the Cuban Missile Crisis.
The way of life of the ancient Greeks may seem foreign to us, Rubio noted, because our way of life has become obsessed with safety, in contrast to their feats. We don’t know the shame of defeat or the glory of victory. In this, he was also channeling the words of Teddy Roosevelt and the concept of the “man in the arena.”
America’s top diplomat talked about how the Western way of life has too often become about rewarding the average and the mediocre. He contrasted this with the Parthenon in Athens. The Greek city-states were filled with conflict and passion. They fought to distinguish themselves, and they worked on art and philosophy.
Rubio’s speech described the Greeks as creating a great civilization. Thumos is the Greek word for “spiritedness.” The US secretary of state contrasted their sense of spirit with how those in the West now teach their children to be ashamed of nationalism.
The West has decayed. We have transferred our sovereignty in some cases. “As the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and rivals only became more assertive,” Rubio said.
Today the West is at a crossroads. “The next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century,” he noted, querying whether the West will maintain its place at the head of the world or decline and find itself in servitude.
Act now, Rubio urged.
He said that under US President Trump, America is working toward national power and to rebuild its defense industrial base (DEB).
The United States will rebuild the economy and master new technologies such as chips, cyber, and drones. A new age of exploration in space is coming, Rubio added, in the ultimate expression of the Trump doctrine.
Willingness to use military force
The American politician also discussed the willingness to use force, referring to “the classical understanding of politics and statecraft that the Trump admin hopes to reclaim for our country and civilization.”
Rubio said he believes Europe can awaken from its slumber and rekindle its spirit. This means increasing defense spending and incorporating new manufacturing.
He praised modern Greece, noting that it has been a model ally of the US and saying that he hoped Europe would follow Athens’ example. This relates to Greek defense spending and its work on migration and other issues.
Recently, Greece began work on what it calls the Achilles Shield, a major defense initiative. Athens signed a deal with Israel in late August to acquire air defense systems such as Spyder, David’s Sling, and the Barak MX system.
The point that the US secretary of state was making is also linked to American history. He described how the US developed across the European continent: “Born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world.”
Rubio spoke about an inflection point in our civilization, adding, “The threats we face today are every bit as real as on the dramatic stage of antiquity.”
With the new competition between great powers and the wars, the US wants to rebuild institutions and alliances, Rubio said.
Today, Greece is one of America’s key allies in the Eastern Mediterranean. Another is Israel. Turkey is also a NATO ally of the US. The Trump administration has excellent relations with Saudi Arabia, Syria, and many other countries, too.
Rubio's speech helps show where the US administration's path
Rubio’s speech lit one more light along the dark road of the current global crisis. It helped point the way to where the US wants to go in the future.
He has tended to focus on certain parts of the Trump administration’s policies in particular. For instance, he has focused less on the Iran conflict and more on the doctrine in Latin America. He has focused less on Russia and more on other policies in Asia and Europe.
Yet in the Athens speech, Rubio explicitly criticized the “radical mullahs of Iran.”
He is one of the most articulate of the Trump administration’s top officials, in terms of explaining the president’s doctrine and harnessing history to it.
What does the Athens speech tell us?
In a world where the film Odyssey has been a resounding success, there is an appetite for learning about the ancient Greeks.
The Greeks are also not lost on discussions in Israel.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has spoken about the country becoming a kind of “super Sparta.” Israel channels many of the values that Rubio praised, such as being a nationalist country that defends its borders and has a strong defense industrial base.
Israel, as the country of the Jewish people, also has connections to both Western civilization and older civilizations in the Middle East.
Rubio’s speech in Athens was aimed primarily at a Western European audience. The idea of Europe waking from its slumber is not new. The continent has slumbered before, for instance in the years after the Great War (WWI), as well as in earlier centuries, such as the Dark Ages after Rome and during periods in the Medieval era.
Each time, Europe has managed to recover, just as Rome recovered after its sacking in the fourth century BCE.

“Given the incidents, it was acknowledged that there are serious challenges to protecting critical infrastructure. These threats are a direct consequence of the lack of prospects for a peaceful resolution to the military conflict''.
Iliana Iotova said CCNS members had also agreed to continue implementing the measures adopted by the Council of Ministers to counter risks and threats. ''The Consultative Council on National Security agreed on proposals to the executive and legislative branches, with the proposals being adopted by a three-quarters majority. Three parliamentary groups voted against. We condemn the attacks on merchant ships and call for an investigation to establish those responsible for the attacks”, Iliana Iotova added.
“An immediate ceasefire is the strongest guarantee of our security. Bulgaria must play an active role in this process,” the president also said.
“Bulgaria should urgently hold consultations with Romania and Türkiye on joint action to halt attacks on merchant ships in the Black Sea and ensure the safety of navigation. Bulgaria should take an active role in negotiations and in finding consensus among the countries bordering the Black Sea: Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia and Türkiye”, Iliana Iotova added.
PHOTO BGNES
It is also necessary to strengthen maritime situational awareness through the use of unmanned aerial systems for reconnaissance and surveillance, as well as to accelerate the modernization of the armed forces with the aim of acquiring counter-drone systems with kinetic capabilities, in close cooperation with NATO and the European Union.
According to the participants in the meeting, Russia’s war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration in the security environment in the Black Sea region.
Premier Rumen Radev
PHOTO BGNES
Following the meeting, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said that, at this point, there are no grounds for Bulgaria to categorically say that Russia was responsible for the strikes on vessels in the country’s exclusive economic zone. According to him, determining the origin of the drones used in the attacks should be based on concrete evidence rather than hypotheses.
The Prime Minister said that the government would propose coordination with Türkiye and Romania, while also seeking support from the US partners to investigate the area where the strikes occurred.
Particular attention will be paid to the vessel Able, which is still afloat, in order to determine the origin of the drones, Rumen Radev explained. He also announced that Bulgaria had had contacted the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) to request a free examination of debris from the sunken vessel. “Only then can we say what kind of drone it was and who carried out the attack”, Premier Radev stated firmly.
The Prime Minister stressed that, at present, there is no immediate threat to Bulgaria’s national security. “I cannot say that there is an immediate threat to national security. Of course, there are risks. A war is being waged not far from us. As I said, it is expanding its geographical scope. It has also entered the exclusive economic zone of the Republic of Bulgaria. But at this point, I can say that there is no direct threat to Bulgaria’s national security”, said Rumen Radev.
Ivaylo Mirchev
PHOTO BTA
“What became clear from the Consultative Council on National Security is that there are sufficient indications of clear Russian involvement in the sinking of one of the vessels”, said Ivaylo Mirchev, co-chairman of Democratic Bulgaria. He added: “I don’t remember anyone at the table having doubts that Russia was behind the attack.”
The MP also said that the text adopted by the Consultative Council on National Security was not supported by four parliamentary groups - Democratic Bulgaria (DB), We Continue the Change (PP), Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) and Vazrazhdane.
Stanislav Atanasov
PHOTO BTA
“The issue on which there was no consensus was who the aggressor is, and that is abundantly clear”, said Stanislav Anastassov of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS) parliamentary group following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security (CCNS).
Kostadin Kostadinov
PHOTO BTA
Vazrazhdane is calling for Bulgaria to act as a mediator in the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, rather than participate in policies that, according to the party, fuel the hostilities, said the party’s leader, Kostadin Kostadinov, following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security.
Nikolay Denkov
PHOTO BTA
Nikolay Denkov of We Continue the Change (PP) highlighted the vote on the CCNS statement, noting that four of the six parliamentary parties had voted against the document. Regarding the question of who was behind the attacks on the vessels, he stressed that the investigation should be completed before any definitive conclusions are drawn. According to him, the participants in the CCNS were united in their view that the investigation must be completed and that its findings should be provided to the relevant authorities.
The GERB–SDS parliamentary group was represented by GERB leader Boyko Borissov, who made no comment following the meeting of the Consultative Council on National Security.
The meeting was attended by the Speaker of Parliament, the prime minister, the ministers of defence and interior, the heads of the security services, and representatives of the parliamentary groups. The CCNS’s decisions are purely advisory and consultative, serving to foster political consensus and make recommendations on strategic matters related to the country’s security.

Four in five Russians view Putin as one of world’s most influential leaders — poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:09:47 UTC
03:09:47 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. An overwhelming majority of Russians (80%) consider Russian President Vladimir Putin one of the world’s most influential leaders, according to a study by the Analytical Center of the Russian Public Opinion Research Center (VCIOM).
The telephone survey was conducted on October 6, 2026, among 1,600 Russians aged 18 and over.
"Today, the Russian president celebrates his 74th birthday. To mark the occasion, the VCIOM Analytical Center conducted a study on the head of state’s role in strengthening the country’s position. An overwhelming majority of Russians recognize Vladimir Putin as one of the world’s most influential leaders (80%)," the center said on its website.
Only 17% of respondents disagreed.
About seven in ten Russians (71%) believe that Russia has become stronger during Putin’s years in office. Meanwhile, 69% said that his policies had prompted the international community to take Russia more seriously, while 68% expressed confidence that the country would overcome all difficulties under his leadership.
"Thus, Russians see the incumbent president as a guarantor of the country’s stability, strength and international influence, entrusting him with resolving the most complex challenges facing the nation," the study said.

Ukraine war latest: Russian attack on Pryluky kills at least 20, including 5 children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

Ukraine war latest: Russian attack on Pryluky kills at least 20, including 5 children
Key developments on Oct. 7:
- Russia slams Ukraine with missiles, drones on Putin's 74th birthday, at least 26 dead including 5 children
- Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
- EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
- Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, intelligence says
- Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin
At least 26 people have been killed in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities on Oct. 7, coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In the city of Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building, killing at least 20 people, including five children, and wounding at least 55, including seven children.
Three of the dead children, named Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhiy, were only one year old, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media. The other child was an eight-year-old named Maksym, he added.
A fifth child was killed by the Russian strike, as Ukraine's state emergency service (DSNS) said as of 7:13 p.m. local time.
"Today, as a 'birthday gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said.
"It was an ordinary five-story apartment block. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," he added.
Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said that on Putin's birthday, he hopes "the Russian dictator ends up in custody in The Hague or in hell."
"That is all he deserves."
Pryluky resident Halyna Osovyk, 55, woke up, and soon after, her flat was shaken by an explosion, she told the Kyiv Independent. Then came more strikes, smoke, and shattered windows. Across the road, two entrances of a neighboring apartment building were destroyed, and rescuers were searching the rubble for people.
The woman herself was still shaking as she spoke. Her hands and legs trembled.
"It was just sheer horror. And the sound of the missiles — you simply cannot put it into words," Osovyk said.
She knew some of those affected. One family was trapped under the debris – the mother, grandmother, and one child were killed, while another child was rescued and taken to the hospital. Another woman and her child were also pulled from the rubble and hospitalized, Osovyk said. As rescuers continued clearing the ruins, people waited for news of relatives who were still missing.
Pryluky had experienced Russian attacks before, she added, but never a morning like this. Asked what she would wish for Putin on his birthday, she replied: "I wish he could have what we are going through now."

Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia's Samara Oblast, according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.

EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
The European Commission announced the disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) of defense support to Ukraine on Oct. 7, part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv.
"Today's disbursement will help strengthen Ukraine's defense industry. And Ukraine's ability to defend itself. To protect people and infrastructure," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a press statement.
"The money will be spent on drones, drone interceptors, drone ammunition, and missiles manufactured by Ukrainian entities," reads the press release.
The EU's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, was intended to provide two-thirds of Kyiv's financial and defense needs until the end of 2027.
In 2026, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) was earmarked for defense, and Ukraine's plans for how to spend that money have all been submitted and approved by Brussels.

Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, intelligence says
Russia has stepped up efforts to disrupt Danish companies involved in supplying weapons to Ukraine, Denmark's intelligence service representative told Reuters on Oct. 7.
Josefine Christensen, an analyst at the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), said Russia was increasingly focusing on targets directly connected to Western military support for Ukraine.
According to Christensen, Russia planned a lot of operations in spring but carried out "very little," while in early summer they started to carry out "a lot more."
She added that Russia's operational boldness is growing as it is now trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line, meaning weapons production.
Russia is relying on individuals recruited online to conduct such operations. Some are first tasked with gathering information or photographing potential targets before being offered more serious assignments.
European drone manufacturers and suppliers have attracted particular attention. Christensen cited a list released by Russia's Defense Ministry in April that included European companies involved in producing drones and related components.

Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 7, telling him Turkey is ready to contribute to efforts for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, and stressing the importance of the safety of navigation in the Black Sea, according to Erdogan's office.
The two Presidents discussed bilateral relations, as well as regional and global issues, Turkey's Directorate of Communications said.
Erdogan also congratulated Putin on his birthday and his party's success in the latest Russian parliamentary elections, the office said.
The security situation for Black Sea shipping has worsened over the past weeks.
On Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.

68-year-old Russian who swam to Lithuania in search of asylum gets six years in prison after being returned home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:05:47 UTC
03:05:47 KST

The Baltic Fleet Military Court in Kaliningrad has sentenced 68-year-old Igor Odintsov to six years in a penal colony on charges of “publicly calling for terrorism.” In September, he tried to avoid a prison term in Russia by swimming across the Neman River and seeking asylum in Lithuania. Lithuanian border guards detained Odintsov and returned him to Russia.
A news release on the court’s website dated Oct. 1 identifies the defendant only by the first letter of his surname: “O.” The independent Russian news outlet Mediazona reported that the description could only match the case of pensioner Igor Odintsov, a resident of the town of Neman, located just across the Neman River from Lithuania.
“O.” was sentenced under Part 2 of Article 205.2 of Russia’s Criminal Code, which covers public calls for terrorism. The case reached the military court in September, but proceedings were suspended in the middle of the month after the defendant fled.
On Sept. 18, Lithuania’s border service reported that a “68-year-old Russian citizen” had swam across the river into Lithuania the previous day. Local border guards detained him at about 1:50 p.m., and he asked for political asylum. However, that evening at around 7 p.m., he was returned to Russia through a border checkpoint:
“There was no information indicating that he faced danger, had any special status, or might be admitted to the European Union, and he did not fall into the category of vulnerable persons… A decision was made not to admit him,” Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service said at the time.
Four days later, the court proceedings resumed. On Oct. 1, the man was sentenced. Sigitas Šamborskis, head of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad, confirmed to the Lithuanian newspaper Lietuvos Rytas that it was Odintsov who had been convicted earlier in the month:
“This is yet another betrayal. It’s very disgraceful on Lithuania’s part. It’s not just disgraceful, it’s downright criminal,” the newspaper quoted him as saying.

Two German parties draft resolution on ending aid to Ukraine and lifting Russia sanctions
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
21:05:00 EEST
03:05:00 KST

Two German parties draft resolution on ending aid to Ukraine and lifting Russia sanctions
Two German political parties, Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the Alliance for Social Justice (BSW), plan to pass a resolution in the regional parliament of Saxony-Anhalt calling for an end to military and financial aid to Ukraine and the lifting of economic sanctions against Russia.
Source: European Pravda, citing Der Spiegel
Details: Under the draft resolution, the state parliament (Landtag) should acknowledge that the policy of sanctioning Russia and providing weapons and financial aid to Ukraine has failed. An extraordinary session is to be held to pass the resolution.
The resolution calls on the regional government "to use all available means, including through an appropriate initiative in the Bundesrat, to make efforts to prevent further escalation of the conflict in Ukraine and to implement a policy aimed at establishing peace". According to the draft, the main focus should be on diplomacy. "An immediate ceasefire and the start of peace negotiations with Russia are necessary," the draft resolution states.
The normalisation of economic relations with Russia and the immediate lifting of economic sanctions against the Russian Federation are stated to be among Germany's objectives.
The effect of the resolution would be largely symbolic, as the main authority regarding aid to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia is held by Berlin and Brussels.
AfD politician Ulrich Siegmund, who intends to run for Minister-President of Saxony-Anhalt in December, said the parties are at last able to increase pressure on Berlin, "forcing it to finally make efforts to end the war rather than prolong it, and to spend billions in taxpayers' money on the people in our country and not weapons for the battlefields in Ukraine".
BSW founder Sahra Wagenknecht said Germany should focus on dialogue with Moscow "instead of contributing to an escalation that will sooner or later end in war". She accused German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of travelling to Kyiv with a "suitcase of money".
Background:
- BSW parliamentary group leader Thomas Schulze told the dpa news agency that a peace motion had been one of the party's election pledges: "We are now keeping this campaign promise. Magdeburg is sending Berlin a signal for a policy of peace."
- The extraordinary session of the state parliament is scheduled to take place on 14 October. Under the rules of procedure, such sessions must be convened if requested by a quarter of members.
- On 6 October, the state parliament held its first session in Magdeburg. AfD politician Tobias Rausch became the new speaker.
