Rubio urges West to rebuild strength as great-power competition returns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:03:38 UTC
03:03:38 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday warned that weakened militaries, outsourced industries and declining confidence had left the West vulnerable as the "great-power competition" returns.
Rubio argued that Western countries allowed rivals to gain ground by surrendering control of critical industries and transferring decisions to international institutions.
“In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay,” he said at the Acropolis in Athens.
As Western confidence faltered, adversaries became more assertive, building their wealth and power, he added.
“There is new competition between great powers again,” said Rubio, warning that states continued to compete for territory, technology, resources, markets and energy.
He said decisions taken in the next decade would determine whether the West retained its global position or faced decline.
Under President Donald Trump, Washington had chosen to restore control of critical supply chains, reindustrialize its economy and rebuild its defenses, he said, highlighting ambitions in artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, space exploration and military technology.
Europe urged to strengthen defenses
Rubio encouraged Europe to revive its ambitions, pointing to rising defense spending, expanded manufacturing and new partnerships following commitments made in The Hague last year.
“We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago,” he said.
He praised Greece as a “model ally” on defense, energy and migration, expressing hope that other European countries would follow its example.
Despite tensions between Washington and European capitals, Rubio urged both to preserve ties and strengthen an alliance capable of confronting shared threats.
He said institutions and alliances should defend the sovereignty of their members, adding that countries could recognize common interests while retaining distinct national identities.
Greenland deal presented as cooperation model
Rubio cited an agreement last month between the US, Denmark and Greenland as an example of his vision for transatlantic cooperation.
He said the deal would “reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO,” arguing that all three partners benefited and that Europe and the US emerged stronger.
“We want to win together. We must win together,” he said.
Drawing extensively on ancient Greek history, Rubio framed his appeal around national loyalty, ambition and a willingness to defend Western civilization, saying diplomacy must be backed by military capability and the credibility to use it.

Spanish unions call general strike over housing before snap election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:02:47 UTC
03:02:47 KST

Maricarmen dies at 87 after eviction sparked Spain housing protests
The general strike is the first to be jointly backed by Spain’s two largest unions in 14 years.
An 87-year-old woman whose eviction helped stoke nationwide protests over housing has died, Madrid’s tenants’ union said, as trade unions announced a general strike next month over housing issues, which helped prompt a looming snap election.
Maria del Carmen Abascal, known across Spain as Maricarmen, was evicted on September 23 after an international investment fund bought her building and raised her rent by more than 200 percent to roughly $1,880 a month, a move aimed at pushing out the long-term tenant to make way for lucrative tourist apartments.
Maricarmen had been hospitalised after being carried out on a stretcher from the apartment where she had lived for seven decades. Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez offered his condolences in a post on X.
“All my love to Maricarmen’s family and loved ones,” he wrote. “A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today.”
Following Maricarmen’s eviction, the Madrid Tenants’ Union organised protests and encampments in Madrid’s central Puerta del Sol square, drawing tens of thousands of demonstrators before spreading to dozens of other cities.
Strike ahead of snap election
Trade unions on Wednesday announced a nationwide general strike over housing issues for November 11, a few weeks before a snap election in which rising rents and evictions have become major campaign topics.
The country’s two largest unions, the Workers’ General Union (UGT) and Workers’ Commissions (CCOO), said the planned date still needs to be ratified by other unions. It will be the first general strike jointly backed by Spain’s two largest unions in 14 years.
“We cannot ignore the fact that housing is where most of our wages go. What is the point of raising the minimum wage if housing costs are rising three, four or five times faster?” Madrid Tenants’ Union spokesperson Valeria Racu said.
Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the Bank of Spain. The average rental price of 1,176 euros ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7 percent of a young person’s average monthly salary in Spain, Youth Council of Spain figures show.
In addition to protests, the failure last week by Spain’s government to pass emergency measures aimed at tackling the crisis prompted Sanchez to call an early election for November 29.
Sanchez’s main rival, conservative Popular Party (PP) leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, is seeking a chance at forming a government, while far-right Vox leader Santiago Abascal is positioning his party as a potential kingmaker.
The 54-year-old prime minister, who has been in power since 2018, goes into the election with opinion polls consistently putting him behind Feijoo. The conservative leader suffered a major setback when the party finished first in the 2023 general election without securing enough support from other parties to form a government.
Polls suggest Feijoo will not win an outright majority, meaning he will need support from Vox to govern.

EU reportedly agrees major expansion of Russia sanctions blacklist

EU member states agreed Wednesday to place more than 1,600 additional individuals and organizations under sanctions over Russia's war in Ukraine, Euronews reported.
The agreement reached by EU ambassadors would add 743 people and 826 entities to the bloc's blacklist over their alleged role in supporting Russia's war.
Another 77 lawmakers are set to face restrictions after standing in September's State Duma election in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, according to the report.
The decision followed weeks of negotiations and legal checks and is due to receive formal approval from EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg on Monday.
Those designated will face asset freezes and travel restrictions, while EU individuals and companies will be barred from making funds available to them, according to the report.
The agreement comes as European governments confront a series of suspected hybrid attacks which they attributed to Russia.
Brussels is also considering further designations following a drone incident at Leipzig airport in Germany.
The latest expansion will bring the total number of names in the EU's Russia-related sanctions list to nearly 4,650, according to the report.

The Guardian view on Conservative conference: struggling to break out of the comfort zone | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:02:22 UTC
03:02:22 KST

For a party that keeps losing elections, the Conservatives have enjoyed a remarkably upbeat conference in Birmingham this week. A party with a strong regicidal impulse is united behind Kemi Badenoch. Opinion polls show the leader’s personal ratings, while not spectacular, outperforming the wider Tory brand. Mrs Badenoch exuded confidence in her keynote speech on Wednesday, setting out what she believes is a path back to power.
The strategic focus is the economy. The Conservative leader expects Andy Burnham’s honeymoon to come to an end when his chancellor delivers a painful budget later this month. A spending review will then compound the pain, forcing grim trade-offs on a prime minister who has a reputation for deferring hard choices.
Mrs Badenoch presents herself as made of sterner stuff. By that she means she is prepared to say that an overgrown state does too much for too many people. What the Tory leader imagines to be fiscal courage is really ideological complacency pitched at her party’s comfort zone. The Conservative conference generated multiple commitments to cut taxes, mostly for upper-middle- and high-income families, alongside pledges to boost spending on defence and prison places, while also reducing the national debt. This is affordable, according to Mrs Badenoch, thanks to £70bn of “savings” the Conservatives claim to have identified in cuts to the civil service, regulators and working-age benefits.
It is a phoney equation that doesn’t account for the increase in costs to government once the social consequences of austerity become apparent. But the proposed reallocation of resources from mythical undeserving benefit-claiming idlers to enterprising but overtaxed middle-class families is a trusted campaign device.
Mrs Badenoch presents this agenda as “something for everyone”. In reality, she is trying to reach two particular audiences. The Tories need to attract voters in their former “blue wall” heartlands, now held by Liberal Democrats, and people who backed Boris Johnson in 2019 and then switched to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. These groups have very different attitudes, crudely represented by the polarised political identities that coalesced into leave and remain blocs – one nationalistic, the other more liberal – on the question of Brexit.
Mrs Badenoch spent two years courting the former camp with hardline positions on immigration and hostility to net zero climate policy. She has belatedly noticed the existence of people who are appalled by Mr Farage’s agenda. A significant passage in her speech on Wednesday rebuked Reform UK politicians who use a narrow ethnic definition of Englishness.
But mostly the Conservative leader talked about tax cuts, because she believes they appeal across the spectrum. That is often a reliable assumption, although the same plan didn’t help the Tories in 2024. Reckless pre-election giveaways succeeded only in poisoning the fiscal well for Keir Starmer.
The problem for the Conservatives then was that people didn’t trust them to govern responsibly or competently. This hasn’t changed. Mrs Badenoch thinks victory is available by attaching her personal brand to a classic Tory formula, unrevised for decades. Judging by the mood in Birmingham, her MPs and members agree. This is what happens when a party speaks to itself. A much harder test awaits when they have to speak to a country that remembers Conservative government well enough to be disinclined to listen.

Brain scans reveal opposite reward responses in ADHD and autism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:00:59 UTC
03:00:59 KST

Individuals with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and those with autism spectrum disorder both experience atypical responses to rewards, but their brain activity patterns differ in opposite ways. A new analysis reveals that while the two conditions involve the same deeper brain structures, they feature distinct patterns of heightened or reduced activity that could help explain their differing symptoms. The findings were published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry.
Processing rewards is a basic function that drives learning and survival. When a person receives a reward, specific brain networks evaluate its value and influence future motivation. Atypical responses within these systems are common in several neurodevelopmental conditions.
People with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, often show a high sensitivity to immediate rewards. This sensitivity is associated with impulsive behavior. When an individual with ADHD receives a reward, their brain may over-register the immediate gratification, making it difficult to wait for delayed outcomes.
In contrast, individuals with autism spectrum disorder, or ASD, frequently exhibit a reduced drive for specific rewards. This includes a lower sensitivity to social rewards, which can affect social engagement and interaction. They may not experience the same internal reinforcement from a smile or verbal praise that a neurotypical person does.
Because ADHD and ASD often occur together and share overlapping symptoms, researchers wanted to know if their reward-processing differences stem from the same underlying brain mechanisms. A research team led by Chunhong Zhu, Ting Xu, and Tingyong Feng at Southwest University in China conducted a systematic review to map these patterns. They sought to identify exactly how brain activity diverges when individuals with either condition experience a reward.
The researchers first performed a meta-analysis of 29 existing brain imaging studies. This combined dataset included 468 patients with ADHD, 424 patients with ASD, and 1,027 control participants. Each original study used functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan participants’ brains while they received either a monetary or social reward.
The team used specialized software to map areas of the brain that consistently showed abnormal activity across the studies. They found that both conditions involve altered activity in the amygdala and the putamen. These are deep subcortical brain regions that help process emotions and motivation.
The amygdala is generally responsible for recognizing motivationally important stimuli. The putamen helps the brain gauge sensitivity to a received reward. However, the nature of the alterations went in entirely opposite directions for each diagnosis.
In individuals with ADHD, these subcortical areas showed abnormally high activity during reward delivery. In individuals with ASD, the same regions exhibited unusually low activity compared to healthy controls. The two conditions also featured entirely distinct changes in the outer layers of the brain, known as the cortex.
Participants with ADHD displayed reduced activity in the prefrontal cortex and other areas responsible for impulse control and decision making. Participants with ASD showed heightened activity in medial prefrontal regions that assign subjective value to specific interests. To better understand these biological differences, the researchers conducted a second level of analysis using an independent database of healthy brain scans.
They looked at how the altered amygdala and putamen regions functionally connect with the rest of the brain. The brain regions that are hyperactive in ADHD were heavily linked to circuits that drive motivation and emotional responses. The regions that are hypoactive in ASD were more strongly wired to social and cognitive networks.
The team also used a large database called Neurosynth to match the abnormal brain maps with specific cognitive functions. Neurosynth contains data from thousands of published studies, allowing the researchers to see which psychological terms frequently overlap with certain brain areas. The hyperactive regions in ADHD matched with terms related to intense emotions.
The hypoactive regions in ADHD aligned with attention and executive control. For ASD, hyperactive regions were linked to social and value-related terms. The hypoactive regions in ASD matched with novelty and basic affective processing.
These patterns suggest that reward responses in ADHD are tied to emotional regulation challenges. In ASD, the responses point toward difficulties in integrating social and affective signals. Finally, the researchers compared their brain activity maps with known distributions of chemical messengers in the human brain.
They examined positron emission tomography scans showing where receptors for dopamine and serotonin are most densely located. Dopamine helps drive immediate reward-seeking behavior. Serotonin helps manage long-term goals and impulse inhibition.
The team found that the hyperactive regions in ADHD overlap with areas heavily populated by both dopamine and serotonin receptors. This chemical overlap in hyperactive emotion centers, combined with underactive impulse control centers, provides a physical map for impulsive behavior. The imbalance between a highly sensitive reward center and a weakened prefrontal control system makes delayed gratification difficult.
In ASD, the overactive value-processing regions sat in areas with very low serotonin transporter density. This might reflect a compensatory mechanism where the brain over-processes certain social or restricted reward signals. The underactive subcortical regions in ASD mapped onto areas rich in both dopamine and serotonin receptors, pointing to a general biological desensitization to rewards.
These findings provide a biological framework for understanding divergent behaviors in ADHD and ASD. However, the research does face a few limitations. The initial meta-analysis included a moderate number of studies, and it grouped different types of rewards together.
Social and monetary rewards may trigger slightly different biological pathways. Because of a limited amount of available data, there were not enough original studies on ASD to separate the reward types mathematically. Additionally, the brain connectivity analysis relied on scans from healthy individuals rather than patients with the conditions.
Mapping these exact networks directly in patient populations will be an important next step. Future research could also explore whether separating distinct reward types yields even more specific brain signatures.
The study, “Distinct neurobiological alterations during hedonic experience of rewards in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder: Multimodal evidence from neuroimaging meta-analyses,” was authored by Chunhong Zhu, Mercy Chepngetich Bore, Xueke Wang, Ting Xu, and Tingyong Feng.

The firm designs and manufactures its own range of radio accessories and distributes products from specialist manufacturers including OTTO Communications.

Jonathan the giant tortoise, 194, offers up insight into secrets of longevity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:00:02 UTC
03:00:02 KST

The ancient quest to extend human lifespan has received a boost after scientists analysed the genetic code of the world’s oldest living land animal, a giant tortoise called Jonathan.
The tortoise, which lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the governor of Saint Helena in the South Atlantic, is believed to be 194 years old, making him a contemporary of Queen Victoria and Charles Darwin.
Analysis of the animal’s DNA revealed a host of genetic variants in most of the biological pathways for ageing that scientists have discovered. Together, they help organisms to survive by repairing damaged DNA, regulating their metabolism and fending off cancer.
But more intriguing to the researchers were chemical patterns on Jonathan’s genes that appear to protect the healthy functioning of his mitochondria, the tiny battery-like structures that power biological cells. Ailing mitochondria have been strongly linked to ageing and age-related diseases.
“We’re still trying to work out how ageing occurs and Jonathan gives us a real window on to what happens over a long period of time,” said Stephen Clark, a senior researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation. “His mitochondria must be especially stable and that’s an insight into longevity in general. It’s important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.”
The insight came when the international team, led by Benjamin Vaisvil, looked at chemical tags that attach to DNA, creating patterns that change over time. The tags, known as methyl groups, typically silence the genes they latch on to.
Writing in Science Advances, the researchers describe how they compared the methylation patterns on Jonathan’s genes with those from other giant tortoises. The patterns on many of his genes were similar to those of other old tortoises, but the patterns on genes linked to mitochondrial function matched those from much younger animals.
It is unclear whether, or how much, the chemical patterning contributes to Jonathan’s impressive lifespan. Clark said the team now needed to validate the finding. “How do we test this idea?” he said. “Is there a way that makes the mitochondria young, or can we replace the mitochondria and see if it extends longevity? That’s one of the next steps.”
The former senior veterinary officer of Saint Helena, Joe Hollis, took over Jonathan’s care in 2009. He was not faring well at the time. Cataracts had left him blind, he had lost his sense of smell and his beak was soft and crumbly, making it hard to forage. Hollis began hand-feeding him and six months to a year later, the tortoise had regained weight and sported a hard, serrated beak.
In April, Jonathan was caught up in a viral crypto death scam when a message from a fake X account posing as Hollis claimed the tortoise had died. The news spread around the world before the Guardian made contact with Nigel Phillips, the governor of Saint Helena, who interrupted his bedtime routine to check on Jonathan. He found him asleep under a tree but “very much alive”.
Jonathan certainly appears to be enjoying life. A few months ago, he was found mating with Emma, who shares his paddock. Shortly afterwards, the wife of the governor, who is also called Emma, checked on Jonathan and found him upside down. “Emma [the tortoise] has a very semicircular shell,” said Hollis. “So if you slip sideways fast enough the momentum will flip you right over. It’s phenomenal though. He’s 194. You’re going to have an accident, aren’t you, at 194?”

What Singapore really thinks of Australian solar power export plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

What Singapore really thinks of Sun Cable, the Australian solar power export plan
Australia and Singapore are neighbours, but not exactly close.
As the crow flies, the distance from Darwin, the capital of Australia's Northern Territory, to the South-East Asian island nation is 3,400 kilometres — by most standards, a very long way.
And yet it is this distance over which an Australian energy company is vying to lay the world's longest subsea electrical cable in the hope of tapping into a green dream.
That company is Sun Cable, a renewable energy developer backed by Australian tech billionaire Mike Cannon-Brookes.
Sun Cable aims to generate colossal amounts of solar power in the endless, sun-drenched expanses of Australia's Top End, supplying Singapore's 6 million consumers via a 4,300km transmission cable through the Indonesian archipelago.
"I'm not aware of too many other projects on this scale," James Bowen, an energy and geopolitical analyst, said.
"I think we could safely call it a mega-project."
Ambition without equal
Indeed, the exact scope of Sun Cable's $35 billion ambition is hard to comprehend.
It would involve building solar panels to produce up to 10 gigawatts across as much as 12,000 hectares — an area twice the size of Manhattan.
Battery storage on a similarly massive scale would back up the solar farm when the sun was not shining.
Electricity would be transported 800km from the desert to Darwin, where some of it would support the local grid.
The vast majority, however, would be sent onwards to Singapore.
There, Sun Cable would supply up to 1.75 gigawatts of power, or about a quarter of the country's typical demand.
Amid persistent questions about the feasibility of Sun Cable's grandiose plans, the ABC travelled to Singapore to speak to potential customers.
Puah Kok Keong, chief executive of the Singapore Energy Market Authority, is the regulator of the nation's power and gas industries and one of its most senior energy officials.
Puah said his country's energy needs were intense.
He said air-conditioning in the famously steamy climate ran around the clock while industry chewed up as much as 80 per cent of power demand.
Added to the challenge of meeting that demand, he said Singapore wanted to become carbon-neutral.
Plus, Singapore is tiny — at fewer than 750 square kilometres, it is 13 times smaller than greater Melbourne.
"We have set for ourselves a goal of reaching net zero by the year 2050," Puah told the ABC.
"You can imagine for a small country like Singapore how difficult that can be."
'Cables, not pipelines'
Singapore, Puah said, was doing what it could within its own borders.
Solar panels are being installed everywhere — on roofs, on car parks and even on the city's reservoirs as floating installations.
But he acknowledged it was a strategy with severe limits.
Even with the feverish activity, Puah said solar only supplies about 3 per cent of Singapore's power, a figure unlikely to increase by much more than double.
To reach net zero by the middle of the century, he said Singapore had started to look further afield.
"We are also looking at importing electricity from around the region," he said.
"We have set for ourselves a target of importing up to around 6 gigawatts of clean energy from the region by the year 2035."
It is into this equation that Sun Cable hopes to insert itself.
Currently, Singapore gets about 95 per cent of its electricity from natural gas, more than half shipped into the country as liquefied natural gas (LNG).
The rest is sourced via pipelines from neighbouring Malaysia and Indonesia.
Christophe Inglin from the Sustainable Energy Association of Singapore said the island state would have to do with renewable electricity what it had long done with fossil fuels.
"We've imported the oil and gas," Inglin said.
"We can now import electrons.
"So instead of pipelines, we need copper cables. It's about transmission."
According to Inglin, Singapore already imports some electricity from Malaysia through a high-voltage transmission line, but these imports do not amount to much.
There are plans to dramatically increase the amount through a regional "super grid" that would much more closely weave together the electricity systems of South-East Asia.
Under such plans, Inglin said Singapore would be able to source hydro power from Laos, wind from Vietnam and huge amounts of solar from Malaysia and Indonesia.
"Without the regional grid, it wouldn't work," he said.
"So, it's very important.
"Obviously, the political will and the technology have always been there. They go round and round.
"But I think we're seeing breakthroughs coming now. It's in the interests of both the exporting countries and the importing countries, Singapore."
Stretching for the sun
Inglin said a South-East Asian network did not preclude Sun Cable, which declined to be interviewed for this story.
Australia borders the region, but he said the company faced long odds.
"I think the Singapore government and the EMA [Energy Market Authority] keep a very open mind on that," he said.
"They say, 'If you can do it, bring it in … there's a market here for that.'
"Of course, they face enormous challenges. The sunshine is the least of them. They've got that.
"But how do you build that subsea cable for a viable enough price to bring it to Singapore? So, let's see."
Warnings about the viability of such an immensely long cable are not lost on observers.
Bowen, who is the industrial decarbonisation lead for Australia at the Institute of Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, said the theoretical neatness of the cable idea ran into harsh geopolitical realities.
Besides being six times longer than the world's longest subsea electrical cable — the Viking Link between Denmark and England — Bowen said the Australia to Singapore cable would face arguably greater risks.
For one, it would run through the waters of another country, Indonesia, which is also one of the globe's most seismically active.
He said Singapore may also be unwilling to rely on a single cable responsible for the supply of so much of its electricity.
"Any time you have a single piece of infrastructure a country would be dependent on for its energy … there are risks to interdiction," Bowen said.
"We've always seen this around energy in general.
"Energy is just an inherently geopolitical concern, and countries are very careful … about how they calibrate their energy security strategies."
Puah from the Energy Market Authority echoed the comments.
"I think Sun Cable certainly faces quite a lot of challenges," Puah said.
"The distance, besides increasing the cost of the transmission, also means that the regulatory approvals needed for the path where the cable may come by from Australia through Indonesia to Singapore will need a lot of regulatory approvals."
Cost and opportunity
Perhaps more than security, Bowen said costs may be a bigger risk for Sun Cable.
He said people — and countries — were capable of accepting risks to the supply of goods or services, but only for the right price.
"We talk about energy security as being all about the physical security of supply," he said.
"But cost is really a massive factor for most countries, and they will actually take on a lot of risk, including geopolitical risk … if they're assured of low-cost energy."
It was a view shared by Lu Ming Pang, a senior analyst with Rystad Energy based in Singapore.
Lu said Singapore, as one of the richest countries in the world, had fired the starter's gun on a race to provide it with clean energy over the coming decades.
He said Sun Cable was just one horse in that race.
"We do see the supply of renewable energy sources from countries in Indonesia and Malaysia who are willing to supply through shorter grids into Singapore," Lu said.
"So I think also the economics of having close-distance transmission also competes with the Sun Cable."
Despite this handicap, Lu said the dream of exporting solar power from a huge country such as Australia to a tiny, densely populated and wealthy country like Singapore was likely to be an enduring one.
"In the long run, maybe in 10 to 20 years, that might be a possibility," he said.
"I do think that it is a very big opportunity for Australian solar power to be sold into a high-capital Singaporean market.
"The opportunity is there."
Puah Kok Keong, the head of Singapore's energy watchdog, was equally diplomatic.
Puah said the island nation was keeping an open mind and would be happy to take Sun Cable's power.
However, he cautioned it would not do so at any price.
"We will want to go for an energy source or energy technology that can check all the boxes of security, cost, and low carbon," Puah said.
"I think there's a good chance that [Sun Cable] can still happen. But, as I said, there are challenges that we have to overcome."

The New ChatGPT Is More Show Than Tell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

When you ask a chatbot a question, you’ll often get a wall of text back, maybe with an image or two pulled from the web. That may no longer be the case soon, as OpenAI overhauls how ChatGPT answers prompts.
On Wednesday, OpenAI unveiled an “Intelligent UI” update for ChatGPT that generates visual, custom elements—when helpful—for answering a user's questions. The company's new experience is powered by its recent GPT-6 model, which rolls out to paid users today and to free users tomorrow.
I got a quick test of the user interface before launch, and these visual elements felt like a welcome change. When I asked for a diagram of a slug, ChatGPT generated an anatomy-focused visual with buttons I could press for each different part, from the upper tentacles to the muscular foot. I also generated a San Francisco apartment affordability calculator with movable sliders to adjust income and other expenses, showing what percentage of my take-home pay different units would cost.
My favorite part of this quick hands-on with ChatGPT’s Intelligent UI was an airplane seat explorer. I’m not a fan of sitting in the exit rows, so I asked ChatGPT to generate a custom tool to compare the cabin layouts between four different Alaska and Delta planes. In its output, I could tap any seat on the map for more details, and ChatGPT highlighted the exit rows in green.
While useful in some results, every ChatGPT answer won’t suddenly include a chart or graphic. “We have a design team that spent a lot of time figuring out when adding a diagram, chart, or buttons adds value versus when it's starting to feel cluttered,” says Aarush Selvan, a product manager at OpenAI. If a user isn’t interested in visuals, they can tell ChatGPT to generate fewer of those outputs.
These visual results are similar to what Google announced earlier this year for Search when it expanded the bespoke results users may see. Google’s version is called “generative UI.” One example: If you want to better understand deep space, Search can output an adjustable graphic that breaks down how black holes work, using multiple sliders.
Chatbot experiences have increasingly become multimodal, meaning that text, images, and voice blend into one user experience. OpenAI's launch of an updated ChatGPT that's easier on the eyes and more interactive for over a billion users signals that the multimodal era is here. However, a larger shift toward generative user interfaces may spark an identity crisis for designers, as AI dictates more of what software looks like for individual users.
With AI tools now able to quickly generate custom software, the future of chatbots is further personalized and attuned to what I want to see, and what I want to see is slug diagrams. Good riddance to walls of text.

This is not an accident or a mistake - it is a deliberate, purposeful policy of terror against one's own people, against families, and against children. The Kiev regime has been killing civilians for years, destroying homes, schools and hospitals, depriving children of their childhood and future. There are lives, destinies and irreparable grief behind every such attack," she said.
Kravchenko said that there can be no justification for such actions. "Sooner or later everyone involved in these crimes will answer for what they have done," she added.
Earlier, Governor Vladimir Saldo said that Alexander and his daughter were killed 120 km from the contact line near the village of Rykovo. In June, Russian President Vladimir Putin personally presented Alexander's wife Tatyana with the Order of the Mother Heroine. She is currently expecting her fourteenth child. The family is known in the Kherson Region thanks to a small bakery they opened, which supplied bread to residents of the surrounding villages.

Israeli banks fear new sanctions over West Bank settlement financing: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:59:44 UTC
02:59:44 KST

Zein Khalil and Rania Abushamala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Israeli banks fear new international sanctions over financing settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank, particularly measures planned by Britain, Israeli daily Haaretz reported Wednesday.
The newspaper said the Association of Banks in Israel had prepared an assessment warning that anticipated British sanctions could affect Israeli financial institutions.
The measures could target entities involved in settlement construction or financing, extending beyond those implicated in violence by Israeli occupiers, according to the report.
Banks are declining to clarify whether they will provide guarantees to contractors seeking to participate in government tenders for the E1 settlement project between Jerusalem and the Maale Adumim settlement.
Located east of Jerusalem, the project aims to connect Maale Adumim to the city through the confiscation of Palestinian land, separating occupied East Jerusalem from the occupied West Bank.
On Sept. 8, 12 countries, including Britain, France, Spain and Canada, announced plans to prohibit trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories.
Britain also announced plans to expand its sanctions framework to cover individuals and entities involved in settlement construction or financing.
According to Haaretz, the British measures require legislation that could take six to nine months to pass.
Representatives of the banking association have met with officials from Israel's Foreign Ministry, central bank and Strategic Affairs Ministry to discuss concerns over the potential consequences.
The association's assessment warned that sanctions, if approved, could affect financial institutions linked to settlement expansion. International financial institutions could also tighten scrutiny of related transactions before the legislation takes effect.
The Bank of Israel expressed concern over the threat of sanctions, saying in a statement that the range of scenarios and implications is broad.
Banks have yet to clarify their position on financing or providing guarantees to construction companies participating in the E1 tenders.
"We have to be patient for another month and hope this issue calms down. Things may look different a week after the elections," Haaretz quoted a banking source as saying, referring to Israel's parliamentary vote scheduled for Oct. 27.
On Sept. 27, Israeli Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara postponed the deadline for submitting bids for the E1 construction tender by one month, leaving the remaining procedures until after the Knesset elections.
Israeli authorities had planned to put 2,167 settlement housing units out to tender on Oct. 25, in addition to 1,234 units included in a separate tender in August, bringing the total to 3,401.
About 750,000 Israeli occupiers live in 194 settlements and 400 settlement outposts across the occupied West Bank, including occupied East Jerusalem, according to official Palestinian figures.
The UN has repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, warning that they undermine prospects for a two-state solution.

The Guardian view on the US midterms: the cost of living is on the ballot, but this is about democracy too | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:59:43 UTC
02:59:43 KST

For once, Democrats and Donald Trump might be in agreement: “Pretend I’m on the ticket,” the historically unpopular president has instructed supporters. Midterms are in large part a referendum on the incumbent, and Trump’s war on Iran and its impact on the cost of living have boosted support for Democrats. With less than a month to go, they have reason to be upbeat. The party has a mountain to climb after the devastating defeats of 2024, and the gerrymandering of Republicans, but surveys give it a lead of about nine points on the generic ballot, which measures preference for parties rather than specific candidates.
Attention has turned from the prospects of seizing the House, where Democrats are forecast a clear majority, to what once seemed like the highly optimistic possibility of taking the Senate too. That would require flipping four seats, with 35 in play. Remarkably, Democrats are prospering in red states from Texas to Alaska. In Kansas – which Mr Trump carried by 16 points, and which has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932 – the race is neck and neck.
Even putting aside the ongoing questions about polling accuracy, there are very good reasons for caution. The first and most glaring is that the Democrats remain unpopular. Voters are being turned off the Republicans rather than drawn towards their rivals; pundits talk of a red undertow rather than a blue wave.
Second, the picture is extremely patchy. Democrats’ striking progress in key races where few had favoured them is tied to standout candidates and especially unpopular opponents – notably in Texas, where the Christian pastor and economic populist James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton, viewed unfavourably by a third of his own party’s supporters. Yet Democrats are struggling in some places where they initially had good reason for optimism, such as Maine. Third, the huge Republican spending advantage is now materialising – with $700m of advertising booked since the start of September.
Mr Trump, who has fared better than his party in elections, is hitting the campaign trail. He may make sure his base turns out. But candidates – including those who benefited from his endorsement – are increasingly distancing themselves from the president because he alienates others. He is visibly more energised by his construction projects than how his voters can pay their bills. His war on Iran looks not only reckless and ineffectual, but is pushing up prices. Strikingly, voters are now more likely to identify Republicans than Democrats as “elitist”. Latino voters who swung to him are changing their minds, with Immigration and Customs Enforcement excesses contributing.
Outrageously, Mr Trump has used taxpayer-funded adverts to laud his presidency. It goes without saying that he cannot be expected to respect the midterm results. The supreme court rejected his efforts to restrict mail-in voting – used by almost a third of the electorate – but he continues to smear it.
Just as he disrupts the electoral process, in office he rejects the norms and restraints that his predecessors recognised, and relies more and more on executive orders – seeking to avoid checks on issues ranging from war to vaccines. But should Democrats manage to take both House and Senate, they would regain both legislative control and investigative powers. In these elections, most votes will be driven by economic stress rather than democratic peril. But their outcome will be critical to the defence of American democracy – or its continued erosion.

Egypt ‘categorically’ rejects invoking Sinai in Israeli finance minister’s remarks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:58:23 UTC
02:58:23 KST

Rania Abushamala
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Egypt “categorically” rejected Wednesday dragging the Sinai Peninsula into remarks by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, an informed source told Egypt’s state-run Middle East News Agency (MENA).
Responding to a query about Smotrich’s statements during the last two days, the source said Egypt “categorically” rejects any attempt to invoke Sinai in his remarks.
The source described the statements as “empty threats,” noting that they coincide with Egypt’s celebrations marking the 53rd anniversary of its victory in the October 1973 war.
The source said the statements “did not warrant any further assurances regarding Egypt’s ability to protect its territory and safeguard its independence against any threats.”
The source described Smotrich’s remarks concerning Sinai and the displacement of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip as “a transparent attempt to use inflammatory rhetoric for electoral purposes.”
“The international community is fully aware that the Israeli occupation bears responsibility for making living conditions in Gaza nearly impossible in an attempt to push residents to leave their homeland and bring the Palestinian cause to an end,” said the source.
Egypt has not and will not accept this, and will not participate in it, the source added.
The source stressed that Egypt rejects having its name drawn into political posturing and maintains its opposition to interference in the internal affairs of any country.
Smotrich said Monday that Egypt would lose the Sinai Peninsula if it attacked Israel.
“What would make Egypt not attack us? The understanding that if they attack us, there will be no Sinai at least,” he said in a video interview from his home.
His comments came on the eve of Egypt’s commemoration of the 1973 war, which paved the way for the eventual return of Sinai following years of Israeli occupation.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said Monday that the Egyptian armed forces remained ready to defend the country, its resources and national security “at all times and under any circumstances.”
Egypt and Israel signed a peace treaty in Washington in March 1979 following the 1978 Camp David Accords. The treaty ended the state of war between the two countries and provided for Israel’s withdrawal from Sinai.

Short trip options
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
20:58:20 EEST
02:58:20 KST

Short trip options
Kyiv • UNN
Kamianets-Podilskyi, Zakarpattia, and Chernihiv region offer fortresses, canyons, thermal pools, and historical landmarks.
The modern pace of life rarely leaves an opportunity to take a full-fledged vacation for several weeks. However, there is no need to wait for summer or a long-awaited break. Short trips lasting 2–4 days are an ideal way to change your surroundings, gain vivid impressions, and emotionally recharge without significant financial expenses or complicated planning. UNN will tell you how an ordinary weekend can turn into a real adventure.
Ukraine has countless amazing places that are ideal for short trips. Regardless of what you are looking for — relaxation in thermal pools, walks through ancient fortresses, or excursions through canyons — Ukrainian routes can surprise everyone.
Kamianets-Podilskyi and Bakota
Kamianets-Podilskyi is famous for its medieval fortress, which seems to rise from the rocky canyon of the Smotrych River. The first day should be devoted to walking around the city, visiting the Old Castle, the Turkish Bridge, observation decks, and cozy cafés.
Kamianets-Podilskyi is famous not only for its castle. In the city, you can visit the Town Hall, the oldest surviving town hall in Ukraine, with a clock tower, dungeons, and interesting museum exhibitions on Polish Market Square.
A unique structure in world architecture is also located here — the Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul. It combines a Christian church, a triumphal arch, and an Ottoman minaret crowned with a sculpture of the Virgin Mary.
You can also descend to the foot of the cliffs to see a picturesque wooden church dating back to the 18th century and admire the steep slopes from the Novoplanivskyi Bridge or Swan Lake.
On the second day, head to Bakota — a flooded village in the Dniester Canyon that has now turned into a real "Ukrainian sea."
A special microclimate prevails here, and the high cliffs offer a panorama of an endless expanse of water. Be sure to visit the region’s oldest monastery, the St. Michael’s Cave Monastery, located directly in the white limestone cliffs.
The Thermal Waters of Zakarpattia
If your goal is maximum relaxation and recovery, Zakarpattia will be the best choice. Visit Palanok Castle in Mukachevo, located on the summit of an extinct volcano, which offers views of the city and the mountains.
Although Palanok Castle is the most famous in Zakarpattia, it is not the only one. St. Miklosh Castle, located in the village of Chynadiiovo, is the medieval "castle of love" of Ilona Zrinski and Imre Thököly, where you can walk through dimly lit corridors and feel the spirit of the era. There is a large park on the castle grounds.
Head to Berehove or Kosyno, which are famous for their thermal pools with a high mineral content. Bathing in hot springs under the open sky offers a feeling of complete relaxation at any time of year.
Of course, you can round off the weekend at a restaurant serving authentic Zakarpattian cuisine to fully immerse yourself in the atmosphere of the region.
Chernihiv Region
For a peaceful vacation filled with history, Chernihiv Region is a good choice. Chernihiv itself is one of the oldest cities in Ukraine. Chernihiv Rampart is the city’s historic heart above the Desna, with 12 cast-iron hetman’s cannons, an ancient collegium, and park alleys.
The Antonii Caves and the Trinity Monastery: an underground monastic complex dating from the 11th–18th centuries, located in the Boldyn Hills, with underground churches, chapels, and unique acoustics.
You can visit the Kachanivka National Historical and Cultural Reserve. It is a magnificent 19th-century palace and park ensemble with a white-columned palace, mirror ponds, and a park where Shevchenko and Gogol were guests.

====================================================================================================

UK Prime Minister Burnham's October 7 op-eds show a gap between rhetoric and reality  - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:57:43 UTC
02:57:43 KST

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has penned two op-eds to mark the third anniversary of October 7 and show support for Jews facing antisemitism, but there is a lack of understanding of where that antisemitism comes from and the way in which his own government has contributed to it.
Writing in The Jewish Chronicle and Jewish News on Wednesday, Burnham acknowledged the pain of the Jewish and Israeli communities.
His language is empathetic: Burnham speaks of those “senselessly killed by Hamas terrorists” and speaks of October 7 as the “deadliest day for the Jewish people since the Holocaust.”
Both pieces speak of the “disturbing” rise in antisemitic behavior in the UK, and incidents such as the Heaton Park synagogue terrorist attack last year.
Burnham reassures the Jewish community that the government stands with them and that “abuse is not tolerated in our streets.”
He then sets out measures being taken by his government to combat Jew hatred, such as increased protection for synagogues, schools and community buildings.
Burnham also acknowledges the role of hostile states “peddling lies and conspiracy theories about minority communities” and the “poison spreading online and teaching young people to recognize attempts to radicalize and divide them.”
Lack of acknowledgment of links between anti-Zionism, antisemitism
On the surface, the op-eds tick all the boxes, but beneath the rhetoric there is a lack of clarity and specificity. The hate, although acknowledged, is not named.
Neither article meaningfully addresses the relationship between antisemitism and contemporary anti-Israel or anti-Zionist activism, despite Burnham’s observation that overseas conflicts can rapidly become domestic sources of hostility. Nor do they examine the political movements, demonstrations or slogans that have generated some of the biggest debates on antisemitism since the Hamas attack.
This, in turn, allows Burnham to frame the issue primarily through the language of security and cohesion while avoiding the more politically divisive debate over Israel and Gaza.
The distinction is also apparent in his treatment of Britain’s Jewish community. In the JC, Burnham addresses Jewish readers directly, offering reassurance that the government will “protect” them. In Jewish News, the Jewish community becomes part of a much broader argument about the status of British society.
Burnham, the political saviour of Jews
The rhetoric correspondingly becomes more sweeping. Burnham argues that “division is a threat to our security” and that allowing antisemitism to take root makes Britain weaker. The article ultimately moves from a promise to protect Jewish communities to a commitment to transform the country itself: “We will do more than just remember. We will change this country.”
This progression places Burnham himself increasingly at the center of the narrative, and the repeated emphasis on “we” will do and “I will act” reinforces his role as the political savior.
Taken together, the two articles serve two overlapping purposes.
The first is to reassure British Jews that their security is being treated as the government’s responsibility. The second is to establish antisemitism as part of a broader political argument about national resilience, foreign interference and social cohesion.
Burnham’s central proposition is that protecting Jewish institutions cannot be separated from protecting Britain as a whole. But what is less developed is how that broader diagnosis translates into confronting the specific political and ideological sources of antisemitism in contemporary Britain.
UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank
The contrast is striking given Burnham’s recent approach to Israel.
In September, his government imposed measures targeting Israeli settlements in the West Bank, with Burnham defending the decision by arguing that continued settlement expansion could make a two-state solution unviable.
The measures came despite repeated and forceful warnings from Jewish community leaders that sanctions could have “unintended consequences” for British Jews.
Burnham has maintained that there is no contradiction between confronting antisemitism and putting pressure on the Israeli government, but that juxtaposition raises a political tension at the heart of his October 7 message: while presenting himself as a defender of British Jews against hatred linked to the conflict in the Middle East, his government is simultaneously adopting increasingly punitive measures against Israel, measures that Jewish communal representatives have warned could feed into the very climate of anti-Israel hostility and the antisemitism he declares he wants to combat.

WATCH: Families of victims of Oct. 7 hold national ceremony in Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:57:38 UTC
02:57:38 KST

The main ceremony organized by the families of victims of the October 7 massacre is being held in Tel Aviv's Yarkon Park on Wednesday.
The ceremony opened with singer Arkadi Duchin performing “Who Loves You More Than Me,” as participants reflected on the lives lost and the memories that have stayed with Israel since.
Duchin was filmed playing a piano placed in the Kipnis family home in Kibbutz Be’eri, where Eviatar “Teri” Kipnis and Lilach Kipnis were murdered, along with Paul Vincent Castelvi, Teri’s devoted caregiver.
Images of those murdered and fallen were projected behind Duchin. Standing beside him was Or-Li Niv, the mother of Staff-Sgt. Omri Niv Feierstein, a soldier in the Home Front Command’s Search and Rescue Brigade who fell in battle at the Zikim military base. Niv read the poem “Mothers” by Osnat Eldar.
Actress and comedian Shani Cohen spoke about what was lost that morning and the memories that have remained with the country ever since.
“And on that Saturday morning, we lost so much,” she said. “We lost some of the innocence we had, and our hearts burned.”
She recalled those who pleaded for help from safe rooms that were set ablaze and from crowded roadside shelters, as well as the desperate messages that became the soundtrack of an unimaginable reality and of people’s final moments.
“Tonight, we will stop to remember everything we lost, and also to ask what has remained within us since then,” Cohen said.
Eli Sharabi spoke of the children who hid for hours inside closets, those who were forced to hold their breath to protect young lives, parents who turned their bodies into human shields, and those who said goodbye in a short text message.
He also recalled neighbors who became like brothers, members of local security teams, and civilians who stepped forward without asking questions.
Sharabi referred to all those who fell in the October 7 war and to “those who saw the abyss open before them and remained human.”
He called on Israelis to remember and tell the story of what happened on the day when “the sky fell on us,” concluding: “We will remember them all and never forget. This is a ceremony of the people, created thanks to the people and held for the people.”
Opening memorial prayer recited by Ido Yakir
Later in the ceremony, Ido Yakir, a member of Kibbutz Magen’s local security team, recited a special Yizkor memorial prayer. Members of the team fought on the morning of October 7 and prevented terrorists from infiltrating the kibbutz. Two members of the team, Ofir Yaron and Avi Fleischer, were killed in the fighting.
“May the people of Israel remember its sons and daughters, the loyal and the brave, people of labor and peace, victims of the massacre of the Black Sabbath of 5784,” Yakir began.
The prayer remembered those murdered in their homes, in the fields, and on the roads of the western Negev, parents who tried to save their children, and partygoers who fled from terrorists.
“Those fallen whose bodies were taken into captivity, and those who were abducted alive and died in captivity,” he recited.
“We will remember the brave-hearted who came to the defense,” Yakir continued, mentioning members of local security teams, female and male soldiers at bases along the border, members of the security and rescue services, and civilians who rushed to help those under attack and were killed.
“We will remember all those who lived along the frontier, civilians and soldiers, strangers, residents, and guests, who with their bodies became our border. May those who fell on the Black Sabbath be sealed in the heart of Israel from generation to generation.”
Alongside the memory of those murdered and killed, the prayer was also dedicated to those left to cope with the loss. Survivors of the horrors, children, those wounded in body and mind, orphans, widows and widowers, and communities that were forced to leave their homes.
“Those rebuilding the ruins, returning to their land like streams in the Negev, and those whom the horrors of the past and the memory of their loved ones do not allow to return,” Yakir recited.
He concluded: “May the mourning neither fall silent nor find consolation nor fade until Israel dwells securely and in peace on its land, from generation to generation.”
Rabbi Beni Kalmanson, father of the late Elhanan Kalmanson, recited the Kaddish. On October 7, Elhanan set out with his brother and cousin to save lives, and fell in the fighting in Be'eri. This evening, his father stood at the memorial ceremony and spoke on his behalf:
"I stand here in the name of my son Elhanan, who sprang into action, fought, and fell for his people and for the sanctification of God’s name," Rabbi Kalmanson said before reciting the Kaddish. "For unity among the people, for overcoming divisions, for mutual responsibility among us, and for the struggle for what is good and worthy in the world."
Recounting those who fought to save others
Later in the ceremony, Shani Cohen and Eli Sharabi dedicated remarks to those who went out to fight and save lives amidst the chaos of the morning of October 7. Cohen described the moments in which, facing the horrific images, there were those who realized the responsibility fell upon them:
“Amid the chaos of the morning of October 7, against the backdrop of images of the border fence being trampled, white pickup trucks driving through Sderot, and heartbreaking live streams of entire families being murdered before our eyes, heroes emerged in the field who realized that if not them, all was lost; it was on them.”
Sharabi continued, describing the decision to head into battle even without organized orders:
“Without organized orders, they took responsibility upon themselves, left their homes, leaving families locked in the safe rooms, rushed out from command posts, police stations, and protected shelters, not out of a sense of heroism, but simply because they understood that this was them, this was what they had to do.”
Cohen mentioned the late Major Ido Shani, deputy commander of the Nahal Reconnaissance Battalion, and the order he relayed over the radio that morning:
“The late Major Ido Shani, deputy commander of the Nahal Reconnaissance Battalion, was, on the morning of October 7, the officer in charge of the Kerem Shalom–Sufa sector. At 6:43 AM, with the first barrage of rockets, he declared over the radio: ‘We are at war. Everyone to defense in their sector, kill terrorists, good luck.’”
Afterward, she spoke about the battle in which he fell, saying, “Minutes later, Ido ran into an ambush against terrorists and was killed in battle facing them.”
Ivri Lider and Eden Golan performed "The Song About the Land" (HaShir Al Ha'Aretz). Later, a video was screened in memory of two transport drivers who set out to rescue civilians on October 7: Abed Al-Karim Nasasra from Kuseife, who was murdered in a terrorist ambush on Route 232, and Haim Ben Aryeh, the legendary transport driver of Gush Katif, who evacuated children from Be'eri to the Dead Sea. The horrors to which Haim was exposed broke his spirit, and he took his own life at the end of October 2023.
After the performance, Youssef Nasasra said his brother Abed set out to rescue partygoers from the Nova festival despite the danger: "It doesn't matter, I know it's dangerous, but these people, they have to be brought back." Irit Ben Aryeh, Haim's widow, shared that she had asked him not to go. His answer was: "If I am needed, I am going."
The ceremony also featured a video honoring Camp Shura volunteers who helped identify those killed on October 7, Maariv reported. Sharabi paid tribute to the soldiers, police officers, emergency personnel, and volunteers who recovered and identified victims and helped bereaved families obtain answers.
Dr. Milkha Chesler, a volunteer dentist in the Israel Police’s casualty identification unit, described feeling a personal connection to every victim. Rabbi Menachem Perl, another volunteer featured in the video, spoke of the lasting emotional toll of the work.
'Without investigating the truth, we cannot repair'
Their testimonies were followed by Omri Shifroni's, a co-founder of the "Kumu" movement, who addressed the ceremony and spoke directly to his family members who were murdered at Kibbutz Be'eri. Shifroni is the uncle of Liel and Yanai Hetzroni and the nephew of the late Aviya and Ayala Hetzroni. Facing the crowd, he recalled the helplessness of that morning:
“My beloved family, you didn't have to be murdered. None of you. You were alone, defenseless, and I couldn't help either.”
From his family’s loss, Shifroni turned to the shattered trust during those agonizing hours waiting for help, saying, “That morning, the systems collapsed; the state failed to function. During those long hours in the safe room, the trust that had anchored us shattered to pieces. But there was also something else. Fighters pressed forward, broke through, and finally arrived. Civilians showed up with all their hearts, and we felt the full power of Israeli mutual solidarity.”
Alongside this mobilization, Shifroni demanded answers. In his words, the path to healing and rebuilding trust requires a full reckoning with what occurred:
“Yet mutual solidarity alone is not enough. To rebuild trust, we also need the truth. We must know what happened. Without investigating the truth, we cannot repair, and we cannot ensure that this will never happen again.”
Later in the ceremony, a video was screened in memory of the late Karin Journo, who was murdered in the “Ambulance of Death” along with 17 partygoers from the Nova festival. Her mother, Inbal, recalled the memories that remained with her: the birth, the first tooth, childhood, and the joy of life. From there, she turned to the final message and the 11 days during which the family still did not know what had become of her.
“I remember the day my Karin was born. I remember her first tooth, suddenly, beneath that little smile, a single white tooth peeked out. And after that came an entire life. A child, a girl, a young woman. School, girlfriends, the army, work, laughter. My Karin grew up, and I remember everything. I also remember the moment she told me she was going to the party, even with a broken leg. I remember the last message, with the last words. I remember the 11 days and nights of suffocating uncertainty and the fear of hoping. I haven’t forgotten for a single second the knock on the door with the shattering news that from my baby girl, whose teeth had only just come in yesterday, only three teeth remained. Three.”
Mother of Siman Tov family says they were 'abandoned and murdered'
Later in the ceremony, a video was screened in memory of the members of the Siman Tov family, who were murdered in their home in Nir Oz. Reuma Kedem, mother of the late Tamar Kedem Siman Tov, was filmed visiting the ruined family home. Against the backdrop of footage of the house, her voice was heard saying, “Enough with war. Enough of this bereavement, enough of the pain. In this burned home, my family, the Siman Tov family, was abandoned and murdered.”
Kedem also spoke of the lives that were meant to continue, of the young girls who should have been starting third grade, and the little boy who should have been going to kindergarten:
“I drift between worlds. I have family in heaven, and I have family on earth. Arbel and Shahar were supposed to enter third grade, and Omriki was supposed to go to the Tut kindergarten. There is no boundary to this pain, and there is no end to the sorrow.”
Yuri and Rosa Yadgarov's testimony
After another musical number, the story of Yuri and Rosa Yadgarov from Ofakim was presented. They had lived together for 55 years and were murdered in front of their only son, Mark. Shani Cohen described how a quiet family morning was shattered by sirens, and how the attempt to reach a shelter ended in the murder of both parents:
“Shabbat, Simchat Torah, Ofakim. Quiet. Yuri and Rosa Yadgarov with their only son, Mark, during a family morning. Suddenly, sirens, relentless rocket barrages. Mark runs outside to open the door of the communal shelter; Yuri and Rosa try to reach him. But a white pickup truck pulls up at the entrance to the building. Yuri is shot first and falls to the ground. Seconds later, they shoot Rosa, and she falls beside him. Mark, whose parents are being murdered before his eyes, is wounded by shrapnel, but manages to flee into the shelter and survives,” Cohen recounted.
'So many love stories cut short'
Eli Sharabi reflected on their 55 years together and on the love stories cut short that day:
“For fifty-five years, Yuri and Rosa lived together. On October 7, so many love stories were cut short, lovers murdered embracing in safe rooms, in living rooms, in the fields, on the dance floor, in vehicles, and on the sides of the road, trying to protect one another until their very last breath.”
Forty-six hostages were taken alive and never had the chance to return: they were murdered by Hamas or mistakenly killed by IDF fire. A segment of the ceremony was dedicated to their memory, opened by Shani Cohen with the words:
“The hands that reached out from the darkness pleading for help returned empty. They were not returned to their homes; they were returned for burial.”
Adi Marciano, mother of surveillance observer (tatzpitnit) the late Noa Marciano, addressed her daughter, speaking of a motherhood abruptly cut short and a grief for which she could never have prepared:
“My beloved Noa, for nineteen years you taught me what motherhood was, but you didn’t teach me what it means to be a bereaved mother. You didn’t teach me how to be a mother to a child who was abducted from us and never returned. Just like me, neither did the mothers of the 17 surveillance soldiers and combat fighters who were murdered and were there with you on that Shabbat, the last time we spoke.”
From her own personal pain, Marciano turned to the other families who had waited for their loved ones' return. She described the vigil beside the phone and the door, and the embrace they envisioned but never received:
“And like you, another forty-five hostages were taken alive and never made it back. They held on for weeks and months. In darkness, in fear. Clinging to life, waiting for someone to come save them. And all that time, their families waited by the phone. By the door. Imagining that moment, that embrace. But the opportunities were squandered. We didn’t get our loved ones back; we received them for eternal rest. And we also received a new family: the family of bereavement.”
The memory of Aryeh and Eli Ozan, who were murdered in a shelter at Zikim Beach
Another video was dedicated to the memory of the late Aryeh Ozan and his son, Eli Ozan, who were murdered in a public shelter (migunit) at Zikim Beach. Lihi Ozan, Eli’s daughter and Aryeh’s granddaughter, was 12 years old when she received the news, a week after October 7. For a moment, hearing they had found her father, she thought he had been found alive:
“They woke me up with the news. My older sister woke me up and said, ‘They found Dad.’ And I thought they had found Dad. But then I realized they had found Dad’s body, not Dad. And I was thrust right into it, boom, at 12 years old, and I didn't know anything about life,” she recounted.
Ron Ozan, Aryeh’s son and Eli’s brother, spoke about the twins he has, named after his father and brother. Alongside the new life, he spoke of the two men who are missing from it: “They aren’t here to see this.”
As Roni Dalumi and Tamir Grinberg performed the song “Regards from Another Life” on stage, hostage survivor Eli Sharabi, hosting the ceremony, addressed the family he lost. He read personal words he wrote to his late wife Lianne and daughters Noiya and Yahel, who were murdered in their home at Kibbutz Be'eri, and to his late brother Yossi Sharabi, who was killed after being abducted to Gaza.
Sharabi spoke of their presence in his life even inside the tunnels, on the day of his release, and now, as he stood on stage. Out of that longing, he spoke of the choice to keep living and remembering:
“My beloved ones, it feels strange to send regards to someone who is no longer with you, but in truth, you never left me for even a single second. You were there day after day with me inside the tunnels; you were with me on the day of my release, and you are with me right now. I promised you we would do everything so you would never be forgotten, and I stand here confident that you hear me. So know this: I do not forget.
Israel does not forget you. You are here every single day, every hour, and every moment. I love you, and I will never stop missing you. You give me the strength to keep living, by choice and out of the conviction that evil must never be allowed to win. I chose life because living means that I remember. Remembering every moment we shared together. Regards from another life.”
Sharabi brought the ceremony to a close with a call to action, imploring people "to remember what happened. To investigate what happened, not to cut corners. Not to let time blur the truth. Not to rewrite history, and not to let history repeat itself."
"Only if we truly remember can we learn," he continued. Sharabi went on to say the Israel "can build a safer, more worthy, better place here. That is our hope."

Mecca defense pact puts Turkey’s commitment to Saudi under domestic scrutiny - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:57:25 UTC
02:57:25 KST

The decision to activate Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan's Mecca Joint Defense Agreement (MJDA) is sparking debate within Turkey. While Ankara is advancing military assistance to defend the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia against attacks from Houthi terrorists, the Turkish opposition is demanding clarification of the legal basis for sending forces and is warning against being dragged into a war in Yemen.
At the same time, a Wednesday report by Middle East Eye reveals details of the planned assistance, from air defense systems and electronic warfare to pilots, aircraft, and the deployment of Turkish commandos.
The dispute sharpened following the emergency meeting held in Riyadh on Monday. The respective foreign ministers, defense ministers, and military chiefs of the three countries decided to immediately begin implementing the mutual defense commitments and prepare for the rapid deployment in Saudi Arabia of the agreed-upon forces and capabilities.
The decision was intended to strengthen preparedness against the threats, military coordination, and the joint defense capability. However, the announcement left key questions unanswered, including how many soldiers will be sent, which systems will be deployed, what each country's contribution will be, who will command the forces, and when the deployment will begin. The duration of the mission and the conditions for either expanding or ending it were also not clarified to the public.
The MJDA has still not been brought before the Turkish parliament for approval, and sources told Turkish media outlets it may be submitted soon. Turkish MP Namik Tan demanded clarification as to whether the document is a binding defense agreement, a memorandum of understanding, or a joint declaration, and asked how it can be implemented before lawmakers approve it.
Turkey's former Israel ambassador queries legality behind Mecca pact before Ankara's parliament approved it
Tan is a member of the opposition Republican People's Party (CHP). He previously served as Turkey's ambassador to both Israel and the US, respectively.
Turhan Comez, a senior member of the Good Party (IYI), warned that the developments could lead to Turkish soldiers being sent to the deserts of Yemen to defend Saudi Arabia against the Houthis, and claimed that the government is acting in violation of the constitution.
Retired Turkish Rear-Admiral Yanki Bagcioglu also warned of an operational risk, namely that if Turkey takes part in offensive activity or direct fighting in Yemen, its forces and commercial ships could become Houthi targets.
Middle East Eye cited two Turkish sources who said that technical teams, air defense systems, and electronic warfare equipment have been in Saudi Arabia since last year, for the protection of critical infrastructure and energy facilities. Ankara is preparing to add equipment, technicians, emergency response teams, and accompanying combat forces.
At a later stage, subject to parliamentary approval, a limited number of Turkish military commandos may be sent, as well as experienced pilots and aircraft to deal with drone and ballistic missile attacks. The described defense targets are Riyadh, the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, and the western section of the East-West oil pipeline, which runs from Abqaiq in the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
Saudi sources said that the activity would be coordinated at a joint base run by Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, alongside a separate base for the Turkish command. A senior Turkish official said that a 2010 training agreement allows a limited technical presence, but that further reinforcement requires parliamentary approval. According to him, approval for sending the forces may be advanced before ratification of the Mecca Alliance. The same official also clarified that there is no plan to send a large force or to intervene directly in Yemen.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said after the meeting in Riyadh that a meeting to advance the alliance's institutions had already been planned, but that the developments between Yemen and Saudi Arabia required an emergency gathering. According to Fidan, they discussed options to support Saudi Arabia's defense alongside ways to resolve the crisis through dialogue. He described the Saudi approach as constructive and noted that the decisions reflect the wishes of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Gular and military chief Selcuk Bayraktaroglu also took part in the meeting. Fidan said that the two contributed to the military, operational, and technical discussions. He noted that the work to establish the alliance's permanent institutions is close to completion. During the meeting, Pakistani Lt.-Gen. (ret.) Nauman Mahmood was appointed MJDA secretary-general for a three-year term.
What is the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, and when was it signed?
MJDA was signed on August 7 by Erdogan, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud, and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
It stipulates that an armed attack on one of the three countries will be considered an attack on all of them, and seeks to expand security cooperation and joint deterrence. At the time of the signing, the Turkish presidency presented the agreement as one that is not directed against any particular country.
In the statement from Riyadh, the three countries condemned the attacks on cities, civilian facilities, and economic infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, as well as attempts to strike Mecca and Medina. They framed the move toward practical measures as a test of the credibility of their mutual defense commitment and a way to strengthen deterrence.
The remaining gap is between the decision to provide assistance and the definition of the mission: the details that were revealed describe the defense of Saudi territory, but questions regarding command, authority, and the scope of involvement still accompany the move. The debate in Ankara is expected to examine how to implement the commitment to Riyadh, and what the limits will be that would prevent it from expanding into fighting inside Yemen.
