The burden of proof is on Chiang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:44 UTC
01:44:44 KST

On Saturday last week, Taipei City Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) wrote on Facebook a post criticizing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator and Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) for a 2014 op-ed on drug policy. The post amassed an astonishing 500,000 comments in less than 24 hours.
Chiang said the flood of activity was orchestrated by the ruling party. If he wishes to make such claims, Chiang cannot simply point to the volume of comments as evidence; he must look a little closer.
Amid the backlash, KMT Taipei City Councilor Chang Szu-kang (張斯綱) shared a DPP supporter’s post on X featuring a screen grab of himself programming a script to comment on the original post to “deal with” the number of comments being deleted. At most, this proves that people could have used bots to leave comments on the post, but there is no indication of what proportion of comments they might account for, how much traffic was due to coordinated behavior, or who implemented any of it. There is also no evidence to suggest that any accounts involved had ties to the DPP.
Chiang claimed that Threads had 90 million registered users in Taiwan, disproportionate to its population size of 23 million.
The Taiwan FackCheck Center has said that the 90 million figure is not from Meta’s official statistics. It was from a miscalculation in a report from the US market research company Resourcera, which mistook Taiwan’s share of traffic as a share of user accounts in its workings. Resourcera has since acknowledged the error and removed the statistic from its Web site.
In sum, Chiang’s first accusation offered no definitive evidence, while his second simply repeated debunked information. We can be certain that 500,000 comments is a startling number. However, we cannot be certain that someone posting about building a comment bot is grounds to dismiss the entire outcry as being the result of green-camp online armies and ruling party power privileges.
As the election heats up, Chiang must accept the burden of proof for his accusations seriously and point to verifiable accounts, coordinated behaviors or official platform data that support his case. Old pieces of misinformation do not suddenly become compelling simply because the mayor quotes them; nor should they be used to give unproven political allegations a second run.
Steve Ho is a retired engineer.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Four are indicted for surveilling Shen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:43 UTC
01:44:43 KST

Prosecutors yesterday sought an 18-month prison term for a man accused of accepting HK$99,950 (US$12,735) from two people in Hong Kong to surveil Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Puma Shen (沈伯洋) in 2024.
Taipei prosecutors sought the sentence for private investigator Cheng Yung-chin (鄭永津), who was charged along with fellow private investigator Hsieh Yi-chen (謝乙辰) and two others over the surveillance of Shen, the DPP’s Taipei mayoral candidate in next month’s local elections.
Cheng, Hsieh and Hsieh’s employees, Chiang Wen-hsin (江文鑫) and Hou Kai-han (侯凱瀚), were indicted on charges of illegally collecting and using personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act (個人資料保護法), prosecutors said.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
Cheng was allegedly hired by Hong Kongers Kuk Kok-yin (鞠覺賢) and Lam Hing (林慶) on Sept. 5, 2024, to surveil Shen, prosecutors said, adding that Cheng received the money via bank transfer that day.
Cheng then subcontracted the job to Hsieh for NT$180,000, and Hsieh assigned Chiang and Hou to conduct the surveillance, prosecutors said.
Hsieh’s employees initially struggled to surveil Shen because Shen had hired personal security, prompting them to propose parking a scooter with a miniature camera under its seat outside Shen’s residence, which Cheng approved, prosecutors said.
The suspects recorded Shen’s and his family’s movements from Oct. 1 to Nov. 8, 2024, and sent the footage via Telegram to Cheng, who forwarded it to Kuk, also using Telegram, prosecutors said.
Chiang and Hou at times stayed in a vehicle outside Shen’s residence to monitor his movements and those of his wife and daughter, they added.
Meanwhile, Kuk and Lam entered Taiwan multiple times starting in September 2024, but are not currently in the country, they said.
Prosecutors yesterday issued arrest warrants for them on the same charges under the Personal Data Protection Act.
After becoming suspicious of the scooter, Shen’s security personnel reported it to the Taipei Police Department’s Daan Precinct in late 2024. It was referred to the prosecutors about a year ago.
Cheng repeatedly downplayed his role during questioning and showed no remorse despite eventually admitting the offense, warranting a harsher sentence, prosecutors said.
As Hsieh, Chiang and Hou admitted to the offenses and expressed remorse, acknowledging that their actions had violated Shen’s privacy, and also said they hoped to have an opportunity to apologize to Shen and seek his forgiveness, prosecutors asked the court to impose appropriate sentences on them.
Shen yesterday said that he has always taken his security seriously, and was saddened by the personal attacks from Taiwanese politicians and influencers who have downplayed China’s surveillance of him.
He said he had told police that he was concerned the incident could be linked to a foreign entity, as he has frequently been criticized or otherwise targeted by China, even before entering politics.
Before becoming a legislator in January 2024, Shen researched and organized international forums on civil defense and national security, activities that he said Beijing strongly disliked.
As an associate professor of criminology, Shen helped establish the Kuma Academy, a nonprofit civil defense organization focused on preparing Taiwanese for a potential Chinese invasion.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office on Oct. 14, 2024, added Shen to its list of “die-hard Taiwanese independence” separatists, citing his role in Kuma Academy.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Taiwan’s urban renewal needs a human focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:41 UTC
01:44:41 KST

As skyscrapers claw at the sky across the nation’s major cities, urban renewal efforts continue. Planners face a daunting environment. Nearly 60 percent of the housing stock is over 30 years of age, with Penghu, Yunlin and Chiayi counties exhibiting the highest average building ages, all over 40 years. In Taipei, 673,000 residences — over 70 percent of all homes — are over 30 years old, with an average age of 39.1 years. Taiwan’s shining office towers conceal a world of aging homes badly in need of replacement.
Rising housing prices are killing more than just the future of Taiwan’s young. They are also making urban renewal projects vastly more expensive and riskier. At the same time, construction costs are rising. The result is that many projects are being abandoned.
ABANDONED PROJECTS
Photo courtesy of the National Housing and Urban Regeneration Center
A recent piece in a United Daily News (UDN) series on urban renewal, “Urban renewal is not what you think,” looked at two typical projects. One was a 140 ping project involving an old building in Taipei’s Daan District (大安). Initially the developer thought the project would go for a good price, but as construction costs rose, the developer abandoned the project and the site was put up for auction.
The second case took place in Taipei’s Songshan District (松山). There the residents had taken it upon themselves to contract out the cost of replacing their building and had all moved out. Their construction company had estimated the project at NT$200,000 per ping, but the cost rose to NT$300,000 per ping, too much for the residents.
Urban renewal projects are more costly for construction companies because of the presence of the residents. In an ordinary project, if the construction firm experiences a NT$10,000 per ping rise in costs, it can just raise the selling price NT$10,000. However, urban renewable projects are often split, with residents receiving two-thirds of the sale price and the construction company one-third. This implies that if costs per ping rise NT$10,000, the price per ping must rise NT$30,000 for the construction firm to cover the cost increase.
Photo courtesy of the New Taipei City Bureau of Urban and Rural Development
INCREASED COSTS
Costs are in fact increasing. The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said early last month that the overall price index for construction projects rose 6.54 percent year-on-year in August, remaining at its highest level since July 2022. The increase was driven by an 8.12 percent year-on-year increase in wages, nearing a five-year high. Demography is having its day: construction industry labor shortages, domestic construction investment and factory construction demand, are pushing up demand for labor and in turn, salaries.
The problems in the two cases discussed above are being replicated across Taipei. The Liberty Times, our sister paper, reported that, based on statistics from the Taipei City Construction Management Office, by the end of July, Taipei had approved 1,079 projects under the dangerous and old buildings reconstruction scheme, while at least 188 approvals (17.42 percent), one in every 5.74 projects, had become invalid.
One problem identified in the UDN series on rising construction costs in Taipei is that the city benchmarks construction costs. Currently the 2024 benchmark cost for a 15 story building, according to a construction industry official quoted, is NT$204,000 per ping. However, the actual cost is NT$285,000.
Moreover, financing rates have risen. Banks face higher risk of non-performing loans in real estate and their provisions for loan non-performance are higher. The result is higher financing costs for urban renewal (The financial industry has proposed lowering the provisioning requirement for qualifying redevelopment loans, but the Financial Supervisory Commission has not endorsed that proposal.) Since urban renewal projects generally take long periods for permitting and construction, the result is rising project costs unforeseen by any of the participants.
A key reason for this is that Taipei’s projects are on average much smaller than those of other cities. Smaller projects are more likely to stall when construction costs rise because their initial construction costs are higher. Out of the 188 dead projects, 132 involved sites 150 ping or less.
The government has established subsidy programs to bring older buildings up to modern earthquake regulations and extend their lives. But only a few thousand buildings have been processed this way, out of well over 5 million needing renewal.
BIRTH RATES
In Kaohsiung the city has integrated its urban renewal program and the semiconductor industry’s southward expansion. According to the Liberty Times, city government officials announced that the program around the R17 World Games MRT station allocates to the city government a 17-story mixed-use building, with housing for industry employees, high class office space, commercial facilities and public childcare. Three other buildings are planned as 21-story residential and commercial facilities, with childcare facilities. A skybridge will connect an adjacent block to the MRT station, and the project calls for taking advantage of the green spaces around Banpingshan (半屏山). The project takes advantage of the large space available for “urban renewal.”
The recognition that child care should have its own designation in the complex is a step forward. But an irony of urban renewal is that demand for housing will almost certainly slump within a decade or two.
Births last year hit a record low of 107,000, with something like 1.8 million for the period 2015-2025. Who is going to live in all those residences needing renewal? Couples from that cohort will not be seeking to purchase homes until after 2050. The government might be better off simply knocking down all the old housing and putting in greenspace, or single family homes where possible. That will help sustain housing prices as well.
The public policy changes proposed by the various parties involved all focus on keeping it sustainable for the construction and real estate firms — rearranging the subsidy regime to maintain things the way they are. If planners view urban renewal as something that markets should determine, then they will get the spaces that markets build: sterile and inhuman, filled with empty immensity. These policy approaches merely replace existing dense housing with updated dense housing, or as Kaohsiung is doing it, with futuristic glass-and-steel building complexes that look like something out of the high-class areas of a dystopian science fiction tale (where, for example, will the street vendors hang out?).
The fundamental program with urban renewal in Taiwan is that it does not address the urgent problems of human living. It does not create livable, walkable environments with enjoyable, energetic atmospheres constructed out of the everyday, organic behavior of its residents, with small shops, street vendors and needed services right at hand, accessible by walking from single family, detached homes.
It goes without saying that those things could increase marriage and birth rates. Shouldn’t that be a foundation of public policy in Taiwan?
Notes from Central Taiwan is a column written by long-term resident Michael Turton, who provides incisive commentary informed by three decades of living in and writing about his adoptive country. The views expressed here are his own.

COVID and flu vaccines should go together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:41 UTC
01:44:41 KST

The Taiwan Association of Family Medicine (TAFM) yesterday urged eligible vaccine recipients to get seasonal flu and COVID-19 vaccines, rather than one or the other, to better protect their lungs and heart.
As the first phase of the government-funded flu and COVID-19 vaccination program began on Thursday last week, the TAFM yesterday invited actor Chen Mei-fen (陳美鳳) and Centers for Disease Control (CDC) Director-General Philip Lo (羅一鈞) to help raise public awareness of the issue.
Lo said more than 1.329 million doses of flu vaccines and 482,000 doses of COVID-19 vaccines have been administered in the past six days, an increase of 24 percent and 55 percent respectively compared with the first six days in last year’s program.
Photo: Pan Shao-tang, Taipei Times
Among older people who received a flu vaccine, about 50 percent also received a COVID-19 vaccine, which is an improvement from about 37 percent in past years, he said.
As the CDC on Tuesday said flu and COVID-19 are still in their epidemic period, and severe flu cases and flu-related deaths confirmed last week were still relatively high, Lo said the high public willingness to get vaccinated is expected to help bring down local viral activity, so the flu epidemic period might end early next month, while the COVID-19 epidemic might end this month.
The CDC purchased 2.3 million doses of COVID-19 vaccines for the program this year, including 200,000 doses of Novavax’s vaccine, which is undergoing lot release testing, and should be available before the end of the month, he said.
Although public vaccination willingness is relatively high this year, Lo said the centers still urge people aged 65 or older and other high-risk groups to get vaccinated against the flu and COVID-19 as soon as possible, as they are more prone to developing severe complications after infection.
The fatality rate of those with severe symptoms from COVID-19 is about one in five people, he said, adding that more than 80 percent of people who died were not up to date on their vaccines.
TAFM chairperson Huang Chen-kuo (黃振國) said some people might recall discomfort from getting a COVID-19 vaccine from a few years ago and are unwilling to get vaccinated, but the new updated COVID-19 vaccine has a smaller dose, reducing physical discomfort.
TAFM member Wu Chih-hsing (吳至行), a medical professor and physician, said the vaccines take about two weeks to build up full protection, so people should not wait until the epidemic worsens to get vaccinated.
Older people and people with underlying conditions are encouraged to get both vaccines, rather than only getting one, he added.
Wu said studies have suggested that contracting the flu or COVID-19 can increase the risk of cardiovascular events, so vaccination not only reduces the risk of severe respiratory illnesses, but also reduces the risk of stroke and myocardial infarction (heart attack) from infection.
There is no telling when one would get infected, Chen said, relating the case of a neighbor who runs a home hair salon and recently contracted COVID-19. They developed serious symptoms, and as their whole family contracted the disease, they had to close the salon for several weeks.
She encouraged those who are eligible for vaccination to “invite each other” to get flu and COVID-19 vaccines together, to “protect their lungs and heart,” as well as earn “health coins.”

Coast guard ships arrive in Palau
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:40 UTC
01:44:40 KST

Two Coast Guard Administration (CGA) patrol vessels have docked at Malakal Harbor in Palau as part of an expedition exercise and diplomatic visit, during which a senior official is expected to meet with Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr, the agency said yesterday.
The two vessels, the 4,000-tonne-class Chiayi and the 1,000-tonne-class Penghu, set sail for Palau from Taiwan last week and arrived on Tuesday at Malakal Harbor, the CGA’s Fleet Branch said in a statement.
The journey marks the second time the CGA has dispatched a “friendship fleet” to another country, after it sent its first-ever goodwill fleet, comprising the Hualien and Taipei patrol vessels, to Palau last year.
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
During the visit this week, a delegation led by CGA Deputy Director-General Hsu Ching-chih (許靜芝) is expected to meet with Whipps and take part in friendly pickleball and swimming competitions with local officials, the statement said.
The two sides are scheduled to attend a banquet aboard the Chiayi, during which a Double Ten National Day reception and a joint flag-raising ceremony are scheduled, it said.
Afterward, the two vessels are to conduct a joint patrol with Palauan law enforcement units as part of a bilateral coast guard cooperation agreement signed in 2019, it said.
The mission included professional training to test vessel performance and coordination between the two ships, the branch said.
The trip is significant for Taiwan’s international maritime cooperation and “coast guard diplomacy,” it said, adding that the CGA will continue to establish international partnerships.

Elon Musk said his business empire would build and operate Terafab independently, quashing speculation about industry leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) swooping in to run his ambitious chipmaking venture.

Freedom is knowing the country is behind you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:38 UTC
01:44:38 KST

The FBI has arrested Wanying “Heather” Zhang, a California real-estate agent who US authorities allege acted at the direction of the Chinese government to surveil and photograph President William Lai’s (賴清德) eldest son and his family.
She is accused of collecting information such as their home address, vehicles and license plate numbers. If the allegations are proven true, it would be transnational repression, something that democratic societies must confront.
The incident has drawn much attention, because it involves Lai’s family, but what is concerning is not simply who was being followed. The issue is whether Taiwanese abroad can be free from surveillance and threats with political motives. Today, it was the president’s family; tomorrow, it could be government officials, businesspeople, academics, international students or even ordinary Taiwanese.
Taiwanese should not be afforded different levels of safety based on their status. Condemnations from the Presidential Office, the Mainland Affairs Council and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs are entirely appropriate. If the government fails to express its stance in the face of cross-border actions that threaten the safety of citizens, the other side could take advantage of its tolerance.
However, condemnation should not be the end of the matter, but a starting point for institutional reform. The US investigation is being carried out under US law; it is not simply acting to protect the Taiwanese government. If a foreign government uses agents to secretly carry out operations and collect information on people in the US, its law enforcement agencies should uphold the rule of law and protect national security. This is a reminder to Taiwan that national security threats do not necessarily involve spies exchanging secrets, as depicted in movies. It could be as little as a person watching someone’s home, or a single cellphone.
Taiwan should establish reporting mechanisms for citizens abroad who are targeted by surveillance or threats, bolster the exchange of security information with democratic partners, and review whether laws are adequate to effectively prevent and hold foreign actors accountable for illegal surveillance, harassment and intimidation. The harm caused by transnational repression is not just that someone is following you; it also has a chilling effect — making people fear that their families could become entangled, and being afraid to speak out, participate in public affairs or live their lives freely.
The difference between democracy and authoritarianism can sometimes be as simple as being able to walk down the street without constantly looking over your shoulder. What Taiwan needs is not louder condemnation, but for every citizen to know that, whether at home or abroad, whenever their freedom is unlawfully threatened, the nation has the institutions, channels and capacity to stand behind them.
Chen Ching-yun is a former director of the Legislative Yuan’s Bureau of Legal Affairs.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Groups urge ministry to expand menstrual leave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:36 UTC
01:44:36 KST

Groups yesterday urged the Ministry of Education to allow students two days a month of menstrual leave, up from the one-day limit.
The one-day policy does not reflect “real bodily experiences,” the groups — including the Taiwan Engagement Association for Youth and the Student Alliance for Gender Equality — told a news conference titled: “Whose period lasts just one day?”
The ministry in 2014 recommended one day per month of menstrual leave, in line with the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women, but the system needs better protections for students, association secretary-general Wang Chi-an (王齊安) said.
Photo: CNA
The number of days allowed, how often leave can be taken and supplementary measures fall short of what students need, Wang said.
The average menstrual cycle varies between 21 and 35 days, and menstruation does not necessarily occur just once per month for shorter cycles, EdYouth Taiwan advocacy officer Wan Yi-fan (萬儀梵) said.
However, menstrual leave can only be taken once per month, meaning students risk poor attendance and grades, and might not be able to take make-up classes or exams, Wan said.
Surveys have showed that although the ministry has petitioned education providers to allow menstrual leave, many have yet to implement the guidelines, Student Alliance for Gender Equality proposal team convener Chen Chia-yi (陳佳儀) said.
Some institutions instead count extra menstrual leave as general sick leave, which requires supplemental documentation, while they do not allow students to take make-up classes or exams, Chen said.
Some students have even been reprimanded for requesting additional days, she said, adding that such policies are not in line with Article 15 of the Gender Equity Education Act (性別平等教育法).
The leave allowance should be increased to two days per month without requiring students to provide supplementary documentation, there should be no required interval between leave days and schools should be permitted to offer more days off, she said.
The ministry should also consider ensuring that education providers do not deduct attendance points or reduce grades over menstrual leave, she added.

Sharp increase in CPI likely temporary: DGBAS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:33 UTC
01:44:33 KST

Taiwan’s consumer prices rose at the fastest pace in 31 months last month, driven largely by a surge in vegetable costs after heavy rainfall, although the government said the increase was temporary and did not signal broad-based inflation.
The consumer price index (CPI) increased 2.73 percent from a year earlier, marking the fifth straight month above the central bank’s 2 percent inflation target, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics (DGBAS) said yesterday.
Vegetable prices contributed 0.53 percentage points to the overall increase, DGBAS Department of Statistics Deputy Director Tsai Hsiu-hui (蔡秀慧) said.
Photo: CNA
Because vegetables can generally be replanted and harvested within about a month, the price shock is likely to fade quickly, she said.
“We expect the increase in inflation to be a short-term phenomenon, with the CPI growth rate likely to ease in October,” Tsai told a news conference in Taipei.
For inflation to be considered entrenched, price increases need to be broad-based, significant and persistent, Tsai said. While some items posted sharp gains last month, the overall data did not meet all three criteria, she said.
Transportation and communications costs rose 4.07 percent, the most among the major CPI categories. Fuel prices jumped 12.72 percent from a year earlier, while airfares rose 13.83 percent as higher fuel surcharges and airport service fees pushed up travel costs amid tensions in the Middle East, Tsai said.
Prices of education and entertainment equipment, including computers and related products, climbed 9.75 percent, the fastest increase in 44 years, as memory prices surged.
However, Tsai said that such products have a relatively small weighting in the CPI and are not purchased frequently, limiting their impact on overall inflation.
Food prices increased 2.64 percent, with restaurant meals up 3.04 percent as heavy rainfall pushed up costs of agricultural products. Housing costs rose 2.38 percent, led by a 1.72 percent increase in rent and higher household gas, electricity and management fees.
Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 2.52 percent from a year earlier, indicating that underlying price pressures remain somewhat elevated.
This month, consumer inflation is expected to ease partly because of a shift in the timing of the Mid-Autumn Festival, which fell in September this year, but October last year, Tsai said.
Even so, CPI growth is likely to remain above 2 percent this month, while the outlook for vegetable prices would depend largely on weather conditions, she said.
Producer prices also accelerated sharply last month, as the producer price index (PPI) rose 18.12 percent from a year earlier, driven by higher prices for petroleum and coal products, computers and electronic and optical products, chemicals, pharmaceuticals and electronic components, the DGBAS said.
Higher natural gas prices charged to industrial electricity users also contributed to the increase, it said.
In the first nine months of the year, CPI rose 1.94 percent from a year earlier, while PPI increased 10.16 percent, DGBAS data showed.

Prosecutors yesterday indicted a university student accused of accessing Taiwan High Speed Rail’s radio communications system and sending a false alarm that prompted four trains to make emergency stops in April.
The Taoyuan District Prosecutors’ Office sought a two-year prison sentence for the student, surnamed Lin (林).
A second man, surnamed Chen (陳), was indicted for allegedly helping Lin access the system.
Photo: Cheng Shu-ting, Taipei Times
Lin used a radio programmed with the system’s parameters to access its TETRA network — a digital radio standard used by railways and emergency services — at Taoyuan High Speed Rail Station at 10:27pm on April 5, prosecutors said.
At 11:23pm that day, while aboard a bus near Taichung High Speed Rail Station, he allegedly transmitted a “General Alarm” signal, they said.
The operations control system automatically relayed the warning to nearby trains, prompting the drivers of three passenger trains and one out-of-service train to manually apply their emergency brakes, they said.
The incident caused delays totaling 48 minutes, they added.
After receiving a report from railway police on April 13, investigators searched three locations associated with Lin on April 28, seizing radio equipment and electronic devices, they said.
Chen allegedly supplied the radio and the system parameters, but prosecutors found no evidence that he knew Lin intended to transmit the alarm.
Lin faces charges under the Railway Act (鐵路法) for allegedly exploiting vulnerabilities in a critical railway communications system and disrupting its operation.
Chen was charged under the Criminal Code with helping Lin gain access to the system.
Prosecutors said Lin acted out of curiosity about radio technology, but his actions disrupted railway operations and affected passengers’ rights.

Unions need better rules: advocate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:30 UTC
01:44:30 KST

Labor advocates yesterday called for reforms to make unions easier to organize in Taiwan, saying that stronger collective bargaining is needed to tackle persistent low pay among young workers beyond annual minimum wage increases.
Speaking at a news conference in Taipei honoring the annual World Day for Decent Work, Taiwan Labor and Social Policy Research Association executive director Chang Feng-yi (張烽益) said Taiwan’s unionization rate among employees has long remained below 10 percent, citing structural barriers, including the 30-person threshold, for forming a union.
“The threshold for workers to join unions is high, and the risks they face are also high,” Chang said.
Photo courtesy of Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Lin Yueh-ching’s office
Chang proposed moving toward a more pluralistic union system in which a union receiving majority support from workers could obtain collective bargaining rights.
Taiwan Labour Front Secretary-General Yang Shu-wei (楊書瑋) said that one change would be to allow outside industrial and professional unions to enter workplaces to recruit members, a practice he said is permitted in some other countries, but not in Taiwan.
Although starting salaries for young workers had gradually risen in the past few years, much of that improvement had resulted from minimum wage increases, he said.
Taiwan’s minimum monthly wage is NT$29,500 and increases to NT$30,900 from Jan. 1 next year. The ministry generally defines young workers as those aged 15 to 29 in its labor statistics.
“Companies need a mechanism for systematic wage increases. This cannot be addressed solely through minimum wage increases,” Yang said, adding that greater wage transparency was one way to support regular pay raises.
Ministry of Labor data cited at the event showed that 17.2 percent of first-time employees last year started at the then-minimum monthly wage of NT$28,590, while the median monthly salary among all first-time employees was NT$36,000.
Yang said unions can help workers negotiate pay raises, but added that Taiwan faced a more fundamental problem than some countries, where unions existed but younger workers might be reluctant to join them.
Democratic Progressive Party legislator Lin Yueh-chin (林月琴) urged the labor ministry to raise the NT$40,000 monthly salary threshold below which employers are required to show the salary range in job postings, saying the threshold should increase as the minimum wage rises.
In a statement issued later yesterday, the labor ministry said the Labor Union Act guarantees workers the right to organize and join unions, adding that workers at companies with fewer than 30 employees can join with other workers to form, or join existing, industrial or professional unions.
The ministry said it would review the union rules after the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade completes the approval procedures, including gathering views from stakeholders and consulting labor and employer groups.
The agreement includes provisions on strengthening labor rights and rules concerning thresholds for forming unions, according to the ministry.
On wages, the ministry said it is studying amendments to raise the NT$40,000 salary threshold below which employers must release pay information in job postings, with the new threshold possibly set at “a certain multiple of the minimum wage.”

Trump’s great oil heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

When the US ousted Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro earlier this year and put him in a New York jail cell, Venezuelans at home and abroad rejoiced. For the first time in 27 years, the country faced a real possibility of regime change. However, removing an autocrat does not necessarily dismantle the authoritarian system that kept him in power, particularly when the man who removed him is an aspiring authoritarian and kleptocrat in his own right.
Nearly nine months after Maduro’s capture by US special forces, the prospect of democratic change is dimming by the day. That was evident last week during the UN General Assembly, where US President Donald Trump warmly welcomed the leader he left in charge of the country, Delcy Rodriguez, who had been Maduro’s vice president. Trump’s backing has prompted several US allies in Latin America to warm to the chavista government, as seen in last month’s meeting between Paraguayan President Santiago Pena and Rodriguez.
This is happening even as the UN’s fact-finding mission on Venezuela reports that the machinery of repression built under chavismo remains largely intact. While some political prisoners have been released, and access to some previously blocked media outlets has been restored, the most recognizable figures of the Maduro regime are still in power. The security services and military high command have not been purged of regime loyalists, and armed colectivos continue to operate with impunity. No matter how US Secretary of State Marco Rubio tries to spin these facts, or how often Rodriguez promises free elections, a democratic transition is not in sight.
Trump’s priorities — energy security, access to low-cost oil and rewarding his business cronies — help explain this authoritarian inertia. Venezuela offers all three, with its vast oil reserves providing US refineries with additional supplies and reducing exposure to energy-market instability. In August, for example, the Trump administration struck a deal with North American Blue Energy Partners, granting the company a 100-year concession to 17 Venezuelan oil fields containing about 65 billion barrels of proven reserves. The US government also acquired a 35 percent stake in the company and the right to buy 20 percent of its production at cost.
And more investment is on the way, as Venezuela’s interim government expects the deal to deliver as much as US$100 billion in infrastructure investments. Chevron is expanding its Venezuelan operations, and ExxonMobil is discussing a return to the country almost two decades after Hugo Chavez nationalized its oil assets.
There is no inherent contradiction between economic recovery and democratization. The two can and should go hand in hand, as they did in countries such as Poland in the 1990s. The problem begins when economic stabilization is put first, without a clear plan for a democratic transition — precisely the Trump administration’s approach. In his first press conference after Maduro’s capture, Trump barely mentioned democracy, but had plenty to say about oil.
A 100-year concession is not an ordinary foreign investment. It assumes the basic arrangement will survive across US administrations. And since the US government has a direct stake in the company, US taxpayers have a vested interest in protecting it.
Trump’s oil deal, brokered by businessman Alejandro Betancourt, a chavista loyalist who has been implicated in multiple corruption scandals, was negotiated with little transparency and no competitive bidding by the Rodriguez government, whose constitutional legitimacy remains contested. The deal places a significant share of Venezuela’s main asset under the control of a foreign government for an extraordinary length of time. Add Trump’s declaration at the UN General Assembly that the US should control Venezuela’s oil, because “to the victor go the spoils,” and it is easy to see why a future democratically elected Venezuelan government might want to revisit the deal.
Nothing requires US oil companies to oppose democracy or deliberately block elections, but billions of dollars in US and foreign investment create powerful incentives to avoid the uncertainty that free elections and a new government would bring. A Venezuelan government that protects contracts, keeps the oil flowing, cooperates with the US government and allows US companies to operate freely is immensely valuable, regardless of how democratic it is.
If this deal does materialize, then those incentives would not disappear when Trump leaves office. Venezuela could end up stable enough for foreign companies to invest, yet never democratic enough to put those investments at risk. The Trump administration has already demonstrated its eagerness to work with the same repressive regime it once bitterly opposed when its interests are at stake.
Before Maduro’s removal, the impoverished chavista government was grappling with collapsing oil production and had few international partners. New oil revenues could ease some of Venezuela’s economic misery and enable the regime to rebuild relations with neighboring countries, making it harder to dislodge.
That leaves the chavista regime with a better chance of survival, while the US gets greater energy security and a pliable ally in Caracas — a win-win for everyone but Venezuelans yearning for political freedom.
Maduro’s removal created an opportunity for democratic change. Trump’s oil heist is turning it into the path not taken.
Cristina Ramirez is an international political analyst for Panama en Directo and CNN en Espanol, and lectures on comparative political economy and the political economy of corruption at King’s College London.
Copyright: Project Syndicate
China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) received two different welcomes within the space of 10 days — one in New Delhi and the other in Washington. Travel spending changing, Mastercard says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:29 UTC
01:44:29 KST

Taiwanese visiting Japan and South Korea are changing their spending patterns and the places they visit, Mastercard’s data and services team said in a statement yesterday.
Data gleaned from Taiwanese travelers in 2024 and last year showed changes in their habits, the team said.
Japan, China and South Korea are the top three tourism destinations for Taiwanese, with 14.5 million people traveling abroad in the first eight months of this year, the statement said, citing Tourism Administration data.
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
Last year, Taiwan-issued Mastercard holders’ in-person spending grew 39 percent in Japan and 44 percent in South Korea compared with the previous year, Mastercard Taiwan managing director Eva Chen (陳懿文) said in the statement.
The figures outpaced the year-on-year growth in Taiwanese tourists’ spending on consumer goods, which were 16 percent in Japan and 35 percent in South Korea during the period, Chen said.
Taiwanese tourists’ spending continued to grow in major cities, while growth was stronger in several destinations outside those centers, although they also showed more interest in exploring smaller towns and cities, she said.
Tokyo and Osaka accounted for a combined 41 percent of Taiwanese visitors’ spending in Japan, but it increased by 66 percent in Fukuoka, 48 percent in Okinawa and 36 percent in Sapporo, she said.
By comparison, Taiwanese tourism spending in Tokyo increased by just 6 percent, she said.
Taiwanese experience-related spending grew 90 percent and 68 percent respectively in Fukuoka, which broadly reflected trends elsewhere in Japan, Chen said.
Last year, Seoul accounted for 61 percent of total spending by Taiwanese tourists to South Korea, down from 64 percent the previous year, she said.
Experience-related spending by Taiwanese in South Korea “grew 102 percent in Jeju and 73 percent in Busan, outpacing their spending on goods, Chen said.
The reverse was true of Incheon and Gyeonggi-do, where Taiwanese tourists’ spending on goods increased by 132 percent and 120 percent respectively, she said.
Taiwanese visiting Japan and South Korea increasingly planned their trips around local concerts, rather than Taiwan’s national holidays, Chen said.
Taiwanese attending South Korean music concerts outspent those who were vacationing in the country four-fold in terms of average daily spending, she said.
The patterns indicate that Taiwanese increasingly favor experiencing a foreign culture over buying consumer products, she added.

As equity investors enter the final stretch of a pivotal year that has propelled South Korea and Taiwan to the forefront of the global artificial intelligence (AI) trade, the latter is emerging as the stronger bet.
The TAIEX beat the KOSPI by about 23 percentage points last quarter, the widest margin since the turn of the century. Earnings upgrades also outpaced those for its South Korean peer for the first time since March last year. About 40 percent of the fund managers surveyed by Bank of America Corp last month said they were overweight Taiwan, versus 25 percent for South Korea.
Driving the optimism are Taiwan’s deeper linkages across the AI supply chain and a more upbeat earnings outlook.
Photo: CNA
“The distinction for us is not simply the amount of AI exposure, but the nature of the earnings supporting it,” M&G Investments (Singapore) Pte Ltd portfolio manager Vikas Pershad said. “Taiwan offers a broader and deeper opportunity set. Its earnings come from volume and that makes its earnings upgrades broader and stickier. [South] Korea’s earnings, in the near-term, are coming from price.”
Taiwan offers investors exposure across chip design and manufacturing, packaging, networking and servers, meaning it has more ways to benefit as AI spending broadens. Meanwhile, South Korea’s market leadership remains heavily concentrated in chipmakers Samsung Electronics Co and SK Hynix Inc, leaving it more vulnerable as doubts emerge over how much longer the current memory upcycle can run.
Up 72 percent this year, the TAIEX is the top performer among more than 90 equity indexes tracked by Bloomberg. The KOSPI is ranked second, with gains of about 63 percent. Taiwan’s lead comes as shares of KOSPI heavyweights Samsung and SK Hynix plunged between 19 percent and 33 percent last quarter.
Earnings estimates for the TAIEX rose about 19 percent in the last quarter, compared with an increase of about 15 percent for the KOSPI, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.
Societe Generale SA is “keeping a preference for Taiwan over Korean equities, given the diverging earnings growth trajectories,” strategists including Rajat Agarwal said.
In terms of valuations, the TAIEX is trading at about 18 times its one-year forward estimated earnings. The KOSPI trades at about 5.5 times, reflecting concern that the memory cycle might be approaching a peak, and in part the longstanding “Korea discount” that has kept the market cheap relative to global peers.
Still, when asked which market would benefit the most from the next phase of the AI cycle, 35 percent of the respondents in the Bank of America survey chose Taiwan. Just 5 percent picked South Korea. The TAIEX is delivering broader gains than its other tech-heavy peers, reflecting a wider range of investment opportunities. About 10 percent of the gauge’s stocks have at least doubled this year through Tuesday, compared with 4.1 percent for the KOSPI and 5.7 percent for Japan’s Nikkei 225.
“The next leg of upside for Taiwan stocks is likely to depend less on broad AI enthusiasm and more on local tech companies that remain exposed to genuine bottlenecks in the AI value chain,” Allspring Global Investments Holdings LLC portfolio manager Gary Tan (譚頌超) said.

Initial public offerings (IPOs), placements and block trades raised US$47.5 billion in July to last month, the biggest haul ever for the period, data compiled by Bloomberg showed. That pushed fundraising this year above US$92 billion and within reach of the US$112.5 billion record set in 2021. AI has been at the heart of Hong Kong’s deal revival, but this summer brought a new level of intensity. Chinese companies raised ever-larger sums

China prefers to win without firing a shot in its bid to strangle Taiwan’s strategic autonomy. Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu (孫子) would have approved. Its central tool at sea is the “cabbage strategy”: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) layers fishing boats, maritime militia, coast guard cutters and warships around Taiwan’s contested waters in overlapping rings. Each layer normalizes daily coercion, narrows Taiwan’s freedom of movement and chips away at its maritime sovereignty — all while staying below the threshold of armed conflict. This is “gray zone” warfare at its most cost-effective — one of Beijing’s most promising

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07

01:44:28 KST

Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight into yesterday, killing at least 12 civilians, including three children, and wounding more than 40 in Moscow’s latest devastating barrage, Ukrainian officials said.
Ukraine had anticipated the attack, with President Volodymyr Zelenskiy warning the previous day that intelligence services had concluded that Russia was building up for a “massive” strike.
Although Ukraine knew about the looming attack, which coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday, it could not fend it off completely.
Photo: Reuters
The deaths and damage illustrated the difficulty Ukraine has in countering Russia’s ballistic missiles and the new jet-powered drones used in Moscow’s escalating bombardments.
Without ammunition for its US-made Patriot air defense systems, Ukraine cannot stop Russian ballistic weapons. It is racing to develop a new generation of interceptors fast enough to catch Moscow’s high-flying jet-propelled drones.
“Ukraine has once again been hit by Russian missiles throughout the night,” Verkhovna Rada Human Rights Ombudsmen Dmytro Lubinets said on Telegram.
“Another sleepless night, another act of terror, after which people still have to plan their working day despite everything,” he added.
A Russian strike destroyed an apartment block in Pryluky, in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, killing nine people, including three children, and wounding 34, Ukrainian Minister of Internal Affairs Ihor Vyhivskyi said.
Deaths were also reported in three other Ukrainian cities, including the capital, Kyiv, Zelenskiy said.
“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively,” the Ukrainian leader said on social media.
Ukraine is looking worldwide for available Patriot missiles, which are in short supply due to the Iran war.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge, and air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity,” Zelenskiy said.
In Kremenchuk, in the Poltava region, two people were killed and seven injured, and a rescue operation was continuing, Poltava Oblast Governor Vitalii Diakivnych said.
“That is exactly what the enemy is counting on — For us to be afraid to fall asleep, to let our children out of our sight, to plan anything, so that everyone thinks: Next time it could be my address,” he said.
The Russian Ministry of Defense said the military carried out a massive strike overnight targeting industrial facilities involved in the production and storage of missiles and drones across Ukraine.
The ministry said that port and ship repair facilities in the southern Odesa region and ships carrying cargo for the Ukrainian military were also hit.
Ukraine has hit back at Russia by launching long-range drones and missiles on oil refineries and storage depots.
Zelenskiy said that Ukraine targeted two oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions of Russia.
Zelenskiy also indicated that Ukraine had struck in the Black Sea. He posted images of a fire said to show an oil tanker burning in the water near the Russian city of Sochi.
It was not possible to independently verify the images.
Some Russian online media late on Tuesday also posted the images. Unconfirmed media reports said it was carrying oil from Novorossiysk to India and was attacked by Ukrainian sea drones.
Additional reporting by Reuters

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:25 UTC
01:44:25 KST

Myanmar’s junta chief-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing arrived in Malaysia yesterday for talks with Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, as the military-backed leader once shunned by regional nations seeks international legitimacy.
The two-day visit comes as Malaysia pushes ahead with a controversial move to repatriate thousands of Myanmar nationals, despite warnings from the UN and rights groups that returnees could face serious danger amid a raging civil war.
“The visit provides the prime minister with an opportunity to sustain his direct engagement with Myanmar,” the Malaysian government said in a statement on Tuesday.
Photo: Myanmar presidential press and information bureau via via EPA
Key bilateral issues include the “voluntary, dignified and safe repatriation of Myanmar nationals of all ethnic groups who have been in Malaysia illegally,” it added.
Myanmar has been in turmoil since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup in 2021, triggering a nationwide civil war that has killed an estimated 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
The military engineered a widely criticized election that allowed Min Aung Hlaing, who is subject to a raft of Western sanctions, to take up a civilian role — a transition that has sparked some moves toward re-engagement with Myanmar.
Although Min Aung Hlaing and other senior Myanmar officials have been excluded from ASEAN summits since 2021 over their failure to implement a peace road map brokered by the group, individual countries in the region have moved to rebuild ties with Naypyitaw.
Since formally becoming president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has visited ASEAN members Thailand, Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam, and also made trips to China, India, Russia and Belarus.
In Malaysia, following a wave of online hate speech and misinformation earlier this year, pressure on undocumented migrants and refugees has grown, particularly against Rohingya Muslims, many of whom fled a brutal 2017 military crackdown in Myanmar’s Rakhine state bordering Bangladesh.
Last month, Anwar said in a podcast that he would invite Min Aung Hlaing for an official visit if Myanmar accepted the return of thousands of Rohingya refugees.
“Under pressure to send refugees back, Anwar needs Naypyitaw’s cooperation, and a visit is the price,” International Crisis Group senior Asia adviser Richard Horsey said. “He says this is not recognition, but Min Aung Hlaing will present it as exactly that.”
Fortify Rights senior human rights specialist Yap Lay Sheng agreed, saying that the Migrant returns are the “only reason” Malaysia wants to engage with Myanmar.
“For so many years Malaysia has shown the military regime the cold shoulder,” he said. “Suddenly there’s a 180 degree about turn to welcome the regime with open arms.”
Malaysia has deported about 10,000 Myanmar nationals since January, according to Anwar, who said Burmese authorities had given assurances those returning would not be harmed.
Although Malaysia has said the repatriations are strictly voluntary, the UN has raised concerns about the move, warning that people sent back to Myanmar might face serious risks.
Rights groups have also urged Malaysia to halt the returns, citing the ongoing violence and risk of forced conscription.
Despite repeated calls for an end to the violence, including from ASEAN, the civil war in Myanmar continues unabated.
The Burmese military has carried out several airstrikes within the last fortnight in Rakhine, where it is battling a rebel group, killing at least 58 people and injuring dozens of others, including at a busy market.
The attack was the deadliest since a hospital bombing in December and drew condemnation from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
ASEAN’s current chair, the Philippines, also expressed concern over the airstrike.
“Nothing in the region’s response gives Naypyitaw any reason to think they will come at a diplomatic cost, including Min Aung Hlaing’s red carpet in Kuala Lumpur,” Horsey said.

01:44:23 KST

Former president Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文) on Tuesday met with US Representative Nancy Pelosi in San Francisco, their first meeting since Pelosi’s high-profile visit to Taiwan in 2022 as speaker of the US House of Representatives.
The two met at the San Francisco hotel where Tsai was staying during her visit to the city.
After the meeting, Pelosi on social media described Tsai as a “courageous champion of democracy” and “a dear friend of America.”
Photo: Screen grab from Nancy Pelosi’s Facebook page
“The bond between the United States and Taiwan is strong, and Congress’ commitment to the Taiwanese people and their freedom remains steadfast,” she said.
Tsai also posted about the meeting on social media, recalling their meeting in Taiwan in 2022, when she presented Pelosi with the Order of Propitious Clouds with Special Grand Cordon, one of Taiwan’s highest decorations, in recognition of Pelosi’s contributions to promoting Taiwan-US relations.
“Over the years, regardless of changes in the international situation, Pelosi has consistently been a staunch friend of Taiwan,” Tsai wrote.
Tsai said she gave Pelosi a silk scarf designed by Chien Chun-yuan (簡君嫄).
The scarf’s design was inspired by the ocean and coral, Tsai said, adding that she hoped the gift would convey to Pelosi the beauty and creativity of Taiwan as a maritime nation.
Tsai arrived in San Francisco on Monday to begin a weeklong visit to the US. She was scheduled to deliver the opening keynote address at Stanford University’s DEFCON’s Technology and National Security Conference yesterday.
Pelosi and Tsai last met in Taiwan in 2022 when the then-speaker visited from Aug. 2 to 3, the first such visit by a sitting US House speaker since 1997.
Pelosi’s visit prompted China to conduct large-scale live-fire military drills around Taiwan, heightening cross-strait tensions.
Tsai’s trip to the US is her first there since leaving office in May 2024 after serving two four-year terms as president.
Separately, a US congressional delegation is in Taiwan for a four-day visit, during which its members are to meet with President William Lai (賴清德) and other senior officials, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Tuesday.

Saudi Arabia: Overturn death sentence against Sri Lankan migrant worker over social media post
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:22 UTC
01:44:22 KST

Saudi Arabia’s authorities must urgently overturn the death sentence issued against a migrant worker on charges of “blasphemy”, said Amnesty International today. The organization is calling on Saudi authorities to release him immediately and unconditionally given his charges stem entirely from his exercise of his right to freedom of expression.
Anojan Sivarasa, a 24-year-old Sri Lankan national, was arrested on 1 July 2026 after posting a comment on Facebook deemed insulting to the prophet Mohammad. He told the judge that he made the comment during a moment of anger, and that he subsequently deleted it and published a video apology expressing remorse. He was prosecuted swiftly and just weeks later, on 27 July, was sentenced to five years in prison and a SAR 3 million fine (around USD 800,000). Less than two months later, this was increased to a death sentence on appeal on 17 September. He was denied access to a lawyer from the moment of his arrest and until his initial sentencing.
“The case raises alarming concerns about the application of the death penalty and the arbitrariness of the Saudi criminal justice system, with his initial sentence of five years transformed into a death sentence less than two months later on appeal. No one should be imprisoned, let alone face execution simply for expressing their views, even if these are deemed insulting or offensive. Anojan Sivarasa was exercising his right to freedom of expression and his execution would amount to arbitrary deprivation of life. Saudi authorities must immediately quash this death sentence, overturn his conviction and release him immediately and unconditionally,” said Heba Morayef, Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa.
“International human rights law restricts the death penalty to the ‘most serious crimes,’ understood to involve intentional killing, yet the Saudi authorities have continued to impose death sentences for conduct that should not be criminalized and to execute people at a startling rate after grossly unfair trials, including for non-violent offenses.
‘Sentencing a man to death over a social media post is a chilling illustration of the Saudi authorities’ willingness to impose this cruel and irreversible punishment, including for acts that should never be criminalized. Saudi authorities should immediately establish a moratorium on the use of the death penalty as a first move towards its full abolition.”
No one should be imprisoned, let alone face execution simply for expressing their views, even if these are deemed insulting or offensive.
Heba Morayef, MENA Regional Director
Saudi Arabia remains one of the world’s leading executioners. As of 5 October 2026, at least 175 people had been executed in Saudi Arabia this year, including many for drug-related offences. Foreign nationals account for a majority of those executed, with at least 94 foreign nationals from more than 20 countries put to death this year alone.
Saudi Arabia’s courts have, in recent years, imposed prison sentences of up to several decades for social media posts, with sentences swinging widely on appeal.
Saudi Arabia has no written penal code: many offences and their punishments are not defined in law but left to the discretion of judges, who rule according to their own interpretation of Sharia. Where written laws do exist, the authorities often rely on vague and overly broad provisions of the counter-terror law and anti-cybercrime law, such as impinging on “public order”, “religious values”, and “public morals,” to criminalize people solely based on their exercise of the right to freedom of expression.
“Saudi authorities must halt this crackdown on freedom of expression and immediately release all those detained solely on the basis of their exercise of human rights,” said Heba Morayef.
Background
On 27 July, the Criminal Court in Al Ahsa sentenced Anojan Sivarasa to five years’ imprisonment and a SAR 3 million fine (USD 800,000), the maximum punishment under Article 6 of the Anti-Cybercrime Law. On 17 September, the Court of Appeal in the Eastern Region increased his sentence to death as a hadd punishment, which is a fixed, mandatory punishment under Sharia. Anojan has appealed the death sentence.
Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all cases without exception regardless of the nature or circumstances of the crime; guilt, innocence or other characteristics of the individual; or the method used by the state to carry out the execution.

Defense company executives underscore autonomous capabilities at forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:44:16 UTC
01:44:16 KST

It is important that Taiwan acquire autonomous capabilities to reduce decisionmaking time during wartime and ensure the efficient use of resources in peacetime, defense company executives told a forum yesterday.
Speaking at the Aerospace and Defense Strategic Forum hosted by the Taiwan External Trade Development Council, Mira Resnick, a senior director at Saronic Technologies, said that Taiwan could be vulnerable to China’s attrition-based tactics.
That vulnerability is based on the armed forces’ current approach, which involves responding to daily harassment by Chinese navy and coast guard vessels, as well as maritime militia vessels operating in the waters near Taiwan, by shadowing them with crewed navy and coast guard vessels.
Photo: CNA
“Every hour a corvette spends shadowing a militia trawler is an hour of hull life, fuel, and, scarcest of all, sailors,” said Resnick, a former US deputy assistant secretary of state for Israeli and Palestinian affairs.
“Taiwan is spending its rarest resource on the least demanding mission. That is the attrition that is happening right now without a shot fired,” Resnick said, adding that China is attempting to fatigue the hulls and crews of Taiwan’s navy and coast guard by “normalizing its presence” in waters close to Taiwan.
Taiwan faces a dilemma in deciding whether to acquire remotely controlled or autonomous uncrewed surface vessels, Resnick said.
China has invested “enormously” in electronic warfare and counterspace capabilities and would target the datalinks of Taiwan’s forces in a war, she said.
“A remotely piloted vessel is a hostage to its link. Sever the link, and you have zero capability,” Resnick said.
She called for the deployment of multi-mission autonomous surface vessels with modular payloads alongside the approximately 1,300 one-way uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) that Taiwan plans to procure.
Such vessels can shadow China’s maritime militia instead of coast guard vessels, track the movements of Chinese vessels and even provide targeting information for one-way USVs should China launch an amphibious invasion, offering Taiwan “a variety of options,” Resnick said.
Meanwhile, Alex Chang (張良治), head of Anduril Taiwan, said that on the future battlefield, commanders could have only seconds to understand an incoming attack and assign an appropriate weapon in response.
However, “no headquarters can manually process every radar track, drone feed, electronic signal and targeting request moving across a contested battlespace at once,” Chang said.
“This is why autonomy matters,” Chang said. “It can turn disparate systems into a coherent fighting force, one that is not paralyzed by missile strikes or electronic warfare.”
Autonomy would also distribute decisionmaking, enabling smaller units to operate independently and present an adversary with “more targets and more dilemmas than it can manage,” he said.
Taiwan should work to connect data across disparate systems so that it has an “integrated data layer” that can continue to inform decisions necessary to accomplishing missions in degraded communications environments, Chang said.
China is exploring ways to use artificial intelligence to “discipline, constrain and replace” elements of human decisionmaking, he said.
Taiwan should pursue the opposite model, giving commanders more options, junior leaders greater awareness and individual units more freedom to innovate toward a shared mission, he said.
The donation of offshore patrol vessel Kinmen to the Philippines includes provisions that protect Taiwanese fishers and facilitate security cooperation across the First Island Chain, officials said yesterday. The security situation for Black Sea shipping has worsened over the past weeks.
Drones reportedly struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper. The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova. The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
On Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
On Oct. 3, Russian forces attacked a civilian cargo ship sailing under the Liberian flag at a port near Odesa in the Black Sea, killing one.
The sailor killed was a motor engineer, and three other crew members were injured in the strike, according to the Ukrainian Sea Ports Authority. 13 other crew members were evacuated from the vessel.
"This is yet another deliberate attack by Russia on civilian shipping," said the Sea Ports Authority. "Russia continues to terrorize the peaceful merchant fleet and sailors who risk their lives every day to ensure the operation of Ukrainian maritime routes."
Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement condemning Russia and calling for Black Sea passage as the U.N. Security Council met, the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Sept. 23, against the backdrop of the U.N. General Assembly.
"As the Security Council meets to discuss the situation in Ukraine, we reaffirm our shared commitment to the principles of the U.N. Charter and peace. We stand in solidarity with Ukraine as it continues to face Russia's war of aggression," Kallas said.

What France's student protesters want – and what the government is offering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:41:57 UTC
01:41:57 KST

What France's student protesters want – and what the government is offering
Staff shortages, rats in the corridors, and a university admissions system that feels like a lottery. As protests sweep France, high school students have drawn up a list of demands to deal with these and other issues. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has promised a government response by the end of October, but whether he can quell the unrest remains to be seen.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Mass protests across France’s high schools roiled the country again on Tuesday, with hundreds of thousands joining the biggest day of the movement so far. Demonstrations began in late September, with the first protest traced back to Saint-Exupéry high school in Créteil, a southern Parisian suburb.
A handful of teachers at Saint-Exupéry went on strike September 17 to lament staff shortages. “We were short a maths teacher, a French teacher, a literature professer, a history teacher and an assistant professor. The school nurse was on sick leave,” Laurent Bessiere, a maths teacher, told French radio station France Inter.
That same evening, students gathered to join the fight and planned a protest for the next morning. Stacking a few bins in front of the school entrance and holding placards, they rose up to make demands alongside their teachers.
“We’re asking for the bare minimum,” a student told France Inter.
Their demands struck a chord with other high schools across the nation, which are suffering from a lack of funding and understaffing.
In response to the protests, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle their demands and send in proposals by the end of the month. But finding spare funds to implement educational reforms will be complicated, given heated debates over France’s already strained 2027 budget.
Read more'We're fed up': Paris students rise up in a movement that shows no sign of slowing
Staff shortages
A union of high school and university students on Monday published a list of 10 “emergency measures” they say could serve as a basis for working with the government, whose response so far has been “repression”, they write.
High on the list is the issue of staff shortages. Students are demanding a large-scale recruitment drive to create additional teaching posts so that each classroom has a person to lead it. They also want to ensure that every establishment has at least one nurse, a psychologist and a career adviser for every 500 students.
More than half of France’s middle and high schools lack at least one teacher, a major trade union representing public school staff found. And 69 percent of schools are short of at least one member of their teaching and support staff. Understaffing means classrooms are overcrowded, regularly packing in 35 students at a time.
Read moreWhy so many French teachers are calling it quits
The numbers do not reflect the optimism that French Education Minister Édouard Geffray expressed before the September start of the new academic year. Speaking on France Inter at the end of August, he insisted that teacher shortages would be “minimal” and that “all indicators” were that things were on track to be “much better” than in previous years.
To meet the demand for teacher replacements, Lecornu referred to a scheme from 2023 encouraging teachers to cover for the short absences of colleagues in a statement published Sunday. As for long-term absences or unfilled posts, Lecornu said he ordered his ministers to prioritise filling them in every regional education authority.
Run-down buildings
Students have also repeatedly sounded the alarm on the dire state of their school buildings. A wave of viral Instagram videos posted by students resurfaced when the protests began. “I’m a student at the Blaise Cendrars high school in Seine-Saint-Denis (a northern suburb of Paris). Of course, I don’t have a roof over my head when I’m in class,” one student ironically said in a video showcasing the deplorable state of her establishment. Others have reported seeing rats and cockroaches scurrying through school corridors and flooded toilets.
To display this content from Instagram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Speaking to French radio ICI on Wednesday, vice president of the Île-de-France region James Chéron rejected the criticism. He said the region’s €6.6 billion, 10-year plan covers almost every public high school and that nearly 400 of its 468 establishments are already new or renovated, with the rest either under works or “being studied”. Chéron added that Seine-Saint-Denis has received the “most investment”.
But students are not convinced. During the successive heatwaves that scorched parts of France this summer, some classrooms reached 38° celsius. Two-thirds of the country’s elementary, middle and high schools have been built before 1970 and cannot withstand rising temperatures brought on by climate change.
Read moreNew timetables, longer holidays: How can French schools adapt to heatwaves?
The maintenance of school and university buildings is number one on the list of demands published by the student union. They are asking that an “emergency plan” be implemented to renovate dilapidated buildings and adapt them to heatwaves by installing air conditioners or cooling systems. They also want the buildings to be well-insulated to face cold spells. Providing “clean and functional toilets” is a key tenet of the request.
On this point, Lecornu said in his statement that the upkeep of public high school buildings, equipment and canteens is the responsibility of regional councils, but that the state would “support” them. Ministers are tasked with setting a timetable on urgent needs and clarify who is responsible for what.
“Studying in run-down premises is an obstacle to education,” Lecornu acknowledged.
Long hours
Timetables have also come under scrutiny. Students say school days are too long, sometimes running from 8am to 6pm due to gaps in their schedule where they don’t have class. They point to a reform adopted in 2019 that allows high school students to choose specialisation courses in their final years as one of the reasons timetables can be disrupted.
“When I was in high school I would start at 8am and finish at 6pm,” recalled Julie, who is now in university. “My schedule was packed, and I still had extracurricular activities on the side.”
“I wake up at 6am because I live far from my high school. It takes me one hour to get home and then I have a tonne of homework to do. I barely spend time with my family,” one student told France 2 in an interview on Sunday.
Though French students tend to spend fewer days in school than the OECD average, they make up for that with longer school days.
Lecornu has asked for improvements to timetables and independent study conditions to be reviewed with public school staff, student representatives and even local transport authorities. He encouraged them to use artificial intelligence to refine the software used to build timetables ahead of the next school year.
A citizen’s convention submitted a proposal to the government in November last year on how to reform public school timetables, but the proposal has so far gone unheeded.
Issues with the Parcoursup platform
France’s national online platform for applying to higher education institutions, Parcoursup, is also in the firing line. A bit like UCAS in the UK, final-year high school students use it to apply to university courses and other programmes, receiving offers based on their school records and applications.
Students argue that the system is opaque and seems arbitrary. Each university course ranks applicants with its own local algorithm and criteria, and students say they cannot see how decisions are made or why they were turned down. Many suspect their applications, including cover letters they spend hours writing, are never really read.
“I wrote about a dozen cover letters without using ChatGPT, but I feel like my applications were not even looked at. When I see people accepted onto the course I wanted with lower grades than mine, it seems completely illogical to me,” Ghjulia told FRANCE 24. The 18-year-old was hoping to start medical school but none of her applications were accepted, despite having solid grades.
But students also say Parcoursup entrenches inequality. A February 2026 report concluded that it helps keep sociocultural inequalities in place. One reason is that courses can see which high school an applicant attended, which can disadvantage students from less prestigious schools or poorer areas. The report drew out 51 proposals to address these issues, including dropping cover letters, hiding the applicant’s school and sharing local algorithms.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Lecornu is promising to make Parcoursup more transparent. Under his plan, students would be told exactly how courses weigh their grades and specialised subjects, how applicants are ranked, and why they were accepted or rejected. Ministers Édouard Geffray and Philippe Baptiste have until the end of October to propose changes for the 2027 admissions round, which opens in January.
The other demands listed by students include financial help, including guaranteeing that students meals are capped at €1, and ending the police violence that has run rampant during the protests.
