President Yotova: Bulgaria Seeks Black Sea Moratorium and Stronger Anti-Drone Defenses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:41:51 UTC
01:41:51 KST

President Yotova: Bulgaria Seeks Black Sea Moratorium and Stronger Anti-Drone Defenses
President Iliana Yotova said Bulgaria will propose a moratorium on hostilities in the Black Sea, seek stronger allied surveillance and anti-drone capabilities, and pursue diplomatic efforts with all Black Sea littoral states following a meeting of the Consultative Council for National Security (CCNS) on the drone attacks against two commercial vessels in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The CCNS meeting, convened by Yotova, focused on current risks and threats to Bulgaria's maritime security and critical infrastructure in the context of the war in Ukraine. Representatives of parliamentary groups, the Speaker of the National Assembly Mihaela Dotsova, Prime Minister Rumen Radev, the ministers of Defense, Interior, Foreign Affairs, Environment and Water, Deputy Minister of Finance Lyudmila Petkova, the Chief of Defense, and the heads of security and intelligence services took part.
The session lasted five hours. Representatives of the special services reported on threats to shipping security arising from the war in Ukraine and assessed the protection of strategic infrastructure against possible drone attacks.
Yotova said the participants had identified a deterioration of the security environment in the Black Sea and an escalation of hostilities between Russia and Ukraine.
"Russia's war against Ukraine has led to a significant deterioration of the security environment in the Black Sea region. The Consultative Council on National Security discussed current risks and threats to the maritime security and critical infrastructure of the Republic of Bulgaria in the context of the war in Ukraine and in light of incidents that have occurred in the Black Sea in recent days. During the meeting, an escalation of hostilities in the conflict between the Russian Federation and Ukraine was noted, threatening maritime security and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea region," Yotova said.
She said the council had also identified a growing number of attacks involving naval and aerial drones against commercial vessels, with consequences including damage to and sinking of ships and loss of life.
"There is a growing trend of attacks using naval and aerial drones against commercial vessels, resulting in damage to and the sinking of ships, as well as the loss of human life. This has led to restrictions on freedom of navigation, a sharp decline in shipping traffic, increased insurance costs, economic losses, and the risk of environmental pollution," the President said.
The council agreed that the growing use of advanced, long-range unmanned systems is increasing threats to Bulgaria's critical infrastructure not only around the Black Sea but throughout the country.
"A consensus was reached that the use of an increasing number of highly advanced, long-range unmanned systems has significantly heightened threats to the Republic of Bulgaria's critical infrastructure - not only in the vicinity of the Black Sea but across the country's entire territory," Yotova said.
The security of strategic facilities in Bulgaria's defense industry was also examined. According to the position presented after the meeting, the country faces serious challenges in protecting its critical infrastructure.
The CCNS linked the current risks to the inability to resolve the military conflict in Ukraine through diplomatic means and agreed to continue implementing measures already adopted by the Council of Ministers. Participants also called for an analysis of the existing regulatory framework and possible amendments needed to implement those measures.
The council adopted a package of proposals for the executive and legislative branches with a three-quarters majority, as required by law. Representatives of three parliamentary groups voted against the proposals.
One of the decisions directly addressed the attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea. The CCNS condemned the strikes as a gross violation of international maritime law and called for an immediate investigation to establish who was responsible and for the government to make the findings public once the investigation is complete.
"The Consultative Council on National Security unequivocally condemns the strikes on merchant vessels in the Black Sea as a gross violation of international maritime law and insists on an immediate investigation to identify the perpetrators. Once the investigation is concluded, the executive branch must inform the public of the findings," Yotova stated.
The proposals also call for Bulgaria to take an active part in diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the war, while continuing government measures against identified risks and threats.
"The greatest guarantee of our security is an immediate ceasefire and the utilization of all political and diplomatic channels to achieve peace. Bulgaria must play an active role in this process," the President said.
The CCNS recommended improving maritime situational awareness through unmanned aerial systems for reconnaissance and surveillance. It also called for faster modernization of the Armed Forces, including the acquisition of anti-drone systems with kinetic engagement capabilities, in close cooperation with NATO and the European Union.
Another proposal requires the executive branch to review the existing legal framework and submit amendments to the National Assembly where necessary, with the aim of supporting physical protection of strategic sites and strengthening the state's ability to ensure maritime security.
"The executive branch should analyze and propose to the National Assembly amendments to the existing regulatory framework in order to support physical protection measures for strategic sites and ensure the country's maritime security," Yotova said.
The council also recommended keeping Bulgaria's national maritime search and rescue system at a high level of readiness.
Regarding NATO, the proposals call for Bulgaria to use its membership in the Alliance and the European Union to protect its security, economic and environmental interests and contribute to stability in the Black Sea region.
"Bulgaria should utilize its capacity as a full member of the EU and NATO to articulate a firm stance and ensure the protection of its security, economic, and environmental interests, as well as regional stability," Yotova stated.
The council said NATO's enhanced vigilance activities along the Eastern Flank provide an opportunity for Bulgaria to seek a greater allied contribution to Black Sea security. The measures could include additional air and maritime surveillance assets, stronger coastal defenses and improved capabilities against unmanned systems.
"There is an opportunity for us to request increased allied contributions to Black Sea regional security, to activate options for deploying additional air and maritime surveillance assets, and to strengthen coastal defense systems and anti-drone capabilities within the framework of NATO’s enhanced forward presence," Yotova said.
The President emphasized that the proposed measures are compatible with the Montreux Convention.
The possibility of seeking consultations with NATO allies under Article 4 of the North Atlantic Treaty was also discussed. Yotova said the council considered such a move counterproductive at this stage because incidents of this kind should instead be discussed within the North Atlantic Council and an Article 4 consultation would not produce new measures.
Bulgaria will also propose that the European Union establish a framework to support free and safe navigation in the Black Sea as part of its strategic approach to the region.
"Bulgaria should propose that the EU develop a framework mechanism for free and safe shipping in the Black Sea as part of its strategic approach to the Black Sea region," Yotova said.
She noted that maritime security is already one of the main pillars of the EU's Black Sea strategy and that a dedicated Black Sea security hub is planned, but said more specific proposals are needed and that Bulgaria could play an active role in developing them.
The proposals include using European satellite surveillance capabilities to identify potential threats at an early stage. Bulgaria could also seek activation of the EU Civil Protection Mechanism if incidents create environmental risks, use monitoring tools of the European Union Satellite Centre to detect threats, and explore financial compensation for losses.
The CCNS called for urgent consultations with Romania and Turkey on coordinated action against attacks on commercial vessels and measures to protect navigation in the Black Sea.
A central diplomatic initiative would involve Bulgaria seeking consensus among all Black Sea littoral states on a moratorium on hostilities at sea and turning the region into a zone of shared security.
"Bulgaria should take an active role in negotiations to reach a consensus among the Black Sea littoral states, Russia, Ukraine, Bulgaria, Romania, Georgia, and Turkey, on a moratorium regarding hostilities in the Black Sea and on transforming it into a zone of shared security," Yotova said.
Bulgaria is also expected to raise Black Sea risks, threats and possible security solutions in all relevant European forums, particularly at the European Union summit on October 15 and 16.
At the United Nations, Bulgaria will seek assistance in clarifying the technical and legal aspects of incidents in the Black Sea and pursue a resolution guaranteeing freedom and safety of navigation. The proposal specifically calls for the involvement of mechanisms of the UN's International Maritime Organization.
The meeting was held after two merchant vessels were attacked inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. The attacks occurred on October 6 approximately 70 nautical miles, or 130-150 kilometers, from the Bulgarian coast, east of Cape St. Atanas and the town of Byala.
One vessel, sailing under the Togolese flag, suffered severe structural damage and sank within three minutes. The other, sailing under the flag of Palau, caught fire.
The fate of the crew of the sunken ship remained unknown. The Bulgarian ro-ro vessel Dioscuria, which was nearby, saw the explosion and went to the scene. An overturned boat, three capsized life rafts and life jackets were found, but no people were located.
The Navy and Air Force deployed assets to the search, including two helicopters and a Su-25 aircraft. All 18 crew members of the second vessel were rescued. Two sailors were injured, including an Indian national who was hospitalized in Varna in serious condition with burns. The Turkish captain suffered injuries to his head, chest and left leg but was discharged after receiving medical treatment.
Following the attacks, President Rumen Radev held an emergency meeting with representatives of the Defense, Interior, Transport and Environment ministries, the Presidency and security services. He described the incident as an "absolutely unacceptable attack" in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone and a "flagrant violation of international law." He also warned that the continuation of the war was widening its geographical scope and increasing risks to security and civilian shipping.
The origin of the drones had not been established immediately after the attack. The Prime Minister said it was not possible at that stage to determine with certainty which country the aircraft came from. Bulgaria notified the European Commission and the European Council, while the issue was also raised with NATO.
Authorities were simultaneously monitoring another vessel considered a potential risk after it was struck in August and left drifting without a crew and with a failed control system. The Air Force carried out aerial surveillance, while relevant institutions said they were ready to act if the vessel moved toward the Bulgarian coast. Possible marine pollution resulting from the attacks was also being monitored.
Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria would send a diplomatic note to the country responsible if the drones were established to be Russian or Ukrainian.
"At the moment, I can say there is no direct threat to Bulgaria's national security." Radev said after attending the CCNS meeting on the attacks against the ships.
He questioned the effectiveness of relying on military action alone and pointed to the continued use of drone strikes by both sides despite spending on defense.
"How many hundreds of billions have been spent on defending Ukraine against drone strikes? Do the strikes continue? They do. How much has Russia spent on defense? Do the Ukrainian strikes continue? They do. There are many tools in the diplomatic arsenal that are not being used; we are relying solely on military action," he said.
Radev said Bulgaria would establish the nature of the drones before identifying their origin and would follow the same procedure used in the case of the drone in Kardam.
"If the drones turn out to be Russian or Ukrainian, we will immediately send a diplomatic note to the respective country. We will do everything to determine the nature of the drones. That is what happened with the drone in Kardam, too. Initially, we did not announce what it was; we only revealed the drone's identity after the necessary checks and analyses. We will proceed the same way in this case," Radev said.
Kostadin Kostadinov, leader of Revival, left the CCNS meeting saying participants had failed to reach consensus on the proposed position. He said he could not support the draft submitted by the Presidency because it dealt with the consequences of the Black Sea situation rather than its causes.
"Clearly, no decision will be reached. There was, of course, a proposal for a position statement from the presidency - one I cannot support because it contains many points that raise more questions than they answer. The entire statement proposed by Ms. Yotova, regarding which we have not, at least for the moment, reached a common decision, discusses the consequences but fails to address the causes of the very situation that prompted the convening of the Consultative Council," Kostadinov said.
He warned that similar incidents could continue as the war develops and said he had serious concerns that the conflict could intensify.
"Ships have been hit in the Black Sea. Unfortunately, this will continue to happen, and I have very serious concerns, shared by others present at the council, that the conflict will intensify and that there will be other such incidents, let’s call them. We cannot convene a Consultative Council on National Security for every single case of this kind," he said.
Kostadinov also argued that the pre-election environment had influenced the decision to convene the meeting, although he said he attended because of his responsibilities as a statesman.
He objected in particular to the proposal that Bulgaria should participate actively in the peace process, arguing that it was inconsistent with the country's actions toward Russia.
"The proposed document stated that Bulgaria should actively participate in the peace process. I asked a question: how can that be, given that just three weeks ago, Bulgaria, represented by Ms. Yotova herself, supported a declaration condemning the actions of the Russian Federation? How can that be, given that Bulgaria is currently participating in discussions on the next package of EU sanctions against Russia?" Kostadinov said.
He also cited Bulgaria's arms exports and argued that the country should instead seek to act as a mediator between Moscow and Kyiv.
"When Bulgaria acts not as a mediator but as an instigator, when it pursues a policy that is clearly failing right now, given that we are currently exporting weapons worth hundreds of millions of euros (exports haven't stopped at all; they are happening this very moment), how can Bulgaria speak of achieving peace while fueling the war? It is monstrous hypocrisy. And for that very reason, I could not support this proposal," the Revival leader said.
Kostadinov said the meeting had also considered a proposal for Bulgaria to formally address Russia over military activity inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
He cited the proposed wording as calling on Bulgaria "to demand that Russia cease and refrain from conducting military or other offensive actions within Bulgaria's Exclusive Economic Zone in the Black Sea."
He said information provided during the closed meeting indicated that there was still no definitive evidence establishing where the drones that struck the two vessels had originated.
Kostadinov also disputed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's statement that the origin of the drones had been established jointly with Bulgarian security services. He said Bulgarian services had requested information but had not yet received an answer.
"I asked a specific question. Our services have requested information. They do not yet have an answer. They will receive one, but they do not have it yet," Kostadinov said.
He accused Zelensky of lying and suggested that the statement could be connected to Bulgaria's pre-election situation, describing this as his political assessment.
Kostadinov said Bulgaria did not have an independent policy on the war and security in the Black Sea. He added that sensitive information had been presented during the closed session that he could not disclose publicly.
"Other things were said as well, things I cannot share, but they are quite alarming regarding our readiness for surveillance, defense, and so forth. Frankly, all of this reflects extremely poorly on the policies pursued by Bulgarian governments in recent years. And by 'years,' I mean more than a decade. In practice, this policy of vassalage rather than sovereignty has failed. We are seeing the consequences of that right now. I am deeply concerned about our country's future," the Revival leader said.
The CCNS is chaired by the head of state and includes the Speaker of the National Assembly, the Prime Minister, the ministers of Defense, Interior, Foreign Affairs and Finance, the heads of key security agencies and structures, the Chief of Defense, and one representative from each parliamentary group.
After hours of deliberations, Deputy Finance Minister Lyudmila Petkova and State Agency for Intelligence (DAR) head Antoine Gechev were the first participants to leave, at around 5:00 PM.

Value-added tax refunds will resume in two to three weeks at best, Finance, Tax and Customs Policy Committee head Danylo Hetmantsev said, confirming a problem that businesses have raised with the committee, as refunds have been halted for the past three weeks.
"The problem is real, and it is serious. At best, refunds will resume in two to three weeks," he said on Telegram on Wednesday.

According to preliminary Finance Ministry data, budget VAT refunds fell to UAH 9.9 billion in September 2026, compared with UAH 15 billion in September last year and UAH 21.4 billion in August.
For January-September as a whole, total VAT refunds were UAH 170.9 billion, compared with UAH 131.2 billion a year earlier, while VAT revenue from goods produced in Ukraine reached UAH 255.2 billion, compared with UAH 231.6 billion a year earlier.
"The situation is the same as with capital expenditure. Everything will be financed as cash becomes available in Treasury accounts," a government source told Interfax-Ukraine about the VAT refunds.

MotoGP to introduce separate Sprint, Grand Prix qualifying in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:40:47 UTC
01:40:47 KST

Halis Sunnetci
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
MotoGP will introduce separate qualifying sessions and starting grids for Sprint and Grand Prix races from the 2027 season, the championship announced Wednesday.
Since Sprint races were introduced in 2023, a single qualifying session on Saturday has determined the starting grid for both races.
Under the new format, Friday will begin with a 45-minute Free Practice 1, followed by a 30-minute Free Practice 2 that will no longer determine which riders advance directly to Grand Prix qualifying.
Friday will end with a 15-minute Sprint qualifying session involving all riders, which will determine the grid for Saturday's Sprint race, MotoGP said.
Saturday will start with a 20-minute Free Practice 3 before qualifying determines the grid for Sunday's Grand Prix.
All riders will compete in a 15-minute Grand Prix Q1, with the fastest 12 advancing to the 15-minute Q2 session.
The Sprint will then take place later Saturday using the grid determined by Friday's Sprint qualifying.
Sunday's traditional MotoGP warm-up will also be removed, according to the championship.
Instead, the pit lane will open for 10 minutes ahead of the Grand Prix, allowing riders to complete multiple sighting laps before the race.
The changes will coincide with MotoGP's new technical regulations for 2027, including a reduction in engine capacity from 1,000cc to 850cc.

Zuckerberg’s Biohub teams with Google, US government in $1.8B push to model human cells with AI
Unknown

2026-10-07

01:39:43 KST

Halis Sunnetci
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Mark Zuckerberg-backed Biohub is joining forces with Google, Meta and the US government in a $1.8 billion effort to generate biological data for artificial intelligence models, the institute announced Wednesday.
Biohub said the US Energy Department (DOE) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) will join its Virtual Biology Initiative, alongside Google DeepMind, Isomorphic Labs and Meta.
The project seeks to generate and standardize vast amounts of biological data needed to develop predictive models of cells.
Google DeepMind, AI drug discovery company Isomorphic Labs and Meta will collectively invest $300 million in the initiative, while the DOE will contribute more than $500 million over five years for biological measurement, modeling and computing.
The NIH will contribute datasets and other resources developed through more than $500 million in previous federal investment, with Biohub working to standardize the information for AI training.
Biohub, a nonprofit research organization co-founded by Zuckerberg and his wife, physician Priscilla Chan, launched the five-year Virtual Biology Initiative in April with a $500 million commitment.
Building 'virtual cell'
The initiative ultimately aims to develop AI models capable of predicting how cells behave and respond to interventions such as drugs or genetic changes, allowing scientists to test possibilities digitally before moving to physical experiments.
"An accurate predictive model of biology could dramatically accelerate scientific discovery by enabling scientists to perform experiments digitally," said Alex Rives, Biohub’s head of science.
Biohub said the resulting datasets will eventually be made available to the wider scientific community.
Commercial partners will have a one-year period of exclusive access to data they help fund before it becomes publicly available, while government-funded data will carry no such restriction, according to Rives.

Gerhard Schröder visits latest Russian employer, Hyperglobus

Gerhard Schröder visits latest Russian employer, Hyperglobus
October 7, 2026
Gerhard Schröder visited one of the Moscow branches of the new Hyperglobus supermarket chain on Wednesday, a few days after being named a member of its supervisory board.
Russian TV footage showed employees at the branch greeting the former German chancellor and his current wife, So-yeon Schröder-Kim, with sustained applause.
Schröder has current or recent links to a series of Russian businesses and to President Vladimir Putin, issues that have become increasingly contentious in Germany in recent years, particularly since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
What is Hyperglobus' link to Germany?
The new Russian supermarket chain Hyperglobus was spun off from Germany's Globus Holding last year.
Last week, Hyperglobus announced that Schröder had been appointed to the supervisory board. The supermarket confirmed that the former chancellor and Social Democrat had visited a branch on the western outskirts of Moscow on Wednesday.
"I'm very pleased to be here, to see this wonderful hypermarket, to see the results of your work and to meet you, my wonderful colleagues," RBC television in Russia quoted Schröder as saying.
Schröder also reportedly called last week for the continuation of remaining trade ties between Russia and countries like Germany amid the sanctions imposed since the start of the war in Ukraine.
"It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow us to hear each other and look for ways forward," newspaper RBK reported him as saying last Friday.
What's the deal with Schröder, Putin, Russia and Ukraine?
Schröder's close ties to Putin came under scrutiny even while he was still in office, notably in 2004 when Schröder responded to a question from a reporter by saying that, yes, he believed Putin was a "flawless democrat" or lupenreiner Demokrat.
Even 22 years ago, this assertion strained credulity in many eyes — not least among opposition groups or in war-torn Chechnya.
On leaving politics, Schröder kept close ties to the Kremlin and took up a series of senior roles, perhaps most famously on the board of the Rosneft energy giant and before that on the board of the Nord Stream gas pipeline project that was majority owned by Gazprom.
In 2014, not long after the annexation of Crimea and as a Russian-backed civil war brewed in Ukraine, Schröder was Nord Stream's guest of honor in St. Petersburg, where he celebrated his 70th birthday in lavish style.
Four years later, after an election many in the West decried as bordering on a sham, Schröder took a prominent place at the 2018 swearing-in ceremony for Putin's fourth presidential term at the Kremlin (pictured above).
Now-deceased Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny once said Schröder was Putin's "errand boy."
In 2024, Schröder was stripped of a state-funded office and staff — typically provided to former chancellors — on the basis that he was no longer fulfilling any obligations tied to his previous role in government.
His party, the center-left Social Democrats, tried on several occasions to eject him as a member. Each attempt failed to clear the high legal bars required, and he remains a member, having joined in 1963.
Putin has often suggested him as a possible peace mediator between Russia, Ukraine and Europe — with Schröder also expressing a willingness to take on the role — even though the reality is he would likely be entirely unacceptable as a mediator to all parties other than Russia, and particularly to Ukraine.

Debt interest exceeds health or education spending in 51 developing countries: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:38:35 UTC
01:38:35 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Some 3.7 billion people live in 51 developing countries where public debt interest payments exceed government spending on health or education, UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) warned Wednesday.
Developing countries paid $995 billion in net interest on public debt in 2025, nearly three times the 2010 level, according to UNCTAD's "A World of Debt 2026: Rising debt costs and stalling development."
The median share of government revenue devoted to net interest reached 8.1%, almost double the level in 2010.
Global public debt climbed to $111 trillion in 2025, including $35 trillion owed by developing economies.
Developed countries held more than two-thirds of the total, although debt has grown faster in developing countries.
Higher costs squeeze development spending
UNCTAD said developing countries face structurally higher interest rates, compounded by recent conflicts and crises.
External financing has also become scarcer as bilateral lenders redirect development assistance toward domestic priorities and private creditors become more cautious.
Borrowing at rates comparable to developed economies could save developing countries around $500 billion annually, UNCTAD estimated.
The agency called for stronger financial safety nets, reversing declines in development assistance, expanding lending by development banks and improving national debt management.
Borrowing countries seek stronger voice
The Borrowers' Platform will hold its first Governing Council meeting in Bangkok on Oct. 12, on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings.
Launched in April, the initiative provides developing countries with a forum to share experience and strengthen cooperation on debt challenges, according to UNCTAD, which serves as its secretariat.
Members are expected to formalize their participation and elect a chair for the 2026-2027 annual cycle.

‘Birthday gift for Putin’: Russian attack on Ukraine kills 21, including four children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:37:00 UTC
01:37:00 KST

Russia launched one of its heaviest aerial attacks on Ukraine in recent months overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, firing dozens of missiles and around 130 drones at a wide range of areas across the country. At least 21 people were killed, including four children, and around 60 were wounded. 
The attack took place on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s 74th birthday — he was born on October 7 — and officials in Kyiv said the deadly destruction was effectively a “birthday gift” for him.
The attack came after weeks in which Russia stepped up its use of fast, jet-powered drones, posing a new challenge to Ukraine’s air defense system. The heaviest toll was recorded in the city of Pryluky in the Chernihiv region, about 135 kilometers (84 miles) east of Kyiv. A Russian missile struck a five-story apartment building directly, destroying large sections of it. According to updated figures released by Ukrainian authorities Wednesday afternoon, 15 people were killed at the site, including four children, and around 50 others were wounded. Rescue crews and residents spent hours digging through the rubble in an effort to find people trapped beneath it and survivors.
The missile struck the building at around 6 a.m., when many residents were still asleep. According to local authorities, two sections of the building were destroyed in the strike. A children’s and youth creative center, a factory and vehicles were also damaged in the city, while a fire broke out in an industrial area following the bombardment. Among those affected was a local police officer who was wounded, while her husband — who until recently served as a police officer on the front — and her mother were killed. Seven children were also among the wounded, including a 3-year-old girl. An 8-year-old boy was among those killed.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy linked the timing of the attack to Putin’s birthday. “On Wednesday, as a ‘birthday gift’ for Putin, the Russian military destroyed a residential building in Pryluky,” he said. “The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile attacks.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha joined in the condemnation, saying Russian generals had given Putin his “favorite birthday gift — war crimes.” He said the Russian president’s truly fitting gift would be to see him stand trial in The Hague.
The strike on Pryluky was part of a large-scale combined attack. Zelenskyy said Russia launched around 70 missiles in total, many of them ballistic. The Ukrainian Air Force said the attack included 48 Kh-101, Iskander-K and Kalibr cruise missiles, as well as ballistic and anti-ship missiles and 130 drones of various types, including Shahed drones. Of those, 46 were jet-powered.
According to Zelenskyy, infrastructure in Kyiv and 12 other regions came under fire. Five residential buildings were damaged in Dnipro and four in Kremenchuk. Two people were killed and seven wounded in Kremenchuk, while additional fatalities were reported in Kyiv and Oleksandriia. The bombardment forced authorities to introduce emergency power outages in five regions as repair work continued throughout Wednesday.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, air defenses managed to shoot down or disrupt 161 targets: five ballistic or other high-speed missiles of various types, 39 cruise missiles and 117 drones. Missile and drone strikes were nevertheless recorded at 18 locations across the country.
Among the areas that came under the heaviest fire were Kyiv, Kharkiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk. Ukraine, meanwhile, reported relative success in countering the jet-powered drones: More than 80% of the 46 such drones launched in the attack were intercepted, compared with an interception rate of around 50% to 60% in recent weeks. The greater threat for Kyiv remains ballistic missiles, which are far more difficult to intercept and require Patriot systems and additional interceptors.
The attack did not come as a complete surprise. On Tuesday, Zelenskyy warned that Ukrainian intelligence had information indicating that Russia was preparing a “massive attack” and urged residents not to ignore air raid alerts. Many Kyiv residents headed to the capital’s deep underground metro stations overnight to seek shelter. Despite the advance warning, air defense systems were unable to stop all the missiles.
” (Photo: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)
Zelenskyy particularly emphasized the difficulty of countering ballistic missiles and again called on Kyiv’s allies to provide Ukraine with additional Patriot systems and ammunition. Shortages of both have made it especially difficult for Ukraine to defend its cities.
“Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. Air defense packages are a vital need for us right now,” he said.
Russia, for its part, confirmed that it had carried out a “massive attack” but claimed its targets were facilities connected to Ukraine’s military industry. The Defense Ministry in Moscow said it struck sites where missiles and drones are manufactured and stored, including facilities linked to Fire Point, which produces, among other weapons, Ukraine’s Flamingo cruise missiles. Russia also claimed it attacked port infrastructure and shipyards in the Odesa region, as well as vessels it said were used by the Ukrainian military.
At the same time, Ukraine continued its long-range strikes inside Russia. Zelenskyy said two oil facilities and a training complex in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions had been attacked over the previous 24 hours. He called the strikes “a justified Ukrainian response to all Russian attacks against our people.”
Zelenskyy also released footage of an oil tanker burning in the Black Sea near Sochi. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the Russian attack, saying that “Russia is pursuing a deliberate strategy of terror” aimed at making everyday life impossible for Ukrainians.

Why it is legitimate to ask whether Zionism is inherently racist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:34:52 UTC
01:34:52 KST

Breadcrumb
Why it is legitimate to ask whether Zionism is inherently racist
The British Green Party's decision to declare Zionism a form of racism was always going to provoke the backlash we are seeing, but we believe that this reaction is unjustified.
The motion passed by 1,022 votes to 813, prompting accusations of antisemitism and condemnation from Israel and several British political and Jewish organisations.
But the vote's significance goes far beyond the Green Party. It reflects a profound shift in public attitudes in Britain and elsewhere after three years of Israel's devastating war on Gaza. Ideas about Israel, Zionism and Palestinian dispossession that were once largely confined to Palestinian, anti-colonial and activist circles are entering mainstream political debate. A much deeper public understanding of the nature of the Israeli state and the ideology underpinning it is crystallising.
Whatever one thinks of every clause in the Green motion, dismissing the proposition that Zionism and racism are connected as inherently antisemitic is therefore neither historically serious nor intellectually defensible.
It is, after all, a debate the international community has had before.
In 1975, UN General Assembly Resolution 3379 determined that "Zionism is a form of racism and racial discrimination". Importantly, the resolution situated Zionism within a wider anti-colonial framework, declaring that international peace required the elimination of "colonialism and neo-colonialism, foreign occupation, Zionism, apartheid and racial discrimination".
The resolution was revoked in 1991 amid the diplomatic negotiations surrounding the Madrid peace conference. But repealing a political resolution did not settle the historical or moral question it raised. Half a century later, the reality produced by Zionism demands that this question be revisited rather than placed beyond permissible debate.
Zionism's intellectual history is far more complicated than the common description of it as simply the national liberation movement of the Jewish people. Long before modern political Zionism emerged among a minority of European Jews in the late nineteenth century, Protestant Christian currents in Europe, particularly in Britain, advocated the "restoration" of Jews to Palestine. Seventeenth-century Christian millenarians promoted Jewish return partly through an eschatological belief that it would hasten the Second Coming.
Christian Zionism remains a powerful political movement today. Historically, such ideas were – and still are – regarded with deep suspicion by many Jews, not least because visions of sending Europe's Jews elsewhere could coexist comfortably with antisemitic desires for a Europe without Jews.
Modern Jewish Zionism itself arose partly in response to very real and murderous European antisemitism. That history must never be trivialised. But the political solution Zionism proposed was the establishment and maintenance of a Jewish demographic and political majority in a land already overwhelmingly inhabited by another people.
That contradiction could not be resolved without dispossession.
In 1948, more than 750,000 Palestinians were uprooted from their homes as Israel was established. They and their descendants were denied return, while immigration laws gave Jews around the world a privileged route to citizenship. Palestinians who remained inside Israel lived under military rule until 1966. After 1967 came occupation, settlement, land confiscation and an increasingly elaborate system in which Jewish settlers and Palestinians living alongside one another were subjected to radically different rights and legal regimes.
These were not merely unfortunate deviations from an otherwise egalitarian project. Maintaining a specifically Jewish state in a country whose indigenous Palestinian population never disappeared has required continuing demographic and territorial engineering.
Israel eventually made the principle explicit. Its 2018 Nation-State Basic Law declares that national self-determination in Israel is "unique to the Jewish people".
Nor can appeals to an abstract Jewish right to self-determination be separated from the political reality that now exists between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean. There is not, in practice, one sovereign Israeli state alongside an independent Palestinian state. One overwhelmingly dominant power controls the territory and the lives of the people within it, but allocates radically different rights according to nationality, ethnicity, and legal status.
Meanwhile, settlement expansion in the West Bank, Israel's continuing control over Gaza, and Israeli military occupation of additional Syrian territory have made the borders of this supposedly settled national project anything but settled.
Within Israeli politics, powerful currents openly advocate permanent sovereignty over occupied Palestinian territory. Self-determination cannot be treated as an unquestionable moral principle when, in practice, its implementation requires another people's permanent subordination.
That is why the apartheid charge can no longer credibly be dismissed as fringe rhetoric.
And neither should Jewish identity be collapsed into Zionism.
Mainstream discussion in Britain too often speaks of "the Jewish community" as though millions of people share a single political view on Israel. Claims about what proportion of British Jews are Zionists, or about what criticism of Israel makes Jews feel unsafe, are frequently reproduced with far less scrutiny than comparable political claims would receive.
This obscures a broad spectrum of Jewish opinion, including anti-Zionist and non-Zionist Jews, Holocaust survivors and their descendants, religious Jews who reject Zionism, and younger Jewish activists who refuse the proposition that Jewish safety must depend upon Palestinian dispossession.
Jewish participation in the Green debate itself also matters: Jewish members were present on different sides of the argument, underlining precisely why no organisation should be permitted to appoint itself the sole authentic voice of Jewish political opinion. Indeed, Jewish Greens themselves acknowledged substantial disagreement within their membership before the conference.
Antisemitism is hatred of or discrimination against Jews because they are Jews. Zionism is a political ideology with a historical record, institutional forms and material consequences. Like any other political ideology, it can and must be examined, criticised and judged by what it has produced.
The Green Party motion should therefore be an invitation to argument, not an excuse to shut one down.
The New Arab Editorial represents the collective voice of The New Arab’s editorial team, presenting views that promote authentic discourses on the MENA region and beyond.
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@newarab.com

She told Israel's Army Radio that the government was trying to make affected families forget what happened on 7 October.
Netanyahu, whose far-right government had been in office for nine months when the attack took place, has refused to accept responsibility for the security failures that preceded it.
Recent reports have indicated that he was warned of a major and imminent security threat in the weeks before 7 October by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed.
Hamas, Islamic Jihad and other armed groups from Gaza launched an unprecedented air, land and sea incursion into southern Israel on 7 October 2023.
Almost 1,200 Israelis were killed in attacks on military outposts and communities in and around the Gaza border, while around 250 people were captured and taken to Gaza. The captives were subsequently released in ceasefire and hostage deals, rescued by Israeli forces, or killed.
The death toll also includes Israelis killed by their own military during the chaotic response to the attack, according to Israeli media reports.
Hamas said its operation, dubbed "Al-Aqsa Flood", was carried out in response to Israel's decades-long occupation of Palestinian territory, violence against Palestinians and raids at the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, Islam's third-holiest site.
Israel responded by launching its devastating assault on Gaza, which has been described as a genocide by several human rights organisations and experts.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli bombardment and ground operations in the enclave, according to Gaza's Health Ministry, with thousands more believed to remain buried beneath the rubble.
Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, are wanted by the International Criminal Court over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Much of the enclave lies in ruins, with recent satellite images showing the scale of the destruction.
The Israeli military continues to control around 70 percent of the territory, while implementation of an October 2025 ceasefire agreement has been slow. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the ceasefire came into effect.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned on Wednesday that extremism was gaining ground inside the country’s legislatures after a lawmaker from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected president of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament.
Tobias Rausch secured 48 votes in Tuesday’s secret ballot, after the AfD emerged as the largest party in last month’s state election.
The result has raised questions over whether lawmakers from other parties, potentially including Merz’s Christian Democrats (CDU), helped secure his victory.
There is no evidence identifying the additional votes because the ballot was secret.
Merz urges parties to maintain AfD firewall
Merz called on politicians to reject cooperation with the AfD, saying its growing presence in state institutions posed a challenge to Germany’s democratic system.
“Extremism is forcefully making its way into our parliaments,” Merz said, warning that lawmakers who supported the AfD were “playing the extremists' game and undermining credibility.”
He said supporting the AfD was incompatible with the values of his CDU and rejected speculation that CDU lawmakers had backed Rausch, while acknowledging that the secret ballot made it difficult to establish who voted for whom.
Merz also cautioned against drawing conclusions without evidence, warning of the possibility of political “false flag operations.”
AfD and BSW push Ukraine and Russia motion
Rausch received more votes than the AfD and the far-left Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) could provide on their own, together holding 44 seats.
The BSW had pledged before the vote to support the AfD candidate. The two parties have opposed mass immigration and called for an end to sanctions against Russia.
After the vote, the AfD and BSW used their new strength in the state parliament to introduce a motion calling on Germany to halt military and financial support for Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia.
The development has intensified debate over the effectiveness of Germany’s so-called firewall, under which mainstream parties have traditionally ruled out coalition agreements or political cooperation with the AfD.
CDU faces pressure over secret ballot
Merz said it would be up to political groups in Saxony-Anhalt to determine whether the circumstances surrounding the vote could be clarified.
His coalition partner, the Social Democratic Party (SPD), has demanded answers from the CDU. SPD parliamentary group leader Matthias Miersch said he planned to raise the issue at a coalition meeting Wednesday evening.
Merz also accused the AfD, BSW and the far-left Left party of seeking to weaken democratic cohesion.
The controversy comes as the AfD’s strong performance in eastern Germany continues to put pressure on Merz’s government and test the long-standing political barriers separating the far-right party from Germany’s mainstream political establishment.

Rubio urges West to return to its ‘civilizational roots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:33:00 UTC
01:33:00 KST

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called for the nations of the West to return to their civilizational roots and restore the values that drove the rise of Europe and North America to global dominance for centuries.
In Athens to discuss deepening economic, energy and security cooperation with Greece, Rubio delivered a speech later Wednesday near the ruins of the Acropolis, a widely recognizable symbol of the city's ancient civilization associated with the creation of popular participatory government and the social contract.
Rubio aimed to remind listeners of qualities he says were born in Greece and later defined the West, such as curiosity, courage, ambition, a restless spirit of exploration and a drive to discover the unknown.
"It has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the 'global community' over one's own people. And I think here, too, we have much more to learn from the men of Ancient Greece. They knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else," Rubio said.
"Today, we find ourselves at a crossroads," he said. "The next decade will write the story of the next century. The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world, or resigns itself to a future of atrophy, and servitude, and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all."
Rubio is seen by many as the gentle face of the Trump administration and has been frequently dispatched to clarify or otherwise address concerns about the president's frequently undiplomatic statements.
Rubio, along with Vice President JD Vance, is seen as one of the leading contenders to assume Trump's mantle at the top of the Republican Party, which faces stiff challenges in next month's congressional midterm elections. Republican Party, which faces stiff challenges in next month's congressional midterm elections.
The Trump administration has repeatedly accused countries in Europe of backsliding on their traditional values and democratic principles by stifling the free speech of conservatives and falling short on commitments to international partners like the United States.
Many of those countries have rejected the complaints and accused the U.S. under Trump of being guilty of similar behavior and worse with its staunch anti-immigration stance that some believe is racist.
Ahead of his visit to Athens, about 1,500 people gathered to protest Rubio's presence and the war in Iran, chanting "American killers!"
The demonstration was organized by a communist labor union and other left-wing groups and was held ahead of extensive road closures planned in Athens. Organizers said similar protests were held in at least 12 other Greek cities. Police banned public demonstrations Wednesday in central.
Rubio is on the second leg of a three-nation tour of NATO allies that has already taken him to Iceland and will end in Portugal on Thursday. The trip is aimed at reassuring U.S. partners that the Trump administration is committed to their success and security despite what has been an often brusque and sometimes rude approach to traditional friends that has stirred unease.
Rubio began emphasizing historical themes on Thursday, when he met Iceland's foreign minister at the site of the landmark 1986 summit between former President Ronald Reagan and then Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, a meeting that many believe marked the beginning of the end of the Cold War and was a catalyst for the eventual dissolution of the Soviet Union.
It remains unclear what impact Rubio's visits will have, although on Tuesday in Reykjavik, he sought to reassure Iceland that President Donald Trump's administration has no designs on the island. Rather, he said the U.S. shares Iceland's deep concerns about Arctic security as tensions between the U.S. and Russia rise in the High North and elsewhere.
Iceland has been uneasy about Trump's intentions toward it after he posted a map showing the colors of the U.S. flag sprawling across all of North America and extending to Iceland and Greenland. That wariness has persisted despite an agreement last month to increase the U.S. presence in the neighboring Danish territory of Greenland that appears to have ended Trump's demands for the U.S. to take full control of the island.
But after Rubio's talks in Reykjavik, those tensions appeared to be on the wane. Rubio said the United States would not do anything in Iceland without Iceland's consent.
Before delivering his speech in Athens, Rubio declined to comment when he was asked about allegations of misconduct leveled at U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle.
At a joint news conference with the Greek foreign minister, Rubio said he would not address the matter while visiting a foreign country, but added: "Suffice it to say our embassy here is doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
The top Democrats on the Senate Foreign Relations and House Foreign Affairs committees, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and Rep. Gregory Meeks, have initiated probes into claims reported last month by the Wall Street Journal that Guilfoyle acted improperly while serving as the top U.S. envoy to Greece.
The Journal reported that Guilfoyle told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings.
Guilfoyle, a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump's son Donald Jr., has denied any wrongdoing, and Rubio has defended her before.

Labour could oversee worst parliament on record for living standards, study warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:30:55 UTC
01:30:55 KST

Soaring energy and housing costs mean Labour is on course to preside over the worst parliament for living standards in modern times, a stark analysis warns.
Three weeks ahead of John Healey’s budget, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation said Britain faces a “dire” outlook unless the government takes “bold policy action”.
The JRF predicts that, after housing costs, average household incomes will be between £440 and £770 lower in real terms in 2029-30 than when Labour came to power two years ago.
Even the lower end of that range would mark the biggest decline in living standards since modern records began in 1961, the thinktank said, and come on top of a tight squeeze in the last parliament.
Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, has been tasked by Andy Burnham to lead the Cabinet Office cross-government taskforces, with two focusing on turning around living standards. One is looking at short-term cost of living measures to help on housing and energy, and the other at big structural interventions such as public control that might alleviate those pressures long term.
Their work will eventually form part of the 10-year plan expected later this autumn, which Burnham began discussions about with cabinet ministers at a Chequers away day this week.
Haigh has repeatedly told officials that there will have to be “trade offs” in order to prioritise alleviating the cost of living and public control.
At the budget, Burnham has promised to offer a “breathing space” to voters and Healey is expected to offer £1bn in additional support to energy consumers; but there are concerns inside government about whether that goes far enough.
Healey is minded to rebuff a call from the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to spend billions more on removing levies from bills altogether. The most likely solution is understood to be increasing the warm homes discount – a £150 discount to energy bills offered to households on certain benefits.
The chancellor is understood to be considering raising this by £100, with the rise funded by taxpayers.
The foundation’s living standards analysis used the Bank of England’s two projections for energy prices – a “central” and an “adverse” scenario.
The thinktank has pointed out that since the Bank set these out in July, real-world events have tracked close to the adverse scenario, with oil prices surging back above $100 a barrel after hostilities resumed in the Middle East.
By driving up the cost of energy, the renewed conflict has also increased expectations that the Bank will raise the base interest rate to tackle resurgent inflation. Markets are now betting on four quarter point increases to 4.75% by the end of next year.
Borrowing costs for homebuyers have already jumped in response to the resulting turmoil in bond markets – with the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hitting 6% this week for the first time in three years.
Chris Belfield, the chief economist at the JRF, said: “Without bold policy action on living standards, families are set to be poorer than they were a decade ago. This is terrible both for families who are just treading water to get by and the more than 7 million families who are already routinely going without essentials like food and basic toiletries.”
Some forecasts have suggested the typical household dual-fuel bill could leap by 16% to the equivalent of £2,000 a year in the first quarter of next year. Given the scale of the looming squeeze, the foundation has argued for a more ambitious package of measures on energy than Healey appears minded to offer.
It would like to see a baseline level of energy offered to all households at a cheaper price, with those in greater need entitled to more of these cut-price units of gas and electricity.
Other recommendations include making benefits more generous by relinking local housing allowance to average rents; and increasing universal credit, as the Conservatives did during the Covid pandemic. This could be paid for via changes such as increasing capital gains tax rates to match income tax, it argues.
The JRF analysis of changes in living standards over time differs from those of the Office for Budget Responsibility and other thinktanks such as the Resolution Foundation because of different ways of accounting for housing costs.
Despite Burnham’s promise to correct 40 years of economic missteps, Healey’s budget is expected to be relatively modest, with important decisions on tax and spending delayed until next year. These include when the UK will implement spending 3% of GDP on defence – a target Healey claimed to be committed to when he resigned as defence secretary earlier this year.
In his 28 October statement, the chancellor is expected to focus on filling the gaps in the defence investment plan announced by Keir Starmer’s government in June; and laying out how the Treasury will devolve some income tax revenue to regional mayors.
A Treasury spokesperson said: “We know families are feeling the impact of higher prices, pushed up by conflicts overseas.
“The chancellor is focused on giving households and businesses a bit of breathing space where we can. That’s why we have removed VAT from electricity bills, capped bus fares in England at £2 in 2027, extended the 5p fuel duty cut, and frozen rail fares and prescription charges.”

Israel bars Palestinian election officials from Jerusalem, Gaza

Breadcrumb
Israel bars Palestinian election officials from Jerusalem, Gaza ahead of November vote
Palestinian election officials have reportedly been barred by Israel from entering Gaza and East Jerusalem ahead of the November legislative elections - the first planned since 2006.
The Palestinian Central Elections Commission was prevented from entering both territories on Tuesday to oversee preparations for the 28 November vote, according to Palestinian news agency Wafa.
This could potentially create a fresh obstacle to the first Palestinian parliamentary elections in decades,
Wafa quoted an unnamed Palestinian official source but provided no further details.
Israeli officials did not publicly respond to the reports that the Palestinan officials had been denied entry.
However, a spokesperson for the Palestinian Central Elections Commission told news agency AFP that the vote could still go ahead.
“The Commission is continuing to organise the electoral process despite the Israeli decision,” said commission spokesperson Farid Taamallah, adding that employees in Gaza had already been trained and were present on the ground.
On Tuesday, EU foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said in a post on X that the bloc was “ready to deploy an Election Observation Mission for the Palestinian legislative polls”.
During a telephone conversation with Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh, Kallas said: “Palestinians have the right to choose their representatives in elections that are credible, inclusive and transparent.”
In a statement posted on X, al-Sheikh called for “European support to help overcome any obstacles to holding the elections, ensuring the participation of all our people in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip in the electoral process.”
The reported incident has raised concerns among Palestinians that the vote could be postponed or cancelled, similar to what happened in 2021.
At the time, President Mahmoud Abbas postponed the election until Israel agreed to allow Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem to participate.
Additionally, an August poll by the Jerusalem Media and Communication Center found that only 29 percent of Palestinians expected the November election to take place as scheduled.
Despite Abbas extending the candidate nomination period from 12 to 18 days because of severe movement restrictions and the difficult security and political situation in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza, the commission said last week that preparations remained on track.
It further stressed that the extension would not affect the 28 November polling date.
Jibril Rajoub, secretary-general of the Central Committee of Fatah, which dominates the Palestinian Authority, told reporters last month that he did not expect the legislative election to be held on time.
He instead called for a presidential election to be held first.
Doing so “would solve a large part of the problem,” he said, arguing that a presidential election would be easier, less costly and could be organised through consensus.
The last Palestinian legislative elections were held in 2006, when Hamas won a majority of seats over Fatah.
A conflict subsequently emerged between Hamas and Fatah and Hamas militarily took control of Gaza a year later, while the PA remained in the West Bank.
The current legislative election process was formally launched in July, when Abbas set 28 November 2026 as the date for elections to the Palestinian Legislative Council in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza.
The Central Elections Commission began accepting nominations on 26 September.
Under the current timetable, campaigning is scheduled to begin on 6 November, followed by a campaign blackout on 27 November and polling on 28 November. Results are scheduled to be announced on 29 November.
The legislative vote is separate from the presidential election.
Abbas has said a presidential election is planned for the first quarter of 2027, although a specific date has not yet been set.

A new civil society alliance is testing Tunisia's one-man rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:29:21 UTC
01:29:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Five years after Kais Saied's power grab, Tunisia's streets are stirring again
Tunis - On 3 September, the Tunisian General Labour Union (UGTT), the National Order of Lawyers, and the Tunisian League for Human Rights launched a joint coordination framework, bringing together three of the four organisations awarded the 2015 Nobel Peace Prize for brokering Tunisia's national dialogue.
The statement was signed at UGTT headquarters by Salaheddine Salmi, the union's secretary general, Boubaker Bethabet, head of the bar association, and Bassem Trifi, president of the human rights league.
It called for dialogue, stronger protection of rights and freedoms, and a review of economic and social policies, citing shortages of medicine, water, electricity, and falling purchasing power.
The framework, led by the UGTT, the country's largest union with more than a million members, has since grown to nine organisations, which have called a national march in Tunis on 17 October, blaming the authorities for worsening living conditions and shrinking freedoms.
Their alliance comes five years after President Kais Saied suspended parliament and began ruling by decree, years in which unions, lawyers, and rights defenders have each come under mounting pressure.
The founders present the framework as a civil society platform that will stay closed to political parties. Analysts say the march will put the new alliance to an early test, as these organisations seek to turn shared grievances into sustained pressure.
The founding statement, titled "Tunisia First, and the People Above All Else," described a deep political, economic, and social crisis that has widened poverty and pushed up unemployment.
Official figures from the National Institute of Statistics put unemployment at 14.9 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, with more than a third being young people.
Meanwhile, inflation rose for a second consecutive month in September, to 5.6 per cent, with food prices up 8.4 per cent.
Saied in late April pointed to his government’s policy of self-reliance, arguing that Tunisia had the resources and national expertise to drive its own development without relying on foreign dictates.
He has also opposed the privatisation of public institutions, framing state control of key sectors as part of his broader approach to economic sovereignty.
A 2026 report by the Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy argues, however, that public anger has grown as government promises have failed to translate into improvements in daily life, while pressure on foreign currency reserves has contributed to shortages of food and medicine.
Why now?
Anger had spilt into the streets this summer, from protests over power and water cuts during a July heatwave to a rally of thousands in Tunis on 25 July, the anniversary of Saied's power grab.
Fuel tanker drivers are among the latest to walk out, after transport companies deducted social security contributions from their wages without paying them into the national fund, leaving the drivers unregistered and their families without the health booklets that cover treatment and medicines, according to Slouane Smiri, an assistant secretary general of the UGTT.
Slim Sahimi, secretary general of the UGTT's General Federation of Petroleum and Chemicals, told The New Arab that the drivers first stopped work spontaneously in August over unpaid social security dues and allowances agreed in May 2019.
"The UGTT intervened to calm the situation in return for a working session with the relevant ministry, which never took place, so the union carried out a strike on September 23," he said.
Badie Mbarek, a senior UGTT official, said the framework was driven by the mounting economic and social pressures facing workers, including rising living costs, declining purchasing power and deteriorating public services.
"Workers are living a difficult reality because of the deteriorating economic and social conditions and the lack of clarity in the policies pursued by the current authorities, along with the decline of freedoms and their restriction through several decrees, such as Decree 54," he told The New Arab.
Zied Dabbar, president of the National Union of Tunisian Journalists (SNJT), warned in January that Decree 54, a 2022 cybercrime law, was increasingly used against journalists and citizens and had become a tool for criminalising opinion, despite Justice Minister Leila Jaffel's assurance to parliament in November 2025 that it had been applied only in cases of defamation, slander, and false news.
On 30 September, a day after the march was announced, Saied replaced the decree's five-year prison term for a first offence with fines of 10,000 to 20,000 dinars ($3,370 to $6,740), though the SNJT wants it repealed.
Mbarek said the recent presidential decree reflected the result of months of the UGTT’s efforts to assert its national role and defend workers’ interests. He argued that the union’s involvement in the emerging framework was part of a broader effort to address the economic and social pressures facing Tunisians.
“The union, he added, “will remain a supporter of the interests of its members and of the Tunisian people.”
From statements to the streets
Six organisations joined the movement on 29 September, including the General Union of Tunisian Students (UGET), the Tunisian Association of Democratic Women, the Union of Unemployed Graduates, the Tunisian Organisation of Young Doctors, the Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights, and the SNJT.
Mbarek had said the UGTT was open to new members but ruled out political parties.
"This framework will include only civil society organisations that aim to serve the national interest and have no political agenda," he told The New Arab.
For UGET, joining was a natural step, said its deputy secretary-general, Liwa al-Nabli, pointing to shrinking freedoms, a worsening economy that weighs on all students, and a troubled start to the academic year in teaching, transport, and university housing.
Students are a core part of society, he said, and the student movement has defended the interests of Tunisians since the colonial era.
"For some time, UGET members have faced repeated harassment, on campus through referrals to disciplinary councils and off campus through arrests, because of their union and political activity," al-Nabli told The New Arab. "Particularly during protests in defence of the Palestinian cause and boycott campaigns."
Who gets a seat?
Iyed al-Mabrouk, a student activist, welcomed the UGET's decision to join, arguing that the student movement's role should not be confined to the faculty and calling the move a true embodiment of the slogan "the student movement is an inseparable part of the popular movement".
Sameh al-Aouiti, another activist, accuses the organisers of deliberately excluding several organisations, among them the Tunisian General Union of Students (UGTE).
"That is unacceptable, because the UGTE has led most national mobilisations," he said, citing its rejection on 28 September 2024 of an electoral amendment that stripped the administrative court of its power over election disputes before that year's presidential vote.
The UGTE, historically close to the Islamist Ennahda movement, issued its own statement objecting to not being invited to the coordination meeting and describing the move as an exclusionary approach at odds with the values of freedom and democracy.
Haythem al-Aouni, a Tunisian political activist and blogger, told The New Arab that the framework is important because it now unites rights defenders, lawyers, and workers with students, the unemployed, and the feminist movement.
"When nine organisations meet, we are no longer talking only about politics in its narrow sense, but about the state, society, rights, and social justice," he said.
He also called for opening space for young people within parties, civil society, and institutions, and for giving them a real chance to run for office and take part in decision-making.
"Tunisia today needs shared spaces like these," he said, "because the danger is not in disagreement, but in disagreement turning into a reason to obstruct dialogue."
Fady Ahmed is a Tunisian journalist covering business, politics and human rights. He uses a pseudonym for safety reasons.

01:27:16 KST

The Italian ambassador to Warsaw, Luca Franchetti Pardo, participated today on the central “Nowy Świat” Street in the Polish capital in the unveiling ceremony of a commemorative plaque dedicated to Luciana Frassati Gawrońska (1902–2007), a figure of extraordinary importance in the history of relations between Italy and Poland in the 20th century, as well as the sister of St. Pier Giorgio Frassati. The event, organized by the Frassati Foundation and held under the honorary patronage of the Italian Embassy in Warsaw, was attended by the Apostolic Nuncio to Poland, H.E. Archbishop Antonio Guido Filipazzi, and was attended by representatives of city institutions and the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as well as an audience of public and private figures close to the Frassati Gawroński family.
                                    
Having formed a bond with Poland and Warsaw through her marriage to a Polish diplomat, Luciana Frassati Gawroński, “the Italian woman who fell in love with Poland” (as the plaque states), traveled to Nazi-occupied Poland no fewer than seven times during World War II, carrying out clandestine and humanitarian activities in support of the Polish resistance.  Thanks to her intervention, some of the professors from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków—who had been arrested by the Germans on November 6, 1939, and sent to concentration camps—were released. ““Luciana Frassati Gawrońska was an extraordinary figure of the 20th century who, through her example and constant civic commitment, bore witness to the deep and enduring friendship that unites Italy and Poland, as well as the values of solidarity, generosity, and altruism,” the ambassador emphasized.

BRÜSSEL — Die EU wird erst dann weitere Öl- und Dieselreserven freigeben, wenn die Internationale Energieagentur (IEA) klargestellt hat, dass ein solcher Schritt die Energiesicherheit der Union nicht beeinträchtigen würde. Das erklärten drei mit der Angelegenheit vertraute Diplomaten gegenüber POLITICO.
Die Gruppe der Sieben – zu der Italien, Japan, Deutschland, Großbritannien, Frankreich, Kanada und die USA gehören – einigte sich am Freitag darauf, 100 Millionen Barrel Öl und Diesel freizugeben. Zuvor hatte die US-Regierung damit gedroht, Dieselexporte zu verbieten, sollte Europa nicht auf seine Ölvorräte zurückgreifen.
Die IEA schien jedoch am Mittwoch zu bestätigen, dass die geplante Freigabe aus den bereits im März zugesagten Vorräten erfolgen und keine zusätzlichen Lieferungen umfassen würde. Mit anderen Worten: Es würde sich keineswegs um eine neue Freigabe handeln, sondern lediglich um die Erfüllung früherer Zusagen.
Advertisement
Bei einem Treffen am Mittwochnachmittag bezogen auch EU-Vertreter diese Position und kündigten an, künftige Entnahmen „bis zu einer klareren Einschätzung der Marktbedingungen und der Risiken für die Versorgungssicherheit durch die IEA“ auszusetzen, so einer der Diplomaten. Die Länder müssten wissen, „wie weit wir gehen können“, sagte ein anderer.
Mit Blick auf die aktuell hohen Dieselpreise warnten einige EU-Länder, dass eine Freigabe der Vorräte zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt sie im Falle einer Versorgungskrise verwundbar machen könnte. Unter den IEA-Mitgliedern gibt es noch genügend ungenutzte Vorräte, um die Zusage zur Freigabe von 100 Millionen Barrel zu erfüllen.
Von den im März zugesagten 400 Millionen Barrel wurden 325 Millionen freigegeben, wobei einige Länder „größere Mengen als ursprünglich zugesagt“ freigegeben haben, teilte die IEA in einer Erklärung im Anschluss an eine außerordentliche Ministerkonferenz mit. Damit verbleiben noch rund 100 Millionen Barrel, die die Länder im Rahmen dieser Vereinbarung noch freigeben können, fügte sie hinzu.
In der Erklärung der IEA heißt es, die neue Zusage stelle eine „Vollendung“ der Vereinbarung vom März dar. Zu den 32 Mitgliedern der IEA zählen wohlhabende Länder aus Europa, Nordamerika und Ostasien.
POLITICO hatte bereits berichtet, dass Frankreich und Deutschland – die über einige der bedeutendsten Vorräte in Europa verfügen – signalisiert hätten, dass sie über die bereits zugesagten Mengen hinaus keine oder nur minimale Mengen freigeben würden.
Es bleibt unklar, welchen Anteil der jetzigen Freigabe die Nicht-EU-Mitglieder der IEA übernehmen werden, nachdem zum Beispiel Japan jegliche weiteren Freigaben ausgeschlossen hat.
Weitere Einzelheiten zur Ölfreigabe durch die G7 sollen nächste Woche bei einer Sitzung des IEA-Verwaltungsrats erörtert werden, sagte der zweite Diplomat.

Iconic penguin colony sees "population collapse," study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:24:36 UTC
01:24:36 KST

Iconic penguin colony sees "population collapse" driven by climate change, study finds
A remote island near Antarctica is no longer home to the world's largest penguin colony as climate-driven changes to ocean food chains likely devastated its once-thriving inhabitants and caused a "population collapse," researchers said Wednesday.
Drone and satellite images showed that the volcanic island of Zavodovski lost more than 680,000 — or nearly two-thirds — of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
"That's a very rapid loss," Norman Ratcliffe, the lead author of the BAS study published in the journal Current Biology, told AFP.
The study's findings raise concerns that chinstrap populations across the South Sandwich Islands, which include Zavodovski and are home to 38% of the species, have fallen.
The scientists, who released video of their research, suggest that the "alarming declines" should lead to chinstrap penguins being redesignated as "endangered" by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
This would be a sharp downgrade from their "least concern" classification, which means they are not currently threatened with extinction.
Surveys in 2011 had concluded that chinstrap populations across the South Sandwich Islands were stable.
But their number on Zavodovski fell from around 1.09 million breeding individuals in January 2011 to 402,000 in 2025, or a 63% decline, according to the study.
The island is also home to a different species, macaroni penguins, whose population rose from around 338,000 in 2011 to 433,000 in 2025 -- and now outnumber chinstraps.
Together, chinstraps and macaronis now total more than 835,000 on Zavodovski.
The researchers said the Adelie penguins of Cape Adare, on the other side of Antarctica, are now the world's largest penguin colony, numbering more than one million as of 2018.
"Most striking change"
Zavodovski island's Mount Curry volcano erupted in 2016, sparking fears that it could wipe out its penguin population.
But the researchers found that the ash cloud was blown northeast over an area not inhabited by the flightless birds.
"The decline in chinstrap colony area was in progress prior to the eruption and continued at a constant rate thereafter," the study said.
"We don't think the volcano is implicated or it's not the main driver (of the population decline) because what we see is a linear decline in the chinstrap penguins," Ratcliffe told AFP.
Instead, the scientists linked the drop in chinstrap numbers to a reduction in the availability of krill -- the tiny shrimp-like creatures that are their main food source.
Warming ocean temperatures have pushed the crustaceans south toward colder waters, which chinstraps do not tolerate.
"We think that climate change operating through food webs is probably the main driver," Ratcliffe said.
The island's chinstrap population has been falling at a rate of 7% per year.
Macaroni penguins have increased in number over the same period as they eat a wider range of prey than chinstraps. Their survival also supports the idea that the volcanic eruption was not a factor in the chinstrap's demise.
"The observed numerical shift from chinstraps to macaronis on Zavodovski represents the most striking change in penguin community composition that has been observed at a single location in Antarctica to date," the study said.
"The most plausible explanation for the observed patterns of population change is that a climate-induced regime shift has occurred that has been detrimental to the maritime Antarctic chinstraps but has favored the subantarctic macaronis."
A study released earlier this year found that warming temperatures are forcing chinstrap, Adelie and gentoo penguins to breed earlier, posing a big problem for the species. The change in habits is setting up potential food problems for young chicks.
The new study comes about six months after the emperor penguin was declared an endangered species.
Researchers from the British Antarctic Survey and University of Southampton said last year that Antarctica's emperor penguin population may be declining faster than even the most pessimistic predictions. Images showed the species, recognizable by their height and yellow patches, declined in Antarctica by 22% between 2009 and 2024.
