Why Saudi Arabia is back at war in Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:22:03 UTC
01:22:03 KST

Why Saudi Arabia is back at war in Yemen
A major escalation in Yemen has brought Saudi Arabia back into military confrontation with the Iran-backed Houthis, ending years of relative calm as tensions rise across the Middle East.
Much of the fighting has taken place along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategically important Bab el-Mandeb Strait, following major Houthi territorial gains and a Saudi-backed counteroffensive. The waterway has become increasingly important as the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupts regional trade and energy routes, particularly through the Strait of Hormuz.
Who are the Houthis?
The Houthis, formally known as Ansar Allah, are a Zaydi Shia armed and political movement that emerged in northern Yemen in the 1990s. Their traditional stronghold is the mountainous province of Saada along the border with Saudi Arabia. The movement emerged in opposition to Yemen’s central government and Saudi and US influence.
They now control much of northern and western Yemen, including areas where most of the country’s population lives.
The Houthis are backed by Iran and describe themselves as part of the Tehran-aligned “Axis of Resistance.”
Over years of fighting, the group has developed an arsenal of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones capable of striking Saudi Arabia and ships in the Red Sea.
How did Yemen’s civil war begin?
In 2014, the Houthis seized Sanaa and forced the internationally recognized Yemeni government from the capital. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year at the head of a military coalition seeking to restore the government and counter Iran’s growing influence.
Years of fighting failed to dislodge the Houthis. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 sharply reduced hostilities and cross-border attacks, and although it formally expired after six months, hostilities remained limited for several years.
Fighting resumed in July, when Yemeni government forces struck the runway at Sanaa airport to prevent an Iranian plane carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The delegation was returning from the funeral of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed in the opening US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic Republic at the end of February. The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airport strike, declared the de-escalation over, and retaliated against the kingdom.
The conflict escalated further in September, when the Houthis made their largest territorial gains in years, taking Mocha and key positions along the Red Sea coast and around Bab el-Mandeb. The group also claimed to have effectively encircled Taiz, a major city linking northern and southern Yemen with the Red Sea coast, after cutting a vital supply route to the southern port city of Aden.
Why is Saudi Arabia involved?
Yemen shares a long border with Saudi Arabia, making the conflict a direct security concern for Riyadh. The Houthis have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to strike deep inside the kingdom.
After years of costly fighting, Saudi Arabia had sought to reduce its direct involvement and pursued talks with the Houthis following the 2022 truce. Their recent advances along the Red Sea coast and renewed cross-border attacks have brought Riyadh back into major military action.
The Saudi-led coalition said on Monday that 100 fighter jets were taking part in Operation Dawn of Yemen, providing air cover for government forces, and claimed to have destroyed 324 “high-value” Houthi targets. Hundreds of fighters have reportedly been killed on both sides since then.
The Houthis have responded with missile and drone attacks on Saudi cities, airports, and military facilities.
What does the Iran war have to do with it?
Iranian advisers helped the Houthis plan and carry out their September offensive along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, according to AP, which reported that Iranian personnel were involved at multiple levels of the operation.
The US has not resumed direct strikes against the Houthis, but American and regional officials reportedly said that Washington is providing Riyadh with intelligence, target identification, and operational planning.
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Türkiye activated the collective-defense provisions of their Makkah Alliance for Defense for the first time on Monday in response to attacks on the kingdom. The pact, sometimes dubbed the ‘Muslim NATO’, was signed in August and commits all three members to respond if any one of them comes under attack.
Who else is involved?
The forces fighting the Houthis are themselves divided. Yemen’s internationally recognized government relies heavily on Saudi Arabia, but government-aligned formations have different political and regional loyalties.
The UAE, once Saudi Arabia’s main coalition partner in Yemen, has backed powerful southern forces, including groups seeking an independent southern state. Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have at times pursued competing goals, although forces aligned with both are now fighting the Houthi advance.
Western countries are also providing military support to Riyadh. The UK has deployed an RAF Voyager tanker to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi defensive operations, while France has announced the deployment of troops, radars, and air-defense systems to help protect Saudi energy infrastructure around Yanbu, a major Saudi oil-export hub on the Red Sea.
Why does Bab el-Mandeb matter now?
Bab el-Mandeb is a narrow strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. Ships traveling between Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal normally have to pass through it.
The strait has become especially important since the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted shipping through Hormuz on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula. Saudi Arabia can bypass Hormuz by moving crude from its eastern oil-producing regions through the East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea.
The pipeline was shut after drone attacks in September that Riyadh blamed on Iraqi militias but has since resumed operations, with flows reportedly reaching 5.8 million barrels per day.
Oil shipped from Yanbu to Asian markets, however, must pass through Bab el-Mandeb, putting the route close to the fighting in Yemen. The Houthis have previously attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea with missiles, drones, and explosive boats and have renewed threats against Saudi-linked vessels.
How does it affect global energy markets?
The renewed fighting in Yemen is adding pressure to already strained global energy markets. Oil prices climbed again on Wednesday, with Brent crude trading above $101 a barrel and US benchmark West Texas Intermediate around $90 amid concerns over global supplies.
Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser has warned that the world’s supply cushion was “scarily thin,” saying nearly 3 billion barrels of regional supply had been lost since the war with Iran began and that depleted stocks could take up to two years to rebuild.
The pressure has been even greater on refined fuels. Nasser said diesel and other fuel prices had risen more sharply than crude. G7 countries agreed last week to release 100 million barrels of oil and refined products from emergency reserves in an effort to ease the squeeze.
US President Donald Trump has blamed the global diesel shortage primarily on Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries rather than the Middle East conflict and has urged Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky to halt the attacks.
What happens next?
Yemen’s government has set a goal of restoring its authority across the country, including retaking the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa. Fighting remains intense, however, with the Houthis launching missiles and drones at Aden International Airport on Wednesday as clashes continued elsewhere.
The conflict is worsening Yemen’s long-running humanitarian crisis. Some 184,000 people had been displaced by the latest fighting as of October 4, according to the International Organization for Migration. The WHO said last week that 838 people had been killed and more than 3,600 injured since August.
Diplomatic efforts are continuing, with the UN urging support for a political settlement and de-escalation.
Russia has also urged restraint and expressed readiness to help mediate if requested. The Kremlin said on Wednesday that Moscow was watching the escalation “with concern.”

Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:19:56 UTC
01:19:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon's Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced
Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, the first significant aid from the group to supporters who bore the brunt of the conflict.
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, the US Treasury Department and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.
But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, an armed group founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982 which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.
AIDING 50,000 FAMILIES
Hezbollah would use the funds to pay an initial $3,000 per family, and priority will go to those whose villages have been destroyed or are inaccessible due to Israeli occupation, the sources said. These number around 50,000 families, one of the sources said.
Iran has maintained financial support to Hezbollah through years of crippling US sanctions: it transferred $1 billion to the group in the first 10 months of 2025, according to the US Treasury Department.
Tehran has never acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran's policy of funding regional proxies has stirred domestic protester anger against the clerical rulers in the past and could prove particularly sensitive at a time of worsening hardship in Iran.
Iran had promised Hezbollah more funding after Tehran signed an interim deal with Washington in June that allowed Iran to sell its oil, Reuters reported at the time. That agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Iran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade to block Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would soon contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations”, without elaborating.
Hezbollah's ability to fund local services and provide post-conflict aid has helped shore up its support in the past. Following a war with Israel in 2006, the group immediately handed out large cash payments to those impacted and moved swiftly to help rebuild Beirut's southern suburbs, a stronghold.
But this time there has been little sign of reconstruction. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that the total reconstruction costs from the two wars since 2024 could exceed $27 billion.
A COSTLY WAR
The two sources provided no details on how the money got to Lebanon.
One of them said it was increasingly difficult for Hezbollah to move funds via financial companies that once processed such transfers. Such firms based in Iraq and Dubai were no longer an option, and they were also now under pressure in Turkey, this source said.
Hezbollah’s foes believed money was currently the group’s “oxygen”, the source added. Despite the difficulties securing funding, the group had not stopped paying its fighters and the family members of those killed in combat, this source said.
In Lebanon, the war has inflicted a heavy price on the Shi’ite Muslim community from which Hezbollah draws support. Israel has razed villages across a swathe of territory it has seized in the south, saying it aims to shield northern Israel from Hezbollah attack.
Israeli attacks in Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March 2, according to Lebanon’s health ministry.
Hezbollah has not disclosed figures on its war dead. Reuters reported on May 4 that several thousand Hezbollah fighters had been killed in the war.

Tunisia blocks 300km 'Dignity March' from reaching capital

Breadcrumb
Tunisia blocks 300km 'Dignity March' from reaching capital
Tunisia's security forces have blocked a march by long-term unemployed university graduates from entering the capital after protesters walked nearly 300 kilometres to demand the implementation of a law promising public-sector jobs.
The "Dignity March" began in Menzel Bouzaiane in the central Sidi Bouzid governorate on 27 September, with participants travelling on foot towards Tunis and the presidential palace in Carthage.
Security forces stopped the protesters at Borj Cedria, on the southern outskirts of the capital, telling them they could not continue towards Tunis as a collective protest, according to participants.
The protesters were reportedly permitted to travel into the capital individually.
Six representatives of the march meanwhile travelled to Carthage after initially being informed that President Kais Saied had agreed to meet them.
However, Khadija Safoufi, a spokesperson for the unemployed graduates, told Al Jazeera Net they instead met one of Saied's aides, who told them the law would be implemented but provided no timetable or details.
Safoufi described the outcome as a "major disappointment" and said protesters intended to continue their march towards the capital despite the police intervention.
The protesters are demanding the implementation of Law No. 18 of 2025, which established exceptional measures to recruit university graduates who have been unemployed for prolonged periods into Tunisia's public sector.
The legislation provides for a digital platform to register and rank applicants according to criteria including age, year of graduation and social circumstances, with recruitment supposed to take place in stages over no more than three years.
Protesters say that months after the legislation was passed, they are still waiting for the government to launch the platform, begin recruitment and provide a clear timetable for implementing the law.
Saied met Prime Minister Sarra Zaafrani Zenzri and Employment and Vocational Training Minister Riadh Chaouad on Monday to discuss its implementation.
The Tunisian president described unemployment as an injustice rather than a choice and reiterated his government's commitment to fulfilling its promises.
The march began with just 23 participants but grew to more than 120 as unemployed graduates from other parts of Tunisia joined along the route, according to its organisers.
Parents also walked alongside their unemployed children, some of whom have spent more than two decades looking for stable work.
Several participants required medical treatment because of exhaustion during the journey, while two were injured after being struck by a motorbike.
The march's starting point carries particular significance in Tunisia.
Sidi Bouzid was where street vendor Mohamed Bouazizi set himself on fire in December 2010 following a confrontation with local officials, triggering protests fuelled partly by unemployment, economic marginalisation and anger at the state.
The demonstrations spread across Tunisia and ultimately forced longtime president Zine El Abidine Ben Ali from power in January 2011, setting off uprisings across the Arab world.
More than 15 years later, unemployment remains a major problem in Tunisia, particularly among graduates and young people.
The country's unemployment rate stood at 15% during the first quarter of 2026, according to Tunisia's National Institute of Statistics, with around 641,700 people unemployed.
For participants in the Dignity March, the journey from Sidi Bouzid towards the capital was intended to turn years of waiting into direct pressure on the government.
Despite being stopped short of Tunis, participants said they would continue attempting to reach the capital.

Israel keeps Palestinian journalist Bushra al-Tawil in isolation for 46 days

2026-10-07
16:16:07 UTC
01:16:07 KST

Israeli prison authorities have continued to hold Palestinian journalist and administrative detainee Bushra al-Tawil in isolation for 46 straight days, Palestinian prisoners’ organisations said on Wednesday.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society, Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, and the Palestine Liberation Organisation’s Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said in a statement that Tawil, 33, was transferred to Ohalei Oz isolation facility in Beersheba in southern Israel.
She was moved there from Neve Tirza prison in central Israel after being held in isolation at Damon prison in Haifa in northern Israel, according to the statement.
The groups said the repeated transfers and continued isolation have prevented her legal team from visiting her, despite several requests submitted by lawyers from the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs.
A lawyer was informed on Wednesday that Tawil had again been transferred to Ohalei Oz, preventing the scheduled visit, the statement said.
The organisations urged international organisations operating in the occupied Palestinian territories, particularly the International Committee of the Red Cross, to urgently intervene to end her isolation and secure her release.
Systematic prisoner isolation
The groups said Tawil’s case highlights “the growing policy of isolating Palestinian prisoners, including women,” noting that the practice has become “systematic” in recent months, leaving detainees unable to know the allegations against them or challenge them, while also causing psychological harm.
The UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, known as the Nelson Mandela Rules, prohibit prolonged or indefinite solitary confinement.
It defines solitary confinement as holding a prisoner for 22 hours or more a day without meaningful human contact, and prolonged solitary confinement as lasting more than 15 consecutive days.
The Palestinian groups said Tawil’s 46 days in isolation exceed that threshold and violate international standards.
Tawil has been held in administrative detention without charge since February, according to the statement.
Calls for release
The groups described her as one of the most prominent Palestinian female detainees to face administrative detention in recent years.
She is the daughter of Jamal al-Tawil, a Palestinian administrative detainee who spent years in Israeli prisons, according to the statement.
The organisations demanded Tawil’s immediate release and an end to her isolation.
Israeli forces carry out frequent raids and arrests in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, amid increased illegal settlers’ attacks against Palestinians.
About 9,500 Palestinians are held in Israeli prisons, including around 90 women and more than 350 children, who face food deprivation, torture and medical neglect, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups.

Five Arab writers shortlisted for 2026 National Book Awards in US
Five writers of Arab origin are among the finalists for the US's 2026 National Book Awards, including Syrian writer and journalist Samar Yazbek, Palestinian-American poet and physician Fady Joudah and Egyptian writer and translator Abdelrahman ElGendy.
Palestinian-American novelist Hannah Lillith Assadi and Cuban-Palestinian American poet Carolina Ebeid are also among the finalists.
The National Book Foundation announced 25 finalists on Tuesday across five categories — fiction, nonfiction, poetry, translated literature and young people's literature.
ElGendy was shortlisted in nonfiction for Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, while Joudah and Ebeid are both finalists in poetry, for Exhibit G: Poems, Essays, and Photographs of Gaza and Hide, respectively.
Yazbek is shortlisted in translated literature for Your Presence Is a Danger to Your Life: Voices of Survival and Witness in Gaza, translated from Arabic by Leri Price, while Assadi is a fiction finalist for Paradiso 17.
In the fiction category, Assadi is competing against Edwidge Danticat for Dèy, Julián Delgado Lopera for Pretend You're Dead and I Carry You, Valeria Luiselli for Beginning Middle End and Morgan Thomas for Mad Eden.
Assadi, born to a Palestinian father and Jewish-American mother, drew inspiration for Paradiso 17 from her late father's life. The novel follows a Palestinian man forced from his homeland as a child during the 1948 Nakba and his decades-long search for home.
The works nominated across the awards explore themes including displacement, memory, family and identity.
Egyptian prison memoir shortlisted
In nonfiction, ElGendy is competing against Colin Asher for The Midnight Special: The Secret Prison History of American Music, Camonghne Felix for Let the Poets Govern: A Declaration of Freedom, Sara Nović for Mother Tongue and Joseph Osmundson for Spawning Season: An Experiment in Queer Parenthood.
In Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, ElGendy recounts his imprisonment alongside his father two years after the Egyptian revolution, following a violent security crackdown on protest.
The memoir traces the six years he spent in prison, including his experiences navigating bureaucracy and corruption, as an account of resistance, survival, and liberation.
Palestinian poets shortlisted
Palestinian-American poet, translator and physician Fady Joudah is among the five finalists in the poetry category.
His nominated work, Exhibit G: Poems, Essays, and Photographs of Gaza, brings together poetry, images, and translations connected to his witnessing of Gaza's destruction.
He is joined on the poetry shortlist by Carolina Ebeid, a Cuban-Palestinian American poet, for Hide.
Joudah and Ebeid are competing against Victoria Chang for Tree of Knowledge, Brenda Hillman for Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation and Susan Stewart for Bramble.
Joudah was previously a National Book Award finalist in poetry in 2024.
Samar Yazbek's Voices from Gaza
Syrian writer, journalist and human rights advocate Samar Yazbek is shortlisted in the translated literature category for Your Presence Is a Danger to Your Life: Voices of Survival and Witness in Gaza, translated from Arabic by Leri Price.
The book, originally published in Arabic as Memory of Absence: Gazans' Accounts of Genocide, is based on interviews Yazbek conducted with hundreds of survivors from Gaza during 2024 about their experiences since 7 October 2023.
Yazbek and Price have both previously been finalists for the award.
The other translated literature finalists are Karl Ove Knausgaard's The School of Night, translated from Norwegian by Martin Aitken; Vicente Luis Mora's Centroeuropa, translated from Spanish by Rahul Bery; Intan Paramaditha's Night of a Thousand Hells, translated from Indonesian by Stephen J. Epstein and Tiffany Tsao; and Mohamed Mbougar Sarr's Pure Men, translated from French by Lara Vergnaud.
In young people's literature, the finalists are Elana K. Arnold for Holloway, Tae Keller for When Tomorrow Burns, Keala Kendall for That Which Feeds Us: A Hawaiian Gothic, David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels for The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America, and Julian Randall for Shook.
The nominated works span subjects including intergenerational trauma, the legacy of colonialism in Hawaii, the AIDS crisis in the United States, and anxiety and adolescence.
A total of 1,912 books were submitted for this year's awards, including 451 in fiction, 727 in nonfiction, 285 in poetry, 159 in translated literature and 290 in young people's literature.
Five judges select the winner in each category. Winners receive $10,000, while each finalist receives $1,000. In the translated literature category, the prize is divided equally between the author and translator.
The strong Arab and Palestinian presence on this year's shortlist follows Lebanese author Rabih Alameddine's win at the 2025 National Book Awards, when The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother) won the fiction prize.
Alameddine's novel follows a Lebanese family across six decades, from the country's civil war to the Covid-19 pandemic.
The winners of the 2026 awards will be announced on 18 November at the 77th National Book Awards ceremony.

The European Parliament is investigating French-Palestinian MEP Rima Hassan after she removed an Israeli flag from an exhibition marking the third anniversary of the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks, with the lawmaker accusing Parliament of applying a double standard to Israel as it wages its genocidal war on Gaza.
A European Parliament spokesperson confirmed the investigation to The New Arab, following calls from pro-Israel lawmakers for Hassan to be sanctioned.
Hassan has defended her protest, confirming that she deliberately removed the Israeli flag while disputing claims that she vandalised the exhibition. Her office said neither the Israeli nor European Union flag was damaged.
Speaking in the European Parliament chamber on Tuesday, Hassan rejected as “factually false” Parliament President Roberta Metsola's claim that she had been filmed “apparently damaging” the exhibition.
Drawing a comparison with Russia's invasion of Ukraine, she questioned why an Israeli flag was being displayed inside Parliament as Israel continues its assault on Gaza, and whether the institution would allow a Russian flag to be displayed under similar circumstances.
Hassan said the exhibition had been organised in partnership with the Israeli embassy and alleged that it featured a map depicting a “Greater Israel”.
She also accused Yaron Bob, an Israeli artist invited to the exhibition, of denying the existence of Palestine and the Palestinian people.
Her office said the EU flag fell as a result of a loss of balance rather than being deliberately removed.
It said Hassan's protest was intended to denounce “the ongoing genocide carried out by the Israeli government” and was “in no way aimed at the people to whom this event was intended to pay tribute, nor at their memory”.
Parliament considers sanctions
Metsola raised the incident after images emerged from Monday evening and vowed that Parliament would take “all appropriate steps”.
“We take this extremely seriously,” Metsola said, adding that the MEP concerned would have the right to give her side of the story.
She said Parliament could not tolerate property damage or actions that could be perceived as intimidation.
A spokesperson for Metsola said procedures under consideration could include sanctions, while another Parliament spokesperson said the next step would involve hearing from Hassan.

The New Arab approached Hassan directly for further comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Hassan, an MEP from France Unbowed (LFI) and a member of the European Parliament's Left group, has become one of the institution's most prominent advocates for Palestinian rights since her election in 2024.
She joined a Gaza humanitarian flotilla mission seeking to break Israel’s blockade of the territory, but the vessel was raided by Israeli forces and Hassan was subsequently arrested and deported.
Hassan has described being abused by Israeli police during her detention, while organisers of the flotilla said she was held in solitary confinement, kept in handcuffs for extended periods and subjected to aggressive body searches.

Haaretz editors and reporters reflect on the stories that have stayed with them through the three years since October 7, 2023, related either to the events of that day itself or the repercussions that have rippled outward ever since.
October 7, 2023Israel at war: Sirens sound in central and southern Israel
Read the first reports of October 7, 2023.
My overnight shift on the news desk from October 6 into October 7 had been one of the quietest I'd ever had until the sirens blared in Tel Aviv just before 7 A.M. I sent out the first push notification – of what would be thousands over the brutal years of war that followed – which simply said the only news we knew for sure at that point: "Sirens sound in central and southern Israel."
From that morning on, Haaretz.com shared our reporting via a live blog, active every single hour of every single day, until early October 2026. I often think back to that first day: sifting through scraps of information to give the world something certain, translating what our reporters were seeing with their own eyes, trying to make sense of what might come next – it felt impossible then, and is unbelievable now.

Firefighting aviation is more than just an aircraft: how XENA organizes international forest-firefighting operations
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
19:13:45 EEST
01:13:45 KST

Firefighting aviation is more than just an aircraft: how XENA organizes international forest-firefighting operations
Kyiv • UNN
XENA deploys the An-32P Firekiller in less than a day and fights fires in Turkey, Georgia, and Montenegro. The aircraft drops 8,000 liters of water.
Forest fires are becoming larger in scale and more intense, so Europe is seeking additional rapid-response capabilities. Under these conditions, the role of aerial firefighting is growing. Behind every sortie lies much more than just a specialized aircraft: crew training, technical support, logistics, coordination with local services, and the readiness to deploy an operation in another country at short notice.
The Ukrainian airline XENA—the world's only commercial operator of the An-32P Firekiller firefighting aircraft—has been participating in international forest-firefighting operations in Turkey, Georgia, and Montenegro since 2021. How this work is organized and what is required for a specialized aircraft to begin fighting a fire within just a few hours of receiving an alert was explained in an exclusive interview with UNN by XENA Director Yevhen Sokol and the company's Chief Operating Officer Ihor Komarov.
From contract to first sortie
When the scale of a fire requires additional aviation resources, a specialized aircraft cannot simply fly into the country and begin operating. First, the operator must be officially engaged in the operation.
XENA operates under contracts awarded through tenders conducted by specialized agencies and authorities. These procedures assess the financial offer, the quality of services, and compliance with safety requirements. Such contracts may be either multi-year or short-term—when an emergency requires a rapid decision.
Once the contract is signed, the operation is deployed directly. A base must be designated, the aircraft supplied with fuel and water, the necessary clearances obtained, operations coordinated with local aviation authorities, and the crew prepared for the flight rules and zones.
Under the contract, the aircraft must be ready to take off within 20 minutes of an alert, and XENA has repeatedly demonstrated its rapid deployment in practice—from arrival to the start of operations, less than a day may pass
During a fire, the aircraft becomes part of the local response system. The areas of operation and priorities are determined by the client and local authorities, while coordination is ensured through joint chains: fire detection, task assignment, and crew support.
Four flight-crew members work on board—the captain, first officer, navigator, and flight engineer. They are joined by a local pilot-observer, who helps maintain communication with ground services and coordinates the drops. On the ground, technicians, a base manager, and specialists responsible for water, fuel, and team support are at work.
Photo credit: Patrick Zweiger, Dalaman, 2026
According to XENA, in Turkey, for example, detection is carried out through a multilayered system—drones with infrared cameras, patrol aircraft and helicopters, and ground-based forestry services.
In the air, the crew simultaneously maintains contact with air-traffic control, with other firefighting aircraft and helicopters on the coordination frequency, and with ground services through the pilot-observer on board specifically to coordinate the drops. One minute before dropping the water, the crew announces its actions over the radio to ensure safety in the drop zone. This has been practiced to the point of becoming automatic—this is how one aircraft operates effectively in crowded airspace alongside dozens of other assets
Flight over the fire: crew requirements
Working abroad means that the crew encounters new conditions each time. The work requires taking into account the terrain, climate, sudden weather changes, local regulations, and the specifics of interaction with other services.
Working in the mountains is particularly challenging.
The An-32P drops water from extremely low altitudes—approximately 40–60 meters above the fire, so the pilots, without exaggeration, "descend into the very heart of hell." In mountain valleys, the wind behaves unpredictably, as in a wind tunnel; smoke "eats up" visibility and is dangerous for the engines. There is virtually no room for error here
Photo credit: Patrick Zweiger, Dalaman, 2026
The requirements placed on crews for firefighting missions are extremely high, and they begin even before the first mission.
XENA is built around its pilots—mostly former military aviators with an average of approximately 20 years of experience. New pilots undergo intensive theoretical and conversion training at the Antonov training center, after which they need up to six months of additional training to fully master the specifics of firefighting flights. Before working in a new country, the crew separately studies the local flight zones, airfields, restrictions, aviation regulations—and even communication practices
The flight over a fire itself also has its own specific features and requires exceptional physical and psychological readiness. The aircraft is flown manually, without an autopilot, at an altitude of 40–60 meters above the flames. In mountainous areas, an instant reaction, excellent vision, and the ability to clearly assess the terrain and see the development of the fire literally several steps ahead are required. High temperatures add to the challenge. On the apron, temperatures can reach +70°C, while in the air they are 40–45°C. During busy periods, a crew may carry out 10–12 sorties a day, so after arriving in a new country, it is important to take the acclimatization period into account as well.
Our operational capabilities are unmatched in high-precision firefighting. Flying at 40–60 meters in challenging conditions requires exceptional skill—and our crews demonstrate the highest level of technical excellence every time
What the An-32P Firekiller can do
One of XENA’s aircraft involved in fighting forest fires in Europe is the An-32P Firekiller. It is a specialized firefighting version of the An-32 transport aircraft.
The company emphasizes that its key advantages are the combination of power, precision, and versatility.
The An-32P takes off and lands in challenging conditions—from unpaved and minimally prepared strips—thanks to its high-mounted engines and low-pressure tires. It operates immediately and at low altitude: it drops 8,000 liters of water or retardant from an altitude of approximately 40 meters at a speed of 230–260 km/h. In a single pass, the aircraft covers a strip measuring 35×160 meters, while two consecutive drops of 4,000 liters each cover an area of 20×300 meters. Its four independent tanks can be filled in 5–8 minutes, providing up to 32,000 liters per hour
Photo credit: Patrick Zweiger, Dalaman, 2026
At the same time, firefighting is not the An-32P’s only function. The aircraft can carry up to 6,700 kg of cargo in a 66 m² cargo compartment, be used as a medical platform for up to 24 stretchers, or deploy up to 27 firefighter-paratroopers. It can also transport and drop emergency equipment.
The aircraft operates at temperatures of up to +55 °C and at airfields up to 4,500 meters above sea level.
It is no wonder that pilots call it a "rocket": its two Ivchenko turboprop engines produce a combined output of more than 10,000 horsepower
XENA’s experience in international missions
The Ukrainian airline XENA has already operated in Turkey, Georgia, and Montenegro. The largest number of missions took place in Turkey: since 2021, the company’s crews have carried out more than 1,000 firefighting missions there and delivered over 7 million liters of water to fire zones. During the 2025 season, XENA carried out 450 missions in Turkey and Montenegro. In Georgia, the company’s work received public recognition from the local authorities.
Montenegro became XENA’s newest destination—the company has been operating there since 2025. This country became an example of how quickly an international firefighting operation can be deployed.
In 2025, during a challenging fire season, an XENA-operated An-32P Firekiller was deployed to Montenegro with the support of the United Arab Emirates.
We deployed to Montenegro in the shortest possible time, fully within the terms of the contract. Less than 24 hours after arrival, the crew was already operating from Podgorica and carried out ten firefighting missions the following day
The aircraft’s commencement of operations was officially announced by Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajić, while the country’s Ministry of Internal Affairs highlighted its professionalism, effectiveness, and compliance with safety and quality standards.
In 2026, XENA is operating in Montenegro again. In particular, the company was involved in fighting a fire that lasted several days in the Orjen area near Herceg Novi, where ground forces have difficulty reaching some of the fire’s hotspots.
What European firefighting aviation will need
Fire seasons in Europe are becoming longer and more intense, meaning that countries need not just individual aircraft, but ready-made aviation capabilities that can be rapidly deployed.
This primarily concerns rapid deployment, a high intensity of operations, and the ability to integrate into the national response system—together with drones, other aircraft, and ground services.
It is precisely this comprehensive capability that makes it possible to use firefighting aviation as a fully fledged part of the response system for large-scale wildfires.

Ancient crocodilian found in rocks that built Great Sphinx: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:12:41 UTC
01:12:41 KST

Dilara Hamit
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Fossils recovered from the same limestone formation used to build Egypt's Great Sphinx belong to a distinct extinct crocodilian that lived about 45 million years ago, researchers said Tuesday.
The animal, named Herugavialis cairensis, inhabited the shallow tropical sea that once covered what is now northern Egypt, according to a study published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
Its remains came from the Mokattam Formation, a thick limestone deposit containing fossils of fish, sharks and early whales, according to the study.
It said stone quarried from the formation was later used in some of ancient Egypt's best-known monuments, including the Great Sphinx and the Giza pyramids.
The key specimen, a nearly complete skull uncovered during the 1920s, had previously been classified as a member of Tomistoma, the genus that includes the modern false gharial of Southeast Asia.
Researchers used computed tomography, or CT, scans to examine the skull's internal anatomy and compared more than 300 features with those of living and extinct crocodilians.
Their analysis found enough differences to place the Egyptian animal in a separate genus.
The name Herugavialis combines "Heru," another name for the ancient Egyptian god Horus, with a term referring to gharials. The species name cairensis reflects its connection to Cairo.
The skull is also missing the end of its snout, an accidental resemblance to the Great Sphinx, which famously lacks its nose.
"Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru, who was possibly the inspiration for this iconic monument," said study co-leader Philip Mannion of University College London.
Gharials are crocodilians distinguished by their long, narrow snouts, according to the study.
Only two species survive today: the critically endangered Indian gharial and the endangered false gharial, both found in parts of South and Southeast Asia.
Their fossil record, however, shows that gharial-like crocodilians once had a much wider geographical range and that some species lived in marine environments.
The identification of Herugavialis cairensis adds to evidence that several gharial species inhabited the Mediterranean region over tens of millions of years.
Researchers said the finding provides a clearer picture of the group's complex evolutionary history.

Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
Far-right and far-left parties gain ground in local elections as Merz’s approval rating sinks.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz has hit out at what he called political “extremism” in Germany after recent stinging defeats in local elections to far-right and far-left parties.
“This is a task for our society as a whole, and it is one I intend to play my part in,” he said on Wednesday at an event in Berlin.
Merz said “extremism” was forcefully making its way into the country’s parliaments, a day after a member of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) was elected president of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt and the Left Party won out in Berlin’s state election last month.
“Anyone who casts their vote for the AfD is playing the extremists’ game and undermining credibility,” Merz said. “In any case, this is incompatible with the values of my party, the CDU [Christian Democratic Union of Germany].”
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority it had had sought. AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch won the presidency of the parliament in the eastern German state Tuesday, backed by the left-populists in a secret ballot.
Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after about a million people fled to Germany in 2015, many of them from war-torn Syria.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with mainstream parties, though most traditional parties have pledged not to enter coalitions with the AfD.
Berlin election
Merz’s comments followed the far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on September 20, in another defeat for the chancellor’s ruling Christian Democrats.
Lead candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through with a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party, which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980, said the increasingly difficult rental situation was the biggest social problem in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations she said drove property speculation, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 percent of voters backed a proposal to promulgate the move.
While the AfD has attracted most attention, the Left Party has also benefitted from a general turn against the mainstream centre-left and centre-right parties.
Meanwhile, Merz has received a record low approval rating. Earlier this month, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his performance, the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
Another major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters are set to elect a new parliament in April.

NEW DELHI: Aiming to expedite transmission projects, power ministry has issued fresh guidelines for determining compensation to landowners for laying inter-state transmission lines, fixing separate rates for the Right of Way (RoW) corridor and land used for tower foundations.Nearly 50GW of renewable energy projects are estimated to be delayed due to the lack of inter-state transmission connectivity needed to evacuate clean electricity. Ratings agency ICRA had also pointed out in July that transmission projects faced significant execution challenges related to land acquisition and RoW issues, leading to delays and grid curtailment. It estimated Rs 5-6 lakh crore of capital expenditure in the sector over the next five years.In a report tabled in Parliament last year, the parliamentary standing committee on energy had pointed out that issues related to RoW compensation, land acquisition and delays in environmental clearances were among the major hurdles in laying transmission lines.Officials said the guidelines will apply to transmission lines of 66 kV and above, unless a state govt has already notified its own compensation policy.
The guidelines are aimed at bringing uniformity in compensation for landowners affected by transmission projects.As per the guidelines, compensation will be based on the prevailing market value of land determined by a market rate committee headed by the district magistrate or deputy commissioner. This will apply in cases where the market value of land is lower than the prevailing circle rate. The committee will include officials from the revenue department, the sub-divisional magistrate, an administrative representative and representatives of the local civic body.
The guidelines also prescribe a mechanism to determine market value where there are disputes. The committee will appoint three valuers selected from a list available through the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India, with valuation carried out along the transmission line alignment. Provisions have also been made for the committee to settle grievances relating to land rates.

====================================================================================================

Danish university study examines antisemitic stereotypes in Agatha Christie’s novels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:09:08 UTC
01:09:08 KST

A new study published in the academic journal Nordisk Judaistik (“Scandinavian Jewish Studies”) examines the recurring presence of Jewish characters and antisemitic tropes across the detective fiction of Agatha Christie.
Written by Sofie Lene Bak, a historian at the University of Copenhagen, the study, titled ‘Whodunit?' Antisemitism as a literary device in the detective works of Agatha Christie, investigates how antisemitism functioned as a deliberate literary device rather than merely reflecting harmless attitudes of the period.
The study is part of Bak’s research project, Code and Conspiracy: Antisemitism in Denmark After 1945, which examines how antisemitic ideas have continued in the period following the Holocaust.
How memory cultures are reproducing classical prejudices
Bak wrote that the study was also prompted by the sharp resurgence of antisemitic tropes following the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israel-Hamas War.
The surge raised questions about how generations raised in memory cultures shaped by the Holocaust are reproducing classical prejudices. She noted that while research on post-1945 antisemitism has largely focused on political extremes, there remains a need to examine popular culture and entertainment where audiences may be particularly susceptible.
Examining Christie’s works, the study notes that out of 70 books, including 66 detective novels, Jewish characters appear in 23 works, with seven novels featuring sufficiently detailed portrayals for deep textual analysis.
Addressing the common defense that Christie’s work must be read purely within its historical context when antisemitic prejudices were socially acceptable, Bak analyzes three distinct interpretive levels to determine how anti-Jewish statements operate.
At the first level, prejudices were utilized according to genre conventions as red herrings to distract readers from the genuine clues leading to the solution of the murder and the identification of the true culprit.
At the second level, Christie placed xenophobic or prejudiced statements in the mouths of fictional characters to signal their narrow-mindedness, snobbery, or social position, though these remarks were rarely challenged within the narrative.
At the third level, where antisemitic statements appear without an omniscient narrator or specific character attribution, Bak points to embedded and potentially unconscious stereotypes belonging to the author herself, providing insight into the cultural-historical context.
Grappling with whether these portrayals gradually disappeared as awareness of National Socialism grew, Bak examines specific texts across a chronological span to test prevailing historiographical claims.
Antisemitic caricatures used in Christie's early works
In Christie’s early works, such as The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1921) and Peril at End House (1932), Jewish characters such as Dr. Bauerstein and Jim Lazarus are marked by prominent physical descriptions and financial associations that cast them as outsiders and suspects.
Bak said that “Christie often uses Jewish characters as red herrings. Readers are meant to suspect them, only to discover in the end that someone else committed the crime. But that mechanism works only if readers already associate these characters with certain negative assumptions,” and they “are depicted as different or foreign. This creates a distance between them and the other characters, and this distance is essential to the role they play in the story.”
Drawing on social psychological research regarding warmth and competence, Bak argues that these figures embody ambivalent antisemitic stereotypes, perceived as cold, arrogant, and excessively concerned with money yet highly competent, which elicits both envy and suspicion.
While historiography has frequently sought to downplay these portrayals by arguing that such tropes receded as Christie became aware of the consequences of National Socialism, Bak’s analysis emphasizes continuity, effect, and the long afterlife of these depictions.
Jewish stereotypes became more 'coded' after World War II
Challenging the assumption of a post-war break, Bak points out that explicit Jewish characters largely vanished after World War II, yet Christie’s writing still contained problematic caricatures.
“It is true that she abandoned the most overt depictions. Instead, the stereotypes became more indirect and coded.” Bak said.
Examples include the dressmaker Madame Alfrege in The Hollow (1946), who is introduced by the narrative voice as a vitriolic little Jewess and depicted as malicious, vulgar, and loud, with a physical description highlighting a thick nose.
Another instance is the traumatized German cook and Holocaust survivor Mitzi in A Murder is Announced (1950), who, despite not being explicitly named as Jewish, is portrayed through coded markers of sallow skin and dark hair while being subjected to constant mockery, cruelty, and ridicule by her household.
Bak said, “No one in the novel likes Mitzi, and it is suggested that she suffers from paranoia and may even exaggerate the suffering she experienced in her homeland. As a result, the other characters portray her as unreliable, ungrateful, and fundamentally ridiculous. It is a brutal caricature. I believe Christie intended her as a comic character, but that does not make the portrayal any less problematic.”
Bak contends that post-1945 antisemitism became coded, indirect, and sarcastic rather than disappearing outright.
She points out that this coded language relied on subtle textual hints, such as foreign origins, German-accented exclamations, fear of the Gestapo, and physical markers previously associated with Jewish characters, where the object of scorn was never explicitly named as Jewish, requiring readers to decode the underlying tropes.
Building on this analysis, Bak further substantiates her findings by examining how these texts persisted across generations through international publishing practices. She argues that while this prejudice became more subtle in later writing, the bias itself endured because decades of reprints and translations preserved the original phrasing verbatim.
To support this claim, the study tracks the publication history of Danish translations, demonstrating that publishers maintained the original antisemitic descriptions and references across multiple reissues spanning decades.
By contrast, Bak highlights that modern film adaptations have consistently omitted or de-emphasized the Jewish backgrounds of characters entirely, proving that the explicit markers were never essential to the narrative plots.
Bak concludes the study by rejecting the notion that these elements can be excused as mere laziness or harmless attempts at comic relief, asserting that such tropes must be confronted directly rather than downplayed as reflections of a different era.
She notes that while an author’s precise psychological intentions remain difficult to reconstruct, the decisive factor is the tangible emotional impact on readers who absorb these embedded stereotypes without conscious challenge.
Read more of Sofie Lene Bak's study here.

Saudi Arabia has launched an air accident probe following last week's cockpit stabbing on a flydubai jet, as experts examine any fallout for aviation safety alongside a separate UAE-led criminal investigation, three people close to the matter said.
Safety probes designed to keep flights safe are normal after accidents but are not mandatory when a deliberate act is involved, such as the suspected attempt by a co-pilot to bring down the Israel-bound flydubai jet on September 30.
Until now, it has remained unclear whether Saudi Arabia would go ahead with such a probe, which experts say could test a system of international co-operation designed to make recommendations for safety without attempting to assign blame.
The people close to the matter said Saudi Arabia had notified specialist aviation agencies abroad that it would carry out a safety investigation under international rules into flight FZ1073, which was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center, which has responsibility for accident investigations, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Saudi government and the country's regulator also did not answer requests for comment.
UAE running a separate criminal investigation
The US National Transportation Safety Board, which would be closely involved in any probe because the Boeing 737 MAX jet that survived a steep plunge was designed and built in the United States, could not immediately be reached for comment.
Officials in the UAE did not respond to requests for comment. Under international rules, the UAE would also automatically be involved because the jet is registered there and the airline is based in Dubai.
The UAE has already opened a separate criminal investigation into the incident, which its prosecutor general has called a "terrorist attack."
Israel, whose citizens made up nearly all the 172 people on board, has offered to take part in any Saudi-led safety investigation but has not so far been invited to take part, the head of the country's air accident agency told Reuters.
"We are still waiting for a notification from Saudi Arabia to invite us to take a part in the investigation," Ofer Vaknin, director of the Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority, said.
Saudi Arabia and Israel do not have diplomatic relations, though experts say the decades-old system of cooperation on preventing accidents, which is widely credited with a sharp reduction in the accident rate, can cross political lines.

China’s High-Tech Ambitions Have a Blue-Collar Status Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:08:00 UTC
01:08:00 KST

As China celebrated its dominance at the Asian Games that concluded days ago in Nagoya, Japan, its achievement at another global sporting festival in Shanghai has been largely overlooked. In the 2026 edition of WorldSkills, what the organizers call an Olympics for vocational skills, the Chinese team topped the medal table with 41 gold, 11 silver, and 4 bronze medals. In fact, the Chinese team has topped the medal table five straight times in the biennial competition, a phenomenon that has been attributed to the country’s unparalleled investments in providing systematic coaching and training for athletes in the same way it does for the regular Olympics.
Beyond simply winning medals, the Chinese authorities felt the need to drum up public interest in the competition. Local and national media, and even governments, covered WorldSkills extensively while it largely went unnoticed in other countries. Given that whatever prestige that China earns from WorldSkills is largely geared toward a domestic audience rather than an international one, it begs the question of why China would even bother with prompting something that leads to little gain in global stature.
The answer to the question may be found in a February 2026 announcement from the Chinese Ministry of Education (MoE) suggesting vocational school reforms. The document criticized the current system’s lack of connection between education and employers, producing few skilled industrial workers essential for driving China’s next generation of high-tech manufacturing.
China’s 2026-2030 Five-Year Plan emphasized that manufacturing remains central in ensuring the technological self-sufficiency underlying long-term economic growth and safeguarding national security. The MoE implied that the country’s vocational schools, without reforms, would be incapable of producing the human resources needed to achieve that goal.
But for vocational schools to urgently produce talent for high-tech manufacturing, they need more than just an appropriate curriculum. They also need the best raw talent that China has to offer. Here is where vocational schools fall short.
China’s university enrollment increased from 1 million in 1999 to 9.6 million in 2020. The country’s brightest increasingly aspire to join the ranks of what used to be a tiny segment of the intellectual elite signaled by a university diploma. The expanding path toward college education has cemented a social hierarchy in which a bachelor’s degree followed by white-collar work is seen as more desirable than a vocational one followed by a career in manual labor, no matter how technically sophisticated.
That norm of high-education aspirations is most clearly seen in study abroad. My primary job as a college admissions consultant leads me to interact with hundreds of Chinese families who are first and foremost attracted to higher-ranked institutions with well-recognized names. In choosing between the likes of the American Ivy Leagues and the British Oxbridge, they care less about what practical skills they can acquire, but whether the degrees indicate a highly competitive environment, and by proxy, the intelligence of successful applicants. Despite much cheaper costs and clear paths for employment, very few indicate interest in English-language higher-education programs in Germany and other European countries anchored by technical apprenticeships.
It is this cultural norm that the MoE must fight against as it seeks to overhaul the vocational school system in China. The proposed collaboration with major manufacturers will help. In a slowing economy, many applicants may be interested in blue-collar work with the likes of Huawei and Xiaomi, rather than a bachelor’s degree that comes with unemployment afterwards. But without changing the cultural norms of seeing technical education as “lower” than the university one, vocational schools in China, no matter how reformed, can still only attract those who are not afraid to be seen as desperate and obtuse enough to work on the factory floor.
Hence the glowing coverage of WorldSkills. The prestige of China’s medalists is about bringing pride not just to the country, but to their professions. And to further bestow status, China is turning hundreds of vocational schools into diploma-granting colleges, slapping bachelor’s degrees on vocational training. If better prospects for jobs do not bring brighter talent into technical education, the hope is that erasing the difference in visual appearance between universities and vocational schools can break down the hierarchical thinking.
It remains to be seen whether China’s dwindling ranks of youngsters will be sufficiently lured by the more attractive job prospects offered by manufacturing. As Chinese firms wow domestic and foreign audiences with fully automated dark factories, the image of grittiness associated with manufacturing is being chipped away. But will that overcome an ingrained educational culture that sees the work of the brain as higher in social status as that of the hand, even if the hand is increasingly replaced by robotics? It will depend on whether the Chinese mentality will evolve as fast as the country’s approach to industrial policies and technologies.

UK to stay in Palestine despite Israel threat to close consulate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:04:06 UTC
01:04:06 KST

Breadcrumb
UK to maintain presence in Palestine despite Israeli threat to close Jerusalem consulate
Israel's upcoming closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem will be "disruptive," but "not the end of the story" for the UK's work in Palestine, Sir Vincent Fean, former British Consul General in Jerusalem, told The New Arab.
Israel is threatening to close the British diplomatic facility, which works with political organisations, NGOs, and economic partners in Palestine on 8 October.
"It is disruptive. It is meant to be disruptive," Fean, who is a trustee of the Britain Palestine Project, which advocates equal rights for Palestinians and Israelis, said.
"The Israeli government wants to disrupt our relationship with the PLO and the Palestinian Authority."
However, the UK will continue to work with Palestinian institutions via the Palestinian embassy in London, which achieved full embassy status in January.
The UK's visa applications in Palestine are handled by an office in Ramallah, which is independent of the consulate. Their work is expected to continue if the consulate closes.
The British consulate is based in East Jerusalem, which is illegally occupied by Israel. The consulate was established in 1838, 110 years before the creation of the state of Israel.
The attempted closure of the consulate is illegal under international law, but the UK has limited legal options to fight Israel's move.
"When we talk about legal challenge, there are not all that many places to go. The international court of justice would be an option, but it's a slow moving mechanism and this is a fast moving story," Fean said.
In September, Israel announced that the Jerusalem consulate would be closed within 30 days in response to the UK adopting limited sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The deadline is 8 October, and while the Israeli government could backtrack, Fean told The New Arab that this is unlikely "until anything changes."
A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office told The New Arab, "We will not go into detail on live discussions about the future of the British Consulate General in Jerusalem. The protection and wellbeing of our staff is our priority."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced that Britain would impose sanctions on Israeli settler groups last month, one of his first major announcements since taking up the post last July. The sanctions came as a response to increasing violence against Palestinians in the West Bank by Israeli settlers.
At least 1,145 Palestinians have been killed and 13,200 injured by Israeli settlers and soldiers in the West Bank since October 2023, according to data from the UN. In his announcement of the sanctions, Miliband referred to "settler terrorism."
The sanctions will ban the import to the UK of goods from Israeli settlements, and act against individuals and companies providing services for settlement expansion.
"Britain has a historic responsibility towards Palestine and the Palestinians," Palestinian ambassador Husam Zomlot told The New Arab at last week's Labour Party Conference regarding the sanctions, "So we are hoping that Britain is going to lead rather than follow a global campaign to end this once and for all."
Britain is reportedly considering expelling Israeli diplomats if Israel carries out its threat to shut the Jerusalem consulate.

High-ranking German politicians marked the anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place in Israel on October 7, 2023.

"We are witnessing rising antisemitism in Germany — antisemitism that far too often goes unchallenged," Merz said, adding that his government "will do everything" to combat it.
"Jewish people must be able to live without fear throughout Germany," Merz said in a statement, also emphasizing Germany's support for Israel. "Our Israeli friends can count on our commitment to ensuring that such a crime never happens again."
'Political action' needed

"Germany must continue to stand up against antisemitism and for Israel’s security, for the dignity and self-determination of the Palestinians, and for the prospect of peaceful coexistence in the Middle East," he said in a statement.

Germany stands with Israel

Rebranded Jaguar unveils its first electric sportscar: The Type 01EV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:03:22 UTC
01:03:22 KST

Hailed as the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the company’s history, it premiered in New York today, targeting a younger, wealthier and mostly American customer base.
Luxury car manufacturer Jaguar unveiled its first new model since its controversial rebrand two years ago at a flashy New York launch party attended by actress and new company ambassador Florence Pugh, in a bid to win over younger, richer and mostly American audience.
The luxury four-door GT Type01EV is Jaguar’s first foray in the electric vehicle (EV) market. Its ultra-modern, brutalist, sharp-edged design is a massive shift from its previously quintessential British elegance.
The radical design is an attempt by Jaguar’s hierarchy to shake off its previously antiquated albeit storied legacy that started as being a car for racing enthusiasts to one for the posh elite. They now have a newer, younger and richer demographic in their crosshairs.
Jaguar says the new model is the first production from its new Jaguar Electric Architecture (JEA), a dedicated platform for the next generation of Jaguar modes, as the company embraces its original motto “Copy Nothing” to create a vehicle they feel is unique.
It’s also gigantic.
Coming in at 5.2 metres long and 2 metres wide, it is longer than most SUVs and too long for most European carparks.
That makes it something of an awkward fit for Europe, where narrow roads are already struggling with the weight and size of today's monstrous vehicles. It would be far more at home on America's vast, endless highways.
But that has not stopped SUV numbers from exploding on EU roads in recent years.
The Type01EV is very low to the ground for its size, standing at only 1.4 metres tall, making it a particularly sleek looking vehicle.
It weighs in at a huge 2700 kilograms, significantly heavier than its competitors such as the Porsche Taycan Turbo GT (2,200kg) and a little more than the Mercedes-Benz EQS (2,585 kg) which shares a similar length.
The Type 01EV’s three motors and battery are extraordinary too. Not only are they powerful, clocking in 1030 horsepower and taking it from 0 to 100 kph in 3.2 seconds, it boasts an impressive 450-mile (720km) range, way above most of its rivals, with only the Porsche Taycan marginally more powerful.
The battery also charges at 350kw, allowing it to charge 200 miles (321km) of range in just 13 minutes and go from 10% to 80% charge in just 22 minutes, making it even more appealing to drivers wishing to make the switch to an electric vehicle.
But it won’t be for everyone.
Base models will start at around €167,470 in Europe, with bespoke specifications and customisations taking it up to €185,470.
Jaguar’s rebranded new car does retain a sense of Britishness though, with the Type01EV designed, engineered and built in the UK, according to their website.
Orders are scheduled to open in early 2027, with the first delivers in Europe expected in the second half of 2027.
Jaguar is a British and global car icon known for models such as the Jaguar E-Type driven by Frank Sinatra, Steve McQueen and described by Enzo Ferrari as “the most beautiful car ever made”.
Before its rebrand in 2024, the company was facing a severe, multi-year identity and financial crisis caused by a failing business strategy that relied on an aging core audience and failed to win over younger consumers.
Jaguar was making cars that were not common enough to compete with BMW and Mercedes nor exclusive or “cool” enough to compete with Porsche or Bentley.
The car company took the plunge with a radical rebrand in 2024, releasing an advert that featured no car at all. Instead, models in brightly coloured clothing spouted slogans such as “live vivid”, “delete ordinary” and “be the jag you are”.
The campaign was criticised by many including political figures such as Donald Trump and Nigel Farage for “going woke,” with Elon Musk asking on social media platform X, “Do you sell cars?”
Jaguar defended the ad campaign, telling Sky News at the time that the company wanted “to be bold and disruptive".
The new model’s launch comes as parent company Jaguar Land Rover recovers from a cyberattack that forced the company to halt production last year. One month later, the company announced it would cut 4,000 jobs as part of a major cost-cutting drive.
Today’s unveiling is the culmination of a years-long strategy to reposition the car manufacturer.
