====================================================================================================

Conservatives’ more rigid thinking styles don’t seem to make them likelier than liberals to toe the party line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:00:47 UTC
01:00:47 KST

People who identify as liberal or conservative often appear worlds apart in how they think, but new research suggests they respond to political endorsements in much the same way. Although conservatives in the study tended to report more rigid thinking styles, liberals and conservatives were largely equally likely to shift their policy views to match the stated positions of their own party. The findings, published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, indicate that at least one key psychological process behind partisan opinion operates similarly across the ideological spectrum.
The research was conducted at Michigan State University by Aymin Triki, then an undergraduate research assistant; Abigail L. Cassario, then a PhD candidate; and Mark J. Brandt, then an associate professor who ran the lab where Triki worked. Triki, the study’s lead author, is now a lab manager at the We-Search Lab at Harvard University, Cassario is a postdoctoral research associate at the University of Illinois Chicago, and Brandt is a professor of political psychology at Tilburg University.
“I’m proud of Aymin for leading this project and writing an excellent paper describing our work together,” Brandt told PsyPost.
The team aimed to explore the psychological mechanisms behind “party cues.” A party cue is a piece of information indicating whether a political party or its leaders support or oppose a specific policy. Learning that your own party supports a proposal generally makes you more likely to support it, while learning that the opposing party supports it makes you less likely to agree.
Psychologists have offered two main explanations for why party cues work. The first is that they act as a mental shortcut, allowing voters to skip the hard work of analyzing complex policies by simply trusting a group that generally shares their interests. The second explanation is that people are motivated to be good group members, and following a party endorsement is a way to express loyalty and protect their social identity.
“There is a long-running argument in political psychology about whether liberals and conservatives are characterized by different psychological processes,” Brandt explained. “That is, rather than just being different in terms of their values and policy positions, also being different in the psychological processes that drive their decisions and attitudes.”
The “asymmetry perspective” proposes that liberals and conservatives differ in deep-seated psychological ways, not just in their values. According to this view, conservative ideology tends to attract people with more rigid thinking styles, such as a stronger desire for firm, definite answers and less inclination to second-guess their first instincts. Some psychologists have argued that this profile, along with a greater emphasis on group loyalty and authority, should make conservatives more likely to rely on party cues.
Whether that rigidity shows up in how people actually handle political information is less settled. A study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that more conservative people updated their beliefs slightly less in response to new factual evidence, though the difference was very small.
An opposing “symmetry perspective” argues that liberals and conservatives process political information using the same basic psychological tools, even if they apply them toward different goals. A 2018 meta-analysis, which pooled the results of 51 experiments, concluded that liberals and conservatives were equally likely to judge identical information more favorably when it supported their side. But the authors of a 2019 commentary argued that the experiments in that analysis often relied on a narrow, unrepresentative set of policy issues, which may have hidden real differences between the two groups.
Triki, Cassario, and Brandt set out to address that criticism by testing party cue effects across a wide range of contemporary issues while also measuring participants’ thinking styles. “Prior work has examined ideological differences in party cues, but we wanted to do a more comprehensive study,” Brandt said. “In particular, we wanted to test these effects across a wide range of issues currently important in American politics. This way we can be sure that our results are not due to the specifics of a given policy and instead we can be confident in understanding how ideology and party cues intersect across a wide range of policies.”
The researchers first re-analyzed data from two earlier experiments, conducted in 2018 and 2020, that together included more than 4,300 participants and more than 80 policy issues. Both samples were recruited with the aim of resembling the U.S. population demographically. Participants rated their support for policies such as raising the minimum wage or privatizing veterans’ health care on a 1-to-7 scale. For randomly selected issues, they first learned where the two parties, or Barack Obama and Donald Trump, stood.
These analyses pointed toward symmetry. Democrats and Republicans shifted toward their own party’s position and away from the opposing party’s to essentially the same degree. On individual issues, conservatives sometimes responded more strongly and liberals sometimes did, in roughly equal numbers. A measure of liberal-conservative self-identification in one dataset also showed no difference between the groups, though that result was less conclusive.
“The overall party cue effect was reliable, but small,” Brandt noted. “It was the equivalent to .3 scale points on a 1-7 scale. However, this is just the average.”
“For some policies, the effect is much smaller (nearer to zero) and for others the effect is much larger (an effect larger than 1 scale point on a 1-7 scale),” he continued. “These larger effects would represent very large effects in the experimental literature on attitude change.”
To test whether particular thinking styles might still make a difference, the researchers ran a third experiment in August 2024 with 1,659 participants recruited through Prolific, an online research platform. This was a convenience sample, meaning participants were not selected to mirror the national population, though the researchers recruited roughly equal numbers of Republicans and Democrats. The experiment used 37 real policy issues on which Joe Biden and Donald Trump took opposing positions. For some issues, participants were told where “Democratic leaders” and “Republican leaders” stood.
The researchers measured ideology in four ways: party identification, self-placement on a liberal-to-conservative scale, right-wing authoritarianism, and progressive values. Right-wing authoritarianism reflects a tendency to defer to established authorities, value tradition, and favor harsh treatment of people who break social norms, while the progressive values scale captures an identity-focused form of left-wing ideology.
To assess thinking styles, participants completed a short reasoning test built around questions where the intuitive answer is wrong. They also completed questionnaires measuring need for closure, which is a desire for firm answers and a dislike of ambiguity, and dogmatism, which is the tendency to treat one’s own beliefs as unquestionably true.
In this sample, conservatives showed the profile that the asymmetry perspective predicts. Compared with liberals, they did worse on the reasoning test and reported a higher need for closure and more dogmatism. Conservatives, whether identified by party or self-placement, were also more responsive to party cues than liberals, as were people high in right-wing authoritarianism, while the progressive values measure showed no difference. Participants with a higher need for closure or more dogmatism also followed cues more closely, though results for the reasoning test were inconclusive.
This result conflicted with the first two analyses. When the researchers limited the analysis to nine issues that also appeared in the 2020 experiment, the difference persisted, suggesting the choice of issues did not explain it. Instead, they suspected the online convenience sample might not reflect the broader population, or that conservatives had become more responsive to party cues since the earlier data were collected.
To find out, the team ran a fourth experiment with 1,389 participants recruited using quotas to match the U.S. population on age, gender, race and ethnicity, and region. It used the same 37 issues and the same psychological measures as the third experiment, with additional attention checks.
Once again, conservatives did worse on the reasoning test and reported a higher need for closure and more dogmatism than liberals. However, the difference in how the two groups responded to party cues disappeared: whether ideology was measured by party or by liberal-conservative self-placement, liberals and conservatives were equally swayed by party endorsements. Reasoning test scores showed no link to how strongly people followed cues, and there was no evidence that need for closure or dogmatism made a difference, although those estimates were less precise. The progressive values measure gave inconclusive results.
“Notably, our core finding is that liberals and conservatives do not differ substantially,” Brandt emphasized. “In other words, the strength of party cue effects does not differ between liberals and conservatives. We do not think there is a practical difference in the size of the effect of party cues between liberals and conservatives.”
The finding that conservatives reported more rigid thinking styles is in line with a study covered by PsyPost in 2022, which found greater cognitive rigidity among Trump supporters than among supporters of liberal candidates, though that study looked at support for specific 2020 presidential candidates rather than general ideology. The overall symmetry in responses to party cues is also in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, in which liberals and conservatives alike rated political opponents as less moral than members of their own party, even after being treated fairly by them in an economic game. That study examined moral judgments rather than responses to party endorsements.
“We found ideological similarities in a specific psychological process. This is not an argument that all ideologies are the same,” Brandt cautioned.
“The liberals and conservatives in our samples differ from each other in other ways,” he said. “They support different policies. They follow different political leaders. And they cared more about different types of policies.”
The exception was right-wing authoritarianism. In both the third and fourth experiments, people scoring high on this measure followed party cues more strongly than those scoring low. The researchers considered whether this reflects a tendency to obey authority figures, but the part of the scale measuring submission to authority did not stand out from the others.
“This measure captures a type of conservatism that is particularly obedient to conservative authorities and aggressive in response to people who violate conservative norms,” Brandt observed. “Although we do not have an explanation for why this measure differed from the other measures of conservative ideology, it may be the case that there are particular types of conservatism that are more susceptible to party cues than others.”
Because the study covered so many issues, the researchers could also explore why differences between liberals and conservatives showed up on some topics but not others. “An advantage to looking at many different issues is that we can see if there are some issues with ideological differences and others without such differences,” Brandt said.
In these exploratory analyses, differences tended to emerge on issues where one group already held stronger views before seeing any cue. On those issues, the group with stronger initial views shifted less, either because they were more committed to their position or because they had little room left to move. In one dataset that also measured how aware people were of each policy, the group that was more aware of a given policy tended to shift less. The authors note that these analyses were not planned in advance and need to be replicated.
“One thing we found is that when an ideological group has a strong opinion on the issue, then they are less likely to be affected by party cues,” Brandt added. “This gives us insight into where we might expect people to be more or less likely to be affected by party cues.”
There are a few other things to keep in mind. The experiments measured how people’s stated attitudes shifted in response to party cues, but not whether those shifts translate into behaviors such as voting or protesting, where liberals and conservatives could still differ. The researchers also used accurate, real-world party positions, so the cues may often have matched what participants already believed. Future studies might examine how people respond to cues that run against their prior views, or to false information about where their party stands.
The conclusions also rest most heavily on three of the four experiments. The authors gave less weight to the third experiment because further analyses suggested that conservatives recruited through Prolific responded unusually strongly to party cues compared with liberals in that sample and with both groups in the other samples. The study also did not include every possible measure of ideology, such as left-wing authoritarianism, and all of the samples were from the United States.
“The goal of my lab is to understand how belief systems work,” said Brandt, who directs The Belief System Lab. “Major ongoing projects in the lab aim to map the structure of belief systems and to use that information to predict and understand the dynamics of political attitudes.”
The study, “American liberals and conservatives have different cognitive styles, but (mostly) respond the same to party cues,” was authored by Aymin Triki, Abigail L. Cassario, and Mark J. Brandt.

US colleges could face $70,000 fee per foreign student seeking work authorisation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:00:44 UTC
01:00:44 KST

The Department of Homeland Security has proposed a $70,000 fee for international students seeking to work in the United States, the latest effort from the Trump administration to crack down on foreign enrollment.
A proposed rule announced on Wednesday would require schools to pay the fee for every student who participates in the optional practice training programme, known as OPT, which allows students to work in jobs related to their major during or after their time in school.
Students are generally eligible for one year of work post-graduation, though certain science, technology, engineering and math majors are eligible for an additional two years.
Schools would be required to pay the $70,000 for each new student's initial application to the programme, and a $30,000 fee for each renewal.
The change would represent a blow to American colleges and universities that heavily recruit students from overseas as a source of tuition revenue, as well as tech companies and other industries that hire many international students for technical roles.
The OPT programme allows international students to gain hands-on experience and fill labour shortages in high-demand STEM fields, said Fanta Aw, CEO of NAFSA, an association that represents international education.
"Driving away the talents, perspectives, and aspirations of international students will only hurt American innovation, economic growth, workforce development, and global leadership," Aw said in a written statement.
Pressure on overseas students
In a statement, DHS described the fee as a response to fraud and abuse of the visa program, which it called a "pipeline for cheap foreign labour."
The public has 60 days to comment on the proposal before DHS can finalise it and put it into effect.
The proposal also could face legal challenges from higher education groups or business associations that could delay it.
President Donald Trump's administration has been putting pressure on international students in many ways as part of its wider efforts to crack down on immigration and reshape higher education.
Last year, the Republican administration began suddenly terminating the legal status of thousands of international students, detaining and deporting many of them.
This summer, the administration finalised a rule that sought to prevent international students from staying in the US for more than four years without approval from the federal government.
The move drew swift backlash from higher education leaders who said it would increase the burden on schools and noted that many programmes are longer than four years by design.
A federal court prevented the rule from taking effect in September.

Whether NATO’s European members can fuel their armed forces out to 2050, in peacetime and in war, has been assessed in a new report drawing on research led from Aberdeen, according to the university.
Dr Alfonso Martinez-Felipe, a senior lecturer in chemical engineering, undertook a fellowship with the NATO Energy Security Centre of Excellence in Vilnius, working on sustainable fuels, energy resilience and the part future fuel supply chains play in defence. The work produced the report Fuelling the Forces to 2050, published under the centre’s Future of Fuel programme, with two postgraduate students from the university’s MSc in Energy Transition Systems and Technologies also contributing.
The report examines how fuel requirements and supply could evolve under different circumstances, covering both peacetime and conflict scenarios.
Dr Martinez-Felipe said: “It has been extremely rewarding to see the work undertaken during the fellowship develop into a published report and to have the opportunity to present our findings directly to NATO stakeholders in Vilnius.”
Ben Cook, the United Kingdom’s senior national representative at the centre, said: “The University of Aberdeen’s support has been invaluable throughout this project. The research and analysis conducted by Alf, Jose-Luis and Ime have helped drive forward this landmark report on fuel security for the Alliance.”
The Energy Security Centre of Excellence in Vilnius is one of the alliance’s accredited centres, which are nationally sponsored rather than funded from the common budget, and its work informs NATO thinking without binding it.

Germany's AfD faces difficulty forming government after Saxony-Anhalt election win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:57:54 UTC
00:57:54 KST

Germany's far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) convened for the first session of the Saxony-Anhalt state parliament on the 6th of October; however, a month after the party's successful election, there is still no clear path to forming a local government, reports Reuters.
Despite achieving its best-ever result in a state election, the AfD fell three seats short of an absolute majority—the goal set by its candidate for state premier, Ulrich Siegmund. Before the the 6th of October session, Siegmund stated he would seek the parliamentary support needed to become Saxony-Anhalt's premier in the first round of voting. As the vote is now scheduled for December, he has more time to secure the necessary backing.
So far, the AfD has failed to garner sufficient support from potential partners or win over enough lawmakers from rival parties; consequently, efforts to form a government have not yielded results. The government formation deadlock highlights a challenge the party has faced for years: how to translate voter support into executive power within a political system where major parties refuse to cooperate with the AfD. 
Founded in 2013 as an initially Eurosceptic movement, the AfD has attracted a large number of voters through its increasingly hardline stance against migration—particularly after the arrival of around a million asylum seekers in Germany in 2015. Since then, the party has become a dominant force across much of eastern Germany.
However, many remain opposed to cooperating with far-right forces.
 On the 6th of October, around 400 peaceful protesters gathered outside the Saxony-Anhalt parliament in Magdeburg; before the parliamentary session, they read the German Constitution aloud, and several protesters held a red banner bearing the slogan "No cooperation with the far right."
The inaugural session on the 6th of October nevertheless delivered a symbolic victory for the AfD. With support from the left-wing populist BSW, 35-year-old real estate entrepreneur and close associate of Sigmund, Tobias Rausch, was elected president of the state parliament. He has thus become the first AfD member to hold such a high-ranking position in German state government. Rausch used his inaugural speech to call on lawmakers to work together, adding that "political firewalls" should be a thing of the past.
The AfD's successes in Saxony-Anhalt and two other federal states have increased pressure on the government of Friedrich Merz, and questions have arisen within his party regarding the effectiveness of the "political firewall."
For several weeks, the AfD has been attempting to woo politicians away from Merz's party, though there have been no reports so far of any politicians defecting to the right-wing camp.
The vote on the 6th of October also served as a test of whether the AfD could rely on the left-wing BSW. It is the only party that has not explicitly ruled out cooperation with the right, although it has rejected the idea of joining the AfD in a coalition government. The BSW has announced that it will abstain from the vote to appoint Sigmund as state premier. Like the AfD, the far-left party also opposes immigration and seeks to restore energy ties with Russia.
Consequently, the AfD might have to form a minority government—a model already in place in Thuringia. However, Siegmund has previously rejected this model, as it would make him overly dependent on smaller parties. The AfD’s candidate for minister-president has suggested that a re-run of the election could be held if sufficient support cannot be secured.
In the secret ballot for the position of parliamentary president, Rausch received 48 votes, meaning he garnered support not only from his own party and the BSW (which together hold 44 seats) but also from at least four lawmakers from other parties.

Launched at the Nantes shipyards in 1934 and acquired by the Italian Navy in 1950 as a training ship, the Nave Palinuro has been sailing “with favorable winds” (as its motto states, “Faventibus Ventis”), playing a vital role in the training of non-commissioned officer cadets, who spend several weeks at sea aboard her, undergoing an intensive program of specialized training. The Nave Palinuro is a recognized traveling symbol of our country and its maritime heritage, and plays a valued role in naval diplomacy. In this context, the majestic sailing ship’s upcoming stop in the port of Koper serves as a further and welcome sign of the strength of the solid bonds of friendship and cooperation that unite Italy and Slovenia. During its stay in port, the crew of the Nave Palinuro, led by Captain Francesco Carriero, will be engaged in a series of institutional and ceremonial activities, including a visit from the Italian Ambassador to Slovenia, Giuseppe Cavagna, the Deputy Chief of the Defense Staff of the Republic of Slovenia, Anže Rodem, and the Italian Consul General in Koper, Simona Ciuffoni. HS: Nokia plans to cut 253 jobs in Finland
Finland
Unknown Publisher

18:57:27 EEST
00:57:27 KST

Nokia plans to cut up to 253 positions in Finland as the network equipment maker seeks to reduce costs and direct investment towards areas including defence, artificial intelligence and data centres, Helsingin Sanomat reported on Wednesday.
The company informed employees about the plans but did not issue a public statement, according to the newspaper. Nokia later confirmed to Yle that it had started the change negotiation process.
The planned reductions affect Nokia operations in Espoo, Tampere and Oulu. Negotiations with employee representatives are due to begin on Monday, 12 October.
Nokia employs about 6,800 people in Finland. The proposed cuts represent about 3.7% of that workforce.
According to HS, Nokia told employees that the changes aim to protect the company’s competitiveness while allowing investment in businesses expected to support future growth.
Nokia Finland country manager Mikko Hautala told employees in an email obtained by HS that the company intends to continue investing in areas regarded as strategically important.
“For Finland, our intention is to continue investing in strategically important areas, including the defence sector and opportunities created by artificial intelligence and data centres,” Hautala wrote, according to the newspaper.
He said the planned changes were necessary as Nokia responds to changes in its operating environment.
The reductions form part of the cost-saving programme Nokia launched in 2023. The company aims to reduce operating expenses by between €800 million and €1.2 billion by the end of this year. Nokia said in its July interim report that it was targeting the upper end of that range.
The latest negotiations follow another round of reductions in Finland earlier this year. Nokia announced in April that it would cut 107 positions in the country.
Employee representative Jari Nummikoski, who represents senior salaried staff, told HS that another round of negotiations had been expected after similar processes in previous years.

Milan looks East: Chinese fashion takes centre stage for traditional craftwork
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:55:30 UTC
00:55:30 KST

Brocade carries centuries of Chinese history, woven with patterns that have long held meanings beyond decoration. Now, the traditional craft is finding a new expression on the Milan catwalk, as designers reinterpret the fabric for a contemporary audience.
There's been a lingering sense of a tide turning since Chinese brand ZHONGFANG.LIJIN unveiled its Brocade Reborn collection for spring/summer 2027 at Milan Fashion Week.
Its starting point was “Jin Mai” (锦脉), the living veins of brocade. The term refers to the warp and weft of the fabric, but also to the continuity of a tradition that evolves with each new generation.
A fashon industry veteran for more than 20-years, He Rong, founder and creative director of ZHONGFANG.LIJIN, is the beating heart of the collection. As a textile engineer, his practice centres on silk and intricately woven brocades, exploring how these traditional textiles can find a place in contemporary design.
In Brocade Reborn, nature takes centre stage. Mulberry leaves, silkworms curled inside their cocoons and butterflies emerge as flowing lines, tactile textures and sculptural silhouettes. Brocade is transformed through pleats, intricate motifs and layered details, bringing a centuries-old craft into a distinctly contemporary wardrobe.
The colour story is equally rooted in Chinese culture. Tianshui Bi evokes the tones of water and sky, Taoyao the delicate pink of peach blossom, Mihe a warm honey hue, Yuebai the soft white of moonlight, and Dailan a deep indigo. Together, the palette draws on Eastern aesthetics and the philosophy of the five elements, Wu Xing.
The Milan presentation was He Rong’s first in the city, organised with the support of Haining China Home Textile City, one of China’s major textile industry hubs. More than a showcase of craftsmanship, it placed traditional Chinese textile techniques within the international fashion conversation, showing how heritage can be reworked for a contemporary runway.
From brocade to the everyday wardrobe
That dialogue between heritage and contemporary fashion continued with the second Chinese label at this year’s Milan Fashion Week. CHEN.1988 presented its “Insieme con Amore” spring/summer 2027 collection last month at Castello Sforzesco, marking a decade of the brand’s creative journey and its evolving approach to everyday dressing.
While ZHONGFANG.LIJIN starts with the story woven into the fabric itself, CHEN.1988 looks to the way clothes are worn today. The collection experiments with asymmetrical cuts, fluid draping, pleats, suede, corduroy and checks. Fitted silhouettes are balanced by looser, more relaxed shapes, while a restrained palette of black, grey, beige and burgundy is enlivened with flashes of green and navy.
Menswear and unisex pieces also take centre stage. The boundaries between womenswear and menswear are increasingly fluid, with the collection focusing less on fixed categories and more on creating clothes that adapt to the person wearing them.
This idea is at the heart of “Daily Attitude”, the phrase CHEN.1988 uses to define its approach to fashion. Rather than saving clothes for special occasions, the collection brings fashion into the rhythm of everyday life, turning versatile pieces into a canvas for personal style and self-expression.
CHEN.1988 was founded in 2016 by designers Chen Long and Fu Zhichen, both affiliated with the Jiangxi Institute of Fashion Technology. In 2025, Chen Long received the 29th China Fashion Designer“Golden Top Award”, one of the country’s most prestigious honours for fashion designers. The Milan show marked another step in the brand’s efforts to establish itself on the Italian fashion scene.
Chinese fashion seeks its own language
The two collections approach Chinese fashion from very different directions. One draws on the richness of traditional brocade and silk, while the other starts with the rhythms of the modern wardrobe. Yet both share the same ambition: to move Chinese fashion forward without turning away from its roots, while refusing to let heritage define its entire identity.
Milan has become a stage for Chinese designers to show more than traditional craftsmanship.Their collections demonstrate how heritage techniques can be reworked, reshaped and woven into contemporary fashion while remaining connected to their origins.

Most French view high school students' demands legitimate: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:52:03 UTC
00:52:03 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
A majority of the French consider the demands of nationwide high school students legitimate, while more than half approve of the protests, according to an Elabe poll for French broadcaster BFMTV published Wednesday.
Some 72% of respondents said the demands were legitimate, including 28% who considered them “completely” legitimate and 44% who said they were “rather” legitimate.
Separately, 55% said they approved of the student mobilization, which began in mid-September because of complaints about staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms and inadequate school facilities. Blockades and demonstrations have since spread to schools in several French cities.
The largely peaceful movement has also seen violent incidents, including fires, property damage and attacks on staff and police, according to authorities.
Some 35% disapproved of the protests, while 10% said they were indifferent.
When asked about the future of the mobilization, however, 55% said it should end.
Another 27% favored continuing the protests at the current level, while 17% supported an escalation involving more and larger blockades.
The distinction was particularly notable among younger respondents.
Among those aged 18 to 24, 33% favored ending the movement, 38% wanted it to continue at its current level and 28% supported an escalation.
Support for the mobilization was higher among parents of high school students, at 71%.
The Education Ministry said Wednesday that 459 schools had experienced full or partial suspension of classes, down from 891 on Tuesday.
Student and youth unions have demanded further demonstrations Thursday in Paris and other cities.

Years After His Death, Vladimir Zhirinovsky Lives Rent-Free in Russians’ Heads
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:43 UTC
00:51:43 KST

In late September, President Vladimir Putin took a moment at a meeting with parliamentary party leaders to remember a familiar face missing from this year’s State Duma elections: Vladimir Zhirinovsky.
“I would like to say that we certainly miss him, especially under the current circumstances. It is a pity that he is gone,” Putin said at the Sept. 28 meeting.
More than four years after his death in 2022 at age 75, Zhirinovsky continues to hold a place in Russia’s popular consciousness, from TikTok to the Kremlin.
His party still campaigns on his image, social media users recast his speeches as prophecies and polling suggests that Russians remember him more fondly than they viewed him during his lifetime.
Meanwhile, the once-fringe nationalist rhetoric he championed has become more prominent in mainstream Russian politics since the invasion of Ukraine.
“Rest in peace, Uncle Vova; you always knew everything,” reads one comment on his official Instagram page.
A fixture in Russian politics for decades, Zhirinovsky led the right-wing populist Liberal Democratic Party (LDPR) from its inception in 1992 and ran no fewer than six failed presidential campaigns.
As a lawmaker, he was better known for his provocative, outlandish speeches and clashes with fellow politicians than for his legislative work.
Among his more notorious statements were calls to use nuclear weapons against other countries and demands to seize Alaska from the U.S., along with numerous abusive comments toward women.
His persona nevertheless became a source of comic relief for many Russians and the inspiration for countless memes, Instagram reels and musical mixes.
Since his death, that trend has only grown. Social media users create AI videos that cast him as an honest politician and a near-prophet, often contrasting him against depictions of corrupt, greedy officials.
A March 2025 survey by state pollster VTsIOM found that 66% of respondents said they had trusted Zhirinovsky, up from 60% in a survey conducted shortly after his death. During his lifetime, trust in Zhirinovsky had usually fluctuated within 15-30%.
As during his lifetime, it can be difficult to tell where the admiration ends and irony begins.
Following reports that an employee at a Siberian anti-plague institute had fallen ill and died last week, excerpts from Zhirinovsky’s speeches about plague resurfaced on social media.
“Zhirinovsky even predicted the plague in Russia,” says the author of one post.
“He just ran his mouth a lot,” came a reply in the comments.
Yet the idea that Zhirinovsky foresaw events others failed to anticipate has become central to his posthumous popularity. Collections of his predictions that appear to have come true regularly circulate online.
One of the most widely cited examples comes from a State Duma speech in late 2021, when he appeared to anticipate Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
“At 4 a.m. on Feb. 22, you'll feel [our new policy],” Zhirinovsky said. “I’d like 2022 to be peaceful. But I love the truth, for 70 years I've said the truth. It won’t be peaceful. It will be a year when Russia once again becomes great.”
Russian troops invaded Ukraine on Feb. 24, two days after the date he had named.
Some of his statements from the 2000s have also been interpreted as forecasts of Russia’s annexation of Crimea. Many more predictions, including claims that the 2024 U.S. presidential election would be canceled and that NATO would collapse, would not come true.
VTsIOM head Valery Fedorov told the RBC news website that Zhirinovsky’s public image has evolved since his death from that of a scandal-prone politician to a symbol of “patriotism and strategic foresight,” a change he linked to the upheavals of recent years that he said have challenged Russians’ worldview.
“In times of fundamental shifts in the very foundations of how we see the world, radical critics of the old order often turn out to be the greatest realists,” Fedorov said. “Zhirinovsky, who fiercely and relentlessly stripped away the illusions surrounding the rulers and ideologues of the ‘unipolar world,’ proved to be a true herald of a new era of ‘warring kingdoms’.”
Exiled political analyst Abbas Gallyamov, a former Putin speechwriter, offered a different explanation.
“Of course, part of it is that people tend to think more kindly of someone after their death than during their lifetime,” Gallyamov told The Moscow Times.
“But the main reason is that Russia now has a kind of political vacuum: people are dissatisfied with the leaders they have, and no new ones are in sight,” he said. “That applies to the gray mass of officials like [State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav] Volodin, to opposition figures and to Putin himself.”
Zhirinovsky’s image has helped fill that vacuum, Gallyamov said.
“In terms of showmanship, no one comes close to him,” Gallyamov said. “Living standards are falling, there’s no gasoline, and none of the politicians are responding to people’s concerns. That’s when you start wistfully remembering the colorful, charismatic Zhirinovsky.”
Putin and ordinary Russians alike associate Zhirinovsky with the 2000s, a period they now recall with nostalgia amid the war in Ukraine and the economic malaise that has stemmed from it, Gallyamov said.
He also argued that Zhirinovsky helped build a constituency for the nationalist rhetoric that Putin later adopted as his own, then yielded his political niche to the president without putting up a fight.
As for the now 74-year-old Putin, remembering Zhirinovsky may also offer reassurance about his own mortality, Gallyamov suggested.
“The president is aging,” Gallyamov said. “He finds the thought of death unpleasant, but takes comfort in the idea that the ‘right people’ are remembered and loved even after they die.”

ADL honors US senators Rosen, Lankford for bipartisan work against antisemitism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:27 UTC
00:51:27 KST

US Senators Jacky Rosen (D-NV) and James Lankford (R-OK) have been jointly awarded the Levenson Family Defender of Democracy Award by the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) in recognition of their sustained, cross-party leadership and efforts to combat the rising tide of antisemitism.
As co-founders and co-chairs of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, the two lawmakers have worked together to advance legislative measures targeting hate and supporting religious freedom.
Their collaborative initiatives include helping elevate the US Special Envoy to Monitor and Combat Antisemitism to the rank of Ambassador, leading the reauthorization and passage of the Never Again Education Act, and introducing both the Holocaust Education and Antisemitism Lessons (HEAL) Act and the bipartisan Jewish American Security Act.
Accepting the honor, Senator Rosen emphasized the ongoing commitment required to protect Jewish communities.
“It is truly an honor to receive the Levenson Defender of Democracy award with my good friend and colleague Senator James Lankford,” Rosen stated. “We promise to continue fighting to ensure that Jewish communities everywhere can practice their religion and participate in society without fear.”
'Protecting Jewish Americans is not a partisan issue'
The ADL highlighted the senators' collaborative impact on social media, posting: “Congratulations to our Levenson Family Defender of Democracy Award honorees, Jacky Rosen and James Lankford.
As co-chairs of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, they've proven that protecting Jewish Americans is not a partisan issue. Their partnership gives us hope for the future.”

Gaza hostages have returned from captivity, but still face fights over govt. rehabilitation support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:23 UTC
00:51:23 KST

Three years after October 7, the question facing many former hostages is no longer how to bring them home. It is what happens after they get there.
That question resurfaced in an N12 investigation broadcast Wednesday, in which former hostages described sleepless nights, difficulty working, housing problems, and families still struggling to function months or years after returning from Gaza.
A Jerusalem Post examination of the government framework raises another question: Money was allocated for some of the very services now said to depend on donations. What happened to it?
Government procurement records show that in September 2025, the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry approved a joint project with Lehoshit Yad, the nonprofit featured in the N12 report, to operate its Shavim LeHaim community for captivity survivors and their families.
The project totaled NIS 3.03 million and was scheduled to operate through the end of 2026. The ministry was to provide NIS 1.515 million, with the organization contributing the same amount.
The ministry’s document said the community then comprised 144 people from 54 families, including 58 children and teenagers who had returned from Hamas captivity.
Yet in its response to N12 this week, the Welfare Ministry said Lehoshit Yad chose to operate outside the formal arrangement and therefore did not utilize the available budget.
The dispute comes as former hostages confront problems extending far beyond their initial medical treatment.
Former hostages face ongoing struggles
N12 interviewed Yosef-Haim Ohana, who spent 738 days in Hamas captivity and said he is still moving between his grandmother’s home and friends’ places while trying to secure housing.
Segev Kalfon described waking at night believing he was hearing explosions. Eitan Yahalomi, who was 12 when he was kidnapped from Nir Oz and is now 15, said he rarely leaves home and spends much of the night on his phone.
One of the few things that regularly draws Yahalomi outside, he said, is the Lehoshit Yad community.
“I can't see myself without the organization,” he told N12.
The difficulty of treating captivity as an individual trauma has been acknowledged by the state itself.
When the National Insurance Institute (NII) and Sheba Medical Center launched a long-term rehabilitation programin March 2025, the institute said existing legal assistance for second- and third-circle degrees of relationship did not fully address the complexities emerging after hostages returned.
Legal framework surrounding support for ex-hostages is still expanding
The Health Ministry says every returning hostage has been assigned a coordinating nurse and can receive continued physical and mental-health treatment. The NII provides automatic disability recognition, rehabilitation assistance, and financial benefits.
The legal framework is still being expanded.
A government bill granting released hostages automatic rights equivalent to 100% disability and state-funded medical treatment without a time limit passed its first reading in May 2025. The Knesset’s Labor and Welfare Committee began preparing it for second and third readings in December.
A separate Knesset discussion in February called for broader recognition of the Gaza captivity’s effects on entire families, as well as for long-term rehabilitation.
Israel built an extensive system to receive people coming out of Gaza: hospitals, psychologists, social workers, grants, and rehabilitation staff. Three years after October 7, the challenge is whether those systems can adapt to needs that are highly individual and can last for years.
For former hostages who cannot work, housing benefits may still leave them unable to rent near their support network.
Parents who were never in Gaza may nevertheless be unable to sleep or return to work. Teenagers may receive professional treatment and still need other former hostage children around them before they are willing to leave their bedrooms.
The next question is whether the state and the organizations surrounding them can build a system designed for the years ahead, after the headlines fade.

Theological beliefs linked more strongly than church attendance to antisemitism in young Christians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:16 UTC
00:51:16 KST

A new survey examining ideological and religious attitudes among young Christian men indicated that specific theological views served as a far stronger predictor of antisemitic attitudes than regular church attendance.
Katie Posey, a PhD student in Antisemitism Studies at Gratz College, conducted the survey. It was funded by the Academic Engagement Network and the Israel Institute at Regent University. Posey detailed the survey’s findings in an op-ed published in The Christian Post on Monday. The survey is not yet published in full.
Posey said in a statement to The Jerusalem Post, “It was during my Quantitative Approaches to Antisemitism course at Gratz College that I started to design this study. Over the last few years, I watched antisemitic conspiracy theories about Jews and Israel gain traction among young Christian men, which was shocking to me, and it was often through popular online voices.”
“So I wanted to know whether what they believed about the Jewish people theologically made any difference. After Oct. 7, I wanted to see more Christian communities engage their young people to confront antisemitism in all its forms, and I noticed that wasn’t happening everywhere—that also led me to certain kinds of research questions,” Posey said.
In early summer, Posey surveyed 1,090 Christian men aged 18 to 30 across the United States. The participants came from diverse backgrounds, representing Catholic, Evangelical, mainline, non-denominational, and other Christian traditions.
Respondents were questioned about their faith, media habits, political views, perceptions of Jewish people, and their level of comfort discussing Israel.
Perspective on God's covenant with Israel the strongest predictor of views on Jews
Posey said the “strongest predictor of antisemitic attitudes was beliefs that God’s promises to the Jewish people have ended. When I compared the factors together, these beliefs were about four times as strong a predictor as political conservatism.
Church attendance, by contrast, did not predict antisemitic attitudes in the study. There was also a hopeful finding. Men who believed that God’s covenant with the Jewish people continues had lower antisemitic attitude scores. That means what churches teach matters. Christians need to ask a basic question: What does Scripture say about God’s faithfulness to the Jewish people?”
To address these theological roots, Posey pointed to Romans 11, with Paul warning Gentile believers not to boast over the Jewish branches and reminding them, “you do not support the root, but the root supports you” (Romans 11:18). Later in the same chapter, Paul points out that the Jewish people are “beloved” and that “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:28–29).
Emphasizing that Christian faith cannot be separated from its Jewish roots, given that Jesus and his first followers were Jewish, and much of the New Testament assumes the story, promises, and Scriptures of Israel, Posey highlighted that theologian Gerald McDermott argues in a new survey that theology is a stronger predictor of antisemitic attitudes among young American Christian men than church attendance.
Ideas heavily shaped by the media landscape
Posey also emphasized that young Christian men's ideas were heavily shaped by what they watched regularly online. Posey said her study revealed distinct patterns in media consumption: respondents who frequently watched media figures such as Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, or Nick Fuentes recorded higher average antisemitic-attitude scores than men with little or no engagement with them. Notably, the study found that about one in six men surveyed watched Fuentes at least monthly.
Posey cautioned that those were not before-and-after scores and do not prove that watching those figures directly caused antisemitism, but rather that engagement with those figures and antisemitic attitudes were closely linked within that demographic. Furthermore, media exposure remained significantly linked to antisemitic attitudes even after controlling for theology, politics, contact with Jewish people, gaming, and church attendance.
Posey highlighted one of the study's most critical findings: men who believed God’s covenant with the Jewish people continues did have lower antisemitic attitudes, but they were not less likely to engage with those media figures. Stronger beliefs about God’s faithfulness did not automatically translate to different media choices.
At the same time, beliefs that God’s promises had ended linked directly to greater engagement with those figures, showing that theology and media habits overlapped, but one did not simply cancel out the other.
Posey noted that the survey revealed a gap in how ready young men felt to talk about Israel. Fewer than half said they felt comfortable discussing Israel in church or ministry, and only 44% said they felt equipped to discuss it from a biblical perspective. Nearly four in 10 respondents indicated they avoided conversations about Israel entirely because they tended to become tense.
Relationships also played a pivotal role in the data. Men who reported no personal contact with Jewish people registered higher antisemitic-attitude scores, with almost half of those surveyed answering “no” or “not sure” when asked whether they personally knew a Jewish individual.
Emphasizing the practical implications of those figures, Posey argued that churches needed to build real relationships with Jewish neighbors and communities.
“Christians also need opportunities to know Jewish people as people, rather than just as names in a Bible lesson or a news story,” Posey said, adding that antisemitism should not be addressed solely as an abstract idea.
Posey concluded that the “study cannot tell us whether this media content causes antisemitism. Because the survey captured one point in time, it is also possible that men who already hold antisemitic ideas seek out voices that echo those ideas. More research is needed to sort out cause and effect. But the practical lesson is already clear: churches need to address both theology and media habits. Good theology does not automatically change what young men watch, and media literacy cannot provide the theology they need.”
Read the op-ed by Katie Posey that this article draws from at: https://www.christianpost.com/voices/the-belief-that-predicts-antisemitism-in-young-christian-men.html

EU countries will release fresh oil stocks only after top agency assessment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:13 UTC
00:51:13 KST

BRUSSELS — The EU will only conduct further releases of oil and diesel reserves after the International Energy Agency has made it clear such a move would not be damaging to the bloc's energy security, three diplomats familiar with the matter told POLITICO.
The Group of Seven — which includes Italy, Japan, Germany the U.K., France and the U.S. — agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after U.S. officials threatened to ban diesel exports if they didn't tap stockpiles.
However, the IEA appeared to confirm Wednesday that that release would draw from stocks pledged under an agreement in March and not include additional supplies. In other words, it would not amount to a new release at all, but would simply fulfil prior promises.
Advertisement
In a meeting Wednesday afternoon, EU officials endorsed the position, pledging to defer any future drawdowns "pending a clearer IEA assessment of market conditions and security-of-supply risks," said one of the diplomats. Countries need to know "how low we can go," said another.
While diesel prices are high as a result of airstrikes on energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East, some EU countries warned that releasing stocks now could leave them vulnerable in the event of a supply crisis.
There remain enough untapped stocks among IEA members to satisfy the pledge to release 100 million barrels.
Of the 400 million barrels pledged in March, 325 million have been released, with some countries releasing "greater volumes than they initially pledged," the IEA said in a statement following an emergency ministerial meeting. That leaves around 100 million left that countries can still release under that agreement, it added.
It said the fresh commitment would represent a "completion" of that March agreement. The IEA's 32 members include wealthy European, North American and East Asian countries.
POLITICO reported earlier Wednesday that France and Germany — which hold some of Europe's most significant stockpiles — had signalled they would release no or minimal supplies on top of those already pledged.
It remains unclear what share of the releases non-EU members of the IEA will accept, after Japan, another member, ruled out any further releases.
Further details on the breakdown of the G7 release will be discussed at a meeting of the IEA's governing board next week, the second diplomat said.

On this day: US, Britain strike Afghanistan over September 11 attacks, kickstart War on Terror
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:51:10 UTC
00:51:10 KST

On October 7, 2001, the United States and Britain began their first attacks on Afghanistan in retaliation for the September 11, 2001, terror attacks, in what would be the beginning of the "War on Terror."
The bombing targeted Taliban and al-Qaeda terrorists and was the launch of Operation Enduring Freedom, which would span over a decade (until December 31, 2014), and be followed immediately by a second operation (Operation Freedom's Sentinel), which lasted until August 31, 2021.
Ahead of the strikes on Afghanistan, the US demanded that the Taliban turn over Osama bin Laden, along with all other al-Qaeda leaders, among several other demands.
The Taliban refused, claiming that it had no evidence that bin Laden was responsible for the September 11 attack, and instead, on October 7, proposed to try him in an Islamic court. The US rejected this proposal.
Bin Laden was killed by US forces on May 2, 2011, when the Naval Special Warfare Development Group, commonly referred to as US Navy SEAL Team Six, carried out a special operation in Pakistan, where the terror emir was living.
US pulls out of Afghanistan after deal with Taliban
The US fully pulled out of Afghanistan on August 31, 2021, when then-president Joe Biden carried out a troop withdrawal deal made with the Taliban by his predecessor, US President Donald Trump.
As the US troops departed, they destroyed more than 70 aircraft and dozens of armored vehicles, and disabled air defenses that had thwarted an attempted Islamic State rocket attack on the eve of the US departure.
Having failed to anticipate the Taliban would prevail so quickly, Washington and its NATO allies were forced into a hasty exit, leaving behind thousands of Afghans who helped them and may have qualified for evacuation and others who feel at risk.
Nearly 2,500 Americans were killed in the conflict. Many of them were just born when the September 11 attacks took place.
Reuters contributed to this report.

Climate change strips island’s title of largest penguin colony: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:50:00 UTC
00:50:00 KST

Climate change strips island’s title of largest penguin colony: Study
- Climate change has cut Zavodovski island’s chinstrap penguins by two-thirds since 2011, ending its status as the world’s largest penguin colony.
- The British Antarctic Survey data show numbers fell from 1.09 million to 402,000, while macaroni penguins rose and now outnumber chinstraps.
- Researchers say shrinking krill stocks, not the 2016 volcano, likely drove the decline, and they urge the IUCN to list chinstraps as “endangered”.
AI generated
PARIS – A remote island near Antarctica is no longer home to the world’s largest penguin colony as climate-driven changes to ocean food chains likely devastated its once-thriving inhabitants, a new study said on Oct 7.
Drone and satellite images showed that the volcanic island of Zavodovski lost more than 680,000 – or two-thirds – of its chinstrap penguins between 2011 and 2025, according to the British Antarctic Survey (BAS).
“That’s a very rapid loss,” Norman Ratcliffe, the lead author of the BAS study published in the journal Current Biology, told AFP.
The study’s findings raise concerns that chinstrap populations across the South Sandwich Islands, which include Zavodovski and are home to 38% of the species, have fallen.
The researchers suggest that the “alarming declines” should lead to chinstrap penguins being redesignated as “endangered” by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
This would be a sharp downgrade from their “least concern” classification, which means they are not currently threatened with extinction.
Surveys in 2011 had concluded that chinstrap populations on the South Sandwich Islands were stable.
But their number on Zavodovski fell from around 1.09 million breeding individuals in January 2011 to 402,000 in 2025, or a 63% decline, according to the study.
The island is also home to a different species, macaroni penguins, whose population rose from around 338,000 in 2011 to 433,000 in 2025 – and now outnumber chinstraps.
Together, chinstraps and macaronis now total more than 835,000 on Zavodovski.
The researchers said the Adelie penguins of Cape Adare, on the other side of Antarctica, are now the world’s largest penguin colony, numbering more than one million as at 2018.
Krill decline
Zavodovski island’s Mount Curry volcano erupted in 2016, sparking fears that it could wipe out its penguin population.
But the researchers found that the ash cloud was blown north-east over an area not inhabited by the flightless birds.
“The decline in chinstrap colony area was in progress prior to the eruption and continued at a constant rate thereafter,” the study said.
“We don’t think the volcano is implicated or it’s not the main driver (of the population decline) because what we see is a linear decline in the chinstrap penguins,” Ratcliffe told AFP.
Instead, the scientists linked the drop in chinstrap numbers to a reduction in the availability of krill – the tiny shrimp-like creatures that are their main food source.
Warming ocean temperatures have pushed the crustaceans south towards colder waters, which chinstraps do not tolerate.
“We think that climate change operating through food webs is probably the main driver,” Ratcliffe said.
The island’s chinstrap population has been falling at a rate of 7% per year.
Macaroni penguins have increased in number over the same period as they eat a wider range of prey than chinstraps. Their survival also supports the idea that the volcanic eruption was not a factor in the chinstrap’s demise.
“The observed numerical shift from chinstraps to macaronis on Zavodovski represents the most striking change in penguin community composition that has been observed at a single location in Antarctica to date,” the study said.
“The most plausible explanation for the observed patterns of population change is that a climate-induced regime shift has occurred that has been detrimental to the maritime Antarctic chinstraps but has favoured the subantarctic macaronis.” AFP

The status of Iran's uranium enrichment programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:44:09 UTC
00:44:09 KST

Explainer-The status of Iran's uranium enrichment programme
VIENNA, Oct 7 - US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters on Monday that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' seven-month war.
The Trump administration has sought to force Iran to denuclearize in slow-moving negotiations to end the conflict. Below is a summary of what is known, and not, about the current status of Iran's uranium enrichment programme, which is at the heart of its nuclear infrastructure.
WHAT DID IRAN HAVE BEFORE THE US AND ISRAEL BOMBED?
Israel launched airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities on June 13 of last year, soon followed by the United States. In a 12-day campaign, they destroyed or badly damaged the three uranium-enrichment facilities that were known to be operating in Iran at the time.
They argued that Iran was getting too close to being able to produce a nuclear weapon, but the UN nuclear watchdog, the International Atomic Energy Agency, said it had no credible indication of a coordinated weapons programme.
Iran was, however, enriching uranium to up to 60% purity, a short step from the roughly 90% of weapons grade.
The IAEA, which had access to all Iran's declared nuclear sites, including its enrichment plants, until the US-Israeli bombing campaign, estimates Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to up to 60% when the first bombs fell.
That is enough, if enriched further, for 10 nuclear weapons, according to an IAEA yardstick. Iran also had stocks of uranium enriched to lower levels.
No other country has enriched uranium to such a high level without producing nuclear weapons. The US and its European allies say there is no civil justification. The IAEA said the enrichment level and quantity produced were of serious concern.
Iran has long held that it does not want and is not seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
WHAT REMAINS?
Iran has not told the IAEA how much of its enriched uranium survived the attacks or informed it of its whereabouts. It has also not let IAEA inspectors return to the bombed sites since they were attacked.
Of the three enrichment plants, the only above-ground one, at the sprawling Natanz nuclear facility, was destroyed, the IAEA has said. The other two, at Natanz and Fordow, were at least badly damaged and are widely believed to be out of action.
The day before Israel attacked, Iran informed the IAEA it was opening a new enrichment plant at Isfahan, which diplomats say is in a network of tunnels there that appears largely unscathed by US bombing. The IAEA says it does not know the status of that plant or whether it contains nuclear material.
While some of Iran's enriched uranium will have been destroyed in the US-Israeli strikes, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said in March his agency believes "a bit more than 200 kg" of Iran's uranium enriched to up to 60% remains in the tunnel complex at Isfahan, with some also still at Natanz.
WHERE DOES THAT LEAVE IRAN'S ENRICHMENT CAPACITY?
Not even Iran's arch-foe Israel alleges Iran is currently enriching uranium. How long it would need to restart is an open question, but as long as a significant portion of its 60% stock remains, it could in principle enrich to weapons grade with relatively little effort and few machines known as centrifuges.
A 2015 deal between Iran and major powers gave the IAEA extra inspection powers, including oversight of the number of centrifuges and parts for them.
US President Donald Trump's withdrawal from that deal in 2018 prompted its collapse and the IAEA lost track of those machines. Their current number and whereabouts is unknown.
WHAT DID VANCE SAY ABOUT IRANIAN ENRICHMENT?
In an interview with Reuters, Vance questioned why Iran had 60% enriched uranium if it claims to not desire nuclear weapons. And he positioned meaningful reductions in "enrichment capacity" as a prerequisite to satisfying US demands and ending the war.
"Sixty percent enriched uranium, you know, I'm hardly a nuclear scientist, but I've learned this: you don't need that for any energy production. You don't need it for anything except to have threshold weapons-grade uranium," Vance said.
"I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity. So far, we haven't seen a long-term commitment to do that."
THEN HOW CAN IRAN REDUCE ITS CAPACITY?
Given that Iran is not currently known to be enriching, any reduction is likely to be compared to its previous capacity, which was significant. A reduction could refer to purity, output or the number of enrichment sites. REUTERS

It should be added
The Pope convened this assembly—a meeting with the heads of Catholic bishops’ conferences from around the world—to mark the 10th anniversary of a major 2016 document authored by his predecessor, the late Pope Francis.
That document, titled "Amoris Laetitia" ("The Joy of Love"), called on the Church to be less strict and more merciful toward "imperfect" Catholics—notably those who have divorced and remarried.
Under current Church teaching, Catholics who have remarried cannot receive Communion unless they abstain from sexual relations with their new partner, since their first marriage remains valid in the eyes of the Church.
Francis appeared to open the way to Communion for such Catholics, noting in a footnote to the 2016 document that they could receive "help through the sacraments," but he never formulated a clear universal policy for the entire Church.
In his speech on Wednesday, Leo did not mention the issue directly, but said that the Church must "discern the action of grace even in situations marked by limitations, wounds, and evident failures."
Bishops from more than 115 countries are taking part in the assembly, including two from China—a country that in 2018 concluded a controversial agreement with Francis regulating the appointment of Catholic bishops in the country after decades of tension. The event is also attended by 11 married Catholic lay couples, who are expected to share testimonies about their lives.
Pope Leo warns that the UN risks turning into a "farce"25.09.26, 17:50 • 4637 views

Yemen war deepens hunger crisis as child malnutrition surges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:42:16 UTC
00:42:16 KST

Breadcrumb
Yemen war deepens hunger crisis as child malnutrition surges
Yemen's escalating war is rapidly worsening an already severe hunger crisis, with more than one in four children screened by UNICEF teams in recent weeks found to be acutely malnourished, the agency told The New Arab.
Of nearly 2,900 children screened in areas where humanitarian workers were able to gain access, more than 200 were suffering from severe acute malnutrition, the deadliest form of malnutrition.
The findings come as nearly 1,000 people have been killed and more than 200,000 displaced in renewed fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and Houthi rebels, while around 18.3 million people across Yemen are facing acute food insecurity.
"The renewed fighting is increasing the risks by displacing families, disrupting health and nutrition services, restricting humanitarian access and further weakening families' ability to secure food and essential care," Ali Qasim Ali, a UNICEF communications specialist in Yemen, told The New Arab.
Even before the latest escalation, more than 2.2 million children under five were projected to suffer from acute malnutrition in Yemen in 2026, including 516,157 children with severe acute malnutrition.
The World Food Programme (WFP) has also warned that hunger is accelerating across the country, with its monitoring in accessible government-held areas finding that 74 percent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs - the highest proportion recorded this year.
The humanitarian deterioration follows the resumption of major fighting in September between Houthi rebels and forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government, backed by a Saudi-led coalition.
The escalation has brought some of the heaviest fighting since a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted the country's previous phase of full-scale war.
Yemen imports around 90 percent of its food, leaving families particularly vulnerable to fighting that disrupts markets and transport while driving up the price of staple goods.
Children face worsening hunger crisis
Severe acute malnutrition is life-threatening, particularly when accompanied by illness or medical complications.
Children suffering from severe acute malnutrition with medical complications are 12 times more likely to die than better-nourished children without timely treatment, according to UNICEF.
The escalation is simultaneously making that treatment harder to obtain.
Since the fighting intensified in September, more than 200,000 people have been displaced, including an estimated 110,000 children, according to UNICEF.
Many families fled with little or no warning, leaving behind their homes, possessions and livelihoods, while some have already experienced multiple displacements.
"The impact is severe and immediate," Ali told The New Arab.
"Displacement often means families lose access to income, food supplies, healthcare and community support systems."
Twenty-seven UNICEF-supported health facilities have had services disrupted because of insecurity and access constraints.
The facilities provide essential healthcare, including treatment for children with acute malnutrition and support for pregnant and breastfeeding women.
"For children already weakened by malnutrition, any delay in accessing health and nutrition services can have serious consequences," Ali said.
The impact is particularly acute in conflict-affected areas and governorates hosting large numbers of newly displaced families, including Taiz, Lahj, Aden, Marib and Abyan.
Children under five suffering from acute malnutrition, those living in displacement sites and those cut off from healthcare and nutrition services are among those UNICEF considers most at risk.
Aid agencies struggle to reach families
The worsening crisis comes as humanitarian agencies face growing difficulties reaching people affected by the fighting.
WFP has reported displaced families arriving around Aden and Taiz after travelling for days without adequate food or water, while escalating insecurity has restricted humanitarian access to parts of the country.
The agency needs $109 million to provide emergency food and nutrition assistance to as many as 1.5 million people affected by the war and has warned that its ability to maintain assistance is under increasing pressure.
The conflict is also compounding Yemen's vulnerability to disease, creating an additional threat to children already weakened by hunger.
"Conditions could worsen very rapidly," Ali told The New Arab.
"Continued fighting risks triggering further displacement, interrupting nutrition treatment, closing more schools and health facilities, and worsening disease outbreaks."
Cholera cases have already tripled in three weeks, according to UNICEF, while measles continues to spread, with displacement increasing children's vulnerability to infection and disease.
Ali said some of the most vulnerable children were living in areas affected by active hostilities, where insecurity is restricting humanitarian access and families' ability to reach essential services or move somewhere safer.
