Air Force Leaders Elevate Point Defense as a Key Air Warfare Mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:41:07 UTC
00:41:07 KST

NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Flying and fixing aircraft remains the Air Force’s reason for being, but protecting air bases from attack is becoming an essential component that makes those possible. Following attacks on air bases across the Middle East during Operation Epic Fury, point defense was among the hottest topics on tap at AFA’s 2026 Air, Space and Cyber conference in September.
The Iranian attacks, such as the March 27 air raid on Prince Sultan Air Base, Saudi Arabia that damaged multiple refueling aircraft and an E-3 Sentry AWACS command and control plane, did not deliver crippling blows. But they did cause injuries, disrupt operations, and destroy some aircraft.
The damage was great enough to convince Air Force leaders to prioritize air base defense—or point defense, as they are calling it—and invest in new weapons and a new career field to man them.
Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink and Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach announced new initiatives at the conference, aimed at improving oversight of point defense acquisitions amid the recent explosion of growth in the counter-drone industry as it responds to increasing Pentagon demand.
Wilsbach pledged that point defense will no longer be treated as a “side hustle” but as a “core function of air and space power.”
The Air Force began ramping up its point defense strategy in late 2023 after unidentified drones were seen flying repeatedly over Langley Air Force Base, Va. Soon the service, along with the rest of the U.S. military, was racing to catch up with the rapidly evolving drone warfare threats and tactics emerging from the war in Ukraine. Then in June 2025, Operation Spider Web, a bold Ukrainian drone attack on strategic bomber bases deep inside Russia, showed Air Force leaders just how vulnerable the service’s own air bases were to this new threat.
But it took the hard lessons from a shooting war with Iran to elevate point defense to a new level of importance at the service’s semiannual Corona summit in June and make it a key focus at this year’s AFA event, said retired Air Force Lt. Gen. David Deptula, dean of the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies.
“The reason why it was announced at AFA is because a decision had been made at the previous Corona to make point defense a mission function of the Air Force,” Deptula said. The conference “was the first opportunity to really make a big splash.”
During the conference, several Air Force generals said that the service’s increased emphasis on point defense is needed after watching Iranian drone and missile attacks strike air bases during Epic Fury.
Air Combat Command Boss Gen. Adrian L. Spain said Epic Fury “laid bare some of those things that have been in front of us for a while, and it just reminded us that we have to get after some of these things.”
“Our bases are under attack; we have to continue to generate air power in spite of that,” Spain said. “We have to be able to be resilient under attack, and we have to be able to sustain the force under those kinds of pressures to win.”
The Air Force’s chief modernization officer, Lt. Gen. Christopher J. Niemi, said the service identified more than a year ago that it would have to “increasingly protect our assets at air bases with investments in point defense but that accelerated … because of some of the experiences that we had over there.”
Prior to Epic Fury, the Air Force appeared to be banking on its agile combat employment strategy to disperse forces from large bases to ad hoc air bases in order to complicate targeting for adversaries and fight through attacks. The service evacuated Al Udeid Air Base, Qatar, before the Feb. 28 launch of Epic Fury, moving aircraft and most personnel to other locations both in the region and back in the United States.
When Iranian forces attacked Al Udeid, destroying the Combined Air Operations Center, or CAOC, there, the facility was empty—the first time it hadn’t participated in air combat operations since the 1990s. Instead, Epic Fury’s air operations were commanded fromShaw Air Force Base, S.C.
“ACE was really birthed out of necessity, [because] I cannot protect these forces any longer,” Spain said. “But if I could perfectly protect all my forces at a location, I would not move. There’s no reason to move. I’m only creating turbulence for myself if I do that.” That turbulence extends to every part of an air operation, he said: “I have a logistics problem I’ve got to worry about. I’ve got a fuel problem I’ve got to worry about. I have a [command and control] problem I have to worry about when I move around more.”
Spain said Iran’s proven ability to threaten a base means the Air Force is returning to “a time well before 9/11, where we were preparing to fight a peer adversary in an existential way. We see what that looks like through the experience of [Epic Fury].”
Air base defense has long been a complex problem for Air Force leaders. Ostensibly, the Army is responsible for protecting air bases from missile attacks, dating back to the 1948 Key West Agreement on roles and missions of the armed forces. That’s why the Patriot ballistic missile defense system is an Army weapon system. But with the rise of low-cost attack drones such as the Iranian Shahed, the scale and scope of threats has grown while the Army’s capacity to defend far-flung bases has not kept pace. In April 2025, the Air Force published new doctrine on “Point Defense of Air Bases,” assuming a more active role for Airmen in defending their air bases.
The lack of hardened shelters at most forward bases contributes to the Air Force’s vulnerability. Investment in such structures and other passive defenses has often ranked low among budget priorities, compared to aircraft and major research initiatives.
Deptula maintains that the Air Force has long been underfunded and that vulnerabilities are the result of calculated risk and budget choices.
“How come hardened aircraft shelters weren’t in place at Prince Sultan Air Base? How come the command-and-control facility at Al Udeid—that the joint force air component commander has been operating from since 2001—wasn’t built underground?” Deptula said. “The answer is money, because it costs more money. The United States military took the risk, understanding that there were threats out there, they were willing to take the risk and not to spend the money to build hardened aircraft shelters, to build underground facilities.”
Now that “the threat has shown itself to be highly capable,” he added, “resources are going to have to be allocated to increase our ability to defend our bases.”
Air Mobility Command Boss Lt. Gen. Daniel H. Tulley said he was encouraged by Wilsbach’s decision to establish a new career field to develop point defense specialists. Wilsbach said the Air Force will start designating Airmen with the new specialty within two years. The Air Force announced it was standing up the new career field in late June after the Corona meeting. As a short-term fix, USAF has established point defense flights, specialized units of roughly 20 Airmen each, trained to rapidly deploy to hotspots and defend air bases against drone attacks.
Tulley saw how unprotected Al Udeid was when he commanded the 379th Air Expeditionary Wing there from 2019 to 2021.
“When I was at Al Udeid, this problem was widely recognized,” Tulley said. “The Air Force has been going after it, but I think our sense of urgency has dramatically increased—which it needs to. We’ve all seen what Operation Spiderweb did in Russia. How do we prevent the same sort of thing, and maintain the sense of urgency?”
The Air Staff and Point Defense Task Force, working with the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401, or JIATF 401, is making headway to identify technologies and field new weapons to counter the drone threat. But it will take years for the service to build up an adequate point defense capability.
“Would I like to get there a lot faster? Yes, but I think we’re getting there,” Tulley said. “I’d like to look back in two years and say, ‘We’re done,’ but I don’t know if we’ll quite be there yet.”
The Air Force relies primarily on the Small Unmanned Air Defense Systems, or SUADS, for countering drones. The system is capable of identifying and tracking enemy missiles or drones of multiple sizes, and downing incoming drones with an electronic warfare weapon. To stop missiles, it uses both electronic warfare and kinetic effectors. It can also interface with commercial counter-drone systems and other air defense systems, depending on the needs of a commander.
It’s available in two variants, one for fixed air bases and one that can be deployed on a pallet for rapid response missions. The Air Force has requested more than $1.5 billion for SUADS in the fiscal 2027 budget, with most of the funding allocated for the system’s missile defense components, according to budget documents.
What remains unclear is how much money is being spent on additional counter-drone systems for the Air Force, which are being acquired with the assistance of JIATF 401. Those buys are difficult to track since they are not listed in the budget request. Both Air Force and JIATF 401 officials declined to provide funding details.
During the conference, leaders said the Air Force is working on initiatives to gain more oversight over the acquisition process to more efficiently manage its counter-drone acquisitions.
Globally, the market is expanding rapidly, The current global counter-drone market is valued at roughly $9 billion and is projected to reach about $30 billion by 2031.
JIATF-401 Director Army Brig. Gen. Matthew Ross cited that figure in a talk with industry members Sept. 15. The U.S. portion of the counter-drone market is currently valued at roughly $2.5 billion and is expected to grow to roughly $8.6 billion by 2030, according to MarketsandMarkets.com a business intelligence firm.
“What that means is that demand is going up really quickly,” said Ross adding that his agency is acquiring “additional arrows to put into the quiver of our warfighters,” but “our supplies just aren’t there yet.”
Meink said the service is also looking at establishing a senior portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to manage the point defense enterprise. PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to get more authority into the hands of fewer leaders in order to maximize acquisition success. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.
Currently, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems oversees counter-drone acquisition efforts and the service’s PAE for Intelligence, Surveillance, Reconnaissance & Special Operations Forces manages offensive drone acquisitions, said Lea Kirkwood, the Air Force PAE for Electronic Systems.
The Pentagon recently stood up the new Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager for Unmanned Systems, or DRPM UxS, with the goal of accelerating the development, procurement, and fielding at scale of autonomous capabilities.
“There’s a lot of considerations across mission areas,” Kirkwood said, adding that the Department of the Air Force is “looking at how do we need to look at our structure to say ‘how can we best support the [Pentagon], the DRPM UxS, and then also within the DAF, both from the offensive and the defensive perspective’—you know, what’s the best way to get after this?”
The Air Force is also creating a “point defense weapon system,” Wilsbach said during his speech. The new system will be designed to formally manage multiple counter-drone systems that range from sensors, radars, and command and control architecture to kinetic and nonkinetic effectors for disabling or destroying incoming drones.
“The point defense weapon system is a way for us to consolidate these capabilities under a single umbrella,” Michael Sheehy, director of future operations under the Air Force deputy chief of staff for operations said during the JIATF 401 industry meeting.
The Air Force is currently writing a program action directive for the weapon system. “That way it’s not this ad hoc approach to this, where it is buying some, trying some pieces of parts and then kind of making up who’s operating the system. … The other thing that it does is it creates a single point for funding within the Air Force,” Sheehy added. “Now I have a program element code for this weapon system, and as funding’s coming in, it’s going to that as opposed to kind of going all over the place.”
Sheehy noted that there was a “vast difference” in the amount of counter-drone innovations on the show floor at the AFA conference this year compared to prior shows.
“There’s a lot of counter-UAS capability that is being developed out there, and … we need to have a more enterprise level approach to doing this,” he said. The Air Force “owes it to our wing commanders to provide that kit, provide that training, provide that organization that is professionalized to get after this really difficult problem.”

French wine industry facing historic low harvest after extreme summer heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:40:11 UTC
00:40:11 KST

France’s wine industry is facing a historic low harvest after the country was hit by a series of summer heatwaves.
At about 35m hectolitres, the total harvest would be down 2% on a mediocre 2025 yield and 14% below the 2021-2025 average, according to estimates published on Wednesday by the ministry of agriculture.
The International Organisation of Vine and Wine, which tracks global statistics on wine production and consumption, said that last year France had recorded its lowest production since 1957.
This latest decline is a result of hot weather, slightly mitigated by recent rain, and a reduction in cultivated areas, which were pared back by 1.9% in the past year.
Some southern areas, already battered by the heat in 2025, have nonetheless seen production rise this year. In Bordeaux, despite a 5% decrease in cultivated areas, production is expected to increase by 10% on 2025, though this is still 11% below the 2021-2025 average.
For the south-west the rise is about 12%, essentially a return to the previous four-year average.
The Champagne region fared less well as growers had to harvest exceptionally early after the extreme heat sped up sugar buildup and hence natural alcohol production.
The harvest there wrapped up in September for the first time, with production down by half on last year and the five-year average.
Claude Mandois, a producer in Champagne, reported harvesting three-quarters of an average yield in terms of volume but added: “In terms of quality visually and in terms of taste we had an exceptional harvest.”
In Burgundy and the Beaujolais region, production is projected to be 30% lower than the five-year average.
“It’s a level of heterogeneity I’ve never experienced before,” said Jérôme Despey, the chair of the wine advisory board at the public agency FranceAgriMer and a winegrower in the southern Hérault department.
He said vines in the south had become more resilient to the climate, with previous intense heat spells causing growers to adapt vineyard management practices such as largely leaving leaves to protect the grapes. Southern regions also benefited from May rainfall.
The ministry and the industry emphasised overall the “excellent health” of the harvest, which was free of fungi and other moisture-related diseases.

The International Classical Music Festival, now in its 35th edition, is underway in Bitola through October 10.
                                    
Since 1992, the Festival has hosted over 110 renowned Italian artists, establishing itself over the years as a major event for the promotion of Italian music and culture in North Macedonia.
                                    
As part of the Festival, which began on October 2, the opening of the Italian Exhibition of Prints and Drawings was also held.
                                    
On the second evening of the festival, held on Saturday, October 3, with the support of the Italian Embassy in Skopje, Italian pianist Bruno Canino performed a concert at the “Oficerski Dom” Palace, in what is considered the concert hall with the best acoustics in North Macedonia, on a Bösendorfer Grand Concert 280 piano.

Costa Rica's Grynspan ahead in race to be next UN chief, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:39:20 UTC
00:39:20 KST

Costa Rica's Grynspan ahead in race to be next UN chief, sources say
UNITED NATIONS, Oct 7 - An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two sources close to the process said.
The fifth secret poll by the 15-member Security Council followed days of intense negotiations among diplomats in New York after four previous ballots did not result in the emergence of one candidate with overwhelming backing.
Although Grynspan is still leading the pack of seven contenders, the support for her weakened slightly compared to the poll last week, suggesting ongoing gridlock, a result that may prompt other senior figures to join the race.
The selection is taking place at a critical time for the 193-member body. Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, cutbacks in American contributions, and the UN's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of many of its agencies.
Former UN official Daniel Safran-Hon said that while Grynspan had a bad day, she is still in the race because she still has the nine votes necessary to get the job.
Under UN rules, a recommendation to the General Assembly for the secretary-general post requires an affirmative vote from at least nine of the 15 council members, although ultimately, the five veto powers — the US, China, Russia, France and Britain — need to agree on a candidate.
"Her unstable support could be seen by potential new candidates as an opportunity to join the race ahead of the next round later this month," said Safran-Hon, adding that the race has not been this competitive in 30 years.
After former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet dropped out of the race last month, seven candidates are vying to succeed Antonio Guterres. The former Portuguese prime minister steps down at the end of this year after two five-year terms.
If the impasse persists, more candidates could enter the race. Diplomats at the UN say several senior figures, including former and current foreign ministers and country leaders, are seriously considering throwing their hats into the ring.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In the straw polls, which are expected to continue for several more rounds, Security Council members are asked on secret ballots if they "encourage," "discourage" or have "no opinion" on candidates.
Grynspan received 9 encourage votes, 6 discourage and 0 no opinion. That was down from 10 encourage votes at the previous vote.
The rest of the candidates, who include Guyana's UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, the high-profile director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, received more discourage than encourage votes, suggesting that the support for them is waning. REUTERS

“Super Intelligence Force” : ce que la Maison-Blanche attend de cette task force sur l’IA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:37:13 UTC
00:37:13 KST

Le directeur du renseignement national Jay Clayton, qui dirigera la task force, lors de son audition de confirmation au Capitole, à Washington, le 15 juillet 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images
L’administration Trump a accordé à la “Super Intelligence Force” une grande latitude pour déterminer comment le secteur de la tech et le gouvernement fédéral devraient répondre aux menaces que fait peser l’évolution rapide de l’IA sur la sécurité nationale et les libertés publiques, selon une charte obtenue par POLITICO.
Trois personnes au fait des discussions concernant cette task force ont confirmé l’authenticité du document. Ces personnes s’expriment sous couvert d’anonymat afin de pouvoir partager des informations qui n’ont pas encore été rendues publiques.
La task force devra définir des “mesures pour améliorer la capacité à la fois du gouvernement et du secteur privé face à se préparer et à répondre aux menaces pesant sur le territoire national et le peuple américain”, précise la charte. Elle rédigera également un rapport sur les risques liés à l’IA, en mettant l’accent sur “les menaces potentielles pour les libertés civiles”, la cybersécurité, les normes applicables aux modèles avancés et les conséquences d’une éventuelle surréglementation.
Advertisement
Le Wall Street Journal a été le premier à révéler les détails de cette charte.
La Silicon Valley et le Capitole ont tous deux été pris au dépourvu par l’annonce faite par Donald Trump concernant la création de cette task force. Quatre représentants du secteur de la tech ont en effet assuré à POLITICO que peu de personnes au sein de la filière en avaient été informées avant la publication du post du président américain sur les réseaux sociaux. Donald Trump préfère parler de “superintelligence” plutôt que d’intelligence artificielle.
Le directeur du renseignement national, Jay Clayton, dirigera cette task force dans le cadre de ses nouvelles fonctions de référent IA de l’administration, aux côtés du sous-secrétaire à la Défense, Emil Michael, du directeur de l’Office of Personnel Management, Scott Kupor, et du président de la Commission fédérale du commerce, Andrew Ferguson, qui occuperont les fonctions de vice-présidents.
Le groupe sera composé notamment de responsables d’administrations fédérales, par exemple de la NSA (l’agence de renseignements électroniques) ou du ministère de la Santé et des Services sociaux. De hauts responsables de la Maison-Blanche, dont le vice-président JD Vance et la cheffe de cabinet Susie Wiles, seront également étroitement associés à ces travaux. L’ancienne secrétaire d’Etat Condoleezza Rice, ainsi que le financier et ex-référent IA David Sacks apporteront également leurs “conseils”, respectivement en matière de sécurité nationale et de technologie.
La task force sera en place pendant cent vingt jours, mais ses activités pourront être prolongées — ou ses missions transférées à un autre organisme public — sur décision de Susie Wiles, selon la charte.
Advertisement
Plus d’opportunités, mais aussi plus de risques
Toujours d’après le document, la task force mènera des travaux portant sur les services financiers, les infrastructures énergétiques, les transports, l’agriculture et les services d’urgence, et collaborera avec le Pentagone, le ministère de la Justice, le ministère de la Sécurité intérieure et la Commission fédérale du commerce afin de formuler ses recommandations.
La charte met également en avant deux domaines à risque qui font l’objet d’une attention accrue depuis quelques mois : la biosécurité et les menaces pesant sur l’approvisionnement en eau. OpenAI a récemment apporté son soutien à une série de projets de loi visant à empêcher les modèles d’IA d’aggraver la menace que représentent les armes biologiques. De son côté, son concurrent Anthropic a révélé plusieurs incidents au cours desquels ses modèles ont été utilisés par des scientifiques de pays étrangers pour mener des recherches sur des agents pathogènes dangereux.
L’administration Trump a également lancé en août un programme visant à protéger les infrastructures hydrauliques américaines vulnérables contre les menaces liées à la cybersécurité, à la suite d’une série de cyberattaques visant des réseaux d’approvisionnement en eau locaux à travers le pays.
La task force sera également chargée d’examiner “les protocoles et mécanismes actuellement en place” permettant aux laboratoires d’IA de signaler au gouvernement les violations de sécurité, les piratages et les jailbreaks (ou débridages), ainsi que de formuler des recommandations visant à améliorer la réponse du gouvernement face à de tels incidents.
Le document décrit cette technologie comme “à la fois un amplificateur et un catalyseur des risques et des opportunités”, mais attribue en fin de compte la responsabilité des risques liés à l’IA aux laboratoires qui développent des modèles avancés.
“Bien que les laboratoires soient en dernier ressort responsables des risques et des opportunités que leurs modèles amplifient et accélèrent, le rôle du gouvernement fédéral est de prendre conscience de cette période de changement et de la comprendre, ainsi que de faire respecter les lois de notre nation afin que les principes fondamentaux de notre République soient préservés et promus”, peut-on lire dans le document.
Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

Russia dismisses transparency calls amid reports of second Siberia plague case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:36:58 UTC
00:36:58 KST

Rospotrebnadzor said nearly 5,000 tests found no dangerous pathogens and saw "no epidemic risk," while the Kremlin called most media reporting "false" and said it had no knowledge of a US demarche formally requesting additional information.
Russia dismissed calls for transparency over the death of a laboratory technician from plague in Siberia on Wednesday, as reports emerged of a second case of infection.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said it saw "no epidemic risk" following the death of a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, identified as Darya Shipilova, who died last week in the town of Shelekhov near Irkutsk.
The agency said Shipilova had been "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with," and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.
More than 90% of those who had contact with her had completed medical monitoring, it said.
The Kremlin dismissed reports of a second suspected plague case in Siberia, telling journalists that most media reporting on the situation was "false".
"The media are reporting a great deal right now, and the overwhelming majority of what the media are reporting around this situation is false information," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, urging citizens to rely solely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements.
Russian authorities have maintained since the start of the week that Shipilova died of pneumonia and that her cause of death remains "undetermined".
International concern persists
US President Donald Trump had a call with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin scheduled for Wednesday to address the plague incident, and his administration sent Moscow a demarche requesting additional information.
"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Peskov said he had no information that the Kremlin had received any US official complaint.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus on Wednesday called on Moscow to clarify the situation over media reports of a second staff member with pneumonia of unclear origin.
"Timely, complete and transparent information-sharing in line with the International Health Regulations is critical," Tedros said.
The WHO said the day before that the possible case posed a "very low" risk beyond Russia's borders, citing the country's reduced contact with the rest of the world due to its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and resulting sanctions.
It noted that the institute studied "dangerous pathogens" and that plague occurs naturally among wild animals in the Irkutsk region.
Pneumonic plague, the most dangerous form of the disease, affects the lungs and can spread person to person through airborne droplets, with an incubation period as short as 24 hours.
It can be fatal without appropriate care, but the chances of recovery are high if identified and treated promptly. Symptoms include shortness of breath, coughing and blood-streaked sputum.
The more common bubonic plague is caused by the bite of an infected flea and can produce purulent ulcers.
If verified, the Siberia case would be Russia's first confirmed plague infection since 2016.

Over 20,000 unaccompanied minors reached Europe in 2025: UN

More than 20,000 unaccompanied minors reached Europe through mixed migration routes in 2025, making up nearly two-thirds of the 31,100 children who arrived during the year, U.N. agencies said.
A joint report by the International Organization for Migration, International Organization of Migration (IOM), UNHCR and UNICEF found overall child arrivals by sea and land fell 25% from 2024.
The share recorded as unaccompanied, however, rose to 67% from 51% a year earlier, according to the report.
The highest proportions were recorded in Italy and Spain, where 86% of child arrivals were unaccompanied.
IOM Director General Amy Pope warned that limited safe pathways leave children exposed to smugglers, violence and exploitation.
"Children are making difficult and dangerous journeys without a parent or guardian by their side," Pope said, calling for greater cross-border cooperation to protect them.
"No child should have to face these risks alone," she said. "Our shared responsibility is to work across borders to protect them, uphold their rights, and provide the care and support they need."
Among more than 4,600 adolescents and young adults interviewed along Mediterranean, West African Atlantic and Western Balkan routes, nearly half of those asked about their experiences reported physical violence.
On the Central Mediterranean route, 28% said they had been held against their will, while 17% reported being forced to work, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the number of children undergoing refugee resettlement procedures to Europe fell to 3,400 in 2025 from 8,900 a year earlier.
Separately, only 199 children were relocated between European states under the Voluntary Solidarity Mechanism, down 67%, the report said.
None of the relocated children was unaccompanied.
The IOM urged EU member states to "put the best interests of the child at the centre of every decision, to guarantee timely access to services, and never to detain children for immigration purposes."
"Unaccompanied and separated children should have immediate access to legal representation," the agency said.

In Brussels, the situation will be discussed at a meeting of the European Union’s Health Security Committee. So does all this attention mean we should be worried about a plague outbreak?
No. It’s odd, to say the least, that Donald Trump has focused on an unconfirmed plague death in Russia: an average of seven Americans are diagnosed with plague each year in the United States, including its pneumonic form. If confirmed, the Russian case would be the country’s first since 2016.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has requested data from Russian agencies about the situation in the Irkutsk region and assesses the risk to residents of Russia as low and the risk to people in Europe as very low. That assessment is well-founded: plague does not spread from person to person all that easily.
Russian authorities have quarantined and are monitoring people who had contact with the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute researcher who died. Antibiotics taken at the first signs of plague are highly effective, and Russia also has a vaccine against the infection.
So why is everyone talking about this?
The main source of global concern appears to be not the possible outbreak itself and its effects, but the absence of clear official comment from Russian authorities.
WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus made that clear in a statement, saying that “timely, complete and transparent information sharing” is important for accurate risk assessment and to “clarify conflicting reports.”
Unnamed U.S. officials complained to The Wall Street Journal that Russian authorities have provided “little information” about what happened. The State Department is preparing a formal diplomatic message requesting additional information about the death of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute employee and the subsequent quarantine measures, according to The Washington Post.

Scientists in Vienna and Beijing create world’s first nuclear clocks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:35:04 UTC
00:35:04 KST

Scientists in Vienna and Beijing create world’s first nuclear clocks
VIENNA – Scientific teams working separately in Vienna and Beijing have developed the world’s first two operating nuclear clocks in what they are calling an important advance in timekeeping that promises wide-ranging practical applications and offers a new tool to investigate fundamental physics.
The two devices represent the next generation of atomic clocks, the ultra-accurate timekeeping machines first created in 1949.
The two research teams, describing their achievements on Oct 7 in scientific papers published in the journal Nature, said nuclear clocks have the potential to outperform the best conventional atomic clocks, but do not do so yet.
They are called nuclear clocks not because they are powered by nuclear fusion or fission, as a layman might surmise, but because time is calculated by monitoring how light – a high-powered laser – interacts with the nucleus of an atom.
The nuclear clocks both are based on a form, or isotope, of the element thorium, called thorium-229, trapped in solid-state calcium fluoride crystals.
“The two teams worked independently and reached operating thorium-229 nuclear clocks at the same time, using different experimental approaches. I think this is very encouraging because it shows that the concept is robust and not dependent on one particular technical implementation,” said physicist Shiqian Ding of Tsinghua University in China, who helped lead the team behind the Beijing clock.
“The creation of a nuclear clock was something that physicists dreamt of for almost 50 years. In my team, we have been working towards this goal since 2008,” said physicist Thorsten Schumm of TU Wien in Austria, who helped lead the team behind the Vienna clock.
Schumm said he envisions uses for nuclear clocks in areas such as satellite-based navigation, synchronisation of data transfer, surveying and metrology, which is the study of measurement and its practical applications.
Conventional atomic clocks measure time by using lasers or microwaves to make subatomic particles called electrons jump back and forth between two energy levels in an atom’s shell, using elements such as cesium or strontium.
The new nuclear clocks measure time by using lasers to make subatomic particles called protons and neutrons jump back and forth between energy levels inside the nucleus of an atom, in this case thorium-229.
The idea is that tracking these transitions inside the atomic nucleus might attain even higher levels of accuracy than tracking them in electrons because an atomic nucleus is much smaller than the shell surrounding it where electrons reside.
Perfecting the technology
Schumm said the nuclear clock is still “far from its target performance”, with the researchers looking to perfect the technology.
“What is really nice here: the Vienna clock has slightly better thorium crystals – higher concentration, better optical properties – while the Beijing team has a stronger laser. So already by putting these components together, we can build a significantly better clock,” Schumm said.
The best conventional atomic clocks can go billions of years losing or gaining only one second. This ultra-accuracy has been vital for applications such as global navigation satellite systems and internet, cellular and fibre-optic communications.
The researchers think nuclear clocks, once perfected, may do the job even better and can be built to be less bulky and delicate.
The nuclear clocks offer promise in probing fundamental physics. The Vienna team demonstrated that their clock could carry out a precision physics experiment, as they sought to detect dark matter, a crucial component of the cosmos that to date has eluded observation. The experiment did not, in fact, detect dark matter but the nuclear clock performed at the level of the best atomic clocks.
“It gives access to a whole new physics universe,” Schumm said. AFP

robotically 3D printed earth bricks wrap multispecies habitat around olive tree
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:35:03 UTC
00:35:03 KST

robotically 3D printed earth bricks wrap multispecies habitat around olive tree
the pavilion combines computational fabrication with dryland agricultural knowledge to create a porous structure that regulates shade, heat, airflow, and moisture while providing niches for plants, insects, birds, fungi, and other species.
178 3D printed earth bricks form porous habitat around olive tree
BUSTAN, meaning ‘orchard,’ is a full-scale earthen pavilion developed by the Material Topology Research Lab (MTRL) at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology and Weizmann Tree Lab for The Circle exhibition at Design Museum Holon. Built from 178 robotically 3D printed earth bricks, the structure is organized around a living olive tree, treated as the pavilion’s primary client. The bricks are made mainly from locally sourced soil mixed with bio-based plant fibers and mineral binders. Each brick is digitally designed and robotically printed with a specific geometry and surface texture, giving it an ecological function related to shade, thermal mass, airflow, moisture, or habitat.
The pavilion forms a porous wall that creates a microclimate around the tree’s canopy and root zone. Certain bricks shade the roots and reduce solar exposure, while thick earthen walls absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Openings near the top promote passive stack ventilation, and the layered soil profile in the planting zone retains moisture through capillary action.
Bespoke brick geometries also create niches for plants, insects, birds, small mammals, fungi, and biocrusts. As the earthen structure weathers and becomes inhabited, the project proposes architecture as part of an evolving living system rather than a fixed object.
BUSTAN, a pavilion of 178 robotically 3D printed earth bricks built around a living olive tree | all images ©Edo Asoulin
Ancient agricultural practices meet robotic earth fabrication
BUSTAN draws on agricultural practices from the drylands of the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East, where shade, soil, water, shelter, and local materials were used to create microclimates for cultivation. The project translates this environmental logic through computational design and robotic fabrication.
The earth is developed into an extrudable paste and deposited layer by layer by a robotic arm through a custom nozzle. Each brick type follows its own toolpath, producing differentiated forms and surfaces according to its ecological role. The process included local soil collection, material testing, binder development, robotic programming, and fabrication at the Technion Advanced Construction Center (TACC).
As part of MTRL’s research into material ecology, robotic fabrication, and landscape, BUSTAN brings these ideas together as a full-scale prototype that tests how computational tools and local materials can support tree cultivation and multispecies habitat.

Google, Unity launch platform to create video games from prompts
- - Google and Unity launched Playground, a new platform that lets adults create and customise video games from text prompts with “no coding required”.
- - Unity Spark will join Playground in 2026, adding “robust, professional-level” mechanics and high-fidelity 3D tools for creators.
- - The move shows Google’s push into world models and AI gaming, with limited market reaction and possible benefits for Unity’s business.
AI generated
Alphabet’s Google and gaming tools developer Unity Software announced a new platform that will allow people to create video games from simple text prompts, marking the latest incursion of generative artificial intelligence into artistic and creative industries.
The initiative, called Playground, will “put game creation in the hands of millions of new creators, and bring new experiences to billions of players worldwide”, the companies said in a statement on Oct 7.
With its debut, Playground will let people 18 and older generate and customise games using natural language prompts, “no coding required”.
Later in 2026, a new expanded creation experience called Unity Spark, will be integrated with Playground, providing “robust, professional-level” mechanics and high-fidelity 3D capabilities.
Creators will be able to build “immersive, superlative experiences” with a simple text prompt, according to the release.
Playground builds on Google’s push into world models, a type of AI that generates virtual environments in real time from text prompts, rather than just video.
Google’s prototype tool for creating such worlds, Project Genie, spooked Wall Street in January and sent gaming stocks sharply lower, as investors parsed the threat of AI tools and their potential to upend video games.
The market reaction on Oct 7 was more muted. Unity shares were little changed while shares in Roblox, a gaming platform where people create their own games, were down less than 1%.
Google had fallen behind rivals including OpenAI and Anthropic on the AI frontier, but its newly announced Gemini 4 Argon model is seen as helping it catch up.
World models and multimodality, the ability of AI to work with inputs including images, audio and video, in addition to text, have long been understood as Google’s technological strengths.
Google and Unity’s partnership “could reduce fears that AI will make Unity’s core game-building software less necessary, while posing limited medium-term risk to Roblox’s advantage as a social gaming platform,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Nathan Naidu wrote in a note to investors.
The introduction of Unity Spark later in 2026 “could broaden Unity’s creator base and support its game-development business”, which represent about a third of sales. BLOOMBERG

The Pentagon Hopes to Speed Up ‘Kill Chain’ AI Buys With 5-Minute Videos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:34:33 UTC
00:34:33 KST

An under-the-radar procurement program led by the Department of Defense has been granting special statuses to would-be defense contractors that make it easier for the government to quickly purchase their AI offerings, based on product videos that must be no longer than five minutes.
It’s part of the Pentagon’s desperate bid to inject competition in a market the United States military itself destroyed.
The initiative, known as Tradewinds, is managed by DOD’s Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office (CDAO.) Companies can submit videos describing how their AI products address one of several different “strategic focus areas” that the government periodically updates. At least once a month, a panel of judges review submissions and decide whether to accept them into the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace, where the videos can then be viewed by government officials.
If accepted, the pitched products are considered “post-competitive.” Many procurement regulations include competitive requirements. The status can let government buyers check off that box and potentially help shave months off of award timelines. A DOD official says that in several instances, the department has been able to make awards using Tradewinds in less than a week. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google are all listed as participants.
OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google declined to comment for this story.
Though the Tradewinds Solutions Marketplace has been around since late 2022, the Trump administration has been far more vocal than its predecessors about the military buying and operationalizing AI. It also hopes to have more money than ever to throw around: As part of its 2027 budget request to Congress, the White House asked for $1.5 trillion for the Department of Defense, citing “historic investments” in AI as a priority.
This year, the military is seeking video pitches for AI tech that can help “enhance force lethality” and those that can “unleash” AI-enabled agents that can assist in the joint targeting process, including so-called kill chain execution.
No longer as relevant? Pitches for products that promote “a culture of responsible AI” and provide guardrails for AI development and use—requests made during the final Tradewinds submissions cycle under the Biden administration. A DOD official says that the 2026 topics were selected to align with a January 2026 AI strategy memo.
“There has never been a better time to build for the Army,” wrote then-sitting US Army secretary Daniel Driscoll as part of a pitch for more defense tech startups included in Y Combinator’s Fall 2026 wishlist of companies to fund. (Driscoll has since resigned from his position and returned to the private sector. He did not respond to a request for comment.)
Opaque Transactions
Acceptance onto the Tradewinds marketplace—and the special “post-competitive” status that comes with it—lets government buyers more easily cut deals using special types of contracts such as “other transaction” agreements, or OTs, which aren’t subject to certain federal acquisition requirements. By law, the Pentagon can spend up to $500 million dollars on a single OT without having to notify Congress.
Procurement experts say that OTs are considered fast and flexible, which can be appealing to startups that don’t want to gamble on whether a months-long procurement process will result in a contract. However, not all agencies publicly report their OT spending, and even when they do, they’re difficult to find on government-run sites that track federal spending, like USASpending.gov and SAM.gov.
“While OTAs offer opportunities to attract new procurement partners and reduce red tape, numerous reviews have raised red flags,” US senator Joni Ernst of Iowa tells WIRED. “These include questionable costs, mishandling of restricted information, a lack of oversight, reduced accountability and transparency, and an inability to track and access OTA outcomes.”
Ernst recently worked to pass the Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025, which will require the Department of Defense and other agencies to report OTs to the public. They’ll have three years to get into compliance.
According to public records, Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI all have OTs with the Pentagon’s CDAO. According to a DOD official, Tradewinds was leveraged along with market analysis and research as part of the department’s AI acquisition strategy, but the three companies did not confirm whether Tradewinds was used for the specific agreements WIRED identified.
Armed Forces Meet Market Forces
One of the key goals of Tradewinds is to bring “nontraditional” players into the defense industry, says Will Roberts, a former acquisition lead for the Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, CDAO’s predecessor, who helped launch the effort. In some ways, it’s an effort to swing the pendulum back to where it was in the past.
Following the Cold War, the Pentagon encouraged defense companies to merge during a now-infamous meeting called the Last Supper, since Congress was preparing to slash defense budgets. Even though it may seem like only having to deal with a few large companies might make things easier, “it actually had a huge impact on market competition,” says Roberts.
Around the same time, explains Sharon Weinberger, a national security reporter and author of the book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War, the personal computer boom meant that Silicon Valley was able to make its own money and with that, set its own research priorities without being beholden to the funding and influence of the military.
Roberts and other defense professionals brought up the military’s historic role in funding—and shaping—technologies like the Internet and GPS. With those investments also came leverage, says Roberts. “We've sort of lost that leverage because there's billions of dollars in AI being invested by companies themselves.”
Weinberger says this has given Silicon Valley titans an immense amount of power over the Pentagon’s technological future. “The amount of money that the Pentagon can put into AI, compared to what venture capital can invest? It's like a drop in the bucket,” she says. “And that's really frightening for the Pentagon. What happens when they can't drive the direction of technology anymore?”
Publicly, this can play out in dramatic and confusing ways. Weinberger points out, for example, that the recent legal battle over Anthropic’s status as a supply chain risk could be seen as the government trying to figure out what legal mechanisms it has to flex its authority over AI companies.
Silicon Valley sensibilities have also been a roadblock in the past, albeit briefly. Roberts recalls how Google employees got “super paranoid” in 2018 about the company’s involvement with the Pentagon’s Project Maven, which eventually led to Google pulling out of the effort. Roberts says the Pentagon spent years trying to “appease” Google with less politically charged projects like those focused on humanitarian aid and veteran health.
Google declined to comment on whether that telling was accurate. One of the Google solutions listed as “awardable” on the Tradewinds site is called “Google for Military Health - Tradewinds,” and in July 2025, the company announced a $200 million deal with CDAO to utilize its frontier AI technology. In a press release, Jim Kelly, a vice president at Google Public Sector said that the company was “committed to advancing the deployment of innovative technology across the defense ecosystem.”

Three years after October 7: What changed for Israel, the Middle East and Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:34:11 UTC
00:34:11 KST

Netanyahu’s October 7 response has no endgame. Russia has a stake in what follows
On October 7, 2023, Israel faced a horrific attack when Hamas killed over a thousand of its citizens and took hundreds of hostages. This atrocity can never be justified.
But there is another fact that we cannot ignore: Israel’s overconfidence and conviction of superiority over its adversaries led to the country’s most catastrophic security failure. Three years later, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government still has no convincing answer as to how the ensuing war is supposed to secure a safer future for the country.
More firepower, no endgame
The Israeli leadership’s main takeaway from the October 7 tragedy was the need to strike earlier, harder, and deeper. Deterrence gave way to destruction and elimination – first of the adversaries’ military capabilities, then of their leaders. The war expanded beyond Gaza, engulfed Lebanon, and finally escalated to a direct confrontation with Iran. Aggression became the guiding principle of regional policy. Yet, the tragedy also demanded a reassessment of the adversary, a sober evaluation of the country’s intelligence, and governmental accountability. Force can punish an enemy, but it cannot rectify the errors that made the attack possible in the first place.
Here, we clearly see the main contradiction of Netanyahu’s policy. Israel can destroy command centers, eliminate commanders, demolish infrastructure, and occupy territory. However, it is incomparably more difficult to shape neighboring societies in a way that would prevent the threat from re-emerging. The government expanded its military objectives but never defined a realistic political outcome. Who will govern Gaza? What kind of international recognition will that authority rely on? How can the daily lives of Palestinians be restored? What will ensure the safety of Israelis once the army withdraws? As long as there are no answers to these questions, every victory necessitates yet another military operation.
It would certainly be a mistake to deny the losses inflicted upon Israel’s adversaries. Hamas leaders Ismail Haniyeh and Yahya Sinwar, and Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah have been killed. In February 2026, Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes. This case is distinct because the strike was linked not to the events of October 7 itself, but to the broader confrontation surrounding Iran and its nuclear program – though the events of October 7 had served as the initial catalyst.
It’s true that the loss of leadership disrupts command structures, severs ties, and hinders the restoration of military capabilities; however, the outcome must be judged by the state of the organizations and the country itself following these strikes. Iran retained its operational capacity; on March 8 – barely a week after the assassination – Mojtaba Khamenei, the son of the late Ali Khamenei, was elected as the new Supreme Leader. The death of the leader did not lead to the collapse of Iran, as both Israel and the US had hoped.
Nothing drives people to become militants like the loss of loved ones and the destruction of their homes and lives. Those who have survived deadly attacks on their families have nothing to lose; such people seek protection, revenge, or at least a sense of purpose – and militant organizations step in to provide all this. Moreover, Hamas and Hezbollah are structured not as armies with a vertical chain of command, but as networks comprising a military wing, social services, schools, charitable activities, family and community ties. A slain commander can be replaced, but such an environment cannot be easily destroyed by bombs.
History has already demonstrated this. Hezbollah emerged in response to the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon; following the 1992 death of its leader, Abbas al-Musawi, Hassan Nasrallah took the helm and strengthened the movement. Hamas lost its founder, Ahmed Yassin, in 2004, yet won the parliamentary elections in Gaza just a couple of years later. Neither Hamas nor Hezbollah may regain their former strength anytime soon: they suffered great losses, and their supply and command capabilities have been crippled. Yet their story does not end with a list of slain commanders; it lives on in those who remain amidst the ruins.
Israel’s victories, the region’s instability
On the third anniversary of October 7, the situation in Gaza reveals the same disconnect between military pressure and political outcomes. The October 2025 agreement secured the return of the surviving hostages, and by January 2026, the bodies of the deceased had also been brought back from Gaza. However, Hamas has not been disarmed (despite Netanyahu describing it as largely disarmed), and the transition to a new governance structure has yet to begin. Israeli strikes continue, and the army reportedly controls about two-thirds of the territory. While Israel retains immense coercive power, it has been unable to establish a sustainable order.
The external aspect proved particularly difficult to handle. In the wake of October 7, Israel was naturally seen as a nation that had endured a horrific attack; everyone sympathized with it. Later, however, the image shifted: the world saw a devastated Gaza, a displaced population driven from place to place, and a humanitarian catastrophe. Now, facing another rainy winter, hundreds of thousands of people in Gaza are living in overcrowded camps where torrential rain floods their tents, or in buildings at risk of collapse. The longer this catastrophe drags on, the less people are willing to believe the explanation offered by Israel – that its actions are merely self-defense.
People all over the world have openly started expressing hostility toward Israel. Such a level of hatred would have been unimaginable just a few years ago. In the spring of 2026, Pew Research Center surveyed residents of 36 countries: on average, 67% held a very negative view of Israel, while only 25% viewed it favorably. Attitudes have deteriorated even in countries that sympathized most with Israel – such as the UK, Italy, Poland, and Australia. While criticism of the government’s actions does not equate to justifying Hamas, global anti-Semitism has risen due to the conduct of Netanyahu and his far-right ministers – Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben-Gvir, who publicly express hateful, dehumanizing statements.
Netanyahu has gradually lost the sympathy of the international community. Public outrage has moved beyond street protests, influencing diplomatic decisions and relations with partners. The stance of Arab states has also shifted. Before the war, they viewed the normalization of relations with Israel as a means of gaining access to technology, investment, and enhanced security guarantees. Now, public fury over the Palestinian tragedy makes direct rapprochement difficult. Saudi Arabia continues to demand irreversible progress toward Palestinian statehood as a condition for normalizing relations with Israel. The assumption that the Palestinian issue could be sidelined by striking deals with Arab governments proved unfounded. The issue could neither be bypassed nor frozen; it has resurfaced in the region in its most destructive form.
The Middle East has become less predictable. The weakening of Iran’s allies has shifted the balance of power but failed to establish recognized rules of coexistence. Regional states are seeking additional external security guarantees and are ramping up their military capabilities. The direct confrontation between Israel and Iran has expanded the scope of potential targets and the number of parties involved in the conflict. Israel’s tactical advantage exists alongside the heightened vulnerability of the entire regional system.
Russia’s stakes in a fractured Middle East
Russia is primarily concerned with Iran’s stability. Tehran is important both as an independent partner and as a participant in Eurasian transport, trade, and energy networks. Strikes on Iranian infrastructure and disruptions to its foreign trade directly affect Russian interests. The North-South Corridor is gaining importance as an alternative transport route, yet it is simultaneously becoming more dependent on Iran’s ability to keep ports, roads, and border crossings operational. Increased demand for the route does not automatically guarantee an increase in its capacity; the war increases the need for connectivity while complicating the task of maintaining it.
The fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in late 2024 significantly expanded Israel’s freedom of action in Syria. Under Assad, Israel had carried out periodic strikes but was compelled to factor in Russia’s presence, leading to a degree of restraint. Following the rise of Ahmed al-Sharaa to power, Israel began acting with far less inhibition: it expanded its military footprint in Syria, continued to dismantle military infrastructure, and began openly dictating terms to Damascus regarding the deployment of its own forces in the country’s south. The weakness of the new government presented Israel with an opportunity to impose limits on its neighbor’s sovereignty. For Russia, this signifies the collapse of the previous regional balance and creates a need to defend its interests in an environment where Israel increasingly seeks to unilaterally define the permissible rules of conduct for its neighbors.
For Moscow, these changes meant that it had to negotiate the terms of its military presence with the new authorities. Agreements reached in August 2026 regarding Russian facilities demonstrate that it is still possible to maintain relations. Exercising regional influence now requires greater flexibility and less reliance on a single political partner.
The economic consequences for Russia are also mixed. Disruptions in Middle Eastern oil supplies could keep global prices high and boost export revenues. However, a protracted war also drives up transport and insurance costs, disrupts payment settlements, and dampens economic activity in countries with which Russia is developing ties. Amidst this turbulence, Moscow’s role is growing. Russia is a major player in the global energy market, a partner in coordinating oil policy, and an independent diplomatic force that maintains contact with opposing sides.
Cooperation with Moscow enables the Persian Gulf states to expand their options and reduce reliance on US security guarantees. Diplomatically, the crisis offers Russia an opportunity to champion a more consistent approach to security. Its support for Palestinian statehood and opposition to strikes against sovereign nations resonate with many non-Western partners. However, political influence is only achieved when a country’s stance is backed by practical action. Moscow needs to maintain channels of communication with Iran, Israel, and Arab nations, facilitate agreements, and safeguard its own projects.
Netanyahu’s policy has failed to ensure long-term security. Despite Israel’s military achievements, the stated objective – long-term security – hasn’t been met, and the costs of the risky venture continue to rise. Three years on, Israel finds itself more capable of delivering strikes, yet less able to convince its neighbors – and even its allies (such as the Trump administration) – that its policies are paving the way to an acceptable future. As long as Israel substitutes these objectives with continued reliance on coercion, the consequences of the war will be felt far beyond its borders.

Deadly drone attacks raise questions over Europe’s Black Sea defences
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:33:43 UTC
00:33:43 KST

The European Union has a plan to safeguard the Black Sea. But days after drones wreaked havoc along Romania and Bulgaria’s coast, sinking commercial vessels and killing two people, questions loom over how Brussels can protect the sea.
Drones have left a trail of destruction across the Black Sea, sinking commercial ships, setting vessels ablaze and killing civilians — exposing the challenge Europe faces in protecting one of its most vulnerable maritime regions.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev described a drone attack on Tuesday, some 130km off the country's coast, as "absolutely unacceptable". One merchant ship sank and another was damaged. Radev did not attribute blame, with an investigation still underway.
Romanian Foreign Minister Oana-Silvia Țoiu described a deadly incident off the country’s coast a day earlier as “a flagrant violation of international law”.
On Monday, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying Ukrainian grain caught fire and subsequently sank off Romania. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the vessel had been attacked by Russian drones. Two people onboard were killed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned both incidents.
"The situation in the Black Sea is increasingly concerning," she said. "Attacks on civilian shipping are unacceptable."
The incidents have renewed scrutiny of Europe's ability to protect shipping and critical infrastructure in the Black Sea, more than a year after the EU launched a strategy to strengthen security in the region.
When the Black Sea Security Strategy was unveiled in May 2025, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that the region was bearing the spillover effects of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"The Black Sea region is the prime target for hybrid actions. The European Union aims to boost cooperation to combat cyberattacks, disinformation, and other hostile actions," she said.
“Recurring airspace violations and attacks on ports and shipping lanes highlight this reality."
The policy was aimed at ensuring the security of this maritime corridor, as well as protecting critical infrastructure and assets, such as offshore installations and subsea cables.
It also promised the development of a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub aimed at coordinating support and boosting coast-guard cooperation, among other activities. The hub would also analyse seabed sensor data and alert allies to potential dangers and incoming threats.
Asked to assess the effectiveness of the policy in light of this week’s recent incursions, European Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said 65 projects worth €200 million had been initiated in the region because of the policy.
“To add in that context, the European Maritime Safety Agency has offered its support to the Romanian and Bulgarian authorities, in line with its role in providing European-level maritime safety and situational awareness support,” he said.
“Romania and Bulgaria requested satellite imagery to enhance situational awareness following the attacks, and we are currently delivering the shots.”
On the Black Sea Maritime Security Hub, Wigand said it is a project led by Romania and Bulgaria that aims to “help enhance maritime situational awareness and reflection of critical infrastructure”.
A European Commission report on the implementation of the EU’s Black Sea Strategy from July confirmed that the two countries had jointly developed a concept for the hub, which aims, among other initiatives, to counter complex hybrid threats.
In the wake of Bulgaria’s incursion, Romania’s foreign minister said on Tuesday the hub will be located in both of the countries’ main ports, Constanța and Varna, respectively.
But a leaked copy of the EU’s landmark Annual Defence Readiness report shows major shortfalls across Europe’s defence capabilities, particularly when it comes to maritime warfare.
The document, prepared by the European Defence Agency with contributions from the Commission and the EU's foreign policy unit, the European External Action Service, assesses whether the 27 member states are on track to achieve defence readiness by 2030.
Although EU governments plan to invest approximately €98.9 billion from 2024-2029 in maritime capabilities, current deficiencies affect a range of naval operations.
“Critical gaps also remain in naval munitions and missile stockpiles, naval Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD), long-range strike capabilities, and the protection of seabed infrastructure,” the report states.
To fix the problem, the report recommends three courses of action: developing maritime domain awareness, balancing investment in large combat platforms with naval strike capabilities, and investing in supporting enablers such as seabed protection.
Mihai Sebastian Chihaia, a maritime security expert at the European Policy Centre, said the Black Sea had received too little attention in Europe's wider defence debate and argued that strategies alone were insufficient.
“We have quite a few strategies, we have quite a few directions, but to really secure the Black Sea, you actually need capabilities,” he told Euronews. These capabilities include intelligence-gathering operations, such as sensors and radars, for example.
Chihaia argued that NATO — the cornerstone of European collective defence — could also develop a dedicated Black Sea strategy.
In light of the drone incidents from earlier this week, Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey have stressed they are coordinating efforts to strengthen security in the region.
But Chihaia said what remained missing was a broader vision for the Black Sea's future security architecture. Despite years of discussion, NATO has yet to produce one. "This hasn't happened," he said.
Chihaia said the Commission's role is to provide directions and ideas for the member states. This may include funding options, such as the Security Action For Europe (SAFE) defence loan programme.
“It’s really to incentivise the member states to work together, to develop new technological solutions, and to integrate them,” he said.
Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Bulgaria and Romania "play a crucial role to defend our eastern flank", adding that the two countries are receiving a combined €20 billion under SAFE.

“Negotiations are underway regarding their return to their homeland,” the ministry added, saying it remained in contact with Russian officials at several levels.

Men say they were deceived and sent to war
The negotiations followed video appeals from young Kazakh men asking their government to help them return home.
Their relatives said the men had traveled to Russia after being offered civilian employment but were instead pressured into joining the Russian military and sent toward the war zone.

Ukraine Working on 5 Ceasefire Tracks With Partners, Foreign Ministry Says
Relatives said geolocation data sent by some of the men indicated that they were in the northern part of the Russian-occupied Luhansk region.
Among the cases under review is that of Miras Tasharganov, whose mother told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Kazakh service that he had traveled to Russia to work in Kursk.
According to her account, Tasharganov and other men complained about their working conditions before being taken to a military enlistment office and forced to sign contracts.

The figure cannot be independently confirmed and does not indicate how many may have enlisted voluntarily or under coercion.
Tokayev tells Putin to stop war but keeps ties close
Kazakhstan has attempted to balance its longstanding relationship with Moscow against growing concern over Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the recruitment of Kazakh citizens.
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev directly urged Russian President Vladimir Putin in July to stop the war and return to negotiations.

Astana has not recognized Russia’s attempted annexation of Ukrainian territories. However, it continues to maintain extensive commercial, political and strategic ties with Moscow.
During Putin’s May visit to Astana, the two leaders signed a declaration setting out “seven principles of friendship”, covering economic cooperation, shared history, regional integration, education and security.
Russia also agreed to help construct Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant since the collapse of the Soviet Union, with Moscow expected to finance most of the project.
Kazakhstan relies heavily on Russian infrastructure to export oil to international markets, while Russia continues to lease the Baikonur Cosmodrome and use it for space launches.
The two countries are also members of the Eurasian Economic Union and share one of the world’s longest land borders.
Kazakhstan has tightened some export controls amid warnings that companies in Central Asia were helping Russia obtain sanctioned goods. Nevertheless, trade and infrastructure links leave Astana economically dependent on cooperation with Moscow.
The attempt to retrieve Kazakh nationals from the Russian military illustrates that difficult balance: Tokayev’s government is publicly calling for the war to end while continuing major energy, space and commercial projects with the country waging it.

For families in Israel and Gaza, neither the pain nor the memory of children lost has faded
Three years after Hamas launched its attack on Israel, killing some 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage, the pain felt by families of some of the youngest victims of the assault and the war it sparked in Gaza has not dulled.
Ofri Bibas Levy said every Oct. 7 brings her family's loss sharply back into focus.
Her brother Yarden, along with his wife Shiri and their sons Ariel, 4, and Kfir, 9 months, was abducted by Hamas militants from Kibbutz Nir Oz exactly three years ago. Yarden Bibas was released in February 2025. Shiri and her boys never came home; they were killed in captivity.
"I'm still living the day, every day, every second," Bibas Levy told CBS News. "Everything else seems pointless."
She said the attack broke something in the country's collective psyche.
"The loss of trust, the loss of security, the feeling that people can come inside my house and kill my family and you're not safe anywhere," she said.
She's still angry, and she said she wants revenge.
"Every member of those organizations, those terror organizations, for me, should be killed," she said.
But she still hopes for a better future, and believes "that conflicts can be solved."
Bibas Levy said she wants to be able to tell her own 7-year-old daughter, who asks if people will come to kidnap her, that she is safe at her home, without feeling like she is lying.
Asked about recent reports that Israel's leaders failed to act on warnings before the attack, she said it was "like a knife in the heart, twisting it every single time, again and again."
"Why didn't they do everything to save my family?" she asked.
Her message three years on: "The world forgot too fast what happened here."
On the other side of the Gaza border, CBS News spoke with Hind Rajab's grandmother.
She said the family still feels the 5-year-old Palestinian girl's presence in every moment.
Hind was trapped inside a car that came under Israeli fire in Gaza City in January 2024. Audio recordings of her desperate pleas for help to Palestinian paramedics were heard around the world. Her body was found 12 days later.
Speaking with CBS News in early October, her grandmother, who has the same name, held up Hind's notebook and the kindergarten graduation gown she wore.
"Hind cannot be forgotten, because what happened to her was very difficult," she said. "She was an innocent child who had a whole life ahead of her, like any other child in Gaza."
She remembered her granddaughter as a little girl who "loved life and had a talent for drawing," and who had dreams of becoming a doctor.
"A person cannot forget their child, someone who is their own flesh and blood," she told CBS News. "Even if an entire lifetime passes, Hind will remain in our memories."
The Israeli military announced in August that it had opened a criminal investigation into Hind's killing, but her grandmother wasn't hopeful.
"We don't expect from this enemy, who deliberately kills our children every day, that justice on their side will be carried out properly or clearly," she said.

Over 20,000 children reached Europe without parent or guardian in 2025: UN agencies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:32:12 UTC
00:32:12 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
More than 20,000 of the 31,100 children who reached Europe along mixed migration routes in 2025 arrived without a parent or guardian, according to UN agencies.
A joint report by the International Organization for Migration, International Organization of Migration (IOM), UNHCR and UNICEF found overall child arrivals by sea and land fell 25% from 2024.
The share recorded as unaccompanied, however, rose to 67% from 51% a year earlier, according to the report.
The highest proportions were recorded in Italy and Spain, where 86% of child arrivals were unaccompanied.
IOM Director General Amy Pope warned that limited safe pathways leave children exposed to smugglers, violence and exploitation.
"Children are making difficult and dangerous journeys without a parent or guardian by their side," Pope said, calling for greater cross-border cooperation to protect them.
"No child should have to face these risks alone," she said. "Our shared responsibility is to work across borders to protect them, uphold their rights, and provide the care and support they need."
Among more than 4,600 adolescents and young adults interviewed along Mediterranean, West African Atlantic and Western Balkan routes, nearly half of those asked about their experiences reported physical violence.
On the Central Mediterranean route, 28% said they had been held against their will, while 17% reported being forced to work, according to the report.
Meanwhile, the number of children undergoing refugee resettlement procedures to Europe fell to 3,400 in 2025 from 8,900 a year earlier.
Separately, only 199 children were relocated between European states under the Voluntary Solidarity Mechanism, down 67%, the report said.
None of the relocated children was unaccompanied.
The IOM urged EU member states to "put the best interests of the child at the centre of every decision, to guarantee timely access to services, and never to detain children for immigration purposes."
"Unaccompanied and separated children should have immediate access to legal representation," the agency said.
