Russia’s war against Ukraine sends the bill to its own companies: bond defaults head for a 17-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:31:58 UTC
00:31:58 KST

More than 50 Russian companies could default on their bonds this year, the most since 2009, a rating-agency analyst told Russian newspaper Izvestia, which reported it on 6 October.
Russia's wartime economy is straining under high interest rates, and the budget is too: the 2026 deficit has nearly doubled from the earlier forecast to a record $88 billion, with more deficits planned for the next three years as Moscow raises taxes to fund the war and plans its biggest defense budget since the full-scale invasion began.
A default is a situation in which a company cannot make promised interest payments to investors on time or repay borrowed money. If a payment is not made by the agreed deadline, the company becomes delinquent, which under certain conditions is recognized as a default.
So far this year, 20 companies have defaulted for the first time, compared with 24 in all of 2025, said Mikhail Nikonov of the Expert RA rating agency. Most of the companies that missed payments are small issuers of high-yield bonds, Izvestia reported.
In 2026, Russian companies have missed payments totaling 41 billion rubles (about $490 million), compared with 34 billion rubles (about $410 million) the previous year, according to investment bank Sinara.
Russia faces a new wave of corporate defaults
By the end of 2026, the number of Russian companies unable to service their ruble-denominated debt on time could reach 40–50, the highest level since 2010, said Pavel Zholobov, junior managing director at the NRA rating agency.
The number of bond defaults in 2026 has already reached its highest level in a decade, Zholobov said. Similar figures were recorded in the mid-2010s: in 2014, 35 companies missed payments; in 2015, 52 did so; and in 2016, there were 44 issuers. This occurred in part after Western sanctions were imposed on Russia over its annexation of Crimea and its war in Donbas, as well as amid a halving of oil prices and a sharp weakening of the ruble.
There were more defaults only in 2009. At the time, amid the fallout from the global financial crisis, more than 100 issuers faced payment problems, while the volume of distressed debt reached nearly 200 billion rubles, Zholobov noted.
High interest rates put pressure on companies
This time, the main reason for companies' difficulties in making bond payments has been the prolonged period of high interest rates, which has continued since 2023. Companies are raising financing at high interest rates but are unable to refinance their debt on more favorable terms, explained Ekaterina Sidorova, head of the Foreign Exchange, Commodities and Debt Markets Department at SberCIB Investment Research.
At the same time, the situation does not yet resemble a systemic debt crisis: defaults are primarily being recorded among companies with low credit ratings and high debt burdens, Sidorova said.
If a company fails to repay bond debt, it is given 10 business days to meet its obligations. If it fails to do so, the company may offer investors a restructuring—for example, by postponing payments in exchange for a higher interest rate.
The number of defaults will remain high in 2027, Sidorova believes.
High interest rates were a response to accelerating inflation in Russia. Domestic demand was outpacing production, Russia's Central Bank said in October 2023. Sanctions over the war and rising defense spending had also hit the economy and the ruble, which had lost about 25% against the dollar that year. The bank raised its key rate from 7.5% in the first half of 2023 to 15% by the fall.
Ukraine targets Russia's oil industry to weaken its war economy
Ukraine is also seeking to weaken Russia's economy as part of efforts to reduce its ability to finance the war. In particular, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said strikes on oil refineries are aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and destroying its military and economic potential. According to the ministry, the attacks have knocked out more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity.
In the first half of July, Russian oil refineries processed about 3.9 million barrels of oil per day—the lowest level since March 2005. Due to the production cuts, Moscow was also forced to restrict fuel exports.

Gaming, binge eating share traits with recognized addictions: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:27:20 CST
00:27:20 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Some everyday behaviors, including excessive gaming, binge eating and compulsive sexual behavior, can share many characteristics with traditionally recognized alcohol and drug addictions, an international study has found.
Researchers found gaming disorder was 98.9 percent similar to gambling disorder, sharing many of the same risk factors, warning signs and underlying characteristics. Binge eating disorder and compulsive sexual behavior disorder also showed a high degree of overlap, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's Flinders University.
The study, published in European Psychiatry, examined almost 250 systematic reviews and meta-analyses comparing gambling disorder with alcohol use disorder and six behavioral addictions.
The findings add to evidence that addiction can extend beyond substances and gambling, while everyday behaviors such as gaming, eating and shopping can make harmful patterns harder to identify and address.
The researchers compared the disorders across 75 factors linked to addiction, including mental health, personality traits, emotional regulation, cognition and brain function, and found striking similarities between many of the conditions.
They said that better recognition of behavioral addictions could reduce stigma, improve access to care and help people get support before significant harm occurs. ■

Roundup: Kenyan president directs enhanced emergency measures after first Ebola case
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
23:27:16 CST
00:27:16 KST

NAIROBI, Oct. 7 (Xinhua) -- Kenyan President William Ruto has ordered health authorities to ramp up emergency measures following the death of a patient confirmed as the country's first imported case of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD).
In a statement issued on Tuesday evening, Ruto directed the National Security Council Committee to convene, assess the situation, and recommend measures to safeguard the country.
He said the government has ramped up surveillance, contact tracing, and public health interventions to curb potential transmission of the virus, with eight family members of the deceased placed under quarantine and undergoing daily symptom monitoring.
He added that 21 healthcare workers who attended to the patient have been quarantined and are being closely tracked by health officials.
"Contact tracing has also been extended to passengers who traveled on the same flight as the deceased into the country," the president said.
So far, 27 passengers who may have had contact with the deceased have been identified and contacted, and appropriate public health measures are being taken, the statement said.
The president said surveillance and rapid response teams are on the ground, building on the preparedness and surveillance systems Kenya has maintained since May, when Ebola outbreaks were declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda.
"Kenya is prepared to deal with this public health emergency. The government will continue to strengthen surveillance, contact tracing, testing and treatment capacity as necessary," Ruto said.
He urged Kenyans to remain calm and vigilant, observe strict hand hygiene, and avoid contact with individuals exhibiting symptoms associated with Ebola virus disease, which include fever, severe headache, muscle pain, weakness, vomiting, diarrhea, and unexplained bleeding.
The Kenyan leader said anyone experiencing these symptoms, particularly following possible exposure to a suspected or confirmed case, should avoid close contact with others and immediately seek guidance and medical care from a recognized health facility.
He assured the public that the government will continue to monitor the situation closely, implement all necessary measures to safeguard citizens, and provide regular updates on any further developments.
The patient, a Kenyan citizen, fell ill while living in the DRC and sought treatment at several local health facilities, according to the Ministry of Health.
The patient subsequently traveled by road to Kampala, Uganda, via Beni in the DRC on Oct. 2, before flying to Nairobi and arriving on Oct. 3.
Upon arrival, the patient was promptly transported to a Nairobi hospital and isolated.
Laboratory samples tested positive for the Bundibugyo virus at both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute.
Despite receiving supportive care, the patient died on Monday night and was buried on Tuesday in accordance with the country's safe and dignified burial protocols for viral hemorrhagic fevers.
Following the confirmation of Kenya's first Ebola case, the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) has called upon pharmacists and personnel across all medication-related care centers to exercise heightened vigilance.
In a statement, the PSK emphasized that pharmacy care teams must be fully prepared to identify potential risks and protect both themselves and patients in the event of a virus surge.
Pharmacists have been strongly urged to remain alert for patients presenting with symptoms associated with the virus.
"Where clinically appropriate, establish relevant recent travel and exposure/contact history early," the PSK said.
Health authorities said Kenya has remained on high alert since May. As of Tuesday, the country had screened over 652,000 travelers entering the nation, tested 267 suspected samples, and trained approximately 5,000 healthcare workers on Ebola prevention and management, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The WHO said Kenya is the fourth country to confirm a case of BVD.
The DRC is currently responding to an ongoing BVD outbreak, while Uganda, where the Bundibugyo virus species was first detected in 2007, brought its latest outbreak to a close in August.
Most cases in Uganda were imported from the DRC, with a small number locally acquired among contacts and healthcare workers linked to those imported cases, according to the WHO. ■

The composition of growth is expected to shift, with a smaller contribution from private consumption and a larger one from exports. Real household income is projected to slow, reflecting wage deceleration and, in 2026, the unanticipated impact of higher prices.
The Bank of Portugal has identified predominantly downside risks to economic activity and upside risks to inflation, with both largely contingent on the evolution of geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. ■

====================================================================================================

The mass killing does not mean Israel’s winning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:25:06 UTC
00:25:06 KST

The mass killing does not mean Israel is winning
Israel’s military might has failed to achieve the political goals in Gaza it was supposed to.
Three years have passed since Hamas’s attack shook Israel and triggered the ongoing genocidal war. The image of the Israeli army as an invincible force was shattered. In response, Israel used all its military power – except the nuclear bomb – and mobilised all its Western allies to unleash an unprecedented campaign of death and destruction that has devastated Gaza.
The Israeli army did not just target military positions and fighters of the Islamic resistance; it set out to punish the civilian population through massacres and mass destruction. By now, it has killed more than 74,000 and injured more than 180,000, starved the entire population, destroyed the healthcare system, devastated the education system, and wiped out most of Gaza’s life-sustaining infrastructure, including water treatment and desalination plants and the electricity grid.
If the purpose of military power is to achieve political objectives, then the measure of success cannot be the number of people killed or the scale of destruction wrought. It has to be whether the conflict has ended on the desired terms.
But three years into this carnage, Israel appears unable to translate its military superiority into a political reality that reflects its stated goals.
From the start, the Israeli government made clear it aimed to free the captives, eliminate the Palestinian resistance, impose security control over the Gaza Strip, and establish an alternative administration. It also tacitly demonstrated it wished to prepare the ground for the eventual expulsion of the Palestinians.
So what has it achieved so far?
First, all captives have been freed. But of the 250 taken to Gaza, the Israeli army managed to free just eight and recovered the bodies of another 12. It shot dead at least three and killed an unknown number of others during bombing operations.
The vast majority of captives – both dead and alive – were released after intense diplomacy and negotiations with Hamas. It is quite telling that the Israeli army’s point man for the captives’ issue recently said they could have been released a year earlier and some of those who died could have been saved. Overwhelming military power clearly failed in the captives file.
Second, Israel has also been unable to end the presence of the Palestinian resistance in the Gaza Strip despite extensive military operations and the assassination of a large number of its leaders. Hamas continues to be in control of parts of the Strip despite facing continuing Israeli bombing campaigns and attacks by pro-Israel Palestinian militias. Israel has now been forced to negotiate Hamas’s disarmament rather than achieve it by force.
Third, the Israeli army has occupied 60 percent of the Gaza Strip, but it has stopped short of a massive operation to take over the rest of the territory. That is because it understands that the political, humanitarian, and military costs of such a decision would be too high.
Fourth, Israel and its foremost ally, the United States, put a lot of effort into the creation of the Board of Peace and a plan for the reconstruction and alternative administration of the Gaza Strip that excludes the UN. However, that effort has largely failed. The administrative committee for Gaza has not entered the territory to take over governing and the humanitarian provisions of the agreement are yet to be implemented.
Finally, the preparation for the expulsion of the Palestinians from Gaza has not made significant progress. Israel has tried to push Palestinians to leave their land through repeated displacement, starvation, the destruction of homes and infrastructure, and various schemes for “voluntary departure”. Destruction has made the Strip unlivable, but the majority of the Palestinian population has made clear it wants to stay. There have even been returnees from Egypt.
At this point, it is clear that Israel faces a “day after” problem in Gaza. Its military is able to raze the Strip, but not build a new political reality that satisfies Israeli aims and desires.
The hope that reducing Gaza to an apocalyptic landscape would push the entire population into such despair that they would give up on their cause and their rights has been quashed.
The continued presence of Palestinians, the continued resistance, and the growing political and international prominence of the Palestinian cause have demonstrated that the Israeli approach of brutal aggression has failed.
Military power can impose a temporary reality, but it cannot produce political legitimacy on its own. Worse still, it can actually destroy legitimacy. And that is exactly what has happened to the Israeli government and the Israeli project as a whole.
When, last month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took to the podium to deliver his speech before the UN General Assembly, representatives of the majority of UN members walked out of the hall.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity.
And it’s not just his international standing that the Israeli genocidal war has destroyed.
Israel is increasingly spurned by the global majority. A Pew Research survey across 36 countries found that 67 percent of adults see the country unfavourably. The populations of key Israeli allies perceive Israel increasingly negatively: the US – 60 percent; Germany – 73 percent; United Kingdom – 69 percent; France – 68 percent.
In Washington, the debate about US support for Israel has intensified to the point that a growing number of lawmakers are supporting bills that propose curbing military aid or imposing sanctions. In European capitals, similar discussions have resulted in the recent imposition of restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli settlements.
Today, Israeli leaders will address their nation, boasting of military successes, celebrating military prowess and promising more revenge.
But the truth is, the Israeli army, one of the strongest in the world, wielding state-of-the-art fighter jets, sophisticated drones, and AI-navigated 900-tonne bombs, launched a genocidal war against a weak non-state actor armed with small arms … and lost.
People can be killed, homes can be pulverised, and territory can be controlled, but a national cause that has resonated with the world for decades cannot be wiped out through military force.

EXPLAINER - What to know about ‘plague’ quarantine in Siberian region of Russia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:25 UTC
00:24:25 KST

- Local authorities say Rospotrebnadzor implements 'comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures,' which later assesses sanitary, epidemiological situation in region as ‘stable’
- World Health Organization says, based on ‘available unofficial information,’ it assesses public health risk in region as low
Local authorities in Russia's Siberian region of Irkutsk have imposed quarantine measures on people and several hospital departments amid reports of a possible "plague" outbreak.
Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology."
The employee died from her illness, according to numerous media reports and official statements, while authorities placed those who had contact with her under medical observation.
Rospotrebnadzor later said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region was "calm."
The developments, however, have raised concerns and public health fears on social media.
Here is what is known about the reported outbreak:
Reported outbreak
On Friday, Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said that he convened an extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission following reports of a suspected "highly dangerous infectious disease" in a local resident.
Kobzev said Rospotrebnadzor organized and was implementing a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures, adding that the watchdog and regional government were closely monitoring the situation.
"I would like to inform you that all identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none of the contacts show any signs of illness, and laboratory test results have come back negative," Kobzev said.
Maxim Modin, mayor of Irkutsk's Shelekhovsky district, said the same day that several departments of the district hospital in Shelekhov suspended patient discharges and admissions.
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighboring Russian Republic of Buryatia, said the woman who died in Irkutsk "possibly from the plague" had not visited his region.
Tsydenov said there were no "plague" outbreaks in Buryatia, including in areas bordering Mongolia.
Two days later, Rospotrebnadzor said no emergencies had been reported while working with pathogenic microorganisms at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute.
It said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was "stable."
The watchdog added that no cases of infectious disease had been reported among employees of the institute over the previous 10 days.
Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "calm."
Media attention intensified after local outlet People of Baikal on Friday reported that the institute employee, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, allegedly broke a test tube containing "pneumonic plague."
The outlet reported that she became ill after allegedly breaking the test tube late last month and was hospitalized in Shelekhov, where she died Friday evening.
High-level reactions
Several high-level officials have commented on the situation, urging people to rely on official assessments from relevant authorities.
"Rospotrebnadzor is the lead agency with competence in this area," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a news conference in Moscow on Monday.
"It is precisely Rospotrebnadzor's official statements that should be heeded, rather than listening to various rumors or speculations," Peskov said.
He added that the watchdog employs top-tier professionals in the field and again urged people to "heed their official statements."
US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the reported case of "pneumonic plague" in Russia and pledged assistance.
"Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger," Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Nebraska.
"But we'll help them. We'll help them," he added.
Responding to Trump's comments, Peskov said it is "always good when mutual assistance is offered."
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it was closely monitoring reports of a "suspected case of pneumonic plague" in Russia that resulted in one death.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia the same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information about the incident with the international community.
The World Health Organization told Russian state news agency Tass that it was maintaining contact with local health authorities over the incident.
The WHO said that, based on "available unofficial information," it assessed the public health risk in the region as low.
What is plague?
While the exact cause of the reported illness remains unclear, official statements have raised questions about plague.
Plague is an infectious illness caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, which spreads through small wild mammals and their fleas, according to the WHO.
The WHO said bubonic plague is the most common form, while pneumonic and septicemic forms are invariably fatal unless treated early.
According to the WHO, pneumonic plague is the most virulent form, with an incubation period potentially as short as 24 hours.
Plague was historically responsible for the "Black Death," a pandemic in Europe in the 14th century that resulted in more than 50 million deaths, according to the WHO.

As NHS workers we will not stop speaking out til Palantir is out
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:09 UTC
00:24:09 KST

Breadcrumb
As NHS workers we will not stop speaking out til Palantir is out
Last Wednesday, a group of health workers stood outside Palantir's London office beside a replica of a destroyed Palestinian ambulance. A coalition of health worker organisations, in collaboration with Amnesty International, had parked it there to send a clear message.
Palantir, the company running the NHS's patient data platform, is the same company whose CEO, Alex Karp, has publicly declared he is “the most publicly supportive CEO of Israel”. That is a state that has decimated the healthcare system across the Gaza Strip and is steadily crippling it across the West Bank.
But Palantir's ties go far beyond words. In January 2024, it signed a strategic partnership with Israel's Ministry of Defence to support its war effort. The UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory has named Palantir as a supplier of AI tools used by the Israeli army in Gaza. The Nordic investor Storebrand dropped the company over concerns that its predictive policing systems help Israel flag Palestinians as potential "lone wolf" attackers so they can be arrested pre-emptively.
In the United States, its software helps target people for deportation.
Following the action outside Palantir's London office, activists called a national day of action. Grassroots groups across the UK organised 45 protests in more than 30 towns and cities. Nurses, porters, GPs, patients and pensioners were all asking the same question. Why is a company accused of complicity in human rights abuses, mass surveillance and genocide being trusted with our most intimate information?
No faith in Palantir
Increasingly, the public is refusing to let that question go unanswered. More than 44,000 people have now filed legal objections under data protection law, asking NHS England to stop Palantir's Federated Data Platform from storing or using their records. The UK’s health innovation minister has warned that mistrust of Palantir is pushing patients to opt out of NHS data sharing altogether.
In August, NHS England was forced to apologise after admitting it had wrongly claimed that only NHS staff could access identifiable patient data. Meanwhile, the platform's projected costs have risen, its promised benefits have been revised down, and Foxglove's freedom of information requests found that nearly a third of trusts using one of its flagship tools performed fewer operations than before.
Judged purely as a product, setting its human rights record aside, Palantir's platform is costing more and delivering less.
The campaign to remove Palantir from our health system has reached a critical point, with the £330m contract due for review early next year. It is the most pressing boycott issue facing health workers today. If we fail, we will be locked in with a company accused of complicity in grave abuses, offering inferior technology, and holding our most sensitive information.
As health workers, we know that none of this is abstract, nor is it disconnected from Israel's ongoing colonisation of Palestinian land. Trust and confidentiality are the foundations of medical care. A teenager will not tell their doctor about self-harm, and a migrant mother will not bring her child to A&E, if they fear where their information ends up. When that trust breaks down, patients always pay the price.
Boycotts work
We are often told that boycotts are empty gestures that change nothing. History says otherwise. Boycotts have a long and honourable history in healthcare. Doctors and nurses helped isolate apartheid South Africa, and the medical profession led the push to divest from tobacco until screening it out became standard practice for the BMA and the Royal Colleges. In each case, we were told it was not our place. Each time, we were proven right. Refusing to profit from harm is not politics. It is first, do no harm, applied beyond the bedside.
The past few weeks have proved the point again. After years of pressure from campaigners across the UK, long before the current genocide began, and most recently from Nurses for Palestine and the wider health worker movement, the Royal College of Nursing ended its commercial partnership with Teva UK.
Teva UK is the British arm of the Israeli drug giant, which is one of the NHS's biggest suppliers. In a letter to campaigners, the chair of the RCN's council said the college should only enter commercial relationships with companies that represent the values of the nursing profession. That sentence matters.
Our professional bodies take sponsorship money, host exhibition stands and lend their credibility to corporations every day. Choosing who they partner with is not neutral. When the world's largest nursing union, home to half a million nurses, decides a company does not reflect its values, every other royal college should take note. Medical colleges and organisations can no longer hide behind medical neutrality.
If boycotts didn't work, nobody would be trying so hard to silence the health workers calling for them. Censorship is not a side effect of this struggle. It is part of the machinery. Palantir is shielded by a contract with 417 of its 586 pages blacked out. Teva's sponsorships are presented as neutral. And those who object are treated as the problem.
So here is what health workers can do. Object to your data being processed on the Federated Data Platform, and help your patients understand that they can too. Ask your royal college, your trust and your union who sponsors them, and what those companies do. Support colleagues who are being pursued for speaking out, and do not let them stand alone.
We became health workers to protect life. That duty does not stop at the hospital door, and it does not fall silent because a regulator, a lobby group, or a tech giant would prefer it to. Outside Palantir's office last week, that ruined ambulance said what too many of our institutions will not. We intend to keep saying it until they listen.
Amira Nimerawi is a senior advocacy policy and research lead in the humanitarian sector and the co-founder and CEO of Health Workers 4 Palestine, a global grassroots movement of health professionals and allies advocating for the right to health and the end of the illegal occupation of Palestine.
Follow Amira on Instagram: @amiranimerawi @healthworkers4palestine

Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:24:08 UTC
00:24:08 KST

Saudi Arabia launches air safety probe into flydubai incident, sources say
Oct 7 - Saudi Arabia has launched an air accident probe following last week's cockpit stabbing on a flydubai jet, as experts examine any fallout for aviation safety alongside a separate UAE-led criminal investigation, three people close to the matter said.
Safety probes designed to keep flights safe are normal after accidents but are not mandatory when a deliberate act is involved, such as the suspected attempt by a co-pilot to bring down the Israel-bound flydubai jet on September 30.
Until now, it has remained unclear whether Saudi Arabia would go ahead with such a probe, which experts say could test a system of international cooperation designed to make recommendations for safety without attempting to assign blame.
The people close to the matter said Saudi Arabia had notified specialist aviation agencies abroad that it would carry out a safety investigation under international rules into flight FZ1073, which was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked the captain with an axe.
One of the people, however, said it was not clear whether Saudi investigators would publish their findings.
Saudi Arabia's National Transport Safety Center, which has responsibility for accident investigations, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Saudi government and the country's regulator also did not answer requests for comment.
The US National Transportation Safety Board, which would be closely involved in any probe because the Boeing 737 MAX jet that survived a steep plunge was made in the United States, confirmed it had assigned a representative to the probe.
Officials in the UAE did not respond to requests for comment. Under international rules known to the industry as Annex 13, the UAE would also automatically be involved because the jet is registered there and the airline is based in Dubai.
The UAE has already opened a separate criminal investigation into the incident, which its prosecutor general has called a "terrorist attack."
Israel, whose citizens made up nearly all the 172 people on board, has offered to take part in any Saudi-led safety investigation but has not so far been invited to join, Ofer Vaknin, director of the Aircraft Safety Investigation Authority, told Reuters.
However, he added that Israel may not need to join, because it was not an operational or safety issue with the aircraft.
REDUCTION IN ACCIDENTS
Saudi Arabia and Israel have no diplomatic ties, though experts say the decades-old UN-backed system of cooperation on safety has demonstrated it can work across geopolitical lines.
The Annex 13 rulebook grants observer status to countries with significant fatalities or injuries, but does not describe what happens where all passengers escape injury as in this case.
By avoiding questions of blame and focusing solely on technical matters, air accident investigations are widely credited with sharply reducing accidents in recent decades.
They have generally stayed below the diplomatic radar, allowing specialists to cooperate regardless of diplomatic ties.
In 2020, despite heightened tensions following the shooting down of a Ukrainian jet by Iran, aviation officials from the US and Iran jointly took part in the playback of cockpit tapes at the offices of France's BEA agency, participants said.
However, there has been growing friction in recent years over access to evidence between civil and judicial probes.
In 2015, France's BEA agency went ahead with a civil safety probe after clashing with prosecutors over access to evidence following the pilot-suicide crash of a Germanwings jet.
Safety officials say that whereas prosecutors take the lead when a crime is suspected, even cases of deliberate action can yield lessons on topics like recruitment or cockpit safety. REUTERS

What to Say When Someone Shows Up Sick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:22:56 UTC
00:22:56 KST

Your colleague has a fever, a packed calendar, and no intention of missing your 2 p.m. meeting. They make all of this clear as they plop down next to you in that stuffy conference room with a door someone has helpfully just closed. You’re less impressed by their work ethic than concerned about spending the next hour breathing the same air—yet saying something makes you feel like the rude one.
Should you suggest they go home? Ask your boss to intervene? Subtly inch toward an open window? And how do you account for the possibility that they don’t feel they have a choice about being there?
The same awkwardness can occur at home, where a friend arrives for dinner and mentions they’ve felt terrible all day—right after you hugged them hello. Asking them to leave can feel like delivering two uncomfortable messages: You did something wrong, and I don’t want you here, says Vanessa Bohns, a social psychologist at Cornell University and author of Should I Say Something?: The Science of What to Share—and What to Keep to Yourself.
“If you say something to someone and you call them out, in a way you’re judging them,” she says. “It threatens their standing as a good person.” Suggesting they head home can also feel like rejecting them—especially if they showed up because they didn’t want to disappoint you.
Still, Bohns says, “it’s worth saying something.” The key is to make your request clear while reassuring the person that you care about them and would like to see them when they’re feeling better.
Here’s what to say when you’re facing a sick coworker, an ailing dinner guest, or some other ill person who insists they’re absolutely fine.
When a coworker—or your boss—shows up sick
Before deciding what to say, consider what you can realistically offer. Could you take notes for your colleague? Help them join remotely? Reschedule a meeting that depends on their participation? Giving someone a way to bow out with grace can make your request easier to accept, says Jodi R.R. Smith, an etiquette expert in Marblehead, Mass.
“I’m going to take copious notes,” she suggests telling a colleague. Offer to send them afterward so they don’t feel they’ll miss out by heading home.
How you phrase that suggestion depends partly on your role and relationship to them, adds Elaine Swann, an etiquette expert in Carlsbad, Calif. A manager can instruct someone to head home; a peer should frame it as a request. Either way, speak privately or send a quick message instead of calling someone out in front of the room.
Dr. Heidi Torres, an infectious-disease physician and assistant professor of clinical medicine at Weill Cornell Medicine, makes it clear to her colleagues that the office can manage without them: “You stay home, you be guilt free. We are fine. We do not need you to be here.”
If you’re the manager, make sure they know who will handle their workload after they leave. Someone who’s worried about an unfinished project may hear “go home” as “finish it from bed,” says Claire Smith, an occupational health psychologist at the University of South Florida who studies working while sick. Discuss what can wait, who can cover urgent tasks, and whether they’re expected to work at all. Working remotely removes the pressure to show up at the office, but it can leave people feeling they have no reason to take a sick day—even when they feel awful.
Too often, Claire Smith says, employees have to decide whether they’re well enough to work and then figure out what to do about the meeting they’ll miss or the deadline they can’t meet. “It’s not a mutual conversation.”
Of course, going home isn’t always as simple as grabbing your coat. Some people can’t afford to miss a shift; others worry they’ll be penalized for calling out. No carefully worded request can fix a lack of paid sick leave or a strict attendance policy, Claire Smith says. Before assuming someone is being inconsiderate, ask what’s keeping them there. If you can take something off their plate, be specific: “Would it help if I handled the client follow-up so you could head home?” That won’t replace a lost paycheck, but it might ease their worry about leaving work unfinished.
What if the sick person is your boss? Bohns suggests framing your request around a shared work goal, especially if your manager treats pushing through illness as a badge of honor. “One of us should stay healthy for this project,” she suggests saying. You can then ask to join from your desk—making it clear that staying well is part of your commitment to the work.
Ideally, conversations like these should start before anyone gets sick. Torres recommends establishing a coverage plan ahead of cold and flu season, so employees know who will take their shift or handle urgent work. Clear expectations also give coworkers something to point to when someone shows up unwell: You can remind them of the sick policy instead of making it a personal request.
Managers need to follow those expectations themselves. Even a workplace that offers paid time off and backup coverage sends a conflicting message when the boss shows up with a fever. “That policy feels more like decoration,” Torres says. “They have to also follow that and lead by example.”
When a friend or guest arrives feeling awful
Your friend may have dragged themselves to your dinner party because they thought you’d be disappointed if they canceled. Start by relieving that pressure, Bohns suggests: “I’m so sorry you’re feeling so lousy.” Then give them explicit permission to leave: “I hope you didn’t feel obligated to show up. You should definitely go home and rest.”
You can soften the departure by packing up a container of dinner or sending them home with dessert. Before they go, make it clear you still want to see them: “We have to catch up. Let’s reschedule when you’re feeling better,” Bohns suggests.
If they seem inclined to stay, be more direct. “I’m concerned about the rest of the guests,” Swann suggests saying privately. Ask them to call it an early evening, and resist announcing their departure to the group. “Allow the person to leave with dignity,” she says.
If you’re a fellow guest, consider how well you know the person. A close friend might appreciate a whispered suggestion to head home and an offer to help arrange a ride, Jodi Smith says. If you barely know them, pull the host aside instead. Assume they’ve been busy serving dinner and greeting people and haven’t noticed what’s going on. Briefly explain your concern, then add: “I wanted to let you know so that you could handle it in the way that you see fit,” she suggests. Leave the decision to them; you can decide whether you’re comfortable staying.
For your next gathering, Bohns suggests giving guests permission to cancel before anyone even has the sniffles. Tell people upfront that they shouldn’t feel pressure to attend if they’re unwell—and that you’ll invite them again. Someone who’s worried about seeming flaky may need to hear that staying home won’t cost them their place in the group. “It doesn’t mean you’re off the list,” she says. “You’re still going to be invited.”
When they insist it’s “just a cold”
You’ve barely finished suggesting your friend or colleague head home when the reassurance begins: It’s just a cold. They feel fine. They’re definitely not contagious.
Instead of arguing, Bohns suggests a reply that keeps the focus on you: “I’m just being extra careful right now.” Then explain what you’re going to do: “I hope you don’t mind if I stay over here.”
Sharing a little context can help, too. Maybe you’re trying to stay healthy for a big upcoming trip, or you need to avoid bringing an illness home to a family member. Explaining that makes your request feel less like a judgment of their decision to show up, Bohns says.
Those circumstances matter: What’s “just a cold” to one person could be a much bigger deal to someone else, Torres says. The person sitting nearby could be immunocompromised, take care of an elderly parent, or have a baby at home.
At the same time, a cough doesn’t tell you everything. Torres says even she can’t always immediately distinguish allergies from an infection. If leaving isn’t an option, you can put on a mask or open a window to bring in fresh air—without needing to settle what’s making someone cough.
When you’d rather leave
If you’re ready to leave, you don’t have to wait for someone else to make the first move. Even if you’re the only person speaking up, you may not be the only one who’s uncomfortable.
“We can see everyone else’s behavior, but we can’t see their feelings,” Bohns says. Your coworkers or fellow party guests might have the same concerns—and be waiting for someone else to say something.
At work, Swann suggests privately messaging your manager or the meeting organizer to explain your concern and ask whether you can join remotely. That gives you a way to stay involved without spending the rest of the meeting next to someone who’s sick.
At a party, you can simply thank the host and say you need to head out—even if they’re the one who’s under the weather. “Thanks for inviting me. I’ll catch up with you later,” Swann suggests. Keep your goodbye warm and brief, without announcing your reasons to everyone at the table.
“If you don’t want to be around a sick person,” she says, “make the move yourself, and don’t try to get other people involved in it.”

Russia creates control system for group of drones using voice, text commands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:22:33 UTC
00:22:33 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 7. /TASS/. Specialists of a resident company at the Ushkuinik Research and Production Center have developed an intelligent system to control a group of unmanned ground and aerial vehicles using voice and text commands, a TASS correspondent reported from a national drone show.
The TASS correspondent familiarized himself with the innovation on the sidelines of the All-Russian Drone Congress 2026 running in St. Petersburg.
"This is software that makes it possible to autonomously control groups of both ground and aerial robotic vehicles with the help of voice or text. The basic scenario envisages entering voice or text data into our app and the system then recognizes the input, verifies the command and transmits it to a drone," a company representative said.
Before giving a command, the system also analyzes the capabilities of a particular robotic vehicle for implementing the assigned mission, he said.
"After a series of such checks, the entire assigned mission is automatically distributed among several robotic vehicles, subsequently awaiting a human operator’s manual confirmation," the company representative specified.
The system allows a human operator to monitor and control a flight, the movement of robotic vehicles and their fulfilment of the assigned mission, he said.
"In case of changes to input data, such an approach helps either to conclude the task or define new missions for the same groups of robotic vehicles," he added.
The All-Russian Drone Congress is running in St. Petersburg on October 7-9. The event has been organized by the RuDrones Center of Unmanned Technology Competences.

EU Approves Record Sanctions Expansion Targeting 1.6K Russian Citizens and Entities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:21:52 UTC
00:21:52 KST

The European Union has agreed to blacklist more than 1,600 people and entities in the single largest expansion of its sanctions regime against Russia since the beginning of the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, diplomats said Wednesday.
The new listings target 743 individuals and 826 entities primarily linked to Russia’s defense industry, according to Euronews.
More than half are concentrated on missile production, Reuters reported Tuesday.
The 22nd package also targets 77 political figures and election officials in connection with last month’s parliamentary elections held in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
Several other Russia-related listings were approved under the EU’s separate North Korea sanctions framework.
The sanctions entail travel bans, asset freezes and prohibitions on receiving EU funding.
EU foreign ministers will formally approve the expanded sanctions list in Luxembourg on Monday, per Reuters, AFP and Euronews. The bloc last approved its 21st sanctions package in July.
The agreement will bring the total number of people and entities under EU sanctions over the war to nearly 4,650.
The agreement follows backlash over the recent removal of oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, concessions made to prevent all other EU listings from lapsing. Usmanov’s removal was linked to the release of a French prisoner in Azerbaijan.
EU officials are reportedly also considering moving toward qualified majority voting for future sanctions to prevent vetoes by single members.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."

US Marine murder arrest sparks protest in Tokyo (VIDEO)
Outrage over the alleged killing of a woman by a US Marine in Okinawa has erupted in Tokyo, where protesters marched on the US Embassy demanding an end to the American military presence in Japan.
The demonstrations follow the arrest of Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, suspected of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel on the island on Saturday and stealing her belongings. Ballard has denied the allegations.
Okinawa is home to several major US military installations and tens of thousands of American service members.
Footage from Tuesday’s rally shows demonstrators carrying placards demanding justice for Yagi and calling for US forces to leave Japan, before marching outside the embassy under a heavy police presence.
“Neither the US military nor the embassy has offered a proper apology. It is only natural to be angry about this,” one protester said.
Another demonstrator said resentment over crimes involving US personnel had accumulated over decades and accused the authorities of ignoring repeated demands to remove American bases.
“It is truly infuriating that the presence of these bases leads to women being killed or raped like this. I cannot forgive it,” the protester said.
Tokyo has lodged a formal protest with Washington over the case. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has described the alleged killing as a “heinous crime” and demanded full US cooperation with the investigation, tighter discipline among American personnel, and measures to prevent similar incidents. Washington has expressed regret over Yagi’s death and pledged to cooperate with the Japanese authorities.
The case has reignited a decades-old dispute over the concentration of US military facilities in Okinawa. The prefecture accounts for just 0.6% of Japan’s territory but hosts around 70% of the land exclusively used by US forces in the country.
Crimes involving American personnel have repeatedly fueled opposition to the bases. In 1995, the abduction and rape of a 12-year-old Okinawan girl by three US servicemen triggered mass protests. In 2016, former Marine and US base worker Kenneth Franklin Gadson raped and murdered 20-year-old Rina Shimabukuro and was later sentenced to life imprisonment.
Further sexual assault allegations involving US personnel have emerged in recent years despite measures introduced by the US military to tighten discipline, including increased patrols and restrictions on off-base drinking.

Decades-long mystery solved as lost bomber crew identified
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:21:24 BST
00:21:24 KST

Decades-long mystery solved as lost bomber crew identified
The graves of four previously unknown World War 2 Airmen have finally been given names at a ceremony in the Netherlands.
Four airmen who died when their Lancaster bomber crashed in Germany in December 1944 were finally honoured by name after an 82-year search uncovered the truth behind one of Bomber Command’s wartime mysteries.
Earlier today at the CWGC’s Venray War Cemetery in the Netherlands a service was held for Flying Officer (Fg Off) Leslie Markland Hough, Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF); Pilot Officer (Plt Off) John Henry Tales, Royal Air Force Volunteer Reserve (RAFVR); Sergeant (Sgt) Henry Charles Burnside RAFVR and Sgt John Lawson RAFVR, whose remains lay in graves marked ‘unknown’ for decades following a series of post-war administrative errors.
On the morning of 8 December 1944, the Lancaster PD374 of No. 218 Squadron RAF departed RAF Methwold in Norfolk as part of a force of more than 130 tasked with attacking the Neerbeck oil plant at Homberg in Germany’s Ruhr region. From the seven man Lancaster crew; three escaped by parachute and were taken as Prisoners of War and the other four lost their lives.
JCCC Caseworker, Tracey Bowers, said:
  Today we honour the British and Australian airmen who served and died together during World War 2. To have so many families present here today has made this occasion especially poignant, and seeing them interacting with members of the local community who have adopted these graves incredibly moving.
Plt Off Tales, born in Attercliffe, Sheffield, on 31 December 1917 was one of eleven children. He worked as a poster writer before enlisting in the RAF in September 1939 where he built an exemplary service record. Despite having already completed a full operational tour, he volunteered to return to frontline operations and joined No. 218 Squadron in August 1944.
John Tales, nephew of Plt Off Tales, who attended the service with other family members said:
  It has been an extremely poignant occasion and we are honoured and quite overwhelmed to have been here. It has been wonderful to learn more about our Uncle John and we would like to thank all those who have made this possible
The Captain of Lancaster PD374 was Australian airman Fg Off Hough RAAF. Eyewitness accounts suggest Hough remained at the controls of the burning aircraft to give others the opportunity to escape.
The two other crew honoured were Sgts Burnside and Lawson. Burnside was known for his professionalism and immaculate appearance, while Lawson, affectionately known as “Geordie”, came from a mining family in County Durham.
Thurston Lawson, nephew of Sgt Lawson who attended the service with his cousin John Lawson said:
  Fantastic day and incredibly memorable. So moving to see so many people here and everyone has been so kind and represented their organisations brilliantly.
The rededication service was conducted by Reverend (Group Captain) Ruth Hake, who said:
  It is my immense privilege to conduct the ceremony for Fg Off Hough, Plt Off Tales, Sgt Burnside and Sgt Lawson today. They gave their lives in defence of our nation, and in dedicating their graves today with their names rightfully in place, we are able finally, to honour that debt that we all owe to them and their loved ones.
Today’s service, held more than eight decades after these men lost their lives, means the crew of Lancaster PD374 will finally be commemorated under their own names rather than as unknown servicemen.
Dr Daniel Seaton, Commemorations Case Officer at the CWGC, said:
  I am delighted that, after so many years, the final resting place of these brave airmen has finally been identified. Their family members, of whom so many were here today, can now visit their known graves in perpetuity. The Commission is pleased to have assisted with this process and will continue to maintain their graves with the utmost care and respect.

US consumers' year-ahead inflation expectations rose in September to their highest level since May 2023, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said Wednesday.
Median one-year inflation expectations increased to 3.9% from 3.6% in August, while three-year expectations edged up to 3.3% from 3.2%, the bank said.
Five-year inflation expectations remained unchanged at 3%, it added.
Expected household spending growth climbed 0.3 percentage points to 5.5%, also its highest level since May 2023, according to the bank.
Consumers expected prices over the coming year to rise 4.8% for gasoline, 5.5% for food and 6.8% for rent, the bank said.
Expected growth in college education costs rose to 7.5%, it added.
Households reported worsening financial situations and greater difficulty accessing credit compared with a year earlier, according to the bank.
Labor market expectations mostly improved, however.
The perceived probability of losing a job fell to 13.5%, its lowest level since December 2024, while the likelihood of finding a new job after losing one increased to 46.1%, the bank said.

5 takeaways from Kemi Badenoch’s fighty Tory conference speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:21:02 UTC
00:21:02 KST

5 takeaways from Kemi Badenoch’s fighty Tory conference speech
The Conservative leader aimed brickbats at Labour, Nigel Farage — and any attempt to “unite the right.” Now she just has to persuade some of the public to vote for her.
BIRMINGHAM, England — Kemi Badenoch used her rare moment in the spotlight Wednesday to promise “a fight coming in British politics; a fight that we have not seen in this country for more than half a century.”
Britain’s opposition Conservative leader, speaking at the close of her party’s annual conference in Birmingham, started as she meant to go on. She attacked Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour Party and her right-wing rivals, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
It was a speech more about positioning the Tories in a five-party system than about policy. What little she did announce was also about positioning.
Advertisement
Badenoch’s flagship pledge was to abolish inheritance tax on a person’s main home, which is currently set at a threshold of £500,000 (or £1 million for a married couple). It will overwhelmingly benefit the wealthiest families — but it’s part of Badenoch’s argument about being unashamedly Tory and pursuing growth.
On her own terms, and those of her members, Badenoch is seeing the conference as a success. This time last year her own party was muttering about her future; now it is united in pursuing a victory at the next general election.
Whether she can achieve that victory is another question. POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the Conservative Party on just 18% in a general election (due by 2029), beneath its historic low in 2024, and behind Reform on 22% and Labour on 26%.
POLITICO crunched the five biggest takeaways as Tory conference closed.
1) ‘Unite the right’ looks dead and buried
With most polls projecting a hung parliament, the shape of Britain’s next government could be decided by one thing: whether the Tories are willing — or able — to form a pact with the rival right-wing party Reform UK.
Badenoch’s speech suggests that they are neither — and made it personal. Badenoch, the first Black leader of a major U.K. political party, took aim at Reform politicians and outriders who have questioned if non-white Brits with foreign heritage can be classed as English.
Advertisement
“I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English,” she said. “We must not let these people take us backwards. That is not the country we are … I am black. I am British. I am proud of my country.”
She added: “To those who say unite the right: We are not uniting with that.”
At the same time, her party is clearly turning its head to middle-class “shire Tories” in the south of England who switched to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Some of the key policies announced this week — such as state-subsidized childcare for workers earning more than £100,000 a year, and scrapping inheritance tax on multi-million-pound family homes — will benefit wealthier voters in London and the south.
That is a very different voter coalition to the industrial heartlands in northern England, where low-income voters have turned to Reform. “None of our voters would benefit from this tax cut for the 2%,” boasted one Reform aide of the Tory inheritance tax policy. “They’ve abandoned going after our voters.” (Tory aides insist they have policies to win back both groups.)
So could Badenoch’s Conservatives form a pact with any other party? The jury’s out on that.
She spent little energy criticizing the hard-right Restore Britain – which could aid her party by splitting Reform’s vote – but Restore’s tally of seats at an election would be minimal.
Advertisement
And while the Tories governed with the centrist Liberal Democrats in 2010, both sides remain scarred from that. Meanwhile, Burnham has already laid out what sounded like a coalition pitch last week, when he argued for closer ties with the EU and electoral reform. Shadow Minister for Policy Renewal Neil O’Brien told a fringe event: “Not since Marilyn Monroe stood on that hot air vent and let her skirts billow have I seen such a ‘come hither’ gesture.”
2) Attack-dog Badenoch is in a fight of ideas
Badenoch’s speech focused overwhelmingly on attacking her rivals and creating clear space between her party and theirs.
Burnham was the “Paddington Bear prime minister who hopes our problems go away”; Tory defector Robert Jenrick was part of an “export boom of drama queens going to Reform”; the Green Party was guilty of “disgraceful antisemitism”; some Reform politicians are “measuring up the curtains for their prison cells.” Her autocue even instructed her to give “side eye” when mocking Farage’s ally George Cottrell, whose links to the Reform leader have come under scrutiny.
It was a deliberate contrast to Burnham’s speech last week, which avoided naming his rivals. In a five- or six-party market, the two leaders are taking opposite approaches to make themselves stand out: Burnham wants to rise above the melee while Badenoch thew the hardest punches.
They are united, though, in seeing politics as a battle of ideas — unlike former PM Keir Starmer, accused of focusing more on process than vision. Badenoch spent more than two months personally writing a 95-page treatise on her ideas about the future, “The Right Way.” She unveiled it on the conference’s first day; extraordinarily, it didn’t leak.
Badenoch also wants to cut through by presenting her party as the voice of fiscal responsibility and defense. The Tories announced what they said would amount to £13 billion a year in welfare cuts on top of £23 billion announced last year. “Our country is running out of money. Almost every other problem flows from this,” said Badenoch.
Advertisement
She added her party would end the “delays” and approve a third runway for Heathrow Airport (though the exact process for this was not clear), halve the 15 percent rate of employers’ national insurance for under-25s and overturn the Labour government’s reforms to employment rights.
The Conservatives are banking on Burnham’s star falling after the Oct. 28 budget and a difficult spending review next year, in which he will have to set out whether Britain spends 3% of its GDP on defense by 2030.
A shadow cabinet minister, granted anonymity to speak frankly, said: “It’s a make-do-and-mend budget; they’ll get through that — but they can’t get through the spending review. [Former Chancellor] Rachel [Reeves] left them a bomb primed to explode.”
3) There are still some no-go areas for the Tories
The ideological chasm being opened up between Badenoch and Burnham is forcing the Conservatives onto uncomfortable territory.
Burnham used his own conference speech to open the door to a possible return to the EU, but Badenoch was clear she didn’t want to take the bait.
“He [Burnham] wants to reopen the Brexit debate. Can you imagine having to go through that again?” the Tory leader said. “So much time lost arguing with ourselves, arguing with the EU, going round and round in circles, businesses not knowing whether they should invest. He wants to do it all again. I think that is a terrible idea.”
Advertisement
Public opinion has shifted in the decade since the EU referendum, which was triggered and implemented by the Conservatives. Renegotiating any new deal with Brussels will be a headache for Burnham and stacked with peril, but it’ll also serve as a reminder of what the Tories — and veteran Brexit campaigner Farage — delivered for the country.
Veteran Euroskeptic MP Bernard Jenkin was even blunter at a fringe event: “Do not defend Brexit. Brexit is toxic with the voters.”
The other big divide that Burnham opened up is on social care. He wants to fund a “national care service” for the elderly in part by changing the “triple lock” on state pensions.
That lock is cherished by many on the right — but there are also the small-state realists who want it axed to curtail the ballooning welfare bill. POLITICO reported that shadow cabinet ministers are debating not coming up with their own substantive offer on how to fix the care system.
“The Tories are ducking the big issues facing our country and instead of showing leadership, Kemi Badenoch is happy to fail a whole generation of older people who have contributed to society all their lives,” Labour Party chair Bridget Phillipson responded.
Whether or not the Tories want to talk about these issues, their rivals will try to ensure they have no choice.
Advertisement
4) The Tories are definitely ready for an election … honest
The Conservatives are living in constant fear of Burnham calling a snap election.
Despite the prime minister insisting he won’t trigger a vote until 2029, Tory figures know it’s within the PM’s gift to go to the polls whenever it suits him best. The right is deeply divided and Burnham may want to seek his own mandate instead of serving out predecessor Keir Starmer’s stifling manifesto. That could catch the Conservatives on the hop.
Badenoch’s top team privately feared that Burnham would announce an election in his conference speech last week, said three senior figures with knowledge of the conversations. That didn’t happen, but it underlines the anxiety the Tories are living under.
Badenoch’s team pulled together a draft manifesto after some “highly stressed” conversations over the summer, said a second shadow cabinet minister. It now sits waiting in a Word document ready to go in case of emergency.
Would-be candidates are already trooping into the party’s new headquarters in Westminster for regular assessment days, while Badenoch’s senior team is holding an election planning meeting once a week on a Wednesday afternoon, a person with knowledge of it said.
“We are ready for an election whenever it’s called,” Badenoch insisted on Wednesday. “We will need many more talented people in the next parliament. People who have had successful careers outside Westminster, not just people who know how to talk a good game, people who know how to get stuff done.”
Advertisement
But deep down the Tories know they’ve got some way to go to be fully prepared.
One party activist told POLITICO a mere 17 campaign managers are in post, despite around 80 being needed for a full-strength election battle. “If we have an election tomorrow we’re f*cked,” they added. (A Tory official said further recruitment would start shortly.)
5) It’s still the Kemi show
“We are under new management. There’s a new captain. There’s a new coach. There’s a new owner, effectively, which is all me,” is how Badenoch put it to GB News.
There’s a reason why she’s taking the “all me” approach. Badenoch easily out-polls her own party, which was unceremoniously dumped out of power by the electorate two years ago. “The party is a drag on Kemi,” as a third shadow cabinet minister put it.
Badenoch knows she must deflect some of that shine onto her colleagues. That’s why they were introduced, if somewhat awkwardly, in a parade into the hall before her speech — where she name-checked ministers who she said had helped trigger government U-turns.
At the same time, the party still feels a need to apologize for the failures that littered its 14 years in power. O’Brien made that point at one event on the conference fringe, arguing that the Tories failed to build enough prison places, failed to “stop the boats” and failed to deport illegal immigrants sufficiently.
The mission, said O’Brien, is to show “that you are serious, that you are different, and it’s not just another round of bullsh*t ‘hope again’ and fantasy … I feel seared by our experiences in government last time round. After we left, I felt a profound sense of disappointment and frankly shame.”
Badenoch put it best in her speech, where she insisted voters are at least peering through the shop window at the Tories. “They like what they see,” she said, “but let’s be honest: not enough of them are buying yet.”

Ukraine is working with international partners on five possible ceasefire formats as Kyiv continues efforts to find a path toward ending Russia’s war, Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi said on Oct. 7.
The proposals include a full and unconditional ceasefire, separate arrangements covering the Black Sea, food exports and energy infrastructure, as well as a US-backed energy ceasefire.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“These are initiatives developed with the involvement of Ukrainian diplomacy. They are realistic and mutually beneficial,” Tykhyi said at a briefing, sourced by RBC-Ukraine.
The five tracks are:
- Full and unconditional ceasefire: Ukraine agreed to a comprehensive ceasefire proposal in March 2025, and Kyiv’s position remains unchanged. Tykhyi said it now awaits a reciprocal decision from Russia.
- Black Sea security: Ukraine, Turkey and Egypt are working on proposals to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea.
- Black Sea food security: Kyiv is working with India on protecting food exports through the Black Sea.
- India-led energy track: India is working to facilitate a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
- US-backed energy ceasefire: Ukraine and the US are discussing a separate arrangement to stop attacks on energy facilities, Tykhyi said.
“It takes two to tango,” Tykhyi said, stressing that Russia must agree to the proposed arrangements.
He said Kyiv considers the proposals both realistic and mutually beneficial.
Tykhyi also pushed back against claims that Ukraine is responsible for the lack of progress toward a ceasefire, calling such arguments an attempt to exploit public fatigue with the war.
“An attempt to shift the blame for the continuation of the war from Moscow to Kyiv is manipulation,” he said.
India has recently increased its involvement in diplomatic efforts between Ukraine and Russia, particularly on Black Sea security and energy infrastructure.
Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar has been involved in efforts to explore an energy ceasefire and a halt to attacks on critical infrastructure, while Kyiv says it remains ready to work with New Delhi on practical proposals.
5 Children, Including Three 1-Year-Old Boys, Among 19 Killed in Russian Strike on Pryluky
Putin rejects proposal for mutual halt to strikes
Moscow has repeatedly rejected proposals for reciprocal ceasefires in different areas of the war.
In one of his latest statements, Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed a proposal under which Russia would stop attacks on Ukrainian vessels if Kyiv halted strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club on Oct. 1, Putin called the proposal “absurd,” arguing that Russia would gain little from stopping attacks on Ukrainian ships carrying civilian and agricultural cargo while its own oil and petroleum exports remain restricted by sanctions.
“We are supposed to stop striking targets that are sensitive to them. Well, it simply looks absurd,” Putin said.
Putin again claimed that Ukraine had initiated attacks on Russian vessels, saying Kyiv began striking tankers and other ships in early July. He claimed that 40 Russian vessels were “knocked out” in the first 10 days and more than 100 had been damaged since.
“We began responding,” Putin said, adding that Russia was now being asked to stop its attacks.
Asked directly whether he would agree to the proposed mutual halt to strikes, Putin replied: “No.”

Platform that sold stolen sexual images of women and girls shut in France-US operation
PARIS - A joint French-US operation has shut down several websites associated with an online platform that sold private sexual content stolen from over 17,000 women worldwide, law enforcement authorities in both countries said on Oct 7.
Two brothers, aged 21 and 25, were arrested in northern France on Oct 6 on suspicion of having been the “main administrators” of the NudeLeaksTeens platform, a statement from the Paris prosecutor’s office said.
The platform sold “packs” of images and videos of thousands of women and girls stolen from sources including hacked accounts on Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
More than 17,000 women of all nationalities were affected, the prosecutor’s office said, some of whom were children.
The US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Virginia said in a separate statement that the site “offered for sale sexually explicit images and videos of children”.
It said the platform sold its content in specific albums, including one advertised as containing “6,200 private nude files” of mostly American teenagers or adults from hacked accounts, including child sexual abuse material.
French investigators also seized digital assets including bitcoin worth more than €700,000 (S$1 million).
Users on the platform were encouraged - in exchange for virtual currency - to provide identifying information about each victim, who were listed individually by their real names and categorised by age, location and occupation.
French prosecutors said the operation was part of a joint effort with US law enforcement to “combat child pornography, as well as the distribution and sale of stolen private sexual content involving women”. AFP

Pope Leo opens Vatican meeting likely to discuss remarriage, gay Catholics
VATICAN CITY – Pope Leo urged an assembly of some 150 bishops from around the world to find “renewed ways” of helping modern families at the start of a week-long meeting at the Vatican, his biggest gathering of Church leaders so far.
The assembly, meeting through Oct 14 to discuss Catholic family life teachings, is expected to touch on contested topics such as the Church’s treatment of LGBT members and those who have been divorced and remarried, although those issues are not formally on the agenda.
Leo asked that God would “give us the freedom to listen to one another, the wisdom to recognise his work among his people, and the courage to follow where he leads us”.
The Pope has called the assembly, a meeting with the presidents of the world’s Catholic bishops conferences, to mark the 10th anniversary of a landmark 2016 document written by his predecessor, the late Pope Francis.
That text, titled Amoris Laetitia (The Joy of Love), urged the Church to be less strict and more compassionate towards “imperfect” Catholics, such as those who are divorced and remarried.
Under current Church teaching, remarried Catholics cannot receive communion unless they abstain from sex with their new partner, because their first marriage is still valid in the eyes of the Church.
Francis appeared to open the door for remarried Catholics to take communion, saying in a footnote of the 2016 document that they could receive “the help of the sacraments”, but never laid out a clear universal policy for the global Church.
Leo did not specifically mention the issue in his remarks on Oct 7 but said the Church must “recognise the work of grace even in situations marked by limits, wounds and apparent failure”.
Bishops from more than 115 countries are taking part in the assembly, including two from China, which negotiated a contested 2018 deal with Francis that normalised appointments of Catholic bishops in the country after decades of tensions.
Also taking part are 11 lay Catholic couples, who are expected to give testimonies about their lives. REUTERS

Ex-Barclays traders jailed for rigging interest rates have convictions quashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:19:25 UTC
00:19:25 KST

Five more former traders who were jailed for rigging interest rates have had their convictions quashed by the court of appeal in London, after a long battle to clear their names.
The court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham – all of whom worked at Barclays.
Their acquittals on Wednesday came just over a year after the UK supreme court overturned a decade-old ruling against the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes.
The five former Barclays traders were jailed between 2016 and 2019 on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now-defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).
The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.
The five former Barclays traders applied to clear their names after Hayes, the first banker jailed for Libor-rigging in 2015, had his name cleared. Carlo Palombo, a former Barclays trader sentenced to four years in prison in 2019 for rigging Euribor, also had his conviction quashed on the same day in July 2025.
The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that had ultimately “deprived” them of a fair trial. They found trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries that found the former traders guilty.
The cases of the American Pabon; Calcutta-born Merchant; Britons Bermingham and Mathew; and French national Moryoussef were referred back to the court of appeal by the Criminal Cases Review Commission in January.
The move came after the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the men, found their convictions “may be considered unsafe” after the supreme court ruling in the cases of Hayes and Palombo. The SFO did not contest the appeals.
Mathew said: “For the last 10 years, the stain of a criminal conviction has been a burden I have carried every minute of every day.”
He added: “Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it’s about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened.”
In a statement, Pabon, thanked Hayes, who he said “refused to let it go and pushed this through for all of us”.
Tom Bushnell, a partner at the law firm Hickman & Rose, which represented Merchant, Mathew and Moryoussef, said: “In Jay Merchant and Jon Mathew’s case, it took over a decade for this wrong to be righted. In Philippe Moryoussef’s case, over eight years.
“Their lives have been turned upside down as a result. All involved in the criminal justice system should now ask themselves not only how this error came to be made and repeated, but also why it took so long to correct.”
Wednesday’s ruling marks a further blow for the SFO, with the unravelling of more of its high-profile prosecutions. It said: “After carefully considering this judgment and the full circumstances, we do not oppose the appeals of five individuals convicted by juries in relation to Libor and Euribor.”
The agency reiterated in a statement that the supreme court had “found that there was ample evidence on which a properly directed jury could have convicted Tom Hayes and Carlo Palombo”.
Jason Williams, the head of division at the SFO, added that it was not deemed in the public interest to seek retrials of Hayes and Palombo.
A further attempted appeal by Christian Bittar, a former Deutsche Bank trader who pleaded guilty in 2018, is expected to be heard on Friday. His case is the only one being contested by the SFO, which argues his conviction was safe.

IEA members back faster oil stock releases, prioritizing diesel
