Ukraine Builds New Stormbird Drone to Strike Where Larger UAVs Can’t Operate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:10:22 UTC
00:10:22 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Ukraine Builds New Stormbird Drone to Strike Where Larger UAVs Can’t Operate
Ukrainian defense company Skyeton has developed the Stormbird unmanned aerial system (UAS), a new strike platform designed for precision missions and already being used by Ukraine’s Defense Forces, the company told Militarnyi on October 7
Stormbird is based on the architecture of Skyeton’s Raybird (ACS-3) reconnaissance system but features expanded payload integration capabilities, allowing it to perform a broader range of missions. According to the company, the system was codified by Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense in early 2026.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The new platform builds on experience gained from more than 350,000 hours of combat operations with Raybird reconnaissance drones. Stormbird retains the Raybird’s endurance, reliability, and resistance to electronic warfare while adding strike capabilities.
Skyeton has developed several payload options for the system, including the Remora glide munition and the Quadremora FPV-type loitering munition. Stormbird can also carry a communications relay designed to maintain connectivity beyond the coverage of ground-based infrastructure.
“With Stormbird, we have taken a step beyond reconnaissance. This UAS combines Raybird’s endurance and low observability with the precision and versatility required for modern strike missions,” Skyeton CEO Roman Kniazhenko said.
“Our vision is to create a comprehensive ecosystem of small fixed-wing UAS capable of performing reconnaissance, detection, and target identification missions, and now also delivering precision strikes in environments where manned aircraft or even larger UAVs cannot operate,” he added.
According to Militarnyi, Stormbird was designed with the low-observability and survivability requirements of modern unmanned systems in mind. Its compact airframe is intended to reduce its radar signature, while a high degree of autonomy allows the system to conduct precision strikes in rapidly changing combat conditions.
The Stormbird is the latest Ukrainian-developed unmanned system to receive approval for military use. On October 5, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported that it had cleared the domestically produced Varkhan unmanned ground vehicle for operational use by the Armed Forces.
Designed primarily for battlefield logistics, the Varkhan can transport weapons, ammunition, equipment, and other supplies. The system was developed by a Ukrainian defense manufacturer in response to operational requirements identified by the military.

Swedbank: Acceleration in inflation was expected  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:09:24 UTC
00:09:24 KST

TALLINN - The prices of goods and services rose by 0.9 percent in September compared to August, and the consumer basket became 3.5 percent more expensive year-on-year. According to Swedbank, this acceleration in price growth was expected and primarily driven by rising energy costs.
"The price increase seen in Estonia in September was one of the lowest in the eurozone, which gives some breathing room to companies that must compete with businesses from other countries where inflation has not been as rapid in recent years, despite their own rapidly growing costs," said Liis Elmik, a senior economist at Swedbank.
According to Eurostat's preliminary comparable figure, the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), inflation in Estonia was 3 percent in September, while the average increase for goods and services in the eurozone was 3.8 percent. Latvia experienced a similar price hike to Estonia, but Lithuania's was significantly faster at 6.1 percent, primarily due to pension reforms and tax increases.
"Nearly half of the monthly price increase was due to the rising cost of motor fuels, which have gone up by about 40 percent over the year. Interestingly, public transport prices have remained unchanged during the same period. While train and bus tickets have become more expensive, airline tickets have actually become cheaper, according to calculations by Statistics Estonia," Elmik said.
In addition to diesel and gasoline, prices for other fuels also increased in September. Gas saw the largest monthly price hike. Elmik forecasts that the price of gas in flexible-rate plans will rise even further in October.
Although the conflict between the US and Iran continues, oil exports from the Persian Gulf have begun to recover. In September, the export volume of oil and petroleum products reached over 80 percent of its pre-war level. However, transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains unsafe, with new attacks on tankers being reported.
"As a result, market participants are quite pessimistic and expect oil prices to remain around 100 dollars per barrel in the coming months. A drop in gas prices is anticipated in Europe next spring, after the heating season ends. By the end of 2027, current forecasts suggest that European gas prices will still be nearly twice as high as they were before the war in the Middle East," Elmik stated.
In September, the prices of clothing and footwear also rose, in addition to energy costs. Over the year, however, apparel has become somewhat cheaper. Cross-border shopping increases competition and helps to lower prices.
"Parents were pleased by the elimination of kindergarten co-payments in Tallinn. However, since the cost of kindergarten constitutes a small share of the consumer price index, the impact of this decision on the overall index was modest," Elmik noted.
Swedbank forecasts a three-percent inflation rate for this year. Next year's price increase is expected to remain below three percent. The largest contributors to this year's inflation are rising energy and transportation costs.

Bank of Estonia: Rising fuel prices account for half of annual inflation  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:09:08 UTC
00:09:08 KST

TALLINN - According to data from Statistics Estonia, consumer prices rose by 3.5 percent year-on-year in September and by 0.9 percent compared to August. The acceleration in inflation was driven by rising energy prices, said Bank of Estonia economist Sulev Pert, adding that excluding energy, price growth remained moderate and does not indicate a widespread strengthening of price pressures.
"Motor fuels alone accounted for almost half of the annual price increase in September. In addition to crude oil being approximately 70 percent more expensive in euro terms than a year earlier, fuel refining margins, which now account for about one-fifth of the fuel price, have also risen this year. Motor fuel prices also rose sharply in neighboring countries in September. In October, Latvia temporarily lowered its fuel excise duty until the end of the year, after which fuel prices dropped to Estonian levels. Among the Baltic states, motor fuels remained the most expensive in Lithuania," Pert noted in a press release.
The economist pointed out that among housing-related energy costs, natural gas saw the steepest annual price increase, rising by 38 percent. The price increase for heat energy remained at previous levels. During the heating season, more expensive gas could raise district heating prices, but the impact depends on the region, as many district heating networks predominantly use biomass or waste heat. In September, the average stock exchange price of electricity remained lower than last year, supported by favorable weather conditions. For consumers, however, electricity was more expensive, as the final price is also affected by the balancing capacity and security of supply fees added this year, as well as changes in monthly fees.
"Food prices continued to curb overall inflation, being lower in September than a year earlier. However, the rise in producer prices for foodstuffs suggests that the recent price decline may not continue. Dairy products, oils and fats, and fruits were still cheaper than a year ago, while vegetables, in contrast, were more expensive. Varying price changes for foodstuffs are influenced by both seasonality and special offers on individual products. An increase in production costs may reach consumer prices with a delay, and its extent also depends on competition in the retail sector," Pert explained.
Excluding energy prices, price growth remained slow in September, he said. "The annual price increase for services has slowed down significantly compared to last year, from 10 percent to 2.3 percent. Persistently high energy prices would increase companies' production and transport costs and gradually raise the prices of other goods and services as well," the central bank economist added.

====================================================================================================

Badenoch made the best of it – but the Tories still have a mountain to climb before any hope of No 10 | Henry Hill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:08:39 UTC
00:08:39 KST

On paper, the traditional role of the journalist at a British party conference boils down to some simple questions: what was the mood of the assembled activists? Did the leader give a good speech? In practice, the changing nature of conferences and the media makes this superficially simple task more complicated than it may initially appear.
Any journalist covering the leader’s speech, for instance, will have watched it in full. But it will reach the vast majority of its intended audience in fragmentary form, through clips – and speeches are increasingly written with that reality in mind. The conference hall is not really the audience, or the full speech really the product. This adds a layer of complexity to the reviewer’s task.
Likewise, it is less meaningful than once it was to talk about the mood of the conference. Thirty years ago, when our political parties were much more robust social institutions than they are today, millions of Britons were party members through thick and thin, and thousands attended annual conference whether they liked the leadership or not.
It was this democratic culture that gave us the spectacular showdowns at Labour conferences in the 1980s, or Tory activists cheering Norman Tebbit’s excoriation of the European Union in the 1990s. But it is unthinkable now: most people disaffected with a party – especially the Conservatives – are simply not members of it; they certainly don’t take time off work and spend several hundred pounds to attend conference.
Even with that caveat, however, there is no doubt that the mood inside the Conservative party is considerably improved on last year’s. Manchester proved that Kemi Badenoch can make good use of a spotlight, even in otherwise extremely challenging conditions, and her position has improved markedly since then. Her personal ratings are up, her party’s polling has recovered (a little), her only real rival for the leadership has defected to Reform UK, and Reform has its own problems.
The policy side of things is helping, too. I was very critical of Badenoch’s decision to go as slowly as she did on policy, and do think that first year of near-radio silence did the Tories serious damage. But the eventual policy announcements have, so far, been generally well-considered; if they still tend to err too much on the side of caution, it is at least better than the alternative, the wild promises of an opposition which has abandoned all hope of office.
Birmingham has also confirmed that the Conservatives have recognised the need for a strategic pivot. Badenoch has come under fire from some quarters for returning to the party’s “comfort zone” on tax cuts and deregulation, rather than trying to reassemble Boris Johnson’s 2019 coalition and go blow-for-blow with Reform.
But that analysis fundamentally misunderstands the current state of play. As much as the gladiatorial spectacle of the “fight on the right” appeals to journalists, so long as the Tories and Reform are polling where they are, they are not really each other’s primary opponent. Reform’s immediate front lies through Labour; of the 98 seats where it placed second in 2024, 89 are held by a Labour MP.
The Conservatives’ front, in contrast, is much more southern, affluent and Liberal Democrat-facing. Many commentators, both inside the party and out, too quickly assume this means “liberal”, because they assume such voters should be Tory by default. This ignores the fact that, by 2024, the Conservatives did not actually have an attractive economic pitch to those voters. Badenoch’s bet is that a substantial number of these voters – both those who defected to the Lib Dems and a large share who party strategists identify as simply having stopped voting – can be wooed back with a strong economic offer on things such as childcare and inheritance tax.
It remains to be seen whether she gets the polling bounce that is the traditional marker of a successful party conference. But based on what I saw over the past few days, I would say this was broadly a positive event for the Tories.
I worry, however, that the party itself is over-reading it. Yes, its situation has improved – but that is clearing the extremely low bar set by two sets of catastrophic local elections in 2025 and 2026. Yes, Badenoch’s personal ratings have improved – but she remains in truth the second least unpopular leader, rather than a particularly popular one.
Tory loyalists can be perhaps forgiven, meanwhile, for playing up the “Kemi bounce”, which has lifted their party from about 17.5% to about 20% in the current polling average, while ignoring the “Kemi slump” that preceded it (she took the leadership when the party was at 26% on that same average). But you would not guess, reading the room in Birmingham, that the Conservatives are still several points shy of their disastrous vote share at the 2024 election.
Yet perhaps this is again a problem of the chimerical nature of conference. The party strategists I spoke to seemed quite realistic about their task at the next election: avoid extinction and remain the largest rightwing party. But the party leadership could hardly make that their top line: it would simply demotivate their remaining troops and be severely punished by the press.
It is therefore their difficult task to consistently strike an optimistic note without entirely falling for it themselves – and ours to try to work out if, or when, they have.
- Henry Hill is political editor of the Critic

MEPs urge tougher action against China as tensions hit ‘critical point’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:07:12 UTC
00:07:12 KST

The resolution calls China “a decisive enabler” of Russia’s war in Ukraine and says the EU should take action against China’s weaponisation of the rare eath minerals that Europe depends on.
The European Parliament has called for tougher action against China’s economic coercion and support for Russia, warning that relations with Beijing have reached a “critical point”.
MEPs backed the resolution by a landslide on Wednesday, urging the EU to consider deploying its powerful Anti-Coercion Instrument if Beijing weaponises Europe’s dependence on critical raw materials.
The vote came as EU Trade Chief Maroš Šefčovič was flying to Beijing for crunch talks aimed at rebalancing the increasingly strained trade relationship.
October is shaping up to be a crucial month for EU-China relations. EU leaders, whose countries now all run trade deficits with China, are pressing the European Commission to deliver concrete results from negotiations with Beijing.
Tensions also extend well beyond trade. The EU has become increasingly alarmed by Beijing’s close relationship with Moscow and its role in sustaining Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“The relations have now reached a critical point, mostly due to China’s unfair economic practices such as dumping and spying and its position on Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine,” the resolution adopted by EU lawmakers reads.
The text was backed by 454 MEPs, with 86 voting against and 110 abstaining.
Lawmakers described China’s role in the Ukraine war as that of “a decisive enabler”, pointing to “Chinese diplomatic backing and material assistance that sustains the Russian military-industrial complex”.
Pressure to use anti-coercion tool
They also call on EU countries and the Commission to “urgently” take action on “the weaponisation of critical dependencies by China.”
Europe felt the vulnerability of those dependencies in 2025, when China restricted exports of rare earths, which are vital to the EU’s automotive, defence and clean-tech industries, amid its escalating trade war with the United States.
The MEPs said the EU should consider using the Anti-Coercion Instrument (ACI) when China instrumentalises such EU dependencies.
The ACI is an EU mechanism that allows the bloc to adopt radical measures – up to restrictions on licences and intellectual property rights – against a third country that uses economic coercion against the EU.
China’s dominance of the production and processing of strategic raw materials has become a major sticking point in trade negotiations, giving Beijing considerable leverage as Brussels seeks to curb its dependence on Chinese imports.
A Commission proposal pushing companies to diversify their suppliers in strategic sectors is in the making and should be presented by the end of the year.
The resolution comes two days after Germany and France harden their stancetowards Beijing, calling for a new trade tool that could allow the Commission to impose measures leading to “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed”.

Kurum urges action to keep 1.5C goal within reach

AA photo.
Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum has urged countries to act on climate pledges and accelerate emissions cuts to keep the 1.5-degree warming goal within reach.
Kurum, the COP31 president-designate, made the call at a preparatory climate meeting in Fiji on Oct. 7. Türkiye will host the U.N. climate summit in Antalya from Nov. 9 to 20.
“When we come to Antalya, we want to discuss what we have done, not what we will do,” he said.
Kurum said exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius of warming above preindustrial levels must not mean abandoning climate action. Decisions taken now could still limit the extent and duration of any overshoot and reduce future risks, he said.
He called for rapid emissions reductions, wider use of renewable energy and greater energy efficiency, alongside efforts to avoid dependence on high-carbon infrastructure.
Cutting emissions and adapting to climate change were complementary tasks, Kurum said, adding that Türkiye and Australia had developed COP31’s action agenda around implementing existing commitments.
He also urged countries to work together on climate finance, saying earlier decisions on access to funding needed to produce results. Supporting a just transition and helping vulnerable countries withstand climate impacts were essential to those efforts, he said.
Scientific findings must be translated into policies, investment and measurable results, Kurum added, calling on governments to fulfill the commitments they make at climate summits.
At the closing session, he said there would be no surprises or decisions imposed from above in Antalya, stressing that the summit must reflect a common international will. He also called for greater attention to the concerns of Pacific island nations and other countries facing the effects of climate change.
During his visit, Kurum held a three-way meeting with Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and European Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra.

The facility is involved in supplying the Russian armed forces.

EU enlargement: European Commission tables reforms to prepare bloc for new members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:05:00 UTC
00:05:00 KST

EU enlargement: Reforms seek to prepare bloc for new members
October 7, 2026
The European Commission wants to inject new momentum into its enlargement process, which has seen some candidate countries waiting for decades to join.
Albania, Montenegro, Moldova and Ukraine are currently the frontrunners to join the bloc, with EU officials expressing the hope that Montenegro could do so as early as 2028.
"A larger union is a long-term investment in Europe's peace, security and prosperity," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told journalists in Strasbourg on October 6.
One key question is how the EU can take in more countries in the near future without becoming harder to run or running the risk of democratic backsliding in new member states.
The Commission's answer to this question is to simultaneously require candidate countries to meet EU standards and get the bloc itself to reform by removing obstacles in the accession process and protecting its democratic values.
Less unanimity, more qualified majority votes
One of the main stumbling blocks in accession negotiations so far has been the need for unanimous decisions across all 27 members. In the past, individual states have often blocked a candidate's progress because of bilateral issues.
The delays caused by Hungary's blocking of Ukraine's negotiation process are a prominent example.
Now — and not for the first time — the Commission is recommending that member states move away from the principle of unanimity for decisions like the opening of negotiation clusters, replacing it with qualified majority voting.
The unanimity dilemma
"Every cluster that you open is subject to three individual decisions, and every single decision is subject to unanimity. It's mind-blowing, and I think this clearly needs to go," a Commission official, who wished to remain anonymous, told journalists on Tuesday.
The catch is that a shift to qualified majority voting would itself require a unanimous decision.
"I have some reservations as to whether there will be unanimous agreement from the member states to move to qualified majority voting," Tinatin Akhvlediani, head of the enlargement program at the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS) told DW, pointing to previous attempts to change voting rules that were shot down by member states.
Gradual access to membership benefits
To incentivize reform in candidate countries, the Commission is proposing gradual integration, which means that these countries could be granted some of the benefits of membership before joining — as long as they meet the EU's criteria.
"Gradual integration is not a substitute for full membership. It is the accelerator for enlargement," Kos said on Tuesday, underlining that the process would stay merit-based.
This could have a motivational effect on candidate countries, Nina Vujanovic, a research fellow at Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, told DW: "Reforms are important, but it is also important to reward that process a little bit earlier, ahead of accession," she said.
Earlier access to EU benefits is not entirely new: Montenegro, for example, already participates in the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) even though it is not yet a member.
Addressing geopolitical realities
The Commission now wants to give candidate countries such early access more systematically and link it to strategic alignment.
"This is not something that will be available [to candidate countries] unless they really orient themselves on the EU," a Commission official told journalists.
Making strategic alignment a condition is new and reflects the EU's efforts to adjust to the geopolitical tensions members and candidates are facing.
Candidates' choice: Russia or the EU?
"The EU is trying to keep candidate countries out of the hands of Russia," Heather Grabbe, a senior fellow at Bruegel, told DW. "Strategic alignment is aimed very squarely at politicians like Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, who has clearly promoted Russian interests," she said.
The new procedures would demand alignment not only with the EU's foreign and security policy, but also with its standards on economic security. "Trading gas with Russia is simply not something that builds trust with the European Union," said Nina Vujanovic.
The lessons the EU learned from Hungary, Poland
To prevent breaches of democratic rules by new member states, the Commission proposes a 15-year period within which it would be easier to sanction new members by cutting financial support or restricting voting rights.
In an interview with The Guardian and other European media, Commissioner Kos made it clear that the EU had learned its lesson from the democratic backsliding it saw in the past in countries like Poland or Hungary: "No more Viktor Orban. We have to have quicker mechanisms than only Article 7."
Double standard or necessary protection?
Critics point out that this safeguard would create unequal conditions within the union.
"It is inherently unfair," says Heather Grabbe. "In the 2040s, why should Montenegro face different conditions than, say, Slovenia?"
Many current candidate countries have a shaky record when it comes to democratic norms, as Tinatin Akhvlediani points out: "They are actually fragile democracies. So, this approach vis-a-vis these countries can be very much justified."
Experts say that while it might be desirable to apply similarly strict rules to all members, it is not realistically feasible as it would have to be approved unanimously and, as Grabbe says, "it's very hard to get turkeys to vote for Christmas."
Although the Commission's push for new rules in relation to enlargement is likely to move the debate forward, it is ultimately up to member states to decide how much of it becomes reality.
The European Council, which is made up of the heads of state or government of the 27 EU member states, the European Council president and the president of the European Commission, is expected to discuss the proposals at its upcoming meeting on October 15–16.
The outcome of those talks will determine how quickly the Commission's new enlargement agenda can move forward.
Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

Russia’s Donbas Advance Goes Into Reverse as Ukraine Retakes Ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:05:00 UTC
00:05:00 KST

Ukraine is retaking territory in Donbas and disrupting Russia’s plans to encircle the region’s remaining Ukrainian-held cities, challenging the Kremlin’s narrative that their capture is inevitable, The New York Times (NYT) reported.
According to the report, Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly claimed that Ukraine’s defenses in the Donbas will collapse and that Russian forces will seize the region faster than Kyiv expects.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Recent battlefield developments, however, point in the opposite direction.
A Ukrainian counteroffensive in northern Donetsk, known as Operation Vivaldi, has pushed Russian troops back, reclaimed settlements, and prevented Moscow’s forces from advancing behind the defensive belt centered on Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
The operation has been underway for several months, but Ukraine kept many of its details secret until September.
Russia’s encirclement plan disrupted
Russia sought to approach Sloviansk and Kramatorsk from the north through the Lyman sector while advancing from the south, creating a wide encirclement of what Ukrainian forces call the Donbas “fortress belt.”
Operation Vivaldi disrupted the northern part of that plan.
Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps said its troops recaptured several settlements, severed Russian logistical routes, and forced Moscow to redeploy units to stabilize the front.
President Volodymyr Zelensky initially said that Ukrainian forces had reclaimed 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) during the operation. In a subsequent interview, he offered a more conservative estimate of between 125 and 140 square kilometers (48-54 square miles).
Ukraine Working on 5 Ceasefire Tracks With Partners, Foreign Ministry Says
“Vivaldi is a very successful operation. It is not finished yet,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine is already preparing a fourth phase of the counteroffensive. The first three phases also inflicted more than 5,000 Russian casualties and resulted in the capture of approximately 250 Russian troops, according to Ukrainian officials.
The battlefield claims cannot all be independently verified because extensive drone surveillance has created wide contested areas where neither side maintains complete control.
Russia’s territorial gains turn negative
Western organizations tracking the front line have produced different figures, but their assessments point to the same general trend: Russia’s advance slowed sharply in 2026 and may have gone into reverse during September.
The Finnish open-source intelligence organization Black Bird Group estimated that the area under Russian control shrank by approximately 190 square kilometers (73 square miles) in September.
“This marks the greatest monthly net territorial loss for Russia in our dataset since June 2023,” the group said.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) produced a more conservative estimate. It assessed that Russian forces captured approximately 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) but lost about 256 square kilometers (99 square miles) in September, leaving Moscow with a net loss of roughly 81 square kilometers (31 square miles).
ISW cautioned that some territory recorded as liberated in September may have been retaken earlier because Ukraine concealed the progress of Operation Vivaldi.
From March through September, Russia lost control of nearly 294 square kilometers (113 square miles) while establishing a presence in approximately 174 square kilometers (67 square miles), according to ISW’s calculation.
Russian forces also suffered more than 46,000 casualties during September while probably making no net territorial gains, the organization said.
Pressure continues in southern Donbas
Ukraine’s success in the north does not mean that the battle for Donbas has ended.
Russian forces continue conducting intense attacks in southern Donetsk and remain capable of putting pressure on Ukrainian defensive lines. Moscow has also attempted to infiltrate Ukrainian positions using small infantry groups rather than relying exclusively on large mechanized assaults.
Ukraine has reorganized its defenses in the area and, according to the NYT, has so far prevented Russian forces from achieving the breakthroughs needed to encircle Donbas cities still controlled by Kyiv.
Russian advances across Ukraine have generally slowed since March compared with the already limited pace recorded during 2025.
Independent estimates differ over the exact amount of territory captured by each side, but analysts broadly agree that Russia has gained only slightly more land than it has lost during 2026 – despite sustaining heavy casualties and repeatedly claiming major battlefield success.
Putin claimed on Oct. 1 that Russian forces had captured 1,301 square kilometers (502 square miles) during September alone. Independent battlefield maps do not support that figure.
Russian commanders face criticism
Ukraine’s gains have also triggered criticism from Russian pro-war military bloggers who accuse commanders of sending misleading reports about supposed advances to their superiors.
ISW said some Russian commentators blamed a culture of “beautiful reports” for leaving senior commanders with an inaccurate picture of the battlefield and helping Ukraine achieve surprise around Lyman.
One prominent Russian military blogger acknowledged that Ukrainian advances had delayed Russia’s planned offensive toward Sloviansk and left the northern flank of a major Russian grouping vulnerable to further counterattacks.
There is no independently verified evidence of “panic” throughout the Kremlin. However, criticism from pro-war Russian commentators and Moscow’s efforts to regain lost positions indicate concern over a counteroffensive that has undermined Putin’s claim that the fall of Donbas is only a matter of time.
Ukraine’s latest official account of Operation Vivaldi says its forces recovered up to 140 square kilometers (54 square miles) around Lyman, while earlier phases liberated several settlements and disrupted Russia’s attempt to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

Lebanon's Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:04:25 UTC
00:04:25 KST

Lebanon's Hezbollah gets $200 million from Iran to help displaced, sources say
BEIRUT, Oct 7 - Hezbollah has received $200 million from Iran to help Lebanese displaced by this year’s war with Israel, two people with direct knowledge of the transfer said, in what would be the first significant aid from the group to supporters who bore the brunt of the conflict.
The US disputed the claim. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement that the money "is not there," accusing Hezbollah of "trying to save face with fake stories about cash influxes from Iran."
A Treasury spokesperson said Iran was “running out of money and ways to move money” and that Tehran “does not have money to fund its campaign of terror.”
Hezbollah received the cash last month despite a tightening US economic chokehold on Iran and increasing difficulties in getting funds to Tehran's Lebanese ally, said the people.
Intermediaries who moved the money charged a 20% fee, reflecting the risks of dealing with the group, they said. One said this was four times the normal fee.
Asked for comment, a Hezbollah official said an amount had been secured and a plan for distributing it would be announced in the coming days, without elaborating on the source of the funds.
The Iranian foreign ministry, Iran's permanent mission in Geneva, and the Lebanese government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Israel’s bombardment and invasion of Lebanon uprooted hundreds of thousands of Hezbollah’s Shi’ite Muslim constituents after the group entered the regional war in support of Iran on March 2.
But those displaced have so far received little to no assistance from Hezbollah, an armed group founded by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards in 1982 which has suffered heavy Israeli blows in two wars since 2024 and is designated a terrorist group by Washington.
The State Department's Pigott said Hezbollah had caused misery for Lebanese and had itself been decimated, while its backer Tehran was suffering under a US blockade of oil exports. "The United States will continue to strangle Hezballah's finances through sanctions while supporting the ability of Lebanon's legitimate government to rebuild the South," Pigott said.
AIDING 50,000 FAMILIES
Hezbollah would use the funds to pay an initial $3,000 per family, and priority would go to those whose villages have been destroyed or are inaccessible due to Israeli occupation, the sources said. These number around 50,000 families, one of the sources said.
Iran has maintained financial support to Hezbollah through years of crippling US sanctions: it transferred $1 billion to the group in the first 10 months of 2025, according to the US Treasury Department.
Tehran has never acknowledged financing Hezbollah. Iran's policy of funding regional proxies has stirred domestic protester anger against the clerical rulers in the past and could prove particularly sensitive at a time of worsening hardship in Iran.
Iran had promised Hezbollah more funding after Tehran signed an interim deal with Washington in June that allowed Iran to sell its oil, Reuters reported at the time. That agreement collapsed in July.
Washington has since intensified economic pressure on Iran, tightening sanctions and imposing a naval blockade to block Iranian oil exports.
Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a speech last month that the group would soon contribute to a project aimed at housing thousands of people displaced by the war, using “available resources and donations”, without elaborating.
Hezbollah's ability to fund local services and provide post-conflict aid has helped shore up its support in the past. Following a war with Israel in 2006, the group immediately handed out large cash payments to those impacted and moved swiftly to help rebuild Beirut's southern suburbs, a stronghold.
But this time there has been little sign of reconstruction. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said last month that the total reconstruction costs from the two wars since 2024 could exceed $27 billion.
A COSTLY WAR
The two sources provided no details on how the money got to Lebanon.
One of them said it was increasingly difficult for Hezbollah to move funds via financial companies that once processed such transfers. Such firms based in Iraq and Dubai were no longer an option, and they were also now under pressure in Turkey, this source said.
Hezbollah’s foes believed money was currently the group’s “oxygen”, the source added. Despite the difficulties securing funding, the group had not stopped paying its fighters and the family members of those killed in combat, this source said.
In Lebanon, the war has inflicted a heavy price on the Shi’ite Muslim community from which Hezbollah draws support. Israel has razed villages across a swathe of territory it has seized in the south, saying it aims to shield northern Israel from Hezbollah attack.
Israeli attacks in Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March 2, according to Lebanon’s health ministry. Its toll does not say how many combatants may be among the dead. Hezbollah has not disclosed figures on its war dead. Reuters reported on May 4 that several thousand Hezbollah fighters had been killed in the war. REUTERS

Spanish unions call general strike for November 11, weeks before snap election
MADRID, Oct 7 - Trade unions in Spain on Wednesday announced a nationwide general strike over housing issues for November 11, a protest that will take place a few weeks before a snap election in which rising rents and evictions have become campaign topics.
The country's two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, said they had agreed on the date, although it still needs to be formally ratified by other unions in a meeting later on Wednesday. It will be the first general strike jointly backed by Spain's two largest unions in 14 years.
The strike will be the latest in a series of demonstrations provoked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, with activists camping on one of the capital's main squares calling for solutions to a mounting housing crisis.
Those protests, along with parliament's rejection last week of decrees aimed at curbing evictions and limiting rent pressures, prompted Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to call an early election for November 29.
Sanchez is seeking to shift the political narrative from his government's handling of a migrant crisis in Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta and a series of corruption cases involving his Socialist Party and his family to the housing crisis, an area in which he believes he can harness growing resentment about rising rents.
Spain has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to the Bank of Spain.
With fewer people able to afford a home, renting has increased sharply, putting pressure on that market. The average rental price of €1,176 ($1,315) is equivalent to about 98.7% of a young person's average monthly salary in Spain, according to the Youth Council of Spain.
"We cannot ignore the fact that housing is where most of our wages go. What is the point of raising the minimum wage if housing costs are rising three, four or five times faster?" said Tenants' Union spokesperson Valeria Racu. REUTERS

Venezuela rejoins national parliaments organization with full rights, parliamentary chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:03:19 UTC
00:03:19 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Venezuelan National Assembly President Jorge Rodriguez said Wednesday that Caracas has rejoined the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU).
“Venezuela has re-entered the Inter-Parliamentary Union with full rights,” Rodriguez wrote on US social media platform X, adding that a Venezuelan parliamentary delegation is representing the country at the IPU’s 153rd Assembly in Tanzania.
The assembly is being held Oct. 5 to 9 in Arusha, bringing together parliamentarians from around the world for discussions on parliamentary diplomacy and international cooperation.
A video by Rodriguez shows IPU President Tulia Ackson reading a document concerning Venezuela’s reinstatement with full rights.
Rodriguez said the process leading to Venezuela’s reinstatement began Sept. 17 during a conversation with IPU Secretary General Anda Filip, according to media reports.
The delegation attending the assembly includes National Assembly Second Vice President Grecia Colmenares and lawmakers Jose Gregorio Correa and Saul Ortega.
Venezuela’s reinstatement follows years of disputes about the country’s parliamentary representation amid its prolonged political crisis.
The IPU previously examined Venezuela’s representation in the organization. In 2021, a delegation led by Rodriguez held meetings with IPU officials in Geneva as part of efforts to restore dialogue with the organization.
Rodriguez has attributed Venezuela’s exclusion from the organization to political polarization and disputes about the country’s parliamentary representation.
Venezuela’s return to the IPU comes as Caracas seeks to strengthen its participation in international organizations and expand parliamentary diplomacy.
The 153rd IPU Assembly agenda includes discussions on governance, inclusion, peace, sustainable development and other issues related to international parliamentary cooperation.
Founded in 1889, the IPU describes itself as the global organization of national parliaments. It promotes parliamentary dialogue, cooperation and diplomacy and has 183 member parliaments.

Germany extradited from Japan a Russian hacker accused of working for the largest ransomware group

Germany extradited from Japan a Russian hacker accused of working for the largest ransomware group
Kyiv • UNN
The 28-year-old Russian is suspected of working for the Qilin group. He was detained in Japan under an international warrant following an investigation in Germany.
German authorities extradited a 28-year-old Russian man from Japan who is suspected of being involved with the Qilin hacking group. The man was detained in Osaka in May, after which he was handed over to Germany for investigation. Bild reports, according to UNN.
Details
The German authorities believe that 28-year-old Russian Vladimir K. is a member of the Qilin hacking group. He was detained in Osaka in May. According to German investigators, he operated under the pseudonym Snake as part of a group of eight people who form Qilin’s core. The group engages in cyberattacks and extortion and has already harmed thousands of companies and government institutions around the world.
The “Albus” special commission of the North Rhine–Westphalia State Criminal Police Office had been secretly investigating the hackers’ activities since mid-2024. German investigators managed to infiltrate the group’s infrastructure and the suspect’s computer, establish his identity, and track his trip to Japan. When the Russian man went on vacation to Tokyo, he was detained under an international warrant.
North Rhine–Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul called the detention “the greatest success by German investigators in the fight against cybercrime.” According to him, this is the first case in which a Russian hacker has been detained outside Russia. The international search for other alleged members of Qilin’s core is ongoing.
The scale of Qilin’s activities is enormous. According to German authorities, 3,954 victims of the group are known worldwide, while the total ransom demands reached $2.88 billion. The victims paid the hackers at least $140 million.

British billionaire warned Epstein was a ‘sexual deviant’ decades before FBI closed in on the abuser
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:53 UTC
00:00:53 KST

For Jeffrey Epstein, the billionaire Goldsmith family was a gateway to elite society and he wanted to be in their circle.
The disgraced financier, who died in prison in 2019 facing sex-trafficking charges, longed for a billionaire’s lifestyle and cultivated the family’s friends, bankers, business associates and advisers.
But Sir James Goldsmith, who was knighted by the Queen in 1976 and became a prominent British politician, remained wary of the American financier and even “despised” him, his daughter Jemima recently told the Guardian.
Two decades before Epstein came under federal investigation, Goldsmith – who died in 1997 – told a confidant that Epstein was a “sexual deviant” who was recruiting children for illicit activities.
Goldsmith “told me not to have anything to do with him, that he was a pervert, and he didn’t want him near any of us. He had four daughters to protect,” recalled the famous French architect Robert Couturier, who designed opulent homes for Goldsmith in New York and Mexico.
Goldsmith’s alleged warning came around 1987, years before complaints about Epstein’s solicitation of young girls for sex began filtering into federal law enforcement. Epstein’s network of pretty “girls” evolved into what authorities describe as a global sex-trafficking ring that catered to the ultra-rich and powerful.
It would become a scandal that touched royals, politicians, businessmen, academics, foreign diplomats and celebrities around the world, and left more than 1,000 victims in its wake.
“That is the pity of it all. It was all preventable,” Couturier told the Guardian. Epstein, born on Coney Island, had been on the radar of New York’s elite since he first surfaced at society events, often on the arm of heiresses, Couturier said.
“He was a charmer and a talker. Lots of rich people are deeply gullible, as protected as they are from reality. No one did anything about it.”
In the mid-1980s, Sir James Goldsmith – known as “Jimmy” – announced he was making a shift in his US business operations. Goldsmith had hired a new chief executive who would open an office for him in Hilton Head, South Carolina, an emerging luxury resort.
Goldsmith’s Hilton Head office is rarely mentioned in writings about his reign as the “lucky gambler”, as Time Magazine called him, an adviser to US presidents who became one of the world’s richest men by betting on undervalued companies. His conglomerate, with command centers in Paris and London, had its US headquarters in New York, close to his elegant Manhattan townhouse where Goldsmith entertained and where the young Epstein trolled for wealthy clients.
Hilton Head at the time was undergoing a chaotic development boom that brought in a rush of speculators, shady operators and vacationers lured by star-studded golf tournaments and tennis matches. Its population, 11,000 in 1980, doubled in a decade. Its tiny airport was suddenly a busy landing strip for private jets, including a $10m Gulfstream owned by Goldsmith’s company that was parked there for quick hops.
Epstein developed a lifelong fascination with Goldsmith, his family and fortune, an investigation by the Guardian found.
Epstein’s connection to Goldsmith, and the presence of the billionaire’s company and his associates on a South Carolina sea island – which was attracting an infusion of investors – is potentially relevant because of an alleged sexual assault that is said to have occurred there in the 1980s. A woman known only as Jane Doe 4 claimed in four FBI interviews after Epstein’s 2019 arrest that he had assaulted her during his visits to the island in the 1980s, when she was still a teenager. She has also claimed the man she only knew as “Jeff” trafficked her to other men, including Donald Trump.
The White House has vehemently denied the allegation about the US president, calling it “completely baseless” and “backed by zero credible evidence”.
The Guardian has been examining records, digging into archives and conducting interviews to explore intersections of Goldsmith and Epstein and try to understand if Epstein, with decades of secretive movements and a web of global financial ties, might have had reason to be on Hilton Head in the 1980s when those alleged assaults by Epstein occurred. This remains a mystery, but Epstein’s relationship with Goldsmith provides some additional clues.
Those who dismiss the claim of Jane Doe 4 – including Epstein’s brother Mark – have cited the lack of a public record of his presence on the island as proof that her story is untrue. Mark Epstein told the Guardian he has “no knowledge of him being in Hilton Head”.
Understanding how Epstein won and retained access to power and privilege throughout his life is important as criminal investigations of his sexual abuse and financial crimes continue around the globe. Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two overseers – Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn – of Epstein’s $577m estate, according to the Wall Street Journal. Both have denied they knew of Epstein’s criminal behavior. The Department of Justice has said that Epstein “harmed” over 1,000 people, including minors who were sexually abused.
The justice department has released about 3.5m documents under the Epstein Disclosure Act, including reams of emails, letters and bank transactions. But the trove includes almost no records from the 1980s, leaving a large gap in the public’s understanding. Epstein’s alleged victims continue to accuse the justice department of a cover-up for holding back documents that might implicate Trump and other powerful men in Epstein’s exclusive circle. Trump has said he ended their friendship in 2004 after a real estate dispute and kicked Epstein out of his Mar-A-Lago club in 2007 for poaching employees.
It is unclear whether Goldsmith’s concerns about Epstein stemmed from specific encounters, and there is no indication that Goldsmith ever reported his concerns to local or federal law enforcement.
It took decades for the FBI to catch up with Epstein’s crimes. Federal investigators in Florida charged him in 2008 with soliciting sex from minors after a two-year investigation in which they interviewed young women, including some minors, who he paid for sexual encounters in his Palm Beach mansion. He served 13 months in jail under a lenient deal cut with federal prosecutors.
Until now, the earliest warning about Epstein’s criminal behavior is believed to have come in 1996, when one alleged victim – an artist named Maria Farmer – claims she alerted authorities that she was sexually assaulted by Epstein, according to a lawsuit she has brought against the FBI. Farmer has also claimed that Epstein stole nude images she had of her two minor siblings, which she kept for her personal use in her artwork. The FBI has said in response to the ongoing litigation, which now includes 34 alleged victims, that agents do not have a duty to investigate “every single tip that comes across their desk”.
A fascination with ‘Sir James’
Since Epstein’s death, Goldsmith has been portrayed as an important influence in his early career.
The New York Times last year described Sir James as a connection Epstein shrewdly calculated was “worth nurturing for the long haul”. It recounted a party scene at Goldsmith’s Upper East Side mansion where Epstein, trained in classical piano, serenaded guests with a piano solo from the grand entry hall.
Goldsmith’s warnings about Epstein came just as Epstein signed one of his biggest clients, the Ohio retail magnate Les Wexner, the founder of Victoria’s Secret, who was then ranked by Forbes as the 10th richest person in the US. Wexner says he severed the relationship with Epstein in 2007 after discovering he had stolen funds from Wexner.
Some questions about Epstein and Goldsmith may never be answered given the secrecy surrounding these events and the refusal of key sources to answer questions.
Meanwhile, the debate over the government’s release of the Epstein files rages on. Attorney general Todd Blanche has declined to release about 2.5m Epstein documents he deemed duplicative. An independent journalist, Katie Phang, is suing Blanche to try to force their release, and Blanche recently quietly turned over some of the documents related to Jane Doe 4 to a federal judge, who is reviewing the documents in his chambers.
Prominent figures caught up in the Epstein controversy include former US president Bill Clinton, former Prince Andrew, former Harvard president Larry Summers and billionaire investor Leon Black. Black was recently held in contempt of Congress for his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee in connection to its Epstein investigation.
Epstein’s emails about the Goldsmiths sometimes suggested bruised feelings and revealed he was watching the family from afar. He was not among the dozens of invited guests in 1997 to Jemima Goldsmith’s grand wedding party to the cricketer-turned-politician Imran Khan, who served as Pakistani prime minister, according to the guest list.
Just before he finished his lenient 2008 sentence for sex crimes in Palm Beach, Epstein scolded a young Romanian admirer for turning down her exclusive invite to a swanky dinner at Jemima’s Oxfordshire estate.
“That was a BIG mistake,” he wrote in an angry 2010 email.
Epstein criticized daughter Jemima’s choice of husband, calling Khan – who is now divorced from Goldsmith and in jail on corruption charges – a “whacko”.
In a 2018 text, Epstein wrote of Imran Khan: “makes donald look like einstein. incapable of truth. , devout islamisist . many nuclear weapons. ( not erdogan or khomeni). he was married to two friends of mine. one daughter of jimmy goldsmith.”
After the family distanced itself from him, Epstein gathered gossip about James’s daughter Isabel’s haughty behavior and joked when a hurricane seemed destined to damage Las Alamandas, her posh Mexican resort.
“hurricane will hit isabel goldsmith resort and bye bye,” he wrote to a friend in 2015.
Epstein elevated his access to the British elite when, in 1990, he started dating Ghislaine Maxwell, the daughter of a British media baron, who hobnobbed with British royals and enhanced Epstein’s standing among upper-crust families like the Goldsmiths. Maxwell became Epstein’s closest partner in recruiting young women, according to her federal indictment. She is serving a 20-year sentence.
Three Goldsmith heirs told the Guardian in emails they never met Epstein and doubted their father had any business dealings with him. Isabel Goldsmith did not respond to messages.
“I’m not sure I had ever heard of Jeffrey Epstein before he hit the news for the first time. So I’m presuming my father did not know him,” said Ben Goldsmith, an environmentalist and investor who was 16 when his father died.
Zac Goldsmith, a conservative member of the House of Lords, said he never met Epstein and was not aware of his fascination with the family.
Jemima Goldsmith Khan, who owns a London-based film production company, said she never met Epstein. “I heard that my father despised him – he was certainly not a friend of his,” she said.
Sir James was a king of US corporate takeovers in a frenetic era of Wall Street deal-making, earning hundreds of millions by seizing control of vulnerable companies and cutting thousands of American jobs. Goldsmith sold his New York investments in 1987 and made a hasty exit back to London after correctly predicting the Black Monday stock market crash.
Epstein was a takeover amateur who concocted his own deals while working as a consultant to a shady Manhattan debt collection company, Towers Financial, whose chief executive, Steven Hoffenberg, was later convicted of running a $450m Ponzi scheme. Before his death, Hoffenberg accused Epstein of masterminding the scheme. Epstein was never charged.
Hoffenberg’s most ambitious effort was an attempted takeover of troubled Pan Am Airlines, the prestigious international carrier Epstein had fantasized as a boy about one day owning, according to an email from one of his friends.
Working from its Hilton Head office, Goldsmith’s takeover team had already analyzed Pan Am’s books and backed off from making an offer. Developer Donald Trump also flirted with a takeover bid but never made it, media reports show.
Couturier met Epstein through Isabel Goldsmith, the titan’s oldest daughter. Jet-setting Isabel became friendly – but not romantically involved – with Epstein, he said, and Isabel and Epstein both socialized in New York City’s nightlife scene. Epstein kept Isabel’s phone contacts at several addresses in his “little black book” later seized by the FBI as evidence.
Couturier had grown close to James Goldsmith and his long-term girlfriend, who hired him in 1981 to renovate a mansion on East 80th Street. Goldsmith cut famous takeover deals around the dining room table, and his catered parties attracted the cream of Manhattan society.
Isabel told Couturier that Epstein wanted to discuss hiring him for another renovation at a huge Upper East Side brownstone purchased by Wexner, he said. Epstein later moved into the restored mansion at 9 East 71st Street, about a half mile from Goldsmith’s, and decorated its dark wooded interior with his private art collection and gaudy fabrics. It became a center of his sexual misconduct, an address where the FBI in 2019 carried out boxes of photographs of alleged victims, massage tables and sex toys.
Wexner also owned a dilapidated historic townhome next door at 11 East 71st Street that needed total renovation. The house was eventually bought through a trust by Trump’s commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, who has said he hardly knew Epstein, his nextdoor neighbor. Under questioning by House investigators, Lutnick acknowledged visiting Epstein for lunch at the predator’s Caribbean island, Little Saint James.
Couturier was approached and interviewed by the FBI in 2010, after Epstein’s first arrest. A record of the interview, which is included in the Epstein files, indicates that Epstein had approached Couturier for a high-paying project on Little Saint James Island, where he was asked to provide “decor and furniture appropriate for teenage girls, with pink furnishings and bunk beds”.
Couturier told the Guardian he remembered Sir Jimmy’s earlier warning. He withdrew from the contract, leading to a legal dispute.
Goldsmith was hardly a prude, Couturier said, but he had no tolerance for inappropriate behavior with children. Goldsmith’s own domestic life was what his daughter Alix once described as “unconventional”, with three wives, numerous girlfriends and eight children. Two children were born in New York to his longtime girlfriend, a French journalist who moved with him to the city.
Another link between Epstein and Goldsmith was Bear Stearns, where Epstein was a junior broker until he was targeted in an internal investigation of his trading practices. He quit in 1981 with an indignant resignation letter that was included in the Epstein files.
Goldsmith remained a major Bear Stearns client, and Epstein, who somehow remained on good terms with the brokerage top brass, invested his own and his clients’ money into the firm, which collapsed in 2008.
Epstein always kept an air of mystery around his business deals. In the 1980s, he described himself to friends as a “bounty hunter” who traveled the world to recover stolen money for rich clients.
He and Goldsmith knew many of the same influential people. The Saudi billionaire Adnan Khashoggi, an international arms dealer, hired Epstein in the 1980s for unspecified work, according to published reports. Khashoggi and Goldsmith were both trusted advisers to President Richard Nixon, who met with them after his 1974 resignation to discuss overseas income opportunities, according to a Nixon biographer.
Epstein became friendly with a wealthy international investor, Jean “Johnny” Pigozzi, who was in Goldsmith’s circle of advisers and is one of the trustees of Goldsmith’s estate, according to published reports. At one point, Epstein’s girlfriend Maxwell emailed Pigozzi to get price estimates for his French estate and nature preserve in Panama, saying she had an interested potential buyer, the emails show.
Pigozzi, an art collector and heir to an auto fortune, is best known in popular culture as the inventor of the “selfie” because of his candid photographs of the rich and famous, including Goldsmith. He did not respond to messages.
Goldsmith’s massive holding company, GOSL, had operations around the world and a corporate office in Manhattan run by his trusted team.
But in 1985, GOSL filed papers with the state of South Carolina seeking authorization to do business in the state, the Guardian found. It opened an office in Hilton Head, the home of Al Dunlap, a notorious corporate raider Goldsmith was hiring to run his US operations.
Dunlap had been living part-time on Hilton Head since the early 1980s when he was running a company that made paper cups. He was among the many corporate bigwigs who had discovered Hilton Head as a sanctuary for executives and government officials who needed privacy. Most exclusive neighborhoods were gated and developed on former rice plantations.
Dunlap – who died in 2019 – had the Wall Street clout to ask investors to come to him. A newspaper account describes one session in 1985 at a new Marriott waterfront resort in Hilton Head where Dunlap pitched a Lily-Tulip stock offering backed by Wall Street firms to 70 out-of-town investors before leaving on a global capital-raising tour.
Some locals say the atmosphere on the island was so frenetic, with investors and deal makers arriving for meetings, that anyone could slip in and out without notice.
Goldsmith’s office in Hilton Head was tasked with selling millions of acres of forest land the company had acquired in takeovers of US paper companies. Its vast new holdings stretched from the Pacific north-west to the Adirondacks, making Goldsmith’s company one of the largest owners of undeveloped US land.
The Guardian tracked down former GOSL executive Phil Lader, who was in charge of land sales, to ask if he recalled seeing Epstein in Hilton Head during the time GOSL had an office there. The short answer was “no”.
Lader was a Hilton Head resident and former chief executive at Sea Pines. In 1981, he founded the prestigious Renaissance Weekends, which drew luminaries to the island for private invitation-only retreats. He was especially close to Bill Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas when he and his wife, Hillary, began coming to Lader’s exclusive gatherings. Other featured guests included Wall Street executives, university and government officials and leaders in the arts and sciences.
Goldsmith hired Lader as a GOSL vice-president in 1986, just after he lost a Democratic party bid for the South Carolina governorship. Lader was appointed Clinton’s deputy White House chief of staff in 1993 and moved to London four years later when he was appointed ambassador to the court of Saint James’s.
Lader said he never met Epstein and “never heard the name Jeffrey Epstein in my years on Hilton Head”. Epstein reportedly made 17 visits to the Clinton White House and later flew Clinton on his private jet.
A partially redacted 2011 exchange in Epstein’s emails shows he was aware of Renaissance Weekends, which are promoted on social media as gathering places for “thought-leaders”. An unnamed friend asked if Epstein had heard of the gatherings.
“Of course,” Epstein wrote. Asked if it was “something i should do?”, Epstein wrote “yes”.
Renaissance Weekends were held in Hilton Head for 20 years, then moved to Charleston. Similar programs are also held in other cities.
The woman who would come to be known as Jane Doe 4 first called an FBI victim hotline to report her alleged abuse on 10 July 2019. It was four days after Epstein’s arrest at a New Jersey airport. The agent manning the phones recommended that she be interviewed in person, near her home in Vancouver, Washington. One of her close friends made a separate call to anonymously report Jane Doe 4’s abuse.
Jane Doe 4’s federal class-action lawsuit, filed later in New York against the Epstein estate, alleges she met Epstein around 1984, when she was a teenager, and had sex with him for several years when he visited the island. She said he rented properties, including a villa at Sea Pines, from her mother’s realty firm.
In four FBI interviews in 2019 she described her abuser’s specific sexual quirks – including his use of butt plugs. Several were seized when the FBI gathered evidence in Epstein’s home in 2019.
Some details squared with accounts given by other young victims who came forward during the previous Florida investigation. She described how he allegedly asked her to recruit friends and took nude photographs of her, also part of a pattern, and repeatedly plied her with drugs and alcohol. The FBI seized thousands of photographs and videos depicting victims when it searched his various properties.
The Marriott hotel on Hilton Head figures heavily in her allegations. She told the FBI about a pool party there with local teenage girls and older males. She claimed the older man she knew as “Jeff” made a brief appearance at the pool before taking her back to his rented villa. She also mentioned a neighbor she had talked with during the period of alleged abuse.
Her local attorney told the Guardian he sat in on the FBI interview and interrupted when she began describing telling other girls about “Jeff”. The lawyer said he feared the FBI might accuse her of aiding her abuser in soliciting other minors.
FBI notes in the case, which were first reported by the Post and Courier in Charleston, South Carolina, repeat the woman’s allegation that at one point, Epstein transported her to New York or New Jersey where she claims he introduced her to Trump, who forced her into a sex act. She estimated she was about 13-15 years old, which would place the dates between 1983 and 1985, but she acknowledged a fuzzy memory. Trump said in a 2002 interview with New York magazine that he had known Epstein for 15 years, which would date their relationship to 1987. The White House has denied Jane Doe 4’s allegations.
Jane Doe 4 also offered names of some of her high school friends who might have seen her with Epstein.
But there is no evidence the FBI ever followed up on the leads Jane Doe 4 gave investigators. Its interest in her case appears to have died abruptly when she asked agents what the point was of her continued cooperation and told them she intended to join a class-action lawsuit, filed by the Bloom Law Firm in December 2019.
A relative of Jane Doe 4 told the Guardian that she had been scarred by “layers of trauma” as a young girl from family tragedies and upheavals. She had spent time in foster care and had just finished elementary school when the family made its way south.
Jane Doe 4 declined to answer questions from the Guardian relayed through the relative, who considers her account “plausible” because she was often unsupervised in her early teens. Three friends contacted by the Guardian did not respond to messages.
Jane Doe 4’s attorney at the Bloom Law Firm told the Post and Courier she ultimately reached a settlement with Epstein’s estate but declined to give an amount.
Court records show a claim she filed with the Epstein victims’ compensation fund, a formal review panel funded by the estate, was denied. The dates of her alleged abuse are much earlier than most other victims who have come forward with claims.
In response to lawmakers’ questions about whether Jane Doe 4 had received a settlement from the estate, an attorney for Epstein’s accountant, Richard Kahn, said he could not recall details of all 60 women who settled with the estate outside of the compensation fund.
The record is far from definitive about whether Epstein ever visited Hilton Head during this time. He did not own a private plane in the 1980s, so no travel logs are available. Epstein did have other real estate development interests at that time, including a long friendship with a developer who was building an oceanfront golf course on nearby Kiawah Island.
Later records in the Epstein files show his plane landing at the nearby Savannah airport several times from 2013 to 2019, for unknown reasons. The emails show a redacted exchange in 2014 suggesting he was on Hilton Head for a March visit.
Kenneth Lannon, a retired FBI expert in child sexual victimization who has trained hundreds of law enforcement agents to investigate abusers, said it was “highly likely” Epstein had victims pre-dating his Florida arrest and that he probably “started out slowly and just got better and better at it as time went on.
The typical child sex abuser, he said, begins targeting and grooming potential victims soon after puberty, although they may come across as “nice guys” in regular social interactions. Money and the ability to travel freely make the crimes easier to pull off, he said.
Child victims are often so starved for attention they become compliant and have more than one encounter with the abuser.
Jane Doe 4 had a troubled life after leaving Hilton Head. She married several times and moved to the west coast. She returned to be with family in Georgia and was arrested in 2023 for stealing money from a dying man. She pleaded guilty and spent a year in jail. Her brothers were well educated; one worked for a few years as a Bear Stearns trader before the brokerage collapsed in 2008.
A family member told the Guardian in June that Jane Doe 4 was “staying off the grid” and lived in fear of retaliation from the Trump administration amid the ongoing controversy over the handling of the case.

Eleven bail hostels due to house early release prisoners in England and Wales closed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:53 UTC
00:00:53 KST

Eleven bail hostels that were supposed to have housed dangerous prisoners during the early release of stalkers and domestic abusers in England and Wales have been closed, the Guardian can disclose.
Seven of the halfway house facilities, known as approved premises, were shut because of a lack of qualified staff and the other four because of problems such as infestations or lack of running water, Whitehall sources said.
The figures have emerged six days after about 700 male offenders, including violent criminals and burglars, were released. Some told journalists they had nowhere to stay and that they were likely to reoffend as a result.
Nearly one in eight approved premises for dangerous prisoners have been closed during the early release scheme, an increase from nearly one in 10 in July.
Martin Jones, HM chief inspector of probation, said the figures were concerning. “Approved premises play a critical role in the safe reintegration of the most complex individuals back into the community,” he said. “It is therefore concerning if there has been an increase in closures at a time when releases are increasing. Action needs to be taken to ensure adequate staffing cover and contingency plans.”
Ian Lawrence, the general secretary of the probation officers’ union, Napo, said his members were concerned that approved premises had been closing because of staff shortages or poor maintenance.
“At a time when we are seeing greater pressure on accommodation needs due to early releases, these closures are adding additional issues for our members to deal with and for those coming out of prison,” he said. HM Prison and Probation Service “needs to urgently address this issue so safe and robust release plans can be made in advance of early releases”.
Approved premises supervise about 2,000 criminals considered too dangerous to release back into the community across England and Wales.
Residents often have drug and alcohol problems and complex mental health needs. They live in the hostels for up to 12 weeks and can be recalled to prison if they refuse to submit to drug and alcohol tests or have their rooms searched.
Staff are required to monitor residents, with rapid enforcement action needed to stop violent incidents, self-harm and overdoses.
Western approved premises, a hostel for 27 offenders in Weymouth, will close on Friday because of staffing shortages.
Bridgewood approved premises in Northampton, which monitors 17 high-risk offenders, was closed earlier this year because of staff shortages, sources said.
A report from the probation watchdog in February found that Bridgewood required improvement. It highlighted “concerns over the workplace culture, training gaps and inconsistent supervision” and found “there were occasions when staffing levels did not meet the requirements for safe and effective operation”.
The government has not publicly named the affected locations, but Lightfoot House in Ipswich, which operates as an approved premises hostel under the East of England Probation Service, is among those to have closed.
Insiders said high stress levels coupled with the expiry of contracts with the private companies Sodexo and OCS, which provided overnight staff cover at the hostels, had led to a staffing crisis.
Security guards have been filling in for qualified staff while dealing with some serious offenders, resulting in formal complaints.
There are 104 approved premises across England and Wales, most of which are for men only. Eight are facilities for women.
The second tranche of early release prisoners are scheduled to leave prison on 13 October. About 2,000 criminals are to be freed over the month, with another 3,000 following in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.
Asked about the Western, Bridgewood and Lightfoot closures, a Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government is fixing the crisis it inherited by investing a record £700m in the Probation Service and recruiting 1,300 new officers this year.
“Prisoners at risk of becoming homeless are offered up to 12 weeks of basic accommodation on release and we will always ensure that those who present the very highest levels of risk are placed in an approved premises.”

‘A worrying decline’: Why penguins are vanishing from this volcanic island 2,000km from humans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:38 UTC
00:00:38 KST

Scientists have blamed human-caused climate change for the decline in chinstrap penguins on the remote Zavodovski Island.
A volcanic island near Antarctica no longer homes the largest penguin colony in the world, as scientists warn that “even the most remote parts of the planet” are not immune to climate change.
Located in the South Sandwich Islands, Zavodovski Island is considered one of the most remote and extreme places in the world to undertake fieldwork – distanced some 2,000 kilometres away from the nearest permanent human settlement.
It took researchers from the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) more than a fortnight to sail across stormy seas to reach the rugged cliffs of this volcanic island, which is around twice the size of Gibraltar.
Using a combination of drone surveys, aerial photography and tracking devices fitted to penguins, scientists uncovered the loss of more than half a million chinstrap penguins.
This loss represents more than a quarter of the island’s penguins, whose numbers are made up almost entirely of chinstrap and macaroni penguins, and cedes the island's title of world's largest penguin colony to Cape Adare in the Ross Sea.
Why are chinstrap penguin populations plummeting?
For years, Zavodovski Island appeared to buck the trend of widespread chinstrap penguin declines that have been reported across Antarctica and the surrounding islands.
Now, researchers warn that it has the highest rate of chinstrap population decline in the world.
By comparing aerial surveys with satellite records, the BAS team found a 63 per cent decline in occupied chinstrap nests from 2011 to 2025, the cause of which can be inferred from the satellite tracking data of individual penguins.
The steady loss of the penguins suggests the island’s volcanic eruption in March 2016, which deposited smoke and ash over the lower slopes of the volcano, is not to blame. Instead, scientists warn that climate-driven changes to the Southern Ocean are disrupting the penguins’ food supply.
“This is a worrying decline for chinstrap penguins, which have specialist diets and specific ocean temperature preferences,” says penguin ecologist Professor Norman Ratcliffe, who led the research.
Ratcliffe explains that chinstrap penguins prefer to forage in cooler waters to the northwest of the island. This is where they would expect to find Antarctic krill, the prey that make up the bulk of their diet.
“The problem is, with waters warming, the krill have moved southwards into the Weddell Sea,” he says. “Sea-ice cover to the south and a lack of suitable islands for nesting prevents chinstraps from following the food.”
Why macaroni penguins are faring better on Zavodovski Island
While the chinstrap population had been declining, the population of macaroni penguins on the island increased – by 28 per cent from 2011 to 2016, where it has remained stable since. Researchers say this can also be attributed to the penguins’ dining habits.
Unlike chinstraps, macaroni penguins have a broader diet and can switch to alternative prey such as fish and crustaceans when krill become less abundant.
Tracking data showed them predominantly foraging in warmer waters northeast of the island, where they were “likely supplementing their diets” with these alternate food sources.
“Our data shows that the cold-adapted Antarctic chinstrap species are no longer thriving beside their sub-Antarctic neighbours,” Ratcliffe adds.
“It’s the biggest change in community composition ever observed at a single location in Antarctica, which provides further evidence of how rapid warming in the Antarctic is impacting unique and sensitive ecosystems.”
The researchers ruled out other explanations for the change, such as competition for nesting space between the two penguin species, or krill fisheries in the region.
This is mainly due to the availability of breeding habitat on the island and the ban of krill harvesting in the Marine Protected Area (MPA) surrounding the island. However, researchers say it is “unclear” how krill fishing in areas connected by currents to this MPA may be affecting wider food availability.
Climate change reaches the most ‘remote’ parts of the planet
The research team is now concerned that such large changes to the chinstrap and macaroni populations could cause wider disruption to marine food webs in the region.
But it's the state of our ecosystems in a changing world that concerns them the most.
The South Sandwich Islands are home to 30 per cent of the world’s chinstrap population. The declines here, coupled with those seen elsewhere in Antarctica, may tip chinstrap penguins into the 'Endangered' category on the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species.
Earlier this year, Emperor penguins were declared an endangered species due to sea ice loss triggering massive population declines in Antarctica.
Dr Peter Fretwell, a BAS researcher who specialises in remote sensing of penguins, says the study is yet another example of a “warming climate impacting even the most remote parts” of the planet.
“The South Sandwich Islands are far from any humans, home to almost a third of the world’s chinstrap penguins – but not even they can escape the impacts of climate change.”
