Can $1B buy victory in US midterm elections? Some Republicans fear the answer is no
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:32 UTC
00:00:32 KST

Republicans are entering the final month of the midterm campaign increasingly anxious that the $1 billion at their disposal may not be enough to fend off sweeping losses as the party reckons with persistent cost concerns, the fallout from the war on Iran and US President Donald Trump's approval at record low.
The cash advantage, spread out across a half-dozen groups, is driven largely by the Trump-aligned MAGA Inc., which had nearly $416 million in cash on hand at the end of August and began stepping up its spending on critical races in September.
But that money may have come too late, forcing the president's group to pay much higher rates because of the shrinking availability of air time.
Four Republican Senate campaign officials said groups that reserved advertising time last spring paid much lower rates than MAGA Inc. and its affiliated groups, AP news agency reported.
Instead, by waiting until September, Trump-connected organisations are sometimes paying more than five times what they would have spent if they acted earlier.
A representative of MAGA Inc. familiar with the group's strategy said its spending has allowed Republicans to keep races more competitive than they would have been otherwise. In some cases, the group has been the only one on the air criticising Democratic candidates.
The MAGA Inc. representative and the Republican Senate campaign officials spoke to AP on condition of anonymity to discuss internal strategy.
The challenge is acute in places like Texas, where Trump will travel on Wednesday for the second time in a week to stump for Republican Ken Paxton's Senate campaign. The state hasn't elected a Democratic senator since 1988, yet MAGA Inc. has spent more than $22 million in the past month, according to the ad tracking firm AdImpact.
Another group, Texas PAC, which is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, has spent more than $83 million on advertising in the past month, an extraordinary amount to protect what's normally a safe Republican seat.
One of those advertisements, which featured Paxton's estranged wife saying she's supporting the full Republican ticket, aired across the United States last weekend during a football game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Houston Texans.
Candidates are charged a lower advertising rate than outside groups, so the late infusion of super PAC cash has come at a steep price.
MAGA Inc., which is running ads primarily on streaming services, has been charged roughly $894 per airing, according to AdImpact, while Texas PAC has been charged roughly $809 for a mix of broadcast and streaming. That compares with about $290 for Talarico's campaign, also on broadcast and streaming.
Those averages mask some of the more glaring disparities.
For example, during a football game last month, Texas PAC was charged $450,000 to air a single spot in the Austin market. Talarico's campaign paid $50,000 for a spot during the same game in the same market, according to AdImpact.
Elections are referendum on power of money
The 2026 campaign is shaping up as a referendum on the power of money in American politics.
Democrats freely acknowledge their disadvantage, relying instead on anti-Trump sentiment among voters and targeted messaging on issues like corruption. Some Republicans, meanwhile, are open about the challenge of trying to spend their way out of a tough campaign at this late stage.
Neil Newhouse, a longtime Republican pollster, echoed concerns that his party was deploying its cash too late.
"After the votes are counted, I think we're going to find the most effective advertising in terms of communicating message and moving voters and poll numbers, the most effective time was advertising that happened well before Labor Day, not after it," he said. "A million dollars of advertising in October is a drop in the bucket."
Thune's group began pulling back in North Carolina last week, a sign of the party's challenge in the Senate race there. The state's outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis has been increasingly vocal about his party's vulnerabilities and recently said that, even with a strong cash advantage, “in the last month, you pretty much have to place your bets.”
"If we have endless resources, then we should spend endlessly in every state," he said. "Absent endless resources, you've got to make data-driven decisions about where you can win."
The midterms mark the first national election since the Supreme Court in June erased limits on how much political parties can spend in coordination with candidates for Congress and president, injecting even more money into a political system already awash in cash.
Money alone doesn't translate into victory
There's plenty of evidence that money alone doesn't translate into victory.
Democrat Kamala Harris entered the final stretch of the 2024 campaign with significantly more money than Trump but went on to lose every critical swing state and the White House.
Elon Musk's $25 million didn't lift his preferred candidate to a Wisconsin Supreme Court seat last year. And Tom Steyer didn't advance to the general election in the California governor's race despite pumping $216 million of his own money into the campaign.
The $1 billion that Republicans have amassed compares to at least roughly $579 million held by a comparable collection of major Democratic groups.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said his party is facing an "obscene" amount of spending that could swamp them in the midterms.
"We're never going to have as much money as them," he said in an interview. "I sum up the election in this sentence: Can a massive Republican advantage in money beat a massive Democratic advantage in better candidates and political climate? I bet it can."
In addition to Texas, Democrats have mounted competitive Senate campaigns in states like Ohio, Maine, Iowa and Michigan. A similar dynamic has emerged in governors' races from Florida and Georgia to Wisconsin, Ohio and Nevada.
Former President Barack Obama is stepping up his involvement in the midterms and will headline a fundraiser for Senate candidates on Wednesday.
In the House, Democrats are growing so confident they can retake the majority that they're expanding their targets deeper into traditionally Republican districts in Arkansas and Tennessee. But a lack of money could limit their gains.
"We absolutely need to spend enough to get our message out," said Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. "And district by district, we are."
Trump turns to his bond with supporters
From his earliest days as an unlikely political figure, Trump has consistently overcome expectations.
Facing daunting prospects heading into the final weeks of his last midterm, he's betting he can again outwit political gravity, relying in large part on the deep bond he's built with supporters.
He has stepped up his campaign rallies in recent weeks, traveling to deep red territory to galvanize the party faithful. At events like the one this past weekend in Vandalia, Ohio, the crowd was enthusiastic and cheered at the lines that have become Trump staples over the years, particularly when he dips into profanity.
The high school gymnasium that held the event was packed, though crowds began emptying out about halfway through the 90-minute rally.
In the closing minutes of a speech on Monday in Grand Island, Nebraska, the president revived his plea that supporters who have stood so fervently by him pretend as if he is on the ballot one more time.
"In a true way, I am running," he said. "We have to keep it going."

Biology and Consciousness: Where’s Your Evidence? The Perversion of the new ‘Silicon Science’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:30 UTC
00:00:30 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
There is an increasingly common trend in the literature for AI consciousness which goes like this. For all those who think consciousness is tied to biology — a group of folks often called ‘biological naturalists’ — you need to show us the evidence for why biology matters (see for example, here)
At this point the biological naturalist’s ability to defend their view is immediately undermined, because this objection is demanding something of them that no scientist can yet offer: compelling evidence for how consciousness works.
It’s just a fact that we don’t have a good understanding of consciousness. It is as true for those who believe complex computation is sufficient for consciousness, as it is for those who think biology is necessary, that they can offer pretty much zero highly compelling evidence for their view. Sure, we can offer arguments for our views, we can gesture at various hypotheses, but that’s about it. It’s not a defect in the scientist’s work. It’s a reflection of the state of current understanding on consciousness.
Yet somehow this objection is always hurled at the biological naturalist, and rarely ever at the computational functionalist.
But the objection being put to the biological naturalist, as opposed to the computational functionalist, is a complete perversion of the methodological order in science.
Generally, for any domain of inquiry to progress in knowledge, certain methodological precepts are accepted as true. For example, in science, it is universally accepted that experiments must be replicable and that hypotheses must be falsifiable.
Another general methodological precept of science —so utterly elementary that it usually goes completely undiscussed — is that science is the study of the natural world.1 Let me repeat that, because it’s so basic you might have missed it. Science studies nature. That is the assumption functionalism now requires that we defend.
Of course, this is not to say that science doesn’t develop artificial tools in an effort to understand the world, or that socio-political forms of hierarchy do not impact those efforts, oftentimes blurring the lines between science and engineering (consider, as an obvious example, the making of the first atomic bomb, which required taking newly understood theoretical physics and transforming it into a massive industrial engineering project).
It is just to say that the scientific enterprise generally assumes as its object of study the organic world.
Arguably, this is the most fundamental assumption science relies on. And clearly, it has proven to be a success (one wonders how far we would have gotten in physics or chemistry if we demanded of these fields that they defended their decision to study matter rather than silicon).
The assumption is more elementary than other precepts, such as falsifiability. At one point, science took for granted that its hypothesis didn’t need to be falsifiable —this was a standard only implemented with Popper — and today, we wouldn’t dream of questioning that methodological assumption. Yet science has always been sure of its object of study: the natural world, and today, we are witnessing an inundation of pressure to prove this precept. To prove that organic material is where natural phenomenon like consciousness come from.
Obviously, this can be hard to do, but it’s actually not because we lack the evidence. It’s because the evidence is so overwhelmingly pervasive it is difficult to point to.
If you must point to something, you’d have to point to the entire history of successful science as one’s ‘proof’. The entirety of science is proof of the biological naturalists basic assumption: that organic matter is what consciousness resides in.
Humans are curious creatures and as part of that curiosity we have come to systematise the study of nature. We call this ‘science’ when it is successful enough that we gain some understanding of how nature works. Sometimes — think physics, chemistry — it works pretty well.
We also have this other thing that curious humans do, whereby they apply the science they have learned —for better or worse — to the real world. This is called engineering.
The conceptual distinction is clear. We all understand it, perhaps with the exception of a small industry of thinking that insists on blurring this distinction, through mechanisms such as demanding that ordinary science justify its own existence, lest we replace it with an engineering task (building AIs) and calling this ‘science’ (claiming they could be conscious).
Because that is essentially what is being asked of the biological naturalist when they are required to show what exactly it is about nature that is important for consciousness. They are being asked to justify the methodological nature of all science.
But this is an absurd ask. And in reality, the opposite should be occurring: it is the computational functionalist that needs to justifying themselves.
Curiously however, that justification is rarely given (I would genuinely love to read a single argument for substrate independence).
Instead, what we usually get is virtue signalling about ‘biological chauvinism’ or some other such vague statement intended — it seems— to shake the moral compass of those who are afraid of being called names, or who don’t have a good understanding of their own moral positions, so, cannot defend themselves.
To the demand that biological naturalists defend the view that biology matters to consciousness, here is my response: the existence of ordinary science is self-justifying, or if you like is vindicated through its past historical explanatory successes.
Granting this, the burden of proof is on those who wish to alter this successful methodological precept, and the evidence, given how well this precept works, should be overwhelming.
I am waiting for AI consciousness enthusiasts to provide it.
I am not saying that it cannot be provided. Another methodological precept of science is that evidence is defeasible, hence, so is the evidence that consciousness is rooted in organic life.
The point is that the demand for the biological naturalist to defend their view is a perversion of what in this debate needs defending. The one claiming that consciousness in silicon is possible is the one who needs to justify their claims.
The biological naturalist is simply doing science.
Biological Naturalism Defended
To make matters even more ludicrous, biological naturalists typically defend themselves pretty well, all things considered.
Consider recent papers from Ned Block and Anil Seth, for instance. Block argues that consciousness may depend on sub-computational processes that arise from biology that computational functionalism (the view that computation is sufficient for consciousness) necessarily ignores.
I think this is a reasonable view considering how in other domains of neuroscience there is work suggesting that the computations underlying memory, for instance, likely require molecular computation to account for the speed at which human memory computes.2
Seth takes a different approach, arguing that consciousness may depend on organic life (a claim that Seth would be entitled to take for granted if he were a physicist, chemist, or biologist, say, but one he has to defend as a neuroscientist).
Because of the outlier norms in cognitive science and AI consciousness debates, it’s incumbent on Seth to give an argument for what exactly it is about life that is so important to consciousness. His argument is that consciousness rests on the autopoietic nature of organic creatures (roughly, that biological creatures regenerate their own material nature).
I’m not sure about this hypothesis, though I certainly think it’s worthy of investigation and further inquiry. But how certain this particular hypothesis is, should be beside the point. Given how little we understand about the brain and about consciousness, it is very normal that current hypotheses are likely false, incomplete or in some other way inadequate.
As such, the only reasonable scientific conversation to be having in my view, is whether Seth’s particular view best explains the nature of consciousness. Instead, given the silicon science assault on rational inquiry, this gets overlooked.
Seth’s arguments, along with others like Block’s, are treated as defending ‘biological naturalism’, instead of viewing them as efforts to explain consciousness.
Up against the monstrous task of defending this basic precept —a precept that no scientist has ever needed to defend before the onslaught of silicon science — the arguments will inevitably seem inadequate.
But their inadequacy is not the problem. The problem is that the arguments are expected to bear this burden of proof to begin with.
I’ll leave you with the wise words of philosopher of science Mazviita Chirimuuta on this issue. In response to the demand that she defend her claim that biology matters to consciousness, she writes:
‘‘The argument here is pretty much like the parable of the search for the lost keys only on the patch of ground where the streetlight is shining. The computational framework offers the brightest sharpest light that researchers have yet had on the question of how ordinary matter can be organised to do cognition-like things. But given that computers are so unlike humans and other animals in their ability to perform the great feats of intelligence without a glimmer of sentience, it is reasonable to think that the keys to consciousness are somewhere in the dark’’
In other words, until someone offers me a serious reason to stop doing science the way it has been done for centuries, I’ll continue on my way respecting its basic methodological percepts. A reasonable view, if you ask me.
Photo by Brecht Corbeel on Unsplash
I am of course, restricting my argument to what we often call ‘the hard sciences’ or at the least omitting certain disciplines like economics, which, if one wanted to call this a ‘science’ would not be included here.
Charles Randy Gallistel and Adam Philip King, Memory and the Computational Brain. Why Cognitive Science will Transform Neuroscience (Malden, MA: Wiley-Blackwell, 2009)

Drone landing system cut from three units to one
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:00:25 BST
00:00:25 KST

A Cambridgeshire firm that lets drones land precisely using radar rather than satellite positioning has cut the equipment needed on the ground from three units to one, and has rebranded under new leadership, according to skyAnchor.
The company, formerly Cambridge Sensoriis, makes the ARC system, which uses patented radar-based radio frequency technology to land and tether uncrewed aircraft, and says its technology has been adopted by partners in more than ten countries over six years of development.
The latest firmware release, ARC 1.4, allows supported applications to land on a single anchor unit rather than the three-unit configuration previously required, which cuts both the cost and the logistical burden of fielding the system. The release also adds support for PX4 moving-landing alongside ArduPilot.
That second change matters chiefly because of who has taken it up. Evolve Dynamics has recently adopted PX4 on its Wolfe platform, a sub-four-kilogram uncrewed aircraft built for rugged use, and the two companies have worked together to tune the integration.
Mike Hall, appointed chief executive earlier this year and with the business since it began, said: “We’re delivering real value to the drone industry right now, by providing a trusted platform for take-off, tethering, and landing. Our customers already have a lot to manage. With skyAnchor, they don’t need to think about this critical phase of operation, they know they can rely on us to handle it with consistency and confidence.”
Landing is where most drone accidents happen, and precision landing without satellite positioning has become a requirement rather than a refinement as jamming has spread. A system that can put an aircraft onto a moving deck or vehicle in weather, without relying on GPS, addresses a problem that affects every operator from the Royal Navy down to a utility company inspecting pylons.
skyAnchor is the trading name of Cambridge Sensoriis, based at Bourn near Cambridge, and specialises in radar antenna, transceiver and signal-processing design, developing collaborative radio frequency systems of low size, weight and power for military and commercial aircraft.
The company is at stand SB24 at Apex Europe in London on Wednesday and Thursday.

Singapore’s air pollution worst in world as haze shuts Malaysia schools

China’s thorium-229 nuclear clock beats Vienna’s on stability, studies show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:00:07 UTC
00:00:07 KST

China’s thorium-229 nuclear clock beats Vienna’s on stability, studies show
Chinese and European teams in ‘fierce but friendly’ competition to develop the next-generation timepieces
Initial results from the world’s first two working nuclear clocks indicate that China’s timepiece is about six times as stable as the one in Vienna, according to papers published this week by the journal Nature.
The clocks were developed independently but both the Chinese team, led by Tsinghua University in Beijing, and the researchers at Vienna’s TU Wien used thorium-229 nuclei embedded in crystals to keep time by the steady rhythm of the atom’s core, rather than the electrons whirling around it, as in atomic clocks.
When Nature reported in June that the two teams had separately developed the radical new devices, Thorsten Schumm, a member of the European team, said that “now we have a fierce but friendly global competition”.
According to the latest papers, the Beijing scientists also showed that two crystals grown separately kept the same time – a sign such clocks could be reliably reproduced, they said. Meanwhile, the Vienna team used its clock to hunt for dark matter, without success.

15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A quake on Mars may have set these rocks rolling
Images show fresh boulder tracks near the source of a possible temblor on the Red Planet
Earthquakes frequently trigger rock falls. Now there’s solid evidence marsquakes can send boulders tumbling, too.
Scientists mined high-resolution imagery of the Red Planet taken shortly after a recent temblor and found hundreds of new imprints left by tumbling boulders, researchers report September 2 in npj Space Exploration. Such rockfalls can be used as a proxy for seismic data, which is difficult to collect across the solar system.
The data were collected with NASA’s InSight lander, which touched down on Mars in 2018. Over the next four years, its seismometer detected more than a thousand marsquakes. Many of those temblors originated in a region known as Cerberus Fossae, just north of the Martian equator. That’s a dynamic landscape riddled with slopes, cracks and rocks on the move, says Vijayan, a planetary scientist at the Physical Research Laboratory in Ahmedabad, India, who goes by a single name. “Thousands and thousands of boulders have fallen.”
Vijayan and his collaborators focused on one well-detected marsquake captured by InSight that occurred in July 2019 just a few tens of kilometers from Cerberus Fossae. By comparing images taken in June 2019 and December 2020, the researchers discovered 27 new linelike features. Each was composed of tens to hundreds of distinct marks. These structures were most likely tracks created by boulders bouncing downhill, the team concluded.
Using historical imagery, the researchers calculated that only about two such features form each year on average in Cerberus Fossae. “We have statistics of previous boulder falls,” says Bivas Das, a seismologist at the Physical Research Laboratory and a member of the research team. Recording 27 new structures over a span of just 18 months is wholly unexpected, Das says. “That’s a big increase.” The nearby marsquake recorded by InSight was probably the instigator, the team concluded.
Mysteries remain, however. All of the rockfalls occurred on the north side of a prominent valley in Cerberus Fossae, despite more boulders being located on the south side of the valley. “That puzzles us,” Vijayan says. The complex landscape of Cerberus Fossae might well alter how seismic waves travel, making it difficult to predict how shaking will impact different areas, he says. “The wave propagation is going to be complicated.”
Looking for such boulder falls elsewhere could help space exploration efforts, the team suggests. Human settlements would do best avoiding areas that are seismically active, and tumbling boulders can be the proverbial canaries in the coal mine, Vijayan says. “They’re like a proxy in the absence of seismic data.”

"I chose education, not 'The Hunger Games'" - Belgian students protest tuition costs; arrests made

Liège Mayor Willy Demeyer told Belgian broadcaster RTBF that he hoped calm would be restored and that "it would be possible to establish a dialogue, and young people would be able to express their grievances peacefully and, if possible, be heard."

New nuclear clocks could become world's most accurate timekeepers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:58:38 UTC
23:58:38 KST

Nuclear clocks could become world's most accurate timekeepers
In short:
Two teams of scientists have built the first working "nuclear clocks", which could become the world's most accurate timekeepers.
The clocks could be used in navigation, mining, earthquake prediction, and potentially discovering new areas of physics.
What's next?
Both clocks are in their experimental stages, but researchers say they will be rapidly improved.
A pair of crystals illuminated with lasers could become the world's most accurate clocks.
Two teams of scientists have made the world's first "nuclear clocks", which keep time by tracking tiny changes in the centre of atoms.
Both clocks are so accurate that if they ran for 30 million years, they would only be off by a second.
This accuracy does not surpass the best clocks in operation right now, but both teams are confident they will be able to improve their clocks significantly.
The researchers have published their work in two papers in the journal Nature.
University of New South Wales physicist Victor Flambaum said nuclear clocks had the potential to become the "most accurate instrument humans have ever built".
Professor Flambaum said the studies, which he was not involved with, represented an exciting step forward.
The clocks could be used to improve technology such as GPS, mining surveys and solve physics mysteries.
How does a nuclear clock work?
Atoms, which compose all the matter we interact with, are made from a "nucleus" containing a dense cluster of protons and neutrons, surrounded by a spacious cloud of electrons.
Atomic clocks, currently the most accurate measures of time in the world, work by tracking changes in the electrons around the nucleus of a caesium atom.
But these clocks are approaching a point where it is physically impossible to make them more accurate.
Nuclear clocks use a similar logic to atomic clocks, but they track even smaller changes in the nucleus of an atom.
"A nucleus is very small compared to [a whole] atom," Professor Flambaum said.
Because it is thousands of times smaller, a nucleus could be used to measure much more subtle changes in time, leading to a more accurate clock.
Why couldn't we build nuclear clocks before?
Nuclear clocks have been theorised for more than two decades, but until recently technological and theoretical constraints have made them impossible to build.
Thorsten Schumm, co-author on one of the new studies and a physicist at Vienna University of Technology, said the main turning point in his team's research came a couple of years ago.
In early 2024 the team used a laser to produce the predicted change in an atomic nucleus that would allow time to be measured.
Professor Flambaum said progress had been "very rapid" since that discovery.
Tsinghua University physicist and study co-author Shiqian Ding said his team needed to solve several different problems to make the nuclear clock.
The problems included making a material with the right clock nuclei inside it and developing lasers precise enough to produce reliable changes.
"There was no single step that suddenly made the clock possible," Dr Ding said.
What is a nuclear clock made from?
A specific type of thorium atom, thorium-229, has the properties to make it usable as a timekeeper.
Both teams grew crystals containing thorium-229, then suspended them under ultra-precise lasers that could produce tiny, nucleus-sized "ticks" in the thorium.
The researchers also have plans to improve nuclear clocks so they can outperform atomic clocks.
Professor Schumm said thorium-229 had potential to be more stable than atomic clocks, meaning nuclear clocks could become very small and practical to move around.
"We envision a chip-scale device," he said.
What would nuclear clocks be used for?
Nuclear clocks could be used to improve navigation systems such as GPS, which has driven military interest in the latest iterations of atomic clocks.
Professor Flambaum said nuclear clocks could be accurate enough to measure the manipulation of time by gravity, per Einstein's theories of relativity.
This could make them useful in mining exploration or earthquake prediction.
"By measuring, accurately, the gradient of gravitational fields, we can see what is under the earth," Professor Flambaum said.
The super-accurate timekeeping could also be used in physics research, particularly in probing mysterious dark matter.
"I am particularly excited about using nuclear clocks to test fundamental physics," Dr Ding said.
Professor Schumm's team has already used their nuclear clock to detect evidence of dark matter, as proof of concept.
He is planning to install a second nuclear clock in Innsbruck within a year, to accompany the clock in Vienna and measure subtle changes in Earth's movement around the Sun.
Professor Flambaum said there was a "race" among several other groups to make practical nuclear clocks and that any one of them could be the first to outperform atomic clocks.
"The progress is so fast, I expect it will be soon," he said.

Why music in Iran is more than just entertainment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:58:00 UTC
23:58:00 KST

Why music in Iran is more than just entertainment
October 8, 2026
After spending 47 years abroad, Iranian musician Bijan Mortazavi returned to his homeland at the end of September.
Mortazavi is one of Iran's most renowned violinists, singers, and composers.
In July 2026, he performed with his famous white violin at the closing ceremony of the FIFA World Cup alongside the New York Philharmonic Orchestra.
In the videos that he and his wife have now posted on social media, the couple can be seen taking walks through the city of the Iranian capital, Tehran, while passersby greet the musician warmly and welcome him.
Singer Mohsen Namjoo also recently returned to Iran after about 20 years in exile.
Internationally renowned for his experimental Persian music, he blends traditional Persian singing and poetic lyrics with elements of blues, rock, jazz and folk.
In 2009, a court in Tehran sentenced Namjoo in absentia to five years in prison.
He was accused of insulting holy sites and mocking verses from the Quran, among other things.
In a video posted online after his return to Iran, Namjoo said he had returned to the country to spend more time with his family and friends.
Return as a political tool
On August 27, Abbas Salehi, Iran's minister of culture and Islamic guidance, said in an interview with the prominent Iranian media outlet Farhikhtegan that his ministry had compiled a list containing the names of more than 100 distinguished Iranians living abroad.
The goal, he said, was to remove obstacles to their travel or return to Iran.
Salehi stressed that even "critics of the Islamic Republic" could return at any time. He added, however, that the return of artists does not necessarily mean they would perform in Iran. Instead, they could simply visit the country, the minister said.
Sina Yousefi, a human rights lawyer, pointed to international law, specifically Article 12 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Iran is also a signatory.
According to this provision, no one may be arbitrarily prevented from entering their own country. This right cannot be made contingent on a citizen's level of loyalty to the government, he told DW.
"The idea of seeking out certain well-known figures — who the reformists, in particular, believe are less likely to cross the red lines — and winning them over to collaborate or bringing them back to the country is not new," said Sepideh Raissadat, an ethnomusicologist who has been studying the history and development of Persian music for years.
As an internationally renowned performer of classical Persian music, she combines her artistic work with scholarly research, with her dissertation focusing on the lives of Iranian female singers since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Between control and resistance
"The 1979 revolution in Iran was a revolution against music. Music was one of the red lines," said Raissadat, referring to statements by the leader of the revolution, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who as early as July 1979 had publicly described music as harmful to society and called for its complete abolition.
In a speech to employees of Radio Darya on July 21, 1979, Khomeini is said to have described music as "a betrayal of the country" and "a betrayal of the youth." A few days later, the Iranian newspaper Keyhan quoted him as saying that music was "like a drug” and must be completely eradicated.
During the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 to 1988, however, music made a comeback in the form of revolutionary and religious songs. It was also used to stir up feelings of national pride and a sense of belonging.
The regime also failed to completely banish the female voice from the public sphere. "They couldn't completely eliminate the voice of women. The female voice returned through choral singing," said Raissadat.
But the conflict between the state and music continued.
For years, musical instruments were not allowed to be shown on Iranian television. Instruments were confiscated or destroyed on the streets. Fearing repercussions, musicians did not carry their instruments in public, while some hid them in their cars.
"Listening to banned music at home was a political act. And when women began to sing, that, too, became a political act," Raissadat noted. The development of Iranian pop music was also part of this political and cultural tension, she underscored. "People began producing new domestic pop music to compete with music from Los Angeles."
Over the past ten years, social media — which is not entirely under government control — has become increasingly important and now wields considerable influence.
This change is particularly evident among young people, with young women now even playing the guitar without headscarves and performing in public.
Music as an expression of protest
Raissadat observes a particular trend among the families of the young people who were killed during the nationwide mass protests in late December 2025 and January 2026.
The demonstrations began on December 28, 2025, and were violently suppressed by security forces.
Human rights organizations report that thousands of protesters were killed, but the exact figures are unknown due to the extensive information blackout imposed by the regime.
"The most important thing we've seen in recent years has been the use of music by the bereaved families of those killed in the protests. This stands in complete contrast to Shiite tradition and our history," said Raissadat.
At some funerals, families turned the memorial service for their loved ones into a new form of protest.
Instead of religious hymns, music played, and the mourners sang and danced along to it. In doing so, they created a deliberate contrast to traditional religious mourning rituals, the musician said.
"Music became a weapon. Those who were mourning were able to connect with it on their own, and at the same time, it stood in opposition to what the political system stands for," Raissadat pointed out, adding, "Dancing in white clothing also became an expression of this resistance."
This article was originally written in German.

Israel isolating Palestinian journalist for 46 days and counting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:57:19 UTC
23:57:19 KST

Qais Abu Samra and Ikram Kouachi
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Israeli prison authorities have continued to hold Palestinian journalist and administrative detainee Bushra al-Tawil in isolation for 46 straight days, Palestinian prisoners’ organizations said Wednesday.
The Palestinian Prisoner Society, Addameer Prisoner Support and Human Rights Association, and the Palestine Liberation Organization’s Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said in a statement that Tawil, 33, was transferred to Ohalei Oz isolation facility in Beersheba in southern Israel.
She was moved there from Neve Tirza prison in central Israel after being held in isolation at Damon prison in Haifa in northern Israel, according to the statement.
The groups said the repeated transfers and continued isolation have prevented her legal team from visiting her, despite several requests submitted by lawyers from the Commission of Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs.
A lawyer was informed Wednesday that Tawil had again been transferred to Ohalei Oz, preventing the scheduled visit, the statement said.
The organizations urged international organizations operating in the occupied Palestinian territories, particularly the International Committee of the Red Cross, to urgently intervene to end her isolation and secure her release.
The groups said Tawil’s case highlights “the growing policy of isolating Palestinian prisoners, including women,” noting that the practice has become “systematic” in recent months, leaving detainees unable to know the allegations against them or challenge them, while also causing psychological harm.
The UN Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, known as the Nelson Mandela Rules, prohibit prolonged or indefinite solitary confinement.
It defines solitary confinement as holding a prisoner for 22 hours or more a day without meaningful human contact, and prolonged solitary confinement as lasting more than 15 consecutive days.
The Palestinian groups said Tawil’s 46 days in isolation exceed that threshold and violate international standards.
Tawil has been held in administrative detention without charge since February, according to the statement.
The groups described her as one of the most prominent Palestinian female detainees to face administrative detention in recent years.
She is the daughter of Jamal al-Tawil, a Palestinian administrative detainee who spent years in Israeli prisons, according to the statement.
The organizations demanded Tawil’s immediate release and an end to her isolation.
Israeli forces carry out frequent raids and arrests in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, amid increased occupier attacks against Palestinians.
About 9,500 Palestinians are held in Israeli prisons, including around 90 women and more than 350 children, who face food deprivation, torture and medical neglect, according to Palestinian and Israeli rights groups.

Exclusive: The Left group wants to halve MEP salaries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:55:35 UTC
23:55:35 KST

The proposal would slash MEPs’ net monthly salary from around €8,800 to almost €4,400, but opponents have dismissed it as a “populist stunt”.
The Left group in the European Parliament is set to demand that MEP salaries are halved, arguing that lawmakers taking home tens of thousands of euros a month are increasingly disconnected from ordinary voters.
MEPs currently receive a net monthly salary of €8,772.70, on top of several allowances that bring their total monthly income to around €18,000.
Under a formal proposal put forward by Belgian MEP Marc Botenga, only the basic salary would be cut, reducing it to around €4,400 a month.
The measure is contained in an amendment to a resolution on next year’s Parliament budget, which is due to be put to a vote during the plenary session in Strasbourg in two weeks.
“MEPs are very disconnected from the people. For the salary they earn, they do not know what it means not being able to pay rent,” Botenga told Euronews.
The Left estimates the cut would save more than €50 million from next year’s Parliament budget.
“At a time when workers face rising costs and pressure on living standards, elected representatives should lead by example and share in the efforts required of society,” reads the amendment, seen by Euronews.
But the proposal is likely to face opposition from other political groups.
“The proposal is a classic case of populism,” Estonian MEP Jaak Madison, from the European Conservatives and Reformists group, told Euronews.
“If the Left’s MEPs wish to demonstrate genuine solidarity with the voters [...] they could for instance simply refrain from signing the attendance register that entitles them to a daily allowance of over €350,” he said.
German lawmaker Daniel Freund of the Greens/EFA group also described the proposal as a “populist stunt.”
“The rules for MEP salaries are quite sensible; they are tied to the developments of salaries in the member states,” he told Euronews.
A similar proposal was already rejected in the Parliament’s Committee on Economic and Monetary Affairs, Botenga said, acknowledging that the initiative would probably be rejected by his colleagues.
Beyond their net monthly salary of €8,772.70, MEPs are currently entitled to a general expenditure allowance of €4,950 per month. This allowance is halved if they attend fewer than half of the plenary sittings in a year without proper justification.
Their mandate also provides for a flat-rate daily allowance of €359, covering accommodation, meals and related expenses for each day spent in Brussels or Strasbourg. MEPs must sign an attendance register to receive the allowance.
Together, these payments can bring total monthly income to around €18,000, although the amount may vary from month to month depending on the Parliament’s working calendar.
On top of their salary and allowances, MEPs receive over €32,000 per month to cover the cost of parliamentary assistants. Former members of the Parliament are entitled to a pension from the age of 63, amounting to 3.5% of their salary for each full year in office.

Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms

Denmark says Russia has conducted sabotage attacks against its defense firms
COPENHAGEN, Oct 7 - Russia has begun sabotage operations against Danish companies supplying Ukraine after concluding that broader disruption efforts failed to curb Western military support for the country, a Danish intelligence official said on Wednesday.
The shift reflects a significant escalation in Moscow's hybrid warfare campaign, the official, from the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), told a homeland security conference in Copenhagen.
"What we saw in the spring was a lot of planning, but very little carried out; what we saw in early summer is that they started to carry out a lot more," the official said.
Russia concluded that its previous broad-spectrum targeting "did not have the effect of deterring the Western (military alliance) NATO from supporting Ukraine," the official added, and while Moscow maintains political control over operations, its operational boldness is growing and Russia is now "trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line. That means weapons production."
Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. The Russian embassy in Copenhagen rejected the allegations on Wednesday, accusing Danish authorities of making unfounded accusations against Russia.
The official cited a Russian defence ministry list of alleged European drone and drone component manufacturers that Moscow said in April amounted to potential military targets, without elaborating further.
Russia is increasingly using untrained proxies — including homeless people and people addicted to drugs — recruited via Telegram and other social media platforms. Recruitment typically starts with low-threshold tasks such as reconnaissance or photography, then escalates toward actual sabotage operations, PET has said.
"It could be anyone just looking for quick money," the official said. "If the first person isn't successful, they'll throw another one at the problem until they succeed."
Denmark's defence intelligence service last month said Russia is likely to intensify hybrid attacks against the West in coming months, after Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August.
In September 2025, before Denmark hosted an EU summit, drones disrupted air traffic at six Danish airports, including Copenhagen, the Nordic region's busiest, in what Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a hybrid attack on her nation. REUTERS

Putin turns 74 today. Officials and kindergarteners across Russia were forced to wish him a happy birthday.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Putin turns 74 today. Officials and kindergarteners across Russia were forced to wish him a happy birthday.
Kindergarten children in several Russian regions were enlisted to congratulate Vladimir Putin on his 74th birthday, while officials received detailed instructions on how to phrase their messages, according to the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo and the independent Russian news outlet Verstka.
Agentstvo identified more than 20 posts describing kindergarten events held for Putin’s birthday. Teachers told children about the “life journey of the head of state” and forced them to record congratulatory messages to Putin.
In Anadyr, children at one kindergarten congratulated Putin while kneeling on one knee. In Ulyanovsk, children thanked him for “peace” and “light.” Children in the village of Sokolovo, in the Volgograd region, made a poster for Putin reading “We congratulate the president.”
Ahead of October 7, officials received instructions on how to take part in the PozdravliaiuPrezidenta (“I Congratulate the President”) campaign. Yevgenia Khalilova, an official in the Vladimir region, posted the instructions on her page. They said Putin should be congratulated only through personal social media pages, and that well wishes posted through public pages “will not be accepted.” Agentstvo counted at least 1,100 posts using the hashtag #PozdravliaiuPrezidenta on VKontakte.
In Bashkortostan, the requirements for birthday messages were stricter. A guidance document reviewed by the Russian Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti said all posts had to go up no later than 2:00 p.m. local time and include a quote from Putin about the region. Each institution had to produce one publication. The outlet counted at least 400 formulaic birthday messages from Bashkortostan within three hours.
Verstka also found that many of the posts from governors, lawmakers, and other officials were worded almost identically. More than 1,600 Telegram posts wished Putin “robust health and boundless energy.” The heads of several regions and State Duma deputies, as well as singer Nikolai Baskov, the Defenders of the Fatherland foundation, and Moscow Zoo director Svetlana Akulova, congratulated him using that same wording.
None of the officials who wished Putin “robust health” mentioned his age.

Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:52:26 UTC
23:52:26 KST

Ex-German spy chief arrested: A history of spooks working for enemy powers
There have been many cases of top spies giving classified information to enemy nations. Here are some of the highlights.
Germany’s former spy chief, August Hanning, has been arrested on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service.
Hanning, 80, headed up the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005.
A federal prosecutor’s statement said it strongly suspected him of “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services since 2010, while working as a private consultant. He is accused of obtaining around 2,000 sensitive documents from a former bureau chief who has also been arrested.
But he isn’t the only high-ranking intelligence officer to have been discovered to have worked for foreign governments over the years.
Here are some of the highlights.
1940s to 1960s – Kim Philby and the ‘Cambridge Five’
Kim Philby was a British intelligence officer who secretly spent decades working for the Soviet Union during World War II and the early Cold War years.
He was recruited by Soviet Intelligence while studying at Cambridge University in the 1930s. He was the most prominent member of the “Cambridge Five” – a spy ring that gave away British secrets to the Soviet Union.
During the war, he joined MI6, where he rose to head its counter-Soviet division, and was later posted to Washington, DC. This gave him access to sensitive information through his close links to the CIA and FBI.
His tip-offs to his Soviet handlers are believed to have scuppered many Western operations and revealed the identities of agents. This included information operations to overthrow Albania’s communist leader Enver Hoxha as part of Western efforts to stop the spread of communism.
Philby came under suspicion in 1951 and was forced out of MI6 when Guy Burgess and Donald Maclean, two other members of the Cambridge Five, defected to the Soviet Union. Philby was suspected of having warned them that British intelligence officers were close to uncovering their identities as double agents for the Soviet Union, before being formally cleared of the allegations in 1955.
Then, in 1963, aware that the net was closing in on him because of his own involvement with Soviet intelligence, he fled to Russia, where he lived with his wife since 1971, Rufina Pukhova, until his death in 1988. Overall, he provided state secrets, the identities of agents, minutes from cabinet meetings, atomic research, diplomatic and military intelligence, and information about counter-intelligence operations to the Soviet Union for nearly 20 years.
Philby is regarded as the most damaging spy in British history.
According to the UK’s National Archives, one of the agents he unmasked to the Soviet Union was Constantin Volkov, a Soviet intelligence officer posted to Turkiye who wanted to defect to the UK in 1945. Volkov and his wife were seized and executed in Moscow as a result. The information he provided to the Soviet Union about a joint CIA-MI6 operation in communist Albania in the late 1940s and early 1950s resulted in the execution of hundreds of anti-communist agents.
1970s and 1980s – Oleg Gordievsky
Oleg Gordievsky was a KGB colonel who spied for British intelligence for more than a decade.
He was the son of an officer in the NKVD, which was the Soviet secret police and the direct predecessor to the KGB.
But he was recruited by MI6 in the early 1970s after becoming disillusioned by the Soviet crushing of mass protests during the Prague Spring in Czechoslovakia in 1968 and the building of the Berlin Wall.
While working for the KGB, he was stationed in Copenhagen and later in London, where he became KGB station chief in 1985.
The intelligence he provided to the British is thought to have revealed the KGB’s deep concerns that NATO’s 1983 Able Archer exercise might be cover for a real nuclear strike. This was invaluable for helping the West understand Soviet fears and to de-escalate.
Gordievsky came under suspicion and was recalled to Moscow in 1985. He was drugged and interrogated but had not yet been charged when MI6 ran a daring operation to rescue him and smuggle him out of Russia in the boot of a car across the Finnish border.
Russia sentenced Gordievsky to death in absentia.
He lived in the UK under protection until his death in 2025.
1980s and 1990s – Robert Hanssen
Robert Hanssen was a high-ranking agent at the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) who spied for the Soviet Union and later for Russian intelligence services between 1979 and 2001.
Hanssen initially studied dentistry at Northwestern University before switching courses and receiving a degree in accounting and information systems. He worked as a police officer in Chicago before joining the FBI in 1976.
He approached Soviet military intelligence in 1979, eventually working with the KGB and its successor, the SVR. He operated using the alias “Ramon Garcia”.
Hanssen never met his handlers in person, instead using “dead drops” when he would leave classified documents in prearranged outdoor locations, including parks, wooded areas, under bridges and on street corners in the Washington, DC area, in exchange for cash or diamonds.
He handed over thousands of pages of classified material, including details about US nuclear war plans and the identities of Russian officials working for the US. At least two of those sources, including Dmitri Polyakov and Valery Marynov were executed.
The arrest in 1994 of Aldrich Ames, another US spy caught working for Russian intelligence, eventually led to his arrest in February 2001.
He pleaded guilty to avoid the death penalty and died in prison in 2023.
2000s – Alexander Yuk Ching Ma
Alexander Yuk Ching Ma is a former CIA officer who was caught spying for China.
He worked for the CIA from 1982 to 1989 and became a US citizen, living in Honolulu.
In March 2001, officers of China’s Shanghai State Security Bureau asked him to arrange a meeting with a now-deceased former CIA officer who served from 1967 to 1983. The two met in a Hong Kong hotel room for three days. In exchange for $50,000, they provided classified information to China.
The FBI became aware of his ties to Chinese intelligence and hired him as a contract linguist in its Honolulu office so that his activities could be monitored.
He was arrested in a sting after admitting to an undercover FBI employee that he had facilitated the provision of classified information to Chinese intelligence.
Ma pleaded guilty in May 2024 and is currently serving a 10-year prison sentence.

Five times deadly pathogens escaped laboratories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:51:40 UTC
23:51:40 KST

Laboratories exist to study the world's most dangerous microbes, and strict biosafety rules exist to keep those microbes contained. The record shows the rules do not always hold.
A review of reports from 2000 to 2024 identified 712 laboratory-acquired human infections and 17 deaths.
Here are five incidents that show how containment can fail.
California microbiologist dies after meningococcal infection
A 25-year-old microbiologist working with meningococcal bacteria in California became infected and died in 2012.
The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said investigators identified several biosafety breaches.
The case showed that even trained scientists handling Neisseria meningitidis in routine conditions can pay with their lives when safety procedures fail. It remains a stark reminder that laboratory-acquired infections are not only a risk of exotic, headline-grabbing pathogens.
Everyday bacteria can be just as dangerous when protocols slip.
Dozens exposed in CDC anthrax and H5N1 lapses
Dozens of workers at the CDC in Atlanta were potentially exposed in 2014 after anthrax was inadequately inactivated.
Separately, material contaminated with H5N1 avian influenza was mistakenly shipped to another laboratory. The CDC said no illnesses or deaths resulted.
The episodes are notable because the agency helps set biosafety standards for laboratories across the United States.
They show that near misses, not only fatalities, can reveal weaknesses in even the best-resourced institutions and raise questions about oversight.
French technician dies of prion disease after needlestick
A research technician in France died in 2019 from variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (vCJD), a fatal brain disorder caused by prions.
French authorities said the infection could have resulted from a laboratory needlestick accident in 2010.
The Ministry of Agriculture made the assessment. Almost a decade passed between exposure and death.
Prions are neither bacteria nor viruses, and standard sterilisation methods struggle to destroy them, which makes accidental exposure particularly hard to guard against.
Lanzhou factory leak infects more than 10,000 people
Improperly disinfected waste gas from a vaccine factory in Lanzhou, China, released aerosolised Brucella bacteria in 2019 and 2020.
More than 10,000 infections were eventually reported, according to published research.
That makes it one of the largest documented accidental pathogen releases. Brucella causes brucellosis, a disease that normally passes from animals to humans and can bring prolonged fever and joint pain.
Unlike the other cases here, this one reached the wider community, not only staff.
Russian lab worker dies as plague link remains unproven
A 28-year-old employee of an anti-plague institute in Irkutsk, Russia, died in 2026 from severe pneumonia.
According to Reuters, reports alleged a laboratory accident involving plague.
Authorities said testing has not established a laboratory link or plague infection. The cause remains undetermined, so this is an open investigation, not a confirmed escape.
It shows how quickly speculation can fill the gaps when information about laboratory incidents is limited.
Laboratory accidents remain rare, but the cases above show the consequences can be severe when they happen. The CDC, French authorities and published research all point to the same lesson: biosafety depends on strict procedures and transparent investigation.
As the Irkutsk case shows, unanswered questions can fuel speculation, so clear and prompt reporting matters as much as containment.

‘All me’: Tory party riding high on Kemi Badenoch’s wave of popularity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:41 UTC
23:50:41 KST

Kemi Badenoch has long said that the Conservatives were “under new management”, but in a TV interview to mark the end of a party conference at which she has been front and centre of more or less everything, she took the analogy further.
“Your viewers will know that sometimes you have a football team that’s disappointing,” the Tory leader told GB News. “There’s a new captain, there’s a new coach, there’s a new owner, effectively – which is all me.”
These are bold words even for a politician known to possess an iron-clad self-confidence. But they are no exaggeration. Badenoch is not only outperforming her party in polling terms, she is busy remaking it in her own image.
The broad ideological direction was already set, with Badenoch saying explicitly at the start of this year that centrist ideas were no longer wanted. Some more moderate figures remain in her shadow cabinet, but they are signed up to a right-leaning agenda, including opposition to net zero and a bonfire of human rights protections.
Those around Badenoch say, however, that her control goes further, with policy decisions such as the move to grant free childcare to people with incomes above £100,000, announced on the eve of the conference, made simply because she believes they are the right thing to do.
“With policies it’s not about chasing certain groups of voters,” one shadow cabinet minister said. “She focuses on what she thinks needs to be fixed, what she feels is wrong.”
Talking her out of a policy decision, they said, was a tall order: “It’s not going to happen – it’s tablets of stone. She’s not going to change her mind. She knows what the policies have to be.”
Many political parties are, to a greater or less extent, a cult based around the leader, but this is particularly the case for the 2026-period Conservatives, where MPs say Badenoch is talked about on the doorsteps with an admiration and respect not accorded to their party more widely.
MPs recount how her name is raised unprompted. One said: “She’s brought up in a positive way. Crucially, in a world where most people couldn’t name more than a handful of politicians, they know who she is.”
This starring role was obvious throughout the Conservatives’ conference in Birmingham, not least Badenoch’s arrival, which saw her greeted by a flag-waving crowd of activists chanting: “Kemi, Kemi.”
Inside the venue, Badenoch was the heroic centrepiece of the party’s “Birmingham tapestry”, shown in mocked-up 12th-century form doing everything from chastising Wes Streeting to sitting in the turret of a tank.
Such veneration is not just wishful thinking by a party eager to move on from a revolving door of previous leaders. While last year’s conference was viewed as make-or-break for Badenoch, even with her party still bumping along at 20% or so in the polls her position is now seen as secure, with the Conservatives more unified than they have been for years.
This is in part the result of some serial malcontents leaving for Reform UK, especially Robert Jenrick, as well as the party’s diminished size in the Commons, which as one shadow cabinet minister notes, is too small for factions: “We could just about fill a corner table in Pizza Express.”
There are still private doubts, including Badenoch’s instinct to lean into culture wars rather than focus on the economy, which those around her believe is the party’s strongest electoral card.
Some party figures also wonder if Badenoch is thinking about election strategy at all with her very personal suite of policy choices, which in Birmingham mainly consisted of giving tax breaks to wealthier people.
This was capped in her end-of-conference speech with the announcement that a Badenoch-led government would exempt people’s homes from inheritance tax, an idea which, given that the levy only begins on property worth more than £500,000, is a largely theoretical idea outside London and the south-east of England.
While such policies could be appealing to prosperous home counties voters who defected to the Liberal Democrats in 2024, this does not seem to be the plan. During another TV interview, Badenoch chided her questioner for suggesting her tax cuts were aimed at bringing back such support.
“I’m very sad that you’re looking at this in crude electoral terms,” she said. “That’s how we’ve all got into this problem where we keep thinking about winning elections rather than thinking about what works.”
One former Tory strategist said there was a risk of incoherence: “I can’t understand what is being achieved with these announcements. Forget lots of the small ones, just use the money and do a big tax cut for middle earners.”
There was, they added, little chance things would change: “People are scared of her, to be honest. I think a lot of her team don’t know how to say no to her.”
However, much like football, politics is not a one-person game, and a star player or manager will only get you so far. And while Badenoch was at pains to praise colleagues in her speech, it is fair to say that the rest of the shadow cabinet is lagging.
Andrew Griffith, Badenoch’s new shadow chancellor, was feted by his boss for his private sector business expertise. But on Monday he gave a speech widely seen as one of the worst delivered to any conference in years.
It is a matter of profile as well as ability. While Badenoch is recognised by 90% of voters, according to YouGov polling, only 22% say they know who Griffith is. A number of his colleagues are on similar ratings, with pollsters saying even these are likely to be inflated by people who don’t want to admit ignorance.
The experienced Tom Tugendhat, now in the foreign affairs brief, does slightly better, on 46%. Laura Trott, the shadow education secretary, hits 50%, but this is because some people mistake her for the Olympic cyclist, now Laura Kenny, formerly of the same name.
There was some unease in Birmingham about Badenoch blotting out everyone else. “Isn’t there a danger we are becoming a one-woman party?” one activist asked a fringe of shadow cabinet members.
Others disagree. “It’s a normal dynamic for an opposition party that is unpopular,” said Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary. “It needs a strong popular leader that can pull it up and we should thank our lucky stars that we have her.”
Either way, most Conservatives now accept that, for now, it is up to Badenoch to chart the Conservatives’ course, whatever it involves. One ally said: “We win elections on the economy but there’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything.”

George Galloway contests London byelection without setting foot in UK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:50:37 UTC
23:50:37 KST

George Galloway has been elected seven times to parliament, but his attempt to succeed for an eighth this week, in the London seat formerly held by Keir Starmer, is undoubtedly his most curious effort yet.
Since the byelection campaign began, the leader of the Workers party of Britain has yet to set foot in the UK, let alone the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, because he is in what he describes as “self-exile” after being questioned by counter-terrorism police at Gatwick airport a year ago.
Prolific social media feeds show that the veteran leftwinger has spent the past few weeks on a speaking tour in South Africa, with his most recent public appearance on Saturday at a pro-Palestine rally in Cape Town, though posts in the last 24 hours suggest he is in Shanghai, China.
Prior to that he was in Moscow, repeatedly making his hostility to Ukraine and Nato as explicit as his support for Palestine and opposition to apartheid.
“The biggest issue in the H&StP byelection is the path leading us to WW3 in Ukraine,” Galloway wrote on X in the middle of September, an argument that has not gained much traction with voters, though he has chosen to repeat it online – the only way he can reach voters personally before Thursday’s byelection.
Meanwhile, social media feeds show handfuls of Workers party activists campaigning in the constituency without their candidate, fighting a peripheral campaign in a byelection considered to be a battle between Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali and Zack Polanski, standing for the Greens.
“Sincere gratitude to my campaigners who are performing miracles on the ground in my enforced absence. Salute to the supporters they are encountering every day. We can win this. And me and my family can come home. Thank you,” Galloway posted at the end of September.
The campaign highlights an anomaly with Britain’s electoral law. Any British, Irish or qualifying Commonwealth citizen over 18 may stand for parliament – as long as they are not bankrupt or members of the police, armed forces, civil servants or judges. There is no requirement to be a registered elector or other residency requirement, according to the Electoral Commission.
Last month, Galloway also revealed he had been “debanked” – his bank accounts suddenly closed – by the Lloyds-owned Bank of Scotland. “Thirty-nine years ago I opened a personal bank account with Bank of Scotland in Byres Rd Glasgow. Yesterday without explanation or notice they closed my accounts,” he posted on 4 September, threatening Lloyds with legal action.
The bank said it would not comment on individual cases, though account closures are rare. A Bank of Scotland spokesperson added: “Our policy is not to close a customer’s account based on political or personal beliefs and we make customers aware if we make the decision to close an account.”
Galloway chose to leave the UK after he and his wife, Putri Gayatri Pertiwi, were stopped for what he said was “a total of 11 hours” in September last year by “five armed police officers” after returning from the Russian city of Nizhny Novgorod and attending a World Youth Festival assembly.
Last month, the former MP said the first question police asked him was: “Why do you admire Mr Lavrov?” They were referring to Russia’s long-serving foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov. Posting on X, Galloway attached a photo of Lavrov smoking and added: “I could have just shown him this picture!”
Galloway told the broadcaster RT, the former Russia Today, in an interview in March this year that officers “took all our stuff and copied everything on our phones”, forcing them to miss a public meeting in London at which, his wife said in a post on Instagram, “the Chinese ambassador [was] waiting for us”.
Neither Galloway nor his wife were subject to any further legal action in a stop that took place under schedule 3 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019. This allows police to detain people to determine if they have been engaged in hostile activity, considered by investigators to be a low bar.
The former MP had appeared on a discussion panel with Lavrov in Moscow in June 2025, at the Forum of the Future, an event described as “far-right” by the Moscow Times, where Elon Musk’s father, Errol, and Alex Jones, the rightwing founder of Infowars, were also speaking.
In Galloway’s March interview with RT, where he had hosted a talkshow for nine years until Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he said he was “now in exile in the east, and I must say that Moscow in the spring is quite the place to be”.
He was in Moscow in late April, speaking at the inaugural conference of Sovintern, an international pro-Soviet socialist network led by the opposition A Just Russia party, where a welcome address from the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, was read out.
In early September, Galloway released a video promoting his online talkshow, filmed from Moscow’s Red Square where he also said he would appear at a roundtable event on security at the city’s “prestigious university”.
On 13 September he participated in a public Sovintern discussion with Zakhar Prilepin, a leading pro-war author and propagandist who has fought in Ukraine and called for “the return of Kyiv to Russia”.
A day later, Galloway was selected as the Workers party candidate, and he shortly afterwards went to South Africa for a speaking and fundraising tour with the leftwing activist and former journalist Yvonne Ridley. He continued to post on social media from South Africa, frequently on international affairs.
He places a particular emphasis on Russia and Ukraine. Earlier this month Galloway posted an anti-Andy Burnham image, with the prime minister dressed in blue and yellow, the colours of Ukraine. “I want you to die for Ukraine. Conscription coming soon!” the caption read.
Particular criticism has also been reserved for Polanski, his most obvious rival for political support. On 25 September, Galloway posted: “I am with Russia Zack is with NATO. I am with an end to the war in Ukraine Zack is with Zelensky and risking WW3.”
Galloway and the Workers party were approached for comment.

UK PM Burnham's Labour Party faces challenge from Greens in Starmer's old seat
LONDON, Oct 8 - Andy Burnham needs to win over voters like tech worker Dani Arbid in a by-election on Thursday if he is to fend off a national threat to his Labour Party from the Greens — and the early signs are encouraging for Britain's new prime minister.
The vote for a parliamentary seat in the inner London electoral district of Holborn and St Pancras, made vacant by the resignation of former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, is a first test of whether Burnham can restore voters' faith in Labour, which saw its popularity among left-wing voters plunge over the war in Gaza.
Many, like Arbid, turned instead to the Greens, helping them to their strongest result ever in local elections in May. Now, he says he is undecided on how he will vote in Thursday's by-election but welcomed Burnham's tougher messaging on Israel and his more ambitious approach to ties with the European Union.
"It's very important to read the room, which I think the current Labour government is doing a lot better job at," Arbid, 38, told Reuters. "There is still room for Labour to kind of claw back some of those losses for sure."
LABOUR TIPPED TO WIN BY-ELECTION
Unlike the national picture, where Nigel Farage's Reform UK poses a serious challenge to Burnham, the by-election is mainly a contest between Labour and the Greens, with thousands of activists from both parties out canvassing in recent weeks.
Burnham hopes to show he can consolidate the left-of-centre vote, strengthening his efforts to take on a British right now split between Reform UK and the Conservatives. But the by-election also offers him a chance to rob the Greens of the momentum they have built up under new leader Zack Polanski.
Polanski himself is the Greens' candidate in Holborn and St Pancras but Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, a local council leader, is tipped to hold the seat for the governing party.
Green gains in areas of London contributed to Labour's dismal local election results in May, which helped set in train a process that culminated on July 20 with Starmer's resignation and his replacement by Burnham.
Since then, however, Labour has rebounded in national opinion polls, while the Greens have suffered setbacks.
At a conference last weekend, Green Party members voted to class Zionism as a form of racism, drawing criticism from British Jewish groups, Israel and even some Green lawmakers. Polanski, who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote.
Burnham's government, which has taken a more critical approach towards Israel and banned the import of goods from West Bank settlements, said the Greens had overstepped a line.
On Camden High Street, an area of London brimming with market stalls and popular with musicians, artists and tourists, Kamran Ahmed, a local resident who works in AI, said Polanski could have managed the issues raised at conference better.
But on a local level he said the Greens had something new to offer, echoing frustration heard around the country that the previously dominant Conservative and Labour parties no longer have the answers.
"Nothing is set in stone, but some of the mainstream parties have over-promised and under-delivered... If you take an area like Camden, it could benefit from some of the fresher thinking that the Green Party offers," Ahmed said.
Damian Lyons Lowe, head of pollster Survation, said the seat was one of the Greens' top targets, and that governments rarely did well at by-elections. But the Greens' anti-Starmer message, which resonated so well in May, was being tested by Burnham.
"Burnham has made direct appeals to Green-minded voters in terms of some of the things they care about," he told Reuters.
"The Burnham vibe check is very different to the Starmer-led Labour government, and that's a problem for the Green Party." REUTERS

Hungary risks situation near energy catastrophe if cut off from Russian gas — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:47:42 UTC
23:47:42 KST

MOSCOW, October 7. /TASS/. Hungary risks finding itself in a situation "bordering on an energy catastrophe" if it is cut off from Russian gas supplies in 2027, Artyom Ilyinsky, a junior research fellow at the Department of European Political Studies at IMEMO RAS, wrote in a column for TASS.
"Technically, Hungary is capable of weaning itself off Russian gas by October 2027. However, this is possible only under the most optimistic forecast. Romanian production must reach planned targets on schedule and without disruption, pipelines must operate at peak capacity, and Budapest will have to cover the shortfall through emergency spot-market purchases. Only in this way can the country bridge the gap to 2028 – the launch date for alternative contracts with Western gas companies," Ilyinsky noted. "For the European Union itself, there is a threat that a member state could find itself in a situation bordering on an energy catastrophe if these bold and optimistic scenarios fail to materialize."
The expert explained that the delivery of major volumes under non-Russian gas agreements is scheduled to begin only in 2028, creating a critical time gap that "will prevent Hungary from navigating the pivotal year of 2027 smoothly."
"At the same time, the stance of external actors – specifically the United States – remains unclear. Hungary has already appealed to the US Congress to avoid the imposition of penalties mandated by the new US sanctions law targeting buyers of Russian oil and gas. Marton Hajdu, head of the Hungarian delegation, stated that he had asked the US side to support the country's transition efforts leading up to 2027 and to allow the continued use of Russian oil and gas for the time being. However, Washington has not yet officially announced its decision. This places Budapest in an awkward position, where the verdict of its transatlantic partner will determine whether the country can weather 2027 or not," Ilyinsky pointed out.
"Hungary has a chance to gradually diversify away from Russian gas. However, an attempt to do so before autumn 2027 – even if new contracts are signed 'here and now' – risks exposing the country to an energy shock. Judging by the cautious tone of the Energy Minister's projections, Budapest might not actually take this painful step," Ilyinsky added.
On September 18, Hungarian Minister of Economy and Energy Istvan Kapitany stated that Hungary's new government, led by Peter Magyar, would be ready to phase out Russian gas by October 2027, the deadline set by the European Union. In an interview with the Telex online news outlet, he noted that negotiations were underway with neighboring countries and LNG suppliers. According to the minister, the necessary cross-border pipeline infrastructure is already in place.
The previous administration under Viktor Orban had launched efforts to diversify supply sources and routes several years ago, citing national security reasons. In 2024, Hungary began purchasing small volumes of gas from Turkey and Azerbaijan, and announced plans to import Qatari LNG starting in 2027. Furthermore, Budapest intends to expand cooperation with Romania to purchase gas from the major Neptun Deep offshore field in the Black Sea. Hungary is connected by gas pipelines to all its neighboring countries except Slovenia.
