EU hopefuls fear new safeguard plans could create second-class members
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:46:54 UTC
23:46:54 KST

EU candidate countries fear safeguards designed to prevent democratic backsliding, like a planned 15-year probation period, could create second-class membership and be used to exert political pressure.
EU candidate countries have raised concerns that new safeguards designed to prevent democratic backsliding after accession could leave them with second-class membership – or give existing member states a powerful tool to exert political pressure.
The concerns follow proposed measures unveiled by the European Commission on Tuesday, including a 15-year probationary period during which new members could lose voting rights if they commit a serious breach of EU values and rules.
"We are counting on the European Union to ensure that the accession process remains ambitious, credible and predictable, and reflects the progress that Ukraine continues to make," Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, told Euronews.
"Our starting point remains full integration into the single market, and any transitional arrangements must be justified, proportionate and time-limited," he added.
Two-tier membership
One of the biggest concerns among candidate countries is that the safeguards could create a second tier of EU membership.
Countries including the Netherlands and France called for tougher safeguards, citing the experience of Hungary under Viktor Orbán and the difficulty of tackling democratic backsliding once a country has joined.
"We do not want a two-tier membership to join our union. Countries need to meet very high standards on the rule of law. We need to be sure that after joining, they never fall below those standards again. And this is what we have learned from experiences in the past," Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said as she presented the measure.
Publicly, candidates have been cautious in their response. Apart from Ukraine, the other three frontrunners – Montenegro, Albania and Moldova – are small countries deeply invested in joining the bloc.
Behind closed doors, however, candidates make no secret of their unease, especially over the 15-year probation period. During that time, newcomers could be stripped of voting rights for serious breaches of EU values and rules. Several had hoped the period would be shorter.
The Commission says this "institutional safeguard clause" is not discriminatory because it is temporary. But while the proposal includes no renewal mechanism, candidates fear member states might push to add one.
"The Commission stresses that this measure is temporary, but there is a significant risk that it might turn into a permanent status. What happens if the probation period gets repeatedly extended or its expiration blocked?" Obrad Kesić, head of Bosnia and Herzegovina's mission to the EU, told Euronews.
Risk of misuse
There is also concern among candidate countries that the safeguards could be used for political purposes, particularly in bilateral disputes with existing member states.
"It is important that the new safeguards should not be abused," said Zlatko Vujović, president of the NGO Centre for Monitoring and Research. "New members should not be blackmailed by old members," he said, pointing to the potential instrumentalisation of bilateral issues.
The threshold for suspending a country's voting rights will therefore be crucial. Candidates want clear safeguards against arbitrary action or attempts to pressure a newcomer into abandoning a strategic national interest.
When the debate over stronger safeguards began, Montenegro's ambassador to the EU, Petar Marković, said any assessment of democratic and rule of law backsliding should rest on objective criteria and systematic breaches.
"We will have very active monitoring precisely in the fields that are covered by the new institutional safeguards," a Commission official told Euronews when asked how such decisions would be made.
The official added that this monitoring would complement an expanded version of the rule of law reports and the information collected under Article 7 of the EU treaty, which allows suspending certain membership rights if a member state seriously and persistently breaches the EU's core values.
The idea is to make triggering easier than under Article 7. That provision allows measures against a member state that undermines the Union's functioning, but only with the unanimity of all the other member states. In Hungary's case, a sympathetic Polish government stood in the way.
Under the Commission's proposal, however, a decision would go through unless opposed by a qualified majority of member states. That prompts fears it would be far too easy to act against a newcomer that does not toe the line.
The procedure could be triggered by the Commission or by a "reasoned request" from member states. But its details, which are crucial for newcomers, will be negotiated only in the accession treaty.
Political bargaining
The Commission's proposals are non-binding and are likely to become a major point of contention in the final stages of accession negotiations.
"The transitional periods have to be negotiated between the member states and the country that wants to become a member of the EU. When it is negotiated, it will become a part of the accession treaty," Kos said.
That means the safeguards will be tailored to each newcomer's circumstances, but also to its bargaining position and its eventual relations with current member states, friends and sceptics alike.
"Our objective remains full accession to the EU, with equal rights and responsibilities," Cristina Gherasimov, Moldova's deputy prime minister for European integration, said on Facebook after the announcement.
The calculation in Brussels is that stronger safeguards could make it easier for enlargement-sceptical countries such as France and the Netherlands to accept new members when the time comes to ratify their accession treaties.
There is also an expectation that Montenegro, first in line to join, may set the blueprint for future accession treaties. But its determination to complete the process may leave it with little leverage to resist tougher conditions.
"Montenegro would accept anything. They are very keen to conclude the process, almost at any cost," a diplomat from a candidate country told Euronews, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Sasha Vakulina contributed to the reporting.

07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Italy’s Chamber of Deputies approved the government’s third and final confidence vote Wednesday on an electoral reform bill, paving the way for a final secret ballot Thursday, according to public broadcaster Rai.
Lawmakers backed the confidence motion on Article 3 by a 228-144 vote, with three abstentions. The provision redraws several electoral constituencies in South Tyrol, including Merano, Bressanone and Bolzano.
The lower house approved confidence motions Tuesday on Articles 1 and 2, covering the electoral systems for the Chamber of Deputies and Senate.
Lawmakers also approved Article 8 on Wednesday in a 214-0 vote, while opposition parties abstained. The provision extends voting away from one’s place of residence to family caregivers. The government did not attach a confidence motion to that article.
The reform, which has passed the Senate and returned to the lower house following amendments, has drawn strong criticism from opposition parties.
Its provisions include voter preferences alongside fixed lead candidates on party lists, as well as changes to electoral rules.
Women’s associations in Modena have appealed to President Sergio Mattarella to return the legislation to parliament if he identifies constitutional concerns, arguing that its candidate selection rules undermine equal access to elected office.
A network opposing the reform also said it was preparing legal challenges to file once the law takes effect, seeking a referral to the Constitutional Court.
The parliamentary votes come amid debate about possible early elections in May. Deputy Prime Minister and Forza Italia leader Antonio Tajani said Tuesday that his party favored completing the parliamentary term.

Satellite images show attack jets at Chinese military facility in Laos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:46:01 UTC
23:46:01 KST

Satellite images show attack jets stationed at a new Chinese military facility in Laos, which opened last week and gives Beijing’s air force its first foothold in mainland south-east Asia.
Images provided by the commercial satellite provider Vantor show eight light attack aircraft positioned at Ban Keun airport alongside what appear to be more than a dozen military vehicles lined up in rows.
The planes’ shape matches that of the Chinese-made Hongdu JL-8 jet, a two-seat trainer that can be deployed in combat to carry bombs. Laos is reported to have four such aircraft, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
In a rare example of Beijing’s overseas military expansion, China opened what it said was a joint “support and training centre” at Ban Keun on 29 September.
The airport, about 30 miles (50km) north of Vientiane, the capital of Laos, has been significantly expanded over the past year. Satellite images taken months ago show farmland and dirt paths where there are now new buildings and a paved runway.
Aside from its island bases in the South China Sea, Beijing does not have a significant network of military outposts in other countries, and the Laos airbase would be its first facility in another country capable of handling fighter jets.
The new satellite images, taken a day after the announcement and first reported by Reuters, show extensive construction work that appears to be focused on a future runway extension, which could make the airport capable of handling larger planes such as bombers.
In its announcement last week, China’s defence ministry said the new centre would “help Laos strengthen the training of its air force pilots” and was not “directed against any third party”.
Governments will be watching closely for signs of deployments or the installation of defence equipment that may serve wider military ambitions. After the announcement, the Singapore-based security analyst Collin Koh said it “may not be wrong to conclude this is the first full-fledged PLA [People’s Liberation Army] overseas base in south-east Asia”.
Over the past two decades, China has built up an extensive network of outposts on islands in the disputed South China Sea, including airbases with air defence installations. Otherwise, its navy’s sole overseas military base is a logistics base in Djibouti, on the coast of the Horn of Africa.
The Laos agreement follows a similar programme established in Cambodia, at the Ream naval base on the Gulf of Thailand, although that facility has no runway.
After years of speculation and denials, China announced in April last year that it had created the “joint logistics and training” facility in Cambodia. It said the centre would support the two militaries in “conducting regional counter-terrorism, disaster prevention and mitigation, humanitarian assistance, joint training and other operations”.
US forces are believed to have used Ban Keun airport in Laos during covert military operations at the height of the Vietnam war in the 1960s and 1970s. Its development will be monitored by Vietnam, which maintains disputes with China over the South China Sea, and Thailand, which shares a border with Laos.
After the announcement last week, Thailand’s defence ministry spokesperson said Bangkok considered itself a close partner of both Laos and China and saw it as Vientiane’s sovereign right to decide whether to grant permission for a Chinese base.
“Nevertheless, Thailand will continue to closely monitor developments and how the matter proceeds, particularly with regard to building mutual trust,” said R Adm Surasant Kongsiri.
China’s government did not mention sending aircraft to Laos in its initial announcement, while the government of Laos has not commented on the project.
The US-based Institute for the Study of War has described the Laos base as the “first PLA overseas military facility focused on air power”. In its assessment, the thinktank said the base was “not yet equipped to provide the PLA with the ability to execute major combat operations, unlike US military bases”.
It said the base would give the Chinese military alternate routes to access to the South China Sea and strategic air routes.
Reuters contributed to this report

Could the UK really rejoin the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:45:52 UTC
23:45:52 KST

It was lobbed into the national conversation without fanfare or warning, almost a footnote in the UK prime minister’s first speech as leader to his governing Labour party’s annual conference last week. But Andy Burnham has kicked off a quiet U-turn on Brexit.
By stating bluntly that the decision to leave Europe’s core political community had done “more harm than good”, Burnham broke a taboo in his own party, in effect, discarding his predecessor’s paralysing ‘red lines’ on Europe, and signalling he will not be bound by these constraints after the next British election.
Over the coming six weeks Burnham will gauge public support before setting out options for the UK’s long term relationship with the UK’s largest market. Rejoining the 27-nation bloc will be one of them. Burnham is opening the door to Britain reversing Brexit.
The famous red lines, or non-negotiables, enshrined by Keir Starmer in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, were meant to reassure Brexit-supporting voters that under Labour there would be no return to a single market, customs union or the free movement of people. But these pledges left Starmer with little room for manoeuvre with Europe, beyond warm words.
The evidence that Brexit has stunted the British economy is not new. Estimates for the damage quitting the single market has already done range from 6% of 8% of GDP. What is new is a prime ministerial readiness to publicly acknowledge that harm and conclude that an ambitious new path is required.
“This is the first time that a UK politician in power has been willing to stand up and say that Brexit is a failure that we must address or redress in some fundamental way,” Joël Reland, an analyst with the UK In a Changing Europe thinktank, told me. “Keir Starmer’s public message was that we will be sticking with Boris Johnson’s [2019] Brexit deal, but we’re going to improve it to make Brexit work. Burnham is saying Brexit doesn’t work and that we need a different form of deal. That has never been said before.”
Burnham is not yet committing himself to fighting the next election on a particular course of action. Much will depend on the response he gets. But all options – Lisa O’Carroll details them here – are on the table, from a customs union to re-joining the single market and becoming, like Norway, a rule-taker, to “going all the way”.
But crucially, Burnham has already departed from the orthodoxy that makes questioning Brexit a heresy. Instead of shutting down the topic to limit his exposure to Eurosceptic attacks, the prime minister is meeting it head-on, Reland said. “Burnham could have done what every other leader before him has done since the 2016 referendum, and take a clear red-lines position against Brexit, but he didn’t. And I don’t see why you would do that unless you wanted to take on the political argument”.
Why would Burnham choose this juncture and risk drawing down what Rafael Behr calls the Brexit curse?
The economic rationale is the obvious one. “Burnham’s ten year domestic agenda promises radical reform of such things as the social care system, and somebody is going to have to pay for that,” argues Reland. “One of the ways you can get economic growth is by rejoining your largest and closest trading partner.”
The modest ‘re-set’ agenda launched by Starmer in May 2025 is stuck, bogged down in disputes, such as that over fees for EU students in the UK. A pencilled-in 20 November summit is still up in the air. Britain’s big impediment from outside the club is its lack of bargaining power. A cherrypicking attempt to coax the EU into a selective single market for goods only (without free movement of people) was firmly rebuffed by Brussels in May. And even if this reset were fully delivered, the government’s own figures estimate it would add at most, 0.3% to GDP by 2040.
Labour meanwhile has lost votes to its left, particularly to the Greens, so a more progressive offer on Europe might be a gamble worth taking. New polling, as Pippa Crerar and Rowena Mason revealed at the weekend, shows that if Burnham’s preference is for rejoining the EU, almost half of the country already agrees.
Gaby Hinsliff noted that among Burnham’s opponents the only one to react to the surprise move with “unfettered glee” was Nigel Farage. Yet, she suggested, the Conservatives, also obsessed with economic growth, may not side with Farage given that most voters think Brexit has made them economically worse off. “It’s not in Tory long-term interests to strangle this at birth” wrote Hinsliff.
A warm welcome?
Events in Europe are also dictating the pace. “Welcome back!” was the French president Emmanuel Macron’s possibly tongue-in-cheek response to Burnham’s remarks. But it is a French-led project called “Made in Europe” that is both concentrating the PM’s mind and could ultimately undermine his ambition.
Made in Europe is a highly protectionist idea for turning the EU into an industrial powerhouse, able to withstand competition from China. UK-made goods, if legally classified as non-European under the law, would be locked out, spelling trade devastation for the British car industry. France, facing its own domestic upheaval and crunch elections next April, is being hardline about Britain’s exclusion: Macron’s ministers insist that if you’re not paying the costs of the internal market you don’t get to claim the benefits. Made in Europe is emerging as a symbol, Reland explained, of how geopolitics is driving the EU’s agenda, and widening its range of competencies to such areas as industrial policy, AI and tech sovereignty. “It is no longer just food and environment policy that is set at EU level but the big, strategic, hard security decisions too,” he said.
The more that EU countries strategically pool sovereignty to respond to shocks such as US trade aantagonism or Russian hybrid warfare, and the more aggressively they protect that cooperation, the steeper the costs of being outside the club become. With Norway and Switzerland, both non-EU members with single market access, now also facing the Made in Europe battle, it’s no wonder Burnham is mulling the full rejoin option.
But, as Mujtaba Rahman’s prescient column advised, the coming debate will need to go beyond the question of whether Britain could contemplate rejoining, to an honest assessment of what Europe has become in the years since it left.

The Quiet, Careful Growth of Philippine-Taiwan Ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:44:00 UTC
23:44:00 KST

On October 2, the Philippine Coast Guard commissioned BRP Sarangani, a retired Taiwanese Coast Guard cutter formerly known as the Kinmen. The transfer is unusual because Taiwan only transfers decommissioned vessels to states that officially recognize Taiwan’s statehood, which the Philippines does not.
Furthermore, the vessel did not sail from Kaohsiung to Manila under the Taiwanese flag, government-to-government, the way Taipei’s other patrol-vessel donations have gone to Palau, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu – states that recognize the Republic of China (Taiwan). Instead, the Philippine nongovernmental organization We Protect Our Seas (WPS) Foundation quietly acquired the Kinmen, renamed it, repainted it, and handed it to the Philippine Coast Guard in a ceremony that never mentioned where the ship had come from.
The reason for this indirect approach is obvious: the Philippines adheres to the One China policy and would not like to provoke China. Unofficial engagements with Taiwan, carried out by states like the United States, France, Singapore, the United Kingdom, and Germany that formally recognize China, are a global default. China explicitly tolerates their economic and cultural relations with Taiwan.
So what makes the Philippines’ engagement with Taiwan different, and why is Manila engaging with Taiwan so extensively now when its relationship with China is tenser than in the past two decades?
The Philippines as a Distinct Case
For most of the above-mentioned states, Taiwan policy is about standing up for democracy and alliance management, conducted at a safe distance – being geographically far away from the immediate threat of military conflict with China. However, the Philippines is in close proximity to Taiwan. The Philippine province of Batanes lies south of Taiwan, near the Bashi Channel, placing it closer to spillover from the Taiwan conflict.
Adding to this are 200,000 Filipino workers currently in Taiwan, whose evacuation during a Taiwan crisis would pose an emergency for the Philippine government. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has publicly stated that Taiwan’s security is inseparable from the Philippines’ own, making clear that Taiwan is a national security question rather than an elective foreign policy stance.
Yet Manila must tread carefully. Anything it does with Taiwan that upsets China is directly visible in Chinese assertiveness in the South China Sea, affecting Filipino sovereignty and fisheries.
The Philippines’ increased engagement with Taiwan predates the Marcos administration. Taiwan is the Philippines’ ninth-largest trading partner, with established cooperation in education, agriculture, and healthcare and growing interest in semiconductors and start-ups. Under Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte (in office from 2016-2022), the Philippines and Taiwan signed a bilateral investment agreement in 2017 – the first major investment agreement in the last 25 years – under Taiwan’s New Southbound Policy, with cooperation extending across trade, investment, education, and labor mobility. But this engagement made sense given that the Philippines was in a state of rapprochement with China.
What has changed now is the strategic significance of Philippines-Taiwan engagement. Economic and cultural ties are increasingly accompanied by institutional and maritime cooperation. In April 2025, the Philippines eased restrictions on official exchanges with Taiwan, facilitating travel for economic and trade-related purposes. This was highlighted by Taiwanese Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung’s visit to Manila, the second such foreign minister visit to the Philippines since 1975. Taiwan’s subsequent proposal to open a second representative office in Cebu to deepen the “Taiwan-Philippine Corridor” further signaled an effort to deepen institutional engagement.
Maritime cooperation has become increasingly apparent. What began as crisis management following the 2013 killing of a Taiwanese fisherman by Philippine personnel has created a basis for maritime cooperation, despite the absence of diplomatic recognition.
The WPS Foundation confirmed that the recently transferred vessel, BRP Sarangani, will support maritime patrols, search and rescue, humanitarian assistance, disaster response, and training. The transfer of vessels between two coast guards without requiring an overt government-to-government transaction demonstrates how institutional informality can create political space for cooperation that formal diplomatic relations might otherwise constrain.
Last year, the Philippine and Taiwanese Coast Guard conducted patrols in the Bashi Channel. Taiwan’s Coast Guard is also planning to send vessels to visit the Philippines in 2027, the first visit since the Philippines switched its recognition from the ROC to the People’s Republic of China in 1975.
But why is the Philippines doing this now, when China has become more assertive? One plausible explanation is that the Philippines sees little benefit in restraining its engagement with Taiwan. Chinese pressure in the South China Sea continued despite Manila’s previously cautious approach to Taiwan, giving Philippine policymakers fewer reasons to believe that restraint will win China’s goodwill.
At the same time, the Philippines cannot match China militarily or economically. Deepening ties with Taiwan offer the Philippines a way to widen its strategic and economic options at a relatively low cost. Manila can strengthen cooperation with a partner that provides investment, technology, and security benefits, while also engaging with an issue that China considers highly sensitive. Whether this amounts to deliberate tit-for-tat is difficult to establish, but the effect is clear: the Philippines has less incentive than before to keep its Taiwan relationship within narrow limits simply to avoid displeasing China.
Keeping It Under the Threshold
While the Philippines has steadily expanded its engagement with Taiwan, it has stopped short of turning that engagement into overt alignment, as seen in the vessel transfer through a non-governmental organization and the Philippine government’s refusal to publicly recognize it as a formerly Taiwanese vessel. Manila has repeatedly affirmed that its One China policy remains “consistent, clear and unchanged” and that “economic, cultural, and functional cooperation with Taiwan” does not violate it. Military and security engagements such as tabletop exercises or patrols are consistently described as “unofficial and informal.” Even the April 2025 easing of visa restrictions excludes visits and exchanges over defense- and security-related issues. Furthermore, no agreements, Memoranda of Understanding (MoU), exchange of notes or similar documents can proceed without clearance from the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) and, where necessary, an authorization from the Office of the President.
This caution reflects Manila’s awareness that spillover from a Taiwan crisis would be unavoidable. Under the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, U.S. forces could rely on Philippine bases to support operations in a Taiwan crisis. Yet Filipino officials have been explicit that they do not want the Philippines drawn into such a conflict – a position echoed by the public, with roughly 86 percent of Filipinos saying that they want the country to remain neutral in a China-Taiwan conflict. Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Thersea Lazaro has said that Manila is open to discussions with China over evacuation plans for its citizens in the event of a Chinese invasion of Taiwan.
The throughline is consistent: Manila wants to preserve its One China policy so Beijing has less reason to treat Philippine security as fair game in any future crisis.

CIS countries concerned by forecast of arms race in outer space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:43:04 UTC
23:43:04 KST

TURKMENBASHI, Turkmenistan, October 7. /TASS/. The CIS Foreign Ministers have adopted a joint statement "on support for practical steps to prevent an arms race in outer space," the Executive Committee of the Commonwealth said.
"The CIS member States express serious concern about the real prospect of an arms race in outer space and its transformation into an arena of military confrontation, which weakens global stability. The parties note that a ban on the deployment of weapons of any kind in outer space, the use of force or threats of force against space objects or with their help could prevent the emergence of a serious threat to international peace and security. The parties also emphasize the inadmissibility of using space systems and related ground infrastructure for purposes incompatible with ensuring international peace, security and confidence-building between states," it said in a statement.
The document noted the crucial importance of immediately taking practical measures to prevent an arms race in outer space, the most effective of which remains negotiations of the international community on a multilateral legally binding and guaranteeing instrument.
"The CIS member states note the broad support for the resolutions Non-Deployment of the First Weapons in Outer Space approved at the 80th session of the UN General Assembly, Further Practical Measures for the PAROS (Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space - TASS) and Transparency and Confidence-Building Measures in Outer Space Activities as evidence that the international community shares their objectives in preventing an arms race in outer space," the statement said.
Meeting of the Council of the CIS Foreign Ministers was held on Wednesday in the Avaza National Tourist Zone. The document was signed by the foreign ministers of Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Russia, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan.

Pro-Palestinian protesters and counter-protesters clashed in central London on Wednesday as police intervened during a demonstration in Russell Square.
Pro-Israel protesters approached students supporting Palestine who wanted to continue the march and hurled insults at them.
British police detained several people from both groups but had not yet released an exact number.
Students from King’s College London, the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), University College London (UCL) and the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS), protesting Israel’s genocide in the Gaza Strip, which has entered its third year, began a march from King’s College London in solidarity with the Palestinian people.
The group organizing the pro-Palestinian protest later told participants to disperse.
The demonstration, which was scheduled to end at 2 pm local time (1300GMT), concluded at around 1.15 pm (1215GMT), with activists saying they would disperse for security reasons.
Marching toward University College London in Russell Square, the students carried Palestinian flags and chanted slogans along the route, including “End the genocide in Gaza” and “Leave the Palestinian people alone.”
When the university students reached Russell Square, they came face-to-face with a pro-Israel group. As the two groups exchanged chants, police officers moved between them and took security measures.
The pro-Israel protesters reportedly approached students supporting Palestine who wanted to continue the march and hurled insults at them.
‘Israeli army soldiers move fully freely’ in London
One of the protesters, speaking to Anadolu, said the rally had been approved by the Home Office and that demonstrators were protesting in support of Palestine and calling for an end to Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
The protester said several people he identified as Israeli soldiers had followed and harassed demonstrators in the streets of London.
“While we rallying for Palestine to stop the genocide and stop the lobby, Zionist lobby to fund Israel, we been attacked by a few Israeli army soldiers in the street of London, they are fully free. They move fully freely, following us, harassing us, saying words, using all bad words, and us as as as we all know, we’ve been we’ve been rallying for like three years.”
“We have zero crime committed. We are abiding by the law. We have followed every single instruction the police give to us,” he said.
He also said that a group of counter-protesters had gathered in advance in an attempt to provoke confrontations and lead to arrests.
Despite the clashes, the protester said demonstrators would continue their march toward the Home Office, adding that they would not abandon their cause.
The protester said activists had been holding demonstrations for around three years and maintained that they would continue to rally in support of Palestine.
The Metropolitan Police imposed strict conditions on the march, warning that anyone who breached them could be arrested.
Deputy Assistant Commissioner James Harman, who leads Met operations including public order policing, said police could not ban the protest unless the risk of serious disorder was so high that it could not be managed through conditions.
“We hear the calls for this event to be banned. The police cannot ban protests and can only ask the Home Secretary to do so if the risk of serious disorder is so high that it can’t be managed by conditions. That high bar is not met here,” Harman said in a statement Tuesday.
He also rejected claims on social media that the Met had banned other protests, including a UKIP march in Tower Hamlets.
“This will be a day of mourning and reflection for many in London and we know the serious concerns that this event has caused Jewish communities in particular,” Harman said.
“We have imposed stringent conditions on those taking part in this march. These will help us manage the event and minimise serious disruption.”
Since October 2023, Israeli attacks have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 in Gaza. About 90% of the territory’s infrastructure has been destroyed.
Despite an October 2025 ceasefire agreement between Israel and the Palestinian group Hamas, Israeli attacks have since killed 1,454 Palestinians and wounded another 5,090, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Genocide and the slow erosion of the family in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Ali Abu al-Ezz, 38, lives with his six children near the “Yellow Line” in Gaza City’s eastern Tuffah neighborhood. His children range in age from 13 to two years old. After they were displaced from their land following the demarcation of the Yellow Line, Abu al-Ezz pitched a tent for his family as close to their home in Tuffah as he could, hoping that one day they would be able to return.
The tent they live in is far from their daily needs and necessities. Food is difficult to reach, humanitarian organizations distributing water and meals are scarce, and medical facilities and schools are far away. When the new school year began last December, Abu al-Ezz did not send any of his children to attend. In fact, he rarely ever leaves the area, preferring to stay close to his wife and children.
Before the war, Abu al-Ezz’s children attended nearby schools regularly, while he worked as a taxi driver, heading out in the morning and driving until sunset to support his family. Today, the war has imposed an entirely different reality.
“The road to the schools is long and difficult, the streets are not fit for walking, and transportation is also hard to find,” Abu al-Ezz said. “I am afraid that if I send my children to school, a quadcopter will shoot and kill them, or their school will be bombed, and they will die. I decided to postpone all of their education until the war ends, when we can feel safe in our own country again.”
The war has affected families beyond their homes and how they obtain food and water. It has altered the very meaning of family life and the roles that parents and children are expected to play within it.
Despite the blockade and hardships that had long shaped life in Gaza before the war, families could still maintain a semblance of an ordinary social order. Children went to school and played outside together. Even if they made playgrounds and football pitches out of busy streets and lots, they still had space to live their childhood.
That balance has been shattered.
For many fathers, parenthood has become an unending attempt to keep their children alive. Mothers cook over open fires and devise ways to keep rodents out of tents while trying to maintain some measure of cleanliness in conditions that make it nearly impossible. And children, among those most profoundly affected by the war, have been forced into roles that once belonged to adults.
“Some days, I leave in the morning to try to make some money or find some work for the day,” Abu al-Ezz said. “By the time I return with whatever I have earned and some food for my children, my eldest sons will have taken care of other things.”
His sons – Ibrahim, 13, and Hassan, 11 – are responsible for finding drinking water for the family.
“These were never my children’s responsibilities,” Abu al-Ezz said. “But the war has forced these children to carry responsibilities far beyond their age, responsibility for the family itself and for finding the things we need to survive.”
The boys fetch water and search the streets and rubble for pieces of wood to burn for cooking. They return during the hottest hours of the day, walking under the sun while carrying jerrycans of water that, their father says, seem to weigh as much as they do after months of hunger.
Before the war, this time of year sounded very different inside Abu al-Ezz’s home. His children would return from school, filling the house with stories about their classmates and teachers. A new school year meant excitement over new books, school bags, and stationery.
“We lived under siege, and our circumstances were difficult, but our lives were beautiful,” he said. “We lived in our homes. We visited our relatives, and they visited us. We went to the sea to relax. Every month, we would have barbecues on the beach or on our roof. We were happy with the little we had, and we thanked God for what He gave us.”
For Abu al-Ezz, deprivation has penetrated almost every aspect of his family’s life. The infants cry from hunger while their parents search for formula, the children suffer as their daily needs cannot be met, and even his wife’s personal necessities have become difficult to obtain.
“We live as if we have been cut off from the world,” he said. “As if we do not belong to this modern age. It feels as though we are living in the Stone Age, not 2026.”
“And the strangest thing of all is that the world watches us and sees this, yet nothing changes in the miserable life we are living,” he continued.
When children dream of food and shelter
The war has changed not only what children do, but also what they dream about.
For Ibrahim, Abu al-Ezz’s 13-year-old son, aspirations have narrowed to the most basic elements of a livable life.
He dreams of leaving behind the makeshift tent his family assembled from scraps of fabric and wood. Every winter, when heavy rain floods the area, the family risks losing their only shelter. On some nights, they sleep sitting upright on plastic chairs to keep themselves above the water flooding the tent from all sides.
Ibrahim dreams of a Qatari tent, the name Gazans commonly use for the dome-shaped tents that are considered better able to withstand winter rain because of their sturdier fabric and construction.
But his dreams extend beyond shelter, for the simplest things. “I dream that one day we will eat three good meals,” Ibrahim said.
He also dreams of going to his grandfather’s house and playing with his cousins, and of having just one more of the evenings his father once organized on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore: the entire family gathered together for a barbecue by the sea.
Now Abu al-Ezz’s extended family has been scattered. Relatives live far from one another, each in a different tent, each confronting their own conditions of displacement and survival.
A family scattered across Gaza
The transformation of family life in Gaza is not limited to children or their parents. The rituals that once held extended families together, from visiting relatives’ homes to evening gatherings to sharing meals and stories, have all been disrupted.
For older women in particular, the contrast between life before and after the war can be stark.
Before the war, many spent their later years surrounded by children and grandchildren, living in established family homes and enjoying the companionship of nearby relatives of their generation.
Hanan Abu Arab, 63, was one of them.
Displaced from eastern Khan Younis and now living in Deir al-Balah, Abu Arab once had a five-story house where her children and grandchildren gathered. In front of it was a garden where she sometimes received close friends and relatives. They would sit beside rose bushes she had planted herself, spending hours together in the evening, talking and drinking tea.
Today, she hesitates to even name her new home as a tent. “It is more like a room wrapped in cloth,” she said. “It is not properly enclosed.”
During the winter, rain enters from every direction. Sometimes, she said, she has to leave and stand by the roadside, searching for any roof or overhang that might shelter her from the rain.
“My house was a landmark in Bani Suheila because of how beautiful it was,” Abu Arab said. “My relatives who lived nearby would come almost every day. We stayed up together, ate fruit, and talked for hours. Everyone who entered my house would tell me how beautiful it was.”
“All of those traditions are gone,” she added.
Abu Arab sees this fragmentation as one of the less visible consequences of the war. Everyone, she said, is pushed toward the same calculation: Protect yourself and your children, stay away from danger, leave the tent as little as possible, and hope that, by doing so, death will pass you by.
“This is one of the hidden goals of this genocide,” she said. “For the Israeli army to tear apart everything that connects Palestinians, everything that creates a social fabric and solidarity in Gaza, and replace it with this constant, urgent need for individual survival.”

Ukraine's 413th Separate Raid Regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces struck the Snizhne Machine-Building Plant in occupied Donetsk Oblast in September, working with other Defense Forces units, the regiment posted on 6 October, sharing a video of the strike. The General Staff reported the strike on the plant on 11 September, saying that the extent of the damage was being clarified.
The strike adds to Ukraine's campaign of long-range attacks on Russian military targets as Russia has begun its winter campaign of strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure. Hitting the suppliers of aircraft parts goes after Russia's ability to keep its attack jets and helicopters flying.
The regiment said the plant works for Russia's military industry, producing engine components for attack aircraft and combat helicopters.
A former Motor Sich plant in occupied Snizhne
The Snizhne plant was a separate division of Motor Sich, a Ukrainian aircraft-engine maker based in Zaporizhzhia, a city that remains under Ukrainian control. Snizhne has been under Russian occupation since 2014. The plant specializes in producing parts for gas-turbine engines, including compressor and turbine discs and blades, the General Staff said. It never built whole engines. In September 2014, months into the occupation, it was machining blanks from Motor Sich's Zaporizhzhia plant into turbine blades and was one of only two plants in the former Soviet Union making such blades for helicopters, a plant worker said.
Motor Sich said in December 2017 that it had lost control of the plant. Weeks later, Viacheslav Bohuslaiev, then Motor Sich's honorary president and a member of parliament, told RFE/RL's Donbas.Realii that Motor Sich still owned the plant and had handed its management to a foreign company, while keeping it under the company's "full control."
In February 2023, Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office served Bohuslaiev a notice of suspicion of aiding a terrorist organization, alleging that Motor Sich shipped blanks to the Snizhne plant and received finished engine parts through foreign-registered companies. The case went to court in October 2023, and Bohuslaiev, who denies the charges, has been in pretrial detention since October 2022 as the trial continues.
Snizhne, which Russia uses as a rear base, has been hit before. In May, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and the Security Service of Ukraine struck a Russian training center for drone pilots in the city, and in September, a strike on energy infrastructure cut power across Snizhne.

Sudan army chief rejects talks with rebels

Sudan army chief rejects talks with rebels
Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has reiterated his rejection of negotiations with the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), vowing to continue the military campaign against the group.
Burhan, who also chairs Sudan’s Transitional Sovereignty Council, made the remarks on Tuesday during a visit to the Amri area in the country’s Northern State.
“We say it again: We have no negotiations with anyone, we are not speaking with anyone, and we have nothing to do with anyone,” Burhan said, according to the Sudan Tribune.
The army chief also reiterated the military’s intention to continue its campaign against the RSF. “We tell the rebels among you that we are coming to you with force,” he said. “We want to uproot the enemy and eliminate it completely.”
The remarks came as fighting continues between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the RSF in Darfur, Kordofan, and Blue Nile. Much of Darfur remains under RSF control, while the army has been seeking to advance into the region.
Burhan has repeatedly rejected negotiations with the RSF during the conflict. In May 2024, he said, “there will be no negotiations, no peace, and no ceasefire” until the RSF was defeated. In April this year, he again ruled out talks with the paramilitary group or its supporters.
Sudan’s conflict erupted in April 2023 following months of tensions between the SAF and the RSF.
Sudan descended into chaos in April 2023 when fighting erupted between the national army, the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict followed months of tension between their commanders, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan and Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, over a planned transition to civilian rule. What began in the capital, Khartoum, as a power struggle has devastated the country, killing tens of thousands, displacing millions, and pushing parts of Sudan into famine.
Regional and international peace efforts, including African Union mediation and Saudi-US talks in Jeddah, have repeatedly stalled. In September 2025, the Quad group – the US, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and the United Arab Emirates – proposed a three-month humanitarian truce leading to a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led political transition. Burhan rejected a subsequent US-led proposal that November, arguing it would dismantle state security institutions while leaving the RSF in place. The paramilitaries said they accepted the truce.
The UAE’s involvement has deepened mistrust of mediation. Sudan’s army-backed government severed diplomatic ties with Abu Dhabi in May 2025, accusing it of supporting the RSF. The UAE denies supplying weapons to the paramilitaries. Relations with Washington deteriorated further in September 2026 after the US questioned both factions’ legitimacy. Sudan rejected the remarks and called for peace efforts free from foreign dictates.
Meanwhile, rival administrations have entrenched Sudan’s divisions. Burhan’s government returned to Khartoum in January 2026 after the army recaptured the capital, having operated from Port Sudan during the fighting. In July 2025, the RSF-aligned TASIS coalition announced a rival government based in Nyala, Darfur, with Dagalo heading its governing council. The UN Security Council and African Union rejected the move.
On Sunday, US senior adviser for Arab and African affairs Massad Boulos met with Burhan in Egypt. “The United States stands ready to support all efforts leading to a comprehensive dialogue among the Sudanese political forces, leading to a preliminary road map of the future of the Sudan,” Boulos said. The meeting, however, followed a dispute over Burhan’s planned trip to the UN General Assembly in New York last month, when the US did not issue him an entry visa. Foreign Minister Mohieldin Salim Ahmed Ibrahim had to address the gathering on his behalf.
In his address, Salim called for international pressure on foreign parties supporting the RSF, saying peace would require the paramilitary group to be disarmed and weapons to remain under the control of state institutions.

Halis Sünnetci
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
 OpenAI's ChatGPT for Teens poses an "unacceptable risk" to children despite recently introduced safety measures, according to an assessment by the Common Sense Media's Youth AI Safety Institute.
The organization urged OpenAI to restrict ChatGPT to users aged 18 and older until it addresses shortcomings researchers identified in parental alerts, crisis responses, learning protections and age estimation.
Researchers tested more than 4,000 prompts on accounts registered to users aged 13 to 17 and had responses reviewed by experts, including child psychiatrists and a pediatrician.
The institute said newly created accounts linked to parents generated no alerts even when testers spent up to an hour discussing suicidal thoughts, self-harm or disordered eating.

OpenAI disputed the assessment, saying much of the testing may have taken place before parental controls were fully activated and therefore did not accurately reflect how its teen safeguards work in practice.
The institute said it had confirmed with OpenAI before testing that the Teen Mode features were fully launched and stood by its findings.

A dietitian explained the benefits of mackerel and how to eat it properly
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:37:46 EEST
23:37:46 KST

A dietitian explained the benefits of mackerel and how to eat it properly
Kyiv • UNN
Mackerel contains omega-3, vitamins D3 and B12, and protein. The dietitian recommends baking fresh fish and limiting salted and smoked varieties.
Mackerel is a source of omega-3, vitamins D3 and B12, and high-quality protein. Dietitian Oleksandr Kushch told UNN in a comment about the benefits this fish can provide to the body, who should limit salted and smoked fish, and how to choose mackerel properly.
Omega-3, vitamins and protein: the benefits of mackerel
Mackerel is a fatty marine fish. At the same time, according to the dietitian, its fat contains polyunsaturated fatty acids that are important for the body. In addition, the fish contains significant amounts of vitamins and protein.
Mackerel is a fatty marine fish, and unlike meat, its fat consists of unsaturated fats—namely, polyunsaturated fatty acids that the fish accumulates in the cold waters of the Atlantic. These are primarily omega-3 fatty acids—very beneficial polyunsaturated fatty acids that have a positive effect on the prevention of atherosclerosis, brain function, cognitive abilities, and the overall condition of the central and peripheral nervous systems. In addition, mackerel is rich in vitamin B12. About 100 grams of mackerel contain the daily requirement of vitamin D3, which is very important for bones and the immune system
In addition, as the doctor explains, vitamin D3 is important for various processes in the body. Another advantage of mackerel is its nutritional value, while the fish also remains one of the more affordable products.
Vitamin D3 is highly multifunctional. In terms of its chemical structure, it resembles hormones and serves as a raw material for the production of sex hormones in our bodies, such as testosterone, progesterone and estrogen. It also affects the state of the immune system, regulates calcium metabolism, and strengthens bones, teeth and ligaments. In addition, mackerel is relatively inexpensive and is an excellent source of protein: 100 grams of this fish contain about 18–20 grams of high-quality protein
Oleksandr Kushch also emphasizes that fish can be a source of protein, vitamins and micronutrients, and this is especially relevant during the cold season, when people receive less sunlight.
Unlike, for example, Scandinavian countries, Ukrainians currently consume very little fish, seafood and seaweed. And everything we obtain from the sea is a source of micronutrients, high-quality protein and beneficial vitamins. Therefore, people should not become fixated on monodiets in which they eat only chicken from morning till night or just buckwheat. It is important to have diverse sources of protein, vitamins and micronutrients. This is especially true in autumn and winter, when we get less vitamin D from sunlight
Can you eat mackerel while losing weight? The doctor separately explained whether people trying to lose weight should be afraid of the fats in mackerel.
There is no need to be afraid of the fat in fish. These are not the kinds of fats that accumulate under the skin and contribute to excess weight. If we fry it in oil, the fish will simply absorb that fat like a sponge, and then, yes, we may consume extra calories and trans fats. But if we cook mackerel properly, all the fats it contains are very beneficial. Therefore, mackerel is quite suitable for people who are watching their weight or trying to lose weight, provided it is not fried in oil or made too salty
At the same time, the dietitian recommends combining different types of fish, meat, eggs and dairy products in the diet.
There is no strict daily or weekly portion of mackerel. I would like people to consume different varieties of fish and meat, eggs and dairy products—all of these are sources of protein. It is better when a person has three to five sources of high-quality animal and plant protein. Then they have enough energy and building material to restore muscles and any cells in the body
In addition, the doctor says, the method of preparation also affects the nutritional value of the product. The dietitian considers fresh fish that has not undergone excessive heat treatment to be the best option. However, one should be careful with salted and smoked mackerel.
The deeper and more intense the heat treatment, the more vitamins we lose, because they are fairly unstable compounds. But this does not apply, for example, to vitamin D3 and the other fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K, because they are less vulnerable to temperature. Fresh fish is the best option there is, and the less time that passes from catching it to serving it, the better. I would recommend baking or stewing fresh fish rather than eating a lot of salted or smoked fish
In addition, Oleksandr Kushch stressed that excess salt can primarily be a problem for people with high blood pressure.
A person can consume too much salt, and this can cause water retention in people with high blood pressure and, consequently, an increase in blood pressure. Therefore, I would not recommend eating excessive amounts of salty foods. During the smoking process, fish absorbs certain resins, and resins are combustion products that can be carcinogenic. If, for example, you are preparing food for children, I would still recommend baking or stewing fresh fish
How to choose and prepare mackerel The doctor also commented on the widespread belief that fish, including mackerel, is a universal remedy for lowering cholesterol. According to him, fish alone cannot replace comprehensive treatment if cholesterol levels are significantly elevated, but its regular consumption can be part of a healthy diet.
One mackerel will not overcome this process and cannot be a panacea. Elevated cholesterol can be caused by various factors: it may be hereditary hypercholesterolemia, impaired liver function, or other disorders, so each case must be examined separately. If a person is prone to elevated cholesterol and the risks of atherosclerosis, their diet should be as free as possible of saturated fats. In general, we always recommend eating more fish and switching to healthy cooking methods
However, Oleksandr Kushch notes that oily fish can provide the body with the necessary amount of omega-3, provided it is consumed regularly. He recommends including it in the diet several times a week.Read also: Flaxseed oil: benefits, harms, contraindications
Regular consumption of oily ocean fish three or four times a week, with a serving of at least 100–150 grams, provides us with a daily portion. In Scandinavian countries, there is an excellent source of various types of oily ocean fish close at hand—sardines, anchovies, salmon, and others. Therefore, they get enough of it in their diet. Fish in general should be a regular part of one’s diet
Special attention should also be paid to frozen mackerel, because proper freezing, according to the dietitian, helps preserve nutrients, whereas refreezing can reduce the product’s quality. Therefore, he recommends buying fish where one can be confident that storage conditions have been properly maintained.
If the freezing is done properly and the rules are not violated—when the fish is caught, cleaned, and deep-frozen—it practically retains all its beneficial substances. But often during transportation the fish partially thaws and is then frozen again; in that case, the water in the tissues in the form of ice literally tears apart the fish’s structure through these processes, and it becomes crumbly. In addition, this can cause bacterial contamination, which may lead to foodborne infections
The doctor also advises against buying such fish at informal markets, while he considers shops with specialized refrigeration equipment a more reliable option.
Fish must be selected very carefully, especially frozen fish, and it should not be bought at informal stalls or markets. It is better to choose a fish store with stationary refrigerators and freezers that can more or less guarantee the quality of the product. We cannot fully trace the journey of this fish, but we understand that it is very long—it is transported to us from the Atlantic Ocean. Therefore, transportation and freezing conditions are of great importance

Countries and international health authorities are pressing Russia for greater transparency over the reported death of a laboratory technician in Siberia, as Moscow insists there is no evidence of an epidemic and says the cause of death remains undetermined.
The international response follows reports that a 28-year-old woman working at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute died on October 2 after being hospitalised with severe pneumonia.
Russian authorities have said she died of pneumonia and that the cause has not been established, while reports that she contracted pneumonic plague have not been independently confirmed.
Russia’s health agency said on Wednesday that there were “no epidemic risks” and rejected suggestions of a confirmed plague outbreak.
Here’s how the international community is reacting to the accident.
US and WHO seek more information
The United States has formally asked Russia for information about the reported death, according to a source familiar with the matter.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called for Moscow to be transparent about the incident, while President Donald Trump said he expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has also requested additional information, including reports of a second employee suffering from pneumonia of undetermined cause.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said transparency was necessary to properly assess any potential public health risk and said the organisation was ready to provide technical assistance if requested.
The WHO said it was following reports that the laboratory worker had died after severe pneumonia and that initial media accounts had suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged accidental laboratory exposure.
EU calls for reliable findings
The European Union has urged Russia to provide “timely and transparent reporting” on the incident.
European Commission spokeswoman Eva Hrncirova said the bloc wanted reliable epidemiological and microbiological findings and was following the situation closely in coordination with experts from the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control.
The EU's response reflects wider concern over the lack of independently confirmed information about the reported case.
China in close contact
China said it remains in close contact with Russia on infectious disease prevention, including plague.
Foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing and Moscow maintain regular cooperation on preventing and controlling infectious diseases when asked whether Russia had sought assistance from Chinese authorities or experts.
China did not indicate that it had identified a public health threat linked to the reported death.
Neighbours step up precautions
Lithuania said it could consider restricting the transit of Russian citizens if a pneumonic plague case were confirmed and posed a threat, although Health Minister Linas Kukuraitis stressed that the reported case had not been independently verified.
Lithuania's National Public Health Centre said there was currently no increased risk of plague infection in the country. Kukuraitis said any response would be coordinated with the EU and that Lithuania had procedures and sufficient medical supplies to respond to a potential outbreak.
Mongolia, which shares a border with Russia, has taken a precautionary approach. Its health ministry ordered increased health surveillance along the border, while stressing that the current risk level remained low.
Border crossings in Selenge Province are operating normally, Mongolia said, with health monitoring measures in place.
Russia says there is no epidemic risk
Russian authorities have sought to calm concerns surrounding the reports, rejecting suggestions that anti-plague measures were being imposed.
The reported death has nevertheless triggered international calls for clearer information, particularly because the woman worked at a facility specialising in plague research.
For now, there is no independent confirmation that the woman died from plague, and the available information does not establish that an outbreak has occurred.
International health authorities are seeking further epidemiological and laboratory data before assessing the potential risk.

Scientists might finally have figured out why weed makes you feel paranoid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:37:08 UTC
23:37:08 KST

Whether you are smoking or eating it, marijuana can be relaxing—or it can cause feelings of anxiety, panic and paranoia. But despite the prevalence of these unnerving experiences—studies suggest frequent cannabis use is associated with higher odds of anxiety—scientists have little understanding as to why they occur.
“From a biological perspective, we really know almost nothing,” says Sachin Patel, a neuroscientist at Northwestern University.
In a bid to understand why one of the world’s most popular drugs summons such negative emotions, Patel and his colleagues investigated its effect on mice. The team’s findings, published last week in Nature Communications, reveal that, when given such a drug, rodents suffer adverse reactions similar to the paranoia human cannabis users feel. The effect is driven by a specific group of neurons in the central amygdala, a brain region that processes fear and anxiety.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The researchers injected mice with varying doses of CP55940, a synthetic cannabinoid that mimics the effects of tetrahydrocannabinol, or TCH, the main psychoactive compound in weed. Then they placed the mice in a cage with a petri dish full of fox urine. As expected, the animals became anxious, either fleeing the threatening odor or freezing in place. These responses were more extreme in mice who received larger doses—a relatable result if you’ve ever found yourself peering suspiciously through the living room blinds after one toke too many.
To tease out a connection between the animals’ behavior and their brain activity, the researchers turned to the central amygdala, which past research has shown to play a role in threat responses. Looking through small microscopes implanted in the mice’s heads, Patel’s team zoomed in on a particular subset of brain cells, called somatostatin neurons, as the animals reacted to the fox urine scent. “The take-home,” Patel says, “was that those cells were hyperactive when combining cannabinoids with the stress exposure.”
The researchers found that cannabinoids suppress the release of a neurotransmitter called gamma-aminobutyric acid, or GABA, which tamps down brain activity. In other words, the drug essentially weakens the central amygdala’s “brake,” Patel says, allowing fear and anxiety to run wild. When the researchers silenced the somatostatin neurons, the mice stopped trying so hard to avoid the threatening odor in their midst.
“This elegantly demonstrates a causal role,” says Ozge Gunduz-Cinar, a neuroscientist at the U.S. National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, who was not involved in the study. She notes, however, that the researchers “examined only a single inhibitory cell type in a single brain region using an innate fear model,” suggesting there may be more to this story.
Humans are not mice, so it is unclear whether our own cannabis-induced anxiety arises in the exact same way. But Patel suspects a similar mechanism, given that stoned mice exhibit a pattern of behavior that might feel familiar to anyone who’s overdone it on edibles. “The fact that we can mimic that behavioral response in animals quite nicely makes me think that the neural data we have has some relevance to what’s probably going on in humans,” he says.
Human relevance might be difficult to prove, though. You could hypothetically get someone high, put them in a brain scanner, make them stare at pictures of scary faces and then look to see how their brain activity changes as dread wells up inside them—but that wouldn’t be very kind. “It’s a little difficult from an ethical perspective,” Patel acknowledges. Still, he believes that a deeper understanding of how marijuana affects the brain could produce new ways to counteract a bad trip.

German spy chief accused of treason, espionage issued formal arrest warrant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:36:19 UTC
23:36:19 KST

A judge of Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued a formal arrest warrant against a former spy chief accused of buying secret documents and using them in an analysis for a foreign intelligence service, the Office of the Federal Prosecutor said on Wednesday.
The case of 80-year-old August Hanning, detained on Tuesday over suspected espionage and attempted treason, has shocked the German intelligence community and lawmakers, and could emerge as one of the biggest leaks of classified documents in Germany since the end of the Cold War.
It has also raised concerns that foreign intelligence agencies could cut Germany off from important information.
Federal prosecutors have not identified the foreign intelligence service, and it is unclear whether Hanning's alleged analysis reached its intended recipient.
Der Spiegel news magazine reported late on Tuesday that investigators were pursuing a possible connection to Azerbaijan. It reported Hanning had been in contact with an agent from the country. Azerbaijan on Wednesday denied any connection.
Lawyer says Hanning did not pass along information 'to detriment of Germany'
Hanning on Tuesday did not respond to a request for comment.
"While it is true that he was in possession of confidential documents, the allegation that he passed on information contained therein to the detriment of Germany, let alone for payment, is incorrect," his lawyer told German newspaper Die Welt on Wednesday.
A judge at the Federal Court of Justice in the southwestern city of Karlsruhe issued the arrest warrant, federal prosecutors said.
The official warrant allows authorities to keep Hanning in custody.
Azerbaijan's Media and Broadcasting Council issued a statement saying the allegations were groundless disinformation.
"The malicious intent of the forces behind this disinformation operation is to damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations," the council said.
A senior Azerbaijani government official told Reuters that Baku had contacted German intelligence services through official channels and had been told that the case had no connection to Azerbaijani intelligence.
German BND Chief of Staff in custody
Hanning was head of the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 to 2005.
Prosecutors allege that in 2010 Hanning agreed to pay for confidential information from an official identified as Manfred D, who served as chief of staff to successive BND heads prior to his retirement in March this year.
His position potentially gave him access to some of Germany's most current intelligence at the time that prosecutors say documents were being siphoned from the service.
Manfred D. was detained on Tuesday and also placed under formal arrest on Wednesday.
Prosecutors on Tuesday said that the investigation centered on suspicion that Hanning received approximately 2,000 documents from D. through June 2022. "Some of these documents were classified," a spokesperson for the prosecution service said.
It is still unclear what level of secrecy the potentially leaked documents had.
Marc Henrichmann, head of the parliamentary committee that oversees the intelligence services, said he was "pretty stunned" by the case.
But he downplayed comparisons to the 1970s case of East German spy Guenther Guillaume, secretary of Chancellor Willy Brandt, who eventually stepped down over the affair.
"I find (that comparison) a bit of a stretch at the moment, because we don't even know exactly what happened there yet," Henrichmann told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk.

Is the world turning against the Islamic Republic of Iran? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:35:54 UTC
23:35:54 KST

On Monday, 10 countries – the United States, Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, the Dominican Republic, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, and Trinidad and Tobago – issued a joint statement condemning what they described as Iranian terrorist activity and malign influence across the Americas.
“These hostile efforts include a range of Iranian and proxy-sponsored lethal plotting, illicit fundraising, political interference and foreign influence activities, and operations meant to bolster terrorist networks, coerce perceived enemies, compromise legal or administrative processes, and harm regional security,” the statement read. “We stand united in our determination to protect our countries and our people against such threats. The Islamic Republic of Iran and its proxies must halt these actions now.”
Three days earlier, an even broader coalition had issued its own warning to the Iranians.
Fifty-six countries, ranging from the United States, Britain, France, and Germany to Bahrain, Morocco, Japan, South Korea, Colombia, Argentina, Paraguay, and Yemen, reaffirmed their commitment to enforcing the UN restrictions restored against Iran last year. The signatories pledged to prevent transfers that could assist Iran’s nuclear, missile, drone, and weapons programs and to increase cooperation against Iranian proliferation.
Taken individually, neither statement marks a fundamental change in the international order or the way the world has tried to contain the Islamic Republic. But taken alongside other developments over the past several months, however, they raise a larger question: Is the world beginning to turn against the Islamic Republic?
South American countries breaking from Iran
Some of the clearest evidence has come from Latin America.
Colombia formally broke diplomatic relations with Iran on September 19, citing Iran’s alleged links to terrorist and narcoterrorist groups, human rights abuses, attacks on countries outside the conflict, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and obstruction of the International Atomic Energy Agency. Days later, the country went even further, designating the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organization and announcing measures aimed at preventing people associated with it from entering Colombia.
What is interesting there is Bogota's change of direction. Colombia has hardly marched in lockstep with Israel in recent years, so this decision cannot be put down to a move by a traditionally pro-Israel government.
There is also a question mark over Venezuela.
Although there has been no official designation of any Iranian entity, nor any statements, it was announced in August that Venezuela’s post-Maduro government is establishing an official consular channel with Israel for the first time in 17 years.
After two wars with Israel in the past 14 months, Iran may worry that its influence in Venezuela, which was secured through the Chavez and Maduro governments, will now be tested.
Elsewhere in the region, Argentina has hardened its stance under President Javier Milei, while Paraguay has emerged as an increasingly vocal opponent of Iranian and Hezbollah activity in Latin America. The October 5 declaration suggests that those individual positions are increasingly becoming a coordinated regional effort.
Europe starts to see Iran as terrorist state
Europe has also begun to put words into action.
In February, before war broke out on February 28 between the US, Israel and Iran, the European Union formally placed the IRGC on its terrorist list, freezing its assets and prohibiting EU operators from making funds available to it. Britain followed in July by moving against the IRGC under its new state-threat legislation.
In June, some 22 Western governments issued another joint statement accusing the IRGC Intelligence Organization, Quds Force, and Iranian intelligence services of lethal plotting abroad, including against Iranian dissidents, journalists, and Jewish and Israeli communities.
Meanwhile, the war has widened the group of countries prepared to confront Tehran.
Middle Eastern nations dragged into conflict, cooperate against proxies
Perhaps nowhere is that more significant than in the Gulf. Before the fighting began, Gulf governments went to considerable lengths to avoid being dragged into an Israel-Iran confrontation and stressed that their territory would not be used to attack Iran.
Iranian missile and drone attacks changed all that. Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Jordan joined the United States in March in condemning Iranian attacks against countries across the region. Later that month, a larger grouping including Egypt, Turkey, Pakistan, Azerbaijan, Lebanon, and Syria condemned Iranian missile and drone attacks on neighboring states.
By July, all six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) members and Jordan were again jointly condemning continued Iranian and proxy attacks against their territory and civilian infrastructure.
Russia, China, other nations maintain relationships with Iran
None of this, however, means that Iran has become internationally friendless.
Russia and China remain crucial counterbalances to Western pressure, helping to provide Iran with military and economic aid, while Iran retains important relationships across parts of Asia, Africa, and the Middle East. Qatar continues to serve as an intermediary between the US and Iran, and even governments furious over Iranian attacks have repeatedly emphasized diplomacy instead of any further escalation.
Nor should every country appearing on a joint statement be interpreted as joining some new anti-Iran alliance. We can ask what each country’s motives are. Some are primarily concerned with nuclear proliferation, others with terrorism, maritime security, human rights, or attacks on their own territory.
What has changed, though, is the breadth of the countries confronting the Islamic Republic regime, and the range of issues bringing them together.
The Islamic Republic now faces European governments treating the IRGC as a terrorist or state-security threat, Latin American governments severing ties and coordinating against Iranian networks, dozens of countries seeking to restrict its nuclear and missile programs, and Arab states publicly condemning Iranian attacks on their soil.
Many of these governments disagree profoundly over many issues, including Israel, Gaza, the United States, and the future of the Middle East. But more and more, they are finding themselves aligned in how they deal with the Islamic Republic.
