Israel has allegedly blocked the Palestinian Central Elections Commission from entering east Jerusalem and the Gaza Strip to monitor the November 28 elections, a Palestinian Authority official told the PA’s official WAFA news agency on Wednesday, as European Commission Vice President and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas renewed Europe’s commitment to deploying an election observation mission.
Though the CEC has yet to issue an official statement on the alleged block, CEC spokesperson Farid Taamallah confirmed the report to Agence France-Presse and insisted that the elections could still go ahead.
Taamallah has not yet responded to The Jerusalem Post’s request.
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed planned elections in 2021 amid a dispute over voting in east Jerusalem. At the time, many of Abbas’s critics accused him of using the dispute as a pretext to postpone the elections and retain power, citing his low levels of support in Palestinian polls.
Experts who have spoken to The Post in recent months, including Prof. Kobi Michael, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) and the Misgav Institute, have suggested that Abbas could use a similar justification to postpone the elections.
Speculations over whether the PA elections will be able to happen
Yoni Ben-Menachem, a senior researcher at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs, has also reported that Hussein Al-Sheikh, deputy chairman of the Palestinian Authority, was pushing Abbas to postpone the elections, using the issue as a justification.
Unlike in 2021, however, the PA has gained international support for Palestinian statehood under the New York Declaration on the condition that it holds democratic elections.
Kallas confirmed she spoke with al-Sheikh on Tuesday, promising that the EU was ready to deploy an Election Observation Mission.
“Palestinians have the right to choose their representatives in elections that are credible, inclusive and transparent,” she wrote on X/Twitter after the call. “After nearly 20 years without a parliamentary vote, these elections would offer a long-overdue opportunity to renew the legitimacy of Palestinian institutions.”
Al-Sheikh also confirmed the call took place, adding that they also discussed the issue of settler violence and humanitarian conditions in the Gaza Strip.
He said on Facebook he called “for European support for Palestinian efforts to overcome obstacles that may hinder the conduct of elections and their implementation, ensuring the participation of all our people in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Gaza Strip in the electoral process.”
With eight candidate lists already submitted, and more expected, Dr. Nabil Kukali, Founder and President of the Palestinian Center for Public Opinion, said he believed there would “certainly” be “frustration.”
Who will Palestinians hold responsible for delayed elections?
Based on the PCPO’s last poll across the territories, 79.4% of Palestinians want the election to go ahead in November. Still, Kukali predicted that “many Palestinians could understand a delay if it becomes clear that the main reason is the inability to hold inclusive elections in east Jerusalem and Gaza.”
“The broader context is also important. Palestinian-Israeli relations are currently under severe strain, with political and economic cooperation greatly reduced and continuing restrictions in the West Bank,” he continued.
“Under these circumstances, public reaction may depend less on the delay itself and more on whom Palestinians hold responsible for it.”
Based on the current status of relations with Israel, Kukali said he “would not assume” that another delay in elections would weaken support for Abbas, especially “if Palestinians believe that Abbas and the Palestinian leadership remain committed to holding elections throughout the Palestinian territories, including East Jerusalem and Gaza, and that the principal obstacle comes from Israeli restrictions, the political cost to him could be limited.”
“Some Palestinians may even view a refusal to hold elections without Jerusalem or Gaza as a defense of the principle that national elections should include all Palestinian territories,” he added.

Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
17:34:36 EEST
23:34:36 KST

The World Health Organization has asked Russia for more information about the death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker at a Siberian institute that studies plague, while Russian authorities say testing has found no cases of the disease and no risk of an epidemic.
Darya Shipilova died on Friday after developing severe pneumonia from a cause that authorities have yet to establish.
Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Her death led authorities to quarantine about 200 people and send senior public health officials to the Irkutsk region.
Russia’s health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said almost 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens among people who had contact with Shipilova. About 90% of those initially placed in quarantine had been released.
The agency said Shipilova had received vaccinations against the dangerous infections she worked with. Authorities have not established what caused the pneumonia that led to her death or how she became ill.
WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organisation had requested further information from Russia about the cause of the pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted public health measures and reports concerning another institute employee with pneumonia of undetermined origin.
“Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential,” Tedros said in a statement on X.
The WHO said Russian authorities had reported that no plague cases had recently been registered in the Irkutsk region. The organisation has assessed the risk as moderate to low within Irkutsk, low for Russia and very low for the wider WHO European region.
Russian authorities told the WHO through an international health notification system that testing had found no dangerous infectious disease pathogens among Shipilova’s contacts.
The Kremlin said Russia had followed established procedures in informing the WHO.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov rejected reports surrounding the case and urged the public and media to rely on information from Rospotrebnadzor.
Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and spreads between people through respiratory particles. The WHO says the disease has an incubation period as short as 24 hours. Treatment is effective when infection is identified and treated in time.
The case has also drawn attention from Washington. US officials have called for more information from Moscow.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he expected to speak to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the case “very soon”. Peskov said on Wednesday that no telephone call between the two presidents had been scheduled.

Students have protested over Belgium’s French-language education system, citing rising education costs, overcrowded classrooms and difficulties accessing study materials. They held signs with slogans including “It’s a mess, we are fighting for a right! Not a privilege!” and “I chose education, not the hunger games!!”.
The unrest follows June clashes between protesters and police in Brussels over education reforms, including a tuition increase for most students in Belgium’s French-speaking Community to €1,194 (S$1,700) from €835.
Videos circulating on social media in recent days showed shattered glass, fires and hundreds of mostly young protesters in Liege, while other footage showed police blocking roads. During the Oct 7 protest, police were seen checking students for weapons.
In touch with French students
Some students told Reuters they were in touch with French counterparts. “We support each other because we’re facing pretty much the same issues,” 19-year-old student Alfred said.
Amelia Di Salve, also 19, who is studying to become a teacher, said Belgium’s student movement began earlier this year and was reignited after students saw the demonstrations in France. “When we saw nothing was changing without protests, we decided we would start... France did influence us a little,” she said.
Liege mayor Willy Demeyer told Belgian broadcaster RTBF he hoped calm would return and “that dialogue can be established and that the young people can express their grievances in a peaceful way and, if possible, have those concerns heard”. REUTERS

With this in mind, the Tokyo office of the ICE Agency, together with the training institution Sanko Gakuen, is bringing Italian cuisine into classrooms in six Japanese cities as part of the 11th Italian Cuisine Week in the World (SCIM), the annual event promoted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation to highlight the excellence and internationalization of Italy’s food and wine sector. The tour has already visited Yokohama, Nagoya, Sendai, Sapporo, and Tokyo, with a stop in Omiya scheduled for late November, involving local enthusiasts and students from vocational schools. In the hands-on sessions, led by professional chefs, participants learn not only how to prepare recipes correctly but also to recognize the value of certified ingredients and authentic “Made in Italy” products. “This year, we wanted to start from the roots,” Gianpaolo Bruno, director of the ICE Agency in Tokyo, explained to ANSA, emphasizing that the selected training centers are where the future leadership of Japan’s top restaurants is being prepared. The chefs show students “what lies behind an Italian dish”: local culture, attention to ingredients and seasonality, and attention to detail. Japanese consumers, Bruno notes, are “connoisseurs” of Italian cuisine, and this opens up vast opportunities for companies targeting the premium segments with products rooted in tradition and regional heritage. Leading the classes in Tokyo was Chef Stefano Dal Moro of Osteria Del Ponte, who presented dishes from the regional cuisine of Veneto, his homeland, to introduce the students to new flavors and highlight values shared by Italy and Japan, such as the joy of dining together, sustainability, and a commitment to quality ingredients. “From young Japanese people,” says Dal Moro, “I’d like to bring to Italy their meticulousness in seeking perfection and in reproducing the same flavor, even without sharing the same culture.” These trade ties are complemented by the widespread presence of Italian restaurants: Tokyo is home to over 5,000 Italian restaurants, with a broad presence throughout the country. For Anna Iele, attaché for agri-food policies at the Italian Embassy in Tokyo, the initiative is a valuable tool for “strengthening collaborations” between the two countries, because cuisine is “a very important vehicle for diplomacy.” This year marks the 160th anniversary of Italian-Japanese diplomatic relations, and celebrating them around the table is, she adds, the most effective way to do so. With an eye already on October 25, World Pasta Day, a symbol of a cuisine recognized as a UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Ethiopian PM reelected despite rebel offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:33:12 UTC
23:33:12 KST

Ethiopian PM reelected despite rebel offensive
Ethiopia’s parliament has re-elected Abiy Ahmed as prime minister for another five-year term, two weeks after armed groups formed an alliance to overthrow his government amid renewed fighting in the country’s north.
Abiy was sworn in on Monday at the inaugural session of the newly elected House of Peoples’ Representatives after his ruling Prosperity Party won a sweeping majority with 438 seats in elections held in June. Addressing lawmakers, Abiy expressed his government’s readiness to confront threats and protect its national interests.
“Getting tripped up by an obstacle once is natural, but stumbling repeatedly is not normal,” he said, urging unity and greater preparedness for domestic and external challenges.
Abiy first became prime minister in 2018 and won the 2019 Nobel Peace Prize for restoring ties with neighboring Eritrea after two decades of hostility following their 1998–2000 border war. His government fought a two-year war against the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) from November 2020. Hundreds of thousands of people were killed before a peace agreement was signed in Pretoria in November 2022.
On September 20, the TPLF, which governs the northern Tigray region, and six other armed groups, including the Amhara Fano National Movement and the Oromo Liberation Army, announced the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival. The coalition unites former battlefield enemies; Fano fought alongside federal troops against the TPLF before turning against Addis Ababa in 2023.
Fighting has since intensified between federal troops and TPLF forces, which seized airports in Tigray’s regional capital, Mekelle, and the cities of Axum and Shire, disrupting commercial flights. On September 24, the army said it had killed 272 rebel fighters and wounded 260. Federal troops and allied fighters retook Mekelle and its airport last weekend, while the TPLF vowed to continue fighting. More than 720 patients wounded in the conflict had been admitted to hospitals in Korem, Alamata and Shire as of September 25, according to Doctors Without Borders.
The fighting has also fueled a diplomatic crisis amid allegations that Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan are supporting the armed groups. All three deny the claims. Addis Ababa closed its embassy in Asmara and expelled ten Eritrean diplomats last week, prompting Eritrea to sever ties. Ethiopia also ordered an Egyptian diplomat to leave, and Cairo retaliated by expelling an Ethiopian Embassy counselor.
During his address following reelection, Abiy renewed his pledge to secure maritime access for landlocked Ethiopia through dialogue and mutually beneficial arrangements. That ambition has strained relations with Eritrea over its Assab Port and with Somalia over Ethiopia’s 2024 coastline deal with Somaliland, which Mogadishu condemned as a violation of its sovereignty. A Turkish-mediated agreement later that year eased the dispute with Somalia.
The African Union (AU) has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels. The AU and UN have also urged federal troops and TPLF forces to halt hostilities and resume talks to safeguard the Pretoria agreement.

Latvian authorities have launched proceedings to declare Riga-based Russian journalist Leonid Ragozin persona non grata, Delfi reported Tuesday.
While Ragozin was not identified by name, Foreign Minister Baiba Braže announced blacklisting proceedings against a Russian citizen based on new information from “competent authorities” and discussions with the prime minister.
Sources familiar with the matter told Delfi that the move targets Ragozin, who has resided in Latvia since around the time of Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014. There was no indication when the decision would be made.
Ragozin drew public ire for comments he made on a podcast hosted by Aaron Maté of fringe far-left outlet The Grayzone, which has been accused of taking a pro-Russian slant.
He argued that Russia was compelled to respond to the West with “brute force,” saying, “[Russia] always consider themselves as the underdogs and as the side that is being under constant pressure from the West, encroaching on its sphere of influence, on its strategic interests. It compels them to respond to hybrid actions, to clandestine actions, to sort of invisible actions that change the landscape in the former Soviet Union.”
Late last month, Latvian Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava urged the foreign ministry to declare Ragozin a persona non grata due to “opinions that are in blatant contradiction to the interests of the Latvian state.”
“His actions can be regarded as ones aimed at steering Western public opinion in a direction favorable to Russia,” Dombrava wrote on Sept. 30.
Ragozin is a former producer for the BBC Russian Service and editor at Russian Newsweek. His freelance commentary has appeared in recent editions of Al Jazeera, Jacobin and The American Conservative.
In an August column for The American Conservative, Ragozin argued that ordinary Russians perceive greater threats from Western nations than from their own government.
On Wednesday, Ragozin thanked supporters while criticizing those reacting to the news of the proceedings to declare him persona non grata with “sadistic glee.”
Latvia has declared dozens of Russian cultural figures, state journalists and commentators personae non gratae since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

West wrong to pin hopes on Russia’s collapse – Fyodor Lukyanov (VIDEO)

Unknown Publisher

West wrong to pin hopes on Russia’s collapse – Fyodor Lukyanov (VIDEO)
The West should abandon the thought that the Ukraine conflict will cause Russia to collapse like the USSR did in 1991, foreign affairs expert and RT contributor Fyodor Lukyanov has said.
Lukyanov, a program director at the Valdai International Discussion Club, moderated a more than three-hour-long session with Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of the club’s annual forum last week. 
Putin said at the event the current tensions with the US and EU stem from the fall of the Soviet Union. Since then, Moscow has repeatedly tried to build good relations with Western countries, but their leaders have persisted in doing “everything they could to truly isolate and further break apart Russia itself,” Putin stressed.
During his appearance on RT’s East Meets West podcast with Olga Bataman and Tara Reade, Lukyanov said that “there are a lot of grounds on our [Russian] side to believe that we can win… by military means” in the conflict with Kiev.
“Paradoxically, Ukraine has the same idea based on another calculation, based on the expectation that the Western support will not stop and that on “a very traditional, old, good belief that Russia at some point will suddenly collapse,” he said.
According to the analyst, the same idea is also prevalent among the Western elites. It’s being “partially inspired by what happened relatively recently in our history, 35 years ago. The collapse of the Soviet Union played a very negative role because they started to believe that it can be repeated,” he noted.
Lukyanov said that he has already given up explaining to his American and European interlocutors that Russia is “different” and that it “will not collapse as the Soviet Union, but people in the West and now in Ukraine, they still believe it’s possible.”
The analyst also suggested the EU’s current hostility towards Russia should be explained by its leader’s trying to “find a way how to consolidate societies” amid “enormous” political, economic and social problems experienced by the bloc as a whole and its individual member-states.
They seek “to blame someone else and to find a menace which, as during the Cold War, can unify Europe,” he stressed.

Premier Giorgia Meloni said Wednesday
that the government was considering a "mobile" mechanism to
reduce fuel duties as a way of helping people and businesses
with soaring energy costs, in order to replace a fixed cut in
diesel duties that elapsed this week.
                                    
The first such cut was approved in March in the wake of the
U.S.-Iran war and in recent months there has been a
17-cent-per-litre reduction in diesel duties, which was
gradually brought down to 12.2 cents and then to 6.1 cents
before being allowed to expire on Tuesday.
                                    
Eni raised its cap on fuel prices in its gas stations as a
consequence of the end of the cut in duties, going from 2.19 to
2.25 euros for a litre of diesel, with the cap for unleaded
petrol remaining at 1.99 euros per litre.
                                    
Encouraged by the government, the State-owned energy giant
brought in the 30-day cap last week and several other companies
running petrol stations in Italy followed suit.
                                    
Under the possible mobile mechanism, the reduction in duties
would be related to the extra yield the State gets from VAT from
higher fuel prices.
                                    
"We remain ready to intervene again, in particular through a
mobile excise-duty mechanism," Meloni said at the end of the
Med9 summit in Split,
"As of September, we have (accumulated) approximately 170
million euros that can be spent toward this goal.
                                    
"We're considering whether it's more effective to spend it
now—while containment measures are still in place—or to keep it
as a reserve for when those measures end.
                                    
"It also depends on how well the price cap holds up.
                                    
"Let's see what happens in the coming hours.
                                    
"I hope that the price cap can be fully restored in the coming
hours; then we'll have to assess the situation afterwards".

Mumsnet denies using AI for content after prompt appears on message board
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:31:04 UTC
23:31:04 KST

Mumsnet has denied using AI to produce content after detailed instructions to help an AI model write one of its popular “am I being unreasonable” (AIBU) posts appeared on a Mumsnet message board.
Users of the long-established forum, which is known for its frank discussions of family tensions, were vexed when the AI prompt appeared in response to a user seeking advice about a family dilemma involving a neurodivergent uncle and a sick child.
The user, called AmIAComplete, had asked for “a sanity check” from other users after an awkward social interaction with their brother’s family but was met with a prompt titled AIBU Response Schema v.1.0.
It instructed an AI to write an “interpersonal reasonableness” post and “give a clear, forum-style ruling plus brief actionable advice”. It included definitions of common Mumsnet abbreviations including AIBU, ND (neurodivergent) and DD (dear daughter).
The prompt said: “do not diagnose anyone; do not demean ND people; do not imply a sick child owes social performance” and said “prioritize compassion, boundaries, and de-escalation”.
Site users called the emergence of the prompt “really creepy”, “crazy” and “so disappointing” and it fed speculation about Mumsnet’s use of AI, with one user saying: “We might as well just go and do something else then.”
Mumsnet was founded in 2000. It faced a 19% drop in its monthly unique user numbers in 2025 to 6.1 million and the number of posts fell by 600,000. It said in its latest annual report that it was “embedding AI tools to improve productivity and enhance the user experience”.
Recent research, published in Nature, has shown that AI assistance in social media risks creating “semantic garbage” and is seen by users as less informative, “robotic” and “generic”.
Soon after the prompt emerged, Mumsnet denied that it used AI to write threads and said it had come from a tool to suggest thread titles which uses an OpenAI model. But users refused to accept this explanation and some copied the prompt into an AI and found it generated a full post.
“We are not idiots,” said one user, MrsBennetsPoorNervesAreBack. “Please can you give us a transparent explanation?”
Mumsnet then said the prompt did not come from them and suggested it had somehow transferred from AmIAComplete’s computer. Again users were unconvinced and speculated the prompt must have leaked from Mumsnet’s internal system.
Mumsnet’s founder, Justine Roberts, joined the thread and confirmed the prompt had come from its system, which sends users’ drafts to OpenAI, which is meant to suggest a title, although this time it sent a prompt for a whole reply. She said it “looks like an error on their side” and said: “We don’t use AI to write threads or replies on Mumsnet.”
This explanation also failed to appease users, who said they were being “fobbed off”.
“Why would OpenAI compel itself to do/try to do something so specific if it’s never been asked to do that before from your side?” said one. “It’s like it’s appeared in the wrong place. Rather than just sprung out of thin air.”
“I just don’t know anymore what’s real and what isn’t sometimes!” they said.
Roberts told the Guardian: “I understand why it looked like it had ‘appeared in the wrong place’. But nothing in our systems asks for, stores or uses anything like it.”
She said Mumsnet had never tested a tool that drafted posts, but it used AI for coding, advertising operations, conversational analysis and flagging potentially problematic posts to moderators.
“Mumsnet works because the people on it are real,” Roberts said. “Members trust that the advice they get comes from other parents, not a machine … This episode was a useful reminder of two things. First, these systems are less predictable than the people selling them like to suggest. Second, users are understandably highly concerned that Mumsnet remains written by humans.”

Türkiye rules out Treasury funding for losses at investment funds under liquidation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:31:01 UTC
23:31:01 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
Türkiye will not use Treasury resources to cover private losses at investment funds undergoing liquidation, Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz said on Wednesday, outlining repayments using fund assets and recovered proceeds.
Briefing the parliament on the Fund Coordination Board, which he chairs, Yilmaz said 131 funds under liquidation represented 4.6% of all funds and 7.7% of their combined portfolio value.
“In other words, the problem has occurred in a limited segment of the fund market,” he said.
Their portfolio value equaled 2.4% of household financial assets as of Oct. 5.
Yilmaz said the financial system faced no systemic risk, stressing that the problem’s limited scope did not diminish its importance.   
Repayments to prioritize small investors
Distributing available resources proportionately to investors’ holdings was the general legal principle governing liquidation, Yilmaz said.
For funds subject to extraordinary liquidation, interim principal repayments of up to 1 million Turkish liras ($20,326) are planned, prioritizing small investors and money market funds.
Existing fund assets will be used first, supplemented by resources recovered from those obtaining excessive or unjust gains and proceeds from sales of assets removed from the system.
“Treasury resources will not be used for private losses arising during this process,” he said, adding that investment funds, particularly high-risk hedge funds, did not carry the state guarantee applicable within the banking system.   
Investigations and preventive measures
Judicial and administrative authorities are examining the case, with those responsible for unlawful gains through speculation and manipulation to be held accountable, Yilmaz said.
The State Supervisory Council has deployed 10 inspectors to review the responsibilities of relevant institutions and independent regulators.
Authorities are also evaluating administrative and legal measures to prevent similar problems, he added.
The coordination board has established a roadmap, with institutions taking steps within their mandates.
Yilmaz pledged transparent, fair and speedy liquidation, reaffirming Türkiye’s commitment to expanding and deepening capital markets.

====================================================================================================

How Oct. 7 Changed Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:30:50 UTC
23:30:50 KST

The world changed when Hamas attacked Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023, catalyzing devastating conflict throughout the region. But within Israel, political sentiments have changed surprisingly little.
To some, the attack fulfilled long-term right-wing warnings that Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza would yield disaster; and the attack was incontrovertible proof that Palestinians will never live in peace with Israel.
Israeli left-wingers, for their part, have long held that a festering military rule over Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, and failure to reach peace, would inevitably lead to violent conflagration. For them, Oct. 7 only proved that they had been right all along.
The standoff raises crucial questions. In three years since Oct. 7, how has the attack changed Israeli society? And how will the answer affect upcoming elections in Israel?
The world after Oct. 7
To be sure, there have been cataclysmic changes in Israel, and the Middle East at large, since Oct. 7. The war in Gaza that began that day has become Israel’s longest war. A relatively stable ceasefire with Lebanon from 2006 to 2023 ended when Hezbollah, a Shi’a militia group, fired on Israel the day after Hamas’ attack; after multiple escalations since then, the current ceasefire is precarious. Israel and the U.S. have waged two full-blown wars with Iran, and the Middle East is still threatened by spin-off conflicts.
The losses Israelis suffered on Oct. 7 and since then have affected the country collectively and profoundly. For two years, many Israelis went from demonstration to demonstration demanding that their government prioritize a deal with Hamas to release Israeli hostages. Hundreds of thousands have spent the last three years in and out of active reserve duty.
Since 2023, Israel has seen record levels of emigration and growing international isolation. Sixty-one percent of Israelis told pollsters for the Israel Democracy Institute (IDI) that the national mood is poor.
Moreover, the destruction of Palestinian life and society, still ongoing, will one day force a terrible reckoning within Israel.
Attitudes towards a two-state solution
What’s less visible, and more surprising, is what has stayed the same. Israelis’ attitudes towards Palestinians, occupation, and conflict have become more extreme. But I would argue that Israeli public opinion today says much more about how Israel had changed prior to Oct. 7. The change in national attitudes since that fateful day has been moderate and consistent with what came before.
In December 2022, almost a year before Oct. 7, support for peace through a two-state solution hit a historic low. In the joint Palestinian-Israeli survey I conduct together with colleagues at Tel Aviv University and the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research, support stood at 39% of Israelis that year—the lowest since the 1990s. Among Jewish respondents, just 34% supported a two-state solution, and 37% believed Israel should permanently annex the West Bank while Palestinians would have limited rights.
When we conducted the study again in mid-2024, Jews were twice as likely to support a single, Israeli-dominated unequal state as they were to support two states.
Palestinian attitudes in 2022 were similar. Just one-third supported two states. Both sides showed a mirror-image majority who distrusted the other. In surveys by the IDI from that same time, 59% of Jewish Israelis defined themselves as right-wing; just 12% said they were left-wing.
When did sentiments shift?
What changed after Oct. 7? This July, the Tel Aviv University Peace Index survey found that support for two states stood at 31%, an eight-point decline in the four years since 2022. Now, IDI surveys find that just over 60% of Israeli Jews describe themselves as right-wing, just a few points higher than late 2022.
Israel has changed, but this change began years before Oct. 7 2023. In 2010, no fewer than 71% of Israelis supported a two-state solution in the joint surveys. The years that followed were plagued by stagnation and dissipation of any peace process, regular wars with Hamas, and a heavily nationalist government in Israel. It stands to reason that these phenomena pushed Israeli society further to the right. Support for the two-state solution eroded slowly, then rapidly by the end of the decade.
That shift was self-reinforcing: the more right-wing Israelis became (primarily the Jewish population), the more elected leaders took ever-more radical positions such as supporting settlement expansion and de facto annexation in the West Bank. In 2019, Prime Minister Netanyahu began referring to extending sovereignty over parts of the West Bank, or de jure annexation. The current government accelerated those processes drastically.
Study after study shows that Arab citizens of Israel have remained the strongest supporters of peace, before and after the current wars. But with Jewish Israeli and Palestinian attitudes so dismal in the years before Oct. 7, the chances of resurgent violence almost seemed inevitable.
In other words, most Israelis did not radically transform their worldview after Oct. 7. In fact, hardline political trends were among the many factors contributing to the terrible escalation to begin with.
The politics of peace
Another thing that hasn’t changed in Israel during the last three years of war: hopes for peace. The number of Israeli Jews who self-describe as left-wing has barely shifted. In a May survey for the Institute for National Security Studies, about 20% of the total population, Jews and Arabs, define themselves as left-wing, and a similar share typically say they are centrist. These groups embrace a commitment to democracy, liberal values, separation of religion and state, and reject the religious fundamentalism of the current government.
The left remains committed to peace via diplomacy and Palestinian self-determination. In a mid-2025 survey I conducted for a peace organization called A Land for All, where I am also an active member, the large majority of self-defined left-wing Israelis, and nearly half of centrists, supported a basic two-state solution.
Do peace attitudes even matter, when there is no peace process? That may be theoretical for now, but elections aren’t. Israelis will be voting on Oct. 27. Polls show the voters deeply divided, just as they were in the elections held between 2019 and 2022.
Netanyahu’s far-right coalition is not doing well. Nearly all polls show his coalition parties well below their actual result in 2022. And most mainstream polls show a consistent majority for today’s opposition parties.
At first glance, these shifts might seem antithetical. Aren’t these ideological and electoral trends moving in contradictory directions: more right-wing, but a majority against the current government?
It turns out that even the Israeli electoral contradiction is not new. During the five elections from 2019 through 2022, a majority of Israelis were right-wing and voted for right-wing parties. But to form a coalition, some of those parties no longer supported Netanyahu and refused to join a coalition under his leadership. Netanyahu therefore commanded only about half the seats in parliament following four of these cycles. Neither side had a clear or firm coalition majority, and the country was thrown into electoral turmoil five times over.
But if all mainstream polls show the anti-Netanyahu parties winning, including right-wing opposition parties, shouldn’t that mean a decisive outcome against him this time? Not quite: no poll shows Israel’s Jewish, Zionist parties reaching a majority in October.
And in Israel’s right-wing, populist discourse, the main opposition party leaders opposed to Netanyahu now, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman, with similar statements from frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot, insist that parties representing Arab citizens must not be part of a coalition after Oct. 7. Together they will likely hold a critical number of parliamentary seats. It’s a view that implicitly (and falsely) connects them with the Hamas attacks.
Those Arab or Palestinian citizens of Israel have been stalwart supporters of peace, and were among the victims of Oct. 7. A large majority, nearly three-quarters of them, want an Arab party to join Israel’s governing coalition, according to polling by the Moshe Dayan Center at Tel Aviv University.
But if Israeli party leaders ultimately prioritize their ideological convictions (or political posturing) against Arabs over their rejection of Netanyahu, their options will be limited since they look unlikely to win a majority of Knesset seats in October.
Netanyahu has much working against him: ongoing corruption trials, the fact that he was the leader who presided over the terrible failures of Israel to prevent Oct. 7, three years of wars, and the unconscionable destruction of Gaza. Yet he could still form the next government if the opposition can’t do it—and lead it.

IMF backs global central bank rate hikes, chief Georgieva says
Unknown

TOKYO, October 7. /TASS/. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) strongly supports benchmark interest rate hikes by central banks worldwide, IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said.
"Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries’ monetary policy – and it is highly appropriate that the U.S. Federal Reserve, the ECB, and the Bank of Japan have all raised rates and spoken firmly, with future policy rate paths repricing accordingly," she said.
"Policymakers had a relatively easy ride over the last 17 years as for all that time interest rates were stuck below GDP growth rate," the IMF chief said. She explained that because economies grew faster than the interest rates they had to pay, debt servicing pressures were mitigated. Now, however, rising interest rates have put an end to that environment.
She was speaking in Singapore ahead of the IMF and World Bank Autumn Meetings, scheduled for next week in Thailand.

New British weapons firm to announce first products
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
15:30:07 BST
23:30:07 KST

A company setting out to become Britain’s next sovereign defence prime, built around producing complex weapons faster and more cheaply than the established manufacturers, will announce its first products at Apex Europe this week, according to Cody Aerospace and Defence.
The firm is pitching itself at a problem it describes bluntly, that long development cycles, constrained industrial capacity and extended replenishment timelines are limiting how far Britain and its allies can build and sustain weapons stockpiles. Its answer is a model built around affordability, attainable production volumes and sovereign supply chains.
In practice that means using qualified commercial and military off-the-shelf components inside designs Cody owns, concentrating its own engineering on system integration, packaging, fire control and launcher architecture. The company says that reduces development risk, shortens lead times and makes production scalable, and that it intends to deliver turnkey solutions to end users as well as build partner companies’ products under licence.
Henry Price, the founder and chief executive, has fifteen years in the industry leading work at aerospace primes and tier one suppliers, and the company says its wider leadership brings experience across systems engineering, propulsion, software and defence procurement.
Entering the complex weapons market is not a small undertaking, and the British end of it has been dominated for two decades by MBDA under the Complex Weapons Pipeline, an arrangement that gives the Ministry of Defence a long-term relationship with a single supplier in return for sustained capability. The war in Ukraine exposed what that arrangement cannot do, which is produce weapons quickly and in quantity when a stockpile runs down, and the gap it leaves is what Cody is aiming at.
The strategy of building around off-the-shelf components rather than bespoke design has worked elsewhere. Anduril has taken a similar route with the Barracuda family, claiming a fraction of the tooling and parts of a conventional cruise missile, and Ukrainian manufacturers have gone further still out of necessity.
Apex Europe runs at The Magazine in London on Wednesday and Thursday.

The Baltic Fleet Military Court on Sept. 30 found Igor Odintsov guilty of publicly calling for terrorism, the regional news outlet Russky Zapad reported. He will serve his sentence in a high-security penal colony.
The court found that Odintsov had posted messages on a messaging app that portrayed the “ideology and practice of terrorism as correct and deserving of support and emulation.”
Investigators also said he held “radical views,” opposed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and had a “negative attitude” toward the Russian authorities.
The Lithuanian news outlet Lrytas identified Odintsov, 68, as the Kaliningrad region resident who swam across the Neman on Sept. 17 and sought asylum, saying he faced persecution in Russia over his social media posts.
Lithuanian authorities detained him at around 1:50 p.m. local time and returned him to Russia through the Panemune border crossing at 7 p.m. that same day.
Odintsov fled to Lithuania on the day he was due to appear in a Russian court over the case.
Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service said at the time that it had received no information about threats against him, any special status he held or arrangements for his admission to the European Union. It said he did not fall into a category of vulnerable people and decided to return him to Russia.
The border service now says it has “doubts” about whether Odintsov’s statement could be considered a request for protection, saying it “was not expressed clearly and understandably.”
Sigitas Šamborskis, chairman of the Lithuanian community in Kaliningrad, said he knew Odintsov and called the Lithuanian authorities’ decision to expel him a “betrayal.”

Attacks on tankers in Hormuz hit highest of any week since start of Iran war, sources say
LONDON, Oct 7 - Attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz hit their highest last week of any week since the Iran war began, according to maritime security sources tracking incidents, amid a bigger export push by Gulf producers.
Attacks, attempted attacks and harassment activity including drone overflights, surveillance and hailing using VHF radio by Iran's Revolutionary Guards have persisted in the strait, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said in a note on Sunday.
"These actions continue to demonstrate Iran’s intent to assert presence along key transit lanes and maintain pressure on transiting vessels," the JMIC said.
In the week of September 28-October 5, there had been at least 12 attacks on oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers around the Strait of Hormuz, according to data from three maritime security sources who analysed incidents based on information received from the area.
That was the highest number of attacks in a single week since the US war with Iran began on February 28, the sources said.
Separate data collated by the UN's shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization (IMO), showed nine incidents involving vessels in the same week.
The UN body tends to take longer to verify and officially record incidents, maritime sources say.
The closest week in terms of comparable incidents was the week of July 13 when there were eight incidents, separate IMO data showed.
Gulf oil exporters topped pre-war levels for about half of September, shipping data showed on Monday, though attacks on tankers and logistical constraints cloud the outlook for sustained higher flows.
India's foreign ministry said on Tuesday that 12 crew members were injured after an unknown projectile struck Panama-flagged oil tanker On Peace while it was passing through the Strait of Hormuz. REUTERS

French-Japanese duo wins Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:25:09 UTC
23:25:09 KST

France's Henri Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai on Wednesday won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for solving the mystery of why only one form of certain molecules appears in nature, a discovery decisive for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals.
The pair were honoured "for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis", the jury said.
Like hands, molecules such as amino acids exist as two mirrored variants, but only one of them is found in the proteins in the body's cells, while the other is rarely found in nature.
The fact that only one appears is a phenomenon known as "homochirality", the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences explained.
"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, told a press conference.
"The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular," Linke added.
Kagan, 95, is professor emeritus at the Universite Paris-Saclay in France while Soai, 76, is a professor at Tokyo University of Science.
Soai, who was out shopping when he received the call from Stockholm, said it was one of "the most exciting days in my life", when he was reached by the Nobel Foundation during Wednesday's press conference.
The Academy had not been able to reach Kagan to give him the news before the announcement.
French President Emmanuel Macron congratulated him on his prize on X, calling his achievement "a tremendous source of pride for the country".
Mirrored keys
The academy in a separate statement likened the chirality conundrum to a locksmith creating keys to order but whenever they produce them they get two mirrored variants.
"Only one of them fits the lock -- and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key."
One example of the potential danger of using the wrong key, or version, was the thalidomide scandal in the late 1950s and early 1960s, when thousands of children were born with birth defects.
"When researchers analysed what had happened, they realised that it was the active substance's mirror image that caused the harm," the academy said.
Phillip Broadwith, an editor at the Royal Society of Chemistry's Chemistry World magazine, explained that the duo's work "goes to the very fundamental level of understanding how we can control which 'hand' of a molecule we make".
Controlling "is crucial for making things like drugs or even flavours and fragrances", Broadwith said.
"It also helps to explain a possible way that all the chiral molecules on earth -– our proteins, sugars and biomolecules, settled into one specific handedness rather than the other," he said in an email sent to AFP by the society.
In the 1980s, Kagan found a new way of manipulating chemical reactions to create an excess of one of the mirror-image forms. Soai later took the next step and in 1995 published a key paper describing the design for "the first ever chemical reaction that had the potential to be homochiral", to create the chosen version of a molecule, the jury said.
In 2003, he succeeded.
"The Soai reaction is considered one of the most elegant chemical experiments ever conducted," the academy said.
Snubbed
Kagan had previously missed out on the Nobel prize.
In 2001, the chemistry prize was awarded to William Knowles, Ryoji Noyori and Barry Sharpless for their pioneering work in asymmetric catalysis.
That sparked controversy, with many French chemists outraged by the absence of the man regarded internationally as the "father" of the technique.
The chemistry prize follows the physics prize, which on Tuesday honoured Belgian physicist Francis Halzen for groundbreaking work using Antarctic ice to capture particles originating in the distant cosmos.
On Monday, the medicine prize was awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. The literature laureate will be revealed on Thursday, and perhaps the most keenly anticipated award — the peace prize — is due on Friday.
The economics prize wraps up the Nobel season on October 12.

Ukraine ready for five ceasefire arrangements, but Russia must agree – Foreign Ministry
Ukraine is ready for five ceasefire arrangements with Russia developed jointly with other countries, but their implementation requires Russia to agree to them.
Source: Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne; Novyny.LIVE, citing comments by Ukraine's Foreign Ministry spokesman Heorhii Tykhyi to journalists
Quote from Tykhyi: "At present, there are five different ceasefire arrangements that Ukraine is ready for and that are being worked on in different formats...
Constructive engagement and steps from the Russian side are needed for this ceasefire to take effect, but on the Ukrainian side there is indeed readiness and a constructive approach in these areas."
Details: The spokesman said diplomats had prepared a broad range of possible solutions.
The first option is a general, unconditional and complete ceasefire, which Ukraine agreed to back in 2025 during talks in Saudi Arabia. Tykhyi said this agreement remains valid and would take effect if Russia agrees to it as well.
Two other proposals, being worked on by Türkiye and Egypt with the involvement of Ukrainian diplomats, concern the Black Sea. Tykhyi described these options as mutually beneficial and realistic, but said they also require the Russian side's consent to be implemented.
The fourth area is India's work on finding solutions concerning food security in the Black Sea and in the energy sector.
During the recent engagements between President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump, the possibility of working towards an energy truce was also discussed. This is the fifth ceasefire option.
Tykhyi concluded by saying that recent attempts to shift blame for the continuation of the war from Moscow to Kyiv were a cynical exploitation of people's fatigue for political purposes.
Background:
- On 2 October, Oleksii Honcharenko, a member of parliament from the European Solidarity party, posted his vision for ending the war and advised negotiating with Russia "about everything under the sun", saying Ukraine is losing the war.
- Commenting on calls from some MPs to halt hostilities and negotiate with Russia, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine could not bend to Russia.
- Meanwhile, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha outlined four possible ceasefire arrangements with Russia. He stressed that Ukraine is ready for different formats, but only if the ceasefire covers both energy infrastructure and the Black Sea.

Eritrean troops drive through northern Ethiopian town, witnesses say

Eritrean troops drive through northern Ethiopian town, witnesses say
Oct 7 - Eritrean soldiers drove through the northern Ethiopian town of Adigrat on Wednesday, two witnesses told Reuters, days after the Horn of Africa neighbours severed diplomatic ties, raising fears of outright conflict.
The sightings of Eritrean troops would be the first confirmation of their presence on Ethiopian soil during the conflict in the country's north between the federal government and a rebel alliance that broke out last month.
Eritrea’s information minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied Eritrean forces were there, calling the witness accounts part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression against its smaller neighbour.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of backing the rebel alliance battling federal government troops since September 23 in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Afar's chief administrator said last week that Eritrean troops were fighting in his region, but Reuters could not confirm that.
Asmara has denied the allegations, which led to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Spokespeople for Ethiopia's government and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
WITNESSES SAW ERITREAN TROOPS DRIVING THROUGH TOWN
Two residents of Adigrat, a town in Tigray about 25 km (15 miles) south of the Eritrean border that has not experienced clashes during the current conflict, said they had seen two trucks with dozens of Eritrean soldiers driving through the town on Wednesday morning.
They said they could identify the soldiers as Eritrean by their off-white camouflage uniforms.
Another Adigrat resident who was not in town at the time said family members had told him they had also seen Eritrean troops.
Reuters could not independently verify their accounts. All spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns related to the ongoing conflict.
The Eritrean information minister Yemane said the allegations were intended to provide Ethiopia with a pretext to attack Eritrea.
For over three years, Abiy and other Ethiopian officials have repeatedly said that sea access is vital for their landlocked country's security and economy. Asmara views those comments as an implicit threat against it, while Addis Ababa has said it aims to gain sea access peacefully.
Ethiopia “has tried to re-package this war agenda in terms of self-defence by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea,” Yemane said. “So we connect the dots.”
NORTHERN ETHIOPIA CONFLICT FUELS FEARS OF WIDER WAR
Eritrean soldiers fought in support of Ethiopia’s federal government during a 2020-2022 civil war in Tigray.
Some of them remained in northern parts of Tigray close to the border well after the war ended, according to Ethiopia’s government, UN experts and human rights organisations. Eritrea denied this.
The fighting that broke out last month has raised fear that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in an increasingly fragile region where other powers are competing for influence.
Tigray has Ethiopia's longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west.
Ethiopia's government has also accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the opposition alliance. Both have denied this.
On Saturday, the US State Department urged Asmara and Addis Ababa to exercise restraint, warning that a conflict would jeopardise US collaboration with both countries.
Eritrea, a former province of Ethiopia, won its statehood in 1993 after a 30-year independence struggle. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 that killed tens of thousands.
They normalised diplomatic relations in 2018, winning Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize, but relations soured once again during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. REUTERS

WHO seeks additional information from Russia after lab worker's death, reports of 2nd pneumonic plague case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:22:39 UTC
23:22:39 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
07 October 2026•Update: 07 October 2026
The World Health Organization (WHO) is seeking additional information from Russia on the death of a laboratory worker from suspected pneumonic plague, as well as reports of a second employee with pneumonia of unknown cause, its chief said Wednesday.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said in a post on the US social media platform X that the worker at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute died Oct. 2 after being hospitalized with “severe pneumonia.”
He said the WHO has requested additional information to clarify the cause of the worker's severe pneumonia, the pathogen that prompted the public health measures and reports of a second employee with pneumonia of undetermined cause.
"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing" is essential to clarify conflicting reports and accurately assess potential public health risks, he added.
Initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an alleged "accidental laboratory exposure," he said.
Russian authorities said no plague cases had recently been registered in Irkutsk Oblast, in response to a WHO verification request under the International Health Regulations.
Authorities told the WHO that an epidemiological investigation was conducted, preventive and control measures were implemented and identified contacts were monitored and tested.
No high-threat pathogens were detected among the contacts, and medical observation of all identified contacts has been completed, according to Russian authorities.
Speaking to reporters in Geneva later Wednesday, WHO officials said the cause of the laboratory worker's death remains unknown and that the information available is insufficient to complete a full assessment of the potential public health risk.
“We don't know exactly how this person died,” WHO's Maria Van Kerkhove said. “We know that she had pneumonia. We know it was a fatal case.”
She said WHO understands that laboratory tests have been carried out but that the causative agent has not been identified. The agency is seeking details on which tests were performed, which pathogens were examined and whether further analysis is underway.
WHO officials said Russia described the illness as “community-acquired severe pneumonia of unknown etiology,” which would indicate that authorities believe the infection did not originate in the laboratory.
Van Kerkhove, however, said WHO still wants to establish both what caused the infection and how the worker contracted it.
The agency is also seeking more information about conditions at the facility, including what pathogens the worker handled, the protective equipment used and whether any laboratory incident occurred.
WHO officials stressed that an initial risk assessment had been based on reports of suspected pneumonic plague, a disease whose risks are well understood. But with the pathogen now undetermined, they said there is not enough information to assess the risk of further spread.
Asked whether Russia should have provided more information, Van Kerkhove said: “The simple answer is always yes.”
“We need transparent and timely reporting from all of our member states,” she said, stressing that such information is necessary for WHO to assess risks and alert other countries when needed.
WHO has offered technical support on infectious diseases and laboratory biosafety and biosecurity and said it could send experts if requested.

From 'vote chori' to 'chita andolan': Street protests return with a new playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:22:19 UTC
23:22:19 KST

Street protests are back, this time with new tools
NEW DELHI: Slogans are ringing out, crowds are turning up and the streets are once again abuzz with protests.On Tuesday, INDIA bloc MPs took their protest against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls to the national capital, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation. The march took an unexpected turn when Rahul Gandhi surprised the police with a last-minute change of course, turning it into a sit-in.A day later, opposition MPs were back with another dramatic flash protest on Janpath streets, where Priyanka Gandhi Vadra lay down on the road and refused to budge until the CEC agreed to meet opposition leaders.
During the INDIA bloc’s protest against the CEC, Priyanka Gandhi lay down on the road, daring anyone to move her.
And more could be coming. Cockroach Janata Party’s Abhijeet Dipke, who rallied young protesters during the anti-NEET paper leak agitation in July, has warned of a “Jantar Mantar 2.0” on October 10 if the CEC does not resign.But Delhi is not the only place, and politicians are not the only ones taking their grievances to the streets. Across the country, protests over very different issues are bringing people out in an attempt to make their voices heard.The protests differ in scale, issue and leadership. But together, they point to something familiar returning to the foreground: street politics.
The street has always been a political stage
Peaceful protests have always been a part of our democracy.
India's politics has rarely been confined to Parliament, party offices or election rallies. The streets have always had a part to play.Mahatma Gandhi turned marches, boycotts and satyagraha into instruments of mass politics during the freedom struggle. Decades later, Jayaprakash Narayan's movement drew students and citizens onto the streets against the Indira Gandhi government.Anna Hazare's anti-corruption protests filled Jantar Mantar and Ramlila Maidan in 2011. The anti-CAA protests saw prolonged sit-ins, while farmers camped at Delhi's borders for more than a year before the three farm laws were repealed.
How social media changed street mobilisation
Street politics, then, is hardly new. What keeps changing are the tools used to trigger, spread and sustain mobilisation. Political analyst Uday Chandra feels social media is making protests more visible while also changing who can start and sustain them.
Protest against CEC over SIR process in Delhi
"Social media certainly makes protests visible to millions, enabling a rapid or viral spread. But it also does something more important: it reduces dependence on political parties, unions and established organisations to mobilise people. A grievance may now turn into a movement before conventional political actors decide how to respond," Uday Chandra says.But the current round of protests goes beyond social-media amplification, feels Chandra."I think something real is happening beyond social-media amplification. Street protest never quite disappeared from politics in India, but for much of the past decade, electoral politics under a highly centralised party machinery overshadowed it. What we are seeing now is, to my mind, the re-emergence of the street as an autonomous political arena," he said.
When the youth lead, parties follow
What stands out in this round of protests is not just the issues being raised, but who is often raising them first.On questions ranging from examinations to electoral rolls, young people have managed to create pressure outside the usual party machinery. Increasingly, political parties have found themselves responding aggressively to issues they did not start.So, have young people and students shown political parties the way back to street mobilisation? The events surrounding the NEET protests in July this year are a case in point.As students protested over the paper leak, Jantar Mantar became the centre of an agitation that continued for weeks. The CJP emerged as the pressure group leading the agitation and eventually ensuring the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union education minister.Many political parties that initially stood on the sidelines scrambled to join the agitation. On July 21, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, Mallikarjun Kharge and other opposition leaders staged a sit-in outside Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence over police action against students protesting the NEET paper leak.
Rahul Gandhi being taken away by police during a Congress protest against police action on demonstrators at Jantar Mantar.
But Chandra argues that the CJP, as a movement, differs significantly from political parties and earlier large movements such as the Anna Hazare agitation or the farmers' protests."CJP is much more decentralised than the two movements you mention. The Anna movement had recognisable leaders and a national campaign/agenda. Likewise, the farmers’ protests rested on strong unions, local organisation, and the economic capacity to sustain mobilisation for months. By contrast, what we see emerging now is networked, relatively leader-light, and often issue-specific," he said.The CJP advantage is also organisational, he feels."Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube and other online platforms can connect previously unrelated groups rapidly. Mobilisation is, therefore, not only faster but more fluid. You do not necessarily need to build and register an organisation before launching a movement. Increasingly, the movement precedes the organisation," Chandra adds.It is perhaps this realisation that has forced political parties to course-correct their mobilisation strategies.Rahul Gandhi, who faced criticism for prioritising his "Chhatron ki Goonj" campaign instead of backing the anti-NEET protests led by CJP, has now made a more direct attempt to help Congress enter the protest space. On October 4, he launched the 'Satyagraha' portal, which seeks to map protests across the country and connect people agitating over different issues.
Rahul Gandhi launched 'Satyagraha' website for information on current protests in India
For Chandra, the move shows that Congress has recognised the risks of ignoring protests that begin online and then spill onto the streets."The Satyagraha platform strikes me as an attempt to situate the INC within an emerging ecology of anti-BJP protests. This is an interesting shift in political organisation. It takes the party from a traditional top-heavy high command structure to a node connecting diverse and dispersed struggles against the status quo."
Beyond Jantar Mantar: The protests away from the spotlight
The high-decibel protests against Gyanesh Kumar or over NEET are only one part of the story, perhaps the more visible one. Away from the national spotlight, peaceful protests have been taking place across the country over a wide range of issues.They may be small, localised and often unconnected: women’s safety, land, displacement, water, facilities in schools, local governance and more. But together, they show how the street remains an important space for people trying to make themselves heard.In Delhi, young women have marched over women's safety after cases of sexual violence. Demonstrations have also spread to cities including Mumbai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad, Patna and Dehradun, with protesters demanding safer public spaces and greater accountability from governments and police.
Protest on women's safety in Delhi
In Madhya Pradesh’s Panna district, families affected by the Ken-Betwa river-linking project have revived their "Chita Andolan". Protesters have slept on funeral pyres, stood in water and gone on hunger strike over compensation and rehabilitation.
Protesters stage the 'Chita Andolan' in Madhya Pradesh's Panna district, demanding compensation and rehabilitation.
In Maharashtra’s Maval, farmers opposing the Pavana closed pipeline project announced a 'jal samadhi' agitation while also demanding rehabilitation for families that surrendered land for the Pavana dam decades ago.Water has also brought farmers onto the streets in Karnataka, where organisations in Krishna basin districts have opposed releasing reservoir water to Telangana, arguing that drought-hit areas within Karnataka should be given priority.At IIT Bombay too, students have turned their protest over the death by suicide of student Sahil Wakode into a hunger strike, with the JNU Students’ Union joining calls for action on the demands raised by protesters.The scale and demands vary sharply. Some protests involve thousands; others are confined to a university campus, a few villages or even a handful of streets. They may target the Centre, state governments, local administrations or institutions, but the impulse is the same: take the grievance to the street.
The street is old, the tools are changing
So, street politics is old, but the mobilisation techniques have changed. Earlier movements depended heavily on student organisations, unions, public meetings and, later, television coverage. Today, a protest can begin on Instagram or X before it reaches Jantar Mantar.Social media has also changed the language of protest. A slogan shouted on the street can become a meme within hours, while posters, one-liners, chants and songs travel far beyond the protest site.Recent demonstrations have offered plenty of examples. At women's protests in Delhi, slogans such as 'Ek kachori, do samosa, in mardon ka kya bharosa' quickly travelled from the street to Instagram reels, using humour and rhyme to make a serious point about women's safety and gender attitudes.At the Mumbai protest against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, placards carried lines such as 'Gyanu must go' and the Bollywood-inspired 'Vote churaya mera, kisne o sanam? Gyanu ne'. Days later, Rahul Gandhi carried the Gen Z-style message "Gyanesh, it's done bro!" during the INDIA bloc's march to the Election Commission. Whether it will culiminate into effective but what it definitely did was make people stop and notice.
And Gen Z may not be the youngest generation learning to protest.In Lucknow, around 200 schoolgirls blocked a road in the rain over a shortage of teachers and a damaged road leading to their school. In Fatehpur, around 1,000 students staged a four-hour protest demanding drinking water and repairs to classrooms. In several cases, authorities acted after the protests.What has changed is not the instinct to protest, but how quickly a grievance can find an audience and become visible. The slogan may now become a meme and the mobilisation may begin on a phone screen. The destination, however, is often still the same: the street.

Often juggling breaking news, long-form explainers and the everyday chaos of the newsroom, she is usually managing stress, chasing clarity and trying to log off on time (rarely successful). She also cares deeply about stories around women’s rights and social change, while two very opinionated dogs make sure she never truly switches off.

Russia’s Wildberries Finding Fertile Ground in Central Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:22:00 UTC
23:22:00 KST

During World War II, Soviet authorities moved industry and people – often forcibly – away from the frontier in Europe into the heartland of Eurasia. The strategic relocation of factories and critical production to the Urals, Siberia, and Central Asia fundamentally changed economies across the union.
Now, amid a different war on the European front, Russian industry is looking again to Central Asia for relative safety to continue conducting business.
Wildberries & Russ, the parent company of Russia’s largest e-commerce retailer, Wildberries, reportedly signed an investment agreement this week with the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry, and Trade to expand its logistics capacity in Uzbekistan. The deal comes in the wake of an early August announcement from Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration that Wildberries would expand its warehouse capacity in that country.
Starting in July 2026, Ukraine began targeting major Wildberries warehousing facilities in Russia. Through mid-August, Ukrainian drones had struck at least 20 Wildberries hubs, many of them near Moscow. According to the Moscow-based e-commerce consultancy Data Insight, as reported by DW in mid-August, Wildberries had lost 480 billion rubles worth of goods ($5.7 billion) and a third of its warehouse space.
As The Diplomat’s Albert Otkjær pointed out in August, WIldberries’ effort to build out its warehousing capacity in Kazakhstan predates the current crisis – though not the February 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Wildberries’ expansion into Kazakhstan began in 2023, when the company opened its first logistics center in Astana, followed by a warehouse complex in Almaty. In September 2023, Wildberries opened a sorting center in Uralsk, the company’s fifth logistics center in the country.
Similarly, in May 2023 Wildberries opened its first logistics center in Uzbekistan, in the Tashkent region, followed by plans for a second in Fergana. In October 2023 Wildeberries announced that it would build another logistics center in the Tashkent region.
The recently announced deal pertains to a planned logistics hub in the Zangiata district of the Tashkent region, to be built on a a 67.3-hectare site. According to the company, the facility will generate at least 7,500 jobs.
As such, the wave of attacks this summer targeting Wildberries is not the sole motivation for its efforts to expand capacity in Central Asia. Those efforts began earlier. The region is, even absent the ongoing conflict, a large market for Russian companies and a bridge deeper into Asia. Factoring in the war in Ukraine only deepens the commercial logic for expansion into Central Asia.
It also deepens the risks. Ukrainian authorities have justified the strikes on an ostensibly civilian enterprise by arguing that Wildberries warehouse are “involved in supplying the Russian military with drone components, navigation equipment, and other gear,” as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in late July.
Similarly, Ukraine justified attacks on Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure near Novorossiysk – in November 2025 and July 2026 – given the critical importance of oil revenues to the Russian war machine. But collateral damage to Kazakhstan’s export of oil through the CPC led to pushback from both Astana and Washington. In February 2026, Ukraine’s ambassador to the United States said that Kyiv had received a formal demarche from Washington. The complaint, Ambassador Olga Stefanishyna said, cited the risks posed to “American investments which are being performed through Kazakhstan.”
In early August, Bloomberg reported, citing a U.S. official, that Ukraine had agreed to not strike CPC infrastructure critical to Kazakhstan’s oil exports in the Black Sea, as well as avoid striking non-Russian vessels – provided they’re not separately sanctioned or carrying Russian cargo.
Could Ukrainian drone strikes target Wildberries facilities in Kazakhstan or Uzbekistan? It’s highly unlikely, though not impossible as the war drags on. Such a strike would mark a significant expansion of the conflict and be ruinous to Kyiv’s relations with the Central Asian states, and likely the United States, too, given Washington’s intercession on Kazakhstan’s behalf in regard to the CPC.

Ukraine Strikes Russia’s Seshcha Airfield, Drone Launch Site and Command Posts
Ukrainian forces struck Russia’s Seshcha airfield and multiple drone, radar, electronic warfare, command, and logistics sites on October 6 and overnight October 7.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the strikes on October 7, stating that the targets were located in Russia and temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff noted that the extent of damage at Seshcha airfield in Russia’s Bryansk region is still being assessed.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian electronic warfare station near Hrynove and a radar station near Elionka in the Bryansk region. The military command added that a site used to store, prepare, and launch Russian strike drones was hit near Donetsk.
The General Staff further reported strikes on Russian drone command posts near Bilotserkivka and Kamianka in the temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia region. It also confirmed a strike on a command post near Hirnyk and command and observation posts near Ukrainsk and Kurakhivka in the Donetsk region.
In the temporarily occupied Luhansk region, the General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck a logistics depot near Krynychne and a fuel and lubricant depot near Kondriuche. "The Ukrainian Defense Forces continue to strike enemy military facilities," the General Staff wrote.
The strikes form part of Ukraine’s broader effort to disrupt Russian rear-area command, drone, surveillance, electronic warfare, and logistics infrastructure supporting combat operations.
Ukrainian forces have repeatedly hit the same categories of Russian infrastructure, including a drone storage and launch site near occupied Donetsk, which was struck on September 14 and overnight into September 15.
That operation also targeted three electronic warfare stations, two radar sites, and a MESH communications relay in the Bryansk region, along with a fuel and lubricant depot in the temporarily occupied Luhansk region.
Separately, a RAM-2X drone struck a Russian Nebo-M long-range radar near the Millerovo airfield in Rostov region, a facility regularly used to launch Shahed-type drones against Ukraine.
The radar was hit roughly 175 kilometers from the line of contact.
