Menopause drug Lenzetto returns to Spanish pharmacies in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:20:19 UTC
23:20:19 KST

Hungarian pharma company Gedeon Richter has told Euronews it expects to resume supply of its menopause treatment in Spain from mid-November, but warns global limits may stop it from meeting demand in 2027.
Lenzetto, one of the most widely used hormone treatments to relieve menopausal symptoms, will once again be available in Spanish pharmacies from the second half of November, its manufacturer Gedeon Richter has confirmed to Euronews.
"We expect the product to be available in pharmacies from the second half of November," the pharmaceutical company said in response to questions from Euronews. Gedeon Richter says it will do "everything possible" to guarantee stable production for the rest of this year and in 2027, although it acknowledges that worldwide supply constraints may prevent it from fully covering current demand.
The company traces the origin of the current shortage of the medicine in Spain to a sharp rise in demand for menopause hormone treatments in Europe. In an email, the company explained that growth has been far higher than expected and that both manufacturing capacity and the supply of the device used to administer Lenzetto, the applicator, could not keep pace with the surge in demand.
Gedeon Richter stresses that the situation is temporary and "is not related to any problem with the quality or safety of the medicine". The issue, according to the company, is simply that high demand has outstripped its production capacity.
To increase the availability of its medicine, the laboratory says it is making full use of its current production capacity and working to expand both the number of suppliers and its manufacturing options. It is also trying to improve the supply of applicators and increase their production capacity, among other measures.
These plans include a new plant and a new production line. In Romania, Gedeon Richter has also launched a dedicated investment project to strengthen its manufacturing capacity. The company warns, however, that expanding pharmaceutical production takes time because of quality controls.
The company also acknowledges that the measures adopted will not resolve the situation overnight. It says it is working so that the changes can improve supply as quickly as possible.
A problem affecting other markets
The shortage of Lenzetto is not limited to Spain. Gedeon Richter confirms that there is currently a global shortage of the medicine, although the severity of the problems varies between markets depending on local demand, forecasting capacity and logistical possibilities.
The situation has for months made it difficult to obtain some hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms. The lack of Lenzetto forced patients and healthcare professionals to turn to other forms of estradiol, which eventually generated a domino effect on some of the alternative treatments.
The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has also identified the Lenzetto shortage and is studying possible coordinated measures at the European level. In Spain, the Spanish Agency of Medicines and Medical Devices (AEMPS) has likewise recorded supply problems affecting other medicines, such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva.
"The supply problem started in April with Lenzetto and has subsequently affected other transdermal hormone therapies such as patches and gels," AEMPS said in a statement (source in Spanish) published in early October. "The Ministry of Health has been in contact with the holders of other hormone treatment alternatives that are currently not reimbursed, to explore their possible inclusion in the pharmaceutical services of the National Health System."
Richter responds to AEMPS criticism
AEMPS has pointed out that some of the supply forecasts previously communicated by Gedeon Richter "have not always been accurate" and that interruptions which could affect the continuous supply of the medicine were not reported with sufficient notice.
Asked by Euronews about these comments, the company does not directly address the allegations, but says it maintains "close contact" with AEMPS and works "in a collaborative manner" with the agency to tackle the situation.
Gedeon Richter adds that it has improved its forecasting systems in response to demand it describes as "unprecedented" and that it continues to provide information to the authorities as new data become available.
The laboratory does not, however, guarantee a full recovery of supply in the short term. The company says its goal is to be able to consistently meet patient demand from the second half of 2027.

Menopause drug Lenzetto back in Spanish pharmacies from November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:20:19 UTC
23:20:19 KST

Hungarian pharma company Gedeon Richter has told Euronews it expects to resume supply of its menopause treatment in Spain from mid-November, but warns global limits may stop it from meeting demand in 2027.
Lenzetto, one of the most widely used hormone treatments to relieve menopausal symptoms, will once again be available in Spanish pharmacies from the second half of November, its manufacturer Gedeon Richter has confirmed to Euronews.
"We expect the product to be available in pharmacies from the second half of November," the pharmaceutical company said in response to questions from Euronews. Gedeon Richter says it will do "everything possible" to guarantee stable production for the rest of this year and in 2027, although it acknowledges that worldwide supply constraints may prevent it from fully covering current demand.
The company traces the origin of the current shortage of the medicine in Spain to a sharp rise in demand for menopause hormone treatments in Europe. In an email, the company explained that growth has been far higher than expected and that both manufacturing capacity and the supply of the device used to administer Lenzetto, the applicator, could not keep pace with the surge in demand.
Gedeon Richter stresses that the situation is temporary and "is not related to any problem with the quality or safety of the medicine". The issue, according to the company, is simply that high demand has outstripped its production capacity.
To increase the availability of its medicine, the laboratory says it is making full use of its current production capacity and working to expand both the number of suppliers and its manufacturing options. It is also trying to improve the supply of applicators and increase their production capacity, among other measures.
These plans include a new plant and a new production line. In Romania, Gedeon Richter has also launched a dedicated investment project to strengthen its manufacturing capacity. The company warns, however, that expanding pharmaceutical production takes time because of quality controls.
The company also acknowledges that the measures adopted will not resolve the situation overnight. It says it is working so that the changes can improve supply as quickly as possible.

All 32 NATO Members Send Military Representatives to Kyiv in First Such Visit in Eight Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:20:13 UTC
23:20:13 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
All 32 NATO Members Send Military Representatives to Kyiv in First Such Visit in Eight Years
NATO’s Military Committee visited Kyiv for the first time in eight years, bringing together military representatives from all 32 NATO member states for talks with Ukraine’s military leadership, according to NATO Military Committee Chair Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone on October 7.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The delegation, led Cavo Dragone, visited the Ukrainian capital on October 6 and met with Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi.
The visit followed a commitment Cavo Dragone made to Drapatyi after their meeting earlier this year. It also came several months after NATO’s North Atlantic Council visited Ukraine in June.
“After an eight-year absence, the NATO Military Committee is back in Kyiv for an official visit. And while we may not have been here physically, Ukraine has always been in our thoughts, discussions, decisions and subsequent actions—every single day,” Cavo Dragone said in a video address.
During the talks, the NATO representatives discussed Ukraine’s current military priorities and lessons gained during Russia’s war against Ukraine, including experience that could help the Alliance strengthen its preparedness for existing and future security threats.
Cavo Dragone said the delegation also sought an updated assessment of the battlefield situation from Drapatyi and discussed what additional steps NATO members could take to support Ukraine.
The 32 military representatives also visited the Wall of Remembrance in Kyiv to honor Ukrainian service members killed defending the country.
The trip marked the first visit by the NATO Military Committee to Kyiv since 2018. Drapatyi had announced plans for the committee’s return in August 2026 following his first meeting with Cavo Dragone.
Earlier, in March, a NATO military command delegation led by Admiral Pierre Vandier, Supreme Allied Commander Transformation, visited Ukraine for the first time since the start of the full-scale war, discussing Ukrainian participation in future NATO exercises and expanded military cooperation.

Police fire teargas as French school protests cause ‘heaviest toll in decades’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:20:00 UTC
23:20:00 KST

Police fire teargas as French school protests cause ‘heaviest toll in decades’
- - Police used tear gas as France’s biggest school protests in decades spread nationwide, with students, teachers and parents angry over poor school conditions and violence.
- - Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said 215 teenagers and 85 staff were injured, while over 700 police were hurt; a 15-year-old lost a hand in clashes.
- - The government plans school repairs and reforms, but faces budget pressure, rising debt and growing political unrest before next spring’s presidential election.
AI generated
STRASBOURG/LYON/PARIS – Police fired tear gas at protesters outside French high schools on Oct 6 as students, teachers and parents took to the streets on the biggest day of what Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu described as the most violent school protests in decades.
The protests, in which a teenager lost a hand on Oct 5, were the latest manifestation of public anger in a country where the far right and far left are surging ahead of a presidential election in the spring.
The government is under pressure to tame public debt amid weak growth, and has struggled with basic tasks such as passing a budget since President Emmanuel Macron’s allies lost their majority in a 2024 parliamentary vote.
Lecornu told lawmakers at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff had so far been injured in clashes, “the heaviest toll in decades paid by the school system”. His office said more than 700 police officers were also hurt.
Macron has convened Lecornu and other senior ministers at an emergency meeting on Oct 6, broadcaster BFM reported.
In Marseille and Nantes, protesters held up signs reading “The state has killed national education”. In Toulouse, parents linked arms at the front of a march through the city.
In Strasbourg, Lyon, Rennes and Paris, the demonstrations at times turned violent, with police firing tear gas and protesters lighting fires in the streets and hurling projectiles.
The Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.
By late afternoon they said they were still clashing with a small contingent of people. Three shopfronts had been damaged.
The protests began in September in the deprived suburbs of Paris, before spreading nationwide.
“There is such a gap between the elites and us,” said Hugo Vetzel, a recent high-school graduate in Strasbourg.
The High School Students Union said more than half of France’s high schools were blockaded or would close for the day. Some local education authorities have tried to move classes online.
Students complain about schools facing basic maintenance problems, from water leaks to rat infestations.
Thousands of arrests
Rights groups, students and parent groups have accused e authorities of using disproportionate force against minors. The government says the protest movement has been hijacked by outsiders and in some places deteriorated into urban violence.
France’s interior ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested since the protests began, the overwhelming majority of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted for unspecified crimes, including 1,483 minors, the justice ministry said.
A teenager’s hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Oct 5. The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police grenade intended to be non-lethal.
“They want to divide the young people into good and bad protesters,” said Omar Slaouti, a high-school teacher in Argenteuil, a north-western suburb of Paris.
Young people were torching things to make their voices heard, he said, including those angry about being excluded from the education system.
“If there were no trash cans on fire, the government would not have stepped back and become aware of the issues at stake. I would add that one can, of course, regret this but the government alone is responsible for this.”
Six months before an election to replace Macron, his government and far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the unrest. LFI denies the accusation.
“All the young people are in the streets. Everywhere there aren’t police, everything is going smoothly,” said Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI’s presidential candidate.
Prime minister promises reponse
Lecornu has ordered his ministers to tackle the students’ leading demands. Those include ensuring absent teachers are replaced, reviewing the length of the 8am to 6pm school day and the need for longer lunch breaks.
The government will also look at repairs needed to ageing school buildings, said Lecornu, who demanded ministers send in their first proposals by the end of October.
Parent Emilie Lhomme said at a protest outside the Helene Boucher school in Paris that the government’s words were not enough.
“That’s all fine and dandy, but that’s not what’s going to change the daily lives of our children,” she said.
Finding spare cash to implement educational reforms will be difficult.
The government is under pressure to try to narrow a ballooning budget deficit as investor concerns about France’s growing debt, weak growth and reluctance to rein in spending push the cost of borrowing higher. The yield on France’s 10-year bonds briefly hit a 24-year high of over 5% last week.
The surge in French borrowing costs has started to spill into the broader euro area, with the sliding euro currency the latest alarm bell for policymakers. Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Oct 6 there was no need for the European Central Bank to step in.
Le Pen, the far-right euro-sceptic populist leading the presidential race ahead of next spring’s election, set out plans to slash public spending if elected, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility as the bond market crisis deepens.
French spending on education has lagged inflation and the country’s students are trailing their OECD peers in overall performance, data from the PISA 2025 assessment shows. REUTERS

Ukraine is ready for 5 ceasefire options — Ministry of Foreign Affairs
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv is considering five ceasefire formats: Ukrainian, Indian, Turkish, Egyptian, and American. Steps by Russia are needed to launch them.
Ukraine has five proposals regarding a possible ceasefire with Russia. In particular, these include the Ukrainian agreement presented in March 2025, as well as proposals from countries such as India, Turkey, Egypt, and the United States. This was reported by Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi, according to UNN.
Details
The other day, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that, as of now, there are five such, essentially different, ceasefire arrangements that Ukraine is ready for and that are being worked on in various formats
According to him, this is primarily a general ceasefire, unconditional and complete, to which Ukraine agreed back in March 2025 in Jeddah.
This Ukrainian agreement remains in force and could take effect if there were, accordingly, a reciprocal agreement from the Russian Federation. The second and third are proposals being developed by Turkey and Egypt concerning the Black Sea. They have positions developed in consultations with Ukraine. In other words, I want everyone to understand that these are not simply proposals from outside being offered to the Ukrainian side; they are the work of diplomats with the participation of Ukrainian diplomacy and with Sybiha's direct personal involvement—the development of modalities that could work
He also recalled that there is a broader proposal from India. There is also another proposal from the United States, which was discussed during the latest contacts between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump.
As of now, I repeat once again, constructive steps from the Russian side are necessary for these ceasefires, concerning the matters I have listed, to take effect. But on the Ukrainian side, there is indeed both readiness and a constructive approach in these areas
We remind you
Ukraine received proposals regarding a possible ceasefire with Russia from India, Turkey, Egypt, and the United States. India proposed the broadest option, while Kyiv is ready to consider various ceasefire formats.

Hungary lifts veto on advancing Ukraine’s EU accession with the opening of new clusters – media
Kyiv • UNN
EU ambassadors paved the way for the start of negotiations on the single market and competitiveness. Hungary abandoned its blockade over minority rights.
EU ambassadors in Brussels on Wednesday, October 7, paved the way for the start of accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova on the single market and competitiveness. Hungary lifted its veto on the talks. Rapporteur reported this, citing EU diplomats, writes UNN.
Details
Hungary had been blocking this step since the summer, demanding that Ukraine adopt legislation concerning the educational rights of national minorities.
The next step is for the bloc's capitals to agree on drafts of the EU's common positions, potentially paving the way for the official opening of two clusters at an intergovernmental conference (IGC) next week, the publication writes.
If they are opened, only two of the six negotiating clusters will remain for Ukraine: Cluster 4, covering digital and industrial policy, and Cluster 5, covering energy and climate.
"Hungary made it clear at the beginning of this week that it would drop its opposition if Ukraine's parliament approved an agreement with Budapest on protecting the rights of the Hungarian minority," the publication says.
The vote in Ukraine's parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, is "scheduled for next Monday," the publication writes. "The following day, the ministers of the EU countries will meet in Luxembourg. Diplomats hope to convene an IGC to officially open the clusters on the sidelines of the meeting," the publication notes.
"Ukraine will adopt legislation in the Rada next week, and we hope that, on this basis, there will be unanimity in the Council on opening Clusters 2 and 3. By the way, the same will apply to Moldova," an EU diplomat said.
The EU opened Clusters 1 and 6 in June and July, but the new Hungarian government led by Péter Magyar slowed further progress until an agreement on minority rights is approved, the publication notes.
On Tuesday, the European Commission presented a broader review of enlargement policy, according to which EU membership candidates will be placed on a 15-year probationary period.
The European Commission proposes new rules for future EU members07.10.26, 12:47 • 2966 views
Under the new "institutional safeguard," the EU may suspend a new member's voting rights in the Council of the EU after particularly serious cases involving violations of EU values or breaches of the principle of "sincere cooperation."

European Commissioner Kubilius calls for ramping up military preparations in EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

23:17:43 KST

BERLIN, October 7. /TASS/. European Commissioner for Defense and Space Andrius Kubilius called for accelerating military preparations in Europe, which, according to him, is not yet able to provide military deterrence to Russia.
"Russia is still not being deterred," he said at a conference in Hamburg broadcast by the European Commission.
"Russia is still outproducing us in military production. Russia is able to rapidly make military technological innovations, like new types of drones."
He admitted that if "day X" comes "in terms of Russia’s possible aggression," the EU will face "a battle-tested Russian army with an ability to use 10 million drones per year or around 30,000 drones per day."
Based on these assumptions, Kubilius demanded that "our defense readiness has to speed up." He called for special efforts to develop "military mobility" in the EU - that is, the ability of EU countries to quickly transfer large masses of troops and weapons across Europe.
Kubilius called for a speedy creation of a military Schengen, a legal system for the free movement of troops throughout Europe in an emergency situation.
Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin called "lies and nonsense" the assumption that Russia wants to attack NATO, and advised anyone who hears such statements to ask the question: "Why does Russia need this?".

Knox posts photo outside Perugia courthouse 15 years after Kercher acquittal
Italy
Unknown Publisher

16:17:18 CEST
23:17:18 KST

Amanda Knox on Wednesday posted a
photo of herself outside a courthouse in Perugia 15 years to the
day since her acquittal in the murder of her flatmate in the
Umbrian capital, Meredith Kercher.
                                    
The 39-year-old Seattle-born author and stand-up comedian, who
recently caused a flap by appearing at the Edinburgh Fringe with
a set that featured her conviction and eventual acquittal in the
November 1 2007 murder of the London-born 21-year-old Leeds
University exchange student, posted on X: "I also visited the
courthouse where I was sentenced to 26 years, and where crowds
of locals chanted 'Shame' when I was acquitted.
                                    
"And I walked through Venice, Milan, and Rome with my head held
high," she emphasized.
                                    
Among the memories she posted was a photo with Father Saulo, the
chaplain at Perugia's prison during her four-year incarceration,
two years before she was found guilty in 2009 and two years
before she was  cleared in 2011.
                                    
"The priest who held my hand during those years when my family
couldn't," Knox wrote.
                                    
Knox was convicted of the murder of Kercher with her former
Italian boyfriend Raffale Sollecito in 2009 and was sentenced to
26 years in prison.
                                    
In 2011, the conviction was overturned and Knox was released,
whereupon she returned to America.
                                    
In 2013, her acquittal was overturned after a successful
prosecution appeal and a retrial was ordered.
                                    
In 2014, an appeals court in Florence convicted Knox of murder
for a second time.
                                    
In 2015, the Italian Supreme Court of Cassation definitively
acquitted Knox of Kercher's murder.
                                    
Knox has since begun a comedy career.
                                    
In 2026, Knox announced a comedy show at the Edinburgh Fringe
Festival called "Cartwheel" that focuses on the events in
Perugia.
                                    
The title referenced a story that had claimed she did cartwheels
in the police station after Kercher's death.
                                    
Ivorian former drifter Rudy Guede is the only person to have
been found definitively guilty of Kercher's murder.
                                    
Guede was released from jail in November 2021 after serving 13
years of a 16-year-term.
                                    
Last November the 39-year-old was indicted on charges of
sexually abusing his ex girlfriend.
                                    
Knox criticised Guede's early release.
                                    
The Italian lawyer representing Kercher's family expressed shock
in August at the news that Knox was telling her story at the
Fringe.
                                    
Francesco Maresca said the show was "a deplorable offence to
Meredith's memory", adding that he had lost all hope of Knox
being able to understand the effect on the victim's family. ,
Knox reportedly said Kercher would have enjoyed the show
because she was intelligent and refined and stressed that she
wasmaking fun of how she was vilified and not at the murder.

Deputy Minister Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski attends meeting of co-chairs of Polish-German Round Table
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
16:16:31 CEST
23:16:31 KST

Deputy Minister Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski attends meeting of co-chairs of Polish-German Round Table
01.10.2026
Four co-chairs of the Polish-German Round Table, established to support the Polish community in Germany and the German minority in Poland, held consultations in Berlin. The meeting took place at the Federal Ministry of the Interior on 30 September.
The hosts were represented by State Secretary to the Federal Minister of the Interior Christoph de Vries and Federal Government Commissioner for Matters Related to Ethnic German Resettlers and National Minorities, Dr. Bernd Fabritius. The Polish side was represented by Secretary of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and Secretary of State at the Ministry of the Interior and Administration Tomasz Szymański. The meeting was also attended by German Ambassador to Poland Miguel Berger and Jan Tombiński, chargé d'affaires a.i. of the Polish Embassy in Berlin.
The meeting’s main goal was to prepare the next session of the Polish–German Round Table, which will be held in Warsaw on 20 January 2027. In a friendly and constructive atmosphere, the attendees summarised the proposals gathered during consultations with the Polish diaspora in Germany and the representatives of the German minority in Poland. 
*** 
Established in 2010, the Polish–German Round Table is a bilateral dialogue forum, the purpose of which is to discuss and implement the provisions of the Polish–German Treaty on Good Neighbourly Relations and Friendly Cooperation of 1991. It aims to support German citizens of Polish descent and Poles in Germany as well as the German minority in Poland in preserving and fostering their cultural, linguistic, and educational identity.

Estonia aims to teach air‑gun shooting to 14‑year‑old students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Estonia aims to teach air‑gun shooting to 14‑year‑old students
The Defense Resources Agency wants as many eighth‑grade students as possible to be able, if they wish, to shoot an air gun. This school year, about 20 schools are offered in‑depth national defense instruction at the end of basic school.
The Defense Resources Agency began this year with a so‑called national defense year project, with which it wishes to bring national‑defense‑related instruction also into the 8th grades of basic school.
At present, national defense instruction is compulsory in high school. The head of the Defense Resources Agency's national defense education bureau, Aare Jamnes, said that in eighth grade it may not be a separate subject. "Basically, in every subject there is something that can be used in national defense or discussed from national defense," he said.
Jamnes said that this school year 23 schools expressed interest in the national defense year, and in the coming years it is hoped that the number of interested schools will keep growing. The goal, however, is that all Estonian schools would implement integrated national defense instruction in eighth grades.
The programme of these roughly 23 schools' eighth grades includes, among other things, national‑defense‑themed quizzes, excursions to Defense Forces units, and also shooting instruction with air guns.
Jamnes noted that in this way Estonia can get more good shooting athletes, but at the same time young people would be somewhat earlier ready also for national defense.
He explained that there are two different ways to organize shooting in schools. One possibility is when the school itself is active and expresses the wish that they would have such an opportunity. For such schools, the state also offers separate shooting‑trainer instruction.
"The other possibility is that when a physical education teacher wishes to go with their group somewhere to a shooting range. Let's take, for example, Elva school, which contacts the sports center, goes a couple of kilometers from the school to the shooting range, there are trainers, equipment, and shooting is done in a safe environment," Jamnes explained.
Jamnes said that in the case of air pistols it would be entirely feasible also for schools to have a separate shooting range. "A safe shooting lane for an air pistol can be set up in any sports hall. Even now there are still very many schools where shooting ranges are in working order or repairable," he said.
Teenage years are turbulent and young people also have more and more mental health problems. Jamnes said that giving young people an air gun, however, rather reduces any danger situations connected with shooting.
"The more physically active young people are and the more they do joint activities with others, learn and gain new experiences, the more anxiety and various mental problems come down. They are not so withdrawn and they have more opportunities to do things together. I find that this does not increase danger situations, but rather in the broad picture does only good for the mental side, when young people can do sports together and learn new things," he said.
And ultimately shooting an air gun is not compulsory for young people. That is, whoever does not wish to, does not have to shoot, Jamnes noted. "If a young person does not wish it or parents do not wish that their child would get experience in a shooting range, then of course no one is forced," he said.
--
Editor: Valner Väino, Argo Ideon

Romania buys 12 H225M helicopters to replace old Pumas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:50 UTC
23:14:50 KST

- Romania signed a contract for 12 Airbus H225M helicopters, financed by the European Union's SAFE program, to begin replacing its IAR-330 Puma fleet.
- Romania's defense ministry valued the purchase order at about €757 million (about $848 million), including initial logistics support and training.
Romania has signed a contract for 12 Airbus H225M Caracal military helicopters, the first step in replacing the Romanian Air Force’s aging fleet of locally built IAR-330 Puma helicopters, Airbus Helicopters said on October 7.
The deal was concluded through France’s defense procurement agency, the DGA, and is financed under the European Union’s Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, loan program. Romania’s defense ministry said in July that its purchase order for the helicopters, including initial logistics support and crew training, is worth about €757 million (about $848 million), within a total approved SAFE project budget of €852 million (about $954 million).
Airbus said the H225Ms will start replacing the Pumas in both conventional and special operations roles. The first helicopter is due 38 months after the order was signed, Romanian news outlet HotNews reported.
“We are honoured that Romania has chosen the H225M to strengthen its defence capabilities. This selection will also bolster Romania’s industrial capabilities through our long term partnership with IAR, Romania’s sole helicopter manufacturer,” said Matthieu Louvot, chief executive of Airbus Helicopters.
The H225M is the military version of Airbus’ largest Super Puma family helicopter, a twin-engine medium-heavy transport used for troop transport, search and rescue and special operations. Airbus says more than 350 H225s and H225Ms are in service and have flown more than 1 million hours. Romania becomes the 13th H225M customer, joining Brazil, France, Hungary, Indonesia, Iraq, Kuwait, Malaysia, Mexico, Morocco, the Netherlands, Singapore and Thailand.
Romania’s state-owned IAR plant in Brasov license-built the Pumas the H225M will replace, starting in the 1970s. The defense ministry plans to buy about 30 more helicopters after 2030 from its national budget, a deal of roughly €2 billion (about $2.24 billion) meant to move H225M production to Brasov, HotNews reported from the ministry’s SAFE procurement list.
The order is Romania’s second with Airbus Helicopters under SAFE. In June, the Romanian Ministry of Internal Affairs ordered seven H160 and five H145 helicopters for emergency response, civil protection and public order missions. Romania also ordered two H215M helicopters in a naval configuration in 2023.
SAFE provides low-interest EU loans for member states to buy defense equipment quickly from European industry. Romania’s allocation is €16.6 billion, the second-largest among the countries that applied, and the H225M deal was approved by the Romanian parliament as part of a wider package that also includes Lynx infantry fighting vehicles and Piranha 5 armored personnel carriers.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, that reaching an agreement with the US is “not out of reach” if Washington adheres to international legal frameworks, according to the Iranian presidency.
The two leaders discussed regional developments, Iran-US negotiations and relations, according to a statement.
Pezeshkian briefed Putin on negotiations between Iran and the US mediated by Pakistan, describing Washington’s “double standards and maximalism” as the biggest obstacle to reaching a fair agreement.
He said Tehran was prepared to reach a “balanced and fair” agreement that would ensure lasting peace and security in the region.
“Our red line is Iran’s national interests and the rights of the Iranian people,” said Pezeshkian, adding that if Washington adhered to international legal frameworks, reaching an agreement would not be out of reach.
The Iranian president also described Gulf countries as Iran’s “brothers” and expressed regret about the use of US military bases in those countries for attacks against Iran.
He said Tehran was ready to cooperate with neighboring countries to achieve regional peace and security without the presence or involvement of powers from outside the region.
Putin reiterated Russia’s support for diplomatic efforts to reach a political settlement to the war and expressed Moscow’s readiness to continue helping to find a diplomatic solution, according to the statement.
He also stressed the need to respect Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, and backed Tehran’s demands for compensation for damage caused during the war and long-term security guarantees against additional attacks.
The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to expanding cooperation under the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty and maintaining close coordination in international forums.
Iran and Russia signed the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty in January 2025 to strengthen cooperation in several areas, including trade, energy, transport and security.
The US-Israel war with Iran erupted in late February with attacks against Iran, followed by Iranian retaliatory strikes in the region.
Washington and Tehran signed an initial agreement in June following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar to halt hostilities and pave the way for negotiations.
Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including on security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

South West Water owner taps investors to fix infrastructure after sewage spills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-07
14:14:35 UTC
23:14:35 KST

The owner of embattled South West Water has slashed its dividend and launched a cash call to investors as it attempts to fund infrastructure investment, days after it was hit by a record £7.9m fine for hundreds of sewage spills.
London-listed Pennon said on Wednesday it would tap investors for £550m, as part of a £1bn investment “to drive improved outcomes for customers and communities”.
Shares in the utility company, which supplies water to about 3.5 million customers across the south-west of England, as well as 380,000 business customers around the UK, tumbled in response to the announcement, making Pennon the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 index.
Pennon’s new chief executive, Keith Haslett, who was appointed in April, said he had conducted a comprehensive review of the business and had identified areas for improvement, including customer service and the company’s environmental performance.
Last month, a judge issued South West Water with the largest fine for environmental offences in the region, at nearly £8m, and said the company’s conduct amounted to reckless failures in management systems and response to known risks. The fine will be paid by shareholders rather than through bill increases.
The company was fined after hundreds of sewage spills during a six-year period at popular bathing spots including the coastal village of Harlyn in north Cornwall and in sensitive habitats, such as the River Camel, which is home to otters and Atlantic salmon and popular with birdwatchers and sailors.
In June, South West Water was fined £1.85m by a judge in a separate case. The company pleaded guilty to the criminal offence of supplying water unfit for human consumption, after a 2024 parasite outbreak in Brixham, Devon, made hundreds of people sick and forced thousands of households to boil their water.
Pennon said on Wednesday it would also slash its shareholder dividend by about 30%, including the impact of the equity raise, as part of its “operational reset”.
Shares in Pennon, which also owns Bristol Water and SES Water, slumped by as much as 22% on Wednesday after the company’s announcement, named “project Proteus”, after a sea god in Greek mythology.
Haslett told reporters the reaction to the company’s plans had been mixed, saying: “Investment is needed to achieve improvements – we’re funding the plans in the right way.”
He added this would not be funded by further increases to customers’ bills and said he was also bringing some critical roles back in-house, including leakage teams that were previously outsourced.
In its recent results for the year to 31 March, Pennon revealed it had incurred outcome delivery incentives from the water regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, of about £42m for its water and wastewater performance. It said it had faced operational pressures from “exceptional storms and sustained rainfall coupled with a step up in targets and penalty rates”.
The company anticipates it will continue to incur the penalties until 2030 but is aiming to reduce them by at least 50% a year.
On Tuesday, South West Water applied for a ban on non-essential water use for some businesses across parts of Devon and west Dorset, after a lack of significant rainfall after the hot, dry summer. The proposed ban would restrict activities such as vehicle washing, the cleaning of buildings and the filling of non-domestic swimming pools and ponds.
Customers of South West Water are already seeing their bills rise to fuel £2.5bn of investment in infrastructure in the years to 2030.
The number of customer complaints received by South West Water more than doubled over the past year, according to the latest figures from a consumer watchdog. The Consumer Council for Water found complaints to the company soared by 153%, and rated South West Water and Thames Water “poor” for the number of complaints received and how they handled them.
In recent weeks, Andy Burnham has come under further pressure from a cross-party group of MPs to take control of indebted Thames Water.
The MPs are calling for ministers to break off talks with the US hedge funds that are effectively running the company and to consider emergency legislation to take charge of Thames’ financial affairs.
However, the environment secretary, Angela Eagle, has previously suggested a special administration regime – effectively temporary public control – could not be triggered for Thames Water and would require a change in the law.

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek attended the opening of the International Justice Summit, held at Çırağan Palace under the theme “The Future of Justice: A Common Responsibility for Humanity,” and delivered a speech. (AA Photo)
Istanbul on Oct. 8 hosted the International Justice Summit, bringing together justice ministers, members of the judiciary and law professors from various countries, as Turkish Justice Minister Akın Gürlek stressed that international law must be applied equally to all actors.
The summit, which will conclude on Oct. 9, features representatives from more than 70 countries.
A total of 40 speakers are scheduled to address eight separate sessions, while bar associations from 18 countries and more than 30 international organizations are also taking part.

He described as “extremely concerning” the fact that a justice minister had been prevented from attending an international meeting at a platform convened to discuss international cooperation, the rule of law and the universality of justice.
Gürlek stressed that international law can only truly constitute law when it is applied equally to all actors.
“A rule derives its legal character not from being applied only in certain circumstances or to certain actors, but from preserving its universal character. For this reason, we believe the international community must take action without further delay,” he said.
Gürlek also underlined the importance of “effectively investigating allegations of violations, ensuring that those responsible are held accountable, preserving evidence, safeguarding the rights of victims, and supporting independent and impartial judicial mechanisms.”

Katz seeks exclusion orders against activists ahead of West Bank olive harvest
The move follows a Yesha Council appeal citing plans by foreign activists, including participants recruited by the Global Sumud Flotilla organization, to join harvest activities
Defense Minister Israel Katz has directed officials to take steps toward issuing administrative exclusion orders against activists whose activities are found to threaten public order and security during the West Bank olive harvest, i24NEWS learns.
The directive followed an appeal by Israel Gantz, head of the Binyamin Regional Council and chairman of the Yesha Council, on behalf of local authority leaders in the West Bank. Gantz asked Katz to prevent activists he accused of planning provocations and confrontations from reaching harvest sites.
The olive harvest season began this week. According to the statement, the Global Sumud Flotilla organization, which led the Gaza flotilla attended by Greta Thunberg, announced that it was recruiting foreign activists to travel to Israel and take part in activities in West Bank harvest areas.
The appeal also cited organizing by Go Palestine, Protect the Harvest, Faz3a and the International Solidarity Movement.
In response, Katz instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists assessed as posing a threat to public order and security in the area. The statement did not specify how many people could be affected or whether any orders had already been issued.
“The residents of Judea and Samaria are not a backdrop for the campaigns of foreign activists,” Gantz said, using the Israeli designation for the West Bank.
Gantz accused Israeli and foreign activists of seeking to create confrontations and said the olive harvest should not become a means of deliberately generating friction. He thanked Katz for responding to the appeal.

Russian strike on buses kills 30 in frontline Ukrainian city
KYIV – Ukraine on Oct 8 accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians after 30 people were killed when two buses were blown up in the frontline city of Kramatorsk, in one of the deadliest single attacks for weeks.
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky vowed that the attack “will not go unanswered” after photos posted by local authorities showed the burnt-out metal shell of the vehicles, with bodies and debris strewn across the road.
“Russia is trying to destroy all life in (the) Donbas (region) and the world must respond to this,” he wrote on Telegram, warning that the death toll could rise.
Police said the buses were hit with a glide bomb. Three more people were killed in a nearby village as a result of shelling, the emergency services said.
The strikes come just a day after five children were among 22 killed when a Russian missile flattened a five-storey apartment block in Pryluky, in the northern Chernigiv region.
“The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” Donetsk governor Vadym Filashkin said, accusing Moscow of flouting “every conceivable rule of warfare and norm of international humanitarian law”.
Kramatorsk City Council called it “yet another horrific crime committed by the Russian army against the civilian population”.
“Once again, the Russians have struck a location where there are absolutely no military targets,” it added.
Civilian casualties
There has been mounting concern about the increase in civilian deaths and injuries in the nearly five-year conflict, as both sides step up long-range attacks beyond their borders.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Ukraine has accused its forces of deliberately attacking and killing civilians.
The United Nations has verified more than 17,000 civilian deaths throughout the war but says the real number is considerably higher.
Last week, Zelensky said his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin had sanctioned massive attacks on civilian areas, a claim the Kremlin denies.
During a tour of the site of the Pryluky attack on Oct 8, visiting UK foreign minister Ed Miliband said there was “no clearer sign of Putin’s evil, evil intent and strategy in this conflict”.
“Putin once said that he was going to win on the battlefield,” he told reporters, as London announced more sanctions on Moscow. “He is trying to win by terrorising civilians.”
Zelensky urged the US to “raise the pressure” on Russia, including through providing better air defence systems, to force Putin to the negotiating table.
Security worsened
Ukraine’s capital, Kyiv, has come under increasing attack, including on Oct 7 from a barrage of Russian ballistic and cruise missiles, and jet-powered drones.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said three people were killed and 14 wounded on Oct 8.
Key transport bridges in the city, as well as the rail network and energy grid have been hit.
For the first few years of the conflict, Kyiv had been relatively spared from the devastation wrought on the frontline but should now be on a war footing, he argued.
Kramatorsk, which was home to some 150,000 people before the war, is one of the key cities that Russia has not yet captured in the eastern Donetsk region, which Moscow claims as its own.
It has been a logistics and supply hub for the Ukrainian military for much of the war and is part of the so-called “fortress belt” which troops are fighting to keep hold of.
Russian forces have edged close to the city’s eastern fringes, which has prompted calls for the civilians who remain to relocate to safer regions of Ukraine.
Filashkin said the Oct 8 strike represented a “sharp deterioration” in security and ordered the suspension of public transport in Kramatorsk and neighbouring Sloviansk.
Ukraine in September launched a counter-offensive against Russian troops around Lyman – to the north of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk – claiming some success in regaining pockets of territory. AFP

ATHENS, Oct 8 - Greece has agreed to spend up to $4 billion upgrading more of its F-16 fighter jets and buying advanced missiles from the US, two senior sources told Reuters on Thursday, a day after a visit by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Greece had already planned to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to buy US made F-35 fighter jets and helicopters, and to build the "Achilles Shield" a multi-layer anti-ballistic and anti-aircraft system with Israeli-made weapons.
"The agreement includes new advanced missiles and bombs for the F-16 Viper the F-35 fighter jets, and the Black Hawk helicopters. Also the upgrade of old F-16 fighter jets to Viper version," a senior defence Ministry official told Reuters.
The official added that most of the procurements have been included in the government's multi year defence plan and will not put additional pressure to the country's financials.
A senior foreign ministry official confirmed the above, adding that the cost will be spread over several years.
Rubio said on Wednesday in Athens that the two NATO allies had agreed on a joint security plan for counterterrorism information sharing between their law enforcement agencies.
Greece agreed to buy 20 Lockheed Martin F-35 fighter jets and 35 Sikorsky UH-60M Black Hawk helicopters in 2024. Is upgrading about 82 F-16s to Viper version and wants to upgrade 37 more Block 50s to Vipers at a cost of about $1 billion.
The move is part of Greece's bid to modernise its armed forces as it emerges from the 2009-18 debt crisis that led to years of austerity.
Greece spends nearly 3.5% of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many other NATO countries, due to its long-standing dispute with Turkey. REUTERS

Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defence support, rules out offensive role

Turkey’s foreign minister says Ankara weighing Saudi defence support, rules out offensive role
ANKARA, Oct 8 - Turkey is assessing how it can help Saudi Arabia defend against attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants under a joint defence pact with Pakistan, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Thursday, ruling out Turkish participation in offensive operations.
Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August, under which an armed attack on one member is considered an attack on all. The three countries have since held political and military meetings in response to the Houthi attacks.
On Monday, the countries said they had agreed to move immediately to implement their collective defence commitments and ensure the "rapid deployment" of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia.
Speaking at a joint press conference with his Hungarian counterpart Anita Orban in Ankara, Fidan stressed that the pact was defensive rather than offensive, saying military officials were assessing possible contributions, particularly in air defence, electronic warfare and technical support.
"Yemen's legitimate government forces are already continuing the battle on the ground and Saudi Arabia is supporting them," Fidan said.
"But this is a defensive agreement. When a country party to the pact comes under attack, you stand by it in its defence. This is not an offensive agreement. Turkey will not send troops to another country to carry out attacks on its territory," he said.
Fidan said military delegations would determine Saudi Arabia's operational defence needs and what contributions Turkey and Pakistan could make.
On Wednesday, two officials told Reuters that Turkey was sending mainly defensive and technical support to Saudi Arabia to help its fight with Houthi militants.
Turkish officials have said any support provided at this stage would largely be in a bilateral capacity, as Turkey's parliament has not officially ratified the joint defence pact.
Fidan said on Thursday that work was largely completed for the agreement to be submitted for parliament's approval and that they aimed to send it "as soon as possible".
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army and a robust defence industry, has condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, voiced willingness to help meet Riyadh's technical military needs, and agreed to join a Saudi-led coalition to ensure navigational safety in the Red Sea. REUTERS

BBC pays white staff less than ethnic minorities – report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:12:41 UTC
23:12:41 KST

BBC pays white staff less than ethnic minorities – report
White employees at the BBC earn less than their ethnic minority colleagues in six of seven salary grades, according to the British broadcaster’s 2025/26 annual report. The figures have raised new questions about the corporation’s drive to promote ethnic minority staff and its possible impact on pay.
According to the BBC’s 2025/26 pay gap report, highlighted by The Telegraph on Wednesday, black, Asian, mixed-race and other ethnic minority employees earn 13.2% more in median hourly pay than white colleagues in the lowest salary band. Even among the broadcaster’s most senior executives, the gap stands at 5.3%.
White employees came out ahead in just one category, where their median hourly pay was 0.6% higher. Across the BBC as a whole, however, white staff still earned 0.7% more, largely because they held a greater share of the highest-paid jobs.
The pay figures have drawn attention to the BBC’s push to advance ethnic minority employees. The broadcaster runs special mentoring and career development programs designed to help Black, Asian and other minority staff climb the career ladder, raising questions about whether the drive could be contributing to the pay gaps.
The corporation has set a target for ethnic minorities to make up 20% of both its workforce and senior leadership. The BBC insists these are goals rather than quotas and says they have no bearing on pay decisions.
Former UK Culture Secretary John Whittingdale questioned the BBC’s pay practices, telling The Telegraph that the broadcaster “ought to be paying staff entirely on the basis of the value and merit they contribute for the job they are doing.”
He said the BBC had previously moved to correct gender pay disparities and should apply the same principle of “fair pay” regardless of race, sexuality, or gender.
The broadcaster has faced repeated scandals over unequal pay. In 2020, journalist Samira Ahmed won a landmark employment tribunal case after judges found that she had been paid less than male presenter Jeremy Vine for equivalent work.
In 2024, four female BBC presenters accused the corporation of sex and age discrimination following a shake-up of its news division. In November 2025, the BBC disclosed six internal equal pay cases, including two appeals.
The BBC has rejected suggestions that the latest figures demonstrate unequal treatment, saying it is “committed to fair and equal pay for all.”

Italy’s parliament gives final approval to contested electoral reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:13:45 UTC
23:13:45 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
08 October 2026•Update: 08 October 2026
Italy’s Chamber of Deputies gave final approval on Thursday to a contested electoral reform backed by Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government, in a 227 - 164 vote, public broadcaster Rai reported.
The lower house approved the legislation in a secret ballot on its third reading, following amendments adopted by the Senate.
Meloni welcomed the result as evidence of unity within her ruling center-right coalition.
“And to those who hoped to see the center-right divided, today we respond with action: we are united, united, and determined to fulfill the commitments we made to the citizens. Let’s keep going,” she wrote on US social media company X.
The reform provides for a proportional electoral system with a seat bonus for the leading political force or coalition reaching at least 42% of the vote. It also requires coalitions to identify their candidate for prime minister before the election.
Other changes include the return of preferential voting alongside party-selected candidates heading electoral lists, and provisions allowing voters away from their registered place of residence, including family caregivers, to cast ballots.
Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani said the vote demonstrated that the majority remained solid and intended to seek another five years in government.
Opposition parties, however, criticized the provisions on candidate selection and women’s representation.
Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein said fewer than one in five lawmakers would be elected through preferential votes, arguing that party-selected list leaders would limit voters’ choices.
Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte similarly alleged that party leaderships would determine more than 80% of the next parliament’s membership. He also warned that list leaders could all be men.
A network opposing the reform has announced plans to file legal challenges once the legislation takes effect, seeking a referral to the Constitutional Court.

Three years of genocide: How Gaza war has changed Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:10:15 UTC
23:10:15 KST

Three years after Israel launched its war on Gaza, the consequences extend beyond the devastated territory, reshaping Israeli society, its political debate and its relationship with the world.
Former Israeli diplomat Alon Liel told Anadolu the war has hardened attitudes toward Palestinians and pushed peace further from mainstream politics, with implications that could outlast Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government.
“The Israeli public, especially the Jewish public, moved towards nationalistic attitude. More hatred, more fear, more feelings of revenge,” he said.
For Liel, a former director general of Israel’s Foreign Ministry and ambassador to South Africa, the transformation is reflected in both public attitudes and what politicians are prepared to discuss.
Beyond the immediate consequences, Liel sees a deeper change in the prospects for peace with Palestinians.
“The word peace disappeared ... Nobody is speaking about the peace today among the Israeli politicians,” he said.
A Pew Research Center report published Sept. 15 found that only 17% of Israelis believed Israel and an independent Palestinian state could coexist peacefully. For the first time in Pew’s polling, a majority, 56%, considered it impossible.
Liel believes that pessimism limits the prospects for a negotiated settlement, even under a different government.
“I don't see the future coalition working for peace because this is the public attitude and politicians do not speak about peace because they feel that the public doesn't want and doesn't believe in peace.”
“So politicians who speak in the election campaign about peace are in danger of losing votes.”
Israel’s rightward shift predates the war. An Israel Democracy Institute survey in 2022 found that 62% of Israelis identified with the right.
Before October 2023, the government’s proposed judicial overhaul had also exposed deep political divisions, bringing huge crowds onto the streets.
However, Liel believes the war has reinforced the rightward shift.
“In terms of left and right, the Israeli public moved in the last 3 years more to the right.”
The fallout from Oct. 2023 remains central to electoral politics.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey published in September found that 68% of Israelis considered the attacks a central factor in deciding how to vote, with foreign affairs and security narrowly outranking the economy and living costs among their priorities.
Yet this does not necessarily mean stronger support for Netanyahu.
Polls ahead of the Oct. 27 election have pointed to losses for his coalition, with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot emerging as a leading rival.
The conflict has spread beyond Gaza, drawing Israel into renewed fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon and direct war with Iran.
Israeli forces have also occupied areas of southern Lebanon, while fighting has continued despite ceasefire efforts.
An Israel Democracy Institute poll in early March found that 82% of Israelis supported the military operation against Iran.
Liel fears the rightward shift will sustain confrontation across the region.
“If this trend to the right will continue, we will go on with wars ... not only with the Palestinians, also with Lebanon and Syria and Iran and the Yemenites.”
The election campaign has exposed tensions over Palestinian political participation in Israel.
Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh withdrew his candidacy after the Supreme Court indicated it would likely uphold his disqualification.
Adalah, the legal rights organization representing him, said he withdrew to avoid a ruling that could set a damaging precedent for Palestinian political participation.
Four Arab parties also faced exclusion from the election until Israel’s Supreme Court last week overturned the Central Elections Committee’s September decision to bar them.
The war has also sharpened divisions between Israel’s Jewish and Arab citizens.
Human Rights Watch reported in January 2024 that Israeli authorities held thousands of workers from Gaza incommunicado for weeks after the Oct. 2023, subjecting some to inhumane and degrading conditions.
Christian communities in Israel and surrounding communities have also reported a spike in violence and hate incidents.
The Rossing Center, an Israeli nonprofit, documented 155 incidents against Christians in Israel and occupied East Jerusalem in 2025, including 61 physical attacks. Recorded incidents included spitting, verbal harassment and attacks on church property.
Artists critical of the Gaza war have also faced pressure.
In September, Culture Minister Miki Zohar threatened to seek the revocation of Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s citizenship, accusing them of betraying their country through their documentary ‘NAZA.’
The film, which won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, draws on testimony from 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel about the Gaza campaign.
Speaking to Spanish daily El Pais, Abraham described hostility toward their work and the difficulty of confronting public attitudes.
“It’s painful to see so many people losing the most basic moral and human principles,” he said.
The consequences of the Gaza war have also extended into the occupied West Bank, where rising occupier violence and Israeli military operations have intensified pressure on Palestinian communities.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded more than 1,600 attacks by Israeli occupiers causing Palestinian casualties or property damage between January and August 2026.
The attacks affected 275 Palestinian communities, averaging 6.7 a day, up from five in 2025. Damage included water supplies, farmland, homes and other infrastructure.
Military operations have displaced tens of thousands more.
A UN human rights report released in September said more than 33,000 Palestinians had been displaced from the Jenin, Nur Shams and Tulkarem refugee camps during an Israeli operation launched in early 2025 and remained barred from returning.
The war has also raised questions about Israel’s ability to retain its younger and highly educated population.
Figures presented at a Knesset hearing in June showed that about 40,500 Israelis emigrated annually on average between 2009 and 2021.
The number rose sharply to 59,400 in 2022, 82,800 in 2023 and 69,500 in 2024.
About 18,800 Israelis returned in 2024, the lowest figure in recent years.
The report found emigrants were more highly educated than the population overall, with an average age of about 32.5 in 2023.
The hearing reflected growing concern about the long-term demographic and economic consequences of increased emigration.
The changes inside Israel have also coincided with a deterioration in the country's international standing.
Pew polling this year found unfavorable views among 78% of respondents in Spain, 73% in Germany and 65% in Canada. In the US, 60% viewed Israel unfavorably, up from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022.
An Israel Democracy Institute survey marking two years since October 2023 also found that 73% of Israelis believed their country’s international standing had worsened.
Liel believes the damage extends particularly to Israel’s image as a democracy and its association with the pursuit of peace.
“Israel is much weaker now internationally,” he said.

Rubio says military clash between Turkey, Greece ‘unthinkable’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-08
14:20:48 UTC
23:20:48 KST

ATHENS, October 8. /TASS/. A military conflict between Turkey and Greece stemming from their disagreements over the Aegean Sea is unfathomable, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in an interview with the Greek newspaper Kathimerini.
Rubio was asked whether the United States would intervene if relations between Greece and Turkey in the Aegean Sea or in Cyprus deteriorated sharply, and whether it would prevent such a deterioration.
"It seems unthinkable to me that something like this could happen. These are two allies and two NATO partners - so it simply can’t happen. It won’t benefit anyone," Rubio replied.
"It won’t benefit Turkey or Greece, but it also won’t benefit the United States. So instead of even thinking about it, I would just say that for me it is unthinkable, something that we will never allow, and I do not believe that this will happen."
Turkey has not signed a UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, under which countries can expand their territorial waters up to 12 nautical miles. In 1995, during the ratification of this convention by the Greek parliament, Ankara said that if Greece expanded its territorial waters from six to 12 nautical miles in the Aegean Sea, it would be considered a violation of Turkey's national sovereignty and a casus belli. In recent years, Turkish politicians have continued to threaten Greece with war if it expands its territorial waters to 12 nautical miles in the Aegean Sea.
Turkey does not recognize Greece's 10-mile air zone around the islands, considering that Greek airspace, like territorial waters, is limited to six nautical miles. This is why Turkish fighters with weapons on board invade the Greek airspace and flight information area without providing a flight plan, and Athens raises its planes to intercept them. After a reduction in such violations in 2023 and a complete cessation in 2024, there was an upward trend in the last two years.
